student-wants-only-one-favourite-song.body:
Every piano teacher meets this moment sooner or later. A student sits down, eyes bright, and says there is only one song they want to play. It might be a film theme, a tune from a game, a song a grandparent used to hum, or something from a playlist. Scales, method books and other pieces feel like obstacles in the way. It is tempting to see this as a problem to fix. It is more useful to see it as a door that is already open.

## Why one song can matter so much

A favourite song usually carries a feeling, a memory or a sense of identity. Playing it is not just a musical goal; it is a personal one. When a student says "only this one", they are often saying "this is why I came". Respecting that reason builds trust, and trust is what later allows a teacher to suggest something new.

Brushing the request aside can quietly send the message that the student's taste does not count. Families notice this too. A gentler path is to agree to the song openly and then plan how it will teach as many skills as possible.

## Turning the song into a full lesson plan

Almost any piece can be broken into building blocks. The teacher's job is to find them and make each one visible.

- **Melody:** learn the main tune with one hand, at a simplified level if needed.
- **Rhythm:** clap and count the trickiest pattern before playing it.
- **Harmony:** identify the three or four chords that support the tune.
- **Reading:** write out a short version so the student sees the notes they already know by ear.
- **Expression:** decide where the song gets louder or softer, and why.

Each block becomes a small win. Without noticing, the student is practising reading, rhythm, chords and phrasing, all through music they care about.

**Arrange it in layers**
Start with a very simple arrangement: melody only. Then add single bass notes. Then add simple chords. Each new layer is a reason to return to the song, and each one introduces a skill the student will use in every future piece.

![Colourful cartoon poster of a grand piano surrounded by stars](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8a8pox-d4ler.webp)

## Widening the circle without shame

Once the favourite song is going well, the student has proof that practice works. That is the right time to widen the repertoire, and the way it is done matters.

**Use bridges, not replacements**
Suggest a second piece that shares something with the first: the same key, a similar rhythm, the same mood, or the same composer or artist. Say why. "This uses the same left-hand pattern you already learned" is far more inviting than "now it is time for real music".

**Keep the favourite in the rotation**
Do not retire the song too quickly. Let it stay as a warm-up or a reward at the end of a session. Knowing it will not be taken away makes it easier for the student to try something unfamiliar.

**Let the student choose between two options**
Offer two new pieces and let the student pick. Choice keeps ownership with the learner, which is exactly what the favourite song gave them in the first place.

## What families can do at home

Parents and carers can help a great deal without any musical training. Ask the student to play the favourite song for the family and to explain one thing they learned from it, such as a chord name. Celebrate progress on the song, then show equal interest when a new piece appears. Avoid comparing the student to siblings or friends who play different music.

## When the song is too hard

Sometimes the chosen piece is well beyond the student's current level. Honesty helps here, delivered kindly. A teacher can say the full version is a long-term goal and offer a short, simplified version now. One kind option is to keep the original recording as a "someday" target while the student enjoys an easier arrangement today. That way the dream stays alive and the student still experiences success this week.

## FAQ

**Q: Is it wrong to learn mostly by ear from one song?**
A: Not at all. Learning by ear is a real skill. Add reading gradually by writing down what the student already plays.

**Q: How long should a student stay on one favourite song?**
A: There is no fixed rule. Move on when the student feels proud of a version and is curious about the next layer or a new piece.

**Q: What if the student refuses every new piece?**
A: Look for a piece closer to the favourite in style, or let the student suggest a second song. Interest usually grows with confidence.

**Q: Can an app help with a single song?**
A: A practice app can help with steady rhythm and note accuracy, while a teacher helps choose the arrangement and next steps.

polonaise-rhythm-piano-stately-three-bea.body:
The polonaise is a dance in three beats with a distinctive rhythmic figure that often energises the first beat. On piano it appears in teaching pieces and in larger concert works. You do not need advanced technique to learn the basic pulse. You need a clear count, a firm yet unforced first beat, and a left-hand pattern that supports the dance without turning it into a waltz lilt.

## The characteristic rhythmic idea

A common polonaise rhythm places a sixteenth-note pair or a similar short–short idea inside the first beat, followed by clearer longer notes. Exact notation varies by arrangement, but the ear hears a decorated, proud first beat rather than a soft waltz sway.

Count “one-ee-and, two, three” or another subdivision that matches your score. Speak the count while tapping before you play. The speech pattern prevents the first beat from collapsing into a single heavy thump.

- Tap the rhythm on your knees for one minute.
- Play it on one repeated pitch.
- Then place it into a simple five-finger melody.

![Watercolour white grand piano with sheet music and flowers beside a stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3ewmbd-9v84q.webp)

## Left-hand support

Many student polonaises use a bass note on beat one and chords or lighter bass moves on beats two and three. Keep beat one clear, but do not crush it. Beats two and three should stay alive; if they go limp, the dance loses dignity and starts to limp.

Compare the same left hand played as a waltz (lighter beat one, floating feel) versus a polonaise (more ceremonial first beat). The contrast teaches style faster than adjectives alone.

## Practice plan

- Day 1–2: rhythm speaking and single-note taps with a slow metronome.
- Day 3: right-hand rhythm on a five-finger pattern in G major.
- Day 4: left-hand bass and chord skeleton alone.
- Day 5: hands together at a walking tempo.
- Day 6–7: add dynamics that grow slightly through a short phrase, then cadence calmly.

Keep the tempo moderate. Speed without rhythmic clarity erases the dance identity.

## Listening focus

When you hear a polonaise-style piano piece, ask where the first beat is decorated and how long the phrases breathe between cadences. Notice that even in soft dynamics the pulse stays upright. Transfer that listening into your touch: firm fingers on the rhythmic figure, flexible wrist between gestures.

## FAQ

**Q: Is a polonaise just a waltz with a different name?**
A: No. Both use three beats, but the accent design and rhythmic figures differ. Waltz often sways; polonaise often strides.

**Q: Which hand learns the rhythm first?**
A: Usually the hand that carries the decorated figure in your piece — often the right. Still practise the pulse in both.

**Q: Can children learn a polonaise rhythm?**
A: Yes, with short tapping games and slow tempos.

**Q: How do I stop beat one from sounding harsh?**
A: Prepare the hand early, use arm weight instead of finger stabbing, and keep the follow-through soft.


## Polonaise character words and touch

Choose two adjectives before you play, such as “proud” and “calm”. Reject adjectives that push you toward hardness. Play a phrase, then ask whether a listener would guess those words. Adjust touch, not only speed. Character words keep rhythm practice connected to music rather than to maths alone.

In ensembles, agree on the adjectives so everyone aims at the same dance attitude. Shared language reduces conflicting accents.




## Character word pair of the day

Choose two character words before each polonaise run-through and write them at the top of the page. After playing, rate from one to three how well the take matched the words. Low ratings mean adjust touch, not only metronome numbers. Word pairs keep dance rhythm tied to attitude.


## Left-hand alone days for dance pulse

Twice a week, practise the polonaise left hand alone for five minutes while counting aloud. Removing the melody exposes whether the ceremonial first beat is truly clear. Add the right hand only after those five minutes. Players who always practise hands together often hide a vague left hand under a busy tune.


## Short orchestration imagination

Imagine a soft drum on beat one and lighter steps on beats two and three while you play a basic polonaise left hand. The imagination often improves accent honesty without extra force. If the imaginary drum makes you pound, replace it with an imaginary deep string short note instead. Mental orchestration is a touch tool, not a volume contest.

boogie-woogie-left-hand-patterns.body:
Boogie-woogie is a blues piano style built on a left hand that never stops: eight bass notes in every bar, usually swung, repeated over the chords of a 12-bar blues. To start, learn one left-hand pattern on the C chord, move it to F and G, add a simple right-hand riff, and keep the groove steady before you think about speed.

This article is a practical starter kit. It gives you a short history, four left-hand patterns from easiest to hardest, a right-hand vocabulary, and a one-week plan for putting everything together.

## Where boogie-woogie comes from

Boogie-woogie grew out of the blues in the American South in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, often linked to Texas and to pianists who played for working communities. It spread to cities such as Chicago, and in 1928 Pinetop Smith recorded "Pine Top's Boogie Woogie", one of the recordings that helped give the style its name.

The style reached a much larger audience after the "From Spirituals to Swing" concert at Carnegie Hall in New York in December 1938, where pianists Albert Ammons, Meade Lux Lewis and Pete Johnson performed. Its driving bass later fed into rhythm and blues and early rock and roll.


![Sepia drawing of an upright piano keyboard seen at an angle](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvwyzzdv-nmacj.webp)

## The 12-bar map you need first

Almost every boogie-woogie piece uses the 12-bar blues. In C, the chords run like this:

- Bars 1–4: C, C, C, C
- Bars 5–6: F, F
- Bars 7–8: C, C
- Bar 9: G
- Bar 10: F
- Bars 11–12: C, then C or G as a turnaround

Say the chord names aloud while tapping a steady beat before you play a note. If you know where the chord changes fall, your left hand will not panic when it has to jump.

## Four left-hand patterns, easy to hard

**Pattern A: root and fifth**
Play C and G together, then C and A together, alternating on each beat. This "rocking" shape is gentle on the hand and already sounds like boogie.

**Pattern B: the broken sixth**
Play single notes C, E, G, A, B♭, A, G, E as eight even notes across the bar. This climbing and falling line is the classic sound most people imagine.

**Pattern C: walking octaves**
Play broken octaves that climb through the chord: low C to high C, then E, G, A and back. Each note is played as an octave split into two quick notes. It is powerful but tiring, so keep the wrist loose.

**Pattern D: the shuffle with a blue note**
Like Pattern B, but slide from E♭ to E on the way up. That small crush gives the bass a darker blues edge.

Learn each pattern on C first. Then move the same shape to F and G without changing the fingering. Most of the work is the jump at bar 5 and bar 9.

{{IMG:piano-b-4.webp}}

## Swing: the long-short feel

Boogie-woogie is usually played with swung eighth notes. Each pair of eighths is split long-short, roughly like the first and third notes of a triplet. If you play the eight notes perfectly evenly, the pattern sounds mechanical. Try saying "dooo-ba, dooo-ba" while you play, and let the hand copy the voice.

Some players keep the left hand slightly straighter while the right hand swings harder. Listen to recordings and decide what you like, but stay consistent inside one piece.

## A right-hand vocabulary

Keep the right hand simple at first. Your job is to sit on top of the bass, not compete with it.

- **Off-beat chords:** strike a C7 shape on beats two and four, short and light, like a hand clap.
- **The crushed note:** play E♭ and slide it to E with the same finger. This "crush" is the signature blues sound.
- **Repeated riffs:** choose a two-bar riff and repeat it over the changing chords. Repetition is part of the style.
- **Tremolo:** rock quickly between two notes of a chord, such as G and C, for a shimmering build.
- **Turnaround lick:** in bar 12, walk down chromatically from C to G to lead back to the top.

## A one-week practice plan

**Day 1:** tap the 12-bar form, then play Pattern A through the whole form, slowly.
**Day 2:** learn Pattern B on C only, until the little finger lands without looking.
**Day 3:** move Pattern B to F and G; practise only the jumps.
**Day 4:** add the right-hand off-beat chords, hands together at half speed.
**Day 5:** add one crushed-note riff in bars 1–4.
**Day 6:** record one full chorus and listen for rushing at the chord changes.
**Day 7:** play two choruses in a row, keeping the same tempo.

Ten to fifteen focused minutes a day is enough. When the left hand starts to feel automatic, you can raise the tempo a little at a time.

## Why this style is worth learning

Boogie-woogie is one of the clearest workouts for hand independence. One hand must keep a pattern running while the other plays riffs and rhythms against it. That skill carries over to pop accompaniment, jazz comping and classical pieces with busy left hands. It is also a cheerful way to learn piano, which matters: a groove you enjoy is a groove you practise.

If you learn piano online, the left-hand loop is ideal for recording, because it is short and repetitive. An online piano lessons app that listens to your timing can show where the notes bunch up, usually just before a chord change, so you know exactly what to slow down.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is boogie-woogie hard for beginners?**
A: The simplest left-hand pattern is manageable for early players. Start slowly, learn one bar at a time and keep the tempo steady.

**Q: Should I play boogie-woogie swung or straight?**
A: Most boogie-woogie is swung. Some modern players use straighter eighths, but the swung long-short feel is the traditional sound.

**Q: What is the difference between boogie-woogie and the blues?**
A: Boogie-woogie is a piano style within the blues tradition. It usually uses the 12-bar blues form, with a repeating eight-to-the-bar left hand.

**Q: My left hand gets tired. What should I do?**
A: Lower the tempo, relax the wrist and choose Pattern A or B instead of octaves. Take short breaks and avoid forcing speed.

**Q: Can an app help me with the left-hand groove?**
A: Yes. An app that shows your timing note by note makes uneven spots visible, which helps you practise them on purpose.

lydian-mode-piano-raised-fourth.body:
The Lydian mode is a major scale with one change: the fourth note is raised by a semitone. On the piano you can hear it instantly by playing only the white keys, starting and ending on F. That single B natural, where F major would have B flat, gives the sound a bright, open, slightly unresolved glow that composers often use for wonder, space and flight.

This guide treats the Lydian mode as a sound you can build, test and use in your own playing, rather than a definition to memorise. You will compare it with the major scale, find it in any key, try three short experiments at the keyboard and learn how to spot it in music you already know.

## Lydian in four quick facts

- **Formula:** whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half. Three whole steps in a row at the start is its fingerprint.
- **White-key home:** F to F. In C, the Lydian scale is C D E F♯ G A B C.
- **The colour note:** the raised fourth (♯4). It sits a tritone above the home note, which is why it shimmers instead of settling.
- **The chord it suggests:** a major seventh chord with an added ♯11, written Cmaj7♯11 in C.


![Watercolour grand piano with the lid open in soft grey and violet tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvwyzeqi-7d3mn.webp)

## Why one note changes the mood

In a normal major scale the fourth degree pulls gently down to the third. That small pull is part of what makes major music feel settled and "at home". Raise the fourth and the pull disappears. Instead, the ♯4 leans upward toward the fifth, so the melody seems to lift off the ground.

Try this comparison. Play C E G in your left hand and hold it. With your right hand, play F, then F♯, over the chord. The F rubs against the E and wants to resolve. The F♯ floats above it and sounds like light coming through a window. That contrast is the whole Lydian idea in two notes.

{{IMG:piano-5.webp}}

## Finding Lydian in any key

You do not need to learn twelve new scales. Use one of these shortcuts:

- **Raise the fourth.** Start from any major scale and sharpen its fourth note. D major becomes D Lydian with G♯ instead of G.
- **Borrow a neighbouring key.** A Lydian scale uses the same notes as the major scale a fifth above. C Lydian has exactly the notes of G major, just starting on C.
- **Think fourth degree.** Lydian is the mode that begins on the fourth note of a major scale. That is why F Lydian lives inside C major.

Each shortcut is useful at a different moment. The first helps when you are improvising over a chord. The second is handy when reading, because you can reuse key signatures you already know. The third explains the theory behind the sound.

## Three keyboard experiments

**Experiment 1: the drone test**
Hold a low C with the sustain pedal, or repeat it gently in the left hand. With your right hand, play the C major scale up and down, then the C Lydian scale. Listen only to the moment you reach the fourth note. Notice how your ear reacts differently to F and F♯ over the same bass.

**Experiment 2: the one-note melody swap**
Pick a simple tune you can already play in C major, for example a children's song. Every time an F appears, play F♯ instead. Some phrases will sound strange; others will suddenly sound like a film score. Keep a note of which ones you like.

**Experiment 3: the two-chord vamp**
Alternate C major and D major in the left hand, two beats each. Because D major contains F♯, this pair of chords outlines C Lydian. Improvise slowly over it with the right hand using only the notes of C Lydian. Land on F♯ now and then, and hold it, rather than rushing past it.

Spend about five minutes on each experiment. Recording yourself helps, because it is easier to hear the colour of the ♯4 when you are not busy playing.

## Where you may have heard it

Lydian appears in many styles, and you may already recognise the sound:

- **Television and film:** the theme from The Simpsons by Danny Elfman is often cited as a Lydian melody, built around that raised fourth near the start.
- **Rock guitar:** "Flying in a Blue Dream" by Joe Satriani uses a Lydian colour throughout.
- **Jazz:** the Lydian Chromatic Concept by George Russell, first published in 1953, treated Lydian as a central scale for harmony and improvisation.
- **Classical:** the slow movement of Beethoven's String Quartet Op. 132 is written in the Lydian mode.

When you listen, try to catch the moment the melody touches the ♯4. Once you can hear it, you will notice it in game soundtracks, pop bridges and adverts too.

## Common mistakes with Lydian

**Resolving the ♯4 down too quickly**
Many players treat F♯ as a passing note and drop straight to E. That turns the mode back into ordinary major with a decoration. Let the ♯4 breathe.

**Losing the home note**
Without a clear root in the bass, C Lydian can sound like G major. Keep the root present, either as a drone or as the lowest note of your chords.

**Overusing it**
A Lydian colour works because it is special. In a longer piece, save it for a section where you want lift, and contrast it with plain major.

## How modes fit into learning

Modes are a great test of whether theory has become sound. If you can hear the difference between major and Lydian, you are doing real ear training. That is why a structured piano course often introduces modes through listening and improvising before naming them. Good piano teaching works the same way: when you learn piano through sound, theory stops being a list of rules and becomes a set of moods you can choose from whenever you play piano or play music with others.

Practice tools can help. An AI piano teaching app can listen as you improvise and show which notes you used and how long you held them, which makes it easy to check whether you are really landing on the ♯4 or skipping over it.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Lydian a major or minor mode?**
A: It is a major mode. It has a major third above the home note, like the major scale, but its fourth degree is raised.

**Q: Which white keys make the Lydian mode?**
A: Play the white keys from one F to the F an octave higher. The B natural is the raised fourth.

**Q: What chord goes with the Lydian mode?**
A: A major seventh chord with a raised eleventh, such as Cmaj7♯11, or simply a major triad with the ♯4 in the melody.

**Q: Can beginners use Lydian?**
A: Yes. The two-chord vamp of C major and D major is simple enough for early players and gives the Lydian sound right away.

**Q: Can I learn modes when I learn piano online?**
A: Yes. Listening exercises, drones and short improvisations work well at home, especially if you record and review your playing.

two-short-sits-on-the-same-piece.body:
A long sitting on one piece often starts well and then wanders: the same bars are repeated without a plan, or new pages are opened because the first ones feel tired. Two short sits on the same piece, separated by a break, give the hands a chance to return to a written aim while they are still fresh. The method is simple, but it only works if both sits are planned, and if the second sit does not become a vague run-through of the whole movement.

## Give the first sit a small, written aim

Before you begin, write one job in the score: a phrase to loop, a tempo, a fingering seam, or a pedal change. Work only on that job for a modest stretch of time, then stop while the playing is still controlled. Do not "use up" the remaining minutes by raking through later pages. Leave the score open at the same place, with the aim still visible, so the second sit can start without a hunt.

## Take a real break, then begin the second sit from the same bars

Stand, look at something else, or work on a different piece, then return. The second sit should begin with the same bars, at the same or a slightly more flowing tempo, and should ask whether the aim now holds. If it does, you may extend a little on either side of the phrase. If it does not, stay with the original loop rather than adding new work. The value of the break is a clearer second look, not a chance to change the agenda.

## What not to do in the second sit

Do not raise the tempo far beyond the first sit in a single jump. Do not add a new technical problem from later in the piece. Do not play a full run as a test unless the written aim was that run. A full run can be a third, later event, or a task for another day. The two-sit plan is for deepening one place, not for covering the whole work twice.

A short take in TIGA ALPHA at the end of the second sit can capture whether the same bars now sit more calmly, provided you compare it with the aim you wrote, not with a general wish to play more.

## Using the plan in a busy week

On a short day, two sits of modest length still outweigh one tired marathon. If only one sit is possible, keep it as the "first sit" and make the next day's first job the "second sit" on the same bars. Teachers can also assign this shape: one aim, two visits, a brief note of what changed. The piece then has a memory of work, not only of time spent at the piano.

- Write one aim for the first sit and stop while the work is still controlled.
- Leave the score marked at the same bars.
- After a break, start the second sit on those bars, not at the beginning of the piece unless that is the aim.
- If the aim holds, widen the window slightly; if it does not, loop the original bars again.
- Note what changed between the two sits, in a few words, for the next day.

![Silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdlh8l4-8c5jy.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: How long should each sit be?**
A: Long enough to work the aim carefully, short enough that the playing stays controlled. The exact minutes will vary with age and with the piece.

**Q: Can the second sit be later in the same day?**
A: Yes. A gap of some hours can work as well as a gap of some minutes, so long as you return to the same marked bars.

**Q: What if I want to use the second sit for a different piece?**
A: Then you no longer have this plan. The point is a second visit to the same work. Another piece can have its own pair of sits.

**Q: Should a complete run occupy the second sit?**
A: Only if the written aim was that run. Otherwise the run can wait, and the second sit should test the original bars.

**Q: How do I remember what the first sit achieved?**
A: A few words in the score or in a notebook, plus the unmoved marks on the page, are enough. The second sit then has a starting point.

finger-substitution-piano-legato.body:
Finger substitution is a piano technique in which you change the finger holding a key without releasing it, so the next note can be reached smoothly. For example, you might play a note with finger 3, silently replace it with finger 5 while the key stays down, and then use the now-free finger 3 for the following note. The result is a connected legato line even when there are not enough fingers for an ordinary fingering. It is common in slow melodies, chorale-style pieces and inner voices that must sound joined.

Pedal can hide gaps, but it also blurs harmonies. Substitution lets the fingers create the connection themselves, which keeps the texture clean.

## When substitution is the right tool

- A melody needs to stay connected while the hand moves to a new position.
- Two voices are played by one hand and one voice holds a note while the other moves.
- The music is slow and exposed, so even a tiny break would be heard.
- The pedal must change often or cannot be used, for instance in music where clarity matters.

In fast passages, a regular fingering or a quick shift is usually more practical. Substitution is a tool for slow, singing music.

## How to perform the exchange

Hold the key with the first finger. Bring the second finger next to it, touching the key surface. Slide the second finger onto the key as the first finger moves away, without letting the key rise. The key should not move at all; if it rises even slightly, the damper may touch the string and shorten the sound.

**Silent practice first**
Press a single key down and swap fingers back and forth without any sound changing. Try 3 to 5, 4 to 1 and 2 to 1. This trains the control needed before using it in music.

![Black-and-white pointillist sketch of a grand piano beside a window with trees outside](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvzq0lzp-zfo4h.webp)

## A practice routine for real pieces

- Mark each planned substitution in the score, for example "3–5" above the note.
- Play the passage very slowly, pausing on each substitution to check the key stays down.
- Remove the pauses but keep a slow tempo, listening for complete connection.
- Increase the tempo gradually, keeping the exchange calm and early rather than rushed.
- Play once with eyes closed to rely on touch rather than sight.

## Listening for true legato

Legato is a sound, not only a movement. Listen to how one note fades into the next. In a good legato, the end of one note and the beginning of the next meet without a gap and without an obvious overlap. Some pianists add a tiny overlap, called finger legato, to make melodies sing even more. Recording a few bars helps you notice small breaks that are hard to hear while playing.

**Where beginners meet substitution**
Simple chorales and slow pieces in method books often include it. Even a single substitution in a melody can teach the hand a new level of control.

## Troubleshooting a substitution that slips

If the key rises during the exchange, slow down and keep more weight on the original finger until the new one is in place. If the hand twists, choose a different substitution pair. If the passage still feels awkward, discuss alternative fingerings with a teacher; there is often more than one good solution.

Substitution also helps when a phrase ends on a long note and the next phrase begins nearby. Changing to a more convenient finger on the held note prepares the hand without any break in sound, so the new phrase can start relaxed. Think of it as quietly repositioning the hand while the music continues.

## Planning fingering before you need it

Substitution works best when it is planned rather than improvised. Before learning a slow piece, look ahead through each phrase and ask where the hand will run out of fingers. Mark those points in pencil, then test two possible solutions and keep the one that feels calmer. Writing the plan down prevents the hand from choosing a different fingering each day, which slows learning and weakens memory.

## FAQ

**Q: Is finger substitution the same as changing fingers on repeated notes?**
A: No. Repeated notes are played again with different fingers; substitution swaps fingers while the key stays down.

**Q: Do I still need the pedal?**
A: Sometimes. Substitution keeps lines clean, and the pedal can add resonance where the harmony allows.

**Q: Which pieces are good for practising it?**
A: Slow melodies, hymns written in four parts and lyrical studies are ideal.

**Q: Can children learn substitution?**
A: Yes, once they can hold a steady hand shape, the silent swap exercise works well as a game.

choose-a-realistic-performance-tempo.body:
After listening to recordings by some pianists, many people want to play a piece as fast as the recording. But a pianist's tempo can be controlled only after many years of training. If you push to reach that tempo, you often end up tense, unclear, or even making mistakes. For most learners, it matters more to choose a tempo at which you can play steadily, clearly and musically than to chase a very fast one. That tempo can gradually rise as you improve.

## Your Tempo Need Not Follow Anyone Else's

Everyone's level and hands are different, and there is no need to compare tempos with others.

That someone else can play very fast does not mean you must play that fast too.

Finding a tempo that suits you and expressing the music sincerely is what matters most.

## Tempo Can Be Raised Gradually

The tempo you choose now is not fixed for ever.

As practice accumulates, your hands become more skilled, and the tempo you can control will rise.

After a while, you can try a slightly faster tempo again.

## A Musical Tempo

A suitable tempo should also leave you enough energy to express the music, such as changes in dynamics and the rise and fall of phrases.

If all your attention goes into playing the right notes, you have no energy left to express the music.

A slightly slower tempo often lets the music be more expressive.

## Reading Tempo Terms in the Score

The tempo terms in a score, such as Allegro and Andante, give a rough range.

Within this range, you can choose a tempo that suits you.

For example, Allegro can be a fairly fast allegro, or a moderate allegro.

- A recording's tempo is not necessarily right for you
- Pushing for speed easily leads to tension and mistakes
- Choose a tempo that is steady, clear and musical
- Raise it gradually as you improve

## Ask Your Teacher to Help Check the Tempo

When choosing a performance tempo, you can talk it over with your teacher.

The teacher can suggest a suitable tempo based on your level and the character of the piece.

If you are going to take an exam or enter a competition, you can also find out whether there are tempo requirements.

## Break the Tempo Goal into Steps

If the tempo you finally want is still far from where you are now, you can break it into several steps.

For example, if you can now play steadily at eighty beats per minute and the goal is one hundred, you can set ninety as the next goal.

Each time you reach a step, note it in the score, and see yourself getting closer to the goal step by step.

![A watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6ytcu-p3g9i.webp)

## A Steady Tempo

A suitable performance tempo must first of all be one you can hold steadily, without speeding up and slowing down from beginning to end.

If you have to slow down in the difficult places, the overall tempo may be too fast.

Take the tempo at which you can stay steady in the hardest few bars of the whole piece as the baseline for the whole piece.

## The Problem with Pushing for Speed

If you play at a tempo beyond your ability, your hands become tense and the sound becomes unclear.

Some notes may be skipped, and the rhythm may become unsteady.

It may sound fast, but the quality of the music has actually dropped.

## Performance Tempo Summary

A recording's tempo is only a reference; pushing for speed easily leads to tension and mistakes, so choose a tempo at which you can play steadily, clearly and musically.

Refer to the tempo terms in the score, try with a metronome, talk with your teacher, and leave a little margin for performance.

Tempo can rise gradually as you improve, slower can sound lovely too, and there is no need to compare yourself with others.

## Finding a Tempo with a Metronome

You can try several different tempos with a metronome and see at which one you can play the whole piece steadily and clearly.

Write this tempo in the score as your present performance tempo.

Later, when you have improved, you can try raising it slightly.

## Tempo in Performance

In performance, many people play faster without noticing because they are nervous.

So the performance tempo you practise day to day can be a little slower than the fastest you can reach, leaving a little margin.

Then even if you speed up a little in performance, you are still within the range you can control.

## Slower Can Sound Lovely Too

Many pieces sound just as lovely, or even have more character, played at a slightly slower tempo.

Listeners care whether the music moves them, not only how fast it is.

A clear, steady, expressive performance moves people more than one that is fast and messy.

## Using Recording Tempos as a Reference

Listening to recordings is a good way to get to know a piece, but the tempo in a recording is chosen by the performer according to their own ability and understanding.

Even for the same piece, different pianists may choose very different tempos.

So a recording's tempo is only a reference, not a standard that must be reached.

## A Clear Tempo

At a suitable tempo, every note should be clearly audible.

Fast groups of notes do not blur together, and staccato can be played short and clear.

**Look closely**

If you record yourself and find that some notes are not clear, you can slow the tempo down a little.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Should I play at the tempo of the recording?**
A: Not necessarily; a recording is only a reference.

**Q: What is the problem with pushing for speed?**
A: Tension, lack of clarity and a greater chance of mistakes.

**Q: What makes a tempo suitable?**
A: Steady, clear and musical.

**Q: Why leave a margin in performance?**
A: When nervous, people tend to speed up without noticing.

**Q: Does the tempo stay the same for ever?**
A: No, it can rise as you improve.

bach-coffee-cantata-leipzig-coffeehouse.body:
When people think of Bach, many picture church organs and solemn Passions. In fact, in Leipzig Bach often led a group of students and musicians in public concerts held in a coffeehouse. Around 1734 he wrote a light secular cantata about a father who wants his daughter to give up coffee, which later generations called the Coffee Cantata (BWV 211). This little work shows us Bach's humorous, down-to-earth side.

## Summary of Bach's Coffee Cantata

From 1729 Bach directed the musical society in Leipzig, often giving public concerts in a coffeehouse. Around 1734 he completed the secular cantata BWV 211, later called the Coffee Cantata.

**A quick note**

The libretto was written by Picander. It tells of the father, Schlendrian, who urges his daughter Liesgen to give up coffee; she appears to agree but secretly demands that her marriage contract allow her to drink coffee, and the closing chorus ends the story with humour.

This work shows Bach's down-to-earth, humorous side, and some of his keyboard concertos may also have been performed at these concerts.

## Concerts in the Coffeehouse

According to records, the society's winter concerts were held indoors in the coffeehouse, while in summer they may have been held outdoors in a garden.

Besides cantatas, the programmes included instrumental works such as concertos and suites.

Some of Bach's keyboard concertos were very likely performed at these concerts too.

![A person in futuristic clothes playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7r8wp-4iwub.webp)

## Coffee in Leipzig at the Time

In the eighteenth century coffee was becoming more and more popular in European cities, and Leipzig had several coffeehouses.

Coffeehouses became places to chat, read the newspaper and listen to music.

Some people at the time also grumbled about the new habit of drinking coffee, which made it perfect material for a comedy.

## The Daughter Fights Back

At first the daughter takes her father's threats lightly, and even sings an aria in praise of coffee, saying it is sweeter than a thousand kisses.

Only when she hears that she will not be allowed to marry does she pretend to agree to give up coffee.

But secretly she announces that whoever wants to marry her must write into the marriage contract that she may drink coffee.

## Another Side of Bach

In church, Bach wrote many deep and solemn works.

At coffeehouse concerts, he could write a light little comedy like this.

This reminds us that even great composers lived in the ordinary life of a city.

## From Cantata to Piano

Some arias in the Coffee Cantata have lovely melodies, and some people have arranged them as instrumental pieces.

When you play Bach, think about the kind of occasion this music was first performed on, and you will feel it differently.

Some music was written for worship, and some for friends gathering happily in a coffeehouse.

## Leipzig's Musical Society

In the early eighteenth century, Leipzig had a "musical society" (Collegium Musicum) made up of university students and music lovers.

From 1729 Bach took over the direction of this society and led them in regular concerts.

These concerts were open to the public, and were often held in a coffeehouse in the city or in its garden.

## The Closing Chorus

At the end of the cantata, three singers sing a lively chorus together.

The words say that a cat cannot give up catching mice, and girls cannot give up their coffee.

This humorous ending fills the whole work with the flavour of everyday life.

## A Stage for the Keyboard Concertos

Bach wrote a number of concertos for one or several keyboard instruments and orchestra.

Scholars suppose that many of these works were arranged for the musical society's concerts.

For pianists, these concertos are still important repertoire today.

## Understanding the Life Behind the Music

Behind a work there is often the city, the people and the habits of daily life of its time.

The Coffee Cantata is like a window, letting us see the everyday life of people in eighteenth-century Leipzig.

Learning about this background while you learn the piano can make the music feel closer.

**Another way to look at it**
- Bach directed the "musical society" in Leipzig
- The society often performed in a coffeehouse
- Around 1734 he wrote the Coffee Cantata, BWV 211
- It is a comic story of a father urging his daughter to give up coffee

## A Name Given Later

The name "Coffee Cantata" was not given by Bach, but is a popular name that later generations gave it based on its content.

Its original title is the first line of the libretto, meaning "Be quiet, stop talking."

With this line the narrator asks the audience at the opening to quieten down, so that the story can begin.

## The Story of the Coffee Cantata

The libretto of this cantata was written by the poet Picander.

In the story, a father named Schlendrian cannot stand his daughter Liesgen drinking coffee every day, and tries everything to make her give it up.

He threatens that if she does not give up coffee, he will not let her go out and will not buy her new clothes, and finally he says he will not let her marry.

## What Is a Secular Cantata?

A cantata is a vocal work performed by soloists, chorus and orchestra.

Most of Bach's cantatas were written for church services, but he also wrote some secular cantatas, for celebrations, gatherings and concerts.

**Practice order**

The Coffee Cantata is one of the light and humorous secular cantatas.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What group did Bach direct in Leipzig?**
A: The musical society (Collegium Musicum).

**Q: Where did the musical society often perform?**
A: In a coffeehouse in the city.

**Q: Roughly when was the Coffee Cantata written?**
A: Around 1734.

**Q: What is the story about?**
A: A father urging his daughter to give up coffee.

**Q: Did Bach give it this name?**
A: No, it is a popular name later generations gave it based on its content.

practice-15-minutes-5-methods.body:
Practising piano every day but feeling stuck? The problem is rarely too little time. It is usually **practising the wrong thing**: playing the whole piece from the start again and again when you only slip in two bars. Here are five methods that fit into 15 minutes a day.

# 1. Slow first, fast later
Play slowly enough that you make no mistakes, then speed up a little at a time. Playing fast before you are accurate trains your hands to remember the mistake. In the app you can practise below normal speed, for example in Play Along, where the song speed is adjustable.

# 2. Repeat only the bars you missed
Do not play the whole song every time. Find the bar you slipped on and repeat just that until it passes three times in a row. After a round, TIGA ALPHA's practice mode shows which notes you miss most and offers a drill for exactly those.

# 3. Train your ear alongside
Pianists who can hear what a sound is learn new songs much faster. Spend two or three minutes in Ear Gym listening to intervals and chords, and guess before you check.

# 4. Play one song you love, every day
If you only drill technique you will get bored and quit. Save the last couple of minutes for music you really want to play. The app has more than 10,000 songs and Play Along makes practice feel like a game.

# 5. Have something tell you what to practise next
The biggest problem of practising alone is not knowing what to work on. TIGA ALPHA's **AI Daily Mentor** looks at your actual practice data and tells you where your weak spots are, what to do today and for how long.

# A 15-minute plan to try today
- 3 min: warm up with a slow scale
- 6 min: repeat the missed bars (methods 1 and 2)
- 3 min: ear training or note reading
- 3 min: play a song you love

Most important: short practice every day beats one long session a week.

ravel-bolero-long-crescendo-story.body:
Ravel's Boléro, first performed in Paris in 1928, is built on one simple idea: a single rhythm repeated by the snare drum from start to finish while the music grows from a whisper to a full orchestral roar. For pianists, its story is a masterclass in patience, because the hardest part of a long crescendo is not getting loud, but getting loud slowly enough.

This is the story of how a deliberately repetitive piece became one of the most recognized works of the twentieth century, and what it can teach anyone who wants to control dynamics at the keyboard.

## A commission from a dancer

In 1928 the dancer Ida Rubinstein asked Maurice Ravel for music for a new ballet with a Spanish setting. Ravel chose an unusual experiment. Instead of developing themes in the usual way, he would keep the same rhythm and two alternating melodies throughout, and let orchestration alone create the drama. Each repetition hands the tune to a different instrument or combination of instruments, adding color and weight bit by bit.

The ballet premiered at the Paris Opéra in November 1928, and the score soon found a much larger life in concert halls. Ravel himself is often reported to have been surprised by its popularity and to have regarded it as an exercise in orchestration rather than a showpiece.

## The architecture of one long build

Boléro stays in C major for almost its entire length. Near the end, the music suddenly lifts into E major for a few bars, a shock after so much sameness, and then falls back to C before a brief, crashing ending. Everything before that moment is one long, carefully measured increase in volume and density.

That structure only works because the rhythm never wavers. The snare drummer has one of the most exposed jobs in the orchestra: the same pattern, very quietly at first, with no room to rush as the excitement grows. Orchestral players often describe the challenge as keeping the tempo absolutely steady while everyone around them gets louder.


![Bold red, orange and yellow ink illustration of a grand piano on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvllarl-t3nd2.webp)


## What pianists can learn from Boléro

Most of us crescendo too early. We hear "get louder" and reach full volume in a few bars, leaving nowhere to go. Boléro shows the opposite approach: plan the whole arc, save the loudest moment for the end, and make each step only slightly bigger than the last.

At the piano, the same thinking applies to any long build, whether in a pop ballad's final chorus or a classical development section.

**Map the arc before you play.** Mark the start and end dynamic of the passage, then divide it into stages. If a passage moves from piano to fortissimo over sixteen bars, decide which bars reach mezzo-piano, mezzo-forte and forte.

**Keep the tempo independent of volume.** Many players speed up when they get louder. Practise the crescendo with a metronome and notice whether you push ahead.

**Use texture as well as force.** Ravel grew the sound by adding instruments. Pianists can do something similar by adding octaves, fuller chords or more pedal, rather than only pressing harder.

**Keep something in reserve.** The final climax should be the strongest moment. If you are already at your limit halfway through, restart the plan with a quieter beginning.

## A short crescendo exercise

Try this with any simple chord progression, such as C, A minor, F and G:

- Play the four chords as quarter notes for sixteen bars.
- Begin as softly as you can while keeping every note sounding.
- Raise the volume a little every four bars, never more.
- In the last four bars, add the left-hand octave and fuller right-hand voicing.
- Record the result and check whether the growth is even or arrives too soon.

Repeat the exercise on another day at a slower tempo. Controlling volume at slow speeds is harder, and that is exactly why it builds skill.

## Practising dynamics with modern tools

Dynamics are hard to judge from the bench, because we hear our playing differently while concentrating on the notes. Recording is the simplest honest mirror. An online piano teaching application can add a steady pulse and help you notice whether your tempo creeps upward during a crescendo.

TIGA ALPHA, an AI piano teaching app from Thai founders, runs its lessons in English as well as Thai and Mandarin. Its CEO, Teacher Aum, has 20 years of piano teaching experience, and the company positions itself as a high-tech education-innovation business. Piano teaching with AI is useful for this kind of practice because the app keeps the tempo steady while you focus on sound. A studio piano course, a broader piano learning course or other live music teaching can then add feedback on tone and balance.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why is Boléro so repetitive?**
A: Ravel designed it as an experiment: the same rhythm and melodies throughout, with change coming from orchestration and a steady increase in volume.

**Q: Can I play Boléro on piano?**
A: Piano arrangements exist at various levels. The main challenge is keeping the rhythm steady while gradually building volume and texture.

**Q: How do I stop rushing during a crescendo?**
A: Practise the build with a metronome, start softer than you think, and record yourself. Most rushing disappears once you notice it.

**Q: Is dynamics practice useful if I learn piano online?**
A: Yes. Recording yourself with an online piano lessons app or during an AI online piano course is an easy way to check whether your volume grows evenly.

Download it on the [TIGA ALPHA landing page](https://www.tigaalpha.com/landing-en/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=seo&utm_campaign=ravel-bolero-long-crescendo-story), find studio lessons at [TIGA Studio](https://www.tigastudio.net/), and learn more about the company at [tigaalpha.com](https://www.tigaalpha.com). A piano teaching app helps you play piano and play music with patience, one careful step louder at a time.

example-scenario-studio-recital-sign-ups.body:
Recitals are a joy, but organising them can be a headache. This article walks through an example scenario of a small music studio that moves recital sign-ups from paper slips to a simple online form. The scenario is invented for illustration and does not describe any real studio, and no figures are claimed.

## The problem with paper slips

In the example, the studio used to hand out paper slips at the end of lessons. Some slips were lost, some were returned late and some had unclear handwriting. The teacher spent evenings sorting them.

- Slips were easy to lose between the studio and home.
- Handwriting made names and pieces hard to read.
- Changes meant crossing out and rewriting.

## Designing the form

The studio decides to use a short online form. The aim is to ask for only what is needed.

**What the form asks**
- The student's first name, or a name the family is happy to share.
- The piece and approximate length.
- Any accessibility needs, such as a lower stool.
- A parent's contact for reminders.

**What it does not ask**
It does not ask for photos, home addresses or anything unrelated to the event.

![Watercolour upright piano with open sheet music and a wooden bench](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwiax068-jhejl.webp)

## Explaining the purpose

At the top of the form, a few plain sentences explain why the information is collected, who can see it and when it will be deleted. This builds trust and keeps the studio within privacy expectations.

- Say who will read the answers.
- Say that the details are used only for the recital.
- Give a way to ask for changes or deletion.

## Reminders that feel gentle

The studio sends one reminder a week before and another the day before. Each message repeats the date, time, place and what to bring. There are no countdown words. Parents say the reminders are useful and not annoying.

## Handling families without easy internet access

The studio keeps a paper option for any family who prefers it. The teacher enters those answers into the same list. This keeps the process fair, and nobody is left out.

## What the studio learns

In the scenario, the teacher saves time and sees the programme earlier, so there is more room to plan the order of pieces. Families appreciate the clear information. The studio also notices that a few questions on the form could be clearer and rewrites them for next time.

## Connecting the recital to practice

A recital is a good goal for practice. Teachers often suggest short, regular sessions in the weeks before. Some learners use TIGA ALPHA, an AI piano teaching app that follows notes and timing, to check a passage between lessons. The studio treats this as a personal choice and keeps the focus on enjoyment, not on perfection.

## Checking the form before it goes out

Before sending the link, the teacher tests it on a phone and on a computer. A friend fills it in and points out confusing questions. The teacher checks that the confirmation message says what happens next, such as when the running order will be shared. Small tests like this prevent many questions later.

## Looking after the list afterwards

When the recital is over, the teacher exports the answers for the programme, then deletes the form responses as promised. A brief record of which questions confused people will make the next event smoother. Families notice when a studio keeps its word about data, and that quiet reliability becomes part of the studio's good name.

## Small touches on the day itself

On the day, the teacher prints a single page with the running order, so nobody needs the form again. A volunteer parent greets families, and a quiet corner is kept for nervous young performers to breathe and listen to the music in the room. The teacher thanks everyone at the end and reminds families that photos should only include children whose parents have agreed.

## FAQ

**Q: Is an online form necessary for a small recital?**
A: No, but it can save time. A paper option should remain for families who prefer it.

kalimba-mbira-thumb-piano-keyboard-playe.body:
A kalimba or mbira is a lamellophone, often called a thumb piano: a set of thin metal tines fixed over a bridge on a wooden board or box, plucked with the thumbs and sometimes a finger. Each tine sounds one pitch, set by its vibrating length. The mbira has deep roots in Southern African music, where it is played in long, interlocking cycles, while the modern kalimba is a simplified, widely available form of the same idea. For a keyboard player, it is a small instrument with surprisingly big lessons about layout, pattern and listening.

## What makes a lamellophone sound

When a thumb pushes a tine down and lets it go, the tine vibrates above and below the bridge. A longer free length gives a lower pitch; a shorter one gives a higher pitch. Players tune by sliding a tine slightly in or out.

**The body**
A flat board instrument sounds quieter and more intimate. A hollow box or a gourd resonator makes the tone fuller and louder.

**The buzz**
Traditional mbira often carry small rattling attachments, such as shells or metal pieces, that add a soft buzzing halo to every note. To many listeners this buzz is part of the music, not a fault.

- Tines ring for a long time, so the instrument has a natural sustain.
- Each note starts with a soft click from the thumb, then blooms.
- Overlapping notes blur gently into a cloud of harmony.

## The zig-zag layout explained

The most surprising thing for a pianist is the order of the notes. On a typical modern kalimba, the lowest tine sits in the middle, and the notes alternate outwards: one step to the left, the next step to the right, and so on. Moving up the scale means zig-zagging between the thumbs.

That layout has a clear logic. Notes that sound well together, such as a chord built in thirds, often sit side by side, so one thumb can sweep two neighbouring tines and produce a pleasant interval. Scales are split between the hands, so both thumbs share the work evenly.

On the piano, by contrast, pitch rises in one straight line from left to right. Trying both layouts makes it clear that a keyboard design is a choice, not a law of nature.

![Cartoon of a person in headphones at an upright piano in the evening](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdzxjo3-l1cvh.webp)

## Interlocking parts in mbira music

In many mbira traditions, music is built from short repeating cycles. Two parts often interlock: one player plays a basic pattern while another fills the spaces between its notes, so together they create a melody that neither plays alone. Listeners can hear different inner tunes appear depending on which notes their attention follows.

This is close to ideas pianists meet in other settings:

- The left and right hands of a piano part sharing one line between them.
- Ostinato patterns that stay the same while the music around them changes.
- Duets in which two players divide a texture so that it sounds richer together.

Listening to recordings of interlocking mbira music with this in mind is a useful ear exercise. Try to follow one strand for a full cycle, then switch to another.

## What a pianist can practise on a kalimba

A small kalimba is affordable and quiet enough for travel, and it can support skills that carry back to the keyboard.

**Thumb independence**
Alternating thumbs builds a feel for evenness between hands, similar to balancing a melody against an accompaniment.

**Playing by ear**
Because the layout is unfamiliar, the ear has to guide the hands. Picking out a simple folk tune trains pitch memory.

**Listening to resonance**
Letting tines ring makes the player notice how notes overlap, which is useful when learning to judge the sustain pedal on piano.

## From thumb piano to digital tools

The thumb piano also shows how musical interfaces evolve. Instrument makers have built electric versions with pickups, and some digital controllers borrow the idea of a non-linear layout so that harmony falls under the fingers.

Learning technology follows a similar path of rethinking the interface. An AI piano teaching app such as TIGA ALPHA listens to a learner on a standard keyboard and responds with feedback, so the instrument stays familiar while the way of practising changes. Whatever the tool, the musical goals remain the same: steady time, clear melody and attentive listening.

## FAQ

**Q: Is a kalimba the same as an mbira?**
A: They belong to the same family. The mbira is a traditional instrument with its own repertoire and tunings, while the kalimba is a modern simplified design found in many music shops.

**Q: Is notation reading required before picking up a kalimba?**
A: No. Many players learn by ear or from simple number and letter charts, though reading notation helps if you want to share music with pianists.

**Q: Can I play piano pieces on a kalimba?**
A: Simple melodies and some easy accompaniments work well. Pieces with fast chromatic notes or wide ranges usually need rearranging.

**Q: Why does my kalimba buzz on one note?**
A: A tine may be touching something or sitting unevenly on the bridge. Checking its position and pressing it gently into place usually helps.

ai-stem-separation-music-learners.body:
AI stem separation is a technique that takes a finished stereo recording and estimates the individual parts inside it, such as vocals, drums, bass, piano and everything else. The software does not unlock hidden tracks; it predicts what each instrument would sound like on its own, based on patterns learned from many examples. For musicians and learners, it can make the piano part of a dense mix much easier to hear and study.

## Why splitting a mix used to be so hard

When a song is mixed, all the instruments are added together into one waveform per speaker. Many sounds overlap in pitch and time, so there is no simple way to subtract one of them. Older tricks, such as cancelling whatever sits in the centre of a stereo image to remove a vocal, worked only in special cases and often left strange, hollow artefacts.

Machine learning changed the approach. Instead of following fixed rules, a model learns statistical differences between voices, drums and other sources by training on recordings where the separate parts are known.

## How the models work in plain terms

Most systems turn audio into a spectrogram, a picture of which frequencies are present at each moment. A neural network then predicts a mask for each source, deciding how much of each small time-frequency region belongs to the vocal, the bass or another part. Applying those masks and turning the results back into sound produces the separated stems.

- Some models work on the spectrogram, some directly on the waveform, and some combine both.
- Research teams compare systems on shared test sets using objective measures, alongside listening tests.
- Quality depends heavily on the style of music and how similar it is to the training data.

## What it gets right and where it struggles

Separation is often impressive for vocals and drums, which have distinctive patterns. It is harder for instruments that share a range and timbre, such as a piano and a guitar playing chords together, or synth pads blended with strings.

**Common artefacts**
Listen for watery or metallic textures, faint bleed from other instruments, and missing note attacks. These are signs that the model was unsure where a sound belonged.

**Why the piano can be tricky**
Piano notes contain a sharp hammer attack followed by a long decay rich in overtones. Those overtones overlap with many other instruments, so separated piano stems sometimes lose sparkle or pick up traces of the vocal.

![Futuristic keyboard with light lines](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbdosa9-1tuhy.webp)

## Practical uses for piano learners

Used thoughtfully, separated stems can support ear training and arranging.

- Isolate the piano or keys part to transcribe a chord pattern more accurately.
- Remove the original keyboard part and play along with the remaining band as a backing track.
- Slow the stem down to study a fast fill or voicing.
- Compare your own recording with the separated part to notice differences in rhythm and touch.

These uses sit comfortably alongside AI feedback tools. For instance, a learner might work out a pattern from a separated stem and then use TIGA ALPHA to check note accuracy and timing as the pattern is practised on the keyboard.

## Respecting rights and permission

- Private study and practice: generally the safest use.
- Sharing or selling stems: needs permission from the rights holders.


A separated stem is still derived from someone else's recording. Using it privately for study is very different from uploading it, selling it or building a new release on top of it. Copyright rules vary by country, and many recordings involve several rights holders. When in doubt, use stems only for personal practice, or choose tracks that their creators have released for remixing.

## Where the technology is heading

Researchers continue to improve separation for more instrument types and for live, real-time use. Real-time separation could one day let a learner mute a single instrument during a streamed performance, or let a teacher highlight one line during a group lesson. As with any AI tool, the result should be treated as an aid to listening, not as a perfect copy of the original parts.

## FAQ

**Q: Does stem separation recover the original studio tracks?**
A: No. It produces an estimate of each part, which can contain artefacts and traces of other instruments.

**Q: Can I use separated stems in my own release?**
A: Not without permission from the rights holders. For personal practice and study, the situation is different, but rules vary by country.

**Q: Why does the separated piano sound thin?**
A: Piano overtones overlap with many instruments, so the model may assign some of them elsewhere. Results vary by recording.

**Q: Do I need a powerful computer?**
A: Some tools run in a browser or online, while others run locally. Local processing is slower on older machines but keeps audio files on your device.

bartok-kodaly-folk-song-collecting-1906.body:
In the early twentieth century, the Hungarian composers Bartók and Kodály took a phonograph into the Hungarian countryside, recorded the folk songs that peasants sang, and then carefully wrote them down in notation. In 1906 the two published Twenty Hungarian Folk Songs together, written for voice and piano, with each arranging ten. This was the beginning of their long work collecting folk songs, and the songs deeply influenced their later compositions.

## Learning From the Music Around You

The story of Bartók and Kodály reminds us that the folk music around us is also very good learning material.

**Common misconception**

Every place has its own folk songs, and learning to play them on the piano is an interesting kind of practice.

Trying to add a simple accompaniment to a song from your hometown can also train your sense of harmony.

## Pentatonic Scales and Ancient Melodies

In the course of collecting, they found that many old Hungarian folk songs use the pentatonic scale.

The structure of these melodies is very different from the popular music of the cities, and they sound more archaic.

This discovery gave them a new understanding of the origins of Hungarian music.

**Slow down**
- In the early twentieth century, they took a phonograph to the countryside to record folk songs
- They carefully wrote the recordings down in notation
- In 1906 they published Twenty Hungarian Folk Songs together
- The folk songs influenced their later compositions

![Art Deco style illustration: someone practising at a deep red upright piano under a lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5asd9-qd8p7.webp)

## Playing Folk Song Arrangements

When you play Bartók's folk song arrangements, first learn to sing the melody well, and feel the natural rise and fall of the folk song.

Some rhythms are irregular, so count them carefully and do not play them as neat, regular rhythms out of habit.

The harmony sometimes sounds unusual, and that is exactly the character of Bartók's music.

## Summary of Bartók and Kodály's Folk Songs

In the early twentieth century, Bartók and Kodály took a phonograph into the countryside to record folk songs, then carefully wrote them down in notation.

In 1906 they published Twenty Hungarian Folk Songs together, each arranging ten, beginning their long work on folk songs.

The folk songs influenced their compositions and their ideas about education, and also remind us to learn from the music around us.

## Two Hungarian Composers

Béla Bartók was born in 1881 and died in 1945. Zoltán Kodály was born in 1882 and died in 1967.

Both studied music in Budapest, were close in age, and later became good friends and collaborators.

Both were very interested in Hungarian folk music.

## Folk Songs Become Piano Pieces

Bartók arranged many folk songs as piano pieces, such as For Children and the Romanian Folk Dances.

These works keep the melodies and rhythms of the folk songs, and add Bartók's own harmony.

For piano learners, these works are a good way into Eastern European folk music.

## The Difficulty of Notation

The rhythms and pitches of folk songs often differ from the rules in textbooks.

Some notes are slightly higher or lower than the standard pitch, and some rhythms are very free, making them hard to write down in ordinary notation.

Bartók was extremely careful in his notation, using special symbols to mark these details.

## Not Only Hungary

Bartók later also collected folk songs from Romania, Slovakia and other places, and even travelled to North Africa.

In his lifetime he recorded a very large number of folk tunes and left behind a great deal of material.

Kodály, for his part, put more of his energy into Hungarian folk songs and music education.

## The "Folk Songs" Heard in the City

Much of the so-called Hungarian music popular in the cities at the time was in fact adapted tunes with an urban style.

Bartók and Kodály wanted to know what kind of songs people in the countryside really sang.

So they decided to go to the countryside themselves to find the answer.

## Kodály and Music Education

Kodály placed great importance on music education. He believed children should begin learning music with the folk songs of their own people.

His educational ideas later influenced music classrooms in many countries.

Singing, music reading and ear training are important parts of his teaching method.

## A Serious Approach to Recording

When they collected folk songs, they insisted on recording the real sound, rather than changing it according to their own imagination.

This serious attitude is why their material is still valuable today.

When learning the piano, listening carefully and recording accurately is also a very important skill.

## The 1906 Collection

In 1906, Bartók and Kodály published Twenty Hungarian Folk Songs together, written for voice and piano.

Each arranged ten, using piano accompaniment to set off the melodies of the folk songs.

The collection did not cause a great stir when it was published, but it marked the beginning of their folk song work.

## Taking the Phonograph to the Villages

They took the phonograph and wax cylinders of the time and visited many villages.

When the peasants sang, they recorded the singing, and also noted down the words and information about the singers.

**A different angle**

After returning to the city, they listened to the recordings again and again and carefully wrote the melodies down in notation.

## FAQ

**Q: What nationality were Bartók and Kodály?**
A: Hungarian.

**Q: How did they collect folk songs?**
A: They took a phonograph to the countryside to record, then wrote the songs down in notation.

**Q: What was published in 1906?**
A: Twenty Hungarian Folk Songs, for voice and piano.

**Q: How many did each of them arrange?**
A: Ten each.

**Q: Which piano pieces did Bartók arrange from folk songs?**
A: For example For Children and the Romanian Folk Dances.

matching-tone-in-repeated-chords.body:
Repeated chords are common in accompaniments and in some climactic passages, and they easily lose evenness. One repeat is louder, the next is thinner, or an inner note drops out. Matching tone across the set means choosing a voicing, a place in the key, and a weight you can repeat, then practising the set as a controlled series rather than as a burst. The musical plan, including any written crescendo or accent, comes after the default evenness is in place.

## Choose the voicing and the part of the key you will repeat

**Match one chord first, then repeat the same shape**

Play one chord and decide which note should speak most clearly, often the top, and how deep in the key you will go. Repeat that same shape at a slow tempo, listening for the same balance and the same attack. If the wrist locks after a few repeats, shorten the loop and release between groups. A written fingering that you can keep from chord to chord will help the shape remain constant.

## Practise the set in small groups with a click

Divide a long chain of repeats into groups of two, three or four, matching the beat. Play a group, release, and begin again, with a click on the pulse. Listen for an accent that you did not plan on the first chord of a group, or a fade on the last. Those faults are easier to hear in a short group than in a whole page of repeats. When two groups match, join them at the same tempo.

- Fix a voicing and a depth in the key, and repeat that shape slowly.
- Group the chords by beats and loop one group at a time.
- Listen for unplanned accents or missing inner notes.
- Join groups only when the tone still matches at the seam.
- Apply a written crescendo or accent after the even set is secure.

![Cartoon of a person in headphones at an upright piano by candlelight](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdlf8oa-poebm.webp)

**Release between groups until the arm can repeat the shape freely**

## Put the even set back under the melody or the phrase

If the repeated chords accompany a line, add that line only after the set is even. The melody should not force a sudden heavy repeat, unless the score asks for it. If the repeats are themselves the main texture, shape the phrase with a planned dynamic once the default match is there. Pedal changes should follow the harmony, not smear a set that is already uneven.

A short listen in TIGA ALPHA can reveal an unplanned accent in the middle of a set, provided you judge the take against the grouping and voicing marked in the score.

## When the harmony of the repeated chords changes

A new bass note or a new inner tone is a new shape, not only a new volume. Practise the change as a seam between two matched sets: the last chord of the old harmony and the first of the new one, slowly, with the voicing still clear. Then return to grouped repeats on each side of the seam. The ear should hear the harmonic change, not a bump in tone that has no musical cause.

In a soft dynamic, matching tone is often harder than in a loud one, because a thin repeat is easy to miss until you listen for inner notes. Keep a few loops at a soft level once the moderate set is even, and do not raise the volume only to hide the mismatch.

## FAQ

**Q: Should every repeated chord be exactly the same volume?**
A: Only as a starting default. After the set is even, you can add a written or planned rise and fall. The default prevents accidental accents.

**Q: What if the top note keeps disappearing?**
A: Slow the group and give that note a slightly clearer attack, without making the whole chord suddenly loud. Check that the finger on the top note is not collapsing.

**Q: Is a stiffer wrist the way to keep repeats even?**
A: Usually the opposite. A free, repeatable motion, with releases between groups, is more reliable than a locked arm.

**Q: How should I practise repeats that also leap?**
A: Separate the jobs: first match tone on a repeated shape in one place, then add the leap as a landing into the next set.

**Q: Can I use the pedal to glue uneven repeats together?**
A: Pedal will not fix an uneven attack. Match the tone first, then add pedal where the harmony and the style want it.
