contrafactum-new-words-old-melody.body:
A contrafactum, as scholars call it, is a song whose melody is kept while only the words are replaced with new ones. The practice is very old: in the Middle Ages, people set religious words to the melodies of troubadours' love songs; and during the Reformation in the sixteenth century, many German chorales also borrowed popular secular melodies of the time. Later, the same melody with different words travelled through different places and eras, which became almost the norm for folk songs and pop songs. For example, the melody of "Aura Lee" (1861) was later given new English words and became a pop song of the 1950s.

## Why People Do This

Contrafacta became popular because a good melody is easy to remember, while new words can express new content.

People do not have to learn a new melody; they only need to remember the new words in order to sing.

This lets songs spread quickly among people.

**Summary**
- Known academically as a contrafactum
- The melody is kept and new words are put in
- Already common in the Middle Ages and at the Reformation
- The same melody travelled through different eras with different words

## The Reformation Period

In the sixteenth century, the German Reformation leader Martin Luther wanted ordinary people to be able to sing in German.

He and his colleagues wrote many German chorales for the church, and some of these borrowed popular secular melodies of the time or old Latin chant melodies.

These chorales later became an important part of German church music, and Bach often used them.

## Contrafacta in Chinese

Chinese songs also have many examples of contrafacta.

For example, after some foreign folk songs reached China, they were given new Chinese words, some with a meaning completely different from the original.

There are also old tunes that were given local dialect words in different places.

## Contrafactum Summary

A contrafactum, in academic terms, keeps the melody and puts in new words. In the Middle Ages, some people set religious words to the melodies of troubadours' love songs; in the sixteenth-century Reformation, some of the German chorales written by Martin Luther and others borrowed secular melodies or old chant melodies, and Bach later often used them. Some melodies were given different words in different countries, and "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", the "Alphabet Song" and "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" use the same melody, which comes from an eighteenth-century French song.

"Aura Lee" of 1861 had its words changed twice, once by military academy cadets and once for a pop song of the 1950s, and in Chinese there are also examples of foreign folk songs given new Chinese words. In setting words, the rhythm, the stresses and the syllables have to fit together. On the piano you can play "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" and sing different words, or make up a new set of words yourself.

You can play with contrafacta together with Teacher Aum.

## The Melody Stays, the Words Are New

The idea of a contrafactum is very simple: the melody stays the same, and only the words change.

Take a melody everyone knows, set new words to it, and it becomes a new song.

Because the melody is already so familiar, the new song is easy to learn and to spread.

## Playing a Melody on the Piano

First play the melody of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" on the piano.

Then try singing different words, such as the words of the "Alphabet Song", and then sing a set of words you made up yourself.

You will find that the same melody, with different words, feels completely different.

## The New Life of Aura Lee

"Aura Lee", published in the United States in 1861, later had its words changed several times.

A US military academy changed the words, and it became a song the cadets sang at graduation.

In 1956, the same melody was given a new set of English words and became a hit again.

## Make Your Own Contrafactum

Choose a song you know well and try writing a new set of words for it, for example describing what you saw on your way to school today.

As you write, make sure the number of syllables in each line matches the number of notes in the melody.

When you have finished, sing it while you play, and see whether it flows naturally.

## A Familiar Example for Children

Some of the nursery rhymes children often sing are also examples of contrafacta.

For example, "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", the "Alphabet Song" and "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" all use the same melody, just with different words.

Its source is a little tune that was already in print in France around 1761.

## One Melody, Many Sets of Words

Some melodies are especially popular and have been given many different sets of words in different eras.

For example, there is an old British melody that was given the words of different national anthems or patriotic songs in different countries.

The same melody has completely different meanings in different places.

## The Art of Setting Words

Putting new words to an old melody also takes some care.

The new words need to fit the rhythm and stresses of the melody, and the long notes should fall on important syllables where possible.

If the fit is poor, it will feel awkward to sing.

## Playing with Contrafacta in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you and Teacher Aum can write new words for a simple melody, with one of you playing and the other singing.

You can also ask your teacher where your own words fit the stresses of the melody well and where they could still be adjusted.

From one old melody, you can sing a new story.

## Contrafacta in the Middle Ages

In the Middle Ages, the love songs of the troubadours were very popular, and many people could sing them.

Some people kept the melodies of these love songs and set words in praise of the Virgin Mary or of religious festivals.

**Listen**

In this way, religious content spread by means of popular melodies.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a contrafactum?**
A: A song whose melody is kept while only the words are replaced with new ones.

**Q: What is its academic name?**
A: Contrafactum.

**Q: How are German chorales of the Reformation related to changing words?**
A: Some borrowed popular secular melodies of the time or old chant melodies.

**Q: Which songs use the same melody as "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star"?**
A: The "Alphabet Song" and "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep".

**Q: What should you watch for when setting new words to an old melody?**
A: The new words must fit the rhythm and stresses of the melody.

brahms-lullaby-wiegenlied-piano.body:
Brahms's Lullaby was originally a German art song, the fourth in his Op. 49, published in 1868. The melody is simple and gentle, in triple time, and the accompaniment often sways softly like a cradle. When playing this piece on the piano, the key is to make the melody connected and soft like a singing voice, to keep the left-hand accompaniment in a steady three-beat pulse, to keep the volume low overall, and to let phrase endings settle naturally, without playing too loudly or too hurriedly.

## Choosing the Tempo

A lullaby should not be too fast, so choose a calm, settled tempo.

**A little slower**

Keep the tempo of the whole piece steady, and do not speed up as you play.

In the last phrase you can slow down very slightly, so that the music ends naturally.

## Playing One for Your Family

The Lullaby is a piece that is well suited to playing for your family at home, especially on a quiet evening.

Once you have learned it, you can add it to your repertoire and play it whenever you like.

A gentle melody can bring a sense of calm and warmth to the home.

## Chord Changes

The harmony of this piece is not complicated, and it mainly moves around the tonic, dominant and subdominant chords.

When playing the accompaniment, you can write the chord for each bar on the score to help you understand the direction of the harmony.

Once you know the chords, memorising and improvising an accompaniment both become easier.

## Sing First, Then Play

You can first find a recording of the original song and listen to how the singer shapes each phrase, where she breathes and where she pauses slightly.

Then hum the melody softly yourself, and go to the piano and imitate the breathing and rise and fall of the voice.

This method of singing first and playing afterwards is especially suited to piano works adapted from songs.

![A cartoon character with glasses and headphones looks at sheet music and plays an upright piano in a room at night, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1f7cw-ziigk.webp)

## The Three-Beat Left Hand

In the piano version, the left hand often plays simple broken chords or a three-beat accompaniment pattern, for example the bass on beat one and the chord on beats two and three.

The left hand should be steady and even, and softer than the right, giving the melody a gentle background.

You can practise the left hand alone first, so the three-beat pulse becomes steady, and then add the right hand.

## Brahms and Op. 49

Johannes Brahms was a composer of the German Romantic period, who lived from 1833 to 1897.

His Lullaby is an art song written for voice and piano, included in Op. 49 as No. 4.

The song was published in 1868, and has since been arranged for all kinds of instruments and become one of the lullaby melodies familiar to people all over the world.

- Originally a German art song, Op. 49 No. 4
- Published in 1868
- Triple time, with a simple, gentle melody
- The left hand keeps a steady three-beat pulse

## Soft Pedalling

When playing the Lullaby, a little right pedal helps the harmony of the accompaniment join together softly.

Change the pedal as soon as the chord changes, so that the harmonies before and after each stay clean.

Do not press the pedal too deep or too long, and keep the sound clear and soft.

## Versions for Different Levels

The Lullaby has many piano arrangements, and some have only a simple melody and accompaniment, suitable for beginners.

Others add richer harmony and ornaments, suitable for people with some foundation.

You can choose a version that suits your level and ask your teacher to help recommend one.

## Features of the Melody

The melody of the Lullaby does not rise and fall much, and is mostly stepwise motion with small leaps, so it is very easy to remember and sing.

The rhythm of the melody is also very simple, often alternating long and short notes, as if humming softly.

When you play, you can first sing the melody through to feel its breathing and rise and fall.

## The Sway of Triple Time

This piece is in triple time, with three beats to a bar, the first beat slightly stronger and the second and third weaker.

This pattern of strong and weak gives the music a feeling of gentle swaying, like a cradle rocking from side to side.

When performing, do not play the first beat too heavily, but let it be like a soft push.

## Making the Melody Sing

Because it was originally a song, the melody on the piano should also be as connected as a singing voice.

You can use legato fingering so that each note joins naturally to the next, leaving room to breathe between phrases.

Imagine someone softly singing this song, and your right hand is that voice.

## Volume and Tone

The character of a lullaby is quiet and gentle, so the overall volume should be low.

When touching the keys, keep your fingers close to them and press in a soft way, so that the sound is round and warm.

The highest point of a phrase can be slightly fuller, but do not let it pop out suddenly and break the quiet mood.

## Phrase Endings

At the end of every phrase, let it settle naturally and fade slightly, like a voice slowly stopping.

Do not cut off suddenly at the end of a phrase, and do not rush into the next one.

**Summary**

This kind of delicate handling makes the whole piece more tender and moving.

## FAQ

**Q: What was the Lullaby originally?**
A: A German art song, Op. 49 No. 4.

**Q: When was it published?**
A: 1868.

**Q: What is the time signature?**
A: Triple time.

**Q: How does the left hand accompany?**
A: With a steady three-beat pulse, softer than the right hand.

**Q: How should the melody be played?**
A: Connected and soft, like a singing voice.

**Q: How fast should the tempo be?**
A: Calm and settled, and kept steady.

program-music-vs-absolute-music-listenin.body:
Program music is instrumental music meant to suggest a story, scene, character or idea from outside music, while absolute music is instrumental music meant to be heard on its own terms, as patterns of sound, harmony and form. The difference shaped a famous debate in the nineteenth century, and it still offers a helpful pair of lenses for listening. Most pianists play both kinds, often without thinking about which is which.

## What counts as program music

A piece becomes program music when the composer connects it to something beyond the notes. That connection can be a title, a poem printed in the score, a written story or a detailed description.

- Antonio Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, published in 1725, came with sonnets describing birds, storms and winter ice, matched to passages in the music.
- Hector Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830 followed an imaginative storyline, with a recurring theme representing a beloved person.
- Modest Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition, written for piano in 1874, portrays a walk through an art exhibition, with a "Promenade" theme linking the scenes.
- Franz Liszt developed the symphonic poem, a single-movement orchestral work based on a literary or visual source.

Piano character pieces with descriptive titles, such as many by Robert Schumann or Claude Debussy, often belong in or near this category too.

## What counts as absolute music

Absolute music offers no external story. Its interest lies in how themes develop, how keys move, how textures change and how a form unfolds. Titles tend to be generic: sonata, fugue, symphony number, prelude in a given key.

Johann Sebastian Bach's fugues and many sonatas and symphonies of the Classical era are often cited as examples. The music may still feel joyful, tense or tender, but those feelings arise from musical events rather than from a named scene.

## The nineteenth-century debate

In 1854 the critic Eduard Hanslick published an influential essay arguing that the beauty of music lies in its "tonally moving forms", not in representing feelings or stories. Supporters of program music, often associated with Liszt and Richard Wagner, believed music could and should connect with poetry, drama and ideas.

Both sides produced passionate writing, and the argument helped clarify what each approach values. Today most listeners and musicians see the two as ends of a spectrum rather than rival camps.

![Concept art of a modern piano with digital light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9prb6s-uw7zy.webp)

## The grey zone in between

Many pieces sit somewhere in the middle.

**Beethoven's Pastoral Symphony**
Ludwig van Beethoven gave its movements descriptive titles, including a brook scene and a storm, but noted that it was more an expression of feeling than painting. It is descriptive, yet it also follows symphonic form closely.

**Titles added later**
Some popular nicknames, like "Moonlight" for Beethoven's Sonata Op. 27 No. 2, came from others after the composer. The music was not written to depict moonlight, though the nickname now shapes how people hear it.

**Debussy's placement of titles**
In his piano Préludes, Debussy printed each title at the end of the piece rather than at the start, inviting players to hear the music first and the image afterwards.

## Listening with two lenses

You can practise switching lenses with any instrumental piece.

- First listening: ignore the title. Notice themes, repetitions, contrasts and the moment where something returns.
- Second listening: read the title or program. Ask which musical choices support the image: tempo, register, articulation, harmony.
- Third listening: combine both. Hear how the story and the structure support each other.

This method keeps you from treating program music as sound effects and from treating absolute music as abstract and cold.

## What it means for pianists

When you learn a descriptive piece, an image can guide tone and timing. A piece about water might suggest smooth, even arpeggios; a dance might suggest crisp accents. When you learn a sonata or fugue, the structure becomes your story: where the theme enters, how tension builds, where the music comes home.

It can be worthwhile to invent your own private image for an abstract piece, or to study the form of a descriptive one. Both habits deepen interpretation. Practice support from an app such as TIGA ALPHA can take care of note accuracy and rhythm, leaving more attention for these musical decisions.

## FAQ

**Q: Is film music program music?**
A: It shares the idea of connecting music to images and stories, though it is usually discussed as its own field.

**Q: Can music with lyrics be program music?**
A: The term normally applies to instrumental music. Songs already carry meaning through their words.

**Q: Is one approach more serious than the other?**
A: No. Great works exist on both sides, and many composers wrote in both ways.

**Q: How do I know which a piece is?**
A: Check the title, any notes from the composer and the history of the work. When in doubt, it may be somewhere in between.

ai-performance-rendering-expression-bare.body:
AI performance rendering is the task of taking a bare score or a plain MIDI file, with little or no expressive information, and producing timing, loudness, articulation and often pedalling that resemble a human performance. The starting material may be a file in which every note sits exactly on a grid and every velocity is the same. The output is a version in which a phrase leans forward, a cadence breathes, a melody stands above its accompaniment, and a pedal changes the resonance. The aim is not to invent a new composition. It is to give the existing notes a plausible spoken shape.

## Why a bare score sounds flat

Standard music notation is already a rich set of instructions, yet much of what a pianist does is only hinted at. Even when a score includes crescendos, dots and pedal marks, it rarely specifies the exact millisecond of a delay or the exact force of each inner note. A MIDI file exported from notation software is often even plainer: grid-aligned onsets and a single default velocity. Played back as written, the result can feel stiff, because human playing is full of small, structured deviations.

Rendering software tries to supply those deviations in a musical pattern, not at random.

## How rendering models learn expression

**Examples of real playing**
Systems are trained on recordings or MIDI captures in which the same pieces, or similar textures, have already been performed. The model sees both the plain score and the expressive choices, then learns relationships such as "the last note of a phrase often arrives a little late" or "an inner accompaniment stays quieter than the melody".

**Local shape and larger form**
Useful rendering looks beyond single notes. It considers phrase length, repeated material, harmonic arrival points and the difference between a melody and a filler voice. A delay that sounds natural at a cadence can sound nervous in the middle of a rising run.

**Controls a user can still set**
Some tools let a person choose a general character, such as a more restrained or a more flexible result, or lock certain parts of the file so that only the rest is rendered. The file remains editable, which is important if the suggestion is only partly right.

This is different from simple MIDI humanizing, which nudges notes by small random or fixed amounts to avoid a mechanical grid. Rendering aims at patterns learned from actual performances, including coordination between the hands and the use of the sustain pedal.

![Piano keys and score in soft focus](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwfgh3eb-yo6vo.webp)

## Where the suggestion should not have the last word

Rendered expression can be a helpful sketch, especially for a draft arrangement or a first listen to a new score. It still needs a musician's review.

- The model may shape every repeat in the same way, even when a player would change the second telling.
- A learned habit from one style can be applied where it does not belong, for example a romantic swell inside a texture that should stay almost even.
- Pedal marks may blur a line that needs to stay dry, or leave a gap where resonance should continue.
- The system does not know the instrument, the room, or the hand comfort of the person who will play the piece.

Think of the output as a colleague's suggestion written in pencil.

## Using a rendered file as a practice mirror

A thoughtful way to use rendering is to compare it with your own choices rather than to copy it blindly.

- Render a short piece, then play the same score yourself and record both.
- Listen once for timing: where does the model breathe, and where do you?
- Listen again for voicing: which notes are raised, and do you agree?
- Change one phrase on purpose, against the model's suggestion, and decide whether your version says something clearer.

TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app that listens in the other direction. Instead of adding expression to a dead file, it hears the notes and rhythms you actually play and shows where they depart from the score. Rendering can suggest a shape; a practice app can tell you whether your hands realised the shape you intended.

## FAQ

**Q: Is performance rendering the same as composing with AI?**
A: No. Rendering starts from an existing score or MIDI file and adds expressive detail. It does not write a new melody or chord progression.

**Q: How is this different from humanizing a MIDI track?**
A: Humanizing often adds small random or rule-based shifts so the grid is less obvious. Rendering tries to apply patterns learned from real performances, including phrasing and pedalling.

**Q: Can I use a rendered file as a practice model?**
A: You can use it as one listening reference, then keep or reject its choices. It should not replace a teacher's guidance or your own musical decisions.

**Q: Does rendering work only for solo piano?**
A: Piano has been a common test case because of the amount of data and the importance of pedalling, but the same idea can be applied to other scored music.

two-note-slurs-drop-roll-beginners.body:
A two-note slur is one of the first expressive shapes beginners meet in piano music. On the page it looks small: a curved line joining two notes. In sound, it should feel like a sigh or a spoken word with the stress on the first syllable, such as "MA-ma" or "HEL-lo". The first note is fuller, the second lighter and slightly shorter. The physical motion behind that sound is often called "drop and roll", and it is easier than it looks.

## What the two-note slur asks for

When two notes are joined by a short slur, the general convention is to connect them smoothly, give the first note a little more weight and release the second note gently. The second note is often played a touch shorter, so that a small space appears before whatever comes next. Teachers sometimes describe it as "strong, weak, lift".

**Listening comes first**
Before working on the motion, play two notes and say "sigh" out loud as you do it. Many learners find the sound they want simply by matching the shape of the spoken word.

## The drop: sending weight into the first note

The first note begins with a relaxed drop of the wrist and arm. Imagine your hand as loose and heavy, held just above the key. Let it fall gently so the weight of the arm, not a push from the finger, makes the sound.

- Keep the shoulder low and the elbow free.
- Let the wrist dip slightly as the key goes down.
- Keep the fingertip firm enough to carry the weight, but not stiff.

The result should be a warm, rounded tone rather than a sharp hit.

## The roll: rising out of the second note

For the second note, the wrist moves upward and slightly forward while the next finger plays. It feels as though the hand is rolling off the key and floating away. Because the arm is rising, the second note is naturally softer. When the wrist reaches the top of its motion, the hand lifts off the key completely, which creates that small release at the end.

**Think of a single movement**
The drop and the roll are not two separate actions. They are one smooth down-up curve, like a small wave. Practising the wave away from the keyboard, on a tabletop or your knee, helps make it feel natural.

![Painterly wooden upright piano with a green stool on a dark teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8aa5a4-u1y5w.webp)

## Common beginner tensions and how to release them

**Pressing the second note too hard**
Some learners give both notes equal force. Slow down and exaggerate the upward wrist motion so the arm cannot push.

**Locking the wrist**
A stiff wrist turns the slur into two separate taps. Rest the hand in your lap, let it hang, then return to the keys with that loose feeling.

**Lifting too late**
If the second note is held too long, the sigh disappears. Count "one-and" and lift on "and".

**Raising the shoulder**
Tension often creeps up into the shoulder. Take a breath out on the drop, and check in a mirror or a short video that the shoulder stays down.

## A short practice sequence

Use five minutes at the start of practice for this touch.

- Play slurs on neighbouring keys with fingers 2 and 3 in the right hand, slowly, ten times.
- Repeat with fingers 3 and 4, which often feel weaker.
- Do the same in the left hand.
- Move the slur up and down the keyboard, one step at a time.
- Finally, find the slurs in a piece you are learning and play just those pairs.

## How the touch grows over time

As beginners get comfortable, the motion becomes smaller and quicker. Advanced players still use the same idea, but the wave may be almost invisible. Longer slurs over three or four notes build on it too: the arm drops at the start, carries weight through the middle and rolls off at the end. Getting two-note slurs right early lays down a habit that supports phrasing for years.

**Getting feedback**
A teacher can watch the wrist and arm and spot tension quickly. A practice tool like TIGA ALPHA can help you check whether notes are steady, while you focus on the feel of the motion. A useful reminder is that the sound should guide the movement, not the other way around.

## FAQ

**Q: Should the second note always be shorter?**
A: Usually a little, but style and tempo matter. Follow your teacher's advice and listen to recordings of the piece.

**Q: Can I use the drop and roll on fast music?**
A: Yes, with a much smaller motion. Learn it slowly first so the shape is clear.

**Q: What if my wrist feels tired?**
A: Stop and shake out the hand. Fatigue often means too much effort; the motion should feel light.

**Q: Is a two-note slur the same as a tie?**
A: No. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound. A slur joins different pitches.

ticketed-livestream-concerts-online-busi.body:
A ticketed livestream concert is a performance broadcast online that is open only to paying viewers, who typically purchase an online pass that unlocks a private stream at a set time, sometimes with a replay window afterwards. The format grew rapidly in 2020, when venues closed and artists needed new ways to reach audiences. Large productions such as BTS's online concert "Bang Bang Con The Live", streamed in June 2020, showed that fans around the world would pay for a professionally produced stream, while thousands of independent musicians tested smaller paid shows from homes and empty venues.

This article explains how paid livestreams work, why fans buy them and how musicians and teachers can plan a simple, well-run online recital.

## From free streams to ticketed events

Free live videos had been common for years, but they mostly served as promotion. When touring stopped, artists needed income. Ticketing tools that restricted access to paying viewers turned the stream into an event with a clear value: a scheduled performance, shared in real time with other fans, often with features that a recording cannot offer.

## What fans are paying for

**Liveness**
Knowing that the music is happening now creates excitement and a sense of occasion.

**Community**
Live chat lets viewers react together, greet each other and send messages to the performer.

**Access**
Fans in other cities or countries can attend shows they could never travel to.

**Extras**
Multiple camera angles, behind-the-scenes segments, question-and-answer sessions or exclusive songs add value.

## The basic technical chain

- Sound: a clean audio feed is more important than perfect video. Use a decent microphone or a direct line from a digital piano or mixer.
- Video: one stable camera framed to show the performer and the hands works well for piano.
- Encoding: software or hardware converts the feed into a stream.
- Platform: a service handles ticket sales, access control and playback.
- Internet: a wired connection with a speed test before the show reduces dropouts.


![Watercolour grand piano with its lid open in soft grey-violet tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvyav63h-7nw79.webp)

## Planning a small online recital

- Set a clear date and time, including time zones for international viewers.
- Keep the programme shorter than an in-person concert; forty to sixty minutes suits many online audiences.
- Do a full technical rehearsal at the same time of day as the show.
- Prepare a short welcome and introductions between pieces.
- Assign a helper to watch the chat and handle technical questions.
- Offer a replay window for ticket holders who miss the start.

## Pricing and fairness

Ticket prices for online shows are often lower than for physical concerts, reflecting the different experience. Some artists offer a sliding scale so supporters can pay more if they wish, or include a digital programme or download with each ticket. Being transparent about what the ticket includes, such as live only or live plus replay, avoids disappointment.

## For piano teachers and student showcases

Studios can run ticketed or free online recitals for families who live far away. Keep students' privacy in mind: share links only with invited viewers, avoid displaying full names, and get permission from parents before recording or replaying. A recorded showcase can also become a keepsake for families and a reflection tool for students, who can watch their own performance and notice what to work on next.

## What has stayed after 2020

Physical concerts returned, but livestreams did not disappear. Many artists now add a paid stream to selected tour dates, run online release parties or offer subscriber-only sessions. The format works best as a complement to live venues, extending reach rather than replacing the room.

## Handling problems gracefully

Even careful setups fail sometimes. Prepare a short message to post if the stream drops, keep a backup internet option such as a phone hotspot ready, and decide in advance whether a replay will be offered to make up for interruptions. Audiences are usually understanding when performers communicate quickly and calmly.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a ticketed livestream concert?**
A: An online performance that viewers pay to access, usually through a digital ticket for a scheduled stream.

**Q: Why did paid livestreams grow in 2020?**
A: Venues closed, so artists needed new ways to perform and earn, and fans wanted live experiences at home.

**Q: What matters most technically for piano streams?**
A: Clean sound first, then a stable camera angle that shows the hands, plus a reliable internet connection.

**Q: How long should an online recital be?**
A: Shorter than an in-person concert; around forty to sixty minutes suits many audiences.

tarantella-piano-quick-dance.body:
A tarantella on the piano is a fast dance, often written in a compound metre such as six-eight or twelve-eight, in which a larger dotted beat holds a spinning surface of quicker notes. The name recalls a southern Italian dance tradition; piano tarantellas are usually concert or salon pieces that keep the sense of a rapid, circling motion. The technical task is to feel those larger beats, to keep repeating figures even, and to reach a lively tempo without losing the downbeats.

![Musician at an open grand piano on a rainy neon street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdehw38-21jbu.webp)

## Compound time at a speed you can still count

In six-eight, two dotted-crotchet beats in a bar are usually more useful than six small counts, especially as the tempo rises. Clap the two larger beats, then tap the three inner notes of each beat, then play a simple repeating figure in one hand with the same grouping. If you only count six, the dance can feel busy and small; if you only feel one rush per bar, the inner groups can collapse.

A first counting check:

- Clap two larger beats in a bar.
- Tap three inner notes on each beat.
- Play one repeating figure with the same grouping.


Mark the opening beat of every bar, and also the half-bar, in a few difficult passages, so the eye has a landing place.

## Repeating figures that must stay even

Many tarantellas use circling accompaniment patterns or repeating right-hand figures. Practise a single bar, then two, until the figure is even at a modest speed. A bump on the same finger every time will become very obvious when the dance is fast. If a rotation of the hand or a slight shift of position makes the figure smoother, write that in and reuse it.

**The left hand is a motor, not a series of surprises**
When the left hand is the repeating figure, it should be learned until it can run quietly while attention stays on the tune or on a sudden contrast. When the right hand is the spinner, the left hand often marks the larger beats. Either way, one layer should be predictable enough to support the other.

## Building speed without losing the dance

Use a ladder of tempos: exact at a modest speed, then a little quicker, then back down if the downbeats slip. Do not jump to the final tempo with a hope that excitement will carry the notes. Accent-planning helps: a small sense of arrival on the larger beats, with inner notes lighter, keeps the spin organised.

After a first page is even, a short session in TIGA ALPHA can hold one repeating figure at the current honest tempo. The grouping into dotted beats should already be settled at the keyboard.

## Contrasts, slower corners and a final stop

Some tarantellas include a more lyrical middle, a sudden piano, or a brief slower indication before the dance returns. Practise those corners as carefully as the fast figuration, and practise the restart of the quick tempo, which is often where control is lost. The ending should be planned: a clear final pattern, a last downbeat, and a still hand, not a vague tumble off the last page.

If you programme a tarantella after a quiet piece, leave enough silence, then start from the inner count, so the first bar is already in the dance metre.

## A short order for learning a tarantella

- Clap the larger dotted beats, then the inner groups.
- Learn one repeating figure until it is even.
- Keep one hand as a stable motor under or over the other.
- Raise tempo in steps, protecting the downbeats.
- Practise lyrical corners and the restart of the fast dance, plus a clear ending.

## FAQ

**Q: Should I always feel two beats in a six-eight tarantella?**
A: Two larger beats are a useful default. In a very broad middle section you might feel the inner groups more clearly, then return to the two-beat dance.

**Q: What if my repeating figure always speeds up?**
A: Practise it with a click on the dotted beats, then without, and return to a slower exact version as soon as the downbeats slip.

**Q: Is a tarantella meant to sound out of control?**
A: It should sound lively and circling, not careless. Excitement comes from speed plus evenness, not from lost beats.

**Q: How much pedal is useful?**
A: A little may warm a lyrical corner. In the spinning figures, too much pedal smears the groups. Try those bars without pedal first.

**Q: Can I start practice at the final tempo for a short burst?**
A: A short burst can be a check later. It should not replace a slower, exact version of the same figure.

measurable-piano-practice-goals-children.body:
Measurable practice goals tell a child exactly what to achieve, such as "play bars 1 to 4 three times in a row with no stops", instead of only how long to sit at the piano. Time-based instructions like "practise for 20 minutes" often lead to watching the clock, playing the easy parts again and again, or rushing through the piece. A countable goal gives the session a clear purpose and a clear end, so children can see their own progress and feel proud when they reach it.

Parents do not need musical training to support this approach. They only need to help the child choose a goal and notice when it is reached.

## Why minutes alone do not work well

Twenty minutes can contain a lot of useful work or very little. A child may spend most of the time on a favourite section that is already secure, avoiding the tricky bar that really needs attention. Clock-watching also teaches children that practice is something to endure. When the goal is a result rather than a duration, the child naturally spends time where it is needed.

**Combine both if needed**
Some families like a time frame for routine. That is fine; simply add a goal inside the time, such as "in today's 15 minutes, make the left hand of line two smooth".

## Five types of goals that children understand

- Repetition goals: "Play this bar correctly three times in a row."
- Tempo goals: "Play the scale with the metronome at the next speed up."
- Accuracy goals: "Play the first line with all the correct notes and fingers."
- Musical goals: "Make the last phrase get softer like it is falling asleep."
- Independence goals: "Play the piece from memory to the end of the first page."

Rotate the types through the week so practice does not become repetitive.

## A simple tracking chart

A paper chart on the piano works well for younger children. Each day, write one or two goals in simple words and leave a box to tick. Stickers or coloured stars make the chart attractive. Older children may prefer a notes app or a small notebook. The important part is that the goal is written before practice starts, not decided afterwards.

![Cartoon of a person in headphones and glasses at a white upright piano with fairy lights and a neon TIGA STUDIO sign](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvzq4fy6-17ieu.webp)

## Making goals the right size

A good goal is challenging but reachable within one session. If a child fails repeatedly, the goal is too big. Break it into smaller parts, such as one hand alone or two bars instead of four. If the goal is reached in two minutes, raise it slightly next time. Teachers can suggest suitable sizes, and many will happily write weekly goals in the lesson notebook.

**The "three in a row" rule**
Playing a passage correctly once may be luck. Three correct runs in a row show the skill is becoming reliable. Count aloud together so the child feels the achievement.

## How parents can respond

Praise effort and specific results: "You kept the rhythm steady even in the hard bar" is more useful than "Great job". Avoid correcting every note during practice, since that can feel like a test. Instead, ask the child to tell you the goal and show you when it is reached. If the child is frustrated, suggest a short break and a smaller target.

- Ask: "What is today's goal?"
- Listen: let the child show you without interruption.
- Notice: mention one specific improvement.
- Celebrate: tick the box together.

## Keeping motivation over months

Measurable goals add up. After a few weeks, the chart becomes a visible record of progress, which can be motivating on difficult days. At the end of each month, look back at the chart together and choose one piece to play as a small home performance. Linking daily goals to a bigger musical event gives the effort meaning.

Children also enjoy choosing some goals themselves. Offer two or three options and let them pick, which builds ownership and independence. Over time, the aim is for children to set sensible goals without help, a skill that is useful far beyond the piano.

## FAQ

**Q: How many goals should a child have per session?**
A: One to three is enough. More goals make sessions feel crowded.

**Q: What if my child reaches the goal quickly?**
A: Celebrate it, then either finish early or add a small bonus goal. Raise the challenge slightly next time.

**Q: Should I stop using practice time completely?**
A: Not necessarily. A regular time slot helps routine; goals simply make that time more productive.

**Q: Can apps help track goals?**
A: Yes. Some learning apps show completed steps, accuracy or tempo, which makes goals easy to see.

ethical-student-testimonials-consent-mus.body:
Student testimonials can help new families decide whether a music studio is right for them, yet a testimonial is only valuable when it is genuine, specific and shared with clear permission. An ethical process asks politely, explains where words will appear, protects personal data and lets people change their mind. Following that process protects your students, respects privacy law and makes your marketing more believable than polished slogans ever could.

## Why honest testimonials matter

Families comparing music lessons often feel unsure. They cannot judge teaching quality from a website alone, so they look for signs that real people have had a good experience. A short, honest comment from another parent or adult learner answers that need. Exaggerated praise has the opposite effect: readers sense when words have been written for them.

**Specific beats glowing**
"My daughter now practises without being reminded" tells a reader much more than "Amazing teacher, highly recommended". Specific details make a testimonial useful.

## Asking at the right moment

A good time to ask is shortly after a positive moment, such as a recital, the end of a term or a learner finishing a piece they cared about. Ask in a relaxed way and make it easy to say no. Never link a request to lesson prices, grades or performance opportunities.

Good prompts to offer:

- What did you hope to get from lessons when you started?
- What has changed in your playing or practice since then?
- Is there a moment in lessons you particularly remember?
- What would you tell a friend who is thinking about starting?

These open questions invite real stories instead of generic praise.

## Recording permission properly

![Cartoon of a learner at a white upright piano with fairy lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw6v3tea-7a62b.webp)

Consent must be clear and recorded. Explain where the words will appear, such as your website, social media or a printed brochure, and for how long. For learners under the age of consent, ask a parent or guardian. Decide together whether to use a full name, first name or initials. Under privacy laws such as Thailand's PDPA, people have the right to withdraw consent, so keep a simple record and remove content promptly when asked.

**Photos need separate permission**
A written quote and a photo are different things. Ask separately for each, and never use a child's image without explicit permission from a guardian.

## Editing without changing meaning

Light editing for grammar or length is acceptable, but the meaning must stay the same. Send the edited version back for approval before publishing. Never combine comments from different people into one quote, and never invent a testimonial, even as an example on a website.

## Presenting testimonials honestly

Place testimonials near the information they support. A comment about beginner confidence fits on a beginner course page. A comment about recital preparation fits near your concert information. Show a mix of voices rather than only the most enthusiastic ones, and avoid implying that every learner will have the same result.

**Avoid outcome promises**
If a testimonial mentions an exam result or a competition, add context so readers understand that results vary with effort, time and individual goals.

## Keeping testimonials fresh

Review your testimonials once or twice a year. Remove old ones from students who left long ago if they no longer reflect how you teach. Ask current families for new perspectives. A living collection shows that your studio is active and growing.

## Letting learners tell it in their own words

Some learners prefer to speak rather than write. Offer a short conversation after a lesson and take notes, then send the written version for approval. Adult learners and older students may enjoy writing a few lines themselves. Either way, the words should sound like the person, not like your marketing copy.

## When feedback is negative

Not every response will be positive, and that is useful. Thank the person, consider what they say and make changes where needed. Never pressure anyone to change a review. Handling criticism calmly often builds more trust than a page full of praise.

If a comment points to a real gap, such as unclear scheduling or slow replies, share what you changed with the person who raised it. That small act of follow-through is often remembered longer than the original problem.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I use a testimonial from a group chat message?**
A: Only after asking the writer directly and getting clear permission for public use.

**Q: Should testimonials include full names?**
A: Not necessarily; first names or initials are often safer and still credible.

**Q: How long can I keep a testimonial online?**
A: As long as consent allows, and remove it promptly if the person withdraws consent.

**Q: Can I edit a testimonial?**
A: Light edits are fine, but send the final version back for approval.

**Q: Are video testimonials better?**
A: They can feel personal, but they need extra consent and care, especially for children.

sight-reading-one-bar-ahead.body:
Sight-reading at the piano often stalls because the eyes stay on the notes the fingers are already playing. By the time a new bar arrives, there is no plan for the next harmony or the next leap. Looking one bar ahead is a practical habit: the hands play the present bar while the eyes take in the next, and the pulse continues even if a finger is approximate. The skill can be practised on music well within reach, not only on difficult new scores.

## Choose music simple enough that the eyes have spare attention

Use a slow piece, a hymn-like texture, or a short study whose rhythm you can count. If the present bar already consumes all your attention, there is no room to look ahead. Set a modest tempo with a click and decide that the pulse will not stop. Wrong notes may occur; a stopped pulse is the larger fault in this exercise.

## Practise a deliberate look into the next bar

At the start of each bar, play what is already in the hands, then move the eyes to the next barline and take in the new bass, the new melody note, or a leap. You can even say the next bass note while still playing the present bar. Do this for a few lines, then rest. The habit is tiring at first. Mark a reminder at a few barlines, such as a small arrow, and remove the marks as the look becomes regular.

## Recover on the next beat, not by restarting the line

When a chord is wrong, the useful response is to arrive in time for the next beat, even if the wrong notes are abandoned. Restarting the line every time trains the opposite of sight-reading. Practise this recovery on purpose: play a line, allow a miss, and require the next downbeat to be on time. Looking ahead makes that recovery possible, because the next bar is already partly known.

A short reading task in TIGA ALPHA can be used the same way if you treat a first pass as a moving pulse, and judge it by continuity rather than by a perfect note count.

## When the texture thickens or the page turns

In a busier texture, look ahead for the next bass and the next right-hand landmark, not for every inner tone. For a page turn, the look-ahead must include the first notes of the new page, so the turn is prepared like any other shift. Practise the turn on the same simple piece until the pulse survives it. The aim is still a flowing first reading, not a polished performance.

On a first reading of a new line, you can also decide in advance which voice you will protect if the texture becomes busy: usually the bass and the melody. That choice makes the look-ahead smaller, and it keeps the pulse from stalling while the inner parts wait for a later pass.

![Futuristic grand piano and crystal synths on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdlg9sr-haxaw.webp)

- Choose a simple texture and a tempo you can keep without stopping.
- Keep a click running, and do not halt for a missed note.
- At each bar, glance at the next bass or the next leap while still playing.
- After a slip, rejoin on the next beat rather than restarting the line.
- End the sitting while the look-ahead is still possible, not after the eyes have tired.

## FAQ

**Q: Should I always look a whole bar ahead, even in very short bars?**
A: In a very short bar, a beat or two may be enough. The idea is that the eyes are not stuck on the notes already under the fingers.

**Q: What if I lose my place when I look ahead?**
A: The music may still be too hard, or the tempo too fast. Simplify, and point to the next barline as a landmark until the return to the present bar is easy.

**Q: Is it all right to skip an inner note in order to keep the pulse?**
A: In a first reading, yes. Keep the bass and the melody if you can, and accept a thinner middle, so the line continues.

**Q: Should I practise sight-reading at performance tempo?**
A: Start under the tempo at which the look-ahead is possible. A slower, continuous reading teaches more than a fast reading that stops every bar.

**Q: How long should a sight-reading sitting last?**
A: A few minutes of fresh reading is often enough. Tired eyes stop looking ahead, and the habit does not improve after that point.

house-concerts-piano-students-guide.body:
Before concert halls became common, much music was played in homes for friends and family. House concerts revive that tradition. A small audience gathers in a living room, a student or group of students plays a short programme, and everyone shares conversation and refreshments afterwards. For piano students, house concerts offer an intimate, friendly setting to perform, and for families they are a way to celebrate progress together.

## Why house concerts work for students

House concerts sit between a lesson and a formal recital. The audience is small and familiar, the space is comfortable and the atmosphere is warm. Students can:

- perform a full programme of several pieces, not just one
- speak briefly about the music, building communication skills
- experience playing on a different piano in a different room
- receive personal responses from listeners afterwards

These experiences prepare students for larger performances while keeping pressure manageable. A living room also removes the distance of a stage, so students see faces, smiles and reactions, which many find encouraging once they get used to it.

## Choosing a host home

The host home needs a playable piano, ideally tuned shortly before the event, and space for a small audience. A family in the studio may volunteer, or the teacher's own home may work. Agree on details with the host: the date, number of guests, seating arrangements, refreshments and how long the event will last. Respect the host's privacy and house rules.

![Watercolour white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbhfuu5-g2y88.webp)

## Planning the programme

**Keep it short**
Thirty to forty-five minutes of music is enough for a living-room audience.

**Mix moods**
Alternate lively and gentle pieces, and include a variety of styles and periods.

**Feature each performer**
If several students play, give each a short set of two or three pieces rather than one piece each, so listeners get to know their playing.

**Add a shared moment**
End with a duet or a piece that involves more than one performer.

## Talking to the audience

One special feature of house concerts is the chance to speak. Encourage students to introduce their pieces with one or two sentences: why they chose the piece, what to listen for or a fact about the composer. Practise these introductions in lessons. Speaking helps listeners engage and gives students confidence beyond the keyboard.

## Preparing the instrument and space

Visit the home before the concert to try the piano. Every instrument feels different, and students benefit from a short rehearsal on it. Check the bench height, lighting on the music stand and whether pedals work well. Arrange chairs so the audience can see the performer's hands if possible, and leave a clear path to the piano so performers can walk on and off without squeezing past guests.

## Hosting with care

Plan a simple schedule: arrival and greetings, the concert, then refreshments and conversation. Print a short programme with piece titles and performers' names. Remind guests to silence phones. If recording or photographing, ask permission from performers and families in advance and follow the studio's privacy approach.

## When the music ends

Encourage guests to talk with the performers. Their questions and comments are often memorable for students. In the next lesson, discuss how the concert felt, what went well and what the student would like to try next time. Some studios hold house concerts once or twice a year, rotating hosts so different families can take part.

## Variations on the idea

House concerts can take many forms: a themed evening of music from one country, a programme of student compositions, a family concert where parents and children play together, or an afternoon event for grandparents. The common thread is a small, warm setting where music and conversation sit side by side.

Students preparing a house concert programme with TIGA ALPHA can practise run-throughs of their full set, which builds the stamina needed for several pieces in a row.

## FAQ

**Q: How many guests should a house concert have?**
A: Usually fifteen to thirty, depending on the space available.

**Q: Does the piano need to be tuned?**
A: Ideally yes, shortly before the event, so performers and listeners hear the music at its clearest.

**Q: Should students speak about their pieces?**
A: A short introduction helps listeners engage and builds the student's confidence.

**Q: How long should a house concert last?**
A: Thirty to forty-five minutes of music, plus time for conversation afterwards, works well.

corelli-clash-cadential-dissonance.body:
In some Baroque cadences, a very short moment occurs: one voice already has a dissonant note that needs to resolve, while another voice sounds the resolution of that note at the same time. The two notes briefly overlap, sounding like a gentle bump, and then separate and close. This way of writing is often called the Corelli clash, because it is quite common in the style associated with Corelli, although similar progressions may also appear in the works of others of the same period. When learning it, first identify the dissonant note and its resolution separately, then see whether they overlapped in the same place for a beat or less. When listening, the point is not to play this moment harshly, but to let the brief overlap be heard and then leave cleanly. If the two notes are fully staggered, the clash disappears; if the overlap is dragged out, the cadence becomes muddy. This article is only about this brief overlap at a cadence, and does not call every dissonance a clash. When practising, you can enlarge and slow down this moment, and once you can clearly hear the overlap and the departure, put it back into the complete cadence at the original tempo. The name is a later generalisation, meant to help us recognise a specific sound, not a rule that must be applied everywhere.

## Two Opposite Faults

If you stagger the two notes completely, the clash is gone; if you drag the overlap out too long, the cadence turns muddy.

When practising, deliberately slow down at first and find the point where the notes overlap and then leave at once.

Then put it back at the original tempo and check that it is both audible and not muddy.

**Remember this**
- At a cadence, a dissonant note and its resolution briefly overlap
- It sounds like a gentle bump, followed by a separation and a close
- It is quite common in the style associated with Corelli, and similar progressions may appear in the works of others of the same period
- When practising, first slow down to hear the overlap clearly, then put it back at the original tempo, neither removing it nor dragging it out

## How to Handle This Moment in Playing

The overlap should be heard, but it need not be stressed into a harsh blow.

Keep the duration short and the departure clean, so that the cadence is still clear.

Control the touch of both lines, so that it is possible to tell which one goes first and which one goes after.

## How to Understand the Name

The name was given later to identify a common way of writing, and it does not mean that Corelli was the only one who wrote this way.

Treat it as a label for recognising a sound, and there is no need to inflate it into a rule named after a person.

When you hear a similar overlap, you can recognise it in the same way, without first arguing about the name.

## Marking the Overlap in the Score

Make a small mark at the short spot where the overlap happens, and mark which note is the dissonance and which is the resolution.

That way it is also hard to slide past this moment at the original tempo.

Keep the mark small, so it does not make the score hard to read.

## Take Extra Care with the Pedal

This moment is most afraid of a long pedal that keeps the two notes soaked together.

You can pedal briefly or not at all, letting the fingers make both the overlap and the departure clear.

Going through it without pedal often tells you at once whether your foot has been getting in the way.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashing paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdkxeu0-ndqt3.webp)

## Asking Teacher Aum in a Lesson Whether the Clash Is Clear but Not Muddy

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and tell you whether the overlap at the cadence is audible and whether the departure is clean.

If somewhere is soaked by the pedal, you can also ask your teacher to help you lift your foot first and listen to whether the clash is clear.

From this brief clash at a cadence, you can practise letting both the dissonance and the resolution be heard in the same very short moment.

## How It Appears in a Cadence

One voice still rests on the note that needs to resolve, while another voice has already sounded the resolved note.

The two briefly coexist, then the dissonant one leaves and the cadence is completed.

First circle the two notes separately, then see in which very short spot they overlap.

## What to Remember About the Corelli Clash

It is the way of writing in which, at a cadence, a dissonant note and its resolution briefly overlap and then separate.

The name is meant to help us recognise a sound, and does not mean only one person wrote this way.

When playing, let the clash be heard but do not drag it out, and take special care with the pedal.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does the Corelli clash refer to?**
A: At a cadence, a dissonant note in one voice and the resolution in another voice briefly overlap, then separate.

**Q: Does the name mean only Corelli wrote this way?**
A: No. It is a later label, and similar progressions may also appear in the works of others of the same period.

**Q: How should I handle this moment in playing?**
A: Let the overlap be heard, keep the duration short and the departure clean, and do not slam it into a harsh blow.

**Q: What are the two common faults?**
A: Staggering the notes completely, so the clash disappears; or overlapping for too long, so the cadence turns muddy.

**Q: What should I watch for with the pedal?**
A: Do not hold a long pedal, which would soak the two notes together; you can try without pedal first to check whether the clash is clear.

slash-chords-piano-bass-note-reading.body:
Slash chords are chord symbols with a forward slash, such as C/E, G/B or F/C. The letter before the slash names the chord; the letter after it names the note that should sound lowest. C/E therefore means a C major chord with E in the bass. For pianists this is a practical instruction for the left hand, and once you can read it quickly, chord charts start to produce smoother, more professional-sounding accompaniments with very little extra effort.

## Two kinds of slash chord

**Inversions**
When the bass note already belongs to the chord, the slash chord is simply an inversion. C/E is C major in first inversion; C/G is second inversion. The harmony stays the same, but the bass line moves more gracefully.

**Other bass notes**
Sometimes the bass note is not part of the chord at all. D/C, for example, places a C under a D major triad. These shapes create richer, sometimes tense colours and often appear in film and pop arrangements, where the bass holds still while chords change above it.

## How to read them at speed

Treat the symbol as two separate jobs. The right hand reads the part before the slash and plays the chord in any comfortable shape. The left hand reads only the letter after the slash and plays that single note, or that note in octaves. Splitting the task like this stops you from searching for a complicated two-hand chord shape and lets you play at the speed of the chart.

## Common slash-chord bass lines

Most slash chords exist to make the bass move by step. A few patterns appear again and again:

- C, G/B, A minor, A minor/G, F: a bass line falling step by step from C to F
- C, C/E, F, G: the bass climbing from C through E to F and G
- F, F/A, B-flat, C: the same rising idea in another key
- A minor, A minor/G, D/F-sharp, F: a descending line often heard in ballads

Play only the bass notes of each pattern first and sing along. Once the line feels natural, add the right-hand chords above it.

![Cartoon of a learner reading sheet music at an upright piano at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbgh2qs-ff6ej.webp)

## Keeping the right hand still

A useful trick is to let the right hand move as little as possible while the left hand walks. In the first pattern above, the right hand can hold C, E, G for C, slide to B, D, G for G/B, then to A, C, E for A minor, keeping several fingers on shared notes. The listener hears a smooth descending bass under a stable middle register, which is exactly the effect the arranger intended.

## Practising slash chords in steps

**Bass only**
Play the bass notes of a chart in a steady rhythm, one per bar, and listen to their direction.

**Chords only**
Play just the right-hand chords, staying close to middle C and keeping the voice leading smooth.

**Together, slowly**
Combine the hands at a slow tempo, checking that the bass note and chord land together.

**Add rhythm**
Once it is secure, try a simple pattern such as bass on beat one and chord on beats two and four.

When practising with TIGA ALPHA, you can work through a progression bar by bar and check that the left-hand note arrives in time with the chord, a common slip when the hands are thinking about different things.

## Writing your own slash chords

You can create slash chords even when a chart does not include them. Take any progression and ask where the bass could move by step instead of jumping. If the chords go C to F, try C, C/E, F. If they go G to E minor, try G, G/F-sharp, E minor. Small changes like these make simple songs sound arranged rather than strummed, and they train your ear to hear bass lines as melodies in their own right.

## FAQ

**Q: Is C/E the same chord as C?**
A: Yes, it uses the same notes, but with E as the lowest sound, which changes the bass line and the feel of the progression.

**Q: What if the bass note is not in the chord?**
A: Play it anyway. The combination is intentional and gives a fuller or more tense colour than a plain triad.

**Q: Should the left hand play octaves?**
A: Octaves give more weight in louder passages, while a single note is clearer in quiet or fast sections.

**Q: Are slash chords used in classical music?**
A: Classical scores rarely use the symbols, but the same inversions and moving bass lines appear constantly in the written notes.

andalusian-cadence-four-descending-chord.body:
In flamenco, in many pop songs and in film scores, you often hear a group of chords that step down from high to low, one degree at a time. In A minor, they are A minor, G major, F major and E major. This chord progression is often called the "Andalusian cadence" or "Andalusian progression", and the name comes from Andalusia in the south of Spain. The bass descends through four notes and finally rests on a bright major triad, which sounds both sad and full of unresolved tension.

## In Classical Music

This descending four-note bass line appeared very early in classical music too, and is often linked with the "lament bass".

**Summary**

In the Baroque period, composers often used a descending four-note bass to express sorrow.

The Andalusian progression can be seen as one specific form of this descending bass.

## A minor, G, F, E in Pop Songs

You can hear this descending group of chords in many pop and rock songs.

It often comes back again and again as the chord loop of a verse or chorus.

Because the chords are simple and the bass line is clear, it is very suitable to play on guitar and piano.

## Adding a Flamenco Rhythm

In flamenco, this progression is often paired with strong rhythms and accents.

You can try playing these chords with a powerful syncopated rhythm, imitating the strumming of a guitar.

You can also stay on the E major triad and add some decorative melody.

## Playing It in Other Keys

After learning the Andalusian progression in A minor, you can move it to other minor keys, for example E minor: E minor, D major, C major, B major.

Note that the last chord must use the raised leading note, to make a major triad.

Playing it in different keys deepens your understanding of the structure of this progression.

## Another Way to Understand It

From the flamenco point of view, this progression is sometimes seen as a progression in E Phrygian mode, with E as the destination.

Understood this way, the descending semitone from F to E is a typical Phrygian cadence.

Both ways of understanding it make sense, depending on the style and context of the music.

## Improvising with It

This group of chords is very good for improvising.

You can play the four chords again and again with the left hand, and improvise a melody with the right hand using notes of A harmonic minor or A minor.

On the E major triad you can use the raised G in particular, to bring out the colour of the chord.

## How the Chords Are Built

The Andalusian progression is made up of four chords: in A minor they are the A minor triad, the G major triad, the F major triad and the E major triad.

In Roman numerals it is often written i, VII, VI, V.

The roots of the four chords, A, G, F and E, descend one step at a time.

## Playing the Andalusian Progression at the Piano with Inversions

With the left hand play the bass notes A, G, F, E, and with the right hand play the triads A minor, G major, F major and E major in turn.

You can have the right-hand chords use inversions to reduce movement, for example A-C-E, G-B-D, F-A-C, E-G♯-B.

Play it a few times in a row and feel the mood of this progression.

## The Final E Major Triad

The last chord of the progression is the E major triad, which is the dominant chord of A minor.

Because it uses a raised G, that is, the leading note, this chord is a major triad and sounds fairly bright.

After all that minor colour, this bright major triad brings a strong tension.

## Recognising the Andalusian Progression by Ear

When you listen to music, if you hear the bass step down four notes and finally rest on a bright chord, it is very likely an Andalusian progression.

You can try singing along with the bass to confirm that it descends.

Listen to several pieces in different styles and your ear will become more and more sensitive.

**Order of practice**
- A descending i, VII, VI, V progression in a minor key
- In A minor it is A minor, G, F, E
- The bass descends four notes
- It ends on a major triad, with tension

![A black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8n7ns-p68jw.webp)

## The Name Andalusia

This progression is very common in the flamenco music of Andalusia in southern Spain, and so it got its name.

In flamenco, the final E major triad is often treated as a resting place at the end, and does not have to return to A minor.

This differs from the habit in classical harmony that the dominant chord must resolve.

## The Descending Bass

The most obvious feature of this progression is that the bass starts on the tonic and descends four notes by step, arriving at the dominant.

This descending bass line sounds like sinking and sighing.

In A minor the bass is A, G, F, E.

## The Andalusian Progression in Brief

The Andalusian progression is a descending chord progression of i, VII, VI, V in a minor key; in A minor it is A minor, G, F, E, with the bass descending by step from the tonic to the dominant.

The final E major triad is bright because of the raised leading note and brings tension. The name comes from flamenco music, and it can also be understood as a progression on E Phrygian.

**Try it**

It is common in pop, rock and classical music and is related to the lament bass. At the piano you can play it with inversions, move it to other keys, add a rhythm or improvise over it.

## FAQ

**Q: Which chords make up the Andalusian progression in A minor?**
A: A minor, G, F, E.

**Q: How is it written in Roman numerals?**
A: i, VII, VI, V.

**Q: Why is the last chord bright?**
A: It uses the raised leading note and is a major triad.

**Q: Where does the name come from?**
A: Andalusia in southern Spain.

**Q: How does the bass move?**
A: It descends four notes by step from the tonic to the dominant.
