delibes-pizzicati-sylvia-1876-ballet.body:
Pizzicati is a piece of music from the ballet Sylvia by the French composer Léo Delibes, which premiered in Paris in 1876. In this music the string instruments are not bowed but plucked with the fingers, producing a light, bouncing sound that goes with the dancer's nimble steps. Delibes also wrote another ballet, Coppélia, which premiered in 1870. It is said that the Russian composer Tchaikovsky admired the music of Sylvia. This pizzicato piece is often arranged for piano, and it is good material for practising light staccato.

## Pedalling in Pizzicati

For most of Pizzicati your foot can stay off the pedal.

**Details to notice**

The pedal joins staccato notes together and loses the feeling of plucked strings.

Only in the legato melody of the middle section can you use a little pedal, gently.

## Tchaikovsky's Admiration

It is said that Tchaikovsky admired the music of Sylvia very much after hearing it.

In his letters he praised Delibes' music as beautiful and charming.

The ballets that Tchaikovsky later wrote himself were also influenced by French ballet music.

## Playing Pizzicati on the Piano

To play Pizzicati on the piano, use staccato to imitate the sound of plucked strings.

Every note should be short and light, with the fingers springing up quickly.

Do not play too loudly. It should feel like fingers lightly plucking strings.

## The Legato Middle Section

In the middle section, which imitates woodwind instruments, change to a legato touch.

The melody should be fluent and connected, in contrast to the staccato before and after.

This contrast between staccato and legato is where the fun of the piece lies.

## The Dancer's Steps

This music goes with the dancer's nimble, lively steps.

The dancer touches the floor lightly with the tips of her toes, in small, precise movements.

The sound of plucked strings and the lightness of the steps match each other very well.

![Wooden upright piano, green piano bench and orange books against a deep teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaeup1n-9fgnf.webp)

## Staccato Technique

Keep the wrist loose and let the fingertips touch the key and leave at once, so that the sound is crisp like a plucked string.

Do not drop the whole arm down, because the sound will be too heavy.

Imagine your fingers touching something hot and springing away immediately.

## Asking the Teacher to Listen to Your Staccato in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and tell you whether your staccato is light and even.

Piano scores of Pizzicati vary in difficulty, and which one to choose can also be decided together.

From Pizzicati, you can practise light staccato and contrasts of tone colour.

## Summary of Pizzicati

Léo Delibes was born in 1836 and died in 1891. He wrote ballets and operas, and his opera Lakmé contains the Flower Duet. Coppélia, which premiered in 1870, tells of a mechanical doll that can dance. Sylvia, which premiered in Paris in 1876, is based on ancient Greek mythology and tells of a nymph in the service of the goddess of the hunt and a shepherd. Pizzicato means plucking the strings with the fingers instead of using the bow.

Pizzicati is in Act III and is a solo for the female dancer. The strings play a bouncing melody in pizzicato, and in the middle section the flute and other woodwinds play a flowing melody. It is said that Tchaikovsky admired this ballet. On the piano, imitate the plucking with short, light staccato, keep the wrist relaxed, change to legato in the middle section, and use very little pedal. You can compare it with the third movement of Tchaikovsky's Fourth Symphony and Strauss's Pizzicato Polka.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your staccato is light.

## Comparing Other Pizzicato Pieces

In Tchaikovsky's Fourth Symphony, the third movement is played entirely in pizzicato by the strings.

Johann Strauss also wrote a Pizzicato Polka.

Listen to these pizzicato pieces side by side, and you will hear how differently the "plucking of fingers" on strings can be done.

## Coppélia

In 1870, Delibes' ballet Coppélia premiered, telling the story of a mechanical doll that can dance.

The ballet was very popular and made Delibes a famous ballet composer.

Six years later, he wrote Sylvia.

## The Music of Pizzicati

Pizzicati appears in Act III of the ballet and is a solo for the female dancer.

The strings play a light, bouncing melody in pizzicato, like drops of water leaping.

In the middle there is a section in which the flute and other woodwind instruments join in, playing a flowing melody in contrast to the plucking.

- Music from Delibes' ballet Sylvia
- The ballet premiered in Paris in 1876
- The strings are plucked with the fingers
- Practise light staccato on the piano

## What Is Pizzicato?

String instruments are usually played with a bow, which gives a connected, sustained sound.

Pizzicato means plucking the strings with the fingers instead of using the bow, producing a short, light sound.

In the score the Italian word for "plucked" is used, and the player puts down the bow and plucks with the fingers.

## Who Was Delibes?

Léo Delibes was born in 1836 and died in 1891. He was a French composer.

He wrote many ballets and operas, with beautiful music and rich colours.

His opera Lakmé contains a duet, the Flower Duet, which is still often sung today.

## The Story of Sylvia

The story of Sylvia is taken from a pastoral theme in ancient Greek mythology.

Sylvia is a nymph in the service of the goddess of the hunt, and a shepherd falls in love with her.

After many twists, the two are finally united.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which ballet is Pizzicati from?**
A: Delibes' Sylvia.

**Q: In what year did the ballet premiere?**
A: In 1876, in Paris.

**Q: What is pizzicato?**
A: Plucking the strings with the fingers instead of using the bow.

**Q: What is Delibes' other ballet?**
A: Coppélia, from 1870.

**Q: What kind of touch imitates pizzicato on the piano?**
A: Light staccato.

digital-piano-built-in-recorder-self-che.body:
Many digital pianos have a recording function: press the record button to record what you play, then press play to hear it straight away. The exact buttons and steps differ from model to model, so check the instrument's manual. Compared with recording on a phone, recording inside the piano is not affected by noise in the room, and on playback you can hear it directly through the piano's speakers or headphones. Recording a passage, listening to it once, finding one or two things to improve and then recording again to compare is a simple way to check yourself.

**Practice routine**
- Many digital pianos have a recording function
- The exact steps differ by model, so check the manual
- Not affected by noise in the room
- Record a passage, listen once, improve, record again

## The recording function of a digital piano

Besides playing, many digital pianos have some extra functions, and one common one is recording.

**In brief**

With a recording function, you need no extra equipment: you can record your own playing right on the piano.

However, the recording method and functions differ between brands and models of digital piano, and some pianos may not have this function.

## Checking the manual

To find out whether your digital piano has a recording function and how to use it, first check the instrument's manual.

The manual usually explains where the record button is, how to start and stop recording, and how to play it back.

If you cannot find a paper manual, many brands also provide an electronic version on their websites.

## Just record a short passage

To check yourself with the recording function, you do not need to record the whole piece every time.

You can record just a small passage you are practising, for example eight or sixteen bars.

This makes the playback shorter, and makes it easier to concentrate on the details.

## The right mindset when recording

When they press the record button, many people suddenly become nervous and play worse than usual.

This is actually very good practice, because it feels a little like performing on stage.

You can record several times and slowly get used to staying in your usual state while recording.

## What to listen for on playback

When you play the recording back, you can first listen through once and get a feel for the overall effect.

Then listen carefully for a few things: whether the rhythm is steady, whether the notes are right, whether the dynamics vary, and whether the phrases are clear.

Focus on only one or two things each time; you do not need to find all the problems at once.

![A black grand piano and stool against a gold and red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4hjf2-tbr6z.webp)

## Recording inside the piano in summary

Many digital pianos have a recording function, and the exact steps differ by model, so check the manual.

Recording inside the piano is not affected by noise in the room and plays back clearly, so it is good for checking your playing.

Recording a passage, listening once, finding one or two things to improve and recording again to compare is a simple and effective way to check yourself.

## Finding one or two things to improve

After listening to the recording, find one or two things that need improving, such as a spot where the rhythm is unsteady, or where the left hand is too loud.

Mark these places in the score, then practise them specifically.

When you have improved them, record again and compare the difference between the two takes.

## Recording hands separately

Some digital pianos can record the left-hand and right-hand parts separately and then play them back together.

For example, you can first record the left-hand accompaniment, then play the right-hand melody yourself during playback, to practise how the two hands fit together.

Not every piano has this function, so you need to confirm it in the manual.

## Sharing with your teacher

If your digital piano can export recordings, you can also send them to Teacher Aum to listen to.

The teacher can give you some suggestions based on the recording, so you can practise with more direction.

In lessons you can also listen to the recording with the teacher and discuss what can be improved.

## The difference from phone recording

Recording on a phone is also a common method, but a phone records the other sounds in the room along with the music.

Recording inside a digital piano captures the signal from the piano itself, so it is not affected by noise in the room.

On playback you can also hear it directly from the piano's speakers or headphones, and the sound is fairly clear.

## Playing back with headphones

If you do not want to disturb others when practising at home, you can play the recording back through headphones.

With headphones you can also listen more carefully and notice small problems more easily.

However, be careful about the volume if you wear headphones for a long time, and do not turn it up too high.

## Do not rely only on recording

Recording is a very good checking tool, but it cannot replace practice itself.

Time spent listening to recordings should not be longer than time spent practising.

You can treat recording as part of practice: for example, before the end of each session, record a passage, listen to it once, and note what to improve next time.

## Comparing before and after

One benefit of recording is that you can compare your playing from different times.

Some digital pianos can store several recordings, so you can compare your playing from a week ago with now to see whether you have improved.

**Try it**

If your piano can store only one recording, you can also export the recording to a computer or phone to keep it.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can all digital pianos record?**
A: Not necessarily. It depends on the model and the manual.

**Q: How is it different from recording on a phone?**
A: Recording inside the piano is not affected by noise in the room.

**Q: Do I have to record the whole piece every time?**
A: No, just record the small passage you are practising.

**Q: What should I listen for on playback?**
A: Rhythm, accuracy of notes, dynamics and phrasing, focusing on one or two each time.

**Q: What if I get nervous when recording?**
A: Record several times and slowly get used to it.

diminished-seventh-arpeggio-minor-thirds.body:
The diminished seventh chord is a very special chord: all four of its notes are separated by minor thirds, for example B, D, F, A♭. Because every pair of neighbouring notes is the same distance apart, the diminished seventh chord is perfectly symmetrical on the keyboard, and has the same shape whichever note you start from. It sounds tense and uneasy, and Romantic composers loved to use it to colour a moment of tension. Practising diminished seventh arpeggios helps your hand get used to this even shape, and also trains your sense of mixed black-and-white key positions.

## Diminished Seventh Arpeggios at a Glance

The four notes of a diminished seventh chord are all a minor third apart, for example B, D, F, A♭. From the root to the top note is a diminished seventh, and the chord is often built on the leading note of a minor key. Because of the symmetry, there are only three different diminished seventh chords among the twelve semitones.

A diminished seventh chord sounds uneasy and unresolved, and is often used to express tension and to modulate. The fingering is quite regular, commonly using fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4, with the thumb placed on white keys wherever possible. When black and white keys are mixed, the hand needs to shift back and forth. You can first play it as a block chord, and keep the thumb crossing smooth.

You can use diminished seventh arpeggios to train your ear, look for diminished seventh chords in Romantic pieces, and practise slowly first and then faster. You can ask Teacher Aum to help plan your practice.

## How a Diminished Seventh Chord Is Built

The secret of the diminished seventh chord fits in one sentence: stack minor thirds upwards, all the way up to four notes.

For example, starting from B, a minor third up is D, another is F, and another is A♭.

A minor third above A♭ brings you back to B, forming a cycle.

## Training Your Ear with Diminished Seventh Arpeggios

The diminished seventh chord has a very distinctive sound, and when you play the arpeggio you can listen closely to its colour.

Try comparing it with a dominant seventh chord, a major triad and a minor triad, and hear how they differ.

Once you are familiar with it, you will recognise a diminished seventh chord more easily when you hear one in a piece.

![Watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac3ty6-eq18q.webp)

## Why It Is Called "Diminished Seventh"

From the root B to the top note A♭ is a diminished seventh, which is why it is called a diminished seventh chord.

A diminished seventh is a semitone smaller than a minor seventh, so it sounds more tense than a dominant seventh chord.

In harmony, it often appears in minor keys, built on the leading note on the seventh degree.

## Keep the Thumb Crossing Smooth

After finger 4, the thumb tucks under and lands on a note that is still a minor third further on, so the span does not grow.

When crossing, do not suddenly raise the wrist; keep the movement smooth.

You can first practise the crossing position on its own, and then join it up.

## What Are the Three Diminished Seventh Chords?

First: C, E♭, G♭, A (A can also be written as B♭♭).

Second: C♯, E, G, B♭.

Third: D, F, A♭, B.

## The Sound of the Diminished Seventh Chord

A diminished seventh chord sounds uneasy and unresolved, as if waiting for an answer.

In many pieces, composers use it to express tension, surprise or dark moods.

It is also often used at modulations, because it can resolve to several different keys.

## Only Three Different Diminished Seventh Chords

Because the diminished seventh chord is symmetrical, only three different diminished seventh chords can be formed from the twelve semitones.

For example, B, D, F, A♭ and D, F, A♭, B are actually the same set of notes, just in different inversions.

This means that once you have practised the three sets well, you have mastered every diminished seventh chord.

## Finding Diminished Seventh Chords in Romantic Pieces

In the works of composers such as Chopin, Schumann and Liszt, diminished seventh chords appear very frequently.

They often turn up at the most tense and agitated moments in the music.

In a Romantic piece you are practising, try looking for where the diminished seventh chords are.

**Practice sequence**
- All four notes are minor thirds apart
- Perfectly symmetrical on the keyboard
- Sounds tense and uneasy
- Often used to create drama

## Asking Your Teacher to Plan Diminished Seventh Arpeggios in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to plan diminished seventh arpeggio practice, for example starting with the three sets of diminished seventh chords.

Your teacher can also help confirm the fingering for each set, especially the thumb position.

Once you have mastered diminished seventh arpeggios, you will also react more quickly when you meet this kind of chord while reading music.

## Fingering for Diminished Seventh Arpeggios

Because the four notes are the same distance apart, the fingering for diminished seventh arpeggios is quite regular, commonly using fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4.

But exactly which note the thumb starts on depends on where the black and white keys fall, and the thumb is generally placed on white keys wherever possible.

Different method books and exam syllabuses may give different fingerings; go by the one you are using.

## The Challenge of Mixed Black and White Keys

A diminished seventh chord often contains both black and white keys, so the position of the hand needs to shift back and forth.

When playing a black key, reach a little further into the keys; when playing a white key, you can play nearer the edge.

Finding a position where your fingers feel comfortable makes the arpeggio smoother.

## Press Diminished Sevenths as an Evenly Spaced Hand Shape First

Before practising the arpeggio, you can first press all four notes together and feel the shape of your hand.

Because neighbouring notes are the same distance apart, your fingers will spread out very evenly.

Once you remember this "evenly spaced" hand shape, your hand will not panic when you break it into an arpeggio.

## The Speed of Diminished Seventh Arpeggios

At the start, practise diminished seventh arpeggios at a slow speed, making sure every note is even and clear.

Because the shape is regular, once you are fluent, diminished seventh arpeggios can be played quite fast.

**Common mistake**

When speeding up, take care to keep your hand and arm relaxed.

## FAQ

**Q: What interval is there between neighbouring notes of a diminished seventh chord?**
A: A minor third.

**Q: How many different diminished seventh chords are there?**
A: Three.

**Q: What does a diminished seventh chord sound like?**
A: Tense, uneasy and unresolved.

**Q: On which degree of a minor key is a diminished seventh chord often built?**
A: The leading note on the seventh degree.

**Q: Where is the thumb generally placed in diminished seventh arpeggios?**
A: On white keys wherever possible.

do-re-mi-song-solfege-1959.body:
"Do-Re-Mi" is a song from the 1959 musical The Sound of Music, with music by Rodgers and lyrics by Hammerstein. In the show, the governess uses this song to teach the children the solfege syllables: starting from "do", they sing up one note at a time, and each syllable is given a memorable line of lyrics. In the second half of the song, the syllables are shuffled and recombined into a new melody. For piano learners, this song is a good helper for getting to know the major scale and solfege, and its simple melody is also very suitable for beginners to play.

## Playing Do-Re-Mi on the piano

Beginners can start with the right hand from C, singing the syllables as they play.

**Think again**

Each time you play a note, sing its syllable, linking the sound with the name.

Once you are fluent, try playing the full melody of the song.

## Singing it in another key

Once you can start from C, you can try playing the same melody starting from G.

Now do is G, and the scale is G, A, B, C, D, E, F♯, G, which needs one black key.

Sing it with movable-do syllables, and the feel of the melody stays the same, only the pitch changes.

## What solfege is

Solfege is the set of names used to sing the notes of a scale, most commonly do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si (or ti).

In fixed-do, do is always C; in movable-do, do is the tonic of each key.

"Do-Re-Mi" uses the movable-do idea, singing up one note at a time from the tonic.

![Glowing digital interface on a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwad1y1k-n5m28.webp)

## A line of lyrics for each syllable

In the original English lyrics, each syllable is paired with a word that sounds similar, such as "deer" and "sun".

The Chinese version also has matching lyrics, to help children remember each syllable.

This method makes the abstract syllables concrete and easy to remember.

## The song's scene in the show

In The Sound of Music, the new governess finds that the children cannot sing.

She takes the children up onto a hillside and starts teaching from the most basic syllables.

"Do-Re-Mi" is the song she uses to teach them, relaxed and fun.

## Solfege and fingering

When the right hand goes up the scale from C, the thumb usually passes under the third finger after playing E and lands on F.

In the melody of "Do-Re-Mi" you can use similar fingering.

Once the fingering is steady, the melody will play more smoothly.

## Adding the left hand to Do-Re-Mi

Once you know the melody, you can add a simple left hand, for example with the three chords C, F and G.

Change chord every bar or every two beats, choosing according to how the melody moves.

This helps beginners get to know the most basic chords.

- A song from the 1959 musical The Sound of Music
- Built from the solfege syllables "do-re-mi"
- A memorable line for each syllable
- Good for getting to know the major scale

## Practising sight-singing with Do-Re-Mi

"Do-Re-Mi" is also good material for practising sight-singing.

You can first look at the score and sing the melody with the syllables, then play it on the piano and check whether you sang it correctly.

Practising this way over time improves both your reading and your ear.

## Summary of Do-Re-Mi

"Do-Re-Mi" is the song in the 1959 musical The Sound of Music in which the governess teaches the children the solfege syllables, with music by Rodgers and lyrics by Hammerstein. The syllables are do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si (or ti); in fixed-do, do is always C, while in movable-do, do is the tonic of each key, and the syllables can be traced back to the method of an Italian monk of the eleventh century.

Each syllable has a memorable line of lyrics. The first half goes up the major scale from do to high do, and the second half shuffles and recombines them into a new melody. On the piano you can start from C, singing as you play, with the right-hand thumb passing under on F; you can also move to G major, accompany with the left hand using the chords C, F and G, and use the song for sight-singing practice and solfege games.

For solfege practice, you can ask Teacher Aum to help with this song.

## The scale from do to do

In the first half of the song, the melody goes up the major scale one note at a time, from do to high do.

On the piano, if you start from C, that is C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, all white keys.

This is a perfect chance to get to know the C major scale.

## Asking the teacher to use Do-Re-Mi for solfege in lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to use "Do-Re-Mi" to help you practise solfege and scales.

The teacher can also explain the difference between fixed-do and movable-do.

Starting from a fun song, you get to know the most basic things in music.

## The history of solfege

The method of singing a scale with syllables can be traced back to medieval Europe.

It is said that an Italian monk of the eleventh century used the syllable at the start of each line of a hymn to help students remember pitches.

Later, these syllables gradually developed into today's do, re, mi.

## Playing solfege games with children

Parents can sing "Do-Re-Mi" with their children, doing actions as they sing.

One person can also play a note while the other sings its syllable, to see who gets it right.

Little games like this let children learn solfege through play.

## The shuffled syllables

In the second half of the song, the syllables are shuffled and recombined, for example "do mi mi, mi sol sol".

These combinations become a new melody, like a musical game.

**Practice order**

This shows that the same few notes, arranged differently, can become different melodies.

## FAQ

**Q: Which work is Do-Re-Mi from?**
A: The 1959 musical The Sound of Music.

**Q: What are the solfege syllables?**
A: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si (or ti).

**Q: What is do in movable-do?**
A: The tonic of each key.

**Q: On which note does the thumb pass under in the right-hand ascending scale?**
A: F.

**Q: Which black key does the scale starting on G need?**
A: F♯.

digital-piano-storm-and-power-cut.body:
If a thunderstorm or power cut hits while you are using your digital piano, first switch it off and unplug it, then plug it back in once the weather has calmed and the power has returned. Before turning it on again, check that the volume knob is turned down and the headphones are plugged in properly, and after switching on, check that the sound and settings are back to what you normally use. These small steps reduce surprises and get your practice back to normal sooner.

## Everyday habits

After each practice session, switch the digital piano off, and unplug it if it will not be used for a long time.

Do not put cups of water or plants on the instrument, to stop liquid spilling into the keyboard or the electronics.

Wipe the body and keys with a dry cloth from time to time to keep them clean. If you notice problems such as it not starting properly, keys with no sound, or unusual noises, contact the seller or a repair technician to have it checked.

## Restarting after the power returns

Once the power is back, wait a few minutes to be sure the voltage is stable, then plug the instrument back in.

Before switching on, turn the volume knob down low. Some digital pianos return to a default volume when they start, and if it is very loud the sudden sound can be a shock and may disturb the family.

If you practise with headphones, make sure they are plugged in properly before you switch on.

If the power cut was a long one, first check whether the other appliances in the house are running normally before you turn on the digital piano.

- Switch off and unplug when there is thunder
- After a power cut, confirm the supply is stable before reconnecting
- Turn the volume down before switching on
- After switching on, check the sound, metronome and other settings

![A cartoon character with glasses and headphones in a night-time room, reading music and playing an upright piano, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9x0lza-3frae.webp)

## Turn the interruption into a chance to practise

A power cut or storm interrupting your practice is not necessarily a bad thing. Practice away from the keyboard also helps you understand a piece better.

For example, write out the note names of a melody on paper, or close your eyes and recall the structure of the whole piece. Both deepen your memory.

When the power returns and you go back to the piano, you may find some passages are clearer than before.

Note these no-power practice methods in your practice notebook, so you can use them straight away the next time the power goes out.

## Why unplug during a storm

During thunderstorms the power grid can see voltage fluctuations. The manuals of many appliances recommend disconnecting them from the mains during a storm, to reduce the chance of the electronics being affected.

A digital piano contains circuit boards and many electronic components, so like a computer or a television it is an appliance worth protecting.

Unplugging takes only a few seconds, and building the habit is much less worrying than wondering afterwards whether the instrument was affected.

Families living where storms are frequent will find it especially useful to make this step part of their practice routine.

## Tidying the power and cables

Plug the digital piano into a socket that is easy to reach, so that you do not have to crawl behind the instrument to unplug it.

Keep the power cable separate from the pedal cable and the headphone cable, run it along the wall to avoid tangles, and so that nobody trips on it.

If you use an extension lead, choose a reliable product, and do not share one socket with many high-power appliances.

## Checking your usual settings

Some digital pianos return to factory defaults after losing power, such as the sound, reverb, metronome tempo and touch sensitivity.

After switching on, play a few notes and listen to whether the sound is the one you normally use. Turn on the metronome and see whether the tempo needs to be set again.

If your digital piano has a memory function, you can save your usual settings and restore them with one touch after a power cut, which is much more convenient.

## What to do during a power cut

When the power suddenly goes out, the digital piano goes dark straight away. Switch the power off first, then unplug it, to avoid a surge of current hitting the instrument the moment the power returns.

While the power is out you can use the time for practice that needs no electricity, such as reading the score, tapping rhythms, miming fingerings on a tabletop, or singing the melody you are working on.

**Listen**

If you also have an acoustic piano at home, a power cut is a good moment to practise on it instead.

## FAQ

**Q: Does an acoustic piano need special care during a storm?**
A: An acoustic piano uses no electricity, so it generally does not need unplugging, but keep an eye on the humidity in the room on rainy days.

**Q: Can I use a surge protector with a digital piano?**
A: Depending on the electrics in your home, you can consider a suitable voltage stabiliser or surge protector. Ask an electrician or the seller for details.

**Q: What if the digital piano will not turn on after a power cut?**
A: First check the plug, the socket and the power switch. If it still will not start, contact after-sales service or a repair technician.

**Q: The sound is strange after switching on. Is it broken?**
A: The settings may simply have returned to their defaults, so check the sound and effects settings first.

**Q: Can a power cut hurt my ears when I practise with headphones?**
A: During a power cut the sound simply disappears. Turning the volume down before switching on after the power returns avoids a sudden loud sound.

**Q: Can I use a battery-powered keyboard in a storm?**
A: You can follow the product instructions, but safety still matters, and pausing practice during severe lightning is the safer choice.

double-escapement-action-1821-repetition.body:
In 1821, a French piano-making workshop patented a "double escapement" action. Before this, the key had to rise almost all the way back up before the hammer could strike the string again; with the double escapement, the key only needs to rise part of the way to sound the same note again. This improvement made fast repeated notes and trills much easier, and the action of the modern grand piano still uses this principle today.

## How the double escapement works

Put simply, when you press a key, the hammer is pushed towards the string and bounces back straight after striking.

**Summary**

But it does not fall straight back to its resting place. Instead a device catches it and holds it at a point not far from the string.

At this moment the key only needs to rise part of the way, and when you press again, the hammer can strike the string once more.

## Piano workshops in the early nineteenth century

In the early nineteenth century there were many piano workshops in both Paris and London. They made pianos and harps at the same time, and also competed with each other in technology.

The makers in these workshops often talked with players to learn about the difficulties they met in performance.

Many improvements to the instrument slowly appeared through exchanges and repeated experiments like these.

## Virtuoso pianists and the new action

In the first half of the nineteenth century, Paris drew many young pianists known for their technique, and Liszt was one of them.

An action that was responsive and could repeat quickly suited this technically brilliant style of playing very well.

Exchange and cooperation between pianists and makers was not unusual at the time.

## Seeing your own instrument through history

Knowing the story of the double escapement can give us a little more understanding of the piano we play.

Behind every key, many parts work together, and these designs were built up by generations of makers.

Looking after your instrument and having it serviced regularly is also a way of respecting what they accumulated.

## The patience behind an improvement

From noticing the problem to designing a reliable action, makers spent a long time trying things and improving them.

The double escapement did not appear overnight, but was built on the experience of many people before.

This also reminds those who learn the piano that progress often comes from steady small improvements.

![Sepia sketch of an upright piano keyboard seen from an angle](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2kw8a-dxaff.webp)

## The effect on composers

The improved action let composers write more passages that needed fast repeated notes and trills.

Many virtuoso works of the nineteenth century have a great deal of this kind of writing.

The growing ability of the instrument and the development of musical style often pushed each other forward.

**Practice order**
- The invention came from French piano workshops in the early nineteenth century
- In 1821 a patent was filed for the double escapement action
- The key only needs to rise part of the way to strike again
- Modern grand pianos still use this principle

## Feeling repetition on the piano

If you get the chance to play a grand piano, try repeating a note quickly on one key without letting the key rise all the way.

Slowly feel at which position the key rises to when the note can sound again.

This experience can help you understand how the action works, and also help you play repeated notes with less effort.

## Ways to practise repeated notes

When playing fast repeated notes, finger changes are often used, for example the third, second and first fingers taking turns on the same key.

Keep the wrist relaxed and the fingers close to the keys, and do not lift the hand high every time.

Start slowly, make sure each note is clear, then gradually speed up.

## The patent of 1821

In 1821, a French piano workshop took out a patent in England for a new action, an invention often called the "double escapement".

According to records, the patent was filed in London by the nephew of the workshop's founder.

In this design, after the hammer strikes the string, it is first held in a low position, waiting for the next strike.

## Repeated notes become easy

With the double escapement, a player can sound the same note again before the key has fully risen.

This makes fast repeated notes much easier, and trills can be played faster and more evenly.

The player's fingers no longer have to wait for the key to return all the way to the top each time.

## The problem pianos had at the time

Before the double escapement appeared, the piano action had a limit: after the hammer struck the string, the key had to rise almost all the way before it could strike again.

This meant that to repeat the same note quickly, the finger had to wait for the key to come up to the top, so the speed was limited.

For music that needed fast repeated notes and trills, this was an obvious difficulty.

## The difference between grand and upright pianos

Today's grand pianos generally use an action based on the double escapement principle, and repeat the same note fairly fast.

The action of an upright piano is built differently, with the hammer striking the string vertically, and its repetition is generally somewhat slower than a grand piano's.

This is one reason why many players find it easier to play fast repeated notes on a grand piano.

## FAQ

**Q: Who invented the double escapement?**
A: A French piano workshop patented it in 1821, in the early nineteenth century.

**Q: What problem did it solve?**
A: It lets the key strike again after rising only part of the way.

**Q: What is the benefit for playing?**
A: Fast repeated notes and trills become much easier.

**Q: Is it still used in pianos today?**
A: The action of the modern grand piano still uses this principle.

**Q: Is an upright piano the same?**
A: Its structure is different, and its repetition is generally somewhat slower than a grand piano's.

example-scenario-family-ten-minute-pract.body:
The family and child below are imaginary, invented only to show one possible way to set up a short practice routine at home. In the scenario, a family agrees on ten minutes of piano practice at a regular time, with a small checklist on the wall and some flexibility for busy days. The goal is a habit that feels light enough to keep, not a strict timetable.

## The family at home

Imagine a family with a child called Nok, who has just started piano lessons. The teacher has suggested short practice sessions between lessons. At first the family tries to practise at random times, but evenings are busy and the piano is often forgotten. So the family sits down together one weekend to agree a plan.

All details are invented for the example; real families will have their own rhythms.

## Choosing a time that already exists

Rather than adding a new slot to a crowded day, the family looks for a moment that already happens.

- Right after changing out of school clothes.
- Just before dinner, while a meal is being prepared.
- After a short rest, before homework.

In the scenario they choose the time right after a snack, because the child is usually at home and relaxed then. Connecting practice to an existing habit makes it easier to remember.

## A routine with three small parts

The plan has three parts that fit into ten minutes.

- **Warm-up** (about two minutes): a few easy notes or a familiar tune.
- **Focus** (about six minutes): the one thing the teacher asked for, such as a tricky bar played slowly.
- **Play for fun** (about two minutes): any song the child likes.

Ending with something enjoyable leaves a pleasant memory of the session.

![Modern piano under cool futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwo0pm5c-gdg0d.webp)

## A checklist everyone can see

A paper checklist near the piano shows the three parts as small boxes. The child ticks each part with a pencil or sticker. It is not a reward system, only a visual reminder of what comes next. The family agrees that a missed day is not a problem; the next day simply starts again.

- Keep the checklist short, with at most three items.
- Place it where the child can see it from the bench.
- Let the child decorate it, so it feels like theirs.

## The role of the adults

In the scenario, the adult's job is to be nearby and curious, not to correct every note. A parent might sit in the room, listen and ask the child to explain what they are practising. When a mistake happens, the parent says, "Can you try that bar again slowly?" instead of pointing out the error. If the family does not read music, the child can teach them a short piece, which often builds confidence.

## Handling difficult days

Some days the child is tired or upset. The family has a simple rule: on those days, play one familiar song and stop. The routine continues, but the pressure is lowered. Talking with the teacher about weeks that feel hard helps too, because the teacher can adjust the assignment.

## A weekly look back

Once a week the plan gets a gentle review, because what works in one month may not work in the next.

At the weekend, the family looks at the checklist together. They talk about what felt easy, what felt hard and what they want to try next week. This takes only a couple of minutes and keeps the plan flexible.

A family might also add a practice app between lessons. TIGA ALPHA, for example, gives short lessons with feedback after each attempt, and it can be used alongside the plan agreed with the teacher.

## Ideas to adapt

- Younger children may prefer five minutes twice a day.
- Older learners may enjoy a longer focus block.
- Busy weeks can use a "mini session" of just one song.

## FAQ

**Q: Is ten minutes enough for a beginner?**
A: For many beginners, short regular sessions work well. The teacher can advise the right length.

**Q: What if the child resists practice?**
A: Lower the pressure, shorten the session and talk with the teacher about what feels difficult.

**Q: Should parents sit in the room?**
A: Many families find it helpful to be nearby, as listeners rather than correctors.

**Q: Is this a real family?**
A: No. The scenario is imaginary and meant only as an example to adapt.

diatonic-versus-chromatic-notes-in-key.body:
In a key, the seven notes that belong to the scale of that key are called diatonic notes, and notes that do not belong to the key are called chromatic notes. For example, in C major, C, D, E, F, G, A and B are diatonic notes, while notes that need an accidental, such as F♯ and B♭, are chromatic notes. Diatonic notes make music sound stable and clear, while chromatic notes bring new colour and tension. Telling the two kinds of note apart helps us understand melody and harmony more quickly.

## Where chromatic notes tend to go

Chromatic notes often have their own tendencies: a raised note usually wants to move up, and a lowered note usually wants to move down.

For example, F♯ often moves to G, and B♭ often moves to A.

Knowing this tendency helps us anticipate the direction of the melody, and also reduces wrong-note mistakes in reading.

## Chromatic notes as passing notes

Sometimes a chromatic note is just a passing note in the melody, for example going from F through F♯ to G.

This kind of chromatic note does not change the harmony, but only makes the melody smoother.

When playing, you can let it pass lightly, without any special emphasis.

## Feeling it on the piano

You can first improvise a melody on the piano using only the white keys of C major, to feel the stability of diatonic notes.

Then add one or two black keys and listen to how the colour of the music changes.

This kind of contrast practice helps our ears tell diatonic and chromatic notes apart.

## What "diatonic" means

The term diatonic refers to the seven notes that naturally belong to the scale of a key.

Taking C major as an example, the white keys C, D, E, F, G, A and B on the piano are all its diatonic notes.

In G major, the diatonic notes become G, A, B, C, D, E and F♯, and F♯ is originally part of the key signature.

**Common misconceptions**
- Diatonic notes: the seven notes of the scale of the key
- Chromatic notes: notes outside the key, often needing an accidental
- Diatonic notes are stable and clear
- Chromatic notes bring colour and tension

![A high-angle view of an open black piano being played on a neon street in the rain](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5s5pn-5lg1l.webp)

## The colour chromatic notes bring

The appearance of a chromatic note often makes the colour of the music change suddenly.

For example, an F♯ appearing in a C major melody may hint at a move to G major, and a B♭ may hint at F major.

This change of colour makes the music more interesting and more expressive.

## Diatonic scales and the chromatic scale

A scale made up only of diatonic notes is called a diatonic scale, and both major and minor scales belong to this kind.

If you arrange all twelve semitones in order, you get a chromatic scale, which includes both diatonic and chromatic notes.

On the piano, starting from C and playing all the white and black keys in turn through an octave gives a chromatic scale.

## Special cases in minor keys

In minor keys the sixth and seventh degrees are often raised, such as F♯ and G♯ in A minor.

Although these notes need accidentals, they are very common in minor keys and are often seen as part of the minor key.

So when deciding between diatonic and chromatic notes in a minor key, you have to take into account the habits of harmonic minor and melodic minor.

## Use in improvisation and arranging

In improvising and arranging, chromatic notes are a good tool for adding colour.

For example, in a simple C major melody, adding a passing C♯ or E♭ can immediately bring a touch of jazz or blues.

But do not use chromatic notes too much, or the key will become blurred.

## What "chromatic" means

Any note that is not in the scale of the key is called a chromatic note.

On the score, chromatic notes usually have to be written with accidentals; for example, a C♯ popping up in a short piece in C major needs a sharp written to the left of the note.

So when you see an accidental while reading, you have often met a chromatic note.

## Chromatic notes as chord notes

Sometimes a chromatic note belongs to a special chord, such as a secondary dominant.

In C major, the chord D, F♯, A contains the chromatic note F♯, and it leads to the G major triad.

This kind of chromatic note changes the direction of the harmony, and when playing you can give it a little extra attention.

## Diatonic and chromatic notes in summary

Diatonic notes are the seven notes of the scale of the key, played according to the key signature; chromatic notes are notes outside the key and usually need accidentals.

Diatonic notes make music stable and clear, while chromatic notes bring colour and tension; some are only passing, and some belong to special chords.

Watching the direction of chromatic notes while reading and improvising helps us understand and express the music better.

## The key signature and diatonic notes

The key signature tells us which notes are to be raised or lowered, and the notes played according to the key signature are the diatonic notes of that key.

For example, the key signature of D major has F♯ and C♯, so F♯ and C♯ are diatonic notes in D major, not chromatic ones.

To decide whether a note is diatonic or chromatic, first look carefully at the key signature.

## Help when reading music

Knowing about diatonic and chromatic notes gives you a better sense of direction when reading.

Most notes are played according to the key signature; when you meet an accidental, stop and think: where is this chromatic note going?

Reading this way is not just recognising notes, but understanding the music.

## Analysing a melody

Choose a familiar song melody, first work out its key, then circle the chromatic notes in it.

Look at where these chromatic notes appear and where they go afterwards.

After analysing several melodies this way, you will find that chromatic notes follow many common patterns.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are diatonic notes?**
A: The seven notes belonging to the scale of the key.

**Q: What are chromatic notes?**
A: Notes that do not belong to the scale of the key.

**Q: Is F♯ a chromatic note in D major?**
A: No, it is in the key signature, so it is a diatonic note.

**Q: What do chromatic notes do?**
A: They bring colour and tension.

**Q: Where do raised chromatic notes usually go?**
A: Upwards.

digital-audio-workstation-record-edit-mi.body:
Many pieces of music, from simple practice recordings to complete songs, are made in a kind of software called a "digital audio workstation", abbreviated DAW. It sounds a little complicated, but you can think of it as a small recording studio inside your computer.

## What a workstation is made of

The interface differs from one program to another, but most include a few basic parts.

- Tracks: each instrument or each piece of sound sits on its own track, like layers of transparent film.
- Timeline: a horizontal time axis showing when a sound starts and when it ends.
- Mixer: adjusts the volume, left-right position and effects of each track.
- Effects: add processing such as reverb and equalisation to the sound.
- Transport controls: buttons for play, pause, record and so on.

## The basic recording process

**Step one: preparation**
Connect your microphone or digital piano, make sure the sound comes in normally, and keep the room quiet.

**Step two: recording**
Create a new track, press the record button and start playing. Most programs let you try a run-through first, so you can check the volume is right before recording for real.

**Step three: playback and choosing**
After recording, listen back and pick the version you are happy with. If you are not satisfied you can record again, without affecting the other tracks.

![The side of a piano in a room, with light and shadow](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwjqylsc-hdio4.webp)

## Editing: treating sound like building blocks

On the timeline you can cut a recording into pieces, move them around, or delete the parts you do not need. It is just like editing a video. For example, if a practice session begins with someone talking, you can simply cut it out; and two good takes can be joined together.

## Mixing: putting every sound in its place

When there are several tracks, the job of mixing is to make them work together. Adjust the volumes so the main melody is clear, adjust the left-right positions so the sound has a sense of space, and add a little reverb in moderation to make the sound more natural. Mixing is a craft that needs your ears. There is no need to hurry; it comes gradually with plenty of listening and trying.

## MIDI tracks and audio tracks

There are two common kinds of track in a workstation. Audio tracks record real sound; MIDI tracks record performance information such as "which key was played, for how long, and how hard". A digital piano connected by MIDI can record the performance information, and afterwards you can even change the instrument sound or edit individual notes.

## How piano learners can use it

- Record your practice each week on your phone or computer, and compare versions from different times to see your progress.
- Record the left hand and the right hand, then layer them together and listen to check how they fit.
- Use a click track and practise against a steady beat.

This kind of record builds the habit of listening back, and your ears become more discerning and your confidence grows.

## Pairing it with practice software

TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app that gives feedback on pitch and rhythm while you play. You can use it for daily practice first, and then use a workstation to record the version you are happy with as a keepsake. The two tools each have their use: one helps with checking and the other takes care of recording; as for expressiveness, that needs plenty of conversation with a teacher.

## Starting with a simple small project

You can give yourself a small task: record one study, add just a touch of reverb, export it as a sound file, and send it to your teacher to listen to. Once you have completed one whole process, you will find this kind of software is not mysterious. Later you can slowly try adding a click track, multiple tracks, or simple accompaniment for your child's playing. If each step is a little smaller, progress is actually steadier.

## A reminder for parents

When children use recording software, parents should choose trustworthy products together with them, find out where the data is stored, and avoid uploading children's voices and photos carelessly. When something needs to be shared, first get the family's agreement.

## Small tips for getting started

- Start with free or basic software and get familiar with the simplest recording and playback.
- Keep your files tidy and give them clear names.
- Save often to avoid accidental loss.
- Learn only one new function at a time, and do not rush to master everything.

## Good habits for saving and sharing

After recording, store the original files and the exported sound files separately, and write the date and the title of the piece in the file name. When you need to share with a teacher or family, first make sure the other person agrees, then send it in a trustworthy way. A child's practice recordings are a precious record of growth; keeping them safe also makes listening back an easy thing to do.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do I have to buy expensive equipment?**
A: No, you can start experimenting with a phone or an ordinary computer.

**Q: Can children use it?**
A: Yes, with a parent present, starting from simple recording and playback.

**Q: What is the difference between MIDI recording and ordinary recording?**
A: Ordinary recording captures the sound itself, while MIDI captures the performance information, which can be edited afterwards.

**Q: Does it take a long time to learn?**
A: Basic recording and playback are quick to pick up, and the advanced functions can be learned gradually.

digital-piano-split-layer-voices.body:
A digital piano's split function divides the keyboard into a left and a right zone, each with its own sound. For example, your left hand can play bass while your right hand plays piano. The layer function makes a single key sound two voices at once, such as piano plus strings, for a fuller tone. Many digital pianos and keyboards have both. They suit accompaniment, band rehearsals and creative practice. Used well, they let one player produce a much richer effect, but for classical piano repertoire you would normally stick to a single piano sound.

## How to use split

- First choose split mode; the keyboard usually divides near a default note
- Set the split point, which is the key that separates the left and right zones
- Choose a sound for the left zone and one for the right zone
- Adjust the volume balance between the two zones
- Some instruments let you set the left zone to its own octave, so the bass sounds lower

The split point is usually placed near middle C, but you can move it to suit the range of the piece.

## How to use layer

**Choose two sounds**
Common combinations are piano plus strings, piano plus electric piano, and piano plus choir. The first sound is the main voice and the second is the support.

**Adjust the balance**
The layered sound should be quieter than the main sound, otherwise it will cover the clarity of the piano. Many instruments let you set the volume of the second sound separately.

**Mind the difference in attack**
Strings and choir sounds start slowly, while the piano starts quickly. Layering strings over fast passages can make them sound blurred, so it works best for slow passages and long notes.

## Common situations to use them

**Accompanying a singer**
Play root notes in the left hand with a bass sound and chords in the right hand with a piano or electric piano sound. This can imitate a small band.

**Intros to slow songs**
Piano layered with strings suits the intros and interludes of ballads, giving the sound more space.

**Writing and arranging sketches**
Using split to quickly try out different instrument combinations is a handy way to capture arrangement ideas.

![Illustration of an electronic keyboard being played under neon lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3f6a5c-qajnv.webp)

## Things to watch for when practising

**Core technique still uses the piano sound**
Scales, studies and classical pieces train your touch and tone control on the piano. Layering other sounds hides the details, which makes it harder to hear your own problems.

**Split limits your range**
After splitting, each hand has fewer keys available. If a piece needs both hands to cover a very wide range, split is not suitable.

**Where the pedal applies**
On some instruments the sustain pedal affects both zones at once, and a sustained bass sound can become muddy. Check the manual and set the pedal to affect only the right zone.

## A small use in lessons

A teacher can use split to play duets with a student: the student plays the melody in the right zone, and the teacher plays an accompaniment in the left zone with a different sound, so the two of them play together on one instrument. Children often become more interested when they hear different instrument sounds. Once a student knows a piece well, they can also try adding layer to it and hear how the same melody changes with different sounds.

## A little history of split and layer

Early electronic organs already had a split function, so one player could play accompaniment and melody together. As digital sampling developed, sounds became more realistic, and layering moved from simple synthetic sounds to results close to real instruments. Today many stage keyboardists use split and layer together, switching between several combinations in one song so that a single instrument covers several parts of a band. For learners, knowing where these functions come from also helps in understanding how modern pop music is made.

## Saving your favourite settings

Many digital pianos have a registration memory function that stores the split point, the sound combination and the volume balance. If you often accompany the same song, you can save one setting per song and switch with one touch during the performance, rather than adjusting slowly on the spot. Once they are saved, write down on paper which number belongs to which song, so you do not press the wrong one on the day.

## FAQ

**Q: Do all digital pianos have split and layer?**
A: Not every model does. Entry-level models may have only one of the two, so check the manual before buying.

**Q: Can I set the split point wherever I like?**
A: On most instruments you can choose the split key. Usually you hold the setting button and press the key you want; check the manual for the exact method.

**Q: Does layering make practice less accurate?**
A: It hides some detail, so for core technique work use only the piano sound and keep layering for performing and creating.

**Q: Can the left hand play chords when split?**
A: Yes, but chords on a bass sound usually come out muddy. A single note or octaves in the left hand is generally clearer.

**Q: Is it right for children to play with these functions?**
A: They are fine as a way to explore for fun, and changing sounds now and then adds enjoyment, but everyday practice should still use the piano sound.

double-exposition-concerto-form.body:
The double exposition is a common arrangement in the first movement of a classical concerto: the orchestra first states the main material, then the soloist joins and states it again, often bringing new phrases or more brilliant passagework. The two expositions are not a simple repeat. The orchestra's exposition usually stays steadier and more completely near the home key, while the soloist's exposition often takes the contrasting material to the dominant and shows off what the instrument can do. A listener who does not know there are two openings may wonder, "why is the theme coming round again?" For someone playing a concerto on the piano or reading a reduced score, telling apart which part is the orchestra's statement and which is the statement after your own entry helps both memory and the planning of dynamics and the position of the cadenza. In practice, you can remember the two expositions separately, then work specially on the phrase where the soloist enters. When listening to a full recording, it also helps to make a clear mark at the place where the soloist first enters.

## Asking Teacher Aum to mark the entry in a lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to mark on the score the place where the soloist really enters, and to listen together to how that phrase should begin.

How the two expositions should differ in dynamics and character can also be compared on the spot.

From this arrangement of the double exposition, practise remembering the opening of a concerto's first movement clearly.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesiser and drums on a neon street, with a crystal tower behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjb8js-6vy9y.webp)

## Features of the soloist's exposition

After the soloist enters, the material already heard is often told in a more personal way, or given new links and passagework.

Contrasting material is also more often taken to the dominant, preparing for the development that follows.

This is both a part of the structure and a place to show off the solo instrument.

## And the place of the cadenza

Traditionally, a larger cadenza often comes later in the movement, rather than all the technique being used up in the double exposition.

Knowing the structure helps you keep your strength for the places where it should develop and where it should end.

In the two statements at the start, the first job is to state the theme clearly.

## Not every concerto does this

Later works may shorten, merge or rewrite the way the exposition is handled.

With concertos of the nineteenth century and after, go by the particular work all the more.

The classical double exposition is an important starting point, and it is not the case that every period can only use this one template.

## How the two differ

If you play them exactly the same, the audience loses the freshness of "the soloist has arrived".

If no connection can be heard at all, the unity a concerto should have is lost.

On material that can be recognised, you should make the changes that the entering player should make.

## An exercise in hearing the double exposition

Choose the first movement of a classical piano concerto and mark specifically: orchestra begins, soloist enters, development begins, recapitulation and ending.

Just making this one timetable will give you a concrete impression of the double exposition.

On a second listen, hear the similarities and differences in the material.

## Features of the orchestra's exposition

This section is usually fairly orderly, with the main material set out clearly in the home key.

Even when a contrasting theme appears, it does not necessarily travel as far as it later will.

When listening, you can treat it as "first spreading out the map".

## Why say it twice

A concerto needs to let the audience first become familiar with the material about to be developed, and also needs to give the soloist a formal entrance.

With the orchestra opening first and the soloist then restating, both can be done at once.

This arrangement is quite stable in first movements of the Classical period.

**Quick tips**
- The first movement of a classical concerto often has two statements of the theme
- The orchestra states it first, then the soloist joins and states it again
- The two are not a simple repeat, and the key and material may differ
- First tell apart the two openings, then plan the entry and dynamics

## Summary of the double exposition

The double exposition is the arrangement in the first movement of a classical concerto in which the main material is stated first by the orchestra and then by the soloist. The two are not a simple repeat, and the key and the passagework often differ.

When learning, tell apart which bars belong to the orchestra and where the soloist enters, and play the entry phrase steadily; later works may rewrite this tradition.

The place of the entry can be marked on the score by Teacher Aum.

## Practical problems in piano concertos

When playing a piano concerto, practising alone often has only a reduction or an accompaniment track, and it is easy to play the orchestra's exposition as well, or on the contrary to skip it entirely.

You should be clear about which bars the orchestra plays when you perform with it, and where you come in yourself.

The phrase where you enter has to be especially steady, because it is one of the most awaited moments of the whole movement.

## FAQ

**Q: What does double exposition mean?**
A: In the first movement of a concerto, the theme is first stated by the orchestra, and then stated again after the soloist joins.

**Q: Are the two statements exactly the same?**
A: No. The soloist's exposition often has new passagework, and more often takes the contrasting material to the dominant.

**Q: Why is the phrase where the soloist enters important?**
A: Because it is the formal entrance the audience is waiting for, and it needs to be played very steadily and clearly.

**Q: What problems come up when practising alone?**
A: Playing the parts that the orchestra would play, or being unsure where you should come in.

**Q: Do concertos of all periods use this arrangement?**
A: No. It is a common practice of the Classical period, and later works may rewrite it.

dett-juba-dance-in-the-bottoms-1913.body:
Juba Dance is a piano piece by the African American composer and pianist Robert Nathaniel Dett, from his 1913 suite In the Bottoms. The juba was originally a dance tradition accompanied by hand clapping, foot stamping and the rhythms of the body. Dett wrote it onto the piano so that the fingers can also tap out that bright, syncopated pulse. The piece is not a recording of any one particular dance, but uses the language of the piano to come close to this bodily rhythm. When learning it, it is sounder to find the positions of the beats and accents first and talk about tempo and dynamics afterwards, rather than playing it in a lively way right from the start. When listening, you can also first tap out its basic steps lightly with your hands, and then listen to how the piano adds decoration to those steps. Once your tapping is clear, judge whether the accents on the piano fall in the same places. In practice, line up with these positions first and the lively feeling will follow, without having to create atmosphere by playing every note heavily. It can help to step away from the piano and tap the basic steps clearly with hands and feet, then go back to the keyboard and see which notes those steps are written on. If the bodily rhythm disappears once the hands are together, do not add volume first, but find the beat again first. Cheerfulness is the result of getting it lined up, not something piled up with weight.

## What to Remember About Juba Dance

This is a piece from Dett's 1913 suite In the Bottoms, which writes the clapping and stamping tradition of the juba onto the piano.

When practising, line up the beats and accents first, keep your touch springy, and then bring the tempo up gradually.

When listening, clap first, and then hear how the piano adds decoration to those steps.

## How to Hear Beats and Accents

The fun of a dance often lies in this: not every note is equally heavy, but certain beats are stamped more definitely.

You can listen once and only clap, and listen again to see where the piano adds syncopation or short accents.

If a performance plays all the notes equally loudly, the rise and fall of the dance goes flat.

## How the Two Hands Share the Work

Often one hand keeps up the steps while the other sings a short motif or an answer.

First let the hand in charge of the stepping walk steadily by itself, and then gently add the other hand.

If the steps loosen once the hands are together, cut back the decoration for now and find the ground again first.

![Art deco style illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a desk lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjo0k8-h4jkf.webp)

## Asking Teacher Aum in Lessons Whether the Steps Are Clear

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the steps stay clear throughout, and whether the accents are being hammered until they sound hard.

If a passage falls apart as soon as you speed up, you can also ask the teacher to walk through a slowed-down version together with you, clapping along.

From a piano dance of 1913, you can practise rewriting bodily rhythm onto the keyboard.

## Do Not Make the Tempo Lively from the Start

A dance that sounds cheerful live does not demand that you play it through at concert tempo on the first day.

First place the syncopations and accents correctly at a moderately slow tempo, and then move up a little each day.

Liveliness is the result, not the starting point.

## The Suite In the Bottoms

In the Bottoms is a piano suite, published in 1913, and Juba Dance is the one that is more often played on its own.

The whole suite writes about the sounds and scenes of life from different sides, and this piece puts its emphasis on the steps of the dance.

Even if you only learn this one piece, it is worth knowing that it is not an isolated study but one scene within a set of works.

**Quick tips**
- A piano dance from Dett's 1913 suite In the Bottoms
- "Juba" comes from a dance tradition accompanied by clapping and stamping
- The rhythm is bright and syncopated, with a strong bodily feel
- When practising, line up the beats and accents first, then speed up

## What Juba Refers To

The juba is a dance and music tradition that emphasises hand clapping, foot stamping and the rhythms of the body, and it has a long history in African American cultural life.

Dett had professional musical training, and was also interested in how these traditions could enter piano pieces for the concert hall.

Listening to Juba Dance is listening for what is still left, after this bodily rhythm has been rewritten onto the keys, that can catch the ear at once.

## Keep Your Touch Springy

Short notes should bounce but need not be hammered. Keep your palm and wrist able to move, so that the accents come from control rather than from stiffness.

When more connected phrases appear, flatten the touch a little, so that the contrast can be heard.

**A different angle**

Wherever you find yourself playing harder and harder, change to a more unhurried tempo, and let the dance flow again once your arms have relaxed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who wrote this piece?**
A: Robert Nathaniel Dett.

**Q: Which work is it from, and in what year?**
A: The suite In the Bottoms, 1913.

**Q: What did "juba" originally refer to?**
A: A dance and music tradition that emphasises hand clapping, foot stamping and the rhythms of the body.

**Q: Why should you not play all the notes equally loudly?**
A: The fun of the dance depends on the rise and fall of accents and syncopations, and playing everything equally loudly flattens it.

**Q: How should you plan the tempo when starting?**
A: First place the beats correctly at a moderately slow tempo, then speed up gradually. Liveliness is the result, not the starting point.

domenico-scarlatti-555-keyboard-sonatas.body:
Domenico Scarlatti (1685-1757) was born in Naples, Italy, in the same year as Bach and Handel. He spent the second half of his life mainly on the Iberian Peninsula and left about 555 keyboard sonatas. Most of these sonatas have only one movement and are short, often with hand crossing, fast repeated notes and big leaps. In the middle of the twentieth century the American scholar Kirkpatrick catalogued them, which is why today we usually refer to them as "K." followed by a number.

## Born in the same year as Bach

1685 was a very special year in music history, because Bach, Handel and Scarlatti were all born in it.

Scarlatti was born in Naples in southern Italy, and his father, Alessandro Scarlatti, was an important opera composer.

He grew up in a musical family and began learning keyboard instruments very early.

## A few pieces suited to learners

The 555 sonatas vary in difficulty, and some of them are fairly short and suitable for intermediate learners.

You can ask your teacher to recommend a few works with a clear rhythm and not-too-complicated hand crossing as a start.

After you know one or two well, move on to works with higher technical demands.

**Try it**
- 1685-1757, born in Naples
- Born in the same year as Bach and Handel
- Left about 555 keyboard sonatas
- Mostly one movement, often with hand crossing and repeated notes

## Kirkpatrick's numbering

Most of Scarlatti's sonatas were not systematically numbered in his lifetime, and the manuscripts were scattered in different places.

In 1953 the American scholar Ralph Kirkpatrick published a study of Scarlatti and arranged the sonatas into a catalogue.

So when we see "K." followed by a number today, it refers to the number in this catalogue.

## A reported contest

According to accounts, the young Scarlatti once had a keyboard "contest" with Handel in Rome.

The story goes that on the harpsichord the two could not be told apart, while on the organ Handel was the better.

Stories like this may not be entirely accurate, but they show that he was already a very famous keyboard player when young.

## The way of writing hand crossing

Scarlatti's sonatas often have the left and right hands crossing, with one hand reaching over the other to play high or low notes.

This way of writing was very new at the time, and it tests the player's familiarity with positions on the keyboard.

In such passages, the hand has to go over or under the other, and the movement should be light so that it does not bump into the other hand.

![Close-up of grand piano keys and a gold-patterned lid in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2h75x-kei2k.webp)

## Scarlatti's legacy to the piano

Scarlatti's sonatas made many bold experiments in keyboard technique and writing.

These experiments influenced later keyboard music, and they also keep his works on concert programmes to this day.

For learners, these short and lively pieces are another window onto Baroque keyboard music.

## The 555 sonatas

Scarlatti left about 555 keyboard sonatas, a very considerable number.

Unlike the multi-movement sonatas of the later Classical period, his sonatas mostly have a single movement and can be played in a few minutes.

Many sonatas are divided into two parts, and each part is repeated once.

## The years on the Iberian Peninsula

Around 1719, Scarlatti left Italy and worked in Portugal and then Spain.

There he served as a keyboard teacher and wrote a great many keyboard sonatas for his students.

Spanish folk music, such as guitar strumming and dance rhythms, also often appears in his works.

## Fast repeated notes

His works also contain many fast repeated notes, where different fingers take turns on the same key.

For example, changing quickly between the third, second and first fingers makes the repeated notes fast and clear.

When practising slowly, first get the order of the finger changes clear, then gradually speed up.

## Playing Scarlatti on the piano

Scarlatti's sonatas were originally written for the harpsichord, but today many pianists also play them on the piano.

When playing on the piano, you can use a clear, light touch to come closer to the sound of the harpsichord, and use the pedal sparingly.

At the same time, you can also use the piano's ability to vary dynamics to give the music more layers.

## Hearing Spain in the sonatas

When listening to Scarlatti's sonatas, listen for chords that sound like guitar strumming and rhythms that sound like castanets.

These elements give his music a distinctive Iberian colour.

If you compare these features with the works of Bach, his contemporary, you will find a big difference in style between the two composers.

## The Essercizi of 1738

In 1738, Scarlatti published a collection of thirty sonatas, titled "Exercises for the harpsichord".

In the preface, he asks the player not to expect any deep learning in them, but to regard them as an ingenious game.

**Summary**

This remark captures well the light and nimble side of his works.

## FAQ

**Q: In what year was Scarlatti born?**
A: In 1685, the same year as Bach and Handel.

**Q: How many keyboard sonatas did he write?**
A: About 555.

**Q: How many movements do his sonatas have?**
A: Mostly just one.

**Q: What does the "K." number mean?**
A: It is the catalogue number from the catalogue compiled by Kirkpatrick.

**Q: What should I watch for when playing on the piano?**
A: A clear, light touch, and little pedal.
