debussy-first-arabesque-e-major-triplets.body:
Debussy's Deux Arabesques were written between 1888 and 1891 and published in 1891, and they are early piano works of his. The first is in E major. It opens with strings of triplets in the right hand, rising and falling like flowing water, and in many places the left hand plays evenly divided eighth notes at the same time, creating a "three against two" rhythm. To play this piece well, keep the triplets fluent and light, without being thrown off by the left-hand rhythm, and give the phrases a natural rise and fall.

## The Lingering Ending

The end of the piece gradually grows softer, and the last few chords are like ripples slowly fading away.

After the last chord is pressed, you can hold the pedal and let the sound disappear naturally.

Do not hurry to lift your hand or foot before the sound has completely gone.

![Cartoon character with glasses and headphones reading music and playing an upright piano in a night-time room, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4w3ma-is59k.webp)

## The Four Sharps of E Major

The first Arabesque is in E major, with four sharps in the key signature: F, C, G and D.

The middle of the piece passes through other keys too, with quite a few accidentals, so slow down when reading and look carefully.

Before you begin, play the E major scale and arpeggio a few times, so that your fingers get used to the positions of these black keys.

## Summary of the First Arabesque

Debussy's Deux Arabesques were written between 1888 and 1891 and published in 1891. The first is in E major.

The piece is characterised by flowing triplets and a three-against-two rhythm. When practising, clap first, then work hands separately, and finally put the hands together at a slow tempo.

Find the melody, follow the markings for flexible tempo, and use pedal and touch to bring out soft colours.

## Flexible Tempo in the Arabesque

Debussy wrote quite a few tempo changes in the score, such as slowing down slightly and returning to the original tempo.

These changes make the music rise and fall like breathing, so do not play it in a mechanical, constant tempo.

But the tempo changes should not be too free either. Follow the markings in the score and the structure of the phrases.

## Listening Together with Early Works

These two arabesques are among Debussy's earlier works, and their style is clearer and easier to approach than that of his later music.

You can listen to them alongside Debussy's later piano pieces and feel how his style changed.

For learners who want to begin playing Debussy, this piece is a good starting point.

**Practice order**
- Two arabesques, written 1888 to 1891
- Published in 1891, an early work by Debussy
- The first is in E major
- Right-hand triplets against left-hand eighth notes make three against two

## Hands Separately First, Then Together

At the three-against-two places, before putting the hands together, make sure you have mastered each hand separately.

The right-hand triplets should flow evenly all the way through, and the left-hand eighth notes should be steady.

When the hands play together, cut the tempo to about half, and raise it only when the crossing points on every beat line up.

## Pedalling in Debussy's Music

The triplets in the Arabesque need the sustain pedal to join into a shimmer of water.

But the pedal also has to be renewed as the harmony changes, or the sound becomes blurred.

In some places you can use half-pedal, pressing down only partly, so that the sound is connected without becoming too full.

## Impressionist Tone Colour

Debussy's music is often called impressionist, and it values changes of tone and colour.

When playing this piece, try different kinds of touch, so that the sound is sometimes clear and sometimes soft.

If your fingers stay close to the keys and press slowly, the sound is softer. If they fall a little faster, it is brighter.

## The Turn in the Middle Section

In the middle of the piece, the character of the music changes, the rhythm becomes steadier and the melody more definite.

You can treat the middle section as a contrasting part and play it with a slightly different tone colour.

After the middle section ends, the opening triplets return, forming a structure where the end echoes the beginning.

## The Melody Hidden in the Figures

The melody of this piece is sometimes hidden within the groups of triplets, sometimes in the left hand, and sometimes passed between the two hands.

When playing, first find where the melody is, and bring out the melody notes slightly.

Lightly circle these hidden melody notes in the score, and you will not miss them next time you reach them.

## The Opening Triplets

From the very start, the right hand has strings of triplets flowing downward, like clear water running gently from a height.

These triplets should be even and light, with every note clear but no obvious accents.

The wrist can move gently with the direction of the figures, letting the fingers fall naturally onto the keys.

## The Name "Arabesque"

"Arabesque" was originally a term in decorative art, referring to patterns of curves that twine and continue without a break.

Debussy used it to name piano pieces, and the melody and accompaniment really do spread out like a pattern, circle after circle.

The two pieces were written between about 1888 and 1891 and published in 1891, when Debussy was not yet thirty.

## The Three-Against-Two Rhythm

In this piece there are often places where the right hand plays triplets while the left hand plays two eighth notes. This is "three against two".

The first notes of both hands land together, and then the second note of the left hand falls exactly between the second and third notes of the right hand.

You can start by clapping slowly, three beats with one hand and two with the other, and feel where they interlock.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: When was this piece written?**
A: Between 1888 and 1891, and it was published in 1891.

**Q: What key is the first Arabesque in?**
A: E major, with four sharps.

**Q: What is three against two?**
A: One hand plays three notes while the other hand plays two at the same time.

**Q: How do I practise three against two?**
A: Clap first, then master each hand separately, and finally play hands together at a slow tempo.

**Q: How should I use the pedal?**
A: Renew it with the harmony, and use half-pedal where necessary.

dry-cloth-key-cleaning.body:
Before you practise, wipe the keys once, gently, from back to front with a clean, dry, soft cloth. This takes away surface dust and the oil left by your hands. It takes only a few dozen seconds, yet it makes the keys feel fresher, and it also reminds you to switch from whatever you were doing to practice mode. It is a small daily habit worth building.

## Choosing a cloth

A suitable cloth is soft, clean and lint-free, such as a fine microfibre cloth or a soft pure cotton cloth. A rough cloth may leave tiny scratches on the key surface, and a cloth that sheds lint will leave fibres in the gaps between the keys.

You can keep two cloths, one just for the white keys and one for the black keys. After long rubbing, some of the colour coating on certain black keys can be carried onto the white keys, so using them separately is safer.

After a while, wash the cloth and let it dry, so that you do not wipe dust back onto the keys.

If you do not have a dedicated cloth to hand, a clean glasses cloth can stand in for the time being, as long as it is soft and has no cleaning fluid left on it.

## The right direction to wipe

When wiping the keys, work from the back end, near the body of the piano, towards the front end, nearest you, one key at a time or a few keys at a time. This way the dust is pushed to the front edge of the keys rather than into the gaps between them.

Keep your touch light; there is no need to press hard. Rubbing hard from side to side can make the keys sound, and may also push dust into the gaps.

Black keys are narrower, so you can wrap the cloth around a finger and wipe along the length of the key.

## What to do after wiping

When you have wiped the keys, go and wash your hands and dry them thoroughly. Clean hands and clean keys work together, so your fingers will not slip as you practise and will not dirty the keys again right away.

While you are at it, you can check the music stand and the lid for dust and give them a pass with the dry cloth. The whole process takes less than two minutes.

Put this little routine before every practice session, and in time wiping the keys will feel as natural as opening the lid, a signal that you are getting into practice mode.

Before you start playing, slide your fingertips lightly over a few keys and feel whether the surface is dry. This is also a way of getting your hands used to the piano.

- Use a clean, soft, lint-free cloth
- Wipe from the back of the keys to the front; do not rub hard from side to side
- You can use different sides of the cloth for white keys and black keys
- After wiping, wash and dry your hands, then start practising

## Making cleaning a fixed routine

You can keep the dry cloth in the piano bench or in a fixed spot at the side of the piano, within easy reach. If you have to look for a cloth in another room every time, it is hard to keep the habit going.

The routine can be very simple: open the lid, wipe the keys, wipe the music stand, go and wash your hands, sit down and begin. Once the order is fixed, your body remembers it and you hardly need to think.

If there is a child learning piano at home, you can let the child take charge of wiping the keys. A child who looks after their own piano with their own hands often cherishes it more and is more willing to sit down and practise.

## Why keys need wiping often

Your fingers touch the keys every day, and the oil on your skin, sweat and dust in the air gradually build up on the key surface. Over time the edges of the white keys can turn grey and the surface of the black keys can get sticky, so the feel under your fingers is no longer fresh.

Wiping regularly with a dry cloth reduces this build-up. A piano shared by several people at home, or kept in a living room or near doors and windows, gathers more dust and needs cleaning more often.

Cleaning is also a chance to look over the instrument. As you wipe, you can notice whether any key is slow to return or makes a stray noise, and catch problems early.

![A person in futuristic clothing plays a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wokzf-ziyuw.webp)

## When to call a professional

If there is a stain on the keys that is very hard to remove, or if liquid has been spilled into the keyboard, do not take it apart yourself or clean it with a lot of water. Ask a piano tuner or repair technician to look at it.

Keys that stick, return abnormally or make an obvious rubbing sound when pressed all have to do with the internal mechanism. Surface cleaning cannot fix them and they need a professional check.

Everyday dry-cloth cleaning together with regular tuning and maintenance keeps a piano in better condition and makes it more pleasant to play.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I wipe the keys with a wet wipe?**
A: It is not advisable to use wet wipes directly. Moisture and cleaning ingredients can seep into the gaps between the keys, so a dry cloth is the safer choice.

**Q: How often should I wipe?**
A: A light wipe before each practice session is enough. Closing the lid when you are not playing also reduces dust.

**Q: Do I wipe the keys of a digital piano the same way?**
A: The method is similar. Switch the power off before wiping, and again keep liquid out of the keyboard.

**Q: Can yellowed keys be wiped white?**
A: Some yellowing comes from the ageing of the material, and wiping the surface will not change it much. You can ask a professional.

**Q: The piano makes a sound when I wipe the keys. Is that normal?**
A: An occasional sound from a key being pressed during a light wipe is normal. A gentler touch will reduce it.

**Q: Can I use the same cloth for the keys and for furniture?**
A: It is better to keep them separate. A cloth used on furniture may carry furniture wax or cleaning products that are not suitable for piano keys.

dominant-seventh-arpeggio-four-notes.body:
After learning triad arpeggios, many method books and exam syllabuses add the dominant seventh arpeggio. A dominant seventh chord is made of four notes; in C major, for example, it is G, B, D, F. Playing these four notes one after another across several octaves gives you the dominant seventh arpeggio. Compared with a triad arpeggio, it has one more note, and the hand shape and fingering are different. Practising it well not only makes your fingers more agile but also helps you get to know a chord that is very important in harmony.

## The Role of the Dominant Seventh in Harmony

The dominant seventh chord has a strong tendency to "want to resolve", and often goes straight back to the tonic chord.

For example, G7 followed by a C major triad sounds very natural and stable.

Many pieces end with a dominant seventh moving to the tonic.

## Fingering for the G7 Arpeggio

When playing the root-position G7 arpeggio, the right hand often uses fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4 for G, B, D, F, and then the thumb crosses to the G an octave higher.

Going up, the left hand often uses fingers 4, 3, 2, 1, and then finger 4 crosses over the thumb to the next octave.

Fingerings in different method books may differ slightly; go by the one you are using.

## Dominant Seventh Arpeggios at a Glance

The dominant seventh chord sits on the fifth degree: a major triad with a minor seventh stacked on top. In C major the dominant seventh is G, B, D, F, and it has a strong tendency to resolve, often returning to the tonic chord.

A dominant seventh arpeggio has four notes per octave. The right hand often uses fingers 1, 2, 3, 4 and then the thumb; the left hand uses 4, 3, 2, 1 and then finger 4 crosses over. The thumb crossing covers a greater distance than in a triad arpeggio. You can first play it as a block chord, start from different inversions, practise it in different keys, play hands separately before together, and keep the sound even.

You can look for dominant seventh chords in your pieces, and also use them in accompaniment. Teacher Aum can confirm the fingering and the keys to practise.

## Starting from Different Notes

The dominant seventh chord has a root position and three inversions, and the arpeggio can start from different notes.

For example, G7 can start from B, D or F.

Practising from different starting positions helps your hand get to know the shape of this chord better.

## Where the Thumb Crosses

In a dominant seventh arpeggio, the thumb crosses over a greater distance than in a triad arpeggio.

When crossing, keep the wrist steady, and do not suddenly raise or twist it.

You can first practise the change from finger 4 to the thumb on its own, until it becomes smooth.

## Finding the Dominant Seventh in Different Keys

Change the key and the dominant seventh changes too: in G major it becomes D, F♯, A, C.

The dominant seventh in F major is C, E, G, B♭.

You can practise key by key, according to what your method book or exam syllabus asks for.

## How the Dominant Seventh Is Built

The dominant seventh chord sits on the fifth degree of the scale: a major triad with a minor seventh stacked on top.

In C major, the fifth degree is G, so the dominant seventh is G, B, D, F.

G to B is a major third, B to D is a minor third, and D to F is also a minor third.

## Hearing the Dominant Seventh in Pieces

After learning the dominant seventh arpeggio, you can look for dominant seventh chords in the pieces you are practising.

It often appears just before the end of a phrase or section.

Being able to recognise the dominant seventh helps you understand the harmonic structure of a piece.

![A black grand piano and stool in front of a golden-red pointillist background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac2ure-mp864.webp)

## Dominant Seventh Arpeggios and Improvised Accompaniment

Once you are comfortable with the dominant seventh arpeggio, you can use it in simple accompaniments.

For example, when accompanying a song, play the dominant seventh as a broken chord.

This makes the accompaniment flow more and sound richer.

- The dominant seventh chord has four notes
- In C major the dominant seventh is G, B, D, F
- Playing the four notes one after another gives the dominant seventh arpeggio
- The hand shape and fingering differ from a triad arpeggio

## From Triads to Four Notes

A triad arpeggio has three notes per octave, and a dominant seventh arpeggio has four.

Four notes fit four fingers exactly, which makes the fingering quite regular.

But the hand has to spread more evenly, and you need to get to know the distance between each pair of notes.

## Hands Separately Before Together

Dominant seventh arpeggios also need to be practised with hands separately first, so that the fingering of each hand is secure.

When you put the hands together, the two hands cross at different places, so take particular care.

Start at a slow speed and make sure the two hands stay accurately together.

## An Even Sound

When playing arpeggios, keep the volume and length of the four notes even, so that no note is especially loud or short.

The crossing points are where unevenness often creeps in, so slow down and listen carefully.

You can also practise with different rhythm patterns to help your fingers stay even.

## Press G7 as a Single Block First

Before breaking G7 apart, let all four notes land together and listen to the sound of the whole block.

This helps your hand get to know the shape of the chord and the position of the keys.

Once the four fingers on G, B, D and F are firmly placed, release them one by one and travel upwards.

## Asking Your Teacher to Confirm the Fingering in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to confirm the fingering of the dominant seventh arpeggio, especially where the thumb crosses.

Your teacher can also decide which keys to practise according to the requirements of your exam or method book.

**Give it a try**

Once your hand shape and thumb crossing are steady, gradually raise the speed.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the dominant seventh chord in C major?**
A: G, B, D, F.

**Q: On which degree is the dominant seventh chord built?**
A: The fifth degree.

**Q: How many notes per octave does a dominant seventh arpeggio have?**
A: Four.

**Q: What chord does the dominant seventh often lead to?**
A: The tonic chord.

**Q: What is the dominant seventh chord in F major?**
A: C, E, G, B♭.

desirable-difficulties-bjork-varied-cond.body:
Playing smoothly at home but badly once you change to another piano or a different setting is very common. The psychologist Robert Bjork put forward the idea of "desirable difficulties". It holds that adding a moderate amount of variation and difficulty to practice may seem harder in the short term, but may leave memory and adaptability better in the long term.

## Adding Moderate Variation to Practice

You can try changing the order of your practice, for example not always starting from the beginning but starting from a passage in the middle or at the end. This lets you check whether each section is really mastered, rather than relying on the momentum of what came before.

**Slow down**

You can also change the conditions of practice, such as using different tempos, different dynamics, or practising at different times. When conditions vary, your playing does not adapt to just one situation.

If you get the chance, play on other pianos, for example your teacher's piano or a school piano. If you get used to different feels in advance, you are less likely to panic at a performance or a lesson.

Keep the variation moderate. If something is so hard that you cannot complete it at all, it turns into frustration. Start with small changes and increase them gradually.

## Changing the Conditions of Practice

You can change the tempo, for example practising at a tempo much slower than the target, or slightly faster.

You can change the dynamics, for example playing a phrase that is originally loud softly, or the other way round.

You can change the rhythm, for example practising even eighth notes as dotted rhythms.

You can change the setting, for example practising at different times and in different rooms, and playing on another piano when you have the chance.

These changes keep your playing from adapting to only one situation, so you are calmer when facing a new setting.

You can also try closing your eyes while playing a familiar piece, or playing along with a recording by ear without looking. These exercises keep your hands and ears steady under different conditions.

- Practice that is too smooth may lead you to overestimate how well you have mastered a piece
- Moderate variation helps long-term memory
- You can vary the order and conditions of practice
- The difficulty should be moderate, and harder is not always better

## Smooth Practice Does Not Mean Firm Learning

Practising on the same piano at home, at the same time and in the same order, the piece gets smoother and smoother and you feel you have mastered it. But once you change to another piano or play in front of other people, mistakes come easily.

This shows that smoothness in practice sometimes depends on fixed conditions and does not fully represent real mastery.

The psychologist Robert Bjork put forward the concept of "desirable difficulties". He argues that adding some moderate difficulty to practice may give a worse performance than smooth practice in the short term, but long-term memory and transfer are often better.

Here "desirable" means that these difficulties are good for learning, not that any difficulty helps.

This way of thinking can help you rethink how you plan your practice.

## Changing the Order of Practice

A simple approach is not to always start from the beginning. You can start from the middle, the end, or any section.

This lets you check whether each section can start on its own, rather than relying on the momentum of what came before.

When practising several pieces, you can also alternate between them instead of finishing one before moving on to the next. In research this approach is often called interleaved practice.

With interleaved practice, every switch makes you call up your memory again, which is exactly the kind of helpful difficulty.

It may feel less smooth at first, but after sticking with it for a while you will often find the pieces more stable.

## Getting the Level of Difficulty Right

The difficulty should be moderate. If it is so hard that you cannot complete it at all, it becomes frustration rather than a helpful challenge.

Start with small changes, for example only changing the starting place, and add other changes once you have adapted.

You can also combine varied practice with regular practice, for example practising normally a few times first and then adding some variation.

If you find that a certain change makes things very hard, you can step back for now and try again when your foundation is firmer.

What matters is to watch the long-term effect, and not only whether a single practice session goes smoothly.

In your practice log you can note how each variation felt and how well it worked, and after a while you can look back and find the combination that suits you best.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lttdi-9z74x.webp)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Are desirable difficulties better the harder they are?**
A: No. The difficulty has to be within what you can overcome. If it is too hard, it gets in the way of learning.

**Q: Is this kind of practice suitable for a new piece I have just started?**
A: You can lay a foundation first, and once you are basically familiar with it, add variation step by step.

**Q: Will starting from the middle disturb my memory?**
A: On the contrary, it lets you check whether each section is mastered on its own and helps form a more stable memory.

**Q: Does desirable difficulty mean the harder the better?**
A: No. The difficulty should be moderate, at a level you can complete but that takes effort.

**Q: Is interleaved practice suitable for beginners?**
A: You can start with simple alternation, such as practising two pieces in turn.

**Q: What if I play worse after adding variation?**
A: That is normal in the short term. You can look at the effect after a few weeks before judging.

debussy-reverie-1890-early-piano-piece.body:
Rêverie is a short piano piece in F major written by the French composer Debussy around 1890. The melody is gentle and flowing, and the broken chords in the left hand lap softly like ripples, making it very easy to lose yourself in it. Interestingly, Debussy himself did not value this piece. It is recorded that when he later learned it was to be published, he wrote in a letter that it was a hastily written and unimportant work. Yet after it was published in 1905 it became very popular and has often been arranged in many versions. Compared with Debussy's later works, its style is closer to Romanticism, which makes it good material for getting to know his early style.

## Asking your teacher to listen to the left hand of Rêverie

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your left-hand broken chords are even and soft.

**Take it slowly**

The timing of the pedal changes and whether the right-hand melody sings enough can also be adjusted phrase by phrase in the lesson.

From Rêverie, step into Debussy's piano world.

## How Debussy saw Rêverie

It is recorded that Debussy was not pleased when he later learned that Rêverie was to be published.

In a letter he said it was a piece written in a hurry, just to meet a need, and not important.

He may have felt that it did not represent the mature style he developed later.

## And yet it was popular

Whatever Debussy himself thought, Rêverie was very popular after its publication in 1905.

Its melody is lovely and the difficulty moderate, so many people enjoy playing it.

It has also been arranged for orchestra and for many instruments, and often appears on all kinds of occasions.

## Who is Rêverie for?

Rêverie is not technically difficult, and an intermediate player can take it on.

It is good material for getting to know Debussy's early style, and a good piece for practising broken-chord accompaniment and bringing out a melody.

Once you have learned it, other works by Debussy will become easier.

## The melody in F major

Rêverie is in F major, and the right-hand melody is gentle and flowing, like a quietly sung song.

The melody rises and falls very naturally, with long phrases, as if floating slowly in a dream.

There are some repeated notes and small variations in the melody, which give a faint, hazy feeling.

## Rêverie in summary

Debussy wrote Rêverie around 1890, when he was in his twenties. Money was tight then, and he wrote small piano pieces to sell to publishers. It is recorded that he later said in a letter that it was a hastily written and unimportant work, but it became very popular after its publication in 1905 and was arranged for orchestra and many instruments. The piece is in F major, the right-hand melody is gentle and flowing, and the left-hand broken chords lap like ripples.

The style is close to Romanticism and the harmony is fairly traditional, though there are already hazy shifts. You can compare it with Clair de lune, conceived in his early years, and with The Girl with the Flaxen Hair, from his mature period. The middle section is a little more agitated, then the opening melody returns. The pedal should be changed finely, and you can use half-pedalling. The melody should float above the broken chords, the tempo should be unhurried, the difficulty is moderate, and it suits an intermediate level.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the left-hand broken chords are even.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaf3u18-7v6ty.webp)

## The swell of the middle section of Rêverie

In the middle section of Rêverie the music becomes slightly more agitated and the harmony richer.

The melody climbs to a higher register, and the emotion deepens with it.

Then the music slowly calms again, and the opening melody returns.

## The rippling left hand

The left-hand accompaniment is a stream of broken chords, flowing evenly and softly.

These broken chords lap like ripples, carrying the right-hand melody.

When you play, the left hand must be very even and light, with no single note standing out.

## The young Debussy

Around 1890 Claude Debussy was still a young composer in his twenties.

He was still exploring his own style, and his living conditions were rather poor.

He wrote some small piano pieces to sell to publishers in exchange for some income, and Rêverie was one of them.

- A piano piece Debussy wrote around 1890
- F major, with a gentle, flowing melody
- Debussy himself did not value it
- Very popular after its publication in 1905

## The pedal in Rêverie

The sustain pedal, pressed with the right foot, is what joins up those rippling broken chords.

But the pedal must be changed finely, in time at every change of harmony, to avoid a muddy sound.

You can try half-pedalling, so that the sound is both connected and clear.

## An unhurried tempo

The tempo of this piece is not fast, and it should be played calmly and without hurry.

Do not play too quickly just because there are many broken chords in the left hand.

The title itself is a hint: it is like daydreaming, being lost in thought, not rushing along.

## A style close to Romanticism

Compared with Debussy's later works, the style of Rêverie is closer to Romanticism.

Its harmony is fairly traditional, and the melody is clear and complete.

But you can already hear some of Debussy's characteristic colours, such as hazy harmonic shifts.

## The Rêverie melody floats on top

When playing Rêverie, the right-hand melody should float clearly above the left-hand broken chords.

Play the melody notes with a fuller tone, singing with the weight of your fingers.

The left-hand broken chords should be light, like a distant background.

## Comparing it with later works

You can listen to Rêverie together with Debussy's later works, such as Clair de lune and The Girl with the Flaxen Hair.

Clair de lune was also conceived in his early years, but its harmony is more refined.

**Something to think about**

The Girl with the Flaxen Hair, on the other hand, is a work from his mature period, with a simpler and more individual style.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who wrote Rêverie?**
A: The French composer Debussy.

**Q: Roughly when was it written?**
A: Around 1890.

**Q: What key is the piece in?**
A: F major.

**Q: What did Debussy himself think of it?**
A: He thought it a hastily written and unimportant work.

**Q: In which year was it published?**
A: 1905.

debussy-la-mer-1905-three-sketches.body:
La mer is an orchestral work written by the French composer Debussy between 1903 and 1905, with the subtitle "three symphonic sketches". Interestingly, when he began it he was living in Burgundy, inland France, far from the sea; he said he preferred to depict the sea from memory and imagination. In October 1905 La mer had its premiere in Paris, and audiences and critics reacted in different ways. The cover of the first edition of the score used the woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa by the Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai. Today it is one of the most frequently performed orchestral works.

## Listening to the sea with your ears

When you listen to La mer, you can close your eyes and imagine the changing surface of the water.

Notice which instruments portray the light, the spray and the sound of the wind.

Different orchestras bring out different tone colours, so you can compare performances.

## The orchestration of the sea

Debussy cared deeply about instrumental tone colour, and in La mer he planned the entrance of each instrument with great care.

For example, he uses the harp and celesta for the glitter on the water, and muted brass for distant sounds.

These delicate colours make the music like a richly coloured painting.

**Details to notice**
- Written by Debussy between 1903 and 1905
- Subtitle: "three symphonic sketches"
- He began writing it in Burgundy, far from the sea
- Premiered in Paris in October 1905

## Three symphonic sketches

La mer has three movements, which Debussy called "symphonic sketches".

The word "sketch" shows that, like a painter, he wanted to capture an impression of the sea in music rather than tell a specific story.

The titles of all three movements relate to the sea and describe different faces of the water over the course of a day.

## Debussy and the sea

Claude Debussy was born in 1862 and died in 1918. He was a French composer.

He loved the sea from childhood and once said he might have become a sailor.

In many of his works you can hear traces of water, wind and light.

![A glowing abstract digital figure with a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadidlq-e8ugx.webp)

## First movement: From dawn to noon on the sea

The first movement describes the sea changing from dawn to midday.

The music begins with low, hazy sounds, like the sea before daybreak.

Then the instruments join in layer by layer, the light grows brighter, and finally the music reaches a brilliant climax in the midday sun.

## Second movement: Play of the waves

The second movement describes the play of the waves, and the music is light and shimmering.

The instruments appear and vanish like spray, constantly changing.

The rhythm and colour of this movement are very flexible, like sunlight dancing on the water.

## Writing about the sea inland

In 1903, when Debussy began La mer, he was living in Burgundy, in central-eastern France.

In a letter to a friend he said he had countless memories of the sea, and that these suited his music better than the view with his own eyes.

Later he completed part of the revisions of the work in the English seaside town of Eastbourne.

## Third movement: Dialogue of the wind and the sea

The third movement describes a dialogue between the wind and the sea, with intense, grand music.

The low instruments are like rolling waves, while the woodwinds and strings are like the howling wind.

At the end the music builds to a magnificent climax and closes on powerful chords.

## The harmony of the sea

In La mer Debussy uses many unusual harmonies, such as the whole-tone scale and the pentatonic scale.

These harmonies lack the strong sense of direction of traditional major and minor keys, and sound hazy and fluid.

It is exactly this haziness that makes the music as changeable as the sea.

## Playing Debussy on the piano

Debussy himself arranged La mer for piano four hands, so two people at one piano can get hold of those wave-like chords.

Many of Debussy's piano pieces, such as Reflets dans l'eau (Reflections in the Water), also have similar images of water.

When playing these works, pay attention to changes in tone colour and to the use of the pedal.

## The reaction at the premiere

In October 1905 La mer had its premiere in Paris.

At the time, some critics found it too hard to understand, while others admired its novelty.

This was also connected with changes in Debussy's private life, which led some people to hold opinions against him.

## Hokusai's print

The cover of the first edition of La mer used the print The Great Wave off Kanagawa by the Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai.

The print shows an enormous wave whose crest curls like a claw.

Debussy loved Japanese art, and this cover also reflects his taste.

## La mer in summary

Claude Debussy, born in 1862 and died in 1918, who said he might have become a sailor, wrote La mer, subtitled "three symphonic sketches", between 1903 and 1905. He was living in Burgundy, far from the coast, when he began it, and believed memories suited his music better than what he saw with his own eyes. Part of the revisions were completed in Eastbourne, England, and the premiere took place in Paris in October 1905 to mixed reactions.

The three movements are From dawn to noon on the sea, Play of the waves, and Dialogue of the wind and the sea. The first edition's cover used Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa, the work uses the whole-tone and pentatonic scales, harp, celesta and muted brass create its colours, the composer wrote a four-hand version, and his piano piece Reflets dans l'eau also has an image of water.

You can talk about the three movements with Teacher Aum.

## Talking about Debussy's sea in a lesson

In a lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the three movements of La mer and how Debussy describes the sea in music.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend a Debussy piano piece through which to experience his harmony and tone colour.

This work is a very good way to understand the characteristics of Impressionist music.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who wrote La mer?**
A: The French composer Debussy.

**Q: What is its subtitle?**
A: Three symphonic sketches.

**Q: Where was Debussy living when he began writing it?**
A: In Burgundy, far from the sea.

**Q: In which year was it premiered?**
A: October 1905, in Paris.

**Q: Whose artwork was used on the cover of the first edition?**
A: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa.

delibes-flower-duet-lakme-1883.body:
The Flower Duet is a duet for two female voices in Act 1 of the opera Lakmé by the French composer Delibes, which premiered in Paris in 1883. In the story, the heroine Lakmé and her maid gather flowers by the river. Their voices, one high and one low, often sing together a third or a sixth apart, like two threads twisted together. This melody was later used extensively in films and advertisements, so many people have heard it without knowing its name. Played on the piano, it is a way to practise balancing two voices in the right hand.

## Other works by Delibes

In Delibes' ballet music Sylvia there is a very famous Pizzicato.

**A different angle**

Coppélia tells the story of a doll that moves, with lively, light-hearted music.

These works also have piano arrangements, so you can get to know Delibes through them alongside the Flower Duet.

## Delibes, the composer of Lakmé

Léo Delibes (1836-1891) was a French composer, known for his ballet music and operas.

His ballets Coppélia and Sylvia are still performed on stage today.

The opera Lakmé was his representative work of his later years.

## A barcarolle-like rhythm

The accompaniment rocks gently, like a small boat floating on water.

This kind of rhythm is often used in music that describes water and boats, and is called the barcarolle style.

It gives the whole duet a relaxed, dreamy feeling.

**In brief**
- Act 1 of Delibes' opera Lakmé
- Premiered in Paris in 1883
- Lakmé and her maid gather flowers by the river
- The two voices are often a third or sixth apart

## One voice high, one voice low

In this duet Lakmé usually sings the higher part and her maid the lower part.

The two voices are often a third or sixth apart and move together in the same rhythm.

Thirds and sixths are intervals that sound very sweet and harmonious, which is why this music is so soft.

## The rocking left-hand accompaniment

The left-hand accompaniment should imitate the rocking of a barcarolle, played lightly and evenly.

The first bass note of each bar can be a little clearer, and the notes after it should be light.

Change the pedal with the harmony so that the accompaniment is soft and connected.

## The Flower Duet in summary

The Flower Duet comes from Act 1 of the opera Lakmé by Delibes (1836-1891), which premiered in Paris in 1883. The story is set in nineteenth-century India, where Lakmé and her maid gather flowers by the river. The two voices often move in the same rhythm a third or a sixth apart, the accompaniment is a barcarolle-like rocking rhythm, and in the late twentieth century the piece was adopted by many films, television programmes and advertisements.

In the piano version the right hand has to play two voices at once, with the upper one slightly more prominent. You can first practise thirds on scales, and the left hand gently imitates the barcarolle's rocking. The two voices must breathe together. Delibes also wrote Sylvia and Coppélia.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the balance of the two voices.

## The breathing of a duet

The two voices in a duet must breathe together, beginning and ending every phrase together.

On the piano, the two voices in the right hand must also behave like two singers, starting at the same time and releasing at the same time.

Do not cut off the end of a phrase suddenly; draw it back gently.

![A person with blue-purple hair in a futuristic jacket playing several glowing synthesizers on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbi28rw-ur5j9.webp)

## Gathering flowers by the river

In Act 1, Lakmé and her maid come to the river, ready to gather flowers and bathe.

The two sing the Flower Duet, and the words describe thick shade, and jasmine and roses in bloom.

The music is like slowly flowing river water, quiet and beautiful.

## Practising fingers with thirds

There are many parallel thirds in this music, so you can first practise thirds on scales.

For example, with the right hand use fingers 1-3, 2-4 and 3-5 to play the thirds of the C major scale.

Once the thirds are steady, going back to the piece will be much easier.

## Checking the upper and lower voices of the Flower Duet in a lesson

You can play for Teacher Aum in a lesson and ask the teacher to judge whether the volume of the upper and lower voices is balanced.

If your right hand cannot sustain both lines, you can temporarily give the lower line of thirds to the left hand.

From a single duet, feel the beauty of two melodies singing together.

## Playing two voices on the piano

In a piano arrangement, the right hand often has to play two voices at once, one above and one below.

The upper voice should be a little more prominent and the lower one lighter, but both must be connected.

You can first play each voice separately, and put them together once you are familiar with them.

## The story of Lakmé

The story of Lakmé is set in nineteenth-century India, and Lakmé is the daughter of a priest.

She meets an English officer, and the two fall in love, but are caught in difficulty by their different status and culture.

The opera carries the European imagination of the East at that time, and the music has many exotic colours.

## The Flower Duet in films and advertisements

In the late twentieth century this melody was used in many films, television programmes and advertisements.

Because it is used so often, many people know only the melody and not that it comes from a nineteenth-century opera.

Starting from a familiar melody and getting to know the whole opera is also an interesting way to listen to music.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which opera is the Flower Duet from?**
A: Delibes' Lakmé.

**Q: In which year did this opera premiere?**
A: 1883, in Paris.

**Q: Who sings the duet?**
A: Lakmé and her maid.

**Q: What interval are the two voices often apart?**
A: A third or a sixth.

**Q: What is the rhythm of the accompaniment like?**
A: A barcarolle, like a small boat rocking on the water.

debussy-girl-with-the-flaxen-hair-1910.body:
The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is the eighth piece in Book 1 of Debussy's Preludes, written between 1909 and 1910 in G-flat major. It is short, with a gentle melody, and it is one of the first Debussy pieces many learners play. Interestingly, Debussy wrote the title of each prelude at the end of the piece rather than at the beginning, as if he wanted the player to hear the music first and read the words afterwards. Below are the background to the piece and some playing tips.

## The unaccompanied melody at the start

The piece opens with the right hand singing a single line, with no accompaniment at all.

Most of this melody uses notes of the pentatonic scale, which sounds fresh and simple.

Play it very softly, but make every note clear, like someone humming quietly to themselves.

## The quiet ending

At the end, the melody returns as it was at the beginning, then slowly fades away over very soft chords.

Lower the final chord gently and hold it until the sound dies away naturally.

Take your hands off the keys slowly too, so you do not break the quiet atmosphere.

## How G-flat major feels under the hands

G-flat major has six flats, so many of its notes fall on the black keys.

The black keys are higher and narrower, so as the melody moves over them the hand can stay fairly relaxed on the keyboard.

Before you start practising, get to know the scale and main chords of this key on the black keys.

## The title at the end of the piece

Debussy placed the title of each prelude at the very end of the music, written in brackets with an ellipsis.

This way, the player and the listener can first imagine something from the sound alone, and only then see the hint the composer has given.

When you play this piece, you can also set the title aside and simply listen to how the melody makes you feel.

## Practising The Girl with the Flaxen Hair in four parts

You can divide the piece into the opening melody, the section of parallel chords, the high point and the ending.

Learn each hand separately first, then put the hands together, paying special attention to how the hand shape moves in the parallel chord section.

Once each part is secure, join them up, taking care over the transitions between sections.

## Comparing it with the other preludes

You might also listen to other preludes from Book 1, such as The Sails and The Sunken Cathedral.

Comparing them, you will notice that The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is written in a more traditional way, and its melody is the easiest to remember.

This piece is a gentle doorway into Debussy's piano music.

## The colour of parallel chords

In the middle of the piece there is a passage where several chords keep the same shape and move up and down together. This is the "parallel chord" technique that Debussy often used.

This writing ignores the traditional rules of voice leading, yet it creates a hazy, floating colour.

When you play it, keep the hand shape unchanged and move it as a whole, with an even, soft sound.

## Debussy's two books of Preludes

Debussy (1862-1918) wrote two books of piano Preludes, twelve pieces in each.

Book 1 was written between 1909 and 1910 and published in 1910, and The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is the eighth piece in it.

Each prelude has a vivid, picture-like title, such as mist, sails, wind, or footprints in the snow.

![A wooden upright piano, a green piano stool and an orange book against a deep teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7ehyt-npybi.webp)

## Clear layers of volume

Most of this piece lies between soft and very soft, with just one slightly stronger high point in the middle.

Even within the very soft range, create layers: let the melody stand out a little and keep the chords lighter.

Do not play the high point too loudly; it is only a little brighter than its surroundings.

## Flexible tempo

The tempo marking of this piece is "very calm, gentle and expressive".

The tempo can stretch a little naturally, but it should not turn into random speeding up and slowing down.

You can ease off slightly where a phrase ends, then return to the original tempo as the next phrase begins.

## The Girl with the Flaxen Hair in summary

The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is the eighth prelude of Debussy's Preludes, Book 1, written in 1909-1910 in G-flat major, with a title that comes from a poem and is written at the end of the piece.

The unaccompanied opening melody has a pentatonic colour, there are parallel chords in the middle, most of the piece lies between soft and very soft, and even the high point should not be too loud.

Change the pedal with the harmony and check it with your ears, let the tempo stretch naturally, practise in sections, and listen to it alongside the other preludes.

## Debussy's pedalling

Debussy's music often needs the pedal to create a hazy sound, but the score does not always mark it in detail.

When Debussy's harmony stays in place, you can hold the pedal a little longer; when the harmony moves, your foot moves with it.

Keep checking with your ears, and if the melody becomes blurred, change the pedal in time.

## The title comes from a poem

The title "The Girl with the Flaxen Hair" comes from a poem by the French poet Leconte de Lisle.

The poem describes a girl singing in the sunshine, in a bright and peaceful mood.

Knowing this picture helps you grasp the simple, gentle character of the piece.

- Prelude No. 8 from Book 1, 1909-1910
- G-flat major, with a gentle melody
- The title is written at the end, in brackets
- Pentatonic colour and parallel chords

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which work is this piece from?**
A: It is the eighth prelude in Debussy's Preludes, Book 1.

**Q: When was it written?**
A: Between 1909 and 1910.

**Q: Where is the title written?**
A: At the end of the piece.

**Q: What are parallel chords?**
A: Chords that keep the same shape and move up and down together.

**Q: What is the volume like across the piece?**
A: Mostly between soft and very soft, and even the high point is not very loud.

descending-fifths-chord-sequence.body:
There is a kind of chord progression in which the root of each chord is a fifth lower than the one before. In C major, for example: C, F, Bdim, Em, Am, Dm, G, C. This progression is called a descending fifths sequence, and is also often called the circle-of-fifths progression. It sounds natural and flowing, as if the harmony is pushing forward step by step and finally returns to the tonic chord. You can hear this progression in baroque music, classical music, jazz and many pop songs.

## Adding Seventh Chords

The chords in a descending fifths sequence can also all be replaced with seventh chords, for example Cmaj7, Fmaj7, Bm7b5, Em7, Am7, Dm7, G7, Cmaj7.

**Summary**

Seventh chords make the sequence richer, and the connections between the voices smoother.

The seventh of each chord often moves down by step to the third of the next chord.

## The ii–V–I in Jazz

The ii–V–I that jazz uses so often is in fact part of a descending fifths sequence.

In C major, for example, Dm7, G7, Cmaj7: the roots go from D to G to C, each time falling a fifth.

In many jazz standards there are longer chains of descending fifths, with the harmony travelling all the way to the tonic.

## Alternating the Left-Hand Bass Up and Down in a Descending Fifths Sequence

When playing a descending fifths sequence, the left-hand bass can alternate between jumping down a fifth and jumping up a fourth, which keeps the bass in a comfortable register.

If you keep jumping down a fifth, you will quickly end up at the lowest part of the piano.

For example, C goes up a fourth to F, F goes down a fifth to B, B goes up a fourth to E, and in this way the bass can move back and forth in the middle register.

## In Pop Songs

You can hear similar progressions in some pop songs too, for example Am, Dm, G, C.

This passage is exactly the second half of the descending fifths sequence, and it sounds smooth and natural.

Try playing these chords on the piano, and you will find that they sound good and are easy to join to a melody.

## The Feeling of Sequence

A descending fifths sequence often goes together with a melodic sequence, that is, the same melodic shape repeated at different pitches.

With each change of chord, the melody moves down a step, creating a regular descent.

The listener can anticipate the direction that comes next, so the music sounds both regular and forward-moving.

![Piano scene with futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa64vhe-lqajw.webp)

## In Baroque Music

In the music of the Baroque period, descending fifths sequences are very common.

In works by Vivaldi, Bach and Handel, you can often hear the harmony travelling down by fifths all the way.

This way of writing gives the music a drive that keeps moving forward.

## In Improvisation and Arranging

When improvising, or arranging a song, the descending fifths sequence is a very useful tool.

If you want to get from one chord back to the tonic, you can follow the descending fifths direction and go back slowly through a few chords.

This kind of connection sounds very natural and also adds variety to the harmony.

## Roots Falling a Fifth

The characteristic of a descending fifths sequence is that the root of each chord is a fifth lower than the root of the chord before.

From C, for example, a fifth down is F, from F a fifth down is B, and from B a fifth down is E.

On the piano, a bass that jumps down a fifth can also be written as jumping up a fourth, with the same effect.

**Practice order**
- Each chord root is a fifth lower than the previous one
- In C major you can go through all seven degrees
- It sounds natural, flowing and forward-moving
- Common from baroque to pop music

## Hearing the Descending Fifths

When listening to music, if you feel that the harmony is moving down regularly, step by step, pushing towards the ending, it may well be a descending fifths sequence.

You can try singing along with the bass to see whether each time it goes down a fifth or up a fourth.

With practice, it becomes fairly easy to hear this progression.

## Going Through the Descending Fifths in G Major and Other Keys

You can practise playing the complete descending fifths sequence in a few common keys.

For example, G major gives G, C, F#dim, Bm, Em, Am, D, G.

Practising in many different keys helps us become familiar with the chords of each key.

## Why It Sounds Natural

A root falling by a fifth is one of the most powerful movements in harmony.

The dominant chord moving to the tonic is a root falling a fifth, for example G to C.

The descending fifths sequence links this movement together one after another, so it sounds very natural and flowing.

## Connecting in the Right Hand

When the right hand plays the chords, keep the common notes where possible and move the other notes to the nearest ones.

This makes the connections between chords very smooth, and the hand moves less.

For example, from C to F, the C in the right hand can stay where it is, while E and G move to F and A.

## Summary of the Descending Fifths Sequence

A descending fifths sequence is a progression in which each chord root is a fifth lower than the previous one. In C major it is C, F, Bdim, Em, Am, Dm, G, C.

It sounds natural and flowing, often goes with melodic sequences, and is common in baroque music, in the jazz ii–V–I and in pop songs.

Alternating the left-hand bass up and down, keeping common notes in the right hand and practising in different keys can help us master this progression.

## The Complete Sequence in C Major

In C major, going around once with the chords of the key gives C, F, Bdim, Em, Am, Dm, G, C.

Here Bdim is a diminished triad, and F to B is an augmented fourth rather than a perfect fifth. This is an adjustment made to stay within the key.

**Common misunderstanding**

Going through the whole circle passes exactly through the seven chords of the key and finally returns to the tonic.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a descending fifths sequence?**
A: A progression in which each chord root is a fifth lower than the previous one.

**Q: What is the complete sequence in C major?**
A: C, F, Bdim, Em, Am, Dm, G, C.

**Q: Which progression in jazz belongs to it?**
A: The ii–V–I.

**Q: How should the left-hand bass be handled?**
A: Alternate between jumping down a fifth and jumping up a fourth.

**Q: How should the right hand connect the chords?**
A: Keep the common notes and move the other notes to the nearest ones.

debussy-engulfed-cathedral-prelude-1910.body:
Among Debussy's twenty-four piano preludes, The Sunken Cathedral (La cathédrale engloutie) is the tenth piece in Book 1, which was written between 1909 and 1910 and published in 1910. The piece comes from an old legend of Brittany, in north-western France: a city sank beneath the sea, and its cathedral slowly rises out of the early-morning mist, with bells and singing sounding, before sinking back into the sea. With hollow low fifths, chords moving in parallel and long stretches of sustained sound, Debussy paints this picture of sound moving from far to near and near to far again. It is a very good piece for practising layers of tone colour and pedalling.

## Summary of The Sunken Cathedral

The Sunken Cathedral is the tenth prelude of Debussy's Préludes, Book 1, which was written between 1909 and 1910. Its title is printed at the end of the piece, preceded by an ellipsis. It comes from the legend of the sunken city of Brittany. It opens with hollow fifths marked "Profondément calme", the parallel chords carry a medieval flavour, the bells draw closer and reach a climax in great C major chords, and then the cathedral sinks back to the sea floor.

**Details to notice**

Debussy's piano-roll recording from around 1913 has some passages roughly twice as fast, which is related to how the time signature is converted. The pedal should be changed carefully where the harmony changes, and half-pedalling is possible. The tone colour should separate far from near. It suits intermediate to advanced learners better.

The legend and the writing can be talked through with Teacher Aum.

## Putting the Title at the End

Debussy's preludes have a distinctive habit: the title of each piece is printed not at the start but at the end of the music.

An ellipsis is also placed before the title, as if to say "this is only a hint".

He seems to have wanted the player to hear the music first and only then think of the picture in the title.

## The Cathedral Sinks Again

After the climax the music gradually fades, and the chords return to a hazy low register.

The opening theme appears again, but more distant, as if heard through a layer of water.

At last the bells grow quieter and quieter, and the cathedral sinks once more into the depths of the sea.

## Debussy's Twenty-Four Preludes

Debussy's piano Préludes are divided into two books, which together make exactly twenty-four pieces.

Book 1 was completed between 1909 and 1910, and Book 2 between 1912 and 1913.

The Sunken Cathedral is the tenth piece of Book 1, in the same book as The Girl with the Flaxen Hair.

**Common misunderstandings**
- Debussy, Préludes, Book 1, No. 10
- Book 1 was written between 1909 and 1910 and published in 1910
- It comes from the Breton legend of a sunken city
- Hollow fifths, parallel chords and long sustained sound

## Separate Far from Near in Tone

The most important thing in playing The Sunken Cathedral is to separate far from near in sound.

The distant mist and sea water should be played very lightly and softly, while the nearby bells should be played thick and weighty.

The same chord sounds completely different when you sink into it slowly with the weight of your arm and when you touch it lightly with your fingertips.

## The Tempo Puzzle in the Composer's Recording

Debussy himself recorded this piece on piano roll around 1913.

In that recording some passages are played about twice as fast as the score looks.

Many people think this is related to how the time signature in the score is converted, and pianists today still understand this point differently.

## Talking About The Sunken Cathedral in Lessons

Before playing this piece, you can talk with Teacher Aum in lessons about the Breton legend and Debussy's way of writing.

How to play the C major chords at the climax broadly without harshness can also be tried out bit by bit in lessons.

From a single piece, you can step into the world where Debussy paints with sound.

## The Hollow Fifths at the Start

The piece opens marked "deep and calm", with the left hand playing empty fifths and octaves in the low register.

The right hand plays equally open chords softly in the high register, leaving a lot of space in the middle.

These chords without thirds sound ancient and hazy, like a sea surface in mist.

![Glowing digital interface on a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbhu4bb-3f2w0.webp)

## Chords Moving in Parallel

In The Sunken Cathedral, many chords move up or down as whole blocks, in parallel.

This way of writing recalls the parallel organum of the Middle Ages, with the air of a church and ancient singing.

It is rarely written like this in traditional harmony, but in Debussy's hands it becomes a colour for painting a picture.

## The Legend of the Sunken City in Brittany

In Brittany, in north-western France, an old legend is told.

In the legend, a city sank into the sea, and its cathedral was swallowed by the water along with it.

It is said that on a calm morning people can see the cathedral rise out of the mist, hear the bells and the monks' singing, and then watch it slowly sink back to the bottom of the sea.

## Pedalling in The Sunken Cathedral

Almost every section of this piece needs the sustain pedal, so that the bass bells can ring on and on.

But if you keep the pedal down without changing it, the chords become muddy, so change it carefully wherever the harmony changes.

Sometimes you can change only halfway, leaving a little of the bass resonance while making the chords above clear.

## What Level Is It Suitable For?

The notes in this piece are not especially fast, but the stretches are wide and the chords thick, so a fairly good hand span is needed.

The demands on tone colour and pedalling are very high, so it suits intermediate to advanced learners who already have a certain foundation.

Beginners can first listen to different pianists and feel the process of slowly rising and slowly sinking.

## The Bells Draw Nearer

As the music develops, long notes like great bells appear in the low register, ringing one by one.

The volume slowly grows and the register slowly widens, like the cathedral rising bit by bit from the sea floor.

At the climax of the whole piece, great C major chords are played at full strength, as though the cathedral has completely emerged from the sea.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which work is The Sunken Cathedral from?**
A: Debussy's Préludes, Book 1, No. 10.

**Q: When was this book written?**
A: Between 1909 and 1910, and it was published in 1910.

**Q: Where does the story of the piece come from?**
A: The legend of the sunken city in Brittany, France.

**Q: Where did Debussy print the titles of his preludes?**
A: At the end of each piece, preceded by an ellipsis.

**Q: What key is the climax of the whole piece in?**
A: Great C major chords.

ebbinghaus-forgetting-curve-review.body:
Forgetting a well-practised piece within a few days is something many adults learning the piano run into. The "forgetting curve" from psychology shows that forgetting is fastest in the period just after learning, and then gradually slows. Following this pattern, spreading reviews over several intervals is often easier on memory than practising for a long time in one go.

## What the forgetting curve says

Between 1880 and 1885, the German psychologist Ebbinghaus ran experiments on himself, memorising meaningless syllables and then testing how much he still remembered after different intervals.

**In brief**

He published his results in 1885, and the data was later drawn as a curve known as the "forgetting curve". The curve shows that forgetting is fastest in the period just after learning, and then the speed of forgetting gradually slows.

His research also found that relearning something already forgotten is usually quicker than learning it the first time, which shows that the memory has not disappeared completely.

Many later studies have looked at this phenomenon under different conditions. The details differ, but the general pattern of "forgetting fast at first, then slowly" is often cited.

For people learning the piano, this pattern can help explain why a well-practised piece becomes rusty after a few days.

![Electronic devices and an audio waveform in blue-purple light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8llj8i-9tvz6.webp)

## Keeping reasonable expectations

Forgetting is a normal phenomenon and does not mean learning has failed. A piece becoming rusty after a few days is memory changing naturally.

Through review, memory becomes firmer each time, and you get it back faster and faster.

A review plan does not need to be complicated. What matters is carrying it out regularly.

You can find a rhythm that suits you according to your time and the number of pieces.

If you keep it up over the long term, you will find that more and more pieces can be played at any time.

If practice is interrupted for a while, do not be discouraged. Arrange your reviews again in the same way, and you will usually recover faster than when you first learned it.

## The idea of spaced review

Since forgetting is fastest just after learning, reviewing while not much has yet been forgotten lets you bring the memory back in less time.

After each review the memory becomes firmer and the next forgetting is slower, so the interval before the next review can be made longer.

This method of reviewing at gradually lengthening intervals is often called spaced review or distributed practice.

Compared with one long session, spreading the same amount of time over several days often keeps the memory for longer.

This does not mean that a long session is useless, only that the way reviews are arranged matters too.

## Arranging review in your practice

You can prepare a simple record sheet and write down each new section you learn and the date you learned it.

Then arrange a short review on the next day, three or four days later, a week later and two weeks later, and each time you only need to play it a few times.

When reviewing, you can first try playing without the music and then check against the score, so it is both a review and a practice in recall.

If a section goes smoothly in review, the interval before the next one can be longer; if you keep getting stuck, shorten the interval.

Put the review at the start of each day's practice and spend a few minutes on it, and you can take care of both new and old material.

For pieces you already know very well, you can also take them out every so often and play them through, so that they stay ready to perform at any time, instead of waiting until you need them and picking them up again from scratch.

- Forgetting is most noticeable in the short time after learning
- Spaced review helps consolidate memory
- The intervals between reviews can gradually lengthen
- Each review does not need to take long

## Putting spaced review into your practice plan

You can write down the sections you have newly learned and mark the date you learned them. Then review each once on the next day, a few days later and a week later, playing it only a few times and confirming you can still get through it smoothly.

When reviewing, you can try playing once without the music, then check against the score. This is not only review but also practice in recall, which helps make the memory firmer.

A simple way is to keep a practice log and look through what needs reviewing before each day's practice. That way new and old material are both looked after in the same session.

**Another way to look at it**

If a section keeps getting stuck when you review it, you can shorten the interval before the next review and give it a little more attention. When it is stable, go back to the original interval.

## FAQ

**Q: How long should the intervals be?**
A: There is no fixed standard. You can start with a day or two and gradually lengthen them to a week or more.

**Q: Is it better to practise the same section every day?**
A: Daily practice helps with new material, but suitably spaced review makes memory last longer.

**Q: Does forgetting mean I did not practise well?**
A: Forgetting is normal, and relearning is usually faster than the first time.

**Q: Must the intervals follow a fixed number of days?**
A: Not strictly. You can adjust them flexibly according to how well you remember.

**Q: How many times should I play it in each review?**
A: A few times is usually enough. The point is to confirm that you can still get through it smoothly.

**Q: Is spaced review suitable for memorising music?**
A: Yes. It helps memorised material last longer.

four-against-three-polyrhythm.body:
If you have practised three against two, meeting four against three often makes your fingers feel tied in knots. In the same span of time, one hand plays four even notes and the other plays three even notes, and the two hands line up only at the start. This rhythm appears in works by Chopin, Debussy and other composers. Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu, for example, has four in the right hand against three in the left. Once you break it into twelve small cells, it is not so mysterious.

## Four Against Three: Summary

Four against three means that in the same span of time one hand plays four even notes and the other plays three, with the hands lining up only at the start. You can work it out with twelve equal divisions: the four-note hand lands on cells 1, 4, 7 and 10, and the three-note hand on cells 1, 5 and 9.

Learn the order in which the two hands interlock, use words or clapping to help, practise each hand separately until steady, then put the hands together very slowly. Once it is secure, drop the counting and let the two lines flow on their own.

Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu is the famous example. Do not force the notes to line up, and if it feels too hard, start with three against two.

## From Mechanical to Fluent

At first, playing by the twelve divisions will feel somewhat mechanical.

Once you are secure, gradually drop the counting and let each hand keep its own flow.

It should sound like two independent lines, not one complicated jigsaw puzzle.

## Start With Three Against Two

If four against three feels too hard, you can start by practising three against two.

The principle is the same, only worked out with six equal divisions.

Once you are familiar with three against two, four against three becomes much easier.

## Using Words to Help You Remember

Some people use a phrase to help them remember this rhythm, saying it aloud in the order in which the two hands interlock.

You can also clap it: three claps with the left hand and four with the right, slowly against the twelve small cells at first.

Once familiar, bring this feeling to the piano.

## What Is a Polyrhythm

When the two hands play different numbers of even notes in the same span of time, a polyrhythm is formed.

Common ones include two against three, three against four and so on.

They make the music sound more fluid and more complex.

## The Principle of Four Against Three

Four against three means that in the same span of time one hand plays four even notes and the other plays three even notes.

The two hands play together at the start of this span, and after that none of the notes line up.

Only at the start of the next cycle do the two hands play together again.

## Don't Force Them to Line Up

A common mistake in four against three is forcing the notes of the two hands to line up, which produces an uneven rhythm.

It may seem as if it has "come together", but in fact neither hand is even any more.

Check with your ears to make sure the notes of each hand are even.

## Working It Out With Twelve Divisions

The least common multiple of four and three is twelve, so you can divide the span into twelve small cells.

The hand playing four notes lands on cells 1, 4, 7 and 10; the hand playing three notes lands on cells 1, 5 and 9.

This lets you see clearly where every note sits.

![Purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8qjhg-r7lzi.webp)

## How the Two Hands Interlock

By the twelve divisions, the notes of the two hands appear in a fixed interlocking order.

After the first note, which is played together, the order is: four-note hand, three-note hand, four-note hand, three-note hand, four-note hand.

Learning this order well is the key to playing four against three accurately.

## Four Against Three in Other Works

Debussy and other composers also often use polyrhythm to create hazy, flowing effects.

In some Romantic nocturnes and etudes, you can also find four against three or similar writing.

When you meet such places, you can practise them the same way.

## Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu

Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu is a famous example of four against three.

The right hand plays fast sixteenth notes, four to a beat, and the left hand plays triplet broken chords, three to a beat.

This piece is very fast, so you need to make the four-against-three feeling very steady at a slow tempo first.

- Four notes against three in the same span of time
- The hands line up only at the start
- It can be worked out with twelve equal divisions
- First steady each hand, then put the hands together slowly

## Hands Together, Slowly

When putting the hands together, the tempo must be very slow. Count by the twelve divisions and confirm the position of every note.

At first it may feel awkward, and the two hands easily affect each other.

You can start by playing just one cycle, and move on to the next once it is accurate.

## Steady Each Hand Separately First

Before practising four against three, first make the rhythm of each hand steady on its own.

Use a metronome to mark the start of a cycle, with one hand playing four even notes and the other playing three.

Once both hands can keep even independently, put them together.

## FAQ

**Q: What is four against three?**
A: One hand plays four notes while the other plays three in the same span of time.

**Q: Where do the two hands line up?**
A: Only at the start.

**Q: How many equal divisions are used to work it out?**
A: Twelve.

**Q: Which work is a famous example?**
A: Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu.

**Q: What can I practise first if it is too hard?**
A: Three against two.
