first-sustain-pedal-hands-first.body:
When first learning the sustain pedal, it is best to get your hands steady on the keyboard first, then add the foot. The pedal is normally changed after the new chord has been played: press the keys, lift the pedal, then press it down again straight away, so the sounds before and after do not blur together. Practise hands and feet separately until they are comfortable, then combine them.

- Keep your heel on the floor and use the ball of the foot on the pedal
- Hands first, foot second: change the pedal after the new chord is down
- Make the lift and the press crisp
- Practise pedal changes repeatedly on two simple chords

## Common Pedalling Mistakes

One common mistake is holding the pedal down without changing it, thinking the sound is more beautiful that way. In fact, if you do not change the pedal when the harmony changes, the sounds of different chords pile up and become muddy.

Another mistake is moving hands and foot at the same moment, lifting the pedal just as the keys are pressed. This creates a gap between chords and loses the smooth connection. The correct order is to press the keys first, then change the pedal.

Some players also lift the whole foot off the pedal. The movement is too large, it can make noise, and it is hard to control. Keep your heel on the floor and control the pedal with the ball of the foot, and the movement will be steadier.

Learning the pedal takes cooperation between hands, foot and ears, and feeling awkward at first is normal. Practise slowly, step by step, and once the movement becomes a habit your sound will be both connected and clear.

![Colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jeie6-f31lm.webp)

## Judging a Clean Pedal Change by Ear

Whether a pedal change works is ultimately decided by your ears. If the sounds of two chords overlap, you probably released the pedal late or did not lift it far enough. If there is a gap between the chords, the pedal may have gone down too early.

When practising, slow down and listen carefully to every pedal change. You can also record yourself and compare how different ways of changing sound.

Sometimes the score marks where to pedal, and sometimes the player has to judge. As a beginner, follow the score or your teacher's instructions first. As your ear becomes sharper, you can gradually learn to change the pedal according to the harmony.

## What the Pedal Does and Common Blurring Problems

When the sustain pedal is down, the dampers lift away from the strings, so the sound keeps ringing after you release the keys. It can make chords sound fuller and more connected, but if the chord changes while the pedal is still down, the old resonance piles into the new sound and it turns muddy.

When practising, try alternating just a C chord and an F chord, and listen closely to the moment of the pedal change. If you can still hear the old chord inside the new one, you lifted the pedal late or not completely. Aim for hands and foot that are each relaxed yet working together, and only then bring the pedal into a piece.

Some learners pencil the pedal changes into the score to remind themselves on which beat to change. Once the movement is familiar, make small adjustments according to what you hear.

## Practise the Foot Alone First

In the beginning, let your hands rest and train the foot alone. Keep the heel firmly on the floor, press the pedal down with the front of the foot and let it return, feeling the depth and the spring-back of the pedal. The movement should be smooth: do not stamp down, and do not let your foot leave the pedal.

Then play a simple chord, hold it, press the pedal, release your hands, and listen to whether the sound continues. Then lift the pedal and listen to the sound stop. This exercise helps you understand what the pedal does to the sound.

Once the foot movement is familiar, practise the order "keys first, pedal after": play the new chord, lift the pedal right after, then press it down again at once. This movement is often called syncopated pedalling (legato pedalling), and it keeps chords connected without blurring.

**One more thing to think about**

Before adding the hands, you can practise pedalling to a metronome, for example changing the pedal every four beats, so the foot gets used to a steady rhythm. Once the foot has a sense of rhythm, coordinating with the hands becomes easier.

## FAQ

**Q: There are no pedal markings in the score. Can I add them myself?**
A: You can use it sparingly according to the style of the piece, but it is best to have your teacher listen first so the sound does not become too blurred.

**Q: What if a child's foot cannot reach the pedal?**
A: Leave out the pedal for now, or ask your teacher to suggest a suitable aid, and practise it when the child is tall enough.

**Q: How should I handle it when a small child's foot cannot touch the pedal?**
A: You can skip the pedal for the time being, or ask your teacher to recommend a suitable pedal extender.

**Q: Should the pedal be pressed all the way down?**
A: Generally yes, but some pieces use half pedalling, which you can practise under your teacher's guidance.

**Q: Does every piece need the pedal?**
A: No. It depends on the style of the piece and the markings in the score. Some pieces need very clean sound.

**Q: What is syncopated pedalling?**
A: It means pressing down the new note or chord first, then quickly lifting and pressing the pedal again so the sounds connect without blurring.

film-music-piano-motif-storytelling.body:
In film scores, the piano often uses a short, memorable fragment of melody to stand for a character, a place or a mood. This fragment is called a "motif". The composer lets the same motif return again and again in the film, but each time changes the tempo, harmony, register or accompaniment, so the audience feels the story changing without noticing. For example, Summer, written by the Japanese composer Joe Hisaishi for the film Kikujiro, runs a light piano melody through the whole film. Learning to notice how a motif changes will not only make watching films more rewarding, but will also give you plenty of inspiration for your own piano playing and improvisation.

## What is a motif

A motif is a musical unit shorter than a complete melody, usually only a few notes or one or two bars. It must be distinctive enough to leave an impression after one hearing.

- Rhythmic feature: for example long-short-long, or a run of staccato notes
- Interval feature: for example a clear upward leap
- Directional feature: for example an arc that goes up and then down
- Harmonic colour: for example always stopping on a somewhat unstable chord

A good motif is like a person's signature: even if only half of it appears, the listener can recognise it.

## One motif, five moods

**Change of tempo**
Slowed down, it feels like memory or longing; sped up, it feels lively or tense.

**Major to minor**
Lower the third of the motif by a semitone and a bright theme at once turns sad. Many films use this technique when characters part or meet difficulties.

**Change of register**
In the high register it feels light and distant; in the low register it feels heavy and serious.

**Change of accompaniment**
The same melody feels steady with block chords, gentle with flowing broken chords and relaxed with syncopated rhythms.

**Change of instrumentation**
A solo piano feels intimate, and with a string background it feels broad. When playing on the piano, you can create a similar sense of space by thickening the chords and using the pedal.

![A person with headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two city-night windows](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvyb3ihv-q9bg5.webp)

## Why the piano suits film scores

The piano has a wide range, and one person can play melody, harmony and bass at once, so composers often finish their first sketches on the piano. The piano's sound also has a strong "narrative" quality: each note fades away after it is played, with rises and falls like speech, which suits inner monologues and flashback scenes.

In addition, the piano has a wide dynamic range, from a barely audible pianissimo to a full forte, so it can follow the picture in fine detail.

## A three-step arranging exercise: turn a motif into a little story

**Step 1: write down the motif**
Choose the first two bars of a piece you know, or make up four to six notes yourself. Play it until it is secure and make sure it has a clear rhythmic character.

**Step 2: make three versions**
Version one is played as it is; version two is in the minor key and slower; version three moves to the high register, with the left hand changed to broken chords. Play each version twice and feel the difference in mood.

**Step 3: put them in order**
Arrange the three versions as "beginning, change, return", with one or two bars of transition in between. That makes a very short little piece with its own ups and downs.

## Tips for listening to film scores

- When you first watch a film, notice which melody keeps coming back
- Write down the scene and character on screen each time it appears
- Go back to the piano and try to play the first few notes of the melody
- Compare how its tempo and harmony differ in different scenes

This way of listening can help you go from "sounds nice" to "understanding it", and it is a very good kind of ear training for anyone learning music.

## Giving the motif different harmonies

The same melody note can be given different chords, producing completely different feelings. For example, if the melody stops on E, a C major triad feels settled, an A minor triad feels soft, and an F major seventh chord has a touch of dreaminess. Film composers often keep the melody unchanged when the lead character's mood changes and quietly swap the chord underneath. The audience may not be able to say why, yet they feel the atmosphere has changed.

You can try an experiment at the piano: play the same motif again and again with the right hand, and change the chord each time with the left hand, then record it and listen back. This kind of exercise helps you understand how harmony affects mood, and later, when you accompany songs, you will also know better how to choose chords to match the words and the picture.

## FAQ

**Q: Are piano scores of film music difficult?**
A: The originals are often fairly hard, but many themes have easy arrangements, and beginners can start with the melody plus simple chords.

**Q: Can I arrange a motif without having studied composition?**
A: Yes. As long as you can change the tempo, switch between major and minor and change the accompaniment pattern, you can already make a clear difference in mood.

**Q: What is the difference between a motif and a theme?**
A: A motif is shorter and is the smallest unit of a theme; a theme is usually a more complete melody.

**Q: Is this exercise suitable for children?**
A: Yes. Let the child make up a little motif for a favourite story character and play it in different ways, and the practice becomes more fun.

five-against-four-polyrhythm.body:
Divide the same span of time into four and into five, then let the two hands play these two divisions at once, meeting only at the start of each group: this is four against five. It belongs to the same family of layerings as two against three, only the grid is denser, and the crossing points in between are harder to see at a glance. When learning it, do not expect to get through this density by "bluffing"; first make the hand playing four round and even on its own, make the hand playing five round and even on its own, and then layer them onto the same starting point. When listening, first play hands separately to confirm that neither side speeds up or slows down, then listen to how they meet at the start and cross each other in the middle of the grid. If one hand quietly accommodates the other, both divisions lose their evenness and the crossing can no longer be heard. This article discusses only this way of practising four layered with five on the piano, and does not present it as the whole of complex rhythm. Drawing a grid of twenty equal parts can help you see where each side falls, but when playing you do not need to count to twenty in your head; in the end you still rely on each hand running round on its own. When practising, you can first take one group quite leisurely, confirm that the starting point always lines up, and then bring it back little by little to the tempo the score asks for.

## What a diagram can help with

If you divide a line into twenty equal parts, you can see at the same time where the four notes and the five notes each fall.

This is for understanding; it does not mean you have to count to twenty in your head while playing.

Once you are fluent, you should drop your dependence on the diagram and return to listening for whether both hands are round.

**Listen**
- In the same span of time, one hand divides into four and the other into five, meeting only at the start of each group
- Same family as two against three, but the grid is denser and the crossings finer
- First make each hand run round on its own, then layer them onto the same starting point, and do not let one hand accommodate the other
- You can use a more leisurely tempo to settle one group first, then bring it back little by little to the tempo of the score

## What to remember about four against five

This is a notation in which, within the same span of time, one hand divides into four and the other into five, meeting only at the start of each group.

It is the same family as two against three, only denser, and it needs even more that you first separate the hands to get them even.

When you layer them back, hold on to the starting point; if one hand starts accommodating the other, separate them and redo it, and in the end rely on listening rather than guessing the crossing points.

## Why the middle does not need to line up

The lowest common multiple of four and five is twenty, so most of the notes in between do not fall at the same moment anyway.

If you force the middle to line up too, both kinds of evenness are spoiled.

Just hold on to the note at the start of each group, and let the other notes follow their own grid.

## It is the same kind of thing as two against three

Both involve playing different even divisions within the same span of time, meeting only at the head of the group.

Four against five just makes the numbers on the two sides denser, so it is even more necessary to make each hand run round on its own first.

If you can already layer two against three steadily, approaching four against five with the same principle will go more smoothly.

![An electronic keyboard and a screen in neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdl1y2h-t6anb.webp)

## Why separate the hands first for four against five

First practise the hand playing four until it is very steady and even, then practise the hand playing five until it is just as steady.

If either side is not yet steady, it will pull the other off course when you layer them.

You can first play against a steady beat, making the four and the five round separately, before thinking about layering.

## How to layer the two hands back together

First line up the starting point shared by each group, and let the other notes follow their own division.

You can also take one group quite leisurely first, saying four and five aloud separately, and then add speed back little by little to the tempo of the score.

Do not rely on guessing the crossing point in the middle anew each time.

## How to step back when one hand accommodates the other

As soon as you notice one hand accommodating the other, separate them at once, return each to evenness, and then layer them again.

When you rush more and more, also play the same group several more times at a more leisurely tempo.

Stepping back is not failure; it rebuilds the crossing on top of evenness.

## In the lesson, ask Aum, your teacher, to listen for whether both hands are still even

In the lesson you can ask Aum, your teacher, to listen to whether the hand playing four and the hand playing five are both still round, and whether one is quietly accommodating.

If the starting point of some group never lines up, you can also ask the teacher to ease the tempo with you and point out where the crossings fall.

**Try it**

With a denser layering like four against five, practise letting each hand run in its own grid, meeting only at the start.

## FAQ

**Q: What does four against five mean?**
A: Within the same span of time, one hand plays four notes evenly and the other plays five notes evenly, meeting only at the start of each group.

**Q: How is it related to two against three?**
A: It belongs to the same kind of layering, only the grid is denser and the crossings finer.

**Q: Why do the notes in the middle not need to line up?**
A: Four and five mostly do not fall at the same moment anyway, and forcing them to line up would spoil the evenness of both sides.

**Q: Why separate the hands first when practising?**
A: Let each side run very evenly on its own first, then layer them back, and they are less likely to pull each other off course.

**Q: What if one hand gets pulled off course after layering?**
A: Separate them at once, return each to evenness, and then play the same group several more times at a more leisurely tempo.

dvorak-slavonic-dances-op46-1878.body:
The Slavonic Dances, Op. 46, are a set of eight dances written in 1878 by the Czech composer Antonín Dvořák. They began as piano duets for four hands and were arranged for orchestra the same year. The set was commissioned by a publisher on Brahms's recommendation, and it was so popular after publication that Dvořák's name spread all over Europe. The melodies are the composer's own, but the rhythms and style come from Czech and Slavic folk dances, such as the fiery furiant and the lyrical dumka. Eight years later he wrote a second set, the Slavonic Dances, Op. 72.

## Brahms's Recommendation

Dvořák had applied several times for a scholarship that the Austrian government offered to young artists, and Brahms was one of the judges.

**Practice order**

Brahms admired Dvořák's talent and recommended him to his own publisher.

The publisher then asked Dvořák to write a set of dances, and that set is the Slavonic Dances.

## Modelled on the Hungarian Dances

The publisher asked Dvořák for dances because the piano-duet version of Brahms's Hungarian Dances had sold extremely well.

Dvořák's Slavonic Dances also took the form of piano duets.

Unlike Brahms, however, who borrowed existing tunes, Dvořák composed all of his melodies himself.

## The Piano-Duet Version

The first score Dvořák handed in was for one piano and two players.

In the nineteenth century, before recordings existed, people often enjoyed orchestral works at home as piano duets.

The duet version of these dances suited both home entertainment and concert performance.

## Playing the Slavonic Dances with Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to play part of the music and play a Slavonic Dance together with you.

You can also start by clapping and counting the shifting accents of the furiant together with your teacher.

One set of dances is enough to feel the energy of Czech folk music.

## Fame Overnight

When the Slavonic Dances were published in 1878, they were an instant hit, and the sheet music sold well.

The same year, the orchestral version was performed in many places, and Dvořák's name quickly spread across Europe.

From then on, his works were highly regarded in Germany, Britain and the United States.

## The Other Dances

Among the eight dances there are also a polka, a sousedská and a skočná, each a different Czech folk dance.

Every one has its own rhythm and character: some fiery, some graceful, some playful.

The whole set is like a colourful folk ball.

**Listen for**
- Written by Dvořák in 1878, eight dances
- First written as a piano duet
- Recommended by Brahms and very popular after publication
- Rhythm and style come from Slavic folk dances

## The Furiant

The first dance is a furiant, a fiery, fast Czech folk dance.

The furiant's best-known feature is its alternation of accents in groups of two and three beats, which makes the rhythm sound as if it has been thrown off balance.

The piece opens with strong chords that pull you straight into a lively dance.

## The Dumka

The dumka is a lyrical song form from Slavic folk music that often moves back and forth between sadness and joy.

The second dance is a dumka. Its opening melody is slow and sorrowful, and then it suddenly turns light and lively.

This shift of mood is the hallmark of the dumka and a trait of Slavic music.

## Dvořák's Early Years

Antonín Dvořák (1841-1904) was born in a small village in Bohemia, where his father ran a small inn and also worked as a butcher.

As a young man he played viola in an orchestra and organ in church, and life was not comfortable.

In his thirties he was still only a composer with a modest local reputation.

## Who the Slavonic Dances Suit

In the piano-duet version, each part is roughly intermediate to upper-intermediate in difficulty.

Some of the dances are very fast and need two players who work well together.

You can also begin with a slower dance, such as the opening section of the second one.

## The Second Set of Slavonic Dances

In 1886 the publisher asked Dvořák for a second set of Slavonic Dances, catalogued as Op. 72.

The second set also has eight dances, again written first as piano duets and later arranged for orchestra.

Together the two sets make sixteen dances, among Dvořák's most popular works.

![Digital music scene made of glowing lines of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbic4os-o079y.webp)

## Playing the Slavonic Dances as a Duet

When playing a piano duet, the two players' rhythm must match exactly, especially where the furiant's accents alternate.

You can start by clapping the rhythm together, then move to the piano.

The upper and lower parts must listen to each other, and whichever part has the melody should come out a little more.

## Summary of the Slavonic Dances, Op. 46

The Slavonic Dances, Op. 46, are eight dances written by Dvořák (1841-1904) in 1878, first as piano duets and arranged for orchestra the same year. Brahms, a judge of the scholarship, admired Dvořák and recommended him to a publisher, who commissioned the set after the success of Brahms's Hungarian Dances, though all the melodies are Dvořák's own, and its publication made his name known across Europe.

The first dance, a furiant, alternates accents in twos and threes, and the second, a dumka, moves between sadness and lightness. There are also polkas and other dances, and for a duet you should first clap the rhythm together. In 1886 he wrote a second set, Op. 72, and the two sets together total sixteen dances.

**Before you start**

You can ask Teacher Aum to play together with you in lessons.

## FAQ

**Q: In which year were the Slavonic Dances, Op. 46, written?**
A: 1878.

**Q: What form were they first written in?**
A: Piano duet.

**Q: Who recommended Dvořák to the publisher?**
A: Brahms.

**Q: What is distinctive about the furiant?**
A: Its alternation of accents in groups of two and three beats.

**Q: What is the opus number of the second set of Slavonic Dances?**
A: Op. 72, written in 1886.

fanny-hensel-das-jahr-1841.body:
Fanny Hensel (1805-1847) was a German composer and pianist, and the elder sister of the composer Felix Mendelssohn. In 1841 she completed the piano cycle Das Jahr (The Year), which uses twelve pieces to portray the twelve months of the year, with a postlude added at the end. Most of her music was not formally published in her lifetime, and some early songs were even published under her brother's name. Today, Das Jahr appears more and more in concerts and recordings, helping people to rediscover this composer.

## The Position of Women Composers at the Time

In early nineteenth-century Europe, women who wanted to compose professionally and perform in public faced many limits set by social attitudes.

Although Fanny's family supported her musical studies, they did not much approve of her making composition a public career.

So most of her works were played only within the circle of family and friends during her lifetime.

## The Farewell of 1847

In 1847, Fanny died suddenly in Berlin, at only forty-one.

A few months later her brother Felix died too, so the two siblings left the world in the same year.

She left several hundred works, many of which were only published gradually, up to the late twentieth century.

## A Composer Rediscovered

Since the late twentieth century, more and more researchers and performers have turned their attention to Fanny's music.

Her piano pieces, songs and chamber music have been published and recorded one after another, and Das Jahr has also found its way into concerts.

Today she is regarded as an important German composer of the nineteenth century.

![Sketch of a golden grand piano on a cream background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2bv3x-hlvh2.webp)

## Sunday Concerts at Home

After her marriage, Fanny hosted a series of Sunday concerts at her home in Berlin, inviting musicians and friends to perform and listen.

At these concerts she was the organiser, and she often played the piano and conducted herself, performing her own works and those of others.

These home concerts became an important stage on which she could show her musical talent.

## The Piano Writing in Das Jahr

Many of the pieces in Das Jahr place considerable technical demands on the player, with fast figuration as well as rich harmony.

They show Fanny's ability as a pianist and her careful command of piano tone.

Learners at intermediate level and above can pick a few of the shorter pieces to try.

## What Her Story Brings to Mind

Fanny's story reminds us that in the history of music there are many more composers whose works are waiting to be heard.

When learning the piano, besides the familiar names, you can also make a point of looking for less often played works.

This kind of exploration broadens your musical horizons.

## How Learners Can Get to Know Her Music

You can start by finding a recording of Das Jahr and listening month by month, picking out a few pieces you like.

You can also listen to her short piano pieces and works in the style of songs without words, and compare how they are similar to and different from her brother's music.

While learning the history, getting to know a composer with your ears is often the most direct way.

**Listen For**
- 1805-1847, German composer and pianist
- Sister of Felix Mendelssohn
- Completed the piano cycle Das Jahr in 1841
- Twelve pieces for twelve months, plus a postlude

## Inspiration from the Trip to Italy

From 1839 to 1840, Fanny travelled in Italy with her family for some time.

According to records, this trip gave her many fresh impressions and inspiration for composing.

After returning to Berlin, she completed the piano cycle Das Jahr in 1841.

## Songs Published Under Her Brother's Name

According to records, several songs Fanny wrote in her early years were included in song collections published by Felix, under his name.

Later research revealed who the real composer of these songs was.

This history is often used to show how the works of women composers were hidden at the time.

## Poems and Illustrations in the Manuscript

According to records, in the manuscript of Das Jahr, the piece for each month is accompanied by a line of verse, along with a small illustration drawn by her husband, the painter Wilhelm Hensel.

Music, verse and pictures together form a very personal work.

This combination also shows that the cycle held a special meaning for her.

## The Elder Sister in a Musical Family

Fanny was born in 1805, the eldest daughter of the Mendelssohn family, and her brother Felix later became a famous composer.

The two studied music together from childhood, and according to records Fanny's talent for piano and composition was equally outstanding.

Throughout their lives they kept up close musical exchange, often listening to each other's new works and giving opinions.

## Musical Pictures of Twelve Months

Das Jahr consists of twelve piano pieces, each corresponding to one month, with a postlude at the end.

Some pieces are quiet and lyrical, some are passionate and cheerful, portraying the scenery and moods of different seasons.

**A Different Angle**

Listening to them one after another is like walking through a whole year with the music.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who was Fanny Hensel?**
A: A German composer and pianist, the sister of Felix Mendelssohn.

**Q: In which year was Das Jahr written?**
A: It was completed in 1841.

**Q: How many pieces does Das Jahr have?**
A: Twelve, for the twelve months, plus a postlude.

**Q: Why was so little of her music published in her lifetime?**
A: Social attitudes of the time limited women's public careers as composers.

**Q: Can learners play her music?**
A: At intermediate level and above, you can pick a few of the shorter pieces to try.

florence-price-rediscovered-composer.body:
Florence Price was an American composer, pianist and organist. In 1933 her Symphony in E minor was premiered by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, making her the first African American woman composer to have a work performed by a major American orchestra. After her death, her name was for a time forgotten, until in 2009 a large collection of manuscripts turned up in an old house, abandoned for years, near the small town of St. Anne, Illinois. Her music then returned to concert halls and to the music stands of piano learners.

This article follows the composer's life in chronological order, then looks at what Price's piano works can offer learners today.

## Key Facts at a Glance

- Born in 1887 in Little Rock, Arkansas (some sources give 1888), and introduced to the piano in early childhood by her mother, a music teacher
- Entered the New England Conservatory in Boston in 1903, double majoring in piano pedagogy and organ performance, and graduated in 1906
- Around 1927 moved with her family to Chicago, where she made a living by teaching, accompanying silent films and writing radio jingles while continuing to compose
- In 1932, her Symphony in E minor won first prize in the Wanamaker competition
- In 1933, during the Chicago World's Fair, the symphony was premiered by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra under Frederick Stock
- The scores rediscovered in the St. Anne house in 2009 included the Fourth Symphony and two violin concertos


![Pointillist-style painting of a person playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvwz7cgw-z33sa.webp)

## From Little Rock to Boston

Price began learning piano with her mother at around the age of three, performed in public very early, and published her own works in her teens. When she entered the New England Conservatory, she studied composition and counterpoint at the same time, building a solid classical foundation. After graduating she returned to teach in the American South, and for a time headed a music department at a university in Atlanta.

But the American South was then racially segregated, and for an African American woman to establish herself in music was extremely difficult. Price struggled to find suitable work in her home region, and in the end, like many Southern families, she went north to the industrial city of Chicago to look for new opportunities.

## Finding Her Own Voice in Chicago

The musical and cultural atmosphere of Chicago opened a new world for Price. She went on studying orchestration and composition with teachers in the city, and formed a deep friendship with the young pianist and composer Margaret Bonds. Life was not comfortable. The composer had to accompany silent films and write advertising songs under a pseudonym to supplement the household income, but the writing of serious works never stopped.

The competition of 1932 became a turning point. The Symphony in E minor won first prize and was premiered the next year by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra during the Chicago World's Fair. Within the framework of the European symphony, this work weaves in the melodic character of African American spirituals, and the third movement directly uses the rhythm of a folk dance called the "Juba dance", with syncopations that leap like footsteps.

{{IMG:piano-4.webp}}

## Manuscripts in an Old House

Price died in Chicago in 1953. Over the following decades, as musical fashions changed, her works were gradually performed less and less. In 2009, dozens of scores and documents were discovered in a dilapidated house on the outskirts of St. Anne, which had once been Price's summer home.

These manuscripts were later edited, published and recorded one after another. In 2018, the American critic Alex Ross wrote in The New Yorker, describing that old house as a powerful symbol of how a nation forgets its own cultural history. Today Price's symphonies, concertos and piano works appear more and more often on concert programmes.

## What Piano Learners Can Take From Price

**Notice the syncopation**
Many of Price's short piano pieces carry the rhythmic character of spirituals and dances. When practising, first clap the syncopated rhythm with your hands and feel the spring of accents falling on weak beats, then go back to the keys.

**Hear the singing quality in the melody**
Spirituals were originally meant to be sung. When playing this kind of melody, try humming it first, find the natural places to breathe, and then let your fingers imitate the rise and fall of the voice.

**Start with short pieces**
Price wrote a great many short teaching pieces for piano. Early and intermediate learners can ask their teacher to help pick pieces of suitable difficulty from among them, which builds technique and also introduces a stretch of music history that rarely appears in teaching books.

**Write the background into the score**
Note the year of composition and the stylistic sources in the margins of the score, and you will have a clearer idea of what you are expressing when you play.

## FAQ

**Q: Why is Price important in music history?**

A: In 1933 her Symphony in E minor was premiered by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, making her the first African American woman composer to have a work performed by a major American orchestra.

**Q: How were the manuscripts discovered?**

A: In 2009, someone turned up a large number of scores and documents in an uninhabited, dilapidated house on the outskirts of St. Anne, Illinois, which had once been the composer's summer home.

**Q: What are the stylistic features of Price's music?**

A: She received a European classical training, but made extensive use of the melodies of African American spirituals and dance rhythms such as the Juba dance, creating a distinctive American style.

**Q: Are Price's works suitable for beginners?**

A: Price wrote many short piano pieces, and quite a few suit early and intermediate levels. It is best to listen to recordings first, then choose pieces according to your own level.

dvorak-new-world-symphony-1893-premiere.body:
In 1892 the Czech composer Dvořák came to New York to serve as director of a conservatory. While living in America he wrote his Ninth Symphony, subtitled "From the New World". The symphony premiered in New York on 16 December 1893 and was warmly received. The slow melody played by the cor anglais in the second movement was later given words and became a widely sung song.

## The influence of folk music

Musicologists have different views on how many elements of American folk music the symphony actually uses.

**Notice the details**

Dvořák himself said that he did not quote folk songs directly, but wrote melodies that carried the spirit of such songs.

Others think that many of the melodies in the work are closer to the folk music of Bohemia.

![A close-up of the keys of a grand piano and a lid with a gold pattern in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7zavk-o7vv1.webp)

## The New World premiere in summary

Dvořák went to New York in 1892 as director of the National Conservatory, took an interest in American folk music such as spirituals, and in 1893 completed his Ninth Symphony in E minor, "From the New World".

It was premiered by the New York Philharmonic on 16 December 1893 and was a great success. The cor anglais melody of the second movement was later fitted with words by a student as "Goin' Home" and became widely sung.

Themes in the work run through its movements. There are different views about the influence of folk music. He returned to his homeland in 1895, and on the piano you can start by playing the melody of the second movement.

## The horn call of the first movement

The first movement has a theme played by the horn, with a strong, energetic rhythm.

This theme returns several times in later movements and ties the whole symphony together.

Writing a theme that runs through the whole work in this way makes the structure more unified.

## The fiery finale

At the start of the fourth movement, a few notes in the strings gradually speed up, and then the brass play a powerful theme.

In this movement the themes of the earlier movements come back one by one, and it ends in grand chords.

This opening is also often used in films, television and advertisements.

## The premiere in New York

On 16 December 1893, the symphony was premiered by the New York Philharmonic.

According to reports, the audience applauded warmly after each movement, and Dvořák had to rise several times to acknowledge them.

The success of the premiere soon led to performances of the work all over Europe and America.

## Coming to America

Antonín Dvořák (1841-1904) came to New York in 1892 to serve as director of a national conservatory.

America at the time wanted to develop a music of its own, and invited him to help train composers.

He lived in America for about three years in all.

**Common misconceptions**
- Dvořák went to New York in 1892 as director of a conservatory
- The Ninth Symphony, "From the New World"
- Premiered in New York on 16 December 1893
- The cor anglais melody of the second movement became widely sung

## An interest in American music

In New York, Dvořák developed a strong interest in American folk music.

His student Harry Burleigh often sang African American spirituals to him, and Dvořák listened, fascinated.

He believed that American composers could find their own style in this folk music.

## How to listen to a symphony

The first time you listen to this symphony, you can start with the Largo of the second movement and then the finale of the fourth.

When you are familiar with them, listen to the whole work from start to finish, noticing how the themes appear in the different movements.

Listening step by step in this way makes a longer work easier to understand.

## The writing of the New World Symphony

In 1893, in New York, Dvořák completed his Ninth Symphony, in E minor.

On the score he wrote the subtitle "From the New World", meaning music sent back from a new continent.

The work holds both the fresh impressions that life in America gave him and his longing for his homeland of Bohemia.

## The cor anglais in the second movement

The second movement is a slow Largo, and it opens with a few solemn chords in the brass.

Then the cor anglais plays a calm melody full of longing for home.

The cor anglais is a woodwind instrument with a lower, softer sound than the oboe.

## "Goin' Home"

This melody from the second movement was later fitted with English words by one of Dvořák's students, under the title "Goin' Home".

The song became widely known in America, and many people thought it was an old folk song.

In fact, its melody comes from Dvořák's symphony.

## Returning to his homeland

In 1895 Dvořák returned to Bohemia and went on composing and teaching.

While in America he also wrote the famous "American" string quartet and his Cello Concerto.

The three years in America were an important period in his creative life.

## The New World on the piano

The cor anglais melody of the second movement has many piano arrangements, with a difficulty suited to early and intermediate learners.

When playing it, let the melody flow slowly and smoothly, like a quiet song.

**Tip**

Keep the left-hand chords light so that the melody has room to sing.

## FAQ

**Q: In what year did Dvořák arrive in New York?**
A: 1892.

**Q: Which symphony is the New World?**
A: The Ninth Symphony, in E minor.

**Q: On what date was the premiere?**
A: 16 December 1893.

**Q: Which instrument plays the melody of the second movement?**
A: The cor anglais.

**Q: What song did this melody later become?**
A: "Goin' Home".

fortepiano-versus-modern-piano-sound.body:
The piano we know today and the instrument people sat down to play in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries belong to the same family, yet they differ clearly in sound and touch. The earlier instrument is often called a fortepiano (forte-piano), meaning that it could already play loud and soft, but still had lighter hammers, thinner strings, a resonance that faded sooner, and often a narrower range. The later piano gradually became louder, with longer resonance, a wider range, and keys that were deeper and heavier. Knowing these differences is not about deciding which is "more correct", but about hearing that works from different periods were written for sounds that were not the same. If a learner uses the very loud, very long sound of today's instrument to imagine phrases from early Beethoven or the age of Mozart, the dynamics in the score can suddenly seem not enough, when in fact the point of reference has changed. When you get the chance to hear a recording of a restored fortepiano, or visit an exhibition, first notice how quickly the sound closes off, then go back to the modern piano and try to leave a similar space in your touch. This article talks only about changes in the instrument itself and does not mention the name of any maker.

## The Range Changed Too

The range of early pianos was usually narrower than the eighty-eight keys common today, and some works never reach the lowest or highest notes.

Later, as the range expanded, composers gradually began to use the more distant notes as new colours.

In works from around 1800 to the early nineteenth century, the end of the score may still lie inside today's keyboard, and this is normal.

## Loud and Soft in the Name

The name forte-piano stresses that the instrument could already play both louder and softer sounds, unlike the harpsichord, which cannot freely vary dynamics.

Names in early sources were not consistent. Today "fortepiano" is used for the earlier pianos to distinguish them from modern instruments.

What matters is not the name but hearing the difference between the two sounds.

## Resonance and Volume

On earlier pianos, the sound came up quickly and faded quickly, and rarely held a chord for a long time as the modern piano does.

The upper limit of volume was also more restrained, better suited to smaller rooms.

So a forte in the score does not automatically equal a very loud sound on today's instrument.

## What to Listen for Between the Fortepiano and the Modern Piano

If you can find a reliable recording of a fortepiano, first listen to how the same short piece ends and is layered on the two instruments.

Notice not which version is more ornate, but how fast the sound fades, how high the loud notes can go, and how much pedal is used.

After comparing, you will often find it easier to decide where to leave a space when you return to your own piano.

## What to Remember About the Fortepiano and the Modern Piano

They belong to one family, but the early instrument has a shorter resonance and a more restrained volume, while the modern piano is louder, longer-sounding and wider in range.

The aim of understanding the differences is to give you a more suitable sound reference when reading a score, not to rank them.

On today's piano you can also use less pedal and more measured loudness to come closer to earlier phrasing.

## How to Use This Understanding in Practice

You do not need to own a fortepiano. On a modern piano you can try to make the sound close off more cleanly, with shorter resonance.

For example, use less pedal, do not open up to full volume at once where there is a forte, and let the phrase speak for itself.

The aim is not to imitate exactly, but to make the phrasing of older works make more sense.

## Touch and Hammers

Lighter hammers and a shallower key depth make many fast figures and fine gradations easier to achieve with smaller movements.

The touch of a modern piano is usually deeper and heavier, and producing the same clarity of layers often takes some getting used to.

Knowing something about both kinds of touch makes it easier to see why some early fingerings feel hard work on today's piano.

- Early pianos and modern pianos belong to one family, yet differ in sound and touch
- Early instruments have shorter resonance, more restrained volume and often a narrower range
- Later pianos are louder, with longer resonance, a wider range and deeper touch
- Knowing the differences helps place older works back in the sound they may originally have had

![High-angle view of an open black piano being played on a rainy neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdka0oa-hjd8s.webp)

## Trying Shorter Resonance With Teacher Aum in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the same phrase comes closer to earlier phrasing with less pedal.

If a passage sounds too full or the resonance too long on today's piano, you can also ask your teacher to try bringing the dynamics down a notch together.

From the differences between the two kinds of piano, practise placing older works back in the sound they may have had.

## FAQ

**Q: Are the fortepiano and today's piano completely different instruments?**
A: No. They belong to one family, but differ clearly in sound, touch and range.

**Q: What is the most noticeable difference in sound for early pianos?**
A: The resonance is shorter, the volume more restrained, and forte does not mean today's very loud.

**Q: Is understanding these differences meant to prove which piano is better?**
A: No. It is to place works from different periods back in the sound they may originally have been written for.

**Q: Without a fortepiano, how can I come closer on a modern piano?**
A: Use less pedal, do not open up to full volume at once where there is a forte, and let the phrase speak for itself.

**Q: Why might the range of early works not reach both ends of today's keyboard?**
A: Instruments then often had a narrower range, and some notes were not yet on the keyboard.

faure-apres-un-reve-op7-art-song.body:
Après un rêve (After a Dream) is an art song written early in his career by the French composer Fauré, Op. 7 No. 1, composed around the late 1870s. The words are a French translation of a Tuscan folk poem from Italy, about a person who sees their beloved in a dream, and on waking is left only with loneliness, and so calls the dream to return. The piano supports the voice with a series of soft chords, and the melody is long and broad. It was later arranged for cello, violin and solo piano, among many other versions, and it is a good piece for practising singing melodies.

- Fauré's Op. 7 No. 1, an art song
- Written around the late 1870s
- The words are translated from an Italian Tuscan folk poem
- Arrangements exist for cello, violin and solo piano, among others

## What Is an Art Song

An art song is a poem set to music by a composer, usually performed by a singer and a pianist.

**Before You Begin**

Unlike a pop song, in an art song the piano plays an important role, often expressing the mood of the poem together with the voice.

In France the art song is called the "mélodie", and Fauré is one of the important composers in this field.

## A Meeting in the Dream

The words tell of a person who sees their beloved in a dream, and the two leave the earth together and walk towards the light.

In the dream, everything is so beautiful and so tender.

But in the second half of the song, the dream ends, and the loneliness of reality returns.

## Read the Words First

When playing an arrangement of an art song, first understand what the words mean.

Once you know where the sweetness of the dream is and where the loss on waking is, you can find the right tone colours as you play.

If possible, you can also listen to several singers' versions first.

## Who Was Fauré

Gabriel Fauré (1845-1924) was a French composer, organist and teacher.

He wrote many art songs, piano pieces and chamber works, in an elegant and delicate style.

He later became the director of the Paris Conservatoire, and his students included composers such as Ravel.

## Après un rêve in Brief

Après un rêve is Op. 7 No. 1 among the art songs of Fauré (1845-1924), written around the late 1870s. The words are a French translation of an Italian Tuscan folk poem. It tells of meeting a loved one in a dream, loneliness on waking, and calling on the night to let the dream return. The piano part is gently repeated chords, and the melody, in C minor, is long and broad.

It was later arranged for cello, violin, flute and solo piano, among others. In the piano version the melody should be full, the chords light, and the pedal should change with the delicate harmony. Before playing, you can read the words first. Fauré also wrote more than a hundred art songs, as well as nocturnes and barcarolles.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the long phrases and the pedalling.

## The Pedal in Après un rêve

The right foot's pedal is responsible for joining that series of gentle chords into one.

But Fauré's harmonic changes are very delicate, and the pedal must change in time with the harmony, or the sounds will blur together.

You can listen as you play, and whenever the sound turns muddy, it is time to change the pedal.

## From Song to Cello

Players of low bowed strings especially love this song, and the cello version has almost become its second identity.

The cello's sound is deep and warm, very well suited to expressing the sadness of this song.

There are also arrangements for violin, flute and many other instruments, and a solo piano version too.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Long Phrases of Après un rêve

You can play for Teacher Aum in your lessons, and ask your teacher to judge whether the long phrases are connected and whether the melody floats above the chords.

If the pedal changes are never clean, you can also ask your teacher to show you how to change while listening.

From one art song, you can experience how poetry and music come together.

## Fauré's Other Songs

Fauré wrote more than a hundred art songs in his life, and among them Les berceaux and Clair de lune are also very popular.

He also wrote collections of piano pieces, such as the thirteen nocturnes and thirteen barcarolles.

Once you know Après un rêve, you can go on to listen to his other works.

## The Piano's Chordal Accompaniment

The piano accompaniment is a series of soft, repeated chords, like a calm heartbeat in the night.

The chords change very delicately, often moving into another key without you noticing.

This accompaniment gives the voice a quiet, hazy background.

## The Long Lines of Après un rêve

The vocal melody is very long and broad, often sung over many bars in a single breath.

The melody is in C minor, with a faint sadness, and becomes very passionate at the climax.

When playing the piano version, you should join each long phrase together, like a singer.

![High-angle view of an open black piano being played on a neon-lit street on a rainy night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbi373a-fmdk5.webp)

## The Call After Waking

After waking, the person in the song is unwilling to accept that the dream has ended.

At the very end of the song they call the night to return, so that the dream can appear once more.

This change of feeling, from sweetness to loss and then to longing, is what makes the song so moving.

## How to Play the Solo Piano Version

In the solo piano version, the right hand plays the melody, and sometimes also plays part of the accompanying chords at the same time.

The melody should be played full with the weight of the fingers, and the chords should lie lightly underneath.

**Notice the Details**

The left hand plays the bass and the other part of the chords, and should be steady and soft.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who wrote Après un rêve?**
A: The French composer Fauré.

**Q: What is its opus number?**
A: Op. 7 No. 1.

**Q: Where do the words come from?**
A: A French translation of an Italian Tuscan folk poem.

**Q: What key is the vocal melody in?**
A: C minor.

**Q: What versions was it later arranged into?**
A: Cello, violin, flute and solo piano, among others.

family-music-lesson-plan-bundle-design.body:
A family lesson plan is a lesson bundle that a music school designs for several members of the same family learning at the same time, for example siblings learning the piano together, or a parent and child enrolling together. A well-designed family plan is not just a simple discount. It is built around the family's real needs, with arrangements for scheduling, learning content and communication, so that learning goes more smoothly for the whole family. Below, the design thinking is introduced through lesson structure, pricing communication, scheduling and fairness.

## Start by Understanding the Family's Real Needs

When a family enrols, price is often not their only concern. Whether drop-off and pick-up are convenient, whether the children will compare themselves with each other, and whether a parent has time to sit in on practice all affect their decision. At the enquiry stage, a school can ask a few more questions to understand the family's situation.

- How many members want to learn, and what are their ages and levels.
- How many pianos the family has, and how practice time is shared.
- Whether parents want to join the lessons or have lessons separately.
- Which times of the week suit the whole family.

Recommending a lesson bundle after learning this is more helpful than simply handing over a price list.

## Common Ways to Combine Lessons

Depending on the family's needs, several different bundles can be designed:

**Individual lessons in back-to-back slots**
Siblings each have a one-to-one lesson, scheduled at adjacent times. Parents only need one drop-off and pick-up, and each child can keep to their own pace of learning.

**Parent-child lessons**
A parent and child take lessons together and learn simple ensemble pieces. This format suits young children, and also parents who want to grow alongside their child.

**Family group lessons**
Members of the same family form a small group to learn theory, rhythm or ensemble playing. The atmosphere is relaxed, and it works well as a supplement to individual lessons.

## Be Clear About Pricing

The price of a family plan should be simple and easy to understand. Avoid complicated calculations, so that parents can see at a glance how much they need to pay each month and which lessons are included. The pricing information should also state clearly the rules for absences, make-up lessons and withdrawal.

![Close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw735rhh-cjf4j.webp)

If you offer a family discount, explain the conditions that apply, for example that members must be enrolled at the same time, or pay under the same account. Do not use phrases such as "limited places" or "ends soon" to create pressure; give parents enough time to think it over.

## Fairness: Avoid Comparisons Between Children

When siblings learn the piano together, comparisons easily arise. An older child may progress quickly, and a younger child may feel frustrated. Teachers and parents should both avoid direct comparisons, for example not saying "Look, your brother can already do it".

**Each Child Has Their Own Goals and Pace**
A teacher can set different goals for each child, and in feedback compare a child only with their own past. At a family recital, each child can choose a piece they like, instead of everyone playing the same piece.

## Arranging Practice at Home

Many families have only one piano, so practice time needs to be coordinated. A school can offer parents some suggestions, such as making a simple weekly practice timetable so that everyone takes turns at the piano, or having one person do rhythm exercises or listen to music while another practises. That way everyone has something to do, and there is less waiting and arguing.

When a parent is present, it helps to observe more and intervene less. A simple remark such as "the rhythm in this section is much steadier than yesterday" often makes a child more willing to keep practising than correcting mistakes does.

## Reviewing and Adjusting the Plan

The explanatory materials for a family plan also deserve care. A simple one-page diagram can show how lessons work and how they are scheduled under different bundles, so that parents can talk it over at home with the other family members. Avoid technical terms in the materials, and add a short explanation where necessary.

After a family plan has been running for a while, you can review it with the parents: whether the lesson bundle suits them, whether the children's interest has been maintained, and whether the scheduling is convenient. Family circumstances change, for example when a child changes school or a parent's work changes, and the plan needs to be adjusted flexibly. When a school keeps communication channels open, families trust it more.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can siblings have the same teacher?**
A: Yes. A teacher who knows the family background can communicate more easily, but each child should get individual attention.

**Q: Can parents with no experience join parent-child lessons?**
A: Yes. Parent-child lessons usually begin with simple rhythms and ensemble playing, and suit parents who are complete beginners.

**Q: If one child wants to pause and the other continues, does it affect the discount?**
A: This needs to be written into the rules in advance, so that the family understands the fees after any change.

**Q: What age are family group lessons suitable for?**
A: Generally for children who can already concentrate for a period of time. You can try one lesson first to see.

**Q: Can we enrol if we have no piano at home?**
A: Yes. You can start with a digital piano or the school's practice room, and decide later whether to buy an instrument.

fishing-boats-sing-at-dusk-guzheng-piano.body:
Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk is a widely known guzheng piece that portrays fishing boats returning full-laden as the sun sets, with the fishermen singing out loud. It is generally believed to have been adapted from an old tune by the guzheng player Lou Shuhua around the 1930s. The title comes from a line in a famous Tang dynasty essay. The piece begins with a lilting slow section, gradually speeds up, and ends in a lively, joyful mood. It also has many piano arrangements, which are well suited to practising pentatonic melody and building up tempo step by step.

- A guzheng piece adapted around the 1930s
- Depicts fishing boats coming home at dusk
- From slow to fast, building layer by layer
- The piano version imitates the guzheng's slides and sweeping glissandi

## The Pentatonic Colour of the Fishermen's Song

The melody of this piece is built on the pentatonic scale, which gives it a distinctly Chinese character.

**Another way to look at it**

The mode of the whole piece has a bright colour, and the melody unfolds broadly.

Before playing it on the piano, you can play through the pentatonic scale it uses to get familiar with its notes.

## The Slow Opening

The piece opens with a lilting, gentle melody, like a calm lake at sunset.

The melodic line is soft and full of decorative slides.

When playing this section, take your time and let every note sing.

## The Lively Ending

The ending is very fast, with repeated figures and an excited atmosphere.

It finishes with a rising sweep, like boats reaching the shore as everyone cheers.

When you reach this part, keep the rhythm clear and do not let the speed make it fall apart.

## Listen to the Original Guzheng Version First

Before you start on the piano version, find a recording of the original guzheng piece and listen a few times.

Notice how the slides, the sweeps and the tempo changes are handled.

With the sound of the original in your ear, you will have a clearer direction when you play the piano version.

## Imitating the Guzheng's Slides

When playing the guzheng, the left hand often presses the strings to make slides, giving the pitch an expressive rise and fall.

The piano cannot make true slides, but you can imitate them with ornaments or grace notes.

Play the ornaments lightly, and land on the main notes at exactly the right time.

## Piano Arrangements of Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk: Easier and Harder

Piano arrangements of Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk come in different levels of difficulty.

Beginners can start with the slow opening section to get to know the melody.

As you improve, you can take on the full version with its fast passages.

## The Rising Sweep Before the Boats Reach Shore

On the guzheng, a sweep is made by running a finger quickly across the strings, producing a sound like flowing water.

On the piano, you can let your fingers run up or slide down along the pentatonic scale in one go.

The sweep should be light and smooth, with dynamics going from soft to loud or loud to soft, like ripples on water.

## Where the Title Comes From

The four characters of the title, "Yu Zhou Chang Wan", come from a famous line in a well-known parallel-prose essay of the Tang dynasty.

The original line describes the evening, when singing drifts from the fishing boats all the way to the distant shore of the lake.

The piece borrows these words to express the calm and joy of boats coming home on the lake at dusk.

## Where the Piece Comes From

Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk is a solo piece for guzheng.

It is generally believed to have been adapted from an old tune by the guzheng player Lou Shuhua around the 1930s.

Today almost everyone who learns the guzheng plays it, and versions for piano, Chinese folk ensemble and more appear one after another.

## The Left-Hand Sustained Notes of the Evening Return

In the piano version, the left hand often plays broken chords on the pentatonic scale, or sustained notes.

Keep the left hand light, leaving room for the right-hand melody.

In the fast passages, keep the left-hand rhythm steady to support the right hand.

## The Gradually Quickening Middle Section

In the middle section the tempo gradually speeds up and the rhythm becomes livelier.

This suggests the boats rowing faster and faster and the fishermen growing more cheerful.

When playing, mind the step-by-step build-up of speed rather than a sudden jump.

## Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk: A Summary

Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk is a guzheng piece adapted from an old tune by Lou Shuhua around the 1930s. Its title comes from a famous Tang dynasty essay. It portrays fishing boats coming home at dusk and the fishermen singing, moving from a lilting slow section that gradually speeds up and ends in a lively mood.

The melody is built on the pentatonic scale. In the piano version, you can imitate the slides with ornaments and the sweeps with fast pentatonic runs. Practise the tempo build-up in sections until each is steady and then join them, and keep the left hand light and steady.

You can begin with the slow section, and listen to the original guzheng piece before playing. Choosing an arrangement and deciding how to shape it can be discussed with Teacher Aum in lessons.

## Discussing Interpretation in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to help you choose a suitable arrangement.

You can also discuss with your teacher how to bring out the guzheng's character on the piano.

For the passages where the tempo builds, you can ask your teacher to check whether the rhythm is steady.

## Practising the Tempo Build-Up

Because the piece has clear tempo changes, you can practise it in sections.

First get each section steady at a speed you can control, then link several sections together.

**Watch the details**

When linking, make sure the tempo changes transition naturally.

## FAQ

A: The guzheng.

**Q: When is it generally believed to have been adapted?**
A: Around the 1930s.

**Q: How does the tempo change in the piece?**
A: From slow to fast, building layer by layer.

**Q: How can the piano imitate slides?**
A: With ornaments or grace notes.

**Q: How can the piano imitate sweeps?**
A: With fast pentatonic runs up or down.

fantasia-free-form-keyboard-genre.body:
Among piano repertoire there is a kind of work called the "fantasia". Unlike a sonata or a rondo, a fantasia has no fixed form, and its tempo, key and mood can change at any time, so it often sounds as if the player is improvising. Bach's Chromatic Fantasia and Fugue, Mozart's Fantasia in D minor and Schubert's Wanderer Fantasy are all famous examples. Knowing the features of the fantasia helps us, when we play this kind of piece, to keep a sense of freedom without losing the overall direction.

## Bach's Chromatic Fantasia

Bach's Chromatic Fantasia and Fugue, in D minor, is one of the best-known works among his keyboard music.

The fantasia part has fast scales, broken chords and passages as free as recitative.

It is followed by a fugue, and the free fantasia and the strict fugue form a sharp contrast.

## Free Changes of Tempo

In a fantasia, the tempo often changes too, slow and fast, and sometimes there is a free cadenza.

The score will mark different tempo terms, and you need to distinguish them clearly when you play.

The rhythm of a cadenza is fairly free, but it still needs direction, and should not be played in a scattered way.

## Ask Your Teacher to Help Sort Out the Sections of a Fantasia

When playing a fantasia, you can ask Teacher Aum in your lessons to go through the sections and direction of the piece with you.

Your teacher can also help judge how to handle the tempo of cadenzas and free sections.

When freedom and structure are combined, a fantasia will be more convincing.

![Sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angle, in sepia tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacbo2w-pqjrj.webp)

## Writing That Sounds Like Improvisation

Many fantasias open as if the player had sat down at the piano and casually tried a few chords and ran off some scales.

This kind of writing comes from the improvising tradition of keyboard players at the time.

In the composers' day, many players could improvise a fantasia on the spot.

## Direction Within Freedom

The problem most likely to appear when playing a fantasia is being "too scattered", sounding as if it has no direction.

You can first analyse the sections of the whole piece, and see where the music comes from and where it is going.

Once you find the climax and the ending of each section, the free music has a skeleton.

## Play It Like Telling a Story

You can imagine a fantasia as a story: the opening is an introduction, there are ups and downs in the middle, and at the end there is a conclusion.

Each section is a scene or a mood in the story.

This kind of imagining helps join the sections into one whole.

## Schubert's Wanderer Fantasy

Schubert's Wanderer Fantasy was written in 1822 and is a large work with very high technical demands.

Its name comes from an early Schubert song, Der Wanderer, and one section of the fantasy uses the melody of that song.

The sections of this work are played without a break, and one rhythmic motif runs through the whole piece.

## The Fantasia in Brief

The fantasia is music that arises freely from the imagination. It already existed in the sixteenth century, has no fixed form like a sonata or rondo, and often opens as if trying out a few chords on the spur of the moment, coming from the improvising tradition of keyboard players.

Bach's Chromatic Fantasia and Fugue contrasts freedom with strictness. Mozart's Fantasia in D minor, K. 397, was written around 1782, and its last few bars were added by someone else. Schubert's Wanderer Fantasy of 1822 uses the melody of one of his songs. The key and tempo of a fantasia change freely, and the commonest problem is being too scattered, so analyse the sections first and play it like telling a story.

You can start with Mozart's Fantasia in D minor and feel the pauses with your ears, and you can ask Teacher Aum to go through the sections with you.

## Free Changes of Key

In a fantasia, the key often changes unexpectedly, turning suddenly from one key to another.

This kind of change brings surprise and colour to the music.

When playing, you can notice these modulations and let the listener feel the change of colour.

- No fixed form
- Tempo, key and mood change at any moment
- Sounds like improvisation
- Bach, Mozart and Schubert all wrote famous fantasias

## Feeling the Pauses with Your Ears

Fantasias often have fermatas and rests that bring the music to a temporary stop.

These pauses are like silences in a story, giving listeners time to think and to anticipate.

There is no fixed answer for how long to pause. You need to feel it with your ears, so that the pause is natural and meaningful.

## The Name "Fantasia"

The name "fantasia" means music that arises freely from the imagination.

As early as the sixteenth century, there were fantasias written for the lute and for keyboard instruments.

Over several centuries, the fantasia has kept freedom as its central feature.

## Mozart's Fantasia in D Minor

Mozart's Fantasia in D minor, K. 397, was written around 1782 and is a piece many learners like.

It opens with a slow broken chord, followed by a melancholy melody, with a fast cadenza in the middle, and finally it turns to a bright D major.

Mozart did not finish this fantasia in his lifetime, and the last few bars that are commonly played today were added by someone else later.

## Start with a Short Fantasia

For learners, Mozart's Fantasia in D minor is a very good starting point.

It is not long, the technical demands are moderate, and it contains the main features of the fantasia.

Once you can play it well, go on to try longer and harder fantasias.

## How It Differs from Other Forms

A sonata has an exposition, development and recapitulation, and a rondo has a theme that keeps returning.

A fantasia has no such fixed structure, and the composer can arrange the sections as they wish.

Some fantasias consist of several sharply contrasting sections, and others are like one continuous improvisation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does a fantasia have a fixed form?**
A: No.

**Q: What is the catalogue number of Mozart's Fantasia in D minor?**
A: K. 397.

**Q: In which year was the Wanderer Fantasy written?**
A: 1822.

**Q: What problem most often appears when playing a fantasia?**
A: Being too scattered, with no direction.

**Q: Which fantasia can learners start with?**
A: Mozart's Fantasia in D minor.

digital-piano-volume-neighbors.body:
In an apartment, you can reduce the impact of a digital piano on your neighbours by turning the volume down, using headphones, placing a vibration-damping pad under the instrument, and avoiding early mornings and late nights. Note that even with headphones on, the sound of the keys and pedals can still travel through the floor and walls. Staying on friendly terms with your neighbours and telling them roughly when you practise will also put everyone's mind at ease.

- Turn the volume down or practise with headphones
- The thud of keys and pedals can travel too
- Put a vibration-damping pad under the piano and pedals
- Pick suitable times and talk to your neighbours

## Using Headphones

Practising with headphones means that, for the most part, only you can hear the piano. It is a very common approach in apartments.

**Before you start**

Choose headphones that are comfortable, so they do not feel tight during long practice sessions.

Do not set the headphone volume too high, and take them off for a rest now and then after practising for a while.

![Glowing abstract digital graphics with a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9y5fxr-e5ak3.webp)

## Talking to Your Neighbours

If you can, say a quick hello to your neighbours, let them know you are learning the piano, and tell them roughly when you will practise.

You can also ask them to let you know if the sound ever feels too loud, and that you will do your best to adjust.

Most neighbours are understanding, and talking in advance is usually better than explaining afterwards.

## The Case of the Acoustic Piano

If you use an acoustic piano in an apartment, the sound is much louder than a digital piano's, so you need to be even more careful.

Consider a piano with a silent function, or add some sound-absorbing touches around the piano, such as carpets and thick curtains.

Be even more careful about when you schedule practice, too.

## Choosing the Right Practice Times

Try to avoid early mornings and late nights, when your neighbours may be resting.

It is worth looking up the rules of your apartment building, as some places set clear requirements for noise at certain times.

If evenings are the only time you can practise, choose a time that is not too late and use headphones.

## Harmony for Your Playing and Your Neighbours

Learning the piano in an apartment calls for a little more consideration and planning.

With volume control, vibration damping, sensible timing and good communication, you can usually find an arrangement that suits both you and your neighbours.

That way, practising can become a lasting and enjoyable part of your life.

## Adding a Vibration Pad

Placing a vibration-damping pad or a rug under the digital piano's stand and pedals can reduce the vibration that travels through the floor.

If the digital piano stands against a wall, move it a little away from the wall to reduce the sound travelling through it.

These measures usually cost little, yet they can noticeably improve how sound travels.

If possible, you can also lay a thicker rug under the digital piano, which damps vibration and also cuts down on echo in the room.

## Turning the Volume Down

One advantage of a digital piano is that you can adjust the volume. When practising in an apartment, set it so that you can hear yourself clearly without being too loud.

Try standing at the doorway or by the window and listening, to judge whether the sound carries too far.

You can use different volumes at different times of day: a little louder in the daytime and lower in the evening.

## The Challenges of Practising in an Apartment

A room in an apartment is often separated from the neighbours by just one wall or one floor, so sound travels easily.

Although a digital piano's volume is adjustable, it can still disturb your neighbours' rest if you are not careful.

By understanding in advance how sound travels and taking a few simple measures, you can practise with peace of mind and your neighbours will not be disturbed.

## Keeping Practice Effective

Practising only with headphones over a long period may affect how you perceive real tone and volume.

At suitable times in the daytime, you can occasionally practise through the speakers to hear the real sound.

If you have the chance, you can also practise on an acoustic piano from time to time and compare the touch and sound of the two.

## The Sound of Keys and Pedals

Many people think that with headphones on there is no sound at all, but the sound of the keys hitting the bottom, and of the pedals being pressed, can travel through the stand and the floor to the flat below.

This sound can be quite noticeable in the quiet of the night.

**Before you start**

Try a more relaxed way of touching the keys, avoiding pressing all the way down hard every time, and press the pedals as lightly as you can.

## FAQ

**Q: Can neighbours still hear me if I practise with headphones?**
A: You will hardly be heard playing, but the sound of the keys and pedals may carry.

**Q: Do vibration pads help?**
A: They usually reduce the vibration travelling through the floor.

**Q: After what time in the evening is it not suitable to practise?**
A: You can follow the rules of your apartment building and take your neighbours' routines into account.

**Q: Does practising only with headphones have any effect?**
A: It can affect how you perceive real tone, so practise through the speakers now and then.

**Q: What if a neighbour complains?**
A: First find out what is bothering them, then adjust your practice times and methods.

**Q: Can I use an acoustic piano in an apartment?**
A: Yes, but you need to pay closer attention to volume and timing.
