dual-coding-memorize-music.body:
Dual coding theory was proposed in the 1960s and 1970s by Allan Paivio, a psychology researcher from Canada. The core idea is simple: when the brain processes information, one system handles language and another handles images. If the same content is stored in both ways, in words and in images, there is an extra route to it when you try to recall it, so it is often remembered more firmly. Memorising piano music is a good place to use this. Do not rely only on your fingers playing it over and over; give each section of music both a name you can say and a picture you can see.

Many students memorise using only the muscle memory of their fingers. They play smoothly in everyday practice, but when nervous they suddenly forget the next phrase. One reason is that the memory has only one channel, and once it breaks there is no way back. The five methods below help you build two sets of cues, words and images, for the same piece of music.

## What are word cues and image cues?

**Word cues**
Information you can put into words, for example "this section is in C major, and the left hand goes from tonic to dominant", "the right hand goes up five notes, then down three", "the second time differs from the first only in the last note".

**Image cues**
Pictures you can see in your mind, for example how the music looks on the page, the shape of your hand on the keys, what kind of curve the rise and fall of the melody makes, or even a scene you imagine for that section.

The two kinds of cue complement each other. Word cues tell you the logic of the music, and image cues let you grasp its overall shape in an instant.

![A colourful cartoon grand piano poster surrounded by stars](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvx1y2ly-xq6q8.webp)

## Method 1: Give every section a name

Divide the piece into phrases or sections and give each one a short name. The name can be a musical description, such as "climbing the stairs", "echo" or "turning to the minor", or it can be a fun comparison. The process of choosing a name forces you to look closely at what is special about the section, and that in itself is a kind of processing.

- Keep names short, three to five words works well
- Give similar sections related names, such as "echo one" and "echo two"
- Write the names in pencil above the music

## Method 2: Draw the shape of the melody

Take a blank sheet of paper and, without looking at the keys, only at the score, draw one line showing the rise and fall of the right-hand melody. Draw upwards for rising notes, downwards for falling notes, and a flat line for long notes. When you have finished, this "melody map" is an image cue. Think of the line as you play, and many students find they know more clearly where the next phrase goes.

## Method 3: Take a photo of your hand shape

Stop at key places and look at the shape of your hands on the keys: which fingers are on black keys, how far apart your hands are, what angle your wrists are at. You can close your eyes and "take a photograph" in your mind. The next time you reach this spot, recall the photograph first, then play the notes.

## Method 4: Say the harmony and imagine colours

If you have already learned some theory, you can say the chord progression aloud, for example "one, four, five, one". At the same time, imagine a colour or a brightness for each chord, such as bright for a major triad and darker for a minor triad. That way a passage of harmony has both a name and a picture. Students who have not learned theory can use colours alone, such as "this sounds blue here and yellow there".

## Method 5: Rehearse in your mind away from the piano

After memorising, step away from the piano, sit in a chair, close your eyes and recall the whole piece. First use the word cues: say the name of each section in turn. Then use the image cues: picture the score, the melody map and the hand shapes. If you can walk through the whole piece in your head, both sets of cues have been built.

## Putting the methods into daily practice

**Week 1: word cues only**
Each day, when you practise a new section, spend two minutes first giving it a name and writing a sentence or two describing it, such as the key, the hand position and how it relates to the previous section.

**Week 2: add image cues**
Draw a melody map for the sections you have already named, and "take photos" of the hand shapes at key places.

**Week 3: check both sets of cues together**
Rehearse the whole piece in your mind away from the piano, then pick a section name at random and start playing from there.

Taking it in stages like this does not add too much of a burden all at once, and it is easier to keep up.

## Checking how firmly it is memorised

- Start playing from the name of any section, instead of only being able to start from the beginning
- See whether you can hum a section from the melody map alone
- Close your eyes and say the name of the next section, then open them and play it
- Play it again a day later and see which section is the easiest to get stuck on, then add cues to that section

These checks find the "weak links" that are held only by your fingers, so you can strengthen them in time.

## FAQ

**Q: Is dual coding suitable for children?**
A: Very much so. Children especially love naming sections and drawing melody lines, and memorising through drawing adds to the fun.

**Q: Will this take too much time?**
A: It does take somewhat more time at first, but the memory is more stable, and the time you spend playing it over and forgetting it again afterwards drops a great deal.

**Q: Do I still need to add cues to a piece I already know well?**
A: If you tend to get nervous before a performance, it is worth adding them. One more cue gives you one more bit of security.

**Q: Can I use only images and no words?**
A: You can, but the two together usually work better. The whole point of the theory is to use both channels at once.

dowland-lachrimae-seven-tears-1604.body:
John Dowland was an English lutenist and composer of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. In a song book he published in 1600 there is a song called "Flow, My Tears". Its melody steps down from a high note, like tears falling, and it soon spread across Europe. In 1604 he published a collection of instrumental music in London called Lachrimae, or Seven Tears. He took the falling melody that opens the song and wrote seven solemn pavans from it, for five viols and a lute. Dowland often let a trace of melancholy show in his work, and he is said to have given one piece the title "Semper Dowland, semper dolens", meaning "Always Dowland, always melancholy".

## Seven kinds of tears

All seven pavans use the same falling motif, but each one develops it differently.

**Think again**

Some are sadder, some bring a little comfort, and some feel more solemn.

Heard one after another, the seven pavans sound like seven different reflections on the idea of "tears".

- John Dowland, English lutenist and composer
- The song "Flow, My Tears" of 1600
- Lachrimae published in London in 1604
- Seven pavans, for five viols and a lute

## Flow, My Tears

In 1600, Dowland published a song book that included a song called "Flow, My Tears".

The melody of this song starts high and steps down note by note, like tears falling one by one.

It soon spread across Europe, and many musicians made arrangements of it.

## What is a pavan?

A pavan is slow and stately, usually in duple time, and in the sixteenth century it was danced all over Europe.

When people danced a pavan, they lined up and walked slowly forward.

Composers also often wrote pavans that were not meant for dancing, only for listening.

## Playing the tear motif on the piano

On the piano, you can play four descending notes slowly with your right hand, for example "la, sol, fa, mi".

Play them smoothly and softly, like a sigh.

Then add a simple chord in the left hand and listen to the mood the motif creates.

## Always melancholy

Dowland wrote a piece whose title means "Always Dowland, always melancholy".

He is said to have liked using this kind of self-mocking humour to show his sensitive, sentimental nature.

Yet he also wrote many light, lively dances and songs.

## The tears of 1604

In 1604, Dowland published a collection of instrumental music in London called Lachrimae.

The collection opens with seven pavans built on the "tear motif".

Each one has a subtitle, such as "Old Tears" and "New Tears".

## A fashion for melancholy

In Dowland's day, English poets and musicians loved to express melancholy.

Melancholy was seen as a deep and sensitive temperament.

Dowland's music expressed this fashion of the time perfectly.

## Chat with your teacher about Dowland's tears in your lessons

In your lessons, you can talk with Teacher Aum about Dowland's Lachrimae.

You can also ask your teacher to listen to a short piece you wrote using the falling motif and tell you whether it flows smoothly.

Starting from a single four-note motif, you can feel how music expresses emotion.

## Dowland's Lachrimae in summary

John Dowland was an English lutenist and composer of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. The first four notes of "Flow, My Tears" in his 1600 song book, stepping down one by one, are known as the "tear motif". In 1604 he published the instrumental collection Lachrimae in London. It opens with seven pavans written on this motif, scored for five viols and a lute, and each has a subtitle.

A pavan is a slow, solemn dance in duple time. The viol is a bowed string instrument with a fretted neck and a soft sound. Melancholy was fashionable in Dowland's time, though he also wrote lively dances. On the piano you can play "la, sol, fa, mi" to feel the tear motif, and you can also write a little piece from a single short motif.

You can talk about this bit of history with Teacher Aum.

## Viols and lutes

Lachrimae was written for five viols and a lute.

The viol is a bowed string instrument that looks a little like today's cello, but its neck has frets and its sound is soft.

Five viols make up five voices of different pitches, and the lute adds chords among them.

## A four-note descent

The opening of "Flow, My Tears" is four notes stepping down one at a time.

The falling melody made by these four notes later came to be called the "tear motif".

In that period, falling melodies were often used to express sadness and sighing.

![A high-angle view of an open black piano being played on a neon street at night in the rain](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbja5o7-6r6sa.webp)

## Dowland the lutenist

John Dowland was an English lutenist and composer of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries.

The lute is a pear-shaped plucked instrument that was very popular in Europe at the time, with a standing a bit like that of the guitar today.

Dowland's playing was famous, and he worked in several places across Europe.

## Writing a little piece from a motif

Dowland wrote seven pieces from the same motif, and we can try writing a little piece from a small motif too.

For example, repeat the four falling notes several times, starting on a different pitch each time or changing the rhythm.

This is a very good way to learn about composing.

## FAQ

**Q: What instrument did Dowland play?**
A: The lute.

**Q: In what year was "Flow, My Tears" published?**
A: 1600.

**Q: In what year was the instrumental collection Lachrimae published?**
A: 1604.

**Q: How many pavans open Lachrimae?**
A: Seven.

**Q: What is a pavan?**
A: A slow, solemn dance that was popular in sixteenth-century Europe.

digital-vs-acoustic-piano-first-instrume.body:
When deciding whether to buy a digital or an acoustic piano first, you can think about your living situation, budget, practice time and learning goals. For families in apartments who need to practise in the evening, a digital piano lets you control the volume with headphones; if circumstances allow and you value the touch and tone of an acoustic instrument, an acoustic piano is also worth considering.

## What to Look for in a Digital Piano

If you choose a digital piano, look at whether the keyboard has the standard eighty-eight keys, whether the keys have a weight close to a piano's, and whether it comes with a usable sustain pedal. These factors affect how you practise finger strength and pedal technique.

**A different angle**

An acoustic piano needs regular tuning, and you also need to watch the humidity and temperature of the room it sits in, especially in damp climates. Before buying, find out what upkeep is required, and whether the floor level and the neighbours are a problem.

Whichever you choose, you can try playing before you buy, with your child or on your own, to get a feel for the keyboard and the sound. You can also ask a teacher for advice and pick the instrument that suits your stage of learning.

- First assess the space and soundproofing of your home
- Consider your family's routines and practice times
- A digital piano with a weighted keyboard and pedals feels closer to a piano
- Try playing in person before you buy whenever you can

## Decide After Trying Them Out

Before buying, visit a music shop or showroom and try several different instruments yourself, feeling their touch and sound.

When you try them, play some pieces you know, and notice whether the changes in loudness are clear and whether the keys spring back naturally.

If you are choosing for a child, let your child try them too, and see which one they are more interested in.

Taking environment, goals, budget and how the instruments felt into account, choosing an instrument that suits your own family matters more than chasing a single standard answer.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a synthesizer set with crystals in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8k175x-6o89x.webp)

## Thinking About Your Living Space

Families in apartments, or close to their neighbours, often need to think about practice volume. A digital piano has adjustable volume and can be played through headphones, which is more convenient for evening or early-morning practice.

An acoustic piano is loud, and you cannot simply turn it down. If you choose an acoustic piano, think about the times of day you will practise, and whether you need some soundproofing measures.

Space for placing the instrument is also a factor. An upright piano needs a stretch of wall space and is heavy, so moving it takes professionals. A digital piano is usually lighter and takes up less room.

In damp environments or those with big temperature swings, an acoustic piano needs more care. A digital piano is affected somewhat less by the environment, but it too should be kept away from damp and direct sunlight.

## Thinking About Your Learning Goals

If your goal is long-term, systematic study of classical piano, an acoustic piano offers a richer experience in touch and tonal variety, which helps develop fine control.

If you mainly play for fun, play pop songs, or need flexible practice times, a good-quality digital piano can also meet your needs.

When choosing a digital piano, look at whether it has a full eighty-eight keys, whether the keyboard feels weighted, and whether it comes with a sustain pedal. These factors affect how well your practice works.

Whichever you choose, you can talk to your teacher to find out which type of instrument suits your current level and goals.

## Thinking About Budget and Long-Term Use

Instruments come in a very wide price range, so you can choose according to your family's budget. There is no need to buy an expensive instrument at the start, but make sure the instrument's basic quality is good enough for practice.

An acoustic piano needs regular tuning and maintenance, which is a long-term expense. A digital piano usually does not need tuning, but its lifespan and the need to replace it eventually are also worth considering.

Some families start with a digital piano and, once their child's interest and level have settled, think about switching to an acoustic piano. This is a fairly common approach.

You can also consider a second-hand instrument, but before buying it is advisable to have someone knowledgeable or a piano tuner check its condition.

## FAQ

**Q: Will a digital piano affect playing an acoustic piano later?**
A: If the keyboard feels close to a piano's, the effect is usually small, but it is still advisable to play an acoustic piano whenever you get the chance.

**Q: Can I buy a second-hand piano?**
A: You can consider it. It is advisable to have someone knowledgeable check its condition, and to find out about tuning and repairs.

**Q: Will a digital piano affect how well I learn?**
A: A digital piano with a well-weighted keyboard and good tone is generally enough for practice at the beginner stage.

**Q: Is an acoustic piano always better than a digital piano?**
A: Each has its strengths, and which suits you depends on your environment, goals and budget.

**Q: Does a digital piano need tuning?**
A: Generally not, but take care of it and keep it away from damp.

**Q: Can I rent a piano first?**
A: Yes. Some places offer piano rental, which is a good way to try before committing to long-term study.

double-sharp-double-flat-symbols.body:
The double sharp is a symbol that looks like a small "×" and raises a note by two semitones, which is a whole tone; the double flat is written as two flat signs, "♭♭", and lowers a note by two semitones. For example, F double sharp is played on the piano as G, and B double flat as A. The reason it is not simply written as G or A is that in some keys and chords, note names must follow the letter order of the scale or chord, so that the harmonic relationships are clear.

## In G♯ harmonic minor

The G♯ harmonic minor scale is G♯, A♯, B, C♯, D♯, E, F double sharp, G♯.

The seventh degree would originally be F♯, but to form the leading note it has to be raised by another semitone, which makes it F double sharp.

This way each letter appears only once in the scale, and the structure is clear.

## Why not simply write another note

Since F double sharp is just G, why not write G directly?

The reason is that in some keys and chords, every letter has to appear in order, without being skipped or repeated.

For example, in G♯ minor the leading note is F double sharp. If it were written as G, the scale would have two Gs and no F, which would look confusing.

## How far it lasts within a bar

Like ordinary sharps and flats, a double sharp or double flat stays in effect on the same note within the same bar.

In the next bar, it goes back to what the key signature specifies.

If a tie carries the note across the barline, the tied note stays double sharp or double flat.

## A method for reading

When you see a double sharp or double flat, first find the original note, then go two semitones to the right or left on the keyboard.

For example, on seeing F double sharp, first find F; one semitone to the right is F♯, and one more semitone to the right is G.

With a little practice, you will quickly find the matching key.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashed paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa33ewl-2lm8l.webp)

## An example in a chord

Some chords also need a double sharp or double flat in order to keep the letter relationship of stacked thirds.

For example, the D♯ major triad is D♯, F double sharp, A♯, and here the F double sharp is the third of the chord.

If it were written as G, it would no longer look like a chord built from stacked thirds.

## Double flats in flat keys

In keys with many flats, double flats appear.

For example, in some harmonies in C♭ major, or in the altered notes of flat minor keys, you may see B double flat or E double flat.

These spellings, too, are to keep the order of the letters and the harmonic relationships.

## First, a review of sharps and flats

A sharp pushes a note up a semitone, a flat presses it down a semitone, and a natural brings it back to its original position.

On the piano, raising a semitone means going right to the nearest key, and lowering a semitone means going left to the nearest key.

The double sharp and double flat are, on this basis, one more raise or one more lowering.

## How to cancel a double sharp or double flat

If after a double sharp you want to return to a single sharp, some scores write a natural plus a sharp, while others simply write one sharp.

To cancel it completely, write a natural.

When reading, watch for these details, so you are clear which key the note finally is.

## Where they often appear

Double sharps and double flats mostly appear in keys with many sharps or flats, or in Romantic and late Romantic works with many altered notes.

In beginners' pieces they appear fairly rarely.

When you start playing more complex works, you will see them more and more often.

## What the double flat looks like

The double flat is written as two flat signs side by side, also placed to the left of the note.

It means lowering the note by two semitones, which is a whole tone.

For example, E double flat is played on the piano as the key D.

## Practising double sharps and double flats

You can write out a few double-sharp and double-flat notes, such as C double sharp, G double sharp, A double flat and D double flat, and find each one on the piano.

You can also try writing out the G♯ harmonic minor scale and finding the F double sharp in it.

This kind of practice means you will no longer feel confused when you actually meet these symbols.

## Understanding enharmonic equivalents

F double sharp and G, B double flat and A are different names for the same key, which is called enharmonic equivalence.

On the piano you play the same key, but in music theory they do different jobs.

Understanding this helps you follow complex harmony and key changes.

**Listen**
- The double sharp looks like an "×" and raises a whole tone
- The double flat is two flats and lowers a whole tone
- F double sharp plays G, and B double flat plays A
- It keeps the letter order of scales and chords

## What the double sharp looks like

The double sharp looks like a tiny "×" and is written to the left of the note.

It means raising the note by two semitones, which is a whole tone.

**Before you start**

For example, C double sharp is played on the piano as the key D.

## FAQ

**Q: What does the double sharp look like?**
A: Like a small "×", and it raises a whole tone.

**Q: What does the double flat look like?**
A: Two flat signs, and it lowers a whole tone.

**Q: Which key does F double sharp play?**
A: The key G.

**Q: Why not simply write G?**
A: To keep the order of the letters in the scale and chord.

**Q: Does a double sharp last within a bar?**
A: Yes, and after the barline you play according to the key signature.

dominant-seventh-resolution-v7-to-i.body:
The dominant seventh chord (V7) is a major triad on the dominant with a minor seventh added; in C major it is G, B, D, F. It has a strong tendency to "go home" and usually resolves to the tonic chord. There are two key notes in the resolution: B (the leading note) goes up a semitone to C, and F (the seventh) goes down a semitone to E. Once you understand where these two notes go, V7 to I will sound smoother and more natural when you play it.

## The Shortened Form of the Dominant Seventh

In actual playing, you do not always play all four notes of the dominant seventh chord. A common approach is to leave out the fifth, D, and play just G, B, F.

**Remember this**

Because the fifth plays a smaller role in the chord, the character of the chord is still very clear without it, and the load on your hand is lighter.

When accompanying, beginners can start with the form without the fifth and make the resolution of the leading note and the seventh clear.

## The Seventh Goes Down

The F in the chord is the seventh of the dominant seventh, and it is only a semitone from E.

In the resolution, F usually goes down a semitone to E, which is the third of the tonic chord.

With the leading note going up and the seventh going down, the two notes seem to move in towards the middle together.

## Where the Root and the Fifth Go

The root of the dominant seventh, G, usually leaps to the tonic, C, in the bass voice.

The fifth, D, is freer: it can go up to E or down to C.

Sometimes, to make the voices smoother, the tonic chord leaves out its fifth and uses three Cs or repeats other notes instead.

## The Dominant Seventh in Minor Keys

In the harmonic minor, the dominant seventh chord exists too; for example, in A minor it is E, G♯, B, D.

Here the G♯ is the leading note, and it goes up to A in the resolution.

This is why the harmonic minor raises the seventh degree: so the leading note can resolve to the tonic more strongly.

## The Leading Note Goes Up

The B in the chord is the seventh degree of C major, also called the leading note, and it is only a semitone from the tonic, C.

In the resolution, B usually goes up a semitone to C.

This step gives a feeling of being pulled towards the tonic, and is a very important part of the resolution.

## When It Does Not Resolve

Although the dominant seventh usually resolves to the tonic chord, composers sometimes deliberately avoid the usual resolution.

For example, resolving to the vi chord gives an unexpected effect, which is the interrupted cadence.

Knowing the usual resolution lets you appreciate these surprises better.

## Playing It Slowly at the Piano

You can play B, D, F with the right hand and G with the left, and then move slowly to the tonic chord.

In the right hand, B goes up to C, F goes down to E, and D goes to C or E; in the left hand, G leaps to C.

Play it slowly a few times, listen clearly to how each voice moves, and feel the tension turn into relaxation.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon street, with a crystal tower behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2qujq-kql1z.webp)

## What the Dominant Seventh Is Made Of

The dominant seventh chord is built on the fifth degree of the key, which in C major is G.

It is the major triad made of G, B, D, plus F, a minor seventh above G.

Together these four notes make a sound that is both stable and tense.

- Dominant seventh in C major: G, B, D, F
- The leading note B goes up a semitone to C
- The seventh F goes down a semitone to E
- V7 usually resolves to the tonic chord I

## Inversions of the Dominant Seventh

The dominant seventh chord can also appear in inversions, for example with B or F as the lowest note.

Different inversions change how the bass moves in the resolution, making the bass line smoother.

In many accompaniments, using inverted dominant sevenths means your hand has to move less.

## Use in Accompaniment

In the accompaniment of pop songs, the dominant seventh often appears at the end of a phrase, leading into the start of the next.

For example, if one phrase ends on G7, the next starts from C, which sounds very natural.

Learning to add the seventh where it is needed can give the accompaniment more forward drive.

## Why "Resolve"?

There is a tritone in the dominant seventh chord, the distance between B and F, and it sounds unstable.

This instability naturally makes you expect a stable chord to follow.

In tonal music, that stable chord is usually the tonic chord.

## Getting to Know Cadences Through the Dominant Seventh

The dominant seventh resolving to the tonic makes up the most common kind of cadence in music, called the perfect cadence.

Many phrases, and the endings of whole pieces, are closed with this kind of cadence, which sounds complete and definite.

When playing a piece, pay attention to the end of each phrase, and you will often find a dominant seventh leading the music back to the tonic.

## Memorising Where the Dominant Seventh Goes by Ear

You can ask someone to play a dominant seventh chord and then its resolution, so that your ear remembers the feeling of tension turning into relaxation.

Then listen to the effect of different chords following the dominant seventh, and compare which one sounds most like "going home".

This kind of practice helps you judge the direction of the harmony more quickly when listening to music.

## Finding the Dominant Seventh in Different Keys

Every major key has its own dominant seventh chord; in G major, for example, it is D, F♯, A, C.

You can first find the fifth degree of the key, and then build it up with the method of a major triad plus a minor seventh.

Once you are fluent, whenever you see a key you can quickly find its dominant seventh chord.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the dominant seventh chord in C major?**
A: G, B, D, F.

**Q: How does the leading note resolve?**
A: B goes up a semitone to C.

**Q: How does the seventh resolve?**
A: F goes down a semitone to E.

**Q: Why is the dominant seventh chord unstable?**
A: There is a tritone between B and F in the chord.

**Q: Are there dominant seventh chords in minor keys?**
A: Yes, the raised seventh degree of the harmonic minor is the leading note.

direct-modulation-new-key-without-pivot.body:
When modulating, composers often use a chord that belongs to both keys as a "bridge", letting the music slide smoothly into the new key. This is called pivot chord modulation. But there is a more direct way: the previous phrase ends in the original key, and the next phrase begins already in the new key, with no transition in between. This is called direct modulation, sometimes also known as "abrupt modulation". Its effect is sharper and more striking. Below are the features of direct modulation and its common uses.

## How Direct Modulation Works

Direct modulation does not need a bridge chord like that.

**Remember this**

The previous phrase ends completely in the original key, and the next phrase begins directly in the new key.

As soon as the tonic or dominant chord of the new key appears, the listener knows the key has changed.

## Recognising Direct Modulation from Key Signatures and Accidentals

To spot direct modulation, watch for a change of key signature, or a sudden flood of accidentals.

Then look at the cadences of the phrases before and after: if the previous phrase ends completely in the original key and the next begins directly in the new key, it is very likely a direct modulation.

Sometimes a composer does not change the key signature and uses only accidentals to indicate the new key.

## Trying Direct Modulation at the Piano

Play a simple melody in C major, ending with a perfect cadence.

Then play the same melody directly in D major, with no transition in between.

Next, try adding a D major dominant chord between the two sections, and compare the effect of the two kinds of modulation.

## Direct Modulation to a Related Key

Direct modulation can also go to a closely related key, for example straight from C major to A minor.

Because these two keys share many notes, it does not sound too abrupt even without a transition.

This kind of modulation is often used between sections, bringing a change of mood.

## Semitone and Whole-Tone Upward Shifts

A direct modulation up a semitone makes a very noticeable change, with a feeling of being suddenly "lifted".

Raising it by a whole tone is slightly gentler, but it can still make the music brighter.

Sometimes a composer adds a dominant chord of the new key before the modulation to make the rise smoother, but that is no longer quite a direct modulation.

## Using It in Improvisation and Arranging

When arranging an accompaniment for a song, you can try using a direct modulation up a semitone in the final section.

First practise the accompaniment in the original key until it is fluent, then practise the accompaniment in the new key, and finally join the two sections together.

At the moment of modulation, the accompaniment can be strengthened slightly to bring out the new colour.

## Playing Direct Modulation

When playing a direct modulation, you can hold back slightly at the cadence before the change, giving the listener a pause.

When the new key begins, you can use a new tone colour or dynamic to make the change clearer.

But take care to keep the whole coherent, and do not pause too long, or the music will break up.

## First, a Look Back at Pivot Chord Modulation

In pivot chord modulation, you find a chord that exists in both the original key and the new key, so that it belongs to both keys at once.

For example, both C major and G major contain the A minor chord, so the music can "change" to G major starting from the A minor chord.

This kind of modulation is very smooth, and listeners barely notice it.

## Direct Modulation at a Glance

Direct modulation does not borrow a pivot chord: the previous phrase ends in the original key and the next begins directly in the new key. It often happens at the boundary between phrases or sections, and its effect is striking.

The upward shift of a semitone or whole tone before the final chorus of a pop song is often a direct modulation. Modulating to a related key is more natural, while modulating to a distant key has more impact.

To recognise it, look at the key signature, the accidentals and the cadences before and after; when playing, hold back slightly before the change and use a new tone colour in the new key. You can also try using it in your arrangements.

- Goes straight into the new key without a pivot chord
- Often happens between phrases
- The familiar "key change" in pop songs
- Striking and impactful

## Direct Modulation Mostly Happens at Phrase Boundaries

Direct modulation often happens at the boundary between phrases or sections.

Because the previous phrase has already reached a cadence, the listener has had a pause, and the arrival of the new key seems reasonable.

If the key changes suddenly in the middle of a phrase, the effect is even more jarring.

## Key Changes in Pop Songs

Many pop songs raise the whole song by a semitone or a whole tone before the last chorus.

This kind of key change is often a direct modulation: the previous section ends in the original key, and the next begins directly in the key a semitone higher.

It makes the final chorus sound stronger and more exciting.

![High-tech illustration of a glowing keyboard being played on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa85k1u-dyyjp.webp)

## Direct Modulation to a Distant Key

If you modulate directly to a more distantly related key, for example from C major to A♭ major, the effect is very striking.

This kind of modulation is often used to create surprise or strong contrast.

Romantic composers loved this kind of sudden change of colour.

## Direct Modulation and Mood

Direct modulation often brings a change of mood, such as suddenly becoming brighter, more agitated or more subdued.

Composers use it to mark a new section, or to push the music towards a climax.

When listening to music, noticing these sudden shifts helps you feel the emotional ups and downs of a work.

## FAQ

**Q: How does direct modulation differ from pivot chord modulation?**
A: It does not use a pivot chord and goes straight into the new key.

**Q: Where does direct modulation often happen?**
A: At the boundary between phrases or sections.

**Q: What is the direct modulation often heard in pop songs?**
A: A rise of a semitone or whole tone before the final chorus.

**Q: How can I recognise it in the score?**
A: Look at the key signature, the accidentals and the cadences before and after.

**Q: How should I handle it when playing?**
A: Hold back slightly before the change, and use a new tone colour or dynamic in the new key.

dominant-ninth-chord-v9-color.body:
The dominant seventh chord is made of four notes on the dominant, for example G, B, D, F in C major. If you stack another third on top and add A, you get a dominant ninth chord. This extra ninth makes the chord's colour richer and gives it more tension. In a major key, the ninth is a major ninth above the root; in a minor key, a minor ninth is often used. The dominant ninth chord is common in Romantic music, jazz and pop. Below we look at how it is built and how it is used.

## Resolving the Dominant Ninth

Like the dominant seventh, the dominant ninth chord usually resolves to the tonic chord.

**Common mistake**

When resolving, the ninth generally moves down by step, for example A to G; the seventh, F, goes down to E; and the third, B, goes up to C.

That way every voice has a clear direction, and the result sounds natural and flowing.

## The Dominant Ninth in Jazz and Pop

In jazz and pop music, the dominant ninth chord is used very widely, often replacing the plain dominant seventh, especially in relaxed, harmonically colourful ballads and blues.

It sounds softer and more modern than the dominant seventh.

In some styles, the dominant ninth does not even have to resolve and can simply stay where it is.

## Where the Ninth Sits

In traditional harmony, the ninth is usually placed higher than the root, often in the top voice.

If the ninth is too close to the root, for example only a second apart, the sound becomes muddy.

So when voicing the chord, keep a good distance between the ninth and the root.

## Writing Chord Symbols

In pop and jazz chord symbols, a dominant ninth with a major ninth is often written G9.

A dominant ninth with a minor ninth is written G7(♭9).

When you see these symbols, know that both are a dominant seventh chord with a ninth added.

## The Dominant Ninth at a Glance

A dominant ninth chord is a dominant seventh with another third stacked on top, made of the root, third, fifth, seventh and ninth. Major keys mostly use the major ninth and minor keys mostly the minor ninth, written G9 and G7(♭9) respectively.

On the piano the fifth is often left out, and the ninth is placed high to keep its distance from the root. When resolving, the ninth moves down by step, and sometimes it first descends to make a dominant seventh before resolving.

The dominant ninth is common in Romantic, jazz and pop music, and in accompaniment you can swap it for the dominant seventh now and then to add colour.

![Night-time city lights and buildings](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa83tae-asy27.webp)

## The Dominant Ninth in Romantic Music

Nineteenth-century composers often used the dominant ninth chord to add colour to their harmony.

In some lyrical short piano pieces, the dominant ninth makes the melody sound warmer and more yearning.

When playing these works, watch out for dominant chords with an extra note.

## Swapping In a Dominant Ninth When Accompanying Pop Songs

When arranging an accompaniment for a pop song, you can try replacing some dominant seventh chords with dominant ninths.

For example, add the ninth to the dominant chord before the chorus to build anticipation.

But do not add it to every chord, or the accompaniment will become too complicated.

**Take it slowly**
- Stack a third on a dominant seventh chord
- Major keys mostly use the major ninth, minor keys the minor ninth
- Five notes, and on the piano the fifth is often left out
- When resolving, the ninth usually moves down by step

## Hearing the Dominant Ninth

When listening to a dominant ninth chord, notice the extra note at the top of the chord.

It adds a layer of colour beyond the dominant seventh, and often makes the chord feel "thicker" or "brighter".

After listening a few times, your ear will gradually learn to tell the dominant seventh and dominant ninth apart.

## Early Resolution of the Ninth

In some music, the ninth descends to the octave, the root an octave higher, before the chord has changed.

That way, the dominant ninth first becomes a dominant seventh and then resolves to the tonic chord.

This writing makes the ninth sound more like an ornamental note.

## Leaving Notes Out on the Piano

A five-note chord is not easy to play with one hand on the piano, so some notes are often left out.

The fifth is usually the first to go, because it has little effect on the character of the chord.

A common voicing is the root in the left hand and the third, seventh and ninth in the right hand.

## How the Dominant Ninth Is Built

A dominant ninth chord has five notes: root, third, fifth, seventh and ninth.

In C major, the dominant is G, so the dominant ninth is G, B, D, F, A.

The ninth, A, is a ninth above the root, G, which is an octave plus a second.

## Comparing G7 and G9 at the Piano

In C major, first play the dominant seventh G, B, D, F, then the dominant ninth G, B, F, A (leaving out D).

Then resolve both to a C major triad and compare the difference.

Next try the minor ninth version, G, B, F, A♭, and listen to its more tense colour.

## Major Ninth and Minor Ninth

In a major key, the ninth of a dominant ninth chord is usually a major ninth above the root, for example G to A.

In a minor key, because the sixth degree of the key is lowered, the ninth is often a minor ninth, for example G to A♭ in C minor.

A dominant ninth chord with a minor ninth sounds more tense and darker.

## FAQ

**Q: How many notes does a dominant ninth chord have?**
A: Five.

**Q: What is the dominant ninth chord in C major?**
A: G, B, D, F, A.

**Q: Which note is often left out on the piano?**
A: The fifth.

**Q: How does the ninth resolve?**
A: Usually down by step.

**Q: How is the minor ninth symbol written?**
A: G7(♭9).

draw-the-phrase-shape.body:
Drawing a line in pencil on paper, or above the music, that follows the contour of the melody is an intuitive way to understand the shape of a phrase. When the melody goes up, the line rises; when it goes down, the line falls; when the music gets louder the line gets thicker, and when it gets softer the line gets thinner. Play it after drawing, and your fingers will know more clearly where the phrase begins, where it reaches its peak and where it ends.

**Listen first**
- Sing or listen to the melody first, then draw
- The height of the line matches the pitch of the notes
- The thickness of the line can show loud and soft
- When you have finished, play it again with the score

## Why draw a phrase?

When we read music, our eyes often take it one note at a time, so it is easy to notice the notes themselves and miss the shape they make together.

Drawing a line lets you see a melody as a whole: does it unfold steadily, or leap up suddenly and then settle slowly down?

With that overall picture in mind, it is easier to give your playing a natural rise and fall, instead of making every note equally flat.

## Finding the peak of the phrase

Most phrases have a high point of emotion or pitch. As you draw, you can mark the peak with a star or a circle.

The peak is not always the highest note. Sometimes it is where the harmony is most tense, or where the melody lingers longest. Listen a few times and talk it over with your teacher.

Once you have found the peak, let the notes before it lead towards it little by little in your playing, then relax slowly afterwards, and the phrase will have direction.

## Markings in the score that relate to phrases

The slurs in the score often mark the extent of a phrase: one long arc from start to finish shows that these notes belong to the same sentence. When you draw your line, you can first find these arcs and use them as the start and end of each stretch of line.

The crescendo and diminuendo "hairpin" signs correspond exactly to where the line gets thicker and thinner. Dynamic markings such as p, mf and f can set the overall thickness of the line.

Comparing these hints from the composer with the line you have drawn helps you see more clearly why the phrase rises and falls the way it does.

## How to start drawing

Start with a fairly short melody, say four to eight bars. Sing it or play it once and feel which way it goes.

On a blank sheet of paper, draw a line from left to right. When the melody goes up, the line goes up; when it goes down, the line goes down; when the same note repeats, the line stays level.

It does not need to be precise. A rough shape is enough. What matters is that the act of drawing makes you notice how the melody changes.

## Drawing the line on the score

Once you are used to this method, you can draw the phrase line lightly in pencil directly above the music.

Keep the line faint so that it does not cover the notes and markings already there.

After plenty of practice you can rub the line out and see whether you have the shape of the phrase in your head, and whether the rise and fall in your playing is still clear.

## Playing with the score

When you have finished drawing, put the line drawing next to the score and play while looking at it. Notice whether your fingers change dynamics and speed along with the rise and fall of the line.

After playing, you can record yourself and listen back, comparing whether the rise and fall of the sound matches the line you drew.

If you find that one passage sounds flat while the line rises and falls, there is more expression to be found there.

## Adding loud, soft and tempo

Once the basic shape is drawn, you can use the thickness of the line to show loud and soft. Draw the line thicker where the music gets louder and thinner where it gets softer.

If the melody slows down somewhere or has a fermata, you can stretch that part of the line out longer, or draw a small dot above it.

In this way a single line holds information about pitch, dynamics and tempo, like a simple map of the phrase.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon street, with crystal towers behind them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9x4cim-bkuri.webp)

## A way to play for children

For children, drawing phrases can become a little game. Use coloured pens: draw a rising line as a hillside, a falling line as a slide, loud places as a big sun and soft places as little stars.

When the child has finished drawing, let them play while looking at the picture, and ask: "Did your slide slide down?"

This helps children connect abstract music with concrete pictures, and makes their playing more imaginative.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need to be able to draw to draw a phrase?**
A: No. All you need is to draw a rough high and low and thick and thin.

**Q: Do I have to draw every phrase?**
A: No. Choose a few phrases that matter or that tend to come out flat.

**Q: Can I draw the accompaniment too?**
A: Yes, but it is usually best to start with the melody, since the shape of the accompaniment is generally steadier.

**Q: What if my drawing differs from my teacher's understanding?**
A: Show it to your teacher and talk about the different ways of shaping it together. That is itself a very good way to learn.

**Q: Should I keep my line drawings?**
A: Yes. You can tuck them into the score and take them out when you review, and you will quickly recall how you shaped the phrase.

**Q: What pieces suit this method?**
A: Pieces with strong melodies suit it especially well, such as lyrical pieces and arrangements of songs.

digital-piano-usb-midi-computer.body:
Many digital pianos and electronic keyboards have a USB or MIDI port, so they can be connected to a computer or tablet. Once connected, what the keys send out is not sound, but playing information such as which key was pressed, how hard, and for how long. Software on the computer then uses that information to make sound, record your playing or display a score. The ports and supported functions differ between models, so before connecting, read the manual to confirm which cable you need and whether a driver has to be installed.

## Tablets and phones

Besides computers, many tablets and phones can also connect to a digital piano through an adapter cable.

The connection method and supported apps vary, and some need a specific adapter.

Before using one, check device compatibility in the same way, so you do not buy the wrong cable.

## The latency problem

Sometimes after connecting to a computer, there is a small delay between pressing a key and hearing the sound, which affects how playing feels.

Latency may be related to the computer's settings, the software or the audio device. Check the software's documentation and adjust the relevant settings.

If you are only practising, you can also use the digital piano's own sound directly and avoid the effect of latency.

**Quick tips**
- Many digital pianos have a USB or MIDI port
- What is sent is playing information, not sound
- Computer software makes sound, records or displays based on that information
- Before connecting, check the manual for the cable and driver

## Safety and protecting your equipment

When plugging and unplugging cables, be gentle and do not pull hard, so that you do not damage the ports.

When connecting or disconnecting, you can turn the volume down first to avoid a sudden loud sound.

When not in use, put the cables away, so they are not tripped over or chewed by pets.

![Illustration in Bangkok city poster style, with tall buildings and busy street traffic](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0nkos-9ea9p.webp)

## Where the sound comes out

When connected by MIDI, what the piano sends to the computer is information, and the sound the computer makes comes out of the computer's speakers or headphones.

If you want the sound to come out of the piano's speakers, or to send the computer's sound back to the piano, you need to check whether the piano supports audio transfer.

These details differ a great deal from model to model, so see the audio and MIDI sections of the manual.

## What MIDI is

MIDI is a standard that lets electronic instruments and computers communicate. It carries not the sound itself but the information about the playing.

For example, when you press middle C, the piano sends a message telling the computer that middle C has been pressed and how hard; when you release it, it sends another message saying middle C has been released.

After the computer receives these messages, it can play them back with its own sounds, or record them.

## What you can do once connected

Once connected, you can use recording or music production software on the computer to record your playing, then play it back, edit it or save it.

You can also use other sounds on the computer, such as orchestral instruments or synthesiser sounds, so the keys give different effects.

There is also learning software that can show a score or rhythm information based on your playing. The exact functions depend on the software itself.

## Preparing before you connect

Before connecting, confirm which cable you need, for example whether the USB connector type matches both the piano and the computer.

Some instruments are recognised straight away when connected to a computer, while others need a driver supplied by the manufacturer.

This information is usually in the manual or on the manufacturer's official website, so read it through before you start.

## USB ports and traditional MIDI ports

Newer digital pianos often have a USB port, and a single USB cable can connect directly to a computer and carry MIDI information.

Some older instruments use the round traditional MIDI port and need a dedicated MIDI cable or an adapter to connect to a computer.

First look at which ports are on the back or side of your piano, then read the manual to learn what they are for.

## When something goes wrong

If the connection does not work, first check that the cable is plugged in properly, that the computer recognises the device, and that the correct input is selected in the software.

You can also restart the piano and the computer and try again.

If it still cannot be solved, check the manufacturer's support page or contact their customer service.

## The benefit of recording your playing

Playing recorded by MIDI lets you see on the computer the position, length and strength of each note.

This can help you check more objectively whether your rhythm is even and whether your dynamics vary.

However, this data is only a reference. Whether music is good still has to be judged by ear.

## Do not forget the practice itself

Connecting to a computer opens up many interesting possibilities, but it is also easy to spend a lot of time on settings and software.

You can set yourself a rule, such as finishing the day's practice first and only then exploring the functions on the computer.

**Listen**

Technology is a tool to help learning, but real progress still comes from steady, focused practice.

## FAQ

**Q: Does MIDI carry sound?**
A: No, it carries playing information such as keys, strength and length.

**Q: What is the difference between USB and MIDI ports?**
A: USB can often connect straight to a computer, while a traditional MIDI port needs a dedicated cable or adapter.

**Q: Do I need to install a driver?**
A: Some models do. Check the manual to confirm.

**Q: What can I do once connected?**
A: Record your playing, use other sounds, work with learning software and more.

**Q: What if there is latency?**
A: Adjust the computer and software settings, or use the piano's own sound directly.

**Q: What if the connection fails?**
A: Check the cable and settings, and contact the manufacturer if necessary.

double-dotted-notes-three-quarters-longe.body:
A single dot adds half of the note's original length to it; for example, a dotted crotchet lasts a beat and a half. A double dot means two dots after the note: the first dot adds half of the original value, and the second dot adds half of the first dot. So a double-dotted crotchet equals a crotchet plus a quaver plus a semiquaver, which is the length of seven semiquavers. A double-dotted note is usually followed by a very short note, creating a sharp contrast of long and short.

## The Rules of Double Dots

If a note has two small dots to its right, it is called a double-dotted note.

**Common mistake**

The first dot adds half of the original value, and the second dot adds half of the first dot.

Together, the two dots make the note three quarters longer than it was.

## The Double-Dotted Crotchet

Take the crotchet as an example: its original value is one beat, which is four semiquavers.

The first dot adds two semiquavers, and the second dot adds one more semiquaver.

In all that comes to seven semiquavers, which is one and three quarter beats.

## Double Dots at a Glance

The double dot simply adds a little more value on top of the single dot, and the rule is straightforward.

It does not appear very often in scores, but when it does it usually carries a sharp rhythmic character.

Mastering how to count and play it will give you more confidence when you meet this rhythm.

**Take it slowly**
- Single dot: adds half the original value
- Double dot: adds half of the first dot as well
- Double-dotted crotchet = seven semiquavers
- Often followed by a very short note

## The Effect of Long-Short Contrast

A double-dotted note together with the short note after it creates a very sharp contrast of long and short.

This rhythm sounds tighter and more forceful than a single dot, and is often used to express solemnity and resolve.

It is used a great deal in some marches and in Baroque overtures.

## Common Mistakes with Double Dots

The most common mistake with double dots is to play them like a single dot, so that the short note comes too early.

Some people also play the short note too heavily, which interferes with the accent on the next note.

When practising, you can first use a metronome, tapping out the semiquaver subdivision, to confirm where the short note falls.

## Keyboard Practice for Double-Dotted Rhythms

You can first practise the double-dotted rhythm on a single note: hold the long note down and play the short note lightly and quickly.

Then put the rhythm on a simple scale or chords, for example playing note by note up a C major scale.

Once you are fluent, look for this rhythm in pieces and handle it the same way.

## How to Count Double-Dotted Rhythms

When counting a double-dotted rhythm, you can divide the beat into four semiquavers and count "1 e & a".

A double-dotted crotchet starts on "1" and carries on until the "&" of the next beat, and the short note is played on the "a".

At first you can count slowly out loud, and once you are used to it, count in your head.

## The Short Note After It

A double-dotted note is usually followed by a very short note, which fills out the beat.

For example, a double-dotted crotchet followed by a semiquaver adds up to exactly two beats.

This short note is often played quickly, like a little springboard to the next note.

## First, a Review of the Single Dot

Adding a small dot to the right of a note is called dotting it, and the note becomes half its own length longer.

For example, a crotchet is one beat, so a dotted crotchet is a beat and a half.

A dotted minim is two beats plus one beat, three beats in all.

## The Relationship with Ties

A double-dotted note can in fact also be written with ties, for example a crotchet tied to a quaver and then to a semiquaver.

But the double-dot notation is more concise, and it is also easier to see the overall rhythm when reading.

Understanding how the two notations correspond helps you read rhythms faster.

## The Double-Dotted Minim

The original value of a double-dotted minim is two beats.

The first dot adds one beat, and the second dot adds another half beat.

So a double-dotted minim lasts three and a half beats in all.

## Hearing Double Dots

You can ask your teacher to play single-dotted and double-dotted rhythms and compare the difference.

You will notice that with the double dot the long note is longer, the short note is shorter, and the rhythm feels tighter.

After listening a few times, your ear will learn to tell the two rhythms apart.

## Dotted Rhythms in Baroque Overtures

In some Baroque overtures, a very characteristic dotted rhythm often appears, with a long note followed by a very quick short one.

When playing this music, performers sometimes play a single dot as if it were a double dot, to make the long-short contrast stronger.

This was a historical performance habit, and different performers and scholars have different views about it.

![A wooden upright piano, green stool and orange books in front of a deep teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa326o8-g80qn.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What is a double dot?**
A: Two dots after a note, increasing its value by three quarters.

**Q: How long is a double-dotted crotchet?**
A: Seven semiquavers, which is one and three quarter beats.

**Q: What often follows a double dot?**
A: A very short note, to fill out the beat.

**Q: What is the common mistake?**
A: Playing it like a single dot, so the short note comes too early.

**Q: How do I count a double-dotted rhythm?**
A: Divide the beat into four semiquavers and count them.

fix-the-first-mistake-before-the-rest.body:
When you play a piece, you often find problems in several places. If you play from beginning to end every time and just glide past the errors, the problems tend to stay. A more effective approach is to find the first place where something goes wrong, fix it, and only then look for the next one. Solve them one by one and the problems will steadily shrink, because later mistakes are sometimes caused by earlier ones.

## Write the Problems Down

While looking for mistakes, you can mark the trouble spots in the score with a pencil.

When marking, note what the problem is, such as "fingering", "rhythm" or "sharp".

That way, the next time you practise, you can see at a glance where to pay attention.

## Play It Correctly More Often

A passage that has been played wrongly many times needs to be played correctly even more times before the right way is remembered.

So when fixing a mistake, do not be satisfied with playing it right once. Play it correctly several times in a row.

The next day, check again to see whether it has really stuck.

## Earlier Mistakes Cause Later Ones

Sometimes a later mistake is actually caused by an earlier one.

For example, if you use the wrong fingering early on, your hand ends up in the wrong position later, and a new mistake appears.

Solve the earlier problem first, and the later problem may disappear on its own.

- Find the first place where something goes wrong
- Fix it before moving on
- Later mistakes may be caused by earlier ones
- Solve them one by one

## Don't Fix Too Much at Once

If you try to fix many places at once, your attention scatters and none of them gets fixed well.

Focusing on one problem at a time works better.

Each problem you solve also builds your confidence for the next one.

## Then Look for the Next One

Once the first mistake is fixed, keep playing on and find the second place where something goes wrong.

Again, stop, work out the problem, and practise it specifically.

Moving forward one at a time like this, the problems in the whole piece gradually decrease.

## Summary: Fix the First Mistake First

Playing from beginning to end makes mistakes repeat. Instead, find the first mistake, work out the problem, practise it slowly until you play it correctly several times in a row, and then look for the next one.

Later mistakes are sometimes caused by earlier ones. Focus on one problem at a time and mark them in the score.

Alternate between fixing mistakes and playing the whole piece, stay patient, and solve problems one by one.

## Go Slowly When Fixing

When fixing a mistake, you must slow the tempo right down, slow enough to play it correctly every time.

If you use the original tempo, you will most likely keep making the same mistake.

After playing it correctly slowly several times, speed up gradually.

## The Hidden Risk of Playing From Bar One to the End Every Time

Many people practise by playing from beginning to end every time, carrying on whenever they hit a mistake.

This does make you familiar with the whole piece, but the mistakes are repeated every time and become more and more ingrained.

After a few days, those mistakes may have turned into habits.

## You Still Need to Play the Whole Piece

Fixing mistakes one by one does not mean you no longer need to play from beginning to end.

After fixing a few places, you can play through from the start and check that those places also work within the whole piece.

Alternate the two kinds of practice, and the piece will be both accurate and connected.

## Types of Mistakes

Common mistakes fall roughly into a few types: wrong notes, inaccurate rhythm, unsettled fingering, and missed accidentals or dynamic markings.

Different types of mistakes call for different fixes. For example, rhythm problems can be clapped first, while fingering problems need a fingering to be chosen and written down.

First work out which type of problem it is, then choose a suitable method, and the fix will come faster.

## Stay Patient

Sometimes a spot needs many repetitions before it is fixed, and that is normal.

Do not skip a passage just because it is hard. The places you skip will cause trouble later.

Solving them patiently one by one will get you improving faster in the long run.

![A long-braided person playing a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with drones in the sky](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6878m-wckgf.webp)

## Practise Only This One Spot

After finding the first mistake, practise just that short section, which may be only a bar or two.

First play it correctly slowly several times, then start from a little earlier and link it up.

Once this spot comes out right several times in a row, play on.

## Find the First Mistake

First play slowly from the beginning, and stop at the first place where something goes wrong.

Think about what is wrong here: a wrong note, wrong rhythm, or wrong fingering?

Only when the problem is clear can you apply the right remedy.

## Compare With Your Teacher's Reminders

Problems your teacher points out in lessons can be handled this way too.

Put the problems your teacher mentioned in the order they appear in the piece, and start solving from the first.

**Another way to look at it**

At your next lesson, tell your teacher which problems are fixed and which still need help.

## FAQ

**Q: Why fix the first mistake first?**
A: Later mistakes may be caused by earlier ones.

**Q: What should I do once I find a mistake?**
A: Stop, work out the problem, and practise it slowly and specifically.

**Q: Can I fix many places at once?**
A: Focusing on one problem at a time works better.

**Q: Is playing it right once enough?**
A: No. Play it correctly several times in a row.

**Q: Do I still need to play from beginning to end?**
A: Yes, alternating with fixing mistakes.

faure-pavane-op50-1887-flute-melody.body:
In 1887 the French composer Gabriel Fauré wrote a short orchestral piece, Pavane, Op. 50, in F♯ minor. At the start, the strings gently pluck, and above them a flute plays an elegant, slightly wistful melody, like a procession walking slowly. The following year Fauré added an optional chorus to it. The pavane was originally a stately slow processional dance in sixteenth-century Europe, and Fauré borrowed the name and character of this old dance to write a piece with a very late nineteenth-century French flavour. It is also often arranged as a piano solo.

## The flute melody

Over the plucked accompaniment, the flute plays a long melody.

The melody rises and falls gently, with a touch of melancholy, and is very elegant.

On the piano, make this melody as smooth and rounded as a flute, and do not play it too heavily.

## The possibility of piano duet

The Pavane also works well arranged for piano four hands.

One player takes the flute line, and the other takes the plucked-style bass and chords. Each side looks after its own tone colour, which makes it easier to control.

Playing with a friend or family member is a very good kind of ensemble practice.

## The colour of F♯ minor

The Pavane is in F♯ minor, a key with three sharps, so you play more black keys on the piano.

F♯ minor sounds soft and slightly hazy, which suits the atmosphere of this piece very well.

Before you play, practise the F♯ minor scale and its main chords.

## The emotional swell in the middle of the Pavane

In the middle section of the piece, the music becomes more agitated, the dynamics grow stronger and the harmony becomes richer.

This part is like a wave of feeling passing through the procession.

Afterwards, the opening melody returns, and the music goes back to its original calm.

## Fauré and 1887

Fauré was a French composer, known for his songs, chamber music and piano works.

In 1887 he wrote this Pavane, originally for a small orchestra.

The next year he added a chorus, with words describing love and teasing among a group of people at a ball, which can be used or left out in performance.

![Purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabydwj-1x6jh.webp)

## Summary of the Pavane

The pavane was a stately slow dance in sixteenth-century Europe. Fauré wrote his Pavane, Op. 50, in F♯ minor in 1887, originally for a small orchestra, and added an optional chorus in 1888. At the start, plucked strings accompany, and a flute plays an elegant, slightly wistful melody.

F♯ minor has three sharps, and the tempo is a moderately slow Andante. Some think Fauré wanted to keep the feeling of walking forward. The middle section has an emotional swell, then the opening melody returns, and Fauré's harmony is delicate and soft.

On the piano, keep the left hand light, imitating plucked strings, and make the melody as smooth as a flute. Do not let the pedal cover the accompaniment. You can choose an arrangement of a suitable difficulty or play it as a piano duet. Listen to the original first, and Teacher Aum can help you choose the score.

- Written by Fauré in 1887, Op. 50, in F♯ minor
- Plucked-string accompaniment, with a flute playing the melody
- An optional chorus added in 1888
- The pavane was a stately slow dance of the sixteenth century

## Listen to the original orchestral version

Before playing the piano version, listen to the original orchestral version, and to the version with chorus.

Notice the tone of the flute, the sound of the plucked strings and how the atmosphere changes when the chorus comes in.

When your ears are already filled with the sound of the flute and the plucked strings, your fingers have a direction when they imitate them on the keys.

## The tempo of the Pavane

The tempo marking of this piece is a moderately slow Andante.

Some people think Fauré himself wanted it not to be played too slowly, and to keep the feeling of walking forward.

When you play, imagine a group of people walking slowly, not standing still.

## Fauré's harmony

Fauré's harmony is very distinctive, often turning to a new chord in unexpected places.

These harmonic changes are delicate and soft and never feel abrupt.

When playing the Pavane, notice those harmonic turns and let them flow naturally.

## What is a pavane

The pavane is a dance that was popular in sixteenth-century Europe, slow in tempo with stately steps.

People often moved forward slowly in a line, with elegant, restrained movements.

Later, it became a kind of dance in instrumental suites, often paired with a fast dance.

## Using the pedal with care in the Pavane

When playing this piece, you can use some sustain pedal to make the melody more connected.

But take care that the plucked-style accompaniment is not blurred too much by the pedal.

You can change the pedal promptly when the harmony changes, or use a shallower pedal.

## The plucked accompaniment

At the start, the strings pluck with their fingers, producing even bass notes and chords.

This soft plucking sounds like slowly walking footsteps.

On the piano, the left-hand accompaniment should be light and clear, and you can play it slightly detached to imitate the feel of plucking.

## Asking your teacher to choose a Pavane score in the lesson

Which edition of the Pavane to choose for piano can be decided in the lesson, with Teacher Aum taking your level into account.

Your teacher can also help you practise the balance between melody and accompaniment, and the fingering in F♯ minor.

This piece is very good for practising a lyrical melody and a light accompaniment.

## Piano arrangements of the Pavane range from easy to hard

There are quite a few piano arrangements of the Pavane, and their difficulty varies.

Simple versions keep the melody and the basic plucked accompaniment, while harder versions add more harmony and counterpoint.

**Listen closely**

You can choose a version that suits your level.

## FAQ

**Q: In what year was the Pavane written?**
A: 1887.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: F♯ minor.

**Q: Which instrument plays the melody at the start?**
A: The flute.

**Q: What was the pavane originally?**
A: A stately slow dance of the sixteenth century.

**Q: How should the left-hand accompaniment sound on the piano?**
A: Light and clear, imitating plucked strings.

duplet-in-compound-meter-two-in-three.body:
In compound time such as 6/8, a beat is usually divided into three quavers (eighth notes). A duplet fits two even notes into that same beat, and the score shows a "2" above the two notes. It is the exact opposite of the triplet: a triplet puts three notes into a beat that divides in two, while a duplet puts two notes into a beat that divides in three. When practising, first tap out the three-quaver subdivision, then cut the beat evenly in half.

## What is a duplet?

A duplet puts two notes evenly into a main beat that divides in three.

**Remember this**

The two notes are the same length, and each takes half of the beat.

In the score, a "2" is usually written above or below the two notes, and sometimes a bracket or a beam is added too.

## One beat in compound time

In 6/8 there are two main beats in each bar, and each main beat is a dotted crotchet (dotted quarter note).

Each main beat is normally divided into three quavers, counted "one-two-three, four-five-six".

This three-part structure is the basic feature of compound time.

## How to count a duplet

First count "one-two-three" within one main beat and feel the three quavers flowing evenly.

Then keep the length of the beat the same, but count "one, two" instead, cutting it evenly in half.

The second note falls between "two" and "three", exactly at the midpoint of the beat.

## Feeling it with your body

You can tap each main beat with your foot while your hand taps three quavers.

Once you are used to that, keep your foot at the same speed and change your hand to two taps per main beat.

This helps your body feel the difference between a duplet and a three-part rhythm.

## Duplets in improvisation

When improvising an accompaniment to a song in 6/8, you can use duplets in places to vary the rhythm.

For example, at the end of a phrase, play two chords as a duplet to create a broadening effect.

Try adding duplets in different places and listen to what they do to the music.

## Switching to and from the three-part rhythm

Duplets often alternate with the rhythm of three quavers.

When you switch from three notes to two, keep the length of the main beat the same and change only how it is divided.

You can practise the two beats where the switch happens on their own first, and put them back into the piece once they feel familiar.

## Common mistakes with duplets

The most common mistake with duplets is to play them long-short or short-long, so that they are not even.

Some players also unconsciously play a duplet as two ordinary quavers, and the beat ends up too short.

When practising, set the metronome to click once per main beat and check that the two notes are spread evenly across the beat.

## The relationship with two against three

If one hand plays a duplet while the other hand plays three quavers at the same time, you get a two-against-three rhythm.

This kind of different rhythm in the two hands calls for fairly good hand independence.

You can practise each hand alone first, then slowly put them together and find where the notes of the two hands line up.

## Duplets in summary

The duplet is a common rhythmic variation in compound time, and the key to understanding it is to feel the three-part division first and then cut it evenly in half.

It and the triplet are mirror images of each other. Once you have learned one, the other is not hard to understand.

Count a lot, tap a lot and listen a lot, and duplets will become natural.

## How duplets are written

A duplet is often written as two quavers with a "2" above them.

Some scores write it with two dotted quavers instead, which needs no "2" and whose value is also exactly one main beat.

The two ways of writing it sound the same when played.

## Comparing with triplets

A triplet puts three notes evenly into a beat that is normally divided in two, for example three notes in one beat of 2/4.

A duplet puts two notes evenly into a beat that is normally divided in three.

The idea behind the two is the same, only the direction is opposite.

**Notice the details**
- Often found in compound time such as 6/8
- Two even notes in one beat, marked "2"
- The exact opposite of the triplet
- Feel the three-part division first, then cut it evenly in half

## The effect of a duplet

When a duplet suddenly appears in a flowing three-part rhythm, the music seems to "pause" or "broaden" for a moment.

It is like suddenly taking a bigger step while dancing.

Composers often use this device to create rhythmic variety and surprise.

![An Art Deco style illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a desk lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa34ega-wrhtn.webp)

## Recognising them in a piece

In a piece in 6/8, 9/8 or 12/8, if you see a "2" written above two notes, you can be sure it is a duplet.

You can also look out for places where dotted quavers appear in pairs, which often have the effect of a duplet too.

When reading the music, circle these places first and practise them on their own.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a duplet?**
A: Two notes placed evenly in a beat that divides in three.

**Q: In which time signatures does it often appear?**
A: Compound times such as 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8.

**Q: How does it relate to the triplet?**
A: It goes the opposite way: one puts two in the space of three, the other three in the space of two.

**Q: How do you count a duplet?**
A: First count three quavers, then cut the main beat evenly in half.

**Q: What are the common mistakes?**
A: Playing it unevenly, or playing the beat too short.
