finger-pedaling-hold-notes-without-pedal.body:
"Finger pedaling" means using your fingers to hold certain notes down a little longer than written, so that they are still sounding after the next note comes in, giving a connected effect similar to the pedal. For example, in a broken chord, you hold the bass note and a few of the other notes until the chord changes. This method is especially useful in Baroque and Classical works, which often call for little pedal but still need the sound not to seem dry.

## Connection beyond the pedal

The sustain pedal lets all the notes continue together, but sometimes that makes the sound too blurry.

Finger pedaling lets only certain notes continue, while the other notes are released as usual.

This gives a connected effect while keeping the sound clear.

![A piano scene with futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3x6d8-u0hd1.webp)

## Using it together with the pedal

Finger pedaling does not have to replace the pedal completely; it can also be used together with it.

For example, where more resonance is needed, you can use a little half pedal while holding the bass note with your fingers.

This gives finer control over the sound.

## Use in Baroque works

Keyboard instruments of the Baroque period had no sustain pedal, so this kind of music often uses little pedal on the piano.

But if there is no sustain of any kind, the sound can seem a little dry.

With finger pedaling, you can let some chord notes sustain slightly without using the pedal, making the sound warmer.

## Listen to the effect of finger pedaling

After using finger pedaling, listen carefully with your ears to whether the sound has become more connected without becoming too blurry.

If it sounds a bit muddy, hold fewer notes, or release them earlier.

If it is still too dry, try holding one or two more notes.

## The teacher's advice

How to use finger pedaling often depends on the style of the work, the edition and personal interpretation.

In the lesson you can ask your teacher to demonstrate where finger pedaling suits and how long to hold.

Listening to the teacher's demonstration is easier than feeling your way to the right sound on your own.

## Use in Classical works

In Classical works by Mozart, Haydn and others, the pedal is usually used very little.

Here finger pedaling becomes an important way to keep the accompaniment connected.

In the left-hand accompaniment of many Classical works, holding the bass note gives a better effect.

## Do not let the hand tense up

When you hold one note, the other fingers still have to keep playing, which takes some finger independence.

If you tense the whole hand to hold one note, it will affect the playing of the other notes.

You can practise slowly at first, letting the finger holding the note press lightly, without pressing hard.

## Use in right-hand accompaniment

The right hand sometimes plays broken-chord accompaniment too, and finger pedaling can be used there as well.

For example, hold the first note of each broken chord and play the other notes at the written note values.

This makes the accompaniment softer, without joining up the melody as well, as the pedal would.

## Use in broken chords

Broken chords are a very good place to use finger pedaling.

For example, in an Alberti bass such as C, G, E, G in the left hand, you can hold the C until the chord changes.

That way the bass keeps sounding, the harmony sounds more complete, and the other notes stay clear.

## Summary: finger pedaling

Finger pedaling means using the fingers to hold some notes longer, giving a pedal-like connected effect.

It is especially suited to Baroque and Classical works, and to broken-chord accompaniment.

Mastering it lets you play with a warm and clear sound even when using little pedal.

## When to release

The key to finger pedaling is knowing when to release the held note.

In general, when the chord changes you should release the notes of the previous chord, otherwise different chords will blur together.

You can mark on the score the places where the chord changes, as a reminder to release there.

## Getting started with finger pedaling

You can start by finding a simple Alberti bass and practising holding the bass note until the chord changes.

Then look for places in the piece you are working on where finger pedaling can be used.

Use a pencil to draw an extended line on the held notes as a reminder to hold them down.

**A different angle**
- Hold notes down longer than written with your fingers
- Get a pedal-like connected effect
- In broken chords, hold the bass and some of the notes
- Suited to Baroque and Classical works

## What is finger pedaling

Finger pedaling means using the fingers in place of the pedal, holding certain notes a little longer than written.

For example, the score shows an eighth note, but you hold it down past the half beat so that it overlaps with the notes that follow.

These extended notes sound as if they had been kept by the pedal, making the harmony fuller.

## FAQ

**Q: What is finger pedaling?**
A: Using the fingers to hold certain notes longer than written.

**Q: Where is it suitable?**
A: Broken-chord accompaniment, and Baroque and Classical works.

**Q: When do I release the held notes?**
A: Usually when the chord changes.

**Q: Can I use it together with the pedal?**
A: Yes, for example a half pedal together with a held bass note.

**Q: Will holding notes make my hand tense?**
A: Press lightly, without pressing hard.

fengyang-flower-drum-anhui-folk-piano.body:
"Let's talk of Fengyang, tell of Fengyang, Fengyang is a fine place" is how the Anhui folk song Fengyang Flower Drum begins. The flower drum is a folk song-and-dance form from the Fengyang area of Anhui, in which the performers sing while beating a small drum or a small gong. The song has a bright rhythm and a bouncy melody, and its nonsense syllables "de er lang dang piao yi piao" imitate the sound of the drumbeats, which is great fun. When you play Fengyang Flower Drum on the piano, let the left hand play clear "drumbeats" and let the right hand sing a light, lively melody.

## Say the words first, then play

If you know the lyrics, you can first say them aloud in rhythm, especially the nonsense syllables.

Once you have the rhythm in your mouth, play it on the piano and the rhythm will be more accurate.

This helps a lot with mastering dotted rhythms and short, crisp notes.

## Summary of Fengyang Flower Drum

Fengyang Flower Drum comes from the folk song-and-dance form of the Fengyang area of Anhui, in which performers beat a drum while singing. The lyrics are plain and have a spoken, storytelling flavour, and nonsense syllables such as "de er lang dang piao yi piao" imitate the drumbeats. The rhythm is bright, with frequent dotted rhythms and short notes.

The left hand can use short octaves or fifths to imitate the drumbeats, and the right hand's leaping melody should be light. The accompaniment mostly uses notes of the pentatonic scale, and the tempo can be a little fast but must not get messy. You can add variation between the verses.

When you play, imagine the drum and the gong. You can clap the rhythm with children, say the lyrics before playing, and ask Teacher Aum to listen to the left-hand drumbeats.

## What is the Fengyang flower drum

The flower drum is a folk song-and-dance form handed down in the Fengyang area of Anhui.

Performers often hold a small drum in one hand and a drumstick in the other, beating and singing at the same time.

This kind of performance is lively and cheerful, and it is much loved by local people.

## Clapping the rhythm with children

The rhythm of this folk song is perfect for playing with children.

Let the child clap the "de er lang dang" rhythm with their hands while a parent plays the melody on the piano.

You can also swap, with the child playing a simple left hand and the parent singing.

## The drum and gong patterns of the flower drum

In folk flower drum performances, the drum and gong are often struck in set patterns, which people call "luogu jing" (percussion patterns).

The introduction and interludes of a piano version can imitate such a pattern: a few low notes, one high note, then half a beat of rest.

Put a bar like that between two verses, and the whole piece gets an opening and a connecting passage.

## The right hand's leaping melody

The right-hand melody has quite a few leaps, which make it lively and playful.

When you play, keep the wrist relaxed so that every leap is light.

You can use light staccato to bring out the spoken, storytelling feeling.

## How fast should the flower drum go

Fengyang Flower Drum can be played a little fast, with a lively, festive mood.

But the tempo should not be so fast that the rhythm falls apart.

You can first make the rhythm steady at a moderate speed, then gradually speed up.

## Imagining percussion

When you play this piece, you can imagine a drum and a gong accompanying you beside the piano.

The left-hand low notes are like the big drum, and the higher chords are like the small gong.

This imagining helps the left hand produce different tone colours.

## The rhythm of the flower drum

The rhythm of Fengyang Flower Drum is bright, often with short notes and dotted rhythms.

This rhythm is connected with the drum-beating movements of the performance.

When you play, keep the rhythm crisp and clear, without dragging.

## The left-hand "drumbeats"

The left hand can use short octaves or fifths to imitate the sound of a drum.

For example, play a low note at the start of each beat, then a lighter note on the second half of the beat.

The left-hand rhythm should be steady, like a drummer who keeps on beating.

## The lyrics of Fengyang Flower Drum

The lyrics of Fengyang Flower Drum begin with "Let's talk of Fengyang, tell of Fengyang" and tell about the place Fengyang.

The lyrics are plain and direct, with the character of spoken, storytelling song.

After each verse there is often a passage of nonsense syllables imitating drumbeats.

- Folk song-and-dance from the Fengyang area of Anhui
- Performers beat a drum while singing
- The nonsense syllables imitate the sound of drumbeats
- The left hand should play a clear rhythm

## The "de er lang dang" nonsense syllables

Nonsense syllables such as "de er lang dang piao yi piao" imitate the sounds of beating a drum and striking a gong.

These syllables fill the song with rhythm and add to the fun.

On the piano, the sections with nonsense syllables can be played with more spring, bouncing like drumbeats.

## Each verse more lively than the last

This folk song has several verses, with basically the same melody.

When playing the piano version, you can make each verse different in dynamics, register or accompaniment.

For example, thicken the left hand in the last verse to bring out an even livelier atmosphere.

## Asking your teacher to listen to the drumbeats in the lesson

In the lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your left-hand "drumbeats" are clear and steady.

Your teacher can also help adjust the leaping feel of the right-hand melody.

If needed, your teacher can also help simplify or enrich the accompaniment.

## The pentatonic scale and folk flavour

The tune of Fengyang Flower Drum goes round and round on just five notes, and its rustic flavour shows immediately.

The accompaniment chords can also use notes of the pentatonic scale as much as possible.

**Give it a try**

That makes the style of the whole piece more unified.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaa6o5m-4fuc5.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What kind of performance is the flower drum?**
A: A folk song-and-dance form in which people sing while beating a small drum.

**Q: What do the nonsense syllables "de er lang dang" imitate?**
A: The sound of drumbeats and gongs.

**Q: How can the left hand imitate the drumbeats?**
A: With short octaves or fifths.

**Q: What is special about the right-hand melody?**
A: It has quite a few leaps, and is lively and playful.

**Q: What can I do together with children?**
A: Clap the rhythm of the nonsense syllables.

fast-passage-burst-practice.body:
When practising a fast passage, one method is to split it into small groups of notes, play each group quickly in a burst at close to the target tempo, then land on the first note of the next group and stop, relax and prepare, before bursting through the next group. This short-burst way of practising lets your fingers experience fast movement in advance, without getting tense from playing at speed for a long time. Once every group can be played cleanly in a burst, join two groups together, then three, until the whole passage can be played in one go.

## How Much to Practise at a Time

Short-burst practice is fairly intense, so you do not need to do it for long. A few minutes for each difficult spot is enough.

It suits the time just after you have warmed up, when your mind is still fully focused.

When you have finished, you can play the whole passage once more at a moderate tempo to feel the effect of playing it connected.

## Suitable Passages

Scale fragments, arpeggios and cadenza-like fast running passages are all well suited to short bursts.

For chord passages that need a lot of strength, other methods of practice may be needed.

If you are not sure whether a passage suits it, you can ask your teacher for some advice.

## Changing Where You Stop

To make sure every note gets practised, you can change the starting point of the grouping, for example starting the groups from the second note.

That way, the notes that used to be in the middle of a group become the places where you stop, and you can check the state of your hand in different places.

Try several ways of grouping, and the whole passage will become more even and stable.

## Why Slow Practice Alone Is Not Enough

Slow practice helps us build accurate notes and fingering, but the finger movements at slow speed are not quite the same as at fast speed.

When playing fast, the fingers must move more lightly and in smaller movements, and the wrist and arm must work together more flexibly.

If you only practise slowly and then suddenly speed up, your hand may not have time to adapt to this different way of moving.

## What to Do During the Pause

At the end of each burst, when you stop on a note, you can let your wrist and arm relax and feel the weight of your hand resting on the keys.

At the same time, think ahead to the notes and fingering of the next group, so your fingers are ready in advance.

You can pause for longer, until you feel completely prepared, and then begin the next burst.

## Stay Relaxed

When bursting through a passage, the hand easily becomes tense, so pay special attention to the state of your shoulders, arms and wrists.

If you feel tension, relax for a bit longer during the pause, or slow down the speed of the burst.

If your hand or arm feels pain, stop and rest immediately, and do not carry on practising.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline and elevated railway at dusk](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0gunq-1ggo7.webp)

## How to Group the Notes

You can divide a run of fast notes into groups of four, adding the first note of the next group, as one burst.

For example, with eight sixteenth notes, you can first play the first four plus the fifth, and stop. Then start again from the fifth, play to the eighth plus the first note of the next beat, and stop.

The way you group can be adjusted according to the phrase and fingering, for example groups of three notes or six notes.

## Combine It with Rhythm Variations

The short-burst method can also be combined with rhythm-variation practice, for example using dotted rhythms during the burst.

Different methods exercise the fingers from different angles, and you can alternate them so practice does not become monotonous.

Depending on the nature of the difficult spot, you can discuss with your teacher which method is more suitable.

## Joining the Groups Up

Once every group can be played cleanly in a burst, you can join two groups together as a longer burst.

Then three groups, four groups, gradually increasing the length of each burst.

Finally, the whole fast passage can be played in one go, with no need to pause in between.

- Split the fast passage into small groups of notes
- Play each group at close to the target tempo
- Stop on the first note of the next group and relax
- Join the groups together step by step

## The Speed of the Burst

The speed of the burst can be close to the target tempo of the piece, or even slightly faster.

But the condition is that every group is played cleanly and clearly. If you keep making mistakes in the burst, the speed is still too fast, and you need to slow down a little.

Gradually, you will find a burst speed that is both fast and accurate.

## The Idea Behind Short Bursts

The short-burst method lets the hand experience fast movement for a very short time, then stop and rest straight away.

Because you play only a few notes at a time, your hand does not become tense or tired from long periods at high speed.

**A Small Tip**

During the pause, you can also check whether your hand is relaxed and whether the notes and fingering of the next group are ready.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is short-burst practice?**
A: Play a small group of notes quickly, then stop on the first note of the next group.

**Q: Why not just practise slowly?**
A: The finger movements at fast speed are not quite the same as at slow speed.

**Q: How fast should the burst be?**
A: Close to the target tempo, but every group must be clean and clear.

**Q: What should I do during the pause?**
A: Relax your wrist and arm, and prepare the notes and fingering of the next group.

**Q: How do I join the groups up?**
A: Start by joining two groups, then gradually increase the length.

**Q: What if my hand hurts?**
A: Stop and rest immediately.

expressionism-in-music-schoenberg-1912.body:
Expressionism was an artistic movement that emerged in Germany and Austria in the early twentieth century. Painters, poets and composers all wanted to express intense, tense inner emotions in an exaggerated and direct way, rather than depict the outside world. In music, it is often linked with the three Viennese composers Schoenberg, Berg and Webern. Their music often no longer has a clear tonal centre, with sharp harmonies and leaping melodies. In 1912, Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire premiered in Berlin, in which a female voice performs twenty-one poems in a style between speaking and singing called Sprechgesang ("speech-song"), making it one of the landmark works of this movement.

## The sharp harmonies of expressionism

The harmony of expressionist music is often very sharp, with many dissonant intervals.

These harmonies do not resolve into consonant chords but stay tense.

This tense sound is exactly what is needed to express intense inner feeling.

**Slow down**
- An artistic movement in early twentieth-century Germany and Austria
- Expresses intense, tense inner emotion
- Schoenberg, Berg, Webern
- 1912: Pierrot Lunaire uses Sprechgesang

## The inner world

Expressionist artists are not very concerned with what the outside world looks like.

They want to express what people feel inside, especially those intense, tense emotions.

To express these emotions, they often create in exaggerated and distorted ways.

## Pierrot Lunaire

In 1912, Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire premiered in Berlin.

The work is written for one female voice and five instrumentalists, performing twenty-one poems that tell of the fantastical adventures of a clown named Pierrot under the moonlight.

The poems are strange and grotesque, and the music is full of novel sounds.

## Feeling the absence of a tonal centre on the piano

On the piano, you can play a few notes that are far apart at random, without letting them settle into any key.

For example, play a low note first, then leap to a very high note, then play a note a semitone away.

Listen to this centreless sound and notice how it differs from the tonal music you usually play.

## Leaping melodies

The melodies of expressionist music often have very large leaps, jumping from a low note to a very high one in an instant.

The melodic lines are very irregular and not as easy to sing as traditional melodies.

These leaping melodies create a feeling of unease and agitation.

## No tonal centre

One characteristic of expressionist music is that it often no longer has a clear tonal centre.

In traditional music, melody and harmony revolve around a tonic and finally return to the tonic to end.

In these works, all the notes are about equally important, and there is no centre.

## Sprechgesang

In Pierrot Lunaire, the female voice uses a method called "Sprechgesang".

It lies between speaking and singing: the singer glides past the pitch marked in the score, as in speech, rather than singing firmly on the note.

This sound is very distinctive, with a dreamy, grotesque colour.

## Schoenberg's short piano pieces

Schoenberg wrote several sets of short piano pieces, for example the Six Little Piano Pieces, Op. 19, from 1911.

These little pieces are very short, some only a few bars long, but they need very delicate control of dynamics.

If you have some experience, you can find a recording to listen to and get a feel for expressionist piano music.

## The Viennese composers

In music, expressionism is often linked with three Viennese composers: Schoenberg, Berg and Webern.

Schoenberg was the teacher, and Berg and Webern were his students.

They later came to be called the "Second Viennese School".

![Black-and-white stipple drawing of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk2po7-4s1yl.webp)

## What came next

In the 1920s, Schoenberg developed the "twelve-tone technique", a systematic way to organise the twelve semitones.

This method later influenced many composers.

The expressionist movement also gradually developed into other styles.

## Summary of musical expressionism

Expressionism is an early twentieth-century German and Austrian artistic movement that wanted to express intense, tense inner emotion in an exaggerated and direct way. Painters used strong colours and distorted lines. In music it is often linked with Schoenberg and his students Berg and Webern, known as the "Second Viennese School". Their music often has no clear tonal centre, with sharp harmonies that do not resolve and large melodic leaps.

In 1912, Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire premiered in Berlin, with one female voice and five instrumentalists performing twenty-one poems, using Sprechgesang, between speaking and singing. Some of Webern's works last only a minute or two. In the 1920s Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone technique. On the piano you can play a few notes far apart to feel the absence of a tonal centre, and you can also listen to Schoenberg's Six Little Piano Pieces, Op. 19.

You can talk about expressionism with Teacher Aum.

## The painters' work

In painting, expressionist painters often used strong colours and distorted lines.

For example, a sky might be red and a person's face stretched out of shape.

These pictures do not look like reality, yet they let you feel intense emotion.

## Short works

Some works by expressionist composers are very short. For example, some of Webern's pieces last only a minute or two.

They use very few notes to express very concentrated emotion.

Every note matters and needs to be listened to carefully.

## Talking about expressionism with your teacher in the lesson

In the lesson, you can listen to a passage of Pierrot Lunaire together with Teacher Aum and pay attention to the Sprechgesang sound.

You can also ask your teacher to demonstrate the delicate dynamic changes in Schoenberg's piano pieces.

**Before you try it**

Get to know the new sounds of the twentieth century through one intense artistic movement.

## FAQ

**Q: When and where did expressionism appear?**
A: In early twentieth-century Germany and Austria.

**Q: What did it want to express?**
A: Intense, tense inner emotion.

**Q: Which three composers is it often linked with in music?**
A: Schoenberg, Berg and Webern.

**Q: In which year did Pierrot Lunaire premiere?**
A: In 1912, in Berlin.

**Q: What is Sprechgesang?**
A: A way of vocal performance between speaking and singing.

ear-training-echo-intervals.body:
Ear training can begin with a very simple game: listen to a short melody, sing it back with your voice first, then find it on the piano. This "listen, sing, find" echo exercise connects your ears, your voice and your fingers. Once echoing feels comfortable, you can go on to recognise the distance between two notes, called an "interval". This article is split into three stages by difficulty, to help beginners build a foundation in listening step by step.

## Key Points

- Ear training starts not with theory, but with being able to sing back what you hear
- The order of an echo exercise is fixed: listen first, then sing, and play last
- An interval is the distance between two notes, measured in semitones
- At first, tell apart "near and far" before learning interval names
- Shorter sessions done more often usually work more steadily

## What Is an "Echo Exercise"?

An echo exercise is like an echo in a valley: the other person sings a phrase, and you sing it back exactly. In piano learning, "the other person" can be a teacher, a parent, or a short phrase played by an app. The point is to receive the sound by ear alone, without looking at the keys or at the music.

Why sing before playing? Because when you sing, you have to "think" the pitch of the note in your head first. If you just try things at random on the piano, it easily becomes your fingers trying their luck, and your ears are left out.

## Stage One: Short Phrases of Two or Three Notes

**How to practise**
Start with three neighbouring notes near middle C, for example different combinations of Do, Re and Mi. Each time, listen to a three-note phrase, sing it back, then find it on the piano.

**A small tip**
When you cannot find it, first fix the opening note, then decide whether each following note goes "up" or "down". Once the direction is right, you are most of the way there.

## Stage Two: A Wider Range and Rhythm Changes

**How to practise**
Lengthen the phrases to four or five notes and add rhythms of different lengths. You will find that rhythm is also information your ears need to remember.

**A small tip**
You can clap the rhythm lightly while singing, then play it on the piano. Handling melody and rhythm separately makes it easier.

![Grey-purple watercolour grand piano with the lid open, suggesting listening to tone](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvv1y4a2-358s4.webp)

## Stage Three: Getting to Know Common Intervals

When you can echo four or five notes reliably, you can begin to give "distance" a name. On the piano, two adjacent keys (black keys included) are one semitone apart. Starting from C:

- **Major second:** C to D, two semitones, sounds like "taking a step"
- **Major third:** C to E, four semitones, sounds bright
- **Minor third:** C to E♭, three semitones, sounds a little softer
- **Perfect fourth:** C to F, five semitones
- **Perfect fifth:** C to G, seven semitones, sounds open and stable
- **Perfect octave:** C to the C above, twelve semitones, the two notes sound like "a higher and a lower version of the same note"

How to practise: play each of these intervals on the piano, first melodically (one after the other), then harmonically (pressed together), and notice how their "characters" differ.

## A One-Week Ear Training Plan

- Five minutes a day, ten three-note phrases from stage one
- Once you are accurate and steady, switch to the longer phrases of stage two
- Before finishing each day, play the six intervals above once, just listening, not memorising
- At the weekend, take a small quiz: ask someone at home to play intervals at random while you say "far or near"

This kind of small, gradual step is common in music teaching and works as a warm-up in any piano course.

## Three Common Mistakes in Ear Training

**Mistake one: memorising interval names right away**
If you remember the names but your ear cannot tell the intervals apart, ear training has lost its point. Build the "sound sense" first, then put labels on it.

**Mistake two: practising for too long at a time**
Ear training takes a lot of attention, and over a long session the ears tire and judgements become careless. Short and frequent suits better than one long stretch.

**Mistake three: only searching on the piano and never singing**
If you skip the singing step, the connection between ear and voice never gets built. Even quiet humming helps more than not singing.

## FAQ

**Q: I sing out of tune. Can I still do ear training?**

A: Yes. The aim of ear training is not to sing beautifully but to connect your ears with pitch. Singing inaccurately does not matter; try humming first, then check on the piano.

**Q: How does ear training actually help with learning piano?**

A: With sharper ears, it is easier to notice wrong notes when you play, and easier to remember melodies. When reading music, you can also "hear" the notes in your head more quickly.

**Q: Can you train your ears well by learning piano online?**

**Q: Must I memorise the interval names?**

A: There is no rush at first. Tell apart far and near, bright and dark first, and then slowly match them to names. Theory is there so that what your ears feel has a name to be called by.

escape-tone-echappee-step-then-leap.body:
Many notes in a melody do not belong to the chord sounding at the time. They are called non-chord tones. Passing tones and neighbour tones are familiar to most people, and there is another kind called the "escape tone" (French: échappée), which moves in a very distinctive way. It starts from a chord tone and leaves by step, but then, instead of carrying on in the same direction, it leaps in the opposite direction to the next chord tone, as if it had "escaped" from the original path. Recognising this kind of note helps us understand some notes in a melody that seem to be "extra".

## Where Escape Tones Often Appear

Escape tones usually hide behind a weak beat or an off-beat, and carry very little weight.

In melodies of the Classical period, they often appear just before a phrase ending, adding a little decoration to the cadence.

For example, a melody rises one step from the tonic, then leaps down to the leading note, and then returns to the tonic.

## How It Differs from a Neighbour Tone

A neighbour tone leaves a chord tone by step and returns by step to the same note, for example C, D, C.

An escape tone does not return to the original note after leaving; it leaps to a different chord tone.

So to tell them apart, look at whether it leaves by step or by leap, and whether it returns to the original note.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa807qi-wet2q.webp)

## What Is a Non-Chord Tone

In a piece of music, there is usually a chord supporting the music behind every moment.

The notes of the melody that belong to this chord are called chord tones; those that do not are called non-chord tones.

Non-chord tones make a melody flow better and add variety, and there are different kinds, distinguished by how they are approached and left.

## Why It Helps to Understand Non-Chord Tones

Learning the different non-chord tones is not about sticking a label on every note.

What matters more is understanding why these notes make a melody sound smooth, tense or relaxed.

Once you know what they do, you can tell more clearly when you play which notes to bring out and which to pass over lightly.

- The escape tone is a kind of non-chord tone
- It leaves a chord tone by step
- Then leaps in the opposite direction to the next chord tone
- It often appears on weak beats and is common before a cadence

## How to Handle It in Performance

An escape tone is usually a little lighter than the chord tones around it, because it is on a weak beat and is decorative.

When you play it, do not play it too heavily, or the melody will sound abrupt.

But it should not be played too vaguely either; let listeners clearly hear this little "peek out".

## Finding Escape Tones in a Score

To find an escape tone, first work out what the chord is at each point.

Then look at the notes of the melody that do not belong to the chord, and check how they are approached and left.

If the approach is by step and the departure is a leap in the opposite direction, it is very likely an escape tone.

## Escape Tones Compared with Appoggiaturas

An appoggiatura is usually "approached by leap, resolved by step", often falls on a strong beat, and has a feeling of yearning.

The escape tone is exactly the opposite: "approached by step, left by leap", and it mostly appears on weak beats.

You can think of them as a pair of non-chord tones moving in opposite ways.

## Escape Tones and Musical Style

In the time of Bach and Mozart, the directions of approach and departure for escape tones mostly followed the rules.

In Romantic and later music, composers used non-chord tones more freely, and they are sometimes hard to classify strictly.

So be flexible when analysing; the point is to understand what the note does in the melody.

## Escape Tones in Brief

An escape tone is a non-chord tone that leaves a chord tone by step, then leaps in the opposite direction to the next chord tone. It differs from a passing tone and a neighbour tone in how and in which direction it leaves.

It moves in the opposite way to an appoggiatura, mostly appears on weak beats, and in the Classical period is common before a phrase ending. To find one, first identify the chord, then look at the motion before and after the note.

When playing, an escape tone should be lighter than the chord tones but still clear. You can compare a melody with and without the escape tone on the piano, and you can also try writing one yourself.

## Write an Escape Tone Yourself

You can try writing a simple melody and adding an escape tone just before a cadence.

For example, at a "tonic chord to dominant chord" moment, let the melody rise one step from a note of the tonic chord, then leap to a note of the dominant chord.

When you have written it, play it, and listen to whether this small decoration makes the melody more lively.

## How an Escape Tone Moves

The feature of an escape tone is "approached by step, left by leap", and the two motions go in opposite directions.

For example, moving up by step from C to D, then leaping down from D to B, the D here is an escape tone.

C and B belong to the chords before and after, while D does not; it is like the melody briefly peeking outside.

## Playing an Escape Tone in C Major

You can try it in C major: play a C major triad in the left hand and C, D in the right hand, then change the left hand to a G major triad and leap the right hand to B.

Listen to the D. It is a little unstable over the C chord, and then when it leaps to B there is a feeling of landing gently.

Then replace the D by going directly from C to B, and compare the effect of the two melodies.

## How It Differs from a Passing Tone

A passing tone is also approached by step, but it carries on by step in the same direction to the next chord tone.

For example, in C, D, E, the D fills the gap between two chord tones, so it is a passing tone.

An escape tone does not keep going forward; it changes direction and leaps away, so the two sound different.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How does an escape tone approach and leave?**
A: It is approached by step and left by a leap in the opposite direction.

**Q: How does it differ from a passing tone?**
A: A passing tone continues by step in the same direction.

**Q: Is it usually on a strong beat or a weak beat?**
A: Usually on a weak beat.

**Q: How is it related to an appoggiatura?**
A: They move in opposite ways: an appoggiatura is approached by leap and resolved by step.

**Q: How should I play it?**
A: Lighter than the chord tones, but clearly.

focus-practice-big-exam-week.body:
In the week of a big school exam or an important test, it makes sense to cut back on practice time and switch to short, focused sessions, for example ten to fifteen minutes a day, reviewing pieces you already know and keeping your hands in shape rather than learning anything new. Once the exam is over, you can gradually return to your usual practice plan. That way your schoolwork does not suffer, and your piano progress does not come to a complete stop.

## Planning your time in exam week

Exam week is usually the busiest time for students, and revising takes a lot of time and energy.

If you still practise for as long as you normally do, it can feel very stressful, and it is hard to do justice to both.

A more realistic approach is to talk with your family and your teacher ahead of time and adjust the practice plan for this one week.

## Talking to your teacher

If you have a piano lesson during exam week, let your teacher know in advance and discuss whether the content of the lesson should change, or whether the lesson should be rescheduled.

Once the teacher understands the situation, they can set lighter practice tasks, or focus on review in the lesson.

Many teachers understand the pressure students are under during exams, and speaking up early makes the arrangements go more smoothly.

## What parents can do

Parents can help their child plan the time in exam week and keep piano practice relaxed, so that it does not become extra pressure.

If your child wants to play the piano to unwind, support that; if they are too tired, let them rest.

After the exam, you can sit down with your child and make a plan for getting back into practice.

If your child feels anxious in exam week because of the amount of homework, you can turn piano time into a relaxing break rather than another task.

## Find a regular time slot

Between revision sessions, set aside some piano time at about the same time each day, for example after dinner or after an hour of studying.

A regular time slot turns practice into a small rhythm in the daily schedule, and saves you the trouble of deciding each day when to fit it in.

When you practise, put your phone and books aside, play with full attention for a dozen minutes or so, and then go back to your revision.

**Have a listen**
- Practice time can be shortened in exam week
- Focus mainly on reviewing familiar pieces
- Use a regular short time slot to keep the habit going
- After the exam, gradually return to your usual amount of practice

## Balancing schoolwork and music

Schoolwork and music both matter, and at different times you can give more weight to one or the other.

It is perfectly natural to put schoolwork first during exam week and spend more time at the piano during the holidays.

Learning to adjust your plan to the situation is itself a very useful skill, and it comes in handy in other areas of study and life too.

## Focus on review

This week you can concentrate on reviewing pieces you have already learned, rather than starting new, difficult material.

Playing familiar pieces does not take much thinking, and it feels less stressful.

You can also pick one or two technical trouble spots and do a little maintenance practice on them, to hold on to the progress you have already made.

## Shorten, do not stop

You do not have to stop practising completely in exam week. Keeping up ten to fifteen minutes a day helps your fingers from getting too rusty.

A short session also gives a tense revision schedule some variety, letting your brain step away from the books for a moment.

If one day is especially busy, skipping it is fine. The important thing is not to add extra burden for yourself.

## Getting back after the exam

After the exam, there is no need to return to your old practice time straight away. You can build it up over a few days.

On the first day, play familiar pieces to find your feel again; over the next few days, slowly bring in new material.

Returning step by step like this is easier to keep up than suddenly increasing the amount you practise.

![A person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xqucl-irtqe.webp)

## What to do in a short practice session

In those dozen or so minutes in exam week, you can spend two or three minutes warming up with scales, then ten minutes playing one or two familiar pieces.

If there is time left, pick a small tricky spot you have practised before and play it slowly a few times to make sure you still remember it.

This kind of plan is simple and fixed, so you do not have to spend time deciding what to practise. You can sit down and begin, and go straight back to revision when you finish.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is it all right not to practise at all in exam week?**
A: Yes, but a few minutes of practice each day helps you keep your feel for the keys.

**Q: Should I still go to my piano lesson in exam week?**
A: You can talk to your teacher about changing the content of the lesson or rescheduling it.

**Q: Will practising get in the way of revision?**
A: Short sessions at a regular time usually do not, and sometimes they even help you switch moods.

**Q: How long after the exam until I can get back to normal practice?**
A: You can build up the amount of practice gradually over a few days.

**Q: Is exam week a good time to learn a new piece?**
A: It is generally recommended to focus on review and leave new pieces until after the exam.

**Q: Is it all right for my child to play the piano to unwind?**
A: Yes, as long as it does not get in the way of revision and rest.

first-second-ending-brackets.body:
First and second endings are common repeat markings in sheet music. The first time through, play the first ending as written, then go back to where the repeat begins. The second time, skip the first ending and go straight into the second ending. If you draw the route on the score, you will always know which path to take on each pass.

## How the Brackets Are Written and What They Cover

First and second ending brackets are usually drawn above the staff, with a horizontal line and a short downward vertical line enclosing one or more bars, and a number 1 or 2 written inside. The bars the bracket covers are the extent of that ending.

**Summary**

A first ending sometimes covers just one bar and sometimes several. When reading, check where the bracket's horizontal line ends so you know where the first ending finishes.

A second ending bracket sometimes runs on into the next section, or may have no closing vertical line, which means the music simply continues onward.

Seeing clearly where the brackets begin and end is the first step to carrying out the repeat correctly.

## How the Music Changes Between the Two Passes

The first and second endings usually differ in content. The end of the first ending often leads the music back to the beginning, while the end of the second ending often carries the music toward the close or the next section.

Listen to the harmony of the two endings and you will notice that the first ending often stops at a less final point, while the second ending feels more conclusive.

When playing, pay attention to this difference: keep a sense of "going on" at the end of the first ending, and give a fuller close at the end of the second.

Understanding the change between the two passes makes a repeat more than mere repetition: it becomes music that develops.

In ensemble playing, your route through the endings must match your partners'. Before rehearsing, confirm the playing order together so that nobody takes a wrong turn.

## Common Combinations With Repeat Signs

First and second endings are usually used together with repeat signs. A repeat sign is made of two vertical lines and two dots, and the side the dots face shows where the repeat starts. If you cannot find a starting repeat sign, you normally go back to the beginning of the piece.

In some pieces the first ending is long, covering several bars, and the second ending may run on into the next section. When practising, look over the whole structure first and mark the different paths with coloured pens.

Once you are comfortable with first and second endings, learning signs such as D.C., D.S. and Coda becomes much easier. They all tell the player the route through the piece; they just are written differently and jump in different ways.

## Marking Your Score

To avoid taking a wrong turn, draw arrows in pencil on the score: one from the end of the first ending pointing back to the repeat start, and another going around the first ending to the second ending.

You can also use pens of different colours at the start of the first and second endings, so your eyes immediately see the difference between the two routes.

For pieces with a complex structure, you can write the playing order in the margin, for example "Section A twice, first ending the first time, second ending the second time".

Once the markings are clear, you can put more of your attention on the music itself while practising.

Keep the markings simple and clear, and avoid making the score too messy.

![Watercolour of a grand piano with the lid open in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8kj396-vrh13.webp)

## The Order of Play

On the first pass, play in order up to the end of the first ending, then, at the repeat sign, go back to where the repeat begins.

On the second pass, when you reach the point where the first ending begins, skip the whole first ending and go straight on into the second ending.

Some pieces also have a third ending, used in a similar way: on the third pass, skip the first and second endings and go into the third.

If the start of the repeat is not at the beginning of the piece, look for the repeat sign facing right and begin the second pass from there.

**Another way to look at it**

The first time you practise a piece with brackets, play through the route of both passes at a very slow tempo to confirm every turn is correct, then speed up gradually.

- First pass: play the first ending, then go back to the repeat start
- Second pass: skip the first ending and go straight into the second
- Sometimes there is also a third ending, used the same way
- Drawing arrows on the score helps you remember the route

## FAQ

**Q: Can the first and second endings be different lengths?**
A: Yes. The two endings need not be the same length. Just play the bars marked in the score.

**Q: Is there another repeat after the second ending?**
A: Generally not, unless the score has a new repeat sign or another jump marking.

**Q: Can the repeat sign at the end of the first ending be left out?**
A: No. It tells the player to go back to where the repeat begins.

**Q: Can there be another repeat after the second ending?**
A: If the score has a new repeat sign, follow that new sign.

**Q: Should the second pass of a repeat sound different?**
A: Depending on the style and your teacher's advice, you may vary the dynamics or expression a little.

**Q: What if I cannot find where the repeat starts?**
A: If there is no right-facing repeat sign earlier, you normally repeat from the beginning of the piece.

find-the-core-one-goal-practice.body:
When throwing a pot, the first step is to place the clay at the exact centre of the wheel; once it is centred, the shaping that follows is easier. Practising the piano works in a similar way: if the basic rhythm and hand shape of a passage are not yet steady, rushing to add speed and expression often makes it more and more messy. First focus on the single most essential thing, then add other demands step by step.

## How to tell what the core is

When you start a new piece, you can first ask yourself: what is the hardest and most important thing in this passage?

**Think about it**

If it is a fast scale, the core may be an even rhythm and steady fingering.

If it is a lyrical melody, the core may be a connected touch and clear phrasing.

If it is an accompaniment with many chords, the core may be the changes of hand position.

You can also ask your teacher to help you decide; a teacher can often see the key point of a passage quickly.

Sometimes there is more than one core. In that case, first pick the one that most affects the overall result, and deal with the next one after it is steady; there is no need to juggle them all at once.

## Add other demands step by step

Once the core is steady, you can gradually add a second and third goal, such as dynamics, phrasing and tempo.

Add only one at a time, make sure it works well with the core, and then add the next.

If the original core falls apart after you add a new demand, step back and steady the core again.

This process looks slower, but it avoids more mistakes and is more efficient in the long run.

When all the demands are steadily combined, the piece becomes solid and complete.

After you finish a piece, you can look back at what the core was at each stage. Looking back like this helps you judge the focus of new pieces more quickly later on.

## Why find the centre first

Many things need a steady foundation. In piano practice, that foundation might be a steady rhythm, correct fingering or a relaxed wrist.

If the foundation is not yet steady and you rush to add speed, dynamics and expression, problems often pile up, and in the end the whole passage becomes unstable.

First find the single most essential thing in the passage and steady it, and the demands that follow will have reliable support.

This way of thinking makes practice more organised and cuts down the time spent redoing work.

Whether you are just starting out or already have a foundation, and whether you are playing an etude or a piece, this approach works.

## Practising with a focus on the core

Once you have decided on the core, focus only on that one thing while you practise and set the other demands aside for now.

For example, if the core is rhythm, practise slowly with a metronome and listen only for whether the rhythm is even, ignoring dynamic changes for the moment.

Before each practice, you can note today's core goal in your head or on the score as a reminder.

After practising, check whether the goal was met; if it was, you can add a new goal next time.

This way every practice session has a clear direction.

At the end of a session, you can spend a minute thinking about how well today's core goal went and write the result in the margin of the score, so that next time you can pick up where you left off.

![City lights and buildings at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lxigv-0mms7.webp)

## Finding the "centre" of your practice

When you start a new piece, you can first ask yourself: what matters most in this passage? It might be a steady rhythm, correct fingering or a relaxed wrist. Focus only on that one thing for now and set the rest aside.

When the core is steady, add a second goal, such as dynamic changes or phrasing. Adding only one thing at a time keeps practice more organised.

If you find that the original core falls apart when you add a new demand, step back and steady the core again. This process looks slow, but it actually avoids more mistakes.

**Before you start**

This way of thinking applies to learning many skills. Lay a solid foundation first, and what develops afterwards will have reliable support.

**Remember this**
- First identify the single most essential thing in the practice
- Add other demands once the core is steady
- Rushing tends to create more problems
- Focus on one goal at a time

## FAQ

**Q: How do I know the core is steady?**
A: If you can get through it smoothly several times in a row without having to think about it, it is fairly steady.

**Q: Is the core the same for every piece?**
A: No. You need to judge it from the character of the piece and your own situation.

**Q: Can a passage have only one core?**
A: It can have several, but focusing on one at a time usually works better.

**Q: How else can I tell the core is steady?**
A: Play it several times at different tempos; if it holds up in all of them, it is fairly steady.

**Q: Will focusing on the core make me ignore other problems?**
A: You can note the other problems down and deal with them one by one once the core is steady.

**Q: Does this method suit memorising?**
A: Yes. You can steady the structure and chords first, then fill in the details.

ear-training-everyday-melodies.body:
Songs on the radio, music from a little cart on the street and the theme tunes of TV programmes can all become material for training your ears. First hum the melody you heard and decide whether it goes up or down, then find it on the piano one note at a time, and once you have found it, try playing it in a different key. This kind of practice needs no special textbook, yet it slowly improves your ability to recognise pitches and intervals.

## Why Use Everyday Melodies

Dedicated listening exercises can sometimes feel dull, while melodies you hear in daily life already stick in your mind and feel natural to hum. Using them to train your ears gives you stronger motivation and more fun.

**Before you start**

These melodies usually have a simple structure and a narrow range, which suits beginners.

More importantly, this practice builds the habit of paying attention to sound at any moment, so your ears keep "learning" in everyday life too.

## Hum the Melody First

After hearing a melody you want to find, do not rush to the piano. Hum it in your head or softly a few times, until you can sing it through.

While humming, notice a few questions: does it start high or low, are there big leaps in the middle, and does it end on a note that feels settled or hang unfinished?

If you can hum it clearly, the melody is already in your ear, and finding it on the piano will be much easier.

![Piano scene with futuristic light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9x750h-jzjty.webp)

## Listen to the Rhythm Too

A melody is not only pitch but also rhythm. While humming, tap the beat lightly with your hand and feel which notes are long and which are short.

When you play it on the piano, follow the original rhythm as closely as you can, rather than making every note the same length.

If the rhythm is rather complicated, clap only the rhythm first, and add the pitches once it is familiar.

## Find the First Note on the Piano

Sit at the piano, hum the first note, then try to find the note at the same pitch on the keys. You can start near middle C and try one note at a time, going up or down.

Once you have found the first note, you can work out the following notes by asking "up or down, one step or a few steps".

Do not worry if you are slow at first; this is exactly the process of your ear building the link between pitch and keys.

## Find It Step by Step

Each time you find a note, play everything you have found so far from the beginning, then go on to look for the next one. This keeps confirming that the earlier notes are right.

When you cannot find a note, hum the notes before and after it, feel the distance between them, and then try a few possible places on the piano.

If you really cannot find it, skip it for now, find the later notes, and come back to the difficult spot afterwards.

## You Can Add a Simple Accompaniment

Once the melody is familiar, you can try adding a simple chord with the left hand, for example playing the tonic chord at the beginning and end of the melody.

You do not need a complicated harmonisation; it is enough to hear which chord blends well with the melody.

In this way, a melody "picked up" from daily life turns into a little piece you can play all the way through.

## Play It Again in Another Key

After finding the melody, try playing the same melody starting from a different note. For example, if you started on C, now start on G.

When you change key you will meet black keys and have to work out the position of each note again. This helps you understand the interval relationships in the melody rather than just remembering certain keys.

This is also the beginning of transposition practice, which will help with reading music and improvising later.

## Keep a Record as You Go

You can keep a small notebook and write down the melodies you have found, using note names or numbered notation, together with where you heard them.

Flip through the notebook a few months later and you may notice that you find notes faster and can handle more complex melodies.

**Remember this**

You can also take these notes to your lesson, discuss them with your teacher, or ask your teacher to check that the rhythm is accurate.

**Think it over**
- Choose short, easy-to-remember melodies
- Hum first, to confirm the shape and the rhythm
- Start with the first note and try to find it on the piano
- Once found, play it again in another key

## FAQ

**Q: Can I do this exercise if I have no sense of pitch at all?**
A: Yes. A sense of pitch is developed through practice, so just start with very short melodies.

**Q: What if I find the wrong note?**
A: Try again against your humming, or ask a teacher or family member to confirm. Finding wrong notes is part of learning.

**Q: Can I use a phone app to identify the melody?**
A: You can use it as a reference, but trying to find it yourself first trains your ears better.

**Q: Is this suitable for children?**
A: Yes. You can start with nursery rhymes they know and turn it into a note-guessing game.

**Q: Must I write it down?**
A: Not necessarily, but keeping a record helps consolidate and makes later review easier.

**Q: What if the melody has sharps or flats?**
A: Try looking on the neighbouring black keys, and after comparing a few times you will be able to tell them apart.

elgar-salut-damour-1888-engagement.body:
The English composer Elgar wrote Salut d'Amour in 1888 as an engagement gift for his fiancée, Caroline Alice Roberts. The original title was the German "Love's Greeting", and when it was published in 1889 it used the French title "Salut d'Amour", with several versions at once, including solo piano and violin and piano. This little piece is in E major, with a simple, gentle melody. When you play it on the piano, make the melody as warm as a softly spoken word, with the accompanying chords gently holding the melody up.

## An Engagement Gift

In 1888, Elgar became engaged to Caroline Alice Roberts, and he wrote this little piece as a gift for her.

Alice herself also wrote poetry, and she had once written a poem for Elgar; this piece can be seen as his reply.

The work is not long, yet it is full of tender feeling.

![Glowing turquoise grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa51pf7-8an9e.webp)

## Pedalling in a Short Piece

When you play this piece, the sustain pedal can make the melody more connected and mellow.

Change the pedal with the changes in the bass, and change it more often where the melody has passing notes.

If you want the chords to stay light, you can use the pedal more shallowly.

## The Modulation in the Middle Section

The middle of the piece moves to other keys, the mood becomes a little more excited and the melody warmer.

The dynamics of this section can be stronger than at the beginning, and the tempo can push forward a little.

After the middle section, the opening melody returns, and the atmosphere must go back to tenderness.

## Several Different Versions

When the piece was published there were already several versions, including solo piano and violin and piano.

Later came arrangements for cello, orchestra and more, and it can be said to be one of Elgar's most widely circulated short pieces.

Piano learners can play the solo piano version directly, or play it together with a friend who plays the violin.

**Pay attention to the details**
- Written in 1888 as an engagement gift for his fiancée
- The original title was the German "Love's Greeting"
- Published in 1889 under a French title
- Versions for solo piano, violin and piano, and more

## The Melody of Salut d'Amour

The melody starts in the middle register and rises and falls gently, like someone speaking tender words quietly.

The phrases are mostly four bars long, entering softly at the start, opening out a little in the middle and drawing back naturally at the end.

Do not play the melody too loudly; being warm and soft suits the character of this piece.

## The Warmth of E Major

This piece is in E major, with a key signature of four sharps.

E major sounds bright and warm on the piano, and suits this gentle little piece very well.

Before you start practising, get familiar with the positions of the four sharps, and you will be less likely to play wrong notes when reading.

## The Chords That Hold Up the Melody

The accompanying chords are mostly played lightly on the weak beats, as if nodding along gently beside the melody.

The bass falls on the strong beats and gives the melody steady support.

Keep the chords short and light, and do not let them drag on too long, so that they do not cover the melody.

## A Piece to Give to Family

Because the piece is itself a gift, many people play it for their loved ones at family gatherings or on anniversaries.

It is of moderate difficulty and not long, so it suits being kept in your repertoire list as a piece you can play at any time.

When you play for your family, thinking of conveying your feelings to them will naturally make your sound more tender.

## Summary of Salut d'Amour

Elgar wrote Salut d'Amour in 1888 as an engagement gift for his fiancée Alice, and it was published in 1889 under a French title.

The piece is in E major, with versions for solo piano, violin and piano, and more.

When you play it, the melody should be warm and soft, the accompanying chords light and short, the middle section a little warmer, and the ending should close quietly.

## The Soft Ending

The ending of the piece gets softer and softer, and the last few chords are like a quiet farewell.

After the last chord is pressed, you can let it linger a little and let the sound disappear naturally.

Do not rush to lift your hands; let this tenderness stay in the air a little longer.

## Flexibility of Tempo

This little piece suits a tempo with a little flexibility: linger slightly at the high point of a phrase, and slow down slightly at the end of a phrase.

But the flexibility must be natural, so that the listener does not lose the sense of the beat.

You can practise first at a steady tempo until it is familiar, then slowly add subtle changes.

## Playing with a Violin

If you play with a violin, the piano's role becomes accompaniment, and the melody is mainly left to the violin.

The piano must pay attention to the violinist's bowing and breathing, and follow their tempo at long notes and phrase endings.

The two players can first listen to a recording together, and then agree on where the tempo changes will be.

## The Change of Title

Elgar first gave it a German title, meaning "Love's Greeting", because Alice could speak German.

When it was published in 1889, the title was changed to the French "Salut d'Amour", and this French name later became more widely known.

In Chinese it is often translated as "Ai de Lizan" or "Ai de Zhiyi".

## FAQ

**Q: When was Salut d'Amour written?**
A: In 1888.

**Q: For whom was it written?**
A: Elgar's fiancée, Caroline Alice Roberts.

**Q: What was the original title?**
A: The German "Love's Greeting".

**Q: What versions are there?**
A: Solo piano, violin and piano, and more.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: E major, four sharps.

erquan-yingyue-abing-erhu-piano.body:
Erquan Yingyue (The Moon Reflected on the Second Spring) is an erhu solo that almost everyone has heard. It was written by Hua Yanjun, a folk musician from Wuxi in Jiangsu, whom people usually call "Abing". In 1950, the musicologist Yang Yinliu and others travelled to Wuxi specially to record this piece and several other works by Abing. A few months later, Abing died. The "Second Spring" in the title refers to a famous spring on Huishan Hill in Wuxi. The melody is deep and tender, like a person slowly telling their troubles on a moonlit night. Today it can be heard on instruments from the pipa and the violin to the piano.

## Tempo and Flexibility in Erquan Yingyue

The piece is slow, but it should feel as if it is flowing.

**A Different Angle**

When played on the erhu, the tempo is often very free, and the piano version can also have some flexibility.

But the flexibility should be natural, and should not make the music lose its continuity.

## Listen to Abing's Recording First

Before you play, listen to Abing's own recording from 1950.

The sound quality is not what it is today, but you can hear the original style of playing.

Then listen to versions by other erhu players and pianists, and compare how they shape the piece.

## Where the Title Comes From

It is said that Abing at first only called this piece something like "a piece from the heart".

At the recording, Yang Yinliu and the others talked it over with him, and settled on the title Erquan Yingyue, taking its name from a famous spring on Huishan Hill in Wuxi.

The title paints a picture of spring water reflecting moonlight, and it also suits the mood of the music.

- The composer is the Wuxi folk musician Hua Yanjun (Abing)
- Recorded in 1950 by Yang Yinliu and others
- "Second Spring" refers to a famous spring on Huishan Hill in Wuxi
- There is the original erhu version and arrangements for the piano and other instruments

## Development by Variation

The structure of Erquan Yingyue is like many variations on a single theme.

Each time, the melody is extended, the register rises, the dynamics change and the emotion gradually deepens.

In the end, the music gradually calms and finishes in a long, lingering resonance.

## The Melody in the Piano Version

When playing the piano version, make the melody as connected and singing as you can, imitating the sound of the erhu.

Long notes should be held for their full value, and there should be natural breathing between phrases.

You can first sing the melody, or listen to an erhu recording, to find the right feeling.

## From Erhu to Piano

The biggest challenge in arranging an erhu piece for piano is that the erhu's slides and vibrato cannot be done directly on the piano.

Arrangers usually use ornaments, harmonic colour and changes of dynamics to imitate the erhu's expression.

A piano version can also add rich harmony, giving the music more layers.

## Erquan Yingyue in Brief

Hua Yanjun (Abing) was born in 1893 and died in 1950. A folk musician from Wuxi, he studied Taoist music from childhood, lost his sight in middle age and made his living playing in the streets. In the summer of 1950, Yang Yinliu and Cao Anhe used a wire recorder to record six of his works for him, and he died a few months later. The title is taken from a famous spring on Huishan Hill in Wuxi.

The erhu has a soft tone like the human voice. The melody is based on the pentatonic scale, the theme is varied several times as the emotion gradually deepens, and the piano version uses ornaments, harmony and dynamics to imitate the erhu's expression. The melody should be connected and singing, the tempo slow but flexible, and the harmony should serve the melody.

You can listen to Abing's recording first, and you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend a piano score.

## The 1950 Recording

In the summer of 1950, the musicologists Yang Yinliu and Cao Anhe came to Wuxi and used a wire recorder, the equipment of the time, to record Abing.

In all they recorded six pieces played by Abing, three for the erhu and three for the pipa.

A few months later Abing died, and this recording became a precious record that preserved his music.

![A digital music space under neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacwt0z-h5qn1.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Recommend a Piano Score of Erquan Yingyue

If you want to play the piano version of Erquan Yingyue, you can ask Teacher Aum in your lessons to recommend an arrangement that suits your level.

You can also ask your teacher to demonstrate how to "speak" the erhu's slides on the piano.

This piece is very good for practising deep, inward expression.

## The Sound of the Erhu

The erhu is a two-string bowed instrument with a soft, expressive sound, very like the human singing voice.

Players can use slides, vibrato and other techniques to make the melody more tender.

Erquan Yingyue makes full use of these qualities of the erhu.

## Harmonic Colour in Erquan Yingyue

The harmony in the piano version should serve the melody and should not cover it.

The chords and bass notes in the left hand should be soft, creating the quiet atmosphere of a moonlit night.

You can use the pedal to make the harmony warmer, but take care to keep it clear.

## Who Was Abing

Hua Yanjun was born in 1893 and died in 1950. He was a folk musician from Wuxi in Jiangsu, and people usually call him "Abing".

He studied Taoist music from childhood and could play many instruments, including the erhu and the pipa.

In middle age he lost his sight and made his living playing in the streets.

## The Introduction and the Theme

The piece opens with a short introduction, like a deep sigh.

Then the theme slowly unfolds, moving gently through the middle and lower register.

This opening sets a reflective tone for the whole piece.

## The Pentatonic Melody of Erquan Yingyue

The melody is based on the pentatonic scale, deep and tender.

One main phrase returns again and again, changing a little each time, as if someone were telling their story over and over.

**Notice the Details**

The emotion of the music rises and falls gradually, sometimes calm, sometimes stirred.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who wrote Erquan Yingyue?**
A: The Wuxi folk musician Hua Yanjun, known as Abing.

**Q: What year was it recorded?**
A: 1950.

**Q: What does "Second Spring" refer to?**
A: A famous spring on Huishan Hill in Wuxi.

**Q: What scale is the melody based on?**
A: The pentatonic scale.

**Q: How does the piano version imitate the erhu?**
A: With ornaments, harmonic colour and changes of dynamics.

finger-legato-overlap.body:
Finger legato means connecting one note smoothly to the next using only your fingers, without relying on the sustain pedal. The key is the handover: the previous finger lifts just as the next finger presses its key, so there is neither a gap between the two notes nor a long overlap. When practising, slow down first and pass the note back and forth between just two adjacent fingers, listening closely to whether the sound is connected, and then extend it to five-finger patterns and short phrases.

## A few minutes a day

Practising finger legato does not take long; a few minutes a day on the handover is enough.

**Summary**

You can put it in your warm-up and combine it with scale practice, playing scales slowly and legato.

Stick with it for a while and you will find that melodies become easier to play smoothly and with a singing quality.

## Legato and tone

Legato is not only about joining notes; it also affects the quality of the sound. A well-connected melody sounds rounded and warm.

When practising, imagine you are singing with your fingers: each note flows naturally out of the one before, and changes in volume should be smooth too.

If one note suddenly becomes louder or softer, the melody can sound broken even without a gap, so pay attention to evenness of volume as well.

## Record yourself and listen for gaps

Sometimes while playing you feel you are already connected, but when you record yourself you may find small gaps.

You can record a legato exercise on your phone and listen carefully to the connection between each pair of notes.

This kind of check helps you understand your legato more objectively.

## Applying it in phrases

When you meet a slur marking in a piece, you can leave out the pedal at first, play the legato with your fingers alone and listen to the effect.

If your fingers can connect well, add the pedal as needed, and the sound will be cleaner.

In some places the stretch of the hand is too large for the fingers to connect completely, and there the pedal can help.

## Keeping the hand relaxed

When playing legato, keep your hand relaxed and do not press the keys down hard.

After the key is down, you need only a very small force to hold it, letting the weight of your finger rest naturally on the key.

If your hand is too tense, the handover becomes stiff and the sound is hard to connect.

**Practice order**
- Finger legato does not rely on the sustain pedal
- When the next finger presses, the previous finger lifts
- There is no gap between the two notes
- First practise the handover slowly with two fingers

## Why practise finger legato

The sustain pedal can help the sound connect, but it keeps all the notes sounding, which sometimes makes the sound blurry.

Finger legato lets the melody connect clearly while keeping the harmony clean.

Many pieces, especially works from the Baroque period, often need finger legato to bring out clear lines in each voice.

## The timing of the handover

The key to finger legato is the timing of the handover: the previous finger leaves the key at the very moment the next finger presses its key.

If the previous finger lifts too early, a gap appears between the two notes and the sound breaks.

If the previous finger lifts too late, the two notes overlap and sound a little blurred.

## Practise the left hand too

Finger legato is not only a matter for the right hand; left-hand bass lines and inner voices often need legato as well.

You can practise the left hand the same way, starting with the handover between two fingers and gradually extending to patterns and phrases.

Once both hands can play legato, you will feel much freer playing multi-voice works.

![Close-up of the keys of a grand piano and its lid with a gold pattern in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa05wjh-aj2jg.webp)

## Extending to five-finger patterns

Once the handover between two fingers is fluent, try using all five fingers to play an ascending and descending five-finger pattern, for example C, D, E, F, G.

Every note should connect smoothly to the next, with no gap and no obvious overlap.

You can close your eyes and rely on your ears alone to judge whether the legato is even.

## Start with two fingers

You can start with the second and third fingers of your right hand, alternating on two adjacent white keys.

Play slowly, listen closely to whether the two notes are connected, and feel the movement of the handover between your fingers.

When that is fluent, switch to the third and fourth fingers, then the fourth and fifth, and practise every pair of fingers.

## The technique of finger substitution

In places where legato has to be sustained for a long stretch, you can use finger substitution, that is, quietly replacing one finger with another on the same note.

This frees up the right finger for the next note without breaking the sound.

This technique is especially common in organ playing and Baroque keyboard works, and it is useful on the piano too.

## FAQ

**Q: What is finger legato?**
A: Connecting notes smoothly using only the fingers, without the pedal.

**Q: What is the timing of the handover?**
A: The previous finger lifts when the next finger presses.

**Q: What happens if I lift too early?**
A: A gap appears between the notes.

**Q: What happens if I lift too late?**
A: The two notes overlap and the sound is blurred.

**Q: What if my hand cannot reach?**
A: You can use the pedal or the technique of finger substitution.

**Q: How do I check my legato?**
A: Record yourself and listen closely to the connections between notes.
