dvorak-humoresque-g-flat-major-1894.body:
Dvořák's Humoresque is a piano piece many people know, and its lively dotted rhythm is recognisable at once. It comes from the eight Humoresques, Op. 101, that Dvořák wrote in the summer of 1894, and it is the seventh of them, in G-flat major. At the time Dvořák was working in America, and he completed this set while on holiday in his homeland of Bohemia that summer. The piece was later arranged for violin and other instruments and became very widely known. Below we look at the background of the piece and the main points of playing it.

## Choosing an arrangement

Besides the original, the piano score of the Humoresque comes in many simplified editions with reduced difficulty.

**Listen first**

If the key signature of the original is too difficult, you can start with a version transposed into an easier key to get to know the melody.

Once you have some foundation, try the original G-flat major.

## The key signature of G-flat major

G-flat major has six flats, which looks a little frightening, but on the piano many of the notes fall on the black keys, and the position of the hand is in fact very comfortable.

The black keys are narrower and higher than the white keys, so the fingers can move fairly steadily when playing the melody.

Before you start practising, getting to know the G-flat major scale will help you read the music.

## Listening to different performances

You can listen to the original piano version of this piece, and also to arrangements such as the violin version.

Comparing different performances lets you hear how the dotted rhythm and the mood of the middle section are handled differently.

This listening experience helps you find the way of playing that you like.

## Dvořák's Humoresque in summary

The Humoresque in G-flat major is the seventh of the eight Humoresques, Op. 101, that Dvořák wrote in Bohemia in the summer of 1894, when he was working in America.

The piece is known for its bouncy dotted rhythm. The middle section turns to the minor and the colour darkens, then the theme returns, and the black-key positions of G-flat major are in fact very comfortable for the hand.

When playing, keep the short notes of the dotted rhythm light, keep the left hand steady and soft, use a moderate amount of pedal and an unhurried tempo. You can practise in sections, or begin with a simplified version.

## Practising the Humoresque in sections

When practising the Humoresque, divide it into three blocks and polish each separately: the dotted theme, the minor middle section and the return of the theme.

First practise the dotted rhythm and the melody of the middle section hands separately, then put the hands together.

The transitions between the middle section and the opening should also be practised on their own so that the passage is natural.

## Where the eight Humoresques came from

In the summer of 1894, Dvořák went back to Bohemia on holiday and wrote a set of eight piano pieces there, titled Humoresques, catalogued as Op. 101.

Some of the musical ideas in this set are said to have come from melody sketches he noted down while he was in America.

"Humoresque" here means a light, slightly playful piece, not necessarily one that makes people laugh.

## Pedalling in the Humoresque

You can use some pedal in this piece to make the sound rounder, but do not use too much.

The lightness of the dotted rhythm needs clear sound, and too much pedal will blur the short notes.

You can change pedal as the harmony changes, and listen closely to your own sound.

## Returning to the opening theme

After the middle section ends, the dotted theme in G-flat major comes back.

Having heard the melancholy of the middle section, returning here makes the music feel brighter and lighter.

You can play it as lightly as at the start, or vary the details slightly.

![A cyberpunk illustration of a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7caaj-6xtu2.webp)

## Dvořák the man

Antonín Dvořák (1841-1904) was a Czech composer, born in what was then part of Bohemia.

His works often carry the colour of the folk music of his homeland, and his symphonies, chamber music and piano works are all famous.

From 1892 to 1895 he served as director of a conservatory in New York.

- The seventh of the eight Humoresques, Op. 101
- Written in Bohemia in the summer of 1894
- G-flat major, with a bouncy dotted rhythm
- The middle section turns to the minor and the colour darkens

## The left-hand accompaniment

The left hand is mostly an accompaniment of bass notes and chords, and it should support the melody steadily.

The bass notes can be slightly clearer, and the chords played more lightly.

Keep the left-hand rhythm steady so that the right hand's dotted rhythm can bounce lightly above it.

## The lightness of the opening melody

The opening melody should be played in a relaxed, graceful way, without too much force.

You can imagine a leisurely walk, with light and springy steps.

Make the right-hand melody clear and keep the left-hand accompaniment lighter so that it does not cover the melody.

## Why the seventh became the best known

Of the eight, the seventh, in G-flat major, spread especially widely, and when many people today say "the Humoresque", this is the one they mean.

Its melody is simple and its dotted rhythm is light, so it is easy to remember.

Many arrangements later appeared, including versions for violin and piano, which made it even better known.

## The change of colour in the middle section

The middle section of the piece turns to the minor, the colour suddenly gets a little darker, and there is a touch of melancholy.

The melody here is more singing, and the rhythm flows more smoothly than at the start.

When you play it, you can slow down a little and make the tone softer, in contrast with the opening.

## Tempo and freedom in the Humoresque

The tempo of this piece should not be too fast, so that the dotted rhythm keeps its elegance and calm.

At the end of a phrase you can slow down slightly, like a pause in speech.

But the overall pulse should stay steady, without random speeding up and slowing down.

## The dotted rhythm of the Humoresque

What you recognise at once about this piece is the dotted rhythm that runs through the opening, a long note followed by a short one.

When you play it, keep the short note light and not too heavy, as if skipping lightly over it.

Keep the proportion of long note to short note clear, and do not play it as an even rhythm.

## FAQ

**Q: Which set of works is the Humoresque from?**
A: It is the seventh of Dvořák's eight Humoresques, Op. 101.

**Q: When was it written?**
A: In the summer of 1894, while on holiday in Bohemia.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: G-flat major.

**Q: What is the signature rhythm?**
A: A bouncy dotted rhythm.

**Q: What changes in the middle section?**
A: It turns to the minor and the colour darkens.

eleventh-and-thirteenth-chord-extensions.body:
A triad is built from thirds, and a seventh chord is a triad with one more third added. If you keep stacking thirds upwards, you get 9th, 11th and 13th chords. For example, with C as the root, C, E, G, B♭ is C7; adding D gives the 9th, adding F the 11th, and adding A the 13th. These notes are called extensions, and they are often used in jazz and some pop music. In actual playing, you usually do not play all the notes, but choose which ones to leave out.

## How to Divide C13 Between the Two Hands

When playing extended chords, the left hand can play the root and the seventh, and the right hand the third and the extensions.

**Pay attention to the details**

For C13, for example, the left hand plays C and B♭, and the right hand plays E and A.

This arrangement sounds clear and still brings out the colour of the 13th chord.

## Why They Are Called 9th, 11th and 13th

The 9th, 11th and 13th are really the 2nd, 4th and 6th, an octave higher.

They are called the 9th, 11th and 13th because in the chord they sit above the seventh.

These names remind us that the notes are extensions of the chord, and not ordinary passing notes.

## In Jazz

Jazz makes heavy use of 9th, 11th and 13th chords.

These chords make the harmony sound richer and more colourful, and give improvisers more notes to work with.

When learning jazz piano, extended chords are an important part.

## Keep Stacking Upwards

Stack one more third on top of a seventh chord and you get the 9th, which is D when C is the root.

Stack another third and you get the 11th, which is F.

Stack another third and you get the 13th, which is A. At this point all seven note names have been used.

![Glowing turquoise grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa640of-h5s8o.webp)

## Which Register the Extensions Go In

The sound of extended chords is rather complex, and the effect can be very different with different voicings and registers.

Extensions in the low register easily sound muddy, so they are usually placed in the middle or upper register.

Use your ears to judge which voicing is clearest and best fits the needs of the music.

## How Chord Symbols Are Written

In lead sheets, 11th chords are often written C11 or Cm11, and 13th chords are often written C13.

When written C13, it usually means the chord contains the seventh, and sometimes the 9th as well.

If just one note is added without the seventh, it is often written add, for example Cadd9.

## The Sound of the 11th Chord

The 11th in an 11th chord is only a minor ninth, a semitone relationship, from the third, which easily creates friction in a major chord.

So when the 11th is added to a dominant seventh chord, the third is often left out, which sounds like a suspended feeling.

When the 11th is added to a minor seventh chord, the sound is softer and is often used in jazz.

## From Triads to Seventh Chords

A triad is made of two stacked thirds, for example C, E, G.

Stack another third on top and it becomes a seventh chord, for example C, E, G, B♭.

This way of stacking thirds layer by layer is the basic rule for building chords.

## Start Simple

If you are just beginning to learn extended chords, start with the 9th chord, adding a 9th to a seventh chord.

Once you are familiar with that, try adding the 11th and 13th.

Each time you add a note, listen carefully to how the chord changes.

## The Sound of the 13th Chord

The 13th in a 13th chord adds a bright, rich colour to the chord.

The dominant 13th chord is common in jazz and blues, often used just before resolving to the tonic chord.

When playing a 13th chord, you usually keep the root, third, seventh and 13th, and leave out the fifth and some other notes.

## Finding Extended Chords in Lead Sheets

Open a few lead sheets of jazz standards and circle with a pen the chord symbols with the numbers 9, 11 and 13.

Play these chords on the piano and listen to how they work in the song.

This kind of practice helps us get familiar with extended chords more quickly.

## Summary of 11th and 13th Chords

Keep stacking thirds above a seventh chord and you get 9th, 11th and 13th chords; the 9th, 11th and 13th are called extensions.

They are common in jazz and pop. When playing them, you usually leave out some notes such as the fifth, and the dominant 11th chord often leaves out the third.

Starting with the 9th chord, paying attention to voicing and register, and judging by ear can help us make better use of extended chords.

## Which Notes to Leave Out

A complete 13th chord has seven notes, which two hands on the piano can hardly play all at once, and the sound becomes crowded.

Generally, the fifth is the note most often left out, because it has the least effect on the character of the chord.

The root can sometimes be left out too, if a bass player or the left hand is already playing it.

- Keep stacking thirds above a seventh chord
- The 9th, 11th and 13th are called extensions
- Often used in jazz and pop
- In actual playing, some notes are left out

## 9th and 11th Chords in Ballads

9th and 11th chords are also often used in some pop songs and ballads.

For example, using a minor 9th chord in place of an ordinary minor triad sounds softer and more atmospheric.

**Give it a try**

When arranging an accompaniment for a song, you can add extensions here and there to make the harmony richer.

## FAQ

**Q: How is an 11th chord built?**
A: Keep stacking thirds on a seventh chord up to the 11th.

**Q: With C as the root, what is the 13th?**
A: A.

**Q: What are extensions?**
A: The 9th, 11th and 13th.

**Q: Which note is often left out when playing a 13th chord?**
A: The fifth.

**Q: Where are extended chords often used?**
A: In jazz and pop music.

footwear-for-pedaling.body:
Pedalling needs your foot to feel clearly how far down the pedal is, so thin-soled, flat, close-fitting shoes, or simply socks, are best for practice. Thick-soled shoes, high heels, slippers and rain boots can all dull the feel of the pedal and make your pedalling less precise. Before a performance, practise a few times in the shoes you will wear on the day.

**Remember this**
- Flat shoes with thin soles give a clearer feel
- Avoid slippers, thick soles and high heels
- If you practise in socks, watch out for slipping
- Rehearse in the shoes you will wear for the performance

## Keep a consistent habit

Try to wear the same shoes for everyday practice, so your foot's feel for the pedal stays steady.

**Think about it**

If you change shoes often, you have to readjust each time, which can affect how precise your pedalling is.

You can keep a pair of indoor shoes just for practice next to the piano and put them on as soon as you sit down, which is also a small ritual for getting into practice mode.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xn5sm-hbmga.webp)

## Choosing shoes for children

Children's feet are growing, so check the shoe size often. Shoes that are too big tend to shift about when pressing the pedal.

If your child cannot reach the pedals yet, you can use a pedal extender, and again choose close-fitting, flat shoes.

Children's shoes with flashing lights or very hard soles are best swapped for something else during practice.

## Shoes for performances

For a formal performance, many people wear dressier shoes, which may be different from what they wear to practise.

Before the performance, practise at least a few times in the shoes you will wear that day, get used to how the pedal feels, and adjust how hard you press if necessary.

If the soles of your performance shoes are slippery, deal with that beforehand, or choose a pair of dress shoes that are better suited to playing.

## Where your heel goes

When pressing the sustain pedal, the heel usually stays on the floor and the ball of the foot presses the pedal down, which makes the movement steadier.

If your shoes make it hard to keep your heel in place, that will affect how steady your pedalling is.

When you practise, notice whether your heel stays on the floor throughout. This matters more than the shoes themselves.

## Why shoes affect the pedal

The sustain pedal does not have just two states, "down" and "up". How far you press and how fast you release both change the sound.

To control these details, your foot needs to feel clearly where the pedal is and how much resistance it gives.

If the sole is too thick or too stiff, it is as if there were a layer between your foot and the pedal, and delicate control becomes very difficult.

## Shoes that suit practice

Flat shoes with thin soles that fit closely, such as light canvas shoes or soft-soled trainers, are usually well suited to pedalling.

The shoes should fit well and not come loose or slip off when you press the pedal.

The toe should not be too wide or too long, so that it does not touch the neighbouring pedal or the body of the piano.

When choosing shoes, you can put them on and try the pedal at home. If you can clearly feel when the pedal starts to go down, they are a good fit.

Also look at the tread on the sole: very deep treads can catch on the edge of the pedal.

## Changing shoes can be part of getting ready

At home, you can keep a pair of indoor shoes just for practice by the piano stool and put them on as soon as you sit down.

That way the feel under your foot is the same every time you practise, and it is easier to judge how far to press the pedal.

If your teacher's studio asks you to change shoes when you go to lessons, you can bring this pair along, or ask about the studio's rules beforehand.

## Shoes that are less suitable

Slippers easily slide or fall off when you press the pedal, and it is hard to keep your heel fixed on the floor.

High heels change the angle of your foot and raise your heel, making it hard to apply force and control with the ball of the foot on the pedal.

Thick-soled shoes, rain boots and other shoes with very thick or hard soles dull the feel of your foot, making it hard to judge how far the pedal is down.

## Practising in socks or barefoot

When practising at home, some people like to pedal in just their socks, which gives the most direct feel.

When wearing socks, check whether the surface of the pedal is smooth, and if necessary wear socks with non-slip grips to keep your foot from sliding.

**In short**

Practising barefoot is also fine, but pay attention to the cleanliness of your feet and the hygiene of the pedal, and keep warm in winter.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can I practise in slippers?**
A: It is not really recommended. Slippers slide easily and your heel is not stable.

**Q: Can I play in high heels?**
A: Yes, but pedalling will be harder, so practise more before a performance.

**Q: Do thick socks in winter make a difference?**
A: They do reduce the feel a little. You can choose socks that are thin but still warm.

**Q: What if my child cannot reach the pedals?**
A: You can use a pedal extender, and choose close-fitting shoes as well.

**Q: Do I need to think about shoes for the pedals of a digital piano?**
A: Yes, especially for pedals that sense how far they are pressed down.

**Q: What if my performance shoes are too slippery?**
A: Practise in the performance shoes beforehand, and if necessary choose a pair with non-slip soles.

foot-tapping-while-playing-pros-cons.body:
Some piano learners like to tap a foot gently while they play, feeling that it keeps the rhythm steadier; other teachers warn their students not to tap. So should you tap your foot or not? It really depends. When you are learning rhythm or practising music with a strong groove, tapping your foot can help you feel a steady beat. But in music that needs the pedal, in music with a free tempo, or in a formal performance, foot tapping can cause problems. Knowing the pros and cons lets you use it at the right moments.

## In formal performance

At concerts, exams and other formal occasions, it is generally not recommended to tap your foot visibly.

It can distract the audience, and it may suggest that your sense of rhythm depends on outside help.

So gradually practise keeping a steady beat without your foot.

## Why some people tap their foot

Tapping a foot is a very natural bodily reaction.

When they hear rhythmic music, many people nod their head or tap their foot without thinking.

When you tap your foot while playing, your body can feel a steady beat.

## Music with a strong groove

When playing pop, jazz, Latin and other music with a strong groove, tapping your foot can help you get into the groove.

Many musicians who play these styles feel the beat through their bodies.

In this case, foot tapping is a natural form of expression.

## Children tapping their feet

When children are learning rhythm, tapping a foot is a very direct method.

Parents and teachers can let children tap their feet while they learn a rhythm.

But gently guide children, too, to keep the rhythm without their feet once the piece is well learned.

## Moving the beat from your foot to your mind

In practice, you can gradually move the beat from your foot to your mind.

First play a few times while tapping your foot, then stop the foot and count the beats silently in your head.

If the rhythm stays steady, the beat has been internalised.

## When the foot stops, let the metronome judge

Once the foot is still, the metronome becomes the referee, showing whether the beat has drifted.

If you find the rhythm starts to wobble without your foot's help, you can go back to practising with foot tapping.

Slowly reduce your reliance on your foot.

![An electronic keyboard and screen under neon lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9opi0-f08mb.webp)

## The sound of tapping

Tapping a foot often makes a noise, especially in shoes on a hard floor.

That sound mixes into the sound of the piano and disturbs both you and your listeners.

If you do tap, you can simply move your toes lightly, or tap the floor softly with your heel, without making any sound.

## Help when learning rhythm

When you are learning a new rhythmic pattern, especially complex rhythms such as syncopation and dotted notes, tapping a steady beat with your foot is very helpful.

With the foot keeping a steady beat, the hands play different rhythms on top, and you can clearly feel how the two relate.

This works in a similar way to practising with a metronome.

## Foot tapping in short

Foot tapping is a natural bodily reaction, and it is very helpful when learning complex rhythms and playing music with a strong groove, but the right foot controls the sustain pedal and cannot tap; you can switch to the left foot, and when the left pedal is in use the left foot cannot tap either.

The sound of tapping can disturb the playing, so you can move just your toes lightly. In free-tempo music a foot beat limits expression, and in formal performance it is generally not recommended to tap visibly.

You can gradually move the beat from your foot to your mind and check it with a metronome. Children can tap their feet when learning rhythm, and a slight movement of the body is fine too. Whether it suits you is something you can discuss with Teacher Aum.

## Other bodily sensations

Besides the foot, you can feel the beat in other ways, such as a slight movement of the body.

It is very common for the body to sway gently with the beat and the phrases of the music while playing.

But keep the movement small, so it does not affect the steadiness of your hands.

## The problem with pedalling

The sustain pedal on a piano is pressed with the right foot.

If your right foot is tapping, it cannot control the pedal at the same time.

So in pieces that need the sustain pedal, the right foot cannot be used for tapping.

## Free-tempo music

In some music that needs free changes of tempo, such as a ritardando or a free-tempo passage, foot tapping can limit the expression of the music.

If the foot beat is too fixed, it is hard for the music to stretch naturally.

At these moments, put the foot beat aside and let the music breathe with the phrases.

## Tapping with the left foot

Some people switch to tapping with the left foot, leaving the right foot for the pedal.

This is fine in practice, but take care that the movement of your left foot does not upset your balance.

If a piece needs the left pedal, the left foot cannot tap either.

## Talk to your teacher about your foot-tapping habit

If you are not sure whether your foot tapping is appropriate, you can discuss it with Teacher Aum in your lesson.

Your teacher can give advice based on the style of the piece and your own habits.

**Another way to look at it**

Sometimes a teacher will suggest using it in practice and putting it aside in performance.

- When learning rhythm, foot tapping helps you feel the beat
- When using the sustain pedal, the right foot cannot tap
- The sound of tapping can disturb the playing
- Gradually move the beat from your foot to your mind

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: When is foot tapping helpful?**
A: When learning complex rhythms and playing music with a strong groove.

**Q: Why can the right foot often not tap?**
A: It has to control the sustain pedal.

**Q: What is the problem with the sound of tapping?**
A: It disturbs you and your listeners.

**Q: Is foot tapping recommended in formal performance?**
A: Generally, visible tapping is not recommended.

**Q: How can I reduce my reliance on my foot?**
A: Gradually move the beat to your mind, and check it with a metronome.

ear-warm-up-before-practice.body:
Finger warm-ups get the hands ready, and the ears need to be ready too. Before practising, spend two or three minutes "warming up your ears": sing the opening of today's piece, play its tonic note and tonic chord, and hear in your head the tempo and tone you want. Once your ears have a goal, the sound your hands produce has something to be compared with, and it is easier to hear what needs adjusting as you practise.

**Listen first**
- Before practising, do two or three minutes of listening preparation
- First sing the melody of the opening of the piece
- Play the tonic note and tonic chord of today's piece
- Hear the target tempo and tone in your head first

## First find the centre of the key

Every piece has a key, and the tonic note and tonic chord of that key are like the "home" of the piece.

To begin, play the tonic note and listen to it as it sustains for a while; then play the tonic chord and hear whether its colour is a bright major or a soft minor.

You can also play the scale of this key, a little slowly, listening as you play to how each note relates to the tonic.

If the piece changes key in the middle, you can play the tonic chord of the new key as well, to get to know its sound beforehand.

Once your ears know the centre of the key, it is easier to notice a wrong note as you read the music, because it will sound as if it is "not at home".

For keys with many sharps or flats, this step also reminds your fingers which keys are black, and reduces wrong notes at the start.

## Why the ears need preparing too

Many exercises start from the hands: loosening the wrists, playing a few sets of scales. The hands are ready, but the ears are often still on something else.

When you play, it is the ears you rely on to judge whether the sound is good and in tune. If you have no clear target sound in your mind, it is hard to know whether what you just played was right.

The purpose of listening preparation is to build this target in your mind before you start: what the key is, how the melody goes, and what the tempo and tone are like.

With a target, practice becomes "comparing", not just "repeating". Each time you play, you can compare it with the sound in your head.

This preparation takes only two or three minutes, yet it gives the practice that follows more direction.

## Pre-hearing the tempo and tone in your head

The last step before you start is to "pre-hear" the opening in your head: how fast it is, and whether the sound is soft or full.

You can tap the beat lightly a few times, or count a bar in your head, and make sure the tempo is right before you begin, to avoid starting too fast out of nerves.

You can also think about the touch of the first note: pressing lightly from the surface of the key, or sending it out with the weight of the arm.

After the first run-through, compare it with the sound in your head: is the tempo the same, is the tone close, does the phrase rise and fall as it did when you sang it?

Noting down the gaps is the problem this practice session is going to solve. In this way listening preparation and proper practice are joined naturally together.

After keeping this up for a while, you will find it easier to "hear" the music before you play it, which helps with reading new music and with memorising.

## Two or three minutes of listening preparation

Before you start, find the key of today's piece, play the tonic note and then the tonic chord, and listen quietly for a while to let your ears remember the "centre" of the key.

Then, without looking at the keys, sing or hum the first phrase or two of the piece. Where you cannot sing it accurately, you can play the matching note to check.

Then imagine the tempo of the opening in your head, and tap the beat lightly a few times to confirm that the speed is right before putting both hands on the keys.

Play the first time through only when you are ready, and afterwards compare it with the sound you had in your head to see where it is close and where there is still a gap.

## Singing the opening phrase

Next, without looking at the keys, sing the first phrase or two of the piece. It does not need to sound beautiful; humming is fine too.

As you sing, notice where the melody goes up and where it goes down, where the high point of the phrase is, and where you need to breathe.

Where you cannot sing it accurately, you can play the matching note to check, and then sing it again.

When you play after singing, your fingers will know more clearly where the melody is going, and the phrase will be easier to keep connected.

**In brief**

If the piece is for two hands, you can also hum the bass line on its own and listen to how it relates to the melody.

![A cyberpunk illustration of a person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a synthesizer with crystals in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8m1572-5h78k.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: Can warming up and proper practice be combined?**
A: You can warm up with a simpler part of the piece you are working on, but slow down the opening.

**Q: What if my hands are always cold?**
A: Warm your hands first, for example by rubbing them or washing them in warm water, and then begin practising.

**Q: Which scale is right for a warm-up?**
A: You can begin with C major, or choose a scale in the same key as that day's piece, so your hands get to know the black and white keys they will need in advance.

**Q: Can I do listening preparation if I cannot sing?**
A: Yes. Humming or singing silently in your head is fine. The point is to hear the melody first.

**Q: Does listening preparation clash with finger warm-ups?**
A: No. You can do a few minutes of hand exercises first, then two or three minutes of listening preparation.

**Q: Do I have to do it every time I practise?**
A: You can make it a fixed way to begin, especially when working on a new piece or preparing for a performance.

end-practice-on-a-good-note.body:
How a practice session ends often shapes your mood the next time you sit down at the piano. If you always stop on a difficult spot that keeps going wrong, it is easy to leave feeling frustrated. A simple habit is to save the last few minutes of practice for a piece you already play fairly well, or a piece you love, and play it through from start to finish, relaxed. Ending this way lets you leave with a sense of satisfaction and makes you look forward to the next session. The difficult spots can go in the middle of your practice, when your mind is fresh.

## When You Are Not Feeling Your Best

Some days you are not in the right state, and even familiar pieces do not go smoothly.

On those days you can shorten your practice, play just one or two easy pieces, and then stop.

Looking after how you feel matters more than forcing yourself through the practice plan.

## Note Down Today's Progress

Before you finish, take a moment to think about what improved in today's practice, even if it was only a little.

For example, "this bar was smoother than yesterday" or "I remembered the fingering for this passage".

Writing these improvements in your practice notebook lets you see that your effort is paying off.

## The Problem with Stopping on a Difficult Spot

Many people leave the hardest part until last and keep working on it until time runs out.

The result is often that they stop on a problem that is still unsolved and leave with the feeling of "I still can't play it".

When that feeling builds up, it can affect your confidence and motivation to learn.

## Leave the Last Few Minutes Free

In your practice plan, you can set aside the last few minutes for music you already play well.

This could be a section of a piece you are learning that you have already mastered, or a piece you learned before and love.

Play it through, relaxed, and enjoy the pleasure the music brings.

## Choosing Your Closing Piece

You can prepare a few pieces you especially love and play fairly fluently, to choose from as you finish practising.

You can rotate these pieces from day to day, or choose one to suit your mood.

Playing music you love is one of the happiest moments in practice.

## It Is Fine If a Difficult Spot Is Not Fully Solved

Sometimes a difficult spot cannot be solved in a single session. It can take days or even weeks.

If your practice time is up and the difficult spot is still not fully solved, that is fine. Make a note and carry on tomorrow.

There is no need to push yourself to get it right today and then finish tired and frustrated.

## Put Difficult Spots in the Middle

The difficult spots that need the most concentration can go in the middle of your practice, after your warm-up, when your mind is still fresh.

By then your hands are warmed up and your attention is focused, so you will work on the difficult spots more efficiently.

Once you have dealt with the difficult spots, move on to the more relaxed material, and finish with a piece you play well.

## Children's Practice

For children, ending practice with a favourite piece helps them feel more positive about practising.

After your child has worked on the difficult spots, you can encourage them to play their favourite piece and give them sincere praise.

That way, children are more willing to sit down at the piano every day.

![Art Deco style illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a desk lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1uycn-dumdw.webp)

## The Long-Term Effect

If you keep ending practice in an enjoyable way, you will gradually find that your feelings about practising become more and more positive.

That positive feeling becomes a source of motivation, helping you keep learning for the long term.

Music is meant to bring people joy, so let every practice session end on a happy note.

## Echoing the Beginning

You can begin practice with a warm-up and simple scales, to get your hands and your attention ready.

In the middle, work on difficult spots and new material, and at the end, close with a piece you play well.

This way, practice is like a piece of writing, with a beginning, a middle and an ending, and it gives your practice more of a rhythm.

## How You Feel at the End

People's memory of an experience is often shaped by how it ended.

If practice always ends in frustration, the next time you think about practising you may feel a little reluctant.

**A Small Tip**

If practice ends happily, it is much easier to sit down at the piano next time looking forward to it.

**Remember This**
- How you feel at the end affects your mood next time
- Do not always stop on a difficult spot
- Play a piece you already play well in the last few minutes
- Work on difficult spots in the middle of practice

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why end with music I play well?**
A: You leave satisfied and look forward to the next session.

**Q: When should I work on difficult spots?**
A: In the middle of practice, when your mind is fresh.

**Q: What if a difficult spot is not solved?**
A: Make a note and carry on tomorrow. There is no need to force it.

**Q: What should I play at the end?**
A: A passage you have mastered or a piece you love.

**Q: What if I am not feeling my best?**
A: Shorten your practice and play one or two easy pieces.

**Q: Does this work for children too?**
A: Yes, it helps children feel more positive about practising.

family-music-games.body:
Playing some simple music games with your children at home, such as guess the song, find the note, rhythm copycat and improvisation chain, can make learning the piano more fun, and it also trains listening, sense of rhythm and reaction speed. These games need no special props. A piano or just a few pairs of hands is enough, and everyone in the family can join in, whether or not they can play.

**Practice Order**
- Guess the song: play a few notes for everyone to guess
- Find the note: listen to a note and find it on the piano
- Rhythm copycat: clap a rhythm for the other person to repeat
- Improvisation chain: each person plays a short phrase and passes it on

## Combine Games with Practice

You can schedule the games after practice, as a reward for finishing.

You can also pick a few notes from the pieces your child is learning and turn them into guess-the-song or find-the-note questions.

When games and practice are linked in this way, children become more interested.

## Improvisation Chain

Everyone takes turns playing a short phrase on the piano. It can be two or three notes, or a small melodic phrase, and the next person has to carry it on.

You can make it easier by allowing only a few white keys, or only the black keys.

The results are often surprising, and everyone has a great time.

## Guess the Song

One person plays the first few notes of a song everyone knows on the piano, and the others guess what it is.

You can start with very simple children's songs and gradually make it harder, for example by playing only three notes, or by playing the tune with a different rhythm.

The person who guesses correctly gets to set the next question, so everyone has a chance to play.

## High and Low Game

The player plays a note in the high register or the low register, and the others raise their hands when they hear a high note and crouch down when they hear a low one.

You can play faster and faster to see who reacts quickest.

This game is especially good for younger children, helping them understand the ideas of "high" and "low".

## Family Members Who Cannot Play Can Join In Too

Many games do not need anyone to be able to play, such as rhythm copycat, the high and low game and music statues.

Family members who cannot play can clap, sing or guess the song.

Letting your child be the "little teacher" and teach a family member who cannot play a few notes is also a great way to interact.

## Rhythm Copycat

One person claps a simple rhythm, or plays it on the piano, and the other person repeats it.

Start with very short, simple rhythms, such as "long, short, short, long", and gradually make them longer and more complex.

Family members who cannot play can join in too, using clapping, tapping their knees or drumming on the table to show the rhythm.

## Find the Note

One person plays a note on the piano, and the other person, who has their back to the piano, turns round and tries to find that note on the keyboard.

At first you can choose from just a few white keys in the middle, and widen the range once you are fluent.

This game trains your child's ability to tell pitches apart.

![A person in a high-tech jacket playing a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9ymijg-4c3rt.webp)

## Music Statues

One person plays music on the piano and the others move freely to the music. When the music stops, everyone must freeze immediately, like a statue.

The player can change the speed and volume of the music, and everyone changes their movements to follow, for example walking slowly when the music is gentle and taking big strides when the music is loud.

This game lets children feel changes in the speed and dynamics of music.

## A Few Simple Rules for the Games

When playing, there is no need to care too much about winning or losing. The point is that everyone takes part and enjoys it.

You can let your children take turns being the "question-setter", which makes them more motivated.

Do not play for too long. Ten-odd minutes to half an hour is enough, and you should stop while everyone is still having fun.

If your child is a little sad about losing a game, adults can show how to accept the result easily, and then start the next round together.

## Why Play Music Games

Learning the piano takes constant practice, which can sometimes feel dull to a child.

Music games let children meet music in a relaxed atmosphere, training listening, sense of rhythm and reaction speed.

Playing together as a family also builds communication between parents and children and makes music part of family life.

**In Short**

These games are also good to play when friends and relatives visit. Adults and children can all join in quickly, and the atmosphere becomes lively.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How old should children be to play these games?**
A: The high and low game and music statues suit younger children, and the other games can be adjusted by age.

**Q: Can family members who cannot play join in?**
A: Yes, many games only need clapping or singing.

**Q: How long should a game last?**
A: Ten-odd minutes to half an hour, stopping while everyone is still having fun.

**Q: Will the games get in the way of practice?**
A: Schedule them after practice, and they can work as a reward.

**Q: Can we play without a piano?**
A: Rhythm copycat, music statues and others can be played with clapping or other sounds.

**Q: What if my child always wants to win?**
A: Stress taking part and having fun, and let your child take turns setting the questions.

find-a-comfortable-key-for-the-singer.body:
When you accompany someone, you often run into this: in the key written on the score, the singer strains on the high notes or cannot reach the low ones. Everyone's range is different, so the best key for the same song differs from person to person. As the accompanist, you can first ask the singer to sing the highest and lowest lines of the song, listen for where it feels uncomfortable, and then move the key up or down until the singer sings with ease. With the right key, the singing sounds better and the accompaniment fits together more naturally.

## Transposing with chord charts

If you are using a chord chart, transposing simply means moving every chord by the same distance.

For example, if you move the whole song down a whole step, C becomes B♭, G becomes F and Am becomes Gm.

Write out the new chords and you can accompany in the new key.

## Summary: finding a key for the singer

Everyone has a different range, so the right key for the same song differs. First find the highest and lowest notes of the song and ask the singer to try them.

If the high notes strain, move down; if the low notes are out of reach, move up. Look for a balance in the middle, and let the singer compare two or three keys.

Use a chord chart or a digital piano to help with transposing. Have men, women and children try separately, write down the keys that suit them, and let the singer decide.

## Let the singer lead

The purpose of accompanying is to help the singer sing better, so the key should be chosen for the singer.

Even if the original key is more convenient for the accompanist, change it if the singer is not comfortable.

Only when the singer sings with ease will the whole song come across well.

**Think about it**
- Everyone's range is different, so the right key is different too
- First listen to the singer on the highest and lowest lines
- Move the key up or down
- Keep going until the singer sings with ease

## Write down the right key

Once you have found the right key, write it on the score, for example "Sings in B♭ major".

The next time you accompany the same person, you will not need to search again.

If you often accompany several people, you can keep a simple record.

## Range differs from person to person

The highest and lowest notes a person can sing are different for everyone. This span is called the range.

The key written on a score was chosen for one particular range, and it does not necessarily suit every singer.

So when you accompany someone else, the key often needs adjusting.

## Find the balance in the middle

A suitable key usually lets both the highest and lowest notes of the song fall within the singer's comfortable range.

Sometimes you need to find a balance between the high and low notes so that neither end is too much of a strain.

You can try two or three different keys, ask the singer to compare them, and choose the one that feels most natural to sing.

## When children sing

A child's range is usually narrower than an adult's, and it sits higher.

When accompanying a child, take special care not to make them sing too low or too high.

Choose a key in which the child can sing easily and naturally, and they will enjoy singing more.

## Help from a digital piano

If you are using a digital piano, you can also use its transpose function temporarily to try out keys.

That way you do not need to learn the accompaniment in the new key right away, and you can quickly hear the effect of different keys.

Once you have tried them, decide whether to use the transpose function or to learn to play in the new key yourself.

## Ask the singer to try it out

You can first ask the singer to sing the highest and lowest lines in the original key.

Notice whether the singer becomes tense or has to shout on the high notes, and whether the low notes are too weak to be heard clearly.

You can also simply ask the singer: where does it feel uncomfortable?

## When the high notes are too much

If the singer strains on the high notes, try moving the whole song down one or two steps.

For example, moving from D major to C major lowers the whole song by a whole step.

Then ask the singer to sing the high passages again and see whether they feel easier.

## The accompanist's transposing skill

Once you have found the right key, the accompanist needs to play the accompaniment in that new key.

If the accompaniment is simple, such as chords only, transposing is easier.

You can write out the chords of the new key first and then practise them a few times.

## Male and female voices

The ranges of male and female voices usually differ by about an octave, but individuals vary a great deal.

For the same song, a male singer and a female singer often need different keys.

Do not decide by gender alone; always ask the singer to try it.

![Sketch of an upright piano keyboard seen at an angle, in brown and tan tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6zs30-plpmd.webp)

## When the low notes are out of reach

If the singer cannot reach the low notes, you can move the whole song up.

But note that moving up also raises the high notes, so check that they are still singable.

If both the high and low notes are a problem, the range of the song may simply be too wide for this singer.

## First find the song's highest and lowest notes

Before trying keys, look at the melody of the song and find the highest and lowest notes.

The distance between these two notes is the range the song requires.

Once you know this span, you can judge which key suits the song best.

## FAQ

**Q: Why find a key for the singer?**
A: Everyone's range is different.

**Q: What should I look at before trying keys?**
A: The highest and lowest notes of the song.

**Q: What if the high notes are too much?**
A: Move the whole song down.

**Q: How do I transpose with a chord chart?**
A: Move every chord by the same distance.

**Q: Whose needs come first when choosing the key?**
A: The singer's.

faure-dolly-suite-op56-four-hands.body:
Dolly Suite is a set of piano duets by the French composer Gabriel Fauré, Op. 56, in six movements, written over the years from about 1893 to 1896 and published in 1897. "Dolly" was the nickname of a friend's little daughter, and Fauré often gave her a newly written little piece as a present on her birthday or at New Year. The first piece, Berceuse (Lullaby), is said to have been written for her first birthday. Later pieces include a portrait of a little garden, a waltz about a puppy, and a lively final Spanish Dance. The suite has gentle melodies and bright colours, and it is a lovely piece for two people to play together.

## Tendresse

The fifth piece is titled Tendresse (Tenderness). The music is quiet and heartfelt.

**Tip**

Its harmony is delicate, with the soft colours that are typical of Fauré.

After the lively waltz, this piece lets things settle into calm.

## A set of birthday presents

The original title of the Dolly Suite is simply Dolly, the nickname of the little daughter of one of Fauré's friends.

Fauré often gave her a newly written little piece as a present on her birthday or at New Year.

Over the years, these little pieces added up to six, forming this suite.

## The puppy's waltz

The fourth piece is a light waltz whose title is said to come from the name of a puppy in the household.

The music is lively and playful, like a puppy running around the garden.

The light three-beat rhythm means the two players have to work together very closely.

## Dolly's Garden

The third piece is Le jardin de Dolly (Dolly's Garden), said to have been Fauré's present for a New Year.

The music paints a little garden, gentle and bright, like flowers in the sunshine.

In this piece, the melodies of Primo and Secondo weave together beautifully.

**A different angle**
- Piano duet, Op. 56, six pieces
- Written between about 1893 and 1896, published in 1897
- A present for a friend's little daughter, "Dolly"
- The first piece, Berceuse, is said to have been written for her first birthday

## The Dolly Suite, written for four hands

This suite was written for piano four hands, with two players sitting at the same piano.

One player takes the upper part, called Primo, and the other takes the lower part, called Secondo.

In French homes at the time, piano duets were a very popular kind of music-making at home.

## Summary of the Dolly Suite

Dolly Suite is Fauré's piano duet, Op. 56, in six pieces, written between about 1893 and 1896 and published in 1897. "Dolly" is the nickname of a friend's little daughter, and Fauré often gave her new pieces on her birthday or at New Year. The first piece, Berceuse, is said to have been written for her first birthday. The second, Mi-a-ou, is said to come from the way she pronounced her brother's name. Then come Dolly's Garden as the third piece, the puppy's waltz as the fourth, Tendresse as the fifth, and finally the lively Spanish Dance.

In 1906 another French composer arranged it for orchestra, and it was later used for ballet. The Berceuse suits players with two or three years of experience. In a piano duet you should agree on a starting signal, and the player on the lower part usually takes care of the pedal.

You can play the Berceuse together with Teacher Aum.

## Who it suits

The pieces of the Dolly Suite vary in difficulty. The Berceuse is relatively easy and suits players with two or three years of experience.

Some pieces are faster and need better technique and closer coordination.

You can start with the Berceuse and play it with a friend or family member.

## How two players work together

In a piano duet, the two players must listen to each other and match tempo and dynamics.

Before you begin, agree on a breath or a nod as a signal to start together.

The player on the upper part usually takes the melody, and the player on the lower part takes the pedal, so take care that the sounds do not blur together.

## The later orchestral version

In 1906, another French composer arranged the Dolly Suite for orchestra.

The orchestral version gave these little pieces richer colours, and it was later used for ballet performances.

Even so, many people still love it best in its original four-hand form.

## Mi-a-ou

The title of the second piece is Mi-a-ou, which sounds like a kitten's miaow.

The name is said to come from how little Dolly pronounced her brother's name, which sounded like a cat's cry.

The piece is light and lively, full of childlike humour.

![Glowing abstract digital figures and a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbkpr5e-ge7lk.webp)

## Playing the Dolly Suite with your teacher in the lesson

In the lesson, you can play the Berceuse with Teacher Aum, one on Primo and one on Secondo.

After playing, you can swap places and play it again to feel the difference between the two parts.

From a set of presents for a little girl, discover the joy of playing together.

## Spanish Dance

The last piece is the Spanish Dance, with a bright rhythm and lots of energy.

The music imitates the rhythm of a Spanish dance, lively and cheerful.

The whole suite ends in this joyful atmosphere.

## Berceuse

The first piece is the Berceuse, said to have been written by Fauré for Dolly's first birthday.

Primo plays a gentle, quiet melody, while Secondo accompanies with a rocking rhythm.

**Order of practice**

This piece later became one of the most popular in the whole suite.

## FAQ

**Q: What form is the Dolly Suite written for?**
A: Piano duet (four hands).

**Q: How many pieces does it have?**
A: Six.

**Q: Who is "Dolly"?**
A: The nickname of the little daughter of one of Fauré's friends.

**Q: What is the first piece called?**
A: Berceuse (Lullaby).

**Q: What is the last piece called?**
A: Spanish Dance.

fixed-do-vs-movable-do-solfege.body:
When singing from a score, the syllables Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti can be used in two ways. One is called fixed Do: Do is always C, whatever key the piece is in, so C is sung "Do" and D is sung "Re". It is common in France, Italy, Spain and elsewhere. The other is called movable Do: Do follows the key, so the Do of C major is C and the Do of G major is G. It is commonly used in school music education in Britain, the United States and China. Each method has its strengths: fixed Do helps you remember absolute pitch and note names, while movable Do helps you understand each note's function within the key.

## Comparing the Two Systems at the Piano

At the piano, play a G major melody such as "G, A, B, G".

Sung in fixed Do, it is "Sol, La, Ti, Sol"; sung in movable Do, it is "Do, Re, Mi, Do".

Sing it once each way and notice the difference.

**One more thing to think about**
- Fixed Do: Do is always C
- Movable Do: Do follows the key
- Fixed Do is common in France, Italy and elsewhere
- Movable Do is commonly used in schools in Britain, the US and China

![Pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbjua56-on8al.webp)

## How to Sing Sharps and Flats

In fixed Do, a raised or lowered note is normally still sung with its original syllable. For example, F sharp is also sung "Fa".

In movable Do, some teaching systems give raised or lowered notes their own names. For example, a raised "Fa" is sung "Fi".

Practice may differ between countries and teachers.

## Transposing With Movable Do

Movable Do is very useful for practising transposition.

For example, first play a simple song in C major, then play it once each in G major and F major, singing in movable Do as you play.

You will find the syllables stay the same; only the position of your hand on the keyboard changes.

## The Strengths of Movable Do

The benefit of movable Do is that it helps you understand each note's function in the key.

For example, "Sol" is always the dominant and "Ti" is always the leading note; when you hear "Ti", you know it wants to move to "Do".

This helps with learning harmony, ear training and transposition.

## Fixed Do and Movable Do: A Summary

The syllables come from a hymn used by Guido in the eleventh century. Fixed Do keeps "Do" always as C, and in France, Italy, Spain and elsewhere it is often used directly as the names of the notes. Movable Do lets "Do" follow the key, so the tonic of every key is sung "Do", and it is commonly used in schools in Britain, the US and China. The numbered notation marking "1=G" is a movable-Do notation. Fixed Do helps you remember absolute pitch and keyboard positions, while movable Do helps you understand each note's function in the key.

Minor keys and accidentals are sung differently in different systems. Both methods have their uses. At the piano you can sing the G major notes "G, A, B, G" in both systems, and you can also use movable Do to practise transposition.

You can talk about solfège with Teacher Aum.

## The Strengths of Fixed Do

The benefit of fixed Do is that it helps you remember the absolute position and name of every note.

For pianists, seeing a note on the staff lets you sing its name at once and connect it with its position on the keyboard.

Fixed Do is also fairly convenient in music with many changes of key.

## Numbered Notation and Movable Do

The numbered notation commonly used in China, which uses the digits 1 to 7 for the notes, is a kind of movable-Do notation.

When a score is marked "1=G", it means that the "1" of the piece, that is "Do", is the note G.

So singing from numbered notation is naturally singing in movable Do.

## The Movable Do System

In the movable Do system, "Do" follows the key, and the tonic of every key is sung "Do".

The Do of C major is C, the Do of G major is G, and the Do of F major is F.

So whatever the key, a major scale is sung "Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti, Do".

## The Fixed Do System

The fixed Do system ties each syllable permanently to a note name.

"Do" is always C, "Re" is always D, and "Mi" is always E, whatever key the piece is in.

In France, Italy, Spain and other countries, people often use "Do, Re, Mi" directly as the names of the notes.

## Talking About Solfège With Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum which system is normally used for reading music.

You can also ask your teacher to lead you through a melody in both systems.

Starting from the position of "Do", you can understand the relationship between pitch and key.

## Which Is Better

Neither method is absolutely better. Each has its own uses.

Many musicians use both and choose according to need.

For piano learners, knowing both methods allows more flexible reading and listening.

## How to Sing Minor Keys

When singing a minor key in movable Do, there are two approaches.

One is to sing the tonic of the minor key as "La", so A minor, for example, starts on "La".

The other is to sing the minor tonic as "Do" as well, and sing the third note as a lowered "Mi".

## Where the Syllables Come From

The syllables "Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La" first came from a hymn used by the Italian monk Guido in the eleventh century.

Each line of this hymn began on a note higher than the line before, and Guido named the notes after the first syllable of each line.

**Watch the details**

Later, "Ut" was changed to the easier-to-sing "Do", and "Ti" was added.

## FAQ

**Q: Which note is "Do" in fixed Do?**
A: Always C.

**Q: Which note is "Do" in movable Do?**
A: It follows the key and is the tonic of each key.

**Q: Which kind of notation is numbered notation?**
A: Movable-Do notation.

**Q: What are the benefits of movable Do?**
A: It helps you understand each note's function in the key, and makes transposition and learning harmony easier.

**Q: How do you sing "G, A, B, G" in G major in movable Do?**
A: "Do, Re, Mi, Do".

finger-pad-vs-fingertip-tone-color.body:
The same note sounds a little different when played with the fingertip and with the finger pad. The fingertip has a small contact area and a direct touch, and the sound is often crisp and focused; the finger pad has a larger contact area, the finger is relatively flatter, and the sound is often soft and rounded. The piano makes its sound by striking, but the player's control of touch affects how the hammer strikes the string, which brings subtle differences in tone. Learning to use different parts of the finger deliberately gives us one more way to express ourselves.

## Finger pad and fingertip on a digital piano

On a digital piano, tone depends mainly on the speed of the key press, so the difference made by the part of the finger may be small.

But the habit of controlling your touch deliberately helps on any instrument.

When you have the chance, try it on an acoustic piano too.

## Playing with the fingertip

When playing with the fingertip, the finger is more curved and touches the key with the front end of the tip.

The contact area is small, the force is concentrated on one point, and the touch is more direct.

This approach often gives a crisp, bright sound with clearly defined grains.

## Playing with the finger pad

When playing with the finger pad, the finger is relatively flatter and touches the key with the thicker fleshy cushion below the tip.

The contact area is large, and the touch feels softer.

This approach often gives a soft, rounded, singing sound.

## A slow comparison exercise

You can do a comparison exercise on a simple melody: play it once with the fingertip, then once with the finger pad.

Listen carefully to how the sound differs between the two.

You can also record yourself, and the difference is clearer when you play it back.

## Ask your teacher to demonstrate

Tone is a very subtle thing and hard to explain fully in words.

In the lesson you can ask Aum, your teacher, to demonstrate the two kinds of touch so you can listen and watch.

Then imitate it yourself and ask the teacher for feedback.

## Points to watch when using the finger pad

When playing with the finger pad, keep the finger flatter, but do not straighten it completely.

Let the weight flow from the shoulder down the arm to the finger pad, with the finger simply passing it on rather than pressing hard.

When you touch the key, you can imagine "placing" the finger on the key rather than "striking" it.

## Differences between pianos

Different pianos differ in how the keys feel and how the sound responds.

A clear difference in tone on one piano may be less obvious on another.

So judge with your ears, rather than relying only on a fixed method.

## Do not rely on the fingers alone

Changes in tone come not only from the part of the finger, but also from arm weight and the speed of the touch.

If you only change the angle of the finger while the arm is tense, the sound will still be harsh.

Whether you use the fingertip or the finger pad, keep your arm and wrist relaxed.

## Points to watch when using the fingertip

When playing with the fingertip, keep the joints of the finger stable and do not let them collapse as you touch the key.

Keep your nails short, otherwise they will hit the keys and make a noise, and they will also affect your touch.

Keep the finger curved but not stiff, with a natural arch.

## Switching within one piece

A piece may contain both fast runs and lyrical melodies.

When playing, you can switch between fingertip and finger pad according to the character of each section.

You can even use the finger pad for melody notes and the fingertip for accompaniment notes within the same phrase.

## Music that suits the finger pad

Lyrical melodies and slow, singing passages often suit the finger pad.

For example, the melody of a nocturne needs a connected, soft sound.

A finger-pad touch makes the melody warmer and more singing.

![Close-up of the keys of a grand piano and its lid with a gold pattern in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa939v1-tbp9a.webp)

## Music that suits the fingertip

Fast scales, grainy runs and light staccato often suit the fingertip.

For example, the fast passages in sonatas of the Classical period need every note to be clear.

A fingertip touch keeps these notes clean and crisp.

**Slow down**
- Fingertip: small contact area, crisp and focused sound
- Finger pad: large contact area, soft and rounded sound
- Choose according to the character of the music
- Both approaches need a relaxed arm

## Summary: finger pad and fingertip

The tone of a piano comes from the hammer striking the string, and the player's touch brings subtle differences. The fingertip has a small contact area and a crisp, focused sound, which suits fast runs and staccato; the finger pad has a large contact area and a soft, rounded sound, which suits lyrical melodies.

You can switch between them within the same piece, even within the same phrase, but tone also depends on arm weight and the speed of touch. Both approaches need relaxation: with the fingertip, keep the joints stable and the nails short; with the finger pad, let weight carry the finger.

You can compare them slowly on a simple melody and record yourself. Differences between pianos must be judged by ear, the difference may be smaller on a digital piano, and you can ask Aum, your teacher, to demonstrate.

## Where a piano's tone comes from

The sound of a piano comes from hammers striking the strings.

The speed and manner in which the player presses the key affect the force and speed with which the hammer strikes the string.

So although the string for each key is fixed, the player can still change the effect of the sound through touch.

## FAQ

**Q: What does the sound of a fingertip touch have in character?**
A: Crisp and focused.

**Q: What does the sound of a finger-pad touch have in character?**
A: Soft and rounded.

**Q: What suits fast runs?**
A: The fingertip.

**Q: What suits lyrical melodies?**
A: The finger pad.

**Q: Does tone depend only on the part of the finger?**
A: No, it also depends on arm weight and the speed of touch.

falla-ritual-fire-dance-1915.body:
The Spanish composer Manuel de Falla staged El amor brujo (Love, the Magician), a work with singing and dancing, in Madrid in 1915. It includes a piece called the Ritual Fire Dance: in the story, the heroine dances around a fire at midnight, hoping to shake off the shadows of the past. In the music, the bass keeps repeating the same figure, trills in the high register flicker like flames, and the rhythm grows more and more tense. Falla later arranged it as a piano solo, and the piece has since become a favourite encore for many pianists.

## Who Was Falla

Manuel de Falla was born in 1876 and died in 1946. He was born in Cádiz, in southern Spain.

**Practice Order**

He lived in Paris for many years and was in contact with French composers such as Debussy and Ravel.

His music blends Spanish folk music with the new harmony of the early twentieth century.

![A person in a high-tech jacket playing a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacv1zz-dngid.webp)

## The Piano Arrangement

Falla arranged the Ritual Fire Dance as a piano solo, so that it could be played on its own in concerts.

The piano version keeps the original's bass figure, trills and driving rhythm.

The piece is not long, but its effect is powerful, which is why it is so often used as an encore.

## The Foundation You Need for the Ritual Fire Dance

The Ritual Fire Dance is technically demanding. It needs steady trills, strong chords and good stamina.

It suits learners who already have a solid foundation and want to take on an expressive piece.

If you are not at that level yet, you can start with a simplified version.

## Plan How to Practise the Ritual Fire Dance with Your Teacher

If you want to play the Ritual Fire Dance, you can plan your practice steps with Teacher Aum, for example working on the trills first, then the chords at the end.

You can also ask your teacher whether to go straight to Falla's original or begin with a simplified score.

This piece is excellent training for your sense of rhythm and expressiveness.

## El amor brujo

El amor brujo began as a stage work first performed in Madrid in 1915, with singing, spoken dialogue and dance.

Later, Falla revised it into a ballet.

From the story to the melodies, it is full of the flavour of southern Spain, where Cádiz is.

## Trills Like Flames

The high register has many fast trills, like flickering flames.

These trills need to be even and bright, but not too heavy.

You can practise the trills slowly first, getting the two fingers to alternate smoothly, then gradually speed up.

## The Repeating Bass Figure

From the very start, the bass plays the same short figure over and over.

This constant repetition gives the music a feeling of being drawn in and unable to stop.

On the piano this figure goes to the left hand, struck again and again like the unceasing drumbeat beside a fire.

## Rhythm Growing More Tense

As the music develops, the rhythm becomes tighter and the dynamics stronger.

At the end, several powerful chords ring out again and again, like a ritual reaching its climax.

The dance beside the fire stops abruptly, and the last chord is like a flame leaping up.

## The Story of the Ritual Fire Dance

In the story, the heroine feels haunted by the shadow of a former lover.

To free herself from it, she lights a fire at midnight and dances a ritual-like dance around it.

The Ritual Fire Dance portrays this tense and mysterious dance.

**Listen For**
- Falla was born in 1876 and died in 1946
- El amor brujo was staged in Madrid in 1915
- The heroine dances around a fire at midnight
- Falla himself arranged the piano solo version

## The Ritual Fire Dance in Brief

Falla was born in 1876 and died in 1946. He was born in Cádiz and lived in Paris for many years. In 1915 he staged El amor brujo, with singing and dancing, in Madrid, and later turned it into a ballet. The Ritual Fire Dance portrays the heroine dancing around a fire at midnight, trying to shake off the shadow of a former lover.

The bass repeats the same figure, the trills in the high register are like flames, the melody has a Spanish flavour, and the rhythm grows tighter, ending abruptly after strong chords. The piano version arranged by Falla himself is often used as an encore. Repeated chords depend on the wrist, and the dynamics should be planned.

The piece is technically demanding, and you can plan your practice steps together with Teacher Aum.

## How to Play the Repeated Chords in the Ritual Fire Dance

The ending has many fast repeated chords, which need a relaxed wrist and economical movement.

Do not pound them with the strength of your arm; let the wrist lead and keep it springy.

If your arm feels tense, slow down and adjust again.

## Dynamic Layers in the Ritual Fire Dance

The piece has a big range of dynamics from soft to loud, and these need to be planned.

You can play the opening fairly softly and mysteriously, leaving room for the build-up that follows.

Then, at the end, push the dynamics to the climax.

## The Melody of the Ritual Fire Dance

Above the trills and the bass, a melody with a Spanish flavour appears.

The melody often circles around a few notes, with a slightly mysterious feeling.

**Slow Down**

As you play, you can imagine the dancer's figure whirling in the firelight.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which work is the Ritual Fire Dance from?**
A: Falla's El amor brujo.

**Q: When and where was this work staged?**
A: 1915, in Madrid.

**Q: What does the Ritual Fire Dance portray?**
A: The heroine dancing around a fire at midnight, trying to shake off the shadow of the past.

**Q: What are the trills in the high register like?**
A: Flickering flames.

**Q: Who arranged the piano version?**
A: Falla himself.

echo-dynamics-forte-then-piano-repeat.body:
In many Baroque and Classical pieces you will meet this kind of writing: a short phrase is played once, and straight afterwards it is played again exactly or almost exactly the same. A common way to handle it is to play the first time louder and the second time softer, like an echo in a valley. In his French Overture, published in 1735, Bach even named the final movement "Echo". Learning this echo-style dynamic keeps repeated phrases from sounding monotonous.

## Make the Contrast Clear

The echo effect comes from a clear contrast between loud and soft.

If the difference between the first and second playing is too small, the listener cannot hear an echo.

You can exaggerate the contrast at first, then slowly adjust it to a suitable level.

## Echoes in the Baroque Period

In the Baroque period, the volume of many keyboard instruments could not change subtly with the weight of the fingers.

The harpsichord, for example, sometimes has two keyboards, one with a stronger sound and one with a weaker sound.

The player can switch between the two keyboards to create an echo effect with a sharp loud-soft contrast.

## Not Every Repeat Should Be Played Softly

Not every repeat suits the echo treatment.

Sometimes a repetition is for emphasis, and the second time should actually be stronger.

You can decide from the position of the phrase and the mood of the piece, or try several treatments and compare them.

## The Tone Colour of an Echo

An echo is not only a drop in volume; the tone colour can change too.

The second time can be played more softly and roundly, as if from a distance.

Sometimes you can also reduce the accents slightly, to make the echo lighter.

## Asking Your Teacher to Judge Echoes in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to help judge which repeated phrases in a piece suit the echo treatment.

The piano has only one keyboard, so how the two "voices", loud and soft, are made with the fingers is often clear after seeing the teacher demonstrate it once.

Once you have learned echo dynamics, the music will have more layers and more interest.

## A Little Echo Game to Practise

You can play a little echo game with family or friends: one person plays a short phrase and the other repeats it at a softer dynamic.

This game helps you practise controlling dynamics, and it is fun too.

You can also do the "echo" by yourself, with your left and right hands taking turns.

## Echoes in the Classical Period

In some works by Haydn and Mozart you can also often find echo-like writing.

A short motif appears first loud and then soft, adding humour and a sense of conversation to the music.

This kind of writing is common in Classical-period sonatas and minuets.

## How to Express It on the Piano

The piano has only one keyboard, but you can control volume through the weight of your fingers.

When playing an echo, the second time must be clearly softer; you can keep your fingers closer to the keys and make smaller movements.

You can also imagine the sound arriving from far away, with a slightly hazy feeling.

## How to Find the Places for an Echo

In the score, an echo is often a short phrase followed immediately by its repeat, usually one or two bars long.

Sometimes the score marks loud and soft, and sometimes it has no markings at all and the player has to decide.

If a short phrase is repeated twice exactly, you can consider the echo treatment.

## Checking the Echo Effect with a Recording

When practising, you can record the echo passage and listen back carefully to see whether the loud-soft contrast is clear.

Sometimes while playing you feel the contrast is large, but on the recording the difference is not obvious.

Adjust according to the recording, so that the echo effect is clearer.

- When a short phrase repeats, play the second time softly
- Like an echo in a valley
- The last movement of Bach's 1735 French Overture is called "Echo"
- Stop repeats from sounding monotonous

## Summary of Echo Dynamics

Echo dynamics means using a clearly softer dynamic when a short phrase repeats, with a clear, direct loud-soft contrast. Some Baroque harpsichords have two keyboards that can be switched to make an echo effect, and the last movement of Bach's French Overture, published in 1735, is called "Echo".

On the piano you can express an echo through the weight of your fingers. An echo is often a one- or two-bar short phrase repeated exactly, but not every repeat should be played softly. The tone colour of an echo can be softer, the loud-soft contrast should be clear, and after the echo you should return crisply to the original dynamic. Similar writing also appears in the works of Haydn and Mozart.

You can check with a recording, play the echo game with family, and ask Teacher Aum to judge which places suit an echo.

## Bach's French Overture

In 1735, Bach published the second part of his Clavier-Übung, which includes the Italian Concerto and the French Overture.

The last movement of the French Overture is called "Echo".

The score is marked with loud and soft signs, and the alternation is to be expressed with two keyboards.

## Returning to the Original Dynamic After the Echo

After the echo, the music usually returns to its original dynamic and carries on with the next phrase.

This change should be crisp; do not let the soft dynamic drag on too long.

You can prepare the dynamic of the next phrase in advance, at the point where the echo ends.

![Close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac4qe8-uy8lg.webp)

## What Is Echo Dynamics

Echo dynamics means that after a phrase is played once, it is repeated at a clearly softer dynamic.

The first time is like speaking, and the second time is like an echo coming back from far away.

**Practice order**

This loud-soft contrast is clear and direct; it is not a slow decrescendo.

## FAQ

**Q: What are echo dynamics like?**
A: When a short phrase repeats, the second time is played clearly softer.

**Q: Which work by Bach has a final movement called "Echo"?**
A: The French Overture, published in 1735.

**Q: How does a harpsichord make an echo?**
A: By switching between two keyboards.

**Q: Must every repeat be played softly?**
A: No, sometimes the second time should be stronger.

**Q: What should you do after the echo?**
A: Return crisply to the original dynamic.
