fermata-hold-pause.body:
A fermata is a sign drawn above a note or rest, looking like a half-open eye, and it means the note or rest may be held a little longer than its written value. There is no fixed rule for how long to hold it. You decide by considering the tempo and mood of the piece; in slow pieces the hold is often more relaxed, and it helps to understand the tempo terms before you start playing.

## Feeling the power of the pause in practice

A fermata makes you realise that a pause is also part of the music. A well-judged hold lets the music before it have time to resonate, and makes what follows feel more expected.

In practice, you can deliberately listen to how the sound changes during the hold and feel it gradually fading away.

This kind of listening helps develop a sensitivity to musical time, and you will benefit from it in how you handle other places too.

## How to carry on after a fermata

When many people first meet a fermata, what worries them most is not the hold, but how to continue afterwards. One way is to keep counting the beat in your head during the hold, for example counting one or two extra beats, then take a breath before the new phrase begins and come in at the original tempo.

A fermata sometimes appears at the end of a phrase, and sometimes on the very last chord of the whole piece. At the end, the hold lets the sound fade away naturally; in the middle, it is like pausing while speaking, giving the listener time to take it in.

In practice you can first try holding it longer, then try holding it shorter, and listen to which suits the atmosphere of the whole piece better. Discussing your choice with your teacher is also a way of understanding the music.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a synthesizer with crystals in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jng6u-ojdsk.webp)

## Continuing after a hold

After a fermata, pay attention to the start of the next note or the next phrase. If you want to continue at the original tempo after the hold, you can count the beats ahead in your head so that the music restarts naturally.

Sometimes a brief rest follows the fermata, like a breath, before the next phrase begins. This breath can give the music more layers.

If the fermata is at the end of a phrase, hold the note steadily and then close naturally, without letting go suddenly.

In ensemble playing, everyone needs to start together again after the fermata, so pay special attention to the conductor's or your partners' cues.

- A fermata is made of an arc and a dot
- It shows that the value of a note or rest may be extended appropriately
- How long it lasts is judged by the player according to the music
- After the hold, think about how to return to the original rhythm

## How to judge the length of a hold

There is no fixed rule for how long to hold, so you can look to the character and tempo of the music. In a slow, lyrical piece, the hold can be more relaxed; in a light, lively piece, the hold is often shorter.

One common idea is to hold the note for about one and a half to two times its original value, but this is only a guide. More important is to use your ears and judge whether the pause feels natural.

You can listen to how different players handle the same piece and compare how long they stay on the fermata. This helps you build your own judgement.

In practice you can also record several different ways of handling it and listen to which fits the feeling of the piece best.

## What a fermata means in different positions

A fermata can appear over a note, over a rest or over a barline. Over a note, it means the note may be held; over a rest, it means the silence may be held; over a barline, it often means a pause between sections.

In some works, the fermata is also used to mark where the piece ends, often together with markings such as Fine.

In choral or ensemble music, the conductor usually decides how long to hold a fermata and gives the signals to end and to continue. In solo playing, the player judges for themselves.

**Summary**

Knowing where a fermata sits and what it does helps you judge how long to stay there and how to continue.

## FAQ

**Q: Must I hold a fermata for exactly double the time?**
A: Not necessarily. The usual approach is to hold it appropriately, and the exact length depends on the musical context and the player's understanding.

**Q: Can a rest have a fermata too?**
A: Yes, it means the quiet can be held a bit longer.

**Q: Can I hold a fermata for any length I like?**
A: There is some freedom, but it should fit the character of the music, and be neither too long nor too short.

**Q: Should I slow down after a fermata?**
A: Generally you return to the original tempo and carry on, unless the score gives another tempo instruction.

**Q: How do I handle a fermata on a rest?**
A: It means the silence can be held, and again you judge the length by what the music needs.

**Q: Who decides how long to hold in ensemble playing?**
A: Usually the conductor, or a leader agreed in advance.

fortspinnung-baroque-spinning-out.body:
In many Baroque works, a short motif is continued again and again: the same figure is moved higher or lower, or its intervals are slightly changed, yet the listener always hears that it is still moving forward. This way of "spinning out" the material is often called Fortspinnung (spinning out). It is different from the square question-and-answer found in Classical themes: here the emphasis is on continuous motion, and the boundaries of a phrase sometimes become clear only at a fairly definite cadence. When learning it, first pick out the short initial motif by itself, then see how it is attached again and again. This is closer to the nature of the writing than just cutting the score up by bar lines. When listening, you can also follow the figure with your hand, and see after how many sequences it finally stops. If you play every sequence as a brand-new beginning, the feeling of continuous spinning breaks into separate pieces. This article talks only about the spinning writing that is easiest to hear in keyboard works, and does not present it as the only term for analysing all Baroque music. When practising, it helps to first join the motif and its first sequence together at a very slow tempo, make sure a listener can recognise "it is still the same idea", and only then play a longer stretch at the original tempo.

## Practise From Short to Long

First get the motif plus one sequence steady, then add up to three or four, and only at the end play the whole passage as written.

This makes it easier to check, at each join, whether a listener can still recognise the original idea.

If you rush through the whole passage at full speed from the start, you often feel only "lots of notes" and fail to catch the spinning thread.

**Another way to look at it**
- A short motif is continued again and again, often moving in sequence
- Unlike a square question and answer, it stresses uninterrupted motion
- Phrase boundaries often become clear only at a fairly definite cadence
- In practice, first pick out the initial motif, then listen to how it is spun out

## When It Comes to a Stop

A fairly definite cadence, longer notes, or a clear change of the figure into another kind of writing often brings the spinning out to a close.

Hear this pause clearly, and the next phrase will have a place to begin.

Do not push through a real close just to keep things going without a break.

## Ask Teacher Aum in Lessons to Listen to Whether the Joins Still Sound Like One Sentence

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether each sequence can still be recognised, and whether any place that should not break has been cut.

If a place sounds too much like the start of a new sentence, you can also ask your teacher to help rejoin the tone of voice.

From this kind of writing that spins a motif forward, practise keeping a long phrase directed.

## How It Differs From the Period's Question and Answer

Question and answer is more like two symmetrical sentences, with a place to breathe in between.

Fortspinnung often does not give such a square breathing place, and only truly settles at the cadence.

If you cut a long Baroque phrase using the habits of listening to periods, you easily cut where it should not be cut.

## How to Mark the Motif in the Score

First circle the initial motif, then mark the starting point of each of its appearances.

When you see a run of similar figures appearing one after another, you can note in your mind: here it is spinning forward.

Keep the marks few and clear. They are for listening, not for filling the score with drawing.

## What to Remember About Fortspinnung

It is a way of writing in which a short motif is continued again and again, often moving in sequence, and it is common in Baroque works.

Unlike a square question and answer, the breathing place often appears only at the cadence.

In practice, first recognise the motif, then extend outward from short to long, and do not cut the continuous spinning thread.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon street, with a crystal tower behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdkl8ue-vrd5u.webp)

## How to Keep It Unbroken When Playing

Touch and tone of voice should make each sequence feel like a continuation of the previous sentence, not a fresh announcement of a beginning.

Dynamics may have small rises and falls, but it is not advisable to strike every figure with the same weight.

If you use the pedal, do not blur what comes before and after into a directionless mass in the middle of a sequence.

## How to Hear That It Is Spinning Forward

The same figure appears again at a new height or over a new harmony, and the listener can still recognise it.

Only after several continuations does it reach a fairly definite pause.

**Summary**

You can first just follow the figure, ignoring the bar lines for the time being.

## FAQ

**Q: What does Fortspinnung mean?**
A: A short motif is continued again and again, often moving in sequence, so that you hear it is still moving forward.

**Q: How does it differ from the question and answer of a period?**
A: Question and answer is squarer, with a place to breathe in between. Fortspinnung stresses uninterrupted motion and only settles at the cadence.

**Q: What problem is most likely when playing it?**
A: Playing every sequence as a brand-new beginning, so that the spinning thread breaks into separate pieces.

**Q: How can I help myself hear it in the score?**
A: First circle the initial motif, then mark the starting point of each of its appearances.

**Q: Why is it better to practise from short to long?**
A: First make sure a listener can recognise "it is still the same idea", then play a longer stretch. That is clearer than rushing through the whole passage from the start.

edelweiss-1959-musical-waltz-piano.body:
"Edelweiss" is a song written by the American composer Richard Rodgers and the lyricist Oscar Hammerstein for the 1959 Broadway musical The Sound of Music. The edelweiss is a small white flower that grows in the Alps. The melody is simple and gentle, in 3/4 time, and many people think it is an Austrian folk song, or even Austria's national anthem, when in fact it was written specially for the musical. It was also the last lyric Hammerstein wrote; he died the following year. It is a very good song for beginners to play on the piano.

## How Beginners Can Play It

If you have just started learning, first get the right-hand melody of "Edelweiss" under your fingers.

**Slowly**

Then add the left hand, for example one bass note per bar or a simple chord.

Once both hands are fluent, add changes in dynamics.

![Colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacyio2-5dsk9.webp)

## The 3/4 Rhythm

"Edelweiss" is in 3/4 time, with three beats to a bar, the first beat strong and the other two light.

This rhythm has a gently swaying feeling, like a waltz.

While you play, you can count "one, two, three" and feel the pulse of the three-beat metre.

**A small tip**
- Written for the 1959 musical The Sound of Music
- Music by Rodgers, lyrics by Hammerstein
- In 3/4 time, with a simple, gentle melody
- Often mistaken for an Austrian folk song

## The Shape of the Edelweiss Melody

The melody is simple and gentle, with a narrow range, which suits beginners very well.

Many phrases end on a long note, giving a feeling of calm and peace.

The melody has some rising intervals, like looking gently upwards.

## Asking Your Teacher to Help with the Left Hand in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to help write a left-hand accompaniment for "Edelweiss" that suits your level.

Your teacher can also recommend other songs from The Sound of Music that are good to play.

This song is perfect for playing to everyone at a family gathering.

## Listen to Edelweiss in the Musical First

Before you play, listen first to "Edelweiss" in the musical or the film.

Notice how the singer handles the rise and fall of the melody and the breathing.

Bring those feelings to the piano and play the song's tenderness.

## Arrangements at Different Levels

There are many piano arrangements of "Edelweiss" at different levels.

The easy versions have only a simple melody and bass, while the intermediate versions add richer chords and ornaments.

From a one-page beginner's score to an intermediate score with chords, "Edelweiss" comes in all kinds; choose according to your skills.

## Often Mistaken for a Folk Song

Because the melody is plain and the lyrics describe a small Alpine flower, many people think "Edelweiss" is an Austrian folk song.

Some even think it is Austria's national anthem.

In fact, Rodgers and Hammerstein wrote it in 1959 specially for the musical.

## Playing with a Three-Beat Accompaniment

The left hand can go "oom-pah-pah": the bass note falls at the start of each bar, followed by two light chords.

This makes the three-beat pulse of the song even clearer.

Play the chords softly so that they do not cover the right-hand melody.

## The Sound of Music

The Sound of Music had its premiere on Broadway in New York in 1959, and the story is set in Austria in the 1930s.

The show tells the story of a young governess and a large family, and it has many lovely songs.

In 1965 it was made into a film and became known all over the world.

## What the Edelweiss Is

The edelweiss is a small flower that grows high in the Alps, with white flowers covered in fine down.

It is often seen as a symbol of Austria and the Alpine region.

In the song, the edelweiss stands for love and longing for one's homeland.

## Hammerstein's Last Lyric

"Edelweiss" was the last lyric Hammerstein wrote.

Soon after the premiere of The Sound of Music, Hammerstein died in 1960.

This gives the song a special significance.

## Making Edelweiss Sing

When you play this song, you can imagine someone singing softly.

Keep the melody connected, and hold the long notes for their full value.

You can leave a little room to breathe between phrases, like a singer taking a breath.

## Rodgers and Hammerstein

Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein were one of the most famous partnerships in the history of American musical theatre.

Rodgers composed and Hammerstein wrote the lyrics, and together they made many classic musicals.

The Sound of Music was the last work they made together.

## Summary of "Edelweiss"

"Edelweiss," with music by Rodgers and lyrics by Hammerstein, was written for the 1959 Broadway musical The Sound of Music, set in Austria in the 1930s and made into a film in 1965. The edelweiss is a white flower of the Alps. The song is often mistaken for an Austrian folk song or even the national anthem, but it was written specially for the musical, and it was also the last lyric Hammerstein wrote before he died in 1960.

The song is in 3/4 time with a simple, gentle melody. Beginners can play the right-hand melody first, then add a left-hand bass note or chords, using an accompaniment with a bass note on the first beat and chords on the other two. The melody should be kept connected, and there are arrangements at different levels.

You can ask Teacher Aum to help write the left-hand accompaniment.

## FAQ

**Q: What work was "Edelweiss" written for?**
A: The 1959 musical The Sound of Music.

**Q: Who wrote the music and who wrote the lyrics?**
A: Rodgers wrote the music and Hammerstein the lyrics.

**Q: Is it an Austrian folk song?**
A: No, it was written specially for the musical.

**Q: What time signature is it in?**
A: 3/4.

**Q: In what year did Hammerstein die?**
A: 1960.

fonte-and-monte-galant-sequences.body:
In the mid-18th century, a German music theorist gave vivid names to several common chord progressions in a composition textbook written for his students: Fonte (Italian for "fountain") and Monte ("mountain"). A Fonte flows downward like a fountain: a short phrase first appears higher up, then repeats one step lower. A Monte climbs like a mountain path: the phrase rises one step at a time. These patterns are very common in the music of Haydn's and Mozart's day. Recognising them helps us see where the music is heading more quickly on the page.

## Where the names come from

In 1755, the German theorist Joseph Riepel published a composition textbook that taught students to write through dialogue.

**Have a listen**

In the book, he gave several common patterns Italian names, including Fonte and Monte.

In the twenty-first century, scholars of 18th-century music have revisited these names and brought them to a wider audience.

## The chords of the Fonte

In C major, the first part of a Fonte is often A7 to a D minor triad, that is, the dominant seventh to the tonic chord of D minor.

The second part is G7 to a C major triad, that is, the dominant seventh to the tonic chord of C major.

The two parts have the same shape, except that the second part sits one step lower overall.

- Named by a German theorist in the mid-18th century
- Fonte means "fountain": the phrase repeats one step lower
- Monte means "mountain": the phrase repeats one step higher
- Very common in the age of Haydn and Mozart

## Ask your teacher to find Fonte and Monte in your lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to help you find Fonte and Monte in the classical pieces you are learning.

Your teacher can also explain what they do in the piece.

Once you know these common patterns, reading music gets faster and your understanding gets deeper.

## The sequence behind Fonte and Monte

Fonte and Monte are both "sequences": the same small shape, played again at a different height.

For example, a two-bar phrase played first on C and then on D is an ascending sequence.

Fonte and Monte are both specific kinds of sequence.

![A transparent, futuristic keyboard with beams of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaccj2m-1xlm9.webp)

## Monte: climbing like a mountain

The Monte goes in the opposite direction to the Fonte: the phrase rises one step at a time.

In C major, a common Monte is C7 to an F major triad, then one step higher, D7 to a G major triad.

To the ear, the music gets higher and higher and gains more and more momentum, like a climb up a mountain.

## Where a Fonte often appears

A Fonte often appears in the middle of a piece, for example right at the start of the second part of a minuet.

It lets the music leave the home key for a while, then return to it naturally.

You can find it in many Classical-period minuets and sonatas.

## Fonte: flowing down like a fountain

A Fonte has two parts: the first part is in a minor key, and the second part, one step lower, is in a major key.

Take C major as an example: the first part heads to D minor, and the second part, one step lower, heads to C major.

To the ear, there is a touch of melancholy first, then a return to brightness, like water flowing down from a height.

## Finding them on the page

Open a minuet by Haydn or Mozart and first look for two bars that look the same, only shifted by one step.

If the second one is a step lower than the first, and goes from minor to major, it is very likely a Fonte.

If the second one is a step higher than the first, it may be a Monte.

## Playing a Monte at the piano

In the same way, you can play a Monte: C7 to F, then D7 to G.

Listen for the feeling of the music rising one step at a time.

You can also play it in other keys. In G major, for example, a Monte is G7 to C, then A7 to D.

## What a Monte does

A Monte is often used to build tension and push the music toward a high point.

It also often appears in the middle of a piece, or just before the main theme returns.

After the climb, the music often arrives at an important chord and then comes back to the home key.

## Recognise the fountain and the mountain, then memorise

Because Fonte and Monte are both repeated shapes, memorising becomes easier once you recognise them.

You only need to remember the shape of the first statement, and whether the second one goes a step higher or a step lower.

That takes far less effort than remembering note by note.

## Fonte and Monte in short

In 1755 the German theorist Riepel gave common patterns Italian names in a composition textbook. A sequence is a short fragment repeated at different pitches. Fonte means "fountain": the first part is in a minor key and the second part, one step lower, is in a major key; in C major it is often A7 to D minor, then G7 to C, and it often appears at the start of the second part of a minuet.

Monte means "mountain": the phrase rises one step at a time; in C major it is often C7 to F, then D7 to G, and it is used to build tension. On the page, look for short phrases with the same shape in different places. You can play them at the piano to get familiar with the sound. The return of a Fonte can be played in a settled way, and the rise of a Monte can be matched with a crescendo. Recognising them makes memorising easier.

You can ask Teacher Aum to help you find the Fonte and Monte in your pieces.

## Playing a Fonte at the piano

You can play a Fonte at the piano with simple chords: the right hand plays A7 to a D minor triad, then G7 to a C major triad.

The left hand plays the roots, A, D, then G, C.

Play it a few times to get familiar with its sound, and you will find it easier to hear in pieces later on.

## Play the fountain settled, the mountain with a crescendo

Recognising Fonte and Monte helps you understand the direction of the music.

The second part of a Fonte is a return to the home key, so you can play it in a more settled way.

A Monte pushes upward, so you can use a crescendo to go with the rise of the music.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does Fonte mean?**
A: It is Italian for "fountain".

**Q: What does Monte mean?**
A: It is Italian for "mountain".

**Q: Which chords does a Fonte often use in C major?**
A: A7 to D minor, then G7 to C.

**Q: Which direction does the phrase of a Monte go?**
A: It rises one step at a time.

**Q: Who gave these names?**
A: The German theorist Riepel, in 1755.

fauxbourdon-parallel-sixths-15th-century.body:
Fauxbourdon is a way of writing harmony in fifteenth-century European church music. The name comes from French and means roughly "false bass". The composer writes out only two parts: the highest part is a chant melody, and the lowest part moves in parallel a sixth below it, becoming an octave at the ends of phrases. The third, middle part is not written out, and singers improvise it a fourth below the top part. Together, the three parts form a string of parallel 6-3 chords, with a soft, bright sound. The composer Dufay is thought to have used this technique in works from around the 1430s.

## Dufay's works

The composer Dufay, from northern France, is thought to have used fauxbourdon in works from around the 1430s.

**Listen closely**

He often used this method in hymns and other liturgical music.

Later, fauxbourdon became popular in fifteenth-century church music.

## The sixth below

Beneath the chant melody, the composer writes another part that, most of the time, stays a sixth away from the melody.

This part moves along with the melody, like its shadow.

At the beginning and end of a phrase, it usually becomes an octave away from the melody.

## Trying fauxbourdon with your teacher in the lesson

In the lesson, with Teacher Aum, one of you can play the melody and the sixth below, while the other improvises the middle fourth.

You can also ask your teacher to explain what a 6-3 chord is called in today's harmony and how it is used.

From a fifteenth-century improvisation method, you can see how harmony developed.

## A soft, bright sound

Before fauxbourdon, medieval polyphony was often built mainly on fifths and octaves, with an open sound.

Fauxbourdon makes heavy use of thirds and sixths, so the sound becomes soft and full.

This sound is thought to have had an important influence on the later development of harmony.

## The improvised middle part

The third part of fauxbourdon is not written out by the composer.

The singer looks at the melody in the top part and sings along a fourth below it.

In this way, writing only two parts is enough to produce three-part music.

## Listening to a string of 6-3 chords

After playing, listen to this string of parallel 6-3 chords and notice how soft it sounds.

Then take out the middle notes and play only two parts, and compare how the sound changes.

You will find that although the middle part is not written out, it makes the sound much fuller.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, suggesting sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbjwd3t-0rcy8.webp)

## The English influence

Some scholars think the sound of fauxbourdon may have been influenced by English music.

In the early fifteenth century, English music often used thirds and sixths, with a very sweet sound that musicians on the Continent admired.

England also had a similar improvised way of singing, often compared with fauxbourdon.

## Use in arrangements today

Parallel 6-3 chords are still very common in piano arrangements today.

For example, when harmonising a melody, you can use a string of first-inversion chords in the right hand to make the sound flowing and soft.

Knowing about fauxbourdon helps us understand where this way of writing comes from.

- A harmony technique of fifteenth-century church music
- The name comes from French and means roughly "false bass"
- Only two parts are written, and the middle part is improvised a fourth below the top
- It forms a string of parallel 6-3 chords

## Parallel 6-3 chords

With the three parts together, the lowest note and the middle note are a third apart, and the lowest note and the top note are a sixth apart.

This kind of chord is called a 6-3 chord, which today we call a first-inversion triad.

Fauxbourdon is a string of such chords moving in parallel.

## Playing fauxbourdon on the piano

On the piano, you can play a simple melody with the right hand, for example "Mi, Re, Do, Re, Mi, Mi, Mi".

With the left hand, play a sixth below each note. For example, when the melody is "Mi", the left hand plays the low "Sol".

Then use the right-hand thumb to add the middle note a fourth below the melody.

## False bass

The name fauxbourdon comes from French and means roughly "false bass".

Scholars have different explanations for why it is called "false bass".

One view is that the lowest part looks like a bass, but the real melody is in the top part.

## Melody on top

In fauxbourdon, the main chant melody is placed in the highest part.

This is different from much earlier polyphony, where the chant melody was often placed in a lower part.

With the melody on top, listeners can hear it more clearly.

## Summary of fauxbourdon

Fauxbourdon is a harmony technique of fifteenth-century church music. The name comes from French and means roughly "false bass". The composer writes only two parts: the top part is a chant melody, and the lowest part mostly moves in parallel a sixth below it, becoming an octave at the beginning and end. The middle part is improvised by singers a fourth below the top part, forming a string of parallel 6-3 chords, which are what we now call first inversions.

It makes heavy use of thirds and sixths, with a soft, full sound, and it may have been influenced by English music. Dufay is thought to have used it around the 1430s. On the piano you can play the melody with the right hand, the sixth below with the left hand, and add the note a fourth below with the thumb. Strings of first-inversion chords are also common in arrangements today.

**Think about it**

You can try fauxbourdon together with Teacher Aum.

## FAQ

**Q: What does the name fauxbourdon mean?**
A: It is French and means roughly "false bass".

**Q: In which part is the main melody placed?**
A: The highest part.

**Q: How far apart are the lowest part and the melody most of the time?**
A: A sixth.

**Q: How is the middle part produced?**
A: Singers improvise it a fourth below the top part.

**Q: What kind of chords does fauxbourdon form?**
A: A string of parallel 6-3 chords.

explain-your-piece-aloud-to-family.body:
When you are learning a piece, here is a small method to try: before you play it for family or friends, spend two or three minutes "telling" them about it. Talk about how many sections it has, where the climax is, where it changes key, what mood the composer wanted to express and which part you find hardest. To explain it clearly, you first have to think through the structure and details of the music. Often, when you play after explaining, you will find your thinking much clearer and your memorising more secure.

## Explaining to yourself works too

If nobody is around, you can talk into your phone's voice recorder and pretend you are introducing the piece to a friend.

Listen back and see whether you explained it clearly and whether you left out any important section.

This also helps you organise your thoughts.

## Explaining to Teacher Aum in the lesson

In the lesson, you can first spend two or three minutes explaining the piece you are learning to Teacher Aum, and then start playing.

Your teacher can add to or correct your explanation, for example how the sections divide or where the key change happens.

Combining talking and playing also makes better use of lesson time.

## Summary: explaining your piece to family

Before playing a piece, spend two or three minutes explaining it to family or friends. Talk about the composer, the period, the sections, the mood, and the parts you love and fear. Beforehand, mark the sections and key spots on the score as an outline.

When explaining to someone who does not know music, use everyday comparisons and play short snippets as you go. Any spot you cannot explain clearly is a spot you do not understand enough, and you need to go back to the score to sort it out. When there is no one around, you can talk to your phone.

A piece you have explained has signposts for memorising and more vivid expression. Children can give the sections names, adults can talk about harmony and background, and you can explain each new piece once or twice. You can also explain it to Teacher Aum first in the lesson.

- Before playing, spend a few minutes explaining the piece
- Talk about sections, climax, key changes and mood
- To explain clearly, you first have to understand it yourself
- Play after explaining, and both your thinking and your memorising will be more secure

## Explaining and memorising

When you memorise using only finger memory, it is easy to get stuck when you are nervous.

After you have explained a piece a few times, you will have a clear structure in your head: what the first section is about, what the second is about, where the key changes.

This structure works like signposts for memorising. If you forget a note, you can still find where you are heading next.

## Prepare on the score first

Before explaining, you can use a pencil to mark the sections on the score, writing letters such as A, B, A.

Then mark a few key spots, such as where the key changes, where the dynamics reach their peak and where the tempo changes.

These marks are your outline for the explanation.

## Play short snippets as you explain

When you reach a certain section, you can play a short passage for your listener, for example "this is the opening theme, and it will come back later".

Then play the place where the theme returns and ask your listener whether it sounds the same.

This kind of small interaction makes the explanation more lively, and it helps you confirm where the theme appears.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, suggesting sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabq813-g2rjc.webp)

## Explaining and expression

When you explain a piece, you often need words that describe feelings, such as "gentle", "tense" or "spacious".

Once you have said those words, you will also try more deliberately to express them when you play.

A passage you used to play flatly may gain shape and colour.

## Explaining your piece as an adult

Adult learners can go deeper in their explanations, for example the changes in harmony, the composer's life or the background to when the piece was written.

You can look up reliable sources and add what you learn to your explanation.

The more specific your explanation, the deeper your understanding of the music.

## Explain each new piece once

You do not need to explain every day. You can do it once when you are halfway through a piece and can basically play it through.

Then explain it again when you are about to play for others or before an exam.

Between the two explanations, you will notice your understanding of the piece has changed.

## What you can say about a piece

You can say the name of the piece and the composer, and roughly what period it was written in.

You can say how many sections it has and how the mood of each differs.

You can also say which part you like best when you play it, and which part you fear most.

## Why explaining is useful

People often say that you only truly understand something when you can explain it to others.

Practice is the same: your fingers being able to play does not mean you have a clear picture of the piece in your head.

Explaining the piece forces you to organise scattered impressions into one complete map.

## Explaining to someone who does not know music

Your listener does not need to know music. Older relatives or young children are fine.

Precisely because they do not know music, you have to use simple words, such as "here it sounds like rain starting to fall" or "here it suddenly gets very angry".

When you explain with everyday comparisons, your own feeling for the music becomes more vivid too.

## The parts you cannot explain are the parts to practise

While explaining, if you cannot get a certain spot across, for example "here... I think it modulates to another key?", that is a spot where your understanding is not yet enough.

Such spots are also the ones where mistakes or memory slips often happen in performance.

After explaining, you can go back to the score and sort out those vague spots.

## An explaining game for children

For children, explaining a piece can become a little game.

For example, ask the child to give each section a name: "the little rabbit goes out", "a strong wind comes", "back home again".

**Think about it**

When children play after telling the story, they often play with more involvement, and parents find it easier to understand what the child is practising.

## FAQ

**Q: What are the benefits of explaining a piece?**
A: It forces you to think through the structure and details of the music.

**Q: What can I talk about?**
A: The composer, sections, mood, difficult spots and so on.

**Q: What should I prepare before explaining?**
A: Mark the sections and key spots on the score.

**Q: What does it mean if I cannot explain a spot clearly?**
A: Your understanding there is not yet enough, and you need to go back to the score to sort it out.

**Q: What if nobody is there to listen?**
A: Record yourself on your phone and explain it to yourself.

five-four-time-uneven-groups.body:
5/4 time has five quarter notes in each bar, and the usual feeling is to divide the five beats into two groups, "three plus two" or "two plus three". So it does not sound as square and steady as 4/4, but has a slightly tilted, forward-driving pulse. When counting, you can count "1 2 3, 1 2" or "1 2, 1 2 3", and first find where the strong beat is. Some twentieth-century works, film music and jazz have used this time signature.

## The beat that is easy to miss in five

When they first play 5/4, many people unconsciously play it as 4/4 and miss a beat.

**Slow down**

Others pause after the fifth beat, which makes the pulse disconnected.

Setting a metronome to one click per beat and accenting the first beat can help you keep the correct count.

## The three-plus-two grouping

One common grouping is to divide the five beats into "three beats plus two beats".

Here the first beat is the strong beat and the fourth beat is a secondary strong beat, counted "1 2 3, 1 2".

It sounds like a bar of three followed by a bar of two.

## A counting chant for five

Some people use words to help remember the feeling of "three plus two" or "two plus three".

For example, say a three-syllable word and then a two-syllable word, over and over, and the sense of rhythm comes out.

Combining this kind of chant with the bass on the piano helps you get used to five-beat time more quickly.

## Summary: learning five-beat time

The key to 5/4 is to find the grouping inside the five beats and the positions of the strong and secondary strong beats.

Once the grouping is clear, counting and playing both become simple.

Listen to more music written in five, and you will find that this asymmetrical pulse has a unique charm.

## Improvise a bit of 5/4

You can improvise in 5/4 with two chords, for example Am and G.

In "three plus two", play Am on the first three beats and G on the last two, and repeat a few times.

With the right hand, play some simple melody above using notes of A minor, and enjoy the fun of an asymmetrical time signature.

## Other asymmetrical time signatures

Besides 5/4, there are other asymmetrical time signatures such as 7/8 and 5/8.

7/8 is often divided into "two plus two plus three" or "three plus two plus two", which sounds livelier.

Once you have learned the way of thinking for 5/4, you can understand other asymmetrical time signatures in the same way.

## The two-plus-three grouping

Another grouping is "two beats plus three beats", where the first beat is the strong beat and the third beat is a secondary strong beat.

Counted "1 2, 1 2 3", it sounds like a bar of two followed by a bar of three.

The same 5/4 with a different grouping gives the music a different feel.

## Five-beat time is uncommon

The time signatures we meet most often have two, three or four beats, and five-beat time is rarer.

5/4 has five quarter notes per bar, and the first beat is the strong beat.

Because five is an odd number, it cannot be divided evenly into two halves, so the pulse sounds very distinctive.

## Five-beat time in classical works

Since the late nineteenth century, composers have gradually written five-beat time into their works.

For example, in some symphonies one movement is written in 5/4, with a slightly unsteady waltz-like feeling.

These works show composers exploring new rhythms.

## How to tell the grouping

When reading a score, you can observe where the accents of the melody and the bass fall.

If the left hand plays bass notes on beats one and four, it is most likely "three plus two"; if on beats one and three, most likely "two plus three".

Sometimes the composer gives a hint in the score with dotted lines or beam groupings.

![An electronic keyboard and a screen in neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3774y-l34zu.webp)

## Feeling 5/4 on the piano

With your left hand you can play the bass on the strong beats of "three plus two", for example C on beat one and G on beat four.

With the right hand, play a chord on every beat, counting "1 2 3, 1 2" as you play.

After a few repetitions, your body will gradually get used to this asymmetrical pulse.

## Asymmetrical time signatures in folk music

In the folk music of Eastern Europe and the Balkans, asymmetrical time signatures such as five and seven beats are common.

To local listeners these sound perfectly natural, and they are often used for dancing.

Composers such as Bartók drew inspiration from this folk music and wrote many works in asymmetrical time signatures.

## 5/4 in jazz and film music

In the mid-twentieth century, a very famous jazz piece was written in 5/4, and it made many people notice this time signature for the first time.

In film scores, 5/4 is also often used to create a tense or uneasy atmosphere.

When listening to this kind of music, you can count along and feel the cycle of five beats to a group.

**Tips**
- Five quarter notes per bar
- Often divided as "three plus two" or "two plus three"
- An asymmetrical pulse with a forward-pushing feel
- First find the position of the strong beat

## FAQ

**Q: How many beats are there in each bar of 5/4?**
A: Five quarter notes.

**Q: What are the usual groupings?**
A: "Three plus two" or "two plus three".

**Q: How do I tell the grouping?**
A: Look at which beats the bass and accents fall on.

**Q: What are the common mistakes in 5/4?**
A: Unconsciously playing four beats, or pausing after the fifth beat.

**Q: What other asymmetrical time signatures are there?**
A: 7/8, 5/8 and others.

ear-training-intro-high-low-long-short.body:
Learning the piano is not only about training your fingers; you need to train your ears too. Ear training means telling sounds apart by listening: high or low, long or short, loud or soft. For beginners there is no need to start with anything complicated. Begin with the simplest ideas, "high and low" and "long and short", and a few minutes a day will slowly build up your sensitivity to sound. This article introduces a few simple games suitable for children and adults.

## Why train your ears?

The ear is the way in to music. If your ear can tell which note is higher and which is longer, your fingers have more direction when they look for a position on the keyboard. Many people learning the piano find that once they can hear clearly, reading music and playing both become easier.

- If you can hear high and low, you find notes faster.
- If you can hear long and short, your rhythm is steadier.
- If you can hear loud and soft, your playing has more layers.

## Step one: telling high from low

**Comparing two notes**
Ask someone at home to play two different notes on the piano, and you say which is higher. At the start, make the two notes far apart, for example one on the left and one on the right, and bring them gradually closer as you get used to it.

**Let your body help**
When you hear a high note, slowly raise your hand; when you hear a low note, slowly lower it. The movement of the body helps the brain remember the direction of the sound.

**Swap roles**
Let the child play and the parent guess. The child will feel more of a sense of achievement and listen more attentively.

![A close-up of hands practising on the keys](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwib9x6p-8z4te.webp)

## Step two: telling long from short

Play one note and let it ring for a long time, then play a very short note, and ask the student to tell them apart. You can imitate them by clapping: for a long note, slowly draw your hands apart; for a short note, clap once. You can also use words, saying "long" as "aaah" and "short" as "ta".

- First listen to two notes and decide which is longer.
- Then listen to three notes and decide which is the shortest.
- Finally, let the student play one long note and one short note by themselves.

## Step three: play what you hear

Choose three notes, starting with "do", "re" and "mi", and let the student listen and then try to find them on the piano. It does not matter if they cannot find them. Listen a few more times, or ask the teacher for a hint, such as "the first note is just left of the two black keys". Practise for only a few minutes at a time, and finish with one specific word of encouragement, for example "You heard that the second note went up."

## When playing listening games with a child

- Do not require the child to be right the first time; a wrong answer is part of learning too.
- Keep a relaxed tone, and do not turn listening into an exam.
- If the child feels bored, switch to another game, or take a break.

## Small exercises in daily life

Ear training does not have to happen at the piano. When you hear a car horn on the road, you can guess whether it is high or low; when you hear a doorbell, you can wonder how many notes it is made of. Turn everyday sounds into little games, and your ears will become more sensitive without your noticing. Do this only where it is safe, and stay aware of your surroundings.

## Practising with an app

Some students use an AI piano teaching app such as TIGA ALPHA to check at home whether the notes they play match what was asked. It listens to pitch and beat and then suggests the next practice step, helping students connect what the ear hears with what the fingers play. Of course, the teacher's demonstration and your own feeling remain the core, and the app is only an aid.

## A small secret for sticking with it

Choose a fixed time, for example five minutes after dinner. Write the practice on a calendar and draw a small mark when you have done it. After a few weeks, look back at the marks along the way and you will find that you have in fact come a long way. Progress in listening builds up slowly, every person's ears grow at a different speed, and it is quite normal not to hear accurately one day. Just try again, relaxed, the next day.

## Listening to loud and soft: a third little game

Once high and low and long and short are fairly familiar, you can add a game of "loud and soft". Play a very soft note, then a louder one, and ask the student to say which is louder. You can show it with the body: for a soft note, slowly bring your palms together; for a loud note, open your arms. Take care not to strike too hard, so as not to hurt your hands, and not to disturb the neighbours. Practising loud and soft makes students begin to notice the "expression" in music, which helps a great deal later in playing pieces with layers.

## A ten-minute plan

Spend the first two minutes on the high and low game, then three minutes on the long and short game, three more minutes listening to loud and soft, and finally two minutes of free playing of notes you like. Each part is very short, so the child is unlikely to get bored. At the end say something specific, such as "Today you heard three long notes", so that the child leaves the piano with a small sense of achievement.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I train my ear without perfect pitch?**
A: Yes. Ear training is mainly about learning to tell the relationships between sounds, and most people can improve with practice.

**Q: At what age can a child start?**
A: As long as the child is willing to listen and to play, you can start in the form of games.

**Q: How long a day is right?**
A: A few minutes are enough. The point is to do a little every day.

**Q: Do I need to buy special teaching materials?**
A: Not necessarily. The piano at home, voices and everyday sounds can all be used for practice.

granados-goyescas-1911-maiden-nightingal.body:
Goyescas is a piano suite completed in 1911 by the Spanish composer Enrique Granados. It was inspired by the work of the eighteenth and nineteenth-century Spanish painter Goya and portrays the lives and loves of men and women on the streets of Madrid. The best known of its pieces is the fourth, Quejas, ó la maja y el ruiseñor (The Maiden and the Nightingale), with its lingering melody and, at the end, a cadenza that imitates a nightingale's song. Granados later reworked the music of the suite into an opera of the same name, which premiered in New York in 1916. On the way home, the ship he was travelling on was attacked in the English Channel, and he and his wife died.

## Goyescas in Brief

Enrique Granados was born in 1867 and died in 1916. He was born in Lleida, studied and worked in Barcelona, and loved Goya's paintings of ordinary people in Madrid. In 1911 he completed the piano suite Goyescas, which portrays the love and life of majos and majas. It is in two books of six pieces in all, and El pelele is often played with it.

The fourth piece, Quejas, ó la maja y el ruiseñor, has a lingering melody said to come from a folk song. At the end, the trills and ornaments in the right hand imitate the nightingale, and the piano writing often has three or four voices. The suite was reworked into an opera of the same name, which premiered in New York in January 1916, with the intermezzo added shortly before the premiere. In March 1916, on the way home, his ship was attacked in the English Channel, and he and his wife died. To get to know him, you can start with the Twelve Spanish Dances.

You can talk about Granados' works with Teacher Aum.

## The Tragedy on the Way Home

After the opera's premiere, Granados and his wife set off to return to Europe.

In March 1916, the ship they were travelling on was attacked in the English Channel.

According to accounts, Granados jumped into the sea trying to save his wife, but both of them died.

## The Nightingale's Cadenza

At the end of The Maiden and the Nightingale, there is a cadenza that imitates a nightingale's song.

The right hand plays a string of light trills and ornaments in the high register, like a nightingale calling from a branch.

This cadenza calls for very light, agile fingers.

## The Men and Women of Madrid

Goya's paintings often show the fashionable men and women of Madrid's streets, the men called "majos" and the women "majas".

They wear splendid costumes, and are passionate and bold in character.

Granados' suite portrays the love and life of these people.

## Who Was Granados?

Enrique Granados (1867-1916) was both a composer and an excellent pianist.

He was born in Lleida in Spain, and later studied and worked in Barcelona.

He wrote many piano pieces, such as the Spanish Dances, which have a strong Spanish flavour.

## The Opera's Intermezzo

Among the music written for the opera is an intermezzo that was added only shortly before the premiere.

This intermezzo has a beautiful melody and is often played on its own afterwards, with many arrangements.

Arrangements for cello and piano are especially common.

## The Structure of the Suite

Goyescas is divided into two books, with four pieces in the first and two in the second.

Each piece has its own title and portrays a scene or a feeling.

Later, Granados wrote El pelele, which is often played together with this suite.

![Piano scene with futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaeobw1-h4aym.webp)

## Talk About Granados with Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons you can talk with Teacher Aum about the relationship between Goyescas and the painter Goya.

You can also ask for your teacher's opinion on which of the Twelve Spanish Dances to pick first.

Through the works of Granados, you can get a feel for the colours of Spanish piano music.

## Reworked as an Opera

After the suite was published it was very popular, and Granados decided to rework its music into an opera.

The opera is also called Goyescas and uses many of the melodies from the suite.

In January 1916, the opera premiered in New York and was well received.

## The Difficulty of the Piano Writing

The piano writing in Goyescas is complex, often with three or four voices moving at once.

The melody is often hidden in the middle, surrounded by many ornaments and chords.

Sorting out these layers calls for quite mature hand technique.

## The Painter Goya

Francisco Goya was a Spanish painter of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

He painted the lives of many ordinary people of Madrid, such as men and women in the street and festival scenes.

Granados loved Goya's paintings, often went to museums to see them, and drew inspiration from them.

## Starting with the Spanish Dances

Goyescas is very difficult, so if you want to get to know Granados first, you can start with his Spanish Dances.

There are twelve Spanish Dances, and some are of moderate difficulty, suitable for intermediate players.

Among them, the fifth, Andaluza, has often been arranged for guitar.

## The Maiden and the Nightingale

The fourth piece of the suite is Quejas, ó la maja y el ruiseñor, which portrays a young woman listening to a nightingale's song at night and pouring out her troubles.

The melody is lingering and tender, with a touch of sadness.

It is said that this melody comes from a folk song Granados heard in Spain.

**Slow down**
- A piano suite Granados completed in 1911
- Inspired by the paintings of Goya
- The end of The Maiden and the Nightingale imitates a nightingale's song
- Reworked as an opera and premiered in New York in 1916

## The Works He Left Behind

Granados was only forty-eight when he died, and he had many plans unfinished.

But the works he left behind, such as Goyescas and the Spanish Dances, are still often played today.

They let people feel the passion and romance of Spanish music.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote Goyescas?**
A: The Spanish composer Granados.

**Q: In which year was it completed?**
A: 1911.

**Q: What was the inspiration?**
A: The paintings of Goya.

**Q: Which piece ends by imitating a nightingale?**
A: The fourth, Quejas, ó la maja y el ruiseñor.

**Q: Where did the opera of the same name premiere?**
A: In New York, in 1916.

ginastera-danza-de-la-moza-donosa.body:
Danza de la moza donosa ("Dance of the Graceful Maiden") is the second of the three pieces in Danzas argentinas, Op. 2, by the Argentine composer Alberto Ginastera, written in 1937. The two outer dances have stronger, faster steps, but this middle one slows down, with a long melody and harmony that carries a touch of bitterness, as if it singled out one quiet person in a lively scene. It is not a dance for racing through with your hands, but one in which you need to sing each phrase to its end at a slower pace. When learning it, first join up the melody on its own, then let the accompaniment support it at a softer volume. When listening, you can follow only the main melody the first time through, then pay attention to how the bass moves slowly. If a certain phrase keeps breaking off halfway, plan the breathing place in advance, rather than pushing the volume up suddenly to force your way through. In practice you can listen to and practise this piece separately from the ones before and after it, to feel specifically why the middle one has to slow down. If a phrase always breaks at the same spot, pencil the breathing place into the score and sing it twice in a row before playing. The completeness of a slow dance matters more than any surface decoration of tenderness. The slowness of this middle piece is the breathing of the whole set of dances; play it completely, and the speed of the pieces before and after has something to be set against. You do not have to learn all three on the same day; getting the long phrases of the middle one on solid ground is already a very complete achievement. A slow and complete phrase is exactly what this piece has to carry among the three dances.

## How It Contrasts with the Outer Dances

After learning this one, listen to the first and third dances, and it will be clearer why the middle one needs to leave space.

**Listen**

The contrast is not only fast against slow but also touch: the middle piece is more connected and more restrained.

There is no need to rush through all three together; getting the phrases of this one on solid ground is already a good gain.

![A poster-style illustration of the city of Bangkok, with tall buildings and busy traffic in the streets](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjp5i7-fypja.webp)

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen for Whether the Phrases Are Complete

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether the main melody breaks off halfway, and whether the chords underneath cover it.

If the ending of a particular phrase sounds stiff, you can also ask your teacher to listen to two different phrase endings side by side.

From the middle piece of this 1937 set of dances, practise singing out a slow, complete phrase.

## Level and Where to Start

If you can already play a fairly slow melody all the way through and are not flustered by pedal changes, this Danza de la moza donosa is a suitable piece to add to your practice.

Set the tempo by what lets you sing the phrase to its end, and do not chase the faster recordings.

It saves more time to read the phrasing in the score clearly before you start than to keep groping around.

## This Piece's Place in the Set of Dances

Danzas argentinas has three pieces: the two outer ones have stronger steps, and the middle one draws in both the tempo and the tone.

This arrangement gives the whole set room to breathe, rather than three equally lively dances.

Even if you only learn the second one, it is worth listening first to the ones before and after, to understand why it has to be so slow.

## Left-Hand Movement in Danza de la moza donosa

The left hand often has slow harmonic progressions, which should move steadily, without an accent on every beat.

The changes of bass note are often the pivots of the phrases, so you can mark these pivots out separately first.

Change the pedal with the harmony, and change it cleanly, so that the slightly bitter colour can be heard without blurring into one wash.

- The second of Ginastera's Danzas argentinas, Op. 2, of 1937
- The set has three pieces; this one is slower and more singing
- A long melody, with harmony that carries a touch of bitterness
- In practice, first sing the phrase through completely, then add a softer accompaniment

## What to Remember About This Dance

This is the second of Ginastera's Danzas argentinas, written in 1937, slow and singing in character.

When playing, first keep the melody and its breathing places, and change the pedal cleanly with the harmony.

When listening, first follow the main phrase, then hear how it contrasts with the two faster dances before and after.

## How to Sing the Melody

First play only the main melody with one hand, smoothly, singing along aloud to find the breathing places.

Then bring the chords underneath gently back in, and check whether the song is still there.

You can run the same phrase through twice in a row and see which time the ending settles more naturally.

## How to Hear "Graceful" in the Title

The title points to a poised, slightly reserved way of moving in a dance, not a quick stamping of the feet.

The direction of the melody often matters more than rhythmic impact, and the phrase needs both a rise and a settling.

**Before you start**

If you play it in a hurry, or add a heavy accent to every note, this reserve disappears.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which work is this piece from?**
A: Ginastera's Danzas argentinas, Op. 2, of 1937.

**Q: Which piece in the set is it, and what is its character?**
A: The second; slower and more singing than the ones before and after.

**Q: Why sing the melody first when practising?**
A: Once the breathing places and the rise and fall of the phrase are clear, the accompaniment knows where to give way.

**Q: How should the pedal work?**
A: Change it with the harmony, and change it cleanly, so that the slightly bitter colour can be heard.

**Q: How should I set the tempo?**
A: By what lets you sing a phrase to the end; do not chase the faster recordings.

half-tempo-full-run-through-once-a-week.body:
Once a piece is well learned, we often fall into playing it at the normal speed, or even faster and faster. At speed, many small problems are hidden by the tempo. A good habit is to pick one day a week and play the whole piece from beginning to end at about half speed. Slowed down, every note, every fingering and every pedal can be seen clearly, places that had become blurred become clear again, and the piece is kept from getting faster and messier.

## Checking the Fingering

When playing at half speed, you can also check whether the fingering is still the one you originally chose.

**Order of practice**

Sometimes fast playing lets your fingers quietly change the fingering, and slowing down lets you spot it.

If you find the fingering has changed, think about whether the original fingering was poor or whether your habit has changed.

## After You Find Problems

Problems found during a half-tempo run-through can be marked in the score.

In the practice of the next few days, you can deal with these places specifically.

At the next half-tempo run-through the following week, see whether the problems have been fixed.

**Listen**
- Once a week, at about half speed
- Play it all the way through from start to finish
- Let problems hidden by speed show themselves
- Stop the piece from getting faster and messier

## Which Day to Do It

You can choose a fixed day each week, such as Sunday, as your half-tempo day.

Practice on this day can be used mainly for this, with no need to practise a lot of other material.

A fixed schedule is easier to keep up.

## Playing All the Way Through

In a half-tempo run-through, play the piece all the way from beginning to end, not just the difficult places.

The easy places may also have problems that you simply have not noticed.

Playing the whole piece lets you do a full check of it.

## What Half Speed Means

Half speed means about half the original tempo. For example, if the original is a hundred and twenty beats per minute, now use about sixty.

It does not need to be exact. The key is to slow down clearly, slow enough that you can think each note through.

You can use a metronome to help you keep a steady slow tempo.

## Which Pieces Deserve a Weekly Half-Tempo Pass

This method is especially suited to pieces you have learned well and are preparing for a performance or an exam.

For a new piece you are still learning, you normally practise slowly anyway, so you do not necessarily need to schedule it separately.

Memorised pieces are also a good fit, because slow playing lets you check whether your memory is secure.

## Why Pieces Get Messier

When a piece is well learned, the fingers run ahead on their own, and the speed often creeps up without your noticing.

At speed, some notes are not played clearly and some fingerings quietly change, but you do not easily notice.

Over time, the piece becomes less and less stable.

## Returning to the Normal Tempo

After a half-tempo run-through, if you play at the normal speed the next day, it often feels clearer and steadier.

That is because slow playing lets the hands and the mind re-confirm every detail.

This feeling helps us keep up the quality of the piece.

## Checking Pedal and Dynamics

When playing slowly, you can hear more clearly whether the pedal changes are clean and whether the dynamics follow the score.

You can pay special attention to the dynamic markings in the score and see whether you have done them all.

Sometimes you will find that some crescendos and diminuendos have been overlooked.

## Seeing Every Note Clearly

Once slowed down, you can look at the score and check whether every note matches it.

Sometimes you will find that a certain note has always been played wrong, or that an accidental has been ignored.

These small problems are hard to spot when playing fast.

## Half-Tempo Run-Through in Brief

A well-learned piece easily gets faster and faster, with problems hidden by the speed. Once a week you can play it all the way through at about half speed.

At the slow tempo, check each note, fingering, pedal and dynamic, while keeping the feel of the phrases, mark the problems you find, and deal with them specifically afterwards.

Do it on a fixed day. It suits pieces for performance and exams especially well, and returning to the normal tempo the next day will feel clearer and steadier.

## Slow but Not Loose

Playing at half speed does not mean playing casually. You need to keep the direction of the music and the feel of the phrases.

Even at a slow tempo, let the phrases rise and fall and breathe.

Slow playing like this lets you check the details without losing the feel of the music.

## How Much Time to Set Aside

A half-tempo run-through takes about twice as long as usual: a piece of five minutes takes about ten.

If the piece is very long, you can split it over two days.

**Before you start**

What matters is to play attentively, not to rush against the clock.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a half-tempo run-through?**
A: Playing the whole piece once at about half speed.

**Q: Why do it?**
A: To reveal problems hidden by speed.

**Q: How often?**
A: About once a week.

**Q: Can I play casually when slow?**
A: No. Keep the phrases and the feel of the music.

**Q: Which pieces is it for?**
A: Pieces you have learned well and are preparing for performance or exams.

give-the-piece-a-story-image.body:
When you can play all the notes of a piece correctly but do not know how to make it expressive, try giving it a simple story or picture: the opening like a path in the early morning, the middle like a sudden rain, the ending like the sky clearing after the rain. With a picture, your choices of tone, tempo and dynamics have a basis: the morning sound is light and bright, the rain is more urgent, and after the rain stops it slowly calms again. The story does not need to be complicated, nor does it have to be what the composer intended; it only needs to help you find the feeling of the music.

## Summary of Story-Making Practice

Making up a story or picture for a piece can help you choose tone, tempo and dynamics, so that your playing has more expression.

The story does not need to be complicated, nor the composer's original intention; it only has to match the character of the music.

The next time you play a new piece, you might first ask yourself: what kind of story is this piece telling?

## Pictures Help You Choose the Tempo

A picture can also help you decide on the tempo and its changes.

For example, if someone is taking a slow walk, the tempo is unhurried; if they suddenly break into a run, the tempo speeds up.

This kind of imagining makes tempo changes more natural, rather than mechanically following the markings.

## The Title Is a Good Clue

If a piece has a title, such as "Raindrops" or "Lullaby", the title is a good clue for making up a story.

You can imagine a picture from the title, and then enrich the story with the changes in the music.

Even if there is no title, you can give the piece a name yourself, based on the character of the music.

## Making Up Stories with Children

Making up stories is a very good method when a child is learning the piano.

You can listen to the piece together with your child, ask what it sounds like to them, and then make up a little story together.

With a story, children come to like the piece more, and are more willing to express it.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa41u7w-xdats.webp)

## Learn About the Background of the Work

If you want the story to stay closer to the work, you can first find out about its background, for example the circumstances in which the composer wrote it.

This background knowledge gives your imagination more material.

But do not be limited by the background; the feeling the music itself gives you is just as important.

## The Notes Are Right, So What Next?

When learning a piece, you first need to play the notes, rhythm and fingering correctly; that is the foundation.

But once they are right, many people feel something is still missing, and it sounds as if they are "reading" notes rather than "speaking" music.

At this point, making up a story for the piece can often help you find a direction for expression.

## The Story Does Not Have to Be Complicated

The story you make up does not need to be long or complicated; a few sentences are enough.

For example, "A little bird is singing in a tree, suddenly flies away, and then flies back."

A simple story is easier to remember, and easier to recall when you are playing.

## Pictures Help You Choose the Tone

With a picture, it is easier to choose the tone.

For example, if you imagine morning sunlight, the sound can be light and bright; if you imagine a street late at night, the sound can be soft and dim.

Changes in tone come from the speed and weight of your touch, and the picture can help you find the right feeling.

## Listen to the Character of the Piece First

Before making up a story, listen to the piece first, or play it through slowly yourself.

Feel its overall character: is it light, quiet, sad or agitated?

Also notice where it changes, for example a sudden speeding up, a sudden loud passage, or a change of key.

**Summary**
- Make up a simple story or picture for the piece
- The picture helps you choose tone, tempo and dynamics
- The story does not need to be complicated
- It does not need to be the composer's original intention; it only has to help you find the feeling

## Pictures Help You Choose the Dynamics

In a story, a quiet scene calls for soft dynamics and an intense scene for strong dynamics.

If the story has a climax, for example the moment the storm is at its fiercest, that is the dynamic high point of the piece.

Planning your dynamics with a story gives a stronger sense of the whole than just looking at the markings.

## Write It on the Score

Once you have made up the story, you can write it on the score in a few keywords, for example "morning" over section A and "rain" over section B.

Each time you practise, seeing these words lets you recall the picture at once.

These words can also help you stay focused when you play.

## It Does Not Have to Be the Composer's Intention

The story you make up is not necessarily what the composer was thinking when writing the piece.

It is only a tool to help you understand and express the music.

As long as the story fits the character of the music and helps you play with a more expressive sound, it is useful.

## Divide the Piece into Scenes

You can divide the story into scenes according to the sections of the piece.

For example, section A is the beginning of the story, section B is the development or a turning point, and the return of section A is a return to where it began.

**Listen**

Each scene can have a simple picture or mood.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why make up a story for a piece?**
A: It helps you find a direction for expression and choose tone, tempo and dynamics.

**Q: Does the story have to be complicated?**
A: No, a few sentences are enough.

**Q: Does the story have to be the composer's original intention?**
A: No, it only has to fit the character of the music.

**Q: What if the piece has a title?**
A: The title is a good clue for making up a story.

**Q: Is this a good way for children to practise?**
A: Very much so; you can listen together and make up the story together.

fp-fortepiano-and-rfz-rinforzando-marks.body:
Besides the familiar f and p, you will see marks such as fp and rfz in scores. fp means loud then soft: one note or chord is played loudly and immediately followed by a drop to soft. rfz is short for rinforzando and means a sudden reinforcement, emphasising one note or a short stretch of music. Both marks are to do with accents, but their effects differ, so when you play you need to tell them apart.

## Contrast practice at a slow tempo

You can first practise fp slowly: play the first note loudly, pause, then play the following notes very softly.

**Remember this**

Once you are comfortable, slowly shorten the pause until you can make a clear contrast at the normal tempo.

You can practise rfz in the same way: first practise the emphasised note on its own, then put it back into the phrase.

## What fp means

fp is a combination of two dynamic marks: f means loud and p means soft.

Together, they mean that the note is played loudly and then immediately changes to a soft dynamic.

It is often written under a long note or a chord, and the notes that follow all have to be played very softly.

## What rfz means

rfz is an abbreviation of the Italian word rinforzando, and is sometimes also written rf or rinf.

It means reinforcing, and shows that a note or a short stretch of music should be suddenly strengthened.

Compared with sfz, rfz is sometimes used for a group of notes, not just one note.

## Why dynamic contrast matters

Both fp and rfz depend on dynamic contrast to take effect.

If the surrounding notes are played too loudly, these emphases do not stand out; if the surroundings are quiet enough, the emphasis can be heard even if it is not very strong.

So the key to playing these marks well often lies in controlling the notes around them.

## Comparing with accent marks

The common accent mark in scores is a small wedge-shaped symbol written above or below a note.

Accent marks, sfz, rfz and fp are all related to emphasis, but each has its own meaning.

The accent mark is general emphasis, sfz is sudden emphasis, rfz is reinforcement, and fp is loud then soft.

## A long note after fp

If fp is written on a long chord on the piano with no other notes after it, all you can do is play it loudly and let the sound fade naturally.

Some pianists, after playing the chord, use the pedal or a change of the fingers to make the sound seem to fade faster.

More important is that the next phrase starts very softly, so that the listener feels the contrast.

## fp on the piano

On a violin or a wind instrument, a long note can start loud and then become soft, because the player can control how the sound is sustained.

But on the piano the sound begins to fade naturally as soon as the key is struck, and the same note cannot be made loud and then suddenly soft.

So on the piano, the effect of fp is mainly shown by the notes that follow: the first note is played loudly, and the very next note is played very softly straight away.

## fp and rfz in short

fp is loud then soft. On the piano it is mainly shown by a loud first note and very soft notes immediately after it. rfz is rinforzando, meaning a sudden reinforcement of a note or a short stretch.

They are related to accent marks and sfz in being about emphasis, but each is different, and how you handle them depends on the context and style.

The key to playing these marks well is to control the dynamics around them, keep the arm relaxed, and check the contrast with your ears.

## fp and sfz in Beethoven's scores

In works by Beethoven and other Classical composers, both fp and sfz are very common.

These marks often appear in unexpected places, such as on weak beats, giving strong drama.

When you play these works, taking every mark of emphasis seriously makes the music livelier.

## Relaxing the arm

When playing an emphasised note, many people use too much force and the arm becomes tense.

You should in fact keep the arm relaxed and let the weight fall naturally onto the keys, and the sound will be fuller.

After playing, relax the hand immediately, ready for the softer notes that follow.

## Checking the effect with your ears

Record yourself on your phone, and when you play it back listen especially for the fp and rfz, to hear whether the contrast with their surroundings is enough.

If you cannot hear the contrast, play the notes around them more softly, or give the emphasised notes more weight.

Checking with your ears is more reliable than just watching what the hands do.

## The difference between rfz and sfz

sfz is short for sforzando and means a sudden emphasis on one note, usually quite short and sharp.

rfz also means reinforcement, but in the usage of different composers it sometimes means reinforcing a short stretch of music, and sometimes means much the same as sfz.

How to handle it depends on the context and the style of the work.

## Handling rfz

Where there is an rfz, make the emphasised note or phrase stand out more than what comes before and after it.

But the degree of reinforcement has to fit the surrounding dynamics. If the surroundings are p, an rfz does not need to be as loud as an f.

It is a relative reinforcement, not a fixed volume.

![A watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5nooe-w2zg3.webp)

## How to play fp

When playing fp, the first note or chord needs clear weight, and should be played with a full sound.

The notes that follow must lighten immediately, with the fingers barely touching the keys.

**Have a listen**

The clearer the contrast between the two, the more obvious the effect of the fp.

**Pay attention to the details**
- fp: loud first, then immediately soft
- rfz: a sudden reinforcement of a note or a short stretch
- Both are about emphasis, but with different effects
- On the piano, fp has to be shown through the notes that follow

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does fp mean?**
A: Loud first, then immediately soft.

**Q: How do you show fp on the piano?**
A: The first note is loud, and the notes after it are immediately soft.

**Q: What is rfz short for?**
A: Rinforzando, which means reinforcing.

**Q: Is rfz the same as sfz?**
A: They are similar, but the usage varies with the composer and the context.
