gounod-funeral-march-of-a-marionette-187.body:
Funeral March of a Marionette is a piano piece written in 1872 by the French composer Charles Gounod, and in 1879 he arranged it for orchestra. The piece tells a humorous little story: a marionette is broken in a duel, the other marionettes hold a funeral for it, and halfway along the procession everyone stops to rest and have a bite to eat, and then goes on again. The music is in D minor, with a swaying rhythm like the stiff steps of a puppet. In the middle of the twentieth century it was used as the opening theme of a television programme, so that many people recognise it as soon as they hear it.

## A Rest Halfway

The middle section of the piece turns to the major, and the music becomes relaxed and cheerful.

According to the story's description, this is where the marionettes at the funeral have reached the halfway point, stop to rest, and have something to eat and drink.

This middle section makes you laugh, because it is so different from the atmosphere of a funeral.

## Playing the Marionette on the Piano

The original piano version of this piece is of moderate difficulty, suited to players of intermediate level.

The left-hand accompaniment should be regular and springy, like the steps of the marionettes.

The right-hand melody should be clear, with a touch of comedy and exaggeration.

## On the Move Again

After the rest, the procession goes on, and the D minor march melody returns.

But this time the marionettes seem to be in more of a hurry, or a little absent-minded.

In the end the procession moves away into the distance, and the music ends quietly.

## A Television Theme

In the middle of the twentieth century, an American mystery television programme used this piece as its opening theme.

The programme ran for many years, and the piece became a household name because of it.

Many people know the melody without knowing that its composer is Gounod.

**Try it**
- A piano piece written by Gounod in 1872
- Arranged for orchestra in 1879
- A humorous story of a marionette's funeral
- In D minor, with a rhythm like a puppet's steps

![A pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaetpji-cl0xn.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Tell the Marionette Story in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to tell the story of each section of Funeral March of a Marionette.

You can also ask your teacher to help you polish the left hand's jerky, stop-and-go motion and the relaxed feeling of the rest halfway along.

From this little piece, get a feel for humour in music.

## The Marionette Story

According to Gounod's note on the score, the story goes like this: a marionette is broken in a duel.

The other marionettes carry it and line up in a procession to hold a funeral for it.

The story is humorous in itself, because marionettes are not real people.

## The Marionette's Staccato and Legato

There are many staccato notes in the piece, showing the stiff, jerky movements of the marionettes.

There are also some legato sections, showing the marionettes weeping or the relaxation of their rest.

When you play, tell the staccato and legato clearly apart.

## Comparing It with Other Humorous Pieces

There are many other humorous works in music, such as Anderson's The Typewriter and Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals.

Listen to several of them together and see what each composer does to make the listener laugh.

For example, unexpected sounds, exaggerated rhythms, or a contrast between form and content.

## Funeral March of a Marionette: A Summary

Charles Gounod was born in 1818 and died in 1893. He is most famous for the opera Faust, first performed in 1859, and he also set an Ave Maria over Bach's Prelude in C major. He lived in London between 1870 and 1874. In 1872 he published the piano piece Funeral March of a Marionette, and in 1879 he arranged it for orchestra. The story is that a marionette is broken in a duel and the other marionettes hold a funeral for it.

After a short introduction comes a swaying march in D minor. In the middle section, in the major, the marionettes rest halfway and eat; then the march returns and the procession moves away. Telling a comic story in the solemn form of a march creates a contrast. In the middle of the twentieth century an American mystery television programme used it as its opening theme. The original piano version suits intermediate players; the left hand should be regular and springy, staccato and legato should be clearly distinguished, and you can compare it with The Typewriter and Carnival of the Animals.

You can ask Teacher Aum to tell the story of each section.

## The Funeral Procession

At the start of the piece there is a short introduction, like the moment the marionette is broken.

Then the funeral march begins, its D minor melody swaying like a marionette walking stiffly.

The left-hand accompaniment beats out regularly, like the steps of the marionettes landing one by one.

## Bringing Out the Story

When you play this piece, you can imagine the story of the marionette's funeral as you play.

The introduction at the start should be sudden, the march stiff and solemn, the middle section relaxed and cheerful, and the ending gradually moving away.

When you bring out the story, the listener can feel the humour in it.

## A Piece Written in London

Between 1870 and 1874, Gounod lived in London, England.

Funeral March of a Marionette was written during this time, and published in 1872 as a piano piece.

Later he returned to France, and in 1879 arranged it for orchestra.

## Telling a Joke with Music

Funeral March of a Marionette is an example of expressing humour with music.

It tells a comic marionette story in the solemn form of a funeral march, creating a contrast.

This contrast is the source of the humour.

## Who Was Gounod?

Charles Gounod was born in 1818 and died in 1893. He was a French composer.

His most famous work is the opera Faust, first performed in 1859.

**Tip**

He also wrote an Ave Maria, setting the melody over Bach's Prelude in C major, which has been very widely performed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who wrote Funeral March of a Marionette?**
A: The French composer Gounod.

**Q: In what year was the piano version published?**
A: 1872.

**Q: In what year was the orchestral version arranged?**
A: 1879.

A: D minor.

handel-and-bach-never-met-1685.body:
Handel and Bach were both born in 1685, in Halle and Eisenach, not far apart, both in what is now central Germany. They later took very different paths: Handel went to Italy and then settled in London, becoming famous for opera and oratorio; Bach stayed in Germany, holding musical posts in churches and cities. According to the records, Bach twice tried to visit Handel when he came home to see family. The first time, Handel had just left when Bach arrived; the second time, Bach sent his son in his place. In the end, the two never met even once.

## The First Miss

Around 1719, Handel went back to his home town of Halle to visit his family.

According to the records, Bach heard about it and made a special trip to Halle, hoping to meet this famous composer of his own age.

But by the time he arrived, Handel had already left the day before.

## Handel and Bach in Brief

Handel and Bach were both born in 1685, in Halle and Eisenach, both in central Germany, and Scarlatti was born the same year. Handel went to Italy and later settled in London, becoming famous for opera and English oratorio. Bach worked in Germany all his life and from 1723 was music director at St Thomas Church in Leipzig. Around 1719, when Bach reached Halle, Handel had left the day before, and in 1729 Bach asked his eldest son to extend an invitation in his place, which also failed.

Handel's music is grand and bright, with memorable melodies, while Bach is known for intricate, finely worked polyphony. Both wrote keyboard suites. On the piano you can play one short piece by each and compare their styles, keeping the rhythm steady and the ornaments light. You could begin with the minuets from the Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach.

You can chat with Teacher Aum about the story of these two men born in the same year.

## The Second Miss

In 1729, Handel returned to Halle once again.

At that time Bach happened to be ill and could not go himself, so he sent his eldest son, Wilhelm Friedemann, to invite Handel to Leipzig in his place.

Handel did not accept the invitation, and once again the two missed each other.

**Something to think about**
- Both were born in 1685
- Their birthplaces, Halle and Eisenach, are both in central Germany
- Handel settled in London, while Bach stayed in Germany
- Bach tried twice to visit Handel and never saw him

## Talk About These Two Contemporaries in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about the story of how Handel and Bach missed each other twice.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend one short piece by each of them, and compare the difference in style.

From the story of two men born in the same year, you get to know two faces of Baroque music.

## How to Play Baroque Music

When playing music of the Baroque period, keep the rhythm steady, like an accurate pendulum.

Eighth notes without slurs can be played slightly detached, so that each note is distinct.

Ornaments should be played lightly and should not cover the main melody.

## Different Styles

Handel's music is often grand and bright, with tuneful, memorable melodies, well suited to performance in a large hall.

Bach's music is known for its intricate, finely worked polyphony, with several voices interwoven.

Their styles differ, yet both represent the summit of Baroque music.

## Later Comparisons

After the two died, people often compared them together.

In the nineteenth century, Bach's music was rediscovered and came to be valued more and more.

Today, piano learners often end up playing works by both.

## Handel's Path

As a young man, Handel went to Italy and studied Italian opera style.

He later settled in London, where he wrote many Italian operas, and in his later years many English oratorios.

He was very famous in England, and later took British nationality.

## Their Keyboard Suites

Both men wrote a good number of keyboard suites, each stringing together dances such as the allemande, courante and sarabande.

Among Handel's suites, a set of variations later known as The Harmonious Blacksmith is very popular.

Bach wrote several sets of suites, such as the French Suites and the English Suites.

## Comparing the Two on the Piano

On the piano, you can play one short piece by Handel and one by Bach, and compare their styles.

Handel's short pieces often have a prominent melody and a fairly simple left-hand accompaniment.

Bach's short pieces often have independent melodies in both hands, so you have to look after two voices at once.

## Born in the Same Year

In 1685, Handel was born in Halle in central Germany, and Bach was born not far away in Eisenach.

The Italian composer Domenico Scarlatti was also born in the same year.

All three of these composers later became very important figures in the Baroque period.

## Bach's Path

Bach worked all his life in central and northern Germany, serving in turn as organist and music director in several towns.

From 1723 he was music director at St Thomas Church in Leipzig until his death.

He wrote a great deal of church music, keyboard music and instrumental music.

![Lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbjh6xq-6ifi5.webp)

## Start with Bach's Short Pieces

Bach put together a notebook of short pieces for his wife, Anna Magdalena, with many short keyboard pieces in it.

Some of the minuets in it are very good for people just starting Baroque music.

Handel also has some short dances suitable for beginners.

## FAQ

**Q: In which year were Handel and Bach born?**
A: 1685.

**Q: Where did Handel later settle?**
A: London.

**Q: In which city did Bach work from 1723?**
A: Leipzig.

**Q: Why did Bach not meet Handel the first time he went to Halle?**
A: Handel had already left the day before.

**Q: Whom did Bach send to invite Handel the second time?**
A: His eldest son, Wilhelm Friedemann.

grade-exam-scale-hand-positions.body:
When you practise scales before a grade exam, it is better to fix the hand shape and fingering for each key than to keep pushing the speed. Once your fingers know where to go, you are more likely to get the first note right in the exam room, and your hands have a familiar routine to rely on when you are nervous. Many teachers give this same advice before exams.

## Building Up Speed Step by Step

Raise the speed of your scales gradually. Use a metronome to set a tempo you can play accurately without effort, and once several runs in a row feel steady, nudge it up a little. If mistakes creep in after you speed up, go back to the previous setting.

As you practise, check that every note has the same volume and length. Scales are not just about moving your fingers; they are also a great chance to train an even touch. Try recording yourself and listening back to see whether any note is especially heavy or light.

As the exam approaches, you can simulate the exam room: pick a key at random and play it straight away without preparing. This shows whether you really know it, and it makes a surprise request in the exam feel less unfamiliar.

After each session, jot down the tempo you reached and the keys that felt steady, so you can pick up from there next time.

- Check the black keys from the key signature first, then work on the fingering
- At a slow tempo, make every note clear and even
- Practise the thumb-under and crossing points separately a few extra times
- In the final week, aim for steadiness and avoid major fingering changes

## Why Hand Shape Comes First in Scales

A scale looks like a simple string of notes going up and down, but every key has different black keys and a different moment for the thumb to turn under. If you work out the fingering on the spot each time, your hand tends to hesitate and falls apart once you speed up. Fixing the hand shape first is like giving yourself a familiar map for every key.

Start with hands separately at a slower tempo, keeping the volume and length of each note as even as you can. Once the thumb-under points no longer catch, raise the speed bit by bit. Recording one run and listening back often reveals unevenness you do not notice while playing.

In the days before the exam, play each key you will be tested on in exam order to rehearse the rhythm of walking in, but do not play until you are exhausted every day.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jbppn-o2mvp.webp)

## Getting Mentally Ready for the Exam Room

Feeling nervous in an exam is very common. Run through the whole thing at home several times, including walking into the room, sitting down, adjusting the piano stool and starting to play, until the whole process feels familiar.

Before you begin a scale, pause for a second or two to think about the key name, the hand shape and the position of the first note, then start. That short moment of preparation makes the opening steadier.

If you make a mistake along the way, do not panic; carry on to the end as you do in practice. Examiners usually care more about your overall command, and finishing calmly is better than stopping to start again.

Beyond the exam itself, a solid foundation in scales also helps with harder pieces later on. If you treat scales as a long-term basic skill rather than a last-minute task, you will gain much more from them.

## Organising Scales by Key

Grade exams often ask for scales in several keys, and practising them all at once can get confusing. Start by grouping them by the number of sharps or flats, begin with keys whose hand shapes are similar, focus on just two or three keys at a time, and add new ones once those feel secure.

For each key, first find the black keys and set your hands on the keyboard without making a sound, simply feeling which keys your fingers land on. Once the hand shape is clear, play the scale slowly and make sure the fingering is the same every time.

For keys where the fingering is easy to mix up, write down in a notebook which notes the thumb lands on. The thumb position is often the key to a scale's fingering, and once you remember it, the other fingers are easier to work out.

**Have a listen**

Once you have your groups, make a small card for each key, with the key name on the front and the sharps or flats and the thumb positions on the back. Drawing a few cards before you practise helps you quickly recall what is special about each key.

## FAQ

**Q: How fast do scales need to be for a grade exam?**
A: It depends on the exam requirements and your teacher's advice. First make them even and steady, then raise the speed gradually.

**Q: What if my hands shake from nerves in the exam?**
A: Before you start, rest your hand on the first note, pause, take a deep breath, and then begin with the hand shape you have practised.

**Q: Do exam scales have to be played very fast?**
A: The speed should meet the exam requirements, but accuracy and evenness usually matter more than speed alone.

**Q: How should I practise scales with both hands together?**
A: Practise hands separately until they are secure, then put them together at a very slow tempo, paying attention to when each thumb turns under.

**Q: Do I need to practise every key every day?**
A: Not necessarily. You can rotate a few keys each day so that every key is covered within a week.

**Q: Do I need to memorise the fingering for scales?**
A: Yes. A fixed fingering gives your hands more confidence in the exam and also helps when you play pieces later.

galliard-renaissance-leaping-dance.body:
The galliard was a lively triple-time dance popular in sixteenth-century Europe, with many leaps in its steps. It often followed a slow, stately duple-time pavane, and the two were played as a pair. In the dance manual published by the Frenchman Thoinot Arbeau in 1589, the steps of the galliard are described in detail, and the most basic group is called the "cinque pas" (five steps). English composers such as Byrd and Dowland wrote many galliards for keyboard and lute. Its music often has a rhythm that alternates between three and two beats.

## Try dancing it

You can try dancing to galliard music, stepping lightly five times over six beats and leaping on the last step.

**Try this**

This helps you feel the rhythm and the leaping character of the galliard.

If you bring that feeling to the piano, your playing will have more energy.

## Two faces of the same melody

Sometimes the melody of a galliard is the same as that of the pavane before it, only with the rhythm changed from duple to triple time.

So the same melody first appears slowly and with dignity, and then appears again, quick and leaping.

This was a common method of variation in the Renaissance.

## The pavane and the galliard

In the sixteenth century the galliard often followed a pavane, and the two were played as a pair.

The pavane is in duple time, slow and stately, like a procession moving slowly along.

The galliard is in triple time, lively and leaping, and forms a sharp contrast with the pavane.

## Playing a galliard at the piano

When you play a Renaissance galliard at the piano, the rhythm should be light and springy.

The strong beats of the triple time should be clear, and the leaping feeling obvious.

Use the pedal sparingly so the sound stays clear, close to the sound of keyboard instruments of the time.

## The cinque pas

In Arbeau's manual, the most basic group of steps in the galliard is called the "cinque pas" (five steps).

Over six beats of music, the dancer makes five movements, and the last movement is a leap and a landing.

This group of steps can be varied in many ways.

- A lively triple-time dance popular in the sixteenth century
- Often played in pairs after the pavane
- Arbeau's 1589 dance manual describes the steps
- Byrd and Dowland wrote many galliards

## Byrd's galliards

William Byrd was a sixteenth-century English composer who wrote many keyboard works.

His pavanes and galliards often appear in pairs, with beautiful melodies and rich variety.

These works were included in keyboard collections of the time and have survived to this day.

## Dowland's galliards

John Dowland was an English composer and lutenist at the turn of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

He wrote many galliards for the lute, and some were given words and became songs.

One of them is often called the "Frog Galliard", with a light and charming melody.

## Alternating three and two

In the music of the galliard, there is often a rhythm that alternates between three beats and two beats.

For example, two bars of triple time sometimes sound like three bars of duple time.

This change of rhythm makes the music livelier and more interesting.

## The galliard in short

The galliard is a lively triple-time dance popular in sixteenth-century Europe, with many leaps. It often follows the slow, stately duple-time pavane as a pair, and sometimes the melody is the same with only the rhythm changed to triple time. The dance manual published by Thoinot Arbeau in 1589 describes the steps in dialogue, and the most basic "cinque pas" has five movements over six beats, the last being a leap and a landing.

The music often alternates between three and two beats. Byrd's keyboard pavanes and galliards often come in pairs, and Dowland wrote many lute galliards, one of which is often called the "Frog Galliard". In keyboard galliards each strain is often played plainly first and then repeated with ornaments. At the piano, keep it light and springy, use little pedal, and you can play it together with the pavane or step the five steps along with it.

You can chat with Teacher Aum about the history of the galliard.

## Ornamented repeats

In Renaissance keyboard galliards, each strain is often played once, and then played again with ornamentation.

In the second time through, the melody gains many quick passing notes and ornaments.

So each strain has two faces, a plain one and an elaborate one.

## A dance of leaps

The steps of the galliard include many leaps: the dancer jumps high, makes some movements in the air, and then lands.

This dance was a real test of the dancer's stamina and skill.

Young people in the sixteenth century often danced the galliard to show off their vigour.

![A high-angle view of an open black piano being played on a rainy neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaecewh-5rbk1.webp)

## Arbeau's dance manual

In 1589, the Frenchman Thoinot Arbeau published a dance manual.

In dialogue form, the book introduces many of the dances popular at the time, including the galliard.

The book also includes the melodies of the dance tunes, matched to the steps, and is an important source for understanding Renaissance dance.

## Playing it together with a pavane

You can find a pavane and galliard pair and play them one after the other at the piano.

First play the pavane slowly and with dignity, then play the galliard lightly and with leaps.

Feel the contrast in tempo and character between the two dances.

## Chat with your teacher about the galliard in your lesson

In your lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about the history of the galliard and its relationship to the pavane.

Your teacher can also recommend an arrangement of a galliard by Byrd or Dowland as a piece to practise.

**Another way to look at it**

From the galliard, you can get to know the dance music of the Renaissance.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What time is the galliard in?**
A: Triple time.

**Q: What kind of dance does it often follow?**
A: The pavane.

**Q: In what year was Arbeau's dance manual published?**
A: 1589.

**Q: What is the most basic group of steps called?**
A: The "cinque pas" (five steps).

**Q: Which of Dowland's galliards is often mentioned?**
A: The "Frog Galliard".

gregorian-chant-neumes-single-line.body:
Gregorian chant is the Latin liturgical singing of the Western church tradition. It has a single melody, no harmony and no fixed beat, and its rhythm flows naturally with the syllables of the text. It is named after Pope Gregory I of the late sixth century, but today's scholars believe most of these chants were formed in the eighth and ninth centuries, when the traditions of Rome and the Frankish lands merged. To help memory, scribes around the ninth century drew small marks above the words, called neumes, which gradually developed into staff notation with lines, one of the sources of today's five-line staff.

## Try the Modes of Gregorian Chant in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate a medieval-mode melody on the white keys.

You can also talk with your teacher about how neumes, the four-line staff and the five-line staff are related.

From one ancient melody, you can see where today's music notation came from.

## Gregorian Chant in Brief

Gregorian chant is the Latin liturgical singing of the Western church tradition. It is monophonic and unaccompanied, with a rhythm that flows naturally with the syllables of the words. It is named after Pope Gregory I of the late sixth century, though scholars believe most of it was formed in the eighth and ninth centuries from a merging of Roman and Frankish traditions. Around the ninth century, scribes drew neume marks above the words, later added lines, and commonly used a four-line staff, which developed into today's five-line staff.

Chants can be syllabic or melismatic and use the medieval modes. On the piano you can play a free-rhythm melody using only the white keys, starting on D. Later, people added a second melody to a chant, which led to polyphonic music.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the medieval modes.

## Neume Marks

Before music notation was invented, chant was passed down from singer to singer by ear and memory.

Around the ninth century, scribes began to draw small marks above the words to show the rise and fall of the melody. These marks are called neumes.

The earliest neumes could only remind singers roughly where the melody was heading, and could not show pitch precisely.

## From One Voice to Many

Later, people added a second melody above or below the chant melody, and polyphonic music slowly developed.

Many medieval and Renaissance works are built on the melody of a chant.

You could say that Gregorian chant is one of the starting points of the development of Western music.

## One Source of the Five-Line Staff

The four-line staff kept developing and became the five-line staff we know today.

So the staff you read when playing the piano has, as one of its sources, the small marks that medieval scribes drew above chant.

Next time you read music, think about this history, and it will feel rather interesting.

## A Rhythm That Follows the Latin

Gregorian chant has no fixed beat, and is not counted bar by bar like today's songs.

Its rhythm flows naturally with the syllables and stresses of the Latin text.

Singing it feels like reciting the scripture with a melody.

**Quick tips**
- Latin liturgical singing of the Western church tradition
- A single melody, with a rhythm that follows the words
- Named after Pope Gregory I, but mostly formed in the eighth and ninth centuries
- Neume marks are one source of the five-line staff

## The Name Gregorian

This kind of chant is named after Pope Gregory I of the late sixth century.

A legend later spread that he received inspiration while praying and personally compiled these chants.

Today's scholars think the name is more of a tribute, and that the chants took shape much later.

![Close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbj5z55-d9vpp.webp)

## A Single Melody

Gregorian chant has only one melody, and everyone sings the same notes together. This is called monophonic music.

It has no harmony and no accompaniment, only voices echoing in the church.

This simple sound gives a feeling of quiet and solemnity.

## The Flavour of the Modes

Gregorian chant does not use today's major and minor keys but several medieval modes.

For example, playing only the white keys from D up to the D an octave higher gives one common mode.

These modes give chant its old, distant flavour.

## From One Line to Four

Later, people drew a single line above the words to stand for one fixed pitch, and neumes were written above and below the line, which made pitch much clearer.

After that, the lines became two, then three, and finally four lines were most commonly used.

The notation of Gregorian chant is still often written on a four-line staff today.

## Playing a Chant on the Piano

With your right hand, you can slowly play a melody on the white keys only, starting on D, without counting beats, as if reading a poem.

The melody moves mostly by step, with an occasional leap, and ends by returning to D.

This lets you feel what monophonic, free-rhythm music is like.

## The Merging of the Eighth and Ninth Centuries

Scholars believe that most Gregorian chant took shape in the eighth and ninth centuries.

At that time, the singing tradition of Rome spread to the Frankish lands and merged with the local tradition.

The merged chant then spread to churches throughout western Europe.

## Syllabic and Melismatic

In some chants, only one note is sung to each syllable. This is called syllabic, and it sounds like recitation.

In others, many notes are sung to a single syllable and the melody unfolds like a flower. This is called melismatic.

The two styles often alternate within the same chant.

## FAQ

**Q: How many melodies does Gregorian chant have?**
A: Only one. It is monophonic music.

**Q: What is its rhythm like?**
A: It has no fixed beat and flows naturally with the syllables of the words.

**Q: When do scholars think it mostly took shape?**
A: In the eighth and ninth centuries.

**Q: What are neumes?**
A: Small marks drawn by scribes above the words to show the direction of the melody.

**Q: What is it called when many notes are sung to one syllable?**
A: Melismatic.

fux-species-counterpoint-1725-five-steps.body:
Species counterpoint is a classic method for learning to write counterpoint. It comes from the Latin treatise Gradus ad Parnassum, published in 1725 by the Austrian composer and theorist Johann Joseph Fux. In the book, written as a dialogue between teacher and student, counterpoint is divided into five "species": starting from one note against one note, building up to two notes and four notes against one, and then learning syncopation and free, florid counterpoint. Composers such as Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven all studied this book. Even today, people learning harmony and composition often use this method to build a foundation, and for pianists, knowing about it also helps you hear the relationships between voices more clearly.

## Starting simple

The advantage of species counterpoint is that it breaks the complex task of writing counterpoint into simple exercises, step by step.

Each step teaches just one new thing, and only when that is comfortable do you move on to the next.

This approach, from the simple to the complex, also applies to many aspects of learning the piano.

## Third species: four notes against one

In third species counterpoint, every note of the fixed melody is matched by four notes of the new melody.

The rhythm of the new melody is faster, and more passing notes and neighbour notes can be used.

This species teaches the student to write more flexible, more varied melodic lines.

**Quick tips**
- A method from Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum of 1725
- Written as a dialogue between teacher and student
- Five species, increasing in difficulty step by step
- Studied by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven

## The cantus firmus

Every species counterpoint exercise begins with a "cantus firmus" (fixed melody).

The cantus firmus usually consists of whole notes, moves very slowly, and is like a steady foundation line.

The student writes a new melody above or below it that fits with it.

## Species counterpoint in short

Species counterpoint comes from Gradus ad Parnassum, published in Latin by Johann Joseph Fux in 1725. Fux was born around 1660 and died in 1741, and worked for a long time in Vienna. In the book the teacher represents the style of Palestrina and guides the student through dialogue, and the exercises all begin with a cantus firmus made of whole notes.

First species is note against note, using consonant intervals and avoiding parallel fifths and octaves. Second species is two notes against one, where the second note can be a passing note. Third species is four notes against one. Fourth species is offset by a half beat to form a suspension that resolves down by step. Fifth species is florid counterpoint with mixed rhythms. Haydn taught himself from it and used it for teaching, Mozart and Beethoven studied it too, and at the piano you can practise it with the cantus firmus in the left hand and a melody in the right.

You can ask Teacher Aum to explain the rules of the five species.

## Fux and his book

Johann Joseph Fux, born around 1660 and died in 1741, was an Austrian composer and music theorist.

He worked in Vienna for a long time and wrote a great deal of sacred music.

In 1725 he published Gradus ad Parnassum, written in Latin, and its section on counterpoint has been very influential.

## Fourth species: syncopation and suspensions

In fourth species counterpoint, the notes of the new melody are offset from the cantus firmus by a half beat, creating syncopation.

With the offset comes the suspension: a note held over from the previous beat meets a new note in the cantus firmus, first "clashing" to make a dissonance, then moving down a step to settle.

The suspension is an important device in a great deal of music for creating tension and resolution.

## First species: note against note

In first species counterpoint, every note of the cantus firmus is matched by one note of the new melody.

The two melodies move together, and every note forms a consonant interval, such as a third, a sixth, a fifth or an octave.

The point of this species is to learn to choose consonant intervals and to avoid parallel fifths and octaves.

## The dialogue between teacher and student

Gradus ad Parnassum is written as a dialogue, with a teacher guiding a student step by step.

The teacher in the book is cast by Fux as representing the style of the sixteenth-century Italian composer Palestrina.

The student does the exercises, and the teacher points out mistakes and explains the reasons, so it reads like a series of lessons.

## Second species: two notes against one

In second species counterpoint, every note of the cantus firmus is matched by two notes of the new melody.

The first note has to be consonant with the cantus firmus, while the second can be a dissonant passing note, but it must move by step.

This species makes the melody flow more, and begins to teach how to handle dissonance.

![A Bangkok city-poster style illustration of tall buildings and busy traffic in the streets](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadwck7-0v8a1.webp)

## How the composers learned

Haydn taught himself from Gradus ad Parnassum when he was young, and later used it to teach his own students.

Mozart and Beethoven also studied this book, and Beethoven worked through many species counterpoint exercises with his teacher.

This shows that even great composers need to start with basic exercises.

## How it helps with playing Bach

Knowing about species counterpoint helps you understand the polyphonic music of Bach and other composers.

In Bach's works you often hear suspensions, passing notes and free, florid melodies.

Once you know where these devices come from, you can show the relationships between the voices more clearly when you play.

## Fifth species: florid counterpoint

Fifth species counterpoint mixes the rhythms of the previous four species together, and is called florid counterpoint.

The new melody can have long notes, short notes, syncopation and ornaments, like a free singing voice.

This species is the closest to real musical writing.

## Species counterpoint at the piano

Pianists can also try species counterpoint at the keyboard.

The left hand plays a slow cantus firmus, and the right hand adds a melody note against note, following the rules of first species.

Play slowly and listen to whether each interval is consonant or dissonant.

## Ask your teacher to explain species counterpoint in your lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to explain the rules of the five species and demonstrate them at the piano.

Your teacher can also give you a cantus firmus and let you try adding a first-species melody.

Starting from species counterpoint, you can get to know the basics of polyphonic music.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which book does species counterpoint come from?**
A: Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum of 1725.

**Q: In what form is the book written?**
A: A dialogue between teacher and student.

**Q: What is first species counterpoint like?**
A: Note against note, using consonant intervals.

**Q: What is learned in fourth species counterpoint?**
A: Syncopation and suspensions.

**Q: What is the fifth species called?**
A: Florid counterpoint.

hands-on-knees-reset.body:
When you keep making mistakes and getting more hurried, stop, put both hands back on your knees, count slowly to five, look at the place in the score where you will restart, and then return your hands to the keys. This simple reset breaks the cycle of rushing and lets you start again with a clear idea, rather than repeating the same mistake over and over while tense.

## It Works in Front of Family Too

When family members are listening to you practise, a mistake can make you more nervous and eager to get it right immediately.

**A Different Way to Look at It**

In that moment you can do the same thing: put your hands back on your knees, count to five, then start again. When your family sees you do this, they will understand that you are adjusting yourself.

If a child uses this method while practising, parents can give them encouragement, because being able to stop when feeling rushed is itself a sign of progress.

## The Steps of the Reset

When you notice that you keep making mistakes in the same place, or you start to feel hurried, first take your hands off the keys.

Rest your hands lightly on your knees, sit up straight and count slowly to five.

Then look at the score, confirm where you will restart and what the notes and fingering are there, and put your hands back on the keys.

## Treat Mistakes as Part of Practice

Making mistakes is a perfectly normal part of learning, and everyone meets them.

What matters is not never making mistakes, but knowing how to adjust after you make one.

Putting your hands on your knees is a way of telling yourself: it's all right, pause for a moment, think it through, and start again.

**Summary**
- Stop when you keep making mistakes
- Put your hands on your knees and count to five
- Make clear where you will restart
- Restart at a slower tempo

## Why Do You Get Worse the More You Play?

After one mistake, many people immediately start again from the beginning, and they usually play faster and more hurriedly.

When you are rushing, the fingers tense up and your attention drifts to worrying about not making another mistake, which makes mistakes more likely.

Repeat this a few times and you have not solved the problem. You may even have made the wrong movement more fluent.

![A watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xt4yw-986we.webp)

## Slow Down When You Restart

When you restart, you can play more slowly than when you made the mistake, giving your fingers time to move the right way.

If one particular spot keeps going wrong, start only one or two bars before it, rather than from the beginning every time.

After playing it correctly slowly a few times, gradually return to the original tempo.

Before you restart, you can sing the phrase through in your head first, check the rhythm and the notes, and then place your hands on the keys.

The slower tempo does not need to be very slow, just slow enough for you to play every note calmly.

## Find the Reason for the Mistake

Those few seconds of stopping are also a good chance to think. Was the fingering wrong? Did you not read the notes clearly? Or was the tempo too fast?

Once you find the reason, practising in a targeted way is more effective than simply repeating.

You can make a small pencil mark in the score to remind yourself to take care at that spot next time.

## Teaching Children This Method

Children often get anxious or even angry when they make a mistake. Parents and teachers can teach them this simple movement and count along with them.

Gradually, children learn to stop themselves when they feel rushed, rather than keep repeating.

This is not only a practice technique, but also a way of learning to manage emotions when facing difficulty.

## Why on the Knees?

Putting your hands on your knees is a very clear action, which lets both your hands and your brain know "we are paused now".

It takes your fingers off the keys, so you do not press down again in a hurry before you have thought it through.

You can do this anywhere without any equipment, in practice, in lessons, and even before a performance.

## Before a Performance Too

Before a performance, when you sit down at the piano, you can first put your hands on your knees, think about the tempo of the opening and the feel of the first phrase, and then begin to play.

This kind of preparation makes the opening steadier and gives you a short moment to settle in.

**Remember This**

If you get used to it in daily practice, the movement will come naturally on stage too, and you will feel calmer.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Do I have to count to five? Can I count longer?**
A: You can adjust it as needed. The point is to really stop.

**Q: Can I use it several times in one piece?**
A: In practice you can use it at any time. In a performance, try to keep playing.

**Q: Should I stop if I make a mistake during a performance?**
A: In a performance, it is generally better to keep playing, and use the reset in practice.

**Q: What if my child does not want to play after stopping?**
A: You can shorten this part of the practice and play a familiar piece first before coming back.

**Q: Should I practise the mistake spot separately?**
A: Yes. Once you have found the reason, practise it slowly on its own a few times, then put it back into the whole piece.

**Q: Does this method work for adults?**
A: Yes, it works just as well. Adults also often get worse the more they play because they are rushing.

french-overture-dotted-then-fugal.body:
The French overture is a form of overture from the Baroque period. It took shape in France in the seventeenth century and later spread across Europe. It usually has two parts. The first is slow and stately, full of dotted rhythms, like a grand entrance. The second is faster and is often written in imitation or as a fugue, with the voices entering one after another. Sometimes the music returns to a slow section at the very end. The overture to Handel's Messiah, Bach's French Overture BWV 831, and the opening of Bach's fourth keyboard partita are all examples of the French overture.

## Bach's Fourth Partita

Bach's fourth keyboard partita is in D major, catalogued as BWV 828.

**Listen**

Its first movement is called "Ouverture", and it is a French overture.

It begins with a stately dotted rhythm, followed by a lively fugue.

## Handel's Messiah Overture

Handel's oratorio Messiah, written in 1741, opens with a French overture.

The first part is in E minor, slow and stately, with dotted rhythms.

The second part is a fast fugue in which the voices enter one after another.

**Try it**
- An overture form that took shape in France in the seventeenth century
- The first part is slow and stately, with dotted rhythms
- The second part is faster and often written as a fugue
- Both Handel and Bach wrote them

## The Quick Fugue Section

The second part of a French overture is often written in imitation or as a fugue.

One voice plays a theme first, and the other voices enter one after another, imitating it.

This section is light and lively, a contrast to the stateliness of the first part.

## French Overture: A Summary

The French overture took shape in France in the seventeenth century. It usually has two parts. The first is slow and stately, with dotted rhythms in which long notes are made longer and short notes shorter (opinions differ on how sharply the dots should be played). The second is faster and written in imitation or as a fugue, and sometimes the music returns to a slow section at the end. The Italian overture, by contrast, is fast, slow, fast, and later developed into the symphony.

The first part of the overture to Handel's 1741 Messiah is in E minor and the second part is a fugue. Bach's French Overture BWV 831, published in 1735, was written for a two-manual harpsichord and is followed by dances such as the courante, gavotte and sarabande. The first movement of the fourth partita, BWV 828, is also a French overture. On the piano, the long dotted notes need weight, and in the fugue section the voices need to be clear.

You can ask Teacher Aum to explain the structure of the French overture.

## The French Overture as an Opening

An overture is a piece of instrumental music that opens an opera, a ballet or a suite.

It works like a curtain-raiser, getting the audience ready to enter the world of the music.

In the Baroque period there were two main kinds of overture: the French overture and the Italian overture.

## Bach's French Overture

In 1735, Bach published a set of keyboard works that included the Italian Concerto and the French Overture BWV 831.

The French Overture is a suite for a two-manual harpsichord, and it begins with a French overture.

It is followed by several French-style dances, such as the courante, the gavotte and the sarabande.

## Playing the Fugue Section on the Piano

When you play the fugue section of a French overture, make every voice clear.

Each time the theme enters, you can bring it out slightly so the listener hears which voice it is in.

Keep the rhythm steady and light, in contrast to the stateliness that came before.

## How Long Should the Dots Be?

In a French overture, dotted rhythms are often played more "sharply" than they are written.

That means the long note is held a little longer and the short note made a little shorter.

Performers and scholars disagree about exactly how sharp they should be.

![A watercolour-style upright piano with open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwae7sck-54cz0.webp)

## The Dotted Footsteps of the French Overture

The most distinctive feature of the first part of a French overture is the dotted rhythm.

A dotted rhythm is a long note followed by a short one, the long made longer and the short made shorter, like firm footsteps one after another.

This rhythm makes the music sound stately and ceremonial.

## The Contrast Between the Two Parts

The two parts of a French overture differ in tempo, rhythm and writing.

When you play, bring out this contrast.

Make the first part stately and weighty, and the second part light and clear.

## The Two Parts of a French Overture

A French overture usually has two parts.

The first part is slow and stately, and the second is faster and livelier.

Sometimes, after the second part, the music returns to a slow, stately passage to close.

## How It Differs from the Italian Overture

The Italian overture has a different order from the French overture: three parts, fast, slow, fast.

The Italian overture later developed into the symphony of the Classical period.

The French overture, on the other hand, often serves as the first movement of a suite.

## Ask Your Teacher About the French Overture in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to explain the structure of the French overture and how to play the dotted rhythms.

Your teacher can also suggest the overture of Bach's fourth partita as a goal for when your level is higher.

From the French overture, you can discover both the stateliness and the liveliness of Baroque music.

## Playing Dotted Rhythms on the Piano

When you play the dotted rhythms of a French overture on the piano, give every long note weight.

Keep the short notes light and crisp, leading straight into the next long note.

**Tip**

You can start by practising slowly with a metronome to get the dotted rhythm accurate, and only then think about whether to play it more sharply.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is the first part of a French overture like?**
A: Slow and stately, with dotted rhythms.

**Q: What kind of writing is usually used in the second part?**
A: Imitation or fugue.

**Q: What is the order of an Italian overture?**
A: Fast, slow, fast.

**Q: What is the catalogue number of Bach's French Overture?**
A: BWV 831.

**Q: What key is Bach's fourth partita in?**
A: D major, BWV 828.

glissando-slide-keys.body:
Glissando (Italian, often abbreviated gliss.) on the piano means sliding quickly from one note to another with your finger or the back of your fingernail, playing all the white keys or black keys in between in a continuous run. In the score it is usually shown by a straight or wavy line joining the first and last notes. A glissando creates a brilliant, flowing effect, but you need to watch the angle and force of your hand, to avoid hurting your fingers or producing an uneven sound. When you are starting out, you can first practise slowly over a short distance.

## White-Key Glissando

The most common piano glissando is played on the white keys, because the white keys lie flat and the fingers slide over them easily.

**Remember this**

For an upward glissando, you usually use the back of the right-hand third fingernail, or of the second and third fingernails, with the wrist slightly lowered, letting the nail slide along the surface of the keys.

For a downward glissando, you usually use the side of the right-hand thumbnail, or the pad of the third finger, and the direction of the hand is different from going up.

## Where You Often Meet It

The glissando is fairly common in jazz, pop and some modern works, and is often used to create a brilliant or playful effect.

You can also find glissandos in some classical works, for example where certain composers included octave glissandos.

The handling and effect of a glissando differ from style to style, and you can listen to more recordings to get a feel for it.

## Speed and Rhythm

A glissando is usually very fast, but it must be completed in a set amount of time, for example one beat or two beats.

You can first slide slowly to feel the whole distance of the slide, then gradually speed up to fit the beat of the piece.

You can also use a metronome to make sure the glissando starts and ends at the right time.

## Protect Your Fingers

When you glissando there is friction between your fingers and the keys, and if you practise too much or press too hard, your nails or skin may feel uncomfortable.

When practising, limit the number of repetitions, doing only a few each time, and do not slide again and again in a row.

If your fingers hurt, rest right away, and if necessary ask your teacher to adjust your method.

- A glissando is a quick slide from one note to another
- In the score, a straight or wavy line joins the first and last notes
- It is usually played with the back of the nail or the side of the finger
- When starting out, practise slowly over a short distance first

## Practice Methods for Beginners

When you first start learning the glissando, you can practise over a short distance of within one octave, slowly feeling the angle and force of your hand.

Once you are comfortable, gradually lengthen the distance of the slide, for example to two octaves or even more.

The glissando is a very fun technique, and once you have mastered it, it can add a lot of colour to your playing.

## Glissandos on Keyboards and Digital Pianos

On a digital piano or electronic keyboard, the surface and weight of the keys may differ from an acoustic piano, and the feel of the glissando will differ a little too.

Some electronic keyboards have fairly light keys, so be careful not to press too hard when sliding.

Before practising a glissando on a different instrument, you can first try a few light slides to get to know the feel of the keys.

## How a Glissando Is Notated

In the score, a glissando is usually shown by a straight or wavy line joining the first note and the last note, with gliss. written beside it.

Sometimes only the first and last notes are written, and the notes in between are not, and the performer plays them naturally in the slide.

When you see this mark, prepare to slide from the first note all the way to the last, with no pause in between.

## Black-Key Glissando

The black-key glissando is rarer, because the black keys are not laid out flat and there are gaps between them, which makes the slide harder to control.

A black-key glissando is usually played with the side of the palm or the flat of the fingers, and sounds like a pentatonic scale.

If the score asks for a black-key glissando, you can try it slowly at first and find a suitable hand shape.

## Hand Angle and Force

When you glissando, the angle of the hand is very important: the nail should lie against the keys, and you should not press straight down with the fingertip, otherwise it easily catches or hurts your finger.

The force should be even; do not start with a lot of force and have no sound left at the end. You can imagine your hand gently gliding over a smooth tabletop.

If your fingers feel uncomfortable, stop and adjust the angle, and do not force it.

![An electronic keyboard and a screen under neon lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9zowsn-yrr9t.webp)

## The First and Last Notes Must Be Accurate

Both the first note and the last note of a glissando must be clear and accurate, especially the last note, which often lands on an important spot.

You can first practise the positions of the first and last notes on their own, then add the slide in between.

As you reach the last note, you can add a little emphasis, so the glissando has a definite landing point.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does glissando mean?**
A: A quick slide from one note to another, playing the notes in between in a continuous run.

**Q: How is it shown in the score?**
A: A straight or wavy line joins the first and last notes, with gliss. beside it.

**Q: Which part of the finger is used?**
A: Usually the back of the nail or the side of the finger.

**Q: Can a glissando hurt your hand?**
A: A wrong angle or too much practice may cause discomfort, so limit the number of repetitions.

**Q: Can you glissando on the black keys?**
A: Yes, but it is harder to control, and the side of the palm is often used.

**Q: How should beginners practise?**
A: Start slowly within one octave, then gradually lengthen the distance.

green-concert-tour-innovation.body:
Behind a large tour are tonnes of stage equipment, transport between cities or even countries, a whole night of electricity for lights and sound, and the travel of a large audience. In recent years, more and more musicians and production teams have begun to pay attention to the environmental impact of touring and to try new ways of reducing the burden: powering shows with renewable energy, letting the audience's dancing help generate electricity, cutting down on single-use materials, and encouraging travel by public transport. These measures are both a responsibility to the environment and a new form of brand expression: audiences may identify more strongly with a band because they like its environmental values. Green touring has therefore become a direction worth watching in music business innovation.

## Environmental Innovation Centres on Four Areas

**Energy**
Use renewable energy or storage batteries to power the stage and reduce reliance on diesel generators. Some shows have tried laying floors at the venue that turn the energy of footsteps into electricity, or setting up bikes that audience members pedal to generate power, turning participation into an interactive experience.

**Transport**
Combine equipment transport routes as far as possible and choose lower-emission methods; in publicity, encourage audiences to take public transport, or work with local transport services to provide shuttles.

**Materials**
Stage sets can be reused and designed in modules; merchandise and promotional materials can use less plastic and choose recyclable materials.

**Audience behaviour**
Provide water refill points and encourage people to bring their own bottles; set up sorted recycling points at the venue and use simple signs to guide the audience to take part.

## Transparency Matters More Than Slogans

The criticism green tours meet most easily is that they are "only slogans". So more and more teams publish their plans before a tour, report on how they were carried out afterwards, and invite a third-party organisation to assess them when necessary. Even if some goals are not fully reached, explaining honestly why and how they will improve earns more audience trust than exaggerating results. For a music brand, verifiable action is itself very persuasive promotional material, whereas exaggerated environmental claims can bring reputational risk and, in some regions, may even break advertising rules.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in a high-tech coat playing a glowing keyboard installation on a neon street, with a crystal tower behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw166flc-j8vb1.webp)

## Small Music Events Can Do It Too

You do not need a large tour to put environmental ideas into practice. Community concerts, school performances and student concerts at a music studio can all start small:

- Make programmes digital, using a QR code instead of paper
- Choose reusable stage decorations and use them year after year
- Encourage parents and audience members to walk, cycle or carpool
- Provide drinking water on the day to cut down on single-use bottles
- Choose daytime or times with plenty of natural light to reduce lighting electricity

These measures do not cost much, yet they let participants feel the care that has gone into the event.

## Environmental Values and Brand Image

For music education brands and technology companies, environmental care can also be part of the brand story. For example, online lessons in themselves reduce the travel needed to get to class, and digital teaching materials reduce paper use. When telling these stories, be factual: do not exaggerate emission savings or use numbers you cannot prove. Real, specific small actions move people more easily than empty slogans.

## How the Audience Can Take Part

As an audience member, you can also play a part in a green show: choose public transport where you can, bring your own bottle, sort your rubbish as directed, and when buying merchandise choose things you will really use for a long time. Music brings people together, and it can also help everyone form more environmentally friendly habits together.

## New Possibilities from Technology

Digital technology is also lightening the load of live shows. E-tickets reduce the printing of paper tickets, digital screens at the venue can replace some single-use promotional materials, and live streaming lets audiences who cannot attend take part, cutting long-distance travel. Stage lighting is gradually switching to more energy-efficient fixtures, and the efficiency of sound systems keeps improving. In music education, online lessons and practice apps let learners get feedback at home, so they do not have to make a trip to the studio for every small question. Technology is not the goal in itself; the key is to use it to make music activities more convenient while wasting fewer resources.

## FAQ

**Q: Will green tours make tickets more expensive?**
A: Not necessarily. Some environmental measures need investment, but others save money, depending on how the team plans.

**Q: Does pedalling to generate power at a concert really help?**
A: The electricity generated by this kind of interaction is limited; its greater significance is in increasing the audience's sense of involvement and environmental awareness.

**Q: How can I tell whether a show is really environmentally friendly?**
A: Look at whether the organisers publish specific plans and results, rather than just using environmental slogans.

**Q: How can a music studio start making its events greener?**
A: Just start with simple steps such as digital programmes, reusable decorations and encouraging green travel.

hanon-virtuoso-pianist-60-exercises-1873.body:
The French piano teacher Charles-Louis Hanon (1819–1900) published The Virtuoso Pianist in 1873, a collection of 60 finger exercises. Most of them are a short pattern that climbs step by step up the white keys and then comes back down, with the aim of training finger independence, strength and evenness. Many teachers still pick out some of these exercises today, but they also remind students that repeating them mechanically is no substitute for listening, so stay relaxed and pay attention to your tone.

## The Right Way to Practise

When you practise Hanon, keep your wrist, arm and shoulder relaxed. Do not let the whole hand become stiff just to play with more force.

**Quick tip**

Start slowly, and listen to check that every note is even and clear.

If your hand feels tense or uncomfortable, stop and rest straight away. Do not push through it.

![A cartoon character with glasses and headphones reads music at an upright piano in a night-time room, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2mv0s-6rvw9.webp)

## Transposing the Exercises

The Hanon exercises are originally written in C major, using only white keys.

Some teachers ask students to move the exercises into other keys, such as G major or D major, which brings in the black keys.

This trains the fingers and also helps students get to know the layout of the keyboard in different keys.

## How Long Each Day

Many teachers suggest that Hanon needs only a few minutes a day, as part of a warm-up.

Keep most of your practice time for pieces, sight reading and musical expression.

That way your fingers stay in shape without practice becoming monotonous.

## The Goal of the Training

The goal of the Hanon exercises is to let every finger play independently and evenly.

The fourth and fifth fingers, for example, are often the weaker ones, and the exercises use them again and again, so they get stronger.

When the exercises are practised well, finger control and flexibility improve.

## An Old Book Today

Hanon's book was published about a hundred and fifty years ago, and piano teaching methods have kept developing since then.

Today's teachers combine this old book with other kinds of exercises and with pieces.

For learners, what matters is to understand the purpose of each exercise and to check the results with the ear.

## The Structure of the 60 Exercises

The book has 60 exercises in three parts, with the difficulty rising gradually.

The first part is the most basic, the second adds more finger variations, and the third makes higher demands, including trills, repeated notes, scales and arpeggios.

Many learners have only worked through the first part and already feel what it does for their fingers.

## Different Rhythms and Dynamics

To keep the practice from becoming mechanical, you can play the same pattern with dotted rhythms or triplets.

You can also vary the dynamics, for example playing everything softly, everything legato, or with a crescendo and diminuendo.

In this way the same pattern teaches you more, and your ears tire less easily.

## Who Hanon Is For

Learners who have already mastered the five-finger position and basic note reading can try Hanon exercises under a teacher's guidance.

Children should practise for short periods, with an adult or teacher watching hand shape and relaxation.

Adult learners can choose a few exercises that suit their needs as a daily warm-up.

## Combining It with Pieces

The technique built with Hanon exercises is meant to be used in real pieces in the end.

If a particular finger feels especially weak in a piece, you can find a Hanon exercise that targets that problem as a supplement.

Afterwards, go back to the piece and see whether that spot has improved.

## A Pattern Moving Along the White Keys

The most typical Hanon exercise is a short pattern of a few notes that starts on C and moves up the white keys one step at a time.

After reaching the top, a mirrored pattern brings you back down step by step to the starting point.

This structure means learners do not have to spend much effort reading the music and can focus on their fingers.

- Hanon, 1819–1900, French piano teacher
- Published in 1873, 60 exercises
- Patterns climb the white keys step by step and then descend
- The focus is finger independence and evenness

## Different Views on Hanon

In the piano teaching world, opinions on the Hanon exercises differ.

Some think they train the fingers effectively and make a good basic exercise; others worry that long mechanical repetition trains only the fingers and not the ear.

A more balanced approach is to treat it as a warm-up or a supplement rather than the whole of your practice.

## A French Piano Teacher

Charles-Louis Hanon lived from 1819 to 1900 and was a French piano teacher and organist.

He wrote several teaching books in his lifetime, and the best known is this collection of finger exercises.

**Common misconception**

In the more than a hundred years since it was published, the book has been translated into many languages and can be found in practice rooms all over the world.

## FAQ

**Q: In which year was the Hanon exercise book published?**
A: 1873.

**Q: How many exercises are there in total?**
A: 60, divided into three parts.

**Q: What do these exercises train?**
A: Mainly finger independence, strength and evenness.

**Q: How long should I practise each day?**
A: Many teachers suggest just a few minutes as a warm-up.

**Q: What should I watch for while practising?**
A: Stay relaxed, start slowly, and listen to every note.

golden-snake-dance-1934-folk-ensemble.body:
Golden Snake Dance (Jin She Kuang Wu) is a piece for Chinese folk instrument ensemble, arranged by the composer Nie Er in 1934 from the folk tune Dao Ba Ban. It is fiery and joyful, with gongs and drums resounding, and is often played at festivals and celebrations. The most interesting thing about it is the call-and-response of antecedent and consequent phrases in the middle section: each phrase is shorter than the last, the answers come ever tighter, and in the end the two merge together, like a golden snake dancing faster and faster amid the sound of gongs and drums. The piece has many piano arrangements and is a good example for getting to know the structure of Chinese folk music.

## An Ensemble of Folk Instruments

Golden Snake Dance is usually played by Chinese folk instruments such as the erhu, pipa, dizi (bamboo flute) and yangqin, together with gongs and drums.

Each instrument has a different tone colour, and together they make a very rich palette.

Later it was also arranged for orchestra, for piano and for various other instruments.

## Arranged from a Folk Tune

The melody of Golden Snake Dance comes from a folk tune called Dao Ba Ban.

Dao Ba Ban was made by playing the melody of a traditional piece backwards, as a variation.

On the basis of this folk tune, Nie Er reworked the structure and the instrumentation and wrote this ensemble piece.

- Arranged by Nie Er in 1934
- Based on the folk tune Dao Ba Ban
- A piece for Chinese folk instrument ensemble
- A call-and-response of ever-shorter phrases

## The Name of the Golden Snake

The name "Golden Snake Dance" calls to mind a golden snake dancing joyfully amid the sound of gongs and drums.

The name matches the fiery, joyful atmosphere of the music very well.

Many people hear this piece and think at once of the New Year, celebrations and lively scenes.

## Golden Snake Dance: A Summary

Golden Snake Dance is a piece for Chinese folk instrument ensemble, arranged by Nie Er in 1934 from the folk tune Dao Ba Ban, which was made by playing a traditional piece backwards as a variation. The piece is fiery and joyful, with gongs and drums resounding. In the middle, the call-and-response of antecedent and consequent phrases gets shorter each time and the answers come ever tighter, until the two merge together. This structure is called "luosi jieding", the tip of a snail shell.

The gongs and drums often answer the melodic instruments. The piece is usually played by erhu, pipa, dizi and yangqin with gongs and drums, and later versions for orchestra and for piano appeared. In the piano version the left hand imitates the gongs and drums with chords, the call-and-response sections are told apart by register, and simplified versions suit elementary to intermediate players.

You can ask Teacher Aum to explain the "luosi jieding" structure.

## The Role of the Gongs and Drums

In Golden Snake Dance, the gongs and drums are not just accompaniment, but often answer the melodic instruments.

A melodic instrument plays one phrase, and the gongs and drums strike one back, passing back and forth in a very lively way.

The rhythm of the gongs and drums also fills the whole piece with drive.

## A Fiery Opening

At the start of the piece, the gongs and drums and the various instruments play a fiery, joyful melody together.

The rhythm is strong and the tempo fairly fast, like people beating gongs and drums at a festival.

The first few bars are like a temple fair striking up, with the bustle rushing straight at you.

## The Snail Shell's Tip

This structure, in which each phrase is shorter than the last, has a vivid name in Chinese folk music: "luosi jieding", the snail shell's tip.

It is like the shell of a snail, each turn smaller than the one before, finally narrowing to a point.

Once you understand this structure, it is easier to grasp the charm of Golden Snake Dance when you listen to it.

## Playing the Tightening Call-and-Response

When you reach the "luosi jieding" section, make the call-and-response more and more compact.

As the phrases get shorter, you can slightly increase the dynamics, letting the tension build up slowly.

When the two voices finally join together, play full and strong.

## Nie Er and Folk Instrumental Music

Nie Er did not only write songs; he was also interested in Chinese folk instrumental music.

While he was in Shanghai, he took part in collecting and arranging several folk instrumental pieces.

Golden Snake Dance is the most widely circulated of them.

## The Ever-Tighter Call-and-Response

In the middle of the piece there is a special call-and-response of antecedent and consequent phrases: one voice plays the antecedent and another voice plays the consequent.

With each exchange the phrase is a little shorter than the last, and more and more compact.

In the end the two voices come together and form a fiery climax.

## Ask Your Teacher About the Structure of Golden Snake Dance in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to explain the "luosi jieding" structure and what it looks like in the score.

You can also ask your teacher to demonstrate how the call-and-response sections are told apart by register.

From one folk ensemble piece, get to know the wisdom of Chinese folk music.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbil8ge-5fas1.webp)

## Which Version of Golden Snake Dance to Start With

Entry-level arrangements simplify the gongs and drums into a few bass chords, and can be managed after a year or two of lessons.

The full concert arrangement has many fast figures and heavy chords, and is more difficult.

You can start with the simple version to get to know the melody and the structure.

## Playing Golden Snake Dance on the Piano

In the piano arrangement, the right hand plays the joyful melody, and the left hand often imitates the gongs and drums with strong chords.

Play the melody clearly and with spring, and keep the rhythm steady and strong.

**Practice order**

In the call-and-response sections, you can use different registers to tell the antecedent phrase from the consequent one.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who arranged Golden Snake Dance?**
A: Nie Er, in 1934.

**Q: Which folk tune is it based on?**
A: Dao Ba Ban.

**Q: What is the call-and-response structure in the middle called?**
A: Luosi jieding, the snail shell's tip.

**Q: What does "luosi jieding" mean?**
A: Each phrase is shorter than the last, and in the end they merge together.

**Q: What does the left hand often imitate in the piano version?**
A: The gongs and drums.
