group-piano-class-management.body:
The key to managing a piano group class is giving every student something clear to do every minute, rather than having them queue up waiting for their turn to play. A group class usually has four to eight students, each with a different level of progress, personality and attention span. If the teacher looks after only one person at a time, the others quickly get bored, distracted or even noisy. With sensible seating, tiered tasks and a well-paced lesson, a group class can be both orderly and fun.

## How Group Classes Differ from One-to-One Lessons

In a one-to-one lesson, the pace is set by the teacher and one student and can be adjusted at any moment. A group class needs planning in advance, because if any one part gets stuck, it affects everyone. On the other hand, group classes have advantages of their own: students can listen to and learn from each other and play ensemble pieces together, enjoying a sense of togetherness that a one-to-one lesson can hardly offer.

**Turn "waiting" into "taking part"**
The biggest challenge in a group class is waiting time. A good lesson design makes sure students who are not playing at the moment are still doing something connected with learning, such as listening, tapping rhythms or looking at the score to find mistakes.

## Seating and Equipment

If the room has several digital pianos, each with a pair of headphones, students can practise at the same time without disturbing each other. The teacher can use equipment that can switch the monitoring, or walk around between students to listen. If there is only one piano, you can add a few small keyboards or paper keyboards for the desk, so that students can practise fingering while they wait. Seats can be arranged in a semicircle so that every student can see the teacher and the keys being demonstrated.

![Several hands resting on piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw6vcib5-1a0wf.webp)

## The Basic Flow of a Lesson

For a sixty-minute group class, you can use the structure below as a reference and adjust it to the students' ages:

- Opening, five minutes: everyone taps rhythms together or sings a short song to get into the mood.
- New material, fifteen minutes: the teacher demonstrates a new technique or passage, and everyone practises it slowly together.
- Group practice, twenty minutes: students practise on their own with headphones, while the teacher listens to each one in turn and gives advice.
- Ensemble, ten minutes: different parts are given to different students, and they play an ensemble piece together.
- Wrap-up, five minutes: review the key points of the day and set the home practice.
- Buffer, five minutes: left for the unexpected or for students' questions.

## Tiered Tasks: One Piece, Different Levels of Difficulty

There will always be students who are faster and slower in a group. The teacher can design the same piece at different levels: a beginner plays only the single notes of the melody, a student in the middle adds a simple left hand, and a faster student plays the full accompaniment or improvises embellishments. Everyone is playing the same piece, yet each one is challenged.

**Let the faster students be little helpers**
Faster students can occasionally help their classmates, for example by demonstrating a rhythm. But take care not to make them helpers all the time, because they need room to progress too.

## Class Rules and Signals

A group class needs simple, clear rules. For example, when the teacher raises a hand, everyone takes off their headphones and takes their hands off the keys; during a demonstration, everyone just watches and does not play. There is no need for many rules, three or four are enough, and what matters is sticking to them in every lesson. For younger children, a fixed musical pattern can serve as a "gathering signal" and works better than calling out "stop".

## Encourage Listening to Each Other

A unique value of a group class is that students can listen to each other. You can set up a "mini concert" section in which two or three students play a short piece for their classmates each time, and the others name one strength and one suggestion. The teacher should guide students to use kind, specific language, such as "Your rhythm is very steady" or "The ending could be a little slower", to create a supportive atmosphere.

## A Short Summary for Parents After Class

Parents of group-class students are often not in the room, so the teacher can send a short lesson summary from time to time, saying what was learned in this period and how to practise at home. When photos or videos of students are involved, get the parents' consent in advance and take care to protect students' personal information.

## FAQ

**Q: Are group classes suitable for complete beginners?**
A: Yes. Starting together as complete beginners can actually make it easier to build confidence.

**Q: What if the gap in progress is too big?**
A: You can use tiered tasks. If the gap stays large, consider changing the groupings.

**Q: Can I teach a group class with only one piano?**
A: Yes. With rhythm exercises, paper keyboards and taking turns to play, students can still take part.

**Q: How many students per class is about right?**
A: Four to six is generally easier to manage, depending on the room's equipment and the students' ages.

harmonic-interval-melodic-interval-diffe.body:
The distance between two notes is called an interval. If the two notes are played at the same time, it is a harmonic interval; if one note is played first and the other after it, it is a melodic interval. For example, playing C and E together gives a harmonic major third; playing C and then E gives a melodic major third. The two have the same interval name but sound different: a harmonic interval lets us hear the notes blending, while a melodic interval lets us hear the direction the notes travel.

## Sight-Singing Practice

When you meet a melodic interval in sight-singing, first imagine the sound of that interval, then sing it.

**Remember this**

For example, when you see an ascending third, think about how that interval feels, then sing the second note.

This kind of practice links reading the score with listening.

## Ascending and Descending

A melodic interval has a direction: going from a low note to a high note is ascending, and going from a high note to a low note is descending.

For example, C followed by G is an ascending fifth; G followed by C is a descending fourth or fifth, depending on which C it is.

A harmonic interval has no direction, only a distance.

## Remembering Melodic Intervals with Songs

Many people remember melodic intervals by the opening of familiar songs.

For example, if a certain song begins with an ascending perfect fourth, hearing that interval will bring that song to mind.

You could make a small table listing the distance between the first two notes of a few songs you often sing.

## Ways to Recognise Harmonic Intervals

To recognise a harmonic interval, try separating the two notes in your head: sing the low note first, then the high note.

This turns the harmonic interval into a melodic one, which is easier to judge.

With practice, you will be able to hear the size of a harmonic interval directly.

**Notice the details**
- Notes sounding together make a harmonic interval
- Notes sounding one after the other make a melodic interval
- Same name, different sound
- Melodic intervals can ascend or descend

## Melodic Intervals in a Melody

A melody is made up of a string of melodic intervals, some moving by step and some by leap.

A step is a movement of a second, and a leap is a movement of a third or more.

Analysing the intervals in a melody helps us read and remember music faster.

## Harmonic Intervals in Chords

A chord is made up of several harmonic intervals; a major triad, for example, contains a major third and a minor third.

Knowing harmonic intervals helps us recognise chords faster.

When you play a chord, you can also notice the interval between each pair of notes.

## Summary: Harmonic and Melodic Intervals

Two notes sounding together form a harmonic interval, and two notes sounding one after the other form a melodic interval; both are counted in the same way.

A harmonic interval lets us hear blending and has no direction; a melodic interval lets us hear movement and can ascend or descend.

Comparing them on the piano, remembering intervals with songs, and singing the notes of a harmonic interval separately all help us tell the two kinds apart.

## How They Sound Different

A third sounds warm and blended as a harmonic interval, but like a small step of a melody as a melodic interval.

A seventh sounds rubbed and tense as a harmonic interval, but like a big leap as a melodic interval.

So the same interval name can give quite different impressions in the two cases.

## The Two Kinds in Ear Training

In ear training, harmonic and melodic intervals are often practised separately.

Melodic intervals are easier to identify, because you hear one note first and then the other.

Harmonic intervals are harder, because the two notes sound together and you have to pick out two notes from a single sound.

## Harmonic Intervals

When two notes are played at the same time, they form a harmonic interval.

On the score, the two notes of a harmonic interval are lined up vertically, written in the same position.

When you listen to a harmonic interval, your ear hears the two notes combined into one sound.

## Reading Intervals in the Score

When reading music, you can judge an interval quickly by looking at the positions of the two notes.

If both notes are on lines or both are in spaces, the interval is usually an odd number, such as a third or a fifth.

If one is on a line and the other in a space, the interval is usually an even number, such as a second or a fourth.

## Comparing on the Piano

Try a comparison on the piano: first play C and G together and listen; then play C first and G afterwards and listen.

Then do the same with C and E, and with C and B.

This kind of practice helps us feel the difference between harmonic and melodic intervals.

![Lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5ymvc-owm39.webp)

## What an Interval Is

An interval is simply how far apart two notes are, and we usually describe that distance as a certain number, such as a third.

To work out the number, count from the low note to the high note, including both ends.

Take C to E: counting both the first and last notes, three note names are involved, so it is called a third.

## Melodic Intervals

When two notes are played one after the other, they form a melodic interval.

On the score, the two notes of a melodic interval sit one after the other, side by side.

**Listen**

When you listen to a melodic interval, your ear hears the sound travelling from one place to another.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a harmonic interval?**
A: Two notes sounding at the same time.

**Q: What is a melodic interval?**
A: Two notes sounding one after the other.

**Q: Does a melodic interval have a direction?**
A: Yes, it can ascend or descend.

**Q: Which is easier to recognise?**
A: Usually the melodic interval.

**Q: How do I recognise a harmonic interval?**
A: Separate the two notes in your head and sing them one at a time.

fur-elise-opening-practice.body:
Beethoven's Für Elise is a piece many people want to learn. Its formal title is Bagatelle in A minor, catalogued as WoO 59. It was written around 1810 and was not published until 1867, when the scholar Ludwig Nohl edited it. The piece is in 3/8, and its opening melody rocks back and forth between E and D♯ before settling on the A minor tonic chord. The key to playing the opening well is to make the alternating arpeggios of the two hands join into one flowing line, played softly, without giving every note the same weight.

## The Left-Hand Arpeggio

As the right hand lands on A, the left hand plays an A minor arpeggio in the bass register, flowing upward through A, E, A.

Then the right hand takes over and continues upward with C, E, A, so the two hands alternate and form one continuous line.

This alternation between the hands is the most distinctive feature of the opening of Für Elise.

## About the Title

Researchers have different theories about who the "Elise" of the title was, and there is still no settled answer.

The original manuscript was later lost, so many details are now hard to confirm.

For a piano learner, what matters more is understanding the musical character of the piece itself, rather than tracing where the name came from.

## Where the Piece Comes From

Für Elise is a short piano piece by Beethoven. In musical classification it is a bagatelle, a short piece of light character.

Its catalogue number is WoO 59. WoO is short for the German "Werk ohne Opuszahl", meaning "work without opus number", which shows that Beethoven did not give it an opus number in his lifetime.

The piece was not published during Beethoven's life. It was later edited from the manuscript by the scholar Ludwig Nohl and published in 1867.

## Pedalling in the Opening

The arpeggios at the start are often combined with the sustain pedal, to make the harmony fuller and more connected.

The pedal change usually comes where the chord changes, so that the sound of two chords does not blur together.

You can first practise the hands without the pedal, then add it in, and ask your teacher to check where the pedal changes go.

## The Opening Melody

At the start, the right hand rocks between E and D♯ several times, then plays E, B, D, C in turn and finally lands on A.

This run of notes sounds as if it is hesitating and wandering, and then finally finds its direction.

When you play these notes, keep them soft and connected, like a gentle whisper.

- The formal title is Bagatelle in A minor, WoO 59
- Written around 1810 and not published until 1867
- The piece is in 3/8
- The opening melody rocks between E and D♯

## Keep the Volume Low

The dynamic marking at the start of Für Elise is piano (soft), and many people unconsciously play too loudly.

Use a light touch, keep your fingers close to the keys, and keep the sound within a gentle range.

You can add a little emphasis at the high point of a phrase, but the overall character should stay soft.

## What Level Is It For?

The opening of Für Elise is relatively easy, and many people who have been learning for a little while can try it.

However, the middle sections have fast figures and larger leaps, and need more technical preparation.

You can learn the opening theme first, and learn the full version once your level has improved.

## Practice Suggestions

You can first practise the right hand and left hand separately, getting to know each one's notes and fingering, and then practise the places where the hands alternate.

Start slowly with a metronome and gradually speed up to a light tempo, keeping the volume soft.

You can also listen to several different performances to get a feel for the gentle, slightly wistful character of the piece.

## Making the Alternation Sound Like One Hand

When the hands alternate, a common problem is a tiny pause at the handover, or a sudden change in volume.

When practising, play slowly at first and listen carefully for any gap at the moment one hand passes to the other.

The goal is for the listener not to sense the change of hands, as if one hand were playing a single flowing arpeggio.

![A sepia-toned sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angle](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1darm-gy32n.webp)

## Changes in the Middle Section

After the opening theme, Für Elise brings in several sections of different character, some bright and some agitated.

After these sections, the opening theme returns, forming a rondo-like structure.

Understanding this structure can help you plan your practice in sections, and also give your playing more shape.

## The Feel of 3/8

Für Elise is in 3/8, with three eighth notes in each bar and the eighth note as the beat.

Because the tempo is fairly light, many people feel each bar as one big beat, with a gently swaying feeling.

The opening has an upbeat, that is, the piece starts on the last beat of a bar, so be careful when counting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is the formal title of Für Elise?**
A: Bagatelle in A minor, WoO 59.

**Q: When was it published?**
A: In 1867, edited by the scholar Ludwig Nohl.

**Q: What is the time signature?**
A: 3/8.

**Q: What is the opening melody like?**
A: It rocks back and forth between E and D♯.

**Q: What should I watch for when the hands alternate?**
A: Keep the handover smooth, so it sounds like one hand.

**Q: Can beginners play it?**
A: You can start with the opening theme; the middle section needs more preparation.

grieg-notturno-op54-no4-1891.body:
Notturno is a short piano piece by the Norwegian composer Grieg. It appears in Book 5 of his Lyric Pieces, Op. 54, published in 1891, and is the fourth piece of that book. It is in C major. At the start the right hand plays a quiet, gentle melody while the left hand softly plucks out broken chords, like the not-quite-dark sky of a Nordic summer night. In the middle section the music grows gradually more agitated, and then strings of trills and short figures appear in the high register, often heard as the calls of night birds. Finally the opening melody returns and the piece ends in quiet. It is not long, and it is a good piece for practising a singing melody and delicate tone colour.

## Grieg's Piano Language

Grieg's short piano pieces often combine the flavour of Norwegian folk music with Romantic harmony.

He liked to use unexpected chords that give the music a cool Nordic colour.

In Notturno, too, you can hear this kind of delicate, distinctive harmony.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Birdsong in Notturno

In lessons you can play for Teacher Aum and ask your teacher to judge whether the trills are light and clear.

You can also ask for help listening to the balance of volume between the melody and the left-hand chords.

From a short Nordic piece, you can play out the calm of a summer night.

## The Agitation in the Middle of Notturno

In the middle of the piece the music gradually becomes agitated, the harmony richer and the dynamics louder.

This passage is like a sudden surge of feeling in the night.

But the agitation does not last long, and the music soon quietens again.

- It appears in Lyric Pieces Book 5, Op. 54
- Published in 1891, the fourth piece
- In C major, with a quiet, gentle melody
- The trills in the high register of the middle section sound like night birds

## The Calls of the Night Birds

After the middle section, strings of trills and short figures appear in the high register.

These sounds are often heard as the calls of night birds, answering one another in the quiet night sky.

When you play these trills, play them lightly and clearly, like birdsong coming from far away.

## Practising the Trills

When playing birdsong-like trills, keep your fingers relaxed and alternate two notes quickly with your fingertips.

Do not use too much force, or the trill will become heavy and uneven.

You can practise slowly first and then gradually speed up.

## Grieg's Notturno in Brief

Grieg's Notturno is in Book 5, Op. 54, of the ten books and sixty-six Lyric Pieces. It was published in 1891 and is the fourth of the six pieces in this book. In C major, it is often thought to describe a Norwegian summer night when the sky does not quite go dark. At the start the right-hand melody is quiet and gentle while the left hand softly plucks broken chords; the middle gradually becomes agitated, then trills and short figures in the high register sound like night birds, and finally the opening melody returns and the piece ends gently in C major.

Grieg often combined the flavour of folk music with Romantic harmony. This piece suits someone who has played for two or three years, can play clear trills and knows how to use the pedal. The trills should be relaxed and light, the melody should be sung before it is played, and the layers should be distinct.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the birdsong-like trills.

## The Left-Hand Broken Chords in Notturno

The left hand softly plays broken chords, flowing slowly as if through the night.

These chords should sound very light, keeping a distance from the right-hand melody.

You can use the sustain pedal to join the chords together, but change the pedal as the harmony changes.

## Let the Melody of Notturno Sing

When you play the melody of Notturno, you can sing it first to feel the breathing of each phrase.

Keep the fingers of your right hand close to the keys and let the weight of your arm send the sound out naturally.

There should be layers of volume between melody and accompaniment, with the melody on top and the accompaniment below.

## Lyric Pieces, Book 5

From 1867 to 1901, Grieg published ten books of Lyric Pieces in succession.

Book 5, Op. 54, was published in 1891 and has six pieces.

Notturno is the fourth of them and is one of the pieces from this book that is often played.

## A Nordic Summer Night

In Norway, summer nights often do not get completely dark, and the sky keeps a faint glow.

Grieg's Notturno is often thought to describe such a quiet, bright summer night.

There is no darkness or sorrow in the piece, only a gentle, peaceful atmosphere.

## The Melody Returns

After the birdsong, the gentle melody from the beginning returns.

This time it unfolds slowly in an even quieter atmosphere.

Finally the piece ends softly on a chord of C major, like the night slowly sinking into stillness.

## How Hard Is Notturno?

Notturno is not long, but it requires delicate control of tone colour and steady trills.

Someone who has played for two or three years, can play clear trills and knows how to use the sustain pedal can generally start trying it.

The opening and ending are fairly easy, while the middle section and the birdsong passages need a little more time.

![Cartoon character with glasses and headphones in a room at night, playing an upright piano from sheet music, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbknq7p-i6pqf.webp)

## The Gentle Opening Melody

At the start of the piece, the right hand plays a quiet, gentle melody, like speaking softly.

The melody has few notes and a calm rhythm, and each phrase has its own natural rise and fall.

**Try it**

When you play, let the melody sing, but do not let the sound become too loud.

## FAQ

**Q: Which work of Grieg's contains Notturno?**
A: Lyric Pieces Book 5, Op. 54.

**Q: In which year was it published?**
A: 1891.

**Q: What key is the piece in?**
A: C major.

**Q: What are the trills in the high register after the middle section often heard as?**
A: The calls of night birds.

**Q: How many Lyric Pieces did Grieg write in all?**
A: Sixty-six.

french-diapason-normal-435-hz.body:
Today many people are used to treating one fixed frequency as the standard that every instrument should match. Historically, the situation was not so simple. In the mid-19th century, France fixed a reference pitch at 435 Hz, called at the time the "normal diapason" or something similar, so that orchestras, theatres and instrument makers had a pitch they could all refer to. This number did not exist from ancient times, nor was it the only such agreement in the world afterwards. In earlier periods, the reference pitch of different places and ensembles could be higher or lower; in later periods, other widely adopted numbers appeared. The point of knowing about 435 Hz is to understand that the "standard" of pitch has a history of its own: works written in different eras and different cities were not all sounding against the same reference. Piano learners do not need to change the pitch of their pianos, but when listening to recordings of old instruments or reading related notes, they can know that a sound that is higher or lower overall does not mean the playing is out of tune. This article does not present any modern convention as a final point that can never be changed; it simply puts the number once adopted in France back into its own time.

## Setting aside the idea of "there has always been one standard"

A standard sounds like an unchanging ruler, but in fact it is something agreed upon, and it can be replaced by new agreements.

Learning about 435 Hz means seeing one such agreement that was clearly written down.

This helps us avoid mistaking today's most common practice for a law of nature that has always held.

## Why a number was agreed on then

Without a shared reference, the pitch of different ensembles and different cities could differ by an audible amount.

For singers, wind instruments and keyboard instruments that had to work together, this caused real difficulties.

Agreeing on a number was meant to reduce this confusion, not to end all discussion about pitch.

![A watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdkdhf9-x1h43.webp)

## Do piano learners need to change their piano

Usually not. Everyday practice can carry on at the tuning of the instrument you use now.

All you need to know is that the note names on the page describe relationships, and that absolute pitch has moved in history.

When you need to play with a particular old instrument or a particular convention, tune to what is required on the spot.

- In the mid-19th century France fixed a reference pitch at 435 Hz
- The aim was to give orchestras, theatres and instrument makers a shared reference
- The number did not exist from ancient times, and it was not the only agreement afterwards
- Knowing about it helps avoid treating some modern pitch as the way things have always been

## What to remember about 435 Hz

It is a reference pitch that France adopted in the mid-19th century, to give the cooperation of the time a common starting point.

It was neither the first number at the beginning, nor the only agreement afterwards.

When learning the piano you generally do not need to change your own instrument, but you should know that absolute pitch has moved in history.

## How this helps when listening to old recordings

Some recordings of historical instruments sound higher or lower overall, which does not necessarily mean "out of tune"; they may be tuned to the reference of their time.

First ask which reference this performance uses, and then judge whether it is stable and consistent with itself.

A shift of the whole and unevenness within are two different things.

## Ask Teacher Aum in your lesson to listen to overall height versus internal evenness

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen with you to two recordings that differ in overall pitch but are each even within themselves, and to tell these two things apart.

You can also ask your teacher to point out which recording is simply higher overall, and which is truly uneven.

From this historical agreement of 435 Hz, practise bringing "standard pitch has a history too" into your habits of listening.

## 435 was not the beginning of history

Before this agreement appeared, different places already had their own customary pitches, some higher and some lower.

So it is best not to imagine 435 Hz as "the first time humans began tuning A".

It was simply a reference formally adopted in one region during one period.

## Nor was it the end of history

Later, over a wider area, other widely used reference frequencies appeared.

The pianos and orchestras we hear today are not all exactly the same as those of mid-19th-century France.

Projecting one modern number back onto all old works is not accurate.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In what context was 435 Hz adopted?**
A: In mid-19th-century France, to give orchestras, theatres and instrument makers a shared reference pitch.

**Q: Was it a standard that existed from ancient times?**
A: No. In earlier periods the pitch was not uniform from place to place.

**Q: Was it the only such number in the world afterwards?**
A: No. Other widely adopted reference frequencies appeared later.

**Q: If an old recording sounds higher or lower overall, is it necessarily out of tune?**
A: Not necessarily. It may be tuned to the reference of its time, and this should be judged separately from whether it is even within itself.

**Q: Do piano learners need to change the pitch of their piano because of this?**
A: Usually not. Everyday practice can follow the tuning of the instrument you use.

grieg-piano-concerto-a-minor-1868.body:
In the summer of 1868, the Norwegian composer Grieg was on holiday in the Danish countryside, where he wrote his Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16. He was only twenty-four that year. The following spring the concerto premiered in Copenhagen and was a great success. At the very start, the timpani play a roll, and the piano then rushes down from the high register with a series of powerful chords; this opening later became very famous. Grieg completed only this one piano concerto in his life, and over the following decades he revised it again and again.

## Folk Music Elements in the Opening

The descending figure in the piano at the start is often thought to carry features of Norwegian folk music.

One of them, a descending minor second followed by a descending major third, can also be heard in other works by Grieg.

This figure gives the music a distinctive Nordic colour.

## The Three Movements of Grieg's Concerto

The concerto has three movements: the first is a moderately fast Allegro, in A minor.

The second is an Adagio in D-flat major, with a calm and deeply felt melody.

The third is an Allegro whose opening is like a Norwegian folk dance, and it ends in the brilliance of A major.

## Excerpts for Learners

The complete concerto is too difficult for most learners, but you can look for simplified excerpts to play.

For example, the descending chords of the opening or the lyrical melody of the second movement both have easy arrangements.

Playing these excerpts helps you sense the atmosphere of the work.

## Grieg's Piano Concerto in Brief

Grieg was born in Bergen in 1843. In the summer of 1868, aged twenty-four, he wrote the Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16, in the Danish countryside. It premiered in Copenhagen in April 1869; he did not attend himself, and the performance was a great success.

The opening is a timpani roll and chords rushing down from the high register of the piano, with the colour of Norwegian folk music. The three movements are an Allegro in A minor, an Adagio in D-flat major and a dance-like Allegro, ending in A major. In 1870 Liszt played from the manuscript in Rome and encouraged him, and over the following decades Grieg revised the work again and again.

The complete concerto is hard, so you can listen to a recording first and then play simplified excerpts. You can ask Teacher Aum to help find a suitable edition.

## Listen to the Complete Concerto First

Before playing excerpts, listen to a recording of the complete concerto first.

Pay attention to the opening of the timpani and piano, the calm of the second movement and the dance rhythm of the third.

With an overall impression, you will have a better feel for the excerpts when you play them.

## The Story of Liszt Sight-Reading the Score

In 1870, Grieg visited Liszt in Rome and brought the score of the concerto with him.

According to Grieg's description in a letter, Liszt played from the manuscript on the spot and gave him warm encouragement.

This meeting greatly inspired the young Grieg.

## The Colour of A Minor

A minor has no sharps or flats and looks simple on the piano, but the technical demands of this concerto are very high.

In the first movement, the piano has a very long cadenza that calls for great technique and expressiveness.

This concerto is a common piece in pianists' concerts.

## Revised Again and Again

After the concerto was finished, Grieg did not stop revising it.

Over the following decades he adjusted the orchestration and some details many times, and was still revising it in his later years.

The version commonly used today is the one he revised late in life.

## The 1869 Premiere

In April 1869, the concerto premiered in Copenhagen, with a Norwegian pianist as soloist.

Grieg himself did not attend the premiere because of other engagements in Norway.

The performance was a great success, and the work soon spread across Europe.

## The Summer of 1868

In 1868, Grieg had only recently married, and his daughter was also born that year.

In the summer, in a country residence in Denmark, he concentrated on writing this piano concerto.

It was a large-scale work from his youth, full of youthful passion.

**Think it over**
- Written in the summer of 1868 in the Danish countryside, Op. 16
- Grieg was twenty-four at the time
- Premiered in Copenhagen in the spring of 1869
- Opens with a timpani roll and descending chords in the piano

![Glowing digital interface against a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac05qk-ycehf.webp)

## Who Was Grieg?

Grieg was a Norwegian composer, born in 1843 in Bergen on the west coast of Norway.

As a young man he went to Leipzig in Germany to study music, and later lived in Copenhagen for a time.

The flavour of fjords, valleys and country dances is often hidden in his melodies, and the Lyric Pieces and the incidental music for Peer Gynt are examples.

## The Dance of the Third Movement

The theme of the third movement has a sharp rhythm, like a fast Norwegian folk dance.

In the middle there is a lyrical melody played by the flute, which later in the ending is played grandly by the whole orchestra.

The change from minor to major fills the ending with brightness and joy.

## The Opening of Timpani and Piano

At the very start of the concerto, the timpani first roll softly and then grow louder.

Then the piano goes down from the high register, playing a series of powerful chords and octaves, rushing all the way to the low register.

This opening is grand in scale, and many people can recognise it at once.

## Ask Your Teacher to Find Excerpts of Grieg's Concerto in Lessons

If you want to play excerpts of Grieg's concerto, you can ask Teacher Aum in lessons to find a suitable arrangement for your level.

If your level is not yet enough, you can also start with simpler pieces from Grieg's Lyric Pieces.

**Summary**

Build up slowly, and take on a fuller version in the future.

## FAQ

**Q: In which year did Grieg write his piano concerto?**
A: The summer of 1868.

**Q: How old was Grieg then?**
A: Twenty-four.

**Q: Where was the premiere?**
A: Copenhagen, in April 1869.

**Q: How does the concerto begin?**
A: With a timpani roll, and the piano rushes down from the high register in a series of chords.

**Q: Who played it from the manuscript in 1870?**
A: Liszt.

grieg-wedding-day-troldhaugen-op65.body:
In June 1892, Grieg and his wife Nina reached their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary. For the occasion Grieg wrote a piano piece, which was later included in Book 8 of the Lyric Pieces as Op. 65 No. 6, published in 1896 under the title Wedding Day at Troldhaugen. Troldhaugen was their home near Bergen in Norway. The opening is like a group of guests coming to offer congratulations, stepping lightly closer; the middle section is quiet and tender, like the couple's memories. Today this piece is one of the most often played of the Lyric Pieces.

## Lyric Pieces, Book 8

Grieg published ten books of Lyric Pieces in all, sixty-six short piano pieces.

**Summary**

Book 8, Op. 65, was published in 1896 and contains six pieces; this one is the last.

It is also one of the longer pieces in the whole set of Lyric Pieces.

## The Middle Section: Tender Memories

In the middle section the tempo slows and the music becomes quiet and lyrical.

The melody is soft and deeply felt, like the couple, after all the festivity, quietly looking back over the twenty-five years they have walked together.

This section forms a sharp contrast with the liveliness of the opening.

## Troldhaugen, the Home

Troldhaugen is near Bergen, and it was the home Grieg and his wife moved into in 1885.

The house stands on a hillside by a lake, surrounded by woods and fjord scenery.

Grieg spent a lot of his later years here and wrote many works.

![Stippled painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacqtpe-1tt5p.webp)

## The Wedding Day Returns

After the middle section, the march from the opening returns and the mood becomes lively once more.

At the end the music grows louder and louder and finishes on joyful chords.

The whole piece is like a story that goes from festivity to warmth and back to festivity.

## The Flavour of Norwegian Folk Music

Like many of Grieg's works, this piece has the colour of Norwegian folk music.

For example, some open-fifth bass notes and ornamented melodies bring to mind country musicians.

These details give the music more local character.

- In 1892 the Griegs reached their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary
- Included in Lyric Pieces Book 8 as Op. 65 No. 6
- Published in 1896
- Troldhaugen was their home near Bergen

## Plan Your Wedding Day Practice with Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to judge whether your level suits this piece.

Your teacher can also help plan the order of practice, for example practising the lyrical melody of the middle section first and then the chords of the opening.

This piece is very suitable to play at family celebrations.

## Big Dynamic Changes

This piece has big dynamic changes, from very soft to very loud.

Be patient where there is a crescendo, adding a step at a time, and do not use up all your strength at the start.

Layers of dynamics make the pictures in the music more vivid.

## The Chords at the Start of Wedding Day

The chords at the start should be played crisply and with spring, like light footsteps.

Do not play them too heavily, or they will seem clumsy.

You can practise the left-hand chords slowly first to make the rhythm steady.

## Twenty-Five Years of the Griegs

Grieg's wife Nina was a singer and also his cousin, and they married in 1867.

Nina often sang Grieg's songs and was an important partner in his music.

In June 1892 they reached their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary, their silver wedding.

## How Much Skill Does Wedding Day Take?

Wedding Day at Troldhaugen has a technical demand that is medium to somewhat high, with chords, octaves and fairly large leaps.

It suits learners who already have some foundation and can play the simpler pieces among the Lyric Pieces.

You can start with other Lyric Pieces by Grieg and then take on this one.

## Wedding Day at Troldhaugen in Brief

Grieg and his wife Nina married in 1867. In June 1892 they reached their silver wedding anniversary and Grieg wrote this piano piece, whose original title means "The well-wishers are coming". It was included in Book 8 of the Lyric Pieces, published in 1896, as Op. 65 No. 6, and Troldhaugen is their home near Bergen, where they moved in 1885.

The opening in D major is like a march of well-wishers, the quiet, lyrical middle section is like the couple's memories, and then the march returns and the piece ends in joy. It has the colour of Norwegian folk music: the opening chords should be crisp and springy, the middle melody smooth and soft, and the dynamic changes should have layers.

The technical demand is medium to somewhat high, and you can ask Teacher Aum to judge whether it suits you.

## The Singing of the Middle Section

The middle section needs a completely different touch, with a smooth, soft melody.

You can use more of the sustain pedal to make the sound warmer.

The tempo can be a little freer, but do not lose direction.

## The Original Title

The original title of this piece means "The well-wishers are coming".

It portrays the scene of friends and neighbours coming to Troldhaugen on the day of the anniversary to offer congratulations.

When it was published, the title was changed to Wedding Day at Troldhaugen.

## The Opening: The Procession of Well-Wishers

The piece begins in D major with a march-like rhythm, lively and spirited.

The left-hand chords are like the guests' footsteps, and the right-hand melody is like everyone chatting happily.

The music gradually grows stronger, like the procession getting closer and closer until it reaches the door.

## FAQ

**Q: What was this piece written for?**
A: The Griegs' twenty-fifth wedding anniversary in 1892.

**Q: Which book of the Lyric Pieces is it in?**
A: Book 8, Op. 65 No. 6.

**Q: In which year was it published?**
A: 1896.

**Q: What place is Troldhaugen?**
A: The Griegs' home near Bergen.

**Q: What is the character of the middle section?**
A: Quiet and lyrical, like tender memories.

handel-messiah-dublin-premiere-1742.body:
Handel's oratorio Messiah is one of the most famous works in Western choral music, and almost everyone has heard its "Hallelujah" chorus. Its first performance was not in London, where Handel lived for many years, but in Dublin, Ireland, on 13 April 1742. It was a charity concert, and the audience was so large that the organisers asked ladies beforehand not to wear hooped skirts and gentlemen not to wear swords, so that more people could fit in. Here is the story of the work's premiere.

## The "Hallelujah" Chorus

The second part of Messiah ends with the "Hallelujah" chorus, which is grand in scale, with a simple and powerful melody.

This chorus is often sung on its own and can be heard on many occasions.

The voice parts sing "Hallelujah" in turn, a fine example of polyphonic and homophonic writing combined.

## A Score That Kept Changing

In later performances Handel often altered parts of Messiah to suit his singers.

As a result, the work survives in many different versions.

Performers today have to choose among these versions.

## The Journey of a Work

From three weeks of writing in the summer of 1741, to the charity premiere in Dublin, to the annual performances in London, Messiah has had an unusual journey.

Today it is performed regularly in concerts all over the world.

This history also reminds us that the fate of a work is often closely tied to the setting in which it is performed.

## Accompanying a Choir

Many choirs rehearse Messiah with a piano in place of the orchestra.

The piano accompaniment must give the rhythm and harmony clearly, to help the choir come in.

This kind of accompanying is also one way for piano learners to meet choral music.

- In the summer of 1741, Handel wrote the full score in about three weeks
- First performed in Dublin on 13 April 1742
- The premiere was a charity concert
- The "Hallelujah" chorus is still performed today

## Written in a Little Over Three Weeks

The words of Messiah were compiled from scripture by Charles Jennens.

In the summer of 1741, Handel finished the full score in a little over three weeks.

Such speed was not unusual among composers of the time, but the scale and quality of the work have astonished later generations.

## An Invitation to Dublin

In the autumn of 1741, Handel was invited to Dublin to give a series of concerts.

He travelled to Ireland with the newly written Messiah and spent a concert season there.

Dublin audiences welcomed his performances warmly.

## Practising Polyphony with Messiah Arrangements

Quite a few melodies from Messiah have been arranged for piano, such as the "Hallelujah" chorus and some of the arias.

When you play these arrangements, think about how the different voices enter and answer one another in the chorus.

Bringing out the layers of several voices on the piano is excellent practice.

## 1743: Messiah Comes to London

In 1743 Messiah was performed in London, and at first the response was not as warm as in Dublin.

Some people thought it unsuitable to perform a religious work in a theatre.

Later, Handel performed Messiah every year for a charitable foundling hospital, and only then did it gradually become a household name in London.

## Summary of the Messiah Premiere

Handel wrote Messiah in a little over three weeks in the summer of 1741. It was first performed in Dublin on 13 April 1742 as a charity concert, and the organisers asked the audience not to wear hooped skirts or swords so that more people could fit in.

The premiere was a great success. The early London performances met with a lukewarm response, but through annual charity performances the work gradually won people's hearts.

The "Hallelujah" chorus is still performed today. Handel kept revising the score and left several versions, and piano learners can meet the work through arrangements and choral accompaniment.

## The Reception of the Premiere

According to reports at the time, the premiere was a great success and the audience was deeply moved.

The newspapers praised the music and the performance, and the proceeds helped charitable causes.

This success laid the foundation for the later performances of Messiah in London.

![A glowing digital interface against a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7pd43-98qse.webp)

## The Tradition of Standing

In some places the audience stands during the "Hallelujah" chorus, a custom said to go back to the eighteenth century.

There are different accounts of where the custom came from, and no definite record confirms any of them.

Today, whether people stand often depends on local performing tradition.

## Handel's Situation in London

Handel (1685-1759) was born in Germany, later settled in London and became famous for Italian opera.

By the late 1730s, Italian opera was no longer so popular in London, and Handel turned to writing oratorios in English.

An oratorio needs no stage sets or costumes. It is performed by soloists, chorus and orchestra, and its subjects are mostly drawn from religious stories.

## A Charity Premiere

The premiere of Messiah was set for 13 April 1742, with the proceeds going to charity.

Even the rehearsal drew a large crowd, and once word spread, everyone wanted to hear the first performance.

To let more people into the hall, the organisers asked ladies not to wear hooped skirts and gentlemen not to wear swords.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Where was Messiah first performed?**
A: In Dublin, Ireland.

**Q: On what date was the premiere?**
A: 13 April 1742.

**Q: How long did Handel take to write the full score?**
A: A little over three weeks.

**Q: Why were ladies asked not to wear hooped skirts to the premiere?**
A: So that more people could fit into the hall.

**Q: In which part is the "Hallelujah" chorus?**
A: At the end of the second part.

grandmas-penghu-bay-1979-campus-folk.body:
Grandma's Penghu Bay was written, words and music, by Ye Jiaxiu and first sung by Pan Anbang in 1979. It is one of the representative songs of Taiwan's campus folk era. Penghu is a group of islands in the Taiwan Strait, and Pan Anbang is said to have lived there with his grandmother as a child; the song is about those seaside memories. The rhythm is lively and the melody bright, and the lyrics mention the beach, the waves, cacti and the setting sun. It suits the piano well for practising light rhythms and broken-chord accompaniment.

## The Pictures in the Lyrics of Penghu Bay

The lyrics have the evening breeze, the beach, the waves, cacti, and Grandma beneath the setting sun.

**Think it over**

These images are simple and vivid, and one hearing is enough to picture the seaside.

The song puts both the joy of childhood and the longing for Grandma into these pictures.

**Remember this**
- Words and music by Ye Jiaxiu
- First sung by Pan Anbang in 1979
- One of the representative songs of Taiwan's campus folk era
- It sings of childhood memories by the sea in Penghu

## Grandma's Penghu Bay in Brief

Grandma's Penghu Bay was written, words and music, by Ye Jiaxiu and first sung by Pan Anbang in 1979. It is one of the representative songs of Taiwan's campus folk era of the 1970s. Pan Anbang is said to have lived in Penghu with his grandmother as a child, and Ye Jiaxiu wrote the song based on his childhood stories. Penghu is a group of islands in the Taiwan Strait, and the lyrics have the evening breeze, the beach, the waves, cacti and the setting sun.

The rhythm is lively and the melody bright. On the piano you can imitate the guitar with broken chords, and in the right hand you should pay attention to the dotted rhythms and syncopation. Let the chorus grow a little stronger while keeping it fresh. After a year or two of lessons you can play an easy arrangement, and it is especially fun to play and sing at the same time.

You can ask Teacher Aum to teach you the broken-chord accompaniment.

## The Lively Rhythm of Penghu Bay

The rhythm of Grandma's Penghu Bay is lively, with a little bounce, like a sea breeze.

The melody is bright and mostly in a major key, so it sounds cheerful.

When you play, keep the rhythm relaxed and springy, and do not play too heavily.

## The Right-Hand Melody of Penghu Bay

Play the right-hand melody clearly and brightly, as if you were singing happily.

The melody has some dotted rhythms and syncopation, which should be played accurately and naturally.

You can first sing along with the original recording to get to know the rhythm, and then play it on the piano.

## What Kind of Place Is Penghu?

Penghu is a group of islands in the Taiwan Strait, with many beaches and bays.

The islands get plenty of sunshine and strong winds, and many cacti grow there.

What the lyrics describe is exactly this picture of sunshine and waves.

## Ask Your Teacher to Show You the Broken Chords in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to show you a broken-chord accompaniment pattern that suits this song.

If you want to play and sing at the same time, you can also ask your teacher to help you find a key that suits your voice.

Through one campus folk song, you can feel the childhood and sunshine in the music.

## Campus Folk Songs

In the 1970s, a wave of campus folk songs appeared in Taiwan.

Many university students wrote their own songs and sang them with their own guitars; the songs were simple and fresh, and sang of the life around them.

Grandma's Penghu Bay is one of the representative works of this period.

## Ye Jiaxiu

Ye Jiaxiu is a Taiwanese songwriter and singer who wrote many campus folk songs.

His songs often portray the countryside, the fields and childhood, with simple, friendly melodies.

When people mention Ye Jiaxiu, many think first of Grandma's Penghu Bay.

## Playing and Singing Together

The melody of this song is simple and catchy, so it is well suited to playing and singing at the same time.

At first you can play only the left-hand accompaniment and sing the melody yourself.

Once that is comfortable, add the right-hand melody, or ask family members to sing along.

## The Brightness of the Chorus

In the chorus the melody rises and the mood becomes more cheerful.

When you reach the chorus, you can add a little more strength to make the music brighter.

But do not play too loudly; keep that fresh, natural feel of a campus folk song.

## Guitar-Style Accompaniment

Campus folk songs mostly used guitar accompaniment, and this song is no exception.

On the piano, you can use broken chords in the left hand to imitate the sound of plucked guitar strings.

The broken chords should be even and light, like fingers gently plucking the strings.

## Turning Penghu Bay into a Small Chorus

If there are several people at home, you can split into two groups, one singing the verse and the other taking over the chorus.

The person at the piano takes care of the introduction and interludes and gives everyone their starting note.

In this way a song becomes a small family performance.

## Pan Anbang and His Grandmother

Pan Anbang, who first sang this song, is said to have lived in Penghu with his grandmother for a time as a child.

Ye Jiaxiu wrote the song based on the childhood stories he told.

The grandmother and the bay in the song are what childhood looks like to many people.

## Who Should Play Penghu Bay?

Someone who has been learning for a year or two and can read chord symbols will find an easy arrangement of Grandma's Penghu Bay just right.

It lets you practise broken-chord accompaniment, dotted rhythms and syncopation.

**Order of practice**

It is also very good for practising playing and singing at the same time.

A: Ye Jiaxiu, words and music.

A: Pan Anbang, in 1979.

harmonic-reduction-to-understand-passage.body:
Some passages look packed with notes, with fast broken chords, ornaments and passing notes, and they are hard work to read. In fact, many such passages rest on just a few simple chords. An effective method is "harmonic reduction": sum up the notes of each beat or each bar as one chord and play it as a block chord. See the harmonic skeleton clearly first, then go back to the original notes, and reading and memorising become much easier.

## Change Pedal Where the Harmony Changes

After the reduction, you can clearly see where the chords change.

**Try it**

In pieces that need the sustain pedal, these places are often where the pedal should change.

You can mark them in the score to help your pedalling practice.

## Summary: Harmonic Reduction

Many complex passages rest on just a few simple chords. Harmonic reduction means removing the non-chord notes and summing up the notes of each beat or bar as a block chord. Broken chords are straightforward to reduce, and notes that fall on strong beats or are held longer are more likely to be chord notes.

Playing the reduced harmonic skeleton helps you understand the structure. Going back to the original notes then makes reading, memorising and fingering easier, and the places where the harmony changes are often where the pedal changes too.

You do not need to know the chord names to do a reduction. Start with simple pieces, and ask Teacher Aum to help you analyse complex passages.

## Help with Fingering

When you play a block chord, your hand naturally finds a comfortable shape.

That shape often suits the original broken chord as well.

So harmonic reduction can also help us choose fingerings.

## Help with Reading

Once you have seen the harmonic skeleton, going back to the original notes makes reading much faster.

That is because we know which chord each group of notes belongs to, and the hand already has a rough position.

All that is left is to find the exact notes within that position.

## Start with a Simple Piece

You can begin practising harmonic reduction with a simple piece, such as a short one with broken chords in the left hand.

Once you are familiar with the method, use it on more complex passages.

Gradually, you will see the harmony naturally as you read.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothes plays a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a synthesizer with crystals in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa92d9k-iw1as.webp)

## Start with Broken Chords

Passages with broken chords are straightforward to reduce.

For example, if the left hand plays C, G, E, G, you can reduce it to a single C major triad.

Play each group of broken chords as a block chord, and you can see the harmonic progression.

## Ask Your Teacher to Help Analyse in Lessons

When you meet a passage whose harmony is complex and hard to judge, you can ask Teacher Aum to help analyse it in your lesson.

The teacher can point out which notes are chord notes and which are not, and how the chords progress.

Once you have learned the method of analysis, you can gradually do it yourself.

## You Do Not Need to Know All the Chord Names

To do a harmonic reduction, you do not have to know the name and degree of every chord.

It is enough to be able to sum up the notes as a few notes pressed down together.

Of course, if you can name the chords, your understanding will go deeper.

## The Chords Behind a Complex Passage

Many complex passages are actually built from a few simple chords.

Composers use broken chords, passing notes, ornaments and other devices to make the chords richer and more colourful.

If you can see the chords behind it, the passage is no longer so complicated.

## Finding the Non-Chord Notes

A melody often contains non-chord notes such as passing notes and neighbour notes.

A key step in reduction is to sort each note of the melody: keep those that belong to the chord, and set aside those that are just passing through.

Generally speaking, notes that fall on strong beats or are held longer are more likely to be chord notes.

## What Harmonic Reduction Is

Harmonic reduction sums up the notes of a piece of music as a chord for each beat or each bar.

Non-chord notes such as passing notes and ornaments are removed, and only the notes of the chord are kept.

Then these chords are played as block chords, with the notes pressed down together.

## Help with Memorising

When you memorise a piece, remembering the chord progression is much easier than remembering every single note.

If you forget a note during a performance, knowing the chord can help you find it again.

Harmonic reduction is a very practical way to memorise.

- Sum up a complex passage as a few block chords
- See the harmonic skeleton first
- Then go back to the original notes
- It helps with reading, memorising and fingering

## Playing a Progression of Block Chords

Playing the reduced chords in order gives you the harmonic skeleton of the passage.

As you play, listen to how the chords connect, and whether any progression repeats.

**Remember this**

This helps us understand the structure of the music.

## FAQ

**Q: What is harmonic reduction?**
A: Summing up the notes of a passage as a block chord for each beat or bar.

**Q: What is removed in a reduction?**
A: Non-chord notes such as passing notes and ornaments.

**Q: Which notes are more likely to be chord notes?**
A: Notes on strong beats and notes held longer.

**Q: What does harmonic reduction help with?**
A: Reading, memorising, fingering and pedalling.

**Q: Do I have to know the chord names?**
A: Not necessarily.

grieg-to-spring-op43-no6.body:
To Spring is the sixth piece of the Lyric Pieces, Op. 43, by the Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg. The piece is not long, but it is written very brightly: the right hand often sings out an open melody while the left hand supports it with flowing or light figures, as if the air had suddenly turned transparent after the ice and snow melted. It is not a narrative piece describing a particular event; instead it writes the feeling of "spring arriving" as singable phrases and bright harmony. When learning it, first let the melody really sing, then keep the left hand flowing without rushing ahead; this is closer to its colour than pushing the volume full from the start. When listening, you can first follow only the right-hand phrases, and then hear whether the left hand is pushing things along or has already covered the song. If some passage becomes just a sparkling mass of notes and you cannot grasp the main phrase, loosen the tempo further and draw the main phrase out again. When practising, you can warm up by singing the main phrase alone, then let the left hand go through at almost inaudible volume to check whether the flow still rushes ahead. If some passage is only a cluster of bright notes, slow down and use your fingers to draw out the main phrase again. The transparency of spring depends on layers, not on opening up all the notes. You can listen to the ending separately a couple more times to see how the brightness is held in or gently opened up again, which is very helpful for planning the dynamics. Once the left hand truly makes way, the open phrases of the right hand will bring the air of spring by themselves. Once the layers are separated, the brightness appears by itself.

## Where the Brightness of Spring Comes From

A higher register, a more open melodic direction and harmony that is not gloomy all bring this feeling.

**Small tip**

If you play all the notes thick and heavy, the brightness turns into crowding.

You can listen once, paying special attention to how the ending tidies the colour or opens it up a little more.

## Keep the Dynamic Shaping Fine

The arrival of spring can be full of radiance without announcing itself with sudden heavy blows.

Leave room overall at first, and send the sound out only at the places where it should really brighten.

Wherever it gets fuller and fuller, go back to a medium dynamic and find the shape of the phrase again.

![Black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjtf1k-hx4xq.webp)

## How the Left Hand Flows Without Rushing

The left hand should be even and light, like air moving, rather than another melody just as loud.

If the left hand sounds so loud that you cannot hear the right, take the left hand down another notch first.

Change the pedal with the harmony, and change it a little shallower, so that the flow stays connected without blurring.

## How the Right Hand Sends Out the Phrase

The melody needs a rise and a release; long notes should stand firm and not leave early because there is a flowing figure underneath.

You can sing the main phrase alone before playing it, to check that the breathing places are still where they were.

Ornaments or passing notes should not run ahead of the main phrase; they are radiance, not the skeleton.

## How to Arrange Your Practice of To Spring

If you can already play a singing phrase steadily, adding this short piece by Grieg to your practice is a good fit.

Start with hands separately: the right hand fixes the phrases, the left hand fixes evenness, and then put the hands together to check the layers.

Set the tempo by whether the phrases can be sung to the end; there is no need to chase a recording that is very bright and fast.

## What to Remember About To Spring

This is the sixth piece of Grieg's Lyric Pieces, Op. 43, with a bright, singing character and a modest length.

When playing, first protect the main phrase, keep the left hand flowing without rushing and change the pedal a little shallower.

When listening, first follow the right hand, then judge whether the sparkling notes have covered the phrase.

## This Piece Within the Lyric Pieces

Grieg wrote many sets of Lyric Pieces, and each piece captures one mood or a small scene.

In Op. 43, To Spring is strongest in brightness and openness, and does not win by a complicated structure.

Listening to it in the context of the set makes it easier to understand why it is written so directly.

## Ask Teacher Aum in Lessons to Listen for Whether the Main Phrase Is Still There

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the right-hand phrases are complete, and whether the left hand has turned radiance into crowding.

If the pedal is too long in some passage, you can also ask your teacher to change it together with you to a shallower, more frequent change.

Through this piece from Op. 43, practise putting brightness and singable phrases together.

- The sixth piece of Grieg's Lyric Pieces, Op. 43
- Bright, singing character, modest length
- The right hand often has an open melody, and the left hand supports it with a flowing accompaniment
- When practising, first protect the main phrase, then let the accompaniment stay light and keep moving

## FAQ

**Q: Which set of Grieg's works does this piece come from?**
A: It is the sixth piece of the Lyric Pieces, Op. 43.

**Q: What is its overall character?**
A: Bright and singing, and it does not win by a complicated structure.

**Q: What is a common problem with the left hand?**
A: The flowing figure is too loud and covers the main melody.

**Q: Why should it not be played very heavily?**
A: A sound that is too thick turns brightness into crowding, and the transparency of spring is lost.

**Q: How should I set the tempo?**
A: By whether the phrases can be sung to the end; there is no need to chase a very fast recording.

half-pedal-partial-depth.body:
Half pedalling means not pressing the sustain pedal all the way down, but only part of the way, so that the dampers lift just slightly from the strings. The sound then carries on a little, but not as fully as with the pedal fully down, where every note is kept. You can use it in fast runs, where the bass is thick, or wherever you want clarity with a little resonance left over. There is no fixed standard for how deep a half pedal should be: you adjust it by ear and by the feel of your foot, and different pianos respond differently.

## How to Find the Half-Pedal Position

First play a chord on the piano, then press the pedal down slowly and listen carefully for the point at which the sound starts to carry on.

**Try it**

The area around the point where the pedal first starts to work is the half-pedal range.

Every piano's pedal responds differently, so when you move to another piano you need to feel out this position again.

## How the Sustain Pedal Works

Above each string in a piano there is a damper, which normally rests on the string, so that the sound stops at once when you release the key.

When you press the sustain pedal, all the dampers lift off the strings, so the sound carries on even after you let go of the keys.

A half pedal lets the dampers lift only a little, so the strings are gently pressed, and the sound carries on but fades fairly quickly.

## Control with the Foot

Half pedalling needs very fine control of the foot. You cannot press all the way down at once, and you cannot press so shallowly that nothing happens.

Keep your heel resting firmly on the floor and use the front of your foot to control the depth of the pedal gently.

At the start, you can practise just pressing the pedal without playing, to feel the resistance at different depths.

## Do Not Depend on the Pedal

Half pedalling is an aid, and it must not be used to cover up unclear or uneven fingerwork.

When practising, you can first leave out the pedal and get the finger work right, then add the half pedal to adjust the sound.

Only when fingers and pedal work well together will the sound be both clear and colourful.

## Changing the Pedal Quickly

Sometimes in a passage you need to switch often between half pedal and no pedal, or make quick, small pedal changes.

These quick little pedal changes can keep the sound clear while still giving a little connection.

When practising, you can do it slowly at first and make sure the timing of every pedal change is right.

## Trying It on Different Pianos

If you get the chance to play on different pianos, pay special attention to how the half pedal feels different.

On some pianos the pedal is very sensitive, and pressing just a little gives a clear effect; on others you have to press deeper.

Trying many pianos helps your foot and ear adapt more quickly to different situations.

![A transparent futuristic keyboard with light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa08fxk-gmxgz.webp)

## Let Your Ear Decide the Depth

There is no fixed standard for the depth of a half pedal, and the most important thing to judge by is your ear.

As you play, listen closely: is the sound clear, is the resonance suitable, and are the notes blending together?

If the sound is too muddy, press a little more shallowly; if it is too dry, press a little deeper.

- Half pedal presses the sustain pedal only part of the way
- The sound carries on, but not every note is kept
- Useful where you want clarity with some resonance
- The depth is adjusted by ear and by the feel of the foot

## Half Pedal on a Digital Piano

Some digital pianos have pedals that support half-pedal effects, with the sound carrying on differently at different depths.

Some simple pedals have only two states, on and off, and cannot produce a half-pedal effect.

If you want to practise half pedalling, check your digital piano's manual to see whether the pedal supports this feature.

## Talk with Your Teacher

How you use the half pedal depends on the style of the piece, the condition of the piano and the venue, so you need to handle it flexibly.

In lessons you can ask your teacher to demonstrate it, and listen to the effect of half pedalling in different places.

You can also listen to many good recordings and notice how the performers handle the pedal.

## The Sound of the Half Pedal

Compared with full pedal, half pedal sounds clearer, and the notes before and after do not blend together as much.

Compared with no pedal, half pedal adds a little resonance and afterglow, and the sound is warmer.

This in-between effect is very useful in a lot of music.

## When to Use the Half Pedal

In fast scales or passing passages, using no pedal at all may sound a bit dry, while full pedal makes the sound a smear. This is where you can try half pedal.

When chords in the bass register are thick and heavy, half pedal lets the bass resonate without becoming too muddy.

**Common pitfalls**

In some modern works, composers sometimes specifically ask for half pedal to create a hazy effect.

## FAQ

**Q: What is half pedalling?**
A: Pressing the sustain pedal only part of the way.

**Q: What effect does it have?**
A: The sound carries on, but is clearer than with full pedal.

**Q: When do I use it?**
A: In fast runs, thick bass passages or where a hazy effect is wanted.

**Q: How deep should I press?**
A: There is no fixed standard. Go by your ear and the feel of your foot.

**Q: Can I half pedal on a digital piano?**
A: Some pedals support it. Check the manual.

**Q: Can I use half pedal to cover up mistakes?**
A: No. Get your fingerwork right first.

four-hands-duet-agree-tempo.body:
When a piano duet keeps rushing, the most common reason is that the two players have different tempos in their heads. Agree on the speed before you start and count in one bar together. While you play, let the player with the melody lead the pulse and let the other player listen closely, so that both pairs of hands set off from the same beginning. Agreeing in advance is far more useful than arguing after a mistake.

## A few small agreements before playing together

In a duet the two players sit very close, and their hands may cross or come near each other in the middle. Deciding beforehand who sits on the upper (treble) side and who on the lower (bass) side, which player's part leads in each section, and that you will not stop at a wrong note but keep going together, can save a lot of confusion in the moment.

**In short**

When you practise, you can first play together at a slower tempo, record it and listen back together to see where the rushing starts. Very often the problem is only in one or two bars, and repeating just those bars together a few times is more efficient than starting the whole piece from the top again.

Playing together is also practice in listening to each other. When it goes well, tell each other what worked smoothly, and you will be keener to practise together next time.

![A person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jivga-0l0ih.webp)

## Things to agree on before playing

Before you start, the two of you can agree on a few things: what tempo to use, who gives the signal to begin, and what to do when a mistake happens. For example, you can agree not to stop when you slip, but to keep playing and line up again at the start of the next phrase.

You can check the tempo with a metronome first, listening to a few beats together before you begin. Or the player with the melody can softly count one bar in, and the other player comes in after it.

You should also say who will use the pedal. In a duet the pedal is usually looked after by the player of the lower part, and settling this beforehand avoids a muddy sound.

Before playing together, you can also play the hardest passage once slowly together, to confirm that you match in tempo and dynamics there. Once the difficult spots are lined up, the whole piece goes much more smoothly.

## Learn to listen to your partner while you play

One of the most important skills in duet playing is hearing the other player while you play your own part. First learn your own part well separately, then play together at a slow tempo, and consciously listen to what the other person is playing.

If you keep rushing, you can try having one player play just a few key beats while the other follows those beats. Once you have found a shared sense of rhythm, go back to playing the full parts.

Pay attention to the volume balance too. The melody should be clear, while the accompaniment and bass support it without covering it. You can record yourselves and listen back to see which parts are too loud or too quiet.

Eye contact is also very useful when playing together, especially at the beginning, at the end and wherever the tempo changes. A simple nod can get the two of you to start or finish at the same moment.

After practice, the two of you can look back together at what worked well and what still needs adjusting.

## Choosing duets that suit you

Duets come in different levels of difficulty and suit different pairings. Depending on the level of the two players, you can choose an arrangement in which both the upper and lower parts are at a suitable level, so that both of you can concentrate on playing together.

Beginners can start with simple duets, for example one player on the melody and the other on a simple accompaniment. Once you are comfortable, try pieces in which both parts take turns with the melody.

Duets are not only practice, but also a way to enjoy music. Playing with a partner at home or in a lesson helps build listening and cooperation skills.

**Remember this**

Playing together takes patience from both people. Give each other a little more room to listen and fit in, and the process of playing together will bring a lot of enjoyment in itself.

**Order of practice**
- Softly count in one bar together before you start
- Agree who gives the starting beat and who ends
- First learn your own part well on your own
- When playing together, listen to your partner rather than just staring at your own score

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What if brothers and sisters playing together tend to quarrel?**
A: Take turns being the one who counts in, and agree not to blame each other for mistakes, so that attention goes back to the music.

**Q: Do we need a metronome for piano duets?**
A: A metronome is very useful for lining up the tempo when you first play together. Once you are comfortable, try switching it off and keep the rhythm by listening to each other.

**Q: Who uses the pedal in a piano duet?**
A: Usually the player of the lower part, though it can also be decided by the instructions in the score or by your teacher's advice.

**Q: Should we stop if we play a wrong note?**
A: It is best to agree beforehand not to stop, but to keep playing and line up again at the next phrase.

**Q: Can two players of different levels play duets together?**
A: Yes. Choose a suitable piece and let the less advanced player take the relatively simpler part.

**Q: Who turns the pages when playing duets?**
A: You can agree this beforehand. It is usually the player of the upper part, or you can mark the page turns in advance.
