group-fast-runs-into-fours-for-clarity.body:
A long run of fast sixteenth notes looks like an endless line, and it is easy to get tangled up in it, with no idea where to breathe. A practical method is to split the notes into groups of four: make the first note of each group slightly clearer, and think of it in your head as a small unit. The long string then becomes a few small chunks, which are easier for both hands and mind to handle. Once you are comfortable, you can also try moving the start of each group to the second note, practising the same run from a different angle.

## Fast Passages Where Groups of Four Help

This method suits studies, the fast movements of Bach, and scale-like phrases in classical sonatas.

Whenever you have a long string of regular fast notes, you can practise it by grouping.

It can also help you read fast runs more quickly when sight-reading.

## The Relationship with the Beat

When you practise moving the starting point, remember that the beat in your head does not change.

You are only putting your attention on different notes during practice, not changing the rhythm.

In the end, return to the normal grouping and play according to the beat.

## Matching the Hand Position

Sometimes grouping by the beat and grouping by the hand position coincide, for example when each group is exactly one hand position.

Sometimes they do not, and the hand has to move in the middle of a group.

You can mark the places where the hand has to move and practise them separately.

## Practise One Group at a Time

When practising, you can first play just the first group of four notes and stop on the first note of the next group.

Then play the second group and stop on the first note of the third group.

Go group by group, and check your hand position at each pause.

## Adding Rhythm Variations

Group practice can be combined with rhythm variations, for example playing each group with a dotted rhythm, alternating long and short.

Or play the first two notes of each group fast and the last two slow.

These variations make your hands more familiar with the notes of each group.

## Think in Groups as You Play

As you play, think of moving forward "group by group" instead of thinking note by note.

This lightens the load on your mind and lets your hands relax more.

At fast speeds, this way of thinking is especially helpful.

## Moving the Start of the Groups

Once you are comfortable, you can try moving the start of each group to the second note, that is, counting four notes starting from the second note of each beat.

The note that used to be tucked in the middle and easy to overlook now becomes the leading note.

Practising from different angles lets every note get attention.

## Groups of Four in Brief

A long string of fast notes is easy to get tangled in. You can split it into small chunks of four, with the first note of each group slightly clearer on the beat.

Practise group by group, stopping on the first note of the next group, then join them up, and once you are comfortable move the start of the groups, while the beat in your head stays the same.

Decide whether to group in threes or fours according to the beat, mark the groups in the score, match them to your hand positions, think in groups as you play, and add rhythm variations if you like.

## Then Join the Groups Together

Once each group is smooth, try joining two groups together, and then four groups together.

When joining, make sure there is no pause between groups.

Slowly, the whole string of notes will flow smoothly.

## When You Group in Threes

If the notes are triplets or in compound time, you can group them in threes.

For example, the eighth notes in 6/8 naturally divide into groups of three.

The way you group depends on the beat.

**Notice the details**
- A long string of fast notes is easy to get tangled in
- Split it into chunks of four
- Make the first note of each group slightly clearer
- You can also move the start of the groups

## Splitting into Fours

In a piece where the quarter note gets the beat, sixteenth notes come four to a beat.

If you look at them in groups of four, each group is one beat.

The long string of notes is then divided into many small chunks, each easier to handle.

## The Difficulty of a Long String of Notes

A fast run, such as a whole line of sixteenth notes, has many notes and no obvious pauses.

Your fingers and eyes must keep following it all the way, and it is easy to lose your place.

If you make one mistake in the middle, everything after it often falls apart.

![Close-up of grand piano keys and a golden patterned lid in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6xrjk-o42hw.webp)

## The First Note of Each Group

The first note of each group falls exactly on the beat, and you can make it slightly clearer.

It does not need to be played as an accent, just given a tiny bit of weight as the starting point of the group.

This helps us find the beat at speed and keep the rhythm steady.

## Draw Short Lines Between Sixteenth-Note Groups

In the score, you can use a pencil to draw a small dot above the first note of each group, or a short line between groups.

Then you can see the grouping at a glance when you read.

Once you are comfortable, you can rub these marks out.

## FAQ

**Q: Why are fast runs easy to get tangled in?**
A: They have many notes and no obvious pauses.

**Q: How do you group sixteenth notes?**
A: In fours, with each group one beat.

**Q: How should the first note of each group be played?**
A: Slightly clearer, but not as an accent.

**Q: What does moving the start of the groups mean?**
A: Counting four notes starting from the second note of each beat.

**Q: How do you group triplets?**
A: In threes.

gentle-listening-habit-before-bedtime.body:
After a busy day, many people like to listen to a little quiet music before bed. It may be only a small habit, but it can give the day a gentle ending. Below are several common listening practices, covering choosing pieces, volume, timing and surroundings. First, a note: this is a sharing of everyday experience. It is not medical advice, and it is not a way of treating any health condition.

## Why some people like music before bed

For many people, bedtime is one of the quieter times of the day. You put on a familiar piece and let your attention drift slowly away from work, screens and messages, toward the sound itself. Like reading a few pages of a book or drinking a glass of warm water before bed, it is a small personal ritual.

- A familiar piece makes you feel at ease.
- A fixed time lets the body know the day is nearly over.
- A simple melody does not make your thoughts too complicated.

## How to choose a bedtime playlist

**Slow tempo, very little ups and downs**
Solo piano, gentle strings or instrumental music without lyrics are common choices. Avoid pieces with a strong beat or sudden changes.

**A moderate length**
Choose one or two pieces; there is no need to play for a long time. You can set a timer so the music stops by itself at the right moment.

**Respect your own taste**
No single piece suits everyone. Choosing a piece you really like and feel comfortable with matters more than following other people's recommendations.

![Two hands resting on piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwibhrae-smzdx.webp)

## Volume and the atmosphere of the room

- Keep the volume low, low enough that you can still hear the quiet of the surroundings.
- If you live with family, consider using headphones or turning the volume down so as not to disturb others.
- If you fall asleep with headphones, check that the cable and the fit are comfortable, and switch to a small speaker if necessary.
- Dim the lights in the room and keep your phone a little further away, to reduce the distraction of the screen.

## Listening with children

If you have children at home, you can pick a short piece before bed and listen to it quietly together. The adult does not need to say much, and the child does not need to "understand" anything; you are simply keeping each other company. If the child wants to talk, answer softly. A small ritual like this gives children a warm memory of the time before bed.

## If you cannot fall asleep

Sleep is affected by many things, including daily routine, stress and health. Listening to music cannot guarantee that everyone will sleep well. If you have slept badly for a long time, or you feel troubled in your body or your emotions, please consult a doctor, and where needed a licensed professional, and do not rely on music or your own guesses to judge.

## Play in the daytime, only listen at night

Some people, after hearing a piece they like, want to try playing it. When you have time in the daytime, you can sit down at the piano and find the first few notes of the melody. An AI piano teaching app such as TIGA ALPHA can give you hints about the pitch and beat of what you play, so you can get familiar with it step by step at home. Note that learning should be done in the daytime, when you are more alert, and before bed it is better to focus on quiet listening.

## Build your own bedtime playlist

You might build a small playlist of three to five pieces that you find comfortable, and write one simple line about how each feels, for example "good for a rainy night" or "good for after clearing the table". After a few months, this list becomes a little keepsake album. When the list needs updating, you can replace pieces gradually, without changing many at once.

## Small preparations in the daytime

The quiet before bed often has to do with how the day is arranged. Fewer caffeinated drinks after the evening, a walk after dinner, and less screen time in the hour before bed are all common habits. These are only general lifestyle suggestions; everyone's situation is different, and there is no need to copy them exactly.

**Small things you can try**
- Take a slow walk downstairs after dinner.
- Put your phone somewhere out of reach before bed.
- Make the lights in the room softer.

## Being with your own feelings

Sometimes music brings back memories and stirs up all kinds of feelings, which is also quite natural. There is no need to hurry to push these feelings away, nor to force yourself to "relax". If it feels too heavy, you can turn the music off, write a few lines, or talk with someone you trust.

## A simple evening sequence

You can arrange it like this: first put out what you need for tomorrow, then wash up and change into comfortable clothes, and finally listen to one piece in a room with the lights dimmed. Once the order is fixed, your body gradually becomes familiar with the routine. If one day you do not have time, there is no need to make up for it; just carry on the next day.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is listening to music before bed sure to help?**
A: Not necessarily. Everyone feels differently, and music is only one optional everyday habit.

**Q: Can I listen to songs with lyrics?**
A: Yes, but lyrics may make attention more focused, so if needed choose pieces without lyrics.

**Q: Is it good to play music all night?**
A: It is generally recommended to set a timer to stop, let the room return to quiet, and pay attention to how you feel.

**Q: What should I do if I have slept badly for a long time?**
A: Please consult a doctor. Music cannot replace professional medical advice.

furusato-japanese-school-song-1914.body:
"Furusato" ("Hometown") is a Japanese song that was included in a Japanese sixth-grade singing textbook in 1914, with words by Tatsuyuki Takano and music by Teiichi Okano. The lyrics recall the hill where the singer chased rabbits as a child and the river where they fished for little crucian carp, think of parents and friends far away, and finally say that one day they will return to their hometown of green hills and clear water. The melody is in triple time and uses only five notes of the major scale, so it sounds simple and soft. For more than a hundred years it has often been sung by choirs at graduation ceremonies and farewells, and at the piano it is a lovely little lyrical piece that is easy to get started on.

## Singing it at graduation ceremonies

In Japan, "Furusato" is often sung by choirs at graduation ceremonies and farewells.

Classmates are about to part and head off to their own distant places, and this song gives voice to exactly that feeling.

Many people, once grown up, are reminded of their school days the moment they hear it.

## Verse three: one day I will go back

The third verse says that when the singer's ambitions have been fulfilled, one day they will return to their hometown.

There, green hills and clear water are waiting.

This verse turns the whole song from memory toward hope.

## Verse one: the hill where I chased rabbits

The first verse recalls childhood, chasing rabbits on the hill and fishing for little crucian carp in the river.

These are the most ordinary games of a country child.

Yet after growing up and leaving home, these pictures keep coming back in dreams.

## Ask your teacher to listen to the triple time of Furusato

You can play it for Teacher Aum in your lesson and ask whether the strong and weak beats of the triple time sound natural.

You can also ask your teacher to demonstrate how much to slow down at the end of a phrase.

From one small song, play out the longing for somewhere far away.

## A melody of five notes

The melody of "Furusato" uses only five notes of the major scale: do, re, mi, sol and la, with no fa or ti.

This way of writing was very common in Japanese singing textbooks at the time.

With two notes missing, the melody comes across as even simpler and calmer.

## The sway of triple time

"Furusato" is a song in triple time, with three beats to a bar, like a gentle rocking.

Triple time gives a tender, nostalgic feel, and suits memories very well.

When singing, you can feel the first beat of each bar as slightly heavier, and pass lightly over the other two.

**Try this**
- Included in a Japanese school singing textbook in 1914
- Words by Tatsuyuki Takano, music by Teiichi Okano
- Triple time, using only five notes
- Often sung by choirs at graduations and farewells

## How hard is Furusato to start on

"Furusato" has a simple rhythm and a calm tempo, and someone who has been learning for about six months and can play a triple-time accompaniment can try it.

As a next step, you can try playing broken chords in the left hand to make the accompaniment flow more.

You can also play it with family, one person playing and one singing.

## A song from the primary school textbook

In the early twentieth century, Japanese primary schools had a dedicated "singing" class, and the textbooks included many new songs written for children.

"Furusato" was one of those included in the sixth-grade singing textbook in 1914.

It was originally meant to be sung by primary school pupils, but it later became a song that several generations can sing.

## Improvising with five notes

Because "Furusato" uses only five notes, you can try improvising a melody of your own at the piano using only those five notes.

Play slowly in triple time, and imagine a place from your own childhood.

This is a good way to get to know the pentatonic scale, and it can also build an interest in improvising.

## Playing Furusato at the piano

At the piano you can play "Furusato" in F major or C major, with the right hand on the melody and the left hand on a simple triple-time accompaniment.

If the left hand plays one low note in each bar and then two light chords, you will get the sway of triple time.

The melody should be connected like singing, and at the end of a phrase you can slow down slightly and play more softly.

## Furusato in short

"Furusato" is a song that entered a Japanese sixth-grade singing textbook in 1914, with words by Tatsuyuki Takano and music by Teiichi Okano. Its three verses recall the hill where the singer chased rabbits and the river where they fished for little crucian carp as a child, send greetings to parents and friends far away, and look forward to returning to the hometown of green hills and clear water once their ambitions are fulfilled. The melody uses only do, re, mi, sol and la, in triple time, and is often sung by choirs at graduation ceremonies and farewells.

At the piano you can use F major or C major, with one low note and two light chords in the left hand, a melody connected like singing, and a slight slowing at the end of each phrase. You can also improvise using only these five notes, and you can try it after about six months of learning.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the strong and weak beats of the triple time.

![A digital music space under neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbiurnt-unqxw.webp)

## The two authors

Tatsuyuki Takano, who wrote the words, was a scholar who studied Japanese literature and folk songs, and wrote many of the lyrics in the textbooks.

Teiichi Okano, who wrote the music, was a music teacher who spent many years in schools teaching pupils to sing and to play the organ.

The two worked together on several songs in the singing textbooks, and "Furusato" is the most widely loved of them.

## Verse two: relatives far away

The second verse asks whether the parents back home are well, and whether the friends are safe.

Whenever the wind blows and the rain falls, the singer thinks of them.

**Think about it**

The lyrics do not lecture at length; they are just one plain line after another of caring.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In what year was "Furusato" included in a Japanese primary school singing textbook?**
A: 1914.

**Q: Who wrote the words and who wrote the music?**
A: Tatsuyuki Takano wrote the words and Teiichi Okano wrote the music.

**Q: How many notes does the melody use?**
A: Five: do, re, mi, sol and la.

**Q: What time is the song in?**
A: Triple time.

**Q: On what occasions is it often sung by choirs?**
A: Graduation ceremonies and farewells.

handel-harmonious-blacksmith-air-hwv430.body:
In 1720 Handel published a set of harpsichord suites in London. The final movement of the Suite in E major is a theme with five variations. The piece later gained a catchy name, "The Harmonious Blacksmith", along with a story that Handel took shelter from the rain in a blacksmith's forge and found his inspiration in the sound of the hammering. But the name only appeared many years after Handel's death, and the blacksmith story is generally thought to have been invented later. Either way, these variations have a friendly melody and a clear structure, which makes them a fine piece for learning Baroque keyboard music.

- A suite published in London in 1720
- The last movement of the Suite in E major
- A theme with five variations
- The name and the blacksmith story both came later

## The Melody of the Theme

The theme is a simple, friendly melody in E major, divided into two repeated sections.

The melody moves mostly by step and the rhythm is steady, so it is easy to remember.

The theme itself is like a plain, unadorned song.

## The 1720 Collection of Suites

In 1720 Handel published his first collection of harpsichord suites in London, eight suites in all.

These suites include movements such as the prelude, allemande, courante and gigue.

The Suite in E major is the fifth, and its last movement is this "Air with Variations".

## The Trills in the Blacksmith Theme

The theme and variations contain some ornaments, such as trills.

Baroque trills usually begin on the note above and should be played lightly.

For the exact way to play them, see the notes in your edition or ask your teacher.

## Where the Name "Harmonious Blacksmith" Came From

Handel himself called it only an "Air" and never gave it a name.

The name "The Harmonious Blacksmith" only began to circulate in the early nineteenth century.

It is said to be linked to a publisher, who used the amusing title to attract people buying the sheet music.

## Taking the Five Variations One at a Time

Each of the five variations has its own technique, so you can practise them one by one.

Learn the theme well first, then the first variation, then the second.

Once each one is secure, join them together and play the whole piece.

## Two Hands Taking Turns

In these variations, fast figures often pass back and forth between the two hands.

In one variation the right hand is busy, and in the next it is the left hand's turn.

This is excellent practice for developing both hands evenly.

## Handel and London

Handel was born in 1685 and died in 1759. He was born in Germany and later lived and worked in London for many years.

He is best known for his operas and oratorios, and Messiah is his most famous work.

He also wrote a good deal of harpsichord music, mainly for teaching and performance.

## Listen to a Harpsichord Recording First

Before you play, listen to a harpsichord recording to get a feel for the original sound.

Then listen to a piano version and compare the two.

This will help you find a suitable touch and style on the piano.

## Summary of "The Harmonious Blacksmith"

Handel was born in 1685, died in 1759, and lived in London for many years. In 1720 he published his first collection of harpsichord suites, and the last movement of the fifth suite, in E major, is an "Air with Variations". Handel himself never named it. The name "The Harmonious Blacksmith" only spread in the early nineteenth century, and there is no reliable evidence for the story of sheltering from the rain in a forge.

The theme is simple and friendly, divided into two repeated sections. In the five variations the notes grow busier, and fast figures pass between the two hands. It was written for the harpsichord, so on the piano aim for a clear, clean sound and use little pedal. Trills usually begin on the upper note. You can practise section by section, using a tempo at which you can play the last variation steadily.

Start by listening to a harpsichord recording, and ask Teacher Aum to check the ornaments and fingering.

## The Style of the Harpsichord

The instrument Handel had was the harpsichord. Its strings are plucked, so the sound is crisp, but the volume cannot be changed much by how hard the fingers press.

When you play it on the piano, keep a clear, clean touch and use little pedal.

You can still vary the dynamics, but with restraint, and not with the wide swings of Romantic music.

## Planning the Tempo

You can keep roughly the same basic tempo throughout the whole set, because the notes grow busier and the music naturally feels faster.

Do not play the theme too slowly just because of the later variations, and do not start too fast.

First find a tempo at which you can play the last variation steadily.

![A collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city backdrop](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacp0sx-31jip.webp)

## The Idea Behind the Five Variations

After the theme, Handel wrote five variations, each with busier notes than the one before.

The first two variations use sixteenth notes, in the right hand and the left hand respectively.

The later variations use triplets and faster figures, and the music becomes more and more lively.

## The Blacksmith Story

Later, someone told a story: Handel was caught in the rain, stepped into a blacksmith's forge, heard the rhythm of the hammers and found his inspiration.

The story sounds vivid, but there is no reliable evidence for it.

Scholars generally believe it was made up after the name became popular.

## Ask Your Teacher About the Ornaments in the Harmonious Blacksmith

If you want to play "The Harmonious Blacksmith", ask Teacher Aum in your lesson to check how to play the ornaments and the fingering.

You can also ask for advice on which of the five variations to tackle first.

**A Little Tip**

This piece is excellent for practising balance between the two hands and a Baroque touch.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: In what year was this piece published?**
A: 1720, in London.

**Q: Which suite is it a movement of?**
A: It is the last movement of the Suite in E major.

**Q: How many variations are there?**
A: Five.

**Q: Did Handel choose the name "The Harmonious Blacksmith"?**
A: No. It only began to circulate in the early nineteenth century.

**Q: Where do Baroque trills usually begin?**
A: On the note above.

funiculi-funicula-1880-vesuvius-song.body:
Funiculì, Funiculà is a cheerful Neapolitan song with music by Luigi Denza and words by Peppino Turco, written in 1880. It was written to celebrate the opening of the first funicular railway on Mount Vesuvius. The song was so popular as soon as it was published that the German composer Richard Strauss later mistook it for a folk song and wove it into his orchestral work Aus Italien (From Italy). When you play this song on the piano, aim to capture its light, lively, ever-climbing feel.

- Written in 1880 for the opening of the Vesuvius funicular
- Music by Denza, words by Turco
- Richard Strauss once mistook it for a folk song
- Light rhythm and a lively chorus

## A Cheerful Rhythm

The rhythm of Funiculì, Funiculà is light and bouncy, like a cable car climbing steadily upward.

It is usually in six beats to the bar, with each bar divided into two big beats, giving a feeling of rolling forward.

When you play, keep the rhythm springy and driving.

## Funiculì, Funiculà: A Summary

Funiculì, Funiculà is a Neapolitan song with music by Denza and words by Turco, written in 1880 to celebrate the opening of the funicular on Mount Vesuvius. It became popular extremely quickly, and in 1886 Richard Strauss, believing it to be a folk song, wrote the melody into Aus Italien.

The song is usually in six beats to the bar with a light rhythm. You can play the verse staccato and the chorus legato, with a bouncing bass-then-chord accompaniment in the left hand. The mood climbs all the way up, but keep the tempo steady with a metronome.

It can be paired with O sole mio and Santa Lucia as a set, and it also suits piano duet. For editions and rhythm, you can ask Teacher Aum for help.

![A transparent, futuristic keyboard with beams of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaa8l3f-axvdx.webp)

## Staccato and Legato in the Right Hand

The verse melody can be played with a light staccato, expressing a playful, talking quality.

The long notes of the chorus can be played legato, making the melody broader.

The contrast between the two kinds of touch gives the music more layers.

## A Song Written for a Cable Car

In 1880, a funicular railway opened on Mount Vesuvius near Naples in Italy.

To celebrate and promote it, the composer Luigi Denza and the lyricist Peppino Turco wrote this song.

The "Funiculì, Funiculà" in the title is derived from the word for funicular.

## Good for Piano Duet

The melody and accompaniment of this song are clearly divided, which makes it very suitable for arranging as a piano duet.

One person plays the melody and the other plays the bouncing left-hand accompaniment.

In a duet version, the lively atmosphere is even more noticeable.

## Richard Strauss's Mistake

The song became popular very quickly and soon spread across Italy.

In 1886, the German composer Richard Strauss used the melody of this song in his orchestral work Aus Italien.

It is said that he thought it was a traditional Neapolitan folk song, and only later learned that it had an author.

## What the Lyrics Are About

The lyrics are in the voice of a young man inviting his sweetheart to ride the funicular up to the top of the volcano.

The song says that once you board the cable car you will soon reach the summit and see the view in the distance.

The words are light and humorous, full of youthful energy.

## Bringing the Cable Car Song to Your Lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether your rhythm is steady and whether the left-hand jumps are light.

Your teacher can also help you plan the contrast between staccato and legato.

If you would like to play it as a duet with someone, you can also ask your teacher to recommend a suitable edition.

## Controlling the Tempo

This song easily gets faster and faster, because the rhythm itself has so much drive.

You can check with a metronome and keep the tempo steady.

When the tempo is steady, the cheerful feeling actually comes through more clearly.

## The Left-Hand Bouncing Accompaniment

In the left hand you can use a "bass then chord" bouncing accompaniment, playing the bass at the start of each big beat and then the chord.

This kind of accompaniment adds spring to the rhythm.

When jumping, look ahead to the position in advance, relax your wrist and keep the movement light.

## Simple and Complex Scores of the Cable Car Song

The piano versions of this song come in different levels of difficulty.

A simple version keeps only the melody and basic chords, while a complex version has a rich accompaniment and ornaments.

You can choose according to your own level.

## Playing It with Other Neapolitan Songs

Funiculì, Funiculà, O sole mio and Santa Lucia are all famous Neapolitan songs.

Their styles differ: one is cheerful, one passionate, one peaceful.

You can put them together to make a small set of Neapolitan songs.

## A Mood That Keeps Climbing

The mood of the song rises gradually as the cable car climbs the mountain.

You can make each chorus a little more spirited than the one before.

The last section can use fuller dynamics, as if you have reached the summit.

## From Invitation to Cheering: The Two Parts of the Cable Car Song

The melody of the verse sits in a lower register, as if telling a story and extending an invitation.

The chorus repeatedly sings "Funiculì, Funiculà", with a bright, lively melody.

**Common mistake**

When you reach the chorus, you can increase the dynamics to express the scene of everyone cheering together.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What was this song written for?**
A: To celebrate the opening of the funicular on Mount Vesuvius.

**Q: What year was it written?**
A: 1880.

**Q: Who wrote the words and music?**
A: Denza wrote the music and Turco wrote the words.

**Q: Which composer mistook it for a folk song?**
A: Richard Strauss.

**Q: What accompaniment can the left hand use?**
A: A bouncing bass-then-chord accompaniment.

gongche-notation-chinese-characters.body:
Gongche notation is a system in traditional Chinese music that writes down pitches with Chinese characters. Its name comes from two of those characters, "gong" and "chi". It uses the characters He, Si, Yi, Shang, Chi, Gong, Fan, Liu, Wu and Yi to stand for different pitches, which roughly correspond to today's sol, la, ti, do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. The beat is marked with the symbols for "ban" and "yan". Gongche notation was widely used from the Ming and Qing dynasties onward: Kunqu opera, regional operas, folk instrumental music and Buddhist and Daoist music were all written down in it, and many traditional pieces have been preserved only thanks to gongche notation. Today's musicians often have to "translate" it into numbered notation or staff notation.

## Talk About Gongche Notation in Lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum about how gongche notation differs from the notation in common use today.

You can also ask your teacher to help translate a short passage of gongche notation into staff notation and play it on the piano.

From a few characters, see how traditional Chinese music was written down.

## Singing and Playing Gongche Notation on the Piano

You can try this on the piano: let "Shang" equal do, so that "Chi" is re, "Gong" is mi, and "Liu" is the high sol.

Try singing and playing "Shang, Chi, Gong, Chi, Shang, He", that is, do, re, mi, re, do, low sol.

This gives you a feel for singing from notation written in Chinese characters.

## Written Vertically

Gongche notation is usually written vertically like an ancient book, from top to bottom, with the columns arranged from right to left.

The lyrics are written alongside, with the pitch characters on the right of the lyrics.

When reading gongche notation, you need to get used to reading vertically in this way.

## Ban and Yan

Gongche notation uses "ban" and "yan" to mark the beat.

"Ban" is the strong beat and "yan" is the weak beat, usually written beside the characters with symbols such as a small dot or a circle.

For example, "yi ban yi yan" (one ban, one yan) is one strong beat plus one weak beat, equivalent to duple time.

## The Habit of Singing the Notation

People who learn gongche notation often sing the score out first, for example "Shang, Chi, Gong, Chi, Shang".

Being able to sing the notation first and then play it on an instrument is an important method in learning traditional music.

This is very similar to the way we sing the notation first and then play when learning the piano today.

![A glowing digital interface on a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk7zvn-7bvpu.webp)

## Kunqu Opera and Regional Opera

From the Ming and Qing dynasties onward, gongche notation was widely used for Kunqu opera and regional operas.

Many Kunqu songbooks were written down in gongche notation.

Actors and musicians learned the vocal lines and the accompaniment through gongche notation.

**Tip**
- Writes pitches with Chinese characters; the name comes from "gong" and "chi"
- He, Si, Yi, Shang, Chi, Gong, Fan, Liu, Wu, Yi
- The beat is marked with "ban" and "yan"
- Widely used from the Ming and Qing dynasties onward for Kunqu, regional opera and folk instrumental music

## Translating into Numbered Notation

When today's musicians study traditional music, they often have to "translate" gongche notation into numbered notation or staff notation.

This involves fixing the key, matching each pitch character, and turning ban and yan into bars and beats.

This work has made many ancient pieces available to be played and studied by more people.

## Higher and Lower Notes

To show a higher or lower note, gongche notation adds a mark beside the character.

For example, adding the person radical on the left of the character shows a note one octave higher; adding a short left-falling stroke at the end of the character shows a note one octave lower.

In this way a few characters can write down a very wide range.

## The Ten Characters

The pitch characters commonly used in gongche notation are He, Si, Yi, Shang, Chi, Gong, Fan, Liu, Wu and Yi.

They are arranged from low to high, and roughly correspond to today's sol, la, ti, do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti.

Exactly which note each stands for also depends on the key of the piece.

## Writing Pitch with Characters

Gongche notation is a notation that uses Chinese characters to show pitch.

Each character stands for one note, for example "Shang", "Chi" and "Gong".

Because the two characters "gong" and "chi" appear most often, people call it gongche notation.

## Gongche Notation: A Summary

Gongche notation is the traditional Chinese way of writing pitch with characters. Its name comes from "gong" and "chi". The characters He, Si, Yi, Shang, Chi, Gong, Fan, Liu, Wu and Yi are commonly used from low to high, roughly corresponding to sol, la, ti, do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. Adding the person radical shows a note an octave higher, and a short left-falling stroke added at the end shows an octave lower. "Ban" shows the strong beat and "yan" the weak beat, and the phrase "yi ban yi yan" comes from here. It is usually written vertically from top to bottom.

From the Ming and Qing dynasties onward it was widely used for Kunqu, opera and folk instrumental music such as Jiangnan sizhu, Cantonese music and Xi'an drum music. Ornaments and details were passed on by word of mouth, and today it is often translated into numbered notation or staff notation. On the piano you can let "Shang" be do and sing and play "Shang, Chi, Gong, Chi, Shang, He".

You can talk about gongche notation with Teacher Aum.

## Where "Yi Ban Yi Yan" Comes From

In Chinese today the phrase "yi ban yi yan" is often used to describe doing things conscientiously and in an orderly way.

This expression comes from the ban and yan of music.

In singing and playing you had to follow the ban and yan strictly and not get them wrong, and later the phrase was extended to mean doing things properly and carefully.

## What Is Not on the Page

What gongche notation writes down is mainly the skeleton notes and the ban and yan.

Many ornaments, slides and subtle changes of rhythm are not written in the score, and have to be passed on by a teacher by word of mouth.

So the same gongche score may not be played in exactly the same way by different musicians.

## Folk Instrumental Music

Besides opera, folk instrumental music was also often written down in gongche notation.

For example, Jiangnan sizhu, Cantonese music and Xi'an drum music all have traditional pieces written down in gongche notation.

**Think about it**

Many older folk musicians can still sing out the tunes in gongche notation today.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which two characters does the name gongche notation come from?**
A: "Gong" and "chi".

**Q: What does gongche notation use to show pitch?**
A: Chinese characters, such as He, Si, Shang, Chi and Gong.

**Q: What do "ban" and "yan" mean?**
A: "Ban" is the strong beat and "yan" is the weak beat.

**Q: How is gongche notation usually written?**
A: Vertically from top to bottom, with the columns arranged from right to left.

**Q: If "Shang" is do, what is "Gong"?**
A: Mi.

grieg-lyric-pieces-arietta-op12.body:
The Norwegian composer Grieg wrote 66 Lyric Pieces in his lifetime, gathered in 10 books and composed from 1867 to 1901. Book 1 (Op. 12) opens with Arietta, a little piece in E-flat major that runs to just over a page: the right hand sings a gentle melody, and flowing broken chords pass between the two hands. Interestingly, in the last piece of the final book, Grieg brings this melody back once more, rewritten as a waltz, so that the whole set comes full circle.

## Pedal for a Warmer Sound

This little piece suits the pedal, which makes the harmony fuller, but change it promptly as the chords change.

**Quick tip**

If you change the pedal too late, the melody notes blur into the previous chord and sound muddy.

You can first practise without the pedal to get your finger legato right, then add the pedal and hear the difference.

## The Name Arietta

An aria was originally a solo passage in an opera, and an arietta is a little piece that sounds like a solo song.

The name reminds the player that the right-hand melody should sing like a human voice, with breath and rise and fall.

Before playing, try singing the melody first to feel its natural phrase length.

## Flowing Between the Hands

In this piece the broken chords sometimes begin in the left hand and are then taken up by the right, forming an unbroken flow.

The point where the hands hand over must be especially smooth, so that no one can hear the "change of hands".

In slow practice, you can play just those handover notes, again and again, until they sound as if one hand played them.

## A Melody Hidden in Broken Chords

A feature of this piece is that melody and accompaniment are often interwoven, so the right hand has to play the melody and also part of the broken chords.

Bring out the melody notes with a slightly deeper touch, and keep the other notes light, like a background.

You can first play only the melody notes, leaving out the others, to hear clearly where the melody is going, and then add the accompaniment back.

![A black grand piano and bench in front of a golden-red pointillist background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa290lk-8q12s.webp)

## The Rise and Fall of Phrases and Breath

The whole piece is made of several phrases of similar length, and each has its own high point.

Move forward slightly as you approach the high point, then relax gradually once you have passed it.

Leave a tiny breath between phrases, like a singer taking air, and the music will feel more natural.

## What Level Is Arietta For?

The piece does not have many notes, but it asks you to layer melody and accompaniment and to master the basic use of the pedal.

It generally suits learners who have studied for a while and can play simple Romantic pieces.

If you find it difficult, start with simpler singing pieces, build a solid foundation, and then try it.

## Other Pieces in the Lyric Pieces

The Lyric Pieces contain many works familiar to learners, such as little pieces depicting birds, butterflies and folk dances.

Their difficulty varies: some are easier than Arietta, and others need more advanced technique.

You can choose a few with your teacher as repertoire for learning the Romantic style.

## A Norwegian Composer's Musical Diary

Grieg was a Norwegian composer and pianist who lived from 1843 to 1907.

He wrote the Lyric Pieces over more than thirty years, and each book holds several little pieces in different styles, like a musical diary of life and moods.

These works are short and have moving melodies, and many are suitable for intermediate learners.

**A different angle**
- 66 Lyric Pieces in 10 books, 1867 to 1901
- Arietta is the first piece of Op. 12
- E-flat major, only just over a page long
- The last piece brings this melody back as a waltz

## Rubato in the Romantic Style

Romantic works often allow some freedom in tempo, stretching and relaxing to make the music more expressive.

But this flexibility should be natural, and you should not speed up and slow down in every bar; the basic beat must stay steady.

You can first play it at a steady tempo until it is familiar, then slow down slightly at the high points and endings of phrases.

## Details in a Short Piece

Because the piece is so short, every detail matters: the weight of a note, the end of a phrase, a change of pedal.

When practising, you can focus on just one aspect at a time, for example listening to the melody today and to the pedal tomorrow.

Get these details right one by one, and even a piece of just over a page can sound like complete music.

## An Echo After Thirty Years

In the last piece of the final book of the Lyric Pieces, Grieg uses the melody of Arietta again.

This time the melody is written in waltz rhythm, and it sounds like a memory of a work from his youth.

After learning the opening piece, find the last piece and listen to it, to hear how the same melody feels in a different state of mind.

## The Three Flats of E-flat Major

E-flat major has three flats, B-flat, E-flat and A-flat, so many notes fall on black keys.

Before you start, it helps to play the E-flat major scale up and down a few times and press the tonic triad a few times, so your fingers remember these black keys.

**Common pitfalls**

When there are many black keys, move your whole hand a little deeper into the keyboard, and your fingertips will stand more firmly.

## FAQ

**Q: How many Lyric Pieces are there in total?**
A: 66, in 10 books.

**Q: Which book is Arietta in?**
A: It is the first piece of Book 1, Op. 12.

**Q: What key is the piece in?**
A: E-flat major, with three flats.

**Q: Does its melody appear again later?**
A: Yes, the last piece of the final book brings it back as a waltz.

**Q: What should I watch for when playing the melody?**
A: Touch the melody notes slightly deeper, and keep the accompaniment notes light.

holst-the-planets-suite-1918.body:
Between 1914 and 1916 the English composer Holst wrote the orchestral suite The Planets. It has seven movements, from Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter and Saturn to Uranus and Neptune, and each movement portrays the "character" of one planet. Holst's inspiration came from the way planets are described in astrology, not from astronomy. On 29 September 1918 the work was given a private first performance in London, conducted by Boult. There is no Earth in the suite, and Pluto, discovered later, was not included either.

## The Planets Suite at a Glance

Holst wrote The Planets between 1914 and 1916. It has seven movements, from Mars to Neptune. Its inspiration was the character of the planets in astrology, not astronomy, which is why there is no Earth.

Mars uses a five-beat metre and strikes the strings with the wood of the bow, the middle melody of Jupiter was later adapted into a hymn tune, and Neptune ends with an offstage women's chorus fading until it cannot be heard. The private first performance was conducted by Boult in London on 29 September 1918. Pluto was only discovered in 1930, and in 2000 Matthews wrote a Pluto movement to add to the suite.

On the piano you can play the melody of Jupiter or the five-beat metre of Mars. Count every beat clearly first, imagine the instruments of the original, listen to the whole suite first, and ask Teacher Aum to help choose an arrangement.

## Playing Excerpts from The Planets on the Piano

There are piano arrangements of The Planets, and Holst himself also wrote a version for two pianos.

On the piano, you can try the broad melody in the middle of Jupiter, or the five-beat rhythm of Mars.

When playing the five-beat metre, count every beat clearly first, then speed up slowly.

![Illustration of the Bangkok city skyline at dusk with an elevated train line](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaahjk1-15u1d.webp)

## Holst and the Planets

Holst was an English composer, born in 1874.

Around 1913 he became interested in astrology and began to think about the "character" each planet stands for.

These ideas became the inspiration for The Planets.

## Listen to the Whole Suite First

Before playing the piano arrangements, it helps to listen to the whole suite from beginning to end.

Notice the character of each movement and the contrasts between them.

You can also pick just one or two movements you like and listen to them again and again.

## The Story of Pluto

Pluto was discovered in 1930, long after The Planets was finished.

Holst died in 1934 and never wrote a movement for Pluto.

In 2000 the English composer Colin Matthews added a Pluto movement to the suite, but it is not Holst's original work.

## The Middle Melody of Jupiter

The fourth movement, Jupiter, is cheerful and lively, with a broad, stately melody in the middle.

Later, Holst adapted this melody into a hymn tune.

Today this melody is often played on its own on many occasions.

## Talking About The Planets with Your Teacher

In a lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the story of The Planets and the characteristics of the five-beat metre.

There are several piano editions of the Jupiter melody, and you can discuss in person which one to choose.

Your teacher can also help you practise irregular metres.

## Imagine the Tone Colours

The orchestration of The Planets is very rich, with many distinctive tone colours.

When playing an arrangement on the piano, you can imagine the instruments of the original, such as the brilliance of the brass and the softness of the strings.

This helps you bring more variety of colour to the piano.

## Astrology, Not Astronomy

Note that The Planets does not describe the scientific features of the planets, but the symbolic meanings given to them in astrology.

For example, Mars stands for war, Venus for peace and Jupiter for joy.

So the subtitle of each movement is a character or a mood.

## Why There Is No Earth

There is no Earth in The Planets because in astrology Earth is where the observer stands, and it is not treated as an "astrological planet".

So Holst wrote only the other seven planets.

This again shows that the work comes from an astrological point of view.

## The 1918 First Performance

On 29 September 1918, The Planets was given a private first performance in London, conducted by the conductor Boult.

The performance was a gift to Holst, and the audience was mainly invited friends and people from the music world.

Later the work was performed in public one movement after another, and it quickly became popular.

## The Seven Movements

The suite has seven movements: Mars (the Bringer of War), Venus (the Bringer of Peace), Mercury (the Winged Messenger), Jupiter (the Bringer of Jollity), Saturn (the Bringer of Old Age), Uranus (the Magician) and Neptune (the Mystic).

Each movement has its own style, tempo and orchestration.

Playing the whole work through takes about fifty minutes.

- Written between 1914 and 1916
- Seven movements, each portraying one planet
- Inspired by astrology, not astronomy
- Private first performance in London on 29 September 1918

## The Fading Ending of Neptune

The last movement, Neptune, is mysterious and ethereal.

At the end, a women's chorus hidden offstage slowly enters and then gradually fades away.

Holst asked in the score for the sound to keep fading until it can no longer be heard.

## The Five-Beat Metre of Mars

The first movement, Mars, uses a five-beat rhythm, and the string instruments strike the strings with the wood of the bow, making a cold, hard sound.

The music grows louder and louder, creating the tension of war drawing near.

This movement is often thought to foreshadow the war that came not long afterwards.

## FAQ

**Q: When was The Planets written?**
A: Between 1914 and 1916.

**Q: How many movements does it have?**
A: Seven.

**Q: What was the inspiration?**
A: Astrology.

**Q: Why is there no Earth?**
A: In astrology, Earth is where the observer stands.

**Q: On what date was the first performance?**
A: 29 September 1918, in private.

haydn-surprise-symphony-no94-london-1792.body:
Haydn's Symphony No. 94 is often called the Surprise Symphony. He wrote it during his first visit to London, and it premiered there on 23 March 1792. The second movement opens with a quiet, simple melody, played softly twice, and then the whole orchestra suddenly plays a very loud chord, making the audience jump, which is how the symphony got its name. Haydn later said that he wanted to surprise the audience with something new.

## Haydn and London

Joseph Haydn was an Austrian composer, born in 1732 and died in 1809, and he wrote more than a hundred symphonies.

**Think again**

In 1791 Haydn was invited to London for the first time, where he gave a series of concerts and wrote new symphonies for them.

London audiences were enthusiastic, and Haydn's concerts were a great success.

## Listen to the Orchestral Version First

Before you play a piano arrangement, listen to the original played by an orchestra.

Notice where the loud chord comes and feel the sound of the orchestra.

Then think about how you could express that surprise in your own way on the piano.

## Haydn's Explanation

There are various stories about why he wrote that loud chord, for example that it was meant to wake up dozing listeners.

But according to Haydn's biographers, Haydn himself said he wanted to surprise the audience with something new and make his concerts stand out.

Whichever story you prefer, this passage shows Haydn's sense of humour.

## The Twelve London Symphonies

Haydn visited London twice and wrote twelve symphonies for London in all, Nos. 93 to 104.

These symphonies are often called the "London Symphonies", and they are important works of his late years.

Besides the Surprise, they include works with nicknames such as the Military and the Clock.

- Symphony No. 94, known as the Surprise
- Written during Haydn's first visit to London
- Premiered in London on 23 March 1792
- In the second movement, a quiet melody is followed by a sudden loud chord

## Haydn's Humour

Haydn's music often has touches of humour, such as sudden pauses and unexpected modulations.

The loud chord in the Surprise Symphony is one of the best-known examples.

When you play Haydn's piano sonatas, you can also look out for these humorous moments and make your playing more fun.

![A pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5820a-638ig.webp)

## The Loud Chord

This loud chord is played by the whole orchestra together, with a heavy stroke on the timpani as well.

It comes at the end of a very quiet phrase, so the contrast before and after is very strong.

Listeners, caught unprepared, naturally jump, and that is exactly the charm of this passage.

## The Power of Dynamic Contrast

This symphony shows us that dynamic contrast is a very effective means of expression in music.

A sudden loud sound after a very quiet passage immediately catches the listener's attention.

In piano playing we can also use dynamic contrast to make the music more alive.

## Try It on the Piano

There are many piano arrangements of the theme of this movement, and they are not difficult, so they suit beginners.

When you play, try playing the opening melody very softly and then suddenly playing one loud chord.

When you play the loud chord, keep your arm relaxed and let weight bring out the sound, rather than hitting hard with your fingers.

## Summary: The Surprise Symphony

Haydn's Symphony No. 94 was written during his first visit to London and premiered there on 23 March 1792.

In the second movement a sudden loud chord follows a quiet melody, which is why the symphony is called the Surprise.

The story shows the power of dynamic contrast and Haydn's humour, and reminds us that quiet playing must really be quiet for the loud playing to have its effect.

## The Melody of the Second Movement

The second movement is an Andante, and the opening melody is very simple, like a children's song, with most of its notes in the tonic chord.

The orchestra first plays it softly, then repeats it even more softly.

Just as the audience feels the music growing ever quieter, a very loud chord suddenly appears.

## Quiet Must Really Be Quiet

For the loud chord to bring a surprise, the quiet playing before it must really be quiet.

Many people still play the soft passages too loudly, so when the loud chord comes, the contrast is not obvious.

In practice, deliberately play the soft places more softly and widen your range of dynamics.

## The Premiere of the Surprise Symphony

Symphony No. 94 was written in 1791 and premiered in London on 23 March 1792, with Haydn himself at the keyboard leading the orchestra.

The premiere was a success, and the sudden loud chord in the second movement left a deep impression on the audience.

Later, this symphony came to be called "Surprise" in English and "the stroke of the timpani" in German.

## The Structure of the Variations

This movement is a set of variations: the opening melody is the theme, followed by several variations.

Each variation keeps the outline of the theme but changes the rhythm, orchestration and mood.

**Common misconception**

As you listen to this movement, notice how the theme is changed in each variation.

## FAQ

**Q: Which symphony is the Surprise?**
A: Haydn's Symphony No. 94.

**Q: When did it premiere?**
A: 23 March 1792, in London.

**Q: Why is it called the Surprise?**
A: A sudden loud chord follows a quiet melody in the second movement.

**Q: How did Haydn explain the loud chord?**
A: According to his biographers, he wanted to surprise the audience with something new.

**Q: How can it be expressed on the piano?**
A: Make the earlier quiet playing really quiet, and keep the arm relaxed for the loud chord.

improvise-feelings-piano-expression.body:
Some feelings are hard to put into words: a restlessness with no clear cause, or a joy you can't quite describe. The piano offers another way to express them: without a score, using just a few notes, some dynamics and a tempo, you play out how you feel right now. This kind of improvisation doesn't need to sound good or be correct. It is more like keeping a diary in sound. This article describes a general approach for anyone who is interested, and it makes no health claims of any kind.

## You Can Start Without Technique

Many people think improvising takes advanced technique, but the simplest improvisation can begin with the black keys alone. The five black keys form a scale, and however you combine them, they never clash harshly, so even beginners can play with confidence.

**Start with one note**
Choose one note and repeat it several times, changing the dynamics and the speed: softly and slowly, or louder and faster. Listen to what feeling these changes bring to mind.

**Then add a second note**
Alternate between two notes and you already have the beginnings of a melody. Try making them sound like a conversation, one asking and the other answering.

## Matching Musical Elements to Feelings

Different musical elements often bring different feelings to mind. These associations vary from person to person, and the following are only some common examples:

- Low register, slow tempo, soft sound: may suggest calm or reflection
- High register, leaping notes, a light touch: may suggest ease or curiosity
- Dynamics that swing between loud and soft: may express a changeable mood
- Long pauses: may express hesitation or waiting

You can choose according to your own feelings; there are no rules to follow.

![A person playing a glowing piano on a neon-lit street in the rain at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw4176tl-jky1n.webp)

## A Simple Practice Routine

Step one: sit at the piano, think quietly about how you feel now, and describe it with a single word. Step two: spend two or three minutes improvising the feeling of that word. Step three: stop, and describe how you feel after playing with another word.

You don't need to record these three steps or play them for anyone. If you like, you can write the two words, before and after, in a notebook, and gradually you may become a little more aware of how your emotions shift.

## Playing Together with Children

Children take to improvised expression very easily. Parents can play a "guess the mood" game with their child: one person plays a short piece and the other guesses which mood it expresses. Children discover that sound can tell a story, and they become more willing to use music to express themselves.

Teachers can also set aside a few minutes for improvisation now and then in lessons, asking students to use the few notes they have just learned to play "today's weather" or "the mood on the way home from school". Activities like this show students that music is not only playing from a score; it can also be their own voice.

## Things to Keep in Mind

Improvised expression is a personal musical activity and is no substitute for professional support. If certain emotions last for a long time or affect your daily life, it is advisable to talk to a doctor or a suitable professional in good time. Also watch your volume when you improvise, especially at night; you can use headphones to avoid disturbing your family and neighbours.

## From Improvising to Composing

Once you are used to expressing yourself through improvisation, you may find a melody you particularly like and want to keep. You can record it, or write it down on paper in a simple way. Gradually, these small fragments may grow into a little piece of your own. Composing doesn't have to be complicated; one sincere melody is a very good start.

## Adding a Little Structure to Improvisation

If completely free improvisation leaves you not knowing where to begin, give yourself a small framework, such as "slow at the start, fast in the middle, back to slow at the end", or "use only three notes, but vary the dynamics". A framework is like a container that gives your expression a starting point. When you are comfortable, loosen the framework bit by bit and let the sound flow more freely.

## Sharing Improvisation in Lessons

If students are willing, they can also share their improvised fragments in lessons. The teacher doesn't need to judge whether it was good or bad, and can simply ask: "What did you want to express?" and "Which sound came closest to how you felt?" A conversation like this helps students connect vague feelings with specific musical elements, and later, when they play pieces from the score, their playing will have more expression.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I improvise if I can't play the piano at all?**
A: Yes. A few notes on the black keys are enough to start.

**Q: What if my improvisation sounds terrible?**
A: This kind of practice isn't about sounding good. The point is to express how you feel.

**Q: Can improvised expression solve emotional problems?**
A: This article makes no such promise. If emotional difficulties persist, please seek help from a professional.

**Q: Do I need to do it every day?**
A: No. Just sit down and play for a few minutes whenever you feel like expressing something.

hildegard-von-bingen-12th-century-chant.body:
Hildegard of Bingen was born in 1098 and died in 1179. She was a nun in medieval Germany, and later became an abbess. She wrote not only poems and theological works but also set many of her own poems to music. More than seventy of her monophonic chants survive today, as well as a musical morality play, Ordo Virtutum (The Order of the Virtues). Her melodies have a wide range and often sing a long string of notes on a single syllable, which is very different from the ordinary chant of her time. In the later twentieth century her music was recorded and performed again, and aroused the interest of many people.

**Try it**
- Born in 1098, died in 1179
- A nun and abbess in medieval Germany
- More than seventy monophonic chants survive
- She wrote the musical morality play Ordo Virtutum

## Her Song Collection

Hildegard set many of her poems to music, and these were later gathered into a song collection.

More than seventy monophonic chants survive today, including hymns, antiphons and responsories.

This is a large number for a medieval composer, and the composer's name is also clearly recorded.

## Declared a Saint by the Church

In 2012, Hildegard was formally declared a saint by the Catholic Church.

In the same year she was also given the title Doctor of the Church, an honour that very few people receive.

This shows that her ideas and writings are still valued today.

## A Many-Sided Nun

Hildegard wrote many theological works, recording the visions she described and her reflections.

She also wrote books about nature, describing plants, animals and stones.

She corresponded with many people across Europe at the time, and several hundred of her letters survive.

## Playing a Single Melody on the Piano

You can try playing Hildegard's melodies on the piano, using only the right hand for the single line.

Notice the rise and fall of the melody and the long melismas, and keep every note smooth and natural.

This can help you get a feel for the flavour of medieval music.

## Ordo Virtutum

Ordo Virtutum is a musical morality play written by Hildegard, probably in the middle of the twelfth century.

In the play, a soul struggles between the various Virtues and temptation, and in the end chooses virtue.

Interestingly, the tempter in the play only speaks and never sings, showing that he has no place in beautiful music.

## A Wide-Ranging Melody

Hildegard's melodies have a wide range, often more than two octaves.

The ordinary chant of the time usually had a narrower range, with the melody moving among just a few notes.

Her melodies sometimes soar high and sometimes fall deep, full of expression.

## Medieval Notation

Hildegard's songs were written down in medieval neume notation.

This notation uses small signs to show the rise and fall of the melody, but it does not record rhythm as precisely as notation does today.

Today's singers have to decide the rhythm and tempo of the songs on the basis of research.

## Long Melismas

Hildegard often sings many notes on one syllable, creating long melismas.

This kind of writing makes the melody seem to wheel in the air, very ornate.

The singer needs very good breath control to sing these long melodies well.

## Summary: Hildegard of Bingen

Hildegard was born in 1098 and died in 1179. She was sent to a convent as a child, later became abbess, and founded a new convent near Bingen. She wrote theological works and books about nature, left several hundred letters, and more than seventy monophonic chants set to her own poems survive, including hymns, antiphons and responsories.

Her melodies often span more than two octaves and have long melismas. In the musical morality play Ordo Virtutum the tempter only speaks and does not sing. Her songs were written in neume notation, and their rhythm has to be worked out through research. They were recorded and performed again in the later twentieth century, and in 2012 she was declared a saint by the Catholic Church and given the title Doctor of the Church. On the piano you can play a single line with the right hand, then add a sustained bass note as an exercise.

You can also talk with Teacher Aum about Hildegard's life and music.

## Monophonic Chant

Hildegard's songs are monophonic, which means they have only one melody and no harmony.

These songs were usually sung by the nuns in the services of the convent.

A monophonic melody lets people focus on the rise and fall of the melody itself and on the meaning of the words.

## Hildegard's Life

Hildegard was born into a family in Germany, and as a child she was sent to live and study in a convent.

She grew up in the convent, where she learned to read and write, to chant and to sing.

Later she became abbess of the convent, and also founded a new convent near Bingen on the Rhine.

![A glowing turquoise grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadluxc-8i5rp.webp)

## Rediscovery in the Twentieth Century

In the later twentieth century, Hildegard's music was recorded and performed again.

These recordings let the voice of this medieval nun be heard by many people once more.

Her music aroused wide interest, and her life has been written about in books and made into films.

## Talk About Hildegard in Lessons

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about Hildegard's life and music.

You can also ask your teacher to explain medieval modes and notation, which helps you understand her melodies.

From the singing of one medieval nun, you can see the early face of music history.

## Adding a Long Note to the Melody

Once you know the melody, you can add a sustained bass note in the left hand, for example holding down the tonic of the melody throughout.

This technique is called a drone, and it can add a little colour to a single-line melody.

**Quick tip**

But note that the original has no accompaniment, so this is only a practice method.

## FAQ

**Q: When did Hildegard live?**
A: From 1098 to 1179.

**Q: How many chants did she leave?**
A: More than seventy monophonic chants.

**Q: What is her musical morality play called?**
A: Ordo Virtutum.

**Q: What are the features of her melodies?**
A: A wide range and long melismas.

**Q: What is special about the tempter in the play?**
A: He only speaks and does not sing.

high-mountains-flowing-water-zhiyin-stor.body:
"High Mountains, Flowing Water" comes from a very old story. In the Spring and Autumn period, the qin player Boya played while thinking of high mountains, and his listener Zhong Ziqi said, "It sounds like towering Mount Tai." When he thought of flowing water, Ziqi said, "It sounds like a mighty river." After Ziqi died, Boya felt that no one in the world understood his music any more, so he smashed his qin, broke its strings and never played again. This story is recorded in ancient books such as the Annals of Lü Buwei (Lüshi Chunqiu), and the Chinese word zhiyin ("one who understands the music", a kindred spirit) comes from it. Later, both the guqin and the guzheng came to have pieces called "High Mountains", "Flowing Water" or "High Mountains, Flowing Water", and the guqin piece Flowing Water was even recorded on a disc sent into space in 1977.

- The story of Boya playing and Zhong Ziqi listening
- Recorded in ancient books such as the Annals of Lü Buwei
- The word zhiyin (kindred spirit) comes from it
- The guqin piece Flowing Water was recorded on a disc sent into space in 1977

## Flowing Water Sent into Space

In 1977 the United States launched two space probes, each carrying a golden disc with sounds and music from Earth.

The disc includes a recording of the guqin piece Flowing Water, played by a famous guqin player.

In this way, this ancient piece flew off with the probe into distant space.

## The Guzheng Piece High Mountains, Flowing Water

The guzheng also has a piece called High Mountains, Flowing Water, but it is a different work from the guqin's Flowing Water.

The guzheng version comes from scores handed down in the folk schools, and its melody is smoother and brighter.

The same story has produced different music on different instruments.

## What the Guqin Is

The guqin is a very old Chinese plucked instrument with seven strings and thirteen marks on its surface, called hui, that indicate pitch positions.

Its sound is deep and distant, and it was often used by scholars to cultivate the mind and express feeling.

In 2003, the art of the guqin was recognised by UNESCO as a protected piece of the world's cultural heritage.

## Where "Zhiyin" Comes From

The word zhiyin comes from this story, and it means "someone who understands my music".

Later, zhiyin came to mean a friend who truly knows and understands you.

Even today people often say that a zhiyin is hard to find, to describe how rare it is to find a real soulmate.

## Feeling the Mountains and Water on the Piano

The piano has none of the guqin's glissandos, but you can use different registers and tone colours to express mountains and water.

For example, use heavy chords in the low register for the mountains and flowing arpeggios in the high register for the water.

A small exercise like this helps you understand how music paints pictures.

## Summary: High Mountains, Flowing Water

The story of High Mountains, Flowing Water tells how, in the Spring and Autumn period, Boya played the qin and Zhong Ziqi could hear whether he was thinking of towering mountains or a mighty river. After Ziqi died, Boya smashed his qin, broke its strings and never played again for the rest of his life. The story is recorded in ancient books such as the Annals of Lü Buwei and the Liezi, the word zhiyin comes from it, and the word later came to mean a friend who understands you.

The guqin has seven strings and thirteen hui. In 2003 the art of the guqin was recognised by UNESCO. The guqin piece Flowing Water imitates the flow of water with glissandos and harmonics, is already recorded in Ming dynasty scores, and in 1977 was recorded on the golden disc carried by a space probe. The guzheng piece High Mountains, Flowing Water is a different work. On the piano you can use low chords and high arpeggios to express mountains and water.

You can talk about this story with Teacher Aum.

## Be a Good Listener

The story of Boya and Ziqi tells us that music needs not only good performers but also good listeners.

When you listen to music, try to think about what picture or mood the performer wanted to express.

Learners can also play for friends in turn and say what they heard.

## Talk About the Story of Zhiyin in Lessons

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the story of Boya and Ziqi and what zhiyin means in music.

You can also ask your teacher to improvise a "mountain" and a "water" piece at the piano, and guess which is which.

From one ancient story, you can feel the understanding between listening and playing.

## Smashing the Qin and Breaking the Strings

Later, Zhong Ziqi died, and Boya was extremely sad.

He felt that there was no longer anyone in the world who could understand his music, so he smashed his qin, broke its strings and never played again.

This ending shows how precious a friend who truly understands you is.

## Towering and Mighty

When Boya played with high mountains in mind, Ziqi said, "How wonderfully you play, as towering as Mount Tai."

When Boya had flowing water in mind, Ziqi said, "How wonderfully you play, as mighty as a great river."

Whatever Boya had in mind, Ziqi could hear it in the sound of the qin.

## The Guqin Piece Flowing Water

The guqin has a piece called Flowing Water, which describes a mountain spring gathering into a stream and then into a river.

The piece has many glissandos and harmonics that imitate the sound of flowing water, sometimes murmuring and sometimes surging.

Both High Mountains and Flowing Water are already recorded in qin scores of the Ming dynasty.

![An Art Deco illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a desk lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbiq1c4-u76h6.webp)

## Boya and Ziqi

Legend says that in the Spring and Autumn period there was a qin player named Boya who played very well.

One day he was playing in the hills when a woodcutter named Zhong Ziqi sat quietly listening nearby.

Although Ziqi was only an ordinary man, he could understand the meaning of Boya's music.

## What the Ancient Books Record

The story of Boya and Ziqi is recorded in the Annals of Lü Buwei, compiled at the end of the Warring States period.

Similar accounts, with slightly different details, appear in ancient books such as the Liezi.

Because it is such an old story, it is more a legend that has been handed down than history that can be verified in detail.

## FAQ

**Q: Who plays the qin in the story of High Mountains, Flowing Water?**
A: The qin player Boya.

**Q: Who is the listener?**
A: Zhong Ziqi.

**Q: What does the word zhiyin mean?**
A: Originally someone who understands the music; later, a friend who understands you.

**Q: In which ancient book is the story recorded?**
A: The Annals of Lü Buwei and other ancient books.

**Q: In which year was the guqin piece Flowing Water recorded on a disc sent into space?**
A: 1977.
