how-fast-piano-progress-realistic.body:
How long it takes to see progress at the piano has no fixed timetable, because everyone's starting point, practice frequency and goals are different. Instead of expecting big changes in a short time, it is better to watch some small things: whether you read music a little faster, whether a difficult spot has become smoother, whether your posture and hand shape are more relaxed. These small changes add up, and that is real progress.

## What Affects the Speed of Progress

Progress at the piano is affected by many factors, such as how many times you practise each week, how focused each session is, the learning method, the difficulty of the pieces, and the learner's existing musical background.

**Listen**

Regular practice is usually better than a long session every few days. A small amount of focused practice every day keeps your fingers and brain familiar with the music.

The learning method matters too. Practising difficult spots slowly, practising in sections and checking with recordings often make the same time work better.

Because these factors differ from person to person, the speed of progress differs too, and there is no fixed timetable.

## Set Specific Small Goals

Instead of vaguely hoping to "play better", set specific small goals, such as "play this piece with both hands by next month" or "play a two-octave C major scale steadily this week".

Specific goals are easier to measure, and finishing them brings a bigger sense of achievement.

A goal should be somewhat challenging, but reachable. If it is too easy you will lack motivation, and if it is too hard it is easy to feel discouraged.

You can set goals together with your teacher, who can give suitable advice based on the learner's level.

After reaching a small goal, take a moment to look back, then set the next one, so your learning keeps a clear direction.

## Take the Ups and Downs Calmly

On the way to learning the piano, progress is often not a straight line upward. It is sometimes fast and sometimes slow, and sometimes you may even feel stuck. This is a normal part of learning.

When progress feels slow, look back at your recent practice methods and see whether they need adjusting, or whether you should try something new.

Remember to acknowledge the progress you have already made. Compared with when you started, many abilities you now take for granted were built up step by step.

Keeping your interest in music and your patience matters more than chasing a result by a certain date.

- The speed of progress differs from person to person, so avoid comparing
- Regular practice matters more than an occasional long session
- You can use recordings and practice notes to see change
- Place your expectations on specific abilities you can observe

## Make Practice Time Better Quality

The same amount of practice time can give very different results. Before you start, think about what problem you want to solve today. This is more rewarding than playing through aimlessly a few times.

During practice, you can stop at regular moments to listen to the sound you just made, judge whether it met your goal, and then decide what to practise next.

Before you finish, briefly review what you gained today and write down what to continue tomorrow, so that sessions connect with one another.

As these small habits add up, your practice becomes more efficient step by step.

## How to Record Visible Progress

A simple way is to keep a practice notebook. After each session, write the date, what you practised, what improved and what is still difficult. When you look back after a few weeks, you will find many changes you did not notice at the time.

Regular recordings help too. Once a month, record the same piece or the same set of scales, and compare the changes in speed, rhythm and tone. For children, hearing the difference between a month ago and now is often more convincing than an adult's praise.

**Practice order**

Parents can also stay in touch with the teacher, to learn what the child is focusing on now and what changes can be expected over the coming period. Expectations like this are closer to reality and easier to meet.

![Watercolour of a grand piano with the lid open, in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8k3yl3-7gvbo.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: Is it normal for a child to still play only simple pieces after a year?**
A: Progress depends on the weekly practice time and the method. You can review the goals and the practice schedule together with the teacher.

**Q: Do adults progress more slowly than children?**
A: Not necessarily. Adults are better at understanding and planning, and with regular practice they can also make clear progress.

**Q: How long do I need to practise each day to improve?**
A: There is no fixed time. Regular, focused practice matters more than simple length.

**Q: If progress is slow, does that mean piano is not for me?**
A: No. Everyone has their own pace, and after adjusting the method you will usually see change.

**Q: How can I tell whether I am improving?**
A: You can watch for it through regular recordings, practice notes and your teacher's feedback.

**Q: Do exams show progress?**
A: Exams are one reference, but progress also includes many abilities beyond exams, such as note reading and expression.

horn-fifths-classical-part-writing.body:
"Horn fifths" refers to a kind of two-part motion common in the Classical period: two voices move in intervals like those a natural horn can play, and between them appears a progression that sounds like parallel fifths but was accepted by the style of the time. The natural horn was limited by the harmonic series, so many intervals could only be joined in particular ways. Composers wrote this kind of motion into the inner or outer voices of piano and orchestral music, and the idiom has stayed with us. It is not a pass to write parallel fifths at will, but a specific pattern with an origin and a shape. For piano and harmony students, recognising horn fifths avoids treating every fifth progression as the same mistake, and also explains some places in Classical works that seem "irregular". Playing the two voices slowly on their own at the keyboard is clearer than just hunting for fifths on paper. At typical cadences or transitions, it is especially worth looking at how the outer voices move.

## Exercises for Hearing Horn Fifths

Choose a slow movement or an ending from the Classical period and listen only to the outer voices. When you reach a moment that sounds open and is then immediately filled in, stop and look at the score.

After listening several times, this kind of motion starts to feel familiar.

You can also compare it with passages of parallel fifths that really should be avoided.

## Horn Fifths: Summary

Horn fifths are a two-part motion in Classical style that imitates the way a natural horn joins notes. They may pass through fifths that the style accepted, but they are no excuse for using parallel fifths freely.

It is clearer to identify them in the score together with their context, to listen slowly to the two voices separately at the keyboard, and to compare them with the parallel fifths that must be avoided.

You can ask Teacher Aum to mark specific examples with you.

## How to Play Them on the Piano

Both voices should be clear, but there is no need to play the fifth as a sudden accent.

Just let the shape of the motion be heard; do not bang it out to "stress the theory".

If the texture is full, practise those two voices first, marked out, and then add the other notes back.

## Why Are They Called Horn Fifths?

The natural horn relied mainly on the harmonic series, so the notes and connections available to it were limited.

When composers imitated this kind of connection in two voices, the motion later called horn fifths took shape.

The name points to the origin; it does not require the piano to imitate all the colour of the horn.

- A two-part motion in Classical style that comes from natural-horn writing
- The motion may contain a fifth that the style accepted
- Not an excuse to use parallel fifths at will
- On the piano, listen slowly to the two voices separately

## What It Looks Like

A common shape is two voices starting from a consonant interval such as a third or a sixth, passing through a fifth, and then moving to another consonant interval.

For a moment it sounds open, and then it is filled back into a fuller sound.

Playing the two voices on their own makes it easier to catch the shape than looking at all the chords.

## How It Differs From Forbidden Parallel Fifths

In traditional teaching, parallel fifths between independent voices are usually avoided, because they can make the voices lose their independence or make the sound too empty.

Horn fifths are a specific progression recognised by Classical style, with fairly regular position, direction and surrounding intervals.

So you cannot judge something wrong just because you see a fifth; nor can you conclude the opposite, that all fifths are fine.

## Where They Often Appear

They often appear in transitions in the outer voices, near cadences, or wherever a little open, horn-like colour is wanted.

In an orchestra they may really be given to the brass; in a piano piece they may be written between the top and bottom voices.

Looking at the bars before and after is more accurate than picking out two notes in isolation.

## How to Recognise Them in the Score

First look at the motion of the two outer voices, or the two main voices: does it pass through a fifth, with intervals such as thirds or sixths before and after?

Then see whether it appears in a Classical-style context, rather than as a random string of empty parallel fifths.

If you are unsure, copy out the two lines on their own and sing them.

![A watercolour of a white grand piano with a score and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdj3pxk-08uat.webp)

## How It Relates to Study and Counterpoint Exercises

In counterpoint or harmony coursework, if the teacher allows horn fifths, they will usually explain the conditions.

Do not extend this to all fifth progressions on your own in coursework.

First write according to the rules of the course, then observe how composers use it in real works.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Mark the Voices in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to mark one instance of horn fifths in a Classical piece and compare it with a parallel fifth that must be avoided.

You can also try on the spot how to play the two voices clearly without banging.

**Quick tip**

Use a voice-leading pattern with a clear origin to practise reading the outer voices more carefully.

## FAQ

**Q: Where does the name "horn fifths" come from?**
A: From the typical voice connections that arose from the natural horn's limits under the harmonic series.

**Q: Does it mean parallel fifths can be written at will?**
A: No. It is only a specific motion with an origin and a shape.

**Q: What should I look at first when identifying it?**
A: The outline of the two main voices, and the Classical-style context it appears in.

**Q: What should I pay attention to when playing it on the piano?**
A: Make the two voices clear, but there is no need to bang the fifth as an accent.

**Q: How do I deal with it alongside the rules in my coursework?**
A: First follow the course's rules on fifth progressions, then observe this specific pattern in works.

home-sweet-home-bishop-payne-1823.body:
"Home! Sweet Home!" comes from the opera Clari, which premiered in London in 1823. The music is by the English composer Henry Bishop, and the words are by the American playwright John Howard Payne. The song says that wherever you roam, however splendid the place, nothing compares with your own humble home. The opera is rarely performed today, but the song has lived on for two hundred years and has been translated into many languages, including Chinese. The melody is simple and warm, and it is lovely to play on the piano.

## Variations and Arrangements

In the nineteenth century, many composers wrote piano variations and fantasias on this song.

These pieces keep the melody but add rich ornamentation and virtuosic passages.

More advanced players can look for one of these arrangements as a challenge.

## The Opera Clari

Clari is an opera that premiered in London in 1823. It tells the story of a young woman who leaves her home and longs for her family.

The opera is rarely staged today, and many people do not even know its name.

But the song from the opera is far better known than the opera itself.

## The Melody of Home! Sweet Home!

The melody is in a major key, at a gentle tempo and in a comfortable range, so it is easy to sing along with.

The phrases rise and fall evenly, as if speaking quietly.

The melody of the refrain lifts a little, then settles slowly back onto the tonic, giving the settled feeling of coming home.

## Around the World

In the nineteenth century the song spread across Britain and America, and was later translated into many languages.

During the American Civil War, soldiers on both sides are said to have loved singing it, thinking of their distant homes.

In China it also has Chinese lyrics and is often known by names such as "Home Sweet Home".

## The Warmth of the Refrain

The refrain, "Home, sweet home", is the heart of the whole song.

When you reach it, you can add a little more volume so the melody feels fuller.

But do not play too loudly; keep it warm and affectionate.

![A watercolour-style upright piano, an open score and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwad6sx5-rd2ja.webp)

## Sing the Song First

Before you play, try singing the song in Chinese or English.

As you sing, notice the breath and the rise and fall of each phrase.

Then go back to the keys and let your right hand follow the way you sang it, and the song will come alive.

- From the opera Clari, premiered in London in 1823
- Music by Henry Bishop, words by John Howard Payne
- A song of longing for a humble home
- The opera is rarely staged, yet the song has lasted two hundred years

## The Tempo of Home! Sweet Home!

The tempo should be gentle but never dragging.

Imagine someone singing softly on a quiet night, longing for home.

You can slow down a little at the end of a phrase to leave a lingering feeling.

## Ask Your Teacher to Help With the Chords in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to help you accompany "Home! Sweet Home!" with the three chords I, V and IV.

Your teacher can also explain what these three chords do in a major key.

This song is very good for practising basic chord accompaniment.

## John Howard Payne

John Howard Payne (1791-1852) was an American actor and playwright.

He wrote the words of "Home! Sweet Home!" while wandering in Europe, far from home.

The song's popularity did not make him rich, and he spent most of his life in foreign lands.

## Playing Home! Sweet Home! on the Piano

Beginners can start by playing the melody with the right hand and feeling its even rise and fall.

The left hand can accompany with the tonic, dominant and subdominant chords, the three basic chords of a major key.

When the chords change smoothly, the accompaniment sounds warm and settled.

## Home! Sweet Home!: Summary

"Home! Sweet Home!" comes from the opera Clari, premiered in London in 1823. The composer Henry Bishop lived from 1786 to 1855, and the lyricist John Howard Payne from 1791 to 1852; Payne wrote the words while wandering in Europe. The opera is rarely performed today, yet the song spread across Britain and America, and soldiers on both sides of the American Civil War are said to have loved it.

The lyrics sing that no splendid place can match a humble home. The melody is in a major key, gentle and even, and the refrain rises a little before settling back onto the tonic. On the piano you can accompany it with the three chords I, V and IV, using broken chords in the verse and block chords in the refrain, with a little more emphasis in the refrain while keeping it warm. In the nineteenth century many composers wrote variations on it.

You can ask Teacher Aum to help with the three-chord accompaniment.

## Henry Bishop

Henry Bishop (1786-1855) was an English composer who wrote many works for the stage.

He is said to have borrowed from a tune he had published earlier when writing the melody of this song.

He wrote a great deal in his lifetime, but the work people remember best today is this song.

## The Lyrics of Home! Sweet Home!

The lyrics mean that even when you wander through splendid places, nothing compares with your own humble home.

There seems to be a warmth from the sky that makes home sacred, something you cannot find anywhere else.

The refrain repeats "Home, sweet home", expressing a deep longing for home.

## Accompaniment Patterns for Home! Sweet Home!

Once you are familiar with the chords, you can change the left hand to alternate between broken chords and block chords.

Broken chords make the music flow, while block chords make it steady.

You can use broken chords in the verse and block chords in the refrain to create contrast.

## FAQ

**Q: Which opera is "Home! Sweet Home!" from?**
A: Clari, which premiered in London in 1823.

**Q: Who wrote the music and the words?**
A: Henry Bishop wrote the music and John Howard Payne wrote the words.

**Q: What do the lyrics express?**
A: That no splendid place can match a humble home.

**Q: Which three chords can accompany it?**
A: The tonic, dominant and subdominant chords.

**Q: Where was Payne when he wrote the words?**
A: Wandering in Europe, far from home.

harpsichord-plucked-strings-vs-piano-ham.body:
In a museum or at a concert, you may sometimes see a keyboard instrument that looks like a piano but sounds much crisper. It is called the harpsichord. Like the piano, it has keys and strings, but the way it makes sound is very different. Understanding the difference helps you see why the piano can vary its volume.

## What the Two Instruments Share

Both the harpsichord and the piano have a row of keys. Pressing a key sets a mechanism in motion that touches the string and makes it vibrate. The vibration of the string is amplified by the soundboard in the body of the instrument and becomes the sound people hear. In appearance, both have a long lid and a set of strings.

- Both have a keyboard played with the fingers.
- Both make sound through vibrating strings.
- Both rely on a soundboard and the body of the instrument to amplify the sound.

## The Harpsichord: Plucking the Strings

In a harpsichord, each key is connected to a small strip of wood, and a tiny plectrum is fixed to the strip. When you press the key, the strip rises and the plectrum gently plucks the string, much as a finger plucks a guitar string. The plectrum can be made of quill, leather, plastic or other materials.

**The Character of the Sound**
A plucked string gives a crisp sound with a clear attack and a short decay. Whether the key is pressed hard or softly, the string is plucked in essentially the same way, so the range of volume is fairly limited.

**How to Create Variety**
Players can express themselves through ornaments, flexibility of rhythm and different combinations of tone. Some harpsichords have two keyboards, or let you switch between different sets of strings, to change the thickness of the sound.

![Several hands resting on piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwjqt9bx-4xv7n.webp)

## The Piano: Striking the Strings with Hammers

In a piano, each key is connected to a felt-covered hammer. When you press the key, the hammer strikes the string and then rebounds, leaving the string free to vibrate. The speed at which the hammer strikes decides the volume: press quickly and the sound is loud, press slowly and it is soft.

This is why the piano has such a rich range of loud and soft, and it is where the instrument gets its name. The full name of the piano is "pianoforte", meaning "soft-loud", because it can be played both loudly and softly.

## The Difference in Feel

The two instruments feel different under the fingers. The keyboard of a harpsichord is usually light, and pressing a key gives almost no feedback in terms of force. A piano keyboard has some weight, and the speed and force with which you press a key directly affect the sound. So when you move from one instrument to the other, your fingers need to adapt again.

- Harpsichord: light keys with a direct response, expressing more through rhythm and ornaments.
- Piano: weighted keys, expressing more through the depth and speed of touch.

## A Listening Exercise

You can find two recordings, one of a harpsichord and one of a piano, and let your child listen: which one sounds crisper? Which one has a richer variety of volume? Describing what you hear aloud, or drawing it, makes an enjoyable listening game.

## What This Means for Learning Piano

Understanding the harpsichord helps explain why touch matters. On the piano, the speed of the finger decides the volume, so a relaxed arm and a steady wrist are essential. When you practise, listen to how your volume changes and think about how to draw loud and soft with your fingers. TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app that students can use at home to practise repeatedly and keep an eye on whether the notes and rhythm are steady. The subtle feel of touch, however, needs a teacher to demonstrate in person in a lesson.

## Questions from Young Children

Children often ask: why do these two instruments look alike but sound different? You can answer in simple words: one "plucks" and the other "strikes". Then ask the child to gently pluck and then strike the tabletop with a finger, and feel the difference between the two actions.

## The Two Instruments on the Page

In piano music, the score often carries markings for loud and soft, such as signs for gentle and strong playing, reminding the player to use different kinds of touch. In music written for the harpsichord there are relatively few such markings, and players rely more on ornaments, the handling of rhythm and the arrangement of figures to make the music rise and fall. Comparing the two kinds of score helps piano learners see that the character of an instrument influences how music is composed and performed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can a harpsichord play loud and soft?**
A: The volume range from key pressure alone is very limited, so players mainly express themselves in other ways.

**Q: Did the piano develop from the harpsichord?**
A: Each instrument has its own construction. The piano appeared relatively later and makes sound in a different way.

**Q: Do I need to know this to learn piano?**
A: It is not essential, but understanding how the instruments work helps you grasp the link between touch and sound.

**Q: Should an ordinary family buy a harpsichord?**

holiday-season-music-marketing.body:
The holiday season is when music schools and families can grow closest. During New Year, school holidays and various festivals, people have more time with their families and are more willing to join events with some warmth. The heart of holiday music marketing is not big discounts, but the feeling of "enjoying music together with family": designing holiday-themed concerts, parent-child workshops, gift lessons and warm content. Done well, it makes existing students feel valued and lets new families meet your school for the first time.

## Where Holiday Marketing Starts

During the holidays, advertisements compete for people's attention. If a music school only sends out discount messages, it is easily drowned out. Sincere content is much easier to remember: a holiday song played by students together, a New Year letter from a teacher to students, an afternoon inviting grandparents to hear their grandchildren play. This kind of content is worth sharing in itself.

**Set the holiday calendar first**
At the start of the year, list the important festivals and holidays, and begin preparing one or two months ahead. Different regions and families celebrate different festivals, so respect a variety of cultures when choosing, and avoid centring everything on a single festival.

## Holiday-Themed Concerts

A student concert can include holiday touches. For example, with the theme "New Year, New Sounds", each student plays one piece connected to the season. You can invite parents, relatives and friends, and end the concert with a song that everyone sings or plays together. Afterwards, with permission, post selected clips on social media with warm words.

- Repertoire: traditional public-domain melodies, short pieces arranged by students, or short original pieces by teachers.
- Venue decoration: simple lighting and decorations are enough, with no need to spend much.
- Timing: keep it to about an hour, so families with small children can come.

![Black-and-white stippled sketch: a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw1j0vlc-wpip4.webp)

## Parent-Child Music Workshops

The holidays are a good time for parents and children to learn together. You can design a parent-child music workshop: parent and child learn a simple piano duet together, or make rhythm instruments from everyday objects and tap along with the music. At the end, each family can record a short video as a keepsake. This kind of activity lets parents experience their child's learning first-hand, and leaves families with a good impression of the school.

## Designing Gift Lessons

During the holidays, some people want to give music lessons as a gift to family or friends. A school can design a gift card or a trial-lesson package, stating what it includes, how long it is valid and how to use it. The packaging can be simple but thoughtful, for example with a handwritten card. When introducing gift lessons, state the conditions clearly. Do not use anxiety-inducing phrases such as "limited-time rush", and do not promise learning results.

**A gesture for existing students**
Giving current students a small holiday gift, such as a piece of holiday sheet music or a practice record card, lets them feel cared for. This kind of gesture often keeps students better than a discount does.

## The Rhythm of Holiday Posts

Two to three weeks before the holiday, you can start posting teaser content: teachers sharing tips for playing holiday songs, behind-the-scenes clips of students rehearsing, and event sign-up details. On the day itself, post greetings and concert clips. After the holiday, post thank-you messages and an event recap. This forms a complete story, rather than a single advertisement on the day.

## Involve the Teachers Too

Holiday events are not only the work of the administrative team. Teachers know the students best. They can recommend students and pieces that suit a concert, and can record a short holiday greeting video. When teachers take part personally, the content has more warmth, and students and parents feel closer to it. At the same time, plan teachers' workload sensibly, so that too many events over the holidays do not affect regular lessons.

## Avoid Common Pitfalls

A few things to watch in holiday marketing: do not overuse holiday elements, or it will look forced; do not send a large number of messages in a short time; make sure the music and images you use are properly licensed; and plan the safety and order of holiday events in advance. Staying sincere is the most important principle of holiday marketing.

## FAQ

**Q: Our music school is small and the budget is limited. How can we run holiday events?**
A: Start small, for example with a half-hour student mini-concert at the school. What matters is the atmosphere and participation.

**Q: Should we offer discounts during the holidays?**
A: You can decide according to your situation, but we do not suggest making discounts the whole of the event. Offering a meaningful experience matters more.

**Q: Can holiday concerts use pop songs?**
A: You need to check the copyright requirements for performing and for posting recordings. Where necessary, choose public-domain works or obtain permission.

**Q: How can holiday events bring in new students?**
A: Let students invite relatives and friends, and offer a way to book a trial lesson after the event, but do not push a sales pitch on the spot.

## Keep Playing After the Holidays

hear-chord-qualities-major-minor-dim-aug.body:
Triads fall into four qualities according to how the thirds are stacked: major, minor, diminished and augmented. They differ in the distance from root to third and from third to fifth. A major triad is a major third plus a minor third, and sounds bright and stable. A minor triad is a minor third plus a major third, and sounds soft and a little darker. A diminished triad is two minor thirds, and sounds tense, as if it wants to move on. An augmented triad is two major thirds, and sounds suspended, a bit like a dream. Once you can tell them apart by ear, you will be quicker at working out songs, improvising and reading music, and you will better understand where the changes of mood in music come from.

## The Structure of the Four Triads

- Major triad: a major third plus a minor third, for example C, E, G
- Minor triad: a minor third plus a major third, for example C, E♭, G
- Diminished triad: a minor third plus a minor third, for example C, E♭, G♭
- Augmented triad: a major third plus a major third, for example C, E, G♯

It is also handy to remember them in semitones: a major triad is four semitones plus three, a minor triad is three plus four, a diminished triad is three plus three, and an augmented triad is four plus four.

## Give Each Chord an Image

**Major triad: a sunny day**
The sound is open and steady, like sunlight coming into a room. Many nursery rhymes and marches are built mainly on it.

**Minor triad: a cloudy day**
The sound is soft with a touch of sadness, but still stable, like an afternoon of light rain.

**Diminished triad: a tightly wound spring**
The sound is compact and uneasy, as if it might head somewhere else at any moment. It often appears where the music needs a push.

**Augmented triad: floating mist**
The sound expands outwards with nowhere to land, and is often used to create a feeling of mystery or transition.

These images are only tools to help you remember. Everyone may feel them differently, and you can use your own comparisons.

![A blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of water on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvybgx5h-bv76i.webp)

## Comparing Them at the Piano

**Comparing from the same root**
With C as the root, play the major, minor, diminished and augmented triads in turn, holding each chord for two seconds. Repeat a few times. Each time only one or two notes change, but the change of colour is very clear.

**Break it up, then put it together**
First play the three notes of each chord one by one from the bottom up, then press them all together. When broken up, each interval is easier to hear. When played together, the overall colour is easier to feel.

**Change the root**
Do the same exercise on roots such as F, G and D, so that your ear does not depend on one fixed pitch.

## A Five-Minute Daily Listening Game

- Ask a family member or friend to play a random triad, and say its quality with your eyes closed
- With no partner, record ten random chords on your phone, then listen and answer the next day
- Practise only major and minor at first, and add diminished once your accuracy is steady
- Finally add augmented, and complete the four-way listening test
- Record the number of correct answers each time and watch how it changes over a few weeks

Starting with two kinds and adding more gradually builds confidence more easily than mixing all four from the start.

## Finding Them in Songs

When you listen to songs, major and minor triads are the most common, and most songs are built mainly on them. A diminished triad usually flashes by, appearing between two chords as a link. An augmented triad is rarer, and often appears when a melody is about to turn in a new direction.

When you hear a moment in a song that is especially tense or especially floating, you can go back to the piano and try to find that chord, and see whether it is diminished or augmented. This kind of practice lets your ear and your fingers grow together.

## Common Confusions and How to Tell Them Apart

**Major and augmented are easily confused**
The two share the same third, and differ only in the fifth. The fifth of an augmented triad is raised by a semitone, and it sounds more "spread out". Play a major triad first, then raise only the fifth, and compare again and again.

**Minor and diminished are easily confused**
The two share the same third, and the difference is also in the fifth. The fifth of a diminished triad is lowered by a semitone, and it sounds tighter. Compare them several times in the same way and your ear will be able to tell them apart.

## Connecting Listening and Playing

After a listening exercise, go straight back to the piano and play the chords you have just heard. For example, if you identified a minor triad, play one on each of several different roots, while singing the root, third and fifth. In this way, what the ear hears becomes linked with where the fingers press, and later, when you see a chord symbol, you can first "hear" its sound in your head, making working out songs and improvising smoother.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Do I need perfect pitch to identify chords?**
A: No. Telling chord qualities apart depends on relative pitch, and most people can learn it with practice.

**Q: At what age can a child start practising?**
A: As long as they can tell a "happy" sound from a "sad" one, they can begin with the contrast between major and minor.

**Q: What if I still cannot tell diminished from minor after a long time?**
A: Slow the tempo down, play each note one at a time, compare the fifth on its own, and then gradually put them back together.

**Q: Can I practise seventh chords this way too?**
A: Yes. Once you are familiar with triads, use the same method to practise major sevenths, dominant sevenths, minor sevenths and half-diminished sevenths.

impressionism-in-music-monet-debussy.body:
The name "Impressionism" first came from painting: in 1874 a critic, seeing Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, used the word "Impressionists" to mock this group of painters. Later, people borrowed the word for music, to describe some works by several composers in Paris around the turn of the century. Debussy and Ravel are two often mentioned among them. This music does not stress clear melody and firm structure. Instead it uses hazy harmony, unusual scales and delicate tone colours to paint the feeling of light, water, clouds and wind. Interestingly, Debussy himself did not like his music being called this.

## The Whole-Tone Scale

Impressionist composers often used a scale called the whole-tone scale.

In this scale each pair of neighbouring notes is a whole tone apart, with six notes in all, for example C, D, E, F♯, G♯, A♯.

Because there are no semitones, the whole-tone scale sounds as if it is floating in the air, with no direction.

## What the Painters Painted

Impressionist painters liked to paint outdoors, catching the changes of light and colour in a moment.

Their brushwork is loose and their outlines blurred, so the picture looks like an impression.

Reflections on water, morning mist and gardens in sunlight were their favourite subjects.

## The Pentatonic Scale

Impressionist composers also often used the pentatonic scale, the five notes you get on the black keys of the piano.

It is said that Debussy heard Indonesian gamelan music at the Paris World's Fair of 1889 and was greatly inspired by it.

The pentatonic scale gave his music a touch of Eastern colour.

## Parallel Chords

You can also try Impressionist parallel chords: play a triad with the right hand, then keep the hand shape and move it up or down together.

For example, move from C, E, G to D, F, A, and then to E, G, B.

Play with the pedal down and listen to the chords sliding past like colours.

**Before you start**
- The name comes from Monet's Impression, Sunrise of 1874
- It is used to describe the works of Debussy, Ravel and others
- Hazy harmony, unusual scales, delicate tone colours
- Debussy himself did not like the label

## Debussy Did Not Like It

Interestingly, Debussy himself did not like people calling his music "Impressionist".

He felt the word was not accurate, and once expressed his dissatisfaction in a letter.

Even so, the label stayed in use.

## Titles That Paint Nature

Many works by Debussy and Ravel have titles that depict nature.

For example Debussy's Clair de lune, Reflets dans l'eau and Voiles, and Ravel's Jeux d'eau.

These titles help listeners imagine the pictures the music describes.

## Playing the Whole-Tone Scale on the Piano

You can play a whole-tone scale on the piano: starting from C, play C, D, E, F♯, G♯, A♯, and return to the high C.

Play slowly with the sustain pedal down, and listen to the feeling of floating in the air.

Then play an ordinary C major scale, and compare the two scales.

## A Painting of a Sunrise

In 1874 an exhibition was held in Paris, showing the work of a group of young painters.

Among them was a painting by Monet depicting a sunrise over a harbour, called Impression, Sunrise.

A critic who saw it used the word "Impressionists" to mock this group of painters, and unexpectedly the name lasted.

![A digital music space in neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk1n29-srccf.webp)

## Trying Impressionist Colours with Your Teacher in a Lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the whole-tone scale and parallel chords, and the use of the pedal in Debussy's works.

The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is not long, and is the first Debussy piece many people meet. Your teacher can help you judge whether you can start learning it now.

From a name borrowed from painting, you can see the colours of music.

## Hazy Harmony

One feature of Impressionist music is hazy harmony, often not resolving according to traditional rules.

Composers liked to move chords in parallel, like patches of colour sliding across a canvas.

The sound and colour of a chord itself matters more than where it goes next.

## Not Only France

Although Impressionism is represented by French composers, it also influenced musicians elsewhere.

Some composers in Britain, Spain and America, for example, used similar techniques in their works.

Later jazz and film music also took many harmonic colours from it.

## Borrowed for Music

Later, people borrowed the word "Impressionism" for music.

It was used to describe the works of some French composers from the end of the nineteenth century to the early twentieth, such as Debussy and Ravel.

Like Impressionist paintings, this music likes to depict the feeling of light, water, clouds and wind.

## Delicate Tone Colours

Impressionist music values tone colour highly, and composers choose instruments and registers carefully.

In piano works they often use the pedal to blend sounds together, like a thin mist.

The dynamics are often very soft, with many subtle changes.

## Musical Impressionism at a Glance

"Impressionism" comes from Monet's Impression, Sunrise at the Paris exhibition of 1874, which a critic used to mock the painters. Impressionist painters caught the fleeting changes of light and colour. Later the word was borrowed for the music of Debussy and Ravel, though Debussy himself did not like it. This music has hazy harmony, with chords moving in parallel, and often uses the whole-tone and pentatonic scales. Debussy is said to have been inspired by gamelan music heard at the 1889 Paris World's Fair.

It values tone colour, often uses the pedal to make the sound like a thin mist, and its titles often depict nature, such as Clair de lune, Reflets dans l'eau and Jeux d'eau. It later influenced jazz and film music too. On the piano you can play the whole-tone scale and parallel chords with the pedal down.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate Impressionist colours.

## FAQ

**Q: Where did the name "Impressionism" first come from?**
A: Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise of 1874.

**Q: Which composers is it often used to describe in music?**
A: Mainly Debussy and Ravel.

**Q: Did Debussy like the label?**
A: No.

**Q: How many notes does the whole-tone scale have?**
A: Six, with each pair of neighbouring notes a whole tone apart.

**Q: Where is Debussy said to have heard gamelan music?**
A: At the Paris World's Fair of 1889.

haydn-farewell-symphony-1772.body:
In 1772 Haydn was Kapellmeister at the country palace of his employer, the Esterházy family. That summer the employer stayed there much longer than in previous years, the musicians' families were left elsewhere, and everyone longed to go home. So Haydn wrote a symphony in F sharp minor. In its last movement, as the score directs, the musicians stop playing one after another, snuff out the candles on their music stands, stand up and leave, until only two violinists remain. It is said that the employer understood the hint and let the musicians go home the next day. The work came to be known as the "Farewell" Symphony.

## Summary of the "Farewell" Symphony

In 1772 Haydn was Kapellmeister at the Esterházy family's country palace. His employer stayed especially long that summer, and the musicians missed the families they had left elsewhere, so Haydn wrote Symphony No. 45 in F sharp minor to express this tactfully. This key was very unusual for symphonies at the time.

In the last movement, a presto gives way to an adagio, and the musicians, following the score, snuff out their candles and leave one by one, until only two violinists remain, said to be Haydn himself and the leader of the orchestra. According to the record, the employer understood the hint and let the musicians go home the next day, though the details come from recollections made many years later and may have been embellished.

Today's performances often keep the walking-off, and on the piano you can feel the effect of voices gradually dropping away. Haydn's sonatas are full of humour too, and you can choose one with Teacher Aum in a lesson.

## Expressing Himself Through Music

As Kapellmeister, Haydn could not easily make a request to his employer directly.

So he decided to express the musicians' feelings cleverly through a new symphony.

This is the Symphony No. 45, later known as the "Farewell" Symphony.

## The Last Two Violinists

It is said that the two violinists who stayed to the end were Haydn himself and the orchestra's leader.

They played the final notes and snuffed out their candles.

The whole hall slowly grew quiet and dark.

## Haydn's Piano Works

Haydn wrote many piano sonatas, and quite a few are suitable for intermediate learners.

His sonatas are likewise full of humour and surprises, such as sudden pauses or unexpected modulations.

You can pick one of them to feel Haydn's musical character.

## Feeling the "Fading Away" Effect on the Piano

You can also feel the effect of voices dropping away on the piano.

For example, play a passage of four-voice chords, then remove one voice every few bars until only one voice remains.

Listen to how the mood changes as the sound goes from full to thin.

## Performances Today

Today, when many orchestras perform this symphony, they still let the musicians leave one by one in the original way.

Some orchestras even light real candles on the music stands, or use small lamps instead.

Seeing the musicians leave, the audience often smiles knowingly.

## The Final Adagio

The first movements proceed in the usual way, and the fourth movement also begins with a presto.

But when the presto ends, the music does not finish as usual and instead turns into an adagio.

In this adagio, the instruments stop playing one by one.

## Leaving One by One

As arranged in the score, each musician, after playing their last few notes, snuffs out the candle on the music stand, picks up the instrument and leaves.

First the oboes and horns go, then the other instruments, and the orchestra grows smaller and smaller.

At last only two violinists remain on stage, quietly playing the final few notes.

![A piano scene with futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabiz95-08xfy.webp)

## Talking About Haydn's Humour in Lessons

In a lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the story of the "Farewell" Symphony and the humour in Haydn's music.

If you would like to play Haydn, you can also choose a suitable sonata together.

Knowing a composer's character makes your playing more lively.

## The Rare Key of F Sharp Minor

This symphony is in F sharp minor, which was very rare for symphonies at the time.

The key has many sharps, and it was not commonly used by the instruments and players of the day.

The opening movement is hurried and agitated, with an uneasy mood.

## The Summer of 1772

In 1772, the employer stayed at the country palace much longer than in earlier years.

Most of the musicians' families were left elsewhere, and the palace had no room for them to live there too.

As time went on, the musicians missed their families badly and hoped to return sooner.

## Humour in the Music

Haydn was a composer with a great sense of humour, and many of his works contain surprises.

The "Farewell" Symphony tells its story through the music itself, not through words.

This clever idea has made it one of the best-loved stories in music history.

## The Employer's Reaction

According to later accounts, the employer understood the meaning of the symphony.

The next day the musicians were allowed to leave the palace and go home to be with their families.

The story has been widely told, but its details come mainly from recollections made many years later and may have been embellished.

- In 1772 Haydn was Kapellmeister at his employer's country palace
- The musicians missed their families and wanted to go home sooner
- In the last movement the musicians snuff out their candles and leave one by one
- Only two violinists remain at the end

## Haydn and His Employer

From 1761 Haydn worked for the Esterházy family of Hungary, and later became Kapellmeister.

He was responsible for composing, rehearsing the orchestra and managing the musicians, and his work was very busy.

The Esterházy family built a large palace in the countryside, where they often stayed for several months in summer.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: In what year was the "Farewell" Symphony written?**
A: 1772.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: F sharp minor.

**Q: Why did the musicians want to go home?**
A: The employer stayed too long, and their families were elsewhere.

**Q: What happens in the last movement?**
A: The musicians snuff out their candles and leave one by one.

**Q: How many musicians are left at the end?**
A: Two violinists.

haydn-the-creation-oratorio-1798.body:
The Creation is an oratorio by the Austrian composer Haydn, written between 1796 and 1798 and premiered in Vienna in 1798. Haydn had heard large-scale performances of Handel's oratorios in London and was deeply moved, and he wrote this work after returning to Vienna. The text draws on the Book of Genesis in the Bible and on the English poet Milton's long poem Paradise Lost. The work opens with an overture describing "chaos", with hazy music that has no direction; then, when the chorus sings "and there was light", the whole orchestra and chorus suddenly sound a loud C major chord, the unforgettable moment of the whole work.

## What an Oratorio Is

An oratorio is a large vocal work with soloists, chorus and orchestra.

**Before you start**

It is somewhat like opera and also tells a story, but usually without sets, costumes or acting.

The subjects of oratorios often come from religious stories.

## And There Was Light

After the overture, the chorus sings softly that God says let there be light.

At the word "light" in "and there was light", the whole orchestra and chorus suddenly sound a loud C major chord.

The move from hazy C minor to bright C major is a moment many listeners cannot forget.

## Talk About the Light of Creation in Lessons

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the musical portrayal of the move from chaos to light in The Creation.

The teacher can also explain the contrast between minor and major, and how Haydn uses instruments to portray animals.

Through one oratorio, you can feel the power of musical description.

## Playing The Creation on the Piano

The Creation has a piano reduction, so you can play the orchestral parts on the piano.

You can experience both the chaos of the overture and the moment of "and there was light" on the piano.

At a more advanced level, you can also try playing accompaniment for the chorus or for a soloist.

## Where the Text Comes From

The text of The Creation draws on the story of the creation of the world in the Book of Genesis in the Bible, and on the English poet Milton's long poem Paradise Lost.

It is said that the text was first written in English and later translated into German in Vienna.

Haydn set the German text to music, and when the work was published, both German and English texts were printed.

## The Overture of Chaos

The work begins with an overture describing "chaos", when the world has not yet taken shape.

The music is in C minor, with hazy, blurred harmony and a broken melody with no clear direction.

In this way Haydn expresses a world without order.

## London and Handel's Oratorios

In the 1790s, Haydn went to London twice, gave concerts and was warmly received.

In London he heard large-scale performances of Handel's oratorios, such as Messiah.

A chorus and orchestra of hundreds playing Handel's works moved Haydn deeply.

## Adam and Eve

The third part of the work describes the life of the first couple, Adam and Eve, in paradise.

In a duet, the two express their thanks to their Creator and their love for each other.

This music is tender and lyrical, like a pastoral poem.

## Music That Describes Animals

In the passages describing the creation of the animals, Haydn uses many amusing musical depictions.

The lion's roar is given to the low trombones, the horse's gallop to fast figures, and the crawling of insects to soft strings.

These depictions let listeners almost see the different animals.

## From C Minor to C Major

The move from C minor to C major at the start of The Creation is an example of expressing feeling through key.

Minor often feels hazy and sad, while major feels bright and joyful.

On the piano, try playing a C minor chord first and then a C major chord, and feel the contrast between them.

## The Premiere and Its Spread

The Creation premiered in Vienna in 1798, and was performed publicly the following year.

The work quickly spread across Europe and was widely loved.

It became one of Haydn's most important late works.

**Think again**
- Haydn's oratorio, written between 1796 and 1798
- Premiered in Vienna in 1798
- Inspired by hearing Handel's oratorios in London
- The loud C major chord at "and there was light"

## The Six Days of Creation

The first two parts of the work describe the six days of creation: heaven and earth, the seas, plants, the sun and moon, birds and fish, animals and humans.

Haydn describes each created thing vividly in music.

For example, low instruments depict the waves of the sea, and the flute depicts the song of birds.

## The 1808 Performance

In 1808, to celebrate Haydn's birthday, a performance of The Creation was held in Vienna, and the aged Haydn came to attend.

It is said that when the orchestra played "and there was light", the audience applauded warmly and Haydn pointed excitedly to the sky.

This was one of the last few public appearances Haydn made in his lifetime.

Haydn went to London twice in the 1790s and was deeply moved by large-scale performances of Handel's oratorios. After returning to Vienna he wrote the oratorio The Creation between 1796 and 1798. It premiered in Vienna in 1798 and was performed publicly the following year. The text draws on the Book of Genesis and on Milton's Paradise Lost, and it is said to have been written in English first and then translated into German, with both texts printed at publication.

The first two parts describe the six days of creation, with trombones, fast figures and soft strings depicting animals, and the third part is the duet of Adam and Eve. hum-first-note-before-playing.body:
Many pieces sound unsteady at the start because the hands have already pressed down while the mind has not yet decided what tempo and sound it wants. Before you start playing, you can sing the first phrase in your head, or softly hum the first note, work out the tempo, dynamics and mood, and only then put your hands on the keys. These few seconds of preparation make the opening steadier and give it more direction.

**Common mistakes**
- Sing the first phrase in your head before playing
- Think through the tempo and dynamics of the opening
- You can softly hum the first note
- Be ready before you begin, and do not rush to press the keys

## Make It a Habit in Practice Too

This preparation is not only for performances. You can do it every time you start from the beginning in everyday practice.

If you restart from a spot in the middle during practice, you can also sing that phrase in your head once before continuing.

Once this becomes a habit, you will find that each time you begin to play, you feel more sure inside.

![A person with blue-purple hair in a futuristic jacket playing layered glowing synthesisers on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xwvqd-10spi.webp)

## Decide on the Sound and Mood

The same notes, played with different dynamics and touch, feel completely different.

Before you begin, think: is this piece gentle or lively? Does the first phrase start softly or strongly?

Once you have decided, your fingers will more naturally use the right dynamics and tempo when they press the first note.

## Record the Opening and Listen

You can record your opening and compare how it sounds when you first sing it in your head and then play, and when you start playing straight away.

Often the prepared opening has a steadier tempo, and the sound of the first phrase has more direction, so listeners enter the mood of the piece more quickly.

If the opening on the recording is still unsteady, take the first phrase out on its own, sing first and then play, and repeat it several times until the opening becomes natural and calm.

## Practising with Children

Children are often in a hurry to start. Parents and teachers can remind them: "Sing it once in your head first."

You can hum the first phrase softly together with the child, and then let the child begin to play.

This little ritual helps children learn to think before playing, rather than just pressing the keys mechanically.

## When the Hands Are Faster Than the Mind

Many people sit down at the piano, glance at the score, and their hands are already playing.

At that moment, their mind may not yet have worked out how fast the piece should go, or whether the first phrase should be soft or loud.

The result is often that after a few bars they find the tempo is wrong, and have to stop and start again, or adjust slowly along the way.

## Why the Opening Matters

The opening of a piece is like the first sentence of a speech. It gives listeners their first impression.

If the tempo of the opening keeps speeding up and slowing down, or the dynamics do not match the mood of the piece, much more effort is needed to put it right afterwards.

Spending a few seconds to get the opening ready often makes the whole piece go more smoothly.

## Place Your Hands on the Keys

When you are ready, gently place your hands at the position of the first note, and do not press yet.

You can pause for a second or two, letting your fingers feel the keys and confirming the position is right.

Then, carrying the phrase you have already sung in your head, begin to play.

## Decide on the Tempo

While singing the first phrase in your head, you can also feel the speed of the beat at the same time.

If the piece has faster passages later on, do not set the opening tempo too fast, or you will not keep up later.

You can also listen to a few beats of the metronome to confirm the tempo, then turn it off and start playing, keeping that tempo in your head.

If the tempo changes within the piece, you can also think before you begin about how the tempo of the first section relates to the later sections.

## Softly Hum the First Note

If singing in your head is not clear enough, you can softly hum the first note, or even the first phrase.

Humming lets you feel the direction of the melody and the place to breathe more concretely.

If you do not sing very accurately, that is fine. The point is to feel the rhythm and mood, not the pitch.

## Sing the First Phrase in Your Head

Before you start playing, look at the score and sing the first melodic phrase through once in your head.

As you sing, notice its tempo, rhythm and rise and fall, and imagine what sound you want to hear.

If the piece has an introduction, or the left hand enters first, you can also first "hear" the feel of the introduction in your head, and then decide how the right hand will come in.

## FAQ

**Q: How long does singing in my head take?**
A: A few seconds is usually enough. Just sing the first phrase.

**Q: What if I cannot sing?**
A: You do not need to sing accurately. The point is to feel the rhythm and mood.

**Q: Should I do this in performances too?**
A: Yes, it helps you start more steadily on stage.

**Q: What if the piece starts with chords?**
A: Imagine the sound and dynamics of the chords, then begin to play.

**Q: What if my child does not want to hum?**
A: They can just count the beats in their head, or an adult can hum for the child first.

**Q: Should I sing every time I start from the middle?**
A: Yes, we suggest it. It makes restarting smoother.

harmonic-series-many-notes-inside-one-no.body:
When you press a piano key, you hear one note. But if you listen closely as it slowly fades away, you may notice higher, thinner sounds hidden inside it. These sounds are overtones. Arrange the overtones in order from low to high and you have the harmonic series. It is the key to understanding tone colour, and the foundation of a great deal of music theory.

## How a String Vibrates

When a string is struck, it does not simply swing as a whole. At the same time it also divides into two parts, three parts, four parts and so on, each vibrating separately. The vibration of the whole string produces the lowest note, called the fundamental. The vibration of the parts produces higher notes than the fundamental, called overtones.

- The whole string vibrating: produces the fundamental.
- Dividing into two parts: produces a sound an octave above the fundamental.
- Dividing into three parts: produces a still higher sound, and so on in turn.

The single note we normally hear is really a blend of the fundamental and many overtones.

## How the Harmonic Series Is Arranged

The harmonic series follows a regular pattern. Starting from the fundamental, the first overtone is an octave higher, the second is higher again, and the gaps get smaller as you go up. The first few overtones correspond to intervals we know well, such as the octave, the fifth and the third. This is why chords sound harmonious: their notes are already related inside the harmonic series.

**Chords and Overtones**
The notes of a major triad can be found among the first few positions of the harmonic series, which is why they sound so well blended.

![A close-up of piano keys and hands playing](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwjqxrqx-y8ma0.webp)

## Overtones and Tone Colour

Different instruments have different tone colours, and one reason is that their combinations of overtones differ. Some instruments have many high overtones and sound bright, while others have fewer and sound soft. The piano's sound also has its own overtone character, depending on the thickness and length of the strings and the point where the hammer strikes.

## Hearing Overtones on the Piano

Here is a small experiment you can try at home.

- Gently press and hold the C one octave above middle C, without making it sound.
- Play the low C below middle C firmly, then quickly release it, keeping your finger on the upper key.
- Now the upper string will vibrate faintly through resonance and give out a delicate sound.

This happens because the overtones of the low C include a sound an octave higher, which makes the corresponding string vibrate in sympathy. For this experiment, the room should be quiet and your ear close to the piano so you can hear it clearly.

## How This Helps Your Playing

Understanding the harmonic series can make your ears more sensitive. When you play a long note, learn to listen to the way the sound rings on, and notice whether it fades away evenly. When you play a chord, listen to whether the notes blend together. This kind of listening practice gradually improves your judgement of pitch and tone colour. TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app developed by a team in Thailand. When students play at home, it can help check whether the notes are accurate and the beat is steady. Learning to hear the layers inside a sound, however, takes time with a teacher's demonstration.

## Games for Children

- "Find the echo": play a long note and ask the child to put an ear close to the piano and listen to how the sound changes.
- "High or low": play a low note and a high note, and ask the child which one sounds "thicker" and which one sounds "brighter".
- "Draw the sound": ask the child to draw what a note looks like from the moment it starts until it disappears.

## A Few Reminders for the Experiment

During the experiment, do not press too hard, and do not tap the strings with your hand. Children should do it with a parent beside them, taking care of the instrument. If you cannot hear the overtones, there is no need to worry. Everyone's ears and surroundings are different, and you will discover something after a few more tries.

## Overtones and Tuning

Piano tuners often use overtones to judge whether two notes agree. When the overtones of two notes line up, the sound is steady. When they do not line up, you hear "beats", a wavering between louder and softer. Children can listen for these subtle fluctuations when two neighbouring strings sound slightly different pitches, and so experience how sharp the ear can be. Of course, this kind of fine listening takes time, so there is no need to hurry.

## From Overtones to Harmony

The first notes of the harmonic series are the octave, the fifth and the third, which matches the basic make-up of a chord. When a child later learns triads, you can recall this little experiment: the notes of the chord were already present inside a single note. Connecting new knowledge to what the ear has experienced makes abstract theory feel friendly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does every note have overtones?**
A: Most instruments produce notes that contain overtones, just in different strengths.

**Q: Are overtones the same thing as tone colour?**
A: Overtones are one important reason for differences in tone colour, but there are other factors, such as the attack and the decay.

**Q: Is it normal not to hear the overtones?**
A: Yes. You need a quiet room and a little patience, and it gets easier after a few more listens.

**Q: Do I have to understand the harmonic series to learn piano?**
A: It is not essential, but understanding it can help you understand tone colour and chords.

hazel-scott-1950-television-show-pianist.body:
Hazel Scott was a pianist known for blending classical and jazz styles. In 1950 she hosted a television show named after herself. She often arranged famous classical pieces and played them in a jazz style with a swing rhythm. Getting to know her music can help learners understand what is distinctive about classical and jazz, and how the two can be combined.

## Blending Classical and Jazz

Arranging a classical work in a jazz style requires being very familiar with both the melody and the harmony of the original. The player keeps the theme of the original while changing the rhythm and adding new harmonic colour, so that the piece appears in a different light.

**Listen**

For learners, you can try experiencing this blend in a simple way. For example, take a familiar melody, change the left hand to a swinging accompaniment rhythm, and listen to how the effect changes.

When learning jazz, a sense of rhythm is especially important. Listen to more jazz piano recordings, notice their groove, and then slowly try imitating it at the piano.

Getting to know musicians like Hazel Scott can also show us the variety of piano music and spark an interest in trying different styles.

## Developing a Jazz Sense of Rhythm

One key to the jazz style is a sense of rhythm, especially the swing feel.

Listen to plenty of jazz piano recordings, and notice how the rhythm flows and where the accents fall.

You can start by clapping or tapping along with a recording to feel the emphasis on beats two and four.

Then practise this rhythm at the piano with simple chords, and get used to it gradually.

Getting to know musicians like Hazel Scott shows us the variety of piano music and can spark an interest in trying different styles.

When learning a new style, be patient with yourself. The rhythm may feel awkward at first, but with more listening and practice your body will gradually find the groove.

## Blending Classical and Jazz

Arranging a classical work in a jazz style requires being very familiar with the original, including its melody, harmony and structure.

When arranging, the player usually keeps the theme of the original while changing the rhythm, for example adding a swing feel, or using richer harmony.

In this way the familiar melody appears in a new light, with the structure of classical music and the freedom of jazz.

When listening to this kind of playing, first find the melody of the original, then notice what has changed in the rhythm and harmony.

This way of listening helps us understand what is distinctive about each of the two styles.

**Try it**
- Hazel Scott was a pianist and singer
- She was known for arranging famous classical pieces in a jazz style
- In 1950 she hosted a television show under her own name
- She was born in Trinidad and moved to New York as a child

![A sketch of a golden grand piano on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8luqd7-hol0g.webp)

## Trying a Simple Arrangement Yourself

For learners, you can experience this blend in a simple way.

Choose a familiar melody, keep the original melody in the right hand, and change the left hand to an accompaniment with a swing rhythm, for example alternating bass notes and chords.

You can also change some of the even quavers (eighth notes) in the melody into a long-short swing rhythm, and listen to how the effect changes.

If you are comfortable with harmony, you can try adding the seventh to chords to give the sound more of a jazz colour.

There is no need to aim for anything complicated at first; what matters is experiencing the change of style.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend some jazz piano books suitable for beginners, starting from basic rhythms and chords and gradually building an understanding of the style.

## Biographical Overview

Hazel Scott was born in Trinidad in 1920, moved with her mother to New York in the United States as a child, and died in 1981.

She studied piano from an early age and began performing in clubs and on the radio when she was very young.

She became known for playing famous classical pieces arranged in a jazz style, and she was also a singer and actress.

In 1950 she hosted a television show under her own name, which was rare in American television at the time, so it is often mentioned in the history of television.

**Order of practice**

Her playing was relaxed and full of skill, and it left a deep impression on many listeners.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need to learn classical before learning jazz piano?**
A: Not necessarily, but a classical foundation helps with reading and technique, and the two can complement each other.

**Q: How do I start trying jazz rhythm?**
A: Start by listening to plenty of recordings, then practise the swing feel with a simple melody.

**Q: Where was Hazel Scott born?**
A: She was born in Trinidad and moved to New York in the United States as a child.

**Q: Do I need a high level to arrange classical pieces?**
A: You can start with simple rhythm changes and try more step by step.

**Q: How do I practise the swing rhythm?**
A: Start by clapping along with a recording, then practise at the piano with simple chords.

**Q: Are her recordings easy to find?**
A: Some of her recordings can be found on music platforms or in library collections.

humid-season-piano-practice.body:
In the rainy season the air is damp and muggy, and the piano, the sheet music and the hands that play are all affected: keys may feel sticky, paper goes soft and wrinkled, and fingers sweat and slip more easily. Watching the room with a hygrometer, dehumidifying moderately, keeping sheet music in a box with desiccant, and washing and drying your hands before practice are a few things that make practice in the rainy season go more smoothly.

## Planning Practice on Rainy Days

If you use a digital piano in thunderstorm weather, you can switch it off and unplug it when there is thunder, and carry on after the storm has passed.

**Watch the details**

When it rains the noise can be loud, and rain on windows or the roof can make it hard to hear details. At those times you can practise things that do not need fine listening, such as scales, rhythm or memorising.

With more time at home on rainy days, you can also use it to listen to recordings, read scores and tidy your practice notebook, making your practice richer.

## Points to Note When Dehumidifying

The aim of dehumidifying is to keep humidity steady, not to make the air as dry as possible. A large change in humidity over a short time can harm the wood more than steady dampness does.

Do not point a dehumidifier directly at the piano. The air outlet should keep some distance from the instrument.

When the rainy season ends and the weather turns dry, also take care that the room does not become too dry, and adjust how you use the equipment according to the hygrometer reading.

## Take Care of Your Sheet Music

Damp air makes paper soft, and music left for a long time may curl, wrinkle or even go mouldy.

You can lay sheet music flat in a storage box with a lid, put a packet of desiccant in the box, and replace it regularly. Put the score you are using back after use, and do not leave it open on the music stand for long periods.

If a score has already absorbed moisture and gone soft, you can place it between sheets of dry blotting paper, press it under a few books, and let it dry slowly in a ventilated place.

## Have a Professional Check It Regularly

Before and after the rainy season is a good time to check the state of the piano. A tuner can adjust tuning and touch according to the change of season, and tell you whether the piano has been affected by humidity.

If some keys clearly become sticky or stuck, or the piano makes unusual sounds, do not open it up and deal with it yourself. Contact a professional as soon as you can.

With regular observation, seasonal maintenance and a suitable room environment, the piano can stay in fairly good condition through the rainy season.

**Common mistakes**
- Use a hygrometer to find out the actual humidity of the room
- Consider dehumidifying when it stays damp for a long time
- Keep sheet music in a sealed box or a drawer with desiccant
- Wash and dry your hands before practice, and keep a dry towel by the piano

## First Find Out the Humidity of the Room

Judging humidity by feel is often inaccurate. You can put a hygrometer by the piano, look at it every day, and note the rough range.

If humidity stays high for a long time, you can use a dehumidifier or the dehumidifying function of an air conditioner to keep the air in the room fairly steady.

For the humidity range that suits your piano, you can ask the tuner at tuning time, and set it according to the condition of the instrument.

![Sketch in sepia tones of an upright piano keyboard from an angled view](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wyovb-dto7p.webp)

## How the Rainy Season Affects the Piano

The wood, felt and strings of an acoustic piano change with the humidity of the air. When humidity stays high for a long time, the wood absorbs moisture, the keys may become sticky or slower to return, and the tuning may also change.

These changes are usually gradual and do not happen overnight, but if the whole rainy season is damp, they are worth watching.

The electronic parts of a digital piano also do not like damp surroundings, and a room with high humidity over a long period needs attention as well.

## Take Care of Your Playing Hands

In hot, humid weather your hands sweat more easily. Washing them with warm water before practice and drying them thoroughly can reduce slipping on the keys.

Keep a dry towel by the piano, and wipe your hands after each piece.

**Before you start**

For practice you can choose a cooler time of day, such as early morning or evening, when the body feels comfortable and it is easier to concentrate.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I put desiccant next to the piano?**
A: You can put it in the music storage box, but we do not recommend putting it inside the piano. For moisture protection inside the piano, ask your tuner.

**Q: Is it good for the piano to run the air conditioner every day?**
A: Moderate use of an air conditioner helps steady temperature and humidity, but the air outlet should not point at the piano, and the temperature should not change sharply and often.

**Q: Do I need to tune more often in the rainy season?**
A: It depends on the piano and the room. You can ask the tuner to advise according to the actual condition.

**Q: Is a digital piano afraid of damp?**
A: Electronic equipment should not be left in damp surroundings for long either. When it is not in use, cover it with a cloth, and open the windows often to air the room.

**Q: Can I still use sheet music that has gone mouldy?**
A: Slight mould spots can be stored separately and kept dry, but for heavily mouldy music we suggest preparing a new copy.

**Q: What if my hands keep sweating and it affects my practice?**
A: Keep the room cool and ventilated, wash and dry your hands before practice, and wipe them after each piece.
