fourth-and-fifth-finger-melody-notes-sup.body:
In many pieces, the right-hand melody falls on the outer side of the hand, that is, it is played with fingers 4 and 5, while the thumb and the other fingers play an inner voice or the accompaniment. But fingers 4 and 5 are often weaker, and the melody they play can easily sound thin and unclear. To make the melody notes on fingers 4 and 5 sing, you cannot rely on finger strength alone. Let the palm and arm support them: tilt the hand slightly toward the outside, so that the weight falls onto the outer fingers.

## Listen for whether the outer-finger melody sings

When practising, use your ears to judge whether the melody sings out clearly and whether the inner voice is light enough.

**Pay attention to the details**

You can record yourself and listen back to the balance between the two voices.

If the melody is covered by the inner voice, you need to adjust again.

## Support from the palm

Keep the arch of the palm stable, especially on the side nearest fingers 4 and 5.

If the palm collapses, fingers 4 and 5 have nothing to support them, and the force cannot get through to them.

You can imagine the palm as a little bridge, holding up every finger.

**Common mistakes**
- The melody often falls on fingers 4 and 5
- The outer fingers need support from the palm and arm
- Tilt the hand slightly outward
- The inner voice should be softer than the melody

## The outer finger of the left hand

The left-hand fifth finger often plays the bass, and it needs similar support.

The bass is the foundation of the harmony, so the notes of the left-hand fifth finger should be deep and weighty.

Here too, you can tilt the hand slightly outward so the weight falls onto the fifth finger.

## Tilting the hand outward

When playing melody notes, you can tilt the hand a little toward the little finger.

That way more of the weight of the arm falls onto the outer fingers.

The tilt does not have to be large. It is enough to feel the weight shifting.

## Keep the inner voice light

Another way to bring the melody out is to play the inner voice more softly.

The notes played by the thumb and fingers 2 and 3 should be quieter than the melody.

You can first play only the inner voice and practise playing it very lightly.

## The joints of the fifth finger

When you play the melody with the fifth finger, make sure the joints of the fifth finger do not collapse.

The fifth finger can be slightly curved, touching the key with the side of the fingertip.

When the joints are stable, the sound is focused and clear.

## Do not rely on finger force alone

To make the notes of fingers 4 and 5 louder, some people press hard with these two fingers.

This easily makes the hand tense, and the sound hard.

A better way is to let the palm and arm support them.

## Keeping the melody connected

When playing a connected melody with fingers 4 and 5, you often need to alternate between these two fingers, or use finger substitution.

For example, on the same note you change from the fifth finger to the fourth, so that you can reach the next note.

These fingerings need to be worked out ahead of time to keep the melody connected.

## The melody on the outside of the hand

In many piano pieces, the right hand plays the melody and an inner voice at the same time.

The melody is often the highest voice, played with the fourth or fifth finger.

The thumb and fingers 2 and 3 play the harmony notes or accompaniment notes below.

## Fourth and fifth finger melodies in short

The right-hand melody often falls on fingers 4 and 5. These two fingers are shorter and less independent, so you cannot rely on finger strength alone. Tilt the hand slightly outward so that the weight of the arm falls onto the outer fingers, keep the arch of the palm stable, and do not let the joints of the fifth finger collapse.

Play the inner voice more lightly. You can practise the melody and inner voice separately and then put them together, use finger substitution to keep the melody connected, and do slow, relaxed outer-finger exercises from time to time. The left-hand fifth finger needs similar support when it plays the bass.

Use your ears and recordings to judge the balance between the two voices, and ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the details of hand shape in your lesson.

## Ask your teacher to look at your hand shape in the lesson

The tilt and support of the hand are subtle movements that are not easy to explain in words.

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to look at your hand shape and demonstrate how to shift the weight onto the outer fingers.

With a clear demonstration, your practice will have a better sense of direction.

## Practising the two voices separately

You can practise the melody and the inner voice separately.

First play only the melody with fingers 4 and 5 and make it sing; then play only the inner voice and practise a light touch.

Then put them together, and take care to keep the difference in dynamics between the two voices.

## Strengthening the outer fingers

From time to time you can do some exercises to strengthen fingers 4 and 5, for example patterns in a five-finger position.

While practising, keep your hand relaxed, and do not use too much force for the sake of strengthening.

Playing slowly and evenly is more helpful than playing fast and forcefully.

## Characteristics of the outer fingers

Fingers 4 and 5 are a little shorter than the other fingers, and they are also relatively less independent.

The fourth finger in particular is linked by tendons to the third and fifth fingers, so its movement is often affected by its neighbours.

So playing the melody with these two fingers needs extra attention.

A: Fingers 4 and 5.

A: Tilt the hand slightly outward so that the weight falls onto the outer fingers.

A: Keep a stable arch.

A: More softly than the melody.

A: Yes, because it often plays the bass.

Handel's Suite in D minor, HWV 437, contains a sarabande with a solemn melody and rich harmony. Today it is often played on its own and has appeared in many films and television programmes. The sarabande is a slow dance in triple time, common in Baroque suites, and its characteristic accent often falls on the second beat. This suite is included in Handel's second set of keyboard suites, published in 1733. Below we look at the features of the sarabande and the key points for playing this piece on the piano.

## The Accent on Beat Two

When you play this sarabande, pay special attention to the weight of the second beat.

In many bars there is a long note or dotted note on beat two, so the music seems to linger there.

You can count "one, two, three" as you play, giving a little extra weight and length to "two".

## Variations After the Theme

In the original suite, the theme of the sarabande is followed by two variations.

The variations keep the original harmony, but the rhythm becomes busier, with more notes.

If you find the variations too difficult, you can begin by playing only the theme.

## The Solemnity of D Minor

D minor sounds solemn and deep in this piece.

The harmony has a number of descending bass lines, which add to the sense of calm and weight.

As you play, listen to the direction of the left-hand bass and let it support the chords firmly.

## Summary of Handel's Sarabande in D Minor

Handel's Suite in D minor, HWV 437, is part of the second set of keyboard suites, published in 1733. Its sarabande is a slow dance in triple time, with the accent often on beat two.

The theme is made up of rich chords. Play them together, use the weight of the arm, let the melody at the top of the right hand float out, and let the left-hand bass give steady support.

Keep a sense of direction in the slow tempo, with moderate dynamic levels, and use the pedal sparingly, changing it cleanly. You can start by playing only the theme, then try the variations and ornaments once it is secure.

## Handling Baroque Style

Keyboard instruments of the Baroque period differed from the modern piano, and their dynamic range and sustaining power were limited.

On the modern piano you can shape several levels of loud and soft, just without the wide swings of Romantic music.

Use the pedal sparingly, mainly to join chords, and change it cleanly.

## Controlling a Slow Tempo

The sarabande is very slow, and playing slow music takes more patience than playing fast music.

Each chord must be held for its full value, and the music must not lose its direction simply because it is slow.

Imagine the phrase moving gently forward, heading towards a goal.

## Ornaments in Handel's Sarabande

Baroque music often adds ornaments on repeats, and this sarabande has the same tradition.

As a beginner, first make the theme secure, then try adding some simple ornaments with your teacher's guidance.

Ornaments must suit the style and must not disturb the accent on beat two.

## What Kind of Dance Is the Sarabande?

The sarabande is a slow dance in the Baroque suite, in triple time.

Its characteristic accent often falls on the second beat, and it sounds stately and calm.

In a suite, the sarabande usually follows the faster courante, creating a contrast in tempo.

**Summary**
- From the Suite in D minor, HWV 437
- The second set of keyboard suites, published in 1733
- Sarabande: a slow dance in triple time, with the accent often on beat two
- Rich chords, with variations after the theme

## The Sarabande on Screen

The solemn atmosphere of this sarabande has led to its frequent use in films and television.

Many people first hear it on screen, and only later learn that it comes from Handel's suite.

As you play, you can also think about why it creates such a serious mood.

## Separating the Sarabande's Chords into Voices

You can take the chords apart and practise the upper melody, the middle voice and the bass separately.

Learn each voice on its own, then put them back together.

This lets you hear more clearly where each voice in the chords is going.

## The Melody at the Top of the Chords

Although they are chords, the top note of the right hand is usually the melody.

When you play a chord, press slightly more firmly with the upper finger and the melody will float out of the chord.

You can play only the melody first, then add the chords, and compare the two sounds.

## Rich Chords

The theme of this sarabande is made up of many chords, and both hands play several notes at once.

Play the chords together, with all the notes sounding at the same moment.

You can use the weight of your arm rather than tapping with your fingers, which gives a fuller sound.

## Handel and His Keyboard Suites

Handel (1685-1759) was born in Germany and later lived and worked in London for many years.

He is best known for his operas and oratorios, but he also wrote a good deal of keyboard music.

He published two sets of keyboard suites: the first in 1720, and the second, which contains HWV 437, in 1733.

A: Beat two.

A: Together, using the weight of the arm, with the melody at the top.

A: You can begin by playing only the theme.

glenn-gould-goldberg-variations-1955.body:
In June 1955, the twenty-two-year-old Canadian pianist Glenn Gould recorded Bach's Goldberg Variations in New York, and the record, released in 1956, caused a great stir. The work consists of an aria and thirty variations, and before this very few pianists had played it complete on record. Gould's distinctive tempos and clear voices led many people to see Bach's keyboard music in a new light. In 1981 he recorded it again, with a tempo and character very different from his youth.

## The 1981 Re-Recording

In 1981, Gould recorded the Goldberg Variations again, and this version was released around the time of his death in 1982.

Compared with his youth, many of the variations are slower this time, and the opening of the aria is calmer.

Listening to the two records together is like seeing the thinking of the same performer at different stages of life.

## What Gould's Story Offers Piano Learners

Gould's story reminds us that the same piece can be played in many valid ways.

When learning, you can listen to the versions of several performers, and there is no need to imitate only one.

Building your own view of the music slowly, on the basis of understanding the score, is a very interesting part of learning the piano.

## Leaving the Stage for the Recording Studio

After 1964, Gould no longer gave public concerts, and put all his energy into recording, broadcasting and writing.

He believed the recording studio allowed a performer to refine things again and again and reach a better result.

This decision was very rare at the time, and sparked discussion about the relationship between live performance and recording.

## An Unexpected First Record

At the time, choosing such a large and not often performed work of Bach for a first record was a bold choice.

After its release the record quickly drew the attention of critics and listeners, and sold well too.

It spread Gould's name quickly, and also led more people to listen to this work.

- Recorded in New York in June 1955, released in 1956
- The work consists of an aria and thirty variations
- Gould was twenty-two at the time
- Recorded again in 1981, in a very different style

## Habits in the Recording Studio

When recording and performing, Gould often sat on a very low chair, which is said to have been adjusted for him by his father.

He would often hum along with the music as he played, and his voice can faintly be heard on some recordings.

These habits became his trademark, and made many people curious about him.

## A Personal Approach to Tempo and Rhythm

In the 1955 recording, many of the variations are fairly fast and the rhythm is full of energy.

This treatment was very different from the "solemn Bach" in many people's minds at the time, and felt fresh.

However, some people thought certain places were too fast, which shows that views on performance style itself differ.

![A person wearing headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2ctkl-ijubs.webp)

## A Young Canadian Pianist

Glenn Gould was born in Toronto, Canada, in 1932. He studied the piano from childhood and showed musical talent very early.

In his early twenties he was already giving recitals in Canada and the United States, and drew attention with his distinctive playing style.

In 1955 he signed with a record company, and for his first recording he chose Bach's Goldberg Variations.

## The Influence of Gould's Recordings

Gould died in 1982, but his recordings are still listened to and discussed by many people today.

The 1955 Goldberg Variations is often mentioned as one of the most influential classical records of the twentieth century.

It also turned this Bach work from something rarely played into a piece that many pianists are willing to take on.

## Clear Voice Lines

One thing that makes a strong impression in Gould's playing is that every voice is very clear.

Even where several voices move at the same time, the listener can tell the direction of each melody.

This clarity comes from his precise control of touch; many notes are played clean and short, with almost no pedal.

## How to Listen When Comparing the Two Versions

You can start with the opening aria, listen to the two versions one after the other, and notice the differences in tempo, tone and mood.

Then pick a few variations with clearly different characters, for example a fast one and a quiet one, and make the same comparison.

This kind of comparative listening helps learners understand how much room there can be in the interpretation of a performance.

## Voice Practice When Playing Bach

If Gould inspires you to play Bach, you can start with the easier two-part inventions.

First get each voice well learned on its own, listening for its direction, then put the two voices together.

Letting each melody be heard clearly is an important goal when playing Bach.

## What Kind of Work Are the Goldberg Variations?

The Goldberg Variations is a keyboard work by Bach, published around 1741 and originally written for a two-manual harpsichord.

The whole work consists of an aria at the beginning, thirty variations, and the aria appearing again at the end.

The variations are built on the bass and harmony of the aria, and a canon appears every few variations.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: In what year did Gould record the Goldberg Variations?**
A: He recorded it in June 1955, and it was released in 1956.

**Q: What does the work consist of?**
A: An aria and thirty variations, with the aria returning at the end.

**Q: Did he record it again later?**
A: Yes, in 1981, in a clearly different style.

**Q: What is distinctive about his playing?**
A: Clear voices, clean touch, and very individual tempos.

**Q: What can piano learners take from this?**
A: The same piece can be played in many valid ways.

grieg-morning-mood-peer-gynt-piano.body:
Grieg's Morning Mood is a melody many people recognise at once: a flute plays a simple phrase first, an oboe answers it, and the music rises like the sun, little by little. It was originally written by the Norwegian composer Grieg as incidental music for Ibsen's dramatic poem Peer Gynt, and it was first performed in February 1876 in Christiania, which is today's Oslo. Grieg later placed it in the Peer Gynt Suite No. 1 as the first piece. Today it has many piano arrangements suited to players of different levels.

## Morning Mood in Brief

Grieg's Morning Mood was originally written as incidental music for Ibsen's dramatic poem Peer Gynt. It was first performed in February 1876 and depicts a morning in Morocco in the play; it later became the first piece of Suite No. 1.

In the orchestral version, a flute and an oboe answer each other at the start, and the melody rises and falls in 6/8 time, gradually building to a climax like the sun coming up.

Choose a piano arrangement to suit your level. As you play, feel the sway of two big beats, keep the left-hand accompaniment light, grow to the climax with a crescendo and then return to calm, and change the pedal with the chords.

## The Dialogue of Flute and Oboe

In the original orchestral version, the opening melody is played first by the flute and then taken up by the oboe.

The two instruments take turns with the same phrase, like two voices answering each other in the morning light.

On the piano, you can try to show the two instruments with different tone colours: a lighter touch for the flute, and something a little rounder for the oboe.

## The Composer Grieg

Edvard Grieg was a Norwegian composer and pianist, born in 1843 and died in 1907.

His music often carries the colour of Norwegian folk music, with fresh melodies and delicate harmony.

Besides Peer Gynt, he also wrote a piano concerto and ten books of Lyric Pieces.

## Keep the Left Hand Light

In piano arrangements, the left hand often plays a sustained bass or broken chords.

This accompaniment should be light and even, supporting the melody like morning mist.

If the right-hand melody comes out a little more, the two hands will have layers of sound.

## Dynamics at the Climax

When you reach the climax, you can gradually increase the dynamics to make the sound fuller.

As you build, use the weight of your arm and keep your wrist relaxed, so that the sound does not suddenly become very loud.

After the climax, remember to bring the dynamics back slowly, to the quiet feeling of the opening.

## The Shape of the Melody

The melody of Morning Mood is in E major and 6/8 time, moving up and down among a few notes like gently rocking waves.

The phrases are short and easy to remember, which is one reason the piece is so well known.

Before playing, hum it a few times and feel how each phrase rises and falls in an arc.

## From Incidental Music to Suite

After the play's performances, Grieg chose several pieces from the music and arranged them into two orchestral suites.

Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, Op. 46, was published in 1888, and Morning Mood is its first piece.

Freed from the drama, the suite could be performed on its own in concerts, which helped Morning Mood spread more widely.

## Ibsen's Peer Gynt

Peer Gynt is a dramatic poem by the Norwegian playwright Ibsen, telling of the wanderings of its hero, Peer Gynt.

To bring the poem to the stage, Ibsen asked Grieg to write the music.

Grieg wrote more than twenty pieces of music, which were first performed with the play on 24 February 1876.

## Music Like a Rising Sun

As the piece develops, the melody keeps moving into new keys and the sound of the orchestra grows fuller and fuller.

At the climax, the whole orchestra plays the theme together, as if the sun had fully risen and its light filled the land.

After that the music slowly calms, and the ending returns to a quiet mood.

## Whose Morning Is It?

Many people think Morning Mood depicts a sunrise over a Norwegian fjord, but in the play it appears at the start of Act IV.

At that point Peer Gynt is in Morocco, in North Africa, and the music depicts the morning there.

Even so, the fresh quality of the music leads many listeners to think of Nordic natural scenery.

## Pedalling in Morning Mood

The harmony of Morning Mood is broad and suits the pedal, which joins the sound together.

Change the pedal every time the chord changes, to avoid the harmonies before and after blurring together.

Where the melody moves by step, also take care that the pedal does not turn the notes into a smudge.

## Choosing a Piano Arrangement

Morning Mood has many piano arrangements, from easy versions for beginners to harder concert versions.

Beginners' versions usually keep only the melody and simple chords, and suit learners who have just learned to read music.

When choosing an arrangement of Morning Mood, pick one you can play through comfortably, with energy left over to care about tone.

- Written by Grieg for Ibsen's dramatic poem Peer Gynt
- First performed in February 1876 in what is now Oslo
- Later became the first piece of Suite No. 1
- Many piano arrangements exist

## The Flow of 6/8

The 6/8 of Morning Mood should be felt in two big beats, like a small boat rocking gently from side to side on the water.

In each group of three small notes, the first one stands a little firmer and the other two glide along after it like ripples.

This is how the melody gets its flowing feeling, like a morning breeze.

## Getting to Know Grieg Through the Lyric Pieces

If you like Morning Mood, you can go on to Grieg's piano works, the Lyric Pieces.

These pieces are short and varied in style, and many suit intermediate learners.

**Something to think about**

From incidental music to piano miniatures, you get a fuller picture of Grieg's musical style.

## FAQ

A: It is from the incidental music to Ibsen's dramatic poem Peer Gynt.

**Q: When was the music first performed?**
A: In February 1876, in what is now Oslo.

**Q: Whose morning does it depict?**
A: A morning in Morocco, in North Africa, in the play.

**Q: Which suite is it the first piece of?**
A: Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, Op. 46.

**Q: Which two instruments answer each other at the start of the original?**
A: The flute and the oboe.

gossec-gavotte-rosine-1786.body:
Gossec's Gavotte is a little piece familiar to many people who learn the violin and piano. It comes from Rosine, an opera of 1786 by the French composer François-Joseph Gossec. Almost nobody stages the opera today, but its light gavotte has been arranged for all kinds of instruments and often turns up in beginners' teaching books. Gossec was born in what is now Belgium and later worked in Paris. He lived to the age of ninety-five, lived through the French Revolution, and wrote a great deal of music for the large celebrations of the revolutionary period.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Gavotte's Upbeat

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your upbeat and staccato are light.

**Summary**

Your teacher can also help you practise how to play the ornaments.

From this little dance, practise a light style and a clear touch.

## Gossec's Gavotte on the Piano

To play this gavotte on the piano, the right hand plays the melody and the left hand plays a simple accompaniment.

The staccato in the right hand should be light and clear, and the ornaments quick and natural.

The left hand simply accompanies the dancers, with light steps, letting the gavotte's melody go in front.

## The Gavotte for Violin and Piano

This gavotte is very good for playing together with a violin.

If you have a friend who is learning the violin, one of you can play the melody and the other accompany on the piano.

One bows and one plays, and both of you have to keep your ears open.

## Gossec's Gavotte: A Summary

François-Joseph Gossec was born in 1734 and died in 1829, living to the age of ninety-five. He was born in a village in what is now Belgium and came to Paris as a young man. He wrote dozens of symphonies and is an important author of early French symphonies. After the Revolution he wrote choral and wind music for outdoor performance at the large celebrations, and he helped found the Paris Conservatoire. His 1786 opera Rosine is rarely performed today, but the gavotte from it has been handed down.

The gavotte is a duple-time dance of French origin that often enters on the third beat. This gavotte has a light, playful melody with staccato and ornaments, and a contrasting section in the middle, and it often appears in beginners' teaching books. On the piano the right-hand staccato should be light; the first two notes are an upbeat; staccato and legato must be clearly distinguished; the ornaments can be left out at first and added later; and it is very good for playing together with a violin.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your upbeat and staccato.

## The Gavotte in Teaching Books

This gavotte has a simple, pleasant melody and is of moderate difficulty, which makes it very suitable for beginners.

Many beginners' teaching books for violin and piano include this piece.

Many students have played it in their first year or two of learning.

![A blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaevl0c-9mgqe.webp)

## What Is a Gavotte?

The gavotte is a dance of French origin, in duple time, at a moderate tempo with a light rhythm.

Its phrases usually set off from the middle of a bar; in four beats, that means coming in on the third beat.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the gavotte often appeared in suites and operas.

## Starting on the Third Beat

When playing this gavotte, remember that it starts in the middle of the bar.

The first two notes are an upbeat, and they should be brought lightly into the first beat of the next bar.

Each phrase also often starts in the middle of a bar, so find the starting point of each phrase accurately.

## A Forerunner of the Symphony

Gossec wrote dozens of symphonies and is an important author of early French symphonies.

In his time the symphony as a genre was still developing.

His work had some influence on the development of French symphonic music.

## Staccato and Legato in the Gavotte

In this piece there are staccato notes and legato notes.

Staccato should be short and light, and legato connected and flowing.

Look carefully at the markings in the score, and tell the two ways of playing apart.

- The opera is rarely staged today, yet the gavotte is widely known

## The Opera Rosine

In 1786, Gossec wrote an opera called Rosine.

Rosine has almost vanished from the stage today, and its name is rarely mentioned.

But one gavotte dance from it has been handed down.

## Ornaments in the Gavotte

There are some ornaments in the piece, such as the grace note and the turn.

Ornaments should be played quickly and lightly, without affecting the rhythm of the main melody.

You can leave out the ornaments at first, get the melody well learned, and then add the ornaments.

## Music of the French Revolution

After the French Revolution broke out in 1789, Gossec wrote music for many of the large celebrations of the revolutionary period.

This music was often written for large choruses and wind bands, and was played outdoors.

He also took part in founding what later became the Paris Conservatoire, where he taught.

## The Melody of Gossec's Gavotte

The melody of Gossec's gavotte is light and playful, with many leaping notes.

The melody often has short staccato notes and ornaments, like light dance steps.

In the middle there is a contrasting section, and then the theme comes back again.

## Who Was Gossec?

François-Joseph Gossec was born in 1734 and died in 1829, living to the age of ninety-five.

He was born in a village in what is now Belgium and came to Paris as a young man.

**Common mistake**

In Paris he wrote many symphonies, operas and sacred pieces, and was a very important French composer of his time.

**Q: Which opera is Gossec's Gavotte from?**
A: Rosine, of 1786.

**Q: How old did Gossec live to be?**
A: Ninety-five.

harmonic-rhythm-how-often-chords-change.body:
In a piece of music, the chords sometimes change several times in a bar and sometimes stay the same for several bars. How fast the chords change is called harmonic rhythm. It is different from the rhythm of the melody: the melody may be busy while the chords change slowly, or the melody may be slow while the chords change quickly. Paying attention to harmonic rhythm helps us understand the structure and mood of a piece, and makes our accompaniment more fitting.

## Harmonic Rhythm in Pop Songs

Many pop songs have a fairly regular harmonic rhythm, for example one chord per bar or one chord every two bars.

**Notice the details**

The chorus sometimes speeds up the harmonic rhythm to lift the mood.

When you listen to a song, try clapping along with the chord changes to feel the harmonic rhythm.

**Common misconception**
- How fast the chords change is the harmonic rhythm
- It is different from the rhythm of the melody
- It often speeds up before a cadence
- It affects the mood and structure of a piece

## Harmonic Rhythm and the Sense of Tempo

Interestingly, harmonic rhythm affects how fast we feel the music to be.

Even if the tempo stays the same, music sounds faster when the chords change quickly and more unhurried when they change slowly.

Composers often use this to change the atmosphere of the music without changing the tempo.

![An illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, expressing the power of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5h6iw-z322u.webp)

## Slow Harmonic Rhythm

When the chords change slowly, the music feels steady and broad, and sometimes seems to float.

In many lyrical slow pieces, a chord is often held for a long time, so that the melody can unfold slowly above it.

In such cases, the pedal can also be held longer.

## Fast Harmonic Rhythm

When the chords change quickly, the music feels tense and driven.

At the climax or ending of some pieces, for example, the chord may change on every beat or even every half beat.

A speeding-up of the harmonic rhythm often makes listeners feel the music is heading somewhere important.

## Different from Melodic Rhythm

The rhythm of the melody is the length of each note, while harmonic rhythm is the length of each chord, and the two are not necessarily the same.

For example, the right hand of an étude may play fast semiquavers (sixteenth notes) throughout, while the chord changes only once a bar.

Telling the two rhythms apart helps us see the skeleton of the piece.

## Speeding Up Before a Cadence

In a lot of classical music, the harmonic rhythm speeds up as a cadence approaches.

For example, the earlier bars may have one chord per bar, and then before the end it becomes one chord every two beats, before landing on the tonic chord.

This speeding-up makes the ending more powerful, and tells the listener that a section is about to close.

## Summary: Harmonic Rhythm

Harmonic rhythm is how fast the chords change. It is different from the rhythm of the melody, and it can keep changing within a piece.

A slow harmonic rhythm feels steady and broad, a fast one brings tension and drive, and it often speeds up as a cadence approaches.

Noticing harmonic rhythm helps us analyse sections, use the pedal and arrange accompaniments.

## How to Find the Harmonic Rhythm

When analysing a score, you can start by looking at the bass in the left hand; where the bass changes is often where the chord changes.

Then look at the notes above to confirm whether the chord has really changed.

Mark how many beats each chord lasts in the score, and you can see the harmonic rhythm clearly.

## Harmonic Rhythm and the Pedal

Understanding harmonic rhythm is very helpful for pedalling.

Generally, the pedal needs to change when the chord changes, and it can be held when the chord stays the same.

So where the harmonic rhythm is slow, the pedal can be longer; where it is fast, the pedal needs to change more often.

## Harmonic Rhythm and Accompaniment

Harmonic rhythm also matters when you arrange an accompaniment for a song.

If the chords change too fast, the accompaniment will feel busy and chaotic; if they change too slowly, it may not fit the melody.

A good starting point is one chord per bar, then speed up in certain places according to what the melody needs.

## Practising Feeling the Harmonic Rhythm

You can choose a familiar piece and play only the bass line in the left hand, listening for when the chords change.

Then tap out the places where the chords change with your hand on a table, and see whether there is a pattern.

This kind of practice helps us become more sensitive to the flow of the harmony.

## Finding Sections with Harmonic Rhythm

Changes in harmonic rhythm are often connected with the sections of a piece.

When a new section begins, the harmonic rhythm may slow down; when a section is about to end, it may speed up.

When analysing a piece, noticing changes in harmonic rhythm can help us find where the sections divide.

## What Harmonic Rhythm Means

Harmonic rhythm refers to how frequently the chords change, that is, how long each chord lasts.

If the chord changes every bar, the harmonic rhythm is one change per bar; if it changes every beat, it is one change per beat.

Harmonic rhythm can keep changing within a piece.

## FAQ

**Q: What is harmonic rhythm?**
A: How fast the chords change.

**Q: Is it the same as melodic rhythm?**
A: No, the two can be very different.

**Q: How does harmonic rhythm often change before a cadence?**
A: It speeds up.

**Q: How do I find the harmonic rhythm?**
A: Start by looking at where the bass in the left hand changes.

**Q: How are harmonic rhythm and the pedal related?**
A: Change the pedal when the chord changes; where the rhythm is slow, the pedal can be longer.

graphic-notation-when-notes-not-enough.body:
Graphic notation is a way of writing music down using lines, shapes, colours and positions in space to represent sound. Standard staff notation is good at recording definite pitches and rhythms, but some music is concerned with the texture, density and process of change in sound, such as a cloud of sound that slowly thickens, a slow glide, or a passage left open for improvisation. In such cases, composers draw pictures, and performers work out what to do from the height, thickness and length of the shapes. Graphic notation is not meant to replace staff notation; it offers another way of communicating where the five-line staff cannot express something.

## The Strengths and Limits of Staff Notation

Staff notation can tell a performer precisely which note to play, how long to play it and when, which matters a great deal for works that need many players or repeated performances. Its limit is that it assumes music is made of separate individual notes.

When a composer wants to express "sound slowly changing from very sparse to very dense", or "pitch rising and falling like waves, where the exact notes do not matter", staff notation becomes clumsy, filled with detail, and the performer may still not grasp the overall feeling. Graphic notation exists to resolve this contradiction.

## Common Shapes and What They Mean

Graphic notation has no single set of rules used all over the world, and each composer usually adds an explanation before the score. Still, some ways of drawing are fairly common, and readers can first get to know their general meaning.

- Left to right usually stands for the flow of time.
- The higher the vertical position, the higher the pitch, usually.
- The thicker the line or the darker the colour, the stronger or denser the sound often is.
- A wavy line may mean pitch rising and falling, or a trembling.
- Scattered small dots are like occasional short notes.
- A large patch of shading may mean many notes sounding at once.

**The explanation page matters more than the shapes**
The same dot may be a short note in one score and a tap in another. The first step in reading graphic notation is always to read the composer's instructions carefully.

![A piano studio lit up at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8ai63o-kz2pj.webp)

## The Timeline: A Framework That Leaves Room for Freedom

Many graphic scores draw a timeline above or below the page, marking approximate seconds or sections. Performers can decide the details freely, but must complete a certain change within the stated time range. This keeps room for improvisation while letting several players roughly line up.

Another approach uses arrows and boxes to show order: play the box on the left first, then choose the next step according to the arrows. The route a performer takes may differ each time, so the piece sounds different every time.

## How Performers Read a Graphic Score

Faced with a graphic score, a performer first has to "translate" the shapes into the language of their own instrument. On the piano, a thick line sloping upwards can become a run of notes sliding from the low register to the high; a patch of shading can be played by pressing many neighbouring keys with the palm or forearm; sparse small dots can be played as very light single notes.

**One score, different answers**
Graphic notation accepts many reasonable interpretations. When two pianists play the same graphic score, the sound may be very different, and as long as both respect the direction, density and timing of the shapes, both are valid performances.

## Playing with Graphic Notation in Class

Graphic notation is very well suited to early music education because it does not require knowing the staff first. A teacher can first let children listen to a sound and ask them to draw it, or the other way round, first draw a picture and ask children to perform it on the piano, by clapping or with their voices.

- Draw a wavy line and let students follow the ups and downs with their voices.
- Use dots of different sizes to represent notes of different strengths.
- Have two students each read one line of shapes to experience a simple ensemble.

Activities like this help children connect "the shapes they see" with "the sounds they hear", and when they later learn the staff, it is easier to understand the up and down of pitch and the before and after of time.
## Graphic Notation and Improvisation

Graphic notation is often discussed together with improvisation, but the two are not quite the same. Pure improvisation has almost no written prompts, and the performer plays freely according to how they feel at that moment; graphic notation gives a broad framework of direction, density and timing, and the performer makes choices within it. You could say graphic notation is a kind of "guided freedom". For learners used to playing note by note from the staff, starting with graphic notation is often easier than facing a blank sheet of paper when approaching improvisation, because the shapes give a starting point and show which way to go first.

## FAQ

**Q: Does graphic notation have a standard answer?**
A: Generally there is no fixed answer, but you should respect the composer's instructions and the basic direction of the shapes.

**Q: Do I still need to learn staff notation after learning graphic notation?**
A: Yes. They serve different purposes, and staff notation is still an important tool for learning and playing in ensembles.

**Q: Is graphic notation used only in modern music?**
A: It appears mainly in modern works and improvised music, and is also often used in early music education and creative classes.

**Q: Can I design my own graphic score?**
A: Yes. Remember to write a clear explanation so that performers know what each shape stands for.

keyboard-role-in-a-band.body:
Unlike playing solo, when you play keyboard in a band you are not the only one responsible for harmony and rhythm: the bass takes care of the low notes, the guitar is also playing chords, and the drummer holds the rhythm. If the keyboard still plays like a solo, with the left hand on bass and the right hand playing full chords, the sound overlaps with everyone else and gets crowded. A better approach is to play little or no bass with your left hand, keep chords in the middle and upper register, use mostly simple rhythm patterns, leave space for the other instruments, and keep listening to the drums and bass.

## Simple Rhythm Patterns

In a band, the keyboard's rhythm patterns do not need to be complicated. Simple and clear matters more.

For example, you might hold a single long chord for a bar, or just tap a short chord on beats two and four.

Leave the complicated rhythms to the drummer. The keyboard only needs to lock in with the drums.

## Band Keyboard Summary

Playing keyboard in a band means shifting from solo thinking to ensemble thinking.

Play less bass, put chords in the middle and upper register, keep the rhythm simple, keep listening to the drums and bass, and leave space.

Play a little less and listen a little more, and the band will sound better.

## Balancing the Volume

The keyboard's volume needs to be balanced with the whole band. It should not be so loud that it covers the other instruments, or so quiet that it cannot be heard.

At rehearsal, you can ask someone to stand out front and listen, to see whether the volume of each instrument is right.

Adjust the keyboard's volume and the way you play based on their feedback.

## Choosing the Right Sound

In a band, the keyboard does not have to use only a piano sound. You can also use an electric piano, an organ or a string pad.

Different sounds suit different songs and sections.

You can try them out with your bandmates to find the sound that suits the song.

**Take it slowly**
- In a band, the bass, guitar and drums share the work
- Play little or no bass with your left hand
- Keep chords in the middle and upper register
- Listen to the drums and bass, and leave space

## Do Not Overlap with the Bass

In a band, the bass takes care of the low notes. If the keyboard's left hand also plays in the low register, it will overlap with the bass.

When two sets of low notes are mixed together, the sound becomes muddy and the notes may even clash.

So in a band, the keyboard's left hand often plays little bass, or none at all.

## Leaving Space

In a band, sometimes not playing is a choice too.

For example, while the singer is singing, the keyboard can play very little, adding just a touch of filler between phrases.

Leaving space makes the singer and the other instruments clearer.

![An illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with an elevated train line](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3z0r7-dky62.webp)

## Staying Out of the Guitar's Way

The guitar often plays chords too. If the keyboard and guitar use the same register and rhythm, the sound is doubled.

You can talk with the guitarist. For example, the guitar strums while the keyboard holds long pad notes, or the guitar plays broken chords while the keyboard plays short, crisp chords.

This division of roles gives the band's sound more layers.

## Communicate at Rehearsals

At band rehearsals, talk with the other members and discuss who is responsible for what in each song.

For example, the keyboard plays the intro, pads under the chorus, and the guitar takes a solo in the instrumental break.

A clear division of roles makes the band play more tightly together.

## Choosing Chord Inversions

When you play chords in a band, choosing a suitable inversion makes the connection between chords smoother.

For example, keep the top note of the chords in a similar place so that it forms a steady line.

This smooth chord voice leading sounds more comfortable in a band.

## Solo versus Ensemble

When playing solo, the piano is responsible for melody, harmony and rhythm: the left hand plays the bass, and the right hand plays the melody and chords.

In a band, these jobs are shared among different instruments, and each player takes only part of them.

So a keyboard player needs to adjust the way they play and find their place in the band.

## Keep Listening to the Drums and Bass

When you play in a band, keep listening to the drums and bass. They are the foundation of the whole band's rhythm and harmony.

Your chords need to fit with the bass notes, and your rhythm needs to match the drummer's groove.

If you focus only on your own part, it is easy to lose touch with the band.

## Keyboard Fills in a Band

Between the phrases of a song there is often a gap of a beat or two, and the keyboard can play a short fill there.

For example, a simple rising figure or a decorative chord.

Fills should be short and soft, and should not cover the singer's next line.

## Chords in the Middle and Upper Register

Putting chords in the middle register or slightly higher avoids the main range of the bass and guitar.

That gives the keyboard its own place in the sound, so it does not get crowded in with the other instruments.

You can try putting chords around middle C or a little higher.

## FAQ

**Q: Should my left hand play bass in a band?**
A: Usually play little or none, to avoid overlapping with the bass.

**Q: Which register should I put chords in?**
A: The middle register or slightly higher.

**Q: Do the rhythm patterns need to be complicated?**
A: Simple and clear matters more.

**Q: Which instruments should I listen to?**
A: Keep listening to the drums and bass.

**Q: Is it fine not to play?**
A: Yes, leaving space is a choice too.

keep-piano-out-of-direct-sunlight.body:
Many families like to put the piano by a window, where the light is good and playing is a pleasure. However, if sunlight shines directly on the piano for long periods, it can cause some problems: the wood heats up, the finish fades, and the strings and parts are affected by changes in temperature. A piano is an instrument made of many materials, including wood, metal and felt, and it is quite sensitive to its surroundings. When placing a piano, paying attention to where the sun falls can help keep it in better condition.

## Keeping a Piano Out of the Sun in Summary

A piano is made of wood, metal, felt and other materials and is sensitive to its environment. Long hours of direct sun can make the wood heat up and dry out and the finish fade, and repeated changes in temperature can also affect the tuning.

Before placing it, you can observe the path of the sun, shade it with curtains or a cover, keep it away from heaters and air conditioners, and watch the humidity. An upright piano can stand against an inside wall with a gap behind it, and a digital piano should also avoid direct sun.

Avoiding the sun does not mean putting it in a dark place, since playing needs soft light. Have a tuner check it regularly, reconsider the position when you move house and use professionals to move it, and talk to Teacher Aum if you have any questions.

## When Moving House or Changing Position

If you are moving house or changing the position of the piano, you can use the chance to reconsider where to place it.

It is best to ask professionals to move a piano, because pianos are very heavy and easily damaged in transit.

Once it is in its new place, let the piano "settle in" for a while before asking a tuner to tune it.

## What a Piano Is Made Of

A piano is made of wood, metal, felt, leather and many other materials.

The soundboard, case, keys and other parts are mostly wood, while the strings and the iron plate are metal.

These materials react differently to changes in temperature and humidity, which is why a piano is sensitive to its environment.

![A watercolour painting of a grand piano with its lid open, in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9bqz3-ny645.webp)

## Observing the Path of the Sun

Before placing the piano, you can first observe where the sun falls in the room.

At different times of day the sun reaches different places, and in different seasons its angle changes too.

Choose a position where the sun will not shine directly for long periods.

## Position Against a Wall

An upright piano is often placed against a wall, and you can choose an inside wall rather than an outside wall.

An outside wall is more affected by the temperature outdoors, while the temperature of an inside wall is relatively stable.

Leaving a small gap between the piano and the wall helps air circulate.

## Talking with Your Teacher

If you find that the tuning of the piano changes quickly, or the keys are not very responsive, you can talk with Teacher Aum.

Your teacher can help judge whether it is related to the environment, and suggest whether a tuner should be called to check it.

When you take good care of the piano, practising feels better too.

## Shading with Curtains

If the piano can only go by the window, you can draw the curtains when the sun is strong.

A thin voile curtain can also soften the direct sun.

When you are not playing, you can also cover the piano with a cover.

## The Effects of Direct Sun

When sunlight shines directly on a piano for a long time, the parts it falls on get hotter.

Wood that heats up may dry out, and over time it may warp or crack.

The finish on the surface of the piano may also fade or change colour because of ultraviolet light.

## Humidity Matters Too

Besides temperature, changes in humidity also have a big effect on a piano.

If it is too damp, the keys may become sluggish, and if it is too dry, the wood may crack.

You can put a hygrometer in the room to watch changes in humidity.

## Light and Playing

Avoiding direct sun does not mean the piano must be put somewhere very dark.

When playing you need enough light to read the score, and you can use the natural light of the room or a desk lamp.

The light of a lamp should be soft, shine on the music, and not directly into your eyes.

## Keep Away from Heaters and Air Conditioners

Besides sunlight, radiators and air-conditioner vents can also cause large temperature changes around a piano.

A piano should not face these devices directly.

Air from an air conditioner blowing straight onto the piano may also dry out the wood.

**Keep this in mind**
- Avoid long periods of direct sun on the piano
- Sun can heat the wood and fade the finish
- Temperature changes may affect the tuning
- You can use curtains or adjust the position

## Have a Tuner Check It Regularly

Wherever the piano is placed, it needs regular tuning and maintenance.

When tuning, the tuner can also help check the condition of the piano, to see whether there are any problems caused by the environment.

You can also ask the tuner which place in your home suits a piano.

## Temperature Changes and Tuning

When sun shines on the piano its temperature rises, and when the sun leaves it falls again.

This repeated change in temperature may affect the tension of the strings and make the tuning unstable.

So a piano standing in the sun may need to be tuned more often.

## Digital Pianos Need Care Too

Although a digital piano has no strings, its case and electronic components are also unsuited to long periods of direct sun.

High temperatures may affect the electronics, and sun may also fade the case.

**Practice order**

So a digital piano can be placed following the same principles.

## FAQ

**Q: What effect does direct sun have on a piano?**
A: The wood heats up and dries out, the finish fades, and the tuning may be affected.

**Q: What if the piano can only go by the window?**
A: Shade it with curtains, and cover it with a cover when you are not playing.

**Q: What else should I avoid besides sunlight?**
A: Radiators and air-conditioner vents.

**Q: Which wall suits an upright piano?**
A: An inside wall.

**Q: Does a digital piano need to avoid the sun?**
A: Yes.

l-istesso-tempo-meter-change.body:
In some pieces the time signature changes partway through, for example from 2/4 to 6/8. At that point the score sometimes carries the Italian term l’istesso tempo, which means "the same speed". It tells the player that although the time signature has changed, the length of each beat stays the same. For example, a quarter note in 2/4 equals a dotted quarter note in 6/8. Understanding this term helps us keep the music flowing smoothly when the time signature changes.

## Why we need this term

When the time signature changes, players may be unsure whether the note values stay the same or the length of the beat stays the same.

**Listen**

For example, when 2/4 changes to 6/8, does a quarter note equal a quarter note, or does a quarter note equal a dotted quarter note?

L’istesso tempo states clearly that the length of the beat stays the same.

## From 3/4 to 2/4

L’istesso tempo can also be used when the number of beats changes, for example from 3/4 to 2/4.

Here the length of each quarter note stays the same, and only the number of beats per bar changes from three to two.

When playing, keep the speed of the quarter note steady.

## Practising time signature changes

When practising a time signature change, you can first use the metronome to tick the speed of the main beat.

Keep the metronome speed the same before and after the change, and change only how each beat is divided.

For example, first count "one-and, two-and", then "one two three, two two three".

## Telling it apart from other tempo changes

L’istesso tempo is different from a tempo: a tempo returns to the original speed after a change of tempo.

L’istesso tempo, on the other hand, keeps the speed of the beat unchanged when the time signature changes.

Both have to do with tempo, but they are used in different situations.

## Finding l’istesso tempo in a piece

In pieces that switch time signatures back and forth, l’istesso tempo and note equations appear especially often.

You can look through the piece you are learning for places where the time signature changes and see whether there is such a marking.

If there is no marking, think about what the composer intended.

## L’istesso tempo summary

L’istesso tempo means "the same speed". It appears where the time signature changes and shows that the length of each beat stays the same. For example, when 2/4 becomes 6/8, a quarter note equals a dotted quarter note: the main beat stays the same, and the division within each beat changes from two to three.

Composers sometimes write a note equation directly, which means the same thing. It is different from a tempo, which returns to the original speed, and it can also be used when the number of beats changes. In theme and variations it is often used to keep the tempo connected.

When practising, use the metronome to hold the main beat, or clap out the main beat and the divisions with your hands. You can write the note equation in the score, and you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the tempo at the point where the time signature changes.

## Clapping the rhythm by hand

You can also step away from the piano first and clap the rhythm before and after the time signature change.

Clap the main beat with one hand and the divisions within each beat with the other.

Once you are comfortable, go back to the piano and play it.

## How to write a note equation

Sometimes the composer does not write l’istesso tempo but writes a note equation directly.

For example, at the point where the time signature changes, you might see "quarter note = dotted quarter note".

This way of writing it is more direct and means the same as l’istesso tempo.

## What l’istesso tempo means

L’istesso tempo is Italian for "the same speed".

It usually appears where the time signature changes.

It tells the player that in the new time signature, each beat is as long as before.

## Asking your teacher to listen to the change in a lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and check whether your tempo stays steady at the point where the time signature changes.

Your teacher can also help explain how to understand the change of time signature when there is no marking.

How you handle the tempo at a time signature change matters a great deal for the continuity of the music.

## Use in theme and variations

In a set of variations, different variations often use different time signatures.

Sometimes the composer writes l’istesso tempo so that the speed stays connected from one variation to the next.

This makes the whole set of variations sound more unified.

- It means "the same speed"
- When the time signature changes, the length of each beat stays the same
- For example, a quarter note equals a dotted quarter note
- Sometimes it is shown with a note equation

## From 2/4 to 6/8

In 2/4, one beat is a quarter note, holding two eighth notes.

6/8 also has two beats per bar, but each beat is a dotted quarter note, divided into three eighth notes.

Under l’istesso tempo, the length of the quarter note equals the length of the dotted quarter note, so the eighth notes in each beat become busier.

![A person wearing headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab4wfe-ml0t3.webp)

## A reminder in the score

If the l’istesso tempo in the score is easy to miss, you can write the note equation beside it in pencil.

For example, write "quarter note = dotted quarter note".

With this small note, your hands won’t panic at the moment the time signature changes.

## What it sounds like

In a change like this, the pulse of the beat stays the same, but the division within each beat changes from two to three.

It sounds as if "one two, one two" has become "one two three, one two three", while the speed of the main beat stays the same.

**Tip**

This change turns the rhythmic feel of the music from steady to flowing.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does l’istesso tempo mean?**
A: The same speed.

**Q: Where does it usually appear?**
A: Where the time signature changes.

**Q: What is equal when 2/4 changes to 6/8?**
A: A quarter note equals a dotted quarter note.

**Q: How is it different from a tempo?**
A: A tempo returns to the original speed, while l’istesso tempo keeps the speed of the beat when the time signature changes.

**Q: What do composers sometimes use instead?**
A: A note equation.

lament-bass-descending-tetrachord.body:
When expressing sorrow, Baroque composers often used a fixed bass line: starting on the tonic and descending step by step through four notes to the dominant, for example D, C, B♭, A in D minor. This bass is often called the "lament bass" or the "descending tetrachord". Sometimes it is filled in with semitones, becoming a chromatic descent of D, C♯, C, B, B♭, A, which sounds even sadder. It is often repeated over and over while the melody above keeps changing.

## The chromatic version

Another version descends chromatically, passing through every semitone from tonic to dominant, for example D, C♯, C, B, B♭, A.

The semitone descent makes the music sound more anguished and tense.

This version is often used in works expressing deep grief.

![A colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8or8o-6u8o5.webp)

## What is a tetrachord

A tetrachord is a segment of a scale made up of four adjacent notes, spanning a perfect fourth.

The lament bass is a descending tetrachord from the tonic to the dominant.

In a minor key such as D minor, it is D, C, B♭, A.

## Purcell’s example

In the opera Dido and Aeneas by the English composer Purcell, Dido’s Lament is a famous example.

The bass of this aria is a chromatic descending tetrachord, repeated many times.

The melody above is sorrowful and deeply felt, and is often considered one of the most moving passages in Baroque vocal music.

- Four notes descending from tonic to dominant
- Often used by Baroque composers to express sorrow
- There is also a chromatic version
- Often used as a repeating ground bass

## Playing the lament bass at the piano

With your left hand, play D, C, B♭, A in D minor, two beats on each note, and repeat several times.

With your right hand, you can start with simple chords, such as D minor, C major or an inversion of A minor, B♭ major and A major.

Then try the chromatic version and compare the two colours.

## The natural scale version

One common version is the descent along the natural scale, for example D, C, B♭, A in D minor.

Each step is a whole tone or a semitone, and it sounds steady and heavy.

It is often paired with simple chords to form a repeating harmonic cycle.

## As a ground bass

The lament bass is often used as a ground bass, repeated again and again.

The bass does not change, while the melody and harmony above it keep changing.

This kind of writing is closely related to variation forms such as the passacaglia and the chaconne.

## Bach’s examples

Bach also often used descending chromatic basses to express sorrow.

For example, in some of his cantatas and Mass settings there are choral passages built on a chromatically descending bass.

These passages are solemn and deep, with the descending bass running all the way through.

## Lament bass summary

The lament bass is a bass line that descends four notes from the tonic to the dominant. In D minor it is D, C, B♭, A, and there is also a chromatic version. Baroque composers often used it to express sorrow.

It is often used as a repeating ground bass and is closely related to the passacaglia and the chaconne. Dido’s Lament from Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas is a famous example.

It is still common in later music and in pop songs, and it is related to the Andalusian cadence. At the piano you can play the bass, add chords and improvise over it.

## Improvising a melody above it

Once the bass is familiar, you can let your left hand repeat the lament bass while your right hand tries to improvise a melody.

The melody can use the notes of D minor, or C♯ over the A major chord.

Try to make the melody a little different each time, and feel what variation is like.

## The link with the Andalusian cadence

In the Andalusian cadence, A minor, G, F, E, the bass is exactly a descending tetrachord from tonic to dominant.

So you can think of the Andalusian cadence as the lament bass with a particular set of chords.

Both have a sad, sinking feeling.

## Why it is called a lament

In the Baroque period, this descending bass often appeared in vocal works expressing grief and parting.

The bass walks downward step by step, like a sigh or heavy footsteps.

That is why later generations called it the "lament bass".

## Hearing the lament bass

When listening to music, if the bass walks downward step by step, covers four notes and then returns to the beginning, it is very likely a lament bass.

You can try singing along with the bass and counting how many steps it descends.

The more Baroque works and pop songs you listen to, the more sensitive your ear will become.

## Let the line of the lament bass keep sighing

When playing a piece with a lament bass, make the bass line clear and connected, like a continuous sigh.

With each repetition, you can vary the dynamics and tone colour a little.

The melody above should sing, but it should not cover the presence of the bass.

## In later music

After the Baroque, composers of every generation continued to use this descending bass.

In Classical and Romantic works, and in many pop songs, you can hear a bass line descending from tonic to dominant.

**Practice order**

It has become a common device for expressing sadness.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Where does the lament bass descend from and to?**
A: From the tonic to the dominant.

**Q: Which notes are they in D minor?**
A: D, C, B♭, A.

**Q: What other version is there?**
A: The chromatic descending version.

**Q: What is a famous example?**
A: Dido’s Lament from Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas.

**Q: In what form does it often appear?**
A: As a repeating ground bass.

kuhlau-sonatinas-op20-c-major.body:
Kuhlau's Sonatinas Op. 20 are a set of three short piano sonatinas by Friedrich Kuhlau, a composer born in Germany who later settled in Denmark, published around 1820. They are short, clearly structured and bright in melody, with a moderate level of technical difficulty, and many learners play them at the intermediate stage. As a boy, Kuhlau lost an eye in an accident, but he still became a prolific composer, writing many flute works and operas. It is recorded that he also met Beethoven, and the two made a word joke on Kuhlau's name and wrote a canon.

## The Singing of Kuhlau's Slow Movements

The slow movements of the sonatinas have gentle, singing melodies.

When you play, make the melody connected, like a person singing.

The left-hand accompaniment should be soft, setting off the right-hand melody.

## Kuhlau Sonatinas Op. 20 Summary

Friedrich Kuhlau was born in 1786 and died in 1832. He was born in Germany and settled in Copenhagen to escape the wars. As a child he slipped on the ice, injured an eye and lost his sight in it. He wrote operas, flute music, piano music and songs. In 1825 he met Beethoven in Vienna, and Beethoven made a joke on his name, which sounds like the German words for "cold" and "warm", by writing a canon.

Sonatinas are short, and the first movement often uses a small-scale sonata form. The three sonatinas of Op. 20 are in C major, G major and F major, each in three movements, fast, slow, fast. The first movement of the first has rising broken chords, the slow movement is lyrical, and the last movement is a rondo. When you play, make the touch clear, use the pedal sparingly and let the phrases breathe. They are often studied together with Clementi's Op. 36.

You can ask Teacher Aum to recommend suitable sonatinas.

## The Structure of Sonata Form

The first movements of Kuhlau's sonatinas are often written in sonata form.

First comes the exposition, with two themes. Then comes the development, in which the themes are varied and developed. Finally comes the recapitulation, in which the two themes return.

Playing these sonatinas helps you understand the structure of sonata form.

## Touch in Kuhlau's Sonatinas

When you play Kuhlau's sonatinas, the touch should be clear and bright, in the style of the Classical period.

Fast scales and broken chords should be even and flowing.

Use the pedal sparingly, so that every note stays clear.

## Phrasing and Breathing

Kuhlau's melodic phrases are regular, often four or eight bars long.

When you play, find the beginning and end of each phrase, and let the phrases breathe naturally.

The high point of a phrase can be brought out slightly, and the ending should be closed off cleanly.

![A digital music space in neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaf04rd-jtrf6.webp)

## Losing an Eye

It is recorded that, as a boy, Kuhlau went out one winter evening, slipped on the ice and injured an eye, and later lost the sight in it.

Even so, he kept on studying music and became an excellent pianist and composer.

His story shows how deep his love of music was.

## Compared with Clementi's Sonatinas

Kuhlau's sonatinas are often studied together with Clementi's Sonatinas Op. 36.

The two composers have a similar style, and both wrote sonatinas in the Classical style.

Kuhlau's works are sometimes more lyrical, with a touch of Romantic colour.

## The First Sonatina, in C Major

The first sonatina of Op. 20 is in C major. The theme of the first movement is bright and light, with rising broken chords.

The second movement is a lyrical slow movement with a gentle, singing melody.

The third movement is a fast rondo with a lively rhythm, full of energy.

## The Prolific Kuhlau

Kuhlau wrote a great number of works, including operas, flute music, piano music and songs.

He wrote many flute works, although it is said that he did not play the flute himself, and these works are still commonly used by flute learners today.

His stage works in a Danish national style were very popular in Denmark.

## The Sonatinas Kuhlau Wrote

A sonatina is a sonata that is shorter and simpler in structure.

It usually has two or three movements, and the first movement is often written in sonata form, but on a smaller scale.

Sonatinas are good material for learning sonata form, and many learners play them at the intermediate stage.

## Meeting Beethoven

In 1825, Kuhlau travelled to Vienna and met Beethoven.

It is recorded that when the two were together, they made a word joke on Kuhlau's name: in German, Kuhlau's name sounds like the two words for "cold" and "warm".

Beethoven even wrote a short canon about it, joking that he was "cold but not warm".

- A set of three piano sonatinas by Kuhlau
- Published around 1820
- Often played by learners at the intermediate stage
- Kuhlau once met Beethoven

## Who Was Kuhlau

Friedrich Kuhlau was born in 1786 and died in 1832. He was born in Germany.

Later, to escape the wars, he came to Copenhagen in Denmark and settled there.

He wrote many works in Denmark and is an important composer in the history of Danish music.

## Ask Your Teacher to Recommend a Kuhlau Sonatina in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend a Kuhlau sonatina that suits your level, starting from the first of Op. 20.

Your teacher can also explain the structure of sonata form, to help you understand the first movement.

With Kuhlau's sonatinas, you step into the world of the Classical sonata.

## The Three of Op. 20

Kuhlau's Sonatinas Op. 20 number three in all, in C major, G major and F major.

Each has three movements, fast, slow, fast.

They have bright melodies and clear structure, and the technical difficulty increases gradually.

## FAQ

**Q: Where was Kuhlau born, and where did he later settle?**
A: He was born in Germany and settled in Copenhagen, Denmark.

**Q: How many are there in Op. 20?**
A: Three, in C major, G major and F major.

**Q: How many movements does each have?**
A: Three, fast, slow, fast.

**Q: In which year did Kuhlau meet Beethoven?**
A: 1825.

**Q: Whose sonatinas are Kuhlau's often studied with?**
A: Clementi's Sonatinas Op. 36.

interval-inversion-rule-of-nine.body:
If you move the lower note of an interval up an octave above the upper note, or move the upper note down an octave below the lower note, you get its inversion. Inversion follows two simple rules. The two numbers always add up to nine, so a third becomes a sixth. And the quality swaps: major becomes minor, minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, diminished becomes augmented, and perfect intervals remain perfect. Knowing this rule lets you work out intervals more quickly, and also helps you understand how intervals change when chords are inverted.

## Make an Inversion Chart

You can make a small table with the original interval on the left and the inversion on the right, for example major second and minor seventh, minor third and major sixth.

Look at it every day, or have a friend ask you intervals at random for you to answer.

Once you are familiar with it, you will be able to name the inversion of any interval quickly.

## The Numbers Add Up to Nine

An interval and its inversion always add up to nine.

A third inverts to a sixth, and three plus six is nine; a second inverts to a seventh, and two plus seven is nine.

A fourth inverts to a fifth, a fifth inverts to a fourth, and a unison inverts to an octave.

**Remember this**
- Move the lower note up an octave or the upper note down an octave
- The numbers add up to nine
- Major and minor swap
- Augmented and diminished swap; perfect intervals do not change

## Why Interval Inversion Is Worth Learning

If you meet two notes written far apart, you can first move them into the same octave and then use the inversion rules to work them out.

Interval inversion is a very practical rule in theory, and two points are enough to remember: "add up to nine" and "quality swaps".

It helps you calculate intervals faster, understand chord inversions, and gives you more choices when writing melodies.

Keep this rule in mind and reading and analysing music become much easier.

## Inversion and Melody Writing

When writing a melody, you may sometimes replace a rising interval with its falling inversion, for example replacing a rising third with a falling sixth.

The pitch position of the melody changes, but the notes used are still the same, and they still fit the chords.

This technique can give the melodic line more variety.

## Intervals Within Chord Inversions

When a chord is inverted, the arrangement of the intervals in it changes too.

For example, a C major triad in root position is C, E, G, and in first inversion it is E, G, C.

The third from C to E has become a sixth from E to C, which is why the first inversion is also called a six chord (a chord of the sixth).

## The Link in What We Hear

An interval and its inversion often sound similar in character.

For example, thirds and sixths are both fairly consonant, and seconds and sevenths both have a rubbing quality.

This is also why, in harmony, thirds and sixths are often regarded as closely related intervals.

## The Name of the Six-Four Chord

Put the fifth, G, at the bottom to get G, C, E: from the bass G to C is a fourth, and from G to E is a sixth.

So the second inversion is also called a six-four chord, and the name comes from these two intervals.

Once you understand interval inversion, you can see how these chord names arise.

## Perfect Intervals Stay the Same

A perfect interval is still perfect after inversion.

A perfect fourth inverts to a perfect fifth, a perfect fifth inverts to a perfect fourth, and a perfect octave inverts to a perfect unison.

This also shows the close relationship between fourths and fifths.

## Using Inversion to Work Out Intervals Quickly

Sometimes a large interval is awkward to calculate, and you can work out its inversion first.

For example, to find the interval from C up to the B above it, first look at B up to C, which is a minor second.

According to the rule, the inversion of a minor second is a major seventh, so C to B is a major seventh.

## Checking the Rule at the Piano

Play a major third at the piano, then move the lower note up and listen to the minor sixth it becomes.

Then play a perfect fifth, move the lower note up, and listen to the perfect fourth it becomes.

Playing it with your own hands makes the rule stick more firmly.

## What Is Interval Inversion?

Interval inversion means swapping the positions of the two notes of an interval, one above the other.

In practice, you move the lower note up an octave, or move the upper note down an octave.

For example, C to E is a third; move C to the top and it becomes E to C, a sixth.

## The Swap of Quality

Besides the number, the quality of the interval also changes on inversion.

A major interval becomes minor after inversion, and a minor interval becomes major.

For example, the major third C to E becomes, after inversion, E to C, a minor sixth.

## The Swap of Augmented and Diminished

An augmented interval becomes diminished after inversion, and a diminished interval becomes augmented.

For example, the augmented fourth F to B becomes, after inversion, B to F, a diminished fifth.

Both are tritones, and on the piano they are the same two keys, only written and named differently.

![A collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa2z498-lzph2.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What is interval inversion?**
A: Swapping the positions of the two notes of an interval, one above the other.

**Q: What is the rule for the numbers?**
A: The original interval and its inversion add up to nine.

**Q: What is the inversion of a major third?**
A: A minor sixth.

**Q: What is the inversion of a perfect fifth?**
A: A perfect fourth. A perfect interval stays perfect after inversion.

**Q: Why is the first inversion called a six chord?**
A: Because the interval from the bass to the root is a sixth.
