heiligenstadt-testament-beethoven-1802.body:
In the summer of 1802, the thirty-one-year-old Beethoven was living in Heiligenstadt, a small town on the outskirts of Vienna. His hearing had already declined noticeably, and he feared he would lose it completely. In October he wrote a long letter there to his two brothers, describing the pain brought by his failing hearing and setting down his determination to go on living for his art. The letter was never sent in his lifetime. It was found only after his death in 1827, and later became known as the "Heiligenstadt Testament".

## Summary of Heiligenstadt

In 1802 Beethoven, whose hearing had clearly declined, was living in Heiligenstadt on the outskirts of Vienna. In October he wrote a long letter to his two brothers, describing the pain and loneliness of his failing hearing, and also setting down his determination to go forward for his art.

The letter was never sent and was found only after his death in 1827. It is called the "Heiligenstadt Testament". He went on composing for more than twenty years afterwards, including the Third Symphony of 1803 to 1804, and in his later years he lived and composed relying on his inner hearing and his conversation books.

Knowing this story helps in understanding the sonatas and symphonies. You can compare works from before and after 1802, and talk about the composer with Teacher Aum in a lesson.

## The Music That Followed

Around the time he wrote this letter, Beethoven's musical style began to change.

Between 1803 and 1804 he composed the Third Symphony, which is grand in scale and full of heroic spirit.

Many people see this period as a new stage in Beethoven's composing.

## The Name "Testament"

Because the letter contains arrangements for the time after his death, later generations called it the "Heiligenstadt Testament".

But judging from its content, it is more like a personal confession and a statement of resolve.

After writing this letter, Beethoven lived on for more than twenty years and wrote a great many works.

## Works to Listen To

You can listen to works Beethoven wrote around 1802, such as the Second Symphony and several piano sonatas.

Then listen to the later Third Symphony and compare the change in style.

This lets you feel the turning point of this period more directly.

## The Long Letter of October 1802

In October 1802, Beethoven wrote a long letter in Heiligenstadt, addressed to his two brothers.

In it he admitted openly that his hearing was failing, and described the loneliness and pain it brought him.

He also explained why he often seemed withdrawn, hoping his family would understand.

## Heiligenstadt Today

Heiligenstadt today still has the house where Beethoven lived, which has become a memorial museum.

Many music lovers visit it to see the place where he wrote the letter.

Nearby there is also a small path named after Beethoven.

## A Letter Never Sent

After writing the letter, Beethoven did not send it, but kept it with him.

Only after his death in 1827, when his belongings were being sorted, was the letter found.

Since then, it has been an important document for understanding Beethoven's inner world.

- In 1802, Beethoven lived in Heiligenstadt, on the outskirts of Vienna
- In October he wrote a long letter to his two brothers
- The letter describes the pain of failing hearing and the resolve to keep composing
- It was found only after his death in 1827

## The Conversation Books

In his later years, when Beethoven communicated with other people, he often asked them to write what they wanted to say in a notebook. These notebooks are known as the "conversation books".

The conversation books that survive today record many of his conversations with friends and students.

These materials are also important sources for studying Beethoven's life.

## Staying for Art

The most important part of the letter is the resolve that Beethoven set down.

He wrote that it was art that kept him going, and that he felt he still had a great deal of music left to write.

This will to go forward for art ran through the rest of his composing career.

## The Town of Heiligenstadt

Heiligenstadt is a small town on the outskirts of Vienna, and has now become part of Vienna.

It has vineyards and fields, and the surroundings are quiet.

In 1802, on his doctor's advice, Beethoven came to stay here for several months, hoping to rest.

## From the Story Back to the Piano

Knowing this story can help us understand Beethoven's music better.

For example, when you play his sonatas, you can feel the struggle, perseverance and hope in them.

The experiences behind the music often give a work more weight.

## Talking About the Composer in Lessons

When you study Beethoven's works, you can talk with Teacher Aum in a lesson about the composer's life.

Knowing when and in what circumstances a work was written gives your playing more direction.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend Beethoven works suited to your level.

## Hearing and Composing

As time passed, Beethoven's hearing grew worse and worse, and in his later years he could hardly hear at all.

But he kept composing, writing works such as the Ninth Symphony, the late piano sonatas and string quartets.

He relied on his inner hearing, "hearing" in his mind the music he wrote down.

![A futuristic illustration of someone playing a glowing keyboard on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaac5o1-mchtj.webp)

## The Trouble of Failing Hearing

From his twenties, Beethoven noticed that his hearing had begun to decline.

For a musician this was a very heavy blow.

He began to avoid social occasions, afraid that others would find out he could not hear well.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: In which year did Beethoven live in Heiligenstadt?**
A: 1802.

**Q: Who was the letter written to?**
A: His two brothers.

**Q: What did the letter say?**
A: The pain of failing hearing and the determination to go forward for his art.

**Q: When was the letter found?**
A: After Beethoven's death in 1827.

**Q: How did he communicate with others in his later years?**
A: He asked them to write in the conversation books.

how-to-listen-to-piano-recordings.body:
Listening to fine piano recordings is a very good supplement to learning the piano, but if you only play them as background music, you often gain little. A more effective way is to listen with a specific question in mind, for example: how does the tempo change in this passage? Where is it very soft and where very loud? How is the volume balanced between melody and accompaniment? Does the pedal make the sound clean or hazy? Focus on one question each time, and when you finish, compare with the score or your own playing. You can also compare two or three players' versions to appreciate different ways of understanding the music.

- Used only as background music, a recording gives little
- Listen each time with one specific question
- The question can be about tempo, dynamics, balance or pedal
- Compare versions by different players

## Questions About Dynamics

You can notice where in the whole piece it is very soft and where very loud, and how big the contrast in dynamics is.

**Practice order**

You can also notice how crescendos and diminuendos are carried out, whether the change is quick or develops slowly.

Compare these observations with the dynamic markings in the score, and see how this pianist reads those markings.

## Questions About Balance

You can notice the volume relationship between the melody and the accompaniment, and whether the melody is always clearly heard.

In passages with several voices, try to tell the different voices apart and listen for which one is brought out.

This kind of listening helps you handle balance better in your own playing.

## Compare Two or Three Pianists

For the same piece, different players treat it differently, for example in tempo, dynamics and expression.

You can choose two or three versions, listen with the same question, and compare the differences.

This comparison shows you that music can be understood in many ways, and helps you form your own ideas.

## Questions About Pedal and Tone

You can notice whether the sound is clean and clear, or carries some hazy lingering resonance.

You can also notice the changes of tone colour in different sections, for example bright in some places and soft in others.

These are related to the use of the pedal and the way of touching the keys, and can serve as a reference for your own practice.

## Choose Reliable Recordings

You can choose recordings recommended by your teacher, or officially released albums and concert recordings.

The quality of recordings online varies, so listen to several and choose a version with clear sound and reliable playing.

When you are not sure, ask your teacher whether they recommend a version.

## Build a Listening Habit

Each week you can set aside some time to listen carefully to a few piano recordings, each time with one question.

You can also listen to the piece you are learning with headphones while commuting or resting.

What you gather by listening will slowly enrich your understanding of music, and will also influence your playing.

## Listen with One Question

Before listening to a recording each time, first set yourself a question, such as "does the tempo change in this passage?"

While listening, concentrate only on this question and leave the other aspects aside for now.

This lets you listen more deeply, and makes it easier to remember what you heard.

## Compare with the Score

While listening, keep the score open in front of you, and let your eyes point to wherever your ears have reached.

This links the sound you hear to the markings in the score, and deepens your understanding.

If you find the player's treatment differs somewhat from the markings in the score, you can think about why, or discuss it with your teacher.

## Questions About Tempo

You can notice where the player slows down slightly and where they speed up slightly.

For example, whether the end of a phrase slows a little, and whether there is a little push before the climax.

These subtle tempo changes are often an important reason why music feels as if it breathes.

![Close-up of grand piano keys and a gold-patterned lid in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1b194-tkj7u.webp)

## Compare with Your Own Playing

After listening to a recording, you can record yourself playing the same passage, and listen with the same questions.

Compare the differences between yourself and the recording, and find what can be improved.

This comparison makes your direction clearer.

## Background Music and Focused Listening

Treating a recording as background music, listening while doing other things, can make you familiar with the music, but it is hard to notice details.

When you listen with focus, you put your attention completely on the music, and hear many things you normally overlook.

**Remember this**

Both ways have value, but if you want to learn from a recording, you need to listen with focus.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the use of listening to recordings?**
A: You learn how tempo, dynamics, balance and other aspects can be handled.

**Q: How can I listen more effectively?**
A: Listen each time with one specific question.

**Q: What questions can I ask?**
A: Tempo changes, dynamic contrast, melody balance, pedal and tone, and so on.

**Q: Should I follow the score?**
A: Yes, link the sound with the markings.

**Q: How many versions should I listen to?**
A: Two or three versions, to compare different treatments.

**Q: What kind of recording should I choose?**
A: A reliable recording recommended by a teacher, or an officially released one.

home-on-the-range-kansas-1870s.body:
Home on the Range is an American Western folk song. Its words come from a poem written in the early 1870s by Brewster Higley, a pioneer living in Kansas, and the tune was set to it by his friend Daniel Kelley. The words describe a wide prairie: deer and antelope play there, a discouraging word is seldom heard, and the sky is not cloudy all day. It was widely sung among Western pioneers and cowboys, and in 1947 it was made the Kansas state song. The melody is a gentle triple time with a wide range, which makes it well suited to practising broad, long phrases on the piano.

## How Hard Is Home on the Range for Beginners?

The rhythm of this song is not complicated, but the melody covers a wide span, so the right hand needs to move between different positions.

**Think about it**

Someone who has learned for about a year and can use the sustain pedal can try it.

You can also play just the right-hand melody first, and add the left hand once you are used to the changes of range.

## A Gentle Triple Time

Home on the Range is a song in triple time, at a gentle tempo, like a slow walk across the prairie.

Triple time gives the melody a flowing, spacious feel.

When you play, do not rush. Let every bar unfold calmly.

## Who Wrote This Song?

In the 1930s, someone claimed to have written the song and even went to court over it.

To settle the matter, people investigated where the song came from, and eventually found the trail leading to Higley and Kelley.

This investigation finally made the song's authors known to everyone.

## From a Log Cabin to the Whole Country

At first the song was only passed around locally, and later it travelled across the West with pioneers and cowboys.

People sang it around campfires and on cattle drives, and different versions of the words gradually appeared.

By the early twentieth century it had become a very well-known Western song in America.

## Long Phrases

The phrases of Home on the Range are fairly long, and one phrase often spans several bars.

When you play, treat a whole phrase as one breath and do not break it in the middle.

You can sing it first to feel where to breathe, then play the same breathing on the piano.

## A Pioneer's Poem

In the early 1870s, a doctor named Brewster Higley moved to the prairie in Kansas and lived in a small log cabin.

He wrote a poem describing his home on the Western prairie.

It is said that his friend Daniel Kelley, a neighbour who played the violin, set the poem to music.

- The words come from a poem by Higley from the early 1870s
- The tune was set by Daniel Kelley
- It became the Kansas state song in 1947
- Gentle triple time with a wide range

## A Wide Range

The melody of this song rises and falls a good deal, sometimes leaping from a low note straight up to a high one.

In particular, in the chorus line "Home, home on the range", the melody opens upward, as if looking at the sky far away.

When you play, let the high notes sing out, but do not play them too hard.

## Home on the Range at a Glance

Home on the Range is an American Western folk song. Its words come from a poem written in the early 1870s by Brewster Higley, who lived in a small cabin on the Kansas prairie, and it is said to have been set to music by his violin-playing neighbour Daniel Kelley. It describes a prairie where deer and antelope play and the sky is clear all day. It spread across the West with pioneers and cowboys, in the 1930s someone claimed to have written it, and only after an investigation was the real author found. In 1947 it became the Kansas state song.

The melody is a gentle triple time with a good deal of rise and fall, the chorus opens upward and the phrases are long. You can play it in F or G major, with a triple-time accompaniment or broken chords in the left hand, changing the pedal with the chords, and using octaves or fifths in the bass. Someone who has learned for about a year can try it.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the long phrases.

## The Kansas State Song

In 1947, Home on the Range was made the state song of Kansas in the United States.

The prairie scenery it describes is just what Kansas looks like.

To this day, many Kansans still sing it on important occasions.

![Illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, expressing the strength of the song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbixvbd-kp077.webp)

## Playing a Sense of Wide Open Space

To bring out a sense of wide open space, let the left-hand bass be a little broader, using octaves or fifths.

The right-hand melody should be smooth and long, like wind blowing across the prairie.

The tempo can be a little slower, leaving room for every note.

## Pictures from the Prairie

The words describe a wide prairie where deer and antelope play freely.

There a discouraging word is seldom heard, and the sky stays clear all day, never cloudy.

These simple lines paint the ideal home in the pioneer's heart.

## Asking Your Teacher to Listen to the Phrases

In a lesson you can play for Teacher Aum and ask them to judge whether the long phrases flow in one breath.

You can also ask the teacher to demonstrate how to change the pedal in triple time.

From a pioneer folk song, play the openness of the prairie.

## Playing Home on the Range on the Piano

F major or G major both sit comfortably on the keyboard. Give the melody to the right hand, and let the left hand carry the triple-time foundation.

The left hand can play one bass note first and then two light chords, or play flowing broken chords.

**Common mistakes**

The sustain pedal can be changed along with the chords, so that the sound is as wide as the prairie.

## FAQ

**Q: Whose poem are the words of Home on the Range from?**
A: Brewster Higley.

**Q: When was the poem written?**
A: In the early 1870s.

**Q: In which year did it become the Kansas state song?**
A: 1947.

**Q: How many beats is the song in?**
A: Triple time.

**Q: How do you play a sense of wide open space on the piano?**
A: Use octaves or fifths in the left-hand bass, and keep the right-hand melody smooth and long.

imitate-nature-sounds-improvise.body:
Imitating rain, birdsong, wind or waves on the piano is a simple and fun improvisation exercise. You do not need a score. Just listen to the sounds around you, then try to express them with short notes in the high register, long notes in the low register, changes of soft and loud, and the pedal. This exercise helps you explore the keyboard more freely, and makes you pay more attention to changes of tone colour and dynamics.

## Why Imitate Sounds from Nature?

Most everyday practice follows the score, and the fingers get used to fixed notes and rhythms. Imitating sounds from nature requires you to look for the right notes and ways of playing yourself.

**Remember this**

This process lets you explore the whole keyboard more freely and discover the many different sounds the piano can make.

It also trains the ear, making you pay more attention to high and low, long and short, soft and loud, and tone colour.

Sometimes imitation exercises can also help you relax, because there is no standard of right and wrong. You are simply playing with sound.

## A Sound Game for Parent and Child

This exercise is especially good to do with a child. A parent names a sound, the child imitates it on the piano, and then you swap roles.

Children often have many wonderful ideas, and may express a sound in unexpected ways.

There is no need to judge right or wrong. What matters is encouraging the child to try boldly and express themselves.

![A black grand piano and stool against a gold and red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xs70f-kjl8z.webp)

## Imitating Waves and Wind

Waves can be played in the low and middle registers with broken chords that go from slow to fast and from soft to loud, then slowly fade, like a wave rushing up and drawing back.

The sound of wind can be made with continuous scales running quickly up or down, together with the pedal, so that it sounds like a gust blowing past.

These imitations do not have to be accurate. It is enough if they remind you of that sound.

## From Improvisation Back to Pieces

After the imitation exercise, when you go back to the piece you are learning, you may find you are more sensitive to tone colour and dynamics.

Many composers have also written works that portray scenes from nature, such as piano pieces on the themes of rain, birds and water.

When you get to know these works, you can think about how the composer used notes to paint these pictures, and compare them with your own improvisation.

## Listen Carefully First

Before you begin, you can spend a minute or two listening to the sounds around you, such as birdsong outside the window, the sound of rain, or wind rustling through leaves.

You can also recall sounds you have heard, such as waves at the seaside or thunder in the distance.

Try to describe the character of these sounds: is it high or low? Continuous or one beat at a time? Gentle or strong?

## Notice Your Discoveries

After each imitation exercise, you can briefly note which methods you used: in which register, with what dynamics, and whether you used the pedal.

Next time, you can try different methods, and compare which one is more like the sound you want to express.

You can also share these notes with your teacher, who may give you some new suggestions or recommend related pieces.

## Imitating Rain

Light rain can be made in the high register by gently touching a few notes irregularly with your fingers, like drops falling on the eaves.

Heavy rain can be made by speeding up, adding more notes, and making the dynamics a little stronger.

Press the sustain pedal so that the notes pile up together, and you will hear a continuous sheet of rain.

## Add a Simple Structure

Once you are familiar with a few sounds, you can combine them to tell a little story. For example, it begins with bright sunshine and birdsong, then light rain starts, the rain grows heavier, and finally the rain stops and the birds begin to sing again.

A structure like this gives the improvisation a beginning, a development and an ending, like a small piece.

You can record your own "story", and it will be a lot of fun to listen back to.

- Listen carefully first, then imitate on the piano
- The high register suits light, bright sounds
- The low register suits deep, heavy sounds
- The pedal can join the sounds into one

## Imitating Little Birds

Birdsong is usually fairly high and fairly short, and can be imitated with light short notes in the high register.

Try playing two or three neighbouring notes quickly back and forth, or play one note followed at once by a higher one, like a bird calling.

**Practice order**

The dynamics can be lighter, and the speed can vary, so that the sound seems more alive.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need to know harmony to improvise?**
A: No. Imitating sounds can start from any note.

**Q: Can I do this exercise on a digital piano?**
A: Yes, and you can also try different tone settings.

**Q: Does a child playing randomly count as practice?**
A: Exploring sound with a purpose is part of practice too. You can guide your child to describe what they want to express.

**Q: What if my imitation does not sound like it?**
A: That is fine. The point is to listen carefully and try boldly.

**Q: How long should this exercise last?**
A: Five to ten minutes is enough, as a change before or after regular practice.

**Q: Are there piano pieces that depict nature to listen to?**
A: There are many. You can ask your teacher to recommend works that suit your level.

hocket-shared-melody-piano-duet.body:
Hocket is the technique of splitting one complete melody into fragments that two or more players perform in turn, each responsible for only some of the notes, so that together they make one continuous melody. The listener hears a single melodic line, but every note actually comes from a different person or instrument. This technique already appeared in medieval European vocal music, and similar practices can be found in folk music, handbell ensembles and modern works around the world. In piano learning, hocket is an excellent cooperative exercise that trains rhythmic accuracy, focused listening and teamwork.

## The Basic Features of Hocket

- One melody is split into several parts
- Each player is responsible for only some of the notes
- The notes must fit together seamlessly, with no gaps or overlaps
- Together, the listener feels one continuous melody
- Accurate rhythm matters more than volume

The biggest challenge of this exercise is that you must keep listening to the others to know when to come in.

## Similar Practices Around the World

**Handbell ensembles**
Each player holds a bell or two of just one or two pitches, and the melody can only be completed when everyone rings in turn.

**Panpipe and bamboo-pipe ensembles**
In the folk music of some regions, two people each hold a set of pipes and play alternately to make one melody.

**Modern works**
Some contemporary composers use hocket in piano, percussion or electronic music to create the effect of sound leaping through space.

These examples show that splitting a melody up and handing it to different people is a way of musical thinking that crosses cultures.

![A pointillist painting of a figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvybdcv9-iuhan.webp)

## Relay Exercises on the Piano

**Preparation**
Choose a simple melody everyone knows, such as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star or Ode to Joy. Two people sit at the same piano, or each uses a keyboard.

**Round 1: one bar each**
Player A plays the first bar and player B plays the second, taking turns. The handover must happen without a pause.

**Round 2: one beat each**
Player A plays beats one and three of each bar, and player B plays beats two and four. Now you need to listen to your partner even more closely.

**Round 3: one note each**
Every note of the melody is played by the two players in turn. This is the hardest version: once the rhythm goes wrong, the melody breaks.

**Round 4: dividing by pitch**
Player A is responsible only for the three notes C, D and E, and player B for F, G and A, and whoever's note comes up plays it. This kind of split is closer to a handbell ensemble.

## What This Exercise Trains

- Inner pulse: even when it is not your turn, you must keep counting the beat in your head
- Listening: you must listen to your partner's notes to come in on time
- Even tone: the two players' volume and touch need to be close for the melody to sound continuous
- Teamwork: when a mistake happens, you adjust together instead of blaming each other

For children, this exercise is like a game; for adults, it is a very good introduction to ensemble playing.

## You Can Practise Alone Too

If you have no partner, you can also do hocket with your two hands: the right hand takes some of the notes and the left hand takes the others, and the two hands play the same melody in turn. This trains independence and coordination between the hands, and lets you feel the melody being "passed" from one hand to the other. You can also record the part of one hand and play along with the recording with the other part, which is like playing an ensemble with yourself.

## Ways to Play at Home and in Class

At home, a parent and child can each take a few notes and complete a children's song together. In class, the teacher can divide the whole class into two or three groups, each responsible for different notes, and take turns playing on simple percussion instruments or keyboards. This approach does not need a high level, yet lets everyone take part and enjoy the pleasure of making music together.

## Checkpoints When Listening to a Recording

After a round of the relay, record it on a phone and listen back, focusing on three things. First, whether the melody is continuous, and whether it breaks off suddenly anywhere. Second, whether the two players' volume is close, and whether one person's notes stand out. Third, whether the tempo is steady, and whether it gets faster and faster. Write down the problems you find, and in the next round work on just one of them. This way of practising makes cooperation more efficient, and lets every participant see their own progress clearly.

## FAQ

**Q: What age is hocket suitable for?**
A: As long as a child can count the beat steadily, they can start with the one-bar-each version.

**Q: Can two people of different levels practise together?**
A: Yes. Let the more advanced player take the harder parts, and the less advanced player the long notes or just a few notes.

**Q: Why can't we ever fit together?**
A: Most likely you are not counting the beat in your head all the time. Turn on a metronome first and have both players follow it.

**Q: Does this exercise help with solo playing?**
A: Yes. It makes you pay more attention to the continuity of the melody and the steadiness of the rhythm, which matter just as much in solo playing.

## Take Cooperative Practice Home

To practise playing together with your family at home, try TIGA ALPHA.

he-luting-shepherd-boy-flute-1934.body:
Shepherd Boy's Piccolo is a piano piece written in 1934 by the Chinese composer He Luting. That same year, the Russian composer and pianist Alexander Tcherepnin launched a competition in Shanghai for piano works in a Chinese style, and this piece won the top prize. It has since become one of the best-known works in Chinese piano music. The piece is in ternary form. Two voices answer each other like a shepherd boy playing a pipe, the melody has a strong pentatonic colour, and the lively rhythm of the middle section expresses the ease and happiness of country life.

## The Composer He Luting

He Luting was a Chinese composer and music educator who lived from 1903 to 1999.

He wrote piano pieces, songs, film music and other kinds of works, and had an important influence on the development of modern Chinese music.

He also worked in music education for many years and trained many musicians.

## The Picture in the Title

The title Shepherd Boy's Piccolo paints a pastoral picture: a boy herding cattle, sitting on the back of an ox and playing a short bamboo flute.

The piece uses the piano to imitate the lilting sound of the flute and the calm of the fields, with a strong country feeling.

As you listen, you can imagine this scene and feel the ease and happiness in it.

## Key Points for Performance

In the first section, pay attention to the balance and smoothness of the two voices. The melody should be lilting and gentle, like the sound of a flute.

In the middle section, pay attention to clear and light rhythm, and do not play too heavily.

The third section returns to the mood of the opening. You can make it more delicate than the first time, letting the music end naturally.

## A Conversation Between Two Voices

The most distinctive feature of the first section is the conversation between the two voices, one above and one below, imitating and answering each other.

This writing draws on the techniques of Western polyphony while blending in the melodic character of Chinese music.

When you play, make sure both voices are clearly heard, like two flutes calling back and forth.

**A Little Tip**
- Composed by He Luting in 1934
- Won the top prize in the competition started by Tcherepnin
- In ternary form
- Two voices answer each other, with a pentatonic colour

## Listening and Learning

It is worth comparing recordings by several pianists to hear how each one handles the two flutes and the leaping middle section.

If you want to learn the piece, you can ask your teacher for advice suited to your level and start by practising the first section.

As you learn, it also helps to find out more about Chinese folk music, which will help you understand the style of the piece better.

## The Colour of the Pentatonic Scale

The melody has a strong pentatonic colour, sounding friendly and simple, with the flavour of Chinese folk music.

The pentatonic scale has no semitones, so the melodic line is steady and flowing.

As you play, you can feel this distinctive modal colour and compare it with Western major and minor music.

## The 1934 Competition

In 1934 the Russian composer and pianist Alexander Tcherepnin came to Shanghai. He was very interested in Chinese music and launched a competition for piano works in a Chinese style.

The competition aimed to encourage Chinese composers to express Chinese musical style on the piano.

He Luting's Shepherd Boy's Piccolo won the top prize in this competition.

## The Development of Chinese Piano Music

In the first half of the twentieth century, many Chinese composers began to try using the piano, an instrument from the West, to express Chinese musical style.

Shepherd Boy's Piccolo is one of the representative works of this period and offered a model for later Chinese piano composition.

Today, Chinese piano works are very rich in both number and style.

## Its Place in Piano Study

Shepherd Boy's Piccolo is often used as a Chinese piece in piano study. It is of moderate difficulty, and someone who has studied for a few years can practise it.

Learning this piece helps students understand Chinese-style piano music and the use of polyphony and the pentatonic scale.

It also often appears in the repertoire of performances and competitions.

![A cyberpunk illustration of a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1qylw-qdakl.webp)

## The Structure of Ternary Form

Shepherd Boy's Piccolo is in ternary form, that is, ABA.

The first section has a flowing, lilting melody, like a shepherd boy slowly playing his flute. The middle section has a lively, cheerful rhythm, like the boy playing in the fields.

The third section returns to the opening melody with some variation, so that the beginning and end of the piece echo each other.

## The Liveliness of the Middle Section

The rhythm of the middle section clearly becomes livelier, with many leaping notes and short rhythms.

You can use a lighter touch here to express the joy of the boy at play.

It contrasts with the flowing first section and gives the whole piece its rise and fall.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who composed Shepherd Boy's Piccolo?**
A: The Chinese composer He Luting.

**Q: When was it composed?**
A: 1934.

**Q: What honour did it win?**
A: The top prize in the competition started by Tcherepnin.

**Q: What form is it in?**
A: Ternary form, ABA.

**Q: What are its special features?**
A: Two voices answer each other, with a pentatonic colour.

**Q: How difficult is it?**
A: Moderately difficult, and you can try it with some foundation.

john-cage-4-33-premiere-woodstock-1952.body:
On 29 August 1952, in a concert hall in Woodstock, New York, the pianist David Tudor gave the premiere of John Cage's 4'33". He sat down at the piano, closed the keyboard lid, watched a stopwatch, and played not a single note across the three movements, only opening and closing the lid at the start and end of each movement. What the audience heard was the wind outside the window, the rain, and the sounds inside the hall. The piece made many people rethink what music is, and what silence is.

## What the Audience Heard

Although the piano made no sound, the concert hall was not completely silent.

**Listen closely**

According to later accounts, at the premiere you could hear the wind outside the window in the first movement, raindrops on the roof in the second, and in the third the audience's own whispers and movements.

Cage hoped people would notice that these sounds, normally overlooked, can also be listened to with real attention.

## The Premiere at Woodstock

On 29 August 1952, 4'33" was premiered in a country concert hall in Woodstock, New York.

The performer was the pianist David Tudor, who at the time specialised in playing new music.

The concert also included other new works, and the audience was mostly people interested in new music.

## A Room Without Sound

Cage once said that in a room built to shut out sound, he still heard two sounds, one high and one low.

From this he concluded that absolute silence does not exist in the world, and that some sound is always present.

This idea influenced him as he composed 4'33".

## The Influence of the Piece

4'33" influenced many later artists, not only musicians but also painters, dancers and performance artists.

It made people notice the sounds in their surroundings, and also think about the relationship between performing and watching.

When modern music is discussed, this piece is often mentioned.

## Rests Are Music Too

For people learning an instrument, this piece can remind us that rests and silence are part of music too.

A rest on the page is not simply "stopping", but the breathing and the space of the music.

When you play, treat every rest seriously, and the music will have more shape.

## What Tudor Did on Stage

Tudor walked onto the stage, sat down at the piano, closed the keyboard lid and began timing with a stopwatch.

At the end of each movement he opened the lid, and closed it again as the next movement began.

For a full four minutes and thirty-three seconds, he did not press a single key.

![A person with a long braid plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon-lit street, with drones in the air](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa55aze-px6ak.webp)

## The Controversy

After the premiere, 4'33" caused a great deal of controversy: some felt it was not music at all, while others found it deeply inspiring.

Even today, people's views of the piece still differ.

But either way, it led many people to ask where the boundaries of music lie.

## Hearing Music in Silence

When we play, our attention is usually all on the notes we are making.

This piece reminds us that sound happens in a space, and that the surroundings also affect the music we hear.

The same piece played in different rooms will sound different, which is also worth noticing.

## The Composer John Cage

John Cage was an American composer of the twentieth century, born in 1912 and died in 1992.

He liked to experiment with new sounds and new ways of composing, for example placing screws and rubber on the strings of a piano to change its tone.

4'33" is one of his most widely known works, and one that has prompted a great deal of discussion.

## Listening to Your Surroundings

You can try a small exercise: sit quietly for four and a half minutes, do nothing, and simply listen to the sounds around you.

You may hear an air conditioner, cars in the distance, or your own breathing.

This exercise can help us become more sensitive, and when we play, we can better hear small changes in sound.

## The Length of the Three Movements

The piece is divided into three movements, and at the premiere their lengths added up to exactly four minutes and thirty-three seconds, which is where the title comes from.

The instruction on the score is for the performer not to play during this time.

Cage later explained that the piece can be performed by any instrument, and by any number of people.

## 4'33" in Summary

On 29 August 1952, the pianist David Tudor premiered Cage's 4'33" in Woodstock, playing not a single note across the three movements and only opening and closing the keyboard lid to mark the movements.

The audience heard the wind, the rain and the sounds inside the hall, and Cage used this to make people rethink music and silence.

For people learning the piano, it reminds us to take rests seriously and to listen more to the sounds around us.

**Try it**
- Premiered on 29 August 1952 in Woodstock
- Performed by the pianist David Tudor
- Three movements, with no note played
- Makes people rethink music and silence

## 4'33" and the Piano

Although the piece can be performed on any instrument, the premiere was on the piano, so people often link it with the piano.

The keyboard lid became a symbol in the performance, its opening and closing telling the audience when a movement began and ended.

Some pianists perform this piece in concerts, as a special kind of experience.

## FAQ

**Q: When was 4'33" premiered?**
A: On 29 August 1952.

**Q: Where was it premiered?**
A: In Woodstock, New York, in the United States.

**Q: Who gave the premiere?**
A: The pianist David Tudor.

**Q: What did the performer play?**
A: Not a single note; he only opened and closed the keyboard lid.

**Q: What does the piece want people to think about?**
A: What music is, and what silence is.

just-intonation-pure-intervals.body:
Just intonation is a tuning system that fixes pitches with simple whole-number frequency ratios. In just intonation, the octave is 2:1, the perfect fifth is 3:2, the major third is 5:4 and the minor third is 6:5. Chords built from these ratios sound very pure, with almost no wobbling "beats". But just intonation has a problem: an instrument tuned this way is hard to transpose, because in different keys the same note needs a different pitch. Today's piano uses twelve-tone equal temperament, while choirs and string quartets, when they sing and play, often drift naturally toward just intonation.

## Feeling just intonation through overtones

On the piano, you can silently press down a high key, then strike a note an octave or a twelfth lower firmly, and release the low note.

The strings of the high note will sound by sympathetic resonance. These are overtones.

The relationships between overtones are exactly the simple ratios of just intonation.

## The pure major triad

In a major triad tuned in just intonation, the frequency ratio of the three notes is 4:5:6.

The notes of such a chord blend together and sound very steady.

Many people who hear a just-intonation major triad for the first time find it "calmer" than the major triad on the piano.

## Just intonation in brief

Just intonation fixes pitches with simple whole-number frequency ratios: octave 2:1, perfect fifth 3:2, perfect fourth 4:3, major third 5:4, minor third 6:5. The major triad is 4:5:6, and it sounds pure, with almost no beating.

But working out the notes this way produces a small discrepancy of 81:80, and a keyboard tuned in just intonation is hard to transpose. Today's piano uses twelve-tone equal temperament, which allows free transposition, though its major third is a little wider than the just one. Choirs, string quartets and barbershop quartets often drift naturally toward just intonation.

At the piano you can feel simple ratios through the overtone experiment, and history offers other systems such as Pythagorean tuning and meantone temperament. You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the overtone experiment in a lesson.

## The basic intervals in just intonation

In just intonation, the octave is 2:1, the perfect fifth is 3:2 and the perfect fourth is 4:3.

The major third is 5:4 and the minor third is 6:5.

These ratios are all simple, which is why the intervals sound so harmonious.

## The compromise of equal temperament

Today's piano uses twelve-tone equal temperament, which divides the octave evenly into twelve semitones.

This makes every key sound the same, so you can transpose freely.

The price is that, apart from the octave, every interval deviates a little from just intonation. The major third, for example, is a little wider than the just one.

## Other tuning systems

Throughout history, besides just intonation and equal temperament, there have been many other tuning systems, such as Pythagorean tuning and meantone temperament.

Different systems make different trade-offs between purity and the ability to change key.

Knowing about them helps us understand the sound of music from different periods.

- Pitches fixed with simple whole-number frequency ratios
- Octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, major third 5:4
- Chords sound pure, with almost no beating
- Hard to transpose, so the piano uses equal temperament

## Just intonation in choirs and strings

Instruments without fixed pitch, and the human voice, can adjust pitch at any moment to suit the harmony.

When choirs and string quartets sing or play chords, they often naturally tune the thirds to be purer.

That is why the triads in a choir without a piano underneath are often especially clear and bright.

## Why piano learners should know about just intonation

The pitch of the piano is set by the tuner, and you cannot change it while playing.

But knowing about just intonation helps us understand why chords on the piano sound different from chords sung by a choir.

When you play with string players or singers, it also helps you understand how they adjust their intonation.

## What are beats?

When two notes are close in frequency but do not quite fit a simple ratio, a periodic swelling and fading appears. This is called beating.

A major third on the piano, for example, has a slight wobble.

In just intonation the beats almost disappear, so the sound is purer.

![A black grand piano and bench in front of a gold and red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab0vbj-5so30.webp)

## Barbershop quartets

In barbershop quartet singing, a choral style from the United States, the singers strive especially for pure chords.

When a chord is sung very accurately, the overtones stack up and produce a "ringing" resonance.

This effect comes precisely from intervals close to just intonation.

## Asking your teacher to play overtones

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the overtone experiment, so you can hear the sympathetic resonance of the piano strings.

You can also ask your teacher about the history of tuning systems and how they relate to piano tuning.

This knowledge gives us a deeper understanding of the sound of the piano.

## Frequency ratios and intervals

The pitch of a sound is determined by its vibration frequency, and the ratio of the frequencies of two notes determines the interval between them.

If two notes have a frequency ratio of 2:1, for example, they are an octave apart.

Just intonation uses simple whole-number ratios to fix every interval.

## The problem with just intonation

The problem with just intonation is that fixing all the notes with simple ratios produces some inconsistencies.

For example, the D worked out from C by a perfect fifth and a major third needs a slightly different pitch in different chords.

The two Ds differ by a tiny interval called the comma, with a ratio of 81:80.

## Hard to change key

Because of this inconsistency, a keyboard tuned in just intonation sounds pure only in a few keys.

Once you move to a distant key, some chords are clearly out of tune.

**Listen**

This is why keyboard instruments gradually adopted other tuning systems.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the frequency ratio of the perfect fifth in just intonation?**
A: 3:2.

**Q: What is the frequency ratio of the major third?**
A: 5:4.

**Q: What is the frequency ratio of a major triad in just intonation?**
A: 4:5:6.

**Q: What is the problem with just intonation?**
A: It is hard to transpose, and it produces a discrepancy of 81:80.

**Q: What tuning system does today's piano use?**
A: Twelve-tone equal temperament.

jianpu-numbered-notation-history.body:
Jianpu is a notation that uses the numbers 1 to 7 for "do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti". It is extremely common in China, and many people first learn to sing by reading it. It was not actually invented in China: in 1742 the French thinker Rousseau proposed a number-based system to the Academy of Sciences in Paris, and in the nineteenth century several French music educators developed similar ideas into a system for teaching singing. The method later reached Japan, then came to China in the early twentieth century with the "school song" movement, and gradually became one of the most widely used kinds of music notation.

## Why It Became So Widespread

An important reason jianpu spread so widely in China is that it is easy to learn and easy to print.

All you need is numbers and a few simple symbols, which can be set in type under ordinary printing conditions.

Many songbooks, newspapers and textbooks used jianpu, so more people could learn to sing new songs.

## Movable-Do Notation

Jianpu is a movable-do system, and the top of the score states something like "1=C" or "1=G".

This means that the "1" of the piece is the note C or G.

To put the same melody in another key, you only change the marking at the start; the numbers stay the same.

## Comparing the Two Notations in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to write a familiar song in both jianpu and staff notation, so you can compare the two.

You can also ask your teacher to check whether your own exercises in turning jianpu into staff notation are correct.

From a few numbers, you can see the journey a notation made across countries.

## How Note Lengths Are Shown

Jianpu uses dashes and underlines to show how long a note lasts.

A dash after a number extends the note by one beat; a line under a number halves its value.

For example, a number alone is one beat, one line underneath makes it half a beat, and two lines make it a quarter of a beat.

## Numbers Stand for Notes

Jianpu uses the Arabic numerals 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 for "do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti".

The number 0 stands for a rest, that is, silence.

As long as you know your numbers, you can learn to read jianpu very quickly.

**Try it**
- Use the numbers 1 to 7 for the seven solfège syllables
- In 1742 Rousseau proposed a number-notation system
- In the nineteenth century French music educators developed it into a teaching system
- In the early twentieth century it came to China with the school song movement

![A high-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a neon-lit street at night in the rain](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk92g6-2vacj.webp)

## High Dots and Low Dots

A dot above a number means one octave higher; a dot below a number means one octave lower.

Two dots mean two octaves higher or lower.

In this way, just seven numbers can show a very wide range.

## Jianpu and Staff Notation

Jianpu and staff notation each have their strengths.

Jianpu is simple and intuitive, and suits singing and single-line instruments; staff notation shows harmony and multiple parts more clearly, and suits instruments such as the piano.

People who learn the piano usually work mainly from staff notation, but it is also useful to know jianpu.

## The Nineteenth-Century Singing System

In the nineteenth century, several French music educators built on similar ideas and developed a system for teaching singing with numbers.

The method was promoted in French schools and choirs, and helped many ordinary people learn to sing from a score.

Later, it spread to other countries too.

## Passing Through Japan

In the late nineteenth century, Japan promoted Western music education in its schools and also adopted number notation.

At that time many Chinese students were studying in Japan, and they came across this convenient notation.

When they returned home, they brought it to China.

## Rousseau's Proposal

In 1742, the French thinker Rousseau put forward a new notation system to the Academy of Sciences in Paris.

He suggested using numbers in place of the notes on the staff, to make learning music simpler.

However, the musicians of the time did not accept his proposal.

## From Jianpu to Staff Notation

If you are already familiar with jianpu, you can compare the two notations when you start learning staff notation.

For example, in C major, the 1 of jianpu is the "do" on the first ledger line below the staff.

Taking a familiar jianpu song, translating it into staff notation yourself and playing it is a very good exercise.

## Jianpu in Summary

Jianpu uses the numbers 1 to 7 for "do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti", 0 for a rest, dots above and below the numbers for higher and lower octaves, dashes to lengthen and underlines to halve note values, and a marking such as "1=C" at the start; it is a movable-do notation. In 1742 the French thinker Rousseau proposed a number-notation system to the Paris Academy of Sciences, but it was not accepted, and in the nineteenth century French music educators developed a system for teaching singing with numbers.

Japan later promoted it in its schools, Chinese students brought it home, and it spread in the early twentieth century with the "school song" movement. Easy to learn and easy to print, jianpu suits singing and single-line music, while staff notation suits multi-part instruments such as the piano, and you can try turning a familiar jianpu song into staff notation and playing it.

You can ask Teacher Aum to compare the two notations with you.

## School Songs

In the early twentieth century, China's new-style schools began to offer singing classes, and many new songs were written for students. This became known as the "school song" movement.

Most of these songs were written in jianpu, and they quickly spread through the schools.

From then on, jianpu took root in China.

## FAQ

**Q: What does jianpu use to show notes?**
A: The numbers 1 to 7.

**Q: What does a dot above a number mean?**
A: One octave higher.

**Q: In what year did Rousseau propose a number-notation system?**
A: 1742.

**Q: How did jianpu reach China?**
A: Through Japan, with the school song movement in the early twentieth century.

**Q: Is jianpu a movable-do or fixed-do notation?**
A: It is a movable-do notation.

kangding-love-song-sichuan-folk-piano.body:
"On the hill where the horses run, a wisp of cloud drifts by, oh." This is the first line of "Kangding Love Song". The song comes from the Kangding area of Sichuan and has the character of the local "liuliu" tunes, with a bright melody, a relaxed rhythm and a touch of playfulness. It spread across the whole country in the mid-twentieth century and is still often sung and arranged today. To play it at the piano, the key is to catch that light step and the speech-like quality of a folk song.

## A light rhythm

The rhythm of "Kangding Love Song" is relaxed and flowing, with the lilt of walking or riding a horse.

When playing, keep a steady beat and do not drag.

Imagine humming a song as you walk, and let the rhythm be natural and light.

**Try it**
- A folk song from the Kangding area of Sichuan
- Has the character of the "liuliu" tunes
- A bright melody and a relaxed rhythm
- At the piano, bring out the manner of a folk song

## Accompanying with simple chords

If you want to make your own accompaniment for "Kangding Love Song", first try the three chords I, IV and V, phrase by phrase.

Find the chord that suits each melodic phrase, and play a bass note or a simple chord with the left hand.

Once you are fluent, try broken chords or bouncing patterns to make the accompaniment livelier.

## The manner of a folk song

Folk songs grow out of speech and singing, and the melody rises and falls with the manner of the words.

When playing the piano, you can think of each phrase as a sentence, with some words stressed and others touched lightly.

A melody played this way is more than a string of notes; it has the flavour of speech.

## Little ornaments

When singing folk songs, singers often add small slides or ornaments on certain notes.

At the piano, you can imitate this effect with short grace notes.

Ornaments should be few and light, and should not make the melody complicated.

## Kangding and this song

Kangding lies in western Sichuan. It is a mountain town surrounded by high mountains and grasslands.

"Kangding Love Song" spread from the folk tunes of this region.

The "liuliu" in the song is a vocable with no specific meaning, but it makes the singing lively and warm.

## What level suits "Kangding Love Song"

The melody of this song is simple. It suits beginners practising melody with a simple accompaniment, and also people who have just learnt a few basic chords and want to try arranging for themselves.

More advanced learners can play a richer arrangement or try making their own.

You can also play with family and friends, one at the piano and one singing.

## The vocable "liuliu"

Chinese folk songs often contain vocables, such as "liuliu", "ya" and "yo", which fill out the melody and strengthen its manner.

When playing at the piano, the notes that carry vocables are usually lighter and quicker, as if tossed off in passing.

You can sing while you play, to feel what the vocables do in the melody.

## Singing and playing together

"Kangding Love Song" is very good for singing with piano accompaniment, because the melody has a narrow range and the words are easy to sing.

You can first choose a key that suits your voice and accompany yourself with simple chords.

When you sing and play together, the accompaniment should follow the singer's breath and not rush ahead of the voice.

## The structure of the melody

The melody of this song is made of several short phrases, and each verse repeats the same melody.

The melody is based mainly on the pentatonic scale, with little rise and fall, so it is easy to remember.

At the piano, you can first learn one verse well, then add the changes of the later verses.

## Keep the pedal clean in "Kangding Love Song"

Because the rhythm is light, this song should not use much pedal.

You can change the pedal once a bar or every two beats to keep the sound clear.

With bouncing accompaniment patterns, playing without pedal is sometimes more springy.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7nl7j-3vg8i.webp)

## The left-hand accompaniment

In piano arrangements, the left hand often uses simple bass notes and chords, or bouncing accompaniment patterns.

The left hand should be light and springy, supporting the rhythmic feel of the melody.

If the left hand is too heavy, the whole song loses its relaxed character.

## "Kangding Love Song" in brief

"Kangding Love Song" comes from the Kangding area of Sichuan and has the character of the "liuliu" tunes. The vocable "liuliu" makes the singing lively and warm, and the melody is based on the pentatonic scale, with each verse repeating.

At the piano, keep a light, steady rhythm, think of each phrase as a sentence, keep the left hand light and springy, and use the tonic, subdominant and dominant chords to make your own accompaniment.

Between verses you can vary the accompaniment pattern and the register. Ornaments should be few and light, the pedal should not be overused, and the song is also very good for singing and playing together.

## Variety between verses

This song has several verses of words with the same melody, so playing it can easily become monotonous.

You can change the accompaniment pattern in different verses, or move the melody to a different register.

For example, keep the first verse simple, add broken chords in the second, and make the last verse a little fuller.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Where does "Kangding Love Song" come from?**
A: The Kangding area of Sichuan.

**Q: What is "liuliu"?**
A: A vocable that makes the singing lively and warm.

**Q: What is special about the rhythm?**
A: It is relaxed and flowing, and must be kept steady.

**Q: Which chords can be used for the accompaniment?**
A: The tonic, subdominant and dominant chords.

**Q: How can the verses avoid monotony?**
A: Change the accompaniment pattern or the register of the melody.

joplin-easy-winners-rag-1901.body:
"The Easy Winners" is a ragtime piano piece published by Scott Joplin in 1901. Like many rags, it usually has a steady pulse in the left hand and a syncopated melody in the right; different sections take turns, like a set of little scenes on the march. Its character is more unhurried than some faster, fancier rags, and the "easy" in the title means a confident, unflustered way of moving along, not playing carelessly. When you learn it, first make the left hand as steady as walking on solid ground, and then let the right-hand syncopations dance on that ground; this is clearer than rushing both hands together. When listening, you can also follow only the bass line first, and then listen to how the right hand slips out of step with it. If both hands rush forward together, the fun of the syncopation gets swallowed by the speed. In practice you may play an unhurried rag more slowly than a recording, as long as the pulse is still there and the off-beat notes are still clear. Once the main section is steady, you can join the repeats and the contrasting sections as the score directs, instead of rushing through from the beginning every time. If a syncopation keeps missing the beat in the same place, take out just that bar, keep the left hand at the original speed, slow the right hand down to line up, and then put them back together. The unhurried character is kept through this kind of alignment. After choosing an edition, also look carefully at the repeat signs, so you do not play a section that should be repeated only once, which would make the structure a little shorter.

## What to Remember About The Easy Winners

This is Joplin's ragtime of 1901, with a steady left hand and a syncopated right hand, and a character that is unhurried and unflustered.

In practice, first line up each hand separately, then put them together, and do not let the pedal cover the pulse.

When listening, first follow the bass, and then listen for the notes that slip away from it.

## Keeping the Left Hand Steady

The left hand should be even; as bass notes and chords alternate, do not let one heavy and one light beat make you lose your footing.

Keep the wrist free, so the hand can move between positions without banging the keys to make the sound.

You can play the left hand alone as one continuous line, to confirm that it can stand on its own.

## The Title Does Not Mean Careless

"The Easy Winners" is closer to an unhurried, confident attitude than to permission to leave out the details.

If you play it rushed and loud, that unhurried quality disappears.

You can first sing the main melody at the speed of speech, and then go back to the score to see where the syncopations are written.

## Lining Up the Right-Hand Syncopation

Syncopation means that some notes come early or off the main beat, but they must still lock into the ground of the left hand.

First slow the right hand down and lightly tap the main beats, to see on which side of the beat the off-beat notes fall.

If the hands do not line up when you put them together, do not speed up both; slow down first and line them up.

## How Ragtime Appears in This Piece

A common ragtime texture is a steady pulse in half notes or quarter notes combined with a syncopated upper voice.

"The Easy Winners" writes this contrast very clearly, and there are also clear repeats and returns between the sections.

When listening, hold on to "steady below, off the beat above", and it becomes easier to follow its structure.

## Asking Teacher Aum to Listen for Whether the Syncopation Locks In

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your left hand is as steady as the ground and whether your right-hand syncopation locks in with it.

If a particular section rushes forward every time it repeats, you can also ask your teacher to slow it down with you by counting the beats.

Use this unhurried 1901 rag to practise making both the pulse and the syncopation clear at the same time.

## Pedal and Touch

The pedal should not blur the left-hand pulse into a haze; usually change it briefly with the harmony, or use a little more only in the more connected phrases.

The syncopated notes in the right hand should be springy, with short notes finished cleanly and long notes allowed to sing.

Keep some dynamic room in reserve overall, and do not play at full volume from the very start.

- A ragtime piano piece published by Joplin in 1901
- A steady left-hand pulse, with a syncopated right hand
- Unhurried in character, not to be played as a flustered show of technique
- Good for practising a steady left hand and clear syncopation

## Hearing the Repeats in the Sections

Ragtime often repeats by section, and listeners smile in recognition when familiar material comes back.

You can also practise section by section: once one section is secure, move on to the next, and finally smooth out the joins.

The return need not be exactly the same as the first time, but the pulse and the main melodic outline should still be recognisable.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote this piece, and in what year was it published?**
A: Scott Joplin, in 1901.

**Q: What is the easiest feature of ragtime to hear?**
A: A steady bass pulse combined with a syncopated upper voice.

**Q: How should "easy" be understood here?**
A: As closer to unhurried and confident, not as permission to play carelessly.

**Q: What should I do when the hands do not line up?**
A: Slow down first, and let the right-hand syncopation lock back into the left-hand ground.

**Q: What should I watch for with the pedal?**
A: Change it briefly and use it sparingly, so the left-hand pulse does not blur.

jingle-bells-piano-beginner.body:
"Jingle Bells" was written by the American composer James Lord Pierpont and first published in 1857, under the title "One Horse Open Sleigh". The song describes dashing through the snow in a sleigh, with a lively rhythm and a tune that is easy to remember, and the chorus has many repeated notes, which makes it very good practice for beginners. At the piano, let the melody in the right hand be light and springy, and let the left hand keep a steady two-beat or four-beat pulse with a simple bass note or chord, to bring out the relaxed, cheerful mood.

## A Lively Rhythm

The rhythm of "Jingle Bells" is bright and lively, usually in 4/4 or 2/2 time.

**Something to consider**

The melody has many quarter notes and eighth notes, ringing out crisply like little bells.

As you play, keep the rhythm steady and springy to bring out the cheerful mood.

## From Singing to Playing

You can start by singing the melody to get to know its rhythm, and then practise the right hand and left hand separately.

Set the metronome slowly at first, then raise it notch by notch to a cheerful speed.

Once you know it well, you can perform it for everyone at holidays or family gatherings and share the joy of music.

## Adding a Little Effect

To suggest the sound of bells, you can add some short ornaments or light chords in the high register.

You can also add a bell-like figure in the introduction or at the ending, for extra fun.

These small touches can give your performance a festive atmosphere.

## A Sleigh Song from 1857

"Jingle Bells" is a song by the American composer James Lord Pierpont, first published in 1857.

At that time it was called "One Horse Open Sleigh", and was only later renamed to the title everyone knows today.

The song was originally about the joy of racing through the snow in a sleigh in winter, and gradually became linked with winter holidays.

## Different Versions

There are many arrangements of "Jingle Bells", from simple beginner versions to versions with a jazz style or richer harmony.

You can start with the simple version and, once you are comfortable, try more challenging arrangements.

You can also try writing a simple accompaniment for the song yourself, as an arranging exercise.

## A Light Right Hand

The melody in the right hand should be light and springy, and not played too heavily.

You can play staccato on some notes to make the sound crisper, like the sound of bells.

Finish the end of each phrase clearly before moving on to the next.

## Contrast Between Verse and Chorus

The verse of this song tells of the sleigh setting off, and its melody rises and falls; the chorus is the familiar "jingle, jingle".

When you play, you can make the verse a little softer, then make the chorus bright and spirited, to create a little contrast.

In this way, even a simple song can be played with shape and depth.

## Singing with Your Family

This song is perfect for singing at home with your family: you can play the accompaniment while everyone sings the melody.

When accompanying singing, pay attention to everyone's tempo and do not play too fast.

Time spent singing together like this lets music become a joy the whole family shares.

## Common Chords

In the C major version, the song mainly uses the three chords C, F and G, with chords such as D7 appearing occasionally.

Knowing these chords helps you understand the harmony of the song, and makes it easier to work out an accompaniment of your own.

You can start by playing only the chords while singing along with the melody, to get used to where the chords change.

## Playing the Repeated Notes

The repeated notes at the start of the chorus are the most distinctive part of the song, sounding like bells jingling.

At a slow tempo you can use the same finger each time, letting the key come back up between notes.

If the tempo is faster, you can also consider changing fingers, and you can talk this over with your teacher.

## Left-Hand Bass Notes on C, F and G

At first, the left hand only needs to play a bass note such as C, F or G at the start of each bar.

Once you are comfortable, you can add simple chords, or use an accompaniment pattern that alternates bass note and chord to add rhythmic drive.

The left hand should stay steady, giving the right-hand melody a reliable pulse.

## A Catchy Chorus on Repeated Notes

The melody of this song is simple and easy to remember, and the chorus has many repeated notes, such as three of the same note in a row.

The melody of the verse rises and falls a little, describing the feeling of the sleigh gliding over the snow.

The range of the whole song is not wide, so a beginner's hand does not need to move very far.

- Written by James Lord Pierpont
- First published in 1857 under the title "One Horse Open Sleigh"
- Lively rhythm, with many repeated notes in the chorus
- The left hand keeps a steady pulse

josquin-des-prez-renaissance-master.body:
Josquin des Prez was a composer of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. He was born in what is now northern France and Belgium and worked for many years in Italian cities such as Milan and Rome. He wrote many masses, motets and secular songs, and his music spread widely during his lifetime. In 1502 a Venetian printer published a book of masses containing only his work, which was very rare at the time. The reformer Martin Luther is said to have remarked that Josquin is the master of the notes: the notes must do as he wishes, while other composers must do as the notes wish.

## A composer from the north

Josquin was born in what is now northern France and Belgium, a region that produced many fine composers in his day.

**Summary**

They often travelled to churches and cities across Italy, bringing the polyphonic techniques of the north to the south.

Josquin is one of the most famous of them.

## The 1502 book of masses

At the end of the fifteenth century, music printing began to develop in Venice.

In 1502 a Venetian printer published a book of masses that contained the work of Josquin alone.

At the time, a book devoted to a single composer was very rare, which shows how famous he was.

## His years in Italy

Josquin worked in Italy for many years and visited cities such as Milan, Rome and Ferrara.

In Rome he sang in the pope's chapel choir.

A name carved into a wall there is said to be his, and it can reportedly still be found in that chapel today.

## The puzzle of authorship

Because Josquin was so famous, quite a few printers of the time published other people's works under his name.

Today's scholars have to work hard to decide which pieces he really wrote.

This, too, shows from another angle how famous he was in his day.

## Josquin in brief

Josquin des Prez was a composer of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, born in what is now northern France and Belgium. He worked for many years in Milan, Rome, Ferrara and other Italian cities and sang in the pope's chapel choir. In 1502 a Venetian printer published a book of masses containing only his work, and Martin Luther is said to have called him the "master of the notes".

He often used imitation, in which one voice sings first and the other voices enter a little later. He cared about matching the music's mood to the words, and he also wrote French secular songs. Because he was so famous, many works by others were published under his name. At the piano, you can play a short melody in the right hand and imitate it in the left hand an octave lower, two beats later.

You can try imitation with Teacher Aum.

## From imitation to canon

If imitation is kept up strictly from beginning to end, it becomes a canon.

The rounds that many children know are a simple kind of canon.

Josquin's imitative writing can be seen as a refined Renaissance development of this technique.

## The master of the notes

The reformer Martin Luther is said to have loved Josquin's music.

He is said to have remarked that Josquin is the master of the notes: the notes must do as he wishes, while other composers must do as the notes wish.

The saying shows that Josquin could use the rules of music freely to express exactly what he wanted.

## Secular songs

Besides sacred music, Josquin also wrote many secular songs in French.

Some are tender and some are humorous, and they were popular in the cities of his time.

Some songs were later arranged for instruments and played on the lute and on keyboard instruments.

## Trying imitation at the piano

You can try imitation at the piano: play a short melody of four or five notes with the right hand.

After two beats, the left hand enters an octave lower with the same melody.

Listen to what happens when the two hands play the same melody, one after the other.

## Words and music

Josquin cared a great deal about the relationship between words and music, letting the mood of the music follow the meaning of the text.

Sad words were set to low, slow music, and joyful words to bright, lively music.

This approach had a great influence on later composers.

## His motets

Josquin wrote many motets, polyphonic choral pieces set to sacred Latin texts.

In one famous motet in honour of the Virgin Mary, the four voices enter one after another in imitation at the opening.

This work is often used as an example when studying Renaissance polyphony.

- A composer of the late fifteenth to early sixteenth centuries
- Worked in Italian cities such as Milan and Rome
- In 1502 a book of masses containing only his work was published in Venice
- Said to have been called the "master of the notes" by Luther

## Trying Josquin's imitation with your teacher

In a lesson with Teacher Aum, one of you can play a melody while the other enters with the same melody two beats later.

You can also ask your teacher to explain the difference between Renaissance polyphony and the later polyphony of Bach.

From a "master of the notes", learn to hear every line in polyphony.

## The technique of imitation

In Josquin's music, a technique called imitation is often used.

One voice sings a melody first, and the other voices enter a little later with the same melody.

Layer by layer, the sound grows richer while every voice stays clear.

![A person with blue-violet hair and a futuristic jacket plays layered glowing synthesisers on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbj9589-18s0v.webp)

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Where was Josquin born?**
A: In what is now northern France and Belgium.

**Q: Which Italian cities did he work in?**
A: Milan, Rome, Ferrara and others.

**Q: What kind of book was published in 1502?**
A: A book of masses containing only his work.

**Q: Who is said to have called him the "master of the notes"?**
A: Martin Luther.

**Q: What is imitation?**
A: One voice sings a melody first, and the other voices enter a little later with the same melody.
