idee-fixe-berlioz-fantastique-1830.body:
The "idée fixe" is the name given to the melody that keeps returning in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830, changing its character from movement to movement. It stands for the beloved person the music tells of, and comes back across the five movements at different speeds, in different orchestrations and with different moods: sometimes graceful, sometimes agitated, sometimes placed in very different scenes. This approach is similar to what is later called the leitmotif: both use one recognisable piece of musical material to run through a larger work. For anyone listening to the symphony or looking at a piano reduction, first humming this melody until it is familiar and then listening to each transformation is the most direct way into the work. It also shows that a theme does not have to appear only once at the beginning, but can carry the story through the whole work. When listening, it is especially helpful to have a sheet of paper and note the tempo and character each time it appears. With this table, the five movements are less likely to fall apart in your hearing.

## The Symphony of 1830

The Symphonie fantastique was completed and first performed in 1830, and is one of Berlioz's most famous early large-scale works.

It has five movements and a storyline that can be told.

The idée fixe is the main musical material that binds this storyline together.

## How to Start Listening

First find only the original form of this melody and listen again and again until you can hum it.

Then listen to the whole work, and each time it appears, note the movement, the tempo and the general mood.

On the second listening it will be much clearer than the first.

## Why Is It Called an Idée Fixe?

The name stresses that one musical idea is "fixed" and used as a means of running through the work.

It is not repeated unchanged every time, but changes its appearance while remaining recognisable.

The point of listening is exactly this: "still recognisable, yet with a different character".

## Help for Understanding Programme Music

This work is often discussed as a programme symphony, because the music is tied to a storyline.

The idée fixe gives this storyline a concrete sound, rather than only a written explanation.

Even without relying on the detailed story, just following this melody lets you feel that the five movements are connected.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Hum the Original Form With You in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to hum the original form of the idée fixe with you until it is familiar, and then listen to a transformation in one of the movements.

You can also mark on the spot which notes to bring out in the piano reduction.

Through this leading melody of 1830, practise following the thread of material that runs through a large work.

- A leading melody that recurs in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830
- Changes tempo, orchestration and character from movement to movement
- Stands for the beloved person the work tells of
- Hum the original form first, then listen to each transformation

## How It Is Transformed

The same melody can be slowed down or sped up, given to different instruments, set with different accompaniment, or placed in different scenes such as a dance or a march.

Sometimes it is fairly complete, and sometimes only its outline remains.

Remember the intervals and rhythmic outline of the original form first, and you can keep up with the transformations.

## Do Not Hear It in Only One Way

If you decide it must always be graceful or always intense, the later transformations will seem "wrong".

A better expectation is to recognise it while allowing it to change with the scene.

This flexibility is exactly the strength of the technique.

![Lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdj7wt8-7inc6.webp)

## Relationship to the Leitmotif

Later, people often used the term leitmotif for similar running material, especially in large stage works.

The idée fixe can be seen as an important example of this approach in the symphony.

When studying, there is no need to argue about which word is more correct; just grasp the point that "recognisable material runs through the work while changing".

## On the Piano Reduction

A piano reduction puts the main melody in a place where it is fairly easy to see, but it may still be surrounded by texture.

You can mark the idée fixe with a coloured pencil and let it be heard a little when you play.

A reduction cannot replace the colours of the orchestra, so you should still listen to a recording for the changes of orchestration.

## The Idée Fixe: Summary

The idée fixe is the leading melody that recurs and is constantly transformed in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830. It stands for the beloved person, and changes tempo, orchestration and character from movement to movement.

When studying, hum the original form first, then note each appearance, mark it in the reduction, and listen to a recording for the orchestration.

You can ask Teacher Aum to hum and listen to the original form and its transformations with you.

## FAQ

**Q: Which work contains the most famous example of the idée fixe?**
A: Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830.

**Q: What does this melody stand for in the work?**
A: The beloved person the music tells of.

**Q: Is it exactly the same each time it appears?**
A: No. It changes tempo, orchestration and character while remaining recognisable.

**Q: What should I do first when I start listening?**
A: Hum the original form until it is familiar, then follow its transformations through the movements.

**Q: How should I use a piano reduction?**
A: Mark this melody and bring it out slightly, while still listening to an orchestral recording for the changes of colour.

landini-cadence-under-third-14th-century.body:
The Landini cadence is a common way of ending a phrase in fourteenth- and fifteenth-century polyphonic music. Before reaching the final note, the top voice does not rise directly from the leading note to the tonic. Instead it first steps down from the leading note to the sixth degree, then leaps up a third to the tonic. For example, in a phrase ending on C, the melody goes "ti, la, do" instead of "ti, do". It is named after Francesco Landini, a fourteenth-century composer and organist from Florence, Italy, because he often used this ending in his works, but many composers of the same period used it too.

## Playing the Landini cadence at the piano

At the piano you can play "ti, la, do" with your right hand and "re, do" with your left hand at the same time.

Play slowly at first and listen to how the two voices open out from a sixth to an octave.

Then compare it with an ending that goes straight from "ti" to "do".

## Listening to medieval songs

You can find recordings of fourteenth-century Italian songs and listen to the ending of each phrase.

In many phrases you will hear this step down, "ti, la, do".

After listening a lot, you will quickly learn to recognise the Landini cadence.

## A softer ending

Because it first steps down, the Landini cadence sounds softer than a direct resolution of the leading note.

It has a graceful, gently winding flavour.

This flavour is common in fourteenth-century Italian songs.

## Not his invention

Although the Landini cadence is named after Landini, he did not invent it alone.

In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, composers in Italy, France and elsewhere often used this ending.

It was named after him only because later generations often saw it in Landini’s works.

## Who was Landini

Francesco Landini was a fourteenth-century composer, poet and organist from Florence, Italy.

He left around one hundred and fifty secular songs, most of them ballatas for two or three voices.

He was famous in his own time and is regarded as one of the representative figures of fourteenth-century Italian music.

## Landini cadence summary

The Landini cadence is a common phrase ending in fourteenth- and fifteenth-century polyphony. The top voice steps down from the leading note to the sixth degree and then leaps up a third to the tonic, for example "ti, la, do", while the lower voice goes from "re" to "do" at the same time, so the two voices open out from a sixth to an octave. It is named after Francesco Landini, the Florentine composer, poet and organist who left about one hundred and fifty secular songs, but many composers of his time used it.

It is softer and more winding than a direct leading-note resolution, and in the late fifteenth century it was gradually replaced by the perfect cadence, with the bass moving from dominant to tonic. At the piano you can play "ti, la, do" with the right hand and "re, do" with the left, or you can write a short melody that ends with it.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the Landini cadence.

## Later changes

By the late fifteenth century, the Landini cadence was used less and less.

Composers increasingly used the cadence with the bass moving from dominant to tonic, which later became the perfect cadence.

But in some later music you can still occasionally hear this stepping-down ending.

## Putting it into a short melody

You can write a short four-bar melody yourself and end the last bar with a Landini cadence.

For example, "mi, re, do, re, mi, re, ti, la, do".

Play it a few times and feel the flavour this winding ending gives the melody.

## What is a cadence

In music, a cadence is the way harmony and melody move at the end of a phrase or piece.

It is like the tone of voice at the end of a sentence, letting people know the sentence is finished.

Different periods have different common cadences.

## Stepping down first

What makes the Landini cadence special is that after the leading note, the melody does not rise straight to the tonic.

It first steps down to the sixth degree, then leaps up a third to the tonic.

That is "ti, la, do", as if taking a small detour before arriving.

## Trying the Landini cadence with your teacher in a lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the Landini cadence and how it differs from the later perfect cadence.

You can also play a short melody you have written for your teacher and see whether the cadence sounds natural.

From one small detour, you can hear the elegance of the Middle Ages.

## Leading note to tonic

In a lot of music, before a phrase ends, the melody often rises a semitone from the leading note to the tonic.

For example, in C major, it goes from "ti" to "do".

The leading note is only a semitone below the tonic and has a strong feeling of wanting to rise.

- A common phrase ending in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries
- The top voice steps down from the leading note to the sixth degree, then leaps to the tonic
- Named after the Florentine composer Landini
- Many composers of the same period used it too

## Working with the lower voice

In the Landini cadence, while the top voice goes "ti, la, do", the lower voice usually goes down from "re" to "do".

The two voices expand from a sixth to an octave, creating an ending that opens outwards.

**Summary**

This is a very typical cadence in medieval polyphony.

![A wooden upright piano, a green piano stool and orange books in front of a dark teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbjvcnv-rfb9t.webp)

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: How does the top voice move in the Landini cadence?**
A: It steps down from the leading note to the sixth degree, then leaps up a third to the tonic.

**Q: What is the melody in a phrase ending on C?**
A: "Ti, la, do".

**Q: Who is it named after?**
A: Francesco Landini, a fourteenth-century composer from Florence.

**Q: Did Landini invent it alone?**
A: No, many composers of the same period used it.

**Q: How do the two voices change at the ending?**
A: They open out from a sixth to an octave.

hungarian-minor-scale-raised-fourth.body:
The Hungarian minor scale is a seven-note scale made by raising both the fourth and seventh degrees of the natural minor. Raising the seventh gives a strong leading note, as in the harmonic minor; raising the fourth as well creates an augmented second in the middle of the scale, which sounds especially sharp and colourful. Many melodies and piano pieces with a Hungarian or related folk flavour use this scale, or draw typical intervals from it. For learners, it is more useful to play the scale slowly at the keyboard, starting from A minor or another key, and listen for where the augmented second falls, and then look for the same motion in pieces, than to just remember a name. It is related to the harmonic and melodic minor, but differs from them in key ways, so they should not be confused. When practising, try it with both hands, and read the accidentals carefully in keys with many sharps. Sing the augmented second in tune on its own and then put it back into the scale, and the scale often steadies at once.

## Fingering on the Keyboard

Because there are several sharps or raised notes, decide the fingering in advance so your hand does not twist on the augmented second.

**Listen**

You can start by practising one octave slowly, hands separately, and then extend to two octaves.

In keys with more black keys, place the fingers ahead of time even more carefully.

## The Hungarian Minor Scale: Summary

The Hungarian minor scale raises the fourth and seventh degrees of the natural minor, so it has a strong leading note and forms an augmented second in the middle, unlike the harmonic minor, which raises only the seventh.

Play it slowly at the keyboard and sing the augmented second in tune, then look for typical motion in pieces, and decide the fingering beforehand.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your intervals are accurate.

**Try it**
- Raise the fourth and seventh degrees of the natural minor
- An augmented second appears in the middle of the scale
- Related to the harmonic minor, but with an additional raised fourth
- Play it slowly at the keyboard first, then look for typical intervals in pieces

## How to Get There From the Natural Minor

Take A natural minor as an example: the original notes are A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

Raise F to F♯ and G to G♯, and you have a Hungarian minor scale.

On other tonics the principle is the same: raise both the fourth and seventh degrees.

## What to Listen For When Practising the Hungarian Minor Scale

Each day, play it slowly up and down in one key, listening especially for whether the augmented second is in tune.

Then circle the same interval in the piece you are learning.

If the piece does not use this scale, there is no need to force an unrelated work to fit.

## Do Not Mix It Up With Other "Style Scales"

Textbooks may also give other scale names that contain an augmented second, and their fingering and note sets are not necessarily exactly the same.

With a specific piece, go by the notes that actually appear in the score.

First master this one clear definition, and then compare it with other names.

## Harmonic Hints

The raised seventh still usually leans towards the tonic, while the raised fourth gives special colour to chords in the subdominant direction or in the middle.

You do not need to analyse all the chords at the start; just being able to hear these two raised notes in the melody is already very helpful.

As a further step, you can look at which chords they appear in.

## Comparison With the Harmonic Minor

The harmonic minor usually raises only the seventh and leaves the fourth unchanged.

The Hungarian minor scale raises both notes, so the colour in the middle is sharper.

Both can have a strong leading note, but the path through the middle is different.

## Where Is the Augmented Second?

After the fourth and seventh are raised, an augmented second often forms between the raised fourth and the original sixth.

This interval sounds fairly wide and sharp, and is one of the easiest features of this scale to hear.

First sing these two notes in tune on their own, and then put them back into the scale.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen to the Augmented Second in Lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether you sing and play the augmented second of this scale accurately, and to compare it once with the harmonic minor.

If a piece contains similar motion, you can circle it together.

Through the Hungarian minor scale, practise recognising that sharp, colourful interval in the middle.

![A watercolour of a grand piano with its lid open, in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjcay8-j6vg7.webp)

## How It Appears in Melodies

A melody does not always run through every note of the scale strictly; usually a few typical motions recur.

For example, a short figure containing an augmented second, or an ornament with a raised fourth.

Listen for these typical intervals, rather than checking whether any note has been left out.

## FAQ

**Q: How is the Hungarian minor scale formed?**
A: By raising both the fourth and seventh degrees of the natural minor.

**Q: What is its most easily heard feature?**
A: The augmented second that often appears in the middle of the scale, and the strong leading note.

**Q: How does it differ from the harmonic minor?**
A: The harmonic minor usually raises only the seventh; this scale raises the fourth as well.

**Q: Does a whole melody have to run through every note of the scale?**
A: Not necessarily. Often a few typical motions containing an augmented second or a raised fourth recur.

**Q: What should I do first when practising?**
A: Choose a key, play and sing the scale slowly, and first sing the augmented second in tune.

keep-score-still-under-fan.body:
Practising under a fan or air conditioner, with the score blown over or its corners lifted by the wind, is a very common small nuisance. Holding both sides with clips, adjusting the fan's direction and speed, and putting loose pages into a clear plastic sleeve can all keep the page steady. When the score stops moving, your eyes and attention can stay on the music, instead of constantly reaching out to hold the paper down.

## What to Practise When It Is Windy

If for some period the fan has to be turned up high, you can put the focus of your practice on pieces you already know by heart, depending less on the score.

**Keep this in mind**

You can also use this time for scales, arpeggios and other technical exercises, most of which do not need you to keep looking at the score, as your hands and ears can manage.

The work of reading a new piece can be scheduled for a time when the wind is gentler, such as early morning or evening, or you can read it through at a table first and make your markings, and then go to the piano to play. That way, even if the score is occasionally blown about, it will not completely upset your rhythm.

## Adjusting the Direction of the Wind

Try not to let the fan blow straight at the music stand. You can place a floor fan to the side and behind you, so the wind blows on your body rather than on the page.

A ceiling fan cannot change direction, so you can turn the speed down a little, or adjust the position of the piano to avoid the spot directly under the ceiling fan.

The same goes for the air-conditioner vent: do not let cold air blow directly at the music stand and the piano. Cold air blowing directly not only makes the score move about, but also makes your fingers cold.

## Fixing with Clips

Music clips are small clips made specially to hold sheet music, usually clipped on both sides of the music stand. Choose a type with soft pads on the jaws, which are less likely to leave dents in the paper.

Do not clip too tightly; leave a little give, so that when you turn the page you can easily slide it out from under the clip.

If you do not have music clips, ordinary binder clips can also be used temporarily, but take care that the clips do not cover any notes.

## Why Scores Get Blown About

Music paper is light and thin, especially photocopied loose pages and paperback books, and even a little wind will lift the corners of the pages. When a fan turns overhead, the wind presses down in gusts, and the page trembles gently in time with it.

If the score is already curled at the edges, or the spine is too stiff to close, a gust makes it even easier to turn over.

In the tropics or in summer, running a fan is almost a necessity for practising, so finding a way to fix the score is more practical than turning off the fan.

If this small nuisance is not dealt with, it interrupts your practice again and again, and makes you more and more impatient.

**Watch the details**
- Clips hold both the left and right sides, with moderate pressure
- Do not let the fan blow straight at the music stand
- Put loose pages in a sleeve or stick them on a stiff board
- Plan in advance the places where you need to turn pages

## You Could Also Consider Digital Scores

A score on a tablet is not afraid of the wind, you can turn pages with a light tap of the finger, and there are also devices that turn pages with a pedal.

However, with digital scores you need to watch the screen brightness, the battery and reflections, and reading for a long time may also tire the eyes.

Paper and digital scores can be used together: use the digital score for practice in windy seasons, and paper when you need to make a lot of markings.

![A person with blue-purple hair and a futuristic jacket plays a multi-tiered glowing synthesiser on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wu4wa-lq9b9.webp)

## Add a Layer of Protection for Loose Pages

For single photocopied sheets, put them in a sleeve and then into a folder with a hard cover; the paper gains weight and stiffness and is less likely to be blown up.

You can also stick two or three pages side by side on a sheet of stiff card to make a small display board; it is very stable on the music stand, and it also means fewer page turns.

Choose matt sleeves, which reduce reflection from the lights and make reading more comfortable.

The size of the card can be cut to the width of the music stand, so that it does not block the lid of the piano and does not wobble back and forth by being too big.

## Plan Your Page Turns in Advance

In a windy room it is easier to get flustered when turning pages. In practice you can first look at where the page turns are, and find a rest or a long note as the turning point.

If a section is hard to leave your hands from exactly where the page turns, you can photocopy the first few bars of the next page and stick them on the edge of the current page.

Once you are used to it, turning the page becomes a natural movement within the music, not an interruption.

## FAQ

**Q: Will music clips damage the score?**
A: Choose clips with soft pads and do not clip too tightly, and they generally will not leave obvious marks.

**Q: Can I stick the score to the music stand with tape?**
A: You can fix it temporarily with tape that is easy to peel off, but do not stick it over the notes, and be careful when peeling it off.

**Q: Must a piano never go under a ceiling fan?**
A: It can, but turn the wind speed down, fix the score with clips, and also pay attention to changes in the temperature and humidity around the piano itself.

**Q: Will the fan make my hands cold?**
A: Wind blowing directly on your hands may make your fingers cold; you can adjust the direction so that the wind blows on your body rather than your hands.

**Q: Will a tablet be blown over by the wind?**
A: A tablet is heavier than paper and generally will not, but make sure the music stand can hold it steadily.

**Q: Is there a way that does not use clips?**
A: Putting the score in a stiff ring binder, or sticking it on stiff card, can also reduce the movement effectively.

keyboard-to-upright-piano-first-week.body:
When you move from a keyboard to an upright piano, it is very common to find the keys heavy and the sound hard to control in the first week. On an upright piano the keys are connected to the action, so the depth and force of each keypress affect the tone. Getting used to the weight of the keys with slow playing and familiar hand shapes helps more than rushing into new pieces. Get familiar first, then speed up.

## Why Acoustic Piano Keys Feel Heavier

On an acoustic piano, pressing a key moves the action inside so that the hammer strikes the string, and the keyboard itself has a certain weight and resistance. The keys of many beginner keyboards are lighter and have no such mechanism, so your fingers feel strained when you first switch.

**Remember this**

The key to adapting is not to pound the keys harder, but to relax your arms and shoulders and let their weight sink naturally into the keys. At first, play plenty of long notes and slow chords, and listen to each note from the moment you press the key until it fades away. Gradually you will find the feel of controlling the volume.

You can also play the same piece on both the keyboard and the piano, and compare the touch and sound of the two instruments. This helps you build new habits of touch more quickly.

## Get Used to the Feel of the New Piano First

When you first switch, do not rush into playing pieces. Spend a few days on scales, simple chords and short pieces you know, and feel the weight, depth and return speed of the keys. Once your fingers are familiar, practising new material will go more smoothly.

The tone of an acoustic piano changes with how you touch the keys. Try playing the same note with different amounts of force and listen to how the sound differs. This kind of practice builds your sensitivity to tone, which is hard to experience on a keyboard.

Your fingers may tire easily at first, which is a normal part of adapting. Split your practice into several short stretches with rests in between, so that your hands slowly get used to the weight of the new keys.

Try playing a very soft melody on the new piano, then a very loud chord, and feel how the keys respond at different levels of force. Knowing the volume range of your new piano will help you control dynamics later.

## Re-learning Familiar Pieces on the New Piano

After switching, pick a few pieces you already play very well and practise them again. Because the notes and fingering are already familiar, your attention can go entirely to the touch and the tone, and you will adapt faster.

On an acoustic piano, changes in dynamics are more obvious. Try deliberately adding contrast between loud and soft in a familiar piece, and feel how arm weight and the speed of your touch affect the sound.

If some passages do not feel smooth on the new piano, slow down and practise them again. This usually just needs getting used to, and does not mean that what you learned before was wasted.

Adapting to a new piano takes a little time, so there is no need to hurry. As long as you practise regularly, your fingers will gradually get used to the new keyboard, and the rich variety of tone on an acoustic piano will become one of the pleasures of practising.

**Pay attention to the details**
- Play familiar, simple pieces first and concentrate on feeling the weight of the keys
- Use the weight of your arm to drive your fingers, rather than relying only on the fingertips
- Press each note all the way down before releasing it
- Daily sessions do not need to be long. What matters is regular contact

![A watercolour painting of a grand piano with its lid open, in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jdkar-zk7qp.webp)

## Basics of Placement and Care

An upright piano is best placed away from direct sunlight and away from air-conditioning vents, to avoid big changes in temperature and humidity. You can leave a little space between the back of the piano and the wall, which helps the sound resonate.

In a humid climate, keep an eye on the humidity in the room, and use dehumidifying equipment if necessary. Damp can affect the touch and tuning of the keys and internal parts, so keeping the piano dry and clean is important.

**Summary**

An acoustic piano needs regular tuning. Generally you can have a professional tuner check it at the recommended interval. After a house move, or just after the new piano is set up, you can also ask a tuner to take a look.

## FAQ

**Q: Is it normal for my fingers to ache after switching pianos?**
A: Some tiredness at first is common. Shorten each practice session and rest in between. If the discomfort continues, stop and ask your teacher.

**Q: Can I keep practising on my keyboard?**
A: You can, as a supplement, but to get used to the feel of the piano, it is best to spend most of your practice time on the piano.

**Q: Will my keyboard practice be wasted?**
A: No. Reading, fingering and sense of rhythm all carry straight over to the piano. You just need to get used to the new touch.

**Q: How often does an acoustic piano need tuning?**
A: Follow your tuner's advice. It is usually once or twice a year, depending on use and the environment.

**Q: What if I get very tired after switching?**
A: Shorten each practice session, practise in short stretches, and pay attention to relaxing your wrists and arms.

**Q: Can I alternate between a digital piano and an acoustic piano?**
A: Yes, but be aware of the difference in touch, and do extra adjustment practice on the acoustic piano when needed.

key-signature-change-mid-piece.body:
When the key signature changes in the middle of a piece, the new key signature is usually written after a double barline. From there on, all the notes concerned must be played according to the new key signature. Marking it in the score in advance and getting to know the scale of the new key helps your hands and eyes get ready, so you do not carry on playing in the old key signature.

## Prepare in advance

When you get a new piece, you can first look through it from beginning to end, find all the double barlines and new key signatures, and circle them in pencil.

**Tip**

About two bars before the key signature changes, you can write a reminder, such as the name of the new key or the notes that will change, so that your eyes see it ahead of time.

In practice, first play the scale of the new key on its own, so your fingers get used to the positions of the new black keys, and then practise the passage before and after the change.

Practise the few bars before and after the change together, again and again, so that the transition becomes natural.

If the key signature change falls right at a page turn, you can copy the new key signature at the end of the previous page ahead of time, to reduce the flurry when turning the page.

![A sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angled view, in sepia tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8kkvxp-7kst0.webp)

## Common mistakes

The most common mistake is not noticing the key signature change and carrying on in the old key signature, so some notes are wrong.

Another mistake is, when changing back to the original key, still keeping the sharps or flats of the new key. Remember that each change of key signature is a new instruction.

Accidentals and key signatures are also easily confused. An accidental is valid only within the current bar, while the key signature affects all the bars that follow.

When you find a mistake, you can strengthen the reminder in the score, and practise slowly and repeatedly until your fingers are used to the new rule.

You can also ask your teacher to listen to the passage with the key signature change and confirm that no sharps or flats have been missed.

## Understanding what a key signature change means

A change of key signature usually means the music has entered a new key, bringing new colour and mood. For example, going from a major key to its relative minor, or to the dominant or subdominant key.

Listening to the music before and after the change and noticing how the mood changes can help you understand what the composer intended.

Some passages with a changed key signature are contrasting sections, after which the original key signature returns. Noticing this structure helps you grasp the layout of the whole piece.

Once you understand what the change means, you can use different tone colours and dynamics to show the different sections in performance.

This kind of listening also helps you remember the piece better.

**Another angle**
- The new key signature usually appears after a double barline
- From the new key signature onwards, play by the new rule
- You can mark it two bars ahead as a warning
- Play the scale of the new key first to help your fingers get used to it

## How a key signature change is written

When the key signature changes mid-piece, the new key signature is usually written after a double barline. If the original sharps or flats are cancelled, naturals are written first, followed by the new sharps or flats.

The new key signature takes effect from this point and lasts until the end of the piece, or until the next change of key signature.

Sometimes the new key signature is also written in advance at the end of the previous line as a reminder. This is called a cautionary key signature.

Knowing these conventions, you can spot key signature changes in good time when reading.

## How to prepare before a key signature change

When you get a new piece, you can first leaf through it from beginning to end and find the position of every double barline and new key signature. Circle them in pencil and write down the name of the new key and the notes that need to change, so you are not caught off guard when you get there.

If the new key signature cancels the original sharps or flats, the score shows this with natural signs. This also needs attention, because your fingers may still be used to the earlier black keys.

In practice you can take the two bars before and the two bars after the change and repeat them on their own, so the transition becomes natural. Once it is fluent, put them back into the whole piece and play it continuously.

For younger learners, you can circle the new key signature with a coloured pen, or put a small mark on the notes that need to change. Once they are familiar, reduce the marks gradually, so their eyes learn to read what the key signature means directly.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between an accidental and a key signature change?**
A: An accidental is valid only within the current bar, while a key signature change affects all the bars after it, until it changes again.

**Q: Does a key signature change always mean a modulation?**
A: It usually means the music has entered a new key, but the exact key must still be judged from the melody and harmony.

**Q: What does it mean when naturals appear in a key signature?**
A: They cancel the sharps or flats of the original key signature, and the new key signature is written after them.

**Q: Do I play the cautionary key signature?**
A: No, it is only a reminder that the key signature changes at the start of the next line.

**Q: Does the tempo change after a key signature change?**
A: Not necessarily. Tempo changes depend on the tempo marks in the score.

**Q: How do I memorise a piece with many key signature changes?**
A: You can divide the piece into sections by key, and remember the key and the opening of each section.

improvise-variations-on-a-familiar-tune.body:
Variation is a very common device in classical music: you play a theme first, then repeat it in different ways. You can try making simple variations yourself. Take a familiar nursery song, for example. Play it exactly as written the first time; the second time, change the rhythm by turning quarter notes into a dotted rhythm; the third time, add passing notes between the melody notes; the fourth time, switch to a minor key, or hand the melody to your left hand. Change just one thing each time, and the theme is still recognisable while the music takes on a new look.

## Change the Accompaniment Pattern

Besides changing the melody, you can change only the left-hand accompaniment.

**Take it slowly**

For example, the first time play long chords in the left hand, the next time play broken chords, and the time after that a bouncing bass with chords.

The melody stays the same, but changes in the accompaniment still give the music a different feel.

## Choose a Familiar Tune

To make your own variations, start with a very familiar tune with a simple melody, such as a nursery song.

The simpler the tune, the easier it is to vary, and the easier it is to hear the theme.

First get the tune comfortable in your right hand, then add simple left-hand chords.

## Write Down Your Own Variations

If you really like one of your variations, you can jot it down simply, or record it.

That way you can play it again next time, or keep improving it.

Little by little, you will build up more and more ways to vary a tune.

## Change Only One Thing at a Time

When making variations, there is a simple principle: change only one thing each time through.

If you change too much at once, the theme may no longer be recognisable, and the variation loses its point.

With only one change, listeners feel "this is still the same piece" and also hear something new.

## Switch to a Minor Key

The fourth time, you can try playing the theme in a minor key.

For example, if the original is in C major, change the E in the melody to E♭ and the A to A♭, and it will sound darker and a little sadder.

This is a very common kind of change in variations, and it can alter the mood of the music dramatically.

**Quick tips**
- Play the theme first, then repeat it in different ways
- Change the rhythm, for example to a dotted rhythm
- Add passing notes, or switch to a minor key
- Change only one thing each time so the theme is still recognisable

## Link the Variations Together

Once you have tried several variations, you can join them in order to make a little set of variations.

You can usually start with simple changes and become richer as you go, then return to the theme at the end or close with a short ending.

This gives the whole set of variations a shape that rises and falls.

## Summary: Making Your Own Variations

To make variations on a familiar tune, start by playing it as it is, then change the rhythm, add passing notes, switch to a minor key or hand the melody to the left hand.

Change only one thing each time so the theme stays recognisable.

Link several variations together, and you have a little set of variations of your own.

## Add Passing Notes

The third time, you can add some passing notes between the notes of the melody.

For example, if the melody leaps from C to E, put a D in between so that the melody moves step by step.

This makes the melody flow more smoothly and sound more ornamented.

![A glowing digital interface against a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4ep3n-hfnuv.webp)

## What Is a Variation?

In classical music, there is a common form called theme and variations.

The composer first writes a theme, then repeats it again and again, changing it a little each time.

Mozart's Variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", for example, takes a French folk song as its theme and builds twelve variations on it.

## First Time: Play It As It Is

Before you make variations, play the theme exactly as it is once, so that both you and your listeners remember it.

Play it clearly and steadily, without any ornaments.

This first time is like the opening of a story, introducing who the main character is.

## Give the Melody to the Left Hand

You can also give the theme's melody to the left hand, with the right hand playing chords or accompaniment.

When the melody appears in the low register it sounds deeper, which is a fresh effect.

When the left hand plays the melody, make sure it can be heard clearly, and play the right-hand accompaniment more softly.

## Rhythmic Variation

The second time, you can change only the rhythm and keep the notes of the melody the same.

For example, change even quarter notes into a dotted rhythm, long then short, and it will sound more bouncy.

You can also split each note into two eighth notes to make the melody flow more.

## Listen to Composers' Variations

You can find some famous sets of variations to listen to and see how composers make their changes.

Besides Mozart's Variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", Bach's Goldberg Variations and many of Beethoven's sets of variations are excellent examples.

As you listen, ask yourself: what has changed in this variation? Is it the rhythm, the harmony or the register?

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a variation?**
A: You play the theme first, then repeat it in different ways.

**Q: How can I change the rhythm?**
A: For example, change quarter notes into a dotted rhythm.

**Q: How do I switch to a minor key?**
A: Lower the third and sixth degrees of the melody by a semitone, for example changing E to E♭.

**Q: How many things should I change each time?**
A: We suggest changing only one thing each time so the theme stays recognisable.

**Q: Which sets of variations can I listen to?**
A: For example, Mozart's Variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" and Bach's Goldberg Variations.

janacek-on-an-overgrown-path-1911.body:
On an Overgrown Path is a set of short piano pieces by the Czech composer Leoš Janáček. The first book has ten pieces, written between about 1900 and 1911 and published in 1911. These little pieces recall his life in his Moravian homeland, and they also carry his longing for his daughter Olga, who died in 1903. Each piece has a very distinctive title, such as Our Evenings, A Blown-Away Leaf, Good Night! and Words Fail! The music is short and plain, the melodies often imitate the intonation of speech, and the harmonic colour is unique, which makes it a good starting point for getting to know Janáček's style.

## The Second Book

Besides the ten pieces of the first book, Janáček wrote several more pieces for a second book.

The second book is similar in style to the first, but was published later.

What is played most often today is mainly the ten pieces of the first book.

## A Blown-Away Leaf

The second piece, A Blown-Away Leaf, has a soft, drifting melody, like a leaf carried through the air by the wind.

The harmonic changes are very delicate, with a faint touch of sadness.

This little piece is very short, but its atmosphere runs deep.

## Summary: On an Overgrown Path

Leoš Janáček was born in 1854 and died in 1928. He was born in a small Moravian village, spent his life collecting and studying Moravian folk songs, and wrote many of his important works after the age of sixty. The ten pieces of the first book of On an Overgrown Path were written between about 1900 and 1911 and published in 1911. The title hints at a return to the past. His daughter Olga died of illness in 1903 at the age of twenty-one, and In Tears and Unutterable Anguish carry his longing for her.

The titles include Our Evenings, A Blown-Away Leaf, Come with us!, Good Night! and The Barn Owl Has Not Flown Away! He often wrote the intonation of speech down as notes, so the melodies sound like talking, and Words Fail! has many pauses. The harmony often uses folk modes and unexpected shifts. The second book was published later, and the technical difficulty is mostly moderate. Before playing, you can first think about what the title means.

You can ask Teacher Aum to recommend a suitable little piece.

## The Intonation of Speech

Janáček paid close attention to the intonation of people speaking, and often wrote down what he heard as notes.

He believed that the intonation of speech holds human feeling.

In this set of little pieces, many melodies seem to imitate the intonation of speech, short and natural.

![Illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, expressing the strength of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaf2wx8-dzrwm.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Recommend a Janáček Piece in Lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend a little piece suited to your level, chosen from the first book.

Your teacher can also explain the way Janáček's melodies imitate the intonation of speech.

Through this set of little pieces, step into Janáček's musical world.

## Playing Janáček on the Piano

The technical difficulty of these little pieces is mostly moderate, suited to players at an intermediate level.

But to play them well, you need some understanding of Janáček's unique style.

When you play, let the melody sound like speech, let the pauses feel natural, and keep the colours of the harmony delicate.

## The Special Titles

Each of the ten little pieces in the first book has a special title.

For example, Our Evenings, A Blown-Away Leaf, Come with us! and Good Night!

There is also one called The Barn Owl Has Not Flown Away!, and in Czech folk belief the barn owl is often linked with bad omens.

## Who Was Janáček?

Leoš Janáček was born in 1854 and died in 1928. He was a Czech composer.

He was born in a small village in Moravia, and the folk music there influenced him deeply.

Many of his important works were written after the age of sixty. When his opera Jenůfa was successfully staged in Prague in 1916, he was already over sixty.

## Distinctive Harmony

Janáček's harmony is very distinctive, often using the modes of folk music and unexpected chord shifts.

Sometimes a chord suddenly moves to a distant key, which comes as a surprise.

This distinctive harmony gives his music a special colour.

## Words Fail

Words Fail! is a very special little piece whose melody often stops, like a person who wants to speak but cannot find the words.

The music has many pauses and halting figures.

This little piece uses music to express a feeling that is hard to put into words.

## Longing for His Daughter

In 1903, Janáček's daughter Olga died of illness at only twenty-one.

The loss hit him very hard, and it is generally thought that some of the pieces in the set carry this deep sorrow.

In Tears and Unutterable Anguish, for example, let us feel a father's longing.

## His Moravian Homeland

Moravia is a region in the east of today's Czech Republic, rich in folk music and dance.

Throughout his life, Janáček collected and studied a great many Moravian folk songs.

Many of the pieces in On an Overgrown Path carry memories of home and the flavour of folk music.

- Short piano pieces by the Czech composer Janáček
- The first book has ten pieces, published in 1911
- They recall life in his Moravian homeland
- They carry longing for his daughter, who died in 1903

## The Name "Overgrown Path"

The name "On an Overgrown Path" sounds like a path that nobody has walked for a long time, grown over with weeds.

It hints at a return to the past, to remember people and things that have gone far away.

This set of little pieces is a series of pictures the composer sees as he walks along the path of memory.

## Read the Title Before You Play

Before playing each little piece, think first about what its title means.

For Good Night!, for example, you can imagine a gentle evening with someone softly saying goodnight.

**Summary**

A title can help you find the mood and picture of the music.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who wrote this set of little pieces?**
A: The Czech composer Janáček.

**Q: How many pieces are in the first book?**
A: Ten, published in 1911.

**Q: What place do these little pieces recall?**
A: His Moravian homeland.

**Q: In which year did Janáček's daughter die?**
A: 1903.

**Q: What do Janáček's melodies often imitate?**
A: The intonation of speech.

kreisler-1935-pastiche-revealed-story.body:
Fritz Kreisler was a very famous violinist in the first half of the twentieth century. For decades, he played many short pieces in concerts, saying he had found them as manuscripts by eighteenth-century composers in old libraries, such as works by Pugnani, Francoeur and others. Audiences and critics loved these "discoveries". It was not until 1935 that Kreisler publicly admitted that the pieces were in fact all his own, written in imitation of the old composers' styles. The story caused a great deal of argument, and it made people ask: does the value of a piece depend on who wrote it, or on the music itself?

## Why Did He Do It

Kreisler later explained that when he was young he needed more short pieces to fill out his concert programmes.

**Before you start**

If the programme was full of his own name, it would seem not modest enough, and might not be taken seriously.

So he borrowed the names of old composers for these works.

## Works Published Under His Own Name

Kreisler also had some works that he published directly under his own name, such as Liebesfreud, Liebesleid and Schön Rosmarin.

These pieces have the style of the Viennese waltz, with beautiful and touching melodies.

They are still often played by violinists today, and there are piano arrangements too.

## The Question Kreisler Left for Listeners

This story makes us think: when we listen to music, are we moved by the music itself, or influenced by the composer's name?

Sometimes a famous name makes us assume in advance that the music is good.

Learning to judge with your own ears is very important.

## The Confession of 1935

In 1935, when a critic questioned him, Kreisler publicly admitted that these works were all his own.

When the news came out, the music world was in uproar.

Some felt they had been deceived, while others thought it was just a harmless joke.

## The Art of Imitating a Style

That Kreisler could write "old works" convincing enough to be believed shows how well he knew the musical styles of the eighteenth century.

He knew the harmony, melody and ornamentation habits of that era, which is why he could imitate them so closely.

Imitating a style is itself one way that composers learn.

## Chat with Your Teacher About Kreisler's Style Game in a Lesson

In your lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about this story and share your own views on the value of a work.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend a short piano piece in imitation of the Baroque or Classical style to learn.

Starting from the story, you can understand musical style more deeply.

## A Batch of "Old Manuscripts"

From the early twentieth century, Kreisler played many short works in concerts.

He said these were manuscripts he had found in old libraries and monasteries in Europe, written by composers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

The programmes carried the names of Pugnani, Francoeur, Vivaldi and others.

## Try Writing a Piece in an Imitated Style

After learning some Baroque or Classical works, you can try imitating their style and write a short melody.

For example, write one using a Baroque sequence, or an eight-bar Classical phrase.

This is one of the most direct ways to understand a style.

## Kreisler Story Summary

Fritz Kreisler was born in 1875 and died in 1962. He was born in Vienna, and from the early twentieth century he played many pieces that he said were "old manuscripts" found in old libraries and monasteries. The programmes carried names such as Pugnani, Francoeur and Vivaldi, for example the Praeludium and Allegro in the style of Pugnani. He explained that he did it to enrich his programmes without seeming boastful.

In 1935 he publicly admitted that he had written them himself, which caused argument, and some criticised him for dishonesty. He replied that the value of the works did not change with the name of the author. He also published works under his own name, Liebesfreud, Liebesleid and Schön Rosmarin. That he could imitate so closely shows how well he knew eighteenth-century style. The story reminds us to judge with our own ears, and you can also try writing a melody in an imitated style.

You can chat about this story with Teacher Aum.

## The Critics' Argument

Some critics criticised Kreisler, saying that what he did was dishonest.

Kreisler replied that the value of these pieces had not changed because the author's name had changed.

He also pointed out that the people who had once praised these pieces were now changing their tune because the author was him, which itself was worth thinking about.

## Kreisler the Violinist

Fritz Kreisler was born in 1875 and died in 1962. He was born in Vienna, Austria.

He studied the violin from childhood, and began touring Europe and the United States while still very young.

His playing was warm and elegant, with a flavour peculiar to Vienna, and audiences loved it.

![A person wearing headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing the city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwad9fx6-0alb1.webp)

## Piano Arrangements of Kreisler's Pieces

Many of Kreisler's violin pieces have arrangements for solo piano or piano duet.

Some arrangements were made by other pianists and are quite difficult.

There are also simplified versions suited to intermediate players.

## Playing Works in an Imitated Style

On the piano, there are also many works in imitation of the Baroque or Classical style.

When you play this kind of work, you can pay attention to its stylistic features, such as Baroque ornaments and Classical clear structure.

Understanding the style helps you bring out a more authentic flavour.

**Think again**
- Kreisler was a famous violinist of the first half of the twentieth century
- He passed off pieces he wrote himself as works by old composers
- In 1935 he publicly admitted he had written them
- It sparked a discussion about the value of a work

## The Praeludium and Allegro in the Style of Pugnani

One of the most widely known is the Praeludium and Allegro, which the programme described as "in the style of Pugnani".

Pugnani was an eighteenth-century Italian violinist and composer.

**Summary**

This piece is majestic, and many violinists have made it one of their concert pieces.

## FAQ

**Q: Who was Kreisler?**
A: A violinist born in Austria, born in 1875 and died in 1962.

**Q: Whose works did he say his own pieces were?**
A: Those of old composers such as Pugnani, Francoeur and Vivaldi.

**Q: In which year did he confess?**
A: 1935.

**Q: Why did he do it?**
A: To enrich his programmes without seeming boastful.

**Q: Which works did he publish under his own name?**
A: Liebesfreud, Liebesleid, Schön Rosmarin and others.

key-signature-circle-of-fifths.body:
To recognise key signatures quickly, two memory rules are enough. Sharps appear in the order F, C, G, D, A, E, B, and flats go in exactly the reverse order: B, E, A, D, G, C, F. When you see a sharp key signature, raise the last sharp (the one furthest right) by a semitone, and that is the tonic of the major key. When you see a flat key signature, the second-to-last flat is the name of the major key (with only one flat, the key is F major). Once you have these two rules, and use the circle of fifths to understand how keys relate to one another, you no longer need to count black keys one by one when reading music.

## Quick summary

- Order of sharps: F C G D A E B
- Order of flats: B E A D G C F
- Sharp keys: last sharp + a semitone = the major tonic
- Flat keys: second-to-last flat = the name of the major key; one flat is F major
- Every major key has a relative minor that shares its key signature, with its tonic three semitones below the major tonic

## What is a key signature, and why recognise it first?

The key signature is written at the start of every staff and tells you which notes in the piece are to be raised or lowered throughout. It decides the "scale map" of the piece.

If you start playing without recognising the key signature, it is easy to make the same mistake again and again on one note, such as every F in G major having to be played as F♯. Spending three seconds to see the key signature clearly saves a great many corrections later. For anyone teaching piano, this is also a very worthwhile step to build into reading habits first.

## Sharp keys: look at the last one on the right

**Rule**
Sharps are added in the order F, C, G, D, A, E, B. Find the last (rightmost) sharp in the key signature and raise it by a semitone, and that is the major tonic.

**Examples**
- One sharp (F♯): F raised a semitone is G, so the key is G major
- Two sharps (F♯, C♯): C raised a semitone is D, so the key is D major
- Three sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯): G raised a semitone is A, so the key is A major

**Memory tip**
You can turn the seven letters into a little rhyme of your own, as long as the order is right. Many students find that a sentence they make up themselves is easier to remember than one someone else gives them.

## Flat keys: look at the second-to-last one

**Rule**
Flats are added in the order B, E, A, D, G, C, F, exactly the reverse of the order of sharps. The second-to-last flat in the key signature is the name of the major key.

**Examples**
- One flat (B♭): this one needs to be remembered separately: it is F major
- Two flats (B♭, E♭): the second-to-last is B♭, so the key is B♭ major
- Three flats (B♭, E♭, A♭): the second-to-last is E♭, so the key is E♭ major

![A grand piano with its lid open, in a dark ink-wash style on a grey-white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvv1zvxs-d208i.webp)

## Why do some keys use sharps and others flats?

The choice of key signature lets every scale keep the rule that each letter appears once. For example, the F major scale is written F, G, A, B♭, C, D, E. If B♭ were written as A♯, there would be two As, which would only confuse the reader. So F major uses a flat, while G major uses a sharp, and in this way each of the seven letters appears once in the scale, the page is clear, and the player can easily judge each note's function.

## The circle of fifths: joining all the keys into a ring

Put C major at the top and go clockwise by a perfect fifth (seven semitones) each time, and you get G, D, A, E, B and so on, with one more sharp in the key signature at each step. Going anticlockwise by a perfect fifth each time gives F, B♭, E♭ and so on, with one more flat at each step.

The value of the circle of fifths is that:

- You can see at a glance how "near" or "far" two keys are; neighbouring keys differ by only one sharp or flat
- You can understand why many pieces modulate to a neighbouring key
- When planning the order of scale practice, you can move forward one key at a time round the circle of fifths

## Relative minors: one key signature, two colours

Every major key has a minor key that uses the same key signature, called its relative minor. To find it, count down three semitones from the major tonic.

- C major → A minor (no sharps or flats)
- G major → E minor (one sharp)
- F major → D minor (one flat)

To decide whether a piece is in the major or in its relative minor, look at the bass or chords at the beginning and end: if it often lands on A, it is most likely A minor; if it often lands on C, it is most likely C major.

## A three-minute daily key signature flashcard drill

- Prepare cards with a key signature drawn on the front, and the major key and relative minor written on the back
- Each day, draw five at random and say the answer within three seconds
- After a correct answer, play that key's tonic triad on the piano
- Put cards you got wrong back at the front, and review them first the next day

This drill can serve as a warm-up in any piano course, and also suits a short quiz before a lesson in music teaching.

## How TIGA ALPHA helps you practise key signatures

TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app built by a team in Thailand, led by its CEO, Teacher Aum, who has 20 years of experience teaching piano; the app can be used in ten languages: Thai, English, Chinese, Arabic, Japanese, Russian, Spanish, French, Hindi and Korean. As an online piano teaching app, it can:

- Schedule a daily key signature review in **Pathway**, recording how many answers you got right
- Use **Daily Mentor** to remind you to confirm the key signature before you practise a new piece
- With **Play Along**, let your ear hear directly whether you have missed a sharp or flat

This way of teaching piano with AI lets "remembering the rules" and "playing them" happen in the same flow.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do I have to memorise all the key signatures before learning the piano?**

A: No. You can start with a few keys such as C, G and F, and learn more as your repertoire grows. Remembering as you play often works more naturally.

**Q: Do the rules for sharp keys also apply to minor keys?**

A: The rules first help you find the major key, then count down three semitones to get the relative minor, and then you judge which of the two it is from the beginning and end of the piece.

**Q: What is the difference between accidentals and a key signature?**

A: The key signature applies to the whole piece; an accidental applies only within the bar where it appears, and after the barline the key signature's rule applies again.

**Q: When learning piano online, how can I check whether I have misread a key signature?**

A: You can record your playing and listen back, or compare with the play-along feature of an online piano teaching app. If it does not sound in harmony with the accompaniment, go back and check the key signature first.

**Q: Do I need to memorise the circle of fifths?**

A: Understanding matters more than rote learning. If you know that "clockwise adds sharps, anticlockwise adds flats", you can work it out yourself when you need it.

## Next step: make key signatures a reflex

Once key signatures are familiar, reading music at the piano goes more smoothly, the theory side of learning music becomes better organised, and you can focus more on expression when you play.

keyboard-geography-eyes-off-hands.body:
If you keep looking down to find the keys, your eyes struggle to stay on the score, and both reading and sight-reading suffer. You can build a sense of keyboard geography by starting with the groups of black keys: the groups of two and groups of three are the landmarks for your hands on the keyboard. When you practise, close your eyes, feel for the groups of black keys with your fingers, and then find the white keys beside them, such as C to the left of the two black keys and F to the left of the three black keys. Once that feels familiar, practise moving to different octaves and hand positions without looking at your hands.

## Finding Other Notes

Once you know C and F, you can find other white keys, such as D between the two black keys, and G and A between the three black keys.

**Common mistake**

You can also find black keys, for example the first of the two black keys is C sharp or D flat.

Each time you find a note, play it, so that your hand, your ear and the note name all connect.

## Finding C and F with Your Eyes Closed

Start by closing your eyes and gently feeling the black keys with the fingers of your right hand, moving from left to right, until you find a group of two.

The white key to the left of the two black keys is C, and the white key to the left of the three black keys is F.

Once you have found one, open your eyes to check, then close them again to find the next C or F.

## Moving Between Octaves

Many pieces need your hands to move between octaves, for example from middle C up to the C an octave higher.

First practise the move while watching your hands, and remember how far your arm travels. Then try it without looking.

After you land, lightly touch the groups of black keys to confirm you are in the right place.

## A Game for Children

For children, you can turn finding keys into a game. For example, a parent calls out a note name and the child closes their eyes to find it.

If they find the right key, they play it. If not, they open their eyes, take a look and try again.

A simple, fun game like this helps children get to know the keyboard as they play.

## Combining It with Sight-Reading

A better sense of the keyboard helps sight-reading in particular, because when you sight-read your eyes need to keep reading ahead.

When you practise sight-reading, remind yourself to look at your hands less. When you are unsure, feel for the black keys first and then play.

Little by little, you will find that your sight-reading becomes smoother.

## Using Your Peripheral Vision

Never looking at your hands at all is not the goal. In some big leaps it is perfectly normal to glance at the keys with your peripheral vision.

The point is to keep your eyes on the score most of the time and only check with a glance when you need to.

As your sense of the keyboard improves, you will need to look at your hands less and less.

## A Little Every Day

Practising keyboard geography does not take long. One or two minutes before each practice session is enough.

You can close your eyes and find a few notes, or play a scale without looking at your hands.

After a while, you will notice that you look down for the keys much less often.

## Black Keys Are Landmarks

The black keys come in groups of two and three, repeating one group after another, and this is easy to recognise both by eye and by touch.

If you lightly run your fingers over them, you can feel that the black keys are higher than the white keys, and that there is a larger gap between groups.

Using these groups as a reference, you can quickly find the position of any white key.

## Why Not Always Look at Your Hands

If you look down at your hands for every note, your eyes have to travel back and forth between the score and the keys.

Each time you look up, you have to find your place in the score again, which easily interrupts the music and slows down your reading.

If you can find the keys without looking, your eyes can stay on the score more, and your playing will be smoother.

**Take it slowly**
- The groups of black keys are the landmarks on the keyboard
- C is to the left of the two black keys, and F is to the left of the three black keys
- Close your eyes and feel for the groups of black keys with your fingers
- Once familiar, practise moving hand positions without looking

## Practising in Dim Light

Some people practise in very low light, for example with only a small lamp on the score so that the keys are hard to see.

This forces you to rely on the feel of your hands to find the keys, which improves your sense of the keyboard.

Be careful about safety, though. Do not practise in complete darkness, so that you do not bump into things or trip.

## Feeling Your Hand Position

When you play a piece, your hands often settle in a fixed position, for example the right thumb on C and the five fingers on C to G in turn.

You can practise placing your hand in this position without looking, then play the five notes and check that they are right.

Little by little, try other positions too, such as G position and F position.

![A cartoon character wearing glasses and headphones plays an upright piano while looking at the score in a night-time room, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa09a2j-16srf.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: Why shouldn't I always look at my hands?**
A: Moving your eyes back and forth interrupts your reading and the music.

**Q: What are the landmarks on the keyboard?**
A: The groups of two and three black keys.

**Q: How do I find C with my eyes closed?**
A: Find the group of two black keys. The white key to the left of them is C.

**Q: Can't I look at my hands during big leaps either?**
A: You can check with your peripheral vision. The point is to look less.

**Q: Does it help with sight-reading?**
A: Yes, your eyes can keep reading ahead.

**Q: How should children practise?**
A: Turn finding keys into a game with eyes closed.

jianzipu-guqin-tablature-reduced-charact.body:
Jianzipu is a notation made specifically for the guqin. It reduces the strokes of Chinese characters and combines them into special symbols, and each symbol records not a pitch but a playing method: which finger of the right hand plucks the string and how, and which finger of the left hand presses which hui (position marker) on which string. It is said to have been compiled in the Tang dynasty by guqin players such as Cao Rou. Before that, guqin scores described the fingering in whole passages of text, which is called "wenzipu" (text notation). Jianzipu generally does not record rhythm, so players have to rebuild a piece from old scores, their teacher's lineage and their own understanding, a process called "dapu".

## Jieshi Diao: Youlan

One of the earliest surviving text scores is a Tang dynasty manuscript, "Jieshi Diao: Youlan" (Orchid in a Secluded Valley), which is kept in Japan.

**Watch the details**

It records the fingering of a guqin piece in detail in writing, running to several thousand characters.

This manuscript lets us see what text notation looked like.

## Dapu

Because jianzipu does not record rhythm, when a guqin player wants to perform an ancient piece, they must rebuild it from the fingering on the score, their teacher's lineage and their own understanding.

This process is called "dapu".

Working out a large piece can sometimes take several months, or even several years.

**Common misconceptions**
- Notation made specially for the guqin
- Reduces the strokes of Chinese characters and combines them into symbols
- Records the playing method rather than the pitch
- Generally does not record rhythm, so "dapu" is needed

## It Records How to Play

Staff notation and jianpu record pitch, telling the player which note to play.

Jianzipu records the playing method, telling the player how to play.

In this sense, it is a little like guitar tablature.

## From Text Notation to Jianzipu

Before jianzipu appeared, guqin scores described the fingering in whole passages of text, which is called "wenzipu".

For example, a single note had to be written as a sentence: press the thirteenth hui with the thumb, pluck the seventh string with the index finger...

Scores like this were very long and awkward to read.

## Different Faces of the Same Piece

Because dapu leaves many points for the player to decide, the same piece worked out by different players may sound somewhat different.

This gives guqin music a strongly personal character.

Listening to different players perform the same piece is a very interesting way to enjoy it.

## Pressed Notes and Harmonics in the Left Hand

With the left hand, a guqin player can press a string to play a pressed note, or lightly touch a hui position to produce a harmonic.

In jianzipu, different symbols show pressed notes and harmonics, and which hui position is used.

The left hand also has sliding and vibrato techniques such as yin, nao, chuo and zhu, and these have their own special symbols.

## Right-Hand Fingerings in Jianzipu

The right hand of the guqin has many fingerings, such as "gou", "tiao", "mo" and "ti", each plucking the string with a different finger and in a different direction.

In jianzipu, each of these fingerings has its own abbreviated symbol.

A skilled player can tell at a glance from the symbol which finger to use and in which direction to pluck.

![A person in futuristic clothing plays a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbka5iv-uh3yf.webp)

## Jianzipu in Summary

Jianzipu is notation made specially for the guqin. It reduces the strokes of Chinese characters and combines them into symbols, and records the playing method rather than the pitch, somewhat like guitar tablature. The upper part of a symbol records the left-hand finger and the hui position, and the lower part records the right-hand fingering and the string number. The right hand has fingerings such as gou, tiao, mo and ti, and the left hand has pressed notes, harmonics, and techniques such as yin, nao, chuo and zhu. Before it came text notation, which described fingering in whole passages of writing, and one of the earliest surviving examples is the Tang dynasty manuscript "Jieshi Diao: Youlan", kept in Japan.

It is said that the Tang dynasty guqin player Cao Rou and others compiled jianzipu. It generally does not record rhythm, so players rebuild a piece from the fingering, their teacher's lineage and their own understanding, which is called "dapu". Working out a large piece can take months or even years, and the same piece worked out by different players has a different character.

You can explore jianzipu together with Teacher Aum.

## No Rhythm Recorded

One feature of jianzipu is that it generally does not record rhythm, or records only very little rhythmic information.

How long each note lasts, and where the music speeds up or slows down, are often not visible on the score.

In the past, this information was passed on mainly by teachers through spoken instruction and demonstration.

## What "Jian Zi" Means

The "jian zi" (reduced characters) of jianzipu means reducing the strokes of Chinese characters.

For example, only part of the character "gou" is taken, and only part of the character "san" is written, and then the parts are put together.

In this way, a single symbol contains the meaning of several characters.

## What Makes Up a Symbol

A jianzipu symbol usually has two parts, upper and lower.

The upper part gives the left-hand information: which finger is used and which hui it presses.

The lower part gives the right-hand information: which fingering is used and which string is played.

## Compilation in the Tang Dynasty

It is said that the Tang dynasty guqin player Cao Rou and others simplified and organised text notation into jianzipu.

Jianzipu is far more concise than text notation, since a single symbol can replace a whole long sentence.

It has been in use ever since, right up to the present day.

## Talking About Jianzipu with Your Teacher

In a lesson, you can talk with Teacher Aum about how jianzipu differs from staff notation and jianpu.

You can also find a picture of a jianzipu score together and try to work out what the symbols mean.

From a single combined Chinese character, you can see the ingenuity of guqin notation.

## FAQ

**Q: Which instrument is jianzipu notation for?**
A: The guqin.

**Q: What does jianzipu record?**
A: The playing method, not the pitch.

**Q: What notation did the guqin use before jianzipu?**
A: Text notation (wenzipu).

**Q: Who is said to have compiled jianzipu in the Tang dynasty?**
A: The guqin player Cao Rou and others.

**Q: What is "dapu"?**
A: Guqin players rebuilding an old score that does not record rhythm, based on the fingering, their teacher's lineage and their own understanding.
