jasmine-flower-pentatonic-left-hand.body:
The key to a left-hand accompaniment for Jasmine Flower is to use fewer "full" triads and more open fifths and open figures with the colour of a second. The melody of this folk song is built on the pentatonic scale, and only when the left hand leaves space can the melody's gentleness and its Jiangnan flavour come through. Beginners can start with the C major pentatonic scale (C, D, E, G, A), beginning with "sustained open fifths" in the left hand and adding step by step to broken figures and bass lines. The four layers go from simple to rich, and each one can stand alone as a complete version.

## A Few Things to Know Before Playing Jasmine Flower

- Jasmine Flower is a widely sung Chinese folk song with several versions in different regions; the one heard most often is the version that circulated around Jiangsu
- The melody mainly uses the pentatonic scale, that is, the five notes do, re, mi, sol and la
- There are no semitone relationships in the pentatonic scale, so if the left hand adds too much "tense" harmony, it easily spoils the original flavour
- This article uses C major as the example so you can practise on the white keys; once you are comfortable, you can move it to other keys
- For the right-hand melody you can refer to a reliable numbered-notation or staff-notation version; this article focuses on the left hand

## Why Triads Make This Song "Lose Its Flavour"

Many piano learners are used to harmonising a melody with "I, IV and V triads", but find that it feels wrong on Jasmine Flower, like painting heavy oils over an ink-wash painting. The reason is that a standard triad contains a third, whose colour is definite and full, while a pentatonic melody is by nature light and full of white space.

Take out the third and keep only the root and the fifth, and the sound immediately becomes transparent. This is what the "open fifth" does: it gives steady support in the bass without stealing the melody's thunder.

## Four Layers, from Simple to Rich

**Layer One: Sustained open fifths**
In the left hand, press C and G on the first beat of each bar and hold them for the whole bar. Where the melody clearly turns to A, you can change to A and E; where it lands on G, change to G and D. This layer uses only three combinations, and suits people who are just getting to know the song.

**Layer Two: Broken open fifths**
Split the two notes of Layer One and play them in the order "bass note, fifth, higher octave bass note, fifth", for example C, G, C, G. The rhythm can be one note per beat, and the sound begins to flow.

**Layer Three: Adding the colour of a second**
On top of the open fifth, add a note a second above the root, for example C, D, G. This figure is very natural in the pentatonic scale and sounds clear, with a slight haze. When practising, play the D more softly than the C and G, like a thin mist.

**Layer Four: A slowly moving bass line**
Between phrases, let the left-hand bass move slowly in the direction of C, A, G or C, G, A, G, following the rise and fall of the melody. Once the bass moves, the whole song has a feeling of "walking", which suits the repeat, the second time through.

![Illustration of a golden pagoda and the Bangkok high-rise skyline against a sunset](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvlsrs6-e87xi.webp)

## Three Details for the Right-Hand Melody

**Touch ornaments lightly**
Folk melodies often have small grace notes or slide-like movements. Play them lightly and quickly, and do not let them be louder than the main notes.

**Leave room to breathe at the end of phrases**
At the end of each line of the lyrics you can soften slightly, leaving a tiny gap before the next phrase, just as a singer takes a breath.

**Don't push the high notes**
When the melody climbs high, many people unconsciously play louder. The high points of Jasmine Flower are better emphasised by "lengthening a little" than by "playing louder".

## The Order for Practising Hands Together

- First sing or hum the melody on its own, to get to know the length of each phrase
- Play the right hand alone until it is familiar, and mark the breathing points of each phrase
- Choose the Layer One accompaniment for the left hand, and play it alone until you can change position without looking at the keyboard
- Put the hands together at a slow tempo, and make sure the left-hand open fifths are always softer than the melody
- Once you are comfortable, use Layer One or Two the first time through, and change to Layer Three or Four on the repeat

Arranged this way, one piece can carry two different moods: plain the first time, richer the second. This idea of "one song, two arrangements" is often used in piano teaching to help students understand the role of accompaniment.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What level of player is Jasmine Flower suited to?**

A: The right-hand melody itself is not hard, and if the left hand uses only the Layer One open fifths, a beginner with some foundation can try it. Layers Three and Four suit people who can already play with the hands independently.

**Q: Can I play it in another key?**

A: Yes. A folk song has no fixed key, and many versions use F or G. When you change key, the five notes of the pentatonic scale move too, and the open-fifth rule for the left hand stays the same.

**Q: Can I use this song at a school event or a family gathering?**

A: Of course. The melody is familiar and the length is moderate, and the Layer One accompaniment is enough to carry a gentle version. Record yourself a few times before the performance and listen back, and you will feel more confident.

**Q: How does the pentatonic scale help in learning music?**

A: The pentatonic scale is the basis of the music of many cultures. Once you have learned it, you will find it easier to understand the melodic features of different cultures, and you will be freer to improvise and arrange.

**Q: Can I learn this kind of folk-song arrangement when learning piano online?**

A: Yes. Practise by layers on your own first, then ask a teacher, or use an app, to listen back to your recording and check whether the left hand is too loud. It is a very practical way to learn.

## Play Gentle Folk Songs on the Piano

klangfarbenmelodie-tone-colour-melody.body:
Klangfarbenmelodie, or tone-colour melody, is an idea Schoenberg put forward at the end of his 1911 Harmonielehre (Theory of Harmony): if a series of notes of different pitches can form a melody, could a series of different tone colours form a kind of "melody" too? Later, people often used the word for an orchestration method: a melody is split into small fragments and handed to different instruments in turn, and the colour changes each time the instrument changes. A famous example of this method is the orchestration that Schoenberg's student Webern made in 1935 of the six-part ricercar from Bach's Musical Offering.

## A Relay of Melody

Later, "tone-colour melody" was often used for an orchestration method.

**Practice order**

The composer splits a melody into small fragments: the first goes to the flute, the second to the clarinet, the third to the violin.

The melody is passed between different instruments like a relay race, and the colour changes with each handover.

## What Is Tone Colour

Tone colour, or timbre, is the colour of a sound.

The same note played on a violin, played on a flute or played on a piano sounds different each time, and this is the difference in tone colour.

We can tell different instruments apart because of their tone colour.

- Schoenberg proposed it in his 1911 Harmonielehre
- A series of different tone colours forms a "melody"
- A melody is split into fragments and given to different instruments
- In 1935 Webern orchestrated Bach's ricercar

![A person with blue-purple hair in a futuristic jacket plays several layers of glowing synthesisers on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbkgic6-rp6wo.webp)

## The Sound of Pointillism

In Webern's music, notes often appear one at a time on different instruments, like a pointillist painting.

Each note is very short and has its own colour.

This way of writing asks listeners to concentrate very closely on every single note.

## The Importance of Tone Colour

The idea of tone-colour melody led composers to pay more and more attention to the role of tone colour in music.

Tone colour was no longer just "clothing" for a melody, but became an important material of music, like pitch and rhythm.

This had a great influence on later twentieth-century music.

## Changing Tone Colour on the Piano

The piano has the tone colour of only one instrument, but you can still bring out different colours in different ways.

For example, a very light touch, the pedal, and different registers all make the sound feel different.

You can try splitting a melody into several parts and playing each part in a different way.

## A Relay in Piano Duet

Two people sitting at the same piano can also play a melody relay.

One person plays the first fragment of the melody, and the other takes over with the second fragment, using different dynamics and touch.

It is like the melody being passed between two "instruments".

## Webern's Bach

In 1935, Webern, a student of Schoenberg, re-orchestrated the six-part ricercar from Bach's Musical Offering.

He split Bach's theme into many small fragments and gave them to different instruments such as trombone, horn, trumpet and harp.

A familiar theme was split into many colours, and it sounds strikingly new.

## Tone-Colour Melody Summary

Klangfarbenmelodie, tone-colour melody, is an idea Schoenberg put forward at the end of his Harmonielehre in 1911, asking whether a series of different tone colours could form a melody just as a series of pitches does. Later the term often meant an orchestration method in which a melody is split into fragments and played in turn by different instruments. In 1935 Webern orchestrated the six-part ricercar of Bach's Musical Offering, giving the theme to trombone, horn, trumpet, harp and others. Schoenberg's 1909 Five Pieces for Orchestra also contains a piece in which a chord changes colour between combinations of instruments.

Webern's music is like pointillism, and tone colour becomes musical material just like pitch and rhythm. On the piano you can change colour with touch, pedal and register, play one melody in sections in different registers, or play it as a relay in piano duet.

You can try tone-colour melody together with Teacher Aum.

## A Melody of Tone Colours

In 1911, at the end of his Harmonielehre, Schoenberg put forward a bold idea.

He asked: if a series of different pitches can form a melody, could a series of different tone colours form a kind of melody too?

He called this imagined music "tone-colour melody".

## Trying Tone-Colour Melody with Your Teacher in a Lesson

In your lesson, you can work with Teacher Aum to split a familiar melody into several parts and play them in turn, using different registers and touches.

You can also listen together to Webern's orchestration of Bach's ricercar, and notice how the theme is passed between the instruments.

From the colour of sound, discover another possibility for melody.

## Schoenberg's Orchestral Pieces

In Schoenberg's own Five Pieces for Orchestra of 1909, there is one piece that is often linked with tone-colour melody.

In this piece, a single chord slowly changes between different combinations of instruments. The pitch changes very little, but the colour keeps changing.

It sounds like light slowly changing on the surface of water.

## A Melody of Pitch

The melody we normally speak of is a series of notes of different pitches linked together in a certain rhythm.

For example, "do, re, mi, fa, sol" is a simple rising melody.

When we listen to a melody, we mainly notice the rises and falls in pitch.

## The Colour of Registers

The low register of the piano sounds deep and full, the middle register warm, and the high register bright.

You can take a simple melody and play the first part in the middle register, the second part in the high register and the third part in the low register.

**Before you start**

After going round the three registers, the same phrase has taken on three different colours.

## FAQ

**Q: Who proposed "tone-colour melody"?**
A: Schoenberg, in his Harmonielehre, published in 1911.

**Q: What is tone colour?**
A: The colour of a sound. For example, the same note sounds different on different instruments.

**Q: How does tone-colour melody work as an orchestration method?**
A: A melody is split into fragments and given to different instruments in turn.

**Q: Which work did Webern orchestrate in 1935?**
A: The six-part ricercar from Bach's Musical Offering.

**Q: How can I change colour on the piano?**
A: Use different touches, the pedal and different registers.

khachaturian-sabre-dance-gayane-1942.body:
The Sabre Dance comes from the ballet Gayane by the Armenian-Soviet composer Aram Khachaturian, which premiered in 1942. It is said that the Sabre Dance was added shortly before the ballet's premiere and was written very quickly. The music is driving, with the xylophone hammering out a ceaseless repeated figure and the brass and snare drum roaring, depicting a fierce dance in which the dancers wave their sabres. It later became one of the composer's most widely known works, often heard in concerts, on television and in sports performances. On the piano, it is excellent material for practising fast repeated notes and strong rhythm.

## Folk Colour in the Sabre Dance

In the Sabre Dance, Khachaturian used many rhythmic features of folk dances from the Caucasus region.

For example, strong accents, fast rhythms and constantly repeated figures.

These features fill the music with an exotic flavour.

## Arrangements of the Sabre Dance

There are many piano arrangements of the Sabre Dance, including solo versions and piano duet versions.

Simplified versions usually lower the speed and reduce the number of repeated notes.

You can choose an arrangement that suits your own level.

## The Figures in the Sabre Dance

At the start of the Sabre Dance, the orchestra hammers out a driving rhythm with strong repeated notes.

The xylophone plays the main melody in the high register, with note after note repeating the same pitch quickly.

This repeated figure is like the quick waving of sabres, full of tension.

## The Saxophone in the Middle Section

Between the fast themes there is a more lyrical middle section, in which the saxophone and cello play a broad melody.

This melody has the flavour of Armenian folk song, and contrasts with the urgency before and after it.

Then the fast theme returns and drives the music to the end.

## Dynamics in the Sabre Dance

The piece is loud for most of the time, but there are changes in dynamics too.

The lyrical melody in the middle section should be played broadly and singingly, in contrast to the urgency before and after it.

The ending should grow stronger and stronger, finishing on a powerful chord.

## The Ballet Gayane

Gayane is a ballet by Khachaturian, which premiered in 1942.

The ballet tells a story set on a collective farm in Armenia, and its heroine is a young woman named Gayane.

The ballet has many dance scenes based on folk dances, with clear rhythms and lots of energy.

## Relaxing Your Wrists in the Sabre Dance

When you play fast, powerful pieces like this, your wrists easily get tense.

Remember to relax your wrists between phrases, and do not keep them rigid all the time.

The power should come from the weight of your arm, not from pressing hard with your fingers.

## Who Was Khachaturian

Aram Khachaturian was born in 1903 and died in 1978. He was an Armenian-Soviet composer.

He was born in Tbilisi, Georgia, and only began to study music formally at the age of nineteen.

His music often blends in elements of Armenian and Caucasian folk music, and is richly coloured.

## The Composer's Frustration

The Sabre Dance became extremely widely known and often appears in all kinds of performances and programmes.

It is said that Khachaturian later felt somewhat helpless about how over-popular the piece became, because its fame overshadowed many of his other works.

His Violin Concerto, Piano Concerto and the ballet Spartacus are equally well worth listening to.

![A sepia sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angled view](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadethf-2pknw.webp)

## Repeated Notes on the Piano

The biggest difficulty in playing the Sabre Dance on the piano is the fast repeated notes.

When repeating the same note quickly, a common method is finger changing, for example using fingers three, two and one in turn on the same key.

Changing fingers keeps every note clear, and your hand does not tire so easily.

- It comes from Khachaturian's ballet Gayane
- The ballet premiered in 1942
- It is said to have been added shortly before the premiere
- The xylophone hammers out a ceaseless repeated figure

## Ask Your Teacher About Finger Changes in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate how to play fast repeated notes using finger changes.

Your teacher can also help check whether your wrists are relaxed and your rhythm is steady.

This piece is very good for practising repeated notes and strong rhythm.

## The Rhythm of the Sabre Dance

The rhythm of this piece is very strong, and every accent needs to be clear and powerful.

First practise slowly with a metronome to get the rhythm accurate, then gradually speed up.

Even when you play fast, keep the rhythm steady and do not let it fall apart.

## Sabre Dance Summary

Aram Khachaturian was born in 1903 and died in 1978. He was born in Tbilisi, only began studying music formally at nineteen, and blended Armenian and Caucasian folk elements into his music. The ballet Gayane premiered in 1942 and tells the story of a woman on a collective farm. The Sabre Dance is said to have been written quickly, shortly before the premiere, at the request of the choreographer.

It opens with strong repeated notes, with the xylophone repeating the same note quickly in the high register. The middle section has a broad melody played by the saxophone and cello. It is said that the composer later felt somewhat helpless about its over-popularity, and his Violin Concerto, Piano Concerto and Spartacus are also worth listening to. On the piano, use finger changes of three, two and one for the repeated notes, keep the rhythm steady and your wrists relaxed, and let the power come from arm weight.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the finger-changing method.

## A Dance Written in a Hurry

It is said that shortly before the ballet's premiere, the choreographer wanted one more lively dance.

Khachaturian wrote the Sabre Dance in a very short time.

**Remember this**

Unexpectedly, this hastily written music later became one of the most widely known parts of the whole ballet.

## FAQ

**Q: Which work does the Sabre Dance come from?**
A: Khachaturian's ballet Gayane.

**Q: In which year did the ballet premiere?**
A: 1942.

**Q: Which instrument plays the main theme at the start?**
A: The xylophone.

**Q: Which instruments play the middle section?**
A: The saxophone and cello.

**Q: How do I play fast repeated notes on the piano?**
A: Change fingers, using three, two and one.

indian-raga-scale-mood-time.body:
The raga is one of the most central ideas in Indian classical music. It is often explained simply as a scale, but it is much more than that: each raga specifies which notes are used, how the melody moves going up and coming down, which notes are emphasised and which typical short phrases belong to it, and it also carries a particular mood. In the North Indian tradition, many ragas are also linked to a certain time of day or a certain season; some suit early morning, for example, and some the depths of the night. Performers improvise within the rules of the raga, and a performance often begins with a slow, free introduction before rhythm and drums are gradually added.

## The Mood of a Raga

In the Indian tradition, each raga carries a particular mood, such as serenity, joy, longing or solemnity.

The performer's task is to bring out this mood gradually through the melody.

It is said that a good performance can immerse the audience completely in that mood.

## Talking About Ragas with Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons you can chat with Teacher Aum about Indian ragas and how they differ from Western scales.

You can also ask your teacher to listen to a short passage you improvised following a set of rules, and tell you whether it has a consistent character.

Through music from far away, you can experience both the rules and the freedom of melody.

- A core concept of Indian classical music
- Sets the notes used, the paths up and down, and typical phrases
- Each raga carries a particular mood
- In the North Indian tradition, many ragas are linked to times of day and seasons

## Which Notes Are Used

Each raga specifies which notes are used. Some use five notes, others six or seven.

Some ragas use different notes going up and coming down; for example, a note may be skipped on the way up but used on the way down.

These rules give each raga its own distinctive sound.

## Set Yourself a Rule

You can also set a "raga" rule for your own improvisation: which notes to use, which note to emphasise, and what kind of signature phrase to have.

Then improvise slowly within that rule, first playing freely and then adding a steady beat.

This lets you get a feel for how an Indian performance moves from slow to fast.

## The Emphasised Notes

In a raga, certain notes are especially important and are emphasised again and again.

Performers often linger on these notes and ornament them, so that listeners feel the centre of the raga.

Other notes are only touched lightly in passing.

## Feeling a Raga on the Piano

The piano is an equal-tempered instrument and cannot fully express the subtle shifts of pitch and the slides of Indian music.

But you can try holding a fifth of do and sol with your left hand while your right hand uses only certain notes, improvising slowly.

For example, your right hand might use only do, re, mi, sol and la, skipping re on the way up and using it again on the way down.

## Summary: Ragas

The raga is a core concept of Indian classical music. It is not just a scale: it also specifies which notes are used, how the melody moves up and down, which notes are emphasised and which signature-like typical phrases belong to it, and it carries a particular mood such as serenity, joy or longing. In the North Indian tradition many ragas are linked to early morning, evening, late night or the rainy season. Indian classical music has two great traditions, North Indian and South Indian, and the North often uses the sitar and the tabla.

A performance often begins with a slow introduction with no fixed beat, then adds the tala rhythmic cycle and the drums. The tanpura plays the tonic and the fifth continuously. On the piano you can play a fifth with your left hand and improvise with your right according to rules you set yourself, experiencing the move from slow to fast.

You can talk about ragas with Teacher Aum.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk5x09-05fei.webp)

## More Than a Scale

Many people who hear about ragas for the first time assume a raga is simply a scale.

In fact, the scale is only one part of a raga.

A raga is more like a "character description" for a melody, telling the performer how this melody should move and how it should express itself.

## A Performance That Unfolds Slowly

A North Indian classical performance often begins with a slow, free introduction with no fixed beat.

In this introduction, the performer reveals the notes and phrases of the raga little by little.

Only later are a fixed rhythm and drums added, the tempo gradually quickens, and the performance reaches its climax.

## Tala

The rhythmic cycle in Indian music is called a tala.

A tala may have sixteen beats, ten beats, seven beats and so on, repeating with a fixed pattern of strong and weak beats.

The performer and the drummer improvise within the tala, and it is thrilling when they land together on the first beat of the cycle.

## Typical Phrases

Every raga has some typical short phrases, like its "signature".

Listeners familiar with Indian music can recognise which raga it is as soon as they hear these phrases.

When performers improvise, they keep coming back to these phrases.

## Ragas for Early Morning and Late Night

In the North Indian tradition, many ragas are linked to a certain time of day.

Some ragas suit early morning, some suit evening, and some suit the depths of the night.

Others are connected to seasons, such as the ragas of the rainy season.

## North India and South India

Indian classical music is divided mainly into two great traditions, North Indian and South Indian.

Both use the concept of the raga, but they differ in many ways in the names of particular ragas, playing styles and instruments.

North India often uses the sitar and the tabla, while South India often uses the veena and the mridangam.

## The Sustained Drone

In an Indian classical performance, one instrument, such as the tanpura, often plays a sustained drone throughout.

This drone is usually the tonic and the fifth, like a steady backdrop.

The melody unfolds freely against this backdrop.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which kind of music is the raga a core concept of?**
A: Indian classical music.

**Q: Is a raga just a scale?**
A: No. It also specifies the melodic paths, the emphasised notes, typical phrases and a mood.

**Q: What are ragas often linked to in the North Indian tradition?**
A: Times of day or seasons.

**Q: What is the rhythmic cycle in Indian music called?**
A: A tala.

**Q: What kind of section does a performance often begin with?**
A: A slow, free introduction with no fixed beat.

instrument-rental-trial-period-model.body:
"My child has only just started. Should we buy a piano first?" This is the first hard question many families face. If you buy and the child doesn't stick with it, that's a waste; if you don't, you worry that having no instrument to practise on will hold back progress. The instrument rental trial period is a business model designed for exactly this hesitation: the family first rents an instrument for a lower monthly fee, and after a trial period decides whether to keep renting, switch to buying, or return it. For instrument shops and music schools, this design lowers the bar for parents and draws more new students in; for families, it is a way to watch a child's interest and practice habits at a smaller cost.

## Forms the Trial Model Can Take

**Pure rental**
Pay rent monthly and return the instrument at any time. Suited to families who are not sure how long the child will learn.

**Rent credited toward purchase**
If you decide to buy within a set period, the rent already paid can be credited in part or in full against the price of the instrument.

**Upgrade exchange**
Rent an entry-level instrument first, and when the child progresses, swap it for a higher-grade model, with the price difference charged separately.

**Seasonal rental**
Rent for a short period for concentrated study during school holidays, and return the instrument when the holiday ends.

## Why This Design Lowers the Bar

When people face a large one-off expense, they tend to be more cautious. Splitting the decision into two steps, "try for a while" and then "decide whether to buy", reduces the pressure at the start. Parents don't have to make an expensive decision before the child's interest is clear, and the shop gets the chance to earn trust through good service during the trial. By the end of the trial, many families have seen how the child practises, so the decision rests on better evidence.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers beside it](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw168fgc-kpx47.webp)

## Details Shops Should Consider When Designing the Scheme

- Inspection and cleaning standards for instruments, confirming good condition before every rental
- Who pays for transport, installation and tuning
- How to tell normal wear from accidental damage
- Credit rules and time limits written in plain language
- A simple returns process with no unreasonable obstacles

Transparent rules reduce disputes and make parents more willing to recommend the shop to friends.

## Questions for Families to Ask Before Signing

How much is the rent per month, and what is the shortest rental term? If the child no longer wants to learn, is there a fee for returning early? If something goes wrong with the instrument, is the repair free, and how quickly will it be dealt with? If you decide to buy, how is the rent credited and what is the final price? In addition, acoustic pianos need regular tuning, while with digital pianos you should check that accessories such as the power supply and headphones are complete. Ask these questions clearly and keep a written contract to avoid misunderstandings later.

## How Music Schools Can Cooperate

A music school can partner with a reliable instrument shop to offer rental information to new students, but it should let parents choose freely and should not force a tie-in. At trial lessons, the school can also help parents understand the characteristics of different types of instrument, such as the touch of an acoustic piano, or the volume control and headphone function of a digital piano, helping families make a suitable choice for their living space and budget. The partnership, and any possible referral fee, should be honestly disclosed to parents.

## The Trial Period Is Also an Observation Period

For a family, the trial period is not only for deciding whether to buy a piano; it is also a good chance to observe the child's learning. You can keep track of how many times a week the child sits down to practise without being asked, whether they enjoy practising, and how they react when they hit difficulties. These observations help parents judge whether the child really likes playing the piano, and make it easier to talk with the teacher about the next steps in learning.

## Business Value Seen from Examples

In many cities, instrument rental has become part of instrument retail. It lets shops build longer-term relationships with families: from rental to purchase, then to tuning, repairs and upgrades, every stage is a chance to serve. Compared with a one-off sale, this relationship depends more on reputation and quality of service, and it pushes shops to take after-sales experience more seriously.

For the music education industry, the lesson from this example is that lowering the bar to entry does not have to mean lowering the price. It can also mean splitting one big decision into several small ones, so that users have the option to step out at every stage. The free trial period of an online course and the trial lesson at a music school follow the same logic.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Is a rented piano suitable for a child's practice?**
A: As long as the instrument is in good condition and properly tuned, a rented instrument supports a child's regular practice just as well.

**Q: How long is a trial period usually?**
A: Different shops set different terms. A few months is common, and you should confirm the exact period before signing.

**Q: Should I rent a digital piano or an acoustic piano?**
A: Think about your living space, volume needs and budget. You can try playing them first and ask the teacher for advice.

**Q: Can the rent be fully credited toward the purchase price?**
A: It depends on the shop's rules. Some credit all of it and some only part, so ask beforehand.

keep-sheet-music-flat.body:
Curled edges, creased corners and loose pages make it hard to find your place when practising and to turn pages smoothly. A few small habits keep scores flat and make it easier for your eyes to find the line you are practising on the music stand: store them flat in a folder, put clear tape on the page corners you turn most, and keep loose pages in a binder.

## Keeping scores flat on the music stand

If the score keeps closing on the stand, you can hold it gently open at both sides with music clips. Do not clip too tightly, or the pages may be marked.

The spine of a newly bought method book is stiff. Before using it, gently press it from the middle out towards both sides a few times so that it opens naturally, but do not press so hard that the spine breaks.

If the music stand is too narrow, you can photocopy two pages and place them side by side, to reduce the number of page turns.

When turning pages, pinch the edge of the corner with your fingers rather than gripping the middle of the page, which also cuts down on creases.

## Ways to store scores day to day

At home, you can set aside a drawer or box just for scores, with everything lying flat. Put the books you are practising on top, so they are easy to pick up.

Photocopied or printed loose pages can go into clear sleeves, and then into a binder. Clear sleeves protect against sweaty hands and dust, and make page turns smoother too.

A small piece of clear tape on the page corners you turn most can reduce wear. Be careful not to put tape over the notes, since the glare can make them hard to read.

You can also put a packet of desiccant in the box or drawer and change it regularly, which is especially useful in damp seasons.

## Why scores get damaged easily

The paper of scores is usually thin, and the corners that are turned often are the first to fray and curl. If you store scores upright on a shelf, over time the whole book bends to one side, and then will not stay open on the stand.

A damp room also makes paper soft and wrinkled. In hot, humid places, scores need to be kept somewhere dry and well ventilated.

When children stuff scores into a school bag, they are often squeezed together with textbooks and water bottles, and a careless moment leaves creases.

Pets and small children may also treat loose scores as toys, so putting them away saves a lot of trouble.

## Borrowed and shared scores

For scores borrowed from a teacher or a library, it is best to keep them in a separate folder so they do not get mixed up with your own, and not to write marks directly on them. If you need to annotate, you can use sticky notes or write on a photocopy.

When several people share one score, you can agree on how to mark it, for example pencil only and in the margins, so that everyone can understand the marks and they are easy to rub out later.

Before returning it, check that none of your own sticky notes or slips of paper are left inside. Keeping the score as it was is a way of respecting the person who lent it.

## Combining digital and paper scores

More and more people read music on a tablet, which has no curling edges and makes page turns easy. But a paper score lets you jot down marks at once and is also kinder to the eyes over long reading, so each has its uses.

One common approach is to use paper for the pieces you are working on closely, so it is easy to mark fingering and breathing, and to keep pieces for sight-reading and review on the tablet, ready to call up at any time.

Whichever you use, make sure the page is clear and steady, and placed at a comfortable height for reading. Once the score is secure, your attention can go to the music.

## What to do with scores that are already curled

A slightly curled score can be pressed between a few heavy books for a day or two, which usually restores it.

Pages that have come loose can be taped back from the reverse side, or the score can be rebound.

If a score has so many marks that it can no longer be read, you can prepare a clean copy and transfer the important marks to it, which makes reading much easier.

When scores are well kept, it is also easier to find the marks and notes from back then when you return to old pieces.

**Common mistakes**
- Lying flat is less likely to curl than standing upright
- Page corners you turn often can have a small piece of clear tape
- Keep loose pages in a binder or sleeves
- Do not put cups or heavy objects on scores

![A high-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a rainy neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wnlbc-iyoob.webp)

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do clear sleeves cause glare?**
A: Some do. You can choose matt sleeves, or adjust the angle of the lamp to reduce glare.

**Q: Can I use a highlighter directly on the score?**
A: Yes, but do not use too many colours, and highlighter cannot be rubbed out, so it is best to try marks in pencil first.

**Q: Should I throw away old scores?**
A: You can keep them as a memento, and they are handy for reviewing later. As long as they are stored separately, they will not take up practice space.

**Q: Can a tablet replace paper scores?**
A: It can be a supplement. A tablet makes page turns easy, but you need to watch the screen brightness and the battery.

**Q: Will tape make the paper yellow?**
A: Ordinary tape may turn yellow over time. You can choose tape marked as suitable for archiving, or stick it only on blank areas at the page corners.

**Q: What if the score gets wet?**
A: First blot the water gently with dry paper towels, then press it flat between sheets of absorbent paper and let it dry. Do not blow hot air directly on it with a hair dryer.

kabalevsky-op27-thirty-childrens-pieces.body:
The 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27, are a set of thirty short piano pieces written by the Soviet composer Dmitry Kabalevsky between 1937 and 1938. The pieces are short and vivid, and each practises one technique or expresses one mood, from simple melodies to fast toccata-style pieces. Among them, the Toccatina, with its bright rhythm and energy, is a favourite with many children who learn the piano. Kabalevsky cared about children's music education all his life, wrote a great many pieces suitable for children to play, and took part in reforming school music programmes.

## Thirty short pieces

The 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27, contain thirty pieces, written between 1937 and 1938.

The pieces are arranged roughly by difficulty, starting with the easy ones and gradually getting harder.

They are all very short, and most fit on a single page.

## Comparing with Bartók's Mikrokosmos

Bartók's Mikrokosmos is also a twentieth-century set of piano works written for learners.

Mikrokosmos makes more use of elements of Hungarian folk music and of various modern techniques.

Kabalevsky's pieces are more melodic and carry the lyrical colour of Russian music.

## Kabalevsky's other children's works

Besides Op. 27, Kabalevsky wrote many other piano works for children, such as the 24 Pieces for Children.

He also wrote an orchestral suite, The Comedians, whose Galop is very famous.

These works are all well worth getting to know and playing for children who are learning the piano.

## The sound of the twentieth century

Although Kabalevsky's children's pieces are simple, they carry the musical colours of the twentieth century.

The harmony contains some unexpected chords and changes of mode, which make the music sound fresh and interesting.

This helps children become familiar with different styles of sound from an early age.

## Asking your teacher to recommend Kabalevsky pieces

Which pieces from the 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27, to learn first can be decided together with Teacher Aum in a lesson.

The division of work between the hands in the Toccatina can also be taken apart and practised slowly in a lesson.

Through Kabalevsky's music, you can enjoy the fun of music while practising technique.

## Caring about children's music education

Kabalevsky cared about children's music education all his life.

He believed that when children learn music, the most important thing is not only technique but learning to feel and understand music.

In his later years he also took part in reforming school music programmes and wrote many books on music education.

## Who was Kabalevsky?

Dmitry Kabalevsky was born in 1904 and died in 1987. He was a Soviet composer and music educator.

He wrote symphonies, concertos, operas and many other kinds of works.

But he is best known for the many piano pieces and songs he wrote for children.

## The Toccatina

The Toccatina is one of the most popular pieces in this set.

The right hand plays short chords without stopping, while the left hand sings the melody in the bass register, with a bright rhythm and plenty of energy.

It is like a little toccata, and it trains finger agility and a steady rhythm.

## The 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27, in brief

Dmitry Kabalevsky was born in 1904 and died in 1987. He was a Soviet composer and music educator who believed that for children learning music, learning to feel and understand it matters most, and in his later years he took part in reforming school music programmes. The thirty pieces of Op. 27 were written between 1937 and 1938, are arranged roughly by difficulty, and each concentrates on one technique or one mood.

In the Toccatina the right hand plays short chords and the left hand sings the melody, with a bright rhythm that trains finger agility and a steady pulse. The pieces have vivid titles, and their harmony carries the colours of the twentieth century. Compared with Bartók's Mikrokosmos they are more melodic. In the Toccatina the right-hand chords should be light, the staccato clear, and each piece's mood should be expressed. Kabalevsky also wrote the orchestral suite The Comedians, whose Galop is famous, and the difficulty runs from beginner to intermediate.

Teacher Aum can recommend suitable pieces.

- Written by Kabalevsky between 1937 and 1938
- Thirty short piano pieces
- Each practises one technique or expresses one mood
- The Toccatina has a bright rhythm and is very popular

## Expressing the mood

When playing this set, besides practising technique, you should express the mood of each piece.

Happy pieces should be played brightly and lightly, and sad ones softly and slowly.

When the mood changes, the weight of touch and the tone colour should change with it.

![A person with headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign in the background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaf4qo2-mlccd.webp)

## What level suits Op. 27

The difficulty of the 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27, runs from beginner to intermediate.

A child who has been learning for a year or two can start with the first few pieces.

Those at a higher level can take on harder pieces such as the Toccatina.

## Vivid titles

Many of the pieces in this set have vivid titles, such as waltz, little song, étude and little sonata.

These titles help children picture the scene and mood of the music.

When playing, you can first think about what the title means, then look for a suitable way to express it.

## Key points for playing the Toccatina

When playing the Toccatina, the right-hand chords should be light and even, and must not drown out the left-hand melody.

The staccato should be clear and springy, and the accents definite.

You can start slowly and speed up, and once the piece is fluent, play it at the bright tempo.

## One thing to practise in each piece

In this set, each piece concentrates on one technique or expresses one mood.

For example, some practise legato, some staccato, and some coordination between the two hands.

**Tip**

Some express joy, some sadness, and some are like a little story.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who wrote the 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27?**
A: The Soviet composer Kabalevsky.

**Q: How many pieces are there?**
A: Thirty.

**Q: When was it written?**
A: Between 1937 and 1938.

**Q: What is special about the Toccatina?**
A: The right hand plays short chords and the left hand sings the melody, with a bright rhythm.

**Q: Which Kabalevsky orchestral suite has a famous Galop?**
A: The Comedians.

joplin-the-entertainer-1902-rag.body:
"The Entertainer" is a ragtime piano piece published by Scott Joplin in 1902, with the subtitle "A Ragtime Two-Step". The whole piece is in 2/4 time, with the left hand bouncing along, a bass note on one beat and a chord on the next, and the right-hand melody full of syncopation. The piece was already published in Joplin's lifetime, and in the 1970s, when a film used it as its soundtrack, it became familiar to many people again. The tempo marking on the score is "Not fast", and when playing it, steadiness matters more than speed.

## Comparing with the Maple Leaf Rag

The "Maple Leaf Rag", which Joplin had published a few years earlier, is also a very famous ragtime work.

Both pieces have a bouncing left hand and a syncopated right hand, but the character of their melodies and sections is different.

You can listen to the two pieces and compare the difference in mood.

- A rag published in 1902
- Subtitle "A Ragtime Two-Step"
- Left-hand bass notes alternating with chords, syncopated melody in the right hand
- The score is marked "Not fast"

![The lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4x2qj-99dz7.webp)

## Go Easy on the Pedal

The bounce of the left hand in ragtime needs to be clear, and if you use too much pedal, the bass notes and chords will blur together.

In most of "The Entertainer", let your fingers play the notes cleanly by themselves, and touch the pedal only at the odd long note.

First get it comfortable without the pedal, and then decide where it is needed.

## The Bounce of the Left Hand in The Entertainer

The left hand of this piece is doing almost the same thing all the time: playing a bass note on the strong beat, and jumping to the middle register to play a chord on the weak beat.

This bounce in the left hand is like the steps of a dance, and it is the foundation of ragtime.

In practice you can first practise the left hand alone, to get used to the distance between bass note and chord, looking ahead to the next position.

## Choosing a Simplified Version

If the original is a struggle, some arrangements keep only the left-hand bass notes and leave out the chords in the middle register, which can serve as a stepping stone.

A simplified version can help you get to know the melody and the structure first.

Once you know them, you can gradually move on to the original writing.

## The "Not Fast" Marking

Joplin wrote the tempo marking "Not fast" on the score.

Many people speed up as they play ragtime, but this makes the bounce of the left hand frantic and the syncopation loses its flavour.

Rather than aiming for fast hands, it is better to give the beat room, so that each syncopated note stands firmly.

## Where the Difficulty Lies

The difficulty of this piece lies mainly in the coordination of the left-hand bounce with the right-hand syncopation.

Before putting the hands together, mark on the score between which left-hand beats each syncopated note falls.

Once you are fluent, speed up gradually, but never go beyond the unhurried tempo the score suggests.

## The Structure of Several Sections

"The Entertainer" is like a string of small linked sections, each with its own tune, and some of them come round again unchanged.

On the score you can mark the sections with letters, such as A, B, C and D, and see clearly the order in which they appear.

Once you know the structure, you can finish the piece one section at a time in practice, and it is easier to memorise too.

## The Entertainer in Summary

"The Entertainer" is a rag published by Joplin in 1902, with the subtitle "A Ragtime Two-Step", in 2/4 time.

The left hand bounces between bass notes and chords, and the right hand plays a syncopated melody.

The score is marked "Not fast": a steady, unhurried tempo matters more than speed, and the pedal should be used sparingly, so that every syncopation is clear.

## Its Later Revival

In the early twentieth century ragtime was very popular, but as musical styles changed it was gradually played less.

In the 1970s, a film used "The Entertainer" as its soundtrack, and many people heard the piece again.

Since then, it has become one of the pieces that many piano learners want to learn.

## The Year of Publication

"The Entertainer" was published in 1902, and is one of Scott Joplin's ragtime works.

The subtitle on the score reads "A Ragtime Two-Step", showing that it is linked to a popular dance step of the time.

Joplin wrote dozens of rags in his lifetime, and "The Entertainer" is one that is widely known today.

## Counting in 2/4

This piece is in 2/4 time, with two beats in each bar and each beat a quarter note.

Because most of the notes are eighth notes and sixteenth notes, when counting you can divide each beat again into two halves or four parts.

Once you have counted the subdivided beats clearly, you are less likely to get the position of the syncopation wrong.

## Dynamics in Ragtime

Ragtime does not need to be loud all the time, and the score also has dynamic markings such as piano and crescendo.

The bass notes in the left hand should be clear and the chords lighter, so that the right-hand melody floats on top.

When a section repeats, you can try playing it more softly the first time and louder the second, to create contrast.

## The Right-Hand Syncopated Melody

The melody in the right hand has a lot of syncopation, with the accent often falling in the middle of the beat rather than at the start.

This syncopation contrasts with the steady bounce of the left hand, and produces the lively feel that is special to ragtime.

**Common misconceptions**

You can first count the beats while tapping out the right-hand rhythm, to confirm the position of each syncopated note.

## FAQ

**Q: When was "The Entertainer" published?**
A: 1902.

**Q: What is its subtitle?**
A: "A Ragtime Two-Step".

**Q: What is the left hand doing?**
A: Playing a bass note on the strong beat and jumping to the middle register for a chord on the weak beat.

**Q: How fast should it be?**
A: The score is marked "Not fast", so an unhurried, steady tempo is enough.

**Q: Why did it become popular again later?**
A: It was used as the soundtrack of a film in the 1970s.

imagine-a-listener-while-practicing.body:
Picturing a specific listener in your mind while you practise, such as a family member, a friend or someone you would like to play for, can give your playing a stronger sense of direction. You naturally start to think: how do I make this phrase clear, how do I get this feeling across? When the music goes from "getting the notes right" to "saying what it means", expression usually follows.

## Different Sections, Different Ways of Speaking

In the same piece, each section can be seen as saying something different to the listener. The opening is like a greeting, the middle like telling of a turn in the story, and the ending like a farewell. Thinking this way makes the contrast between sections clearer.

When practising, you can mark the "tone" of each section on the score with simple words, such as "speak softly", "say with excitement" or "slowly remember". These words do not have to be precise; it is enough that they remind you.

When you are thinking "I want them to hear that it changes here", changes of dynamics and tempo are no longer done mechanically to match the markings, but have a reason.

![A watercolour-style upright piano, an open score and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wqg8a-2lbmo.webp)

## Help for Performances and Exams

Many people are nervous on stage because all they are thinking is "don't make a mistake". If you are used to playing for someone in everyday practice, on stage you can return your attention to that familiar picture, rather than staring at the judgement of the audience.

It is the same in an exam: the examiner is someone who listens to music. It is easier to relax if you treat the performance as telling something to a willing listener than as a test paper to be marked.

This kind of mental preparation needs regular practice; thinking of it at the last minute is usually too late.

- Choose a specific person, not a vague "audience"
- Think about what you hope they will hear
- You can leave the listener out for a while when practising technical passages
- Bring the listener back when you play the whole piece through

## How to Use It in Practice

When working on technique section by section, you can leave the listener out at first and concentrate on fingering and rhythm. Once a section is fairly fluent, imagine that person sitting beside you as you play it.

When you play the whole piece through, think of this listener from the very first note. When you reach the climax, think about what you hope they will feel; at the ending, think about how to let them hear that the piece is over.

After you finish, you can ask yourself: if they had really been listening, would they have understood what I meant? Which phrase was not clear enough?

Sometimes you will forget the listener halfway through, which is quite normal; just bring the picture back in your next run-through.

## Why You Need a Listener

Music is a form of communication in the first place. The composer writes a melody, and the performer brings it to those who listen. If there is nobody in your mind when you practise, playing easily becomes just finger movement: the notes are right, but it is not very moving.

Imagining a listener is like giving yourself someone to speak to. Just as when you tell a story to a person, you pay attention to tone, pauses and emphasis, your playing will gain more rise and fall.

This method does not need anyone to actually be present; it is just a picture in your mind.

Even an étude can be imagined as showing someone the pleasure of a technique.

## How to Choose the Listener

The more specific the better. For example "Grandma, who comes to the house at weekends", or "a friend who likes quiet pieces". A specific person has their own tastes, and you can imagine their reactions more clearly.

Different pieces can have different listeners. A lively piece might be for a small child, and a lyrical one might suit a quiet elder.

Choose someone who makes you feel warm and relaxed, not someone who makes you nervous. The aim is to give the music direction, not to add pressure.

## You Can Also Invite Someone to Really Listen

When a piece has been practised to a certain level, you can really ask a family member to sit down and listen to it once. It does not need to be a formal performance; a few minutes is enough.

After playing, you can ask them a simple question, such as "which part stuck in your mind most?" Their answer can help you see where you came across clearly and where you can strengthen it.

Real listeners and imagined listeners working together make practice feel more and more like making music, and not just completing a task.

## FAQ

**Q: Will imagining a listener be distracting?**
A: You can leave it out during technical practice and add it in run-throughs, so it does not affect your attention to detail.

**Q: What if I do not know who to imagine?**
A: Start with the person closest to you who makes you feel most relaxed.

**Q: Will I get nervous if I keep thinking of a listener?**
A: Choosing someone who makes you feel warm usually makes you more relaxed, not more nervous.

**Q: Can children use this method too?**
A: Yes. Letting a child say who they want to play for often makes them more engaged.

**Q: Does recording something for someone count as a listener?**
A: Yes. Recording a piece and sending it to family or friends also gives practice a clear audience.

**Q: How is imagining a listener different from imagining a picture?**
A: A picture helps you feel the mood of the music, while a listener helps you think about how to get that mood across. The two methods can be used together.

keep-going-after-wrong-note.body:
Many people who learn the piano have a habit: as soon as they play one wrong note, they stop and start again from the beginning. The result is that the start of the piece is polished, but the second half always feels unfamiliar, and the moment a mistake happens on stage or in front of others, everything falls apart. "Not stopping" practice means that in certain practice sessions, whatever mistakes happen, you keep the beat and carry on playing, training continuity in your performance and the ability to respond on the spot.

## Keep the Two Kinds of Practice Separate

Practising actually contains two different kinds of work. One is "repairing": when you find a wrong note, you stop, find the cause and correct it slowly. The other is "performing": you simulate a real occasion and play from beginning to end without interruption. The problem is that many people only repair and never perform.

- Repair sessions: you can stop, repeat and go slowly
- Performance sessions: do not stop, keep the beat, and deal with mistakes afterwards
- You need both, and the proportion can be adjusted to how well you know the piece

## How to Practise "Not Stopping"

**Start with a slower tempo**
Begin at a tempo somewhat slower than usual, so you have room to catch up after a mistake. You can turn on the metronome to remind yourself that the beat must not stop.

**When you slip, protect only the rhythm**
When you play a wrong note, do not go back to fix it; go straight on to the next beat. If you get completely stuck somewhere, play only the left hand or only the bass, and rejoin with both hands at the next place you know well.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a smiling pianist on a rainy street plays a transparent glowing grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw40wlk8-ds5y1.webp)

## Make a List of Mistakes After Playing

After you finish a non-stop run, think back: in which places did you make mistakes? Note them on paper or beside the score. Your next repair session then focuses only on those places. In this way, "performing" helps you find the problems and "repairing" helps you solve them, and the two form a cycle.

## Set "Rejoin Points"

Mark a few rejoin points on the score, usually the start of a phrase or of a section. If you get lost somewhere, you can jump straight to the nearest rejoin point and carry on. In everyday practice you can also start from a rejoin point at random, to make sure every section can start on its own, rather than only from the first bar.

## When This Kind of Practice Is Especially Needed

Before playing for family and friends, before recording a video, or before a student concert, it is a good idea to increase the share of "not stopping" practice. Even at home, treating one complete run now and then as a real performance can gradually ease the nervousness about making mistakes.

## Use Recording to Simulate a Real Performance

When practising "not stopping" at home, the easiest place to slack off is "nobody is listening anyway". Turn on the recording on your phone and tell yourself this is a real concert, and a little tension will naturally arise. This moderate tension is exactly what you meet on real occasions.

After recording, do not rush to delete it. Listen again after some time and note three things: where the mistakes were, whether you could rejoin after them, and whether the overall tempo wavered between fast and slow.

- Where the mistakes were: mark them on the score
- How you rejoined: whether it went smoothly
- Tempo changes: whether you speed up as you go

## Practising with a Teacher or Family

You can ask a family member to sit beside you as the audience, having agreed beforehand that "whatever happens, do not interrupt". For children, having someone listening makes them more serious; for adults, this helps them gradually get used to being watched.

A teacher can also set aside a "little stage time" in the lesson: the student plays the piece they are working on all the way through, the teacher only listens without interrupting, and afterwards first names one thing that went well, then points out one thing to repair. This order makes students more willing to try complete performances again next time.

Gradually, "not stopping even after a mistake" will change from a deliberate exercise into a natural reaction when you perform.

## Small Adjustments in Mindset

When they make a mistake, many people's first reaction is to frown, sigh or shake their head, and these movements make the next beat harder to play accurately. You can try practising a "neutral expression": treat a mistake as if it never happened, and keep your eyes moving forward along the score. Listeners usually remember only the overall musical impression, and seldom notice a single wrong note. Putting your attention back on the next phrase is the adjustment a performer can make.

- Do not frown at a mistake; keep your eyes on the score
- If you get stuck, jump to a rejoin point
- Go back and repair afterwards

Write these three sentences on the cover of your score, and a glance at them while you practise will remind you to keep going.

## FAQ

**Q: If I never stop, won't I get used to the wrong notes?**
A: If you only perform and never repair, you might. So after performing, always practise the mistakes separately and slowly.

**Q: What if I cannot keep playing at all?**
A: Jump to the next rejoin point and carry on, keeping the overall sense of rhythm.

**Q: Is this kind of practice suitable for beginners?**
A: Yes. Start with a very short piece and first practise carrying on after a mistake.

**Q: How often should I do a non-stop run?**
A: Once the piece is basically familiar, you can schedule one or two runs in each practice session.

keyboard-stand-height-stability.body:
When you practise on a keyboard or digital piano with a stand, the height and stability of the stand directly affect your posture and the condition of your hands. A general guide: once you are seated, your forearms should be roughly level with the keys, and your wrists should not tilt up or press down; the stand should sit on a steady floor and not wobble as you play. If the stand is too high or too low, you can adjust the stand, or adjust the height of your chair. Everyone's height is different, so try a few times to find the position where both your shoulders and your wrists feel relaxed.

## Check with Your Teacher

If you are not sure whether your height and posture are right, ask your teacher to take a look and give some advice.

You can also take a photo of yourself playing and look at the position of your arms and wrists from the side.

Once you have found a good setup, you can make a mark on the stand so you can quickly set it back later.

## Problems with Too High and Too Low

If the keys are too high, your shoulders will creep up without you noticing and your wrists will press down, which easily causes fatigue over time.

If the keys are too low, your wrists will tilt up and your back may round, which also makes it harder to play in a relaxed way.

The right height lets your arms rest naturally on the keys, so playing feels easier and it is easier to control the sound.

## The Stand Must Be Steady

If the stand is on uneven ground, or is not locked tight, it will wobble as you play, which distracts you and may even be a safety risk.

Put the stand on flat, solid ground, play a few notes to test it, and see whether it is steady.

If the stand has non-slip pads or adjustable feet, you can use them to make it more stable.

## Pedal Position

If you use a sustain pedal, place it where your right foot can reach it naturally.

Pedals easily slide on the floor, so you can put them on a non-slip mat or against a fixed object.

Keep your heel on the floor as a pivot, and use the front of your foot to press and release.

## Different Types of Stand

Common stands include X-style stands, Z-style stands and table-style stands, and they differ in stability and in how they adjust.

X-style stands are easy to carry but are sometimes a little less stable; table-style stands are usually steadier but harder to move.

Choose the type of stand that suits your needs and your space.

## Adjusting Your Chair

The height of your chair also affects your posture, so choose a piano bench or chair whose height can be adjusted.

If the chair is too low, you can add a firm cushion; if it is too high, you can switch to a lower chair.

When you sit, your feet should rest flat on the floor, or on a stable footrest.

![A blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0lwyl-08a91.webp)

## Adjusting the Stand

Many stands can be adjusted in height. Follow the instructions in the manual to set the stand in a suitable position.

When adjusting, make sure every lock is tightened, so that the stand does not suddenly slide down while you play.

If the stand cannot be set to a suitable height, you can consider adjusting the chair to compensate.

## Children's Changing Height

Children keep growing, so the height of the stand and chair needs to be adjusted from time to time.

Check your child's posture every so often to see whether their wrists and forearms are still in a suitable position.

If your child's feet cannot yet reach the floor, prepare a steady footrest so that they can sit more securely.

**Summary**
- Forearms roughly level with the keys
- Wrists not tilted up or pressed down
- Stand steady, with no wobble while playing
- You can adjust the height of the stand or the chair

## A Reference Height

A common way to check is to sit on the chair, let your upper arms hang naturally, stretch your forearms forward, and see whether your forearms are roughly level with the keys.

With your hands on the keys, the back of your hand, wrist and forearm should form a roughly flat line, without deliberately tilting up or pressing down.

This is only a reference, and you should still adjust according to how it feels to you.

## Checking While You Play

While you practise, pay attention now and then to your shoulders and wrists, and whether they feel tense or uncomfortable.

If you feel discomfort, you can stop, adjust the height or your posture, and then carry on.

Making regular checks a habit keeps you comfortable during long practice sessions.

## Where the Keyboard Sits

When the keyboard is on the stand, place it in the middle, so that one side is not heavier than the other.

The front-to-back position should also be right, so that there is a suitable distance between the front edge of the keys and your body.

Sit roughly in front of the middle of the keyboard, so that both hands can easily reach the registers they need.

## FAQ

**Q: How high should a keyboard stand be?**
A: Once you are seated, your forearms should be roughly level with the keys.

**Q: What should my wrists do?**
A: Stay level with the forearm, neither tilted up nor sagging down.

**Q: What if the stand cannot be set to a suitable height?**
A: Adjust the chair or add a cushion.

**Q: How do I check that the stand is steady?**
A: Put it on flat ground, lock it tight and play a few notes to test it.

**Q: What if my child has grown taller?**
A: Check regularly and adjust the stand and chair.

**Q: What if the pedal keeps sliding?**
A: Put it on a non-slip mat or against a fixed object.

keep-going-after-mistake-performance.body:
Playing a wrong note or missing a beat in a performance or an exam is something many people meet. The better way to handle it is to let the music keep moving forward: do not stop, do not replay, and do not show annoyance on your face. Listeners often care more about whether the music is continuous than about noticing a small mistake. In everyday practice you can consciously practise "carrying on after a mistake", and mark a few places in the score in advance where you can rejoin, so that when something unexpected really happens you can carry on calmly.

## Why not stop

If you stop and replay because of one wrong note in a performance, the audience clearly feels that the music has been interrupted.

**Remember this**

If you keep playing, many small mistakes may not be noticed at all, or are quickly covered by the music that follows.

Keeping the music continuous matters more than correcting a wrong note.

## Let the left hand rejoin first

Sometimes the right-hand melody goes astray. You can let the left hand carry on with the accompaniment first, to keep the music flowing, and let the right hand find its place and rejoin.

Conversely, if the left hand goes astray, you can let the right-hand melody continue, and the left hand can come back in at the next chord.

In practice you can play the whole piece with the left hand alone or the right hand alone, which makes this easier to do in performance.

## Keep a calm expression

When you play a wrong note, do not frown, shake your head or sigh. These expressions make the audience notice the mistake.

Keep a calm expression, as if nothing has happened, and stay focused on the music.

Very often, a mistake that seems obvious to the performer is not noticed by the audience.

## Reflecting after the performance

After you leave the stage, calm down and think about where the mistake happened, and whether it was because of nerves, not enough preparation or a technical difficulty.

Write these places down as the focus of your next stage of practice.

But also remember to acknowledge what you did well, such as being able to carry on playing after the mistake.

## Adjust your breathing

After a mistake, people often get tense, their breathing speeds up, and their hands may stiffen.

On the next long note or rest, you can take a deep breath in and breathe out slowly to calm yourself.

In everyday practice you can also build the habit of breathing naturally between phrases.

## Prepare rejoining points

You can mark a few rejoining points in the score, such as the beginning of each phrase or section.

In practice, try starting from these points, to make sure you can rejoin fluently at each one.

In performance, if you get stuck somewhere, you can jump to the next rejoining point and carry on playing the music.

## Your view of mistakes

Wrong notes are a perfectly natural part of learning and playing, and even experienced performers occasionally slip on stage.

What matters is not never making a mistake, but being able to express the music fully and with feeling after one.

Facing a performance with this attitude makes you feel more relaxed and your playing more natural.

## Talk to your teacher about strategies

You can ask your teacher to help you find the places in the piece where mistakes are most likely, and to design rejoining methods for them.

Your teacher can also share experience of handling surprises in performance, to help you prepare mentally.

With thorough preparation, you will feel more confident on stage.

**Watch the details**
- When you play a wrong note, let the music keep moving
- Do not stop and do not replay
- Listeners care more about whether the music is continuous
- Prepare a few places in advance where you can rejoin

## Keep the beat

When you play a wrong note, the most important thing is to keep the beat steady. Even if you have missed a few notes, play the next note at the right time.

You can keep counting the beats in your head, and let the beat be what you rely on.

As long as the beat is steady, the music will sound continuous and the audience can follow more easily.

## Habits in everyday practice

Many people stop and start again as soon as they make a mistake in practice, and this habit gets carried into performance.

So as a performance approaches, you can consciously practise playing the whole piece without stopping, carrying on even after a mistake.

In this way your hands and your brain gradually get used to "keep going forward" rather than "stop and start again".

![Glowing abstract digits and a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0aydg-p2mtv.webp)

## Practise with mock performances

When you hold a mock performance at home, you can specially practise the ability to carry on after a mistake.

You can even ask family members to make an occasional sound while you play, such as a cough or turning a page, to practise staying focused despite distractions.

This kind of practice makes you better able to cope in the real performance.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Should I stop if I play a wrong note in a performance?**
A: No, let the music keep moving forward.

**Q: What is a rejoining point?**
A: A place where you can rejoin, such as the beginning of a phrase.

**Q: What matters most after a mistake?**
A: Keeping the beat steady.

**Q: What should my expression be?**
A: Stay calm and do not show annoyance.

**Q: How should I practise day to day?**
A: Play the whole piece without stopping, practising carrying on after a mistake.

**Q: Is a wrong note terrible?**
A: No, what matters is being able to express the music fully.

interval-theory-homework.body:
An interval is how far apart two notes are in pitch, usually counted in numbers, so C to E is a third and C to G is a fifth. When doing interval homework, do not just count squares on paper: play each interval at the piano and sing it, so that your ear remembers its sound, and the homework turns from a page of numbers into a set of colours you can hear.

## Link Intervals to Familiar Melodies

A common way to remember intervals is to link each one to the opening of a familiar song. For example, the first two notes of some children's songs are a major second and others a perfect fifth, and each time you hear the start of that song you are reminded of the sound of that interval. Different people can choose pieces they know well.

**Slow down**

When practising at the piano, you can play the lower note first and then the upper note, then play them together, and compare the feeling of separate and simultaneous notes. Gradually your ear will tell major thirds from minor thirds, and perfect fourths from perfect fifths.

Intervals are the foundation for understanding chords and melody. Three notes stacked in thirds make a triad, and the leaps and steps in a melody can all be described with intervals. With this foundation laid, harmony and sight-singing will be much easier later on.

## Recognising Intervals in the Score

On the staff, intervals also follow certain visual patterns. An interval from line to line or space to space is an odd number, such as a third or a fifth; an interval between a line and a space is an even number, such as a second or a fourth.

A third looks on the staff like two neighbouring lines or two neighbouring spaces, while a fifth skips one line or one space. Once you are familiar with these shapes, you can see the direction of a melody more quickly when you read music.

When doing homework, you can first use the visual pattern to judge the number quickly, and then use semitones to confirm whether it is a major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished interval.

## Remember the Sound of Intervals With Songs

Many people remember the sound of intervals with the openings of familiar songs. For example, the first two notes of some songs are a fourth or a fifth apart, and singing it helps you find the feeling of that distance.

You can make a table of your own, matching each interval to the opening of a familiar song. It works better if you choose songs you really know well.

When practising listening to intervals, you can first play two notes at the piano, then sing them and judge how far apart they are. When you are fluent, try listening without looking and say the name of the interval.

- The number of an interval is counted from the lower note to the upper note, including both ends
- The same number can still be major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished
- Thirds and sixths usually sound fairly soft
- Playing the interval and listening is easier to remember than just counting lines and spaces

## How to Calculate Intervals

When calculating an interval, count both the starting note and the end note. From C to E, for example, it passes through C, D, E, three notes, so it is a third; from C to G it passes through five notes, so it is a fifth.

Thirds also come as major thirds and minor thirds. A major third contains two whole tones, such as C to E; a minor third contains a whole tone and a semitone, such as D to F. To tell major from minor, you need to count the semitones in between carefully.

You can count semitones on the keyboard: two adjacent keys, black or white, are one semitone apart. From C to E is four semitones, a major third; from D to F is three semitones, a minor third.

## Use Interval Knowledge at the Piano

Knowing intervals helps you read music faster and find notes. When you see a melody leap up a fifth, your hand knows roughly how far to move, and does not have to look for each note separately.

Intervals are also the foundation for understanding chords. A triad is made of two thirds stacked together, and if you know the difference between a major third and a minor third, you can understand the difference between a major triad and a minor triad.

After finishing your homework, you can play all the intervals in the questions at the piano and listen to their sound. Linking what is on paper with what your ear feels makes memory stronger.

![A colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jqyfn-m9372.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What should I do if I keep miscounting intervals in my homework?**
A: Remember to count both the starting note and the end note. C to D is a second, not a first, for example.

**Q: How do I tell a major third from a minor third?**
A: A major third is a semitone larger than a minor third. You can count the number of semitones at the piano, and then compare the colours with your ear.

**Q: What is the difference between a perfect fifth and a perfect fourth?**
A: A perfect fifth contains seven semitones and a perfect fourth contains five, and they are inversions of each other.

**Q: How can I quickly tell a major third from a minor third?**
A: Count the semitones: four semitones is a major third, and three is a minor third.

**Q: What if I can never tell intervals apart by ear?**
A: You can use the openings of familiar songs, and practise a little every day to build up your aural memory gradually.

**Q: What is an augmented fourth?**
A: It is a semitone larger than a perfect fourth, with six semitones, and it sounds fairly tense.
