joplin-solace-mexican-serenade-1909.body:
"Solace" is a piano piece published by Scott Joplin in 1909, with the subtitle "A Mexican Serenade". Unlike Joplin's fast, bouncy rags, it is slower, its melody sings more, and you can feel a gently swaying rhythm in the accompaniment. If you have learned faster pieces such as "The Entertainer", you might hear "Solace" as the other side of the same composer: it has the same clear beat and syncopation, but is closer to a piece you could sing slowly. When playing, it is better to settle into the slow tempo first and then feel the syncopation and the rise and fall of the melody, than to hurry to get to the end. After playing it through, you can also play just the left hand to walk through the beat, and check whether the sway has quietly sped up. You can also sing each phrase of the melody once more on its own, to see whether the breaths are clear.

## How It Differs from Fast Rags

Joplin wrote many rags at a fairly fast tempo, with very distinct right-hand syncopation.

**Keep this in mind**

"Solace" belongs to his piano works too, but its character is slower and more lyrical.

Listen once through first, then decide on your touch: here what is needed is smoothness and softness, not just crisp, bouncing notes.

## Remember the Structure in Sections

Ragtime and related piano pieces are often made of several fairly complete sections that follow one another, and some sections come back again.

First make a simple mark for each section, noting where there are repeats and where a new melody begins.

Remembering by section is less likely to go astray than memorising the whole piece as one long strip.

## Syncopation at a Slow Tempo

Even when the tempo is not fast, the right hand may still have syncopation, letting the melody slip slightly off the main beats of the accompaniment.

First make the left-hand beat steady, then let the right-hand syncopation land in exactly the right place.

Slow does not mean loose: every syncopation must still be countable.

## Sing the Melody of Solace First

The melody of this piece is fairly long, so it is good to hum it through before playing.

You can open up the high point of a phrase a little and then draw back, avoiding the same volume from start to finish.

Where there is little ornament, you have to rely on the depth of touch to shape the phrasing.

## Asking Teacher Aum to Listen to the Syncopation

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the syncopation at a slow tempo is accurate, and whether your left hand drifts along with the right.

If a phrase does not sing enough, you can also ask your teacher to mark the breaths with you.

Use Joplin's slower side to practise holding on to the beat and the singing at the same time.

## The Sway of the Left Hand

The left hand is usually responsible for the steady pulse and harmony, sometimes with a little sway.

It should be quieter than the right hand, but not so vague that it loses the beat.

You can practise the left hand alone with a metronome first, and then put the hands together.

## Level and Order of Learning

If you can already play simpler rags steadily, learning this slower piece afterwards will help both your syncopation and your phrasing.

If you are still consolidating an even accompaniment, you can also treat it as a piece for practising "slow and accurate".

Take the tempo from the markings on the score and from being able to sing the melody to the end, and do not chase the surface excitement of faster pieces.

## Solace in Summary

Joplin's "Solace" of 1909 carries the subtitle of a Mexican serenade; it is slow and its melody leans towards singing, unlike fast rags, but it still has a clear beat and syncopation.

In practice, steady the left hand first, then sing the right hand, use the pedal lightly and change it in time, and remember the structure by sections.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the syncopation and the phrases.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon-lit street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdiit3y-50z9z.webp)

## The Pedal Helps Connection, but Does Not Blur

Since the melody needs to sing, the pedal can help join the notes; but it must still change when the bass changes.

Where there is a lot of syncopation, a pedal that is too deep wipes out the sharp edges of the rhythm.

First play it through with less pedal to find the phrases that really need to be joined, and then add a shallow pedal.

- Slower in tempo, with a melody that leans towards singing

The subtitle likens the piece to a Mexican serenade, hinting at its singing quality and a certain swaying feel in the accompaniment.

It does not ask you to imitate any particular Mexican folk instrument on the piano.

The title is a clue to get in; what you really rely on is still the rhythm, phrasing and dynamics on the score.

A: 1909.

italian-tempo-terms-piano.body:
The line of Italian at the start of a score is mostly a tempo term: Largo and Adagio mean slow, Andante is like ordinary walking, Moderato is a moderate speed, Allegro is rather fast, and Presto is very fast. They do not just set how fast or slow to play; they also hint at the character of a piece. Read the word before you play, then settle on a tempo together with the metronome number in the score (if there is one), and your playing will not sit in "the same gear" for every piece. This article sorts the common terms into a list you can use directly, in three layers: from slow to fast, modifiers, and tempo changes.

## Three Key Points for Reading Tempo Terms

- A tempo term describes "a rough range of speed plus a mood", not an exact number
- If the score also gives a metronome number (for example "♩ = a certain value"), go by the number and use the term to understand the character
- The same term can mean a different actual speed in different periods and in the hands of different composers
- Modifiers (molto, poco and so on) make the basic term a little faster or a little slower
- Markings that appear within a piece, such as rit. and accel., only affect a passage, and afterwards there is usually an a tempo to return to the original speed

## Layer One: The Basic Terms from Slow to Fast

The terms below are arranged roughly from slow to fast, with a brief English gloss and an association that makes each easier to remember:

- Largo (broad): wide and solemn, like strolling slowly through a great hall
- Lento (slow): slow, with the emphasis on the slowness itself
- Adagio (at ease): unhurried and gentle, often with a lyrical colour
- Andante (walking pace): the pace of ordinary walking, neither rushed nor slow
- Andantino (a little Andante): usually a little faster than Andante
- Moderato (moderate): a moderate speed, steady and even
- Allegretto (a little Allegro): livelier than Moderato, but not yet Allegro
- Allegro (quick, lively): light and bright, like a jog
- Vivace (lively): full of life and spring
- Presto (very quick): very fast, and needs very steady fingers

It should be said that whether Andantino is faster or slower than Andante has been understood differently at different times in history; most textbooks today explain it as a little faster. When you are unsure, you can refer to the metronome marking in the score or to a reliable recording.

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvlr4dv-us4h1.webp)

## Layer Two: Modifiers That Add "More" or "Less" to a Term

**Common modifiers**

- molto: very, for example Allegro molto means very fast
- poco: a little, for example poco Allegro means a little fast
- più: more, for example più mosso means livelier, faster
- meno: less, for example meno mosso means not so fast
- non troppo: not too much, for example Allegro non troppo means fast but not too fast
- assai: quite, very

**Supplementary words with character**

- cantabile: in a singing style, the melody should sound sung
- con brio: with spirit
- dolce: sweetly
- maestoso: majestically

Read the basic term together with its modifiers and you can pick up the "tempo plus expression" the composer wants. Andante cantabile, for example, means a walking pace with the melody sung out.

## Layer Three: Tempo-Change Markings Within a Piece

- accel. (accelerando): gradually faster
- rit. (ritardando) or rall. (rallentando): gradually slower
- a tempo: return to the original speed
- Tempo I (Tempo primo): return to the speed at the very beginning of the piece
- Fermata (an arc with a dot): hold this note or rest longer than its written value

When practising, you can draw a little slope in pencil above these markings: an uphill slope for faster, a downhill slope for slower, and level ground for a return to the original speed. One glance and you know how the tempo is going to move next.

## A Little Experiment: The Same Melody at Three Tempos

Pick a simple melody you already know, such as the first four bars of a nursery song, and play it with three different characters:

**Play it with the feeling of Adagio**
Slow down and let every note sustain fully, closing each phrase gently, like speaking on a quiet night.

**Play it with the feeling of Moderato**
Return to an ordinary walking pace, with even dynamics, so that it sounds natural and steady.

**Play it with the feeling of Allegro**
Speed up and use a lighter, springier touch so that the melody sounds bright and lively.

When you have finished, compare them: the same notes, but with a different tempo and touch, the mood is completely different. This little experiment helps you truly feel that a tempo term describes not only fast or slow but a musical character. Many teachers use similar comparison exercises in lessons to help students connect words with sounds.

## "Thirty Seconds of Tempo Preparation" Before You Play

Sit at the piano, but don't rush to press the first note:

- Read the tempo term at the start and think about what kind of mood it describes
- Sing two bars of the melody in your head, walking through it at that tempo
- If there is a metronome number, turn on the metronome and listen for one bar, then switch it off or leave it on
- Rest both hands lightly on the keyboard, and begin once the beat inside you is steady

This little routine helps you avoid rushing as soon as you sit down. For a child learning the piano, it can also become a fixed "opening ritual" that makes learning music more orderly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Do tempo terms have to be in Italian?**

A: Not necessarily. Italian is the most common traditional choice, but some composers use German, French or English for tempo and expression. When you come across an unfamiliar word, just look it up in a dictionary of musical terms.

**Q: The score says Allegro and I can't play that fast. What should I do?**

A: First play the notes accurately at a slower speed, then speed up gradually. Practice tempo and performance tempo can differ; get it steady first, then fast.

**Q: Which is slower, Adagio or Largo?**

A: Largo is generally considered broader and a little slower, but both are slow tempos, and the difference is more one of character. For the exact speed you can refer to the metronome marking or a recording.

**Q: Do I need to memorise all these terms?**

A: We suggest first remembering the ten or so most common ones, then learning one more each time you meet it while practising a piece. In piano lessons or when learning piano online, writing newly learned terms in your practice notebook makes review easier.

label-sections-abc-in-score.body:
When you get a new piece, a very useful habit is to divide it into sections in pencil and write a letter such as A, B or C at the start of each one. Sections that are the same or similar get the same letter, and places where something changes get a small prime mark, such as A′. Once the piece is divided, you can say "today I'll practise section B" instead of playing from the beginning every time. It also makes talking with your teacher in lessons easier, and when you memorise, the order of the sections helps you remember the whole piece.

## First, look at the shape of the whole piece

When you get a new piece, don't rush to play from the first note. First spend a few minutes leafing through the whole piece.

**Listen**

Notice where there are double barlines, repeat signs, or changes of key signature or time signature. These are often the boundaries between sections.

You can also look for where the melody comes back, and find the "landmarks" of the music.

## Easier communication with your teacher

In a lesson, if the score already has section letters and your teacher says "start from section B", you can find the place straight away.

You can also tell your teacher "the third bar of section C never goes well", which makes your message more precise.

Many teachers are also glad when students make these markings first.

## Practise identical sections once

If section A appears three times in the piece and is exactly the same each time, then learning it well once is like learning it well in three places.

This gives you more confidence in a piece that looks very long.

But check carefully each time it appears for small differences, such as a different ending or different dynamics.

## It doesn't have to be perfect the first time

When you first divide a piece, you may be unsure whether a section should be A or B. That is perfectly normal.

You can divide it according to your own understanding first and discuss it with your teacher in the lesson.

As you gain experience, your sections will become more and more accurate, and you will make them more quickly.

## Plan practice by section

Once the piece is divided, you can plan each day's practice by section, for example section A on Monday and section B on Tuesday.

You can also practise the hardest section first and then the easier ones.

This is more efficient than playing from start to finish every time, and it stops you from knowing the opening very well while the later parts always feel unfamiliar.

![A golden sketch of a grand piano on a cream background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3iysg-labhb.webp)

## Section labelling summary

Labelling the sections of a score takes only a few minutes, but it makes the whole learning process more organised.

Practice can be planned by section, memorising can be done by section, and communication becomes easier too.

Next time you get a new piece, pick up a pencil first and divide it into sections.

## Starting from any section

Once the piece is divided, try picking a letter at random and starting directly from that section.

This skill is very important in performance: if you make a mistake along the way, you can pick up again from the start of the next section.

You can ask a family member to call out a letter at random and then start playing from that section.

## Sections help with memorising

When memorising, you can first learn the order of the sections in the whole piece, for example "A, B, A, C, A".

Then memorise one section at a time, joining each new section to the ones before it as you learn it.

That way, even if you forget something during a performance, you can still find the start of the next section from the order of the sections.

## Counting the bars in each section

Beside each letter you can also write how many bars the section has, for example "A 8 bars".

This helps you estimate how much practice time each section needs, and shows whether the sections are symmetrical.

Some pieces have very regular section lengths, while in others the lengths vary. Knowing this helps a great deal in understanding the music.

## Marking with letters

After finding the boundaries between sections, write a capital letter in pencil at the start of each one, such as A, B or C.

If a later section is the same as section A, write A again. If it is similar to A but with some changes, write A′.

Then, just by looking at the letters, you can see how the whole piece is organised.

**Try it**
- Write a letter in pencil at the start of each section
- Use the same letter for identical sections, and add a prime mark where something changes
- Plan practice by section
- It helps with communication and memorising

## Marking on digital scores

If you read music on a tablet, you can also use the annotation tools to write letters at the start of each section.

The advantage of a digital score is that you can change it at any time and use different colours to tell things apart.

Whether the score is on paper or on screen, the key is to make the markings clear and visible at a glance.

## Mark the places that change

A section marked A′ is similar to section A but not exactly the same, and these changes are where mistakes are most likely.

You can use a pencil of a different colour or a small circle to mark the notes or bars that change.

When practising, pay special attention to these places so that you don't play them as in the original section A.

## Understanding form through sections

Section letters are really a simple analysis of form: "A, B, A" is ternary form, and "A, B, A, C, A" is rondo form.

By dividing pieces into sections yourself, you will gradually become familiar with these common forms.

Later, when you see a new piece, you will be able to spot its structure more quickly.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why divide a score into sections?**
A: To make practice, communication and memorising more organised.

**Q: How do I mark a section that is similar but has changes?**
A: Use the same letter with a prime mark, such as A′.

**Q: How do I practise once the piece is divided?**
A: You can plan it by section and practise a different section each day.

**Q: How does dividing into sections help with memorising?**
A: First learn the order of the sections, then memorise one section at a time.

**Q: What if my sections aren't accurate?**
A: Divide it according to your own understanding first, then discuss it with your teacher.

keep-child-motivated-piano-practice.body:
When a child loses interest in learning the piano, try changing how practice begins, for example by starting with a favourite piece or one very small task, so that the child feels "I did it" the moment they sit down. Interest often comes from a sense of accomplishment, not from facing the hardest part right at the start.

## Add music your child likes

You can talk with the teacher about adding some music your child likes to the practice repertoire, such as easy versions of songs from animated films, pop songs or film music.

Music they love can spark a child's wish to practise on their own, and shows them that piano playing is connected to their own life.

You can also encourage your child to try simple composing, such as making up a short melody from a few notes, or adding a simple accompaniment to a favourite song.

When children find that playing the piano lets them express themselves, their interest often returns on its own.

## Give every practice a relaxed start

Many children do not want to practise because the moment they sit down they must face something difficult. You can replace the opening with something easy to complete, such as first playing a familiar piece they like.

A relaxed opening helps a child settle in quickly and feel the satisfaction of "I can play this", and they are more patient when they move on to new material.

You can also start with a very short small task, such as playing a scale once or clapping a rhythm, and give themselves a small mark when it is done.

The opening does not need to be long. A few minutes is enough. The point is to let the child begin practice in a positive mood.

## Make practice go smoothly from the start

Many children sit down at the piano and face the hardest passage straight away, and after a few failures they do not want to continue. If you change the order, spending a few minutes on familiar, well-liked pieces first, the child's mood and hands both warm up, and the difficult part becomes much easier to handle.

You can also make practice more of a choice. For example, prepare several cards with different tasks, and let your child draw one each day as the opening task, adding a little novelty and initiative.

A drop in interest is sometimes connected to the difficulty of the repertoire. If the pieces stay too hard for a long time, the child never experiences success. Talking with the teacher and adding some pieces of suitable difficulty that the child likes can help bring the motivation back.

- Use a piece your child likes to open practice
- Break practice tasks into small steps that can be done quickly
- Let your child take part in deciding what to practise and in what order
- Record small improvements so your child can see their own progress

## Divide practice into short sections

Long practice sessions easily make a child tired. You can divide the practice time into several short sections, each doing only one thing, with a short rest in between.

Give each section a clear goal, such as "play this line smoothly" or "practise the left hand three times". Once the goal is done you can move on to the next section, and the child will feel more motivated.

You can prepare a small card listing the few things to finish today, with a tick for each one completed. Visible progress adds to the sense of accomplishment.

If your child is not in good form one day, they can finish just one or two of the items. Keeping the habit of practice matters more than one long session.

At the end of practice, you can also leave a minute or two for your child to play freely, so that a pleasant ending makes them look forward to the next time they sit at the piano.

![A cyberpunk illustration of a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8k25pv-c4slj.webp)

## Reduce interruptions during practice

While your child practises, parents can try to cut down on interruptions and corrections along the way. Frequent reminders easily make a child feel watched and lose their initiative in practising.

If you notice a problem, you can wait until your child has played a piece through and then talk about it together, or note the problem down and leave it for the teacher to deal with in the lesson.

Giving your child a quiet, undisturbed place to practise also helps them focus on the music itself.

**Try it**

When a child feels trusted, practice more easily becomes their own business.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What if my child says practising is boring?**
A: You can ask what feels boring, then adjust the way of practising or the repertoire together, so that your child feels involved.

**Q: Should I shorten practice time?**
A: You can shorten it for a while, but keep it regular, and first help your child build a happy practice experience again.

**Q: Should I force my child to practise if they do not want to?**
A: First find out why, and adjust the way and content of practice, rather than simply forcing.

**Q: Should practice time be fixed?**
A: A fixed time helps build the habit, but you can adjust it flexibly according to your child's state.

**Q: Do reward systems work?**
A: They can help as a supplement, but more lasting motivation usually comes from a sense of accomplishment and an interest in music.

**Q: What if my child only wants to play the pieces they like?**
A: You can use the favourite pieces as an opening or a reward, and then add the basic practice that is needed.

interval-quality-major-minor-perfect.body:
An interval has two elements: its number and its quality. The number counts how many note names the two notes span, so C to E is a third. The quality depends on how many semitones it contains: C to E has four semitones and is a major third, while C to E♭ has three semitones and is a minor third. Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are described as "perfect"; seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are described as "major" or "minor"; and when they are a semitone wider or narrower than these, they become augmented or diminished intervals.

## Remembering Through the Major Scale

A handy way to remember is to take the tonic of a major scale as the lower note: the intervals from it up to each degree are all major or perfect.

In C major, for example, C to D is a major second, C to E is a major third, C to F is a perfect fourth, C to G is a perfect fifth, C to A is a major sixth and C to B is a major seventh.

When you meet other intervals, you can first compare them with this standard and see whether the upper note has been raised or lowered.

## Major and Minor Intervals

Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are described as major and minor, and a major interval is one semitone larger than a minor one.

For example, a major second has two semitones and a minor second has one; a major third has four semitones and a minor third has three.

A major sixth has nine semitones and a minor sixth has eight; a major seventh has eleven semitones and a minor seventh has ten.

## Perfect Intervals

Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are usually described as "perfect".

A perfect unison is the same note, with zero semitones; a perfect fourth has five semitones, such as C to F; a perfect fifth has seven semitones, such as C to G; a perfect octave has twelve semitones, such as C to the C above.

Perfect intervals sound open and stable, and in a lot of music they act as a framework.

## Count the Number First

The first step in identifying an interval is to count the number: counting from the lower note to the upper note, how many note names it passes through, including both ends.

From C to G, for example, it passes through C, D, E, F, G, five note names, so it is a fifth; from D to F it passes through D, E, F, three note names, so it is a third.

When counting the number, ignore sharps and flats and look only at the note names. C to G♯ and C to G♭ are both fifths, for example.

## Spelling and What We Hear

The same sound may be written in different ways. C♯ to F and D♭ to F sound the same, but C♯ to F is a diminished fourth and D♭ to F is a major third.

This is because the number is counted by note names, and different spellings give different numbers and qualities.

When analysing a score, judge by the note names actually written, not just by the position on the keyboard.

## Reinforce It With Dictation

After learning the theory of intervals, you can try some listening exercises: have someone play two notes and you work out which interval it is.

At the start, practise telling apart a few pairs of intervals that sound close and are easy to confuse, and gradually extend to more intervals.

When theory and hearing are combined, your understanding of intervals becomes more solid.

## How Intervals Sound

Intervals of different quality sound different too: a major third is bright, a minor third is soft, a perfect fifth is open.

Minor seconds and major sevenths sound fairly tense, while major and minor sixths sound sweeter.

You can play these intervals one by one at the keyboard and notice how each one feels to you, which helps memory.

## Augmented and Diminished Intervals

If a perfect or major interval is made one semitone larger, it becomes augmented; if a perfect or minor interval is made one semitone smaller, it becomes diminished.

C to F♯ is an augmented fourth, with six semitones; C to G♭ is a diminished fifth, also with six semitones.

The augmented fourth and the diminished fifth are in the same place on the keyboard but written differently, and these are enharmonic intervals.

## Then Count the Semitones

Once you have the number, the second step is to count the semitones between the two notes, which is how you judge the quality of the interval.

On the keyboard, two adjacent keys, whether black or white, are one semitone apart.

C to E, for example, passes through C to C♯, C♯ to D, D to E♭, E♭ to E, four semitones in all.

- An interval has two parts: number and quality
- Count note names for the number, and semitones for the quality
- Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are described as perfect
- Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are described as major and minor

![A person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9ztz7l-9nbm9.webp)

## Inverted Intervals

If you raise the lower note of an interval by an octave, or lower the upper note by an octave, you get its inversion.

After inversion, the number and the original add up to nine, so a third becomes a sixth; the quality swaps: major becomes minor, minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, diminished becomes augmented, and perfect stays perfect.

Knowing the rule of inversion helps you work out larger intervals more quickly.

## FAQ

**Q: What are the two elements of an interval?**
A: Number and quality.

**Q: How do you count the number?**
A: Count how many note names lie between the two notes, including both ends.

**Q: Which intervals are described as perfect?**
A: Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves.

**Q: How many semitones does a major third have?**
A: Four semitones.

**Q: Are an augmented fourth and a diminished fifth the same?**
A: They are in the same place on the keyboard, but they are written and named differently.

**Q: How does the number change after inversion?**
A: The original number and the inverted number add up to nine.

liszt-la-campanella-1851-little-bell.body:
La campanella ("The Little Bell") is the third of Liszt's Grandes études de Paganini. The version usually played today is the final one published in 1851, while an earlier version had already been written in 1838. Its theme comes from the last movement of the Second Violin Concerto by the Italian violinist Paganini, where a little bell-like figure gives the piece its name. On the piano, Liszt has the right hand strike the same note over and over in the high register to imitate a clear bell, while the right hand must also leap quickly across wide distances. The set of etudes was dedicated to the pianist Clara Schumann.

## Asking your teacher about the leaps in La campanella

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate how to practise the big right-hand leaps in La campanella.

If the original is too hard, first find a version of La campanella with smaller leaps to warm up with, and your teacher can help you choose one.

Through La campanella, feel how Liszt moves violin effects to the piano.

## The right-hand leaps

One of the main difficulties in playing La campanella is the big leaps in the right hand.

The right hand has to leap quickly between the melody and the bell in the high register, often by more than two octaves.

Leaping accurately and quickly takes a great deal of practice.

## The bell in the high register

The most distinctive feature of La campanella is the right hand striking the same note over and over in the high register, like a clear bell.

This note is often a very high D♯, and it keeps appearing between the right-hand melody.

When you play it, the bell should be clear and bright but not too loud, like a little bell in the distance.

- The third of the Grandes études de Paganini
- Final version published in 1851, an early version in 1838
- The theme comes from the last movement of Paganini's Second Violin Concerto
- The right hand strikes the same note over and over in the high register

## An ever more brilliant ending

Toward the end of the piece the music becomes more and more brilliant, with plenty of fast figures in both hands.

At last it finishes in a flourish of splendid scales and chords.

The whole piece grows from a delicate bell into a brilliant climax, full of drama.

![A collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaerx9x-6h003.webp)

## Paganini's little bell

Paganini's Second Violin Concerto is in B minor, and its last movement is a rondo.

In this movement there is a little bell in the orchestra, answering the violin's high notes.

The movement is therefore called "La campanella", and its theme is light, bouncing and very easy to remember.

## The original and simplified versions of La campanella

The original La campanella is for advanced players.

There are also some simplified arrangements that keep the theme and the bell effect, with the big leaps and the speed made easier.

You can start with a simplified version to get to know the music of the piece.

## Trills and repeated notes

The later sections of La campanella also have many trills and fast repeated notes.

The trills should be even and light, like a bell that keeps on trembling.

For the repeated notes you can use finger substitution, so that every note is clear.

## How to practise leaps

When practising leaps, you can play slowly at first, with your eyes fixed first on the place you are going to land.

The hand should move quickly through the air and then land lightly on the keys, not slam down.

You can practise just the leaping motion first, without sounding the notes, and play them once you are familiar with the distance.

## Two versions

In 1838 Liszt wrote the first version of this set of etudes, which was extremely difficult.

In 1851 Liszt reworked the Paganini etudes, removed several almost impossible passages, and sent the final version to print.

The La campanella played in concerts today is the 1851 version.

## The theme in G♯ minor

La campanella is in G♯ minor, and its theme is light and bright, with a hint of mystery.

This G♯ minor theme returns again and again, each time in a more showy costume.

The variations become more and more splendid, and the difficulty rises too.

## La campanella in brief

The third of the Paganini etudes, La campanella has a theme taken from the little-bell figure in the rondo finale of Paganini's Second Violin Concerto in B minor. Liszt heard Paganini play in Paris in 1832 and was deeply moved. He wrote an extremely difficult first version in 1838, and in 1851 published the simplified final version, dedicated to Clara Schumann.

The piece is in G♯ minor and grows more and more splendid like a set of variations. The right hand repeatedly strikes a very high D♯ in the high register like a bell, which should be clear but not too loud. The right-hand leaps between melody and bell often exceed two octaves; to practise them, find the landing place first, move the hand quickly through the air and land lightly. Later there are trills and repeated notes with finger substitution, and a brilliant ending. Let the melody sing clearly. The original suits advanced players, and there are simplified versions too.

Teacher Aum can demonstrate how to practise the right-hand leaps.

## Dedicated to Clara Schumann

The 1851 version of the Grandes études de Paganini was dedicated to the German pianist Clara Schumann.

Clara was a very famous pianist at the time and the wife of the composer Robert Schumann.

This shows how much Liszt respected her playing.

## Liszt and Paganini

In Paris in 1832, Liszt, still in his early twenties, sat in the audience listening to Paganini play the violin and was completely stunned.

From then on, he wanted the piano to be able to do the incredible things the violin could do.

Later, he arranged several of Paganini's pieces as piano etudes.

## More than technique

Although La campanella is an etude and technically very difficult, it is also a beautiful piece of music.

When you play it, let the melody of the theme sing clearly, and do not let it be drowned by technique.

**In short**

The contrast between the bell and the melody is the most charming thing about this piece.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which number in which set of etudes is La campanella?**
A: The third of the Grandes études de Paganini.

**Q: In what year was the final version published?**
A: 1851.

**Q: Where does the theme come from?**
A: The last movement of Paganini's Second Violin Concerto.

**Q: Who was this set of etudes dedicated to?**
A: Clara Schumann.

**Q: What key is the piece in?**
A: G♯ minor.

li-yinghai-flutes-and-drums-at-sunset.body:
"Flutes and Drums at Sunset" was originally a famous Chinese instrumental piece, often played on instruments such as the pipa, describing the sound of drums and flutes on a river at dusk and the scenery gradually growing quiet. In the second half of the twentieth century, the composer Li Yinghai arranged it as a piano piece, so that these imaginable sounds could unfold on a single piano: sometimes like drumbeats, sometimes like a long breath through a pipe, and sometimes like ripples that the wind makes on water. When you learn it, you do not need to treat it like a Western etude and pursue only even speed. First listen to the original piece or a fairly complete recording of the arrangement, grasp the rise and fall of the sections and the spaces left open, and then begin to play. When listening, you can also notice at first only how it moves from sparser sounds to denser ones and then slowly draws back. If the whole piece is played with the same very full touch, the layers of dusk will be wiped flat. An arrangement is not meant to imitate every instrument of the original exactly, but to let the piano use its own layers to come close to that atmosphere. When practising, you can first listen to the whole piece in three blocks, "sparse, dense, sparse again", and then decide which block to work on today, without tackling the densest passage straight away. If every section is played with the same very full touch, go back to the sparser places and practise specifically leaving the spaces open. The layers of dusk depend on contrast, not on filling everything all the time.

## Space is content too

In a dusk scene, not every moment is filled with sound.

**Quick tip**

Where the score is sparser, do not rush to add many extra notes or press the pedal all the way down to "fill it in".

Leave the spaces open, and the density that follows will seem meaningful.

## How to start practising this arrangement

This is a suitable arrangement for people who can already control different kinds of touch and can organise practice by sections.

First get the map of the whole piece clear by listening, then start with the sparser, slower sections, and do not tackle the densest section first.

Let the tempo follow the breathing of each section, not one uniform fast or slow speed.

## Drumbeats and long phrases

Short, springy notes can come close to a drum, while longer, more connected phrases come closer to the breath of a wind instrument.

Practise the two kinds of touch separately beforehand, and when you put them together there will be contrast.

If the short notes are hammered too dead, the drum becomes a percussion instrument, and if the long phrases are cut into pieces, the breath of the pipe is lost.

## What to remember about this piano arrangement

This is a piano arrangement by Li Yinghai based on a famous instrumental piece, and it is often seen in repertoire from the second half of the twentieth century.

When you play, imagine the drums, the wind instrument and the open spaces section by section, and do not let the pedal blur the layers.

When listening, first grasp the shape of going from sparse to dense and then drawing back, and do not require the piano to imitate every timbre of every instrument.

**A different angle**
- Originally a famous Chinese instrumental piece, often played on instruments such as the pipa
- Li Yinghai wrote the piano arrangement in the second half of the twentieth century
- The sections have drumbeats, long phrases like a wind instrument, and sparser open spaces
- When practising, first grasp the rise and fall and the breathing, and only then pursue density and speed

![A person with headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing the city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdk7r52-tosvf.webp)

## Ask Teacher Aum in lessons to listen for whether the layers are flattened

In your lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the touch for the drumbeats and for the long phrases is separate, and whether the sparse places have been filled in.

If the sustain drags too long in some section, you can also ask your teacher to work through the sections with you and bring your foot back up.

From this arrangement of a river at dusk, you can practise letting the piano use different kinds of touch to come close to different kinds of breath.

## The pedal and the resonance

The piano's resonance can help to come close to water and wind, but a pedal held too long will blur the drumbeats and long phrases together.

Decide how to pedal section by section: in sparse sections you can use a little more to connect, and in dense sections you need to change more often.

First play it once with less pedal and listen to whether the structure is still clear, then add back the resonance you need.

## The relationship between the original and the piano arrangement

The original piece has its own performance tradition and arrangement of sections, and the piano arrangement is a rewriting on top of that tradition, not a simple note-by-note translation.

Listening first to a performance that is not on piano will help you judge which places in the arrangement are closer to drumbeats and which are closer to wind instruments.

Even if you only study the piano score, you should know that what you are playing is an arrangement with a history.

## How the sections rise and fall

A common shape goes from sparse to dense and then gradually draws back, like a river in the evening that is lively first and quiet afterwards.

When you practise, move forward section by section, giving each section one main sound to imagine, and do not use the same touch from beginning to end.

Aim for clarity in the dense places, and dare to leave spaces in the sparse places.

## FAQ

**Q: What kind of playing is the original piece often heard in?**
A: It is often played on Chinese instruments such as the pipa.

**Q: Who made the piano arrangement?**
A: Li Yinghai.

**Q: Is the aim of the arrangement to imitate every instrument exactly?**
A: No. It is to use the piano's own layers to come close to the atmosphere and the rise and fall of the sections of the original.

**Q: Why should the sparse sections not be filled in?**
A: Space is part of the dusk scene, and if everything is filled in, the density that follows loses its contrast.

**Q: How should the pedal be used section by section?**
A: In sparse places you can use a little more to help connection, and in dense places you need to change more often so that the drumbeats and long phrases do not blur together.

left-hand-melody-bring-out.body:
In most pieces the melody is mostly in the right hand, but sometimes the composer hands the melody to the left hand and has the right hand play the accompaniment. To make the left-hand melody clearly heard, you need to adjust the volume balance between the two hands: play the left-hand melody full and connected, and the right-hand accompaniment a little lighter. The sound in the low register is rather thick and heavy, so with a left-hand melody you also need to take care not to play it too heavily or dully. You can use the weight of the arm to bring out a rounded sound, and pay attention to the rise and fall of the phrase.

## The Rise and Fall of the Phrase

A left-hand melody, like a right-hand melody, needs the rise and fall of phrasing, with crescendo, diminuendo and breathing.

You can mark the high point of each phrase on the score, and as you play let the sound gradually grow toward this high point, then fall back naturally.

That way the left-hand melody is not just a string of flat low notes, but an expressive singing voice.

## Training Expression in the Left Hand

From time to time you can do melody exercises for the left hand alone, for example playing the melody of a familiar song with the left hand.

This kind of practice makes the left hand more expressive, so that it can do more than play accompaniment.

When the left hand can sing too, your playing will be richer and better balanced.

## The Right Hand Steps Back

Once the left-hand melody is secure, when you add the right-hand accompaniment, make the right hand clearly lighter.

You can first play the right hand with very little force, so light that you almost only make the keys sound, and listen to whether the left-hand melody is still clear.

Slowly find a suitable balance, so that the accompaniment supports the melody without covering it.

## Left-Hand Fingering

The fingering for a left-hand melody has to consider the need for connection, for example using suitable finger changes and finger crossings.

The span in the low register can be fairly wide, so the hand must move flexibly, but not stiffly.

You can decide the fingering for the left-hand melody together with your teacher, write it on the score, and keep using it.

## Recognising the Left-Hand Melody

When reading the score, if you find the left-hand notes form a rising and falling line while the right hand has repeated chords or broken chords, the melody is probably in the left hand.

Sometimes the score uses words such as "marcato", "espressivo" or "canto" to signal a melody that needs to stand out.

You can first play the left hand alone once and listen to whether it sounds like a song.

![A person with a long braid plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with drones in the air](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0hovs-u0lsn.webp)

## The Tone of the Low Register

The strings in the low register are longer and thicker, and the sound is naturally thick and heavy. If you play with too much force, it easily becomes dull or muddy.

When you play a left-hand melody, let the weight of the arm fall naturally, rather than striking hard with the fingers.

Imagine the sound as rounded and warm, like a low, soft voice singing.

## Handing Over Between the Hands

Sometimes the melody alternates between the two hands, now in the right hand, now in the left.

At these moments take special care over the handover, so that the melody passes naturally from one hand to the other and sounds like one continuous line.

You can mark the melody on the score with a coloured pencil to see clearly where it changes hands.

## Record and Listen

When you play, it is hard to judge the balance between your hands accurately, so you can record yourself and listen back.

If you cannot hear the left-hand melody clearly, either the right hand is too loud or the left hand is not full enough.

After adjusting according to the recording, record again and compare to see whether it has improved.

- Sometimes the melody is given to the left hand
- A left-hand melody should be full and connected
- The right-hand accompaniment should be lighter
- Take care in the low register not to play too dully

## Pedal Under a Bass Melody

When the left-hand melody is in the low register, be especially careful with the sustain pedal, because low notes ring for a long time and easily blur together.

You can change the pedal according to the harmonic changes in the melody, clearing the sound each time the chord changes.

If the sound is too muddy, try a shallower pedal, or change the pedal more often.

## Practise the Left-Hand Melody Alone First

The left hand does not play melodies as often as the right hand does, so it needs special practice to learn to "sing".

You can first play the left hand alone, slowly, making every note connected and working out where each phrase begins and ends.

You can also sing as you play, which helps the left hand find the rise and fall of the melody.

## Learning from Familiar Pieces

Many Romantic piano works have passages with a left-hand melody, such as the middle sections of some nocturnes and lyrical short pieces.

Find a few fine recordings to listen to, and see how pianists make the left-hand melody sing.

This kind of listening experience can help you better understand and shape your own pieces.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How do I know the melody is in the left hand?**
A: The left hand forms a rising and falling line, while the right hand has a repeating accompaniment.

**Q: How do I bring out the left-hand melody?**
A: Play the left hand full and connected, and the right hand clearly lighter.

**Q: Why does the low register easily sound dull?**
A: The strings are long and thick, and the sound is naturally heavy.

**Q: How should I handle the pedal?**
A: Change the pedal according to the harmonic changes, and use a shallower pedal when necessary.

**Q: What should I do when the melody changes hands?**
A: Take care over the handover, so the melody sounds like one continuous line.

**Q: How do I check the balance?**
A: Record yourself and listen to whether the left-hand melody is clear.

liu-tianhua-liang-xiao-erhu-1928.body:
Liangxiao ("A Beautiful Night") is an erhu piece that Liu Tianhua wrote on the night of Chinese New Year's Eve, 22 January 1928. Its original title was Chuye xiaochang ("A Little Song for New Year's Eve"). The piece is not long, with a warm, flowing melody, and it is often one of the first works an erhu player meets after the beginner stage. It was later arranged for piano and other instruments too, so that this small New Year's Eve piece could be heard by more people. If you play a piano arrangement, you can focus on singing the melody smoothly and keeping the breathing of the phrases clear, rather than trying to imitate every erhu technique. Knowing when the original was written and what it was called helps you understand its quiet, warm character. After you have played it all the way through, you can also go slowly through the melody alone and listen to whether each phrase ending closes cleanly.

## The accompaniment should give way to the melody

If a piano arrangement has a left-hand accompaniment, the accompaniment should be quiet and give the melody only a harmonic base.

**Listen for this**

The bass can be a little clearer, while the middle chords or broken-chord figures are lighter still.

After putting the hands together, first listen to whether the melody is complete, and only then adjust the left hand.

## Liu Tianhua and erhu composition

Liu Tianhua was an important erhu player and composer of the early twentieth century, and he also took part in improving erhu playing and teaching.

He wrote a number of works that later became standard erhu repertoire, and Liangxiao is one of the shorter and warmer ones.

These works often combine the feel of traditional melodies with fairly clear notation.

## How to approach playing Liangxiao

As a short piece with a strong singing quality, it can be played in an arrangement by intermediate learners.

First play the melody alone until it is smooth, then add the left hand. Let the tempo be one at which you can finish the phrase, and do not rush.

You might even play the same phrase twice in a row and see which time the ending sounds more natural.

## Liangxiao in brief

Liangxiao is an erhu piece Liu Tianhua wrote on New Year's Eve, 22 January 1928. Its original title was Chuye xiaochang. The melody is warm and the piece is not long, and piano arrangements have often been made of it.

On the piano you rely on touch, phrasing and a quiet accompaniment to keep the sense of continuous breath, and you keep the ornaments light.

Teacher Aum can listen to whether your phrases sound natural.

## Phrasing and breath

You can divide the melody in the score according to the breath, so that each phrase has a gentle beginning and a gentle close.

Do not hurry through the end of a phrase. You can make it a little softer before starting the next one.

Sing the melody slowly once, then go back to the piano and see where the breath points match the phrasing in the score.

## The measure of ornaments and slides

The erhu original often has slides and ornaments, and when it is arranged for piano these details are written as short ornaments or grace notes.

Play them lightly and clearly. They should not push out the main note, and they should not become a blur of notes.

If something is not written in the score, there is no need to add too many glissando effects yourself.

## When this erhu piece moves to the piano

The erhu makes a sustained sound with the bow, and it is easy to join one note to the next. The sound of the piano fades quickly.

So in a piano arrangement you need to rely even more on touch, the arrangement of phrases and a little pedal to keep that sense of continuity.

Do not play every note equally short and equally bright, or the sung breath of the original is lost.

## A small piece written on New Year's Eve

22 January 1928 was Chinese New Year's Eve, and on that night Liu Tianhua wrote this short erhu piece.

Its original title was Chuye xiaochang, and it later spread widely under the name Liangxiao.

"Liangxiao" means a good evening, which suits the family gatherings of New Year's Eve and the short, warm character of the piece.

- Liu Tianhua wrote it on New Year's Eve, 22 January 1928
- Originally titled Chuye xiaochang, later called Liangxiao
- The original is for erhu, with later arrangements for piano and others
- The melody is warm and flowing, and the piece is not long

## Why the melody is easy to get close to

The range of Liangxiao is not very wide, the phrases are fairly short and the progress is smooth, so it is easy to follow after listening once or twice.

It has no long dramatic contrasts, and is more like a little tune that can be sung again and again.

Precisely because the material is simple, a spoiled phrase or notes played too hard will stand out clearly.

## Asking Teacher Aum to listen to your phrasing in lessons

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the melody in your arrangement joins up naturally and whether there are too many ornaments.

Where the breath points could be a little clearer, you can also ask your teacher to mark them in the score with you.

From an erhu piece written on New Year's Eve, practise playing a simple melody warmly and completely.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In what year was Liangxiao written?**
A: On 22 January 1928, which was New Year's Eve that year.

**Q: What was it originally called?**
A: Chuye xiaochang.

**Q: What instrument was the original written for?**
A: The erhu. Arrangements for piano and other instruments came later.

**Q: What matters most when playing an arrangement on the piano?**
A: Sing the melody smoothly and let the accompaniment give way to the main phrase.

**Q: How should the ornaments be played?**
A: Lightly and clearly, without pushing out the main note, and without adding too many effects yourself.

local-instrument-store-collab.body:
When a music studio works with a local music store (an instrument retailer), students find it easier to try, rent or maintain an instrument, and the store gets to know people who are really learning. If the boundaries of the partnership are unclear, though, it can easily turn into competing for customers or exaggerated promises. This article covers several relatively safe approaches: shared goals, a clear division of work and restrained promotion.

## Align on shared goals first

Suitable shared goals include: letting beginners rent for a short time before buying an instrument, helping parents learn the basics of maintenance, and jointly holding a small trial-playing afternoon. Unsuitable goals include: quoting each other's "insider prices" that cannot be honoured, or implying that the other side's service has problems. A partnership starts with a short one-page memo: who is responsible for what, when an activity ends, and how you introduce each other.

- State clearly what each side does not promise
- Agree on the key words of the shared public wording
- Agree on a cap on the number of people at an event
- Agree on how photos and name lists may be used

## How to design joint events more safely

You can hold an open afternoon of "trial playing and posture advice": the store provides the venue and instruments, and the studio provides short coaching. The coaching covers only general methods, does not disparage any brand, and does not replace a professional inspection when advising on a purchase. Afterwards each side follows up its own enquiries, and does not exchange contact details without authorisation.

![An illustration of a glowing transparent piano being played on a neon rainy night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw5frmrc-30uwg.webp)

## Wording for referring people to each other

The studio can say: "If you would like to know about the rental process, you can ask our colleagues at the partner store." The store can say: "If you need systematic lessons, you can look into the trial lesson at the partner studio." The wording stays at making introductions and does not quote prices for the other side. When it comes to piano teaching, stress the learning path; when it comes to buying, stress trying the instrument and matching the budget.

**Benefits and transparency**
If there is a referral fee, it should be written down internally, necessary information should not be hidden from the public, and the general local requirements on advertising and consumer protection should be followed. When in doubt, it is better not to set up a cash commission and instead offer each other trial places.

## Risk checklist

Avoid putting up posters at the other side's counter that exaggerate progress; avoid pushing students who are not ready straight into large purchases; avoid naming and comparing other shops during the partnership. When a complaint arises, first work out where responsibility lies, then reply together, without blaming each other.

## Reviewing the partnership

Within a week after an event, each side writes three sentences: which questions were asked again and again, which steps had too long a wait, and what to cut next time. A review matters more than expanding in scale.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do we have to sign a long contract?**
A: You can try a single event first, then decide whether to renew.

**Q: Can we recruit students in the other side's shop?**
A: Only with their consent, and following the shop's rules, so that customers' quiet is not disturbed.

**Q: What if students are being sold to?**
A: Agree beforehand on "no hard sell", and give students room to say no.

**Q: Is it worth it for a small studio to work together too?**
A: Yes. A small, clear partnership is often more useful than an empty strategic signing.

## A whitelist for joint promotional materials

Make a whitelist beforehand: logos that may be used, a one-sentence introduction that may be written, and promises that may not be made. Each side's materials are seen by the other before they go out. A whitelist reduces misunderstandings of the "I thought you could write it like that" kind. When it comes to the results of learning the piano, write only about methods and services, and make no promise of guaranteed results.

If you jointly film a short video, keep the shots mostly on hands and keys, with few identifiable faces, and confirm authorisation again before publishing. The warmth of a local partnership comes from protecting each other's brands, not from borrowing each other's exaggerations.

Piano teaching studios and music stores have different areas of expertise: one cares about the learning path, the other about choosing and maintaining instruments. Respect the difference, and the partnership will last. For new students who want to play music, a joint event should let them feel the enjoyment first, and only then talk about the next step.

## Physical boundaries between the trial area and the teaching area

During a joint event, try to keep a visible separation between the trial-playing area and the short-coaching area, even if it is only floor markings and signs. When they are mixed together, people trying instruments will think the coaching is a sales pitch, and people receiving coaching will be interrupted by the noise of trial playing. With clear boundaries, both sides look more professional.

Keep the wording on the signs neutral: "Please queue for trial playing", "Please wait here for short coaching". Do not write sentences that urge people to buy or to sign up. If the space is small, you can use time slots: forty minutes of trial playing and advice, then forty minutes of short coaching, with ten minutes in between to clear the area.

After the event, check whether any materials were left in the other side's area, to avoid mixing the brands. Details decide whether you will be invited to work together again.

## A gentle way to end a partnership

If the partnership is not a good fit, submit a written note in advance: until which day the partnership runs, how materials will be taken down, and how already booked joint places will be handled properly. A gentle ending protects both sides' students and customers better than suddenly disappearing. After ending, you can still make friendly referrals, just without holding joint events.

## Reconciling partnership places

The day after an event, each side reports the number of people who actually came, and if the difference is more than two, check by phone, to avoid disputes afterwards.

- Number who attended
- Number who completed a trial
- Materials collected back
- Whether the follow-up list has been anonymised

If photos from a joint event are to be reused for recruitment, the scope of authorisation must be confirmed a second time.

leggiero-con-brio-maestoso-character-wor.body:
Besides terms for tempo and dynamics, a score also has some Italian terms that describe the character of the music. Leggiero means light and nimble, con brio means with vigour and spirit, and maestoso means majestic and grand. These terms tell the player what feeling the music should have. They often appear together with tempo terms, for example Allegro con brio, which means a lively, spirited Allegro.

## Changes of Character Within One Piece

A piece often has more than one character: it may begin marked majestic, turn light in the middle, and return to a spirited state at the end.

The player needs to prepare ahead at these points of change, so that touch and sound change along with them.

You can mark on the score where each character appears, and during practice pay special attention to the bars at the borders.

## Using Imagination to Help Understanding

To understand character terms, you can use your imagination.

For example, for leggiero you can imagine a feather drifting through the air, for con brio an energetic person running, and for maestoso a tall building.

These pictures can help us find the right sound.

## Summary of Character Terms

Leggiero is light, con brio is spirited, and maestoso is majestic. These terms describe the character of the music.

They often appear together with tempo terms, such as Allegro con brio, and when you play you express them through touch, rhythm and sound.

Looking terms up in a dictionary, writing their meanings on the score, using your imagination and listening to recordings can all help us understand these terms better.

## Maestoso: Majestic

Maestoso means majestic and grand.

When you see this term, the music is usually not too fast, and the sound should be broad and full.

It often appears at the opening of a piece or at an important section, creating a solemn atmosphere.

## How to Play with Spirit

When you play a con brio passage, the rhythm should be clear and strong, with firm accents.

The sound can be fairly full, but it must stay springy and not become clumsy.

The music should have a driving momentum forward, as if it were full of energy.

## Other Common Character Terms

Besides these three, there are many other common character terms, for example dolce is sweet and soft, cantabile is in a singing style, and grazioso is gracefully.

Agitato is agitated, tranquillo is calm, and scherzando is playfully.

All these terms tell us how the music should feel.

![A person in futuristic clothes plays a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5lsx2-2e8y9.webp)

## How to Play Majestically

When you play a maestoso passage, the tempo should be steady and not hurried.

The chords in a majestic passage should be solid and full, letting the weight of the whole arm fall naturally into the keys.

Give every important note enough time, so that the music has an unhurried, grand feeling.

## Together with Tempo Terms

Character terms often appear together with tempo terms, forming a complete instruction.

For example, Allegro con brio is a spirited Allegro, Allegro maestoso is a majestic Allegro, and Andante leggiero is a light Andante.

When you read a score, understand the meaning of both words at the same time.

- Leggiero: light
- Con brio: with vigour and spirit
- Maestoso: majestic, grand
- Often appear together with tempo terms

## Leggiero: Light

Leggiero is an Italian word meaning light and airy.

When you see this term, the sound should be nimble and clean, and not too heavy.

It is often found in fast passagework, such as a run of light scales or arpeggios.

## What Character Terms Do

Tempo terms tell us fast or slow, dynamic terms tell us loud or soft, and character terms tell us how the music should feel.

The same Allegro can be light, or strong, or cheerful.

Character terms help the player grasp the atmosphere the composer wanted.

## How to Play Lightly

When you play a leggiero passage, the fingers should be agile and the touch somewhat shallow, and not every note needs to be pressed to the bottom.

The wrist and arm should be relaxed, without pressing down hard.

The pedal is usually used very little or not at all, so that every note is clear.

## Look Up Terms You Don't Know

When you meet an unfamiliar Italian character word, look it up in a small dictionary of musical terms, or ask about it in your lesson.

You can write the meaning of the term in pencil on the score to remind yourself during practice.

As you build up gradually, the common terms will become more and more familiar.

## Character Terms and Physical Sensation

Different characters also feel different in the body as you play.

In a light passage, the body and arms are fairly relaxed, as if just lightly touching the keys; in a majestic passage, the posture is steadier and the arm movements larger.

A spirited passage needs the fingers and wrist to stay springy, ready for the next strong accent.

## Comparing How Several Pianists Play Maestoso and Leggiero

You can find a few recordings of pieces marked with these terms and listen to how different players express them.

Compare their tempo, dynamics and touch, and see where you feel the meaning of the term.

This kind of listening helps us understand character terms more concretely.

## Con Brio: With Spirit

Con brio means with vigour, spirit and fire.

It is often used together with Allegro, as in Allegro con brio.

**Take it slower**

Some of Beethoven's works use this marking, for example the first movement of his Fifth Symphony.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does leggiero mean?**
A: Light, airy.

**Q: What does con brio mean?**
A: With vigour and spirit.

**Q: What does maestoso mean?**
A: Majestic, grand.

**Q: What is Allegro con brio?**
A: A lively, spirited Allegro.

**Q: How do I play leggiero?**
A: Shallow touch, relaxed hand, little pedal.

liszt-liebestraum-no3-a-flat-major.body:
Liszt's Liebesträume ("Dreams of Love") are three piano pieces published in 1850, originally adapted from three songs he had written himself. The third, in A♭ major, is the best known. The words of the original song come from a poem by the German poet Freiligrath. When you play this piece, the melody is often placed in the middle voice, shared by the two hands in turn, with flowing broken chords around it. There are also two cadenzas in the middle of the piece, which need to be light and clear.

## Flowing broken chords

Around the melody is a stream of flowing broken chords, rising and falling like waves.

**Before you start**

These accompaniment notes should be even and gentle. Do not play every note with the same weight.

You can first play each group of broken chords as a block chord, see clearly where your hand sits, and then play it broken.

## Changing the pedal in Liebesträume

This piece needs the sustain pedal, so that the sound of the broken chords blends into one.

You usually change the pedal where the harmony changes, and the change should be clean, so that the chords before and after do not blur together.

If the sound is muddy, check whether you changed the pedal late, or pressed it down too deeply.

## Sing the melody first

Because this piece was originally a song, when you practise you can first sing the melody, or hum it.

As you sing, feel where you need to breathe and where the high point of each phrase is.

After singing, go back to the keys, and the line in the middle voice will find it easier to breathe.

## The words of the third piece

The words of the original third song come from a poem by the German poet Ferdinand Freiligrath.

The gist of the poem is to urge people to cherish those close to them, and to love well while they still can.

Although the piano version has no words, this tender, deeply felt mood runs through the whole piece.

## Handing the melody between the hands

Because the melody is played by the two hands in turn, the places where it passes from one hand to the other easily sound broken or uneven in volume.

You can take out the melody on its own and play it with both hands as divided in the score, to hear whether it is smooth.

Once you are familiar with the handovers, add the accompaniment notes back in.

## From song to piano piece

Liebesträume were first three songs written by Liszt, which he later arranged as piano solos.

The piano version was published in 1850, and the three pieces each have a different character, of which the third is the best known.

Knowing that it was originally a song helps us give more attention to the singing quality of the melody when we play.

## Handling the climax

In the middle of the piece the music gradually becomes more agitated, the melody rises and the dynamics grow, forming a climax.

The climax needs strength, but the sound should still be round, not harsh.

You can bring out the sound with the weight of your arm, rather than striking with force from the fingers.

## What it takes to play Liebesträume

Liebesträume No. 3 asks for a wide hand span, accurate pedal changes and clear separation of voices, and you will find it more comfortable after a few years of study.

If the original seems too difficult, you can first find a simplified version to get to know the melody and structure.

There is a good deal of difference between a simplified version and the original, so you can take both scores to a lesson to compare them.

## Liebesträume in brief

Liszt's Liebesträume are three piano pieces adapted from songs, published in 1850, and the third is in A♭ major.

When playing, let the melody in the middle voice sing, make the handovers between the hands smooth, and keep the broken-chord accompaniment gentle and even.

Change the pedal cleanly with the harmony, and play the two cadenzas lightly and clearly.

![A close-up of the keys and gold-patterned lid of a grand piano in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4pkug-z85wr.webp)

## The melody hidden in the middle register

One characteristic of this piece is that the melody is often not at the top, but in the middle register.

The thumbs of the two hands often take turns playing the melody, with broken-chord accompaniment notes around them.

As you play, make the melody notes played by the thumbs fuller and the other accompaniment notes softer, like a gentle layer of background.

## The key signature of A♭ major

The third piece is in A♭ major, and the key signature has four flats: B♭, E♭, A♭ and D♭.

The piece also moves to other keys in the middle, with quite a few accidentals, so read the score carefully.

Before you start practising Liebesträume, it is worth warming up your hands with an A♭ major scale, so that the four flats settle into your fingers first.

**Think again**
- Three piano pieces, published in 1850
- Adapted from Liszt's own songs
- The third is in A♭ major
- The melody is often in the middle voice, shared by the two hands

## Back to a quiet ending

After the climax, the music gradually calms down and finally returns to the gentle mood of the opening.

At the ending, it should get softer and softer, and the tempo can also slow down a little.

You can let the last few chords fade away slowly, leaving the audience something to savour.

## The two cadenzas

There are two cadenzas in the middle of the piece, fast and light groups of notes, like decorations between the melodies.

The cadenzas do not need to follow the beat strictly. They can have some freedom, but they must be clear and fluent.

When practising, you can first divide a cadenza into a few small groups, practise each group slowly until it is secure, then join them, and finally speed up.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: How many Liebesträume are there?**
A: Three, published in 1850.

**Q: What were they originally?**
A: Songs written by Liszt himself.

**Q: What key is the third in?**
A: A♭ major, with four flats.

**Q: Which voice has the melody?**
A: Often the middle voice, shared by the two hands.

**Q: How should the cadenzas be played?**
A: With some freedom, but light and clear.
