lecuona-malaguena-andalucia-suite.body:
Malagueña is one of the piano pieces from Cuban composer Ernesto Lecuona's suite that is most often played on its own, and it is usually introduced as part of his Andalucía suite. It was written in the late 1920s to the 1930s, and it brings the colour of southern Spanish dance to the piano: a repeating bass, a melody with a Phrygian-mode flavour, and plenty of decisive rhythms and ornaments. It later appeared in song and orchestra arrangements too, but the original piano version is still complete in its own right. When learning this piece, the key is usually to keep the firm rhythm steady and let the colourful melody be heard clearly over the repeating bass. It also helps to listen to it once first and note the order of the main sections before you start playing.

## What "Malagueña" Means

Malagueña was originally a type of song or dance associated with the area around Málaga in Spain.

Lecuona was not making a strict folk record. He used the piano to write down his own imagining of that colour.

The title is only the doorway. What you really need to grasp is the rhythm on the page, the repeating bass and the melody with its minor-second flavour.

## The Composer and the Suite

Ernesto Lecuona was a Cuban composer and pianist who wrote concert piano pieces as well as songs and stage music.

Malagueña belongs to his set of piano works named after Spanish places and dances, and it is often pulled out and played separately.

Knowing that the composer was Cuban helps explain why the piece carries both the vitality of Caribbean music and the modal colour of southern Spain.

## Level and How to Listen

It suits intermediate to upper-intermediate learners who can already keep the rhythm steady and control fairly fast ornaments.

Before you learn it, listen to the original piano version first, then to a song or orchestra arrangement, and compare what was added later.

Let the tempo be whatever lets you settle into the rhythm. There is no need to chase a very fiery recording right away.

**Common misunderstandings**
- A piano piece by the Cuban composer Lecuona
- Often introduced as part of the Andalucía suite
- Written in the late 1920s to the 1930s
- Has Phrygian colour and a firm dance rhythm

## Ornaments and Flourishes in Proportion

In the middle section or near the climax, there are often fairly showy ornaments and fast figures.

They should grow out of the dance rhythm, and must not carry the beat away.

Slow down first to see the notes clearly, then speed up gently to the original pulse.

## The Repeating Bass and the Firm Rhythm

The left hand, or bass voice, often repeats a short figure, which gives the whole piece a steady step.

Play this figure with spring, but there is no need to pound every beat.

Practise the bass steadily on its own first, then add the melody on top, and the rhythm will not fall apart.

## Summary of Malagueña

Lecuona's Malagueña was written in the late 1920s to the 1930s and is often introduced as part of the Andalucía suite. It has Phrygian colour and a firm dance rhythm, and there are later song and orchestra arrangements as well.

In practice, keep the repeating bass steady, play the semitone relationships clearly, use the pedal sparingly and cleanly, and memorise the structure section by section.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your rhythm and colour.

## Memorising the Structure Section by Section

This piece usually consists of several sections that are similar in character yet different, and some material comes back.

Marking where each section begins on the score is clearer than memorising the piece as one non-stop stream.

The repeating bass figure can also serve as a signpost for telling the sections apart.

## Ask Teacher Aum in Your Lesson to Listen to the Dance Rhythm

In your lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the repeating bass is steady and whether the semitones of the Phrygian colour are played clearly.

You can also ask your teacher to point out where the ornaments might carry the beat away and where you should hold back.

With a Spanish-style piano piece by a Cuban composer, you practise making rhythm and colour speak clearly together.

![An illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, conveying the strength of a piece's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdl4po3-n1o0o.webp)

## Don't Let the Pedal Blur the Rhythm

Once a deep pedal goes down, the sharp edges of a decisive rhythm disappear.

Use little pedal in the repeating-bass passages, and use a shallow pedal to help longer melodic phrases stay connected.

Change the pedal whenever the harmony changes, especially in places with chromatic colour.

## A Phrygian Kind of Colour

Many passages give a feeling of the Phrygian mode: the minor second above the tonic gives the melody a sharp, bright colour.

When you play, bring out these semitone relationships clearly and do not gloss over them.

**A detail to notice**

You can also play just the melody first and listen to how the lowered second degree colours the phrase.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who composed Malagueña?**
A: The Cuban composer Ernesto Lecuona.

**Q: Roughly when was it written?**
A: In the late 1920s to the 1930s.

**Q: What kind of modal colour does the piece often have?**
A: A Phrygian flavour, especially the minor second above the tonic.

**Q: What is typically written for the left hand or bass?**
A: A short, springy figure that repeats and gives the whole piece a steady step.

**Q: Why shouldn't the pedal be pressed too deep?**
A: Because once the decisive rhythm and chromatic colour are blurred, both the sharp edges and the colour are lost.

lighting-for-reading-music.body:
Poor lighting or glare when you read music makes your eyes tire quickly, and can even affect how accurately you read the score. A sensible approach is to use soft natural light in the daytime and avoid direct sunlight on the page. In the evening, use one lamp shining on the music stand from above and to the side, and also turn on the room's general lighting, so that the difference in brightness between the page and its surroundings is not too great.

## Lighting for Children's Practice

Children's eyesight is still developing, so lighting during practice needs even more attention. Make sure the page is bright enough, so that your child does not need to lean in close to see clearly.

**Listen**

If you notice your child squinting or putting their head very close while practising, you can check whether the light is sufficient and whether the print on the music is too small.

If necessary, you can photocopy the music enlarged so that your child can see it more easily.

## Choosing a Suitable Colour of Light

The colour of the light also affects how you feel. Light that is too yellow can make the page look blurry, and cold white light can feel harsh when you look at it for a long time.

Many people find neutral white light more comfortable, clear for reading music without being too stimulating.

If your lamp lets you adjust the colour temperature, you can try several settings and find the one that feels most comfortable to you.

## Let Your Eyes Rest Regularly

Even with suitable light, reading music for a long time tires the eyes. During practice you can look up at something in the distance, or close your eyes for a few seconds.

You can take these little breaks between sections, without disturbing the flow of your practice.

If your eyes often feel dry or you cannot see clearly, besides adjusting the lighting you can also consider having an eye test.

## Watch Out for Glare

Glossy paper, clear plastic folders and tablet screens all reflect light easily.

Adjusting the angle of the lamp or the tilt of the music usually avoids the glare.

If you keep your music in a plastic folder, you can choose a matte material. If you use a tablet, you can adjust the screen brightness or use an anti-glare screen protector.

**Try this**
- In the daytime, avoid direct sunlight falling on the page
- In the evening, light the music stand with a lamp from above and to the side
- Turn on the general lighting in the room too
- Watch out for glare from glossy paper or plastic folders

## Arranging Your Evening Light

After dark, there needs to be enough light above the music stand. You can use a small lamp clipped onto the stand, or a table lamp placed beside the piano.

The light should shine down from above and to the side, covering the whole page, without leaving shadows of your hand or head on the music.

The lamp should be bright enough, but need not be too strong. You can choose a lamp with adjustable brightness and adjust it to suit the room.

If the room has both a ceiling light and a table lamp, you can try switching each on separately and see which combination makes the notes on the page clearest, so that your eyes do not feel strained after looking for a long time.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with an elevated light-rail line](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9x923j-t1ps3.webp)

## Using Natural Light in the Daytime

If the room has plenty of light in the daytime, you can practise with natural light. A window is best on your side, rather than directly in front of or behind you.

A window directly in front makes you look straight into the bright light, so your eyes have to switch between light and dark when reading music. Light from directly behind makes your own shadow fall on the page.

When the sun is strong, you can draw a thin curtain to soften the light.

## Light the Whole Room Too

Some people turn on only a music stand lamp in the evening, with darkness all around. Then the page is very bright and the surroundings very dark, and when your eyes switch between the music and the keyboard they have to keep adjusting to different levels of brightness.

If you turn on the main light so that the whole space has basic lighting, with the music stand lamp as a supplement, your eyes will be much more comfortable.

The keyboard also needs to be lit, especially for beginners who often look down at the keys.

## How Light Affects Reading Music

The notes on a score are dense and the lines are fine, so you need clear light to read them accurately. When the light is poor, people unconsciously lean toward the music, tilt their bodies forward, and their shoulders and neck become tense.

If the light is too strong or has glare, bright, harsh spots appear on the page, and your eyes have to keep adjusting and soon feel tired.

Suitable light keeps your eyes relaxed, and lets your attention stay on the music for longer.

## FAQ

**Q: Which is better, a music stand lamp or a table lamp?**
A: Either is fine. The key is that it lights the whole page without causing shadows or glare.

**Q: Can I just use my phone's torch for light?**
A: Temporarily, yes, but the light is concentrated and unstable. For long-term practice, a proper lamp is recommended.

**Q: Will the light affect the piano?**
A: Ordinary indoor lighting has little effect, but avoid keeping lamps that give off heat close to the piano for a long time.

**Q: What colour of light should I use when practising in the evening?**
A: Neutral white light is the most common, and you can also choose a slightly warmer light according to personal preference.

**Q: Does digital sheet music need extra lighting?**
A: A tablet gives off its own light, but the room still needs basic lighting, so that the brightness of the screen and the surroundings are not too different.

**Q: What if my child keeps saying they cannot see the music clearly?**
A: First check the lighting and the print size of the music. If there is still a problem, you can take your child for an eye test.

lunch-break-piano-listening-habit.body:
Ten minutes of piano at lunch means that in the middle of the working day, you put aside your phone messages, put on headphones and listen attentively to a piece of piano music. It is not meant to solve any problem. It is simply a stretch of uninterrupted time in which you put your attention on sound. The method is simple: choose a few piano pieces of suitable length and steady pace in advance, find a relatively quiet corner, listen in the order "melody, bass, tone colour", and do it at a fixed time every day. Many people find that this small habit makes the pace of the afternoon feel calmer, and brings back their interest in music.

## Why the Piano

The piano has a very wide range, from deep and low to clear and bright, and a single instrument can play melody and harmony together. Solo piano has no words, so it does not pull your attention towards a text, which makes it well suited to quiet listening in a short time. There is also a great variety of piano styles, including classical miniatures, jazz ballads, film scores and neoclassical works, so there is plenty to choose from.

To be clear, this is about a personal listening habit and how it feels, not any kind of physical or mental intervention. If you feel tired for a long time or are unwell, please consult a doctor or a licensed clinical music professional.

## How to Choose Pieces

**Moderate length**
Choose pieces of three to five minutes; two or three of them fill ten minutes nicely. Very long works are easily interrupted halfway through.

**Steady pace**
At lunch you can begin with pieces that are not too fast and do not swing too much in mood. Once the habit is established, try a wider variety of styles.

**Prepare ahead**
The evening before, put together a small playlist and play it directly the next day, so you do not spend your lunch break searching for music.

**Rotate now and then**
Change part of the selection every week to keep things fresh. You can also build each week around a theme, such as "waltzes this week" or "piano in the movies this week".

## The Three-Layer Listening Method

On the first listen, follow the melody: follow the highest line and try humming it in your head. On the second, listen to the bass: move your attention to the lowest voice and feel how it supports the whole piece. On the third, listen to tone colour: notice when the sound gets softer and when it gets brighter, and how the piano sound slowly fades under the sustain pedal.

If you only have time for one listen, you can also switch your attention by section within a single piece: melody in the first half, bass in the second.

![A small dark upright piano and its long shadow on an empty grey floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw1ljgxv-oravg.webp)

## What to Do in the Office

- Find a relatively quiet spot, such as an empty meeting room, a rest area by the stairwell or your own desk.
- Use headphones and keep the volume at a comfortable level; do not turn it up to cover noise.
- Set your phone to Do Not Disturb and do not check messages for ten minutes.
- You can close your eyes, or look out of the window into the distance.

**With colleagues**
Some teams listen to a piece together at lunch and then each say one sentence about how it felt. This relaxed exchange sometimes helps people unwind more than chatting over coffee.

## Keeping the Habit Going

**A fixed time**
Put your listening at about the same time every day, such as ten minutes after lunch, to build a rhythm.

**Note down how it felt**
Write a sentence or two in your phone's notes, such as "Today I noticed how warm the left-hand bass was". After a while, look back and you will find your ears have become sharper.

**No need for perfection**
If you miss a day because you are too busy, that is fine. Just carry on the next day.

## Ideas for a Week of Sample Playlists

On Monday you could listen to a gentle waltz and feel the sway of three beats; on Tuesday switch to a piano theme from a film score and imagine the pictures; on Wednesday listen to a jazz-style ballad and notice the colour of the chords; on Thursday choose a short Baroque piece and notice how the two voices talk to each other; and on Friday choose freely and listen to the piece you most want to hear again this week. This kind of plan needs no great knowledge of music, yet lets your ears meet different sounds every day.

## From Listening to Playing

Many people, after building a listening habit, want to play a melody they love themselves. This is a very natural process: you already know how the piece sounds, so learning to play it gives you a clearer goal. You can start with the small section you like best, practise a simplified version, and bring what you felt while listening to the keys.

## FAQ

**Q: Does it have to be classical music?**
A: Not necessarily. Any piano music you like with a steady pace will do, including jazz, film scores and neoclassical works.

**Q: My lunch break is short. What if ten minutes is too long?**
A: Five minutes is fine, with just one piece. The point is to listen attentively.

**Q: Can I listen while eating?**
A: Yes, but your attention is easily divided when you eat and listen at once. If you can, setting aside a few minutes after the meal makes a difference.

**Q: Will listening to piano make me more productive?**
A: Everyone feels differently. Here it is treated only as a restful activity of personal taste, with no promise of any effect.

machaut-messe-de-nostre-dame-1360s.body:
Guillaume de Machaut was a fourteenth-century French poet and composer who served as a canon at Reims Cathedral late in life. His Messe de Nostre Dame was completed around the 1360s. It sets the fixed texts of the Mass for four voices and is one of the earliest surviving Masses written in full by a single known composer. Before this, the musical sections of the Mass were often written by different people. Machaut also cared deeply about preserving his work: late in life he had it gathered into beautiful manuscripts, which is a major reason we can hear his music today.

## Written by One Person

Before Machaut, the polyphonic music for the sections of the Mass was often written by different composers and then pieced together for use.

**Worth noticing**

Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame is one of the earliest surviving examples of a known composer writing these sections as a single, complete work.

This makes the whole Mass more unified in style.

## Beautiful Manuscripts

Late in life, Machaut cared a great deal about preserving his work, and he had his poems and music collected into manuscripts.

These manuscripts were beautifully made, and some were even illustrated.

Thanks to these manuscripts, a large part of his output has survived to the present day.

## Reims Cathedral

In his later years Machaut served as a canon at Reims Cathedral in north-eastern France.

Reims Cathedral is a magnificent Gothic church with an important place in French history.

The Messe de Nostre Dame was quite possibly written for this cathedral.

## The Ars Nova

French music of the fourteenth century is known as the "Ars Nova" period, when rhythm was written in a far more complex way than before.

Machaut is one of the most representative composers of this period.

In the Messe de Nostre Dame you can hear many intricate and ingenious rhythms.

## Isorhythm

In some sections of the Messe de Nostre Dame, Machaut used a technique called "isorhythm".

A rhythmic pattern in one voice is repeated again and again while the pitches of the melody change.

This technique works like an invisible skeleton that holds the whole passage up.

## Four Voices

The Messe de Nostre Dame is written for four voices, a fairly rich texture for its time.

The four voices interweave: sometimes they come to rest together on one harmony, and sometimes each flows on its own.

It sounds both ancient and unusually powerful.

## What Is a Mass Setting?

The Mass is an important Catholic rite, and several of its texts are sung every time, with fixed words.

When a composer sets those fixed texts to music, the result is called a Mass setting.

Over the following centuries many composers wrote Masses, from Bach to Mozart and Beethoven.

## Chat with Your Teacher About Machaut

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about Machaut and the "Ars Nova" of the fourteenth century.

Teacher Aum can play at the piano, side by side, how a bare fifth and a chord with the third added sound different.

From a Mass more than six hundred years old, you can hear the sound of the Middle Ages.

## Listening to the Messe de Nostre Dame

Today there are many recordings of the Messe de Nostre Dame, most of them sung by small vocal ensembles.

As you listen, notice how the four voices interweave and how they come to rest together at the ends of sections.

Its harmony is not quite like the harmony we usually hear today, which gives it a fresh feeling.

## Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame in Brief

Guillaume de Machaut was a fourteenth-century French poet and composer who served as a canon at Reims Cathedral in his later years. The Messe de Nostre Dame was completed around the 1360s and sets the fixed texts of the Mass for four voices. It is one of the earliest surviving Masses written in full by a single known composer. French music of the fourteenth century is called the "Ars Nova", and in some passages he used "isorhythm", in which a rhythmic pattern repeats.

Late in life he had his works gathered into beautiful manuscripts, which is why so much of his output survives. His phrases often end on a bare fifth with no third. On the piano you can feel this by playing do and sol together with the left hand, or try four-voice harmony with two notes in each hand.

You can chat about this piece of history with Teacher Aum.

## Poet and Composer

Guillaume de Machaut was a very famous French poet of the fourteenth century, who wrote many long poems and lyric poems.

Many of his poems were set to melodies by his own hand.

At that time, few people were as accomplished in both poetry and music as he was.

## The Bare-Fifth Ending

Machaut's phrases often end on a harmony with only the root and the fifth, and no third.

This "bare fifth" sounds airy and open.

On the piano, play "do" and "sol" together with the left hand and you will hear it.

![A person wearing headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbj845i-fkhta.webp)

## Playing Four Voices at the Piano

At the piano you can play a simple piece of four-voice harmony with both hands, two notes in each hand.

Play slowly and listen to the direction each voice takes.

Then end on a bare fifth and get a feel for the flavour of the Middle Ages.

**Common misconceptions**
- A French poet and composer of the fourteenth century
- The Messe de Nostre Dame was completed around the 1360s
- Four voices; one of the earliest surviving Masses written in full by a known composer
- Late in life he had his works collected into manuscripts

## FAQ

**Q: Which century did Machaut live in?**
A: The fourteenth century.

**Q: When was the Messe de Nostre Dame completed?**
A: Around the 1360s.

**Q: How many voices does it have?**
A: Four.

**Q: What is fourteenth-century French music called?**
A: The "Ars Nova" period.

**Q: What is a "bare fifth"?**
A: A harmony with only the root and the fifth, and no third.

melody-phrase-arc-twinkle.body:
The key to making a song's melody sound as if it "breathes" is to draw an arc over each phrase: the phrase starts gently, gradually moves towards a high point, then falls back naturally and settles. The notes themselves do not change, but dynamics and note lengths rise and fall slightly along the arc, and the melody turns from "a string of notes" into "a complete sentence". This article uses the familiar nursery song Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star as a demonstration and takes it apart phrase by phrase.

## The short version

- A phrase is like a sentence in speech: it has a start, a high point and an ending
- Find the high point first, then plan the "uphill" towards it and the "downhill" away from it
- Ease the last note of a phrase softly, and do not drop onto it heavily
- Leave a little "breath" between phrases, even if it is only the tiniest pause
- Drawing arcs on the music with a pencil is more reliable than just remembering them

## Why does a melody sound "flat"?

As beginners, most of our attention goes on "pressing the right key at the right time", so every note is played with the same strength, as evenly as typing. The pitches and rhythm are fine, but it still sounds as if something is missing. What is missing is the sense of direction in the phrase.

Singers rarely have this problem, because singing requires breathing, and the breath naturally gives phrases their rise and fall. So a very practical way to draw arcs over a melody is to sing it once and then play it once.

## Putting it into practice with Twinkle, Twinkle

The melody of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star comes from an old French folk song. Its structure is clear, which makes it ideal for practising phrases. In C major, the solfège of the first two phrases is:

- Do Do Sol Sol La La Sol —
- Fa Fa Mi Mi Re Re Do —

**Phrase one: going up, then resting on Sol**
This phrase jumps from Do to Sol, rises to La, and finally returns to a long Sol. The high point is La. How to play it: play the first two Dos a little more lightly; when you jump to Sol, add a little weight; the two Las are the top of the arc, full but not sharp; the final long Sol relaxes and settles, like the pause after finishing a sentence.

**Phrase two: all the way down, coming home**
This phrase goes down step by step from Fa to Do, a "downhill". Let the dynamics get softer as the pitch falls, so the last Do feels as settled as coming home. If phrase one is the "question", phrase two is the "answer", and together they make a question and answer.

**The middle section and the return**
The two phrases in the middle of the song (Sol Sol Fa Fa Mi Mi Re, repeated twice) can be given a slightly different tone colour, for example the repeat can be a little softer than the first time, like an echo. When the first two phrases return at the end, you can play them more calmly than at the start, so the whole song has a feeling of "coming back to where it began".

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers beside it](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvv20qbz-j9zkd.webp)

## Four steps for drawing the arc

- **Sing:** without looking at the piano, sing the melody first, and notice where you naturally breathe
- **Mark:** with a pencil, draw an arc over each phrase on the music and mark the high point
- **Play:** play only the right-hand melody, arranging the dynamics according to the arcs
- **Listen:** record yourself and play it back, and judge whether the high point is clear and the ends of phrases are eased softly

## Three common problems

- **The high point comes too early:** if it is loud from the very start, there is no room to go higher later, and the arc collapses
- **The phrase ending is too heavy:** if the last note is as loud as the notes in the middle, it sounds "cut off"
- **No breath:** if phrases are packed tightly together, listeners cannot tell where one sentence ends

## With the left hand added, is the arc still there?

Many people play beautiful phrases with the right hand alone, but the arc disappears as soon as the left-hand accompaniment is added. The reason is that the left hand takes away attention, and volume too. There are two solutions. One is to keep the left hand one level quieter than the right overall, like laying a soft base colour under the melody. The other is to let the left hand breathe with the phrase too, easing off and settling together at the end of the phrase. You can first play only the bass note of each bar to confirm the arc is still clear, then gradually add back the full accompaniment.

## Using the method on more songs

Once Twinkle, Twinkle is going smoothly, you can use the same steps on melodies with a clear structure, such as Ode to Joy. The longer the song, the more you need to mark out the phrases on the music first. This "divide the phrases first, then shape them" approach is very common in music teaching, and it also suits all kinds of piano courses, as a bridge from "playing it right" to "playing it well".

## How TIGA ALPHA helps you practise phrasing

TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app built by a team in Thailand, and its CEO is Teacher Aum, who has 20 years of experience teaching piano. In this online piano teaching app you can:

- Use **Play Along** to practise the melody with an accompaniment behind it, so it is easier to feel the direction of a phrase
- Use **Pathway** to record which passages of each song you have already divided into phrases and shaped
- Use the questions in **Daily Mentor** to review which phrase's high point you handled more naturally today

Teaching piano with AI does not mean letting a machine decide your musical expression for you. It helps you build a regular routine of "sing, mark, play, listen".

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is the high point of a phrase always the highest note?**

A: Often it is, but not always. Sometimes the high point falls on a longer note in the rhythm or on a tense moment in the harmony. Sing it several times and find the place you most want to emphasise.

**Q: What if the arc conflicts with a dynamic marking?**

A: Treat the markings on the music as the larger frame, and the arc as small rises and falls inside it. For example, if a whole phrase is marked soft, the arc rises and falls within "soft".

**Q: Can young children learning piano understand phrases?**

A: You can use speech as a comparison: "Is this sentence asking a question or answering one?" Children often catch the feeling quickly.

**Q: How can I tell whether my phrasing is good when learning piano online?**

A: Listening to a recording is a very practical method. You can also use the play-along and tracking features of an online piano teaching app, compare recordings from different days and hear how they change.

## Let every song have its own breath

Once you begin to think in phrases, playing the piano is no longer just finishing a task, but telling a small story. The joy of learning music is often hidden in these slight rises and falls, and performing music becomes more moving because of them.

memorizing-multiple-starting-points.body:
When your memory suddenly goes blank on the second page, it is usually because it relies mainly on the momentum of your fingers and has no "footholds" from which to start again. Mark several section starting points on the music and practise starting from each one separately. Then even if you get stuck partway through, you can rejoin at the next familiar place.

## Give memory more than one support

When you memorise, the movement memory of your fingers is important, but it is also the first thing to break when you are nervous. If you also remember the direction of the melody, the changes of chord and the structure of the sections, it is like having several roads ready: if one is blocked, you can take another.

**A small tip**

A common exercise is the "random starting point": ask someone at home, or choose yourself at random, the beginning of a section, and play straight from there. It may be slow at first, but after a few tries every section becomes a small unit that can stand on its own.

Also, you do not have to memorise the whole piece at once. Memorise just a small passage each day. The next day, play yesterday's passage first to confirm it is still there, then add one more. The memory will be more secure and is less likely to break suddenly on the second page.

## Divide the piece into clear sections

Before memorising, you can analyse the structure of the piece: how many sections it has, which parts repeat and which change. Seeing the piece as several named sections is easier to remember than seeing a long string of notes.

You can mark each section on the music in pencil, for example A, B, A′, or with simple words such as "theme", "transition" and "recapitulation". These marks are signposts for your memory.

Every section should be able to start on its own. When you practise, choose a section at random and play from its beginning, to check whether you really remember it, rather than only being able to start from the top.

When one section is always forgotten, split it into smaller pieces, for example just the first four bars, and join them up once they are secure.

- Divide the piece into sections and mark the start of each
- Practise starting straight from the beginning of any section
- Close the music and mentally go through the harmony or the direction of the melody
- Check your memory section by section, not just by playing from the top

## A daily plan for memorising

Memorising can be part of every day's practice, rather than a rush before a performance. For example, each day first memorise a small piece of new material, then review the sections you memorised in the previous days, so that memory builds up gradually.

When you review, you do not need to play the whole piece each time. You can pick a few places that are easy to forget and focus on them.

Every few days, play the whole piece from memory once more and check that the joins between sections are smooth.

![Electronic devices and audio waveforms in blue-purple light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8jktr4-ns3wr.webp)

## Several kinds of memory working together

Memorising on the piano usually depends on several kinds of memory: movement memory in the fingers, aural memory in the ears, visual memory in the eyes, and an understanding of harmony and structure. Relying on only one of them can easily break down when you are nervous.

You can try stepping away from the piano and going through the piece in your head, imagining the position of the fingers and the sound. This kind of mental practice can show whether any part of your memory is blurred.

You can also say the chord progression of a section aloud, or sing the melody, and then go to the piano and play it. Meeting the same material again and again in different ways makes memory more secure.

Some people notice what the page looks like while memorising, for example which line has a special mark. A visual impression can also become a cue for recall.

## A memory check before going on stage

Before a performance, you can do several complete performances from memory, imitating the real situation, without stopping partway. Even if small mistakes happen, keep going to the end, and practise recovering from mistakes.

You can also practise "starting from any section". Ask someone at home to call out the mark of a section at random, and start from there. If every section can be picked up immediately, you will have more confidence on stage.

It also helps to play in different settings, such as on a different piano or in front of other people. A change of setting tests whether your memory is secure.

**Take it slowly**

On the day of the performance, there is no need to practise a lot of new material. Just review the beginnings of a few key sections in a relaxed way, to keep your hands and mind familiar.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do I have to watch my hands when memorising?**
A: There is no need to watch all the time. You can try playing familiar sections with your eyes closed to check whether you really remember them.

**Q: When should I start memorising?**
A: You can begin section by section after you are familiar with the piece, without waiting until the whole piece is fluent.

**Q: Can I look at the music now and then while memorising?**
A: Yes. In the practice stage, look when you hit a place you have forgotten, then try to recall it again.

**Q: Why do I sometimes suddenly forget a piece I know well?**
A: Finger momentum easily breaks when you are nervous, and building several kinds of memory reduces this.

**Q: What is mental practice for?**
A: It helps you find the blurred places in your memory, and lets you review when there is no piano.

**Q: Will memorising in sections make the piece hard to join up?**
A: In practice, pay attention to the joins between sections. You can practise the end of each section together with the beginning of the next.

learn-left-hand-first-sometimes.body:
When learning a new piece, many people are used to practising the right-hand melody first, always leaving the left hand until later and practising it less. The result is often that the right hand is very familiar but the left hand is not steady enough, and problems appear as soon as the hands come together. Sometimes you can do it the other way round and start with the left hand: get familiar with the bass and the chord progression, let the accompaniment settle, and then add the right hand. For pieces whose left-hand patterns are complicated, with many leaps, or whose harmony changes often, practising the left hand first makes the foundation of the whole piece more solid.

- The right hand is often practised first, and the left hand is often neglected
- Sometimes you can start with the left hand
- Get the bass and accompaniment steady first
- Especially suitable for pieces with a complicated left hand

## Then Add the Right Hand

Once the left hand is steady, add the right hand, and first play hands together at a slow speed.

You will find that because the left hand is already very familiar, your attention can go more to the right hand and to how the two hands work together.

If a problem appears when you put the hands together, you can check separately which hand is the cause, and then practise that one specifically.

## Which Pieces Suit Left Hand First

Pieces where the left hand has fast broken chords, big leaps or frequent chord changes are especially suited to practising the left hand first.

In some arrangements of pop songs, the left hand often has a strongly rhythmic bass pattern, and you can also get the left hand steady first.

If your teacher advises practising the left hand first, you can also follow your teacher's plan.

## Ask Your Teacher to Arrange the Order

Every piece has its own characteristics, and you can discuss with your teacher which hand to practise first and how to divide your time.

Your teacher will give suitable advice based on the difficulties of the piece and your own situation.

Adjusting your practice method following that advice often gets a piece learnt faster.

## The Left Hand Is the Foundation of the Music

The bass notes and chords of the left hand decide the harmony and rhythm of a piece and are the foundation of the whole music.

If the left hand is not steady, then even if the right hand plays very well, the whole piece will sound wobbly.

Conversely, if the left hand is steady and clear, the right hand above it sounds freer and more expressive.

## Balancing Time Between the Two Hands

Not every piece has to start with the left hand. The key is to give both hands a balanced amount of practice time.

You can set aside some time for the left hand in your practice plan, for example practising the left hand alone for a few minutes at the start of each session.

Little by little, your left hand will become more and more agile and steady.

## Making the Left Hand Steady on Its Own

You can first play the left hand through completely at a slow speed several times, making sure the notes, fingering and rhythm are all right.

Then use a metronome to speed up gradually, until the left hand can play steadily at close to the original tempo.

During this process, pay attention to the dynamics and tone of the left hand, keeping the bass clear and the chords soft.

## Not Only for New Pieces

Even for a piece you have been practising for a while, you can play the left hand alone from time to time to check that it is still steady.

Very often, when you play hands together, mistakes in the left hand are covered up by the right hand, and you can only find them by playing it alone.

This kind of checking helps you keep up the quality of the whole piece.

## Sing the Melody While Playing the Left Hand

Once your left hand is fluent, you can try playing the left hand while quietly singing the right-hand melody.

This both checks whether the left hand is steady enough and lets you feel in advance how the hands will sound together.

If the left hand falls apart while you sing the melody, it means the left hand still needs more practice.

## Memorising the Left Hand

When memorising, the left hand is often harder to remember than the right, because its patterns may not be as easy to sing as a melody.

Practising the left hand first and understanding its harmony helps you remember the left-hand part more firmly.

You can try playing only the left hand without the score, to check whether you really remember it.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesiser and drums on a neon-lit street, with crystal towers behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0cmio-yf62a.webp)

## Why the Left Hand Is Often Neglected

The right hand usually plays the melody, which is pleasant and easy to remember, so many people are drawn to it from the start and get the right hand familiar first.

The left-hand accompaniment or bass does not sound as interesting when played alone, so it is often left until later.

Over time, the practice time of the left hand ends up far less than that of the right, and its fluency falls behind.

## Understand the Left-Hand Harmony First

Before you start practising the left hand, look at which chords its notes are made of, and write the chord names on the score.

Once you understand the harmonic progression, the notes of the left hand are no longer a string of isolated notes, but patterned groupings.

**Take it slowly**

This makes them easier to remember, and gives your playing more direction.

## FAQ

**Q: Why practise the left hand first?**
A: So that the accompaniment and bass become steady first, and the foundation is more solid.

**Q: Which pieces suit it?**
A: Pieces where the left hand has fast broken chords, big leaps or many chord changes.

**Q: What should I do first?**
A: Understand the left-hand harmony and write down the chord names.

**Q: How can I check whether the left hand is steady?**
A: Play the left hand while singing the melody.

**Q: Must every piece start with the left hand?**
A: Not necessarily. The key is to balance the time between the two hands.

**Q: What if the left hand is hard to memorise?**
A: Understand the harmony, and check by playing the left hand alone without the score.

li-huanzhi-spring-festival-overture-1956.body:
The Spring Festival Overture is an orchestral work written by the Chinese composer Li Huanzhi between 1955 and 1956. It is the first movement of his Spring Festival Suite. The piece opens with lively gongs, drums and yangge rhythms, portraying people dancing the yangge and celebrating the New Year with festive bustle. The middle section is a lyrical, flowing melody with the flavour of folk songs from northern Shaanxi, and at the end the lively music returns. Today, every Spring Festival, this piece is often heard on television and at all kinds of events, and there are many piano arrangements of it.

## Ask Your Teacher to Recommend an Arrangement in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend an arrangement of the Spring Festival Overture that suits your level.

If you want to have it ready before New Year's Eve, you can work backwards and make a table of weekly goals.

From one overture, you can feel the festive excitement of Chinese New Year.

## A Lively Opening

At the very start, the gongs and drums join the whole orchestra in a fiery rhythm, like the gongs and drums of New Year celebrations.

The strings and winds play a quick, joyful melody, like people dancing the yangge.

This lively opening immediately draws you into the atmosphere of the New Year.

## The Yangge of Yan'an

The yangge is a folk song-and-dance tradition widespread in northern China, in which people dance and sing while holding fans and coloured silk.

While he was in Yan'an, Li Huanzhi took part in many yangge events, and he knew the rhythms and melodies of the yangge very well.

These experiences became important material for his later Spring Festival Suite.

## The Rhythm of the Yangge

The rhythm of the opening comes from the gong-and-drum patterns of the yangge.

This rhythm has clearly strong and weak beats and a bouncing feel, which makes you want to move along with it.

When you play it on the piano, bring out these bouncing accents. Do not play it flat.

- Written by Li Huanzhi between 1955 and 1956
- The first movement of the Spring Festival Suite
- Yangge rhythms and gongs and drums
- A middle section with the flavour of northern Shaanxi folk songs

## Summary of the Spring Festival Overture

The Spring Festival Overture is an orchestral work written by Li Huanzhi (1919-2000) between 1955 and 1956. It is the first of the four movements of the Spring Festival Suite. Li Huanzhi became familiar with the yangge in Yan'an as a young man. The opening uses gong-and-drum and yangge rhythms to portray the bustle of the New Year, in the middle section an oboe plays a lyrical melody with the flavour of northern Shaanxi folk songs, and at the end the lively music returns and finishes in jubilation.

It is played by a Western symphony orchestra, yet it has a strongly Chinese character. Piano arrangements exist both for solo and for four hands. In them, low chords can imitate the big drum and big gong, and short high chords can imitate the small gong and cymbals. It is perfect to play for your family at Spring Festival.

Teacher Aum can recommend a suitable arrangement.

## When to Play It

The Spring Festival Overture is ideal for playing to family and friends at Spring Festival.

It is lively and festive, and adds to the joyful atmosphere of the holiday.

The four-hand version can even be played together with family members, which makes it feel even more like New Year.

## A Chinese Flavour in a Western Orchestra

The Spring Festival Overture is played by a Western symphony orchestra, but it sounds strongly Chinese.

This is because the composer used Chinese folk melodies, rhythms and gongs and drums.

This way of combining folk material with the Western orchestra is an important direction in Chinese music of the twentieth century.

## The Spring Festival Suite

The Spring Festival Suite has four movements in all, portraying all kinds of scenes of people celebrating Spring Festival.

The first movement is the Spring Festival Overture, lively and joyful, and the one that is performed on its own most often.

The other movements include lyrical ones and joyful ones, and together they form a picture scroll of the New Year.

![A glowing turquoise grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbif6a4-snzus.webp)

## The Liveliness Returns

After the middle section, the lively music of the opening returns.

The gongs and drums are louder, the rhythm is faster, and the whole orchestra pushes the mood to a climax.

It ends in a burst of jubilation, as if the festive bustle of the New Year had reached its peak.

## Playing the Spring Festival Overture on the Piano

There are many piano arrangements of the Spring Festival Overture, both solo and four-hand.

In the piano version, the opening needs strong chords and a bouncing rhythm to imitate the gongs and drums.

The lyrical melody of the middle section should be played smoothly and expressively, as if singing.

## Imitating the Sound of Gongs and Drums

On the piano, thick chords in the low register can imitate the sound of the big drum and the big gong.

Short chords in the high register can imitate the sound of the small gong and the cymbals.

The contrast in dynamics must be clear, so that the liveliness of the gongs and drums comes through.

## Who Was Li Huanzhi?

Li Huanzhi (1919-2000) was a Chinese composer and conductor, born in Hong Kong, with ancestral roots in Fujian.

As a young man he went to Yan'an to study music, where he came into contact with a great deal of folk music from northern Shaanxi.

Later he wrote many choral, orchestral and vocal works, and the Spring Festival Overture is his best-known piece.

## The Lyrical Middle Section

In the middle section the music slows down, and an oboe plays a flowing, lyrical melody.

This melody has the flavour of northern Shaanxi folk songs, as if someone were singing in the distance.

It contrasts with the lively music before and after it, giving the whole piece more depth.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote the Spring Festival Overture?**
A: The Chinese composer Li Huanzhi.

**Q: When was it written?**
A: Between 1955 and 1956.

**Q: Which work is it part of?**
A: It is the first movement of the Spring Festival Suite.

**Q: Which folk rhythm does the opening use?**
A: The gong-and-drum rhythm of the yangge.

**Q: Which region's folk songs does the middle melody resemble?**
A: Folk songs of northern Shaanxi.

leitmotif-wagner-recurring-themes.body:
A leitmotif is a short melody or harmony used in an opera or other large work to represent a character, object, place or idea. Whenever that character appears, or the idea is mentioned in the drama, this piece of music sounds. The German composer Wagner used this technique extensively and systematically in his large operas, especially in the four-part Der Ring des Nibelungen (The Ring of the Nibelung). The name "leitmotif" was later used by others to describe Wagner's way of writing. Today, many film scores also use leitmotifs to represent characters.

## Design a Motif of Your Own

You can try designing a short motif for a character or a thing.

**Common misunderstandings**

For example, design a light, hopping motif for a kitten, and a low, broad motif for a big mountain.

Then try making the motif change: when the kitten sleeps, the hopping motif becomes slower and softer.

## Changes in a Motif

When a leitmotif appears in a work, it often changes.

For example, the motif representing a hero may become brilliant when he triumphs and dim when he is wounded.

These changes let the music show the development of characters and plot.

## Summary of the Leitmotif

A leitmotif uses a short melody, chord or rhythm to represent a character, object, place or idea. Its forerunners include the idee fixe for the beloved in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830 and the melodies in Weber's operas. Wagner, born in 1813 and died in 1883, used it systematically in his large operas, and the four-part Ring has dozens of motifs, representing the Rhine, the sword, fire, the ring and more.

The name was later used by others to describe his way of writing. Motifs change with the plot and can also appear in combination, and the orchestra can hint at what a character is thinking. Film scores often use them today, and a theme that returns and changes in a piano piece plays a similar role. You can design motifs for a kitten and a mountain and tell a little story.

You can ask Teacher Aum to talk about examples of leitmotifs.

## Forerunners of the Leitmotif

Before Wagner, composers had already used recurring melodies to represent something.

When Berlioz wrote the Symphonie fantastique, he had a melody representing the beloved, which he called the "idee fixe", haunt all five movements.

In Weber's operas, too, there are melodies that represent characters or moods.

## Wagner's Systematic Use

Wagner, born in 1813 and died in 1883, was a German composer.

In his own large operas, he used this technique extensively and systematically.

In his works, leitmotifs do not merely appear now and then, but run through the whole work like a net of music.

## What a Leitmotif Is

A leitmotif is a short piece of music, which can be a melody, a chord or a rhythm.

The composer links it with a certain character, object, place or idea.

When listeners hear this fragment, they think of what it represents.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwae2faq-5qqao.webp)

## Leitmotifs in Film

Today, many film scores also use the method of the leitmotif.

When a character appears, he or she is often accompanied by his or her own melody.

When the audience hears this melody, they can sense the character's presence even without seeing him or her.

## The Name "Leitmotif"

Wagner himself did not often use the word "leitmotif".

The name was later used by others to describe his way of writing, and it quickly became popular.

Today, people use this word to describe a musical fragment that represents something, in all kinds of works.

## Combining Motifs

In Wagner's works, several leitmotifs often appear at the same time, or one after another.

That way the music can show the relationships between several characters or ideas at once.

If listeners are familiar with these motifs, they can hear many details of the plot in the music.

## The Ring of the Nibelung

Der Ring des Nibelungen is Wagner's four-part cycle of operas, and performing all of it takes more than ten hours.

There are dozens of leitmotifs in the cycle, representing all kinds of characters, objects and ideas, such as the Rhine, the sword, fire and the ring.

These motifs keep appearing, changing and combining across the four operas.

## Ask Your Teacher About Leitmotifs in a Lesson

In your lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to talk about examples of leitmotifs, and to play a few of Wagner's motifs on the piano.

Your teacher can also help you design motifs for a little story, and tell it together on the piano.

Through the leitmotif, you learn how music tells stories.

## Telling a Little Story with Motifs

You can use several motifs of your own design to tell a little story on the piano.

For example: the kitten is playing, the mountain is far away, suddenly it starts to rain, and the kitten runs home.

Each character and each piece of scenery has its own motif, and the story unfolds in the changes of the motifs.

## Music That "Speaks"

Leitmotifs let music "speak", sometimes even saying more than the words.

For example, while one character speaks a line, the orchestra may play another character's motif, hinting at whom he is thinking of.

That makes the music part of the storytelling.

**Take it slower**
- A short melody represents a character, object or idea
- The music sounds when the character appears or is mentioned
- Wagner used it systematically in large operas
- Film scores often use it today

## Leitmotif-Like Devices in Piano Music

In piano music, too, there are devices similar to the leitmotif.

For example, a theme returns again and again in a piece, changing a little each time and expressing different moods.

As you play, you can notice how this theme changes each time it appears.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a leitmotif?**
A: A short musical fragment that represents a character, object or idea.

**Q: Who used leitmotifs systematically?**
A: The German composer Wagner.

**Q: How many operas make up The Ring of the Nibelung?**
A: Four.

**Q: In which work does Berlioz's "idee fixe" appear?**
A: The Symphonie fantastique of 1830.

**Q: Where else are leitmotifs often used today?**
A: Film scores.

large-print-scores-older-adult-learners.body:
Many adult and older learners find that the notes on the page are too small and too crowded, and reading them is a strain, especially notes on ledger lines and tiny accidentals. In fact, being able to see the music clearly is one of the foundations of playing well. Making the score a little bigger, the light a little brighter and adjusting the position of the music stand can make reading much easier and practice more enjoyable. These are very simple adjustments, yet they are often overlooked.

## Reading from a tablet

If you read music on a tablet, you can enlarge the page very easily.

**Slow down**

Some score-reading apps can also change the background colour and brightness to make the contrast clearer.

But take care that the screen is not too bright, to avoid tired eyes.

- Scores that are too small make reading a strain
- You can print scores larger
- Adjust the light and the position of the music stand
- Simple adjustments make practice easier

## Printing larger

If you have a digital copy of the score, you can enlarge it when printing, for example to 120 or 150 per cent of the original size.

You can also enlarge a paper score on a photocopier for your own practice use.

After enlarging, one page may have to be split into two, but it will look much clearer.

## Choosing large-print scores

Some published method books and collections come in editions with larger notes, suitable for beginners and older learners.

When buying music, look at whether the font size and layout are clear.

Good layout means suitable spacing between the notes and markings that are clear and easy to read.

![A high-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a neon street on a rainy night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac13cs-exydp.webp)

## Adjusting the lighting

Lighting is very important when practising: if the light is too dim, the score is even harder to see.

You can put a lamp beside the piano that shines onto the score so that it is lit evenly.

Take care that the light does not shine directly into your eyes, and that it does not cause glare on the score.

## Looking at a small section at a time

If a page of music is very dense, you can cover the rest with a sheet of paper and look at only one or two lines at a time.

This helps you concentrate and your eyes tire less easily.

Once you are used to it, gradually look at the whole page.

## Marking small signs with a highlighter

You can use coloured pencils or a highlighter to mark important signs on the score, such as accidentals, places where the hands swap, and dynamic changes.

These eye-catching marks help you notice them more quickly when playing.

But don’t add too many marks, or the score becomes cluttered.

## Adjusting the distance and height of the music stand

If the music stand is too far from or too close to your eyes, reading becomes a strain.

Try adjusting the height and angle of the stand, or the position of the piano stool, to find a distance that is both clear and comfortable.

If you usually wear glasses, check too whether you can see clearly at this distance.

## Asking your teacher to help adjust the score in a lesson

In a lesson you can tell Teacher Aum which scores look hard to read.

Your teacher can recommend editions with a clear layout or suggest an enlargement ratio.

When reading is easy, there is more joy in practice.

## Memorising familiar passages

For passages you already know very well, you can try memorising them to reduce the burden of reading.

Once a passage is memorised, you can concentrate more on your hands and the sound.

When needed, go back to the score to check the details.

## A tip for ledger-line notes

Notes on ledger lines are often the hardest to see when reading.

Beside these notes you can write the note name in pencil, for example "high C".

Once you are familiar with them, gradually rub the names out and practise reading directly.

## Why the score is hard to see

To save paper, many piano scores print the notes quite small and set them quite close together.

Ledger-line notes, accidentals, fingering numbers and dynamic markings are often all small.

For adults and older people whose eyesight has changed, looking at such a score for a long time easily causes tiredness.

## Resting your eyes

After reading music for a long time, you can stop and look into the distance to rest your eyes.

You can also close your eyes and recall in your mind the melody you just played.

Proper rest lets you keep practising for longer.

## Enlarging scores summary

Many scores have small notes set close together, with ledger-line notes, accidentals and fingering numbers all very small, and adult and older learners tire easily when looking at them for a long time. You can print or photocopy them larger for your own practice, choose large-print method books, or use a tablet to enlarge the page and adjust the background and brightness.

Put a lamp beside the piano that shines onto the score, avoiding direct light in the eyes and glare, adjust the music stand and stool, mark important signs on the score with coloured pens but not too many, write note names beside ledger-line notes, look at only one or two lines at a time, rest your eyes, and memorise familiar passages.

When you can’t see clearly, speak to your teacher directly, and you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend editions with a clear layout.

## Say so when you can’t see your teacher’s score

If in a lesson you can’t see your teacher’s score or the writing on the board, you can simply tell your teacher.

Your teacher can help prepare an enlarged score or change the way the lesson is run.

Clear communication makes learning go more smoothly.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why is the score hard to see?**
A: The notes are printed small and set close together.

**Q: How can I enlarge the score?**
A: Print or photocopy it larger, or use a tablet.

**Q: What should I watch for with lighting?**
A: Shine it onto the score, not directly into your eyes, and avoid glare.

**Q: How can I deal with ledger-line notes?**
A: Write the note name beside them in pencil.

**Q: What if a page is too dense?**
A: Cover the rest with a sheet of paper and look at only one or two lines at a time.

listen-pitch-like-language-tones.body:
Mandarin Chinese has four tones and a neutral tone, and Thai has five tones. When people speak, the rise and fall of the voice itself carries meaning. When learning the piano, you can borrow this sensitivity to tones to feel the upward, downward and level movement of pitch in a melody: first hum a phrase of a melody as if you were speaking it, then listen to where it rises and where it falls, and this helps your ears grasp the shape of the melody faster.

## Practising the rise and fall of a phrase through speech

When we speak, a sentence usually has stress and rise and fall, and the end of a question often lifts upward.

When playing a melody you can also ask yourself: does this phrase sound like a statement or a question? On which note is its emphasis?

Playing a melody as if it were a sentence often makes the performance more natural and more expressive.

You can also try reading a line of lyrics aloud in a speaking voice, then listen to the melody of that line, and compare what the rise and fall of the speech and the rise and fall of the melody have in common and where they differ.

## Suitable for different learners

Learners whose mother tongue is a tonal language can make good use of their sensitivity to tones to practise hearing pitch.

Learners whose mother tongue has no tones can also develop a feeling for the direction of a melody by humming, gesturing and drawing.

What matters is to let your ears actively listen, and not just look at the score and press keys.

![High-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a neon street on a rainy night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xpwwg-17ek2.webp)

## Also know how they differ

Tones in language are relative. Everyone speaks at a different pitch, and the same tone does not correspond to one fixed note on the piano.

The pitches in a melody are definite: each note corresponds to a specific place on the keyboard, and the distance between notes is clearly defined.

So tones can serve as an entry point for feeling pitch changes, but when learning a melody you still need to listen concretely and identify every note.

## Finding the melody on the keyboard

Once you are familiar with the shape of the melody, go to the keyboard to find the actual notes. If it goes up, look to the right on the keys, and if it goes down, look to the left.

Find the first note, then try step by step according to the shape, and listen for which note matches what you hummed.

At the beginning you may need to try several times, and with more practice the coordination between ears and hands will get faster and faster.

## Humming a melody as if speaking

When you get a new melodic phrase, do not rush to play it. Hum it first with "la" or "mm".

As you hum, notice: which note is higher than the one before? Which is lower? Where is a note repeated on the same pitch?

You can also gesture in the air with your hand, moving up when the melody goes up and down when it goes down, so that your body also takes part in feeling the pitch.

- Mandarin has four tones and a neutral tone, and Thai has five tones
- Both tones and melody involve changes in how high or low the sound is
- First hum the melody, then decide where it rises and falls
- A tone in language is not the same as a fixed pitch

## Drawing the shape of a melody

After listening to or humming a phrase of melody, you can draw its direction on paper with a line, like drawing small hills and valleys.

When it is drawn, compare it with the score, and you will see that the high and low positions of the notes on the staff are describing the same shape.

This exercise is especially helpful for children who are just starting to read music, because it connects the sound they hear with the symbols they see.

When drawing, you do not need to be precise. Just show roughly the rising, falling and repeating places, and that is already enough to help you remember the phrase.

## What tones are

In Mandarin Chinese, the same syllable said with different tones can mean completely different things, for example mā, má, mǎ and mà.

Thai is also a tonal language, and is generally considered to have five tones.

People who speak these languages have practised telling the height and direction of sounds since childhood, and this ability has some similarities with hearing pitch in music.

## What tones and melody have in common

A tone describes the rise and fall of the voice when a word is said. For example, the second tone in Mandarin lifts upward, and the fourth tone drops downward.

A melody is a series of pitches in order: sometimes going up, sometimes going down, and sometimes staying on the same note.

**Quick tip**

Both need the ear to tell "high" from "low" and "rising" from "falling", so you can use your feeling for tones to help you sense the direction of a melody.

## FAQ

**Q: Is it easier to learn music if I speak a tonal language?**
A: Not necessarily. Everyone is different, and steady practice matters more.

**Q: Which note on the piano does a tone correspond to?**
A: A tone is a relative change of high and low and does not correspond to a fixed note.

**Q: What if my child always cannot tell whether a melody goes up or down?**
A: You can gesture with your hand or draw a line on paper, so that the child feels it while listening.

**Q: Do I need to sing accurately when humming a melody?**
A: Not very accurately. The point is to feel the direction of the melody.

**Q: Is this method suitable for adults?**
A: Yes, people of any age can feel a melody by humming it.

**Q: Do I need special paper to draw the shape of a melody?**
A: Ordinary paper is fine, as long as you draw the highs and lows.

liadov-musical-snuffbox-op32-1893.body:
The Musical Snuffbox is a short piano piece written in 1893 by the Russian composer Anatoly Liadov, catalogued as Op. 32. The piece is very short, like a tiny mechanical music box being opened: the tone in the high register is crisp, the rhythm is neat, and the melody has a touch of toy-like playfulness. It is not meant to express great swings of emotion, but to show clearly a kind of beauty that is limited, delicate and almost a little "mechanical". When you learn it, the focus is often on an even touch and a steady rhythm, not on making the sound thick. When you listen, you can first notice only how the small repeated figures are turned out precisely again and again. If one time is suddenly louder or more hurried than another, that box-like neatness falls apart. In practice, it is better to play it fewer times and count the beat steadily each time than to rush through many repetitions in a row. When practising, you might treat this miniature like a real little device: each time you open it, aim for the same neatness. You can first choose a steady tempo and play it twice in a row, specifically comparing whether the second time is louder or more hurried than the first. If it is, slow down a little more and make the touch in the high register even again. Short does not mean you can ignore the details.

- A piano miniature by Liadov from 1893, Op. 32
- It portrays the crisp, neat sound of a music box being opened
- It is very short, and the touch in the high register must be even
- Good for practising evenness, lightness and restrained pedalling

## What Is the "Snuffbox" in the Title?

In the nineteenth century, some snuffboxes had a set of tiny comb teeth and a cylinder fitted inside the lid, and when you opened it a short piece of mechanical music played.

Liadov wrote the sound of such a device for the piano, so the piece sounds like a toy rather than a large lyrical work.

Understanding this helps explain why it should be played lightly and neatly, and not with great warmth.

## What to Remember About The Musical Snuffbox

This is Liadov's Op. 32 of 1893, using the piano to imitate the sound of a small music box being opened.

When you play it, aim for crispness, neatness and restraint, and do not play it as an impassioned nocturne.

As you listen, notice how the small repeated figures are turned out again and again.

## Where the Mechanical Feeling Comes From

The repeated figures and the very steady beats make you think of a cylinder turning over the same positions again and again.

If the performer suddenly stretches one phrase very freely, that feeling of "the box playing by itself" falls apart.

You can first play twice at a very steady tempo, and then decide where only a tiny breath is needed, rather than large stretches of flexible tempo.

## How the Composer Wrote Pieces Like This

Liadov wrote orchestral music and many short piano pieces, which are often not long but are very carefully detailed.

The Musical Snuffbox shows this side of him, his skill at handling small tone colours, in a very concentrated way.

When you listen, you do not need to look for a long development. Just notice how it repeats a single idea with such refinement.

## Ask Teacher Aum in Your Lesson to Listen for Whether the Box Is Even

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether the high notes are even and whether the beat gets pushed forward anywhere.

If the pedal blurs the grains in some place, you can also ask your teacher to help you change to a shorter, cleaner pedalling.

From a miniature that portrays a music box, practise putting lightness and neatness into your touch.

## How to Play the High Register Crisply

The sound should be bright, but it should not be banged. Keep your fingers close to the keys and let the note come out cleanly, which is closer to a music box than pressing hard to the bottom.

Within the same kind of figure, keep the way you touch the keys close, so that listeners can hear "it is still the same box".

If certain notes keep popping out, play just those a notch lighter and then put them back in place.

![A pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjkq7f-zra34.webp)

## Keep Both the Left Hand and the Pedal Restrained

The left hand is mostly light, short support. Do not use heavy bass to steal the sparkle of the high register.

The pedal can be tapped and released straight away, or used only when you need to join two notes lightly.

If the resonance covers the mechanical grains, first play it through with no pedal at all, and then judge which few places deserve a tiny bit of sustain.

## How to Plan Your Practice of the Snuffbox Piece

This piece is very short, which makes it easy to play roughly because it "doesn't seem difficult".

You can first practise the repeated figures separately until they are even, and then join up the ornaments and the ending as written in the score.

**A common mistake**

Playing a few times with real care each day is more useful than rushing through many times in a row.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote this piece, and in which year?**
A: Liadov, in 1893.

**Q: What does it portray?**
A: The short, crisp music of opening a mechanical snuffbox or music box.

**Q: Why should it not be played very freely?**
A: The charm of a mechanical device lies in the beats and figures being quite regular.

**Q: How should the pedal be used?**
A: Short and sparing. First let the grains be heard, then decide where you need to connect.

**Q: What is easiest to overlook in practice?**
A: Because it is short, it is easy to play roughly. The repeated figures still need to be practised separately until even.

let-us-row-the-boat-1955-song-piano.body:
"Let us row the boat, the little boat parts the waves" is a song many people sang in their childhood. "Let Us Row the Boat", with words by Qiao Yu and music by Liu Chi, was a song from a children's film of 1955. It describes children rowing a boat on a lake, with a broad, bright melody and a rhythm like oars dipping one stroke after another. Played on the piano, it lets you practise a flowing melody and an accompaniment with a gentle rocking feel.

## Singing and accompanying yourself

This song is also very good for singing while you play.

You can start with a simple chord accompaniment and sing the melody yourself.

When you are comfortable, add the melody to your right hand as well.

## Choosing a key for the song

Piano scores of this song commonly come in different keys.

If you want to sing and play together, choose a key that suits your vocal range.

If you only want to play, choose a key with fewer black keys that is easier to play.

## Playing together with a child

This song is also familiar to many parents, so you can play and sing it together with your child.

A parent sings while the child plays, or the child sings while the parent plays the accompaniment.

This kind of teamwork makes practice more fun.

![A person with headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing the city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaa28mg-d8gjl.webp)

## Breathing between phrases

At the end of a long phrase, give the music a little room to breathe.

Let the long note at the end of each phrase fade gently, like lifting the oar out of the water after a stroke.

It is like taking a breath when singing, and it makes the music more natural.

- Words by Qiao Yu, music by Liu Chi, a song from a 1955 film
- A broad melody, with a rhythm like rowing
- The accompaniment can use broken chords to create a feeling of water
- Good for practising a singing melody

## The long phrases

The melodic line is broad and rises and falls naturally, so it is easy to remember.

The phrases are long, like a long sentence said in one breath.

When you play, take care that the phrases are connected and do not break in the middle.

## Ask your teacher to help with the arrangement in lessons

If you want to play a richer version, you can ask Teacher Aum to help arrange the accompaniment.

Your teacher can design a suitable left-hand pattern for your level.

You can also ask your teacher to suggest a suitable key and tempo.

## The picture in the lyrics

The lyrics describe children rowing a little boat on a lake, surrounded by green trees and red walls, with a beautiful white pagoda reflected in the water.

The whole song is full of a relaxed and happy atmosphere.

Close your eyes and think of the lake, the white pagoda and the little boat, and your playing will have sunshine in it.

## The left hand imitating ripples from the oars

The left hand can accompany with broken chords, for example playing the root, the fifth and the third in turn.

The flowing feel of broken chords is just right for imitating the ripples on the water.

Play the left hand lightly and evenly, laying the background colour for the right-hand melody.

## The mood of the second half

The second half of the song has a fuller mood, and the melody also climbs higher.

When you play here, you can add a little more volume to make the music more open.

But do not play too heavily, and keep the song's bright, fresh character.

## Where the song comes from

"Let Us Row the Boat" was a song from a children's film of 1955.

The lyricist was Qiao Yu and the composer was Liu Chi.

The song was later sung widely across the country and became a childhood song in many people's memories.

## Summary: "Let Us Row the Boat"

"Let Us Row the Boat", with words by Qiao Yu and music by Liu Chi, was a song from a children's film of 1955. It describes children rowing a boat on a lake, with a broad melody and a rhythm like oars dipping.

The left hand can imitate ripples with broken chords. If that is hard, start with block chords. The second half has a fuller mood, there should be breaths between phrases, and the key can be chosen as needed.

The song suits singing and playing and parent-child teamwork, you can record a small family performance, and you can ask Teacher Aum to help with the arrangement.

## A rowing rhythm

The rhythm of the song is steady and regular, as if oars were dipping one stroke after another.

Every beat has a sense of moving forward, but without hurry.

You can imagine the motion of rowing as you play and find the right pulse.

## Accompaniment for a simple version

If the left-hand broken chords are too hard, you can start with simple block chords.

Play one chord per bar, or one chord every two beats.

When the melody is comfortable, change to broken chords.

## The interlude

Many piano scores add a few bars of interlude between two verses.

The interlude can repeat the melody of the last line of the verse, or just play the left-hand broken chords.

Keep the tempo unchanged during the interlude so that the next verse comes in steadily.

## Recording a small family performance

Once you can play it well, you can record a small family performance to share with your family.

When recording, you can first say a few words about where the song comes from, and then begin to play and sing.

**Listen**

This is also a very good way to practise performing.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote the words and music of this song?**
A: Qiao Yu wrote the words and Liu Chi wrote the music.

**Q: Which year's film was it a song from?**
A: 1955.

**Q: What accompaniment can the left hand use?**
A: Broken chords.

**Q: What if the left hand is too hard?**
A: Start with simple block chords.

**Q: How is this song best played?**
A: You can sing while you play.
