macdowell-to-a-wild-rose-op51-1896.body:
To a Wild Rose is the first piece of the American composer Edward MacDowell's 1896 piano suite Woodland Sketches, Op. 51. The piece is very short, in F major and slow. The right hand plays a plain, gentle melody, and the left hand supports it softly from below with just a few chords. It has no fast, showy passages, yet it tests control of touch: the sound must be soft, the phrases connected, and the dynamics should not suddenly become heavy. Many learners treat it as a small piece for practising "singing softly". Because the material is simple, practice is better spent on touch, pedalling and the rise and fall of the phrases, rather than adding extra touches.

## What Kind of Work Is Woodland Sketches

Woodland Sketches is a set of short pieces for piano by MacDowell, ten in all, Op. 51, completed in 1896.

Each has a title connected with a little wood, a small animal or a plant, and To a Wild Rose comes first.

The whole set does not pursue grand technique, and is more like a group of musical sketches that you can leaf through slowly.

## Pedal Sparingly and Cleanly

Because the harmony does not change in complicated ways, the pedal can help join the melody, but it should not be pressed too deep or held too long.

Usually change the pedal when the chord changes, letting the sound of the previous chord clear away.

At the ending in particular, clear the resonance cleanly, so that the last phrase comes to rest in quiet.

## Why It Is Called To a Wild Rose

The title compares this little piece to a wild rose growing outdoors: the colour is not strong, but it is quiet and complete.

There is no real scent of flowers or specific description of a field in the score, so you have to approach the image through soft sound and natural phrases.

When you play, there is no need to "act out" a flower in an exaggerated way. Playing the melody cleanly and smoothly is already very good.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen to Your Touch in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether the right hand makes any individual notes too heavy, and whether the left hand covers the melody.

You can also ask your teacher to try two ways of changing the pedal on the same phrase to see which is cleaner.

From one very short piece, practise making the sound lighter and finishing the phrase.

## The Right-Hand Melody Should Be Like Saying a Sentence Softly

The right-hand melody has few notes, so each note should follow on from the one before it, rather than being dropped one by one.

The high point of a phrase can be a little brighter and then drawn back, like the natural stress of speech.

If one note keeps sticking out, first play that beat more slowly and more softly, then return to the original tempo.

## When to Learn It

To a Wild Rose has few notes, and players of intermediate level can begin it.

Its difficulty is not speed but control: the same few chords, played too heavily, lose the feeling of this "wild rose".

You can also use it as a daily piece for practising a light touch: practise the phrases slowly first, then play it through at the slow tempo written in the score. You can play the same phrase three times in a row and compare which time the sound is most even and most connected.

## Summary of To a Wild Rose

To a Wild Rose is the first piece of MacDowell's Woodland Sketches, Op. 51, of 1896, in F major. It is short and slow, with a plain melody and a simple accompaniment, and what it needs most is a soft touch, clear phrases and clean pedalling.

It is suited to practising "singing softly", rather than to practising speed.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your touch and pedalling.

**Listen**
- The first piece of MacDowell's Woodland Sketches, Op. 51, of 1896
- In F major, slow and very short
- Plain melody and simple accompaniment
- Good for practising a soft touch and phrasing

## The Gentle Colour of F Major

F major has one flat, and often gives a feeling of being fairly warm and settled.

This piece stays almost all the time in bright, simple harmony, with no long tense passages.

Precisely because the material is simple, even a slightly heavy touch is especially noticeable.

![Watercolour of an open grand piano in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdi2lrr-ivxir.webp)

## Who MacDowell Was

Edward MacDowell was an American composer and pianist of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

He lived and worked in both America and Europe, and wrote piano pieces, symphonic works and songs.

In his piano miniatures, he often uses a short piece to describe a picture or a mood.

## The Left Hand Should Only Support, Not Take Over

The left-hand chords should be neat and quiet, almost like laying a soft cushion under the melody.

The bass note can be a little clearer, while the chords above it should be lighter still.

**Order of practice**

When putting the two hands together, first listen to whether the right hand can be heard all the way through, and only then adjust the weight of the left hand.

## FAQ

**Q: Which collection does To a Wild Rose come from?**
A: MacDowell's 1896 piano suite Woodland Sketches, Op. 51, where it is the first piece.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: F major.

**Q: How many pieces are there in this set?**
A: Ten.

**Q: What is its main difficulty?**
A: Not speed, but controlling the sound so that it is soft and connected.

**Q: How should the left hand be played?**
A: Neatly and quietly supporting the melody, without covering the right hand.

liszt-un-sospiro-concert-etude-d-flat.body:
Un sospiro ("A Sigh") is the third of Liszt's Three Concert Studies, written between about 1845 and 1849 and published in 1849, in D-flat major. In it, the two hands take turns playing flowing arpeggios across the keyboard, and the melody notes are "handed" from one hand to the other, with the left hand sometimes crossing over the right to play a high note. The Italian title is said not to have been written by Liszt at the outset, but added in later editions. It is a classic piece for practising arpeggios, hand crossing and bringing out a melody.

## The Cadenza-like Passages in the Middle

The middle of the piece has several fast, flourish-like passages that sound like improvised ornaments.

**Slow down a little**

These figures do not need to be played in strict time, and you can take a little freedom.

But keep them light, like a gust of wind passing by, rather than pounding the keys.

![Cyberpunk illustration of a person in futuristic clothes playing a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a crystal synthesiser in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbi48q8-oc1g5.webp)

## Playing the Melody with the Thumb

Many of the melody notes are played with the thumb, which should use the weight of the arm to sound full and clear.

The other fingers play the arpeggios lightly, so they never cover the melody.

This way of singing the melody with the thumb is a hallmark of piano technique in Liszt's day.

## Pedalling in Un sospiro

The flowing arpeggios need the sustain pedal to join the sound into one stream.

But when the melody or harmony changes, change the pedal promptly so the sound does not become muddy.

Imagine the arpeggios as water in the background and the melody as light on the surface: the pedal keeps the water continuous without blurring the light.

## The Climax and the Return

At the climax, the melody is played in octaves and thick chords, with great force.

After the climax, the music slowly calms and the opening melody returns.

The last D-flat major chord falls softly, and the whole piece ends on one long exhale.

## A Melody That Gets Handed Around

As the arpeggios flow, the melody notes are played sometimes by the right hand and sometimes by the left.

At times the left hand has to cross over the right to play a melody note in the high register.

In this way, the melody is like a thread passed back and forth between the two hands.

## Where the Title Comes From

Today each of the three pieces has an Italian title, and the third is called "Un sospiro".

But research suggests these titles were not written by Liszt at the start, and were added in later published editions.

Even so, the name "Un sospiro" suits the mood of the music so well that it has stuck.

## Ask Your Teacher to Look at the Hand Crossing in Your Lesson

You can play for Teacher Aum in your lesson and ask whether your hand-crossing movements are relaxed and well timed.

You can also ask your teacher to listen from the side and judge whether the volume difference between melody and arpeggios is big enough.

Through this piece, you can feel two hands working together to sing a single melody.

## Summary of Un sospiro

Un sospiro is the third of Liszt's Three Concert Studies, written between about 1845 and 1849 and published in 1849, in D-flat major. Its Italian title is said to have been added in later editions. The hands take turns playing flowing arpeggios, the melody is passed from hand to hand, often with the thumb, and the left hand sometimes crosses over the right. The middle has free, flourish-like passages, the climax uses octaves and chords, and the ending is quiet.

Prepare the hand crossings in advance with a relaxed arm, change the pedal with the harmony, and try playing the melody alone first. It is usually an intermediate to advanced piece, so it is best to get ordinary arpeggios solid first.

You can ask Teacher Aum to look at your hand crossings.

## Arpeggios Passed Between the Hands

From beginning to end, the piece is almost all flowing arpeggios played by the two hands in turn.

The left hand plays an upward arpeggio, the right hand picks up the next one, and the sound is as continuous as ripples on water.

The two hands must fit together so seamlessly that it sounds like one hand playing.

## The Hand Crossing in Un sospiro

The movement of the left hand over the right must be prepared early, not left to the last moment.

Keep the arm relaxed, and when you move, let the wrist lead the hand rather than stretching with the fingers.

Practise the crossing slowly first, and speed up once it is comfortable.

## The Three Concert Studies

Liszt wrote the Three Concert Studies in the late 1840s, and they were published in 1849.

All three are both studies for developing technique and pieces that can be performed in concert.

Un sospiro is the third of them, and the most often performed of the three.

## Who Concert Studies Suit

The two hands must fit together exactly and the hand must stretch wide, so Un sospiro is generally learned at an intermediate to advanced stage.

But its notes follow clear patterns, and once you know the arpeggio shapes it is not as hard as it sounds.

It is best to get ordinary arpeggios solid before learning this piece.

- The third of Liszt's Three Concert Studies
- Written between about 1845 and 1849
- In D-flat major, with the hands alternating arpeggios
- The melody is played by the left and right hands in turn

## Play the Melody Alone First

When practising this piece, you can first pick out all the melody notes and play them on their own.

That makes the direction of the melody clear, so when you add the arpeggios you know which notes to bring out.

**In short**

You can also hum the melody softly while playing the arpeggios.

## FAQ

**Q: Which of Liszt's collections does Un sospiro belong to?**
A: The Three Concert Studies, as the third piece.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: D-flat major.

**Q: In which year was it published?**
A: 1849.

**Q: How is the melody played?**
A: It is played by the left and right hands in turn, often with the thumb, and sometimes the left hand crosses over the right.

**Q: Did Liszt write the title "Un sospiro" at the start?**
A: Research suggests it was added in later published editions.

liszt-1840-london-recital.body:
Today we are used to a single pianist performing an entire concert alone, but in the first half of the nineteenth century, concerts usually had several performers taking the stage in turn. Liszt was one of the important figures who promoted the "recital" format, and his 1840 performance at the Hanover Square Rooms in London is often considered an early example of the word "recital" being used for a solo piano concert. It is also recorded that he often placed the piano sideways so that the audience could see the performer's profile, an arrangement that later became common practice.

## Playing from Memory

Liszt was also one of the earlier pianists to play from memory in concerts, which was also a new practice at the time.

His contemporary Clara Schumann was also known for playing from memory.

Playing from memory lets the performer concentrate more on communicating with the music and the audience, and it later became a common habit in recitals.

## A Whole Performance by One Person

In a recital, the pianist has to carry the whole performance alone, which takes great stamina, memory and expressiveness.

With his brilliant technique and strong personal charisma, Liszt proved that one pianist could hold an audience for a whole evening.

This format was gradually adopted by other pianists, and became the most common form of piano concert today.

## Who Was Liszt?

Franz Liszt was born in 1811 and died in 1886, and was one of the most influential pianists and composers of the nineteenth century.

His playing technique was outstanding, and he toured all over Europe, drawing large audiences.

Besides performing, he also composed a great many piano works and arranged many works by other composers.

- In the first half of the nineteenth century, concerts often had several performers in turn
- Liszt was an important figure in promoting the recital format
- His 1840 performance in London is often seen as an early example
- It is recorded that he often placed the piano sideways facing the audience

## Planning the Programme

Liszt's recital programmes often included his own works, his arrangements and works by other composers.

His arrangements brought melodies from operas and symphonies to the piano, giving more people the chance to hear this music.

This rich way of planning a programme also influenced the choice of repertoire in later piano recitals.

## The Influence Today

Today, when we go to hear a piano recital, a pianist sits at a piano placed sideways and plays a whole programme from memory. These habits are all linked to the changes of Liszt's time.

Of course, many other pianists and musicians also contributed to the formation of these practices, and it was not the work of one person.

Knowing this history gives us more to appreciate when we enjoy a concert.

## Placing the Piano Sideways

It is recorded that when Liszt performed, he often placed the piano sideways, so that the audience could see his profile and the movements of his hands.

Before this, there was no uniform custom for placing the piano, and sometimes the performer had his back to the audience.

Placing the piano sideways lets the audience both hear the music and watch the playing, and it later became common practice at concerts.

## The Word "Recital"

The English word "recital" originally meant "reciting" or "telling".

In 1840, Liszt's performance at the Hanover Square Rooms in London was advertised as a "pianoforte recital", which is often considered an early example of this word being used for a solo piano concert.

Different sources describe the details of this history a little differently, but Liszt's role in promoting the recital format is generally recognised.

## Go to a Live Recital

You can look for some of Liszt's piano works to listen to, such as some of his arrangements or his original piano miniatures.

You can also go to a live piano recital and feel the appeal of one pianist carrying a whole performance alone.

As you listen, you will better appreciate the significance of the recital format.

## Inspiration for Student Concerts

For people learning the piano, the recital format also offers some inspiration, such as how to plan the order of a programme and how to stay focused throughout.

In a student concert, each person usually plays only one or two pieces, but you can also think about how to give your performance a complete beginning and end.

As these experiences build up, one day you might hold a small recital of your own.

## Concerts at That Time

In the first half of the nineteenth century, a concert usually did not have just one performer.

The programme often had singers, instrumentalists and small orchestras taking the stage in turn, with a rich variety of content.

For one pianist to play a whole concert alone was rare at the time.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with an elevated light-rail line](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1nz17-jo371.webp)

## A Note of Caution

Historical details often have different versions, and different sources may describe Liszt's performances and habits differently.

If you want to find out more, you can consult reliable biographies and music history books.

What matters is understanding how the recital format gradually took shape and what influence it has on concerts today.

## FAQ

**Q: What were concerts like in the first half of the nineteenth century?**
A: They usually had several performers taking the stage in turn.

**Q: What is Liszt's connection to the recital?**
A: He was one of the important figures who promoted this format.

**Q: What happened in 1840?**
A: His performance in London is often seen as an early example of "recital" being used for a solo piano concert.

**Q: Why did he place the piano sideways?**
A: It is recorded that this let the audience see the performer's profile and movements.

**Q: Did he play from memory?**
A: He was one of the earlier pianists to play from memory.

**Q: Are all these details certain?**
A: Different sources describe them differently, so you can consult reliable biographies.

madrigal-renaissance-secular-part-song.body:
The madrigal is a secular vocal form that arose in Italy in the sixteenth century. It is usually written for four to six voices, with one singer to each part. Its words are mostly Italian love poems or lyric poems, such as those of Petrarch. Composers often used the music to paint the meaning of the words in fine detail, binding words and music closely together. The madrigal developed in Italy for nearly a century, and Arcadelt, Marenzio, Gesualdo, Monteverdi and others all wrote them. At the end of the sixteenth century it reached England, where Morley, Weelkes and others wrote many English madrigals.

## Chat with Your Teacher About Madrigals

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the history of the madrigal and the differences between Italian and English madrigals.

**Little tip**

With a four-voice madrigal, you can play two lines yourself and ask your teacher to play the other two, which is a kind of choral singing too.

Through the madrigal, discover the secular music of the Renaissance.

![An illustration of a colourful grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwae0pmf-zqhzq.webp)

## The Madrigal in Brief

The madrigal is a secular vocal form that arose in Italy in the sixteenth century, sung at home and at gatherings. It is usually written for four to six voices, one singer to a part, who sit around together reading from separate part-books. The words are mostly poems by Petrarch and others, with words and music closely joined. Arcadelt published "Il bianco e dolce cigno" in 1539, Marenzio wrote several hundred madrigals, and Gesualdo used bold chromatic harmony.

Monteverdi's madrigal books move from unaccompanied polyphony to accompanied solo song. In 1588 a collection of Italian madrigals with English words was published in London. Morley's madrigals are light and lively, Weelkes was skilled at painting the words, English madrigals often have a "fa la la" refrain, and madrigals alternate between imitation and chordal writing. At the piano you can play two voices with one hand.

You can chat about the history of the madrigal with Teacher Aum.

## Singing with Friends

The madrigal was originally written for friends to sing together.

If you have a few friends who love to sing, you can try a simple English madrigal.

You can also sing one part yourself while the other parts are played on the piano.

## Marenzio and Gesualdo

In the later sixteenth century, Luca Marenzio wrote several hundred madrigals, with brilliant skill.

The madrigals of Carlo Gesualdo are very distinctive, using a great deal of bold chromatic harmony.

Gesualdo's harmony sounded extraordinarily strange at the time, and it still surprises people today.

## One Singer to a Part

The madrigal is usually written for four to six voices, with each part sung by just one person.

This is different from a large chorus; it is more like a small vocal ensemble.

The singers often sat around a table, each reading from their own part, and sang together.

## Fa La La

Many English madrigals have a "fa la la" refrain, which has no particular meaning.

The refrain is light and rhythmic, and often has several voices chasing one another.

It is great fun to sing and makes the music livelier.

## Poetry and Music

Many madrigal texts came from Italian poets, such as Petrarch in the fourteenth century.

Composers took the meaning of the poem seriously and used music to express every line and every word.

The close union of words and music is what makes the madrigal so appealing.

## Imitation and Harmony in the Madrigal

Madrigals are written in roughly two ways. One is a game of chase, where the same melodic phrase appears in turn from voice to voice.

The other has all the voices singing the same rhythm, forming clear chords.

The two styles alternate, so the music is both interwoven and clear in its words.

## Arcadelt's White Swan

Jacques Arcadelt was a composer of the first half of the sixteenth century who wrote many madrigals.

His madrigal "Il bianco e dolce cigno", published in 1539, was extremely popular at the time.

This madrigal has a smooth melody and clear harmony, and is a good way to get to know the style of the madrigal.

## Arrival in England

In 1588, a collection of Italian madrigals with English words was published in London.

The collection was very popular and made the English fond of the madrigal.

After that, English composers began writing madrigals in English too.

## Monteverdi's Madrigal Books

Monteverdi published several books of madrigals over his lifetime, and his style kept changing.

His early madrigals are traditional unaccompanied polyphony, while later ones add instrumental accompaniment and solo voices.

From his madrigal books you can see music moving from the Renaissance towards the Baroque.

## Songs for the World, Not the Church

The madrigal differs from the motet sung in church: it is a secular song, sung at home and at gatherings.

Its words speak of love, nature and human feeling rather than religious subjects.

This made the madrigal popular with city dwellers and music lovers of the time.

## English Madrigal Composers

Thomas Morley was an important composer of English madrigals, and his madrigals are light and lively.

The madrigals of Thomas Weelkes often paint the words vividly in music.

English madrigals are simpler and merrier than Italian ones, and suit amateur singers.

## The Madrigal at the Piano

The madrigal was written for voices, but it can be moved to the keyboard, where you can still trace each line one by one.

You can play two voices with one hand: first the upper two, then the lower two, and finally put them together.

**Remember this**

This helps you understand how the voices fit together and how the harmony changes.

- A secular vocal form that arose in sixteenth-century Italy
- Usually four to six voices, one singer to a part
- Words mostly Italian lyric poems
- Reached England at the end of the sixteenth century

## FAQ

**Q: In which century did the madrigal arise?**
A: The sixteenth century, in Italy.

**Q: How many voices does a madrigal usually have?**
A: Four to six, one singer to a part.

**Q: Which of Arcadelt's madrigals was popular?**
A: "Il bianco e dolce cigno", in 1539.

**Q: What is distinctive about Gesualdo's madrigals?**
A: Bold chromatic harmony.

**Q: What refrain do English madrigals often have?**
A: "Fa la la".

liszt-waldesrauschen-concert-etude.body:
Waldesrauschen (Forest Murmurs) is a concert study by Franz Liszt that uses fast, light figuration to come close to the continuous rustling of wind passing through a forest. Unlike some shorter pieces that also depict wind or leaves, it is often technically denser, and its layers of sound must stay clear over a very long stretch of motion. When learning it, it is safer to start at a slower tempo, getting the figuration and fingering even, and then gradually bring back the feeling of "the forest sounding", than to chase a very light, very fast demonstration from the start. When listening, first notice whether the continuously rolling notes stay round, and then look for the longer song that surfaces now and then. If the rolling turns into a blur of light spots, with no phrases or bass foundation to be heard, slow down and separate the layers again. The goal of practice is to make technique serve the sound, not to play every note heavily to show how hard it is. In daily practice, take the densest passage and practise it slowly, and also leave one run-through for a fuller line, checking that the layers still hold over a long distance. If only a blur of light remains, slow down and separate the bass and the longer song again. Once the technique is sorted out, still listen to the sound as a forest, not as a string of difficulties.

**Common pitfalls**
- A concert study by Liszt that depicts the sound of wind through a forest
- Within fast, light figuration, audible layers and phrases must remain
- The technique is fairly dense, so practise slowly and evenly first, then gradually speed up
- In practice, let technique serve the sound, and do not use a very heavy touch to show difficulty

## How to Step Back When You Tense Up

As soon as the arm and wrist stiffen, the rolling immediately turns hard.

Do not keep speeding up. Make the movement smaller and make the figuration round again at a slower tempo.

Once you find the position where you are not stiff, nudge the tempo up just a little.

## The Song That Rises to the Surface

Within the rustling, some longer notes often join into phrases.

First pick these notes out on their own, make sure they can be sung, and then put them back into the rolling.

If every note is equally loud, the forest is still there, but the song is gone.

## How the Rustle in the Title Comes About

Continuously rolling figuration is the most direct way to approach the sound of leaves.

The notes must be light and even to sound like wind, not like a string of struck beads.

You can first listen once and judge only whether this wash of sound keeps moving and whether it ever suddenly catches in the middle.

## The Bass and the Pedal

The bass gives this wash of sound a floor: keep it clear, but do not hit it on every beat.

Pedal shallowly and change often, or the leaves will blur into a mist.

First play it once with less pedal, then decide which places really need the sustain to join the sound.

![Watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdk4mm1-oczl6.webp)

## Keeping It Apart from Other "Wind" Pieces

There is more than one piano piece depicting leaves or wind, but this one has its own demands in density and length.

When reading the score, confirm the composer and the title, and do not simply apply the practice approach of another, shorter and lighter piece.

The layers and pedalling habits of each piece should still be decided from this piece's own score.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen for Layers in the Rustle

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your rolling is even, and whether the longer song and the bass are being covered.

If a passage turns hard as soon as you speed up, you can also ask your teacher to help you make the movement smaller and closer to the keys.

With this study evoking a forest, practise keeping dense figuration audible in separate layers.

## Studies and Concerts

It serves to train even, fast touch, and it can also be heard as a complete concert piece.

So it is not enough to pull out the difficult passages and practise only those: you must also keep the layers of sound steady across the whole piece.

Each day you can take a dense passage and practise it slowly, and also set aside time to play through a fuller line.

## What to Remember About Waldesrauschen

This is a Liszt concert study that evokes the sound of leaves: the figuration is dense, yet the layers must stay clear.

In practice, go from slow to fast, pick out the song within the rolling, pedal shallowly and keep your movements free of stiffness.

When listening, first judge whether the rustle is round, then check whether the phrases and the bass are still there.

## FAQ

**Q: Who is the composer of this piece, and what genre is it?**
A: It is a concert study by Franz Liszt.

**Q: What kind of sound is it mainly trying to approach?**
A: The continuous rustling of wind passing through a forest.

**Q: Why is it not enough to practise only the difficult passages?**
A: You also need to keep the layers of sound steady across the whole piece, not just solve a few especially awkward spots.

**Q: How do you find the melody within the rolling?**
A: Pick out the longer notes, join them into phrases, and then put them back into the figuration to check they can still be heard.

**Q: What should you do when it turns hard or stiff?**
A: Slow down, make the movement smaller, and once it is round again, speed up.

lupine-flower-song-1989-film.body:
"Lupin Flower" (Lu Bing Hua) is the theme song of the 1989 Taiwanese film of the same name, composed by Chen Yang with words by Yao Qian. The film is adapted from a novel by the writer Zhong Zhaozheng and tells the story of a child who grows up on a tea plantation and has a great talent for painting. The lupin is a small flower. In Taiwan's tea gardens it is planted to fertilise the tea bushes, and the song uses it as a metaphor for those who give quietly and watch over children. The melody is gentle and heartfelt, and well suited to the piano for practising a singing melody and soft accompaniment.

## A Singing Right Hand

The right-hand melody should be smooth and singing, as if it were being sung.

Let each phrase end softly, like a singer taking a breath after a line.

You can sing the melody first to find the breath of the phrases, and then play it on the piano.

## The Level of Lupin Flower

The easy piano version of Lupin Flower suits players at a beginner-to-intermediate level, with one or two years of lessons.

If chords and ornaments are added to the melody, it becomes a little harder.

You can choose a simple or a richer version according to your own level.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with the elevated light rail](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbii6z9-bncpv.webp)

## Summary of Lupin Flower

"Lupin Flower" is the theme song of the 1989 Taiwanese film of the same name, composed by Chen Yang with words by Yao Qian. The film is adapted from a novel Zhong Zhaozheng published in the early 1960s, about a child with a talent for painting on a tea plantation. The lupin is a small flower of the legume family, planted among the tea bushes; after it fades it is turned into the soil as fertiliser, and the song uses it as a metaphor for elders who quietly watch over children.

The melody is gentle and moves mostly by step, with a calm verse and a chorus that rises. In the piano version the left hand plays even broken chords and the right hand must be smooth and singing. The high point of the chorus can be played full using the weight of the arm. The easy version suits beginner-to-intermediate players, and it is lovely to play for elders.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the breathing of your phrases.

## A Small Flower in the Tea Gardens

The lupin is a small flower of the legume family, with purple, yellow or white blooms.

In Taiwan's tea gardens, lupins are often planted between the tea bushes.

After the flowers fade, they are turned into the soil as fertiliser for the tea.

## Chen Yang and Yao Qian

The song was composed by Chen Yang, who has written music for many films and television dramas.

The words are by Yao Qian, who later wrote the lyrics of many popular songs.

Their collaboration, "Lupin Flower", became a widely loved song.

## A Gentle Melody

The melody of Lupin Flower is gentle and heartfelt, with a range that is not too wide.

The melody moves mostly by step, with an occasional leap that makes the emotion stronger.

The whole song is like speaking softly, or like remembering.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Phrases of Lupin Flower in Your Lesson

You can play for Teacher Aum in your lesson and ask whether the phrases of the melody breathe, and whether the verse and chorus contrast.

Whether the accompaniment covers the melody is often clearer to a listener than to the player.

From one film theme song, feel the warmth in music.

## The Piano Accompaniment of Lupin Flower

In the piano arrangement, the left hand often plays broken chords, giving the melody a soft, flowing background.

The broken chords should be even and gentle, and must not cover the right-hand melody.

Change the pedal with the harmony so that the accompaniment stays connected.

**Common pitfalls**
- Theme song of the 1989 Taiwanese film Lupin Flower
- Music by Chen Yang, words by Yao Qian
- The film is adapted from a novel by Zhong Zhaozheng
- Lupins in the tea gardens serve as fertiliser for the tea bushes

## The Verse and Chorus of Lupin Flower

The song has a verse and a chorus. The verse is fairly calm, as if telling a story.

The melody of the chorus rises, and the emotion becomes stronger.

When playing, keep the verse soft and let the chorus grow a little, but not too loud.

## The Film and the Novel

Lupin Flower began as a novel the writer Zhong Zhaozheng published in the early 1960s.

In 1989 the novel was adapted into a film of the same name and released in Taiwan.

The film tells the story of a child who grows up on a tea plantation and has a great talent for painting, but does not receive the recognition he deserves.

## The High Point of the Chorus

The chorus has a high point in the melody, where the emotion of the whole song is pushed very high.

When you reach it, you can use the weight of the arm to make the note fuller.

But after the high point, let it come back slowly, rather than getting suddenly weaker.

## Playing for Elders

The words of Lupin Flower are about elders watching over children.

At a family gathering, playing this song for the elders is a very thoughtful gift.

You can also sing softly along with your family while you play.

## The Flower Metaphor

The song uses the lupin as a metaphor for those who give quietly, such as the elders at home.

Just as the lupin turns into nourishment so that the tea bushes grow better, elders quietly watch over the growth of their children.

This metaphor is plain and sincere, and moves many people who hear it.

## FAQ

**Q: Which film is Lupin Flower the theme song of?**
A: The 1989 Taiwanese film of the same name, Lupin Flower.

**Q: Who wrote the music and who wrote the words?**
A: Chen Yang composed it and Yao Qian wrote the words.

**Q: Whose novel is the film adapted from?**
A: The writer Zhong Zhaozheng.

**Q: What are lupins used for in the tea gardens?**
A: After the flowers fade, they are turned into the soil as fertiliser for the tea bushes.

**Q: What does the song use the lupin as a metaphor for?**
A: Elders who quietly watch over children.

mark-identical-and-nearly-identical-bars.body:
A new piece in front of you, several pages of dense notes, can make it feel as if it will take a long time to learn. But look closely and you will see that many pieces contain a lot of repeated material: some bars are exactly the same, and some differ by only a note or two. Before learning a new piece, spend a few minutes finding these identical and nearly identical bars and marking them, and you will discover that the part you really have to "learn from zero" is not that large. The nearly identical places are the traps that need particular care.

## Ask your teacher to look with you

The first time you use this method, you can ask Teacher Aum to look for the repeats with you in a lesson.

**A different angle**

A teacher can point out repeats that are hard to spot, such as transposed repeats or similarities in rhythm.

Once you have learned how, you can analyse new pieces on your own.

## Repetition is normal in music

Many musical works are built on repetition and variation.

When a theme appears, it often comes back later, sometimes exactly the same and sometimes slightly changed.

The chorus of a pop song and the recapitulation of a classical work are both examples of repetition.

## Nearly identical bars

Some bars look very similar but differ by one or two notes, or have a slightly changed rhythm.

You can use a different mark for these bars, such as "A′", meaning similar to A but with a change.

Use a pencil to circle the few notes that are different, as a reminder to pay attention.

## Look first, do not rush to play

When you get a new piece, do not rush to start playing from the first bar.

Spend a few minutes looking through the whole piece from beginning to end, noticing which places look alike.

This step may seem like a waste of time, but it actually saves a great deal of practice time later.

## Transposed repeats

Sometimes a passage comes back at a different pitch, with the same shape but higher or lower overall.

You can mark these transposed repeats too, for example by writing "A a fourth higher".

The shape of your hand can stay the same, and only its position changes.

## Identical bars

If two bars have exactly the same notes, rhythm and fingering, they are identical bars.

You can mark them with the same letter or colour, for example both marked "A".

Once you have learned one of them, you have learned the other too.

## Use coloured pencils

You can mark with pencils of different colours, for example blue for identical bars and red for nearly identical ones.

Colours stand out more than letters, and you can see them at a glance.

Remember to use pencil, so you can rub it out or change it later.

- Before learning a new piece, find the repeated bars
- Mark identical bars with one kind of mark
- Mark nearly identical bars with another kind of mark and circle what is different
- The truly new material is less than you think

![Collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9h713-qvfbm.webp)

## Summary: marking repeated bars

Repetition is normal in music. Before learning a new piece, spend a few minutes looking it over and find the identical and nearly identical bars. Mark identical bars with the same mark, and nearly identical bars with a different mark, circling what is different.

The nearly identical places are the traps, so compare and practise them separately. Transposed repeats and repeats of phrases and sections can be marked too. Count how much new material there is, and learn the new material and the changes first.

This kind of analysis is also very helpful for memorising. You can mark with coloured pencils, and the first time you can ask Teacher Aum to look for repeats with you.

## Practise by comparing

For nearly identical bars, you can put them side by side and practise them by comparison.

First play the version that appears first, then the version with the change, and alternate a few times.

Let both your hands and your ears clearly feel the difference between the two.

## Help with memorising

Finding the repeated structure is also very helpful for memorising.

If you remember which places repeat and which places change, you have a clear map when you play from memory.

In performance, you are also less likely to "jump to the wrong track" at a repeat.

## Repeated phrases and sections

Besides bars, you can look for larger units of repetition, such as whole phrases or sections.

Many pieces have an ABA structure, in which the third part is basically the same as the first.

Marking these larger structures gives you a clear picture of the whole piece.

## Learn the new material first

After marking, you can concentrate first on the new material and on the changes within the nearly identical bars.

For the identical parts, learning them once is enough.

Dividing up your practice time this way is more efficient.

## Count how much new material there is

After marking, count how much of the piece truly needs to be learned from scratch.

You will often find that in a piece that looks very long, the new material is only a part.

This gives you more confidence to start learning the piece.

## Nearly identical means a trap

Places that are nearly identical are often easier to get wrong than places that are completely different.

This is because the hands habitually play the way they did the first time and ignore the one or two notes that change.

**Watch the details**

So these places need particular care, and you should take them out and practise them by comparison.

## FAQ

**Q: What should I do first before learning a new piece?**
A: Find the identical and nearly identical bars.

**Q: How do I mark nearly identical bars?**
A: Use a different mark and circle the notes that are different.

**Q: Why are nearly identical places a trap?**
A: The hands habitually play the way they did the first time.

**Q: Which part should I learn first?**
A: The new material and the changes.

**Q: What is this kind of analysis helpful for?**
A: Memorising.

liszt-hears-paganini-paris-1832.body:
In April 1832, the twenty-year-old Liszt heard a concert by the Italian violinist Paganini in Paris. Paganini's astonishing technique and stage charisma deeply shook the young pianist. It is recorded that Liszt then made up his mind to reach on the piano the level that Paganini had reached on the violin, and put in a great deal of practice. Later he wrote a set of piano studies based on Paganini's works, published in 1838 and revised in 1851 as the Grandes études de Paganini, of which the third is La Campanella (The Bell).

## Paris in 1832

In 1832, Paganini came to Paris to give concerts, which was a big event at the time.

**Summary**

In April, the twenty-year-old Liszt went to hear him perform.

By then Liszt was already a pianist with some reputation, but in Paganini he saw an entirely new possibility.

## Paganini the Violinist

Niccolò Paganini was an Italian violinist and composer, born in 1782 and died in 1840.

He was famous for his astonishing violin technique, and could play many passages that were then considered impossible.

His concerts caused a sensation all over Europe, and audiences were often stunned by his playing.

## Learning from Other Instruments

Liszt drew inspiration from a violinist, which also reminds us that piano learners can learn from other instruments.

Listening to a violin, a flute or a singer can help us think about phrasing, breathing and tone colour.

The strengths of different instruments can often give new ideas to piano playing.

![Cyberpunk illustration of a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa574kp-rbcri.webp)

## Summary of Liszt and Paganini

In April 1832, the twenty-year-old Liszt heard Paganini's concert in Paris, was deeply moved, and resolved to reach the same heights on the piano.

He later wrote piano studies based on Paganini's works, published in 1838 and revised in 1851 as the Grandes études de Paganini, of which the third is La Campanella.

This story reminds us that a good performance can inspire people, and that technique must serve the music.

## How to Practise Technique

Liszt is said to have spent many hours every day practising scales, arpeggios, octaves and all kinds of technical exercises.

An ordinary learner does not need to practise for as long as he did, but setting aside a little time each day for technique is very helpful.

When practising technique, also listen carefully, and pay attention to whether the sound is even and whether you are relaxed.

## Changed by One Performance

This story shows that a good performance can deeply influence a person.

Liszt heard one concert, and from then on it changed what he sought in the piano.

When you have the chance, go and sit in a concert hall. Perhaps one evening's performance will change how you think about the piano.

## Listen to the Original and the Arrangement

You can first listen to Paganini's original violin work, and then listen to Liszt's piano study.

Compare the two, and see how Liszt turned the effects of the violin into something for the piano.

This kind of listening can help us understand the relationship between arranging and composing.

## The Resolve After Listening

It is recorded that after hearing Paganini's concert, Liszt was deeply stirred.

He resolved to do on the piano what Paganini had done on the violin, and push piano technique to new heights.

Over the next few years, he spent a great deal of time every day practising technique and studying all kinds of new ways of playing.

**Practice order**
- In April 1832, Liszt heard Paganini in Paris
- Liszt was twenty at the time
- From then on he was determined to raise his piano technique
- Revised in 1851 as the Grandes études de Paganini

## The Paganini Studies

Later, Liszt wrote a set of piano studies based on Paganini's violin works, published in 1838.

These studies were extremely difficult, and in 1851 Liszt revised them into an easier version to play, called the Grandes études de Paganini.

The set has six pieces in all, and is still an important repertoire for pianists to show off their technique.

## Technique and Music

Liszt pursued brilliant technique, but his aim was not just showing off.

He hoped to use technique to expand the expressive power of the piano, so that the piano could express richer feelings and colours.

This is also something we should remember when we practise technique: technique serves the music.

## From Violin to Piano

Paganini's techniques were designed for the violin, such as fast bouncing bowing, double stops and harmonics, and they cannot be copied directly onto the piano.

Liszt had to think about how to achieve similar effects in a piano way.

He tried large leaps, fast repeated notes, wide arpeggios and other kinds of writing, giving the piano a brilliance it had never had before.

## A Pioneer of the Recital

Liszt later became a very popular pianist in Europe, and his concerts were often sold out.

He was also one of the earlier musicians to give "piano recitals", carrying a whole concert alone.

This has some similarity to the image of Paganini standing alone on the stage playing the violin.

## The Study La Campanella

The third of the Grandes études de Paganini is often called La Campanella.

Its melody comes from the final movement of one of Paganini's violin concertos, and the notes repeated again and again in the high register sound like a clear ringing of bells.

Playing this piece needs big leaps for the right hand in the high register, while keeping the sound light and bright.

## FAQ

**Q: When did Liszt hear Paganini?**
A: In April 1832, in Paris.

**Q: How old was Liszt then?**
A: Twenty.

**Q: What did he decide to do after hearing him?**
A: To reach on the piano the level Paganini had reached on the violin.

**Q: What works did he write?**
A: Piano studies based on Paganini's works, revised in 1851 as the Grandes études.

**Q: Which number is La Campanella?**
A: The third of the Grandes études de Paganini.

lisztomania-heine-1844-term.body:
In the 1840s, the pianist Liszt toured all over Europe, and wherever he went the audience's enthusiasm was astonishing: some screamed and fainted for him, and others scrambled to collect the gloves and broken strings he left behind. In 1844, the German poet Heine, in an article reviewing the Paris musical season, gave this phenomenon a name: "Lisztomania" in German, often rendered in Chinese as "Liszt fever". Today the word is often used figuratively for the frenzied adoration of a musician. Heine's tone, however, carried a touch of irony, and he was also thinking about the reasons behind the craze.

- Liszt toured Europe in the 1840s
- Audiences were wildly enthusiastic, collecting gloves and strings
- In 1844 the poet Heine coined the name "Lisztomania"
- Heine's tone carried a touch of irony

## Listening to Music with a Cool Head

Heine's commentary also reminds us that we can keep a calm, thoughtful side when listening to music.

Rather than just following the craze, think about why a piece of music moves you.

Listening this way gives us a deeper understanding of music.

## Think About Stage Presence

Liszt shows us that performing is not only playing the right notes, but also how you communicate with the audience.

When you play for others, think about how to let the audience feel the emotion of the music.

For example, your posture on stage and the stillness before you begin are part of the performance.

## Astonishing Enthusiasm

According to accounts of the time, at Liszt's concerts some listeners were so excited that they screamed, and some even fainted on the spot.

After the concert, people scrambled to collect the gloves and handkerchiefs he left behind, and even strings he had broken while playing.

Some even had his portrait printed on all kinds of small objects.

## Why He Was So Popular

Liszt's playing technique was extraordinary, and he could produce sounds and speeds on the piano that had never been heard before.

He had great charisma on stage, played with passion, and his movements were very expressive.

He also often turned the piano sideways so that the audience could see his profile, which was novel in those days too.

## Talk About Lisztomania with Your Teacher in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about the story of "Lisztomania" and the relationship between performers and audiences.

You can also ask your teacher to pick a lyrical Liszt piece and see whether you could start learning it now.

From one nineteenth-century word, see the birth of the musical star.

## How the Word Is Used Today

Today the word "Lisztomania" is often used figuratively for the frenzied adoration of a musician.

People have found that the kind of craze that music stars cause already existed in the nineteenth century.

This has given people a new understanding of music history.

## The Touring Pianist

From the late 1830s into the 1840s, Liszt toured all over Europe, from Ireland and Portugal in the west to Russia and Turkey in the east.

He is said to have given a great many concerts in those years.

In every city he came to, he caused a sensation.

## From Virtuoso to Composer

In 1847, Liszt ended his touring career and no longer travelled as a solo performer.

He later settled in Weimar, Germany, where he devoted himself to composing and conducting, and taught many students.

And so the age of "Lisztomania" came to an end.

## The Name Heine Gave It

The German poet Heine was living in Paris at the time and often wrote reviews on music and culture for newspapers.

In 1844, in an article reviewing the Paris musical season, he used a new word to describe this phenomenon: Lisztomania.

The word combines "Liszt" with a word meaning "mania".

![Close-up of grand piano keys and a gold-patterned lid in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbjc6nr-thkg4.webp)

## Summary of "Lisztomania"

From the late 1830s into the 1840s, Liszt toured Europe to astonishing enthusiasm: some screamed and fainted, and others collected his gloves, handkerchiefs and broken strings. His concerts in Berlin in the winter of 1841 to 1842 were a high point. In 1844 the poet Heine, then living in Paris, coined the word "Lisztomania" in an article reviewing the Paris musical season, with a tone of irony, and also analysed the reasons.

Liszt had superb technique and strong stage charisma, and turned the piano sideways so that the audience could see his profile. In 1847 he ended his touring and settled in Weimar to compose, conduct and teach. Today the word is often used figuratively for frenzied adoration of a musician, and those with some foundation can begin with a lyrical piece such as the Consolations.

You can chat about this story with Teacher Aum.

## A Tone of Irony

When Heine used this word, his tone carried a touch of irony.

He felt this craze was a bit like an epidemic of collective emotion, hard to understand.

In his article he also tried to analyse why Liszt could cause such a huge reaction.

## The Craze in Berlin

In the winter of 1841 to 1842, Liszt gave a series of concerts in Berlin that caused an especially strong reaction.

It is said that when he left Berlin, many people followed his carriage to see him off.

This Berlin visit is considered a high point of the craze.

## Feeling Liszt at the Piano

Many of Liszt's works are very difficult and need a very high level of technique.

But he also wrote some lyrical, slower pieces, such as the Consolations.

**Remember this**

Those with some foundation can start with these pieces to feel his music.

## FAQ

**Q: Who coined the word "Lisztomania"?**
A: The German poet Heine.

**Q: In which year was it coined?**
A: 1844.

**Q: What did audiences collect at the time?**
A: Liszt's gloves, handkerchiefs and broken strings.

**Q: In which year did Liszt end his touring career?**
A: 1847.

**Q: What was Heine's tone when he used the word?**
A: A touch of irony.

mannheim-orchestra-crescendo-rocket.body:
In the middle of the eighteenth century, the city of Mannheim in south-western Germany had an outstanding orchestra. Led by the violinist and composer Johann Stamitz, it became famous across Europe for its precise playing and delicate dynamic shading, and the composers around it came to be called the "Mannheim School". They often used a long "crescendo" in which the whole orchestra grew slowly from very soft to loud, and listeners are said to have been so thrilled that they rose from their seats. There was also a rapidly rising broken-chord figure known as the "Mannheim rocket". From 1777 to 1778, Mozart spent several months in Mannheim and learned a great deal from this orchestra.

## Why the crescendo was special

Before this, dynamic changes in much music were often sudden, going from soft to loud or from loud to soft.

The Mannheim orchestra's crescendo changed little by little and evenly, which required all the players to work together very well.

The effect was new at the time and left a deep impression on audiences.

## Mozart in Mannheim

From 1777 to 1778, Mozart and his mother stayed in Mannheim for several months on the way to Paris.

He made friends with the orchestra's musicians and heard a lot of their playing.

He is said to have written in his letters that he learned a great deal from this orchestra.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbkkkr1-df922.webp)

## The Mannheim rocket

The Mannheim School also often used a fast, surging melody that climbs up through the notes of a chord.

Like a rocket launching, it is full of energy, and it became known as the "Mannheim rocket".

Similar openings often appear later in the works of Mozart and Beethoven.

## The Mannheim School

The composers who worked around this orchestra were later called the "Mannheim School".

Besides Stamitz, they included Richter, Cannabich and others, as well as Stamitz's two sons.

Their works and style of playing had a great influence on the development of the symphony in Europe at the time.

**Quick tips**
- An orchestra in Mannheim, Germany, in the mid-eighteenth century
- Led by Johann Stamitz
- Famous for its long "crescendo" and the "Mannheim rocket"
- Mozart stayed in Mannheim from 1777 to 1778

## The influence on the symphony

Symphonies of the Mannheim School often have four movements, one of which is a minuet.

This four-movement structure later became the standard form of the Classical symphony.

The symphonies of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven were all influenced by this structure.

## Playing the rocket on the piano

You can also try the Mannheim rocket: with your right hand, play up along the notes of the C major tonic chord, from the low "do" all the way to the high "do".

Play it fast, and let the dynamics go from soft to loud, like a rocket taking off.

Then try the Mannheim sigh: two notes in a group, falling from high to low, with the first note stressed and the second one light.

## Trying the Mannheim crescendo with your teacher in lessons

You can play for Teacher Aum in your lesson and ask whether your crescendo is even and whether there is any place where it suddenly gets louder.

You can also ask your teacher to demonstrate the Mannheim rocket and the Mannheim sigh, and listen to how different their characters are.

From an eighteenth-century orchestra, you can learn to control changes in dynamics.

## The Mannheim sigh

Besides the rocket, the Mannheim School had another common figure, called the "Mannheim sigh".

It is a group of two notes falling from high to low, with the first note stressed and the second light, like a gentle sigh.

This figure gives a melody a soft, wistful flavour.

## Playing a crescendo on the piano

Play a chord repeatedly with both hands, starting so quietly that it is almost inaudible, then push it up little by little.

Take care to add the volume gradually and not to get suddenly louder.

You can count the beats and add a little more every two beats, taking eight or sixteen beats in total to complete it.

## The long crescendo

What the Mannheim orchestra was most famous for was a long "crescendo".

The whole orchestra began with a very soft sound, grew slowly and evenly stronger, and finally reached a very loud sound.

Listeners are said to have been so thrilled by this crescendo that they stood up from their seats.

## Summary of the Mannheim School

In the middle of the eighteenth century, Mannheim in Germany had an orchestra known for its precise playing and delicate dynamics. It was strictly trained by Johann Stamitz, a violinist and composer from Bohemia, and the composers around it, including Stamitz, Richter and Cannabich, were called the "Mannheim School". Its most famous effect was the long crescendo that grew evenly from very soft, which is said to have made listeners stand up in excitement, along with the "Mannheim rocket" that surges quickly up a chord and the "Mannheim sigh" of two notes falling from high to low.

This orchestra was among the first to use the clarinet. Mozart stayed in Mannheim for several months in 1777 to 1778 and later came to love the clarinet. The four-movement structure often used by the Mannheim School influenced the Classical symphony. On the piano you can practise an even crescendo over eight or sixteen beats, and you can play the rocket and sigh figures in C major.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your crescendo.

## Johann Stamitz

The leader of the orchestra was Johann Stamitz, a violinist and composer from Bohemia.

He trained the orchestra very strictly, requiring every player's bowing and dynamics to be uniform.

He also wrote many symphonies for the orchestra and is one of the important composers of the early symphony.

## The Mannheim orchestra

In the middle of the eighteenth century, the city of Mannheim in south-western Germany had an orchestra that was very famous in Europe.

Its players were highly skilled and played together with great precision, and many people praised them.

One English music critic is said to have described it as "an army of generals".

## The arrival of the clarinet

The Mannheim orchestra was one of the first to use the clarinet in a symphony orchestra.

The clarinet's sound is warm and soft, and it added a new colour to the orchestra.

After hearing the clarinet in Mannheim, Mozart came to love the instrument and later wrote many works for it.

## FAQ

**Q: Who led the Mannheim orchestra?**
A: Johann Stamitz.

**Q: What was the Mannheim orchestra's most famous dynamic effect?**
A: A long, even crescendo.

**Q: What is the "Mannheim rocket"?**
A: A melody that surges quickly up along a chord.

**Q: When was Mozart in Mannheim?**
A: From 1777 to 1778.

**Q: Which woodwind instrument did the Mannheim orchestra use early on?**
A: The clarinet.

measure-practice-by-tasks-not-minutes.body:
Many people set their practice goal in time: so many minutes a day. A time goal is simple and clear, but it has a problem: you can spend enough time at the piano without practising what actually needs practice. Sometimes most of the time goes on playing from beginning to end, while the difficult spots stay just as difficult. Another approach is to measure practice by tasks: which few bars to play accurately today, or which passage's fingering to fix in place. When the task is done, the practice has brought real results.

## Combining it with a time goal

Task goals and time goals do not conflict, and you can use them together.

For example, set aside a certain amount of practice time each day and complete a few specific tasks within it.

Time gets you to the piano, and tasks make that time worthwhile.

## What is a task goal

A task goal is a specific thing to be accomplished in one practice session.

For example, "play bars 5 to 8 accurately with the right hand, without looking at the fingering and without mistakes".

When the task is done, it has been a productive practice session.

- Measure practice by tasks, not just time
- Tasks should be specific and checkable
- Completing a task brings results
- Time and tasks can be used together

## The limits of time goals

"So many minutes a day" is a very common goal, and it helps us build the habit of sitting down at the piano.

But when the time is up, it does not mean the practice was effective.

Sometimes we are only repeating what we can already play, or playing absent-mindedly.

## Make tasks specific

The more specific a task is, the easier it is to know whether it is done.

"Learn the new piece well" is too vague, while "play the left-hand leap in bar 12 accurately five times in a row" is very specific.

A specific task also tells us what method to use for practising.

## How many tasks in one session

Each practice session can include two or three tasks, and there is no need for more.

With too many tasks, each one gets only a little practice. With too few, you may finish quickly.

You can adjust according to your time and the difficulty of the piece.

## What if you do not finish

Sometimes a task is harder than expected and is not finished in one session.

This is perfectly normal. You can leave it for the next session, or break the task into smaller pieces.

For example, take a four-bar task and first split it into two bars.

## Tasks should be checkable

A good task can be checked once it is done.

For example, can you play through a passage without stopping, or play it accurately at a certain metronome speed?

When the standard for checking is clear, you will not be left with "I think I got it, but maybe not".

## Setting tasks with your teacher

You can ask Teacher Aum in your lesson to help set the practice tasks for the week.

Your teacher knows your level and can give tasks of suitable difficulty.

At your next lesson, report back to your teacher on how the tasks went.

## Tasks from lesson homework

The content of your tasks can follow the homework your teacher sets.

For example, if your teacher says the fingering in a passage should change, you can make "get this passage comfortable with the new fingering" a task.

This links your practice closely with what you learn in lessons.

## What to do after you finish

If you finish a task early, you can review earlier material or play a piece you like.

You can also think up new tasks for the next session.

There is no need to repeat tasks you have already completed just because the time is not up yet.

## Keeping a record of finished tasks

You can note down in your practice notebook which tasks you finished each day.

At the end of a week, look at how many tasks you completed and you will see your progress clearly.

This kind of record is more satisfying than only noting "how many minutes I practised".

## Summary: measuring practice by tasks

A time goal helps build a habit, but when the time is up it does not mean the practice worked. A task goal is a specific thing to accomplish in one session. Tasks should be specific and checkable, with two or three in each session.

If you finish early, you can review or think up new tasks, and if you do not finish, you can leave it for next time or make it smaller. Tasks and time can be combined, recording finished tasks shows your progress, and tasks for children can be simpler and more fun.

Tasks can come from lesson homework, and do not chase completion at the expense of quality. You can ask Teacher Aum to help set weekly tasks and report back on how they went.

## Do not chase completion alone

When you measure practice by tasks, also pay attention to quality, and do not rush through just to finish.

For example, the standard for "play accurately" should be clear, and it does not count as done if one or two notes are wrong.

While completing the task, also listen to whether the sound and the music are pleasing.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with an elevated light rail](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9fcws-emwrt.webp)

## Tasks for children

Tasks for children can be designed to be simpler and more fun.

For example, "play this line three times, with no mistakes each time", and draw a smiley face for each time completed.

**Slow down**

Parents can help children check whether the task has been completed.

## FAQ

**Q: What are the limits of time goals?**
A: When the time is up, it does not mean the practice was effective.

**Q: What is a task goal?**
A: A specific thing to accomplish in one practice session.

liszt-hungarian-rhapsody-no2-lassan-fris.body:
Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 is one of the best-known of his nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies. It was written in 1847 and published in 1851, in C♯ minor. The piece falls into two sharply contrasting parts: first a slow, solemn "lassan", then a "friska" that grows faster and faster, passionate and unrestrained. This slow-fast, two-part structure comes from a style of dance music popular in Hungary at the time. The piece is technically very demanding, and many orchestral and other arrangements have appeared since.

## Liszt and Hungary

Liszt was born in 1811 in a small village that then belonged to Hungary.

**Practice order**

He left home as a child, studying and performing in Vienna and Paris, and became a famous pianist across Europe.

But he always regarded Hungary as his homeland, and he had deep feeling for Hungarian music.

## The slow-fast dance tradition

This slow-then-fast structure comes from a style of dance music that was popular in Hungary in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

This kind of dance was often introduced by a slow section and then moved on to a fast dance section.

Liszt developed it into a large-scale piano work full of dramatic contrasts.

**Listen for this**
- Written in 1847, published in 1851, in C♯ minor
- One of the nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies
- A slow "lassan" and a fast "friska"
- The slow-fast structure comes from the Hungarian dance style of the time

## The "lassan": slow and solemn

The first half of the piece is called the "lassan". It is slow, with a solemn mood tinged with melancholy.

The melody has many ornaments and a free rhythm, like a violinist in a band improvising.

When you play it, you can let the rhythm be a little flexible to bring out this improvised feeling.

## Imitating the band

In this rhapsody Liszt uses the piano to imitate the sounds of various instruments in a band.

For example, fast repeated notes are like the violin's tremolo, and broken chords are like a struck-string instrument called the cimbalom.

As you play, you can imagine the sounds of these instruments to make the piano's tone colour richer.

## Listen to the rhapsody first

In the same rhapsody, several pianists' "lassan" are often each freer than the last, and it is interesting to compare a few recordings.

Notice the free rhythm in the "lassan" and the changes of tempo in the "friska".

The more you listen, the better you will feel the style of the piece.

## Simplified versions

For learners who are not yet ready, there are also some simplified versions that keep the main melody and rhythm.

Playing a simplified version also lets you feel the charm of the slow-fast contrast in this piece.

When your technique improves, you can take on the original.

## The cadenza

Liszt left a place in the score where the performer can add a cadenza of their own.

Later, some pianists wrote their own cadenzas for this piece.

This reflects the tradition of improvisation among pianists at the time.

## Where the melodies came from

Liszt believed that these melodies came from folk music played by Hungarian Gypsy bands.

He also wrote a book discussing these bands and their music.

Later research found that many of the melodies were in fact popular tunes written by Hungarian composers of the time, which spread widely by being played by the bands.

## The nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies

Liszt wrote nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies in all, and most of the first fifteen were completed between the 1840s and the early 1850s.

The last four he wrote late in life, in the 1880s, and their style is very different from the earlier ones.

These works use many melodies and rhythms that were popular in Hungary at the time.

![A glowing blue-green grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacioom-s6a7q.webp)

## Technical challenges

This rhapsody has many technical difficulties, such as fast octaves, leaps and repeated notes.

The second half of the "friska" is very fast and calls for great stamina and control.

The piece suits learners who already have solid technique.

## From C♯ minor to F♯ major

The piece begins in C♯ minor, and the "lassan" is melancholy and deep.

The "friska" moves to a bright F♯ major, and the mood becomes passionate and joyful.

The change from minor to major takes the music from reflection to revelry.

## The "friska": faster and faster

The second half is called the "friska". It is lively, and it keeps getting faster.

The music is full of energy, with a clear rhythm, like a lively dance.

At the end, both tempo and dynamics reach a climax, and the piece ends in a fiery atmosphere.

## Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 in brief

Liszt was born in 1811 in a small village that then belonged to Hungary. He wrote nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies in all; most of the first fifteen were completed between the 1840s and the early 1850s, the last four were written in the 1880s, and No. 2 was written in 1847 and published in 1851, in C♯ minor.

Liszt believed the melodies came from the folk music of Gypsy bands, and research has found that many are popular tunes written by Hungarian composers of the time. The piece is divided into a slow, solemn "lassan" and an ever-faster "friska", which come from the Hungarian dance tradition. The piano imitates the violin and the cimbalom, there is a place left for a cadenza, the music moves from C♯ minor to F♯ major, and the difficulties include fast octaves, leaps and repeated notes.

You can first listen to different recordings, and if your level is not yet enough, play a simplified version. Teacher Aum can help judge which version suits you.

## Asking your teacher about the version of Rhapsody No. 2 in lessons

If you want to play Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2, you can ask Teacher Aum in a lesson to judge whether the original or a simplified version suits your level.

Your teacher can also help you practise the free rhythm of the "lassan" and the tempo control of the "friska".

This piece is very good for practising strong contrasts and rich tone colour.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In what year was Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 written?**
A: 1847. It was published in 1851.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: It begins in C♯ minor and later moves to F♯ major.

**Q: What kind of section is the "lassan"?**
A: A slow, solemn slow section.

**Q: What kind of section is the "friska"?**
A: A fast section that gets faster and faster.

**Q: How many Hungarian Rhapsodies did Liszt write?**
A: Nineteen.
