left-hand-octave-bass-line-pop.body:
When you play a pop-song or hymn accompaniment, the left hand often plays just one bass note. If you want the bass to have more weight, you can play it as an octave: the thumb and pinky press down two notes an octave apart at the same time, for example a low C and the C an octave below it. When you play octaves the hand opens wide, but the wrist and arm must stay relaxed, not stiffly propped up. People with smaller hands can start by playing only single notes, or play the octave only on important beats, with no need to force it.

## Keep the Wrist Relaxed for Octaves

When playing octaves, many people unconsciously hold the wrist and arm very tight, which tires them easily and makes the sound hard.

After each octave, let the wrist relax gently, and then get ready for the next one.

As you go down into the key, let the weight of the whole arm carry the two fingers down, rather than pressing hard with the fingertips.

## What About Small Hands?

People with smaller hands may find octaves hard work, or may not be able to reach them at all.

In that case, you can start by playing only single notes, or play the octave only on the first beat of each bar and single notes on the other beats.

You can also replace the octave with a fifth, which also makes the bass a little thicker without the hand having to open so wide.

## Summary of Left-Hand Octaves

Playing octave basses with the left hand gives the accompaniment more weight, and it is especially suited to the chorus of a song.

When you play octaves, open the hand, keep the wrist and arm relaxed, use the weight of the whole arm to go into the key, and do not play too heavily.

People with smaller hands can first play single notes or fifths, and play the octave only on important beats.

## Remember to Rest

Octaves need the hand to open fairly wide, and after a long practice session the hand may feel tired.

When you practise octaves, stop every so often and shake out your hands to let them relax.

If you feel pain, stop and rest, and if necessary ask your teacher to check your hand position.

## Moving Between Octaves

In an accompaniment, the left-hand octaves often have to move from one chord to another.

When you move, you can keep the hand in the octave shape and move the whole arm sideways to the new position.

Your eyes can look ahead to the position of the next bass note, so that the hand can land accurately.

## Don't Play Too Heavily

An octave bass is already much louder than a single note, so you do not need to play it with much force.

If the octave is played too heavily, it may cover the right-hand melody or the singer's voice.

Pay attention to the balance between the hands, so that the bass is the support and not the star.

## Using It with the Pedal

In lyrical songs, the octave bass is often used together with the sustain pedal.

After you play the octave and press the pedal, the bass keeps sounding, and the left hand can leave the keyboard to get ready for the next note.

Remember to change the pedal when the chord changes, otherwise several bass notes will blur together.

## Using It in a Song's Chorus

The verse of a song is often quieter, and the left hand can play just single notes.

When the chorus arrives and the music is fuller, switching the left hand to an octave bass gives the accompaniment more weight.

This change from single notes to octaves also lets listeners feel the layers of the song.

- An octave makes the left-hand bass weightier
- Thumb and pinky press two notes an octave apart at the same time
- Open the hand, keep the wrist and arm relaxed
- With small hands, play octaves only on important beats

## Hand Shape and Stretch

When you play octaves, the hand opens until the thumb and pinky can press two keys an octave apart at the same time.

The three fingers in between can lift naturally and slightly, without pressing any key.

The palm should form an arch, rather than pressing flat against the keyboard.

## Starting with a Single Octave

When you first practise, you can play just one octave, such as the low C, over and over a few times to feel the shape and weight of the hand.

Then try moving back and forth between the octaves on C and G, taking care that the shape of the hand stays the same.

Once that is comfortable, add the roots of other chords such as F and A.

![A black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4a1sp-y8ui1.webp)

## Adding a Fifth to the Octave

Once you are familiar with octaves, you can try adding a fifth between the two notes, for example C, G, C.

That way the left hand plays an open chord, and the sound is fuller.

Take note, though, that the hand gets busier with the fifth added, so you can first practise it until it is secure at a slow tempo.

## The Role of the Bass in Accompaniment

In a song's accompaniment, the bass is like the foundation of a house, giving the whole music a steady support.

In many simple accompaniments, the left hand plays only the root of each chord, and that one note is enough to make the harmony clear.

When the song enters a fuller section, such as the chorus, a single bass note can sometimes seem not thick enough.

## What Is an Octave Bass?

An octave bass means the left hand plays two notes of the same name, an octave apart, at the same time.

For example, if the chord is C, the left hand can play the C in the low register with the pinky and, at the same time, the C an octave higher with the thumb.

**Another way of looking at it**

With the two notes sounding together, the bass becomes thicker and has more drive.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is an octave bass?**
A: The left hand plays two notes of the same name, an octave apart, at the same time.

**Q: Which two fingers are used?**
A: Usually the thumb and the pinky.

**Q: What should the wrist be like when playing octaves?**
A: Keep it relaxed and let the weight of the arm fall naturally.

**Q: What if my hands are small?**
A: Play single notes or fifths first, and play the octave only on important beats.

**Q: When do I use an octave bass?**
A: Often in the fuller parts of a song, such as the chorus.

liszt-consolation-no3-d-flat-1850.body:
When people think of Liszt, many think of showpieces with fearsome technique. But he also wrote some quiet, inward piano miniatures, and the Consolations are among the best examples. This is a set of six piano pieces, written between 1844 and 1850 and published in 1850. The third is in D♭ major, at a slow tempo, with a calm and tender melody over gently flowing broken chords, and it is often thought to show the shadow of a Chopin nocturne. Its technical demands are not very high, and for many learners it is their first Liszt piece.

## Tempo and Flexibility

The tempo marking is slow and calm.

**A small tip**

You can allow some free flexibility, such as slowing down slightly at the end of a phrase.

But keep the overall sense of flow, and do not let it drag.

## Pedalling in Consolation No. 3

The wave-like bass notes in D♭ major need to be joined together by the right pedal.

Change the pedal in time when the harmony changes, so that the sound does not run together.

After you change the pedal, listen first to confirm that the resonance of the previous chord has cleared.

## The Right-Hand Melody

After a few bars in the left hand, the right-hand melody enters, calm and heartfelt.

The melody is often in the middle register, surrounded by the broken chords of the left hand.

This song in the middle register needs to be heard, and the left-hand waves are only there to support it.

## The Name "Consolations"

The title "Consolations" is said to share its name with a book of poems by a French writer, published in 1830.

Liszt had read this book of poems and borrowed its name.

These six piano pieces are mostly quiet and lyrical, very different from Liszt's showpieces.

## Listen Before You Play

Before playing, you can listen to several pianists to hear how they handle the quiet atmosphere.

Notice the balance between melody and accompaniment, and the breathing of the phrases.

You can also listen to a Chopin nocturne and compare the similarities between the two.

## When It Was Written

This set was written between 1844 and 1850, when Liszt was gradually bringing his touring life to an end.

From 1848 he settled in Weimar, Germany, and devoted more of his energy to composing and conducting.

The Consolations were published in 1850 and are among his works from this period.

## The Change in the Middle Section

In the middle of the piece, the harmony becomes richer and the melody rises to a higher register.

The dynamic increases slightly, but the overall quiet atmosphere is kept.

After that, the music gradually calms down and returns to the mood of the opening.

## Summary of Consolation No. 3

The Consolations are six piano pieces by Liszt written between 1844 and 1850 and published in 1850. The title is said to borrow the name of a French writer's book of poems of 1830, a time when Liszt was gradually ending his touring and, from 1848, settling in Weimar.

The third is in D♭ major. Its five flats turn out to be comfortable for the hand. The left hand lays a base of slowly flowing broken chords, and a calm, heartfelt melody floats above in the right hand. It is often thought to show the shadow of a Chopin nocturne. The harmony is richer in the middle section, the pedal must change with the harmony, the balance between melody and accompaniment is most important, and the slow tempo should be flexible but not drag.

The technical demands are moderate, and you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the balance.

## The Waves in the Left Hand of Consolation No. 3

At the very start, the left hand plays slowly flowing broken chords over a wide range.

These broken chords are like gentle waves, laying out the background for the melody.

The left hand should be even and soft, with no notes sticking out.

## Where the Difficulty Lies in Consolation No. 3

The technical demands of Consolation No. 3 are moderate, with no very fast figures or difficult leaps.

What it tests more is control of tone, use of the pedal and the singing quality of the melody.

It suits learners who can already play some lyrical miniatures and want to get to know Liszt's music.

## Let the Melody Float in Consolation No. 3

The most important thing in playing this piece is the balance between melody and accompaniment.

The notes of the right-hand melody should be slightly louder than the left hand, but do not strike them hard.

You can first practise the melody alone, then add the left hand, listening to the balance between the two as you play.

## Similarity to Chopin Nocturnes

Many people think this piece calls to mind Chopin's nocturnes.

For example, the wide broken chords in the left hand, the singing melody in the right hand, and the quiet night-time atmosphere.

Liszt and Chopin were friends, and he admired Chopin's works.

**A different angle**
- A set of six, written between 1844 and 1850
- Published in 1850
- The third is in D♭ major, slow and calm
- Often thought to show the shadow of a Chopin nocturne

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Balance in Consolation No. 3 in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your playing of Consolation No. 3 and see whether the balance between melody and accompaniment is right.

Your teacher can also help you practise how to change the pedal and how to shape the phrases.

This piece is well suited to practising quiet, delicate expression.

## The Colour of D-flat Major

The third piece is in D♭ major, with five flats, and most of what you play is on the black keys.

D♭ major sounds soft and warm on the piano, and is well suited to quiet music.

**Remember this**

Although there are many flats, the position of the black keys is comfortable for the hand, and the melody can actually be played more roundly.

![A blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacsi50-2jvlo.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: How many pieces are there in the Consolations?**
A: Six.

**Q: Which year were they published?**
A: 1850.

**Q: What key is the third in?**
A: D♭ major.

**Q: Whose music is the third often thought to resemble?**
A: Chopin's nocturnes.

**Q: What should you pay special attention to when playing Consolation No. 3?**
A: The balance between melody and accompaniment.

london-bridge-is-falling-down-rhyme.body:
London Bridge Is Falling Down is an old English nursery rhyme. Similar words were recorded as early as the seventeenth century, and from the middle of the eighteenth century they began to appear in collections of children's songs. The words tell how London Bridge is falling down, and people think of all sorts of ways to mend it: with wood, with bricks, with iron... and every method seems to have a problem. Children often sing it while playing an "arch game": two people make a bridge with their arms, the others line up and pass underneath, and when the singing stops the "bridge" comes down and catches someone. The melody is simple and very suitable for the piano.

## Adding a Left Hand to London Bridge

Once the right hand is familiar, you can accompany the melody with the tonic and dominant chords.

In C major, use the C chord most of the time, and change to the G chord when the melody lands on D or F.

Play the left hand lightly, to match the bouncy feel of the right.

## The History of London Bridge

London Bridge is a bridge across the River Thames, and over its history it was rebuilt many times.

For a long time it was the main crossing of the Thames in the city of London.

The "falling down" in the rhyme may reflect people's worry about the old bridge.

## The Melody of London Bridge

The melody is in a major key, with a lively rhythm, as if it were skipping along.

The opening melody first climbs a few steps, then comes down, and then repeats.

The last phrase of each verse falls downward, which fits the movement of the bridge coming down.

## Play While You Play

Parents and children can play together: one person plays the piano while the others play the arch game.

When the player suddenly stops, the "bridge" comes down.

This lets children feel the starting and stopping of music through a game.

## Different Stories About Its Origin

Many different guesses circulate about the meaning of the words. Some say it is linked to ancient wars, others to legends about building the bridge.

Most of these claims have no reliable evidence.

We can simply treat it as a fun nursery rhyme, and there is no need to worry about which explanation is right.

## Summary of London Bridge Is Falling Down

This old English nursery rhyme has similar words recorded in the seventeenth century and appeared in children's song collections in the middle of the eighteenth. Other parts of Europe have similar bridge-mending rhymes. London Bridge spans the River Thames and was rebuilt many times in its history. There are many stories about where the words came from, but most have no reliable evidence.

Each verse names a material for mending the bridge and then states its problem. Children often play the arch game, in which two people form a bridge and the others pass through. The melody is in a major key. In C major it begins G, A, G, F, E, F, G, and the hand can sit on C to G or D to A. The dotted rhythms should be clear, and the left hand uses two chords, C and G. You can also play while playing a game, learn about phrases and make up new words.

You can ask Teacher Aum to help you choose a hand position.

**Summary**
- An old English nursery rhyme, recorded as early as the seventeenth century
- Appeared in collections of children's songs in the middle of the eighteenth century
- The words are about mending a bridge with various materials
- Often paired with the "arch game"

## The Rhythm of London Bridge

The melody has some dotted rhythms, which give the music a springy feel.

Play the dotted notes clearly: the long notes a little longer, the short notes a little shorter.

You can clap and say the words first to get used to the rhythm before playing it at the piano.

![Golden grand piano sketch on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwad8kd4-0sog1.webp)

## Singing About Bridge-Mending Materials

You can make up new words with your child by thinking of what else could be used to mend a bridge.

For example blocks, paper or sweets, and each material can have a funny reason.

This sparks children's imagination and their interest in music.

## Playing London Bridge at the Piano

In C major, the opening melody is "G, A, G, F, E, F, G".

The right hand can put the thumb on C, with the five fingers on the five white keys from C to G, and the little finger stretches out slightly for A.

You can also put the hand in the D to A position, so that every note lies under a finger.

## The Words of London Bridge

Each verse of the words proposes a material for mending the bridge, such as wood and clay, bricks and mortar, iron or steel, silver and gold.

But every material has a problem: wood will be washed away, bricks will fall, iron will bend, and silver and gold will be stolen.

This question-and-answer structure makes children more and more interested as they sing.

## The Arch Game

When singing this song, children often play an arch game.

Two children face each other and raise their arms to make a "bridge", while the other children line up and pass underneath it.

When the singing reaches the last line, the "bridge" comes down and catches the child who is underneath.

## Where the Rhyme Comes From

The exact origin of this rhyme can no longer be traced.

Similar words were mentioned in the seventeenth century, and from the middle of the eighteenth century they began to be printed in children's song collections.

In some other parts of Europe there are also bridge-mending rhymes with similar content.

## Learning About Phrases with London Bridge

Each verse of this song is made of a few short phrases, with a clear structure.

Try pausing slightly at the end of each phrase to feel how the phrases divide.

This is a good starting point for understanding musical structure.

## Ask Your Teacher About London Bridge Hand Positions in Your Lesson

Beginners can ask Teacher Aum in their lessons to help choose a hand position that suits them for this song.

Your teacher can also teach you to add a simple left-hand chord accompaniment.

**Mind the details**

Making the bridge, passing under it and the bridge coming down is just right for accompanying a child through the first weeks at the piano.

## FAQ

**Q: How old is this nursery rhyme?**
A: Similar words were recorded in the seventeenth century.

**Q: What do the words say?**
A: London Bridge is mended with various materials, and each has a problem.

**Q: How is the arch game played?**
A: Two people make a bridge and the others pass through; when the singing stops, the bridge comes down.

**Q: What is the opening melody in C major?**
A: G, A, G, F, E, F, G.

**Q: Which two chords can be used for the accompaniment?**
A: The tonic and dominant chords of C major.

liszt-transcendental-etudes-1852-twelve.body:
Liszt's Transcendental Études are a set of twelve piano studies, and the version most often played today is the final edition published in 1852. The set went through three versions: in 1826 the teenage Liszt published a simpler set of studies; in 1837 he expanded them greatly into an extremely difficult version; and in 1852 he made them slightly easier and gave them titles, producing the set we know today. The studies are dedicated to his teacher Czerny, and include famous pieces such as Mazeppa, Feux follets (Will-o'-the-Wisp), Harmonies du soir (Evening Harmonies) and Chasse-neige (Snow Whirlwind).

## A Summary of the Transcendental Études

The Transcendental Études are Liszt's twelve piano studies. A simpler first version was published in 1826, when he was fifteen, and he originally planned forty-eight. In 1837 they were expanded into the extremely difficult twelve of the Twenty-Four Grand Studies, and in 1852 they were simplified, given titles and finalised, with a dedication to Beethoven's pupil Czerny. The keys begin with C major and move through the flat keys, in pairs of a major key and its relative minor.

**Another way to look at it**

No. 4, Mazeppa, depicts a man tied to a wild horse galloping off, and was later reworked as a symphonic poem. No. 5, Feux follets, needs extremely light fingers. No. 9, Ricordanza, must keep the melody singing through the ornaments. No. 11, Harmonies du soir, is all about tone colour, and No. 12, Chasse-neige, ends with tremolos and rapid figuration. Studies can be works of art in their own right, and you can build a foundation with Czerny's studies first.

You can ask Teacher Aum to explain the differences between the three versions.

## Ricordanza

No. 9, Ricordanza (Remembrance), is a lyrical, beautiful study.

The melody is full of rich ornaments, like memories of the past.

The challenge is keeping the melody singing amid the complex ornamentation.

## Feux follets

No. 5, Feux follets (Will-o'-the-Wisp), depicts small flickering lights wandering over a marsh at night.

The right hand has to play extremely fast, light semitones and double notes, like flames flickering on and off.

This study is famous for its difficulty and demands exceptionally agile, light fingers.

## Studies Are More Than Exercises

Liszt's Transcendental Études are not just for practising technique.

Each one has its own picture and emotion, and each can be performed in a concert.

This shows that a study can be a true work of art.

## The Early Draft of His Youth

In 1826, the fifteen-year-old Liszt published a set of twelve piano studies.

They were short and moderately difficult, and showed the influence of his teacher Czerny.

Liszt planned to write forty-eight, covering all the major and minor keys, but he never finished.

## The 1837 Expansion

In 1837, Liszt greatly expanded the set into twelve of the Twenty-Four Grand Studies.

By then Liszt was a pianist of astonishing technique, and the new version was extremely difficult.

Many pianists thought this version was almost unplayable.

## Ask Your Teacher About the Three Versions in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to explain the differences between the three versions of the Transcendental Études.

Your teacher can also arrange Czerny's studies as preparation, according to your own progress.

Start from the studies and see how technique and music are connected.

## The Final Version of 1852

In 1852, Liszt revised the studies once more and simplified some of the passages that were too difficult.

He also gave most of them titles, making them feel more like music with pictures.

This is the Transcendental Études we play today.

## Dedicated to Czerny

The set is dedicated to Czerny, Liszt's teacher in childhood.

Czerny studied with Beethoven, and the hundreds of studies he wrote are still played by young pianists today.

By dedicating this work to him, Liszt expressed his gratitude to his teacher.

- Liszt's twelve piano studies
- Three versions: 1826, 1837 and 1852
- Finalised and given titles in 1852
- Dedicated to his teacher Czerny

![Blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint, symbolising sound and ear training](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadu1iq-lvgtd.webp)

## The Order of Keys in the Transcendental Études

The keys of the twelve studies follow a pattern: C major, then A minor, F major, D minor, and so on, moving through the flat keys.

They come in pairs, one major key followed by its relative minor.

This is a trace of Liszt's original plan to write in every key.

## Harmonies du soir

No. 11, Harmonies du soir (Evening Harmonies), depicts a calm, rich landscape at dusk.

The music has many broad chords and soft tone colours, like the glow of the sunset.

This study is more about tone colour and feeling than about technique alone.

## Chasse-neige

No. 12, Chasse-neige (Snow Whirlwind), depicts snowflakes dancing in the wind.

The music has constantly repeated tremolos and rapid figuration, growing ever more intense.

This study closes the whole set with grandeur.

## Mazeppa

No. 4, Mazeppa, depicts a man tied to a wild horse, galloping across the steppe.

The music has many rapid chords alternating between the hands, like hoofbeats racing across the grassland.

Liszt later reworked this study as a symphonic poem.

## Start With Czerny

If you want to take on Liszt's studies, you can start with Czerny's studies.

Czerny's studies cover all the basic techniques, with the difficulty rising gradually.

**Mind the details**

Once the foundation is solid, take on Liszt's works.

## FAQ

**Q: How many Transcendental Études are there?**
A: Twelve.

**Q: Which versions did they go through?**
A: 1826, 1837 and 1852.

**Q: Who are they dedicated to?**
A: Liszt's teacher Czerny.

**Q: What does Mazeppa depict?**
A: A man tied to a wild horse, galloping across the steppe.

**Q: What is the twelfth study called?**
A: Chasse-neige (Snow Whirlwind).

listen-to-singers-learn-piano-phrasing.body:
Singers need to breathe when they sing, so their phrases naturally have a beginning, an end and a rise and fall in between. The piano does not need breaths, so when playing it is very easy to join one phrase to the next in one long string, with no pauses to be heard. When practising a melody, try singing it first, feel where you need to breathe, and then leave a tiny space at the same place on the piano. You can also listen to singers more often, noticing how they handle the start, the high point and the end of a phrase.

## Singing together with your teacher

In a lesson, you can also ask Teacher Aum to sing the melody through, or sing it to your teacher yourself.

Your teacher can help you find how the phrases divide and where the high points are, and tell you where you can breathe.

This kind of practice gives you a more direct feel for phrases.

## Compare your phrasing with a singer's

You can record yourself playing the melody and compare it with a singer singing the same song.

Listen for whether your phrases have a clear beginning and end, and whether they have a rise and fall.

If it sounds too flat, look again at how the singer handles it and adjust your playing.

**Look closely**
- Singers breathe, so their phrases naturally rise and fall
- The piano easily joins phrases into one long string
- Sing the melody first to find where to breathe
- Leave a little space at the same places on the piano

![An illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, conveying the power of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4bvgq-euty3.webp)

## Inspiration from other instruments

Besides singers, you can also listen to violin, flute and other instruments, which also have to think about phrases and breath.

The places where string players change bow and wind players take a breath are often also the boundaries between phrases.

All of this can inspire your piano playing.

## The end of a phrase

The end of a phrase is usually lighter than the middle, like the voice dropping at the end of a spoken sentence.

Many people, when they reach the end of a phrase, unconsciously play it too heavily, and it sounds as if they are stressing it.

Try making the last note lighter and softer, so that the phrase ends naturally.

## Piano breathing in brief

The piano does not need breaths, so you have to shape phrases all the more consciously, so that the music "breathes".

Sing the melody first, find the places to breathe, leave a little space at the same places on the piano, and pay attention to the high point and the end of each phrase.

Listening to singers and other instruments more often can help you find a more natural way of shaping phrases.

## The piano does not need breaths

People who sing or play wind instruments need to take a breath after every phrase they sing or blow.

The piano is different. The fingers can keep playing and never need to stop for breath.

This is really a convenience of the piano, but it also makes it easy to play one phrase after another with no pause, like talking on and on without taking a breath.

## Leave space on the piano

Back at the piano, at the place marked with a breath mark, lift your hand off the keys a tiny bit and leave a very short space.

This space does not need to be long, and you do not need to change the rhythm. Just make the previous note a little shorter.

It then sounds as if the player is also "breathing", and the gap between one phrase and the next is clearer.

## Building the habit slowly

At first, you may need to sing every phrase before you play it on the piano.

With more practice, you will gradually build the habit, and as soon as you see a melody you can feel the shape of its phrases.

Then your playing will be more like "singing" than like pressing keys.

## How singers sing the peak of a phrase

In a phrase, there is often one note that is the emotional high point. Sometimes it falls on the highest pitch, and sometimes on a note with a very long value.

When singers reach it, they often strengthen it a little or lengthen it a little.

On the piano, you can try putting a little more weight on that note, building up gradually before it and fading gradually after it.

## Listen to how singers shape phrases

In everyday listening, you can listen to more singers, whether classical art songs or pop songs.

Notice how they enter at the start of a phrase, how they strengthen at the high point, and how they close at the end.

Many singers fade a little at the end of a phrase and let the sound disappear naturally.

## What a phrase is

In music, a phrase is like a sentence in language, with a beginning, a middle and an end.

Many melodic phrases are four or eight bars long, and the slurs in the score sometimes also show the extent of a phrase.

Playing a phrase well means letting the listener feel where the sentence starts, where it reaches its high point and where it ends.

## Use lyrics to help you understand

If you are playing a song with lyrics, first look at the lyrics and understand what each line is saying.

The meaning of the lyrics often affects how a phrase is shaped, for example which word to stress and where to pause.

Even in a piano solo, you can imagine the melody having lyrics, to help you find the feel of the phrase.

## Sing the melody first

When practising a melody, you can first step away from the piano and try singing or humming it.

As you sing, you will naturally need to breathe in certain places, and these are often the ends of phrases.

You can mark the places to breathe in the score with a small sign, such as a comma.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why does the piano need to "breathe"?**
A: The piano needs no breaths, so it is easy to join phrases into one long string.

**Q: How do I find where to breathe?**
A: Sing the melody first.

**Q: Does the rhythm change when I breathe?**
A: No. Just make the previous note a little shorter.

**Q: How should I play the end of a phrase?**
A: Usually lighter than the middle, ending naturally.

**Q: What else can I listen to besides singers?**
A: Violin, flute and other instruments.

melodic-dictation-write-down-what-you-he.body:
Melodic dictation means listening to a short melody and writing it down as notation. It is practised in many music courses, and it helps connect your ears with reading music. At the beginning, you can listen to just three or four notes. First work out whether the notes as a whole are rising or falling, then settle the first note and the distance between each note, and finally write the rhythm. You can ask a family member or friend to play on the piano while you take the dictation, and when you have finished, check against the answer to see what you heard correctly and what needs more practice.

## Listen for direction first

When you listen to a melody, the first step is to decide its direction: is it going up, going down, or going up and then down?

**Watch the details**

You can draw the shape of the melody in the air with your hand to help you remember its contour.

Once you know the direction, you are less likely to make big mistakes when you write the notes.

## What is melodic dictation

Melodic dictation means listening to a melody and then writing the pitches and rhythm you hear as notation.

It is the opposite of reading music: when you read, you see the notation and play the sound, and in dictation you hear the sound and write the notation.

Many music courses and exams practise dictation, because it connects the ears with the notation.

- Listen to a short melody and write it as notation
- First decide whether it goes up or down
- Then work out the distances between notes, and write the rhythm last
- Start with three or four notes, and check against the answer when you finish

## Write the rhythm last

Once the pitches are written, write the rhythm.

You can gently clap as you listen to decide how many beats each note has.

You can also first write the number of beats in each bar, and then fill in the note values.

## Ask family to help

To practise dictation at home, you can ask a family member or friend to play a short melody on the piano.

The player can find some simple melodies in a book, or make up a few notes.

When you have finished writing, compare with the original score and see what you got right and what you got wrong.

## Settle the first note

Before dictation, you are usually told what the first note is, or the tonic is played first.

With the first note as a reference, the following notes can be judged by their distance from it.

If you are not told, you can first listen to the tonic chord to work out what key the melody is in.

## Keep a record of mistakes

After each dictation, you can note down the mistakes you often make, such as always hearing a third as a second, or writing the rhythm wrongly.

Once you know your weak points, you can pay special attention to them in your next practice.

You can also ask Teacher Aum to give you some exercises aimed at these spots.

## Judging the distance between notes

Once you know the direction and the first note, you need to judge the distance between each pair of notes.

Is it moving step by step, or leaping a third or a fifth?

At the beginning you can distinguish only between "steps" and "leaps", and when you are more fluent, work out how large each leap is.

## Summary: melodic dictation

Melodic dictation is writing a melody you hear as notation, and it connects your ears with reading music.

First decide the direction, then settle the first note and the distances between notes, and write the rhythm last, focusing on one aspect each time you listen.

Start with three or four notes, ask family to help or practise with a familiar song, keep a record of mistakes, and make progress patiently and slowly.

![A person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4glkt-o1hoy.webp)

## Why practise dictation

Practising melodic dictation makes your ears more sensitive to pitch and rhythm.

Over time, when you look at a score, you can hear its sound in your head, and when you hear a piece of music, you can roughly know what it looks like on the page.

This helps a lot with reading, memorising and improvising.

## Practise with familiar songs

You can also practise dictation with songs you know well, for example by trying to write the opening of a nursery rhyme as notation.

Because you already know the song very well, you can put your attention on turning it into notation.

When you have written it, play it on the piano and see whether it matches the melody in your head.

## Be patient and go slowly

Melodic dictation may feel very hard at first, and writing things wrongly is perfectly normal.

Do not be discouraged by mistakes. Spend a few minutes each day practising and your ears will improve little by little.

You can start with simple examples and keep the habit of practising.

## Start with three or four notes

When you first start practising, the melody should not be too long, and three or four notes are enough.

You can start from the first five notes of C major, for example C, D, E, or E, D, C.

When you can write all these simple melodies correctly, slowly increase the number of notes and the range.

## How many times to listen

In dictation you can usually listen to the melody several times, and you do not need to write it all down on the first hearing.

The first time, listen only for the direction and the general shape. The second time, write the pitches, the third time, write the rhythm, and the last time, check.

Each time you listen, focus on one aspect.

## FAQ

**Q: What is melodic dictation?**
A: Listening to a melody and writing it as notation.

**Q: How long should the melody be at the beginning?**
A: Three or four notes are enough.

**Q: What do I listen for first?**
A: First decide whether the melody goes up or down.

**Q: When do I write the rhythm?**
A: Usually after the pitches are written.

**Q: What if I get it wrong?**
A: Keep a record of the mistakes you often make and pay special attention next time.

listening-practice-on-commute.body:
On your commute, you can use the time for some piano-related listening practice: listen again and again to the piece you are learning, noticing changes in tempo, dynamics and phrasing; compare versions by different performers; try to tell the melody from the accompaniment as you listen to a piece, or count the beats in your head as you follow along. These exercises do not need a piano, yet when you get back to the instrument you will have a clearer idea of the piece.

## Listen to different kinds of music

Besides the piece you are learning, you can listen to other kinds of music too, such as piano works from different periods, chamber music or solos on other instruments.

**Keep this in mind**

Listening widely enriches your understanding of music, and may help you discover new interests.

You can note down pieces you like and try learning them when the chance comes.

- Listen again and again to the piece you are learning
- Notice changes in tempo, dynamics and phrasing
- Compare versions by different performers
- Try to tell the melody from the accompaniment

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yrhxm-bonjf.webp)

## Mind your safety and surroundings

When you listen to music with headphones on your commute, be aware of your surroundings, especially when walking or crossing the road, and do not turn the volume up too high.

On crowded transport, make sure you keep your balance and look after your belongings.

If it is noisy around you, do not turn the volume up too high just to hear better. You can wait and listen when it is quieter.

## Record your thoughts

If you hear something interesting on your commute, you can jot it down briefly on your phone.

For example, "the ritardando in the second section is lovely, I want to try it too", or "this version is faster than the one I am practising".

When you practise at home, looking back over these notes makes your practice more focused.

## Notice the details

As you listen, you can consciously notice some details, for example: is this phrase getting louder or softer? Does the tempo change?

Where does the phrase start, and where does it end? Where does the performer pause for a moment?

Write these details down, and when you practise you can try to bring them out in your own playing.

## Listen again and again to the piece you are learning

Before you leave home, download the audio of the piece you are working on and play it on a loop on the way.

The more times you listen, the more familiar you become with the melody, structure and mood of the piece.

By the time you are back at the piano, you already have the sound of the piece in your mind, and learning it will go faster.

## Tell melody from accompaniment

When you listen to a piano piece, you can try to tell which voice is the melody and which is the accompaniment.

Notice whether the melody is in the high register or the low register, and whether the accompaniment uses chords or broken chords.

This kind of listening practice helps you balance the volume of the melody and the accompaniment better in your own playing.

## Listen for just one thing at a time

Each time you listen, you can set yourself just one focus, for example only the changes in dynamics today, and only the breathing of the phrases tomorrow.

Paying attention to one thing at a time lets you hear it more clearly and remember it more easily.

After a few days, your understanding of the same piece will be more and more complete, and when you return to the piano you will know where to begin.

## Making use of commuting time

Many people spend a stretch of time commuting every day, on a bus, on a boat or on foot.

You cannot play the piano during this time, but you can use it to listen to music and do some piano-related listening practice.

Over time, this listening practice can help you understand music better and give your practice more direction.

## Compare different versions

With the same piece, different performers may shape it differently.

You can find two or three versions and compare how they differ in tempo, dynamics and mood.

After comparing, think about which one you prefer and why. This helps you form your own understanding.

## Let music keep you company on your commute

A commute can sometimes be tiring, and having music with you can make the time more pleasant.

When you turn commuting time into time for learning and enjoying music, you will find you are in touch with the piano more every day.

This kind of accumulation raises your musicianship without your noticing.

## Count the beats as you follow along

As you listen, you can count the beats in your head, feeling the pulse and tempo of the piece.

Where the tempo changes, notice how the performer slows down or speeds up.

**Another angle**

This exercise helps you build a steady sense of rhythm.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does listening to music on my commute help my piano practice?**
A: It can help you get to know the piece and train your ear.

**Q: Which recordings should I listen to?**
A: The pieces you are learning, and versions by different performers.

**Q: Is it safe to wear headphones on my commute?**
A: Be aware of your surroundings, and do not turn the volume up too high.

**Q: What if I cannot tell the melody from the accompaniment?**
A: Start with simple pieces and listen several times.

**Q: Can I listen to other kinds of music?**
A: Yes. Listening widely enriches your understanding of music.

**Q: How do I record the ideas I get while listening?**
A: Jot them down briefly on your phone.

lili-boulanger-prix-de-rome.body:
Lili Boulanger was a French composer of the early twentieth century. In 1913 she won the Prix de Rome in composition with her cantata Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive the prize. Her career was short, but she left many works well worth listening to.

## Listening to the composer's works

The most direct way to get to know a composer is to listen to the music. You could start with her vocal works, choral works or short instrumental pieces, and notice how she uses harmony and tone colour to create atmosphere.

Learning about a composer's life can also help you understand the background of the music. When you listen, though, you can simply let your ears take it in first. There is no need to link every note to a story.

For piano learners, getting to know composers from different eras and backgrounds broadens your understanding of music. You can look for more information in a library or in music reference materials.

Sharing a lesser-known composer in class or in a club is another good way to learn. In preparing to share, you often come to understand the music much better yourself.

**Keep this in mind**
- Lili Boulanger was a French composer
- She won the Prix de Rome in composition in 1913
- The winning work was the cantata Faust et Hélène
- Her older sister Nadia Boulanger was a composition teacher

## Finding reliable sources

To learn more about a composer, you can consult music dictionaries, biographies and scholarly sources, and you can also read the liner notes of recordings.

The quality of information online varies widely. Give priority to libraries, music conservatoires and authoritative publications.

When you share a composer's story, try to use sources that can be traced, and avoid passing on claims that have no basis.

Learning about a life is a way to understand the music better, but listening itself is always the most direct route.

You can organise what you find into a short set of notes and share it with classmates or family.

When you write your notes, record where each piece of information came from, so you can find it quickly if you need to check it later.

## Where to start listening

For a first-time listener, a good place to start is with some of her short instrumental pieces, such as those written for violin or flute with piano. They are brief and easy to get into.

Her vocal and choral works, especially those based on psalms, are often considered among her major achievements.

As you listen, notice how she uses harmony to create atmosphere and how she handles changes of tone colour.

You can find different recordings and listen to them side by side, to appreciate how different performers approach the music.

If you have the score, you can follow it as you listen and pay attention to the structure of the piece.

There is no need to rush to a verdict. Listen once through for the overall impression, note the passages that stay with you, then go back and listen to those places again, noticing how the melodic lines and the accompaniment texture fit together.

## From listening to practising

For piano learners, meeting different composers broadens your understanding of musical style.

Lili Boulanger wrote some piano pieces that are not long, and you can try playing them on your teacher's advice.

When practising these pieces, pay close attention to the colours of the harmony and to the use of the pedal.

You can also listen to her music alongside other French composers of the same period and compare the similarities and differences in style.

Comparing in this way helps you understand what French music looked like in the early twentieth century.

When choosing repertoire, first check the difficulty and length of a piece, pick one that suits your current level, and slowly get to know her musical language.

## Who she was

Lili Boulanger was born in Paris in 1893 and died in 1918, at only twenty-four. Her family had a deep musical background, and her older sister Nadia Boulanger later became a famous teacher of composition.

She was physically frail from childhood, but showed an interest in music very early.

In 1913 she won the Prix de Rome in composition with her cantata Faust et Hélène, the first woman to receive the prize.

The Prix de Rome was an important prize set up in France at the time for young artists, and winners could go to study at the Villa Medici in Rome.

In her short life she left works in several genres, including choral, vocal and instrumental music.

landler-austrian-country-dance-schubert.body:
The Ländler is a country folk dance from Austria and southern Germany. It is in three beats, slower than the later waltz, with steady steps and sometimes stamping and clapping. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries it gradually became faster and lighter in the cities and became one of the forerunners of the waltz. Schubert wrote a great many Ländler and German dances for piano, short and simple, often improvised at gatherings of friends. Later, Mahler also often used Ländler rhythms in his symphonies, bringing in the air of the countryside.

## A steady three beats

The Ländler is in three beats and is slower than the waltz.

**Common mistake**

The first beat of each bar is heavier, like a dancer planting a foot firmly.

Sometimes the dancers also stamp and clap, or sing and whistle.

**Slow down**
- A country folk dance from Austria and southern Germany
- In three beats, slower than the waltz, with steady steps
- One forerunner of the waltz
- Schubert wrote many Ländler for piano

## Don’t play a Ländler as a waltz

When playing a Ländler, it is very easy to play too fast and turn it into a waltz.

Remember that the Ländler is slower than the waltz and its rhythm is steadier.

Imagine dancers in heavy boots, stepping and turning on the grass.

## The German dances of Mozart and Beethoven

Before Schubert, Mozart and Beethoven also wrote German dances.

German dances are very similar to the Ländler: both are country-style dances in three beats.

These works were often written for balls, in versions for orchestra and for piano.

## Dances for gatherings of friends

Schubert often met with friends, and they read poetry, sang and danced together.

At these gatherings Schubert would often sit at the piano and improvise dances for his friends to dance to.

Many Ländler were written, or improvised, on occasions like these.

## Schubert’s Ländler

Schubert wrote a great many Ländler, German dances and waltzes for piano.

These dances are usually very short, around sixteen bars, divided into two sections, each repeated.

Their melodies are simple and warm, with the air of the countryside outside Vienna.

## How it differs from the waltz

The Ländler is slower than the waltz, with a steadier rhythm and a country simplicity.

The waltz is fast and whirls smoothly, with the elegance of the city.

To the ear, the Ländler is like dancing on the grass, and the waltz like spinning in a ballroom.

## Mahler’s Ländler

In the late nineteenth century, the Austrian composer Mahler often used Ländler rhythms in his symphonies.

For example, his First and Ninth Symphonies both contain movements in the style of a Ländler.

These movements combine the simplicity of a country dance with the grandeur of the symphony, sometimes with a touch of irony.

## Starting with Schubert’s Ländler

Schubert’s Ländler are short and not very difficult, and are very suitable for players at beginner to intermediate level.

You can learn several at a time and feel their different melodies and characters.

It is also a good way to get to know Schubert’s musical style.

## The link with the waltz

In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, the Ländler travelled to cities such as Vienna.

In the city ballrooms it gradually became faster and lighter, and the steps became smoother.

This change was one of the sources from which the waltz took shape.

## The left-hand bass of the Ländler

When playing a Ländler, the left hand often plays one bass note followed by two chords.

The bass should be steady and have weight, like the step of a dancer’s foot.

The two chords that follow should be lighter, but not too fast, keeping the steady tempo of the Ländler.

## A country dance

The Ländler comes from the countryside of Austria and southern Germany, a dance that farming people danced at festivals and gatherings.

Its name is related to a region of Austria and means roughly "dance of the countryside".

Dancers dance in pairs, a man and a woman turning together, with steady, strong steps.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothes plays a black grand piano on a neon street, with a synthesizer with crystals in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaedbsh-k4pur.webp)

## The right-hand song of the Ländler

The right-hand melody of the Ländler often has many broken chords and stepwise notes.

Sometimes the melody also has leaps like yodelling.

When playing, keep the melody simple and warm, like singing in the countryside.

## Ländler summary

The Ländler is a country folk dance from Austria and southern Germany, whose name means roughly "dance of the countryside". It is in three beats, slower than the waltz, with a heavier first beat, and the dancers sometimes stamp, clap, sing or whistle. After it travelled to cities such as Vienna in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, it became faster and lighter, and this is one of the sources of the waltz. The Ländler is like dancing on the grass, the waltz like spinning in a ballroom.

Schubert wrote many piano Ländler of around sixteen bars, often improvised at gatherings of friends. Mozart and Beethoven wrote similar German dances, and Mahler’s First and Ninth Symphonies contain movements in Ländler style. In the left hand there is one bass note and two chords, the bass steady and with weight, and the right-hand melody is simple. The tempo should not be too fast, and you can start with Schubert’s Ländler.

You can ask Teacher Aum to recommend Schubert’s Ländler.

## Asking your teacher to recommend Schubert’s Ländler in a lesson

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend a few Schubert Ländler suited to your level.

Your teacher can also explain the difference between the Ländler and the waltz and help you find a suitable tempo.

**Before you start**

Through the Ländler, discover the simple beauty of Austrian country dance.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Where does the Ländler come from?**
A: The countryside of Austria and southern Germany.

**Q: Which is faster, the Ländler or the waltz?**
A: The waltz is faster.

**Q: What is the relationship between the Ländler and the waltz?**
A: It is one of the forerunners of the waltz.

**Q: On what occasions were Schubert’s Ländler often played?**
A: Gatherings of friends.

**Q: Which of Mahler’s symphonies have movements in Ländler style?**
A: The First and Ninth Symphonies, among others.

maria-szymanowska-pianist-composer.body:
Maria Szymanowska (1789-1831) was a Polish pianist and composer. She is regarded as one of the first women of the early nineteenth century to make a profession of performing and to tour across Europe. She wrote piano works including etudes, nocturnes, mazurkas and polonaises, some of which predate Chopin's pieces in the same genres. On her travels she met many figures of the cultural world, and according to records, the poet Goethe wrote a poem for her.

## Inspiration from her story

Szymanowska's life shows a musician's effort to balance performing and composing.

**Before you start**

In the social setting of her time, she held to her own musical path and achieved a respected career.

Learning her story also lets us see a richer musical history as we study the piano.

## Friendships with cultural figures

During her concert tours, Szymanowska met many cultural figures of the time.

According to records, the German poet Goethe admired her playing and wrote a poem for her.

These contacts reflect her influence in European cultural circles at the time.

## Her later years

In her later years, Szymanowska settled in St Petersburg, where she carried on her musical activities and hosted salons of music and literature.

She died in St Petersburg in 1831.

Her daughter later married the Polish poet Mickiewicz.

## Early studies

Maria Szymanowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, and studied the piano from childhood.

She received her musical education in Warsaw and showed her talent for performing very early.

As a young woman she began to perform publicly in Warsaw and gradually built a reputation as a pianist.

## The path of a professional performer

In her day, it was not common for a woman to make a profession of performing and to tour from country to country.

In the early nineteenth century Szymanowska travelled through many European cities, giving concerts in Germany, France, England, Italy, Russia and elsewhere.

Her playing was admired by audiences and musicians of the time, and she is considered one of the early professional women pianists.

Her repertoire included not only her own works but also piano music by other composers of the time, allowing audiences in different places to hear music in different styles.

- Born in 1789, died in 1831
- Polish pianist and composer
- One of the first women to perform as a profession
- Wrote etudes, nocturnes, mazurkas and other works

## Are her works good to learn?

Some of Szymanowska's short piano pieces are not long and are moderate in technical difficulty, suitable for learners with some foundation.

Her etudes can help you practise technique, while her nocturnes can help you practise a singing melodic line.

You can ask your teacher to recommend suitable pieces for your level.

Before learning her works, you can listen to a few recordings first to get a feel for her melodic style and rhythmic character, and then decide which piece to start with.

## Rediscovery

For a long time, Szymanowska's works were played rarely.

In recent decades, as interest in women composers in music history has grown, her works have been republished, performed and recorded.

Today more and more piano learners and listeners are getting to know this early woman pianist.

## The connection with Chopin

Szymanowska and Chopin were both from Poland, and both wrote mazurkas and nocturnes.

Listening to the works of the two and comparing their styles is an interesting way to learn.

Such a comparison can also help you understand how a musical genre developed in the hands of different composers.

## Her piano pieces

Besides performing, Szymanowska also composed quite a lot of piano music, including etudes, nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises and waltzes.

Some of her piano pieces carry the colour of Polish folk music and also show the lyrical style of early Romanticism.

Some researchers point out that some of her etudes and nocturnes predate Chopin's pieces in the same genres, which gives them a certain significance in music history.

## How to study the history

When reading about Szymanowska, you can choose reliable biographies, music dictionaries and the prefaces of printed scores.

Some details may differ between sources, and comparing several sources gives a fuller picture.

**Before you start**

If an anecdote sounds especially far-fetched, check it against several sources before deciding how much to believe.

## FAQ

**Q: What nationality was Szymanowska?**
A: Polish, born in Warsaw.

**Q: When did she live?**
A: From 1789 to 1831.

**Q: What works did she write?**
A: Piano works such as etudes, nocturnes, mazurkas and polonaises.

**Q: What is her connection with Chopin?**
A: Both came from Poland and both wrote mazurkas and nocturnes, and some of her works predate Chopin's pieces in the same genres.

**Q: Did Goethe really write a poem for her?**
A: According to records, yes, and you can check the relevant biographical sources.

**Q: Can piano learners play her works?**
A: Some of the short pieces are of moderate difficulty, and your teacher can recommend them.

left-hand-1-5-10-broken-chord-pattern.body:
A common first left-hand accompaniment is a broken chord inside one octave, such as C, E, G. It sounds clear, but its range is rather narrow and it can sound a little thin. In many lyrical songs and Romantic pieces, the left hand uses a broader broken chord: the root, the fifth, and then a leap up to the third in the next octave, which is the tenth counting from the root. This "1-5-10" pattern spreads the accompaniment wider and makes it fuller, and it is a very practical way to write a left-hand accompaniment.

## Compared with an Ordinary Broken Chord

In an ordinary broken chord such as C, E, G, all three notes lie within one octave.

In a 1-5-10 broken chord, the third is moved up to the higher octave, so the range extends beyond an octave.

The sound feels more open, with sound in both the low and middle registers.

## Stretching the Hand

From the root to the tenth, the distance is more than an octave.

For people with smaller hands, it may not be possible to hold all three notes down at once, but playing them as a broken chord is fine.

As you play, the hand should move from the root toward the tenth, rather than staying stretched open the whole time.

## Why It Is Called a Tenth

Counting up from C, C is 1, D is 2, and so on up to the C an octave higher, which is 8.

Going further, D is 9 and E is 10.

So the E in the higher octave is exactly the tenth counting from C.

## 1-5-10 in a Minor Chord

A minor chord can use the same pattern, for example A minor: A, E, and the C in the higher octave.

The third becomes a minor third, but the shape of the hand is basically the same.

You can practise alternating major and minor chords within the chord progression of a song.

## Don't Keep the Hand Stretched Open

If you play 1-5-10 for a long time, the hand tends to stay tense and spread, and the longer you play the tighter it gets.

In fact, after each note is played, the hand can close up slightly before moving to the next note.

Let the wrist turn gently in the direction of the fingers to help the hand make the move.

## Working with the Sustain Pedal

The 1-5-10 pattern is often used with the sustain pedal, so that the three notes blend into one harmony.

Change the pedal as soon as the root changes, so the lingering sound of the previous chord does not carry over.

You can first play the left hand alone with the pedal to get this coordination comfortable.

- Root, fifth, and the third in the higher octave
- The third sits at the position of a tenth
- A wider range and a fuller sound
- Needs the hand to stretch and to relax

## Ask Your Teacher to Check Your Hand Shape in the Lesson

You can ask Teacher Aum to look at your hand shape and wrist movement when you play 1-5-10.

Your teacher can help spot any over-stretching or tension.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend a few pieces that suit practising this pattern.

## Using It in Song Accompaniment

Many lyrical songs can use the 1-5-10 pattern for the left hand in their piano accompaniment.

First look at the chord symbols of the song, then play 1-5-10 for each chord.

With the right hand playing the melody or chords, you get a full accompaniment.

## Summary of the 1-5-10 Pattern

1-5-10 means the 1st, 5th and 10th counting from the root. With C as the example, that is C, G and the E an octave higher. The tenth is a third plus an octave, and it has a wider range and a fuller sound than an ordinary broken chord within an octave.

A common way to play it is root, fifth, tenth, then back to the fifth. Do not keep the hand stretched open all the time: close it slightly after each note and let the wrist turn with it. Ask your teacher to help choose the fingering, and use it with the sustain pedal.

It works for minor chords too, and can be used in lyrical song accompaniments and Romantic pieces. Start slowly, and ask Teacher Aum to check your hand shape.

## Start Practising Slowly

When you first practise 1-5-10, keep the tempo slow and make sure every note lands accurately.

In particular, for the step from the fifth to the tenth, look at the position in advance.

Once you are familiar with it, gradually speed up.

## Choosing the Fingering

A common left-hand fingering is: 5th finger on the root, 2nd or 1st finger on the fifth, and 1st finger on the tenth.

Depending on the size of your hand and the pattern, the fingering can be adjusted.

You can ask your teacher to help choose the fingering that suits you.

## A Common Way to Play It

A common way to play it is: root, fifth, tenth, then back to the fifth, forming a pattern that goes there and back.

It can also be root, fifth, tenth, fifth, with each note lasting one eighth note.

The exact rhythm pattern can be chosen according to the time signature of the song.

## Examples in Classical Works

In Romantic nocturnes and similar works, the left hand often has broad broken chords, sometimes including leaps of a tenth.

This way of writing lets the left hand cover a wide range and sets off the singing melody in the right hand.

When you play these works, practising 1-5-10 will be very helpful.

## What Is 1-5-10?

"1-5-10" refers to three notes counted from the root: the 1st, the 5th and the 10th.

Taking the C major chord as an example, that is C, G, and the E an octave higher.

**Common misunderstandings**

The tenth is simply a third plus an octave.

![An art-deco style illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9m1gu-5h6cd.webp)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which three notes does 1-5-10 refer to?**
A: The root, the fifth and the third in the higher octave.

**Q: What is 1-5-10 for a C major chord?**
A: C, G and the E in the higher octave.

**Q: Why is it called a tenth?**
A: Because the third in the higher octave is exactly the tenth counting from the root.

**Q: Should the hand stay stretched open the whole time?**
A: No, close it slightly after each note.

**Q: What is it often used with?**
A: The sustain pedal.

meantone-temperament-pure-thirds.body:
Before equal temperament became widespread, keyboard instruments commonly used a tuning method called meantone temperament. Its core idea is to tune the fifths slightly narrow so that the major thirds become pure. The most common version, quarter-comma meantone, was widely used in European keyboard music of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. On an instrument tuned this way, the triads in keys with few sharps or flats are very sweet, but in keys with many sharps or flats there is a harsh "wolf fifth". Understanding meantone helps us understand the choice of keys in early keyboard music.

## The choice of keys

Because of the limits of meantone, most early keyboard works use keys with few sharps or flats.

Keys with many sharps or flats, such as F♯ major or D♭ major, were rarely used.

This is one reason why the keys in early keyboard music look fairly concentrated today.

## Summary of meantone temperament

Meantone narrows the fifths slightly to make the major thirds pure. In the common quarter-comma version, the 81:80 comma is shared equally among four fifths, so C to E is a pure major third and D sits exactly in the middle, which is why it is called "mean tone".

Keys with few sharps or flats have sweet triads, but a harsh wolf fifth is usually left between G♯ and E♭. G♯ and A♭ are not the same pitch, and some old instruments used split keys, which is why the keys of early keyboard works are fairly concentrated.

Later came various irregular temperaments, and in the nineteenth century equal temperament became standard on the piano. Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier has a title meaning roughly "well-tuned keyboard", and you can listen to related recordings together with Teacher Aum.

## What piano learners gain

Understanding meantone helps us see why, in the past, different keys were thought to have different characters.

In unequal temperaments, the intervals in each key are slightly different in size, so each key has a different colour.

On today's equal-tempered piano, that difference has disappeared.

## Bach and the "well-tempered" keyboard

Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier has a German title meaning "the well-tuned keyboard".

It uses all twenty-four major and minor keys, which shows that the tuning of the time could already be used in every key.

However, scholars think that what Bach used was not necessarily today's equal temperament, but possibly some kind of unequal temperament.

## The quarter comma

A major third built from stacked pure fifths is wider than a pure major third by one comma, in the ratio of eighty-one to eighty.

If that comma is shared equally among four fifths, each fifth is narrowed by a quarter of a comma.

That is why this tuning is called quarter-comma meantone.

## Talking about meantone in a lesson

You can ask Teacher Aum in a lesson just how harsh the wolf fifth really is.

You can also listen together to recordings of early keyboard music played in meantone and compare them with the modern piano.

This knowledge gives us a fuller understanding of the history of keyboard music.

## From meantone to equal temperament

From the late seventeenth century into the eighteenth, as music modulated more and more, people began to use various unequal temperaments.

Unequal temperaments made all twenty-four keys playable, though the thirds in each key differed slightly in width, so each key sounded as if it had its own temperament.

In the nineteenth century, equal temperament gradually became standard on the piano.

**Summary**
- Narrow the fifths to make the major thirds pure
- Commonly used in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century keyboard music
- Sweet triads in keys with few sharps or flats
- A harsh "wolf fifth" appears

## The wolf fifth

The problem with meantone is that twelve fifths cannot close perfectly into a circle.

Usually, between G♯ and E♭, a "fifth" is left that is much wider than a pure fifth. It sounds very harsh, like the howl of a wolf, which is why it is called the wolf fifth.

Chords that use this interval are almost unusable.

## Hearing meantone today

Today, some early-music performers use meantone to play early keyboard music.

When you listen to these recordings, notice the purity of the triads and the differences in colour between keys.

It sounds very different from a performance on a modern piano.

## Split keys

To solve this problem, some old organs and harpsichords used "split keys".

A single black key was divided into a front half and a back half, one for G♯ and one for A♭.

That way the player could choose between the two pitches as needed.

## The meaning of "mean tone"

In this tuning, C to E is a pure major third, and D lies exactly midway between C and E.

In other words, C to D and D to E are two equal whole tones, and this whole tone is called the "mean tone".

This is also where the name "meantone temperament" comes from.

## Sweet triads

In meantone, in keys with few sharps or flats such as C major, G major, F major and D major, the major triads are very pure and sweet.

Compared with equal temperament, the major thirds have no obvious beating.

This sound is exactly the ideal tone for much Renaissance and early Baroque keyboard music.

![Watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab1rwb-d5k33.webp)

## G♯ or A♭

In meantone, G♯ and A♭ are not the same pitch.

The keyboard has only one key, so the tuner can choose only one of them when tuning, usually G♯.

That way the E major triad is usable, but the A♭ major triad sounds very unpleasant.

## The starting point of meantone

In just intonation, the frequency ratio of a major third is five to four, and it sounds very pure.

But if you tune with pure fifths one after another, the major third you get from stacking four fifths is wider than five to four.

**Things to notice**

Meantone's solution is to tune every fifth a little narrow, so that four fifths stacked together give exactly a pure major third.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the core idea of meantone?**
A: To narrow the fifths so that the major thirds are pure.

**Q: What does quarter comma mean?**
A: The comma is shared equally among four fifths.

**Q: What is a wolf fifth?**
A: A fifth in meantone that is much wider than a pure fifth and sounds very harsh.

**Q: What are split keys?**
A: A black key divided into two halves, for example G♯ and A♭.

**Q: Why are the keys in early keyboard works fairly concentrated?**
A: Meantone suits only keys with few sharps or flats.

madeline-hunter-lesson-design-seven-step.body:
When there is too much to teach in one lesson, time often runs out halfway through. The educator Madeline Hunter proposed a model of lesson design that is often summed up as a handful of stages: stating the objective, setting the standard, getting attention (the introduction), explaining and demonstrating while checking understanding, guided practice, and lesson closure with independent practice. Piano teachers can borrow this way of thinking to organise a lesson.

- Focus each lesson on one main goal
- Open by saying what the lesson will cover
- After a demonstration, check that the student has understood
- Leave time for the student to practise with guidance

## From Guided Practice to Independent Practice

In the guided practice stage, the student practises under the teacher's eye, and the teacher gives feedback straight away to help the student adjust.

Once the student is fairly fluent, you can let them do it on their own, for example playing the whole piece through, with the teacher giving an assessment only at the end.

Before the lesson ends, you can set specific homework, such as "play the second section slowly three times a day, paying attention to the staccato in the left hand".

Specific homework tells the student what to do at home and makes it easier to check at the next lesson.

In this way the lesson forms a complete cycle.

Sometimes there is not enough time in a lesson for every stage, and that is fine: you can leave the rest for the next lesson. What matters is that each lesson has a clear focus.

## The First Few Minutes

At the start of the lesson, a short activity can help the student settle in, such as playing a familiar piece, doing a rhythm game, or chatting about how practice went this week.

Then, in a sentence or two, state the goal of the lesson, for example "Today we will work on the second section of this piece, focusing on the staccato in the left hand".

Stating the goal lets the student know what the lesson is about and helps them concentrate.

You can also explain why the material matters, for example how it connects with what they have learned before.

The first few minutes are short, but they set the direction for the whole lesson.

## The Thinking Behind Lesson Design

Madeline Hunter was an American educator who worked at the University of California, Los Angeles. The lesson design model she proposed has been widely discussed in teacher training.

The model is often summed up as a handful of stages: stating the objective, setting the standard, getting attention (the introduction), explaining and demonstrating while checking understanding, guided practice, and lesson closure with independent practice.

Its core idea is that a lesson needs a clear goal, and every stage serves that goal.

The model was originally designed for classroom teaching in general, but its way of thinking can be borrowed for piano lessons too.

When borrowing it, there is no need to copy every stage rigidly. You can adapt it to the student and the lesson.

## Explaining, Demonstrating and Checking

When explaining something new, keep the language simple and clear, and cover only one key point at a time.

A demonstration lets the student hear and see directly what the goal looks like. The teacher can play it once and then ask the student to imitate.

After the demonstration, you need to check that the student has understood. You can ask the student to describe the key points, or ask them to play it once and watch whether they manage it.

If the student has not understood, you can explain it again in a different way, or break the material into smaller pieces.

Checking understanding keeps students from going home to practise with a misunderstanding.

When checking, you can ask open questions, such as "How do you think this section differs from the one before?" Letting the student answer in their own words also shows how well they understand.

## Borrowing This Idea to Plan a Piano Lesson

At the start of the lesson, a short activity can help the student settle in, such as playing a familiar piece or doing a rhythm game. Then state the goal of the lesson in a sentence or two.

When explaining something new, you can demonstrate first and then have the student imitate. After the demonstration, use questions or ask the student to play it once to confirm that they have understood the key points.

In the guided practice stage, the teacher can watch from beside the student and give feedback straight away. Once the student is fairly fluent, let them do it on their own, and set specific homework.

The model does not have to be applied rigidly; adapt it to the student. What matters is that the lesson has a clear goal, and that the student knows what they learned and what to practise at home.

![A cartoon-style student wearing headphones sits at a piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lvne1-b6d3f.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: Can a thirty-minute lesson be planned this way?**
A: Yes. Just keep each stage short and focus the goal on one thing.

**Q: Does every lesson need to include all the stages?**
A: No. You can choose flexibly according to the material and the student.

**Q: Does this model suit group lessons?**
A: Yes. Group lessons can borrow these stages to plan the class as well.

**Q: How much homework should I set?**
A: One or two specific tasks are usually enough, so the student can carry them out easily.

**Q: What is a simple way to check understanding?**
A: Ask the student to state the key points, or ask them to play it once and observe the result.

**Q: Does this model suit adult students?**
A: Yes. Adult students also benefit from clear goals and specific homework.
