learn-school-song-melody-chords.body:
To play your school song at the piano, first find or write out the melody and learn it well with your right hand. Then, using the chord markings on the song sheet, or by trying to find suitable chords yourself, accompany with your left hand. Finally, with the needs of group singing in mind, choose a suitable tempo and key so that the singers can keep up and sing comfortably. Once you know it well, it will come in useful at school events or at home.

## Choosing a suitable tempo

When accompanying a choir, the tempo should suit everyone’s singing, neither too fast nor too slow.

You can first listen to a recording of how the school usually sings its song to get a sense of the tempo everyone is used to.

Keep a steady tempo while accompanying, so that the singers can follow your rhythm.

## Features of a school song

School songs usually have a dignified melody and a steady rhythm, suitable for many people to sing together.

Many school songs have a fairly regular structure, with several verses sharing the same melody.

Knowing these features helps you learn the song more quickly and accompany everyone better.

## Preparing an introduction

Before the singing begins, the accompanist usually plays an introduction so that everyone knows the key and tempo and is ready to start singing.

The introduction can be the last line of the song, or a few simple chords.

At the end of the introduction you can use a clear chord or a pause to signal everyone to begin.

## Play it while singing it yourself

Before accompanying everyone for real, you can play and sing it once yourself, to check that the melody, chords and tempo are all right.

As you sing, notice which phrases are long and need a breath in the middle. When accompanying you can play a little more softly in these places, giving the singers some room.

If you find it hard to play and sing at the same time, your accompaniment may not be fluent enough yet, and you can practise the left hand a few more times.

## Choosing a suitable key

If the original key is too high or too low for everyone, you can consider moving it to a more suitable key.

Before transposing, you can discuss it with the music teacher, because the school choir may already be used to a certain key.

After choosing the key, make sure all the chords move along with it.

## Rehearsing with the choir

Before the real accompaniment, you can rehearse a few times with the choir or your classmates.

During rehearsal notice whether everyone can keep up with your tempo and where they tend to sing wrongly, and adjust the accompaniment if necessary.

The volume of the accompaniment should be right: loud enough for everyone to hear, but not covering the singing.

![A collage illustration of hands in high-tech gloves playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yfb20-ltk91.webp)

## Finding the score of the school song

You can first ask the school’s music teacher whether there is a score or a numbered-notation sheet of the school song.

Some schools provide the score of the school song on their website or in the student handbook.

If you can’t find it, you can also work out the melody from memory and recordings and write it down yourself.

- First work out and learn the melody of the school song
- Find the chords from the chord markings or by ear
- Choose a tempo and key suitable for group singing
- Prepare an introduction so everyone knows when to start

## The meaning of playing the school song

Being able to accompany the school song is a way of serving the group, and also a chance to show what you have achieved in learning the piano.

Even if you don’t play at school events, playing the school song at home can bring back many memories.

The process of learning the school song also gives you the basic method of accompanying a song, which you can use for many more songs later.

## Handling several verses

If the school song has several verses, you can play a one- or two-bar interlude between them, giving everyone time to prepare for the next verse.

After the last verse you can slow down gradually on the tonic chord, giving the song a complete ending.

The accompaniment can vary slightly from verse to verse, for example a little stronger in the last verse.

## Learn the melody first

Once you have the score, first learn the melody well with your right hand, paying attention to the rhythm and the length of each phrase.

You can sing as you play, to make sure what you play matches what everyone sings.

If the melody has long notes or pauses, pay special attention, because these are often where everyone breathes.

If a few notes keep going wrong, take that phrase out and practise it slowly, then put it back into the whole song.

## Adding chords to the melody

If the score has chord names marked, you can play them as marked.

If not, you can try the three common chords I, IV and V in turn and listen to which chord best suits the melody in each bar.

The left hand can start with a simple accompaniment, such as one chord per bar, and add variety once you are comfortable.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What if I can’t find the score of the school song?**
A: You can ask the music teacher, or work out the melody yourself from a recording.

**Q: Can I change the key of the school song?**
A: Yes, but it is best to discuss it with the music teacher first.

**Q: How do I decide the tempo for the accompaniment?**
A: Follow the tempo at which the school usually sings the song, and keep it steady.

**Q: How long should the introduction be?**
A: A few bars is usually enough, so that everyone is ready to start singing.

**Q: What if the accompaniment is too loud?**
A: Play a little more softly so that the singing can be heard clearly.

**Q: Can a child accompany the school song?**
A: With some foundation, they can start with a simple chord accompaniment.

live-group-practice-session-model.body:
A live group practice session is one where the teacher goes live online at a fixed time and leads a group of students in practising set material together. Unlike one-to-one lessons, the focus is not on correcting each student in turn, but on creating a "we are all practising together" atmosphere, which helps students build the habit of regular practice. From a music school's point of view, a practice session is a product with controllable costs that can reach more students; for students, it fills the gap of practising alone between formal lessons.

## What problem practice sessions solve

After a lesson, many students put off practising alone at home, or do not know where to start. A practice session provides a fixed time, clear practice content and people to practise with. The teacher demonstrates rhythms and reminds students about hand shape during the live stream, the students practise along, and afterwards they check in in the comments. This structure lowers the barrier to starting practice.

**It cannot replace formal lessons**
A practice session can hardly give detailed guidance on each student's specific problems, so it suits better as a supplement to formal lessons. When presenting the product, this should be stated honestly, so that students do not form unrealistic expectations.

## The structure of a practice session

A practice session usually lasts around thirty to forty minutes, with a clear structure and a steady pace.

A suggested structure:

- Opening few minutes: greetings and the goal of today's practice.
- Warm-up: simple finger exercises or scales.
- Main practice: demonstrated in sections, with students practising along, repeated several times.
- Challenge: a slightly harder variation, to encourage trying.
- Closing: summarise the key points and set a small exercise for before next time.

Choosing one clear theme for each session, such as "left-hand broken chords" or "steady quarter notes", is easier to sustain than a crowded programme.

## Choosing how to charge

![An electronic keyboard and screens under neon lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw5otlpr-uqqnx.webp)

There are several common ways to charge for practice sessions: as an extra benefit for students of formal courses, included in the course fee; as a separate monthly subscription; or bought per session. Which to choose depends on the school's overall product structure. If the main aim of the sessions is to improve retention in formal courses, an extra benefit may suit better; if you want to attract new users, a separate subscription can serve as an entry-level product.

**Be transparent about pricing**
Whichever way you choose, state clearly on the page the price, the number of sessions included, whether replays can be watched and how to cancel. Transparent information builds trust better than any promotional wording.

## Technical preparation

The sound quality of a live stream matters a great deal. If piano sound passes through a phone's noise reduction, it may come out choppy. An external microphone is recommended, with any noise-reduction option that compresses music turned off in the streaming software. The picture should show the teacher's hands and the keys at the same time, which you can do with an overhead angle.

Technical checklist:

- An external microphone placed near the piano, with the volume tested.
- A camera angle that covers the whole keyboard and both hands.
- A stable network, with a speed test before going live.
- A backup device in case of a dropped connection.
- Practice score examples prepared on screen in advance.

## Running the community

Much of the value of a practice session comes from the community. You can set up a student group, share the practice points after each live stream, and encourage students to upload practice clips and encourage each other. The group rules should be written clearly, keeping a friendly atmosphere and avoiding advertising and unrelated content. Teachers and assistants regularly answer questions in the group, so that students feel noticed.

## The teacher's workload

A practice session looks like just one live stream, but there is preparation before and after: choosing the topic, preparing score examples, testing equipment, and after the stream organising the key points and answering community questions. When a school schedules practice sessions, this time should be counted in the teacher's workload and reasonably paid. Several teachers can take turns hosting, each taking the topics they are good at, which both lightens the load and lets students meet different teaching styles.

## Measuring the results

To measure how well practice sessions are working, you can look at a few simple indicators: the number of participants at each stream, the number of consecutive sessions students attend, and the renewal rate among students of formal courses. These figures help judge whether the sessions are really helping students build a practice habit, and let you adjust the schedule and topics accordingly.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Are practice sessions suitable for beginners?**
A: Yes, but choose simple themes and offer options of different difficulty during the stream.

**Q: Can a teacher with no live-streaming experience do this?**
A: They can first try a few test streams on a small scale, and start formally once they are familiar with the equipment and the pace.

**Q: What if students do not turn on their cameras?**
A: Practice sessions usually do not require students to turn on cameras, and you can interact through check-ins in the comments.

**Q: Are replays useful?**
A: Yes. Students who cannot make the time can catch up, but you should say how long replays are kept.

**Q: How many people are right for one stream?**
A: There is no fixed standard. When there are many, an assistant can help answer questions in the comments.

listening-to-rests.body:
A rest marks a period of time with no sound, but it is not a blank in the music. It is part of the music. A good rest lets a phrase breathe and gives the next note more strength. When you play, count the length of a rest as carefully as you would a note, and keep feeling the beat during the rest, so that the quiet parts also have direction.

## Appreciating the Power of Quiet

Quiet in music is often as expressive as sound.

A pause in exactly the right place can make listeners hold their breath, waiting for the next sound.

When you learn to listen to rests and to express them, your playing will have more breath and will move people more.

## A Rest Is Not a Blank

Many people see a rest and treat it as a place to relax and ignore, and often end up playing the rest too short, hurrying into the next note.

In fact, a rest is part of the music, and like a pause in speech, it has meaning.

A good pause gives listeners time to take in what they have just heard, and also makes the sound that follows feel more anticipated.

- A rest marks a period of quiet
- The length of a rest needs to be as accurate as that of a note
- During a rest, keep feeling the beat in your head
- Rests give phrases breath and layers

## Start Practising by Listening

You can find a recording and listen specifically for the rests and pauses in it, feeling the effect they bring to the music.

You can also try playing the rests in your own performance more accurately and more deliberately, and then record yourself and listen back.

Compare the two recordings, and you may find that just by changing the rests, the music becomes clearer and has more layers.

## Rests Let Phrases Breathe

The rest after the end of a melodic phrase is like taking a breath when singing, giving the music room to breathe.

Without these pauses, all the phrases would be crowded together and sound hurried.

When you play, you can imagine that you are singing the melody, and naturally take a breath where the rests are.

![A piano scene with futuristic light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9ya2c0-0ib7m.webp)

## Counting Rests Accurately

In practice, you can count rests just as you count notes, for example "one, two, three, four", to make sure the rest is long enough.

You can use a metronome to check whether the length of the rest is accurate.

Especially for a rest after the end of a phrase, do not shorten it because you are in a hurry to start the next phrase.

After practising a few times with the metronome on, you can turn it off and play again, to see whether you can still keep the rest the same length without the prompt.

## The Sound Before and After a Rest

For the last note before a rest, pay attention to how it ends: whether it is gently released or stopped crisply.

For the first note after a rest, prepare the dynamic and tone so that it enters clearly.

How you handle the moments before and after a rest often decides whether the pause sounds natural or stiff.

## What Is a Rest?

In a score, a rest marks a period of time with no sound.

Rests also come in different lengths, from the whole rest that fills a whole bar to the eighth rest that lasts only half a beat.

Each kind of rest has its own length, and when you play you need to keep silent for exactly the right number of beats.

## Children Learning Rests

When children learn rests, body movements can help them understand, for example putting their hands on their knees during a rest, or giving a gentle clap.

You can also turn it into a game: everyone sings a song together and stops together at the rests, to see who stops most accurately.

This way children find it easier to remember the lengths of rests, and also feel that quiet is part of music.

## Pedal and Rests

When using the sustain pedal, pay attention to where the rests are. If the pedal is still down during a rest, the sound will keep ringing and the rest cannot be heard.

In general, release the pedal at the start of the rest so that the sound stops.

Of course, some pieces deliberately let the sound ring on during a rest, and you need to judge this from the markings in the score and the style of the piece.

## Keep Feeling the Beat During a Rest

During a rest, your hands can leave the keys, but the beat in your mind must not stop.

You can gently nod or count the beats in your head during a rest, to keep yourself in the rhythm of the music.

This way, when the next note begins, you can come in accurately on the right beat.

## FAQ

**Q: Should my hands leave the keys during a rest?**
A: In general they can, but the beat in your head must not stop.

**Q: What if I always play rests too short?**
A: You can count the beats aloud, or use a metronome to help you practise.

**Q: Should I release the pedal during a rest?**
A: Generally yes, to let the sound stop, but it depends on the markings in the score.

**Q: How do I remember the different rests?**
A: You can remember them by comparing them with the lengths of the matching notes.

**Q: What if my child finds rests boring?**
A: You can get them involved with games such as clapping and stopping.

**Q: Do rests have expression?**
A: Yes. The length of a rest and how you handle the moments before and after it both affect the expression of the music.

learn-new-piece-listening-first.body:
When you get a new piece, listening to a recording a few times before you start practising can help you understand its tempo, character, structure and general sound in advance. As you listen, you can follow the score and find where each phrase falls along with the recording, noticing where the climax is, what repeats and what changes. That way, when you begin practising, you already have a picture of the whole in your head, reading is quicker, and you know better which direction each passage is going.

## Don’t rely too much on recordings

Listening to a recording can help understanding, but you shouldn’t depend on it completely to learn a piece, for example by only imitating by ear without looking at the score.

**Watch the details**

The ability to read music has to be built by looking at the score and playing from it yourself.

Use listening as a supplement to practice, not a replacement for reading.

## Notice the structure

When you listen along with the score, notice which sections repeat, which have changes, and where the climax of the piece is.

You can make simple pencil marks on the score, such as section A, section B, climax.

Once you understand the structure, you can plan practice by section, and memorising is also more organised.

## Children learning a new piece

For children, listening to a recording first can make them interested in the new piece and willing to learn it.

Parents can listen together with the child and ask what the piece sounds like, for example rain or dancing.

This kind of playful listening lets children start practising with curiosity.

**Common mistake**
- Listen to a recording a few times before practising
- Get to know the tempo, character, structure and sound
- Look at the score while listening to find your place
- Have a picture of the whole in your head before you start practising

## First listening: the overall feeling

The first time you listen, you can do it without the score, simply listening quietly and feeling the mood and atmosphere of the piece.

Afterwards, think about what feeling the piece gives you and which part you like.

This first impression is often an important starting point for how you will express the piece later.

## When there is no recording

For some pieces you may not be able to find a recording, such as certain études or newly published works.

In that case you can ask your teacher to play it through, or slowly play out the melody yourself first to get a sense of its general shape.

You can also read the score silently in your head and imagine its sound, which is also a very good exercise.

## Why listen first

If you start practising from the score alone, you have to read note by note, and it is hard to imagine the shape of the whole piece all at once.

If you listen to a recording first, you can directly feel the overall effect of the piece and know whether it is lively or lyrical, simple or complex.

With this overall impression, practice has more direction and it is easier to keep your interest.

![A piano scene with futuristic lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0f6yg-jzvhf.webp)

## Notice tempo and expression

When listening to a recording, notice the performer’s tempo and where they slow down or speed up.

You can also notice the changes in dynamics: where it is very soft, where very loud, and where there are crescendos and diminuendos.

Compare these with the markings in the score and see how the performer understands the composer’s intentions.

## Forming your own understanding

The purpose of listening to a recording is to help you understand the music, not to have you copy one performer’s approach completely.

After getting to know several different performances, think about which approach you prefer, or whether you have ideas of your own.

Discuss these ideas with your teacher and gradually form a performance that is your own.

## Choosing recordings

You can choose fairly reliable recordings, such as the edition your teacher recommends or an officially published recording.

If possible, listen to two or three versions by different performers and compare how they handle tempo and expression.

This avoids imitating only one version and helps you form your own understanding.

## Second listening: following the score

The second time you listen, open the score and follow along, finding the position of each bar as you listen.

If you lose your place, you can pause the recording and continue once you have found it.

This kind of practice also trains your reading and makes you more familiar with how the score corresponds to the sound.

## Listening again midway through practice

Midway through practice you can also listen to the recording again from time to time and see whether your understanding has changed.

Sometimes, listening after practising for a while, you will notice many details you missed before.

You can also compare your own recording with the reference recording and see what else could be improved.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why listen before learning a new piece?**
A: To understand the overall tempo, character and structure.

**Q: What kind of recording should I listen to?**
A: One recommended by your teacher or officially published; it helps to hear several versions.

**Q: Should I look at the score while listening?**
A: The first time you can just listen; the second time follow the score.

**Q: Will I rely too much on the recording?**
A: A recording is a supplement; you still need to read the score yourself.

**Q: What if there is no recording?**

melodic-minor-up-down.body:
The melodic minor is one form of the minor scale: going up, both the sixth and seventh notes are raised by a semitone, and coming down it returns to the natural minor. In A minor, the ascending scale is A, B, C, D, E, F♯, G♯, A, and the descending scale is A, G, F, E, D, C, B, A. Written this way, the rising melody moves more smoothly to the tonic, while the descent keeps the soft colour of the minor.

- The melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh notes going up
- Coming down, it returns to the natural minor
- A melodic minor has F♯ and G♯ going up
- Together with the natural and harmonic minor, it is one of three common forms

## Why raise the sixth note

The harmonic minor raises only the seventh note, which leaves a fairly large gap between the sixth and seventh notes, called an augmented second.

This gap is distinctive in harmony, but in a melody it can feel awkward to sing or play.

The melodic minor raises the sixth note as well, filling in that gap and making the rising line flow more smoothly. That is where its name comes from.

## The three minor scales

Minor scales are often divided into three forms: natural minor, harmonic minor and melodic minor.

The natural minor is the most basic form. It uses the same notes as its relative major, just starting from a different note.

The harmonic minor raises the seventh note, while the melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh notes on the way up.

## Melodic minor in jazz

In jazz, the melodic minor often uses the raised sixth and seventh notes both going up and coming down, and is sometimes called the jazz minor.

This differs from the usage in classical music, and shows that the same scale can have different habits in different styles.

As a beginner, first learn the classical rules for going up and down, and look at the jazz variation later.

## The melodic minor going down

Coming down, the melodic minor usually returns to the natural minor, that is, A, G, F, E, D, C, B, A.

The raised sixth and seventh notes are restored on the way down, and the scale brings back the soft, slightly sad colour that is special to the minor.

So the melodic minor is a scale whose ascending and descending forms are different, and that is its most distinctive feature.

## The melodic minor going up

Take A minor as an example. The natural minor notes are A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, all white keys.

Going up in melodic minor, the sixth note F and the seventh note G are both raised a semitone, giving A, B, C, D, E, F♯, G♯, A.

This way, the last few notes of the scale are closer to the structure of a major scale, and the move to the tonic is smoother.

## Melodic minor in pieces

In many minor-key pieces you will see the sixth and seventh notes sometimes raised and sometimes restored, and this is often related to the melodic minor.

Rising melodies often use the raised notes, and falling melodies use the restored ones.

Once you know this, you will not be surprised by these accidentals when you read music.

## Melodic minor in other keys

Any minor key can give a melodic minor in the same way: raise the sixth and seventh notes going up, and restore them coming down.

For example, E natural minor has one sharp, F♯, and going up in melodic minor, C and D are raised too, becoming C♯ and D♯.

Practising the melodic minor in different keys helps you become familiar with the sharps and flats of each key.

## Turning the scale into music

When you practise the melodic minor, do not just play the scale mechanically. You can also try adding changes in dynamics, such as a crescendo going up and a diminuendo coming down.

You can also improvise a short melody with the notes of the melodic minor and feel its colour.

Combining scales with musical expression makes practice more meaningful, and more fun.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon-lit street, with a crystal tower behind them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9zc3te-iatia.webp)

## Hearing the three minors side by side

On the piano you can play A natural minor, A harmonic minor and A melodic minor one after another and compare how they sound.

You will hear that the natural minor is fairly soft, the harmonic minor has a distinctive exotic colour, and the melodic minor going up comes close to the brightness of a major scale.

After comparing them, look at the sharps and flats that appear in your pieces, and it will be easier to understand what the composer intended.

## Practising fingering

The fingering for the melodic minor is usually similar to the other minor forms in the same key, but because the notes going up and down are different, your fingers need to adapt to the change.

When practising, start slowly with one hand, and check that each finger lands on the right key both going up and coming down.

Once you are fluent, practise with both hands together and gradually speed up.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Are the melodic minor going up and coming down the same?**
A: No. Going up, the sixth and seventh notes are raised, and coming down it returns to the natural minor.

**Q: Which sharps does A melodic minor have going up?**
A: F♯ and G♯.

**Q: What is the difference between the harmonic and melodic minor?**
A: The harmonic minor raises only the seventh note, while the melodic minor also raises the sixth note going up.

**Q: Why is it called melodic minor?**
A: Because it makes the rising melody flow more smoothly.

**Q: Does every minor key have a melodic minor?**
A: Yes, it can be made in the same way in any of them.

**Q: Is the melodic minor in jazz the same?**
A: In jazz, the raised notes are often used both going up and coming down.

memorize-piano-three-memory-lines.body:
Many people memorise by playing a piece over and over until their fingers "know the way". This muscle memory comes quickly, but it is also the most fragile: as soon as you are nervous or interrupted, your fingers do not know where to go next. A more reliable way to memorise is to build three lines of memory at the same time: knowing the structure of the piece, being able to hear it in your head, and the movement memory of your fingers. The three support each other, so if one breaks, the other two can still bring you back.

## Structural memory: draw a map of the piece first

Before memorising, look through the whole piece as if you were reading a map. Where is the opening theme? Where does it repeat? Where does something change? You can mark the sections on the music with letters, for example A, A, B, A.

**Find what is the same and what is different**
Many pieces contain a lot of repetition, with only one note or one ending different. Circle these "almost the same" places and write down the difference, for example "the second ending goes up". These are often the places that are easiest to confuse when memorising.

## Aural memory: be able to sing it in your head

Step away from the keys, close your eyes and try to "play" the piece from the beginning in your head. If you cannot continue through some section, your aural memory of it is not yet clear enough. Go back to the piano, play only the melody of that section while singing softly, then leave the keys and try again.

People with good aural memory can hear that "the sound is wrong" even if their fingers slip for a moment, and they quickly find the right note again.

![A small dark upright piano standing alone on a wide grey floor, casting a long shadow](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw40y885-lv367.webp)

## Touch memory: make your movements more stable

Muscle memory is still important, but it needs to be built in a more conscious way. Fixed fingering is the key: use the same finger for the same note every time, so the movement can become stable. If you use finger 2 today and finger 3 tomorrow, your fingers will never remember.

Slow practice also strengthens muscle memory. When you play slowly, you can notice every movement of the hand and every place where it lands, and the body remembers these details more easily than fast repetition.

## Three tests you can do at home

You can check how secure your memory is with these methods:

- Start from the beginning of any section and see whether you can do it without starting from the top
- Play only the left hand from beginning to end without looking at the music
- Step away from the keys and go through the whole piece in your head

If one of the tests fails, you know which line of memory needs strengthening. For example, if playing only the left hand fails, it means you have mainly relied on the right-hand melody to carry the left hand along.

## Memorise in sections, then join them up

Divide the piece into several sections and concentrate on memorising one section a day. The next day, review the previous day's section first, then learn a new one. Pay special attention to the joins between sections, because memory most often stalls at the "change of section". You can practise the last two bars of each section together with the first two bars of the next, so that the join itself becomes a piece of memory.

## Sleep and spacing

Memorising does not have to be done all at once. After a night's sleep you will often find that a passage you barely remembered the day before is clearer. Rather than forcing a piece into your head in one evening, spread it over several days with a short review each day, and give your memory time to settle.

## Write out the story of the piece in words

Another way to strengthen structural memory is to write one simple description for each section, for example "the opening is like a walk", "the second section suddenly turns dark", "the ending returns to the opening theme, but quieter". Words turn abstract notes into pictures with a plot, so when you memorise there is a story line in your head to follow.

These descriptions do not need technical terms. They only need to make sense to you. Children can draw instead of writing, adding a small picture next to each section, such as a sun, a raindrop or a little boat.

## Keeping memorised pieces in good shape

If a memorised piece is not played for a long time, the memory slowly fades. You can put memorised pieces into a review schedule and play one or two each week in rotation. When reviewing, look at the music now and then to make sure you have not drifted into playing something wrong, because after a long time even small mistakes can be "remembered" by the fingers.

You can also change the setting when you review, for example by playing on a different piano or at a different time of day. If you can still play it smoothly after the setting changes, the memory is fairly secure and no longer depends on one familiar situation.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do I always have to memorise?**
A: Not necessarily. It depends on the purpose. Memorising feels freer when preparing for a performance, and playing from the music is perfectly fine for everyday practice.

**Q: Where do people most often forget when memorising?**
A: Usually at the joins between sections, and in repeated sections that are almost identical but slightly different.

**Q: Is memorising different for children and adults?**
A: Children's muscle memory comes quickly, so they most need to add structural and aural memory.

**Q: What if I forget the music when I am nervous?**
A: Jump to the start of the next familiar section and carry on. In practice, rehearse starting from any section.

learn-song-for-family-request.body:
When a family member asks for a song they would like to hear, you can first find or write out its main melody, choose a key that suits your level, then add simple chords with your left hand to make a version you can play all the way through. You don’t need to sound exactly like the original singer. If the melody comes through, the accompaniment is steady, and the beginning and ending are clear, it is a very thoughtful performance.

## Adding chords to the melody

The left hand can start in the simplest way: play one chord on the first beat of each bar, or just the root note of the chord.

First find the few chords the song uses most. Many pop songs use only three or four chords, repeated over and over.

Try playing different chords under the melody and listen to which blends best with it. If you have a chord chart, you can refer directly to the chord names marked on it.

## Preparing the beginning and ending

A song that starts straight into the melody can sometimes feel abrupt. You can play two bars of chords at the beginning as an introduction, so the listeners are ready.

For the ending, after the last line of melody you can slowly settle on the tonic chord, or repeat the last line and gradually slow down.

With a clear beginning and ending, the performance feels complete, like a real piece.

## Get to know the song first

Before you start, listen to the song a few times and notice its main melody, rhythm and mood. Is it light or lyrical? Where is the chorus?

If your family member can sing it, ask them to sing it through, and you will see more clearly which part they know best and most want to hear.

Many songs are quite long, and you don’t have to play the whole song. Choosing the most representative verse and chorus is enough.

## Adding a little variety to the accompaniment

Once the basic chords are secure, you can add some simple variety, such as breaking the chords up and playing them note by note, or repeating them gently to the rhythm of the song.

The verse can be played softer and simpler, and the chorus a little fuller, so that the music rises and falls.

The variety doesn’t need to be complicated; it is enough to give the whole song some layers.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot plays a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xbrm2-t1oxv.webp)

## Choosing a suitable key

The key of the original song may not suit your level. If the original key has many black keys and is hard to play, you can move it to an easier key, such as C major or G major.

When transposing, all the notes move by the same distance, so the melody sounds higher or lower but keeps its shape.

If your family member wants to sing along, also consider whether the key is comfortable for the singer, neither too high nor too low.

## Finding the main melody

If you can find a piano score or a numbered-notation sheet for the song, you can refer to it directly. If not, you can try to find the melody by ear: first hum it, then try it note by note on the piano.

Write down the melody you find, using note names, numbered notation or staff notation, whichever you like.

As you write, pay attention to the rhythm and keep long and short notes distinct. You can compare with the original recording as you go to make sure nothing is missing.

## Practise in sections, then put it together

First practise the right-hand melody and the left-hand accompaniment separately, then slowly put the hands together. For the first few times, it is a good idea to go slowly and listen carefully to whether the chords and melody line up.

Practise the hard places separately a few extra times, then join them up once they are comfortable.

Once the whole song runs smoothly, adjust the tempo and dynamics according to the mood of the song.

## Playing it for your family

When you have practised it, pick a relaxed time to play it for your family. It doesn’t have to be formal; it could be after a meal or on a weekend afternoon.

If your family are willing, you can ask them to sing along while you accompany. This kind of collaboration is often more fun than playing alone.

**Watch the details**

After playing, ask how they felt about it. Perhaps they will request the next song, and that is how your repertoire gradually grows.

**Remember this**
- First confirm the main melody, starting by singing and listening
- Choose a key that is easy for your hands
- Start the left hand with simple chords or single notes
- Prepare a beginning and ending so the performance feels complete

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What if I can’t find the score?**
A: You can find the melody by ear, or ask your teacher to help write a simple version.

**Q: What if I can’t add chords?**
A: You can play just the melody at first, or play only one bass note per bar with the left hand, and learn chords gradually.

**Q: If the song is too long, do I have to play all of it?**
A: No, choose the most familiar section, such as the chorus. Playing one section well is also meaningful.

**Q: Will transposing make the song sound worse?**
A: Transposing only changes the pitch; the shape of the melody stays the same, and with the right key it usually still sounds natural.

**Q: Is this kind of practice suitable for children?**
A: Yes, you can start with songs the child likes, with a teacher or parent helping to simplify them.

**Q: Can I play other people’s songs in public?**
A: Playing privately for your family is fine. For public performances or publishing recordings, be aware of the song’s copyright rules.

mendelssohn-midsummer-overture-1826.body:
In the summer of 1826, the seventeen-year-old Mendelssohn read Shakespeare's comedy A Midsummer Night's Dream. He was deeply drawn to its forest, its fairies and its lovers, and wrote an overture of the same name. He first wrote it as a piano duet, to play with his sister Fanny, and then turned it into an orchestral piece. Seventeen years later, in 1843, he wrote a full set of incidental music for a staging of the play, which includes the Wedding March so often heard at weddings. An overture and a set of incidental music, seventeen years apart, yet the style is completely unified.

## Premiere and spread

In February 1827 the overture was given its first public performance in Stettin (today Szczecin in Poland).

It was soon performed all over Europe and was well received.

Many people were amazed that a seventeen-year-old could write such a mature work.

## Playing the Wedding March on the piano

There are many piano arrangements of the Wedding March, at different levels of difficulty.

When you play it, the opening fanfare should be bright and strong, with the chords together.

The lyrical passage in the middle can be played more softly, for contrast.

## The original piano duet version

Mendelssohn first wrote the Midsummer Night's Dream overture as a piano duet.

He played it at home with his sister Fanny to hear how it sounded.

Only after that did he arrange it for orchestra.

## Unity across seventeen years

The overture was written in 1826 and the incidental music in 1843, seventeen years apart.

But in the incidental music Mendelssohn skilfully quoted themes from the overture, giving the whole set of music a unified style.

This also shows how deeply he always understood the play.

![A person with a long braid plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with drones in the air](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaaifnz-4s9ei.webp)

## The donkey's bray in the overture

In the play, one of the craftsmen is put under a spell and his head is turned into a donkey's head.

In the overture Mendelssohn imitates a donkey's bray with instruments, one high and one low, which is very amusing.

Humorous details like this tie the music closely to the drama.

## Mendelssohn's piano works

Mendelssohn also wrote many piano works, such as the Songs Without Words.

These pieces have beautiful melodies, like songs without lyrics, and suit piano learners very well.

Many of them are short, so they are not too hard to play.

## Light staccato

The music of the fairies flying in the overture needs very light staccato.

To practise light staccato on the piano, start with flexible fingers and a relaxed wrist.

The sound should be light like a feather, so do not play too heavily.

## The 1843 incidental music

In 1843 Mendelssohn was invited to write incidental music for a staging of A Midsummer Night's Dream.

Besides the existing overture, he wrote more than ten further pieces, including a scherzo, a nocturne and a march.

This music was performed with the play in Potsdam in October of that year.

- 1826: wrote the overture at seventeen
- First written as a piano duet, played with his sister Fanny
- 1843: wrote the full incidental music for a staging of the play
- The Wedding March comes from the 1843 incidental music

## The four chords at the start of the Midsummer Night's Dream overture

The overture begins with four long chords from the woodwinds.

These four chords are like opening a door to an enchanted forest.

Then the violins play very light, very fast spiccato, the music of the fairies flying through the woods.

## Talking about Mendelssohn with your teacher

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum about the story of how Mendelssohn wrote this overture as a teenager.

There are more than forty Songs Without Words and quite a few arrangements of the Wedding March, and you can discuss with your teacher which to start with.

Your teacher can also help you practise light staccato.

## The young Mendelssohn

Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg, Germany, in 1809, and showed astonishing musical talent from childhood.

He grew up in Berlin, where his family often held musical gatherings and he had many chances to perform his own works.

In his teens he had already written a number of symphonies and chamber works.

## Summary of the Midsummer Night's Dream overture

In the summer of 1826, the seventeen-year-old Mendelssohn and his sister Fanny read Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, and he wrote an overture of the same name, first as a piano duet and then arranged for orchestra. It opens with four long woodwind chords, followed by light spiccato in the violins, and has humorous details imitating a donkey's bray.

The overture was premiered in Stettin in February 1827. In 1843 he wrote a full set of incidental music for a staging of the play, performed in Potsdam in October of that year, and its Wedding March has since been widely used at weddings. The two parts, seventeen years apart, share one style.

Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words suit piano learners. On the piano you can play the Wedding March and practise light staccato, and Teacher Aum can help you choose the music.

## Reading Shakespeare's comedy

In 1826 Mendelssohn and his sister Fanny read a German translation of Shakespeare's comedy A Midsummer Night's Dream.

The play has fairies in the forest, lovers who lose their way, and a group of craftsmen rehearsing a play, and the story is light and fantastical.

This comedy gave him great inspiration.

## Where the Wedding March comes from

The Wedding March is a piece from the 1843 incidental music, used in the scene where several pairs of lovers hold their weddings.

It begins with a trumpet fanfare, and the melody is bright and festive.

**Try it**

Later, this march came to be widely used at weddings, and it remains popular today.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: How old was Mendelssohn when he wrote this overture?**
A: Seventeen, in 1826.

**Q: What was the original version?**
A: A piano duet.

**Q: Who did he play it with?**
A: His sister Fanny.

**Q: Which year's incidental music is the Wedding March from?**
A: 1843.

**Q: How does the overture begin?**
A: With four long chords from the woodwinds.

memorize-left-hand-part-separately.body:
When memorising, many people mainly remember the right-hand melody, and the left hand is "carried along" by the right. As soon as the right hand makes a mistake, the left hand forgets too, and the whole piece stops. One way to make memorisation more secure is to memorise the left hand on its own: without the score, play through from beginning to end with the left hand alone. The left hand often carries the bass and harmony, and once it is memorised separately, it is like a steady foundation, so that even if the right hand sometimes makes a mistake, you can find your way back quickly.

## The chain reaction when the right hand slips

In a performance, or when you are nervous, the right hand sometimes makes a mistake.

If the left hand depends on the right, then when the right hand goes wrong, the left hand gets confused too.

The result is that the whole piece stops, and it is hard to carry on.

## Ask your teacher to check in lessons

You can ask Teacher Aum in your lesson to listen to you playing the left hand alone.

Your teacher can help find places that you do not remember accurately, such as notes, rhythm or fingering.

You can also ask your teacher to name a passage at random for you to start the left hand from.

## Playing the left hand alone without the score

The method of memorising the left hand alone is simple: without the score, play from beginning to end with the left hand only.

At first you may get stuck in many places, and that is perfectly normal.

The places where you get stuck are the places where your left-hand memory is not independent enough.

## The left hand is the foundation

In many pieces, the left hand takes the bass and harmony and is the foundation of the music.

If the left-hand memory is very secure, then even if the right hand makes a mistake, the left hand can keep playing.

With the left hand's support, the right hand can quickly find its place again.

## Regular spot checks of the left-hand memory

After you have memorised it, do a spot check every few days, letting only the left hand go through from beginning to end.

If you find that some places are starting to blur, practise them again.

This keeps your memory of the piece secure.

## Memorise the right hand separately too

The same method can also be used for the right hand, memorising it separately.

Although the right-hand melody is usually easier to remember, memorising it alone can also reveal some details you did not notice before.

When both hands can be memorised independently, your memorisation is very secure.

## Understanding the left-hand harmony

When memorising the left hand, you can also think about which chord the left hand is playing.

For example, this bar is a C major triad and the next bar is a G major triad.

Once you understand the chord progression, memorising the left hand becomes much easier.

## Summary: memorising the left hand separately

Many people let the left hand depend on the right when memorising, and when the right hand goes wrong the left hand gets confused too. The left hand often carries the bass and harmony and is the foundation of the music, so you can play the left hand alone without the score, and the places where you get stuck are where the memory is not independent.

You can memorise section by section, understand the left-hand harmony, sing the bass line, and once memorised, start from any section and play alone, then put it together with the right hand. The right hand can be memorised separately too.

This method suits pieces that need to be played from memory and pieces with a complicated left hand. After memorising, check regularly, and in lessons ask Teacher Aum to check and to name sections at random.

- Memorise the left hand separately, without depending on the right
- The left hand is the foundation of harmony and bass
- Start from a section and memorise section by section
- Be able to start from any section on its own

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesiser and drums on a neon street, with crystal towers behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9atpo-6m384.webp)

## Sing the bass line

While the left hand plays, hum the bass line as well.

The direction of the bass often has a pattern, such as stepwise descent or a leap to the dominant.

Singing it helps your ears remember the left-hand part too.

## What kinds of pieces it suits

This method suits pieces that must be played from memory, such as pieces for exams or performances.

It is especially helpful for pieces with a more complicated left hand, such as those with many broken chords or an independent melody.

For pieces with a very simple left hand, you may not need to spend much time on it.

## Memorise section by section

You do not need to memorise the left hand of the whole piece at once.

You can memorise the first section first, and when it is secure on its own, memorise the next section.

Join the newly memorised section straight on to the end of the previously memorised one.

## Putting it together with the right hand

When the left hand is memorised on its own, put it together with the right hand.

You will feel the left hand is steadier, and you will have more confidence when playing hands together.

If there are still problems when playing hands together, go back to practising hands separately.

## The left hand being carried by the right

After a piece is well learned, many people find that they can play it from memory, but the left hand is really following the feel of the right hand.

If they play the left hand alone, they may remember only a few bars before they forget.

This shows that the left-hand memory is not independent but depends on the right hand.

## Starting from any section

After the left hand is memorised, you can try starting the left hand alone from any section of the piece.

This checks whether you have really memorised it, and not just the momentum of starting from the beginning.

In performance, this ability is very important if you need to carry on from the middle.

## FAQ

**Q: Why memorise the left hand separately?**
A: To make the left-hand memory independent, not dependent on the right hand.

**Q: What role does the left hand play in music?**
A: It often carries the bass and harmony and is the foundation.

**Q: What does it mean if I get stuck playing the left hand alone?**
A: The left-hand memory is not independent enough.

**Q: How can I check whether I have really memorised it?**
A: Play the left hand alone starting from any section.

**Q: Can the right hand also be memorised separately?**
A: Yes.

long-long-ago-bayly-1830s-song.body:
Long, Long Ago is a song written in the 1830s by the English poet and songwriter Thomas Haynes Bayly, who wrote both the words and the music. The words ask the listener to sing the songs of long ago once more and tell the stories of long ago again, remembering the old days spent with a sweetheart. The song was published in the United States in 1843, after Bayly's death, and quickly became popular. It was later arranged into many instrumental pieces and often appears in beginner violin and piano books. The melody is steady and gentle, good material for practising legato and phrasing.

## Published in the United States in 1843

Bayly died soon after writing this song and did not live to see it become popular.

In 1843 it was published in the United States and quickly spread by word of mouth.

Later it became a well-known old song in both Britain and America.

## Summary of Long, Long Ago

Long, Long Ago is a song with words and music by the English poet Thomas Haynes Bayly in the 1830s. The words ask to be told the stories of long ago again and to hear the songs of long ago sung once more, recalling old days spent with a sweetheart. After Bayly's death it was published in the United States in 1843 and became popular, and it was later arranged into instrumental pieces that often appear in beginner violin and piano books.

The melody mostly moves by step, and the phrases make slow arcs. Each verse ends on the same line, and you can play it differently each time. It is in four-beat time at a relaxed tempo. In the beginner version the right hand plays the melody legato and the left hand plays long bass notes, so it can be played after half a year to a year of lessons, and it is also good for practising sight-reading.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your legato.

## Sing That Song Again

The words of Long, Long Ago sound like speaking to an old friend.

Tell me the stories of long ago again, and sing once more the songs we loved to sing long ago.

Every verse ends on the same line: "Long, long ago, long, long ago."

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to Your Legato in Your Lesson

You can play for Teacher Aum in your lesson and ask whether your legato fingers join the sound into a single line.

You can also discuss with your teacher how to play the repeated closing line differently each time.

From one old song, play a gentle nostalgia.

## Playing Long, Long Ago at the Piano

In the beginner version, the right hand plays the melody, and the left hand plays only a few long bass notes or simple chords.

The right hand must play smoothly, the fingers passing the sound along one after another.

The left-hand bass gently supports, without taking the place of the melody.

## The Level of Long, Long Ago

The beginner version of this piece can be started after half a year to a year of lessons.

Further versions add left-hand broken chords, or have the right hand play two voices.

It is also very good for practising sight-reading, because the melody is easy to guess and the rhythm is regular.

## The Poet Who Wrote the Song, Bayly

Thomas Haynes Bayly was an English poet and songwriter of the first half of the nineteenth century.

He wrote many lyrical little poems, many of which were set to music by himself or by others.

In English homes of the time, people often gathered around the piano to sing the songs he wrote.

## An Old Friend in Beginner Books

The melody of Long, Long Ago is steady and easy to remember, and it was arranged into instrumental pieces very early.

Many beginner violin and piano books include a simple version of it.

Many people played it, on the piano or the violin, in their first year or two of learning.

## The Repeated Closing Line

At the end of every verse, the melody returns to the line "Long, long ago, long, long ago."

The same music appears several times, which is just right for practising playing it slightly differently each time.

For example, play it a little more clearly the first time, and more softly and slowly the last time, like a memory slowly fading away.

## A Steady Melodic Line

The melody of this song mostly moves by step, with only an occasional small leap.

The shape of each phrase is like a slow arc, first rising and then gently falling.

When you play, you can follow this arc, letting the sound grow slightly louder first and then slowly softer.

## Legato Fingers

When playing legato, the previous note is released only after the next note has been pressed down.

That way there is no gap between the two notes, and the sound joins like a single thread.

You can practise slowly at first, listening carefully with your ears for any break between notes.

## Calm in Four-Beat Time

Long, Long Ago is usually written in four-beat time at a relaxed tempo, like telling a story slowly.

Do not hurry, and give every beat time to breathe.

Between phrases you can leave a tiny gap, like a pause in speech.

- Written by Thomas Haynes Bayly in the 1830s
- Words and music both by Bayly
- Became popular after publication in the United States in 1843
- Often found in beginner violin and piano books

![A person with headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbizuj5-ntxbt.webp)

## Memories of Time with a Sweetheart

What the words remember is the old time spent with a sweetheart.

The words said then and the smiles of that time are still clearly kept in the heart.

This gentle nostalgia has no sorrow in it, only tenderness.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote Long, Long Ago?**
A: The English poet and songwriter Thomas Haynes Bayly.

**Q: Roughly when was it written?**
A: The 1830s.

**Q: In which year and where was it published?**
A: In 1843, in the United States.

**Q: What line ends every verse?**
A: "Long, long ago, long, long ago."

**Q: What should the fingers do when playing legato?**
A: Release the previous note only after the next note has been pressed down.

largo-broad-slow-tempo.body:
Largo is an Italian tempo term, meaning very slow and broad. Like Adagio it is a slow tempo, but it puts more emphasis on breadth and dignity of sound. When playing Largo, it is not enough to slow down: each note and chord must unfold fully, keeping the music’s sense of strength.

## What Largo means

Largo is Italian and originally means "broad". As a tempo term it means a very slow, broad speed, usually among the slowest of the tempo terms.

It belongs with Lento, Adagio and Grave as a term for slow tempos, with subtle differences between them. It is generally felt that besides being slow, Largo carries a feeling of breadth and dignity.

Larghetto is the diminutive of Largo and means a little faster than Largo.

There is no fixed standard for the exact speed, and different composers and different periods may understand it differently.

So when you see Largo, besides thinking "slow", also think of the musical character of "broad".

## The challenges of slow tempos

Many people think slow pieces are easier, but slow tempos have their own particular difficulties.

The first is keeping a steady rhythm. At a very slow speed the distance between beats is long, and it is easy to speed up or slow down without noticing.

The second is the continuity of sound. At a slow tempo every note is heard clearly, so the connection between notes and the changes in dynamics are more noticeable.

The third is keeping a sense of direction in the music. In a slow tempo the phrases are long, and without a clear direction the music easily sounds loose.

Facing these challenges calls for more careful listening and steadier control.

- Largo means "broad", very slow and broad
- Usually slower and more dignified than Adagio
- Needs a full, broad tone
- Long notes should be held for their full value

## Common slow tempo terms

From slow to somewhat slow, common tempo terms include Grave, Largo, Lento and Adagio. Grave suggests heaviness and seriousness, Largo is broad, Lento means slow, and Adagio is often rendered as "at ease". The differences between them are sometimes not only about speed but also about the colour of the mood.

When playing Largo, the weight of the arm should be sent steadily into the keys so that chords sound round and full. If you press lightly with the fingers alone, the tempo may be slow but the sound seems thin and weak.

Slow pieces demand just as much sense of rhythm. You can mentally divide each beat into smaller units, for example counting "one and two and", to avoid long notes being unconsciously cut short.

The rise and fall of phrases is also important in Largo. Even at a slow speed the music must still move forward, and you can give every phrase direction through changes in dynamics.

## Subdivide the beat to stay steady

In a very slow tempo you can count each beat in smaller units, for example dividing a quarter-note beat into two eighth notes or four sixteenth notes.

This gives more reference points between beats and makes the rhythm steadier.

When practising with a metronome, you can also set the metronome to the subdivided speed so that it clicks more often.

Once you are comfortable, set the metronome back to the whole beat, or even have it click only on the first beat of each bar, to train your inner sense of rhythm.

The habit of subdividing the beat is useful when playing any slow music.

You can also keep counting the subdivisions in your head while a long note sounds, until the next note arrives, so the long note is not cut short.

## Bringing out the feeling of breadth

The feeling of breadth comes from a full sound and long phrases. Use the weight of the arm to bring out a deep sound, rather than just tapping with the fingers.

Phrases should rise and fall clearly, so that you know where each starts, where it is heading and where it ends.

You can imagine a wide-open scene, such as a plain or a broad river, to help you find the feeling.

You can also listen to Largo pieces played by different performers and notice how they handle tempo and sound.

Bring these ideas into your playing, and slow music will be full of expression too.

**Slow down**

Record your playing and listen back, noticing whether the sound is full enough and whether the phrases have direction, then adjust.

![A cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot plays a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lbll4-c02ns.webp)

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What speed is Largo usually?**
A: Markings differ slightly between editions, roughly between forty and sixty beats per minute; you can refer to the metronome mark in the score.

**Q: What is the relationship between Larghetto and Largo?**
A: Larghetto is a little faster than Largo, meaning a somewhat less broad Largo.

**Q: How do I stop a slow piece from dragging?**
A: Keep a steady beat and give the phrases a clear sense of direction, rather than letting every note linger with the same weight.

**Q: Which is slower, Largo or Adagio?**
A: Largo is generally considered slower, but different composers may understand it differently.

**Q: Does Largo have a fixed metronome speed?**
A: No fixed standard. You can follow the suggestion in the edition, or decide according to the character of the music.

**Q: How do I stop a slow piece from dragging?**
A: Keep a sense of direction in the phrases, and use subdivided beats to help keep the rhythm steady.

mark-practice-pages-bookmarks.body:
When you are working on several pieces from one book, marking the pages you need with bookmarks, coloured tabs or sticky notes lets you open your music straight to the right place every time. Tabs can also be sorted by purpose, such as "learning", "review" and "next lesson", so your practice plan is clear at a glance and you spend less time flicking back and forth.

## Keep the tabs up to date

Once a piece is finished and your teacher has checked it, take the tab off or change it to your review colour.

If a book is covered in tabs, they stop being a useful reminder. Keeping them few and clear is what makes them work.

Set a regular time each week to tidy up, for example after your lesson, and place new tabs according to the new homework.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothes plays a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a crystal synthesizer in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wvzij-43akj.webp)

## Use colour to show purpose

You can give each colour a fixed meaning: for example, red for a new piece you are learning, yellow for an older piece that needs review, and green for a piece to play for your teacher at the next lesson.

The colour system does not need to be complicated. About three colours is enough. Too many rules are hard to remember.

Write the colour key on the inside cover of the book so that parents or teachers can understand it at a glance.

Once the meanings are decided, keep them the same for as long as you can. Changing them often causes confusion.

## Bookmarks for digital scores

If you read music on a tablet, you can also use the bookmark feature in your reading app to save the pages you practise most.

Some apps let you name bookmarks or give them colours, which works much like paper tabs.

Whether paper or digital, the purpose of marking is the same: to help you find what you need to practise faster, so your time goes into real practice.

Whichever tool you use, the key is to keep your markings simple, consistent and up to date, rather than marking as much as possible.

## Using tabs together with a practice notebook

Tabs tell you which page to go to, and a practice notebook tells you what to do on that page. Together they give your practice a clear route.

In the notebook you can write down, by date, which tabbed pieces you practised today, what you worked on in each one, and any problems you met.

Next time you open your music, read the notebook first, then turn to the tabbed pages and pick up where you left off. That way each session connects to the last, instead of starting from scratch every time.

## What to write on a tab

The visible part of a tab can carry a short form of the title or one key reminder, such as "left hand slowly" or "pedal in section two".

Keep the reminder short enough to understand at a glance. Longer details can go in the practice notebook.

When a teacher sets homework in a lesson, they can also write the focus for the week straight onto the tab, giving practice at home a clear direction.

**Think it over**
- Put one tab on each piece you are working on
- Use different colours for different purposes
- Write a short reminder on each tab
- Remove the tab once the piece is finished

## Choosing the right marking tool

Common tools include fabric bookmarks, repositionable coloured tabs, sticky notes and ribbon markers. Coloured tabs are small and stick out past the edge of the page, which suits marking several pieces.

Sticky notes have room for more writing and suit a teacher's reminders, but strongly adhesive ones can lift the paper surface when removed, so low-tack ones are safer.

A ribbon marker suits one main position, such as this week's key piece.

## Why mark page numbers at all

Piano books are usually thick, with dozens of pieces in one volume. If you are working on three or four pieces at once, looking up page numbers in the contents each time takes time and can interrupt the flow of practice.

With tabs, you open the book and go straight to what you need. The convenience seems small, but the few minutes saved every day make it easier to get started.

For children, tabs are also a clear signal: today's practice is the tabbed pages.

**Practice order**

Adult self-learners often work on several pieces at once, and tabs can help you divide your time sensibly between them.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Where on the page should the tab go?**
A: Usually on the outer edge of the page, with a small part showing so it is easy to find. Do not cover any notes.

**Q: Will sticky notes damage the music?**
A: Low-tack sticky notes usually will not. Peel them off slowly, parallel to the paper surface.

**Q: What is the maximum number of tabs in one book?**
A: There is no fixed number, but it is best to mark only the pieces you are learning and the ones you need to review, to keep things clear.

**Q: Will my child treat the tabs like toys?**
A: Let your child be in charge of placing the tabs and explain what each colour means. They usually take better care of them that way.

**Q: How do I mark photocopied loose sheets?**
A: You can sort them into folders of different colours, or write the date and purpose in the top right corner of each sheet.

**Q: Can tabs be reused?**
A: Repositionable tabs can be used many times. Replace them when they lose their stickiness.

loco-after-ottava-sign.body:
An 8va sign with a dotted line means the notes beneath the line are played an octave higher than written. Where the dotted line ends, you will sometimes see the word loco, which means to return to the original pitch position. When you see the end of the dotted line or loco, move your hand back to where the score actually places the notes.

## What the Word Loco Means

Loco is Italian for "in place". In a score it often appears where an octave sign ends, reminding the player to go back to the pitch as actually written, no longer raised or lowered by an octave.

**Remember this**

Octave signs are usually written as 8va or 8vb, followed by a dotted line, and every note under the line is played an octave higher or lower. After the line ends, some scores add loco to make the instruction clearer.

Even when loco is not written, the end of the dotted line also means a return to the written pitch. The word is there only so that the player does not overlook the change while reading.

Knowing this word helps you react faster when reading, so you do not stay in the higher or lower octave after the music has returned to its place.

It is also a reminder that every little word in a score has a purpose, and is worth noticing carefully when you read.

## Why Octave Signs Are Used

When a melody is written very high, many ledger lines are needed above the staff, which makes it awkward to read. With an 8va sign, the notes can be written in a lower, easier-to-read position, while telling the player to play an octave higher.

By the same principle, 8vb or 8va bassa means play an octave lower, and is often used on the bass staff. You may also see 15ma, which means two octaves higher.

When practising, you can mark the octave sign and the end point of the dotted line with a coloured pen, and add a small arrow at the end to remind yourself that your hand must return to its original place.

You can also practise the movement of the hand coming back from the higher octave on its own, so that your arm gets used to the distance. Once it is well practised, the join will feel more natural.

Some scores simply carry on with notes after an octave sign ends, without adding any explanation. So when reading, pay special attention to where the dotted line stops: that is where you return to the original pitch.

## How to Mark and Practise

Before practising, you can use a pencil to draw a small mark where the octave sign begins and ends, such as an arrow, to remind yourself that your hand must move.

First practise only the few bars where you enter and leave the octave sign, repeating the hand's movement between the two registers until it becomes fluent.

Play slowly at first, pausing slightly before the move to confirm that your hand has arrived in the right position before you continue.

Once it is fluent, gradually remove the pause so that the move becomes smooth and natural.

You can also close your eyes and feel the distance your hand travels on the keyboard, which helps build a sense of space.

**Mind the details**
- 8va means play an octave higher
- The dotted line marks the range of the higher octave
- Loco means return to the original pitch
- 8vb means play an octave lower

## Common Problems When Reading

After playing for a while under the dotted line of an octave sign, the hand easily gets used to that register. When the dotted line ends, you may forget to go back and carry on playing an octave higher.

Another situation is when the dotted line ends in the middle of a line. Your eyes watch only the notes and do not notice that the line has stopped, so you play in the wrong register.

A further case is when an octave sign runs across a line break. The new line may repeat 8va at the start or may not, so read carefully.

These problems all come down to attention. The hands follow the eyes, and if the eyes do not see the change ahead of time, the hands can hardly adjust in time.

So when practising a piece with octave signs, you can first spend a run-through just looking at the score and finding every starting and ending point.

![Golden grand piano sketch on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8l48dy-mj115.webp)

## The Sound Effect of a Change of Register

Composers use octave signs mainly to avoid writing too many ledger lines and make the score easier to read. But a change of register also changes the colour of the sound.

The high register is usually brighter and lighter, while the low register is deeper and heavier. When the music returns to its place, the sound changes with it.

When playing, listen for this change so that the audience can feel the music moving from one register back to another.

Sometimes returning to the written pitch also marks the end of a phrase or the start of a new section, and you can shape it together with the structure of the phrase.

**Think about it again**

Once you understand this, reading is no longer just recognising notes, but understanding how the music is designed.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I still return to the written pitch if loco is not written?**
A: Yes. The end of the dotted line means the octave sign no longer applies, and loco is only an extra reminder.

**Q: Can the left hand have 8va too?**
A: It may. The left-hand part sometimes uses 8vb for an octave lower; follow what the score shows.

**Q: What does 15ma mean?**
A: It means play two octaves higher than written, and it is used much like 8va.

**Q: What is the difference between 8va and 8vb?**
A: 8va means play an octave higher, and 8vb means play an octave lower.

**Q: What does 15ma mean?**
A: 15ma means play two octaves higher, and here too you must watch where it ends.

**Q: How can I tell when loco is not written?**
A: Look at where the dotted line of the octave sign ends. After it ends, you are back at the original pitch.
