light-pedal-classical-sonata-mozart-hayd.body:
When playing Romantic music, the sustain pedal is often used a lot, joining the sound into one wash. But when playing Classical sonatas from the time of Mozart and Haydn, the use of the pedal is very different: press it lightly, press it sparingly and change it often, so that every note is clear and the outline of the phrases is distinct. This is because the music of the Classical period emphasises clear lines and refined touch, and the keyboard instruments of that time also sounded lighter and shorter than today's piano. Understanding this helps us get a more Classical sound on today's piano.

## Judge Clarity by Ear

When you use the pedal, listen carefully all the time: Is every note still clear? Are the harmonies running together?

**Something to think about**

If you hear the sound starting to blur, reduce the pedal or change it more often.

You can also record yourself with your phone and check the effect of the pedal when you play it back.

## Change More Often

If a passage of music needs the pedal, change it more often, frequently once per chord or even once per beat.

As soon as the harmony changes, change the pedal, so that the chords before and after do not run together.

In fast passages, rather than changing very often, it is better to leave the pedal out altogether.

![An electronic keyboard and a screen under neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabtx92-ptk27.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen for Classical Pedalling in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether you use too much pedal when you play Classical sonatas.

Your teacher can help you mark which places can take a little pedal and which places must rely entirely on the fingers.

Once you have mastered Classical-style pedalling, your playing will sound cleaner and more stylish.

## Where You Can Use a Little Pedal

In a lyrical slow movement, long melodies and soft chords can take some shallow pedal.

A chord at the end of a phrase, or a bass note that needs resonance, can also have a brief touch of pedal.

Fast scales, staccato and Alberti bass usually take no pedal.

## Contrast with Romantic Pedalling

You can play the slow movement of a Mozart sonata together with a Chopin nocturne.

Chopin nocturnes often need continuous pedal, so that the colours of the harmony blend together.

A Mozart slow movement needs less and lighter pedal, so that the melody is clear like singing.

## The Sound of Keyboards in the Classical Period

The keyboard instruments of Mozart's and Haydn's time had thinner strings and smaller hammers, and their sound was lighter than today's piano and did not last as long.

On such instruments, even with the pedal down, the sound does not blend into one big wash.

Today's piano is louder and its sound lasts longer, so the same pedalling has a much heavier effect.

## Summary of Pedalling in Classical Sonatas

The keyboard instruments of Mozart's and Haydn's time sounded lighter and shorter, and today's piano is louder and longer, so when you play Classical sonatas, pedal lightly, sparingly and change often, to keep the melody, ornaments and Alberti bass clear.

First play a good legato with your fingers and no pedal, and only then consider a shallow or brief pedal. Change it as soon as the harmony changes. Fast scales, staccato and Alberti bass usually take none. The original scores have very few pedal markings, and most of the markings in modern editions were added by editors, so use your ears to judge.

In a big room use even less pedal, and when you change pianos you need to readjust. You can listen to recordings on period instruments, compare with the pedalling in a Chopin nocturne, and ask Teacher Aum to listen for whether you are using too much pedal.

## First Practise Finger Legato Without the Pedal

When playing a Classical sonata, you can first use no pedal at all and play a good legato with your fingers.

The smoothness of a melody depends mainly on the fingers handing over from one note to the next, not on the pedal.

Once finger legato is good, then think about where to add a tiny bit of pedal.

## Listen to Recordings on Period Instruments

You can look for recordings of Mozart and Haydn sonatas played on keyboard instruments from the Classical period.

Notice the light, clear sound, and how sparingly the pedal (or knee lever) is used.

This can help you find a more suitable tone on today's piano.

## The Influence of the Room and the Piano

In a big room with a lot of echo, the pedal can be used even less.

In a small room with a rather dry sound, you can use a little more.

Different pianos also have different pedal sensitivity, so you need to readjust when you change instruments.

## The Shallow Pedal

In Classical sonatas, the pedal often needs to be pressed down only a small part of the way, which is called a shallow pedal.

A shallow pedal makes the sound slightly warmer and rounder, but does not let the notes overlap each other too much.

You can try pressing down just to the depth where it begins to take effect, and listen to how the sound changes.

## The Brief Pedal

Sometimes the pedal is used on just one chord or one long note, pressed and released straight away.

For example, a chord at the end of a phrase, or a bass note that needs to be extended a little.

This kind of brief pedal is like adding a touch of sheen to the sound.

**Remember this**
- In Classical sonatas the pedal should be light and sparing
- Keep the notes clear and the outline of the phrases distinct
- The keyboard instruments of the time sounded lighter and shorter
- Rely mainly on finger legato, and use the pedal only as decoration

## Looking at Pedal Markings in Editions

In the original scores of many Classical sonatas, there are almost no pedal markings.

The pedal markings in some modern editions were added later by editors.

You can refer to these markings, but in the end you must use your ears to judge whether clarity has been kept.

## Clear Lines in Classical Sonatas

Much of the charm of a Classical sonata comes from a clear melody, refined ornaments and a neat accompaniment.

If you use too much pedal, the Alberti bass and fast scales will blur into a mess.

**Practice order**

So the pedal should serve clarity, not make the sound blurry.

## FAQ

**Q: How should the pedal be used in Classical sonatas?**
A: Lightly, sparingly and changed often.

**Q: Why use it this way?**
A: The instruments of the time had a light, short sound, and Classical music emphasises clear lines.

**Q: What does the smoothness of a melody depend on mainly?**
A: Finger legato.

**Q: Where is the pedal usually not used?**
A: Fast scales, staccato and Alberti bass.

**Q: Are there many pedal markings in the original scores?**
A: Very few. Many were added later by editors.

melody-alone-then-add-accompaniment.body:
When you learn a piece with a melody and an accompaniment, start by playing only the melody and treat it as a song: find where each phrase begins and ends, where to breathe, and where the high point of each phrase is. When the melody flows like singing, add the accompaniment, and make it clearly quieter than the melody. A piece practised this way has a melody that floats clearly on top instead of being drowned by the accompaniment.

## Find the structure of the phrases

When you play the melody, first find where each phrase starts and where it ends.

**A common mistake**

You can use a pencil to draw a small curve or comma at the end of each phrase.

Once you know where the phrases are, you can shape them on purpose as you play, instead of playing straight through in one breath.

- Play only the melody first, as if it were a song
- Find the start, end and high point of each phrase
- Add the accompaniment once the melody flows
- Keep the accompaniment clearly quieter than the melody

## The high point of a phrase

Each melodic phrase often has a high point. It may be the highest note, or it may be the most important note.

When you reach the high point, you can add a little more weight, and then ease off gradually after it has passed.

That gives the phrase a shape, instead of a flat, straight line.

## It works for many pieces

This method works for many kinds of pieces, from children's songs to lyrical pieces, and from pop songs to classical works.

As long as a piece has a clear melody, you can play it as a song first.

Once you have this habit, you will find your playing becomes more singing.

## How to add the accompaniment

When the melody is going smoothly, you can play only the accompaniment first, to get to know its chords and rhythm.

Then put the melody and accompaniment together at a fairly slow speed.

When you put them together, keep listening to the melody all the time, and let the accompaniment follow the melody, not the other way round.

## Long notes in the melody

Melodies often have long notes. On the piano the sound dies away little by little, while the accompaniment carries on.

Take special care here that the accompaniment does not cover the fading long note, otherwise the melody sounds as if it has broken off.

After a long note you can make the accompaniment a little softer, or you can touch the key a little deeper at the start of the long note so it lasts longer.

## Check the balance with a recording

Once the hands are together, record yourself and listen to whether the melody floats clearly above the accompaniment.

If you cannot hear the melody clearly, the accompaniment is too loud or the melody is too soft.

Adjust the strength of your two hands according to the recording, then record again and compare.

## Keep the accompaniment soft

The accompaniment should be clearly quieter than the melody, about half as loud.

If the accompaniment is repeated chords or broken chords, be especially careful that the volume does not creep up.

You can first play the accompaniment very softly, then slowly find the right balance.

## The melody is the star of the piece

Most pieces have a main melody, which is the part listeners remember most easily.

The role of the accompaniment is to support and set off the melody and make it sound richer.

If the melody is not played clearly, even the most beautiful accompaniment cannot make up for it.

## Sing it, then play it

If you are not sure how to phrase the melody, try singing it first.

When you sing, you naturally pause where you need to breathe and add emphasis at the high points.

Bring that feeling of singing to the piano, and the melody will be more expressive.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3o53d-rwcfp.webp)

## Summary of melody-first practice

First play the melody as a song, find the phrases, breaths and high points, and then add a soft accompaniment.

This order makes the melody clear and expressive, and the accompaniment can set it off better.

Next time you learn a new piece, try putting the accompaniment aside and spending a little time with the melody alone.

## Different dynamics in the two hands

Playing with different strengths in the two hands takes some practice.

You can start by playing one hand loudly and the other very softly on a simple scale.

Once you are used to the feeling, using it in a piece will be much easier.

## When the melody is in the left hand

Sometimes the melody is in the left hand and the accompaniment in the right, such as in the middle section of some lyrical pieces.

The same method works here: play the left-hand melody alone first, then add the right-hand accompaniment.

Take special care to keep the right-hand accompaniment lighter so it does not cover the left-hand melody.

## The benefit of playing only the melody

Playing only the melody first lets you put all your attention on one line.

You will hear the rise and fall of the melody more clearly, and it is easier to spot where a note is wrong or the rhythm is off.

This step is like learning to sing a song before learning how to accompany it.

## Where to breathe

If this melody were to be sung, where would you breathe?

On the piano, at these breathing places you can lift your hand slightly and leave a tiny gap.

This "breathing" makes the melody sound more natural, more like a person singing.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why play only the melody first?**
A: It lets you focus on one line and bring out a singing quality.

**Q: How do I find the phrases?**
A: Find the start and end of each phrase and the places to breathe.

**Q: How loud should the accompaniment be?**
A: Clearly quieter than the melody, about half as loud.

**Q: What if the melody is in the left hand?**
A: Do the same: play the left-hand melody first, then add a soft right-hand accompaniment.

**Q: How do I check the balance?**
A: Record yourself and listen to whether the melody floats clearly on top.

look-at-ending-first.body:
When you get a new piece, besides reading from the first bar, you can also turn to the end first and see how the piece finishes: the final chord, changes of tempo and dynamics, and whether there is a ritardando or a fermata. Once you know the destination, go back and learn from the beginning, and it becomes easier to understand the direction of the whole piece, and to prepare for the ending deliberately as you practise.

## Tempo and Dynamics at the Ending

Many pieces end by slowing down gradually, or by getting softer, so that the music stops naturally.

The amount of ritardando should be appropriate: too sudden sounds stiff, and too little may not be heard at all.

You can try several different ways of handling it and choose the one that best suits the piece.

![A transparent futuristic keyboard with light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9y2h32-lpc4j.webp)

## Understanding the Direction of the Piece from the Ending

Once you know the ending, look back at the beginning and ask yourself: how does this piece get from the start to the finish?

Is there a climax in the middle? Where is the most tense point, and where does it slowly relax?

With this overall impression, you will understand more clearly what role each section plays in the whole piece as you practise.

You can also listen to a recording of the piece first, paying special attention to how the ending is handled, and then compare it with the score to see how the performer treats those markings.

## What to Look at in the Ending

You can look at the chords in the last few bars, which often tell you the key of the piece.

Look to see whether the ending has a ritardando, a diminuendo or a fermata. These markings decide how the piece feels as it ends.

You can also notice whether the melody at the ending resembles the opening, since some pieces return to the opening theme at the end.

## Carry the Whole Piece in Your Mind

Looking at the ending first is a way to help you understand a piece as a whole.

When you have the shape of the whole piece in your mind, you will know where each section is and where it is going as you practise it.

This gives your playing more direction, and your practice more order.

## How the Ending Echoes the Beginning

The ending of some pieces repeats the opening melody, perhaps with some changes in dynamics, tempo or harmony.

Notice these changes, and when you play you can make the theme at the ending different from the beginning, for example softer and quieter.

This echo makes the whole piece sound more complete.

## Why Look at the Ending First

Many people learning a new piece always start from the first bar and practise onwards, and by the time they reach the ending there is hardly any time left.

The result is that the beginning is very well learned while the ending is never quite secure, and the further on you play, the less confident you are.

Looking at the ending first lets you know from the start where the piece is heading, and you will look after every part more evenly as you practise.

## Leave Time for the Ending

In your practice plan, deliberately leave enough time for the ending.

You can practise the ending on its own in every practice session, rather than reaching it only when you play the whole piece through.

Once the ending is well practised, the overall finish of the whole piece will improve noticeably.

## When Children Learn Pieces

When a child learns a new piece, a grown-up can help the child find the last line first and talk about how the piece ends.

Let the child listen to the sound of the ending first and feel what "finishing" is like.

That way, while learning, the child has a goal in mind and knows where they are playing to.

## Practising in Sections from the End

One practice method is to divide the piece into sections, begin with the last section, then practise the second-to-last, and then join the two.

Adding one section at a time working backwards, the ending gets practised the most, and the further you play, the more fluent you become.

This method is especially suitable before a performance or exam, helping you feel more secure about the ending.

## The Last Note

The last note or chord often needs to be held for a while so that the sound fades away naturally.

If there is a fermata, you can decide how long to hold it according to the mood of the piece.

When you release the keys and the pedal, move gently, so that the sound is not cut off suddenly.

**Listen**
- Turn to the end first to see how the piece finishes
- Notice the final chord and the changes of tempo and dynamics
- Knowing the ending helps you understand the direction of the whole piece
- You can practise in sections working backwards from the ending

## FAQ

**Q: Do I have to look at the ending of every piece first?**
A: Not necessarily, but it is a good way to help you understand the overall structure.

**Q: Won't practising backwards feel strange?**
A: It may feel unfamiliar at first, but it is very helpful for getting to know the ending.

**Q: How much should the ending slow down?**
A: It depends on the mood of the piece, and you can try several ways of handling it.

**Q: How long should the last note be held?**
A: You can let the sound fade away naturally, and when there is a fermata, decide according to the mood.

**Q: Can children understand structure?**
A: Start by listening to the sound of the ending and explain it in a simple way.

**Q: What if I can never play the ending securely?**
A: Practise the ending on its own in every session, and leave it enough time.

mendelssohn-hebrides-fingals-cave-1829.body:
In the summer of 1829, the twenty-year-old Mendelssohn travelled in Scotland with a friend. In August they sailed to the Hebrides, off the west coast. In a letter to his family, Mendelssohn wrote down a short melody, saying he wanted them to know what the islands had made him feel. Those few bars later became the opening of his concert overture The Hebrides, also known as Fingal's Cave. The work puts the sea waves, the sea wind and the scenery of a lonely island into the orchestra.

- Mendelssohn travelled in Scotland in the summer of 1829
- He wrote the first few bars of the overture in a letter
- Finished in 1830, revised and premiered in London in 1832
- In B minor, depicting waves and a lonely island

## The bars in the letter

On 7 August 1829, Mendelssohn wrote to his family from near the Hebrides.

In the letter he wrote that, to make his family understand what the place made him feel, he had thought of the following music, and then he wrote down a few bars of melody.

This melody is the theme that later opened the overture.

## A quiet ending

At the end of the work, the clarinet softly plays a fragment of the second theme, like a calm sea after a storm.

Finally, the wave theme from the beginning returns, and then the music slowly fades away.

The whole piece feels like a journey at sea.

## The overture on the piano

Many of Mendelssohn's orchestral works have arrangements for piano four hands, and The Hebrides is no exception.

When you play the opening theme on the piano, you can imagine the rise and fall of the waves and let the volume increase and decrease naturally with the direction of the melody.

The left-hand bass should be as steady as the deep water.

## The stormy middle section

In the middle of the overture the music becomes agitated, with brass and timpani joining in, as if a storm were rising at sea.

The opening theme is passed between different instruments, getting stronger and stronger.

After the storm, the music gradually calms again.

## What is a concert overture

An overture was originally an instrumental introduction played before an opera began.

In the nineteenth century, composers began to write independent "concert overtures", not for any opera, but only to be played in concerts.

The Hebrides is exactly this kind of concert overture, depicting a scene from nature.

## Summary of Mendelssohn's Hebrides

In the summer of 1829, the twenty-year-old Mendelssohn travelled in Scotland, wrote the first bars of the overture in a letter to his family on 7 August, and also visited Fingal's Cave on the island of Staffa.

He finished a first draft of the overture in 1830, and after revising it in 1832 it was premiered in London. It is a concert overture depicting an island scene.

The B minor theme at the opening rises and falls like waves, the second theme is broad and expansive, the middle section is like a storm at sea, and the ending returns to calm. The work does not rely on a written plot, but describes a feeling in music.

## From first draft to premiere

Mendelssohn finished the first draft of this overture in 1830.

He was not very satisfied with it and revised it further, and the version revised in 1832 was premiered in London.

When the work was published it was given the title The Hebrides.

## Painting without words

In this work Mendelssohn did not write any specific story, and did not add a poem.

He simply used music to express the scenery of the islands and his own feelings.

This differs from some programme music that describes a plot section by section.

## The broad second theme

Next, the cellos and bassoons sing a broad melody, which is thought to be one of the most beautiful passages in the work.

It seems to describe the open sea and sky, and its mood is more relaxed than at the opening.

The contrast between the two themes makes up the main content of the overture.

## Travel and composing

Mendelssohn went to many places in his life, and what he saw on his travels often became inspiration for his composing.

Besides Scotland, his travels in Italy also inspired the Italian Symphony.

When you are learning piano, linking a piece to the composer's experiences makes it easier to understand the atmosphere of the music.

## Fingal's Cave

During the journey they visited Fingal's Cave on the island of Staffa. Its walls are made of hexagonal basalt columns, and the waves surging into the cave echo.

It is said that Mendelssohn was badly seasick on the boat, but the scenery still left a deep impression on him.

The overture was later often called Fingal's Cave as well.

![A person with headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing the city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa7vsdy-vpke7.webp)

## The waves at the opening

As the overture begins, the violas, cellos and bassoons play the rising and falling theme, like waves breaking one after another.

The theme is in B minor, with a touch of gloom and loneliness.

It keeps moving up and down, as if the surface of the sea were rising and falling.

## The young traveller

Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847) was born in Hamburg and grew up in Berlin. As a teenager he had already written a number of mature works.

In 1829 he went to Britain for the first time, and after performing in London he travelled north to Scotland with his friend Klingemann.

**Listen**

The trip gave him a great deal of inspiration, and his later Scottish Symphony is also connected with it.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In which year did Mendelssohn travel in Scotland?**
A: In the summer of 1829.

**Q: Where was the opening theme of the overture first written down?**
A: In a letter to his family.

**Q: What is the work's other name?**
A: Fingal's Cave.

**Q: When was it premiered in London?**
A: In 1832, after revision.

**Q: What key is the opening theme in?**
A: B minor.

leroy-anderson-the-typewriter-1950.body:
The Typewriter is a short orchestral piece written in 1950 by the American composer Leroy Anderson. The most unusual thing about it is that the orchestra really does include a typewriter, "played" by a percussionist: they tap the keys to make a clicking sound, ring a little bell at the end of the line, and then push the carriage back. The whole piece lasts just over a minute, moves at a lively pace and is full of humour. Anderson wrote many similar pieces of light music, such as The Syncopated Clock and Sleigh Ride, which are often played in concerts. This piece is also a fun example for understanding rhythm, accents and musical humour.

## Talk About the Typewriter's Humour in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about Anderson's music and the humour in it.

**Something to think about**

You can also ask your teacher to help you choose a light, witty piano piece to learn.

This piece is a great way to get a feel for rhythm and a relaxed musical style.

## Summary of The Typewriter

Leroy Anderson was born in 1908 and died in 1975. He wrote many witty orchestral miniatures for a light orchestra, and in 1950 he wrote The Typewriter, in which a percussionist plays a real typewriter. The score specifies three sounds: tapping the keys, the bell at the end of a line, and pushing the carriage back. The bell matches the end of a typed line, and the carriage return often lands together with a chord from the orchestra.

The strings play a light, playful melody, and the whole piece lasts just over a minute. Playing the typewriter takes precise rhythm. Anderson also wrote The Syncopated Clock, Sleigh Ride and The Blue Tango. In a piano arrangement, fast staccato notes can imitate the typing, and short notes in the high register can imitate the bell. Keep the staccato short and clear, and you can even write a little piece of music using sounds from everyday life.

You can talk about humour in music with Teacher Aum.

## Practising Staccato

Playing this piece takes a lot of fast, light staccato.

Staccato notes should be short and clear, as crisp as the keys of a typewriter.

Keep your wrist relaxed and let your fingers spring up quickly to make the staccato.

![Illustration of the Bangkok skyline at dusk with an elevated light-rail line](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadojfy-k55xe.webp)

## Humour in Music

Anderson's music is full of humour, which is a rare quality.

He used sounds and scenes from everyday life to write music that makes you smile knowingly.

This shows that music can express deep feelings, but it can also bring lightness and joy.

## What Is a Typewriter?

A typewriter is a machine for typing. Before computers became common, offices were full of them.

When you press a key, a metal hammer strikes the paper and makes a clicking sound.

At the end of a line, the machine rings a little bell, and the typist pushes the carriage back to start a new line.

## Anderson's Other Pieces

Anderson wrote many similar pieces of light music, such as The Syncopated Clock, Sleigh Ride and The Blue Tango.

The Syncopated Clock portrays a clock whose rhythm is a little off, using lots of syncopation.

Sleigh Ride is often played at winter festivals, and uses the sounds of horses' hooves and whips to paint a sleigh racing along.

## Using a Typewriter as an Instrument

Anderson realised that the sound of a typewriter is already very rhythmic.

In the score he specified three typewriter sounds: tapping the keys, the bell at the end of a line, and pushing the carriage back.

In performance, a percussionist sits in the orchestra and "plays" the typewriter following the score.

## The Orchestra's Melody

On top of the typewriter sounds, the strings play a light, playful melody.

The melody fits closely with the typewriter's rhythm, as if the two were in conversation with the typist.

The whole piece is full of energy and humour.

**Remember this**
- Written by Anderson in 1950
- The orchestra really includes a typewriter
- A percussionist taps the keys, rings the bell and pushes the carriage
- The whole piece lasts just over a minute

## Leroy Anderson

Leroy Anderson was born in 1908 and died in 1975. He was an American composer.

He studied music and languages at university, and spoke several languages.

He wrote many short, witty orchestral pieces for a light orchestra, and audiences loved them.

## The Typewriter on the Piano

There is a piano arrangement of The Typewriter, with the melody in the right hand and the accompaniment in the left.

The sound of the typewriter can be imitated on the piano with fast staccato notes.

The bell at the end of the line can be played as a single short note in the high register.

## Just Over a Minute

The Typewriter is very short, lasting just over a minute.

In that short time, Anderson portrays the process of typing in a vivid and entertaining way.

It also shows that good music does not have to be long.

## How Hard Is It to Play the Typewriter?

Playing the typewriter looks easy, but it actually needs very precise rhythm.

The percussionist has to hit every note accurately at a fast pace, and ring the bell and push the carriage at exactly the right moments.

Sometimes the performer adds some exaggerated gestures to make the audience laugh.

## Try Using Sounds from Everyday Life

Think about which other sounds in daily life have a rhythm.

For example, the ticking of a clock, the sound of raindrops, or footsteps.

Try writing a little piece of music on the piano using these rhythms, just as Anderson did.

## The Sound and Rhythm of the Typewriter

The sound of tapping keys is set in a fast rhythm, like a typist working at top speed.

The bell rings at the end of a phrase, matching the end of a typed line.

**Practice order**

The sound of the carriage being pushed back often comes together with a chord from the orchestra, like a full stop.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote The Typewriter?**
A: The American composer Leroy Anderson.

**Q: What year was it written?**
A: 1950.

**Q: Which three sounds does the typewriter make?**
A: Tapping the keys, the bell at the end of the line, and pushing the carriage back.

**Q: How long is the whole piece?**
A: Just over a minute.

**Q: What other pieces did Anderson write?**
A: The Syncopated Clock, Sleigh Ride, The Blue Tango and more.

mensuration-canon-different-speeds.body:
A mensuration canon is a canon in which the same melody moves at different speeds at the same time. One voice goes at the original speed, while another may lengthen every note to twice its value, or follow some other clear ratio, so the voices share the same material yet never land on the same spot at the same moment. This kind of writing has important examples in late medieval and Renaissance polyphony, and it was later still used as an ingenious contrapuntal device. If you study piano or counterpoint, it is wise to learn the theme well at its original speed, then at the lengthened or shortened ratio, and only at the end to put the two on top of each other, which makes it easier to stand on firm ground. It trains not only the fingers but also your sense of proportion in note values. You can set each of the two speeds against the metronome separately, and then look for the beats they share. When you play hands together, always start from such a shared beat, or the hands will drift apart at once. Slow practice matters especially here.

## How to Practise Different Speeds Layered Together at the Piano

First play only the original-speed voice, then play the same theme as the other voice with lengthened or shortened rhythm.

Once both hands are steady, slowly put them together from a shared beat.

As soon as one hand goes wrong, separate them at once, and do not carry on charging ahead in the confusion.

## The Relationship with Augmentation and Diminution

Augmentation and diminution can appear in successive variations, or, as here, happen at the same time.

The special feature of the mensuration canon lies precisely in that "at the same time".

Comparing these two uses helps put the terms back into a concrete context.

## Why You Need a Shared Beat

Two lines at different speeds are still written on the same score with a time signature, so there are always some places where they share the same slot.

Find these slots first, and then putting the hands together has something to rely on.

You can lightly mark these places as alignment points.

![Cartoon-style student wearing headphones sitting at a piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjfhp9-srsqb.webp)

## Mensuration Canon in Brief

A mensuration canon is a technique in which the same melody moves at different, clearly defined speed ratios at the same time. Most commonly the original speed is layered with an augmentation or a diminution, and there are important examples in early polyphony.

When practising, first learn each speed separately, then slowly put the hands together from a shared beat, and begin by choosing a short example with few voices and clear ratios.

You can ask Teacher Aum to mark the shared beats with you.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Line Up the Beats in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to mark with you the beats that the two speeds share, and to put them together once slowly.

You can also first check whether the original-speed voice and the augmented voice are each steady on their own.

From the mensuration canon, practise keeping one melody steady at different speeds at the same time.

## Common Ratios

Doubling or halving the note values is the easier kind to observe.

There can also be more complex ratios, but when learning it is best to start with simple multiples.

The ratio must be clear, or it becomes a vague free imitation and is no longer this technique.

## What to Listen For

First hear that they are the same melody at different speeds, without needing to follow every note at once.

Sometimes they briefly meet at some point, and then part again.

After listening a few times, the overlap of fast and slow becomes predictable.

## How It Differs from an Ordinary Canon

An ordinary canon is often one in which a later-entering voice imitates an earlier one at the same speed.

In a mensuration canon even the speed changes in proportion, so the imitation follows not only in pitch but also in the scaling of note values.

The listener feels the same material both running and walking slowly.

## What to Look at First When Reading a Canon at Different Speeds

Early scores may use different signs to indicate the ratio, while modern notation usually writes out both lines clearly.

Whichever kind of score it is, first confirm the note-value relationship between the voices, and then begin to play.

When you are unsure of a ratio, look up the explanation rather than guess.

## Do Not Pick the Most Complicated Example at the Start

Some works have many ratios and many voices and are not suitable as an introduction.

First find a short example with fewer voices and a clear ratio, and increase the difficulty after you succeed.

Playing a simple example accurately is worth more than playing a complicated one in a muddle.

**Remember this**
- The same melody moves at different, clearly defined speed ratios at the same time
- One voice may be at the original speed, the other augmented or diminished
- It has important examples in early polyphony and was still used later
- First learn each speed separately, then look for a shared beat and put the hands together

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a mensuration canon?**
A: A canon in which the same melody moves at different, clearly defined speed ratios at the same time.

**Q: How does it differ from an ordinary canon?**
A: An ordinary canon mostly imitates at the same speed, while a mensuration canon also scales the note values in proportion.

**Q: Why find a shared beat before putting the hands together?**
A: Because two lines at different speeds are still written in the same grid of one score, and the shared beat is the basis for lining them up.

**Q: What should the order of practice be?**
A: First learn the original speed and the proportionally changed speed separately, then put the hands together slowly.

**Q: What kind of example should a beginner choose?**
A: A short example with few voices and clear ratios, not the most complicated work with many ratios.

messiaen-quartet-end-of-time-1941.body:
In 1940, during the Second World War, the French composer Messiaen was captured and held in a prisoner-of-war camp near Görlitz in Germany. There he met a clarinettist, a violinist and a cellist, and so he wrote a work for these three instruments, plus the piano that he played himself: the Quartet for the End of Time. On 15 January 1941 the work was premiered in the camp, with prisoners and guards as the audience. It was a very special premiere in the history of music.

**Another Angle**
- Messiaen was captured in 1940 and held near Görlitz
- Written for clarinet, violin, cello and piano
- Premiered in the camp on 15 January 1941
- Inspired by the Book of Revelation in the Bible

## Messiaen's Rhythm

Messiaen had many distinctive ideas about rhythm, such as using irregular, asymmetrical rhythms.

**Little Tip**

In the Quartet for the End of Time, the rhythm in some passages is extremely free, and sounds as if time has stopped.

This exploration of rhythm influenced many later composers.

## Legend and Memory

Some stories have circulated about this premiere, for example that the cello had only three strings.

But the cellist Pasquier later said that his cello had four strings.

Details like this are often changed as they are passed on, so when learning about them, take care to tell memory from legend.

## Hearing Messiaen's Harmony at the Piano

Messiaen's harmony is full of colour, and he said he could "see" the colours of chords.

At the piano, you can try slowly playing some chords from his works and listening to their colours.

His music is rather difficult, but you can begin with listening and appreciation.

## The Inspiration for the Quartet for the End of Time

The inspiration for this work came from a passage in the Book of Revelation, in which an angel declares that "there shall be time no longer".

Messiaen was a devout Catholic, and many of his works are connected with his faith.

"The end of time" is meant in a religious sense, and it also relates to his thinking about musical rhythm.

## A Composer Taken Prisoner

Messiaen was born in France in 1908 and was a composer and organist.

After the outbreak of the Second World War, he was called up, and in 1940 he was captured by the German army.

He was held in a prisoner-of-war camp near Görlitz in eastern Germany, known as Stalag VIII-A.

## Quartet for the End of Time in Brief

In 1940 Messiaen was captured in the war and held in Stalag VIII-A near Görlitz in Germany. There he met the clarinettist Akoka, the violinist Le Boulaire and the cellist Pasquier, and wrote the Quartet for the End of Time for these three instruments and piano, inspired by the angel in the Book of Revelation who declares "there shall be time no longer".

The whole work has eight movements, and the third, Abyss of the Birds, is a clarinet solo. It was premiered in the cold on 15 January 1941, with prisoners and guards as the audience. The claim that the cello had only three strings was denied by Pasquier, and the piano's keys would stick. In spring 1941 Messiaen was released and returned to France.

Messiaen has distinctive rhythms and richly coloured harmony, and you can begin with listening; Teacher Aum can introduce twentieth-century piano repertoire.

## After His Release

In spring 1941, Messiaen was released and returned to France.

Soon afterwards, he began teaching at the Paris Conservatoire, where he trained many composers who later became very influential.

The Quartet for the End of Time also became one of the important chamber works of the twentieth century.

![A pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaal5iw-dngzn.webp)

## An Out-of-Tune Piano

At the premiere, Messiaen played an upright piano belonging to the camp, which was in very poor condition.

According to recollections, some keys would stick when pressed and produced no sound.

Even in such conditions, the performance of the work was completed.

## Eight Movements

The Quartet for the End of Time has eight movements, and the combination of instruments differs from movement to movement.

In some movements all four instruments play together, while in others there are only one or two.

For example, the third movement, Abyss of the Birds, is for solo clarinet alone.

## Talking About the Quartet with Your Teacher

In a lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about this work that was born in a prisoner-of-war camp.

You can also ask your teacher to introduce some twentieth-century piano works that you could try at your own level.

Knowing a story like this lets us feel the power of music in hard times.

## A Special Combination of Instruments

The combination of clarinet, violin, cello and piano was rare at the time.

Messiaen wrote according to the instruments and players he had around him.

The work later drew more attention to this combination of instruments too.

## Abyss of the Birds

The third movement, Abyss of the Birds, is a clarinet solo.

The clarinet sometimes plays extremely long notes that swell from soft to loud, and sometimes imitates birdsong.

Messiaen loved birdsong, recorded a great deal of it during his life, and used it in his works.

## The Premiere on 15 January 1941

On 15 January 1941, the Quartet for the End of Time was premiered in the prisoner-of-war camp.

The weather that day was cold, and the audience was made up of the camp's prisoners and guards.

Messiaen later recalled that he had never been listened to by such an attentive, understanding audience.

## Four Musicians in the Camp

In the camp, Messiaen met several musicians who had also been taken prisoner.

Among them were the clarinettist Akoka, the violinist Le Boulaire and the cellist Pasquier.

**Remember This**

With Messiaen himself at the piano, they made exactly a quartet.

## FAQ

**Q: Where was Messiaen held?**
A: In Stalag VIII-A near Görlitz in Germany.

**Q: What instruments was the work written for?**
A: Clarinet, violin, cello and piano.

**Q: On what date was the premiere?**
A: 15 January 1941.

**Q: Where did the inspiration come from?**
A: The Book of Revelation in the Bible.

**Q: Which movement is the clarinet solo?**
A: The third movement, Abyss of the Birds.

example-scenario-parent-sets-up-home-pra.body:
What follows is a fictional sketch, not a report of real events. The parent and child are invented, and the story exists only to show one way of arranging a practice space. In the scenario, a parent called Ploy wants the child to enjoy playing the keyboard at home. Instead of making rules about time, Ploy first improves the corner where the instrument sits, so that sitting down feels easy and pleasant. Small changes in the environment can help practice happen naturally.

## The starting point

Imagine a small flat where the keyboard has been in the living room, beside the television and a pile of laundry. The child often says there is nowhere to put the music. Ploy decides to give the keyboard its own corner, however modest, with light and a place for books.

## Light and seating

First, Ploy moves the keyboard near a window or places a lamp so that the music is easy to read. Then the seat is adjusted. A child should sit with relaxed shoulders and with elbows roughly level with the keys. If the child's feet do not touch the floor, a sturdy box or low stool under them makes sitting more comfortable.

- Good light on the music.
- A stable seat at the right height.
- Feet supported.
- Space for the elbows to move.

## A stand and a small shelf

A music stand holds the book at an easy angle. Beside it, a small shelf or basket keeps the current book, a pencil and a notebook within reach. Ploy labels the basket with the child's name and lets the child decorate it. Having a personal place for the tools gives the child a sense of ownership.

![Watercolour white grand piano with sheet music and flowers in a calm room](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwpg6rzt-7r6qa.webp)

## Quiet and comfort

In the example, Ploy turns off the television during practice and agrees that nobody else will ask the child questions for those minutes. If the keyboard has headphones, they can be used when the home is noisy. The aim is not silence all day, but a short, calm period for focus.

## Simple family rules

Ploy writes three short rules on a card and pins it above the shelf.

- Wash hands before playing.
- Close the lid or switch off when finished.
- Return the book to the basket.

The rules protect the instrument and make the routine predictable. They are friendly rather than strict, and the child helps to write them.

## Making it inviting

A small touch, such as a picture the child likes, makes the corner feel personal. Ploy also keeps a sticker chart nearby, not as a competition, but as a way to remember what has been practised. A short free-play moment at the end of each session keeps the mood positive.

## Keeping the space tidy

A corner stays inviting when it is easy to reset. At the end of each session, the child closes the book, puts the pencil back in the basket and switches off the lamp. This takes thirty seconds, and it means the next visit begins with everything in place. A tidy space also makes it easier for siblings or guests to leave the instrument alone.

## Reviewing after two weeks

After two weeks, Ploy asks the child what feels good and what feels awkward. Perhaps the lamp is too bright, or the seat is a little low. The corner is adjusted accordingly. This review shows the child that their opinion matters and that the space can change.

## Involving the child

The scenario works best when the child helps. Ploy asks the child to choose where the lamp goes, which picture to pin up and what colour the basket should be. Children often take better care of a space they helped to build. The choices can be small, but they send a clear message: this is your place, and it is ready for you whenever you want to play. Many families find that this shared set-up makes starting easier.

## FAQ

**Q: Is this a real family?**
A: No. It is a made-up scenario to illustrate one possible set-up.

**Q: Do I need a separate room?**
A: No. A small corner with light, a stable seat and a place for books can be enough.

**Q: What height should the seat be?**
A: Choose a height where the elbows sit about level with the keys and the feet feel supported.

**Q: Should the child practise with headphones?**
A: It can help when the home is noisy, but listening through speakers sometimes is also useful.

mendelssohn-spring-song-op62-no6.body:
Spring Song is one of the most frequently played of Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words. Its number is Op. 62 No. 6, it is in A major, and its tempo is Allegretto. It was written in the 1840s and is included in Book 5 of the Songs Without Words. The right hand sings a light, connected melody, the left hand supports it softly with broken chords, and crisp ornaments often appear in the middle, like light suddenly brightening in spring. The piece is not long, but it demands a singing melody and even fingers, and it suits learners who can already play a cantabile phrase smoothly. When listening, you can first notice only how the right hand begins and ends its phrases, and then listen to whether the left hand keeps walking steadily underneath.

## How the Right Hand Makes the Melody Sing

The right-hand melody should be connected, with the rise and fall of phrases between the notes, like taking a breath when singing.

Ornaments and quick small figures should not rush ahead of the melody; they are the sparkle, not the main phrase.

You can sing the melody alone once, then return to the piano and see where a phrase needs to be gently closed off.

## Let the Pedal Follow the Harmony

When the left-hand broken chord changes harmony, the pedal usually has to change too, otherwise several chords pile up together.

Sometimes you can change it more shallowly, so the sound stays connected without blurring.

At the end, if the melody gets softer, release the pedal cleanly too, and do not leave a cloud of resonance behind.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen to Your Phrases

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to where your right-hand phrases breathe and whether the ornaments push the beat.

You can also ask your teacher to sit beside you and listen to check whether the left hand is too loud.

Through one short song without words, practise making the piano sound as if it is singing.

## What a Song Without Words Is

A song without words is a kind of short piece Mendelssohn wrote for piano: like a song, but with no lyrics.

He wrote many books of Songs Without Words in his life, six pieces in each, and Spring Song is in Book 5.

When listening, you can imagine the right hand as a singer and the left hand as a quiet accompaniment.

## How the Left Hand Supports the Singing Melody

Most of the time the left hand plays broken chords, which should be even and quiet, without pushing out an accent on every beat.

The bass can be a little clearer, to give the melody a stable base.

Keep the wrist relaxed and let the fingers move along with the chord positions, without hitting every note dead.

**Go a Little Slower**
- Mendelssohn, Songs Without Words Book 5, Op. 62 No. 6
- A major, Allegretto
- Written in the 1840s
- Melody in the right hand, with broken-chord accompaniment in the left

## The Bright Colour of A Major

A major has three sharps, and it is often used for fairly cheerful pieces.

The main melody of this Spring Song is also built on A major, and the harmony moves clearly, so it sounds clean and transparent.

The middle section briefly leaves the original key and then returns to A major, like going out for a walk and coming back.

## Spring Song in Brief

Spring Song is Op. 62 No. 6 in Book 5 of Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, in A major, written in the 1840s. The right hand sings the melody and the left hand accompanies with broken chords; the ornaments should be light and the pedal should follow the harmony.

The piece is not long, and it values singing quality and evenness more than speed, so there is no need to rush at the start.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your phrase breathing and pedalling.

## Ornaments and Light Grain

The score often has short ornaments and fairly fast figures, which should be played lightly, quickly and clearly.

You can first slow the ornaments down, see which main note each one is attached to, and then put them back at tempo.

If the ornaments squeeze the beat out of shape, first steady the beat points of the main melody.

![A group of humanoid robots play piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon-lit street, with crystal towers in the background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdi1i0n-yptby.webp)

## How to Start Learning This Song Without Words

The piece is short and technically not the hardest, but it asks a lot of the melodic line and an even accompaniment.

If you can already play a singing melody smoothly, and your left hand does not cover the right, you can start learning it.

There is no need to chase a fast tempo at the start: first arrange the phrases and pedalling, then gradually return to the Allegretto on the score. You can also practise just the beginning and the ending a few times each day, so that these two spots, the easiest to hear, become steady first.

## The Name Spring Song

"Spring Song" is a title that came into common use later, to describe the bright, light character of the piece.

It is not an art song about spring with sung words, but a song without words on the piano.

The title can help the imagination, but when playing you still need to go back to the phrasing, dynamics and pedalling on the score.

## FAQ

**Q: Which set of works does Spring Song come from?**
A: Book 5 of Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, numbered Op. 62 No. 6.

**Q: What key is it in?**
A: A major.

**Q: What does "song without words" mean?**
A: A short piano piece that is like a song but has no lyrics.

**Q: What does the left hand mainly play?**
A: Even, quiet broken chords.

**Q: How should the ornaments be treated?**
A: They should be light, quick and clear, and must not squeeze the beat of the main melody out of shape.

metronome-one-click-per-bar.body:
When practising with a metronome, most people let it click on every beat and play along with the tick. This helps us stay steady, but it can also make us depend on the metronome, so that once it is switched off we have no idea whether we are fast or slow. A more advanced method is to slow the metronome down so that it clicks only once per bar: for a piece in 4/4, for example, it sounds only on the first beat of each bar. The remaining beats you have to count in your head. That way the metronome is only a checkpoint, and it is we ourselves who really keep the rhythm.

**Quick tip**
- Let the metronome click only once per bar
- Count the other beats yourself in your head
- Move gradually from a click on every beat to every two beats
- Check whether your inner beat is steady

## One Click per Bar in Brief

A metronome that clicks on every beat can make people dependent. Setting it to click once per bar, with the other beats counted by yourself, builds an inner beat. You can first move to one click every two beats, and 3/4 and 6/8 are set according to their pattern of strong and weak beats.

When the metronome comes early or late, it shows whether you have gone fast or slow. Count the beats clearly in your head, and at a more advanced stage you can treat the metronome as a weak beat. This method suits passages you can already play steadily.

A steady inner beat is the basis for controlling tempo changes. You can switch the metronome off step by step, check against a recording, and practise together with Teacher Aum in lessons.

![Watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8w1z7-xz7ag.webp)

## The Relationship with Free Tempo

Some music needs free tempo changes, such as ritardando or free tempo.

Practising with one click per bar is not meant to make the music mechanical.

Rather, you first build a steady inner beat, and on that basis the tempo changes will be under control.

## Checking Your Inner Beat

With only one click per bar, if we play too fast, the first beat of the next bar arrives earlier than the metronome.

If we play too slowly, the metronome sounds first.

That way we can clearly tell whether our inner beat is steady.

## Recording Against the Metronome

You can also record without the metronome, then play back the recording while turning the metronome on to compare.

If the tempo of the recording keeps matching the metronome, your inner beat is very steady.

If there is a deviation, you can find where it begins to speed up or slow down.

## Counting the Beats in Your Head

On the beats where the metronome does not sound, count them clearly in your head.

At the beginning you can count quietly aloud, for example "one, two, three, four".

Once you are familiar with it, switch to counting silently in your head.

## Setting 3/4 and 6/8

For a piece in 3/4, you can set the metronome to one third of the original tempo, with one click on the first beat of each bar.

6/8 is usually counted in two big beats, so you can first let the metronome click on each big beat, then change to one per bar.

Different time signatures can be set according to their pattern of strong and weak beats.

## First Move to One Click Every Two Beats

If you change from a click on every beat straight to one per bar, it may feel very hard.

You can first move to a click every two beats, for example in 4/4 sounding only on the first and third beats.

Once you are used to it, change to only one click per bar.

## Practising Together in Lessons

You can try this method together with Teacher Aum in lessons.

Your teacher can help set up the metronome and can also hear where the rhythm is unsteady.

Once you are home, carry on practising in the way you did in the lesson.

## Switching the Metronome Off Step by Step

When even the one-click-per-bar method is steady, you can try playing once with the metronome switched off completely.

After playing, turn the metronome on again and check whether your tempo has drifted away along the way.

In this way you reduce your dependence on the metronome step by step.

## Letting the Metronome Fall on a Weak Beat

A harder exercise is to have the metronome click once per bar, but treat it as the second or the fourth beat.

This needs us to have already found our own beat before the metronome sounds.

This kind of practice makes your sense of rhythm more independent, and also helps you feel the weak beats.

## The Limits of a Click on Every Beat

A metronome that sounds on every beat is like having someone beside us counting the beats all the time.

What we play this way is steady, but we have not really mastered the rhythm ourselves.

Once the metronome is switched off, the tempo may become fast one moment and slow the next.

## Only One Click per Bar

Set the metronome to click once per bar. For example, for a piece in 4/4 at 80 beats per minute, set the metronome to 20 clicks per minute.

That way the metronome sounds only on the first beat of each bar.

The three beats in between you have to keep steady yourself.

## When to Use This Method

This method suits passages you can already play steadily with a click on every beat.

If a passage is not yet fluent, first practise it steady with a click on every beat.

Once the passage is fluent, use one click per bar to check your rhythm.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What about the other beats when the metronome clicks only once per bar?**
A: Count them yourself in your head.

**Q: What if I cannot do it all at once?**
A: First move to one click every two beats.

**Q: How do I know I have gone fast?**
A: The first beat of the next bar arrives earlier than the metronome.

**Q: What kind of passage suits this method?**
A: A passage you can already play steadily with a click on every beat.

**Q: Will it make the music mechanical?**
A: No, it is the basis for controlling tempo changes.

mock-performance-run-through.body:
Before a real performance, exam or student concert, doing a few mock performances at home is a very practical way to prepare. The rules are simple: play from beginning to end, without stopping and without starting over, as if there really were an audience listening. You can ask family members to sit down as your audience, or record yourself on your phone. Afterwards, look back and see which places need strengthening. This kind of practice lets you get used to the feeling of performing in advance, and it also reveals problems you did not notice when practising in sections.

## The Rules of a Mock Performance

In a mock performance, treat it like a real one, starting from walking up to the piano, sitting down and adjusting the stool.

**Order of practice**

Then play from the first note to the last, and whatever happens along the way, do not stop and do not start over.

When you finish, stand up and bow as you would on stage, and then end the mock performance.

## Review Afterwards

During a mock performance, do not judge yourself as you play. Just concentrate on playing the music through.

When it is over, listen to the recording or think back over your playing, and note what went well and what needs strengthening.

Those places that need strengthening are the focus of your section practice over the next few days.

## Practising Carrying On After a Mistake

A mock performance is also a good chance to practise "carrying on after a mistake". If you play a wrong note, act as if it never happened and keep going.

You can decide in advance on a few "re-entry points", such as the beginning of each phrase. If you get stuck, skip ahead to the next re-entry point and carry on.

After practising this several times, you will be calmer in handling the unexpected when you perform.

## Ask Family to Be the Audience

When people are listening, you feel differently from when you practise alone. You may feel nervous, or you may become more absorbed.

You can ask family or friends to sit down and listen. Even one or two people can create the atmosphere of a performance.

After you finish, you can ask them to say what they heard and which parts they liked.

## The Difference Between Everyday Practice and Performance

In everyday practice, we often stop where we make a mistake and replay it several times until we get it right.

But in a performance, there is no chance to start again, and you have to keep playing even after a mistake.

If you have never practised playing a whole piece without stopping, a small mistake in performance can make you panic, and you may not know how to go on.

## Do It at Different Times

You can do mock performances at different times of day, such as right after getting up in the morning, after dinner, or just after finishing something else.

The time of the real performance is not necessarily when you are at your best, and practising in different states makes you more adaptable.

You can also try starting with no warm-up, to simulate a situation where there is little time to prepare before the performance.

## Scheduling the Mock Performances

You do not need to do mock performances every day. You can start two or three weeks before the performance and schedule a few each week.

For the rest of the time, section practice is still the main work, and the mock performances are used to check the overall effect.

In the last day or two before the performance, you can do one or two relaxed run-throughs to keep your confidence up, without tiring yourself out.

![The lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0a56a-0om1j.webp)

## Mock Performances for Children

For children, you can turn a mock performance into a small family concert, letting the child introduce the piece before playing it.

The family can applaud the child and say what they liked.

This relaxed atmosphere helps children build up stage experience, and it also adds to the fun of learning the piano.

## Try It on Different Pianos

If you have the chance, do a mock performance on a piano at someone else's home, at school or in a practice room.

Different pianos differ in the weight of the keys, the loudness of the sound and the feel of the pedals.

Getting used to an unfamiliar piano in advance means fewer surprises when you perform.

## Looking After Your Feelings

If one mock performance does not go well, do not blame yourself too much. That is exactly the point of a mock performance.

Every mock performance is a chance to learn, letting you find and solve problems before the real performance.

Go about it in a relaxed frame of mind, and you will gradually come to enjoy the process of performing more.

## Record It on Your Phone

If there is nobody to be your audience, you can record audio or video on your phone and treat the phone as your audience.

Knowing that you are being recorded also gives you a little of the feeling of performing.

The recording can be played back again and again, so you can listen to your own playing calmly, like an outsider.

**Listen up**
- A mock performance is played from beginning to end
- No stopping and no starting over along the way
- You can ask family to be the audience, or record yourself
- After playing, find the places that need strengthening

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is a mock performance?**
A: Playing from beginning to end without stopping, just like a real performance.

**Q: Should I start over if I make a mistake?**
A: No. Keep playing.

**Q: What if there is no audience?**
A: You can record audio or video on your phone.

**Q: When should I start?**
A: Two or three weeks before the performance, a few times a week.

**Q: What should I do after playing?**
A: Review the performance and find the places that need strengthening.

**Q: Can children do it?**
A: Yes, it can become a small family concert.

metronome-marking-mm-quarter-equals.body:
Besides an Italian tempo term, many scores begin with a marking like "♩=100", meaning one hundred quarter notes per minute, that is, the metronome set to 100. Some older scores write it as "M.M. ♩=100", where M.M. refers to Maelzel's metronome. Note that the note before the equals sign is not always a quarter note: in 6/8 time a dotted quarter note is common, and then each click of the metronome stands for one dotted quarter note.

## Tempo Changes Midway

Some pieces have a new tempo marking in the middle, showing that the tempo changes from there.

There are also markings written as "♩=♩.", meaning the dotted quarter note of the new section equals the quarter note of the original.

When you meet a marking like this, first find the relationship between the old and new tempo on the metronome, then practise the join.

## Slow First, Then Fast

The tempo marking on a score is often the target tempo for performance, not the tempo at which you begin practising.

When you first learn a piece, you can set the metronome much slower than the marking, to make sure every note is accurate.

Once you are fluent, raise it step by step until you approach the tempo on the score.

## Reading Practice with Metronome Markings

Take out a few different scores, find the tempo marking at the start, and say what the note before the equals sign and the number mean.

Then try each of these tempi on the metronome, and hear the differences between them.

This kind of practice helps you understand tempo markings faster, and gives you a more direct feel for different speeds.

## Tempo Terms and Numerical Markings

Scores often begin with Italian terms such as Allegro or Andante, which describe the approximate speed and character.

A numerical marking such as "♩=100" gives a more specific tempo.

The two often appear together: one tells you the feel of the music, the other tells you where to set the metronome.

## The Note Before the Equals Sign

The note before the equals sign in a tempo marking is important, because it decides what each click of the metronome stands for.

If it is a half note, as in "half note = 60", then each click of the metronome is a half note.

When reading a score, first make out this note clearly, and only then set the metronome.

## Setting the Tempo with a Phone Metronome

Many phone apps can now serve as a metronome, and you can set the tempo just by entering a number.

When setting it, take care to choose the correct time signature and the note value of each beat, especially in compound time.

Some apps can also set accents, helping you feel the first beat of each bar.

**A different angle**
- "♩=100" means one hundred quarter notes per minute
- M.M. means Maelzel's metronome
- The note before the equals sign decides what one beat is
- 6/8 time often uses the dotted quarter note as the unit

## Tempo Markings in Compound Time

In pieces in 6/8, it is often written as "dotted quarter note = 60".

This means each click is a dotted quarter note, which is the length of three eighth notes.

If you mistakenly treat the metronome as eighth notes, the tempo will be much slower, completely changing the feel of the music.

## Tempi Added by Editors

In some classical works, the tempo markings were not written by the composer himself but added later by editors.

In some editions, brackets or explanatory notes show which are the editor's suggestions.

Knowing this can make you more flexible in choosing a tempo.

## No Need to Stick to the Number Rigidly

A tempo marking is a suggestion from the composer or editor, but performers can also make some adjustments according to the instrument, the venue and their own understanding.

For example, in a place with a lot of echo, a slightly slower tempo may be clearer.

What matters is making the music sound right, not mechanically chasing a particular number.

## What M.M. Means

In some older scores you will see the two letters "M.M." written before the tempo marking.

It is short for "Maelzel's Metronome"; Maelzel promoted the mechanical metronome in the early nineteenth century.

Most scores today leave out these two letters and write only the note and the number.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesizer on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa305s0-5ly81.webp)

## Tempo Markings and the Character of the Music

The same hundred beats per minute can sound completely different in different pieces.

In a piece with dense notes, a hundred beats feels very fast; in a piece with many long notes, a hundred beats may feel unhurried.

So after setting the metronome, you still need to use your ears to feel whether the character of the music is right.

## What the Number Stands For: Beats per Minute

The number in the marking tells you how many of that note there are per minute.

"♩=60" means sixty quarter notes per minute, that is, one per second.

"♩=120" is one hundred and twenty per minute, two per second, twice as fast.

## Words Around the Tempo Marking

Sometimes the word "about" or "circa" is written next to the tempo marking, showing that the tempo is only approximate.

Some composers also write a range, such as "♩=88–96", leaving the performer to choose within it.

**Order of practice**

These words remind us that a tempo marking is a reference, not an absolute rule.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does "♩=100" mean?**
A: One hundred quarter notes per minute.

**Q: What does M.M. stand for?**
A: Maelzel's metronome.

**Q: What should I watch for in the tempo marking of 6/8 time?**
A: It is often based on the dotted quarter note, so do not set it by mistake to eighth notes.

**Q: Do I need to practise at the marked tempo from the start?**
A: No. Practise slowly first, then speed up step by step once you are fluent.

**Q: Must tempo markings be followed strictly?**
A: They are an important reference, and can be adjusted a little to suit the music and the venue.

mendelssohn-spinning-song-op67-no4.body:
The Spinning Song is No. 4 of Felix Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, Op. 67, and is sometimes also called "The Bees' Wedding". It is not the same piece as the other short piece that is also often called a spinning song: this one belongs to Mendelssohn's own Songs Without Words, and uses fast, even figures to suggest a spinning wheel or fluttering movement, while a singing phrase still shows through in the middle. When learning it, first get the fast figures even at a moderately slow tempo, then treat the somewhat longer notes as a song; this is safer than chasing a very light, very fast recording from the start. When listening, you can also first notice whether the rolling figures stay round all the way through, and only then look for the melody hidden inside. If the rolling gets more and more rushed, the song gets left behind; when that happens, slow down and first line up the starting points between the groups of figures. Its charm lies in being light, even and always moving, not in playing every note heavily. When practising, first confirm the composer and opus number on the score, so you do not mix up the demonstrations and fingerings of the other piece of the same name. If you cannot find the song in the rolling, pick out the somewhat longer notes alone with a different dynamic, then put them back. Lightness and evenness are the goal; heaviness and rushing often spoil the feeling of the spinning wheel. Write the opus number at the top of the score page, so that you do not mix it up later when you pick up a demonstration of the other piece of the same name.

## Tempo and the Nickname

The nickname "The Bees' Wedding" is something later generations imagined about its light character; it need not be taken as an instruction to play at a dashing speed.

**Before You Start**

The tempo still depends on evenness and on keeping the main phrase clear.

First be able to make both the rolling and the song clear at a moderate tempo, then speed up.

## How to Practise the Rolling Figures

Fast figures in the right hand, or alternating between the hands, should be even, with fixed fingering and small movements.

You can practise in groups, lining up the first note of each group with the beat and keeping the rest of the notes round.

Wherever you always speed up, slow that spot down on its own and repeat it until it stops pushing forward.

## What to Remember About This Spinning Song

This is No. 4 of Songs Without Words, Op. 67, and should be kept apart from the other piece of the same name.

When playing, aim first for evenness and lightness, bring out the song hidden in the rolling, and keep the pedal short.

When listening, first judge whether the movement is round, then look for how the somewhat longer notes join into phrases.

![High-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a rainy, neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdk1drf-noz5g.webp)

## The Song Hidden Inside

The fast figures are not everything: some notes are slightly longer and slightly brighter, and joined together they are the melody.

First pick out these notes alone and sing them through, then put them back into the rolling and check whether they can still be heard.

If every note is equally loud, the spinning scene is still there, but the song is gone.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen for the Song in the Rolling

In a lesson you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and tell you whether the figures are even and whether the somewhat longer notes are getting lost.

If a passage rushes as soon as you speed up, you can also ask your teacher to help you line up the starting points of the groups again.

Through the fourth Song Without Words of Op. 67, practise keeping the phrases alive even in fast movement.

## First, Tell the Two "Spinning Songs" Apart

Among student repertoire there is another short piece also often called a spinning song, and its composer is not Mendelssohn.

This one belongs to Songs Without Words, Op. 67, and is Mendelssohn's own work, so it should not be confused with the other.

When looking at the score, first confirm the composer and opus number before you start practising, and you will avoid many detours.

## Pedal and Lightness

Figures like these do not like long pedal. A short touch, or a shallow change where the harmony changes, makes it easier to keep the grain.

Keep the touch light, with a sound that is bright but not hard.

If the figures get thinner near the end, release the pedal cleanly even earlier.

## How the Left Hand Supports the Spinning Song

The left hand often provides steady harmony or small, short supports, and should not grab attention from the rolling surface.

A clear bass helps you hear the key, but do not add weight to every single note.

**Remember This**

If the layers get muddled when the hands are together, bring the left hand down one more notch.

- The fourth of Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, Op. 67, often called the Spinning Song
- Sometimes also known by the nickname "The Bees' Wedding"
- A singing phrase is still hidden inside the fast, even figures
- When practising, first aim for evenness and then speed up gradually, without losing the main phrase

## FAQ

**Q: Which set of Mendelssohn's works does this piece come from?**
A: It is the fourth of the Songs Without Words, Op. 67.

**Q: Is it the same piece as the other short piece also called "Spinning Song"?**
A: No. The other one has a different composer, so first confirm the composer and number when looking at the score.

**Q: Is "The Bees' Wedding" an instruction to play at a dashing speed?**
A: No. It is a nickname from later generations, and the tempo still depends on evenness and on keeping the main phrase clear.

**Q: How can I find the melody in the fast figures?**
A: Pick out the somewhat longer, slightly brighter notes alone, and joined together they are the song.

**Q: What should I watch for with the pedal?**
A: Keep it short and shallow, so that the rolling does not blur into one wash.
