moscow-nights-1956-song-piano.body:
Moscow Nights was composed by the Soviet composer Vasily Solovyov-Sedoy, with words by the poet Mikhail Matusovsky, and was written for a documentary film in 1955-56. The song describes a summer night when the riverside outside Moscow is quiet and a pair of lovers are reluctant to part. At first it attracted little attention, but after it was well received at an international youth festival held in Moscow in 1957, it spread quickly around the world. The melody is in a minor key, calm and heartfelt, and it suits the piano very well.

## Moscow Nights in Brief

The song was composed by Solovyov-Sedoy, with words by Matusovsky, and was written for a documentary in 1955-56. Its original title referred to "the outskirts of Leningrad". At first it drew little notice, but after it was well received at an international youth festival in Moscow in the summer of 1957, it spread quickly, and it reached China in the late 1950s.

**Summary**

The lyrics describe a pair of lovers reluctant to part by the river on a summer night. The melody is in a minor key, commonly A minor, calm, heartfelt and understated, in 4/4 time with dotted rhythms and syncopation. The phrases end on long notes. The left hand can use gentle broken chords, and the dynamics stay between mezzo piano and mezzo forte. The melody should sound as if it were being sung.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether your broken chords are even.

## A Minor-Key Melody

This song of a summer night is in a minor key, and most piano scores are written in A minor.

The melody is calm and heartfelt, with a faint touch of wistfulness.

It is not as sad as many minor-key songs. It is gentle and understated.

## The Melody Should Sound as if It Is Being Sung

When you play this song, the right-hand melody should be smooth and singing.

Imagine a singer softly singing, with room to breathe between the phrases.

For the long notes by the river, count the beats in full, and let the night linger a little longer.

- Music by Solovyov-Sedoy, words by Matusovsky
- Written for a documentary in 1955-56
- It describes the feelings of lovers by the river on a summer night
- It spread widely after being well received at an international youth festival in 1957

## The Turning Point in 1957

In the summer of 1957, Moscow held a large international youth festival, attended by young people from all over the world.

The song was loved and warmly praised by many people at the festival.

From then on, it spread quickly in the Soviet Union and around the world.

## The Rhythm of Moscow Nights

The song is in 4/4 time, at a moderately slow tempo, with a steady rhythm.

Dotted rhythms and small syncopations are tucked into the phrases, so that the telling of the summer night is not too stiff.

When you play, keep the rhythm flowing and not too mechanical.

![A person wearing headphones practises at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwad13fn-15bzf.webp)

## The Composer and the Lyricist

Vasily Solovyov-Sedoy was born in 1907 and died in 1979. He was a Soviet composer who wrote many lyrical songs.

Mikhail Matusovsky was born in 1915 and died in 1990. He was a Soviet poet.

The song the two wrote together became their best-known work.

## Written for a Documentary

The song was originally written as an interlude song for a documentary, and the original title mentioned "the outskirts of Leningrad".

Later the title was changed to "Moscow Nights".

When it appeared in the documentary, it did not at once attract much attention.

## The Mood of the Lyrics

The lyrics describe a summer night, with the river flowing quietly, everything around calm and only a faint singing in the distance.

A pair of lovers sit by the river, with much to say but unable to say it.

In the end, they promise to remember this beautiful night forever.

## Adding a Left Hand to Moscow Nights

The left hand can play an accompaniment of broken chords to create the calm atmosphere of a summer night by the river.

The broken chords should be gentle and even, like a quietly flowing river.

If your left hand is not yet fluent, first play the chords as blocks, and then slowly break them up into flowing arpeggios.

## How It Spread in China

The song reached China in the late 1950s and was given Chinese lyrics.

Many people learned to sing it when they were young, and it became a shared memory for several generations.

Today it is still often sung at concerts and gatherings.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to Your Broken Chords in Lessons

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the broken chords you play are even and soft.

There are many arrangements of this song, and you can talk together about which version to choose.

This song is very good for practising a lyrical, understated way of expressing yourself.

## The Shape of the Melody

The melody of each phrase does not rise and fall much, like a softly spoken confidence.

The ends of the phrases often rest on long notes, leaving room to reflect.

The range of the whole song is moderate and suits most people to sing.

## The Dynamics of Moscow Nights

The dynamics of this song do not change much, staying overall between mezzo piano and mezzo forte.

The chorus can be slightly stronger, to show the deepening of feeling.

But do not play too loudly, or you will spoil the calm of the night.

## Two Ways of Singing, Russian and Chinese

You can find both the Russian original and the Chinese-language versions to compare.

Notice how they express the gentleness and restraint of the song.

**Common misconceptions**

Then sit back down at the piano and try to let the river and the night flow from your fingertips.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Who composed this song?**
A: Solovyov-Sedoy.

**Q: What was it originally written for?**
A: An interlude song for a documentary.

**Q: What place did the original title mention?**
A: The outskirts of Leningrad.

**Q: In which year did it begin to spread widely?**
A: 1957.

**Q: What mode is the melody in?**
A: A minor key, commonly A minor.

music-app-release-notes-writing.body:
Release notes for a music app should use language users can understand to tell them three things: what changed this time, how it affects their practice, and what they need to do. Many release notes say only "Fixed some issues and improved performance", and after reading them users still do not know what happened. For learners who open the app every day to practise, and parents who sit in on practice, a clear release note reduces confusion and shows that the team is listening to feedback. Writing it well does not need fancy language, only that it is specific, honest and consistent.

## First Think About Who the Reader Is

Users of a music learning app are often very varied: adults starting from zero, children just beginning to read notes, and parents who manage the account for their child. The way a technical team habitually talks, such as "optimised the audio buffering logic", means nothing to most people. A better approach is to start from the situation of use: "The sound delay while playing has been improved, so practising along with the accompaniment will feel smoother."

**A one-sentence test**
After writing each note, ask yourself: could a parent with no technical background read it and understand how it relates to their child's practice? If not, rewrite it.

## Categories Make Information Clear at a Glance

When there is a lot to report, organising by category is easier to read than one long block of text. Common ways of categorising are as follows:

- New features: what has been added and where to find it.
- Improvements: where existing features have become more convenient.
- Fixes: which problems users reported that have been solved.
- Known issues: matters that have not been solved yet and are being worked on.
- Action needed from users: for example, logging in again or updating system permissions.

Keep only the few truly important items in each category, and combine small internal adjustments into a single sentence to avoid information overload.

## Being Honest About Known Issues

Many teams are unwilling to write "what is still not fixed" in the release notes, worried about the impression it makes. In fact, telling users in advance that something is being worked on, and how to get around it for now, is often more reassuring than letting users run into the problem and then go to customer support.

![Close-up of two hands practising on piano keys](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9pu7d6-61xuf.webp)

**Keep the tone calm**
There is no need to apologise repeatedly or to exaggerate the effect of a fix. Describing the current situation, the temporary workaround and how users will be told what happens next is enough.

## Connecting Release Notes to the Product Experience

Release notes do not live only on the app store page. An important new feature can be introduced in the app with a short tip card and a "Try it" entry; a change that affects practice records can get a slightly longer explanation on the website or in the community. For an AI piano learning product that keeps iterating, like TIGA ALPHA, writing each improvement clearly is also a way of explaining the product's direction to users.

- App store: a concise list by category.
- In-app prompt: introduce only one or two new features directly related to practice.
- Website or community: a detailed explanation and FAQ for larger changes.

## Building a Fixed Writing Template

To keep every release note consistent in style, the team can prepare an internal template: fixed categories, fixed tone requirements, a list of words to avoid, and who reviews before publishing. For a multilingual product, you also need to confirm that the content of every language version is consistent, so that one language does not mention a new feature that another leaves out.

## Collecting Feedback to Form a Loop

After the release note is sent, communication has not ended. You can leave a simple feedback entry at the end of the note, such as "Did this change help your practice?", and let users respond in a sentence or two. The team gathers these responses every week, puts recurring problems into the next round of improvement plans, and reports progress in the next release note. In this way the release note changes from a one-way announcement into an ongoing conversation.

- Leave a short feedback entry.
- Go through the responses once a week.
- Report progress in the next update.

**Do not forget the parents who sit in on practice**
Many children's accounts are managed by parents. For changes involving practice records, reminder times or privacy settings, you can write a separate paragraph for parents, explaining why the change was made and what can be adjusted, so that parents can keep supporting their child's practice with confidence.

## FAQ

**Q: Do release notes need a version number?**
A: We suggest including it, so that users can say which version they are using when they contact customer support.

**Q: Does every small update need a detailed note?**
A: Small updates can be short, but should at least say whether the change is a fix or an improvement.

**Q: Can I put promotional information in the release notes?**
A: We do not recommend mixing them. Release notes should focus on product changes, and promotions should be communicated separately.

**Q: When a problem reported by users has been fixed, should it be mentioned specially?**
A: You can simply say "improved based on user feedback", so that the people who made the suggestion know they were heard.

mp-mf-dynamics-levels.body:
mp (mezzo piano, moderately soft) and mf (mezzo forte, moderately loud) both count as "medium dynamics". The difference is that mp leans towards the soft side and mf towards the loud side. They are not fixed volume values but relative levels: within the same piece and on the same piano, mp must be clearly softer than mf, yet not so soft that it becomes p. The key to playing this subtle difference is controlling the speed at which the key goes down, not pressing hard or deliberately softening the fingers. This article uses "speaking volume" as a comparison and offers a complete method, from feeling to practice.

## The Short Answer: How the Dynamic Levels Rank

- The common dynamics from softest to loudest: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff
- Dynamics are relative, so compare them with the other dynamics in the same piece
- Volume depends mainly on the speed of the key going down: the faster it goes, the louder the sound
- The gap between mp and mf is much smaller than the gap between p and f, so it needs finer control
- On different pianos and in different rooms the same dynamic sounds different, so keep adjusting by ear

## Understanding the Six Levels Through Speaking Volume

Imagining dynamics as ways of speaking in different situations is much easier than the abstract "a bit softer, a bit louder":

- pp: whispering to the person beside you in a library
- p: chatting quietly at home in the evening, so as not to wake anyone
- mp: talking normally with a friend across the table in a cafe
- mf: speaking to a small group in a meeting room
- f: addressing the whole class in a classroom
- ff: calling out to a friend far away on the playground

Put side by side like this, you can see that mp and mf are both "normal speaking", only the distance to the listener differs. When playing mp, imagine the sound only has to reach the person across from you; when playing mf, imagine everyone around the table has to hear it clearly.

## Why Do Your mp and mf Sound the Same?

**Reason one: the fingers always go down at the same speed**
Many people get used to one fixed way of touching the keys, so whatever the score says, the keys go down at about the same speed, and naturally no levels can be heard.

**Reason two: thinking only of "soft" and "heavy"**
If you play loudly only by pressing hard, the sound easily turns harsh; if you play softly only by easing off, the sound becomes thin and may not even speak.

**Reason three: no point of reference**
Playing a single mf on its own, it is hard to judge whether it really counts as mf. A dynamic only means something when set against what comes before and after.

![Watercolour grand piano in dusky purple-grey tones with the lid open, symbolising tone and dynamics](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvlrncs-bfhzy.webp)

## Four Exercises to Help Your Fingers Find the Middle Levels

**Exercise one: a volume staircase on one note**
Choose middle C and, with the same finger, play from pp up to ff, two notes at each level, then come back from ff to pp. Keep the wrist and arm relaxed and change only the speed at which the key goes down.

**Exercise two: switching between mp and mf**
On the same note, alternate mp, mf, mp, mf. Before each switch, "hear" the next volume in your head first, then play it. At first the difference can be exaggerated; once you are comfortable, narrow it little by little.

**Exercise three: layering in a five-finger pattern**
With the right hand, play C, D, E, F, G going up and then down, using mp going up and mf coming down, then do it the other way round. This helps you keep consistent dynamic levels across a run of notes.

**Exercise four: dynamic contrast between melody and accompaniment**
Play a simple melody with the right hand at mf and the accompaniment chords with the left hand at mp. Different dynamics in the two hands is the most basic balance requirement in many pieces, and the key to making the melody sing out when you play the piano.

## Recording Check: Your Ears Are More Reliable Than Your Feelings

While you play, your brain "fills in" the effect you have in mind, so you often think the levels are already there. Put your phone beside the piano and record a take, then listen back after a while, and you will often find the difference between mp and mf is smaller than you imagined.

When listening back, ask yourself just one question: with my eyes closed, can I tell which phrase is mp and which is mf? If I cannot, I should widen the gap a little more. This method is common in piano teaching, and it also works as a weekly review when you are learning piano online by yourself.

## A Quick Note on Digital Pianos

Many digital pianos let you adjust touch sensitivity. If it is set to a very "light" mode, a gentle press already gives a loud sound, and dynamic levels become harder to develop. When practising dynamics, set the touch sensitivity back to the standard or usual setting, and use the same setting every time so that you can compare.

## FAQ

**Q: Which is more common, mp or mf?**

A: Both are very common. Many lyrical passages use mp, and many theme melodies use mf. What matters is not which is more common, but that they form a contrast within the same piece.

**Q: My child always plays too loudly. How can I guide them?**

A: Use the "speaking volume" comparison and ask your child, "Is this phrase talking in a cafe, or calling someone across the playground?" Let the child imitate it with their voice first, then go back to the piano. Turning abstract markings into everyday scenes makes learning music easier.

**Q: Are crescendo and diminuendo marks related to mp and mf too?**

A: Yes. A crescendo (cresc. or a hairpin opening to the right) and a diminuendo (dim. or a hairpin opening to the left) indicate a smooth change between two dynamic levels, for example from mp gradually to mf.

**Q: How long should I practise dynamics each day?**

A: A few minutes is enough. Put the volume staircase in your warm-up and keep at it every day; that is more effective than practising for a long time now and then. In piano lessons you can also ask your teacher to listen for you.

molto-poco-non-troppo-modifier-words.body:
Small words are often added before or after the terms in a score to show degree. Molto means "very", poco means "a little" or "slightly", and non troppo means "not too much". For example, Allegro molto is a very fast allegro, poco rit. is a slight slowing down, and Allegro ma non troppo is an allegro, but not too fast. These little words are easy to overlook, but once you can read them, you will judge the proportion of every change in the score more finely.

**Listen up**
- molto: very
- poco: a little, slightly
- non troppo: not too much
- Used together with tempo and dynamic terms

## Marking Them on the Score

When you meet a word of degree, you can pencil its meaning in English on the score, for example "slightly slower", "very fast" or "not too fast".

That way you can see it at a glance when you practise, and it is less likely to be overlooked.

Once you are familiar with them, you no longer need to write them.

## non troppo: Not Too Much

Non troppo means "not too much" or "not excessively".

For example, Allegro ma non troppo is an allegro but not too fast, and Adagio non troppo is an adagio but not too slow.

This term reminds the player to show restraint in a certain direction.

## Degree and Musical Style

Music of different styles also treats degree differently.

For example, in works of the Classical period, even a clearly marked ritardando is usually fairly restrained, while in works of the Romantic period the change can often be greater.

Knowing the period and style of a work helps us judge how far a word of degree should be taken.

## Common Combinations

Combining words of degree with tempo and dynamic terms gives many common expressions.

For example, molto espressivo is "very expressively", poco più mosso is "slightly faster", and sempre più forte is "louder and louder".

Getting to know these combinations lets you understand the score more quickly as you read.

## Practising Control of Degree

You can pick a familiar phrase and play it in two ways, with a "slight ritardando" and with a "big ritardando".

Compare the two effects and feel the difference in degree.

This kind of practice helps us control changes of tempo and dynamics better.

## molto: Very

Molto means "very", showing a large degree.

For example, Allegro molto is a very fast allegro, and molto cresc. is a large crescendo.

When you see molto, you know the change here must be clear and full.

## Degree Is Judged by Ear

Words of degree have no specific numbers, so how much slower or how much louder is left to the player's judgement.

You can decide according to the character of the music, the context and your own understanding.

Listening to recordings by different performers can also help us find a suitable degree.

## Checking the Proportion with Your Teacher

The proportion of a word of degree is sometimes hard to judge by yourself, so you can play for your teacher and ask for some specific suggestions.

You can also record your playing and listen back to hear whether the change is too small or too big.

After a few adjustments, you will gradually find the right degree.

## Words of Degree in Brief

Molto is "very", poco is "a little" or "slightly", and non troppo is "not too much"; they add degree to tempo and dynamic terms.

There are also common words of degree such as poco a poco, più, meno, assai and un poco.

Degree is judged by ear and understanding, and marking the score and practising by comparison can help us express it more accurately.

## assai and un poco

Assai means "very" or "quite", and is close to molto; for example, Allegro assai is a fairly fast allegro.

Un poco means "a tiny bit", slighter than poco; for example, un poco rit. is a slowing down by just a little.

These fine differences have to be felt carefully in performance.

## What Words of Degree Do

Tempo and dynamic terms tell us the direction, while words of degree tell us how big the change is.

For example, the same ritardando can be a little slower or much slower.

Words of degree make the meaning of a term more precise.

## Where Words of Degree Go

Words of degree sometimes come before the term, as in poco rit., and sometimes after it, as in Allegro molto.

Italian word order is fairly flexible, and the meaning is basically the same wherever the word stands.

When reading a score you need not worry too much about position; just recognise the word and know which term it modifies.

## poco: A Little, Slightly

Poco means "a little" or "slightly", showing a relatively small degree.

For example, poco rit. is a slight ritardando, and poco a poco means "little by little" or "gradually".

When you see poco, you know the change should be moderate, not exaggerated.

![Black grand piano and stool in front of a golden-red pointillist background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5mrlb-kseqm.webp)

## poco a poco

Poco a poco is often used with crescendo and ritardando; for example, poco a poco cresc. means getting louder little by little.

This term reminds us that the change should be completed slowly over a longer stretch of time, not arrive all at once.

When playing a passage like this, you can first decide where the end point is, and then move slowly towards it.

## The Meaning of ma

In Allegro ma non troppo, ma means "but".

So the whole term means: allegro, but not too fast.

When reading terms like this, you need to understand the meaning of every little word to understand the whole.

## più and meno

Besides these words, più and meno are also very common.

Più means "more"; for example, più mosso is a little faster. Meno means "less"; for example, meno mosso is a little slower.

**Watch the details**

These words often appear where a section changes, signalling an adjustment of tempo or dynamics.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does molto mean?**
A: Very.

**Q: What does poco mean?**
A: A little, slightly.

**Q: What does Allegro ma non troppo mean?**
A: Allegro, but not too fast.

**Q: What does poco a poco mean?**
A: Little by little, gradually.

**Q: What does più mosso mean?**
A: A little faster.

mozart-and-salieri-myth-and-facts.body:
Antonio Salieri was a composer of high standing in Vienna in the late eighteenth century, and for many years he held important musical posts. After Mozart died in 1791, a rumour appeared in Vienna that Salieri had harmed Mozart out of jealousy. In 1830, the Russian poet Pushkin turned this rumour into a verse drama, Mozart and Salieri, and in the twentieth century there were further adaptations for the stage and the screen, which made the story a household tale. But historians believe there is no evidence at all to support it. In fact, the two once co-wrote a short cantata, and Salieri also taught Beethoven, Schubert and the young Liszt.

## Pushkin's Verse Drama

In 1830, the Russian poet Pushkin wrote a very short verse drama, called Mozart and Salieri.

**Take it slowly**

The verse drama portrays Salieri as a man led astray by envy of a genius.

In 1898, the verse drama was turned into a short opera in only two scenes.

## Playing Mozart on the Piano

Mozart wrote many works for the piano, from simple minuets to sonatas and concertos.

If you have some foundation, you can start with his Sonata in C major, K. 545.

When you play, the sound should be clear and light, and the phrases as natural as singing.

## Mozart and Salieri in Brief

Salieri was born in Italy, came to Vienna as a teenager, and held important musical posts for many years. After Mozart died in 1791, a rumour appeared that Salieri had harmed him out of jealousy. Salieri firmly denied it. In 1830 Pushkin wrote the verse drama Mozart and Salieri, in 1898 it was turned into a short opera, and in the 1970s Peter Shaffer's play was made into a film. But historians believe there is no evidence at all to support the claim.

In 1785 the two, with another composer, co-wrote a short cantata, whose score was found again in the Czech Republic in the early twenty-first century. Salieri taught Beethoven, Schubert and the young Liszt. On the piano you can start with Mozart's K. 545. When reading stories about musicians, we should tell artistic creation apart from historical fact.

You can talk about this misunderstanding with Teacher Aum.

## Twentieth-Century Adaptations

In the 1970s, the English playwright Peter Shaffer wrote a play that told the story of the two men once again.

In 1984 it was brought to the screen, and this version was especially influential.

It was through this film that many people first learned the name Salieri.

## Salieri's Students

Salieri was a very important music teacher who taught many musicians who later became famous.

Beethoven and Schubert both studied composition with him, and the young Liszt also had lessons with him.

It is said that he often taught talented students from poor families for free.

## Salieri's Music

Because of this rumour and the later adaptations, Salieri's music was in fact neglected for a long time.

In recent years, some musicians have begun to perform and record his operas and instrumental works again.

Listening to his music gives a fairer picture of this composer.

## The Relationship Between the Two Composers

In the ten years Mozart lived in Vienna, there was both rivalry and cooperation between him and Salieri.

There were not many musical posts at that time, and it was quite normal for composers to compete with one another.

Mozart also complained about Italian composers in letters home, but this does not show any conspiracy.

## What Historians Say

Historians have studied the sources of the time carefully and believe there is no evidence at all to support the claim that Salieri killed Mozart.

Scholars today have various theories about the cause of Mozart's death, but none of them has anything to do with Salieri.

Plays and films are artistic creations and should not be taken as true history.

![Glowing abstract digital shapes and a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbji62z-g0f5q.webp)

## Who Salieri Was

Antonio Salieri was born in Italy, came to Vienna as a teenager, and spent most of his life there.

He wrote many operas, which were very popular in Europe at the time.

For many years he held important musical posts in Vienna, and he was an influential musician of his day.

## Telling Story from History

The story of Mozart and Salieri reminds us that when we read stories about musicians, we should tell apart what is artistic creation and what is historical fact.

You can read several sources and compare the different accounts.

This habit helps us understand both music and history better.

## How the Rumour Arose

After Mozart died in 1791, a rumour gradually appeared in Vienna that he had been killed by Salieri.

The rumour was brought up again in Salieri's old age and spread more widely.

It is said that Salieri himself was very upset by it and firmly denied it.

## Talk About This Misunderstanding with Your Teacher in Lessons

In your lesson, you can talk with Teacher Aum about the story of Mozart and Salieri and the historical truth.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend a Mozart piano piece, and see whether your current level lets you start learning it.

From a misunderstanding two hundred years old, you can learn to tell story from fact.

## A Work They Wrote Together

In 1785, Mozart and Salieri, together with another composer, co-wrote a short cantata for a woman singer.

The score of this work was missing for a long time, until it was found again in a museum in the Czech Republic in the early twenty-first century.

This shows that the two also had a friendly, cooperative side at the time.

- Salieri was a composer of high standing in Vienna in the late eighteenth century
- A rumour appeared after Mozart's death
- In 1830 Pushkin wrote the verse drama
- Historians find no evidence, and the two even co-wrote a work

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: In which city did Salieri mainly live and work?**
A: Vienna.

**Q: When did the rumour appear?**
A: After Mozart's death in 1791.

**Q: Which poet turned this rumour into a verse drama?**
A: The Russian poet Pushkin, in 1830.

**Q: What do historians think of this claim?**
A: There is no evidence to support it.

**Q: Which famous students did Salieri teach?**
A: Beethoven, Schubert and the young Liszt, among others.

musette-d-major-anna-magdalena-notebook.body:
The Musette in D major is found in the 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach, catalogued as BWV Anh. 126, and who composed it is still not entirely certain. The name "musette" comes from a type of bagpipe, and the piece imitates the bagpipe's continuous drone, with the left hand often leaping back and forth between two Ds an octave apart. In practising this piece, the key points are keeping the left-hand octave leaps steady and the right-hand melody light and lively.

## A family notebook

In 1725, Bach's wife Anna Magdalena owned a music notebook in which many little keyboard pieces and songs were copied.

Some of these pieces were written by Bach, and others were works by family members or other composers.

This Musette in D major is included in it, and the "Anh." before its number indicates that it belongs to the appendix works.

## How fast should a musette be?

A musette is itself a kind of dance, so the tempo should be light but not hurried.

If the left hand cannot manage the leaps, lower the speed first, and raise it once the leaps are steady.

A metronome can help you check whether each leap lands on time.

## The left-hand octave leaps

The most noticeable feature of this piece is that the left hand moves quickly back and forth between the low D and the D an octave above.

When you leap, do not lift the hand too high. Stay close to the keys and use the forearm to carry the hand sideways.

You can first use only the thumb and little finger, moving slowly between the two Ds, and speed up once the position is secure.

## Look first, then leap

Octave leaps often go wrong because the hand moves before the eyes do.

When practising, you can first look at where the next note is, and only then let the hand go there.

Once you are fluent, your hand will remember the distance between the two notes, and your eyes can spend more time on the score.

## The two sharps of D major

D major has two sharps, F sharp and C sharp.

Before you begin, you can play a D major scale to get used to where these two black keys are.

Circling the notes that need to be raised in the score can reduce wrong notes.

## Learning this musette in sections

This piece is divided into a few small sections, and each section has a repeated part.

You can learn the first section first, and once it is well practised, learn the later parts.

Notice whether anything changes when each section is repeated, because in some places the ending is different the second time.

## The countryside feel of the continuous drone

The constantly repeated bass in a musette brings to mind village festivals and outdoor dances, and the music carries a simple joy.

When playing, you can keep this picture in mind, letting the right-hand melody be like people dancing and the left-hand bass like a bagpipe sounding constantly alongside.

With this kind of imagination, even a very short little piece can be played with an atmosphere and character of its own.

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa23r4i-ob5aa.webp)

## What is a musette?

The name "musette" comes from an instrument that can produce a continuous drone while it is being played.

Composers imitated this effect, letting the bass repeat on the same note with a melody added above.

The left hand in this piece is imitating exactly this kind of drone effect.

## Baroque touch

This piece comes from the Baroque period, when keyboard instruments were not the same as today's piano and had a crisper sound.

When playing it on the piano, you can use the pedal little or not at all, so that every note is clearly separated.

The dynamics do not need to be big, and a light, clean sound better suits the style of this kind of piece.

## Coordinating the two hands

Because the left hand is busy leaping, it is easy to get confused when the hands are put together.

You can start at a very slow speed and line up every beat of the two hands.

When you meet a bar that is hard to coordinate, take it out on its own, practise the left and right hands in turn, and then play together.

**Quick tips**
- Included in the 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach
- Catalogued as BWV Anh. 126, composer not entirely certain
- Imitates the continuous drone of a bagpipe
- Keep the left-hand octave leaps steady and the right hand light

## The question of authorship

Because the pieces in the notebook come from different sources, who wrote this musette is still not entirely certain.

Some researchers think it may come from a member of the Bach family, while others think it is the work of another composer of the time.

When playing, there is no need to worry about who the composer was. The lightness and liveliness of the piece itself are the point.

## Other little pieces in the notebook

There are quite a few more little pieces in this notebook that suit beginners, such as several minuets.

After learning this musette, you can pick a few pieces in different styles to learn next.

These pieces can help you become familiar with the features of Baroque music, and also lay the groundwork for playing longer works later.

## The lightness of the right-hand melody

The right-hand melody is bouncy and lively, with many notes detached.

Staccato should be light, with the fingers touching the key and leaving it again, without pressing down hard.

**Summary**

Where there are slurs, join the notes again, so that the melody has contrast.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Was this piece composed by Bach?**
A: The composer is not entirely certain, and the number BWV Anh. 126 places it in the appendix.

**Q: What is a musette?**
A: A dance that imitates the continuous drone of a bagpipe.

**Q: What is hard about the left hand?**
A: Leaping quickly and steadily between two Ds an octave apart.

**Q: Do I need to use the pedal?**
A: You can use it little or not at all, to keep the sound clear.

**Q: Which notebook is it in?**
A: The 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach.

multi-measure-rest-counting.body:
In ensemble or orchestral playing, piano parts often show multi-bar rests: a thick horizontal line with the number of bars to rest written above it. During the rest you need to keep counting bars, while listening to the other instruments for cues, so that you come in accurately at the right moment.

## Listening for Cues

Besides counting, you can use your ears and take the music of the other parts as a cue. In rehearsal, notice what melody the other instruments are playing just before your entry.

You can write cues on the score, such as "come in after the trumpet melody rises", or copy out a few notes from other parts as a reference.

With an aural cue, even if you miscount the bars, you can find your place again from the music you hear.

This ability to count and listen at the same time is a very important skill in ensemble playing.

As rehearsals add up and you grow more familiar with the whole piece, your entries will become more and more accurate.

## How Multi-Bar Rests Are Written

In an ensemble or orchestral part, an instrument may have to rest for several bars in a row. To save space, the music shows this with a thick horizontal line and a number above it, and the number is how many bars to rest.

This notation is called a multi-bar rest. When you see it, you know you will rest for that many bars in a row before coming in again.

In some older scores you may also see special symbols for a two-bar or four-bar rest, combined to show longer rests.

Whichever way it is written, you must count the bars accurately.

A full ensemble score does not usually abbreviate this way; it is common only in the individual parts.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon-lit street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8ktfxp-pl7cs.webp)

## Getting Ready for Your Entry

When the rest is nearly over, bring your hands above the keys one or two bars early and get ready.

The first note of your entry should be on time and clear. If your body is too tense while waiting, the first note may sound stiff, so stay relaxed during the rest.

If you have counted the entry wrongly, do not panic: listen to the other parts to find where you are, and come in again at the start of the next clear section.

After a rehearsal, you can put your entry points and their matching cues into a small table, and review it before the next rehearsal.

After a few rounds of practice, even long rests will feel under control.

## How to Count Bars

When counting bars, you can say the bar number on the first beat of each bar and count the other beats as usual, for example "1 2 3 4, 2 2 3 4, 3 2 3 4". This makes it harder to lose your place.

You can also count on your fingers, folding down one finger for every bar that passes, eight fingers for eight bars.

In passages with many rhythmic changes, take particular care to check whether the time signature changes during the rest.

If the rest is very long, you can count it in groups, for example eight bars as two groups of four, and make a mental note when each group is finished.

Stay focused and do not let your attention wander during the rest.

**Practice order**
- A multi-bar rest is shown by a thick horizontal line with a number
- Keep counting bars throughout the rest
- Counting on your fingers can help your memory
- Remember the cue melody in the other parts before your entry

## What You Can Do While You Wait

When counting bars, you can say the bar number in your head on the first beat of each bar, for example "1 2 3 4, 2 2 3 4, 3 2 3 4", which makes it harder to lose your place. Counting on your fingers is also an intuitive method.

Besides counting, use your ears too. In rehearsal, notice which instrument is playing which melody before your entry, and write a cue on the score, such as "come in after the trumpet rises". That way, even if you miscount, you can find your place by ear.

Stay physically relaxed while waiting, and rest your hands lightly on your lap. As the entry point approaches, bring your hands above the keys one or two bars early and get ready.

Waiting in an ensemble is also a kind of practice. Learning to listen attentively when you are not playing greatly helps your understanding of the structure of the whole piece and how the parts fit together.

After an orchestra rehearsal, you can put your entry points and their matching cue melodies into a small table and read it through before the next rehearsal. After preparing this way a few times, even long rests will feel under control.

## FAQ

**Q: What if I count the bars wrongly?**
A: Do not panic. Listen to the other parts to find where you are, and come in again at the next clear section.

**Q: Do solo pieces have multi-bar rests too?**
A: Rarely. They appear mainly in ensemble and orchestral parts.

**Q: Can I turn the page during a multi-bar rest?**
A: Yes, you can use that time to turn the page, but take care not to lose count of the bars because of it.

**Q: Should I watch the conductor during a rest?**
A: When there is a conductor, watching the conductor's gestures helps you come in accurately.

**Q: Does solo piano music have multi-bar rests?**
A: Rarely. They appear mainly in ensemble and orchestral parts.

minimalism-riley-in-c-1964.body:
In the 1960s, a new style of music appeared in the United States, later known as minimalist music. Its hallmark is the use of very little musical material, with constant repetition and slow change creating a hypnotic effect. In 1964 the composer Terry Riley wrote In C, a work made of just fifty-three short phrases, for any number of players, in which each player decides for themselves how many times to repeat each phrase. It is often seen as one of the early landmark works of minimalist music.

## Links with Other Music

Minimalist music was influenced by many kinds of music, such as the repeating rhythms of Indian music and African drumming.

It also influenced later pop music, electronic music and film scores.

Today you can hear traces of minimalism in the background music of many films and advertisements.

## Playing Phrases from In C on the Piano

You can try playing a few phrases from In C on the piano, repeating each one a few times before moving on to the next.

You can also play with friends, with each person deciding how many times to repeat, and listen to the effect of the layers piling up.

Keep a steady tempo while you play.

## The Power of Repetition

In minimalist music, repetition is not monotony but a way of focusing the mind.

When a pattern repeats again and again, the listener begins to notice subtle changes in it, such as tone colour, dynamics and rhythmic shifts.

This listening experience is very different from traditional classical music.

## Asking Your Teacher to Listen to Repeating Patterns in Lessons

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend minimalist works that suit the piano.

You can also play your own little repeating, changing pattern dozens of times in the lesson and see whether you can keep it steady.

Getting to know this style gives us a broader understanding of music.

## Any Number of Players, Any Instrument

In C does not specify the instruments or the number of players, so any instrument can take part.

Some performances have only a few players, and others have dozens.

This open form has made it a piece that many schools and ensembles love to play.

## Other Minimalist Composers

Besides Riley, important minimalist composers include La Monte Young, Steve Reich and Philip Glass.

Reich's 1967 work Piano Phase has two pianos play the same pattern while one player gradually speeds up, so that the two slip out of phase.

Glass wrote many operas and film scores, and also used minimalist techniques.

## What Is Minimalist Music

Minimalist music is music built from very little material.

It usually uses simple harmony, a steady rhythm and short patterns that repeat again and again.

The music changes very slowly, and the listener gradually notices small differences.

**Common misconceptions**
- It appeared in the United States in the 1960s
- It uses little material, repeated constantly and changed slowly
- In 1964 Riley wrote In C
- In C has fifty-three short phrases, for any number of players

## The "Pulse" on the Piano

In performances of In C, one player on the piano often keeps playing a high C in steady eighth notes.

This sound is called the "pulse". Like a metronome, it keeps everyone at the same tempo.

It is said that this was added during rehearsals for the first performance.

![A colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaaunh2-41cxu.webp)

## Minimalism and In C in Brief

Minimalist music appeared in the United States in the 1960s, using little material that is repeated constantly and changed slowly. In 1964 Riley wrote In C, which has just one page of music and fifty-three short phrases. The players decide for themselves how many times to repeat each phrase, and neither the number of players nor the instruments are fixed. On the piano, a high C is often played continuously in eighth notes as the "pulse".

Other important composers include La Monte Young, Reich and Glass. Reich's 1967 Piano Phase has the patterns of two pianos slowly drift apart. Minimalism was influenced by Indian music and African drumming, and it in turn influenced pop music and film scores.

On the piano you can play phrases from In C and write your own minimalist patterns to practise focus and steadiness, and you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend suitable pieces.

## Slow Change

The changes in minimalist music are often very slow, sometimes one note at a time.

For example, after a pattern has repeated many times, a new note is added, or one is taken away.

This gradual change gives the music a sense of flowing and unfolding.

## Practising Focus and Steadiness

Playing minimalist music takes good concentration and a steady rhythm.

When you repeat the same pattern for a long time, neither tempo nor dynamics can drift.

This is very helpful for practising control.

## The Fifty-Three Phrases of In C

The score of In C is only one page, and on it are fifty-three short phrases.

Some phrases have only one or two notes, and others are a little longer.

All the phrases are arranged in order, and the players go from the first to the last in sequence.

## Players Decide How Many Times to Repeat

What is special about In C is that each player decides for themselves how many times to repeat each phrase.

Because everyone moves forward at a different speed, different phrases pile up on top of one another and form a constantly changing texture.

So every performance sounds different.

## Writing Your Own Minimalist Pattern

Choose four notes such as C, E, G, E, and you have your first minimalist pattern.

Repeat it a few times, then change one note each time and listen to the effect of the slow change.

This exercise helps us feel the relationship between repetition and change.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: When did minimalist music appear?**
A: In the 1960s.

**Q: In which year was In C written?**
A: 1964.

**Q: How many phrases does In C have?**
A: Fifty-three.

**Q: What is the "pulse" on the piano?**
A: A high C played continuously in steady eighth notes.

**Q: What work did Reich write in 1967?**
A: Piano Phase.

metronome-clicks-on-beats-two-and-four.body:
In pop, jazz and many dance styles, beats two and four are often the accented beats, and the drummer's snare mostly falls on these two beats. When practising this kind of music, you can set the metronome to half the original tempo, so that each of its clicks falls on beats two and four, and you feel beats one and three yourself. At first it may feel awkward and you may easily get mixed up, but once you are used to it, your inner rhythm will be steadier and your playing will have more groove.

## Why Beats Two and Four Matter

In classical music, in four-four time the first beat usually carries the most weight and the third beat comes next.

But in pop, rock, jazz and many dance styles, beats two and four are often given special emphasis.

Listen to songs in these styles and you will find that the drummer's snare mostly falls on beats two and four, and that the audience's clapping often lands on these two beats too.

## Practising Swing Rhythm

In jazz there is often a swing rhythm, in which eighth notes are not even, but long then short.

Having the metronome click on beats two and four helps you feel the groove of swing rhythm.

You can first listen to some jazz piano recordings to feel this rhythm, then go to the piano and imitate it.

## Adding Simple Chords

Once you are comfortable counting, you can play a simple chord on the piano, one stroke on each beat.

Make sure the metronome's click lines up exactly with your beats two and four.

If you find the click has drifted onto your beat one or three, stop and start again by counting the beats from the beginning.

## Where It Easily Gets Muddled

When you first start practising, many people unconsciously take the metronome's click for beats one and three.

Then you will find that the accents you play are out of step with the metronome, or you suddenly feel that the metronome is "backwards".

This is completely normal; you can stop first, count "one, two, three, four" again, and then start.

## Not Suitable for All Music

This exercise mainly suits pop, jazz and dance styles.

For a lot of classical music, such as works by Bach or Mozart, the first beat matters more, and this method is not necessarily suitable for practising.

You can choose a suitable way of using the metronome according to the style of the piece.

## Using It on Pieces

After you are comfortable with simple chords, you can apply this method to the pop song or jazz piece you are practising.

Let the metronome fall on beats two and four while you play the complete melody and accompaniment.

You may find that the piece sounds more grooving and no longer so mechanical.

## You Can Also Click Only on Beat One

Besides clicking only on beats two and four, you can also try having the metronome click only on the first beat of each bar.

That way the metronome clicks once every four beats, and you have to keep the rhythm of the three beats in between yourself.

This is another way of training inner rhythm, and suits trying after you have mastered the beats two and four exercise.

**Remember This**
- Pop and jazz often emphasise beats two and four
- Set the metronome to half speed
- Let each click fall on beats two and four
- Feel beats one and three yourself

## Why Practise This Way

When you normally practise with a metronome, it clicks on every beat and you only need to follow it.

If the metronome sounds only on beats two and four, beats one and three have to be counted in your head.

This trains your inner rhythm, so that you can stay steady even without the metronome.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon-lit street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa47984-ydb2d.webp)

## Halve the Metronome Tempo

Suppose you want to practise at one hundred beats per minute; then set the metronome to fifty beats per minute.

The metronome then clicks only once every two beats, and you have to make each click fall on beats two and four.

In other words, when you count "one, two, three, four", the metronome clicks on "two" and "four".

## Start Slowly

As with other rhythm exercises, this one should start slowly.

You can first set the metronome to around forty beats per minute, which corresponds to music at eighty beats per minute.

When you can hold it steadily at this tempo, gradually speed up.

## Practising with a Partner

If a friend is also learning music, you can do this exercise together.

One person claps on beats two and four while the other plays the piano, and then you swap.

This kind of practice is more fun, and it also lets you feel the rhythmic coordination of playing together.

## Count First, Then Play

At the beginning, do not rush to play at the piano; first count the beats along with the metronome.

You can count "one, two, three, four" out loud, letting the metronome's click fall on "two" and "four".

Once your counting is steady, try clapping on "one" and "three" and listening to the metronome on "two" and "four".

## The Two-and-Four Metronome in Brief

In pop, jazz and dance styles, having the metronome click only on beats two and four is a good way to train inner rhythm and a sense of groove.

Set the metronome to half speed, count first and then play, start slowly, and if you get mixed up, count again from the start.

Once you are comfortable, your rhythm will be steadier and your playing will have more groove.

## FAQ

**Q: Why have the metronome click only on beats two and four?**
A: It trains inner rhythm, and suits pop and jazz styles.

**Q: How should I set the metronome tempo?**
A: Set it to half the original tempo.

**Q: What should I do if I get mixed up?**
A: Stop and count "one, two, three, four" again.

**Q: Is this a good way to practise classical music?**
A: Not necessarily; in many classical works the first beat is more important.

**Q: Is there any other similar way of practising?**
A: You can have the metronome click only on the first beat of each bar.

meno-mosso-piu-mosso-tempo-terms.body:
In scores you often see two Italian terms: meno mosso and più mosso. Mosso means "moved", meno means "less" and più means "more". So meno mosso means "less movement", that is, a little slower, while più mosso means "more movement", that is, a little faster. They usually appear where a new section begins and show that the tempo changes from that point, rather than gradually. Knowing these two terms helps us handle tempo changes in a piece accurately.

## Draw an Arrow Next to meno mosso

If you tend to forget tempo changes, you can make a small pencil mark on the score.

**Slower**

For example, draw a downward arrow next to meno mosso and an upward arrow next to più mosso.

Make the arrow stand out, so your eye catches it first when you turn to the page.

## meno mosso and più mosso in Brief

Mosso means "moved", meno is "less" and più is "more", so meno mosso is a little slower and più mosso is a little faster. They usually appear at the start of a new section and mean the tempo changes directly, unlike a ritardando or accelerando.

Afterwards, tempo primo or a tempo is often used to return to the original tempo, and adding poco makes the change more subtle. They are often used in Romantic works to create contrast between sections.

To decide the new tempo, consider the preceding tempo and the character of the new section. You can try it with a metronome, then keep it steady once you have changed. You can draw arrows on the score, and Teacher Aum can help you settle the exact tempo.

## meno and più

Meno means "less" and più means "more".

These two words are very common in musical terms. For example, meno forte means "a little softer" and più forte means "a little louder".

Used together with mosso, they indicate a change of tempo.

## Returning to the Original Tempo

After a meno mosso or più mosso section, the score often says tempo primo or a tempo.

Tempo primo means "return to the first tempo", and a tempo means "return to the original tempo".

Watch for these markings when you play, and return to the original tempo in good time.

## Keeping the New Tempo Steady

Once you have moved to the new tempo, keep it steady throughout the section.

Do not speed up or slow down as you go, unless the score has a marking for a gradual change.

In practice, a metronome can help you stay steady.

## How to Decide the New Tempo

To decide the exact tempo of a meno mosso or più mosso, first find the preceding tempo, then think about the character of the new section.

If the new section is lyrical, you can go a little slower; if it is excited, you can go a little faster.

You can also try a few tempi with a metronome and find the one that fits.

## Listening Practice for meno mosso and più mosso

Find recordings of a few pieces that change tempo in the middle, and when the new section begins, decide whether it has become slower or faster.

Then open the score and check whether it says meno mosso or più mosso there, and whether it matches your judgement.

This kind of practice makes your ear more sensitive to tempo changes, and makes it easier to judge the right amount when you play.

![Sketch of a golden grand piano on a cream background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab40hx-iphif.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Settle the New Tempo in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to help you decide how fast a meno mosso or più mosso section should go.

Your teacher can also help you practise the join between tempo changes so that it sounds natural.

Handling the tempo accurately makes the structure of the piece clearer.

## Where meno mosso and più mosso Often Appear

These two terms often appear where a new section of a piece begins.

For example, a lyrical melody in the middle of a fast piece may be marked meno mosso.

When calm music turns into an excited section, it may be marked più mosso.

- mosso: moved
- meno mosso: a little slower
- più mosso: a little faster
- The tempo changes from here, not gradually

## meno mosso: A Little Slower

Meno mosso means "less movement", that is, a little slower than before.

It is not very slow, only a little slower than the previous tempo.

Exactly how much slower depends on the character of the music and the tempi before and after.

## A Sudden Change, Not a Gradual One

Meno mosso and più mosso usually mean that the tempo changes directly from this point.

This is different from rallentando (gradually slowing) or accelerando (gradually speeding up), which change little by little.

So when you see meno mosso, switch to the new tempo in that very bar.

## A Related Term: poco

Sometimes you will see poco meno mosso or poco più mosso.

Poco means "a little", so poco meno mosso means "slightly, just a little slower".

Such a change is more subtle and needs to be handled with more care.

## più mosso: A Little Faster

Più mosso means "more movement", that is, a little faster than before.

Likewise, it is only a little faster than the original tempo, not suddenly very fast.

It is often used in sections where the music becomes excited or tense.

## In the Works of Chopin and Liszt

You often find meno mosso and più mosso in Romantic works.

In many nocturnes and ballades, for example, the middle section often changes tempo to create contrast.

When playing these works, tempo changes are an important means of expressing emotion.

## The Word mosso

Mosso is Italian and means "moved" or "lively".

It is often used with other words to indicate tempo or character.

**Tip**

For example, allegro molto mosso means "very fast and very lively".

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does mosso mean?**
A: Moved, lively.

**Q: What does meno mosso mean?**
A: A little slower.

**Q: What does più mosso mean?**
A: A little faster.

**Q: How are they different from ritardando and accelerando?**
A: They change the tempo directly, not gradually.

**Q: What does tempo primo mean?**
A: Return to the first tempo.

mendelssohn-rondo-capriccioso-op14.body:
Rondo Capriccioso, Op. 14, is by the German composer Felix Mendelssohn and is one of the best-known piano works of his youth, written and revised between about 1828 and 1830. The piece falls into two parts: it opens with an Andante in E major, like a quiet song without words, then moves into a Presto in E minor, where light staccato notes race along like sprites in the night and recall the overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream that he wrote as a teenager. Many intermediate players like to take on this piece, because it trains the fingers to be light, quick and clear.

## The Young Mendelssohn

Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847) was born in Hamburg and grew up in Berlin.

He showed astonishing musical gifts from childhood, and in his teens he wrote a mature String Octet and the overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream.

Rondo Capriccioso was also written when he was around twenty, and it is full of youthful sparkle.

## How Difficult Is Rondo Capriccioso?

This piece is usually considered intermediate to upper-intermediate.

The introduction is fairly easy, while the presto asks a lot of the fingers in speed and lightness.

If you cannot play the presto fast at first, drop the tempo to half speed and make every note clear before you do anything else.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen to Your Staccato in the Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your presto and tell you whether the staccato is short and light.

If certain bars are never quite steady, you can also ask your teacher to help you find fingering that suits your hand.

Through this piece, you can feel the singing quality and the sparkle in Mendelssohn's music.

## Into the E Minor Presto

When the introduction ends, the music suddenly turns to E minor and the tempo becomes presto.

The right hand plays a stream of light staccato notes and quick figures, while the left hand accompanies with short chords.

The whole passage sounds like little sprites racing across the grass at night, airy and a touch mysterious.

## The Name Rondo Capriccioso

"Rondo" refers to rondo form: one theme keeps coming back, with other sections placed in between.

"Capriccioso" means rather free, with a flavour of improvisation.

Put together, it is a piece with the skeleton of a rondo, but written in a very free and lively way.

## A Brilliant Ending

At the end of the piece, the music grows more and more excited and the dynamics build.

Both hands play fast octaves and chords, and the piece ends in a powerful climax.

The change from lightness to brilliance needs shaping, so do not play too loudly right from the start.

## Rondo Capriccioso in Brief

Rondo Capriccioso, Op. 14, was written by Mendelssohn (1809-1847) in his early twenties, composed and revised between about 1828 and 1830. Its name points to a rondo skeleton with a free way of writing. It opens with an Andante in E major that sings like a song without words, then moves to a Presto in E minor, whose light staccato is written in the same way as the "sprite music" of the overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream. It ends in a climax of octaves and chords.

Staccato should be short, light and clear, and fast figures should be even; you can practise them in different rhythms. The introduction is fairly easy, the presto demands speed and lightness, and practising slowly matters more than practising fast. Afterwards you can play a few Songs Without Words.

You can ask Teacher Aum to look at your staccato and fingering.

## Staccato in Rondo Capriccioso

The presto has many staccato notes, which should be short, light and clear.

Staccato does not mean hitting the key hard; the finger quickly touches the key and then leaves it.

Keep the wrist relaxed and let the fingers act like little springs: the lighter you play, the better you bring out the sprite-like feeling.

## The Sprites of A Midsummer Night's Dream

At the age of seventeen, Mendelssohn wrote the overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream, which also contains light "sprite music".

The presto of Rondo Capriccioso uses the same light, fast, quiet style of writing.

This style was later often called "Mendelssohn's scherzo".

## Slow Practice Matters More Than Fast Practice

Many people rush to play this piece fast, and the notes end up blurred together.

A better way is to practise slowly for a long time, and speed up gradually once the fingers know every figure.

Speed is the result of practice, not a goal to chase from the start.

- Composed by Mendelssohn, opus number Op. 14
- Written and revised between about 1828 and 1830
- An Andante introduction in E major plus a Presto in E minor
- Light staccato like racing sprites

## First, a Song Without Words

The piece begins with an Andante in E major, and the right hand sings a gentle, connected melody.

The left hand supports it softly with broken chords, much like the Songs Without Words Mendelssohn wrote later.

This introduction is not long, but it should be played as if singing, and every phrase needs to breathe.

## Keep Fast Figures Even

The presto has many fast sixteenth notes, and every note should be even and clear.

First slow the presto down to a tempo where you can play cleanly, then raise the metronome just a little each day.

You can also practise in different rhythms, for example long-short-long-short first, then short-long-short-long, so that every finger gets worked.

## Mendelssohn and the Songs Without Words

Over his lifetime Mendelssohn wrote eight books of Songs Without Words, six pieces in each, among the best-loved collections of short pieces in piano history.

The Andante at the start of Rondo Capriccioso can be seen as an early form of this style.

**Common mistake**

After playing Rondo Capriccioso, try a few Songs Without Words, and you will understand Mendelssohn's singing melodies better.

![A person in futuristic clothing plays a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbhw93s-ngl6c.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What is the opus number of Rondo Capriccioso?**
A: Op. 14.

**Q: When was it written?**
A: It was written and revised between 1828 and 1830.

**Q: What key does the piece begin in?**
A: An Andante in E major.

**Q: What key is the presto section in?**
A: E minor.

**Q: Which Mendelssohn work does the style of the presto recall?**
A: The overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream.

mendelssohn-songs-without-words-singing.body:
When you play Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, the heart of it is making the piano "sing like a human voice": the melody should be connected, should breathe, should stand out above the accompaniment, and its phrases should rise and fall. The difficulty is that in many pieces the melody and accompaniment are squeezed into the same hand, so the outer fingers of the right hand must sing while the inner fingers quietly play a supporting role. The solution can be summed up in three steps: first sing the melody to find its natural shape; then practise "two dynamics in one hand"; finally use finger changes and legato technique to link the long phrases. Here they are in detail, in that order.

## Key Points

- Songs Without Words is a collection of piano pieces Mendelssohn wrote over the years, in eight books with forty-eight pieces in all
- "Without words" means the melody has to carry the expression of the lyrics, and be played as naturally as singing
- A common challenge is having both melody and accompaniment in the same hand, so you need to separate the main voice from the support
- Order of practice: sing the melody, separate the voices, put them together, link the long phrases
- Slow down first, so your ear can clearly hear the melody on "top"

## What Are Songs Without Words?

Mendelssohn lived in the first half of the nineteenth century and was one of the important composers of the Romantic period. These short piano pieces are not complicated in structure, but they care a great deal about the singing quality of the melody, so they are often used as teaching material for cantabile playing. Many of the pieces carry titles added later, such as Spring Song and Venetian Gondola Song. These titles help us imagine a picture, but when playing, the line of the melody itself matters more.

For people learning piano, the value of these works is this: the technical demands are moderate, yet they let you concentrate on voice balance, legato and phrase breathing, skills you will use in many musical situations later on.

## One Hand, Two Roles

**The outer fingers carry the melody**
In many Songs Without Words the melody falls on the fourth and fifth fingers of the right hand, and these two fingers are naturally weaker. When playing the melody notes, let the weight of the hand lean slightly to the outside, keep the fingers close to the keys and put them down a little faster, so the sound is rounder and fuller.

**The inner fingers play the supporting role**
The accompaniment notes in the same hand are usually played by the thumb and second finger. They should be lighter and a little shorter, like quietly echoing behind the melody. You can first practise these accompaniment notes alone, extremely softly, so that they almost "disappear".

**The left hand provides the foundation**
The bass notes and broken chords in the left hand should be as steady and soft as the low voices in a choir. The bass note can go a little deeper, and the chord notes after it should be lighter.


![Art Deco style illustration: someone sits playing a deep red upright piano under a table lamp](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvltc16-q1wso.webp)


## Step One: Sing First, Then Play

Do not rush to the piano. First sing the whole melody a few times, even if only softly under your breath. While singing, pay attention to three things:

- Wherever you naturally want to breathe, draw a small comma on the score
- Wherever you want to sing a note brighter, draw a small arc above it
- Wherever you want to fade gradually, draw a decrescendo hairpin

After singing, play, and let your fingers imitate what your voice just did. You will find that a melody that used to "pop out" note by note begins to have a sense of direction. This "sing first, play after" method is widely used in music teaching, because the human voice naturally knows how to express a phrase in one connected line.

## Step Two: Take the Voices Apart, Then Put Them Together

- Play only the melody notes with the right hand, leaving out the others, and practise until it is connected and shaped
- Play only the accompaniment notes with the right hand, very softly, with an even rhythm
- Put the right hand together, keeping the melody at the dynamic you just had and the accompaniment as soft as before
- Add the left hand, slowly at first, with your ear always following the melody

If the melody gets "drowned" once everything is together, go back to the previous step and play the accompaniment even more softly. Often the problem is not that the melody is too quiet, but that the accompaniment is too loud.

## Step Three: Link Long Phrases with Finger Changes

Once a piano note is played it gradually fades, unlike a human voice, which can sustain. To keep long notes and long phrases as connected as possible, you can use two techniques:

**Changing fingers on the same note**
While holding down a note, quietly swap in another finger to take over, freeing the hand to play the next note. This is especially useful when the melody needs to be legato and your hand does not have enough fingers.

**Let the next note catch the tail of the previous one**
The note after a long note should be a little softer than, or about the same as, the volume the long note has faded to. That way it sounds like one continuous breath, rather than suddenly "jumping out".

The pedal can also help with connection, but it should not replace finger legato. Practise connecting with your fingers first, then add the pedal, and the sound will be cleaner.

## FAQ

**Q: What level of learner are Songs Without Words suitable for?**

A: The difficulty varies from piece to piece. Some suit learners with a few years of experience, and others need more mature technique. You can ask your teacher to choose according to your progress, or refer to the repertoire suggestions in a piano study course.

**Q: My fourth and fifth fingers are weak and I cannot bring out the melody. What should I do?**

A: Do not aim for loudness at first. Aim instead for "a slightly faster key descent and a little more hand weight over to that side". Playing a few long notes with the fifth finger alone each day and listening for roundness is more effective than pressing hard.

**Q: Can I use "sing first, play after" if I cannot sing?**

A: Yes. You do not need to sing in tune or sing well; just hum the rise and fall of the melody and the places to breathe, so that you can feel the shape of the phrase.

**Q: How can I check voice balance when learning piano online?**

A: Recording yourself and listening back is the most direct method. You can listen to the melody alone and ask yourself: is every melody note clear? Is the accompaniment covering it? If you build the habit of listening back while learning music, your progress will be more noticeable.

minimalist-music-repetition-listening.body:
Minimalist music emerged in the mid-twentieth century. Its core idea is to take very little material, such as a short pattern, a few chords or a steady rhythm, repeat it for a long time, and let one element change slowly. A first-time listener may feel that it is "just repeating", but if you listen patiently, you will find that the layers, accents and colours of the sound are quietly shifting. The name "minimalism" was borrowed from the visual arts, and it stresses simple structure so that listeners can focus on the process itself.

## What Are the Features of Minimalist Music

- **Steady pulse**: there is often a continuous rhythm that drives the music forward like a pendulum.
- **Short patterns**: the melodic material is often just a few notes, which makes it easy to repeat.
- **Slow change**: each time only a little changes, such as adding a note, changing a chord or moving an accent.
- **Clear harmony**: the harmony is often fairly simple, sometimes staying on the same chord for a long time.
- **The process is the content**: the way the music changes is itself what the piece sets out to show.

## Some Common Techniques

**Additive process**
Start from a very short pattern and add a note every few repetitions, so the pattern grows longer bit by bit. It can also work the other way round, gradually removing notes. The listener can clearly feel something "growing".

**Phasing**
Two voices play the same pattern, with one slightly faster or slower. The two lines gradually drift apart, creating new rhythmic combinations, and after a while they line up again. This technique is often called phase shifting.

**Layering**
Different instruments or voices come in one after another, each repeating its own short phrase, and together they form a rich texture. Take one layer away and the colour of the whole changes.

**Long notes and drones**
Some works use a very long sustained note as a background, over which the changes are extremely slow, so it sounds like a slowly changing landscape of sound.

## How to Listen Without Finding It Monotonous

Minimalist music asks for a slightly different way of listening. Rather than expecting melodic ups and downs and dramatic conflict, treat your ears as a magnifying glass and look for tiny changes.

- **Pick one voice and follow it**: for example, listen only to the bass, or only to the highest line, and notice when it changes.
- **Count the repetitions**: there is no need to be exact. It simply helps you stay attentive while waiting for the change to appear.
- **Notice the overall colour**: sometimes no single note has changed, but a new voice coming in makes the whole sound brighter or darker.
- **Give yourself a full stretch of time**: this kind of music often needs a long time to unfold, and if you listen in fragments, it is hard to feel the process.

![A piano and its keys in the light by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwcl2j2t-w0fmy.webp)

## A Small Experiment on the Piano

You do not need a complicated score to experience the minimalist way of thinking on the piano. The exercise below is for reference only:

**Step 1: Set a pattern**
With your right hand, choose four or five neighbouring white keys and arrange them into a simple loop, for example going up and then down, and repeat it at a steady tempo.

**Step 2: Add a bass note**
With your left hand, play just one low note, once per bar, and keep it unchanged.

**Step 3: Change only one thing at a time**
After every eight repetitions, change one note in the right-hand pattern, or move the accent to another position. Take care to change only one thing each time.

**Step 4: Record it and listen**
Record the whole process and play it back. You will find that when you are no longer busy playing, it is easier to hear those small changes.

This exercise also trains a steady sense of rhythm and long-lasting concentration, because the more repetitions there are, the more it tests whether your tempo stays even.

## The Influence of Minimalism on Music Today

Minimalist techniques were later absorbed in many fields. Film and game scores often use repeating patterns to create lasting tension or anticipation. In electronic dance music, looping rhythms and gradually added layers share the same way of thinking. Many contemporary piano works also use repeating patterns with slow change, so that both the player and the listener can be immersed in a steady groove.

**Links with music technology**
Loop recording, sequencers and digital audio workstations make "repetition with change" much easier to achieve. AI composition tools also often borrow similar patterns when generating looping patterns and gradually changing structures. When learners repeat a pattern in an AI piano learning app such as TIGA ALPHA, they are in fact going through a small "process" of their own: the same few notes get steadier the more you practise and clearer the more you listen.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Is minimalist music just simple music?**
A: The material is simple, but the playing is very demanding. It is not easy to keep a steady rhythm and accurate changes over a long time.

**Q: Why do some people find it relaxing and others find it boring?**
A: How it feels varies from person to person and depends on how you listen and what you expect. You can try focusing on the tiny changes.

**Q: Can beginners play pieces in a minimalist style?**
A: Some works have simple patterns and suit beginners practising a steady rhythm, but many others demand a lot of stamina and concentration.

**Q: What is the difference between minimalism and loop-based music?**
A: Both use repetition, but minimalism puts more emphasis on planned slow change, while looping is only a means.
