mental-practice-without-piano.body:
Even when you are away from the piano, you can do mental practice: look at the score, imagine yourself playing, hear the sound in your head, and feel the movement of your fingers and the fingering. This kind of practice can be done while commuting, waiting or travelling, and it can deepen your memory of a piece and clarify its structure and difficulties. It cannot completely replace practice at the piano, but it can be a very useful supplement.

## Start with Short Passages

When you first start mental practice, you may find it hard to concentrate, or you may run out of steam very quickly.

**A common mistake**

You can start with a short passage, such as a phrase or two of melody, and then slowly make it longer as you get comfortable.

Each session does not need to be long either; a few minutes is enough.

**Slow down**
- Look at the score and imagine the process of playing
- Hear the sound and rhythm in your head
- Imagine the movement of your fingers and the fingering
- Suitable for times such as commuting and waiting

## Practising Without the Score

Once you are familiar with it, you can try recalling the piece in your head without looking at the score.

If you get stuck somewhere, it means your memory there is not yet secure, so you can open the score, take a look and then continue.

This kind of practice is especially helpful for memorising, and it can make you feel more confident in performance.

## What Is Mental Practice

Mental practice means not actually playing the piano, but "playing" the piece through in your head.

You can look at the score or not, imagining your hands on the keys and playing note by note according to the music.

At the same time, you hear those notes in your head, feeling the speed of the rhythm and the changes in dynamics.

## Children Can Try It Too

Children can begin in simple ways, such as singing the piece they have just learned in their head, or "playing" it with their fingers on a table.

Parents can play this game with their children, asking: "Can you play the whole piece in your head?"

For young children there is no need to ask for too much; being able to imagine the melody is already very good.

## Combining It with Practice at the Piano

Mental practice is a supplement and cannot completely replace practice at the piano.

Before practising at the piano, you can first go through the passage you are about to practise in your head, so that your practice is better prepared.

You can also, after practising, recall in your head what you have just practised, which helps consolidate it.

![Sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angle, in tan tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9y1l8o-w5dta.webp)

## Suitable Times and Places

Mental practice does not need a piano, and it can be done in many places, such as on a bus, in a queue or while waiting for someone.

Even if you only have a few minutes, you can go through a passage in your head, or think about the fingering of a difficult spot.

Mind your safety: do not do this kind of practice, which needs concentration, while walking or driving.

## Imagining the Finger Movements

In mental practice, you do not only hear the sound, you can also imagine the movements of your fingers.

For example, imagine which finger you use for which note, when you change fingers, and how the whole hand moves to a new position.

Some people gently move their fingers on their lap or on a table to help them feel the fingering.

If you cannot picture the fingering clearly in your head somewhere, you can write the fingering on the score and check it again when you are back at the piano.

## Practising with the Score

At the beginning, you can do mental practice while looking at the score.

As you look at the music, hear the sound in your head and imagine the movement of your fingers on the keys.

When you come to a place that is unclear, you can stop and look closely, remember the spot, and pay particular attention to it the next time you practise at the piano.

## Practice Everywhere

Once you have learned mental practice, practising is no longer limited to the time you spend sitting at the piano.

On busy days, it lets you keep in touch with the piece, so that it does not become completely rusty for lack of time to practise.

Little by little, you will become more and more familiar with the piece, and your practice at the piano will become more efficient too.

## Why This Kind of Practice Helps

When you practise in your head, you need to know every note and every fingering clearly, which helps you discover which places you are not actually familiar with.

It can also help you understand the structure of the piece more clearly, for example where there is repetition and where there is change.

For pieces you need to memorise, mental practice can help deepen your memory.

Many people only discover through mental practice that there are passages they can play at the piano but cannot say what each note is, and that is exactly where work is needed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can mental practice replace playing the piano?**
A: Not completely, but it can be a useful supplement.

**Q: Do I need to look at the score?**
A: You can look at it at the start, and once you are familiar you can try without.

**Q: When is a good time to practise?**
A: Commuting, waiting and other times when you are sitting quietly.

**Q: What should I do if I get stuck?**
A: Open the score, look at it, remember the spot, and focus on it next time.

**Q: Can children do mental practice?**
A: Yes, they can start by singing the melody in their head and gradually try more.

**Q: How long should each session be?**
A: A few minutes is enough, and you can do it at any time.

mendelssohn-st-matthew-passion-revival-1.body:
On 11 March 1829, the twenty-year-old Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St Matthew Passion in Berlin. After Bach's death in 1750, the work had hardly been performed complete at all. Mendelssohn had come across the score as a teenager, and after careful preparation and some cuts he gave a successful performance at the Berlin Singakademie, then repeated it on 21 March, Bach's birthday. This performance is often seen as an important starting point for the nineteenth-century revival of interest in Bach's music.

## What the Story Tells Us About the Value of Scores

Without a surviving score, Mendelssohn could never have brought this work back to the stage.

**Before you begin**

A score is a record of the music, allowing later generations to play and understand the works of those who came before.

The scores that piano learners read every day carry this same kind of inheritance.

## The Starting Point of the Bach Revival

This performance is often seen as an important starting point for the nineteenth-century revival of interest in Bach's music.

After it, more and more musicians began to study, publish and perform Bach's works.

By the middle of the nineteenth century, a society had even been founded to collect and publish all of Bach's works.

## The Young Mendelssohn and the Score

Mendelssohn was born in 1809 and received an excellent musical education from an early age.

According to the records, as a teenager he was given a handwritten copy of the St Matthew Passion and was deeply drawn to it.

His teacher Zelter was also very familiar with Bach's music, which gave Mendelssohn the chance to study the work in depth.

## Careful Preparation

Staging a large work like this requires a choir, soloists and an orchestra, as well as a great deal of rehearsal.

Mendelssohn and his friends spent a long time preparing, making some cuts to suit the audiences of the day.

After several months of rehearsals, the performance finally took place in the spring of 1829.

## Mendelssohn's Own Music

Mendelssohn was not only a conductor but also an outstanding pianist and composer.

His piano works, such as the Songs Without Words, are still favourites with many piano learners today.

In his music you can also hear how well he knew and loved Bach's counterpoint.

## Bach's Keyboard Works

As interest in Bach's music was renewed, more and more people began to play and study his keyboard works.

The Well-Tempered Clavier, the various suites and the inventions later became important repertoire for piano learners.

When we play Bach on the piano today, we benefit in some measure from the rediscovery of that era.

## Listening to the St Matthew Passion

The St Matthew Passion is very long, and a complete performance takes nearly three hours.

You can begin by listening to a few of the choruses or arias and gradually get to know the work.

As you listen, notice how Bach uses music to express the emotion of the words, which also helps in understanding his keyboard works.

## The Courage of a Young Musician

To organise and conduct such a large work at twenty took great courage and enthusiasm.

Mendelssohn believed the work deserved to be heard by more people, and he put enormous effort into making it happen.

The story also shows us that a love of music can make important things happen.

## The 1829 Performance in Brief

On 11 March 1829, the twenty-year-old Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St Matthew Passion in Berlin, and performed it again on 21 March, Bach's birthday.

The work had hardly been performed complete since Bach's death in 1750, and this performance is often seen as an important starting point for renewed interest in Bach's music.

After that, Bach's works, including his keyboard works, were studied and played more and more.

- Performed in Berlin on 11 March 1829
- Mendelssohn was twenty and conducted
- Hardly performed complete since Bach's death
- Often seen as the starting point of renewed interest in Bach's music

## Cuts and the Original Version

Mendelssohn's performance made cuts to the work, so it was not the complete original.

Today's performances mostly try to follow Bach's original score as closely as possible.

This shows that the way people understand and perform music keeps changing with the times.

![Cartoon-style student wearing headphones sitting at a piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa53hnx-8qzjj.webp)

## The Berlin Premiere of the St Matthew Passion

On 11 March 1829, the performance took place at the Berlin Singakademie, conducted by Mendelssohn, who was only twenty at the time.

According to the records, tickets sold out quickly and many well-known figures came to listen.

The performance was a great success and let many people feel the power of the work for the first time.

## A Second Performance on Bach's Birthday

After the successful first night, another performance followed on 21 March, which happened to be Bach's birthday.

After that, other cities also began to perform the work.

The St Matthew Passion had returned to the concert stage.

## The Forgotten Passion

The St Matthew Passion is a large-scale vocal work Bach wrote for the Good Friday service before Easter, first performed in Leipzig around 1727.

After Bach's death in 1750, many of his large works gradually became rarely performed, and the St Matthew Passion was hardly ever given complete.

By the early nineteenth century, most listeners no longer knew the work.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: On what day was the performance?**
A: 11 March 1829, in Berlin.

**Q: How old was Mendelssohn at the time?**
A: Twenty.

**Q: Why is it called a revival?**
A: Because the work had hardly been performed complete since Bach's death in 1750.

**Q: On what day was the second performance?**
A: 21 March, Bach's birthday.

**Q: What is the significance of this performance?**
A: It is often seen as an important starting point for renewed interest in Bach's music.

nashville-number-system-chord-charts.body:
In the recording studios of Nashville, Tennessee, from the late 1950s onwards, some session musicians developed a way of writing chords as numbers, later known as the Nashville Number System. Instead of chord names such as C, F and G, it uses the numbers 1 to 7 to show each chord's degree in the key. In C major, for example, C is 1, F is 4 and G is 5. A chart written this way can be played straight away, whatever key the singer suddenly decides to move to, with no need to rewrite it. Today the method is still used by many bands and in many studios.

## Showing Rhythm

In the Nashville Number System, one number usually stands for one bar.

**Common misconception**

If a bar contains two chords, the two numbers are written together with a line drawn beneath them, or marked in some other way.

There are also symbols for pauses, held notes and special rhythms, and these may differ slightly from one studio to another.

## Common Number Progressions

The chord progressions of many pop songs come out the same when written as numbers.

For example 1, 5, 6-, 4, or 1, 6-, 4, 5, or 2-, 5, 1.

Remember these number progressions and you can play a large number of songs in any key.

- Developed in the late 1950s among recording musicians in Nashville
- Uses the numbers 1 to 7 for chord degrees
- In C major, C is 1, F is 4 and G is 5
- No need to rewrite the chart when you change key

## Why Use Numbers

In the studio, singers often ask to change key on the spot, depending on how their voice is that day.

If the chart is written as C, F, G, moving to D major means rewriting it as D, G, A, which is a hassle.

With a chart written in numbers, you only need to know the new key. The numbers stay the same.

## Slash Chords and Bass Notes

The Nashville Number System can also show slash chords. For example, 1/3 means the tonic chord with the third degree in the bass.

In C major, 1/3 is C/E.

This is written just like an ordinary slash chord, only with numbers in place of letters.

## Writing Songs in a Minor Key

Songs in a minor key are written in different ways in the Nashville Number System.

Some musicians write the minor tonic chord as 1-, while others write it as 6- of the relative major.

Which method to use is something the band members need to agree on beforehand.

## Training Your Sense of Chords in a Key

Thinking of chords as numbers helps us find them quickly in any key.

Each day, you can choose a key, play the chords from 1 to 7 on the piano in turn, and say their numbers aloud.

This kind of practice deepens your understanding of how keys and chords relate.

## Asking Your Teacher to Practise Number Charts in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to help rewrite a song you are learning as a number chart.

Your teacher can also help you practise playing the same string of numbers in different keys, improving your ability to transpose.

This method is very useful for playing pop songs and accompaniments.

## The Number System and Listening

Once you are familiar with the number system, you can also try identifying chords by number when you listen to songs.

For example, if you hear that a song's chords are 1, 4, 5, you can play it in any key.

This is a great help for working songs out by ear, accompanying and improvising.

![Sketch of an upright piano keyboard from an angled view, in brown tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabaamz-qocqp.webp)

## Marking Minor Chords and Seventh Chords

If you want to write a chord that differs from the default in the key, you need to add a mark.

For example, a minus sign after the number means a minor chord, so 6- is the minor chord on the sixth degree.

Adding 7 means a seventh chord, so 57 is a dominant seventh chord.

## Comparison with Roman Numeral Analysis

The Nashville Number System is very similar to Roman numeral harmonic analysis in classical music.

Roman numerals also show chords by degree, such as I, IV and V, using capital and lowercase letters to tell major and minor chords apart.

But the Nashville Number System is simpler and more practical, designed for playing quickly.

## Numbers Instead of Chord Names

The core idea of the Nashville Number System is to use numbers to show a chord's position in the key.

The tonic chord of the key is 1, the chord on the fourth degree is 4, the chord on the fifth degree is 5, and so on.

In this way, a song's chord progression becomes a string of numbers, such as 1, 4, 5, 1.

## Chords in a Major Key

In a major key, 1, 4 and 5 are major triads, 2, 3 and 6 are minor triads, and 7 is a diminished triad.

In C major, for example, 1 is C, 2 is Dm, 3 is Em, 4 is F, 5 is G, 6 is Am and 7 is B diminished.

Unless there is a special mark, a number usually means the chord that occurs naturally in the key.

## Nashville Number System Summary

The Nashville Number System was developed in the late 1950s among recording musicians in Nashville. It uses 1 to 7 for chord degrees in the key: in C major, C is 1, F is 4 and G is 5, and when a singer changes key on the spot, the chart does not need rewriting.

In a major key, 1, 4 and 5 are major triads by default, 2, 3 and 6 are minor triads, and 7 is a diminished triad. A minus sign marks a minor chord, adding 7 marks a seventh chord, and slash chords such as 1/3 can be written. One number usually stands for one bar. Minor-key songs have two ways of writing, 1- and 6-, so you need to agree on one. It is similar to Roman numeral harmonic analysis but simpler and more practical.

You can write a familiar song as numbers and play it in different keys, remember common progressions such as 1, 5, 6-, 4, play the chords from 1 to 7 in one key each day, and ask Teacher Aum to help you practise number charts.

## Playing Songs with Numbers on the Piano

Pick a familiar song and first write its chords as numbers, for example 1, 5, 6-, 4.

Then play it once in C major, in G major and in F major, and feel how the numbers correspond to the different keys.

When you are comfortable, try quickly playing the string of numbers in any key.

## FAQ

**Q: What does the Nashville Number System use to show chords?**
A: The numbers 1 to 7 show the degrees.

**Q: What chord is 5 in C major?**
A: G.

**Q: What is its biggest advantage?**
A: You do not need to rewrite the chart when you change key.

**Q: What does 6- mean?**
A: The minor chord on the sixth degree.

**Q: Which classical method of analysis is it similar to?**
A: Roman numeral harmonic analysis.

music-course-feedback-survey-loop.body:
Improving a music course often relies on the teacher's instinct: the child seemed a little bored in this lesson, everyone seemed to love that piece. Instinct has value, but it is easily swayed by individual impressions. A well-designed student survey helps music studios and online courses understand more systematically how students and parents feel: which content helps, which arrangements are inconvenient, and why some people are thinking of stopping lessons. More importantly, collecting feedback is only the beginning. The real value lies in making changes based on it and telling everyone about those changes. This back-and-forth forms a feedback loop, so that with each adjustment the course moves closer to what students need.

## Principles of Survey Design

- Short: five to eight questions that take just a few minutes to complete
- Specific: ask "Which part helped you most?" rather than "Are you satisfied?"
- Mixed question types: rating questions are easy to tally, while open questions capture real thoughts
- An anonymous option: people are more willing to say what they are unhappy about
- No unnecessary personal information

## What to Ask

**About the content**
Is the difficulty of the course content right? Which part has helped you most? Is there anything you would like to learn but have not yet covered?

**About scheduling**
Is the lesson time convenient? Is the amount of practice between lessons right?

**About communication**
Is it clear what your child needs to practise each week? Is the teacher's feedback easy to understand?

**Open question**
If you could change one thing about the course, what would it be?

![A dark ink-style grand piano with its lid open against a grey-white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw16afhf-cadko.webp)

## Choosing the Right Time to Send It

The timing of a survey affects the quality of the answers. Sending it in the middle of a term lets you adjust a course that is still under way, while sending it at the end of a term suits an overall review. Avoid the tense period before an assessment or performance, and do not put it in the same message as a payment notice, or people may feel the survey is just for show. For students who have stopped lessons, you can gently invite them to answer one or two questions about why they left. This information is often especially valuable.

## How to Analyse the Answers

Rating questions can be averaged and compared with the previous round. Open questions need to be read one by one, with similar opinions grouped together, for example "I would like to learn more pop songs" or "the practice reminders feel too frequent". Once grouped, pick out the few items that come up most often and are realistic to change, and make them the improvement priorities for the next stage. There is no need to try to satisfy every comment at once, nor to throw out the whole course because of a few negative remarks.

## Telling Everyone What You Did

The step most often forgotten in a feedback loop is telling students "we heard you, and here is what we did". In the next notice you can say simply: based on your comments, we have added a pop song unit and changed practice reminders to once a week. Even when some suggestions cannot be put into practice for now, you can explain why. When students and parents see that their opinions have really brought about change, they will take the next survey more seriously, and their trust in the course will deepen.

## The Full Rhythm of One Loop

A complete feedback loop can be arranged like this: send the survey in the middle of the term and collect answers within a week; spend the following week sorting and discussing them and settling on two or three improvements; use another week to put them into practice and say in a notice what has changed; then, at the end of the term, use a few short questions to check whether those improvements worked. With this rhythm, you can complete at least one loop every term. The teaching team can record each conclusion in a shared document, so that new teachers joining can quickly understand how the course has evolved.

## Feedback Channels Beyond Surveys

A survey is regular, structured feedback, but day to day there can be more relaxed channels too: a small card with two or three questions after a lesson, a poll in the community group, a short chat between teacher and parent. Different channels complement one another and give the course team a fuller picture of how everyone feels.

## Course Feedback vs Teaching Feedback

A student survey collects feedback on the course, but while practising, students also need feedback on their own playing: which note was wrong, where the rhythm was unsteady. The former helps the course team improve its design, and the latter helps students improve their playing. Both matter, and both need to be timely, specific and actionable.

## FAQ

**Q: What if the survey response rate is very low?**
A: Shorten the survey, explain what it is for, and set aside a few minutes in class for everyone to fill it in on the spot. This usually raises the response rate.

**Q: What should I do about sharp criticism?**
A: First thank the person for being willing to speak up, then judge whether there is anything to improve, and if necessary talk privately to understand the details.

**Q: Can children fill in the survey themselves?**
A: Older children can complete a simple version, while younger children can have a parent fill it in for them or answer with emoji faces.

**Q: Should every survey ask the same questions?**
A: Keep a few core questions so that you can compare results, and adjust the rest flexibly according to the focus of the moment.

parent-learns-piano-alongside-child.body:
Some parents start learning a little piano themselves while their child is learning. Learning together can help parents better understand the difficulties their child meets in practice, create an atmosphere of practising together at home, and sometimes even let them play simple duets with their child. One thing to bear in mind: parents' progress and their child's progress do not need to be compared, and parents should not press their own expectations onto the child. Keep the relationship relaxed and mutually encouraging, and learning together will be a happy thing.

## Stay Relaxed

The original purpose of learning together is to enjoy music and to keep your child company, so keep a relaxed frame of mind.

If you find that learning together has brought pressure or conflict instead, you can change the way you do it, for example by practising separately, or by playing together only at weekends.

Only by finding the way that suits your own family can you keep it going.

## A Role Model for Your Child

A parent who is willing to learn something new as an adult is in itself a very good role model for a child.

Children will see from this that learning is a lifelong thing, and that you can start at any age.

This attitude is worth more than learning to play any particular piece.

## Going to Concerts Together

Besides learning together, the whole family can also look for chances to hear a live performance, or put on a record in the living room.

Hearing a piece you are learning performed gives both sides more motivation.

These shared musical experiences can bring the family closer.

## The Parent's Own Way of Learning

A parent can choose the same teacher as their child, or look for a course suited to adults, or start by teaching themselves from a simple beginner's book.

When adults learn, they can choose pieces according to their own interests, such as a favourite pop song or a classic melody.

The important thing is to find a way of learning that you enjoy, rather than forcing yourself to follow your child's pace.

## Arranging Your Time

Parents are usually short of time, and can use odd moments to practise, such as the ten or fifteen minutes after the child has finished.

There is no need to practise for long every day; as long as you keep up a certain frequency, you will see progress.

If you are especially busy for a while, you can also pause, and do not need to put too much pressure on yourself.

## Do Not Become the Teacher

Once parents have learned a little, they may not be able to resist correcting how their child plays, but this easily makes the child feel pressured.

The teaching can be left to the teacher, and the parent's role is to keep company and encourage.

If you notice a problem with your child, you can note it down and raise it with the teacher at the lesson.

## The Practice Atmosphere at Home

If parents also practise, a natural atmosphere of learning music forms at home.

When children see their parents working at practice too, they feel that practising is an ordinary thing everyone does, not something only they are asked to do.

You can arrange some time for parent and child to practise in turns, or to practise separately in the same period.

## Ask Your Child for Help

Sometimes you can let your child be the little teacher for a while and teach you to play a piece they have already learned.

In teaching, the child consolidates what they have learned, and also feels a great sense of achievement.

This swapping of roles can make the parent-child relationship more relaxed and equal.

## No Need to Compare Progress

Children and adults learn piano in different ways and at different speeds: sometimes the child learns faster, and sometimes the adult has an advantage in some respects.

Do not compare the two people's progress, and above all do not say things like "Look, I can already do it, so why can't you?"

Each person moves forward at their own pace, and it is enough to appreciate each other's progress.

- Parent and child learn piano together
- Better understanding of the difficulties in the child's practice
- You can play simple duets together
- No need to compare progress; keep the relationship relaxed

## Playing Duets Together

Once both of you have a little foundation, you can find some simple duets, with one person playing the melody and the other the accompaniment.

Playing together brings a lot of fun, and also trains cooperation and listening.

Performing a duet together at a family gathering is also a lovely memory.

![A black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0t9ei-2hl5b.webp)

## Experiencing the Difficulty of Practice First-Hand

After learning for themselves, parents understand more clearly how hard it is to read music, coordinate both hands and keep the rhythm.

This experience gives parents more patience when keeping their child company at practice, and helps them understand why a child gets stuck in certain places.

When the child says "This part is so hard," the parent can honestly say, "I find it hard too. Let's take it slowly together."

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What are the benefits of parents learning too?**
A: They understand their child's difficulties better and create a practice atmosphere.

**Q: What can we play together?**
A: Simple duets.

**Q: Should we compare progress with the child?**
A: No comparing; each goes at their own pace.

**Q: Can parents correct their child?**
A: Leave the teaching to the teacher; parents mainly keep company and encourage.

**Q: How should parents arrange their time?**
A: Use odd moments, and just keep up a certain frequency.

**Q: What if learning together feels stressful?**
A: Change the way you do it, for example by practising separately or playing together only at weekends.

open-voicing-spread-chords-piano.body:
Open voicing means playing the notes of a chord spread across a wider range, with the distance between neighbouring notes larger than in a close arrangement within an octave. Its opposite is close voicing, where the notes of the chord are packed within the reach of one hand, for example C, E and G played right next to each other. Open voicing often puts the root in the bass and the other notes higher up, sometimes shared between the two hands. Chords played this way sound wider and clearer, and the bass does not turn muddy, so open voicing is common in ballad accompaniment, choral arrangements and film scores. Once you learn open voicing, your accompaniment will immediately sound more layered.

## The difference between close and open voicing

- Close voicing: the chord notes sit side by side, usually within one hand
- Open voicing: the chord notes are spread out, spanning more than an octave
- Sound of close voicing: focused and strong, but easily muddy in the bass register
- Sound of open voicing: wide and clear, good for creating a sense of space
- Use: both are useful; the key is to choose according to register and style

In the low register, notes that sit too close together sound muddy, so the low register generally suits open voicing; in the middle and upper registers, close voicing sounds clear and focused.

## Three common open shapes

**Shape one: root and fifth, with the third in the right hand**
The left hand plays the root and fifth, such as C and G; the right hand plays E a little higher, or E together with the melody note. This is the basis of many ballad accompaniments.

**Shape two: the tenth shape**
The left hand plays the root and the third a tenth above, such as C and the E above the next octave. If your hand is not big enough, you can play the two notes quickly as a roll.

**Shape three: sharing between the hands**
The left hand plays the root in octaves, and the right hand plays the third, fifth and seventh. This voicing is common in jazz and pop ballads, sounding full without being crowded.

![Red, orange and yellow ink illustration of a grand piano on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvybhth2-gdk0p.webp)

## Practising open voicing step by step

**Step one: start with one chord**
Choose a C major triad. Play it first in close voicing, then in shape one, and compare the difference in sound.

**Step two: practise a progression**
Take the four chords C, Am, F and G and play them all in shape one. The left hand plays root and fifth, and the right hand plays the third in the middle register.

**Step three: connect smoothly**
When changing chords, let the right hand move as little as possible, and keep any notes that can stay in place.

**Step four: add the melody**
Add a melody note in the right hand above the third, while the left hand keeps the open root and fifth.

**Step five: try broken chords**
Change the left-hand root and fifth into a broken pattern to make the accompaniment flow more.

## Listening check for open voicing

- Is the bass clear, without any muddiness?
- Is there space left between the middle and upper registers?
- Does the melody sing out clearly on top?
- Are the chord changes smooth, without sudden jumps?

When you listen back to a recording, pay particular attention to the low register. If it sounds like a blur, it is usually because the notes in the low register are too close together; try moving the third higher.

## How it is used in different styles

Ballads often use an open root and fifth, giving the accompaniment a broad background feel; jazz piano often puts the third and seventh in the middle register and leaves the root to a bass instrument or the left hand; choral arrangements often imitate the distribution of human voices, spreading out the bass, tenor, alto and soprano. Knowing these habits helps you find a suitable sound more quickly when accompanying different songs.

## How to play open voicing with small hands

If your hand span is limited, there is no need to force a wide-stretch chord. You can break an open chord into a rolled form, playing the bass first and then the upper notes, and link the sound with the pedal; you can also hand some of the notes to the other hand so that the two hands share. What matters is that it sounds wide, not that every note must be pressed at the same moment.

## Changing voicings within a song

Different sections of the same song can use different voicings to create contrast. In the verse, use a thinner open voicing with just the root and fifth, so that the singing stands out; in the chorus, switch to a fuller voicing shared between the hands to push the emotion to a peak; at the end, return to a simple open voicing and let the music slowly wind down. Adjusting the voicing by section like this lets the accompaniment and melody tell the ups and downs of the song together.

## Three common mistakes

- Three notes crowded together in the low register, making the sound muddy
- The right-hand chord covering the melody so it cannot be heard clearly
- Both hands making big leaps at once when changing chords, so the connection is not smooth

## FAQ

**Q: Is open voicing always nicer to listen to than close voicing?**
A: Not necessarily. Each has its uses: open voicing is used more in the low register, while close voicing is also clear in the middle and upper registers.

**Q: Can beginners learn open voicing?**
A: Yes. Start with a simple shape such as root plus fifth, and you will soon be able to use it in song accompaniment.

**Q: Does open voicing need the pedal?**
A: Usually it does when you roll the chord. You can change the pedal with the chord changes to keep the sound connected but not blurred.

**Q: How do I know which voicing to use?**
A: First listen to the register of the melody and leave space for it, then decide where to place the chord and how to voice it.

music-studio-photo-guidelines-privacy.body:
Promotional photos are an important way for a music studio to introduce itself to the world, but they also touch on the privacy of students and parents. Taking photos should not be a spur-of-the-moment thing; first think clearly about what to shoot, who it is for and who has agreed. A simple set of shooting principles can help a studio capture warm images while holding to its limits.

## Get Clear Consent First

**For adult students**
Before shooting, explain where the photos will be used, such as the website, brochures or social platforms, and ask for clear consent. They may refuse, and may ask for photos to be taken down at any time.

**For students under 18**
You must get the guardian's consent. The consent should be specific, stating the use and scope, rather than a single vague sentence.

**Keep a record of consent**
Store the content and date of the consent in a safe place, viewable only by those who need it.

## Shoot More Hands and Pianos, Fewer Faces

A music lesson offers plenty of good shots that do not show faces.

- Close-ups of fingers on the keys.
- Still lifes of sheet music, a pencil and a metronome on the piano.
- Scenes shot from behind of a student and teacher looking at a score together.
- The light and the piano in an empty classroom.

These images carry a sense of story, and also reduce the impact on personal privacy.

![Hands playing on a piano keyboard](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwgvorv7-3iaz0.webp)

## Watch the Information in the Background

The background is often overlooked when shooting. After shooting, check the following.

- Whether name lists, timetables and contact details on the wall are clearly visible.
- Whether any student information appears on computer screens.
- Whether door numbers, number plates or nearby landmarks reveal places that should not be made public.
- Whether other students' work or practice records have got into the frame.

If you find a problem, crop or reshoot; do not go with the thought "probably no one will notice".

## Prepare Images for Different Uses

**Website home page**
Needs a landscape format and a simple composition, leaving blank space for text.

**Social platforms**
Often need a square or portrait frame, and must be understandable at a glance on a small screen.

**Brochures and posters**
Need higher resolution, avoiding blur.

Images for different uses come in different sizes, so leave some margin when shooting; cropping afterwards will then be easier.

## Light and Tidying

You do not need expensive equipment. Natural light by a window, a clean piano top and a tidy music stand are enough to make the picture look comfortable. Before shooting, put away clutter so that only what you want to express remains in the frame.

## Use and Storage

- Use photos only within the scope of consent.
- Regularly check the photos on the website and platforms, and take down any that are no longer needed.
- If a student leaves the studio and asks for photos to be taken down, deal with it promptly.
- Keep original photos in a place with access control.

## Practice Stories Beyond Photos

Often the most moving picture is not the stage but everyday practice. TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app, and when students practise at home they can get feedback on notes and beats through it. When a studio describes this way of learning, it can use a piano, a pair of hands and a score, and does not need to show people at all, yet readers can still sense the atmosphere of concentration.

## A Simple Shooting Checklist

Before shooting, the team can use a checklist to remind themselves: what is today's theme? Who will be in the frame? Has consent been obtained? Is there information in the background that needs to be covered? Who will select the photos afterwards? Who is responsible for deleting the ones not used? Write these questions on a sheet of paper and post it at the studio door, and nobody will forget.

**On the day of the shoot**
- Tell the people present in advance that photos will be taken today.
- Mark out an area where no photos are taken for those who do not want to be in them.
- Avoid interrupting students during a lesson; wait until the break to shoot.

**After the shoot**
- Check and delete unsuitable photos on the same day.
- Put usable photos into a dedicated folder, and note the scope of consent.

## Talking with Parents About How Photos Are Used

Many parents are happy for their child to take part, as long as they know how the photos will be used. The studio can prepare a short one-page explanation stating the occasion of the shoot, where the photos may appear, how long they will be kept and how to withdraw consent. Put this page with the enrolment materials, and parents can choose as they see fit. If a parent chooses not to consent, also make sure the child does not feel singled out in the activity, for example by asking the child to stand outside the camera's view while still taking part naturally.

## FAQ

**Q: Can we photograph students' work?**
A: First get the consent of the student and the guardian, and explain the use.

**Q: Can consent be withdrawn?**
A: Yes. Students and parents should be told they have this right, and requests should be dealt with promptly.

**Q: Will photos without faces be less appealing?**
A: Hands, pianos and light can be very expressive; the key is a clean, genuine picture.

**Q: What about shooting at events?**
A: Tell people beforehand that shooting will take place, set areas where no photos are taken, and leave a choice for those who do not want to be in the frame.

palestrina-pope-marcellus-mass-legend.body:
In the middle of the sixteenth century, the Catholic Church held the Council of Trent, and some there worried that the polyphony in church was too complicated: several voices sang different words at the same time, and the listeners could not make out the text. According to a story that circulated later, the Roman composer Palestrina wrote a Pope Marcellus Mass in which the voices were clear and harmonious and the words could be understood, convincing the delegates that polyphony could be kept. It is a moving story, but historians think it is mostly a later embellishment. The Mass was published in 1567 and is still one of the works most often studied in Renaissance polyphony.

## The Legendary Mass

According to the story that circulated later, Palestrina wrote a Mass in response to this worry.

**Before You Begin**

Although this Mass is written in polyphony, the voices work together very well and the words are perfectly clear.

Legend has it that after hearing it, the delegates decided polyphony could be kept, and gave up the idea of banning it.

## The Name Marcellus

The Mass is named after Pope Marcellus II.

Marcellus II was pope in 1555 for only three short weeks.

He is said to have asked that church music be dignified and that the words be audible, and perhaps this Mass has some connection with him.

## A Counterpoint Textbook

In the eighteenth century, the Austrian music theorist Fux wrote a counterpoint textbook that took Palestrina's style as its model.

The book was hugely influential, and Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven all studied it.

In this way Palestrina's style became a foundation for learning to compose.

## Words That Could Not Be Heard

Polyphony is beautiful, but it brings a problem: when several voices sing different words at once, it is hard for the listener to tell what is being sung.

In the middle of the sixteenth century the Church held the Council of Trent to discuss many questions, and church music was among them.

Some held that church music should let people hear the words, and that overly complicated polyphony needed to change.

## Smooth Melodies

Palestrina's melodies move mostly by step, with few large leaps.

When there is a leap, the melody usually turns and moves a step in the opposite direction at once, keeping the line balanced.

This way of writing was later summed up as the rules of counterpoint and taught to generations of composition students.

## Pope Marcellus Mass Summary

Palestrina was a sixteenth-century Italian composer who worked for many years in the great churches of Rome. In polyphony, several voices sing different melodies at the same time. At the Council of Trent in the middle of the sixteenth century, some worried that the words could not be heard. According to a story that circulated later, he wrote a Mass named after Pope Marcellus II, who served only three weeks, and convinced the delegates that polyphony could be kept; historians think the story is mostly a later embellishment.

This six-voice Mass was published in 1567. In passages with many words, the voices declaim the text together; the melodies move mainly by step and turn back in the opposite direction after a leap. Fux's eighteenth-century counterpoint textbook took his style as its model, and at the piano you can play a stepwise melody in each hand to get a feel for polyphony.

You can talk about this legend with Teacher Aum.

## Who Was Palestrina

Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was a sixteenth-century Italian composer, whose name comes from his hometown, the small town of Palestrina near Rome.

For many years he held musical posts in several of the great churches of Rome, and wrote more than a hundred Masses and a great many motets.

His works are known for their clear voices and their harmonious, smooth sound.

## Published in 1567

The Pope Marcellus Mass is included in the collection of Masses Palestrina published in 1567.

It has six voices, which made it a choral work of considerable scale at the time.

Over the following centuries it has been regarded as one of the models of Renaissance polyphony.

- The Council of Trent in the mid-sixteenth century discussed church music
- This Mass is said to have allowed polyphony to be kept
- Historians think the story is mostly a later embellishment
- Published in 1567

## Clear Writing for the Voices

One feature of this Mass is that, in passages with a lot of text, the voices often declaim the same words together.

That way, even though it is written in polyphony, the audience can still make out the words.

In passages with fewer words, the voices interweave with one another more.

## What Is Polyphony

Polyphony is when several voices sing independent melodies at the same time.

These melodies interweave like several strands braided together, forming a rich sound.

In the Renaissance, most choral music in church was written this way.

![A watercolour-style upright piano, open sheet music and a wooden stool](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbj4yxe-pgwl5.webp)

## Playing Two Lines at the Piano

At the piano, try playing a simple stepwise melody with each of your right and left hands.

The two melodies can start together, or enter one after the other.

Listen to how the two lines fit together while each stays independent.

## Legend and History

The story that "Palestrina saved polyphony" only spread after his death.

Historians have looked through the records of the Council of Trent and found that the council did not intend to ban polyphony completely.

So the story is mostly a later embellishment, but it shows how much people loved this work.

## Talk About the Palestrina Legend in Your Lesson

In your lesson you can talk with Teacher Aum about the legend and the history of the Pope Marcellus Mass.

When you play one line with each hand, how do you make both lines audible? Your teacher will know as soon as they hear it at the piano.

From one moving legend, get to know Renaissance polyphony.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which period was Palestrina from?**
A: Sixteenth-century Italy, the Renaissance.

**Q: What worried some people at the Council of Trent about polyphony?**
A: Several voices sang different words at the same time, so the words could not be heard.

**Q: Is the story of "saving polyphony" believable?**
A: Historians think it is mostly a later embellishment.

**Q: In what year was this Mass published?**
A: 1567.

**Q: How many voices does it have?**
A: Six.

music-brand-beginner-start-guide.body:
When new users first meet a music course or music app, they are often a little lost: what do I need to prepare? What do I do on day one? Who do I ask when I have a problem? A clear beginner's start guide can answer these questions in advance and make people willing to take the first step. For a music brand, it is also a good chance to show sincerity.

## First, Work Out Who Your Readers Are

Beginners may be parents of a child learning piano for the first time, or adults who want to start again. Their worries differ: parents worry whether the child will stick with it, while adults worry about time and progress. The guide can be divided into two or three subsections by type of reader, each answering in its own language.

## What the Guide Should Contain

**What to prepare**
- A usable keyboard or piano; there is no need to go for expensive equipment at the start.
- A relatively quiet place to practise, at a height that suits sitting.
- A small notebook or digital notes for recording progress.

**What to do in the first week**
- Get to know the layout of the keys and the basic sitting posture.
- Set aside a short time each day; even a very short time makes a habit easier to form than an occasional long session.
- Begin with simple pieces or exercises to get used to the beat and the fingers.

**How to judge progress**
- Write down what you practised each day and how it felt.
- Look back after a week: what feels more familiar, and what still needs practice.
- Do not compare yourself with others.

![Piano with futuristic soft lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwgvwnh4-xzpxl.webp)

## Reminders for Parents

- Keeping company matters more than supervising. Sit nearby and listen, and say what you hear that is good.
- Do not turn practice into a punishment or a bargaining chip.
- If your child is tired, let them rest and keep the atmosphere relaxed.
- If your child runs into difficulty, talk to the teacher rather than scolding at home.

## Who to Ask When Problems Come Up

The guide should state how to get in touch: who to contact, when they can reply, and where the FAQ page is. If an app is used, also explain how to find the help page and how to report problems. Letting new users know that someone is responding is the key to dispelling unease.

## Language and Layout

- Use short sentences and subheadings so people can find the part they want at a glance.
- Avoid too many technical words, and explain them in brackets when necessary.
- Place simple pictures or diagrams in suitable spots to aid understanding.
- Avoid exaggerated promises such as "you will be playing well in no time".

## Connecting the Guide to the Product Experience

What the start guide says should match the actual experience. TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app, and new users can try Premium free for 7 days. State this in the guide, and explain that the app gives prompts on the pitch and rhythm of what you play, so that users know what to expect in the first week. Also remind users that in-person teachers and courses can be combined with the app, each bringing its own strengths.

## Opening with a Story-Like Passage

The guide can begin with a short, plain description in which readers see themselves. For example: "Perhaps you have just bought a keyboard, or perhaps your child has just said they want to learn piano. There is no need to rush; the steps below will help you get off to a smooth start." An opening like this makes readers feel understood rather than sold to. Then lead with clear subheadings so readers know what each part is for. The goal of the whole guide is to make the first week easy, not to put beginners under pressure.

- Do not list too many requirements at the start.
- Use everyday language and explain the purpose of each step.
- Finish with a word of encouragement, but do not exaggerate.

## Following Up After the First Month

Once beginners have finished the first week, the guide can lead them to the second step: review what they have learned, choose a short piece they like, fix a weekly practice time, and ask the teacher or the community when they meet difficulty. At the end of the first month, the brand can send a gentle follow-up email asking about the experience and offering a few related articles. Keep the tone plain, do not rush, and make no promises about results, so that beginners feel someone is beside them without being disturbed.

## Leaving Room for Questions

Beginners have many small questions they feel shy to ask, such as "Is my sitting posture right?" or "Do I need to buy a textbook first?" At the end of the guide, invite them to ask at any time, and explain that common questions will be gathered into articles. When asking becomes an ordinary thing, beginners will not stop for fear of asking something naive, and this too is a way for the brand to show sincerity.

## FAQ

**Q: How long should the start guide be?**
A: Limit it to what the first week needs; one page that can be read through is ideal, and more can go in later articles.

**Q: Does it need a video?**
A: It can have one, but the written explanation should be complete too, for readers with different habits.

**Q: How often should the guide be updated?**
A: Review it every term, or when the product changes significantly.

**Q: What if a beginner has no instrument?**
A: They can first learn about the different types of keyboard and choose one that suits their budget and space, or try a lesson first.

music-school-website-faq-page.body:
The FAQ page on a music studio website brings together the questions parents and adult students ask again and again, and answers them in simple, direct language. A good FAQ page cuts down on repeated enquiries and lets visitors understand how lessons work, what the fees cover, the rules on missed lessons and the practice expectations before they decide to enrol. The key points of writing it are: collect questions from real enquiries, group them by topic, start each answer with the conclusion and then add the necessary detail, and check regularly that the content is still accurate.

## Why It Is Worth the Time

Teachers at many music studios receive similar messages every day: "How old do you have to be to start?" "Can I have lessons without a piano?" "Can I make up a lesson if I miss one?" Replying one by one takes time and the wording is easily different each time. Put these questions on the website, and visitors can look them up themselves at any time, while teachers can put their energy back into teaching.

An FAQ page can also help search engines and various smart assistants understand your studio. A clear question-and-answer structure makes it easier for people to find your answers when they search online for related questions.

## Step One: Collect Real Questions

Do not imagine what parents might ask; gather it from actual conversations.

- Look through chat records and emails from the past few months and note the questions that keep coming up.
- Ask the front desk or teaching assistant to jot down the things they are often asked when they take calls.
- After a trial lesson, ask parents whether they still have any questions.
- Pay attention to the confusions new students often meet in their first month.

Once you have collected twenty or thirty questions, merge those with the same meaning, delete those that appeared only once, and keep the most common ones.

## Step Two: Group by Topic

With many questions, you need categories so visitors can find things quickly. Common groups are:

**Lessons and age**
What age to start, whether adults can learn, how long a lesson is, and the difference between one-to-one and group lessons.

**Fees and payment**
How fees are charged, which payment methods are available, and the rules for missed lessons and refunds. Be clear here, but there is no need to promise anything beyond the offers you actually have.

**Practice and instruments**
What instrument is needed at home, how long a day is suitable for practice, and whether a digital piano is acceptable.

**Scheduling and communication**
How to book, how to ask for leave and make up lessons, and how teachers give feedback on progress.

![A person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw1li6pa-48vun.webp)

## Step Three: Write Clear Answers

**Put the conclusion in the first sentence**
For example, "Yes, you can start lessons without a piano", then explain the reason and give advice. Readers often read only the first sentence, so the first sentence has to answer the question.

**Use the visitor's language**
Avoid too much jargon. If you must use it, explain it as you go. For example, when mentioning "sight reading", you can say "playing straight from a new piece of music".

**Keep it short**
Keep each answer to a few sentences. For content that needs detailed explanation, you can link to a separate page.

**Do not exaggerate**
Do not promise anything about learning results or exam results, and do not use figures without a basis. Down-to-earth answers are more reassuring.

## Step Four: Update Regularly

Lesson arrangements, fees and rules change, and the FAQ page has to change with them. You can check it once a term, delete outdated answers and add new questions. If a question is asked often and is not yet on the website, it needs to be added soon.

## A Sample Answer

Take "Can I start learning without a piano?" as an example. You could write it like this: Yes, you can start. In the early stage, practice can be done on a digital piano with standard-size keys, and once the child or adult student is sure they will keep learning long term, you can consider changing instruments. In lessons, the teacher will plan the practice content around the instrument you have at home. If you are not sure what instrument to buy, you can ask the teacher directly at the trial lesson. This answer gives the conclusion first, then the reason, and finally tells the visitor what they can do next, so it reads clearly and reassuringly.

## Make the Page Easier to Use

- Put a short table of contents at the top of the page, so one click jumps to the matching group.
- Provide contact details at the end of each group, so visitors can keep asking.
- If the studio offers lessons in several languages, you can prepare matching versions for visitors of different languages.

## FAQ

**Q: How many questions should an FAQ page have?**
A: Ten to twenty is usually about right: enough to cover the main questions without making the page too long.

**Q: Can answers state specific prices?**
A: Yes, but make sure they are kept up to date. If prices change often, you can also invite visitors to enquire.

**Q: How is an FAQ page different from a course introduction page?**
A: A course introduction page focuses on showing the content and features, while an FAQ page focuses on answering specific questions.

**Q: Should negative questions be included?**
A: Yes. Answering honestly a question like "What can I do if I cannot keep going?" actually builds trust.

music-brand-visual-identity-system.body:
The visual identity of a music education brand is a complete system made up of the logo, colours, typefaces, photo style and layout rules. Its job is simple: to let parents, students and partners recognise at a glance that a poster, website, social media post, classroom door or lesson handout belongs to the same brand. Many small music schools make only a logo and then produce everything else separately, so every channel ends up looking like a different organisation. Writing the visual rules down and sticking to them is brand work that costs little but works well.

## What a visual identity is made of

A basic visual identity usually has five parts. The logo is the core, but it cannot carry the whole impression alone. Colour sets the mood, typefaces set the tone, photo style sets how real it feels, and layout rules decide whether information is clear. When the five parts work together, the brand looks steady and trustworthy.

**The logo needs different versions**
The same logo needs a horizontal version, a vertical version, a single-colour version and a simplified small-size version. A social media avatar is tiny, and complicated lines blur into a smudge; a sign for the classroom is large, so detail can stay. If different versions are prepared in advance, nobody will stretch or recolour the logo at random when making something in a hurry.

## Colour: choose the main colour first, then supporting colours

A common colour approach for music education brands is one main colour that expresses the brand's personality, plus two or three supporting colours and a set of neutrals. The main colour is used for the logo and key buttons, supporting colours distinguish course categories, and neutrals are used for body text and backgrounds. Too many colours make a layout messy and force the designer to choose again every time.

A colour list can be written like this:

- Main colour: give the exact colour value, used for the logo, headings and call-to-action buttons.
- Supporting colours: one use for each colour, such as children's courses or adult courses.
- Neutrals: dark grey for body text, light grey for backgrounds and dividing lines.
- Forbidden combinations: list pairings with too little contrast that are hard to read.

Contrast is an easily overlooked problem. Light text on a light background is almost impossible to read on a phone screen outdoors. Checking for readability is also a courtesy to older relatives and parents with weaker eyesight.

## Typefaces and tone

![A black upright piano by a window in natural light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw5opvu2-e4113.webp)

Typefaces convey tone. Rounded type feels friendly and suits children's courses; a clean sans-serif feels simple and suits adult courses and online products. If Chinese, English and Thai appear together, choose typefaces that look good side by side and keep the same size hierarchy.

**Write the size hierarchy as a table**
We recommend setting out in a simple table how large and how heavy the type should be for headings, subheadings, body text and notes. That way, whoever makes the poster, the levels of information come out consistently.

## Photo and illustration style

What parents most want to see is a real lesson. For photo style, we suggest keeping light, tone and composition consistent, for example mainly natural light, warm tones and plenty of close-ups of hands and keys. If you photograph students, always get written consent from the student or their parents beforehand and explain which channels the photos will be used on. When faces cannot be shown, you can photograph backs, hands or sheet music, which conveys the atmosphere of the lesson just as well.

Illustrations and icons also need a consistent line weight and corner style. Icons downloaded at random from the internet come in all sorts of styles and look patched together when placed side by side.

## Write the rules into a brand guide

If visual rules are not written down, they soon drift. A short brand guide of a dozen pages is enough, covering how to use the logo, colour values, type hierarchy, photo examples and commonly used templates. Keep the guide in a shared folder the whole team can open, so that new colleagues, freelance designers and partners all work to the same standard.

The most useful part of a guide is often the templates:

- A course poster template, with space reserved for the title, time and QR code.
- Square and vertical image templates for social media.
- Templates for student certificates and concert programmes.
- A website banner template that marks the safe area.

## Review and adjust regularly

A brand grows and its visuals can be fine-tuned, but change them at a steady pace, not on a whim. Every six months, check each channel for outdated logos, drifting colours or inconsistent typefaces. When something needs adjusting, update the guide first, then update the templates, and finally replace online materials one by one. This process keeps change smooth and avoids making long-standing students feel the brand has become unfamiliar.

**Collect real feedback**
At an open day or a parents' meeting, you can ask a few parents to look at the old and new versions of a poster and say which one makes the information clearer. Real feedback is more useful than the team's own tastes.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does a small school need a brand guide too?**
A: Yes, but it can be very simple. A few pages of clear rules can prevent most inconsistencies.

**Q: How do I choose the main colour?**
A: First work out what feeling the brand wants to give, then choose a colour that expresses it and is clearly readable on a phone.

**Q: Can I change the logo often?**
A: We do not recommend it. Frequent changes weaken recognition, and fine-tuning is safer than starting over.

**Q: Can I use student photos directly?**
A: No. You must first get consent from the student or their parents and explain how the photos will be used.

**Q: How do I keep multilingual materials consistent?**
A: Choose multilingual typefaces with a harmonious style, and use the same size hierarchy and layout throughout.

pachelbel-canon-chord-progression.body:
Pachelbel's Canon in D was originally written for three violins and basso continuo. The bass part is made up of eight notes that repeat over and over, while the upper voices unfold layer by layer on top of it. By the common understanding, the chords that go with these eight bass notes are D, A, Bm, F#m, G, D, G, A. When playing an arrangement of the Canon on the piano, you can first get this set of chords well under your fingers, letting the left hand move steadily through round after round, and then add the melody in the right hand.

## Use inversions to make the right hand smoother

If all eight chords are played in root position, the right hand has to make big moves again and again.

**Before you begin**

You can use inversions to keep the right-hand chords as close together as possible, for example D, F#, A for the D chord, C#, E, A for the A chord, and D, F#, B for Bm.

That way the right hand moves very little and the sound is more connected.

## Listen to the original

Before practising the piano version, you can listen to the original string version first, and feel the effect of the three violins entering one after another and chasing each other.

As you listen, notice that the bass keeps repeating while the upper voices grow richer and richer, which is exactly the structural feature of this piece.

With this impression in mind, it is easier to capture the sense of building up layer by layer when you play the piano version.

## Adding the melody

Once you know the chords, you can add the Canon melody in the right hand, while the left hand keeps playing the bass or broken chords.

The melody's opening often starts on F# and descends, step by step, sounding quiet and beautiful.

As the piece develops, the melody becomes richer and richer, with more notes and ornaments added.

## The matching chords

In piano arrangements, these eight bass notes are often paired with this set of chords: D, A, Bm, F#m, G, D, G, A.

In Roman numerals, that is I, V, vi, iii, IV, I, IV, V in D major.

This chord progression sounds warm and flowing, and many later pop songs have used similar progressions.

## Keeping the left hand steady

Because the bass keeps repeating, the steadiness of the left hand is very important; it is the foundation of the whole piece.

The left hand must keep an even rhythm and not lose the beat as the right hand becomes more complicated.

You can practise the left hand alone first, using a metronome to stay steady, and then add the right hand.

## Pachelbel and this Canon

Johann Pachelbel was a German composer and organist of the Baroque period, who lived from 1653 to 1706.

His Canon in D was originally written for three violins and basso continuo, and it often appears together with a gigue.

Today the piece has been arranged in all kinds of versions, and the piano version is one of the most popular.

- Originally written for three violins and basso continuo
- The bass is made up of eight notes, repeated continuously
- The common chords are D, A, Bm, F#m, G, D, G, A
- For a piano arrangement, first get the chords well learned

## Choosing a suitable arrangement

There are many piano arrangements of the Canon, ranging from beginner to advanced.

Beginners can choose a version with just the melody and simple chords, while those with some foundation can choose a richer version.

You can ask your teacher to help recommend a version that suits your level.

## The eight bass notes

The Canon's bass is made up of eight notes, going in the order D, A, B, F♯, G, D, G, A, each lasting two beats.

This set of bass notes recurs throughout the piece, and this way of writing is also called a ground bass.

As you listen, you can try counting along with the bass and feel it cycle round by round.

![Transparent futuristic keyboard with beams of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1ea7t-or7uv.webp)

## From chords to improvisation

Once you are familiar with the Canon's chords, you can also try some simple improvisation over this set of chords.

For example, the right hand can freely combine notes from these chords into a melody while the left hand keeps playing the bass.

This kind of practice helps you understand the relationship between harmony and melody, and it is also great fun.

## What is a canon?

A canon is a way of writing based on imitation: one voice sings out a melody first, and the other voices follow after a time with the same melody.

In Pachelbel's Canon, the three violins enter one after another, playing the same melody, staggered from one another, creating a layered effect.

The bass below keeps repeating, like a solid foundation.

## Building up layer by layer

The charm of the Canon lies in its layer-by-layer build-up: each round adds new variation to the previous one.

In piano arrangements, this build-up is often shown by increasing the density of notes, thickening the chords or raising the register.

When you play, you can let the volume and the emotion grow slowly, round by round.

## Learn the chords first

When practising the piano version of the Canon, you can start by playing only this set of chords, with the left hand on the bass and the right hand on the chords.

Play each chord for two beats, eight chords to a round, and repeat several times until you can play through smoothly without looking at the music.

Once this set of chords is fluent, adding the melody later will be much easier.

## FAQ

**Q: What instruments was the Canon originally written for?**
A: Three violins and basso continuo.

**Q: How many notes are there in the bass?**
A: Eight notes, repeated continuously.

**Q: What are the common chords?**
A: D, A, Bm, F#m, G, D, G, A.

**Q: What is a canon?**
A: One voice appears first, and the other voices follow with the same melody.

**Q: Where should I start with the piano version?**
A: First learn the chords well, then add the melody.

**Q: Can beginners play it?**
A: Choose a simple arrangement.

neoclassicism-stravinsky-pulcinella-1920.body:
After the First World War, many composers grew tired of the huge, intense music of the late Romantic period and looked back to the music of the eighteenth century and earlier. They liked clear structure, simple texture and lively rhythm, and this trend came to be called "neoclassicism". In 1920 Stravinsky's ballet Pulcinella premiered in Paris. He took music said to be by the eighteenth-century Italian composer Pergolesi as his material and added new harmony and rhythm, and the work is often seen as a landmark of this trend. Earlier, in 1917, Prokofiev wrote his Classical Symphony, imagining how Haydn might have written if he were alive today.

## Not Only Stravinsky

Besides Stravinsky and Prokofiev, many other twentieth-century composers also wrote works in the neoclassical style.

For example, some composers of the French "Les Six", and Hindemith in Germany.

Neoclassicism became an important style in the 1920s and 1930s.

## The Borrowed Melodies of Pulcinella

The material for Pulcinella is said to come from works by the eighteenth-century Italian composer Pergolesi.

Later scholars found that some of it was in fact written by other composers, and had merely been put under Pergolesi's name at the time.

Stravinsky kept these melodies but gave them new harmony and rhythm.

## Neoclassicism in Brief

Neoclassicism is a musical trend after the First World War. Composers, tired of the huge, intense style of late Romanticism, looked back to Bach, Haydn, Mozart and the Italian Baroque, liking clear structure, simple texture and lively rhythm, and wrote anew with twentieth-century harmony and rhythm. In 1920 Stravinsky's ballet Pulcinella premiered in Paris, its material said to come from Pergolesi, though some of it was in fact by others.

Prokofiev had already paid tribute to Haydn in 1917 with a short symphony, and Les Six in France and Hindemith, among others, also wrote in this style. On the piano you can add a dissonant note to the chords of a minuet, and when playing, use little pedal and keep the voices clear.

You can talk about neoclassicism with Teacher Aum.

## Weariness with Romanticism

From the end of the nineteenth century to the beginning of the twentieth, many works grew ever larger, orchestras ever bigger and emotions ever more intense.

After the First World War, many composers felt tired of this style.

They wanted music to become clear and simple, and no longer so heavy.

## Talk About Neoclassicism in Lessons

In lessons you can listen to a passage of Pulcinella or the Classical Symphony together with Teacher Aum, noticing how old melodies and new harmony are combined.

You can also ask the teacher to recommend a short piano piece in the neoclassical style, such as the little pieces Prokofiev wrote for children.

From one look back at the eighteenth century, we see another side of twentieth-century music.

## The Classical Symphony

Earlier, in 1917, Prokofiev wrote his first symphony, titled the Classical Symphony.

He said he imagined how Haydn, if he were alive today, would write a symphony.

The work is short, the orchestra is not large, and the melodies are lively, with humorous twists.

## Simple Texture

Neoclassical works often use a small orchestra, with the relationships between the voices very clear.

Composers like every line to be heard, rather than piling up a thick sound.

This simple texture makes the music seem transparent and light.

## Playing Clear Texture

When playing works in the neoclassical style, make every voice clear.

Use the pedal sparingly, to keep the sound clean and transparent.

The rhythm should be steady and springy, like an eighteenth-century dance.

## Clear Structure

Neoclassical works often use eighteenth-century forms, such as the sonata, suite, concerto and fugue.

Their structure is clear and the sections are distinct, so it is easy to hear where the beginning is and where the recapitulation comes.

This is very different from the free, grand structures of late Romanticism.

## Looking Back to the Eighteenth Century

These composers turned their attention to the music of the eighteenth century and earlier, such as Bach, Haydn, Mozart and the Italian Baroque composers.

They liked the clear structure, simple texture and lively rhythm of that music.

But they were not simply imitating; they wrote anew with twentieth-century harmony and rhythm.

## Old Melodies, New Sounds

In Pulcinella, the listener can recognise eighteenth-century melodies and forms.

But some chords suddenly gain an unexpected note, and some rhythms suddenly shift out of line.

This combination of old and new makes the music both familiar and fresh.

![An illustration of a colourful grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbk3ryi-w0bi7.webp)

## Pulcinella

In 1920 Stravinsky's ballet Pulcinella premiered in Paris.

Pulcinella is a character from Italian commedia dell'arte, a clever, mischievous figure.

The story of this ballet is light and humorous, and the music is bright.

## Feeling Old and New on the Piano

At the piano, you can first play a simple melody in an eighteenth-century style, such as the opening of a minuet.

Then add a dissonant note to the left-hand chords, for example adding F♯ to the tonic chord in C major.

**Before you try it**

Listen to what effect a familiar melody gives when combined with new harmony.

**Listen for**
- A trend after the First World War
- Looking back to the eighteenth century, liking clarity and simplicity
- Stravinsky's Pulcinella of 1920
- Prokofiev's Classical Symphony of 1917

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: When did neoclassicism appear?**
A: After the First World War.

**Q: Which era's music did the composers look back to?**
A: The eighteenth century and earlier.

**Q: In what year did Pulcinella premiere?**
A: 1920, in Paris.

**Q: In which year was the Classical Symphony, the tribute to Haydn, completed?**
A: 1917.

**Q: How should the pedal be used when playing neoclassical works?**
A: Sparingly, to keep the sound clean and transparent.
