nine-eight-time-three-dotted-beats.body:
9/8 time means there are nine eighth notes in every bar. But when playing, you do not usually count nine beats. Instead you group them into three sets of three eighth notes, so each bar has three big beats, and each big beat is as long as a dotted quarter note. So 9/8 sounds like 3/4, but inside every beat there are three small notes, which brings a swaying, flowing feeling.

## Common Problems

When playing in 9/8, a common problem is playing all three big beats equally heavily and losing the rise and fall.

**Another angle**

Another problem is playing the three eighth notes in each beat unevenly, so that they turn into a dotted rhythm.

Practise slowly, making sure the three notes in each beat are even and the first note of each big beat is a little heavier.

## The Pattern of Strong and Weak

Of the three big beats in 9/8, the first is the heaviest, and the second and third are relatively lighter.

Of the three small notes that fall within the same big beat, the first stands a little more firmly, and the last two follow on naturally.

This creates two levels of strong and weak, the big beats and the small beats.

## How the Left-Hand Accompaniment Is Written

In piano pieces in 9/8, the left hand often plays broken chords, three notes to each big beat.

For example, on the first big beat it plays the root, the fifth and the octave, and the next two big beats repeat or vary this.

An accompaniment like this gives the music a steady, flowing feeling.

## 9/8 and 12/8

Another compound time in the same family as 9/8 is 12/8, which has four big beats in each bar, each likewise divided into three eighth notes.

If you compare 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 side by side, you will find that they differ only in how many big beats each bar has.

Once you understand one of them, the other two become easy to grasp.

## Comparison with 3/4

9/8 has three big beats in each bar, and 3/4 also has three beats in each bar, so the two have something in common.

The difference is that each beat in 3/4 is usually divided into two eighth notes, while each big beat in 9/8 is divided into three eighth notes.

So 9/8 sounds more flowing, as if every beat were gently swaying.

## Rhythm Patterns Within One Big Beat in 9/8

In a score in 9/8, one big beat may contain three eighth notes joined together, or a long-short combination of a quarter note plus an eighth note.

A dotted quarter note filling a whole big beat is also a very common way of writing it.

When reading a score, first find where each big beat falls, and then look at the rhythm inside each beat.

## Finding 9/8 in Pieces

Some works by Bach use 9/8, such as some preludes and gigues.

Debussy's Clair de lune also begins in 9/8, with music that is calm and flowing.

When listening to these works, you can try counting three big beats along with the music.

## What 9/8 Means

Looking at the time signature 9/8, the 8 underneath says that the counting unit is the eighth note, and the 9 on top says that a bar holds nine of them.

Going by the numbers alone, it seems you would count nine beats in every bar, but in actual playing you rarely count it that way.

9/8 is a compound time, and eighth notes usually come in groups of three.

**Summary**
- Nine eighth notes in every bar
- Usually grouped into three sets of three
- Three big beats per bar, each a dotted quarter note
- Brings a swaying, flowing feeling

## Metronome Settings for 9/8

When practising 9/8 with a metronome, you can set it to click once per dotted quarter note, that is, three clicks per bar.

If the tempo is slow, you can also set it to click once per eighth note, nine clicks per bar.

The first helps you feel the flow of the big beats, and the second helps you play each small note accurately.

## Comparison with 6/8

6/8 has two big beats in each bar, with three eighth notes in each beat, while 9/8 has three big beats.

You can think of 9/8 as 6/8 with one more big beat added.

When playing, feel the rise and fall of three big beats in each bar, not two.

![Close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5okj6-h9dwb.webp)

## The Musical Feel of 9/8

Because each beat is divided into three, 9/8 often brings a swaying, flowing, gentle feeling.

Many lyrical pieces, lullabies and pieces describing flowing water use this kind of compound time.

When playing, let the music flow naturally, and do not play every eighth note equally heavily.

## How to Count 9/8

When you first meet it, you might say the nine small notes as "one-la-la, two-la-la, three-la-la", with the numbers falling on the start of each big beat.

Once you are comfortable, you can count only the three big beats, "one, two, three", and let the small notes flow naturally.

At a slow tempo, you can count nine eighth notes; at a fast tempo, counting three big beats is easier.

## Groups of Three

In 9/8, the nine eighth notes are usually divided into three groups of three.

The first note of each group is the start of that big beat and is a relatively heavy position.

In this way each bar has three big beats, and each big beat is equal to one dotted quarter note.

## 9/8 Summary

9/8 has nine eighth notes in each bar, usually divided into three groups, with three big beats per bar, each a dotted quarter note.

Like 3/4 it has three beats, but each beat is divided into three, so it sounds more flowing and swaying.

Counting the big beats, practising with a metronome, and paying attention to evenness and rise and fall can help us play pieces in 9/8 well.

## FAQ

**Q: How many eighth notes does one bar of 9/8 hold?**
A: Nine.

**Q: How is 9/8 usually grouped?**
A: Three groups of three eighth notes each.

**Q: How many big beats are there in each bar?**
A: Three big beats.

**Q: What is the difference between 9/8 and 3/4?**
A: In 9/8 each beat is divided into three, and in 3/4 each beat is usually divided into two.

**Q: Which work begins in 9/8?**
A: Debussy's Clair de lune.

paganini-caprice-24-variations-legacy.body:
The Italian violinist Paganini wrote twenty-four caprices for unaccompanied violin, published in Milan in 1820 as his Opus 1. The twenty-fourth is in A minor and consists of a short theme, eleven variations and a finale, using almost every difficult violin technique of the time. This short, strong theme later attracted many composers: Liszt, Brahms, Rachmaninoff, Lutosławski and others all wrote piano or orchestral works based on it. It is a vivid example of how one theme can inspire different creations.

## Brahms's variations

Around 1863, Brahms wrote a set of Variations on a Theme by Paganini, Op. 35, in two books.

These piano variations are technically very demanding, and Brahms called them "studies".

Each variation concentrates on practising one piano technique.

## The twenty-four caprices

Paganini's twenty-four caprices were written for solo violin, without accompaniment.

Each one focuses on showing off one or several techniques, such as spiccato bowing, double stops, and fast scales and arpeggios.

This set was published in Milan in 1820 as his Opus 1.

## Paganini's Caprice No. 24 summary

Niccolò Paganini was born in 1782 and died in 1840. His twenty-four unaccompanied caprices were published in Milan in 1820 as Opus 1. The twenty-fourth is in A minor; its theme is only twelve bars long, in two parts each repeated once, followed by eleven variations and a finale, using techniques such as fast scales, octaves, pizzicato and double stops.

Liszt's Grandes études de Paganini, No. 6, is adapted from it. Brahms wrote the two-book Op. 35 variations around 1863. Rachmaninoff wrote his rhapsody of twenty-four variations in 1934, and in the eighteenth variation turns the minor theme into a tender major melody by inversion. Lutosławski wrote variations for two pianos in 1941. On the piano you can play the theme, write variations and try an inversion.

You can ask Teacher Aum to talk you through the various ways of varying a theme.

## Playing this theme on the piano

You can first play the theme of Caprice No. 24 on the piano to become familiar with its melody and rhythm.

Then try writing a simple variation of your own, for example changing the rhythm or adding ornaments.

This is a good way to understand variation.

![Collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadqcer-1no6r.webp)

## The eleven variations

After the theme Paganini wrote eleven variations and a finale.

Each variation uses a different technique, such as fast scales, octaves, pizzicato and double stops.

These variations turn a simple theme into a display of technique.

**Before you begin**
- Paganini's twenty-four caprices, published in Milan in 1820
- No. 24 is in A minor, a theme and eleven variations
- Liszt, Brahms, Rachmaninoff and others took it as their theme
- One theme inspired many different creations

## The theme of No. 24

The theme of Caprice No. 24 is very short, only twelve bars, divided into two parts, each repeated once.

The theme is in A minor, with a strong rhythm and a simple melody that is easy to remember.

Precisely because it is simple, it can be changed into all kinds of different forms.

## Try an inversion

You can also try inverting the theme: find the direction of each note in the melody and turn it upside down.

Play the inverted melody and see how it sounds different.

Flip it upside down and the old theme puts on a new face.

## Comparing several variations

You can find works by Paganini, Liszt, Brahms and Rachmaninoff and compare them.

Notice what the same theme becomes in the hands of different composers.

This helps you understand the styles of different composers.

## Asking your teacher about variations on the Paganini theme in lessons

In lessons you can ask Teacher Aum to explain the various ways of varying this theme.

The scores of Liszt and Brahms are too difficult, so you can ask the teacher to find a simpler version first.

Starting from one theme, you can see the endless possibilities of variation.

## Lutosławski's two-piano version

In 1941, the Polish composer Lutosławski wrote a set of Variations on a Theme by Paganini for two pianos.

This work uses modern harmony, giving the old theme new colours.

Later he also arranged it as a version for piano and orchestra.

## Who was Paganini?

Niccolò Paganini (1782-1840) came from Genoa, Italy, and his skill on the violin was known to everyone at the time.

His technique amazed audiences of the time, and many had never heard violin playing like it.

All kinds of mysterious legends were told about him, but most of them were only people's exaggerated imaginings of his superb technique.

## The magic of inversion

Rachmaninoff's eighteenth variation uses a method called "inversion".

Inversion means turning a melody upside down: where it went up it now goes down, and where it went down it now goes up.

In this way a strong minor theme becomes a tender major melody.

## Rachmaninoff's rhapsody

In 1934, Rachmaninoff wrote the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini for piano and orchestra, made up of twenty-four variations.

Its eighteenth variation turns the theme upside down, becoming a lyrical, broad melody.

This variation is very moving and is often played on its own.

## Liszt's adaptation

When he was young, Liszt heard Paganini play and was deeply struck, resolving to reach the same technical heights on the piano.

He wrote a set of Grandes études de Paganini, adapting several of Paganini's caprices into piano pieces.

The sixth of them is adapted from Caprice No. 24.

## FAQ

**Q: In what year were Paganini's caprices published?**
A: 1820, in Milan.

**Q: How many variations does No. 24 have?**
A: Eleven variations and a finale.

**Q: What is the opus number of Brahms's variations?**
A: Op. 35.

**Q: In what year did Rachmaninoff write his rhapsody?**
A: 1934.

**Q: What method does the eighteenth variation use?**
A: Inversion.

music-course-price-communication.body:
When choosing a music course for a child or for themselves, almost every family weighs the price carefully. Many parents do not think it is too expensive; they simply cannot make sense of it: how much is one lesson, what does the package include, what happens if a lesson is missed, and are materials and exam fees charged separately? The vaguer the price explanation, the more parents hesitate, and they may even suspect hidden fees. For music studios and online courses, the goal of pricing communication is to let parents work out the cost before they decide and to understand what learning each charge corresponds to. Clear, transparent pricing is itself a trustworthy expression of the brand.

## Questions the Price Page Should Answer

- Basic fees: the price of a single lesson, a monthly payment or a term package
- What is included: lesson length, number of lessons, and whether materials or practice tools are included
- Extra costs: whether exams, performances, instrument rental and so on are charged separately
- Rescheduling and missed lessons: how much notice is needed and whether make-up lessons are possible
- Refund rules: how the amount is calculated if someone stops partway through
- Trial options: whether there is a trial lesson or a free trial period

Writing all this down clearly in one place cuts down on repeated enquiries and avoids disputes later.

## Talk About Value, Not Just Price

**Make the abstract concrete**
Instead of writing "professional teachers, quality teaching", explain what a student will learn in a month, for example "learn where five notes sit and play a short piece with both hands". When parents can see concrete learning results, it is easier for them to judge whether the price is reasonable.

Also, if the course offers practice reminders, recorded feedback or online Q&A, this support outside lessons is part of the value too and should be written into the explanation.

**Do not run down other providers in comparisons**
When describing your strengths, say only what you can do, and do not disparage other courses or studios. This is basic professional ethics, and it also avoids unnecessary legal risk.

![Cartoon illustration: a person with glasses and headphones playing an upright piano under a neon TIGA STUDIO sign](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw167rxk-1k8i6.webp)

## Keep Package Design Simple

Many studios launch lots of packages, which only makes it harder for parents to choose. In general, two or three options are enough: for example, pay by the month, pay by the term, and a short-term plan for those who want to try first. The difference between the options should be obvious at a glance, avoiding complicated stacked discounts and hard-to-follow rules. If there is a discount on a long-term package, also explain what happens if someone stops partway, so that parents do not give up for fear of being "locked in".

## Communicating When Prices Are Questioned

When a parent asks "why is it so expensive?", do not rush to defend yourself or cut the price. First find out what they really care about: is the budget limited, are they unsure whether the child will stick with it, or do they want to know how this differs from other ways of learning? For budget, you can introduce a shorter plan; for sticking with it, you can suggest a trial lesson or the trial period; for comparison, you can explain the specific content of the course instead of commenting on others. Patient communication often keeps a family better than a one-off discount.

## Use a Comparison Table to Help Choose

If the course has different plans, you can make a simple comparison table listing each plan's lessons, cost, who it suits and how flexible it is. The table does not need to be fancy; the point is that parents can see the differences within a minute. For example, a short-term plan suits families who want to try first, and a term plan suits students who have decided to learn for the long term. A comparison table is also handy for front desk staff and teachers during enquiries, so that everyone gives the same account and misunderstandings from different wording are reduced.

## Give Notice in Advance When Prices Change

When running costs change, course prices may need to be adjusted. Before adjusting, notify current student families in advance, explain the timing and the reasons, and offer a reasonable transition arrangement, for example honouring the original price for packages already bought until they expire. A sudden price rise seriously damages trust, while early, honest communication lets most families understand. A price-change notice can include:

- The date the new price takes effect
- The main reasons for the change, such as changes in venue or materials costs
- How packages already bought will be handled
- Who to contact with questions

## Price Information for Online Courses

Online courses and music apps also need transparent pricing: how long the free trial lasts, how much per month after the trial, how to cancel a subscription, and how long you can keep using it after cancelling. This information should sit near the subscribe button in clear wording, not be buried in long terms and conditions. When users see the rules clearly before paying, they feel more at ease afterwards too.

## FAQ

**Q: Should prices be published online?**
A: We recommend publishing prices or a price range so that parents have a rough expectation first, then settling on a specific plan through conversation.

**Q: Will a first-time sign-up offer upset existing students?**
A: You can also design a thank-you for existing students who renew or refer others, so that every family feels valued.

**Q: Should fees for missed lessons be refunded?**
A: Handle it according to rules announced in advance. The key is that the rules are clear and applied equally to everyone.

**Q: Is it all right to cut the price when a parent says it is too expensive?**
A: We do not recommend cutting prices casually. First find out the reason, then recommend a plan that suits them better.

music-studio-makeup-lesson-policy.body:
A music studio's make-up and absence rules are an agreement written for parents and students. They explain when a lesson can be missed, how much notice is needed, whether a make-up is possible, how make-ups are arranged and what happens when a teacher has to reschedule. Many studios rely on verbal agreements while they are small, and as student numbers grow, arguments appear such as "You allowed a make-up last time, so why not this time?" A clear written rule both protects the teacher's schedule and lets parents know their options in advance. The keys to good rules are fairness, simplicity and consistent application, together with a gentle tone when communicating them.

## Why Write It Down

The problem with verbal agreements is that everyone remembers a different version. A teacher may, out of kindness, give one extra make-up lesson once, and a parent will take that as the norm; another parent hears about it and makes the same request. Once rules are inconsistent, people easily feel things are unfair, and trust suffers.

**Written rules protect both sides**
Written rules give teachers something to go by when facing a request, so they do not have to judge on the spot every time; parents can also plan ahead and avoid misunderstandings caused by not knowing.

## What the Rules Should Spell Out

A practical make-up policy does not need to be long, but it should cover the most common situations:

- How far in advance absences must be notified, and by what means.
- How advance notice of absence and a last-minute absence are each handled.
- How make-ups are arranged: a fixed make-up slot, or a separately agreed time.
- The deadline by which a make-up must be completed.
- What students get when a teacher is ill or reschedules for some reason.
- How to handle special circumstances such as severe weather.

Write each point in simple sentences and avoid vague phrases such as "depending on the situation". If some flexibility really must be kept, say who decides and on what principle.

![An upright piano and wooden floor in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9pz4ot-c8odn.webp)

## Fair Does Not Mean Rigid

The purpose of rules is not to refuse, but to make sure everyone is treated consistently. When a family has a sudden emergency, the studio can still show care and offer options within what the rules allow, such as switching to an online lesson or providing a plan for independent practice. What matters is that the way exceptions are handled also follows principles and applies equally to everyone.

**Offer an alternative instead of a flat "no"**
When make-up places are full, rather than only saying a make-up is not possible, offer options: join a fixed small-group review session, take a set of after-lesson practice tasks, or complete specified practice in the app and have the teacher check it together at the next lesson.

## How to Publish and Communicate

Once the rules are written, how you communicate them matters just as much. When a new student enrols, send the rules as part of the welcome materials and ask the parent to confirm they have read them. When the rules are updated, give notice in advance, explain the reason for the change and give an effective date, rather than applying it suddenly.

- Provide the rules at enrolment and ask parents to confirm.
- Put the rules somewhere easy to find, such as a parent group announcement or a page on the website.
- When changing the rules, explain the reason and the effective date beforehand.
- Use a standard template when replying to absence messages, with a friendly tone.

**An idea for a reply template**
When an absence message arrives, first thank the person for letting you know in advance, then explain the make-up options and the time range, and finally remind them of a small exercise they can do at home. Three sentences are enough; no long explanation is needed.

## Review the Rules Once a Term

Rules are not fixed once written. At the end of each term, you can look back at the absences and make-ups of that period: which clauses often raise questions, which situations the rules did not cover, and whether teachers felt awkward in applying them. Make small changes based on these observations, and tell parents before the new term starts. Kept up over the long term, the rules will fit the studio's real situation better and better, and parents will also feel that the studio is willing to listen and sincerely improve.

## Use Digital Tools to Cut Back-and-Forth

Many studios use an online booking form or a shared calendar to arrange make-ups, letting parents pick free slots themselves and saving the time of talking to each one. Practice after lessons can also rely on an AI piano learning app such as TIGA ALPHA, so that a student who has asked for leave can keep up at home and not fall behind when they return. Tools are only an aid; rules and attitude are the foundation.

## FAQ

**Q: Can a last-minute absence also be made up?**
A: That depends on the studio's rules. A common approach is that absences notified in advance can be made up, while last-minute absences get practice tasks instead.

**Q: Must a make-up lesson be with the same teacher?**
A: Not necessarily. The rules can state whether make-ups with other teachers are allowed.

**Q: Will strict rules make parents unhappy?**
A: Rules that are clear, applied consistently and come with alternative options are usually easier for parents to accept than vague flexibility.

**Q: How should a teacher's absence be notified?**
A: Give as much notice as possible and explain the rescheduling or make-up arrangements, so parents have time to adjust their plans.

music-education-webinar-planning-flow.body:
A music education webinar is a themed talk that an organisation holds through a video conferencing platform for parents, students or potential users, for example "How to Support Your Child's Practice" or "How Adults Can Start Learning Piano". The talk is mainly about sharing knowledge, letting participants learn about the organisation's teaching philosophy without pressure. A well-designed talk both helps participants solve real problems and builds trust naturally, laying the groundwork for later course enquiries.

## Choosing a Topic: Start from Real Questions

Good talk topics come from users' real questions. An organisation can gather the questions parents often ask in enquiries, or run a simple survey in its community group to see what everyone cares about.

- What age is best to start learning piano.
- How parents who do not know music can support a child's practice.
- How long a complete adult beginner needs to practise each day.
- How to choose between a digital piano and an acoustic piano.

The topic should be specific, not too broad. A title such as "The Meaning of Music Education" is hard to cover clearly in an hour, while "Five Small Ways to Support Your Child's Practice" is more likely to leave people with something useful.

## Preparing the Content

We suggest keeping the talk between forty-five minutes and an hour, with ten to fifteen minutes set aside for answering questions. The content can have a simple, clear structure: first state the problem, then share methods, and finally give a small exercise they can try straight away.

**Add live demonstrations**
The advantage of a music talk is that you can demonstrate live. The teacher can demonstrate a practice method on the piano, or compare two different ways of playing. A contrast you can hear is often more direct than a written explanation.

## Do Not Neglect Technical Preparation

The sound quality of an online talk directly affects the experience. Test in advance how the microphone and the piano pick up sound, making sure the sound is clear and undistorted. We suggest having an assistant to manage the chat, deal with technical problems and note down questions.

![A modern piano in cool-toned lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw7382gk-o4k9g.webp)

Open the room ten minutes before the official start, play soft piano music, and show the talk's topic and start time on screen. These details make participants feel welcome.

## Hosting and Interaction

When hosting, slow down your pace and use plenty of concrete examples. About every fifteen minutes, you can invite participants to answer a simple question in the chat, such as "When does your child practise each day?" Interaction keeps attention and also lets the teacher understand the participants' situations.

When answering questions, if you meet one that can only be answered by learning about the individual, you can invite that person to talk separately after the session, rather than giving a vague answer in public.

## Following Up After the Talk

After the talk, within a day or two you can send participants a thank-you email with a summary of the key points and a link to the recording. If the organisation has a relevant course, you can introduce it briefly at the end of the email and say how to enquire. Keep the introduction to one paragraph, with no pushy wording.

**Respect participants' choices**
Some participants just want to learn something and do not plan to sign up for a course. Respect their choice and do not send promotional messages frequently. The value of a talk lies in sharing, and once trust is built, those who need it will get in touch naturally.

## How to Evaluate a Talk

The pacing of a talk also needs to be rehearsed beforehand. The teacher can ask colleagues to play the participants and run through the whole process, checking that the time allocation is sensible, that the sound in the demonstration section is clear and that the question section runs smoothly. Problems found in rehearsal can usually be avoided in the real talk, so that participants experience something smooth and professional.

A few things to watch: participant attendance, interaction during the talk, feedback in a post-talk survey, and enquiries over the following period. Do not look only at the number of course sign-ups, because the effect of a talk is often long-term.

The questions collected are also a valuable resource. They can serve as topics for the next talk or be turned into an FAQ article.

## FAQ

**Q: Should the talk be paid?**
A: Most introductory talks suit being free, while in-depth specialist talks can be considered for a fee.

**Q: What if few people attend?**
A: With fewer people there is more room for interaction, so you can run it as a small discussion session.

**Q: Can the talk be recorded?**
A: Yes, but tell participants in advance and be careful about personal information in the chat.

**Q: How often is it right to hold one?**
A: Monthly or quarterly are both fine. The key is to keep the content quality up.

**Q: Can I invite parents of students to share too?**
A: Yes. Real experiences are often very popular, but agree the content with them beforehand.

**Q: Can the content of the talk be reused?**
A: It can be turned into articles or short videos to extend the value of the talk.

music-licensing-buyout-vs-subscription.body:
Videos, podcasts, online courses and shop promo films almost all need background music. Using copyrighted songs directly may infringe copyright, so music library services have appeared on the market that provide licensed music for creators and businesses. These services follow roughly two business models: one is a one-off buyout of the right to use a particular track, and the other is a monthly or annual subscription that lets you use the whole library during the subscription. Neither model is absolutely better. What matters is the user's needs, how long the work will be in use and how musicians earn their income. Understanding the two models helps creators choose music legally and lets musicians see how their work can reach the market.

## The Basic Differences Between the Two Models

- One-off buyout: pay once for a track and use it long term within the agreed scope
- Subscription library: pay per period and use a large number of tracks during the subscription
- Scope of licence: both models specify the platforms, uses and regions allowed
- Differences in duration: some subscription licences cover only works published during the subscription, and new works after cancelling cannot use the music

## Who a One-Off Buyout Suits

If you only need a piece of music occasionally, for example choosing a track for a brand promo film or an event video, a one-off buyout is usually less hassle. You pay once and use it according to the licence terms, without worrying about monthly fees. The drawback is that every new track needs a new payment, and the cost builds up with heavy long-term use. Before buying out, read the terms carefully: whether commercial use is allowed, whether you can publish on multiple platforms and whether editing and adaptation are allowed. All these details affect later use.

![A cyberpunk bird's-eye illustration of a person with their back to the viewer playing a black grand piano on a rainy street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw163sob-twc28.webp)

## Who a Subscription Library Suits

**Frequent creators**
For creators who publish several videos every week, a subscription makes choosing music flexible, with no need to buy separately each time.

**Teams that need a consistent style**
A brand content team can choose music of a similar style from the same library, so that all its work sounds more consistent.

**What to watch for**
Works published during the subscription can usually stay up, but the rules differ from service to service. Before cancelling, confirm whether the licence for published content is still valid, to avoid being flagged by a platform later.

## What It Means for Musicians

For musicians, the two models also pay differently. Under the buyout model, musicians often receive a one-off payment when a work is chosen, or a share of sales; under the subscription model, the platform may first pay the musician a production fee and then share income according to plays or usage. Before joining any library, musicians should read the contract for copyright ownership, exclusivity clauses and how income is calculated, and consult a professional familiar with copyright if necessary.

## Practical Steps for Creators Choosing Music

First think clearly about which platforms the video will be published on, whether it will be used for commercial promotion and how long it is expected to be in use; then compare the terms of several services against these conditions, not just their prices. When you download music, keep proof of the licence, such as a licence certificate or order record, and put it in one folder. If a platform raises a copyright question, this proof helps you explain the situation quickly.

## Music Educators Can Learn from This Too

Music teachers making teaching videos also run into the question of background music. The simplest approach is to play public-domain pieces yourself, or use a short melody of your own, which avoids licensing trouble and also shows your teaching style. When you need to use a pop song, find out the platform's rules on cover versions and teaching use.

## A Simple Licensing Checklist

- On which platforms and in which regions the music will be used
- Whether it is used for advertising, selling products or other commercial purposes
- Whether it needs to be edited, sped up or mixed with other sounds
- Where the proof of licence is kept and who is responsible for managing it
- How long the licence lasts and how published works are handled after it expires

Write these items at the start of each project, and team members are less likely to miss key questions when choosing music, which also reduces the trouble of taking works down or changing them later.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I use music freely as long as I credit the source?**
A: No. Crediting the source is not the same as having a licence, and you must still follow the rights holder's licence conditions.

**Q: Will earlier videos have problems after I cancel?**
A: It depends on the terms of service. Before subscribing, confirm the licence status of published works after cancellation.

**Q: Can I use recordings of public-domain music freely too?**
A: Not necessarily. The piece itself may be in the public domain, but a particular recording may still be protected.

**Q: Does a small shop playing music need a licence?**
A: Playing music in a public place usually involves the right of public performance, so we suggest finding out the requirements from your local copyright body.

organ-stops-change-tone-color.body:
Organ stops are, simply put, a set of tone-colour switches. A pipe organ contains many rows of pipes. Each row is called a rank, and the pipes within one rank are similar in shape and material, so they produce a consistent tone. When the player pulls out a stop, the air path to the matching rank opens, and that row of pipes sounds when a key is pressed; push the stop back in and the rank stays silent. By choosing different stops, or combining several stops together, the same key can produce all kinds of sounds: soft, bright, thick or nasal.

## Many pipes behind one key

On a piano, one key usually corresponds to one set of strings, while on an organ one key can correspond to many pipes, one in each rank. Beneath the keyboard is a system of bellows and valves: the key decides "which note", and the stop decides "which ranks". Only when both are open does air flow into a particular pipe.

This design makes an organ something like many instruments built into one body. The player does not need to change instruments; changing stops is enough to change the colour of a whole passage.

## Flue pipes: sounding like blowing a flute

Most pipes are flue pipes. Air blows in from the foot of the pipe, hits the edge of a narrow slit at the mouth and sets up a vibration, and the column of air inside the pipe body then determines the pitch. The principle is similar to blowing a recorder, so flue pipes generally sound rounder and steadier.

**The difference between wide and narrow pipes**
Among flue pipes, those with a wider body usually sound softer and more flute-like; those with a narrower body bring out more overtones and sound brighter, a bit like string instruments. Whether the top of the pipe is closed also changes the tone and the pitch.

## Reed pipes: making a reed vibrate

The other major family is reed pipes. Inside the foot is a metal reed that vibrates rapidly as air flows past, and the resonating tube above shapes the sound. Reed pipes generally sound more edgy, can come close to wind instruments such as the trumpet or oboe, and are often used for melodies that need to stand out.

- Flue pipes: sound produced by air striking the edge of the mouth; rounder tone.
- Reed pipes: sound produced by a vibrating reed; more penetrating tone.
- Pipe shape: width, length and whether the top is closed all affect the tone.
- Rank: a whole row of pipes of the same design, corresponding to one stop.

![Close-up of piano keys](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8ag5z3-9zayl.webp)

## What the "feet" on a stop mean

On the knobs of many stops you will see a number followed by a foot mark, such as 8', 4' or 16'. This is the traditional way of indicating pitch position. An 8' rank sounds at the pitch written on the keyboard; a 4' rank has pipes about half as long and sounds an octave higher; a 16' rank sounds an octave lower.

If the player pulls out the 8' and 4' stops together, pressing one key sounds both the original note and the note an octave above, and the sound immediately becomes brighter and clearer. Add the 16' and the bass gains more weight.

**Mutation stops**
Some ranks are not arranged in octaves but are aimed at the position of a particular overtone. Heard alone they may sound a little strange, but combined with the foundation ranks they give the overall tone a distinctive sheen.

## Combining stops is like mixing colours

Choosing stops is often compared to a painter mixing paint. A few stops suit quiet passages, with a clear, transparent sound; adding more ranks step by step increases volume and thickness together, suiting climaxes. The player decides on a specific combination according to the style of the piece, the echo of the building and the audience of the day.

Experienced players also watch the balance: add too many reeds and the melody may be covered; make the bass ranks too heavy and the harmony turns muddy. A good combination is often not about having more, but about each layer having its own role.

## What this suggests for piano learners

A piano has no stops, but those who play it can also think about "choosing a tone colour". The same chord, played with a light touch and little pedal, is like pulling out just one soft flue stop; played with full weight and sustain, it is like combining several ranks. In practice you can label each section with an imagined tone colour, such as "like a flute" or "like brass", and then use touch and pedal to come closer to that effect.

## Hearing stops change in a space

The same set of stops sounds very different in different buildings. In a large, open, high space the echo is long, and when several ranks are combined the sound blends slowly in the air, so players often need to slow down to give the harmony time to spread. In a smaller, drier space the echo is short and details are clearer, and the player may choose a brighter combination so the sound carries farther. For this reason, organists usually spend a good deal of time testing before a formal performance, playing while a companion walks around the audience area listening, and then adjusting the combination of stops. This habit of adjusting the sound to the space is also a useful reference for piano learners: a piece practised in a small room at home needs to be listened to again and its touch and pedalling adjusted when you move to the performance venue.

## FAQ

**Q: Do electronic organs have stops too?**
A: Many electronic organs imitate the way stops work, using buttons or tabs to choose different combinations of tone colours.

**Q: Are more stops always better?**
A: More stops mean richer choices, but whether the sound is good depends on whether the combination is suitable and on the performance space.

**Q: Do piano learners need to know about the organ?**
A: Not necessarily, but understanding the idea of layering tone colours helps you think about different layers of sound on the piano.

**Q: Can the pitch of an organ be adjusted at any time?**
A: The pitch of a pipe is determined by its body and needs regular tuning by professionals; it is not normally changed at will during a performance.

music-brand-community-ambassador-program.body:
A community ambassador programme is a way for a music brand to invite enthusiastic learners, parents or long-time users to take part, in a formal but relaxed role, in community sharing, welcoming newcomers and organising small events. Its core is not to have ambassadors sell, but to give people who genuinely love learning music a chance to share their experience. For music studios, online courses and music apps, a well-designed ambassador programme can make the community warmer and help new users find a sense of belonging sooner.

## How Ambassadors Differ from Ordinary Referrals

An ordinary referral campaign usually looks only at "how many new users were brought in". An ambassador programme cares more about long-term participation: ambassadors answer new learners' questions in the community, share their own practice methods, and help organise online practice check-ins or in-person sharing sessions. They are part of the community, not an outside promotion channel.

**A clear role lasts longer**
Before starting, the brand must spell out the scope of the ambassador's duties, for example taking part in one event a month and welcoming new members in the community. When duties are simple and clear, ambassadors do not feel overburdened, nor do they mistakenly think they must take on sales tasks.

## How to Choose Suitable Ambassadors

Suitable ambassadors usually share a few traits: lasting enthusiasm for learning music, a willingness to help others, and a friendly way of expressing themselves in the community. When choosing, do not look only at how active someone is, but also at whether their way of communicating makes people comfortable.

- Learners or parents who have long taken part in lessons or used the product.
- Members who have naturally helped others in the community.
- People who can respect learners of different levels and ages.
- People willing to follow the brand's communication principles and privacy rules.

When inviting, you can talk one to one, explain the programme and give the person plenty of time to think. The invited person has the right to decline, and declining does not affect their existing learning service.

## Designing the Rewards

Ambassadors give their time, so the brand should give suitable rewards in return. Rewards can be support with lessons, such as joining a special workshop or receiving exclusive practice materials, or symbolic thanks, such as a handwritten thank-you card or public thanks at an annual event.

![City night scene with lights and streets](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw732xc0-r48e4.webp)

**Transparency matters more than generosity**
If an ambassador receives a reward for sharing in public, the relationship between the two should be clearly disclosed. This respects readers and also protects the credibility of the ambassador and the brand. Do not let ambassadors post exaggerated claims, and do not require them to use fixed promotional wording.

## Examples of Event Formats

There are many events ambassadors can take part in; here are a few common ones that are easy to carry out:

- Welcome session for new learners: ambassadors introduce the community rules and commonly used resources.
- Online practice check-ins: ambassadors lead by sharing their weekly practice notes.
- Repertoire sharing sessions: an ambassador picks a piece and talks about their practice process.
- Parents' exchange time: parent ambassadors share their experience of accompanying children in practice.

Events do not need to be large; a small sharing session of a dozen or so people often feels more like a real exchange than a big event.

## Communication Principles and Risk Management

The brand needs to prepare a concise communication guide for ambassadors, saying what can be shared and what is not suitable to share. For example, do not make other learners' personal information public, do not promise learning results, and do not make comparative judgements about other organisations. When complaints or sensitive issues arise, the person should be guided to contact staff, rather than the ambassador handling it alone.

Regular communication with ambassadors matters too. Each quarter you can hold a short online meeting to hear their suggestions and learn the real needs in the community. This feedback often helps the brand find directions for improving the product or courses.

## How to Evaluate the Programme

Evaluating an ambassador programme should not look only at the number of new people. You can watch whether questions in the community get timely replies, whether new members take part more, and whether feedback on events is positive. A short survey can also show whether new learners feel welcome. Data has to be read together with real conversations to see the full picture.

## FAQ

**Q: Do ambassadors need to sign a contract?**
A: You can use a simple written statement that sets out duties, rewards and how to leave.

**Q: Can underage learners be ambassadors?**
A: Parental consent is needed, they should take part only in age-appropriate activities, and their personal information needs special protection.

**Q: Can ambassadors work for other brands at the same time?**
A: You can agree this in advance; the point is to stay transparent and avoid misleading community members.

**Q: Should the programme have a fixed term?**
A: We suggest half a year or a year per term, after which both sides decide whether to continue.

one-hand-legato-other-hand-staccato.body:
In many pieces, the right hand plays a smooth melody while the left hand plays a light staccato accompaniment, or the other way round, with the left hand legato and the right hand staccato. Using different touches in the two hands at the same time is not easy for many learners: often one hand bounces and the other follows it, or one hand connects and the other connects too. This ability needs dedicated practice, but once you have it, the layers in your music become much clearer.

## Do Not Press Too Hard in the Staccato Hand

The hand playing staccato often presses too hard out of tension, and the sound becomes harsh.

Staccato should be light, like a little ball bouncing off the keys.

Keep the wrist relaxed and use small movements to play staccato.

## Summary of Different Touches in Each Hand

Many pieces need one hand legato and the other staccato. The brain tends to make both hands do the same thing, so they easily influence each other and dedicated practice is needed. First practise each hand's touch separately, then combine the hands slowly with a simple pattern.

Once you are comfortable, swap the touches between the hands, then return to the piece, slowly first and then faster. The staccato hand should be light and relaxed, and the legato hand should keep the connections between notes unbroken. You usually practise without the pedal, check each hand separately with your ears and with recordings, and gradually increase the speed, the chords and the rhythmic difficulty.

To find out whether your two hands' touches are truly separate, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen, and you can also ask the teacher to recommend suitable short pieces.

## Keep the Legato Hand Connected

The hand playing legato must keep hold of its keys while the other hand bounces up.

Pay special attention to the join between each pair of notes, and make sure there is no break.

You can put more of your attention on the legato hand, because it is the one more easily "led astray".

## Swapping the Touches Between Hands

After you are comfortable with right-hand legato and left-hand staccato, swap them: right-hand staccato and left-hand legato.

This lets both hands learn both touches and improves their independence.

After swapping, one side is often clearly awkward. Give that side a few more rounds.

## Start with a Very Simple Pattern

When combining the hands, start with a very simple pattern instead of playing the piece directly.

For example, the right hand plays C, D, E, F, G legato, and the left hand plays C, C, C, C, C staccato.

That way, your attention can go entirely to the difference in touch.

## Why the Two Hands Influence Each Other

When the brain controls two hands, it tends to make them do the same thing.

So when one hand bounces up, the other hand easily leaves the keys as well.

This is perfectly natural and needs practice to make the two hands independent.

## Ask Your Teacher to Check Your Touches in the Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and tell you whether your two hands' touches are really separate.

The teacher can also recommend short pieces or studies suited to practising this skill.

The ability to use the hands independently is the foundation for playing many pieces well.

## Back to the Piece

After you have it down with the simple pattern, go back to the piece.

First choose the section that needs different touches in the two hands, and combine the hands slowly.

Again, slow first and then faster, making sure the touches in the two hands stay different.

## Common Situations in Pieces

In classical short pieces, the right hand often plays a smooth melody while the left hand plays detached bass notes or chords.

In some dances, the left hand is a staccato accompaniment and the right hand is a legato melody.

Sometimes the right hand has a staccato figure and the left hand has legato long notes.

## Listen to the Legato Hand and the Staccato Hand Separately

When practising, listen carefully with your ears: is the melody smooth? Is the staccato clear?

You can record your playing and listen to each hand separately on playback.

If one hand's sound does not meet the requirement, practise that hand again.

![A person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwac1yqw-k5k1h.webp)

## Combine the Hands Slowly

When combining the hands with a simple pattern, the tempo must be very slow.

On every note, watch what each hand is doing: is the right hand still connecting, and is the left hand bouncing?

If you notice they are influencing each other, stop and practise the hands separately again.

## Increase the Difficulty Gradually

When the basic combination is comfortable, you can gradually make it harder, for example by speeding up, adding chords or changing the rhythm.

You can also practise one hand legato and the other non-legato, or one hand staccato and the other holding a long note.

These exercises make the independence of your hands better and better.

## A Note on the Pedal

In this kind of practice, you usually should not use the sustain pedal.

The pedal makes the staccato notes run together too, and then you cannot hear the difference between the touches in the two hands.

Once the independence of your hands is well developed, decide whether to use the pedal according to what the piece needs.

## Practise Each Hand's Touch Separately First

The first step in practice is to practise each hand's touch separately.

Practise legato alone in the right hand, making the melody smooth and rounded, and practise staccato alone in the left hand, making each note light and clear.

**Tip**

Only start combining the hands once each hand's touch is steady on its own.

- Both hands use different touches at the same time
- Common: right-hand legato melody, left-hand staccato accompaniment
- They easily "infect" each other
- Needs dedicated practice in steps

## FAQ

**Q: Why do the two hands influence each other?**
A: The brain tends to make both hands do the same thing.

**Q: What is the first step in practice?**
A: Practise each hand's touch separately.

**Q: What should I use first when combining the hands?**
A: A very simple pattern.

**Q: Why not use the pedal when practising?**
A: The pedal makes the staccato notes run together too.

**Q: Which hand is more easily "led astray"?**
A: The legato hand.

music-studio-teacher-profile-page.body:
A music school's teacher profile page is the main way parents and students get to know a teacher before enrolling. A good profile does not need flowery adjectives; it needs to answer the few questions parents care about most: what this teacher teaches, who they are suited to teach, what the lessons are like, and what experience can be verified. When it is written honestly and specifically, parents feel after reading that they already have a first impression of the teacher, and it is easier to build trust at the first meeting. If it is vague or exaggerated, it makes people suspicious instead.

## The Basic Content of a Profile Page

- The teacher's name and a clear, natural photo
- The main instruments taught and the student ages they suit
- Teaching experience, such as how many years they have taught and what levels of student they have mainly taught
- Verifiable training background or certificates, if there are any
- A paragraph about teaching approach, written in the teacher's own voice
- Available lesson times and the lesson location

The content does not need to be long all at once; it is enough to make each item clear.

## Use Specifics Instead of Adjectives

Words like "patient, professional, experienced" are written by almost every teacher, and parents who read many of them find it hard to tell them apart. A more effective way is to give specific practices, such as "in the first lesson I ask the student to play a piece they know, to see their hand shape and reading habits", or "at the end of each lesson I write a practice sheet telling the student what to practise at home". Such descriptions let parents picture the lesson, and are more convincing than adjectives.

## Photos and Video

**Photos should be natural**
Choose photos of the teacher in the practice room, beside the piano, in bright light with a relaxed expression. Avoid heavy retouching, so that parents find the teacher consistent with the photo when they meet.

**A short video is more direct**
A video of about a minute, in which the teacher briefly introduces themselves and then plays a short piece, lets parents hear the teacher's tone of voice and the sound of their playing.

**Respect student privacy**
If students appear in the video, you must get the parents' consent beforehand, and avoid showing the student's full name and school.

![A person wearing headphones and glasses practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3f1lp0-zhk7f.webp)

## Writing the Teaching Approach Paragraph

This paragraph can be written by the teacher in the first person, in a tone like chatting with parents. You can write why you enjoy teaching piano, what you value most in lessons, and what you do when a student does not want to practise. Real thoughts move people more than standard answers. After writing it, ask a colleague to read it and see whether there is any jargon that is too technical for parents to understand.

## Phrasing to Avoid

**Do not exaggerate results**
Do not write numbers with no source, such as "a very high pass rate in grade exams", and do not use ranking-style or absolute statements.

**Do not compare with others**
The profile page only introduces yourself; it does not judge other teachers or other schools.

**Do not promise outcomes**
Progress in piano differs from person to person; do not write promises such as "you will definitely be able to play a certain piece in a few months".

## Check It Every Six Months

A teacher's experience and teaching focus change over time. You can check the profile page every six months, updating the photo, lesson times and new teaching content. If the teacher starts a new course, such as adult pop piano or parent-and-child music, add it promptly, so that what parents see is always up to date.

## A Short Example

You can take something like this as a model: "I started piano as a child, and began teaching children in the community while at university. In lessons I first listen to the student play a passage, and then we decide together on a small goal for the week. I like to add a little improvisation to lessons, letting students make up a melody of their own from a few notes." A paragraph like this is simple and specific, and after reading it parents can picture the lesson.

## Linking the Profile to the Enquiry Process

At the end of the profile you can put a simple way to enquire, such as "to find out about lesson arrangements, you can first book a meeting for a chat". After reading the profile, a parent who is interested can contact you directly. During enquiries, reception staff can also first ask parents to look at the teacher profile, and then introduce a suitable teacher according to the student's needs, which makes communication smoother.

## FAQ

**Q: Does a teacher profile need to state academic qualifications?**
A: You can, but it is not required. Rather than qualifications, parents often care more about the teacher's teaching approach and the type of student they suit.

**Q: How should a new teacher with little experience write the profile?**
A: Write more about your teaching philosophy and specific practices, and about your own experience of learning piano; a sincere description can move parents just as well.

**Q: How many words should a profile use?**
A: A few hundred words is enough; together with photos and a short video, parents can read it in a few minutes.

**Q: Can we include student reviews?**
A: Yes, but get consent beforehand and keep the original words, without changing or exaggerating them.

**Q: Should the profile pages of several teachers have a uniform style?**
A: The layout can be uniform, which makes it easier for parents to compare; the content should keep each teacher's own voice and character.

**Q: Does a profile page need both Chinese and English versions?**
A: If the school has families from different language backgrounds, you can prepare several language versions so every family can understand.

music-studio-review-invitation-timing.body:
When a family is considering music lessons, they often start by looking at what others say. Reviews are therefore very helpful to a music studio's local reputation. But if a parent is reminded again and again to "go and leave a good review" right after a trial lesson, what they feel is not that they are valued but that they are being hurried. Inviting a review is a piece of communication that needs designing: it should happen after the person has had a real experience, and it should always leave them free to decline.

## Why Reviews Deserve to Be Taken Seriously

Public reviews add information that is hard to see in the official introduction, such as how the teacher explains homework, whether the front desk replies promptly, and whether the classroom is easy to find. Inside the studio, reviews are also a source of feedback and can be read alongside post-lesson questionnaires. Taking them seriously does not mean treating the rating as an enrolment target. Put your energy into teaching good lessons and writing clear communication, and reviews are more likely to appear naturally.

## When Is a Good Time to Ask

A safer moment is when the person has completed an experience they can describe, and their mood at the time is calm. For example: after several lessons, after a public recital is over and everyone has left, or when a parent says unprompted, "we find it very clear here". The following moments are usually not suitable:

- Just after a trial lesson ends, while the person is still putting on their shoes at the door.
- Right when you have just dealt with a complaint or a rescheduling dispute.
- In the middle of a conversation about renewing, paying an extra fee, or agreeing rules for absences.
- When a child has just felt frustrated or nervous in class.

If you are not sure, you can first ask, "If it suits you, may we invite you later to say a few words about how the lessons feel?", leaving the decision with them. If there is no response, do not ask again within a short time.

## How to Word the Invitation Without Pressure

A written invitation should be short, specific and have no conditions attached. You can say which aspects you would like them to share, such as "whether booking went smoothly, or whether your child understands what to practise at home", and attach the link to the review page. Do not hint that a review has anything to do with lesson scheduling, discounts or the teacher's attitude.

![A futuristic piano in soft lighting](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwfgpsqi-2yg12.webp)

- **Do not specify a score**: do not write what star rating or wording you hope to see.
- **Do not set a deadline**: a review is not homework and does not need to be done by a certain day.
- **Offer a private channel**: someone who only wants to tell the studio their views should also be given an email address or a form.
- **Once is enough**: for the same learning experience, one invitation is enough. If you use automatic reminders from a system, they should be possible to switch off, and sent very rarely.

An example of wording: "If you would like to write about how the lessons feel for families who come after you, you can leave a few lines on this page; if it is not convenient, just ignore this message." Written like this, declining is already treated as a normal option.

## Where Reviews Are Posted and Who Decides

Some families are happy to write on a map or local search page, some on the studio's website, and some only want private conversation. When inviting, you can list the possible places and let them choose, and not ask for the same text to be posted on many platforms. Reviews involving children need extra care: do not ask in the invitation for photos showing faces or identifiable names, and remind parents to avoid writing the child's full name or school before posting publicly.

If the studio also uses online practice tools, for example introducing students to an AI piano teaching app such as TIGA ALPHA, the review invitation should separate the in-person lessons from the app experience, so people write only about what they have really used, and later readers do not confuse the two services.

## What to Do After a Review Arrives

Whether it is praise or criticism, it deserves to be seen. Public reviews should be handled according to the studio's existing reply principles: say thank you, respond specifically to the points raised, and move anything needing follow-up to private conversation. Views received privately should go into internal records and be discussed regularly, rather than only keeping the nice sentences for promotion. If you want to quote a review on your website, you must get the person's consent again and handle the credit as they ask.

Do not pick only the most appealing sentences to make a poster. Doing so makes later families feel the reviews are incomplete. If there are few reviews on public channels to begin with, it is better to first write the course descriptions and FAQs more clearly than to keep asking for them.

## Do Not Fixate on the Score

Scores fluctuate, and one review represents only one experience. A studio can look at this in a steadier way:

- Look at which themes recur across different reviews, rather than only at how high the scores are.
- Look at whether you have already improved on the problems raised.
- Look at whether the invitation process made anyone uncomfortable.

When you write "asking for reviews" into your service process, also write "respect the choice not to review". What later readers can trust is often not a screen full of good reviews but clear rules and opinions that are taken seriously.

## FAQ

**Q: Can we invite a review right after a trial lesson?**
A: A safer approach is to wait until they have gone home, and ideally until they have taken a few more lessons and have a real feel for the process. On the day of the trial you can at most ask whether they would be willing to be invited later, without pointing to the review page on the spot.

**Q: Can we offer a small gift in exchange for a review?**
A: We do not recommend it. A material reward makes it hard for later readers to judge whether the review is independent, and it may make the person invited feel awkward.

**Q: If a parent writes an unhappy review, do we still reply publicly?**
A: Yes, and move any details needing verification to private communication. In the public reply, avoid arguing and avoid writing any identifiable student information.

**Q: Can a child write a review themselves?**
A: For public content involving minors, a guardian should decide whether to publish, and details that could identify the child should be avoided.

**Q: Can staff write it for them and ask the parent to confirm?**
A: That is not appropriate. A review should be written by the person who had the experience, in their own words; the studio may at most explain where to post it.

oblique-motion-one-voice-holds.body:
When two voices move at the same time, their relationship can take several forms. If they travel in the same direction, it is called similar motion. If they travel in opposite directions, it is called contrary motion. If one voice stays still while the other moves, it is called oblique motion. Oblique motion is very common in piano music, for example when the left hand holds a long note while the right-hand melody moves above it. It gives the music a steady foundation and a flowing line at the same time.

## Finding Oblique Motion in the Score

Choose a piece you know well and look for places where one voice holds while the other moves.

Mark those places and think about why the composer wrote them that way.

This kind of analysis helps us understand the relationship between voices more clearly.

## Oblique Motion in One Hand

Sometimes oblique motion appears within a single hand, for instance when the right thumb holds one note while the other fingers play the melody.

This asks for a certain amount of finger independence.

When practising, start slowly. Make sure the holding finger stays still while the other fingers move in a relaxed way.

## Hold a Low C and Play a Scale

Try this at the piano: hold a low C with your left hand, and play a scale with your right hand, up from C and then back down.

Listen to how the interval between the two voices changes.

Then try the reverse: hold a high note with the right hand and move the left hand upward from below, and compare the two effects.

## Oblique Motion at a Glance

Oblique motion means one voice holds still while the other moves. It is the counterpart of similar and contrary motion.

It is often found in a melody over a pedal bass, but it can also be the other way round, with the upper voice holding and the lower voice moving, combining stability with flow.

When you play it, the held note must truly be held and the moving voice must be clear. Finding it in the score and trying it at the piano will help you understand it better.

## Holding Notes While You Play

When you play oblique motion, the held note must really be held. Do not release it early.

If you hold it with a finger, be careful not to tense your hand. If you hold it with the pedal, be careful that the moving voice does not become blurred.

Sometimes you will need half pedalling or finger holding to keep the moving voice clear.

## Melody over a Pedal Bass

A very common kind of oblique writing in piano pieces is a long note held in the bass while a tune moves back and forth above it in the treble.

This unmoving bass note is called a pedal point or a pedal bass.

It acts like a steady foundation, leaving the melody above free to move.

## Ways Voices Can Move

In harmony and counterpoint, the movement between two voices can be divided into several types.

When two voices go in the same direction, it is similar motion. When they go in opposite directions, it is contrary motion.

When one voice stays still and the other moves, it is oblique motion.

## Combining with Other Types of Motion

In real music, oblique motion often alternates with similar and contrary motion.

Composers choose different types of motion according to what the music needs.

Understanding these types helps us hear the line of each voice in the music more clearly.

![Close-up of grand piano keys and a golden patterned lid in warm light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5tzwk-cgnqg.webp)

## Relationship to Non-Chord Tones

In oblique motion, the moving voice often creates non-chord tones, such as passing notes or neighbour notes.

Because one voice stays still, each change in the other voice forms a different interval with it, sometimes consonant and sometimes dissonant.

These changes give the music subtle colour.

## When the Upper Voice Holds

Oblique motion does not have to mean a stationary bass. The upper voice can hold while the lower voice moves.

For example, the right hand holds a high note while the left-hand bass steps downward.

This kind of writing often creates a feeling of anticipation, as if waiting for something to change.

## What Oblique Motion Looks Like

On the page, oblique motion looks like one voice written as a long note or a repeated note, while the other voice moves up and down.

For example, the bass keeps holding C while the upper voice goes from E to F and then to G.

The interval between the two voices keeps changing, but one of them stays in place throughout.

## An Example in Studies

Many studies are designed to train this holding and moving within a single hand.

For example, one finger holds a key down while the other fingers play in turn.

This kind of practice helps the fingers become more independent and more flexible.

## The Effect of Oblique Motion

Oblique motion combines stability and flow.

The voice that stays still provides a sense of steadiness, and the voice that moves provides change and direction.

That is why oblique motion is often used in places that call for quietness, breadth or tension.

## In Pop Accompaniment

Oblique motion is also often used in pop piano accompaniment.

For example, the left hand holds a bass note while the right-hand chords change above it, from C to F and back to C.

**Practice order**

This kind of writing gives the accompaniment a feeling of being both steady and changing.

**Remember this**
- One voice holds still while the other moves
- It is the counterpart of similar and contrary motion
- It is common in a melody over a pedal bass
- It combines stability with flow

## FAQ

**Q: What is oblique motion?**
A: One voice holds still while the other moves.

**Q: What is similar motion?**
A: Two voices move in the same direction.

**Q: What is contrary motion?**
A: Two voices move in opposite directions.

**Q: What effect does oblique motion have?**
A: It combines stability with flow.

**Q: What should I watch for when playing it?**
A: The held note must truly be held.

music-course-refund-policy-wording.body:
Before signing up, parents often quietly wonder about one thing: what happens if my child does not settle in, or something comes up at home? A clearly written refund and rescheduling policy can answer that question before sign-up. A policy is not meant to put up obstacles; it lets everyone know the rules, so there are fewer misunderstandings later.

## State the principle first, then the details

At the start of the policy, you can use two or three sentences to explain the overall idea, for example: the studio wants students to learn with peace of mind and also wants teachers' time to be respected, so refunds and rescheduling are handled according to the rules below. That way the reader feels goodwill first and then reads the rules.

**Write in everyday words**
Avoid overly complicated sentences. If you can write "Please let us know the day before the lesson", do not write "Notice must be given in writing no less than twenty-four hours before the lesson".

**Put the key points first**
What parents care about most is usually: can I get a refund, how much, and by when do I need to apply? These three points should appear in the most prominent place.

## Cases that need to be spelled out

- **Before the course starts**: how to handle sign-ups where no lesson has yet taken place.
- **After a trial lesson**: the process if you decide not to continue after a trial.
- **Midway through a term**: how to handle stopping lessons midway because of moving house, a clash of times or other reasons.
- **Rescheduling and make-up lessons**: how much notice is needed for an absence, and the number and deadline of make-up lessons.
- **Changes on the teacher's side**: how the studio will arrange things when a teacher cannot teach for some reason.

For each case, explain in a sentence or two, then add a short example.

![Glowing abstract digital shapes and a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwgvngqw-wud5w.webp)

## Use examples to aid understanding

Examples should use made-up scenarios that involve no real family. For instance: "A parent feels after the first lesson that the time does not suit them, and can contact the studio within the agreed period and proceed in the way described." An example sentence like this is easier to understand than an abstract clause. Avoid specific amounts or percentages in examples unless they really are the studio's own rules and match the sign-up page.

## Tone and wording

- Use polite phrasing such as "we will" and "please", rather than commands.
- Avoid blaming wording, such as "we accept no responsibility after the deadline".
- Do not use exaggerated promises, such as "definitely" or "absolutely".
- For special circumstances, leave a way to talk, for example "If you have special circumstances, please get in touch and we will work it out together".

## Stay consistent with other pages

A refund policy often appears on the sign-up page, the FAQ page and the sign-up confirmation email. The wording in all these places must match, and if one is updated, the others must be updated too. We suggest maintaining the policy in one place and linking to it from the other pages, to avoid contradictory versions.

## A reminder: check against local rules

Different regions have their own rules on consumer rights and prepaid fees. When writing the policy, a studio should check against local law and industry requirements, and consult a professional where necessary. This article is only advice on how to write, and is not legal advice.

## Connecting the policy to everyday practice

Clear rules let students concentrate on practising. TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app that gives students feedback on notes and beats while they play at home, helping them keep their rhythm between two lessons. In its policy, a studio can also gently remind students that even when a lesson is rescheduled for some reason, short regular practice can carry on.

## A small step for polishing the policy

After writing the policy, ask a friend who did not take part in writing it to read it and answer three questions: who should I contact if I want a refund? By when do I need to apply? How much notice is needed to reschedule a lesson? If they cannot answer, that part is not yet clear enough. Then ask a parent friend to look at the tone and say whether it makes them feel trusted rather than guarded against. A test like this takes only a few minutes, but it can reveal many problems you cannot see yourself.

- After each clause, check that there is clear contact information.
- Put the points most likely to cause disputes in a prominent place.
- Before each term begins, read it again and confirm it still applies.

## Internal reminders for teachers and front desk

Once the policy is written, the team also needs the same understanding of it. Teachers and front desk staff should use the same wording when answering parents, and when something comes up that the policy does not cover, note it first and then discuss how to handle it, rather than making a promise on the spot that differs from the policy. At the end of each term, gather the special cases you met into a few points to improve the next version of the policy. A small habit like this makes the policy gradually more complete as it follows real situations, and lets parents feel the studio takes the matter seriously.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: How long should the policy be?**
A: As long as it takes to be clear. A short one-page policy with a few examples is usually easier to read to the end than lengthy clauses.

**Q: Can I just explain it verbally?**
A: We recommend writing it down, and asking parents to confirm they have read it when they sign up.

**Q: Can the policy be changed?**
A: Yes, but give notice in advance and say from when the change applies.

**Q: What about special circumstances?**
A: Leave room for discussion, work it out with the parent according to the actual situation, and record how it was handled.
