music-education-podcast-brand.body:
A music podcast is a mainly audio programme that, through regularly released episodes, talks with listeners about music knowledge, learning experiences and observations about the field. For a music education organisation, the value of a podcast lies in "companionship": listeners tune in while commuting, doing housework or out for a walk, gradually become familiar with the host's voice and views, and come to trust the brand. To make a good music podcast you need clear positioning, a regular segment structure, reliable recording quality, a lawful way of using music, and an update rhythm that is steady without being forced.

## Why Music Education Suits Podcasting

Music is itself an art of sound, so introducing it through the ears is entirely natural. Compared with short videos, podcast episodes are longer and suit exploring a topic fully, for example "Why do adults keep failing to stick with practice?" or "What can parents do when a child does not want to practise?" Listeners who are willing to spend twenty or thirty minutes on an episode have a real interest in the topic, and such listeners are often more willing to find out more about the course too.

In addition, the barrier to making a podcast is fairly manageable. A quiet room, a suitable microphone and basic editing software are enough to start. What matters is not how expensive the equipment is, but whether the content is sincere and useful.

## Define the Show's Positioning

Before you begin, answer three questions: who is the show for, what will they get from listening, and how is it different from other music content? For example, one show could be aimed specially at "office workers who want to take up piano again", solving one specific difficulty each episode, while another could be aimed at parents, discussing the feelings and habits that come up as children learn music. The clearer the positioning, the easier it is to choose topics, and the easier it is for listeners to judge whether the show is for them.

**Give the show a memorable name**
The name should be short, easy to say and related to the theme. Avoid exaggerated words, and do not hint at any promise of guaranteed results.

## Design Regular Segments

A fixed structure lets listeners form expectations and makes production more efficient. An episode can include:

- One-minute opening: a short piano excerpt and one sentence introducing the episode's topic.
- Topic discussion: explore one question and give concrete methods.
- Listener letters: answer one or two questions from listeners.
- This week's mini-exercise: leave a small task they can try straight away.
- Closing: preview the next episode and say where to find more resources.

The segments stay fixed but the content is different each episode. This feeling of "something fresh within the familiar" helps listeners keep tuning in.

![A blue watercolour grand piano with splashes of paint on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw1iyq4w-jife7.webp)

## Recording and Music Copyright

A music podcast often needs to play excerpts of music, and copyright then needs special attention. Using other people's recordings or works may require permission. The safer approaches are: have the teacher play public-domain works live; use a licensed music library that clearly allows commercial use; or invite students to play and obtain their written consent. When recording, choose a quiet room, and hanging fabric on the walls reduces echo. Once recorded, adjust the volume uniformly so that every episode has roughly the same loudness.

## Release Rhythm and Platforms

The update frequency does not need to be high, but it must be steady. One episode every two weeks sustained for half a year usually builds more trust than daily updates at the start followed by a sudden stop. When publishing, put the key points, timestamps and related links in the show notes. You can release the show on several commonly used podcast platforms, so that listeners with different habits can tune in.

**Reuse the content of the show**
One episode can be turned into an article, or a one-minute highlight can be cut as a short video. In this way one piece of content can be seen by more people on different channels.

## From Listener to Student

The aim of a podcast is not to sell courses in every episode but to keep providing value. It is enough to mention naturally at the end of an episode that listeners can book a trial lesson or download a practice tool. You can design a small resource just for listeners, such as a free practice planner that they can get by leaving an email address. Afterwards, follow up with gentle emails introducing course information.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need professional equipment to make a podcast?**
A: Not necessarily. A suitable microphone and a quiet environment are enough to start. The key is content quality and steady updates.

**Q: How long should each episode be?**
A: Twenty to thirty minutes is common. It is long enough to cover a topic and not so long that listeners find it too much.

**Q: Can I play pop songs in the show?**
A: You need to confirm copyright and licensing first. Without a licence, we suggest using public-domain works or a licensed music library.

**Q: How long does it take for a podcast to bring in students?**
A: There is no fixed time. A podcast is more like long-term trust building, and changes are usually seen only after several months or more.

practice-hard-bar-with-one-bar-before-an.body:
Taking a hard bar out and practising it again and again is a common method. But sometimes this happens: played alone, the bar is already smooth, yet when it is put back into the whole piece, you still get stuck there. The cause is often not the bar itself, but how it joins to what comes before and after: the hand has to move over from the previous position, and after playing it has to connect to the next position. So when practising a hard spot, you can bring along the bar before and the bar after, and practise the three bars together.

## First Practise the Hard Spot Itself

If the hard bar itself is not yet familiar, first take it out and practise it alone.

Use slow tempo, hands separately and similar methods, so your fingers get to know the notes and fingering of this bar.

Once the hard spot itself can be played smoothly, add the bars before and after.

![A golden grand piano sketch on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8xvpt-naujn.webp)

## Enter from Different Places

Besides starting from the previous bar, you can also start from the beginning of the phrase or the beginning of the section, and play right through the hard spot.

Entering from different places lets us get through the hard spot smoothly in all kinds of situations.

This helps a lot with steadiness in performance.

## The Join Is the Hidden Difficulty

Between the last note before the hard bar and the first note of the hard bar, there may be a big leap or a change of hand position.

Between the last note of the hard bar and the start of the next bar, there may be a similar problem.

These joins are often overlooked when we practise the hard spot alone.

## Look Ahead to the Next Position

At the joins, your eyes need to look ahead to the next position.

While your hand is still playing the last few notes of the previous bar, your mind should already be getting ready for the start of the next bar.

This kind of advance preparation makes the join smoother.

## Practise the Three Bars Together

You can put the hard bar together with the bar before it and the bar after it as one three-bar practice unit.

Start playing from the previous bar, go through the hard spot, and play on until the end of the following bar.

This way you practise both entering and leaving the hard spot.

## Well Practised Alone but Still Stuck

Many people have this experience: a hard bar is already very familiar when played alone, but playing from the beginning up to it still produces mistakes.

This is because when practising alone, we start from a prepared position.

In the piece, however, the hand has to move over from the position of the previous bar, which is a completely different situation.

## Ask Your Teacher for Help in a Lesson

If a hard spot is still not smooth after practising this way for a while, you can ask Teacher Aum to take a look in a lesson.

The teacher may suggest a different fingering, or adjust how the hand moves.

Sometimes a small change can make the join much easier.

## Record How Many Times You Practise

You can note beside the score how many times each day you practise this three-bar unit, and whether you could play it smoothly.

If you can play it smoothly for several days in a row, the hard spot has been solved.

If it is still unsteady, you can ask your teacher in a lesson to help analyse it.

## Link Them Together at a Slow Tempo

When playing the three bars together, take the tempo slower and make sure there is no pause at the joins.

If you always have to stop at a join, your hand movement is not yet fluent enough.

You can go back to practising just the two notes that make the join.

## Gradually Widen the Range

Once the three bars are familiar, you can gradually widen the range, for example two bars before and after, or a whole phrase.

This way the hard spot slowly blends into the whole piece.

When you finally play from beginning to end, the hard spot is no longer an obstacle that suddenly appears.

- Practise the hard bar together with one bar before and one after
- The problem often lies in the joins
- First practise the hard spot alone, then add the bars around it
- Practise both entering and leaving

## Circle the Three-Bar Unit with Brackets

You can circle the three bars with brackets in the score, to remind yourself that this is a practice unit.

At each practice session, first practise the passages in these brackets, then play the whole piece.

After a few days, see which brackets are no longer needed, and rub them out.

## A Summary of One Bar Before and After

If a hard bar still gets stuck after being practised alone, it is often because the join has not been practised: the hand has to move over from the previous bar and then connect to the next bar. So you can put the hard bar together with one bar before and one after as a three-bar practice unit.

When the hard spot itself is not familiar, practise it alone first. When the join is especially hard, practise only the two notes of the join. Look ahead to the next position with your eyes, link them at a slow tempo, and gradually widen to a whole phrase.

You can enter from different places, mark the practice unit with brackets in the score, record your practice, and ask Teacher Aum for help if it stays unsmooth for a long time.

## Practise Only the Two Notes of the Join

If the join is especially hard, you can practise only the two notes from the last note of the previous bar to the first note of the hard spot.

Practise this movement again and again, until your hand reaches the new position accurately and easily.

**A small tip**

The same method can be used for the join between the hard spot and the following bar.

## FAQ

**Q: Why do I still get stuck after practising the hard spot alone until it is familiar?**
A: Because the join has not been practised.

**Q: What is the three-bar practice unit?**
A: The hard bar plus one bar before and one bar after.

**Q: What if the hard spot itself is not familiar?**
A: Practise the hard spot alone first.

**Q: What if the join is especially hard?**
A: Practise only the two notes of the join.

**Q: How do I widen the range once it is familiar?**
A: Two bars before and after, or a whole phrase.

pop-ballad-right-hand-melody-with-chord-.body:
When you play a pop ballad on the piano, a right hand that plays only a single-note melody can sometimes sound thin. A common remedy is to add one or two chord tones under the melody note. For example, if the melody note is E and the chord is C, add C or G under the E, so that the right hand plays two or three notes. Then let the little finger, or the topmost finger, bring out the melody more clearly, with the chord tones below played more softly. In this way the right hand has both melody and harmony, and together with the bass in the left hand the sound becomes much fuller.

## Summary: Arranging a Ballad

When playing a pop ballad, adding one or two chord tones under the right-hand melody makes the sound fuller.

Start adding them on the strong beats, keep the top melody note clearer, play the chord tones below more softly, and keep the left hand simple.

Adjust the arrangement to the sections of the song and to your own hands, and slowly find a way of playing that suits you.

## Variation Between Sections

A ballad often has two parts, a verse and a chorus, and you can play them differently.

For example, the verse is fairly quiet, so the right hand can play just single notes or only a few chord tones; when you reach the chorus, add more chord tones.

This gives the song a change of layers, and the chorus sounds fuller.

## Making the Melody Clearer

When the right hand plays several notes at once, make the top melody note clearer and the chord tones below softer.

You can shift the weight of your hand slightly towards the little finger side, so that the little finger plays more firmly.

The fingers below press down lightly, as if providing a background for the melody.

## Practising Melody Projection on Its Own

If it is hard at first to make the melody stand out, practise this on its own.

For example, play just two notes, the upper one strong and the lower one weak, and repeat.

You can also play the lower chord tones extremely softly, almost inaudibly, and then gradually make them a little louder.

## Changing the Pedal in a Ballad

In a ballad, using the sustain pedal appropriately makes the sound more connected and softer.

You can usually change the pedal when the chord changes, so that each chord sounds clearly and they do not run together.

If the melody has many passing notes, take care not to hold the pedal too long, or the sound will be too muddy.

## The Idea of Adding Chord Tones

To make the sound fuller, add one or two notes belonging to the current chord under the right-hand melody note.

The right hand then plays two or three notes at once, with the melody on top and the harmony below.

This way of playing is very common in many pop piano arrangements.

## The Limits of a Single-Note Melody

When learning pop songs, many people play the melody with the right hand and chords or bass with the left.

This is a good way in, but sometimes the sound feels not full enough, especially in a quiet ballad.

That is because the right hand has only one voice, and the middle of the range is rather empty.

**Before you begin**
- A right hand playing only single notes can sound thin
- Add one or two chord tones under the melody
- Make the top melody note clearer
- Play the chord tones below more softly

## How to Choose the Chord Tones

First look at the chord symbol written in the score. For C, for example, you know that this beat can use the three notes C, E and G.

If the melody note is E, you can add C or G under it, or both.

If the melody note is not in the chord, say it is D, you can add chord tones only on the important beats and keep single notes elsewhere.

![A digital music space under neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa49494-uiyju.webp)

## Start with the Strong Beats

When you first start practising, you do not need to add chord tones to every melody note; you can add them only on the first beat of each bar.

That way the right hand is not too busy, and the start of each bar gains more weight.

Once you are comfortable, try adding chord tones on beat three or other important notes too.

## The Limits of Your Hand Size

When adding chord tones in the right hand, consider the size of your hand and do not strain to reach a large distance.

If your hands are small, you can add just one chord tone, or choose a note closer to the melody.

In arranging, the principle is comfort and smoothness; there is no need to pursue as many notes as possible.

## Arranging with Your Teacher

If you are not sure how to arrange, you can play your own version for Teacher Aum.

The teacher can help you see whether the chord tones you chose are suitable and whether the melody is clear enough.

You can also ask the teacher to demonstrate different ways of arranging, so that you have more choices.

## Learn from Other People's Arrangements

You can look at piano arrangements of pop songs to see how the arranger adds chord tones under the melody.

You can also listen to pop songs played on the piano and notice whether the right hand sounds like single notes or chords.

Apply these ideas to the songs you play, and slowly form your own style.

## Working with the Left Hand

Once the right hand has added chord tones, the left hand can play more simply, for example just the bass note or octaves.

That way the left hand takes care of the bass, the right hand takes care of the melody and the middle harmony, and each has a clear job.

**Remember this**

If the left hand also plays thick chords, the whole may become too muddy, so watch the balance.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why add chord tones in the right hand?**
A: A single-note melody can sometimes sound thin, and chord tones make it fuller.

**Q: How do I choose the chord tones?**
A: Look at the chord symbol and add notes from that chord under the melody.

**Q: Do I have to add them to every note?**
A: No, you can start from the first beat of each bar.

**Q: How do I make the melody stand out?**
A: Lean the weight of your hand towards the little finger and play the notes below more softly.

**Q: How should the left hand work with it?**
A: The left hand can play more simply, for example just the bass note.

piano-lesson-three-line-notes.body:
A three-line note after a piano lesson is a very short summary the teacher writes at the end of each lesson: the first line says what was learned today, the second says what the student did well, and the third says what to practise at home this week. It is not a detailed lesson plan, nor a report comment, but an "action card" that a student and parent can understand in a minute. Many students still remember the teacher's reminders as they leave the studio, but two days later it has gone hazy; parents who want to help with practice do not know what the focus of the week is. The three-line note is meant to fill this gap between the lesson and practice at home.

## Why Three Lines

The longer a note is, the fewer people read it carefully. Teachers have limited time after a lesson, and a long paragraph is hard to keep up; students and parents faced with a long block of text also find it hard to grasp the main point. The limit of three lines forces the teacher to condense a lesson into its most essential information.

- The first line helps recall the content of the lesson.
- The second line gives specific praise, so the student knows what is worth keeping.
- The third line gives a clear practice task, so they know where to start once home.

## Line One: What We Learned Today

This line should be specific, avoiding vague wording such as "practised the piece". State clearly the title, section or technique, for example "new piece, first section, right hand, met the dotted crotchet". If a new concept came up in the lesson, you can write it in words the student understands, to make reviewing at home easier.

**Use the student's language**
When writing notes for a child, you can reuse the metaphors from the lesson, such as "staccato like a little frog jumping", and the student will recall the scene at once.

## Line Two: What Went Well

Praise should be specific to an action or a sound, not just "great". For example, "the crescendo at the start of the second line was very natural" or "no pause when changing hand position". Specific praise does two things: it lets the student know this way of doing it is right and worth continuing, and it gives the parent something to praise during practice.

**Write just one thing each time**
You do not have to list every strength. Picking the most obvious improvement and writing it clearly carries more weight than a long list.

![The side of a piano indoors, with light and shadow](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwb5ll1y-xzfjk.webp)

## Line Three: What to Practise This Week

This is the most important of the three lines. The task should be doable and checkable, for example "every day, bars three to six in the left hand, slowly, three times, watch that finger 4 does not collapse". If there are several tasks, write them in order of priority: the first is what must be done this week, and the later ones as circumstances allow.

- Say which section to practise, rather than "practise the whole piece".
- Say how to practise, for example slowly, hands separately, or with a metronome.
- Say what to watch for; one reminder is enough.

## An Example

Below is an example of a three-line note written for a beginner child, for format reference only:

**Today:** Met the first line of the new piece "Little Raindrops" and learned to play black keys with finger 3.
**Did well:** All five fingers of the right hand stood on the keys, and the sound was very clear.
**This week:** Every day, play the first line slowly three times with the right hand, clapping the rhythm once before playing.

Notes for adult students can include a little more explanation of the principle, but keep the same three-line structure, so they can read it quickly in a busy day.

## Problems That Often Come Up When Writing Notes

When teachers first start writing three-line notes, they often run into a few problems. First, the third line has too many tasks, five or six at once, so the student does not know which to do first at home and ends up doing none well. Second, the second line turns into polite filler, always writing "did nicely", and students and parents stop caring after reading it many times. Third, too many technical terms are used, parents cannot understand them, and so cannot help with reminders at home. After writing, you can read it from a parent's point of view: if you did not know music, could you tell what to do this week? If the answer is no, simplify it further.

## How to Make Sure the Note Is Actually Used

Writing a good note is only the first step; the key is to make students and parents willing to read it and able to find it easily. You can agree a fixed way of sending it with parents, for example sending it to the same chat window after the lesson, or writing it in the student's practice book. At the start of the next lesson, the teacher first looks at last week's third line and asks how the practice went, so the note forms a cycle. If a student practises at home with an AI piano learning tool such as TIGA ALPHA, you can also compare the practice record in the app with the note, to see whether the task was done and where adjustments are needed.

**Mind privacy**
Write only what relates to learning in the note, and do not write about the student's family situation or other private information. When sending through a group, send each student's note separately, and do not put several students' details together.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need to write one for every lesson?**
A: Every lesson is recommended; once it becomes a habit, it takes only a minute or two each time.

**Q: What if the student is young and cannot read yet?**
A: The note can be written for the parent, who reads it to the child, or you can add a simple picture, such as a star drawn beside the bars to practise.

**Q: What if the student does not complete the third-line task?**
A: First find out why: was the task too much, too hard, or was there a difficulty with scheduling? Then adjust the amount of the next week's task.

**Q: Can a voice message replace the note?**
A: It can be a supplement, but text is easier to check at any time, so keeping a written version is recommended.

part-fur-alina-1976-tintinnabuli.body:
Für Alina is a short piano piece written in 1976 by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, and its score runs to just two pages. Before it, Pärt had spent several years publishing almost no new work, turning instead to the study of medieval and Renaissance music. This piece marks the beginning of a new style that he called "tintinnabuli": one voice moves through the melody step by step, while the other plays only notes of the tonic triad, like distant bells. The piece is very slow and very quiet, with few notes, yet it demands a great deal of listening and control.

## What is the tintinnabuli style

The name "tintinnabuli" comes from the Latin word for "little bells".

**Listen**

Its basic method uses two voices: a melody voice that moves step by step along the scale, and another voice that plays only the three notes of the tonic triad.

Together, the two voices sound as if the melody is slowly unfolding in the ringing of bells.

## Alina's B minor

The piece is in B minor, and the tonic triad is B, D and F♯.

The notes of the triad voice are always chosen from these three, taking the one closest to the melody.

This way, wherever the melody goes, the harmony always revolves around the same chord, which makes it feel very stable.

## Für Alina in summary

Arvo Pärt was born in 1935 and is an Estonian composer. He used twelve-tone technique early in his career, then for several years in the early 1970s published almost nothing while studying Gregorian chant and medieval and Renaissance music. In 1976 he wrote Für Alina, only two pages long, reportedly for a girl from a friend's family who was about to move far away; the performance direction means roughly calm, sublime, listening inwards.

The piece marks the beginning of the tintinnabuli style, whose name comes from the Latin for little bell: one voice moves along the scale, the other plays only notes of the tonic triad. The piece is in B minor, with the tonic triad B, D and F♯. The score has no time signature and no bar lines. It begins with the left hand playing a low B octave with the pedal held down, and it is played very slowly and softly, with the sustain pedal down almost throughout. Pärt later wrote works such as Spiegel im Spiegel.

Whether your tone is even is something you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to.

## Pärt's other tintinnabuli works

After this piece, Pärt wrote many works in the tintinnabuli style, such as Spiegel im Spiegel for violin and piano.

These works are equally simple and serene, and are popular all over the world.

They have given many people a new view of modern music.

![A high-angle view of an open black piano being played on a rainy, neon-lit night street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadbami-bxiwt.webp)

## Alina's pedal

The sustain pedal is held down almost throughout the piece, letting the sounds blend and resonate.

But because there are so few notes, the sound does not become muddy.

Try playing it on different pianos and listen for the difference the pedal makes.

## The opening bass note

At the very start, the left hand plays a very low B octave, and the pedal is pressed so that it keeps ringing.

This low note is like the afterglow of a bell that has just been struck, enveloping the whole piece.

Every melody that follows unfolds within the resonance of this low note.

## Asking your teacher to listen to your Alina

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your playing of this piece and tell you whether the tone is even and soft.

The teacher can also explain how the tintinnabuli style works, to help you understand the relationship between the two voices.

This piece is very good for practising listening and control.

**Try it**
- Written in 1976 by the Estonian composer Pärt
- The score is only two pages long
- Marks the beginning of the "tintinnabuli style"
- One voice carries the melody, the other plays only notes of the tonic triad

## Difficulty in simplicity

The piece looks as if it has very few notes and is technically easy, but playing it well is not easy at all.

It requires very steady control of tone, and a sense of time and space.

You could say it tests your listening, not the speed of your fingers.

## Who is Arvo Pärt

Arvo Pärt was born in 1935 and is an Estonian composer.

Early on he wrote works using modern methods such as twelve-tone technique.

Later, his style changed greatly and became very simple and serene.

## Try writing a bit of tintinnabuli

You can try this at the piano: with the right hand, move step by step up a C major scale, and with the left hand play only whichever of C, E and G is closest to the right hand.

Play slowly and listen to how the two voices work together.

This is the most direct way to understand the tintinnabuli style.

## A score with no time signature

The score of Für Alina has no time signature and no bar lines.

Most of the right-hand notes are not marked with fixed note values, so the player can decide how long each note lasts by feel.

This gives the player a lot of freedom, and also calls for strong listening skills.

## Years of silence

In the early 1970s, Pärt became dissatisfied with the way he had been writing.

For several years he published almost no new work, and turned to studying Gregorian chant and medieval and Renaissance music.

The study and reflection of this period laid the foundation for his new style.

## Playing very slowly and softly

The tempo of this piece is very slow, and the dynamics are very soft.

Each note should be played clearly and gently, and then you listen carefully as its sound slowly fades away.

Do not rush to the next note; wait until the sound is almost inaudible before continuing.

## Written for Alina

The piece is said to have been written by Pärt for Alina, a girl from a friend's family, who was about to leave her homeland to live in England.

The quiet, gentle mood of the piece feels like a farewell and a blessing.

The performance direction Pärt wrote on the score means roughly "calm, sublime, listening inwards".

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote Für Alina?**
A: The Estonian composer Arvo Pärt.

**Q: In which year was it written?**
A: 1976.

**Q: What is the tintinnabuli style?**
A: One voice moves along the scale, and the other plays only notes of the tonic triad.

**Q: What key is the piece in?**
A: B minor.

**Q: What is special about the score?**
A: It has no time signature and no bar lines.

play-passage-an-octave-higher-or-lower.body:
After you have practised a phrase many times, your ears go numb, and sometimes you cannot hear where it is uneven or unclear. There is a simple remedy: move the whole phrase, unchanged, eight white keys to the right or eight white keys to the left, and play it again. When the register changes, the colour of the sound changes too, your ears become sensitive again, and problems you had not noticed come to light. At the same time, playing the same figure in a different position of the hand deepens your memory of the phrase's shape.

## Combine It with Other Methods

Octave-shift practice can be combined with slow practice and rhythm-variation practice.

For example, play slowly in the higher octave and with dotted rhythms in the lower octave.

Different methods check the phrase from different angles, which makes your practice more thorough.

**Slow down**
- After lots of practice the ears go numb
- Move to the higher or lower octave
- The register changes and the ears become sensitive again
- Your memory of the phrase's shape deepens

## Suitable Phrases

This method suits scale-like phrases, arpeggios, melodies and simple accompaniment figures.

If a phrase already sits at the very top or bottom of the piano, you can only move it in one direction.

For a phrase with a very wide span, you can choose just one part of it to move.

## How to Shift Octaves

Choose a phrase you already know fairly well, such as a run of scale notes or a melody in the right hand.

Move the whole thing up an octave and play it once with the same fingering.

Then move it down an octave, below where it started, and play it once more.

## Checking Your Memory

If you have already memorised a phrase, playing it in a different octave is a good way to test your memory.

If it only comes out through the habit of the hand in its original position, you may feel a little unsure in the new octave.

Being able to play it in different octaves shows that your memory of the phrase is fairly solid.

## What to Listen for in the Low Register

In the low register the sound is thicker and fuller, and the effect of legato and the pedal becomes more obvious.

If the legato is not smooth enough, or the pedal change is not clean, it is easier to hear in the low register.

You can use it here to check the connection of the phrase and the clarity of the sound.

## Your Hand Position Changes

In a different octave, the position of your hand and arm changes too, and your body shifts slightly to the left or right.

Playing the same figure in the new position, your hand has to readjust, which lets you feel the shape of the phrase more clearly.

When you return to the original position, you often find it feels easier to play.

## Move the Left-Hand Accompaniment into the Middle Register

The left-hand accompaniment figure can also be played an octave higher.

Hearing the left-hand figure in the middle register often reveals things that were hard to hear in the low register.

For example, one note in a broken chord may be too loud, or the rhythm may not be even enough.

## What to Listen for in the High Register

In the high register the sound is brighter and lighter, and the outline of each note appears clearer.

If a note is played too heavily or too lightly, it stands out especially in the high register.

You can use it here to check whether the notes are even and whether staccato notes are short and crisp.

![A collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa694t6-5k8wt.webp)

## Ears Get Tired Too

When the same phrase is repeated many times, your ears slowly get used to its sound.

Then, even if there are uneven or unclear spots, you may no longer hear them.

Listening in a different way can help your ears focus again.

## How Many Repeats Each Time

Octave-shift practice does not need many repetitions: play two or three times in each octave, listening carefully.

Then go back to the original position, play once, and compare whether the feeling has changed.

Treat it as a small step within your practice, use it now and then, and it will work better.

## Imagining the Sound

When you play in the high register, you can imagine the phrase played by a flute; when you play in the low register, imagine a cello.

Such imagining helps us notice tone colour and the feeling of the phrase.

When you return to the original register, you can carry these ideas with you.

## Summary: Shifting by Octaves

When a phrase has been practised a lot, the ears go numb; move it to the higher or lower octave to make them sensitive again.

The high register suits checking evenness and clarity, the low register suits checking legato and pedalling, the left-hand accompaniment can be practised this way too, and it can also be used to check your memory.

Keep the fingering unchanged, play two or three times in each octave, listen carefully, then return to the original position to compare.

## Be Careful Not to Change the Fingering

When you change octave, the fingering should be the same as the original; do not change fingers just because the position has changed.

That way the benefit of the practice carries back to the original position.

**Look from another angle**

If you find the fingering awkward in the new position, you can think about whether the original fingering needs adjusting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why practise in a different octave?**
A: To make numb ears sensitive again.

**Q: What is the high register good for checking?**
A: Whether the notes are even and clear.

**Q: What is the low register good for checking?**
A: Legato and pedalling.

**Q: Should the fingering change when I change octave?**
A: No, keep it the same as the original.

**Q: Can it be used to check memory?**
A: Yes. If you can still play it in a different octave, you remember it well.

piano-recital-program-order.body:
The order of a student recital programme directly affects whether the audience can keep listening, and also the state of mind of students who play later. Treat length, dynamics and style as labels you can arrange, then place the pieces as opening, middle and close, and the whole concert will be easier to follow. Below are concrete steps for gathering information, ordering the pieces and checking at the rehearsal.

A student recital is not just a matter of putting a list of names into a table. The order of pieces affects the audience's attention, and it affects how nervous the students who play later feel. If you balance length, dynamics, style and age group a little, the whole concert will sound better and be fairer too.

## First, Gather the Basic Information on Each Piece

Before drawing up the programme, ask each teacher to supply: the title, the approximate length, whether the dynamics are on the loud or soft side, whether the style is quiet or lively, and the student's age. With these labels, the ordering has a basis, rather than simply following the order of sign-up.

- Length: under two minutes, two to four minutes, longer
- Dynamics: mostly soft, medium, mostly loud
- Style: lyrical, dance-like, march-like, modern in colour
- Stage experience: first time on stage or already experienced

## Common Ways to Order the Pieces

Three safe ways to open:

- A short, familiar piece at a moderate tempo
- A short lyrical phrase at a medium volume
- A piece by a student who has performed many times

For the opening you can use a short, steady piece that is unlikely to go wrong, to settle the whole room first. In the middle, place pieces that vary in style, avoiding three slow or three loud pieces in a row. Near the end you can put a piece with a slightly brighter mood, but there is no need to aim for a sensational effect. For a child on stage for the first time, try not to place them in the slot that has to follow the hardest piece of the whole programme.

**About a break**
If the programme runs for more than forty minutes, you can plan a short bow or a gap between sets, so the audience can stand up and stretch, and staff have time to tidy the music stands.

![Close-up of piano keys with gold decorative patterns](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3ktwso-t7ivg.webp)

## Students of the Same Teacher Need Not Be Grouped Together

Sometimes, to make changeovers easier, students of the same teacher are placed one after another. If their pieces are too similar in style, the audience may tire. You can mix teachers or age groups, as long as the changeover routine has been rehearsed beforehand.

## State the Essential Information When Printing the Programme

The programme lists the student's name, the title and the composer (if any), and does not need many words of evaluation. Use a large typeface so parents can read it in dim light. If photography is allowed, say when it is allowed and when phones must be silent.

## Run Through in the Real Order at the Rehearsal

Even if there is only one rehearsal, try to follow the real order. Students need to feel who is before them and how much time they have waiting. If you spot a problem, make small adjustments on the spot, and do not leave big changes for the day of the concert.

## Let the Volume Curve Breathe

Imagine the volume of the whole concert as breathing: there is a quiet like an in-breath and a release like an out-breath, but it should not stay at the same level for long. Three loud pieces in a row tire the audience's ears; three very soft pieces in a row may mean those at the back cannot hear. Placing a piece with a slightly brisker rhythm and medium dynamics in the middle often gets the whole room focused again.

If a choir or small ensemble is mixed in, alternating piano solos with group items also changes the atmosphere. Agree the entrance and exit times in advance with the teacher in charge of the ensemble, to avoid the stage being empty for too long.

## Managing the Students' Waiting Area

Put chairs, water and a card showing the order in the waiting area. Have an assistant quietly signal the next student to get ready, so the teacher does not have to announce the pieces and calm nervous students at the same time. For younger children, you can allow one parent to stay near the wings, but agree beforehand on photography and where they may move.

## Time Budget for Announcements and Changeovers

Once the programme is set, allow a fixed number of seconds for the announcement and for each entrance and exit, and time a run-through with a phone. Many overruns are not because the pieces are long but because changeovers are slow. If students are already seated in the wings and their music is already out, you save a great deal of dead time. If there is a host, ask for a short script in advance to avoid a long improvised introduction.

On the day, appoint a "timekeeper" whose only job is to watch the clock and give quiet reminders, with no other duties.

The order of a student recital programme directly affects whether the audience can keep listening, and also the state of mind of students who play later. Treat length, dynamics and style as labels you can arrange, then place the pieces as opening, middle and close, and the whole concert will be easier to follow. Below are concrete steps for gathering information, ordering the pieces and checking at the rehearsal.

## Placing Special Pieces

If someone plays a very modern short piece full of dissonance, you can place it in the middle or later part, with more approachable pieces before and after as a transition. Do not put two experimental pieces back to back, unless the whole concert is a modern-music programme and this has been stated in the publicity.

## FAQ

**Q: Can students choose their own place in the order?**
A: You can collect their preferences, but the teacher makes the final decision according to the effect on the whole concert, and explains the reasons.

**Q: Should a student who makes a mistake start again?**
A: In an ordinary concert they do not start again, unless the organisers have said beforehand that there is a replay segment.

**Q: Can adult students and children play in the same concert?**
A: Yes. Just take care to mix up style and volume, so that no section has all the same mood.

**Q: Should the programme include the teacher's name?**
A: It can. Just use a different type size from the student's name so it does not take over.

ponchielli-dance-of-the-hours-1876.body:
Dance of the Hours is a piece of ballet music from La Gioconda, an opera by the Italian composer Amilcare Ponchielli, which premiered in Milan in 1876. In the opera, this ballet is a performance at a banquet, in which the dancers play the hours of dawn, day, evening and night, showing the changing light of a day through dance. The music begins with a quiet dawn, gradually grows brighter and livelier, and ends with a very fast galop. In 1940 an animated film set it to a comic dance of animals, which made many more people remember the melody.

## The Opera La Gioconda

La Gioconda is an opera in four acts. It premiered in Milan in 1876, and its libretto is adapted from a play by the French writer Victor Hugo.

The story is set in seventeenth-century Venice and tells of the love and sacrifice of a street singer.

The music of the opera is full of passion, with many moving vocal numbers.

## The Hours in an Animated Film

In 1940 a feature-length film that set animation to famous pieces of music turned Dance of the Hours into a ballet of animals.

Ostriches, hippos, elephants and crocodiles dance in tutus, and many in the audience laughed out loud.

This animated sequence made more people remember the music.

## Try Describing a Day

You can try improvising a short piece on the piano that describes different times of day.

For example, use soft high notes for the morning, bright chords for noon and low, deep notes for the evening.

This helps you understand how a composer uses music to show time.

## Summary: Dance of the Hours

Amilcare Ponchielli was born in 1834 and died in 1886, and Puccini was once his student. His four-act opera La Gioconda premiered in Milan in 1876, adapted from a play by Hugo, and set in seventeenth-century Venice. Dance of the Hours is the ballet at the banquet in Act III; it has little to do with the plot and was later often played on its own.

The music begins with dawn played by woodwinds such as the flute, passes through a bright day, a warm evening and a mysterious night, symbolising light overcoming darkness, and ends with a very fast galop in two. In 1940 an animated film set it to a comic ballet of ostriches, hippos, elephants and crocodiles. Piano arrangements often take just the galop section, where the rhythm should be light and springy.

You can talk with Teacher Aum about the character of each hour.

## Who Was Ponchielli?

Amilcare Ponchielli was born in 1834 and died in 1886. He was an Italian composer.

He wrote several operas, and La Gioconda is one of the most widely known.

He also worked as a music teacher, and Puccini was once his student.

## The Ballet at the Banquet

In Act III of the opera there is a grand banquet.

At the banquet, the host invites dancers to perform a ballet, which is Dance of the Hours.

This ballet has little to do with the plot, but the music is lovely, and it is often played on its own.

## The Hour of Night

When night comes, the music becomes deep and mysterious, like darkness covering the earth.

But after the night, the light appears again, and the music turns bright once more.

This symbolises light overcoming darkness.

## Day and Evening

Next the music becomes bright and lively, showing the sunshine of day.

Then it becomes soft and warm again, showing the setting sun of evening.

Each hour has its own melody and colour.

## Describing Time with Music

Dance of the Hours is an example of using music to describe the passing of time.

The composer uses different instruments, tempos and dynamics to show the changing light of a day.

As you listen, you can imagine the sun from sunrise to sunset, and then the night.

## Piano Arrangements of Dance of the Hours

There are quite a few piano arrangements of Dance of the Hours, and they often take just the galop at the end.

The galop is fast and needs agile fingers and a clear rhythm.

There are also simplified versions that keep only the main melody, suitable for players at an elementary to intermediate level.

## Talk About the Hours with Your Teacher in Lessons

In lessons you can talk with Teacher Aum about the musical character of each hour in Dance of the Hours.

You can also ask your teacher to recommend a galop arrangement that suits your level.

This music is a great way to experience describing a picture with music.

## Tips for Playing the Galop

When playing the galop, keep the rhythm light and springy.

Make the right-hand melody clear and the left-hand accompaniment light, and do not let the tempo drag.

You can first practise slowly until it is secure, then gradually speed up to a suitable tempo.

## The Hour of Dawn

The opening of the music is quiet and gentle, like the first light of dawn slowly appearing.

The flute and other woodwinds play a fresh melody, like birdsong in the early morning.

The dancers play the hour of dawn, with light, open movements.

- From Ponchielli's opera La Gioconda
- The opera premiered in Milan in 1876
- Dancers play the different hours of the day
- It ends with a very fast galop

## The Fast Galop

At the end of the ballet comes a very fast galop.

The galop is a quick dance in two, with a lively rhythm, like a pony running.

**Look from another angle**

This music is very lively, and many people recognise it as soon as they hear it.

![A transparent futuristic keyboard with beams of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadfq36-pw46u.webp)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Which opera is Dance of the Hours from?**
A: Ponchielli's La Gioconda.

**Q: In which year did the opera premiere?**
A: 1876, in Milan.

**Q: What does the ballet describe?**
A: The hours of dawn, day, evening and night.

**Q: What dance ends the piece?**
A: A very fast galop.

**Q: Which of Ponchielli's students later became famous?**
A: Puccini.

pedal-marking-ped-asterisk-bracket.body:
There are two main ways of writing pedal markings in a score. The traditional way uses an ornate "Ped." to show that the sustain pedal goes down and an asterisk-like "✻" to show that it comes up. The other way draws a horizontal line beneath the bass staff: it dips down at the start to show the pedal going down, a small "∧"-shaped notch in the middle shows a pedal change, and it turns up at the end to show the pedal being released. The first style is common in older editions, while the second is more precise and is widely used in modern teaching books and scores.

## Pedal markings in summary

Pedal markings come in several forms, such as Ped. with the asterisk and the pedal line, plus written markings like una corda and senza pedale.

**Listen**

Knowing what these markings mean helps you follow the composer's wishes more accurately.

At the same time, check the effect of the pedal with your ears, so that the sound stays clear and resonant.

## Ped. and the asterisk

The traditional pedal marking is an ornate "Ped.", meaning the sustain pedal goes down from this point.

Once it is down, it stays down until a mark like an asterisk, "✻", shows that the pedal comes up.

The two marks usually appear as a pair, and the stretch between them is the span during which the pedal stays down.

## Why the pedal line is more precise

With "Ped." and the asterisk, it is sometimes hard to tell on exactly which beat or note the pedal changes.

A pedal line can be lined up exactly with specific notes, so the player knows precisely where to change the pedal.

That is why many modern teaching books, especially those for beginners, use the pedal line.

## When there are no pedal markings

Some scores have no pedal markings at all, but that does not necessarily mean you cannot use the pedal.

In many Classical and Romantic works, the composer leaves the use of the pedal to the player.

In that case, use the pedal sensibly according to the style, the harmony and the tone you want.

## The marking for the middle pedal

The middle pedal on a grand piano is the sostenuto pedal, sometimes written "Sost. Ped." in the score.

It holds only the notes that are being held down at the moment you press it, and leaves other notes unaffected.

This marking is rare in elementary repertoire and appears mainly in some more complex works.

## Where pedal markings are written

Pedal markings are usually written below the grand staff, that is, beneath the bass staff.

Because the pedal is controlled with the foot, putting the marking at the very bottom means your eyes only need to drop down to see it while reading.

To save space, some scores also write the markings between the two staves.

## Markings for the soft pedal

Besides the sustain pedal, scores also contain markings for the soft pedal, usually written "una corda", meaning "one string".

To cancel the soft pedal, "tre corde" is written, meaning "three strings".

These two Italian terms come up often in playing.

## How the pedal line is written

The other way of writing it is to draw a horizontal line beneath the bass staff.

The start of the line bends down to show the pedal going down, and the end bends up to show it being released.

If a small pointed notch appears in the middle, it means the pedal is quickly lifted and pressed again there, which is a pedal change.

## What senza pedale means

If the score says "senza Ped." or "senza pedale", it means "without pedal".

Usually the composer especially wants this passage to sound dry and clear, with no sustain.

When you see this marking, take your foot off the pedal and use your fingers to control how long the sound lasts.

- "Ped." means the sustain pedal goes down
- The asterisk "✻" means it comes up
- Pedal line: down at the start, a notch for a pedal change, up at the end
- The pedal line is more precise and is common in modern scores

## Practising with the pedal markings

When you first practise a piece with pedal markings, you can leave out the pedal and practise just the hands.

Once the hands are comfortable, add the pedal and practise it marking by marking.

If there is a pedal line, you can trace along the line on the score with your finger to confirm each pedal change.

## How the timing of a pedal change relates to the marking

A notch in the pedal line is usually lined up with the first note of the new chord.

This means you lift and press the pedal at the same moment as, or just after, playing the new chord.

Changing the pedal slightly late like this lets the sounds connect without blurring together.

![A digital music space in neon light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa381ga-vlz5x.webp)

## Watch where the asterisk sits

In some older editions, the position of the asterisk may not line up exactly with where the pedal actually needs to change.

This is because early printing and notation habits were different, and were not always precise down to a particular note.

When this happens, combine the changes in harmony with your own ears to find a suitable place to change the pedal.

## Writing your own pedal markings

If the score has no pedal markings, you can discuss it with your teacher and draw pedal lines on the score in pencil.

Once drawn, change the pedal at the same places every time you practise, so a steady habit forms.

**Think again**

If you want to adjust later, you can always erase and mark it again.

## FAQ

**Q: What does "Ped." mean?**
A: The sustain pedal goes down from here.

**Q: What does the asterisk mean?**
A: The sustain pedal comes up.

**Q: What is the small notch in the pedal line?**
A: It shows a pedal change at that point.

**Q: What does una corda mean?**
A: Use the soft pedal.

**Q: If a score has no pedal markings, can I not use the pedal?**
A: Not necessarily; the player often decides according to style and sound.

pedal-in-bach-sparingly-clarity.body:
In Bach's time, keyboard instruments had no sustain pedal, so when playing his works on a modern piano, many teachers advise using little pedal to keep the individual voices clear. But "sparingly" does not mean "not at all": in some slow movements and places where the harmony changes slowly, a light touch of shallow pedal can make the sound warmer. The key is to press only briefly and shallowly each time, and to change it promptly with the harmony so the voices do not blur together.

## The short pedal method

Besides pedalling shallowly, you can also pedal briefly, for example pressing only on a particular chord and releasing straight away.

This kind of short pedal can make an important chord fuller without affecting the notes that follow.

You can mark in the score the places where a short pedal is needed.

## The instruments of Bach's time

Bach lived from 1685 to 1750, and the keyboard instruments commonly used then were the harpsichord, the clavichord and the organ.

None of these instruments had a sustain pedal like the modern piano.

So when Bach composed, he did not consider the effect of the pedal, and there are no pedal markings in the score.

## Practise well without pedal first

Whether or not you use the pedal in performance, in the early stage of practice keep your foot off the pedal and join the lines with your fingers.

If your fingers can already connect the sound by themselves, the pedal only needs to give a little help.

If you rely on the pedal to connect, then once you take it away the sound will become broken and disjointed.

## The method of shallow pedal

If you want to use the pedal when playing Bach, you can press down only a very little, rather than all the way.

A shallow pedal lets the dampers lift only slightly from the strings, so the sustaining effect is lighter.

This adds a little resonance without making the sound too muddy.

![Cartoon-style student wearing headphones sitting at the piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3y3eq-65zl1.webp)

## Check clarity with your ears

After using the pedal, listen carefully to whether every voice is still clear.

You can concentrate on the bass voice alone and see whether the pedal has blurred it.

If a voice cannot be heard clearly, use less pedal or change it more often.

## Finger pedalling as an alternative

Where you do not want to use the sustain pedal, you can use finger pedalling, that is, hold certain notes down a little longer.

This method makes the harmony fuller without affecting the clarity of the voices.

In Bach's works, finger pedalling is often more suitable than the sustain pedal.

## Ask your teacher to demonstrate pedalling in Bach

The use of the pedal is a question worth discussing with your teacher when playing Bach.

You can ask your teacher to demonstrate the same passage with and without pedal, and listen to the difference between the two.

Decide where to use it according to your teacher's advice and your own listening.

## Where you might consider it

Slow movements where the harmony changes slowly are the places where you can more reasonably consider using the pedal.

For example, slow passages in some sarabandes or preludes.

Fast fugues and inventions, on the other hand, are usually better without pedal, so that every note is clean.

## Why it is advised to use it sparingly

Many of Bach's works are polyphonic, with several melodies going on at the same time.

Once the pedal is pressed, the lingering sounds of the several lines overlap, and the ear finds it hard to follow the direction of each.

That is why many teachers advise relying mainly on the fingers for legato when playing Bach and using little pedal.

## Change with the harmony

If you use the pedal in a passage, you must change it promptly as the harmony changes.

Bach's harmony sometimes changes very fast, possibly every beat or even every half beat.

Where the harmony changes quickly, it is best to use little or no pedal and play legato with the fingers instead.

## Bach pedalling summary

There was no sustain pedal in Bach's time, and when playing his works on a modern piano, it is generally advised to use the pedal sparingly.

But in slow movements and places where the harmony changes slowly, you can use a light, shallow, short pedal and change it promptly with the harmony.

A fairly safe approach is to build the legato well with the fingers first and then let your ears decide how to use the pedal.

**Before you play**
- Keyboards in Bach's time had no sustain pedal
- It is generally advised to use it sparingly, to keep the voices clear
- Slow movements and slowly changing harmony can take a light, shallow pedal
- Press briefly, press shallowly, change often

## Sparingly is not the same as never

However, the modern piano sounds very different from the instruments of Bach's time.

With no pedal at all, some slow passages can sound a little dry on the modern piano.

At such times, using a little pedal where appropriate can make the sound warmer, as long as it does not affect the clarity of the voices.

## Different players' choices

Different pianists make different choices about the pedal when playing Bach.

Some use almost none at all, and some use shallow pedal where appropriate.

You can listen to several recorded versions, compare their sound and find the way you like.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Was there a sustain pedal in Bach's time?**
A: No, and there are no pedal markings in the score.

**Q: Can you use the pedal when playing Bach?**
A: You can use a little, but keep the voices clear.

**Q: What is shallow pedal?**
A: Pressing down only a very little, so the sustaining effect is lighter.

**Q: Where might you consider using the pedal?**
A: In slow passages where the harmony changes slowly.

**Q: What should you practise first?**
A: Without pedal first, building good finger legato.

playing-for-relatives-holiday.body:
At holiday family gatherings, relatives often ask the piano learner to play something. You can prepare one or two pieces you know best and that are not too long, choosing melodies that everyone will enjoy. Before you play, briefly say the name of the piece, and say thank you when you finish. If you do not feel like playing that day, you can politely say so. Think of the moment as sharing, not as an exam, and you will feel much more relaxed.

## Choosing the Right Piece

At a family gathering, choose a piece with a beautiful melody that everyone can enjoy, such as a familiar folk song, a holiday song or a lyrical short piece.

If older relatives are present, playing an old song they know often makes everyone happy.

You can also prepare a lively piece to bring more energy to the room.

If the player is a child, let the child choose the piece. Children usually choose what they love most and are happiest to play for others.

## The Right Mindset While Playing

A family gathering is not an exam. When relatives listen to you play, they are mostly showing care and interest.

Even if you play a wrong note or two, do not stop. Keep going, and people usually will not mind.

Keep your attention on the music and enjoy sharing it with your family.

## Typical Holiday Situations

At Spring Festival, the Mid-Autumn Festival and other holidays, when family and relatives get together, someone often says: "I heard you are learning the piano. Play something for us!"

For children and adults who are learning, this is both a chance to show what they can do and, sometimes, a little nerve-racking.

With some preparation beforehand, you can meet such an invitation more calmly.

## A Small Rehearsal Before the Holiday

A few days before the holiday, do a small rehearsal at home. Ask your family to sit on the sofa, and play the prepared piece all the way through, starting from walking over to the piano.

During the rehearsal, notice whether you speed up when people are listening, and which places make you nervous.

After you find the problems, practise a few more times. On the day of the holiday you will feel much more at ease.

![Bangkok city poster-style illustration with tall buildings and busy street traffic](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yktrm-omdts.webp)

## After You Play

When you finish, you can stand up and say "thank you", or simply smile and nod.

If someone praises you, accept it graciously. If someone offers a suggestion, you can respond politely.

If everyone wants to hear another piece, decide whether to continue according to how you feel.

## Letting Everyone Join In

If the mood is relaxed, you can also play a song that everyone knows and invite your family to sing along.

That way it is not just one person performing; everyone takes part in the music together, and the holiday atmosphere becomes warmer.

Little ones can clap or sway to the rhythm, so the music becomes part of the gathering.

## If You Do Not Want to Play

Sometimes you may not be in the right state, may not have prepared, or may simply not want to play. That is perfectly understandable.

You can say politely: "I am not ready today. I will play for you next time."

Parents should also respect their child's wishes and not force a child to perform when the child does not want to.

## A Short Introduction Before Playing

Before you start, you can simply say: "I am going to play such-and-such a piece."

If the piece has something special about it, for example that you have just learned it, you can mention that briefly too.

An introduction like this gives listeners something to look forward to, and gives you a few seconds to get ready.

## Treat Every Performance as Experience

The more you play in front of family, the more your stage courage grows little by little.

Gradually you will get used to playing in front of others, and the nervousness will ease.

After you get home, you can think about what went well this time and what could be improved, as a reference for next time.

## Preparing Your Repertoire in Advance

Before the holiday, choose one or two pieces you already play fluently as your "gathering pieces".

The pieces do not need to be difficult, and they should not be too long. Around two to three minutes is about right.

The most important thing is that you can play them steadily and are not likely to make mistakes, so you feel more confident.

## The Condition of the Piano

If the gathering is at a relative's home, the piano may be one you do not know, or it may not have been tuned for a long time.

Try a few notes gently first to get a feel for the keys and the sound before you begin.

**Summary**

If the piano is not in good condition, choosing a simple piece is the safer option.

- Prepare one or two fluent short pieces in advance
- Choose melodies everyone will enjoy
- Introduce the title before playing and say thank you afterwards
- If you do not want to play, you can politely say so

## FAQ

**Q: What kind of piece is suitable?**
A: Choose a piece you play fluently that is not too long and has an easy, pleasant melody.

**Q: Do I have to start over if I make a mistake?**
A: No, just keep playing.

**Q: What if my child does not want to play?**
A: Respect your child's wishes. You can politely say that your child will play next time.

**Q: What if the piano at my relative's home has not been tuned for a long time?**
A: Choose a simple piece and try a few notes before you start.

**Q: How many pieces should I prepare?**
A: One or two are enough.

**Q: Can I invite everyone to sing along?**
A: Yes, it makes the atmosphere warmer.

piano-hammer-action-escapement.body:
When you press a piano key, you are actually moving a precise system of levers called the "action". The key works like a seesaw, carrying the force to the back and sending the hammer flying upward to strike the string; just before the hammer reaches the string, a mechanism called the "escapement" lets the hammer break free, so that after striking it can rebound at once instead of resting on the string and muffling the sound. At the same time, the other end of the key lifts the damper, letting the string vibrate freely. When you release the key, the damper falls back onto the string and the sound stops. Understanding this structure helps you see why the speed and timing of your touch matter more than "using force".

## The Five Key Parts of the Action

- Key: the front end is pressed by the finger and the back end rises, like a lever
- Jack: passes the movement of the key to the hammer, and handles the escapement release
- Hammer: a small hammer covered with felt, which strikes the string
- Backcheck: catches the rebounding hammer and stops it from striking the string again and again
- Damper: a felt block resting on the string, lifted when the key is pressed and lowered when it is released

These five parts move one after another in an instant, and all the player feels is "press down, and the sound comes out".

## Escapement: Letting the Sound "Sing"

If the hammer stayed against the string after striking, the string could not vibrate and the sound would at once be muffled. The job of the escapement is to separate the hammer from the part pushing it at the last moment, so that the hammer flies toward the string by inertia and falls naturally back after hitting it.

**What this means for touch**
The hammer strikes by inertia, so what decides the volume is the speed at which the hammer leaves, that is, the speed at which your finger drops the key. If you press hard after the key has reached the bottom, the hammer has long since left, so the sound does not get louder and only your arm becomes tense.

**The feel of the escapement point**
When you press a key very slowly, near the bottom you feel a slight "step", and that is where the escapement happens. The very softest notes are often controlled with fine precision around this point.

![A dark ink-style grand piano with its lid open against a grey-white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvyb2mcq-qm5pa.webp)

## How Fast Repeated Notes Are Possible

When playing the same note repeatedly and quickly, the key does not have time to rise fully. The action of a grand piano usually has a "double escapement" design, so the key only needs to rise partway for the hammer to be ready to strike again. This design appeared in the nineteenth century and made fast repeated notes and trills much easier.

In an upright piano the strings are arranged vertically and the hammers strike horizontally, with springs helping them reset, so the repetition speed is generally not as good as on a grand. That is why some passages feel as if "the key is coming back slowly" on an upright.

## The Relationship Between Dampers and the Pedal

The job of the right pedal is to lift all the dampers together. When the pedal is down, the strings keep vibrating even after you release the keys; at the same time, the other strings that were not played resonate in sympathy, and the sound becomes fuller.

- Release the key, no pedal: the damper falls and the sound stops
- Hold the key, no pedal: only this string sounds
- Pedal down: all strings are free, and the sound is sustained and resonates

Understanding this explains why pedal changes should be "play first, then press": play the new note, then change the pedal, so the old sound is stopped by the dampers and the new sound is kept.

## Three Exercises Related to the Action

**Exercise one: find the escapement point**
On a note in the middle register, press the key down extremely slowly and feel that little step. After a few repetitions, try playing the softest sound you can near that step.

**Exercise two: relax after the key drops**
Play a chord, and at the moment it reaches the bottom let your wrist and forearm relax, with the fingers just resting lightly on the keys. Record yourself before and after relaxing and compare: you will find the volume has not dropped.

**Exercise three: half-key repetition**
On a grand piano, or a digital piano with a similar feel, repeat the same note slowly, letting the key rise only halfway each time. Gradually speed up and feel that the note can sound again without the key rising fully.

## What a Digital Piano Imitates

A digital piano has no real hammers striking strings, but many models build weights or small hammer mechanisms into the keyboard to imitate the weight and rebound of an acoustic piano, and some even simulate the feel of the escapement point. When trying one out, notice whether the weight of the keyboard gradually gets lighter from the low register to the high register, which is also a characteristic of the acoustic piano.

## FAQ

**Q: Why can one person play loudly on the same piano without it sounding harsh?**
A: They use arm weight and the speed of the key drop, rather than pressing hard at the bottom of the key, so the sound is more focused and rounder.

**Q: Does a piano need its action regulated regularly?**
A: Yes. Felt and wooden parts change with time and humidity, so have a professional piano technician check and adjust it.

**Q: Will practising on an upright affect my technique?**
A: Not fundamentally. In practice, pay more attention to controlling repeated notes and very soft notes, and adapt to a grand piano when you have the chance.

**Q: Does my child need to know about this structure?**
A: There is no need to memorise the names, but you can open the lid and let your child watch how the hammers move, which makes them more curious about sound.

piano-and-other-activities-schedule.body:
When a child does piano and other activity classes at the same time, the times often clash. You can start by listing the week's schedule together with your child to see which slots are fairly free; put practice in a fixed, short slot, such as twenty minutes after school or before dinner; practise less on busy days and a bit more on free days. Also ask your child regularly how they feel, and adjust according to their interests and energy; there is no need to fill every slot.

## The reality of many activities

Besides piano, many children also take swimming, painting, dance, ball sports or other academic classes.

Every activity takes time, and with schoolwork on top, a child's week can be packed full.

Piano needs regular daily practice, and in a schedule like this it is often unclear where practice should go.

## Finding out how your child feels

Ask your child regularly how they feel about each activity, what they like and whether they feel tired.

If your child is especially keen on one activity, you might consider giving it more time; if your child feels the load is too heavy, you may need to cut something.

A child's interests and energy change with age, and the schedule can change along with them.

## Adjusting the amount of practice flexibly

On days with lots of classes and homework, you can cut practice down to ten minutes and practise only the most important part.

On days that are fairly free, you can practise a bit more and learn something new.

Adjusting to each day like this keeps the total amount of practice over the week steady.

## Using odd bits of time

Besides the fixed practice slot, you can also use some odd bits of time.

For example, while waiting for another class to start, your child can recall the piece in their head; in the car, they can listen to a recording of the piece they are learning.

These small bits of practice help your child stay familiar with the piece.

## Reviewing the schedule regularly

Every term, or every few months, you can review the schedule with your child to see whether it needs adjusting.

If practice keeps getting squeezed out, think about why: is it a problem with how time is arranged, or has your child's interest changed?

Based on the review, make a new plan and give your child a more balanced life.

![A black grand piano and stool in front of a gold-and-red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yvogp-px1lv.webp)

## No need to fill every slot

It is understandable that parents want their children to learn more, but more activities is not always better.

Rather than learning a little of everything, let your child go deeper in a few activities they are genuinely interested in.

Leave some blank time for your child, so they have a chance to discover their own interests.

## List the week first

Together with your child, write down all the fixed activities in the week, including school, various classes, homework and rest time.

Looking at this chart, you can see clearly which slots are already taken and which are fairly free.

This step helps parents and child face reality together, instead of scheduling by feel.

## Find a fixed practice slot

In the week's schedule, find a fixed slot you can use every day for practice, such as twenty minutes after coming home from school, before dinner.

A fixed slot is easier to stick to than finding time on the spot each day.

If the schedule differs from day to day, you can also set a practice time for each day separately and write it on the chart.

The chart can be put somewhere prominent at home, such as on the fridge or next to the piano, so the whole family can see the week's plan.

## Talk to the piano teacher about lesson times

If the piano lesson clashes with other classes, you can talk to the piano teacher and see whether the lesson time can be changed.

You can also tell the teacher about your child's schedule and ask them to set a suitable amount of practice.

When the teacher understands your child's situation, they can give more practical advice.

- List the whole week's schedule
- Put practice in a fixed short slot
- Practise less on busy days
- Check regularly on your child's feelings and energy

## Leave time to rest

When planning the schedule, do not forget to leave slots where your child has nothing to do and can simply play.

If a child rushes from one class to the next every day, they may feel worn out and lose interest in all of the activities.

**Notice the detail**

With rest, a child has the energy to put into each activity.

## FAQ

**Q: Is twenty minutes of practice a day enough?**
A: For a busy child, regular twenty-minute practice is usually helpful.

**Q: What if there are too many activity classes?**
A: You can assess them together with your child and keep the ones they are genuinely interested in.

**Q: What if practice time keeps getting squeezed out?**
A: Find a fixed slot and write it into the schedule.

**Q: What if the piano lesson clashes with another class?**
A: You can talk to the teacher about changing the lesson time.

**Q: What if my child says they are too tired?**
A: Listen carefully, and cut back on some activities if needed.

**Q: How often should the schedule be adjusted?**
A: You can review it every term or every few months.
