practice-bingo-grid-tasks.body:
Children at home often practise only the pieces they like, and scales, rhythm and note reading are often skipped. Turn the practice tasks into a bingo card: each square is a small task, you colour it in when it is done, and a completed line counts as one finished round. This gamified approach gives every kind of practice a chance to be done.

## Tips for Designing a Bingo Card

When designing the tasks, put the easily skipped practice into the squares, such as scales, rhythm clapping, sight-reading and singing the notes, and also add some fun tasks, such as playing a piece for family.

**A common mistake**

Tasks should be specific and clear, so a child can see at a glance what to do and can finish it in a short time. Tasks that are too hard or too vague make children lose interest.

You can change the content of the card every so often to keep it fresh. You can also let the child help design a few squares, to increase their sense of involvement.

After a line is completed, you can give a simple acknowledgement, such as a mark in the practice notebook, or letting the child choose the next piece they want to learn.

## How to Use It

You can print the bingo card and put it on the piano or stick it on the wall, so it is easy to see every day.

At each practice session, the child can choose one or several squares to complete, and colour them in themselves when done.

After a line is completed, you can give a simple acknowledgement, such as putting a sticker on the card, or letting the child choose the next piece they want to learn.

After a whole card is completed, you can switch to a new one, with the content adjusted to the child's progress.

Parents can encourage from the side, but should try to let the child choose and complete the tasks, to increase the sense of independence.

![Cyberpunk illustration of a silver humanoid robot playing a grand piano and a crystal synthesiser on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lp6gl-f7cgx.webp)

## Key Points in Designing Tasks

Each task should be specific, so the child knows at a glance what to do, for example "play the C major scale twice with the metronome".

Tasks should be completable in a short time, a few minutes is enough, and one square should not take too much time.

The types of task can be varied, including technique, pieces, rhythm, note reading, ear training and singing the notes.

You can also add some relaxed tasks, such as "play a favourite piece for your family" or "make up a four-bar melody yourself".

The middle square can be a free square, letting the child choose what to do.

When designing, you can also adjust the squares according to what the child has recently learned in lessons, so the game keeps pace with the lessons and the practice is more targeted.

- A bingo card breaks practice into small tasks
- Tasks can cover scales, rhythm, note reading and more
- A free square can be added for fun
- Adjust the difficulty of tasks to the child's level

## What a Bingo Card Is

Bingo is a common game. The card has a grid, such as three by three or four by four. You colour in each square as you complete it, and a straight line wins.

Applied to practice, this means writing the practice tasks in the squares and colouring one in each time a task is completed.

This way practice becomes as fun as a game, which is especially suitable for children.

It also helps balance the content of practice. Children often practise only the pieces they like, while scales, rhythm and note reading are easily skipped.

Put these into the squares, and they have a chance of being done.

## Adjust to the Situation

Children of different ages and levels need tasks of different difficulty. You can adjust the number of squares and the content of the tasks according to the child.

If the child finds it too hard, you can reduce the number of squares, or break the tasks into smaller pieces.

If the child finishes very quickly, you can add some more challenging tasks.

You can also invite the child to help design, letting them write a few tasks themselves, to increase their sense of involvement.

A bingo card is only a tool. What matters is keeping practice varied and fun.

**Notice the details**

If you find the child always avoids a certain kind of square, check whether that kind of practice is too hard or not clear enough, and talk with the teacher about how to adjust it.

## FAQ

**Q: Will the bingo card turn into just chasing task completion?**
A: You can add quality requirements to the tasks, such as "play twice at a slow tempo with a steady rhythm", so the child pays attention to how well it is done.

**Q: What age is the bingo card suitable for?**
A: You can adjust the tasks by age, and everyone from primary school children to adult beginners can use it.

**Q: Does it have to be a line?**
A: Not necessarily. You can also count by the number of squares, or by completing the whole card.

**Q: How often should the bingo card be changed?**
A: You can change it every one to two weeks to keep it fresh.

**Q: Can adults use a bingo card?**
A: Yes, just change the tasks to suit yourself.

**Q: What if all the tasks are done but the pieces are not improving?**

pets-and-piano-safety.body:
If you have cats or dogs at home, you can protect the piano with a few small measures: close the lid when you are not playing so pets cannot walk on the keys; do not put food, cups of water or things pets like on top of the piano; clear the hair around the piano regularly; and prepare a special place for pets to rest and play, so they do not always jump onto the piano. That way pets and the piano can both stay safe together.

## Give your pet a place of its own

Not far from the piano, prepare a comfortable bed or a cat tree for your pet, so that they have a position of their own that they like.

**Before you play**

Cats like high places, and with a cat tree they are less likely to jump onto the piano.

When pets rest in their own place, you can give them a reward to help them form the habit.

**Remember**
- Close the lid when you are not playing
- Do not put food or water on top of the piano
- Clear the hair around the piano regularly
- Prepare a dedicated resting area for your pet

![Wooden upright piano, green piano stool and orange books in front of a dark teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yi9wg-robz2.webp)

## Look out for your pet's safety

If the piano lid suddenly closes, it may trap a pet's paw or tail.

Open and close the lid more slowly, and check whether your pet is nearby.

Also take care that pets do not crawl into the gaps behind and under the piano and get stuck.

## Clearing pet hair

Pet hair easily drifts around the piano, even into the gaps between the keys and inside the piano.

You can regularly vacuum the floor around the piano, and wipe the case and keys with a clean soft cloth.

Leave cleaning inside the piano to the professional tuner to handle at the same time as tuning.

## How pets react to the sound of the piano

Some pets may feel nervous or curious when they first hear the piano, and may run over or bark a few times.

You can start with gentle music and let them get used to it slowly.

If your pet seems very uneasy, take them to another room first and wait until they have calmed down.

## Special care with digital pianos

A digital piano has cables and plugs, and pets may chew the cables, which is dangerous.

You can tidy the cables, wrap them in protective sleeves, or put them where pets cannot reach.

When you are not using the digital piano, you can unplug it and put on a dust cover.

## Pets and the piano

Many families keep cats or dogs, and they are often very curious about the piano.

A cat may jump onto the keys or the top of the piano, and a dog may run around the piano or react to the sound.

With a few simple measures, pets and the piano can get along in harmony.

## Close the lid

When you are not playing, form the habit of closing the lid.

That way, when a cat walks on the piano, it will not step on the keys, nor bring hair and dust into the gaps between the keys.

Closing the lid also reduces dust settling on the keys, which protects the piano itself too.

Before you close the lid, look to see whether any hair has fallen on the keyboard, and wipe it gently with a soft cloth before closing.

## Don't put things on the piano

Do not put food, cups of water or toys that pets like on top of the piano.

These things attract pets to jump onto the piano, and if a cup is knocked over, the water may even flow into the piano.

You can also lay a non-slip cover on top of the piano to reduce scratches.

## Tell the tuner about your home

When you ask a tuner to come, you can tell them you have pets and ask them to check while they are there whether there is any hair, dust or small toys inside the piano.

When the tuner opens the piano, it is best to take your pets to another room first, to stop them curiously climbing in or touching the tools being used.

The tuner may also give you some advice on protecting the piano, for example which position is better for the piano.

## Keep practice time cosy too

Some pets stay quietly beside their owner while they practise, which is also a kind of cosy company.

As long as they do not disturb your practice and do not go near dangerous places, you can let them stay beside you.

With protective measures in place, you can enjoy your practice time with peace of mind in the company of your pets.

## The problem of scratching

A cat may scratch the legs or side panels of the piano and leave marks.

You can put a scratching post near the piano to guide the cat to scratch there.

If the cat keeps going for the piano, you can temporarily put something the cat dislikes on that spot, such as double-sided tape, but take care not to damage the surface of the piano.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Will a cat stepping on the keys damage the piano?**
A: An occasional step usually will not, but hair and dust may get into the gaps between the keys.

**Q: What if pet hair gets into the piano?**
A: You can ask the tuner to clean it at the same time as tuning.

**Q: What if the dog barks when it hears the piano?**
A: Start with gentle music and let it get used to it slowly.

**Q: What if the cat scratches the piano legs?**
A: Put a scratching post nearby to guide the cat to scratch it.

**Q: How do you protect the cables of a digital piano?**
A: Tidy the cables and use protective sleeves.

**Q: Can pets stay beside you while you practise?**
A: Yes, as long as they do not disturb the practice and you pay attention to safety.

petrushka-chord-stravinsky-1911.body:
The Petrushka chord is two major triads a tritone apart stacked together. The example most often mentioned is a C major triad and an F♯ major triad sounding at the same time. It takes its name from Stravinsky's 1911 ballet Petrushka, and it stands out in the music that portrays the puppet character. Each of the two major triads is bright on its own, but stacked together they produce a sharp, glittering and slightly unsteady sound, because their roots are a tritone apart, so they do not belong to the same ordinary major key, nor do they form a traditional dominant-tonic relationship with each other. For piano learners, playing the two chords separately on the keyboard and then stacking them to listen is a direct way to get to know this common colour of the twentieth century. It can also help us understand that some "harshness" is not a wrong note, but a composer deliberately stacking two clear chords together. If you circle the notes of the two chords separately, you will see how they interlock. Then listen to the corresponding bars in the original work, and the impression will be even deeper.

## Ask Teacher Aum in lessons to stack them together once

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to play the C major triad and the F♯ major triad first separately and then stacked, to confirm that what you hear is friction and not a wrong note.

**Summary**

If the piece you are learning has a similar kind of writing, you can compare it too.

From this famous sound of 1911, practise hearing the effect of two bright chords stacked together.

## How the Petrushka chord differs from functional harmony

In major and minor keys, two chords are often explained by a relationship such as dominant to tonic.

Two major triads a tritone apart do not have this kind of simple functional relationship.

A more suitable way to hear them is as two opposing colours stacked together.

- Two major triads a tritone apart stacked together
- Often illustrated with C major and F♯ major triads
- The name comes from Stravinsky's 1911 Petrushka
- Best played separately first, then listened to stacked together

## How the two chords combine

Take the C major triad and the F♯ major triad as an example. One is C, E, G, and the other is F♯, A♯, C♯.

When you play them at the same time, on the keyboard you see two groups of notes each tidy in itself but far from each other.

The roots C and F♯ are exactly a tritone apart.

## Related ways of listening

In the twentieth century there were other ways of writing that stack two chords that lie far apart.

Once you know the Petrushka chord well by ear, it is easier to grasp similar stackings when you meet them again.

You should still go by the notes that actually appear in the particular piece.

## No need to memorise many theory terms first

If you can make this sound at the piano and say "two major triads a tritone apart", you have already grasped the core.

Names exist to make discussion convenient.

When you meet other names in analytical articles, you can check them against this clearest description.

## Why it sounds both bright and harsh

A major triad on its own is usually bright and stable.

Put together, the two groups break the stability, and sharp friction appears, while each still keeps its own brightness.

This "brightness that is unstable" is exactly why it is often used.

## How to practise listening at the piano

First play one triad with the right hand and the other with the left, listen to them separately twice, and then press them down together.

You can also first play only the tritone between the two roots, and then fill in each chord's third and fifth.

The volume need not be loud. It is enough to hear the friction clearly.

## What to watch for when playing pieces

If the score has exactly this kind of stacking, you should not change any of the notes just to make it "sound nicer".

Both hands should be together, so that the two chords arrive at the same time.

In the balance, you can bring out one chord slightly, but do not let the other disappear.

![Piano scene with futuristic light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjee87-54t0s.webp)

## Petrushka chord summary

The Petrushka chord is two major triads a tritone apart stacked together, often illustrated with C and F♯. Its name comes from Stravinsky's 1911 ballet, and the sound is bright yet sharp and unstable.

When learning it, first listen to the chords separately and then stacked. When playing, get the two groups of notes together, and there is no need to change notes to wipe out the friction.

You can ask Teacher Aum to make this sound with you at the piano.

## Why it has this name

This chord is called and discussed by this name because of its prominent use in the ballet Petrushka.

The name helps us remember the source, and does not mean that only this one work uses a similar stacking.

First get to know the 1911 work, then notice similar sounds in other twentieth-century music.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Petrushka chord usually made of?**
A: Two major triads a tritone apart, for example a C major triad and an F♯ major triad.

**Q: Where does the name come from?**
A: From Stravinsky's 1911 ballet Petrushka.

**Q: Why does it sound both bright and unstable?**
A: Because each group is a bright major triad, but stacked together they have no traditional dominant-tonic relationship and form sharp friction.

**Q: How do you start listening to it at the piano?**
A: Play the two chords separately first and then press them down together. You can also listen first to just the tritone between the two roots.

**Q: Should you change notes when you meet this kind of writing?**
A: No. You should not change the notes in the score to reduce the friction.

passing-six-four-chord-harmony.body:
A six-four chord is the second inversion of a triad, with the fifth in the lowest voice. For example, the six-four chord of C, E, G is G, C, E with G in the bass. In classical harmony the six-four chord is used with care, and it appears in a few set patterns. The passing six-four is one of them. It appears between two chords, with the bass moving step by step like climbing stairs to link the chords before and after. For example, when the bass goes from C through D to E, the D in the middle carries a passing six-four chord. Understanding this usage helps us make sense of the harmony in a lot of scores.

## Ask your teacher to point out passing six-fours in lessons

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to point out where passing six-four chords appear in the piece you are learning.

Your teacher can also explain how it differs from other six-four chords.

Connecting theory to the pieces you play makes it easier to understand.

## Telling it apart from the cadential six-four

There is another kind of six-four chord that stands guard at the door of the dominant chord and falls on a strong beat. It is called the cadential six-four.

The cadential six-four usually sits on a strong beat and gives a strong sense of expectation.

The passing six-four falls on a weak beat and acts as a link, so the two have different functions.

## How the upper voices fit in

In a passing six-four, the upper voices often stay still or move in the opposite direction to the bass.

For example, when the bass rises from C to E, one of the upper voices can fall from E to C.

This contrary motion makes the voice leading more balanced and fluent.

## Where it comes from: a word on inversions

A triad can be arranged in three ways: root position, first inversion and second inversion.

The second inversion puts the fifth in the bass. For example, in the second inversion of a C major triad, the bass is G.

Because the other two notes lie a fourth and a sixth above the bass, it is called a six-four chord.

## The passing six-four and chord symbols

In lead sheets, the passing six-four is often written as a slash chord, such as G/D.

The chord name comes before the slash and the bass note after it.

When you see this kind of symbol, you know the bass is not the root of the chord.

## Finding passing six-fours in the score

In classical sonatas or minuets, you can often find passing six-four chords.

You can first look for places where the bass moves by step, then check whether the chord in the middle is a six-four chord.

This kind of analysis helps you understand the composer's harmonic thinking.

## Using it when playing accompaniments

When adding an accompaniment to a melody, you can also use a passing six-four to make the bass more fluent.

For example, if you would use a C chord for two bars, you can let the bass go from C through D to E.

An accompaniment like this sounds more lively and does not seem stiff.

## Where the passing six-four sits

The passing six-four appears between two chords and acts as a link.

The most common place is between the tonic in root position and the tonic in first inversion.

For example, in C major, with the bass C, D, E and the chords above being C, G, C, the D in the middle carries a six-four chord of G.

**Things to notice**
- A six-four chord is the second inversion of a triad
- The passing six-four appears between two chords
- The bass moves by step
- It is common between the tonic in root position and first inversion

## Passing between subdominant chords

The passing six-four can also appear between the subdominant in root position and first inversion.

For example, in C major, with the bass F, G, A, the G in the middle carries a six-four chord of C.

The principle is the same: the bass moves by step, and the six-four chord links the two in the middle.

## Passing six-four summary

A six-four chord is the second inversion of a triad, with the fifth in the bass. In classical harmony it is not very stable and is used only in particular places. The passing six-four is one of them: it appears between two chords, the bass moves by step, and the six-four chord falls on the middle step.

It is common between the tonic in root position and first inversion, as with the bass C, D, E, and it can also appear between the subdominant in root position and first inversion. The upper voices often stay or move in contrary motion, and it usually falls on a weak beat with a short value, which makes it different in function from the cadential six-four on a strong beat.

In lead sheets it is often written as a slash chord such as G/D, it can make the bass more fluent when you play accompaniments, and you can ask Teacher Aum to point out passing six-fours in your pieces.

## Stepwise motion in the bass

The key to the passing six-four is the stepwise motion of the bass.

The bass climbs like stairs, rising or falling one step at a time without leaps.

The six-four chord falls on the middle step, like a bridge linking what comes before and after.

## The length of the passing six-four

The passing six-four is usually placed on a weak beat and is fairly short.

That is because it is only a "transition" and not the centre of gravity of the music.

When you play it, you can play it a little more lightly and let it pass naturally.

![Bangkok city poster-style illustration with rows of tall buildings and busy street traffic](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaaq7vu-4n0q8.webp)

## The instability of the six-four chord

In classical harmony, the six-four chord is considered a rather unstable chord.

The fourth between the bass and an upper note is treated in traditional harmony as an interval that needs handling.

That is why the six-four chord is usually used only in particular places.

## Playing the passing six-four on the piano

In C major, you can play a series of chords on the piano: C (root position), G/D (six-four chord), C/E (first inversion).

The left hand plays the bass C, D, E, and the right hand plays the chords.

**Listen**

Listen to how the chord in the middle links the ones before and after.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which inversion is a six-four chord?**
A: The second inversion of a triad.

**Q: Where does the passing six-four appear?**
A: Between two chords.

**Q: How does its bass move?**
A: By step.

**Q: Does the passing six-four usually fall on a strong beat or a weak beat?**
A: A weak beat.

**Q: How is it usually written in lead sheets?**
A: As a slash chord, for example G/D.

play-each-voice-separately-in-fugue.body:
In fugues and other polyphonic pieces, two, three or even more melodies often move at the same time. An effective way to practise is to play each voice on its own first, working out its direction and phrases as if you were singing it; then combine the voices two at a time, and only at the end put them all together. Practising like this trains your ears to pick out every line, and your hands learn which notes belong to which voice, so the layers come through naturally in performance.

## First, Recognise Each Voice

Open the score and find where each voice begins and where it ends.

In a three-voice fugue there is usually a top voice, a middle voice and a bottom voice, and they may be shared between the two hands.

You can use pencils of different colours to lightly mark the notes of each voice.

## Start with Bach's Two-Part Inventions

If you are new to polyphony, begin with Bach's Two-Part Inventions.

Two voices are easier to tell apart than three, and they suit this method well.

Once you feel at home, move on to the Three-Part Inventions and fugues.

## Slow Tempo Is the Key

When you put the voices together, keep the tempo slow, slow enough to hear every voice clearly.

If you play too fast, your ears cannot keep up and the voices blur together.

When you can hear each voice distinctly, then speed up little by little.

## Music in Many Voices

In Bach's inventions and fugues, two or more melodies often move at once, each independent yet fitting together with the others.

This style of writing is called polyphony. Listening to it is a bit like hearing several people talk at the same time, where what each one says matters.

To play this kind of music well, every melody has to be heard clearly.

**Practice order**
- Polyphonic pieces have several melodies moving at once
- First play each voice on its own
- Then combine them two at a time, and finally all together
- Let your ears pick out every line

## Summary: Practising the Voices Separately

Taking each voice out and practising it alone is an effective way to play polyphonic music well.

Alone first, then in combinations, then all together, so that your ears and hands know every line.

Playing practised this way has clearly layered voices and more depth.

## When the Theme Appears

A fugue has a theme that appears in turn in different voices.

You can mark in the score each place where the theme enters, and let the theme stand out a little as you practise.

But do not let the theme get too loud; the other voices still need to stay clear.

## Planning the Fingering

Fingering in polyphonic music is often complicated, because you have to hold some notes while playing others.

You can decide the fingering for each voice first, then check whether it works once the voices are combined.

Sometimes you will need finger substitution, which means quietly swapping one finger for another on a key you are holding down.

## Two Voices in One Hand

Sometimes one hand has to play two voices at once, for example the right hand has the top voice above and the middle voice below.

Then one voice has to be held while the other keeps moving as usual.

You can practise that hand's two voices on their own first, paying attention to which notes to hold and which to release.

## Sing Each Voice

Besides playing, try singing each voice.

Singing helps you feel the direction of the melody more clearly, and it helps your ears remember it.

After singing, when you play it again you will often find you understand the line more deeply.

## Use the Pedal Sparingly in Polyphonic Music

When playing polyphonic music, use very little pedal, or none at all.

With the pedal down, the notes of the different voices run together and become hard to tell apart.

Rely mainly on legato fingering and held notes to keep each melody connected.

## Combining Two Voices

Once you know each voice on its own, you can combine two voices to practise.

For example, play the top and bottom voices first, then the middle and bottom voices.

With each combination, listen for how the two lines fit together: where they move together, and where one rests while the other moves.

## Playing One Voice Alone

Choose one voice and play only that melody from beginning to end, leaving out all the other notes.

As you play, pay attention to its phrases, its rise and fall and its breathing, as if you were singing it.

If the voice passes from one hand to the other, work out where the change of hands happens.

![A person with blue-purple hair in a futuristic jacket plays a layered glowing synthesiser on a neon street](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3kp5i-r452e.webp)

## Record Yourself to Hear the Layers

Record your playing and listen to just one voice, checking whether it stays clear from beginning to end.

Then switch to another voice and check whether anything gets drowned out.

This method helps you find problems that are hard to notice while you are playing and listening at the same time.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why practise each voice separately?**
A: So your ears can pick out each melody and your hands know which voice each note belongs to.

**Q: How do I recognise the voices?**
A: You can mark each voice with a different coloured pencil.

**Q: How should I practise when combining them?**
A: Combine them two at a time first, then put them all together.

**Q: Should I use the pedal in polyphonic music?**
A: Use as little as possible, or none.

**Q: Where should I start with polyphony as a beginner?**
A: You can start with Bach's Two-Part Inventions.

power-chord-root-fifth-piano.body:
In rock music you often hear a simple, powerful chord called a power chord, or a "fifth chord". It has only two different notes: the root and the fifth, sometimes with the root added again an octave higher, for example C, G, C. Because there is no third, you cannot tell whether it is major or minor, and the sound is open and solid. Power chords first became popular on the electric guitar, but you can bring out their strength on the piano too. Knowing about them can help us play rock and pop songs on the piano.

## The Limits of Power Chords

Although power chords are strong, their colour is rather uniform.

**Practice order**

In a lyrical song, using only power chords can sound too empty.

So you can combine power chords with full triads and seventh chords.

## Ask Your Teacher for a Rock Accompaniment in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate how to play a rock song on the piano with power chords.

Your teacher can also help you design the split between the left and right hands, and suitable rhythm patterns.

This is a very good way to practise your sense of rhythm and your control of dynamics.

## Power Chords: A Summary

A power chord has only a root and a fifth, often written C5, sometimes with the root added an octave higher. Because it has no third, you cannot tell major from minor, and the sound is open and solid. It is very clear on a distorted electric guitar, which is why it became a basic chord of rock.

On the piano you can play the root and fifth with the left hand, or an octave in the left hand and a fifth in the right. The shape is fixed, so it is easy to shift. Common progressions include E5, G5 and A5. Much of its appeal comes from rhythm, and it goes well with pentatonic melodies, but its colour is uniform, so in lyrical songs combine it with full chords.

You can compare it with the open fifths of early polyphonic music. Teacher Aum can demonstrate the left-and-right-hand split for a rock accompaniment.

## Why It Became Popular on the Electric Guitar

On a distorted electric guitar, a full triad sounds muddy.

Playing only the root and the fifth makes the sound clear and solid.

So the power chord became a basic chord of rock guitar.

- Only a root and a fifth, often written C5
- No third, so you cannot tell major from minor
- An open, solid sound
- Very common in rock music

## Power Chords and Rhythm

Much of the appeal of power chords comes from rhythm.

You can use continuous eighth notes, or syncopated rhythms, to make the music more energetic.

On the piano, you can keep a steady low note going in the left hand while the right hand plays the rhythm of the power chord.

## How a Power Chord Is Built

A power chord is made of a root and the perfect fifth above it.

For example, the C power chord is C and G.

Sometimes the root is added again an octave higher, giving C, G, C, for a fuller sound.

## Left-Hand Octave Plus Fifth

Another common way to play a power chord on the piano is to play an octave with the left hand and a fifth with the right.

For example, the left hand plays a low C and the C an octave higher, while the right hand plays C and G.

This way of playing sounds thick and heavy, and suits the chorus of a rock song.

![Art Deco style illustration of a person practising at a deep red upright piano under a desk lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaanurt-e601h.webp)

## Pairing with Pentatonic Melodies

A power chord has no third, so it goes with many melodies.

For example, a melody written in the minor pentatonic scale, with power chords underneath, has a rock flavour.

You can try A5, C5 and D5 under a melody in the A minor pentatonic scale.

## Playing Power Chords on the Piano

The easiest C5 on the piano: the left little finger on C and the thumb on G.

You can also play C, G, C with the right hand, or play with both hands together for a wider range.

Play with strength, but keep your arms relaxed, so the sound is solid but not harsh.

## Moving Power Chords

The fingering shape of a power chord is fixed, so it is easy to move.

On the piano, play the fifth with the thumb and little finger, or the thumb and middle finger, and you can slide it to other notes.

For example, moving from C5 to F5 and then to G5 is a common rock progression.

## How Power Chords Are Written

Power chords are often written with a "5", such as C5, G5 and D5.

This "5" means there is only a root and a fifth.

When you see C5 on a chord chart, you know you only need to play C and G.

## Common Power Chord Progressions

Many rock songs use simple power chord progressions, such as E5, G5, A5.

Others use C5, F5, G5, or A5, F5, G5, C5.

When you play these progressions with power chords on the piano, you can use even eighth notes for the rhythm.

## Comparing with Medieval Fifths

In very early Western polyphonic music, people often used perfect fifths and perfect octaves as harmony.

These open fifths have something in common with today's power chords.

But their style and use are completely different, and it is worth listening to them side by side.

## The Effect of Having No Third

The brightness or darkness of a chord depends on the third in the middle. You can hear the difference between E and E♭ at once.

A power chord removes the third, so you cannot tell major from minor.

This makes it sound more neutral, more open and also more powerful.

## FAQ

**Q: Which notes does a power chord have?**
A: The root and the fifth, sometimes with the root added an octave higher.

**Q: How is the C power chord written?**
A: C5.

**Q: Why can you not tell whether it is major or minor?**
A: Because there is no third.

**Q: Why is it popular on the electric guitar?**
A: With distortion, a full triad turns muddy, while the fifth stays clearer.

**Q: How can I make it sound heavier on the piano?**
A: An octave in the left hand and a fifth in the right.

period-versus-sentence-theme-types.body:
When you listen to themes in the classical style, there are two very common ways of organising them, often called the period and the sentence. A period usually works like a question and an answer: the first phrase carries the thought to a place where it cannot quite come to rest, and the second phrase uses similar material to finish the thought. A sentence is more like first stating a short idea clearly, then carrying that idea further forward, and only at the end closing it off. Neither is a hard rule for putting a label on every piece. They are a pair of tools that help the listener grasp the inner rhythm of a theme. When you study, you can first listen to the first half and the second half separately in the score and see whether the second half is answering the first, or is closing up the same motif while pushing it forward. If you only feel that "this passage sounds nice" but cannot say how it walks inside, these two names can give you a more concrete map. This article talks only about the two theme types that are easier to recognise in piano music, and does not present them as the only ways to analyse all music. When practising, it helps to find one clear example of each and listen to the theme alone again and again, without going on to the development after it, which makes it easier to tell the two ways of walking apart.

## How to compare them in practice

Find a typical example of each, play only the theme, listen twice in a row, and compare specifically the direction of the second half.

**Think again**

Then play the two examples one after the other and feel that one is drawing back while the other is pressing forward.

Comparing is harder to forget than memorising definitions on their own.

## How to listen to a sentence

The opening quickly states a short motif clearly, and then, instead of simply repeating it as an answer, carries the motif further forward.

The later part is often denser and moves more forward, and only at the end does a fairly clear closing appear.

The point to listen for is "stand firm first, then set off", rather than "ask, then answer".

## How to mark the score

You can first mark where the theme begins and where it temporarily ends, and then look at whether inside it there are two halves answering each other or one idea being developed further.

There is no need to use many analytical terms at the start. Just write in your own words "this is question and answer" or "this is stand firm, then set off".

Marks are for listening and playing, not for filling up the page.

**Remember this**
- A period is often like question and answer: the first half does not quite come to rest, and the second half finishes the thought
- A sentence is often a short idea presented first, then developed forward and closed
- Both are tools for listening to the inner structure of a theme, not labels to stick on every piece
- When practising, listen to the theme alone first and compare whether the second half is answering or pushing forward

## How to listen to a period

The first half often stops on a note that still wants to go on, and the second half uses familiar material to really close the sentence.

The two halves are often similar in length, sounding like a symmetrical question and answer.

You can listen to only the first half first and ask yourself: does it end like a full stop or like a comma?

## Why tell the two apart

They give a different sense of direction: one is a symmetrical closing, the other a push that keeps moving forward.

When playing, with a period you should pay more attention to whether the two halves answer each other and close symmetrically; with a sentence you should pay more attention to whether the second half really moves forward.

If you expect the wrong thing, you may easily play a place that should push forward too squarely, or a place that should be a reply too aggressively.

## Don't force every piece into a category

Some themes mix the two ways of writing, and some are simply not typical.

When you meet an example you cannot pin down, first get to know it by ear and by hand, then decide whether a name helps.

The tool should serve the person, not make the person fit the tool.

![Digital music image made of high-tech lines of light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdkk62c-gmzv3.webp)

## What to remember about the period and the sentence

A period is often like question and answer, and a sentence is often a presentation first and then development forward.

They are tools for hearing how a theme walks, and there is no need to force every piece into a category.

When practising, first listen to the theme alone, compare the direction of the second half, and then decide on touch and closing.

## Ask Teacher Aum in lessons to judge the direction of the second half together

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the second half of a theme and say whether it is answering the first half or pushing the motif forward.

Where a place is played too squarely or too aggressively, you can also ask your teacher to adjust the tone with you using this map.

From these two common ways of writing themes, practise turning the direction you hear into decisions about how to play.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the easiest feature of a period to hear?**
A: The first half is like a question and has not quite come to rest, and the second half finishes the thought with similar material, often with a sense of symmetry.

**Q: What is the easiest feature of a sentence to hear?**
A: A short idea is stated clearly first, then developed forward, and only closed at the end.

**Q: Why tell the two ways of writing apart?**
A: One puts more weight on answer and closing, the other on pushing on, so what you expect in playing is different.

**Q: Must every piece be put into one of the two categories?**
A: No. Some themes mix them, and when you cannot say, get to know it by ear and by hand first, then decide whether the name is useful.

**Q: How can you compare them more clearly in practice?**
A: Find one clear example of each, listen only to the theme, and compare specifically whether the second half is answering or moving forward.

piano-fingering-numbers-techniques.body:
The small numbers beside the notes in a score are fingering marks: 1 is the thumb, 2 the index finger, 3 the middle finger, 4 the ring finger and 5 the little finger, numbered the same way for both hands. Editors write these numbers so that the hand can find a smooth route between consecutive notes, especially before fast passages, position changes and leaps. At beginner and intermediate level, it is best to follow the fingering in the score as far as possible; once you understand the reasons behind it, you can adjust it to suit your own hand.

Many people playing slowly feel that "any finger will do", and only when they speed up do they find the fingers have "nowhere to go" and have to stop and look for a new position. This is often the result of ignoring fingering early on. Below, starting with how to read the numbers, we go through the common fingering techniques.

## Basic Rules of Fingering Numbers

- Both hands are numbered starting from the thumb: 1 to 5 are thumb, index, middle, ring and little finger
- The numbers are usually written above the note (right hand) or below it (left hand), but different editions of a score may differ
- Editors do not mark a number on every note, only where the position changes or where mistakes are easy
- For notes with no number, the fingering generally continues naturally from the previous one
- Different editions of the same piece may have different fingerings, and this is perfectly normal

![A watercolour-style white piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvwz9wck-3vau4.webp)

## Four Common Fingering Techniques

**Thumb-under**
When playing a scale going up, the thumb passes under the other fingers to reach the next note, so that the hand can keep moving forward. For example, in a C major scale in the right hand, after playing E (finger 3), the thumb passes under to play F.

**Finger-over**
In the opposite direction, the other fingers cross over the thumb. For example, in a right-hand scale going down, after playing F (finger 1), finger 3 crosses over the thumb to play E.

**Finger substitution**
Hold down a key and quietly replace one finger with another, freeing a finger for the notes that follow. This technique is common in legato melodies and polyphonic works, and is often written in the score as two numbers such as "4-3".

**Extension and contraction**
The palm opens slightly so that the fingers cover a range wider than five adjacent keys; afterwards it returns to its natural shape. Extend only moderately, and do not hold the hand stretched for long.

{{IMG:piano-6.webp}}

## Why Did the Editor Write It This Way? Three Ways to Judge

**Look at the notes that follow**
A fingering is often prepared for the next few notes. A note may be given finger 3 instead of 2 because the next four notes go upward and you need to keep enough fingers in reserve.

**Look at the continuity of the phrase**
In melodies that need legato, editors try to avoid using the same finger for two different notes in a row, because that easily breaks the line.

**Look at the natural position of the hand**
The long fingers (2, 3 and 4) are more comfortable on the black keys, and the thumb should stay on the white keys as much as possible. This is the basis of many fingering choices.

## A Four-Step Method for Marking Your Own Fingering

When the score has no fingering, or when you want to check the editor's suggestion, you can mark it yourself with the following steps:

**First find the "must" positions**
Mark the first note of the phrase, the places where the position changes, and the highest and lowest notes; the fingering at these points decides the rest.

**Try two or three options slowly**
In one or two bars where problems are likely, compare different fingerings and pick the one that feels most natural and most connected.

**Write it down in pencil**
Once you have decided, write it on the score and practise with the same fingering every time. Fingers need repetition to build memory.

**Check it at speed**
Play it through at a faster tempo. If it still feels smooth at the original speed, keep it; if it gets stuck, go back to step two and adjust.

## A Small Exercise: One Melody, Two Fingerings

Find a melody of five or six notes that you know well, such as the opening of a children's song. First play it with the most "natural" fingering, then deliberately play it with a different fingering, and compare how the two feel: which connects more smoothly? Which makes the hand move more? Which leaves your fingers with room to spare by the end of the phrase? This kind of comparison takes only a few minutes, yet it lets you really feel how fingering affects the continuity of the sound and the ease of the hand. The next time you see numbers in a score, you will be more willing to ask "why did the editor arrange it this way?" instead of treating them as optional hints.

## When You Can Change the Fingering

- When your hand is rather small or rather large, and the editor's fingering is clearly uncomfortable for you
- When there is a smoother solution for the same passage and you can say why you are changing it
- When your teacher gives a new suggestion based on your hand and playing style

Changing a fingering is not "being lazy"; it is a reasonable choice made after understanding the original fingering. After changing it, stick to the same solution, and do not switch casually each time.

## FAQ

**Q: The fingering in the score is different from what my teacher taught. Whom should I follow?**

A: Generally follow your teacher's suggestion, because the teacher can see your hand shape and habits. You can also ask your teacher to explain the difference between the two fingerings.

**Q: My child never looks at the fingering. What can I do?**

A: You can circle the key fingerings with a coloured pencil together with your child, and "say the fingering aloud" before practising, turning it into a little game.

**Q: I can play with the wrong fingering at a slow tempo. Is it necessary to change it?**

A: Yes. Habits formed at a slow tempo are carried over into fast passages, and changing them then is harder.

**Q: Is the fingering for the left hand the same as for the right?**

A: The numbering is the same, with the thumb as 1. But because the two hands are mirror images, the fingering order for the same scale is usually reversed.

## Start drawing a route map for your fingers

parent-workshop-music-school-marketing.body:
A parent workshop is a small talk-and-experience session of one to two hours that a music school holds for the parents of its students. Typical themes are "how to support your child's practice" and "how to see your child's progress". On the surface it is an educational event, but it is also a gentle form of brand marketing: when parents understand the learning process better, they find it easier to understand the teacher's plans, are more willing to stick with lessons long term, and are happier to share their honest experience with friends. To run a good parent workshop, you need to choose the right topic, design interaction, explain methods clearly, and give parents materials to take home afterwards.

## Why parents need workshops

Many parents have never learned an instrument themselves. When their child gets stuck, loses their temper or slows down while practising, they often do not know how to respond. Some parents push too hard, while others step back completely. Both approaches can make a child lose interest. The workshop helps parents understand the normal rhythm of learning an instrument: progress is rarely a straight line, and there are plateaus and setbacks. Once parents understand this, the way they speak and behave at home becomes calmer.

For the school, parents' understanding reduces misunderstandings. For example, if a teacher slows down the repertoire to build foundations, and parents know the reason in advance, they will not mistakenly think their child "isn't learning anything".

## Choosing a workshop topic

The topic should be specific and, as far as possible, come from parents' real questions. Before registration opens, you can send a simple questionnaire and let parents pick the topics they care about most. Common topics include:

- How long to practise each day, and how to schedule practice time.
- What parents can and cannot say when their child does not want to practise.
- How to read the teacher's practice notes and lesson feedback.
- How to balance exams, competitions and everyday learning.
- How to choose an instrument to practise on when there is no piano at home.

It is more effective for one workshop to go deep on just one or two topics than to cover many things in general terms.

![A watercolour-style upright piano with open sheet music on the stand and a wooden stool beside it](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw1izifb-gqte2.webp)

## Designing the workshop flow

A ninety-minute workshop can be organised like this:

**Opening, ten minutes**: The teacher introduces themselves, explains today's goal, and asks each parent to write down one problem they most want to solve.

**Talk, thirty minutes**: Explain the method around the topic, using real but anonymous situations as examples, and avoid naming any student.

**Hands-on, twenty minutes**: Ask parents to try a simple exercise at the piano themselves, such as playing a five-finger pattern slowly. Parents who have felt for themselves what it is like when "the hands won't listen" are often more understanding of their children.

**Q&A, twenty minutes**: Answer questions from the room; questions you are unsure about can be answered after the session.

**Closing, ten minutes**: Hand out the materials and introduce the next event.

## Materials and follow-up

After the workshop, you can give parents a one-page summary that includes the key points of the day, a few sentences they can use straight away, such as "I heard that you played this section more smoothly today", and a simple weekly practice log. Keep the materials concise so they are easy to stick on the fridge or next to the piano.

A week or two later, you can send a message asking how things have gone at home, and invite parents to share their experience with other parents. Be careful not to let the follow-up turn into a sales pitch; the focus is on caring about the child's learning.

## How teachers need to prepare

A workshop is also a new challenge for teachers. In lessons, teachers face children; in a workshop, they face adults, so their way of speaking needs to adjust: less jargon and more everyday analogies; less theory and more concrete things parents can do. You can ask a colleague to listen to your talk beforehand and point out where it is hard to follow. Preparing one or two short demonstration recordings, such as the same melody practised in a rushed way and in a patient way, helps parents see directly why slow practice matters.

## The word of mouth a workshop brings

When parents feel that the school genuinely cares about their child's growth, they naturally mention the experience when chatting with friends. This kind of word of mouth is more persuasive than advertising. With their consent, the school can invite parents who attended a workshop to write a few honest words about it for the website or social media, but it should not rewrite them into exaggerated claims or promise results.

## FAQ

**Q: How often should we hold a parent workshop?**
A: One or two per term works well, with topics based on the different needs at the start and the end of the term.

**Q: Do workshops need to be paid?**
A: For parents of current students they are usually free; if open to the public, you can charge a small fee to cover the venue and materials.

**Q: Can it be held online?**
A: Yes. Online workshops make it easier for busy parents to attend, but the hands-on part needs to be adjusted so parents try it at home on a phone app or keyboard.

**Q: What if parents disagree with each other?**
A: The teacher can guide everyone to share their experiences, while explaining that every child is different and there is no one-size-fits-all answer.

## Practise together with your child

pause-and-prepare-before-the-hard-spot.body:
When you reach a hard spot, it is often because the hand has not been prepared in time, and mistakes happen in the rush. One practice method is to stop on the note just before the hard spot. While you are stopped, think through the notes that follow, the fingering and the hand position, even move your hand ahead to the prepared position, and then play across. As you become fluent, the pause gets shorter and shorter, until eventually you do not need to stop and the hand can prepare itself in advance.

## Which hard spots it suits

This method is especially useful where you need to change hand position, make a leap or change fingering.

It also suits places where the rhythm suddenly changes, for example from eighth notes to triplets.

Wherever a mistake comes from not being prepared in time, you can practise with this method.

## When both hands are involved

If the hard spot needs both hands to prepare, for example when both hands change position at once, think through the movements of both hands while you are stopped.

You can first practise each hand's preparation separately, then put them together.

When playing hands together, stop and check that both hands are ready.

## Stopping before the hard spot

When practising, stop on the note just before the hard spot and hold it down.

The pause can be fairly long, say two or three seconds, long enough to think through what you need to do next.

This pause gives your mind and your hands time to prepare.

## Marking the score

In the score, you can draw a small pause mark or a circle on the note just before the hard spot.

That way you know to stop and prepare there when you practise.

Once you are fluent, the mark can remind you to prepare ahead of time.

## Stop-and-prepare summary

Mistakes at hard spots often happen because the hand was not ready. You can stop on the note before the hard spot, think through the notes, fingering and position that follow, move the hand over first, and then play across.

Once you are fluent, gradually shorten the pause until you build the habit of preparing in advance. It is especially useful for changes of hand position, leaps and fingering changes.

You can mark the score and combine it with slow practice, and prepare each hand separately, but in the real performance do not leave any extra pauses.

## Let the hand prepare first

While you are stopped, you can let the hand move above the next position, without pressing down yet.

For example, if the next note will be played with the thumb, first move the thumb over that key.

Once you are prepared, play it out, and you will feel calm and unhurried.

![Illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, conveying the power of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6k14e-kcqsx.webp)

## Then play across

When you are prepared, continue from the note where you stopped and play through the hard spot.

Because you have already prepared, this time you can usually play it fairly smoothly.

Repeat this "stop, prepare, then play" a few times, and your hand will gradually remember the preparing movement.

## Don't let it become a habitual pause

The pause is only a stage of practice, so do not stop in the real performance too.

That is why, once you are fluent, you must gradually shorten the pause until you play across without a break.

You can check with a metronome to make sure the final playing has no extra pauses.

## Combining with slow practice

Stop-and-prepare practice can also be combined with slow practice.

First, at a slow tempo, stop and prepare before the hard spot, then play across.

Combining slow tempo with pauses gives your mind and hands more time.

## Gradually shortening the pause

Once "stop, prepare, then play" becomes fairly fluent, you can shorten the pause.

Shorten it from two or three seconds to one second, then to half a second.

In the end you need no pause, and the hand can prepare in advance while still on the previous note.

## The habit of preparing ahead

The ultimate aim of this practice is to build the habit of preparing in advance.

While you play the earlier notes, your mind is already thinking about the notes to come, and your hand is quietly moving towards them.

That way the hard spot does not appear suddenly but is something you expected.

- Mistakes at hard spots often come from an unprepared hand
- Stop on the note before the hard spot
- While stopped, think it through and prepare the hand
- Shorten the pause gradually until it is not needed

## Why mistakes happen at hard spots

When you make mistakes at a hard spot, it is often not because you cannot play it but because the hand was not prepared in time.

For example, a place where you need to change hand position, jump to another register, or use an unusual fingering.

If the hand looks for its position only at the last moment, it is easy to play wrong notes.

## What to think about while stopped

While you are stopped, you can ask yourself in your head: what is the first note that follows? Which finger will play it? Where does the hand need to move?

You can also look at the score and confirm the positions of the next few notes.

Once it is clear in your mind, start to play.

## Say the preparation aloud

When you first start practising, you can quietly say aloud what you are about to do while stopped, such as "thumb to G" or "hand moves right".

Saying it aloud helps your mind remember the preparation steps more clearly.

**Before you play**

Once you are fluent, you no longer need to say it aloud.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why do hard spots go wrong so easily?**
A: The hand was not prepared in time.

**Q: Where do you stop?**
A: On the note just before the hard spot.

**Q: What do you do while stopped?**
A: Think through the notes and fingering that follow, and prepare the hand first.

**Q: Should the pause always be kept?**
A: No, shorten it gradually until it is not needed.

**Q: Which hard spots does it suit?**
A: Places with changes of hand position, leaps and fingering changes.

piano-ballade-genre-chopin-four.body:
The ballade was originally a story-telling poem or song, often recounting legends, love or the adventures of heroes. In the nineteenth century, Chopin used the name "ballade" for solo piano pieces and wrote four large-scale piano ballades; the first, Op. 23, was completed around 1835, and the fourth, Op. 52, between 1842 and 1843. These works have no words, yet they are like a long story, with a beginning, development, climax and ending. Later, composers such as Brahms and Grieg also wrote piano ballades.

## Playing as storytelling

When you play a ballade, or any piece with a feeling of story, you can imagine you are telling a story.

**Notice the detail**

The opening should draw people in, the middle should have ups and downs, the climax should have power, and the ending should leave something to linger over.

This way of thinking helps you plan the structure of the whole piece.

## The time signature of ballades

Most of Chopin's four ballades use a compound metre, such as 6/4 or 6/8.

This metre has a rocking, flowing feel, much like the rise and fall of the voice when telling a story.

When listening, notice the pulse of two main beats in each bar.

## Talking about piano ballades in lessons

In a lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about the characteristics of the ballade and listen together to one of Chopin's ballades.

The teacher can help point out the main themes and how they change.

If the level is right, you can also ask the teacher to recommend a piece worth trying.

## A story-like structure

The structure of a ballade is often like a story: it opens with a calm introduction, then the main "character", the theme, appears.

Next, the theme is changed and developed, the conflict grows more intense, and finally it reaches a climax.

The ending is sometimes tragic and sometimes calm.

## The piano ballade in summary

The ballade was originally a story-telling poem or song. Chopin was among the first to use the name for solo piano pieces, writing four: G minor, Op. 23; F major, Op. 38; A♭ major, Op. 47; and F minor, Op. 52. The first was completed around 1835 and the fourth between 1842 and 1843, and most use 6/4 or 6/8.

They are said to have been inspired by the narrative poems of Mickiewicz, but Chopin did not say which poems they correspond to. Their structure is like a story, with an introduction, development, climax and ending, and the themes are often transformed. Brahms wrote four ballades, Op. 10, in 1854, and Grieg's Op. 24 is a set of variations on a Norwegian folk song.

You can first listen all the way through, then look for the themes and their changes. Chopin's ballades are very demanding; when you play, you can imagine you are telling a story. For help appreciating and choosing pieces, you can ask Teacher Aum.

## The transformation of themes

In a ballade, the same theme often appears in different guises.

For example, a theme that begins gently may later become agitated and grand.

This transformation of the theme is like characters in a story going through different events.

## Chopin's four ballades

Chopin wrote four ballades in all: G minor, Op. 23; F major, Op. 38; A♭ major, Op. 47; and F minor, Op. 52.

The first was completed around 1835, and the fourth between 1842 and 1843.

All four are fairly long, each lasting from about seven to a dozen or so minutes.

## The ballade from sung words to piano piece

Before Chopin, "ballade" mainly meant a song with words.

Chopin was one of the first composers to use the name for purely piano works.

His ballades have no words, yet they keep the feeling of storytelling.

- Originally a story-telling poem or song
- Chopin wrote four piano ballades
- Often in 6/8 or 6/4
- Brahms and Grieg also wrote them

## Brahms's ballades

Brahms wrote four ballades, Op. 10, in 1854.

The first of them was inspired by an old Scottish narrative poem, telling a tragic story.

Brahms's ballades are somewhat shorter than Chopin's, and their style is more deeply sombre.

## How to listen to a ballade

The first time you listen to a ballade, you can leave the score aside and listen all the way through, feeling the changes of mood.

Then find the main themes and notice how they change later on.

Finally, think about what story it tells, if it were a story.

## What it takes to play a ballade

Chopin's ballades are very demanding in both technique and musicianship, and suit more advanced learners.

They require control of a long structure and careful planning of the rises and falls in dynamics and tempo; you cannot use up all your strength at the start.

Intermediate learners can start with listening and analysis.

## The original meaning of the ballade

The ballade began as a story-telling poem, often passed on by word of mouth among ordinary people.

Its content was mostly legends, love, adventure or tragedy, with a clear plot.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, many poets wrote narrative poems, and composers set them as songs.

## The link with poets

It is said that Chopin's ballades were inspired by the narrative poems of the Polish poet Mickiewicz.

This claim comes from accounts by Schumann and others, but Chopin himself never said which poem each piece corresponds to.

So when listening to a ballade, you do not need to look for a specific story, but can feel the plot of the music itself.

## Grieg's ballade

The Norwegian composer Grieg wrote a piano ballade, Op. 24, a set of variations on a Norwegian folk song.

The work is deeply sombre in mood and is regarded as one of Grieg's more important piano works.

**Try it**

It also shows that the ballade can take many forms.

![A Bangkok city poster-style illustration, with tall buildings and busy traffic in the streets](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabs0wd-pu7x9.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What was the ballade originally?**
A: A story-telling poem or song.

**Q: How many ballades did Chopin write?**
A: Four.

**Q: What time signatures do Chopin's ballades often use?**
A: 6/4 or 6/8.

**Q: In which year did Brahms write his ballades?**
A: 1854.

**Q: What is distinctive about Grieg's ballade?**
A: It is a set of variations on a Norwegian folk song.

piano-fills-between-vocal-phrases.body:
When accompanying a singer, there is often a gap of a beat or two after one phrase ends and before the next begins. If the accompaniment just keeps playing the same chord, these gaps can feel a little empty. Experienced accompanists play a short little melody here, called a fill, to link the two vocal phrases. A fill should be short and soft; it must not cover the voice, nor take up the time the singer needs to start the next phrase.

## The Register of a Fill

A fill is usually played above or below the register of the voice, not in the same register as the voice.

**A different angle**

If the singer is in the middle register, the fill can be played in the high register, like a gentle echo.

This way the fill and the voice do not fight each other, and everything sounds clearer.

## Fills: A Summary

When accompanying a singer, you can play short fills in the gaps between vocal phrases to link the two phrases together.

Start from a few notes of the chord or the scale, play outside the register of the voice, keep it soft and short, and do not fill every gap.

Listen to the singer's breathing, match the lyrics, learn from recordings, practise at home first, and talk with the singer.

**Summary**
- There is often a gap of a beat or two between vocal phrases
- Play a short little melody in the gap
- Link the two vocal phrases together
- Keep it short and soft, without covering the voice

## Learn from Recordings

Listen to recordings of pop songs, and notice what the piano or other instruments play in the gaps of the vocal line.

Try playing these fills on the piano, and learn how they are written.

The more you listen, the better you will know which kind of fill suits which kind of song.

## Listen to the Singer's Breathing

When accompanying, listen for the singer's breathing, so you know when the singer is getting ready to begin the next phrase.

If the singer needs a little more time to breathe, the fill can be a bit shorter, or you can simply not play one.

The accompaniment should follow the singer, not make the singer follow the accompaniment.

## Keep It Soft

A fill should be played more softly than the voice; it is only a supporting element, not the lead.

If a fill is played too loudly, it pulls attention away from the voice.

When playing it, you can use a gentler touch.

## Match the Lyrics

The mood of a fill should match the lyrics as far as possible; for example, when the lyrics are cheerful, the fill can be lighter and brighter.

When the lyrics are sad, the fill can be slower and softer.

In this way a fill is not just filling a gap, but helping to express the feeling of the song.

## Talk with the Singer

If you are going to accompany someone, you can talk with the singer and ask whether they like having fills in the accompaniment.

Some singers like a simple accompaniment, others like something richer.

Respect the singer's wishes, and the accompaniment will fit better.

## The Gaps Between Vocal Phrases

In most songs, there is a little gap after each line of lyrics ends, to give the singer a chance to breathe.

These gaps may be only a beat or two, or they may be a whole bar.

An accompanist can use these gaps to keep the music flowing.

## Practise at Home First

Before accompanying a singer, you can first practise at home, singing and playing at the same time, adding fills in the gaps.

You can also play a recording of the song and try playing in the gaps of the recording.

Once you are comfortable, it will feel more natural when you rehearse with the singer.

## Start with Chord Notes

When you first learn to play fills, you can start with the notes of the current chord.

For example, if the chord is C, the right hand can play a few of the notes C, E and G, making a short rising or falling line.

Because these are chord notes, it is bound to sound harmonious.

![A glowing digital interface against a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6mskl-2dvtt.webp)

## Do Not Fill Every Gap

Not every gap needs a fill; sometimes leaving a little silence is also good.

If every gap is filled, the accompaniment can seem too busy, and the voice does not stand out.

You can add fills at important places, such as between sections, or where the mood of the lyrics changes.

## What Is a Fill

A fill is a short bit of melody or figure that the accompanist plays in the gaps of the vocal line.

It is usually very short, only a few notes, like a response to the voice.

A good fill makes the accompaniment livelier, and also helps the singer move naturally into the next phrase.

## Use a Few Notes of the Scale

Once you are comfortable, you can use a few notes of the scale to play a small stepwise melody.

For example, play down from G to C: G, F, E, D, C, which leads straight into the next chord.

This kind of little melody is very natural and is often used in songs.

## Keep It Short

A fill should finish before the singer begins the next phrase; it must not take up the singer's time.

So you need to know clearly how long the gap is, and the fill must not go beyond that length.

**Watch the details**

You can first count how many beats the gap has, and then plan the length of the fill.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a fill?**
A: A short bit of melody or figure played in the gap in the vocal line.

**Q: Which notes should I start learning fills with?**
A: The notes of the current chord.

**Q: In which register should a fill be played?**
A: Above or below the register of the voice.

**Q: Do I need to fill every gap?**
A: No, sometimes leaving space is also good.

**Q: How loud should a fill be?**
A: Softer than the voice.

practice-legato-passage-staccato-first.body:
A fast passage marked legato often comes out as a blur: some notes stick together, some are uneven, and some fingers do not really reach the bottom of the key. A common way to practise is to play the notes of the legato passage staccato first. In staccato, every note has to be prepared and played separately, so the position and movement of the fingers become perfectly clear. Once the fingers know each note well, go back to legato, and the notes are often cleaner and more even.

## Back to Legato

When the staccato is secure, return to legato.

When you return to legato, keep the feeling of every note being clear that you had in staccato.

The fingers still come down one by one; they just no longer lift, and instead hand over smoothly.

- Play a legato passage staccato first
- Prepare and play each note separately
- Keep the staccato light; do not hit hard
- Keep the clarity of staccato when you return to legato

## Alternate Legato and Staccato

You can use the two ways alternately: play once staccato, then once legato.

This gradually carries the clarity of staccato into the legato.

After a few days, see whether the legato passage is cleaner than before.

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen in Lessons

After practising this way for a while, you can ask Teacher Aum in your lesson to listen to the legato.

You can also ask the teacher to check whether your staccato movement is relaxed and free of extra tension.

With the teacher's feedback, your practice will be better targeted.

## Do Not Practise Only Staccato

Staccato is only the scaffolding for legato; the house itself still has to be built with legato.

If you practise only staccato, your fingers get used to lifting, and when you return to legato it comes out less connected.

So after every staccato practice, go back to the legato the score asks for.

## Check Evenness in Staccato

In staccato each note stands alone, which makes it easier to hear which notes are uneven in dynamics and length.

If a note is especially heavy or light, look for the reason, for example whether one finger is weaker.

Take the uneven spots out and practise them a few more times.

## Staccato from Slow to Fast

Staccato practice should also begin slowly, making sure the position and fingering of every note are correct.

When you are familiar with it, gradually speed up.

Fast staccato needs very agile fingers, which is also good training.

## Passages Suited to Staccato Practice

Fast scale runs, broken chords and places where the fingers alternate often respond clearly to being sorted out with staccato.

If a passage always has a few notes sticking together, you can try this method.

For slow, singing melodies, this method does not help as much.

## Why Legato Passages Easily Blur

Legato requires no break between notes, with the fingers passing on one after another.

When the tempo is fast, the fingers easily drag on one another, and some notes are covered by the next before they are played clearly.

Slowing down helps then, but sometimes you need to practise in a different way as well.

## Summary: Practising Legato with Staccato

A legato passage easily blurs at speed. Playing it staccato first makes each note independent and its position clear. Keep the staccato movement light, use the original fingering, go from slow to fast, and use the chance to check evenness.

When it is secure, return to legato and keep the feeling of every note being clear. You can alternate staccato and legato. This method suits fast runs and broken chords and helps less with slow singing melodies.

Staccato is only an aid and cannot replace practising the legato itself. It can be combined with changing the rhythm, and you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the result in your lesson.

## Combine with Rhythm-Variation Practice

Staccato practice can also be combined with rhythm variation, for example changing even sixteenth notes into dotted rhythms.

First play the dotted rhythm staccato, then play the dotted rhythm legato, and finally return to the original rhythm.

Using several methods together makes your fingers more familiar with the passage.

## Staccato Makes Each Note Independent

When you play staccato, each note is lifted immediately after it is played, leaving a brief gap between notes.

That gap gives us time to think clearly about the position and fingering of the next note.

Every movement of the fingers becomes independent and definite.

![A black grand piano and stool in front of a gold-and-red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8v4yi-4y5hj.webp)

## Keep Staccato Practice Light

When practising a legato passage with staccato, keep the movement light; do not hit the keys heavily with your arm.

You can make the staccato with a slight spring of the finger or wrist.

The dynamic can be around mezzo piano; the point is that every note is clear.

## Keep the Original Fingering

When practising with staccato, always use the fingering you use in legato.

The aim of the practice is to make your fingers familiar with the position of each note, and changing the fingering would defeat the purpose.

Sometimes, playing staccato, you will find a spot where the original fingering is awkward, and you can use that to adjust it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why practise a legato passage with staccato?**
A: To make each note independent and its position clear.

**Q: What fingering should I use in staccato practice?**
A: The original fingering used in legato.

**Q: How should the staccato movement be?**
A: Light; do not hit hard.

**Q: Can I practise only staccato?**
A: No, go back to legato after practising.

**Q: What passages suit this method?**
A: Fast runs, broken chords and the like.
