piano-iron-frame-cross-stringing.body:
As the nineteenth century brought a growing demand for pianos that were louder, steadier and could be heard in larger rooms, the strings were pulled tighter, and were often longer and thicker too. A wooden case gradually found it hard to bear such tension alone, so metal frames or braces began to be used inside, spreading the pull of the strings onto a stronger structure. At the same time, many makers also adopted cross-stringing: letting the lower strings run diagonally over the top of the other strings, so that a longer vibrating length is gained within a limited case. These two developments are often discussed together because they answer the same question: how to make a piano sound fuller and steadier without increasing its size endlessly. Learning about them is not meant to help you remember who invented what, but to understand why the inside of today's common piano looks like a small bridge. When a learner opens the lid of a modern piano, they can first recognise that metal skeleton, and then imagine how great the pull on the strings is. This article talks only about changes in structure and in how things sound; it does not name any manufacturer, nor present any one maker's approach as an unchangeable standard.

## Work Backwards from Sound to Structure with Teacher Aum in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen with you to the depth and sustain of the bass, and discuss how this relates to the structure of the modern piano.

If an early piece sounds too full on today's piano, you can also ask the teacher to help you find a more restrained way to play it.

From the frame and cross-stringing, practise linking the sound you hear with the changes inside the instrument.

## What Problem Does Cross-Stringing Solve

If all the strings ran parallel, the case would have to be very long for the bass to reach enough length.

Letting the bass strings run diagonally over the others keeps a longer vibrating length within a relatively compact shape.

In terms of sound, this has a direct bearing on whether the bass can be rich, and whether it can balance with the middle and high registers.

**A common misunderstanding**
- In the nineteenth century pianos gradually adopted metal frames to bear greater tension
- Cross-stringing gives the lower strings a longer vibrating length in limited space
- Both aim to make the sound fuller and steadier without greatly increasing size
- Knowing the structure helps explain why the inside of today's piano looks like a small bridge

## What to Remember About These Two Structures

The metal frame bears the greater string tension, while cross-stringing gives the bass a longer vibrating length in limited space.

Both are meant to give the piano a fuller, steadier sound without making it endlessly larger.

When we play a modern piano today, we are in fact working together with these later-added structures.

![City lights and buildings at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdki0af-l1sku.webp)

## Seeing the Inside Makes It Easier to Remember

If you get the chance, under the guidance of your teacher or a piano tuner, to take a look inside, first recognising the frame and the direction in which the bass strings cross will stay in your memory better than just memorising terms.

There is no need to take the piano apart, and do not touch the parts inside yourself.

After looking once, going back to the score and talking about sound is often more concrete.

## What the Metal Frame Does

The frame or brace bears the pull of the strings, so that the case is less easily pulled out of shape.

In this way tuning can be steadier, and makers are better able to use stronger strings.

Open a piano today and you can often see this layer of metal skeleton; it is not decoration, but part of the structure.

## Why Tension Increased

People wanted a louder sound that could hold its own in larger spaces, and also a wider range and a steadier resonance.

To achieve these, strings often had to be pulled tighter, and sometimes made longer.

Once tension rises, a wooden structure alone is easily deformed, which can even affect the stability of the tuning.

## A Compromise Between Size and Sound

A piano cannot grow without limit, especially as it has to fit into homes or mid-sized halls.

The frame and cross-stringing both seek a stronger, steadier sound within limited space.

So the common shape we see today is in fact the result of a series of structural compromises.

## What This Means for the Player

You do not need to be a maker to understand from this why modern pianos are often louder and steadier than early instruments.

When playing early works, if you feel today's sound is too big, part of the reason is that these later structures support the energy more firmly.

**Slow down**

Controlling the volume is sometimes a matter of cooperating with an instrument designed to produce a very large sound.

## FAQ

**Q: What problem does the metal frame mainly solve?**
A: It bears the greater string tension, reduces deformation of the case, and makes the sound and tuning steadier.

**Q: What does cross-stringing mean?**
A: Letting the lower strings run diagonally over the top of the other strings, so that a longer vibrating length is kept within a limited case.

**Q: Why are these two things often discussed together?**
A: Both answer the question of how to make a piano louder and steadier without much increase in size.

**Q: How does knowing these structures help with playing early works?**
A: It helps you understand why modern pianos are often louder, so you can control volume more consciously.

**Q: Can I open a piano and touch the parts inside myself?**
A: No. If you want to look, do so under the guidance of someone experienced, and do not touch anything yourself.

play-a-piece-cold-once-a-week.body:
In everyday practice, we usually warm up first, then work on the difficult spots, and only when our fingers are fully loosened up do we play the piece through from the beginning. Of course the result is better that way. But in an exam, a performance or when playing for friends, there is often no chance to warm up properly, and you have to sit down and play. To prepare, you can schedule a "cold start" once a week: as soon as you sit at the piano, without warming up or practising the hard spots first, play the piece you are preparing straight through from beginning to end. This genuinely checks whether the piece is stable when you are unprepared.

## Note Down Where It Goes Wrong

Right after the cold start, write down which places had problems.

**Practice routine**

These are the places that go wrong easily when you are unprepared, and they are the risk points in a performance.

In the following week's practice, you can focus on these places.

![Black-and-white stipple sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9qiq7-6diet.webp)

## What Is a Cold Start?

A cold start means that as soon as you sit at the piano, you do no warm-up at all and practise no passages first, but play the piece straight through from beginning to end.

You do not stop in the middle, and you keep going even if you make a mistake.

Just like a real performance.

- Once a week, play the whole piece without warming up
- It simulates the unprepared state of a performance
- Record the places that go wrong during the cold start
- Do not do this every day

## Stability Checks Beyond the Cold Start

A cold start is only one way of checking stability.

You can also check by playing in front of family, playing on different pianos and so on.

Combining several methods gives you a fuller picture of how well prepared you are.

## Choose a Fixed Time

You can choose a fixed time each week for the cold start, for example the first practice on a weekend morning.

A fixed time makes the habit easier to keep up.

You can also occasionally do it at different times to simulate different states.

## Bring Your Cold-Start Notes to Your Teacher

You can tell Teacher Aum the results of your cold start, especially the places that went wrong.

From this information, your teacher can help plan the focus of your next practice.

In a lesson, your teacher can also ask you to do a cold start and watch on the spot.

## Your Playing After a Warm-Up

In everyday practice, after warming up and repeated practice, your fingers are in good shape.

When you play the piece through at that point, you may feel it is already quite fluent.

But that fluency is how you play after full preparation.

## Keep Going When You Make a Mistake

If you make a mistake during a cold start, do not stop and start again.

Practising adjusting quickly after a mistake and carrying on is itself an important performance skill.

You can remember the place where you went wrong in your head and go back to deal with it after you finish playing.

## Once a Week Is Enough

A cold start does not need to be done every day. Once a week is enough.

That is because its purpose is to check, not to practise.

The rest of the time, warm up and practise in the usual way.

## What Happens in a Performance

In an exam, competition or performance, there is often not enough time to warm up.

You may have to sit down at an unfamiliar piano, feeling nervous, and start playing straight away.

If you have never experienced this in your usual practice, you may find the piece suddenly becomes unsteady.

## Compare the Results Each Week

If you do a cold start once a week, you can record each result and compare them.

As your practice progresses, fewer and fewer places go wrong in the cold start.

This gives us more confidence for performing.

## Feelings Before and After a Cold Start

Some people feel nervous doing a cold start, worrying that they will not play well.

That is in fact the point of the practice: to experience a little nervousness in a safe setting.

It does not matter if you play badly. It just tells us which places still need practice.

## The Cold Start in Brief

After warming up in everyday practice, you play in better shape, but in a performance there is often no chance to warm up. A cold start means playing straight through from beginning to end with no warm-up and no practising of passages first, without stopping, and once a week is enough. You can choose a fixed time.

Right after playing, write down the places that went wrong as the focus for next week. You can record yourself and listen back. The first few bars are often unsteady and need more practice. Keep going when you make a mistake, and comparing the weekly results lets you see progress.

A cold start is only one method of checking. Experiencing a little nervousness is exactly the point of practice. You can tell Teacher Aum the results and ask your teacher to watch a cold start in a lesson.

## Recording Helps You Review

You can record during a cold start and play it back after you finish.

Sometimes problems you did not notice while playing are very clear in the recording.

For example, starting too fast or not enough dynamics in a passage.

## The First Few Bars

In a cold start, the first few bars are often very shaky.

Your fingers have not loosened up yet, and you may be a little nervous too.

You can practise the opening of the piece more in everyday practice, so that it starts steadily in any state.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a cold start?**
A: Playing the piece straight through from beginning to end without warming up or practising passages first.

**Q: How often should I do it?**
A: Once a week.

**Q: What should I do after playing?**
A: Write down the places that went wrong.

**Q: Should I stop when I make a mistake?**
A: No. Keep playing.

**Q: Where is it often unsteady?**
A: In the first few bars.

piano-eighty-eight-key-range.body:
Most pianos we know today have 88 keys: from the A at the far left to the C at the far right, spanning seven octaves plus a minor third. This number was not fixed when the piano was first invented. Early eighteenth-century pianos often had a much narrower range, some only about five octaves; after that, makers and composers kept extending both the low and high ends, and by the late nineteenth century 88 keys had gradually become the common standard. Not every surviving piano has exactly this number: some historical instruments have fewer, and occasionally there are pianos wider than 88 keys. For learners, knowing this history helps explain why some early works never reach the highest or lowest keys of today's piano, while later works use those notes as new colours. When you sit down to practise, you can first find middle C on your own piano and then see how far the keyboard extends on either side.

## Limits When Arranging and Transposing

When you transpose a piece, it can sometimes run off one end of the keyboard.

**Practice order**

In that case you need to rewrite the register or choose a more suitable key, rather than forcing yourself to play keys that do not exist.

Knowing the standard range helps you spot this kind of problem early.

## How the Notes at Each End Are Used

The lowest notes are often used to add depth and stability, but in a small room they can sound boomy if played too heavily.

The highest notes are bright and short, well suited as ornaments, though not necessarily for long, forceful playing.

Knowing their character is more useful than just remembering "there are 88 in all".

## 88 Keys: A Summary

The common piano has 88 keys, from low A to high C; early pianos had a much narrower range, this standard only became widespread in the late nineteenth century, and not every piano has exactly this number.

The widening of the range changed the colours available for composing and playing, and it also reminds us to notice the range a piece actually uses when reading music.

You can ask Teacher Aum to point out the notes at both ends on the piano.

## And the Keyboard Diagrams in Textbooks

Many beginner books print a full diagram of the 88 keys and mark the position of middle C.

Get to know this diagram first, then go back to the real piano and explore the two ends; this builds a complete sense of the space.

Even if you only use the middle few octaves for now, knowing where the ends are makes reading music more reassuring.

**Listen up**
- The common piano has 88 keys, from the A at the far left to the C at the far right
- Early pianos had a much narrower range, often only about five octaves
- In the late nineteenth century, 88 keys gradually became the common standard
- Not every piano has exactly this number

## Why the Range Kept Expanding

Composers wanted lower bass notes for support and higher treble notes to shine.

The contrasts a player can make on the same instrument also grow as the range widens.

The expansion did not happen all at once, but gradually, in different periods and different places.

![A piano and sheet music in a bright room](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdiu1ug-8bash.webp)

## There Have Been Other Numbers Too

On the road to 88 keys, other configurations appeared, such as 85 keys.

Today you can still find historical pianos with a narrower range, and a few modern pianos with a wider one.

So a more accurate way to put it is: 88 is a widely adopted standard, not a number set by nature.

## How 88 Keys Became the Common Number

By the late nineteenth century, many newly built pianos used the 88-key layout.

It covers the range from low A to high C, and became the common standard for the many textbooks, works and concert instruments that followed.

"Common" does not mean "always so"; it only means that it has been the most widespread for a little over a century.

## The Narrower Range of Early Pianos

When the piano first appeared, the keyboard was usually shorter than today's, and neither the low nor the high end reached as far as it later did.

A range of about five octaves was already enough for many works of that time.

So we should not imagine eighteenth-century playing with the feeling of today's piano, where there are many unused keys on both sides.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Point Out the Two Ends in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to walk with you from middle C to the lowest and highest notes, and listen to how the two ends differ from the middle.

If an early piece does not use the two ends, you can also discuss whether that has anything to do with the range of the time.

From the story of the 88 keys, we come back to the actual range of the piano in front of you.

## What This Means for Reading Music

With works from the eighteenth or early nineteenth century, both the lowest and highest notes on the page may lie well inside today's keyboard.

With later works, the music may really use keys near the two ends.

**Practice order**

Paying attention to the range as you read can sometimes also help you judge roughly which period a piece's writing belongs to.

## FAQ

**Q: How many keys does a common piano have? From which note to which note?**
A: Usually 88, from the A at the far left to the C at the far right.

**Q: What was the range of early pianos like?**
A: Often much narrower, some only about five octaves.

**Q: Roughly when did 88 keys become the common standard?**
A: It gradually became widespread in the late nineteenth century.

**Q: Do all pianos have 88 keys?**
A: No. Historical instruments may have fewer, and a few pianos are wider than this.

**Q: How does knowing the history of the range help with reading music?**
A: It helps you judge how high and how low a piece is likely to go, and it also helps you spot in advance when a transposition would run off the keyboard.

photograph-score-markings-after-lesson.body:
In lessons, your teacher often writes many markings on the score: changed fingerings, circled hard spots, and reminders about dynamics and pedalling. These markings are very valuable, but a paper score has its inconveniences: sometimes you forget to bring it, sometimes the markings get rubbed out, and when you change to a new score you have to mark everything again. A simple habit is, after every lesson, to use your phone to photograph the pages your teacher has marked and save them by date. That gives you not only a backup but also a clear view of what you learned in each lesson.

## Tell your teacher

You can tell Teacher Aum that you have the habit of photographing the score after every lesson.

**Remember this**

Your teacher may write the markings a little more clearly, or single out which places need extra attention.

Photos taken this way will be more useful.

## A backup when you forget your score

If you are practising somewhere else and forgot to bring your score, you can open the photos on your phone.

Although reading a score on a phone is not as convenient as a paper score, at least you can see your teacher's markings.

If you have a tablet, it will be clearer to look at.

## The inconveniences of a paper score

A paper score is easily lost or damaged, and markings written in pencil may be rubbed out.

Sometimes you forget to bring the score when you go out to practise, and then you cannot see your teacher's markings.

When you change to a new edition of the score, the original markings have to be written again.

## It cannot replace the paper score

Photographing is a backup and a record, and it cannot replace the paper score.

When you practise, you should still use the paper score and keep adding markings to it.

The photos are mainly for review and emergencies.

## The case of online lessons

If the lesson is online, the teacher may mark the score on the screen, or tell you in words what to change.

In that case you can write the markings onto your score yourself after the lesson, and then photograph it and save it.

You can also ask the teacher to send you the marked score file.

**Things to notice**
- After the lesson, photograph the pages that have been marked
- Save them by date for easy review
- You can look at them even if you forget your score
- You can see the progress made in each lesson

## Add a short note

After taking the photo, you can write a few short words beside the photo or in a notes app.

For example, "this lesson mainly changed the fingering in the second section".

That way, when you review later, you can recall what was in the lesson more quickly.

## Mind the copyright

Scores are copyrighted publications, and photographing is only for your own study and backup.

Do not casually share photos of scores online or send them to others.

Respecting copyright is respecting the composer and the publisher.

## Score photo summary

Your teacher's markings on the score are a direct record of what you learned in the lesson, but a paper score is easily lost and the markings may be rubbed out. So after the lesson you can photograph the marked pages, with good light and the score laid flat, and save them by date and piece.

The photos let you see what you learned in each lesson, let you look at them when you forget your score, and let you compare when you change to a new score, but they cannot replace the paper score, and you can add a short note.

Photographing is only for your own study, so mind the copyright. Parents can take the photos for children. For online lessons you can mark the score after the lesson and then photograph it, or ask the teacher to send a file, and you can tell Teacher Aum about this habit.

## Markings on the score

In lessons, the teacher writes many reminders on the score.

For example, a fingering was changed in one place, one section should be softer, and here the pedal should be changed.

These markings are a direct record of what was learned in the lesson.

## A child's score photos

After a child's lesson, a parent can help the child by taking photos of the score.

That way the parent also knows what the child learned in the lesson, and can be more focused when helping with practice.

The photos can also be kept as a record of the child's growth in learning.

## Photographing after the lesson

After every lesson, use your phone to photograph the pages your teacher has marked.

When you take the photo, the light should be good and the score laid flat, to make sure the markings are clearly visible.

If there are several pages, photograph every page.

## See what you learned in each lesson

Put the photos from different dates together, and you can see what new markings were added to the score in each lesson.

This is equivalent to a record of your learning in class.

When you review, you can clearly see your own learning process.

## Save by date

You can save the photos you have taken into an album or folder by the date of the lesson.

You can make a folder for each piece, with the photos arranged by date inside.

That makes them very convenient to find later.

## When you change to a new score

If you need to change to a new copy of the score, for example because the original is too old, you can write the markings back in by comparing with the photos.

That way you will not miss any important reminder from your teacher.

**Listen**

You can also use the opportunity to see which markings are no longer needed.

![Colourful illustration of a grand piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9remp-ijtuw.webp)

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: When should I photograph the score?**
A: After every lesson.

**Q: How do I save the photos?**
A: By date and by piece.

**Q: Can the photos replace the paper score?**
A: No, they are only a backup and a record.

**Q: Can I share photos of the score online?**
A: No, mind the copyright.

**Q: What about online lessons?**
A: Mark the score yourself after the lesson and then photograph it, or ask the teacher to send a file.

piano-lid-open-closed-sound.body:
The big lid of a grand piano can be propped open or lowered; the top lid and front panel of an upright can also be opened or closed. The state of the lid affects how loud and bright the sound is: open, the sound is louder and more spacious; closed, it is softer and more focused. When practising at home, you can choose according to the size of the room, the time of day and your neighbours. For example, a small room or an evening session may call for a closed lid, while you can open it when you need to listen carefully to the tone. Be careful when opening and closing the lid: move slowly to avoid trapping your fingers.

**Things to note**
- The state of the lid affects how loud and bright the sound is
- Open, the sound is louder and more spacious
- Closed, the sound is softer and more focused
- Open and close it slowly to avoid trapping your fingers

## The Effect of Room Size

In a small room, the sound of the piano can easily seem very loud, even a little harsh. In that case you can close the lid or prop it open only a little.

**Remember this**

In a larger room, opening the lid lets the sound fill the space better.

The furniture, rugs and curtains in the room also affect the sound, so take them into account.

## Do Not Put Things on the Lid

Do not put water glasses, vases or heavy objects on the lid, in case they fall or liquid spills into the piano.

If you need to put sheet music or ornaments on the piano, make sure they do not get in the way of opening and closing the lid.

Keeping the lid tidy is part of looking after the piano.

## Choices While Practising

For everyday technical work, or when you will be practising for a long time, you can close the lid to reduce how harsh the sound is on your ears.

When you need to listen carefully to tone and dynamic levels, or are preparing for a performance, you can open the lid to hear a truer sound.

You can also switch flexibly within one session: close the lid for technical work first, then open it to practise expression.

## Try Different Settings

Every piano and every room is different, so try the sound with the lid in different states.

Find a setting where you can hear clearly and your ears are comfortable, and use it as your usual practice setup.

You can also ask your teacher or a piano tuner for advice to help you choose a suitable way.

## Preparing for Performance

If the lid will be fully open at the performance, you can try playing with the lid open in your practice beforehand.

This lets you get used to the louder sound in advance and adjust your control of dynamics.

When you arrive at the venue, you can also pay attention to the state of the lid and its effect on the sound during the rehearsal.

## The Top Lid of an Upright

The top lid of an upright can be opened, and on some pianos the front panel can also be taken off or opened.

With the top lid open, the sound radiates upwards and sounds a little brighter.

With the top lid closed, the sound is softer, which suits practising in a small room or at quiet times.

## Using the Fallboard

Besides the big lid and the top lid, the piano also has a fallboard that covers the keys.

When you are not playing, you can close the fallboard to keep dust off the keys.

Open and close it slowly here too. Some fallboards have a soft-close design, but you still need to watch where your fingers are.

## Think of Your Neighbours When the Lid Is Open

With the lid open the sound is louder, so when practising at home consider how family members and neighbours feel.

In the morning, in the evening or when the family is resting, you can close the lid or play more softly.

Talking with your family and neighbours about practice times can also reduce unnecessary trouble.

## Safety When Opening and Closing the Lid

When opening and closing the lid, move slowly, hold it steadily with both hands and never drop it suddenly.

The big lid of a grand piano is heavy. When propping it up and lowering it, make sure the prop stick is firmly in place, and an adult should do it.

When children are practising, remind them not to pull at the lid, to avoid trapping their fingers.

![Glowing digital interface against a dark background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0y4jh-n6wvj.webp)

## The Difference in Sound

With the lid open, the vibration of the strings travels into the air more directly, and both the volume and the overtones of the sound are richer.

With the lid closed, part of the sound is blocked, so the volume is lower and the tone becomes rounder and gentler.

Try playing the same passage in both states and notice how the sound changes.

## The Lid of a Grand Piano

The big lid of a grand piano can be propped up with a prop stick. There are usually prop sticks of different lengths, so the lid can be raised to different heights.

With the lid fully raised, the sound is reflected towards the audience and sounds loud and spacious. This is the usual state at concerts.

**A different angle**

When practising at home or in a small room, you can use the shorter prop stick, or lower the lid, so the sound is less intense.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the difference between an open lid and a closed lid?**
A: Open, the sound is louder and more spacious; closed, it is softer and more focused.

**Q: Should I open it when practising at home?**
A: Choose according to the size of the room, the time of day and your neighbours.

**Q: How should I prepare before a performance?**
A: Practise beforehand with the lid open.

**Q: What about a small room?**
A: Close the lid or prop it open only a little.

**Q: What should I watch out for when opening and closing the lid?**
A: Move slowly, hold it steadily with both hands and avoid trapping your fingers.

**Q: Can I put things on the lid?**
A: Do not put water glasses, vases or heavy objects on it.

practice-menu-for-short-medium-long-days.body:
The time you can spend practising is not fixed: some days are busy and you have only a little while, while other days are more relaxed and you can practise more. If you decide what to practise on the spot each time, you often waste time, or end up always playing only the piece you like best. A practical method is to prepare several "practice menus" in advance: what to practise on days when time is short, on days when time is medium, and on days when you have plenty of time. When you sit down at the piano, see how much time you have today, pick a menu and follow it.

## Update the Menus Every Week

As your learning progresses, the menus need updating too.

After each lesson, you can adjust the three menus according to the teacher's new assignments.

Parts that are already well practised can move from the menu to the review section.

## The Problem with Deciding on the Spot

If you decide what to practise only when you sit down at the piano, you often hesitate for a long time.

Sometimes you play a favourite piece from start to finish, and the difficult spots never get practised.

On days with little time, you may even feel "there is not enough time anyway, so I will not practise".

## Menus for Children

A child's practice menu can be made more fun, for example by using pictures or stickers for each item.

Each time an item is finished, a sticker goes next to it.

Parents can draw up the menu together with the child, so that the child takes part.

## Three Menus

According to your own life, you can prepare three practice menus: short, medium and long.

The exact lengths differ from person to person and can be decided after talking with your teacher.

Each menu should say clearly what to practise and the rough order of the items.

## The Short Menu: Keep the Essentials

On days with little time, keep only the most essential items.

For example, one simple technique warm-up plus one difficult spot from the new piece.

The point is to stay in touch with the keys so that your fingers do not get rusty.

## Draw It Up with Your Teacher

In lessons you can discuss with Teacher Aum what the three menus should contain.

The teacher knows your progress and can help decide the focus of each menu.

With the teacher's advice, the menus will be better targeted.

## Do Not Always Pick the Short Menu

Once you have three menus, take care not to choose the short menu all the time out of laziness.

You can note in a notebook which menu you chose each day and see whether the spread over the week is reasonable.

If there are too many short menus, think about whether you can adjust your daily schedule.

## Write the Menus in a Notebook

You can write the three menus in your practice notebook or stick them next to the piano.

A glance before each practice tells you what to do today.

You can also record them in a phone notes app and adjust them at any time.

## Short Days Count Too

Many people feel that a short practice has no meaning, but that is not so.

Even with only a little time, practising carefully with the short menu keeps your progress going.

What matters is keeping practice continuous, not practising for a long time every time.

- Prepare a short, a medium and a long menu in advance
- The short menu keeps only the essentials
- The long menu adds review and exploration
- Every menu has clear tasks

## Summary: Practice Menus

The time for practice varies from day to day, and deciding on the spot easily wastes time. Prepare a short, a medium and a long menu in advance: the short menu keeps the essentials, the medium menu is the basic practice, and the long menu adds sight reading, review and exploration.

Every item needs a specific task. Write the menus in a notebook or stick them next to the piano, update them every week from the new assignments, count short days too, but do not always pick the short menu.

A child's menu can use pictures and stickers, the menus can be drawn up with Teacher Aum, and the order can be warm-up, difficult spots, whole piece, ending with a favourite piece.

## The Medium Menu: Basic Practice

On days with a medium amount of time, you can include technique, a few sections of the new piece and a review of an older piece.

This is the menu you will use most often.

The content can be adjusted according to the assignments your teacher sets that week.

## The Long Menu: Review and Exploration

On days with plenty of time, you can add more to the medium menu.

For example, sight read a new, simple piece, review pieces in your repertoire, or try playing a pop song you are interested in.

You usually have no time for these things, and the long menu is exactly the place to schedule them.

![Glowing abstract digital shapes and a grid](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa98zgy-latac.webp)

## The Order Within a Menu

In each menu, you can arrange things in the order of warm-up first, then difficult spots, then the whole piece.

Put the items that need the most attention first, and practise them while your mind is fresh.

At the end you can play a piece you like as a pleasant finish.

## Every Item Needs a Clear Task

Every item on the menu should state a specific task, not just "practise the new piece".

For example, "new piece, bars 9 to 12, right hand, slowly, play the fingering accurately".

**A small tip**

The more specific the task, the more efficient the practice.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why prepare practice menus?**
A: To avoid wasting time deciding on the spot and to give practice more focus.

**Q: How many menus should I prepare?**
A: Three: short, medium and long.

**Q: What goes in the short menu?**
A: The most essential items, such as a warm-up and one difficult spot.

**Q: How often should the menus be updated?**
A: Every week, from the new assignments.

**Q: How can a child's menu be made?**
A: With pictures or stickers.

player-piano-rolls-to-digital.body:
A player piano is a piano that can play music by itself, with nobody sitting at the keyboard. In the early twentieth century it was hugely popular in homes in Europe and America: you loaded a roll of paper full of small holes into the piano, pumped the pedals or switched on an electric motor, and air passing through the holes pushed on the pneumatic mechanism inside the piano, so that the keys went down one by one and the music sounded. The position of each hole on the roll stood for a note, and the length of the hole stood for how long the note lasted. In an age before the gramophone and the radio were widespread, this was almost one of the few ways to hear "human-quality" piano playing at home. Today the same idea lives on in digital form: sensors record the playing, an electronic mechanism reproduces it, and the logic behind it is strikingly similar to the paper rolls of a century ago.

## How a Paper Roll "Remembers" Music

A paper roll is like a very long piece of sheet music, except that it is written not for people to read but for a machine. The roll moves from top to bottom; the position across its width corresponds to the keys, and the length along it corresponds to time. Each time the machine reads a hole, the matching key goes down; when the hole ends, the key is released. Early rolls were mostly punched by craftsmen working from the score, and later methods appeared that could record a pianist's real performance, preserving even subtle changes of tempo and dynamics. These were called reproducing pianos.

![Black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mvzqnyjt-mpkba.webp)

## A Preserved History of Sound

- Many composers and pianists recorded rolls for the player piano, leaving valuable records of their playing
- These rolls let later generations "hear" performance styles from the time when recording technology was still immature
- Some composers even wrote specially for the player piano, using the machine's ability to play dense passages no human hands could manage
- As the gramophone and radio became widespread, the player piano gradually left ordinary homes

Today researchers and enthusiasts still restore old pianos and old rolls, and scan the rolls into digital files so that these sounds continue to be passed on.

## From Paper Rolls to Digital Files

**A change in how music is recorded**
A paper roll records notes by the position and length of holes; modern systems use sensors to record when each key goes down, how fast, and when it is released, and store it as a digital file.

**A change in how it is reproduced**
The pneumatic mechanism has been replaced by electromagnetic drivers, which can control the force of each key more precisely.

**A change in use**
In the past it was mainly home entertainment; now it is also used for teaching demonstrations, remote performance and music research.

## What It Teaches Piano Learners

The player piano tells us something important: a performance can be broken down into a few elements, namely which note, when, how loud and how long. If you can take apart your own playing in this way, it becomes easier to find problems. For example, record a piece of practice and, as you listen back, pay attention to just one element: only the rhythm, or only the dynamics, or only how long the notes last. Focusing on one element at a time is far more useful than a vague feeling that "I played badly".

## If a Machine Can Play, Why Should People Learn?

Some people ask: if a machine can repeat a performance perfectly, what is the point of learning the piano? The answer is that music is not only about "pressing the right keys". When playing, a performer adjusts expression to mood, occasion and audience, and every time is a little different; that is exactly what makes live music moving. Besides, the concentration, patience and sense of achievement that come from learning are things no machine can gain on your behalf. A player piano can be a good teacher and companion, but the person sitting at the keyboard is still the true star of the music.

## Try "Paper Roll Thinking" at Home

Take a sheet of squared paper and write the eight note names from C to C across the top, with each square down the page standing for one beat. With a pencil, fill in the first two phrases of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" as small blocks, as long as each note lasts. Once you have finished, look at this "paper roll" as you play it on the piano, and you will feel directly how rhythm and pitch are recorded.

## Conclusion

From paper rolls to digital files, the technology has kept changing, but people's wish to hold on to music has not.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Are player pianos still made?**
A: Traditional paper-roll types are now rarely made, but modern pianos with digital self-playing features still exist.

**Q: Can old paper rolls still be played?**
A: Well-preserved rolls can still be played on restored player pianos, and some people have scanned them into digital files.

**Q: Can a player piano help with learning?**
A: It can demonstrate how a piece is played and let learners watch the movement of the keys, but you still need to practise with your own hands.

**Q: Can paper rolls record the pedals?**
A: Some more advanced roll systems can record pedal movements, making the reproduced performance closer to the original.

plan-climax-of-piece-dynamics-map.body:
Many pieces sound flat not because of wrong notes but because every section has about the same dynamics. A useful method is to first find the climax of the whole piece, the point where the emotion of the music is pushed to its peak, and mark it in the score; then look at how the dynamics should change step by step from the beginning to the climax and from the climax to the end. Once you have drawn this "dynamics map", you can leave room to build upwards when you play, instead of using up all your strength at the very start.

## Marking the Score

Once you have found the climax, make a clear pencil mark in the score, such as a star.

If there are several high points, you can use marks of different sizes to tell the main one from the lesser ones.

That way, every time you look at the score you are reminded of where the music is going.

## Show Your Dynamics Map to Your Teacher

Sometimes the climax you find may not be the one your teacher sees.

In a lesson, you can show your dynamics map to your teacher and hear their opinion.

The discussion itself can also help you understand the piece more deeply.

## The Climax Is Not Always the Loudest Point

In some pieces, the climax is not the loudest place but the most tense, most emotional one.

For example, in a quiet piece the climax may be just a slight increase in intensity, or the point where the harmony is most tense.

So when looking for the climax, do not rely only on dynamic markings; use your ears to feel the emotion of the music too.

**Remember this**
- First find the climax of the whole piece
- Mark it in the score
- Plan the way up to the climax and the way back down from it
- Leave room to build at the start

## Easing Back After the Climax

After the climax, the music usually eases back slowly and the emotion calms down.

The way back down also needs planning. Do not go from very loud to very soft all at once.

Let the dynamics fade gradually, like a story that has reached its climax and slowly heads towards its ending.

## Check the Ups and Downs with a Recording

Play through the piece following your dynamics map and record it.

Listen to whether the difference in dynamics between the beginning and the climax is clear, and whether the climax really excites the listener.

If it still sounds flat, widen the contrast a little more.

## The Dynamics Map in Brief

Finding the climax of a piece and drawing a dynamics map is an effective way to give your playing shape.

Leave room at the beginning, be patient with the crescendo, ease back slowly after the climax, and let the small high points yield to the main climax.

With this map, you know clearly where the music is going when you play.

## Small High Points and the Main Climax

In a piece, besides the main climax, every phrase and every section also has its own small high point.

The dynamics of a small high point should be weaker than those of the main climax, so that the main climax stands out.

On the dynamics map, you can use small rises and falls for the small high points and a large one for the main climax.

## Do Not Start Too Loud

Many learners play very loudly from the start, and by the time they reach the climax there is no room left to go louder.

Once you have planned your dynamics map, you can consciously start more softly and leave room to build.

That way, when the climax arrives, the music has a real sense of release.

## What Is a Climax?

The climax is the place in a piece where the emotion peaks and the music is most tense.

It often comes in the second half of the piece, and may be the highest note, the loudest chord or the place where the harmony is most tense.

Some pieces have just one obvious climax, while longer pieces may have several high points of different sizes.

![Glowing teal grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa3w7q7-2n4ec.webp)

## Drawing a Dynamics Map

On a sheet of paper, draw a horizontal line to represent the whole piece, then draw the rises and falls of the dynamics on it.

It starts low, rises slowly, reaches its highest at the climax, and then eases back slowly.

This simple diagram helps you see the dynamic structure of the whole piece.

## How to Find the Climax

You can first listen to a recording of the piece a few times and feel where it excites you most.

Then look at the score for the weightiest dynamic marking in the whole piece, the highest note, or the place where a crescendo finally arrives.

Putting these clues together, you can roughly work out where the climax is.

## Be Patient with the Crescendo

The way from the beginning to the climax is often one long crescendo.

This crescendo must not be too fast, or the music will already be loud before it reaches the climax.

You can divide the crescendo into several stages, adding only a little at each stage.

## Why a Piece Sounds Flat

Sometimes a piece has all the right notes and a steady rhythm, but still sounds flat.

A common reason is that the dynamics change too little from beginning to end, so every section is about equally loud.

**Common misconception**

Music is like a story. It needs ups and downs and a climax to keep people listening.

## FAQ

**Q: Why does a piece sound flat?**
A: Often the dynamics change too little and every section is about equally loud.

**Q: How do I find the climax?**
A: Listen to a recording and feel where it excites you most, and combine that with the weightiest dynamic marking and the highest note in the score.

**Q: Why should I not start too loud?**
A: You need to leave room to build towards the climax.

**Q: Is the climax always the loudest point?**
A: Not necessarily. It may be the most tense, most emotional place.

**Q: How do I draw a dynamics map?**
A: Use a line to draw the rises and falls from the beginning to the climax and then to the end.

piano-damper-pedal-early-development.body:
Today the sustain pedal on the right of the piano has become almost the busiest foot in performance. Its job is to let strings that would otherwise stop keep vibrating, so that the sound is prolonged and harmonies can be joined together. This device did not take its present foot-pedal form from the moment the piano appeared. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, many pianos used knee levers or other levers to control the dampers, and the player had to push them with the knees; only later did the foot pedal gradually become the usual method. In the scores of composers such as Beethoven, we can already see requests connected with "lifting the dampers". The point of learning about the early history of the pedal is to understand that the pedal is a tool that helps connect and colour the sound, not a switch to be held down all the time. For learners, this also explains why the pedalling in some early works has to be imagined in light of the instruments of the time.

## How the Foot Pedal Became the Usual Form

As the structure of the piano and the playing posture gradually settled, controlling the dampers with the foot was clearly more convenient.

**Common misconception**

By the nineteenth century the foot pedal had become more and more common, and it finally became the standard fitting on most pianos today.

This change happened gradually. It was not that one day the whole world switched to the same kind of pedal.

![A person in futuristic clothing plays a black grand piano on a neon-lit street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdit0z0-my5d5.webp)

## From an Effect to a Common Technique

At first, lifting the dampers was more of a special sound effect.

Later, it gradually became an everyday way of joining harmonies and helping the music sing.

In today's learning, pedalling is practised systematically from about the intermediate stage, precisely because this use has become so widespread.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Try Two Pedalling Styles in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the same phrase with fewer pedal changes and with frequent pedal changes, and hear how the sound differs.

If an early work has a long pedal marking in the score, you can also discuss together how to handle it more clearly on today's piano.

From the early history of the pedal, we come back to the choice made at every press and release today.

## What Lifting the Dampers Means

When all the dampers are lifted, not only does the note being played last longer, but other strings may also resonate.

So some early markings were not meant as "connect it just a little", but may have meant letting the sound blend over a longer time.

If you followed that idea exactly on a modern piano, pressing deeply without changing, it would often sound muddier than it did then, because later pianos usually have a longer resonance.

## Differences from the Modern Piano

A modern piano's volume and resonance are often greater than those of many eighteenth-century instruments.

So carrying the long pedal markings of early works directly over to today's piano is not always appropriate.

A safer approach is to listen first to the actual reverberation, then decide how often to change the pedal.

## Early Markings in the Score

In the scores of Beethoven and others, instructions connected with the pedal or with lifting the dampers already appear.

These markings remind us that composers of the time already considered this effect part of the music.

As for how deep to press and how often to change, you still have to judge according to the piece and the instrument.

## Knee Levers and Levers

On early pianos, a common method was to push a lever with the knee, thereby lifting the dampers.

The player had to find this position while seated, and the movement was not the same as pressing a pedal with the foot today.

In different instrument-making traditions, the position and sensitivity of the device were not entirely the same either.

## A Short Summary of Pedal History

The sustain pedal is used to control the dampers so that the sound is prolonged. Early pianos often used knee levers, and only later did the foot pedal gradually take over. From the eighteenth to the early nineteenth century there were many kinds of devices, and composers asked for this effect in their scores very early on.

Modern pianos often have a longer resonance, so early markings cannot be copied as they stand. The pedal is always a choice between opening and closing, not a switch to be held down all the time.

Teacher Aum can demonstrate different pedalling on the same phrase.

## Why You Should Not Hold the Pedal Down All the Time

History tells us that the purpose of the pedal is to control the dampers, not to remove every boundary between sounds.

When the harmony changes, you usually need to let the previous group of strings stop.

Knowing about the early devices actually helps you understand that this is a choice that can be opened and also closed.

- The sustain pedal controls the dampers so that the strings keep vibrating
- Early pianos often used knee levers, and the foot pedal came gradually later
- From the eighteenth to the early nineteenth century many kinds of devices were used
- Requests connected with lifting the dampers appeared in scores very early

## How the Sound Stops Without a Pedal

One of the basic principles of the piano is that when the finger leaves the key, the damper makes the string stop sounding.

Without an additional device, the only way to join a series of chords into one wash of sound is finger legato, which is sometimes impossible.

**Common misconception**

So people very early wanted a way to lift the dampers off the strings temporarily.

## FAQ

**Q: Which part of the piano does the sustain pedal control?**
A: The dampers. When they are lifted, the strings can keep vibrating.

**Q: How did early pianos usually lift the dampers?**
A: With knee levers or other levers, pushed with the knees.

**Q: Did the foot pedal become the global standard all at once?**
A: No. It became common gradually during the nineteenth century.

**Q: Why can't the long pedal markings of early works be carried over as they are today?**
A: Because the resonance of a modern piano is often longer, and never changing the pedal would sound muddier than it did then.

**Q: What reminder can learners take from this history?**
A: The pedal is a tool that can be opened or closed, and it usually needs to be changed when the harmony changes.

piano-lesson-warm-up-three-minutes.body:
Many people start playing pieces the moment they sit at the piano, before their fingers are fully "awake", so they tense up easily and play stiffly. Before a lesson or practice, spending three minutes on a gentle warm-up can bring your fingers, wrists and ears into the right state together. This article describes a few simple ways, suitable for children and adults. This is general practice advice, not medical advice.

## Why Warm Up

A warm-up is not any complicated ritual; it simply gives the body and attention a little time to make the transition. Just as you stretch before a walk, moving your fingers before playing makes the practice that follows smoother.

- Start with fingers and wrists in a relaxed state.
- Let the ears settle first, and listen to the sound of the piano.
- Let your mood shift gently from a busy day to practice.

## A Simple Three-Minute Plan

**Minute one: relax the body**
Sit properly, feet flat, shoulders dropping naturally. Take a few slow deep breaths, shake your hands out lightly, then slowly rotate your wrists; every movement should be gentle, with no force.

**Minute two: move the fingers**
Put your hands on the keys and press each finger lightly in turn without making a sound, or play five white keys very softly, from "do" to "sol" and back. Keep the wrists relaxed.

**Minute three: listen to one note**
Choose one note, play it, and listen carefully as it slowly fades. Let your attention gather on the sound, and then begin today's practice.

![Fingers playing black and white keys](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwib7609-88rgi.webp)

## What to Watch For While Warming Up

- Move slowly, and do not chase speed.
- If your fingers, wrists or shoulders hurt, stop and rest straight away.
- If discomfort persists, consult a doctor or a qualified clinical music professional, and do not push through on your own.
- When the weather is cold, you can first wash your hands in warm water, or rub them gently, to warm them up.

## Warming Up Together with Children

For children, a warm-up can become a little game, such as "finger exercises": first let the five fingers "get up" one by one, then "stretch" together. Parents can do it with the child, speaking in a relaxed tone, without requiring the movements to be perfectly correct. Only if the child finds it fun will they be willing to do it every time.

## What to Do After the Warm-Up

After the warm-up, first review what you learned last time, then move on to new practice. This order gives the mind a little familiarity, so you are less likely to meet difficulty right away. If you have very little time that day, you can do just the warm-up and a short review, without forcing more.

## What a Small Tool Can Do

Some students, after warming up, use an AI piano teaching app such as TIGA ALPHA to listen to the pitch and beat of what they play. The app points out which bar needs one more run-through, making it easy for students to check by themselves between lessons. It is a companion to practice; it cannot replace the teacher's guidance, nor replace your own sense of how things feel.

## Turning the Warm-Up into a Habit

Habits take a little time. You can make the warm-up the first thing you do "after opening the piano lid", and fix the time at about the same part of each day. At first you may forget, and you can stick a little note on the piano to remind yourself. After a few weeks, you will find the warm-up has become natural, and your mood on sitting at the piano is steadier too. Everyone has a different rhythm; there is no need to compare yourself with others, nor to blame yourself for missing a day, just start again the next day.

## A Few Tips for Adult Students

Adult students often have time to practise only after a busy day, when the shoulders and neck are stiff. In the warm-up you can first lift both shoulders gently, then lower them slowly, and repeat a few times; you can also support the back of one hand with the palm of the other, to let the wrist stretch out. Keep the movements small and slow, notice where there is tightness, and do not force yourself into any position. The warm-up is just to let the body start more comfortably; it is not a burden on practice, and you need not give up your whole practice plan just because time is short.

## Small Tips While Warming Up

- Put your phone on silent, so these three minutes belong only to you.
- If someone is nearby, quietly tell your family you are warming up, to reduce interruptions.
- When the warm-up is done, take a sip of water before you start practising.

## Linking the Warm-Up to the Piece

After the warm-up, there is no need to go straight to the hardest part. You can first choose a short, familiar melody and play it once at a steady speed, letting your fingers and ears adjust to the day's state together. If a certain place keeps getting stuck, do not force it by repeating over and over; pause first, take a deep breath, then try again at a slower speed.

## FAQ

**Q: Does a warm-up have to be three minutes?**
A: Not necessarily; the time is only a guide. One to five minutes is fine; what matters is that the movements are gentle and your attention is on practice.

**Q: Do adults need to warm up too?**
A: Yes. Adults often have stiff hands after a day's work, and a warm-up makes the fingers more agile.

**Q: What if my hand feels a bit sore during the warm-up?**
A: Stop and rest first, relax your wrists, then try again with a lighter touch; if it still feels uncomfortable, please consult a doctor.

**Q: Is it all right to play without a warm-up?**
A: Yes, but doing a simple warm-up first usually makes practice more comfortable.

phrase-elision-end-and-start-overlap.body:
Normally, one phrase ends and only then does the next begin, with a small pause in between. But sometimes a composer lets the last note of one phrase also become the first note of the next. That way there is no pause between the two phrases, and the music runs on in one breath. This way of writing is called phrase overlap, and in English it is commonly called an elision. It can make the music more continuous and give it more momentum. Below we look at the features of phrase elision and how to handle it in performance.

## How to play an elision

You can let the overlapping note have a clear landing, like the cadence of the previous phrase.

At the same time, from this note on, the direction of the music must turn at once to the new phrase, and the dynamics or tone colour can change a little.

Do not linger too long on this note, or the momentum of the overlap disappears.

## Finding elisions in the score

To find an elision, first find the cadences in the piece and see where the cadence note falls.

Then look at the start of the new phrase and see whether it is also on the same note or in the same bar.

If it is, and there is no pause between the two phrases, it is very likely an elision.

## Elision summary

In an elision, the closing note of one phrase also becomes the opening of the next, with no pause between the two. It often makes the bar counts asymmetrical, for example two four-bar phrases taking up only seven bars.

It often appears at the boundary between sections or on the way to a climax, making the music tighter and giving it more momentum, which differs from the sense of rest in an ordinary cadence.

When playing, the overlapping note needs a clear landing, while also turning at once to the new phrase without lingering too long. You can look for examples in classical sonatas.

## Looking for it in works

In the sonatas and symphonies of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, you can meet links where two phrases share one note everywhere.

You can take a movement from a sonata you know and look carefully at the links between sections.

After finding the places where phrases overlap, listen to recordings and hear how the performers handle them.

## The effect of an elision

An elision makes the music seem tighter and reduces the slackening that a pause brings.

The listener has only just felt one phrase end when the new one has already begun, and feels the music constantly moving forward.

This technique is often used to increase tension and continuity.

## The difficulty of playing an elision

When playing an elision, you need to give the previous phrase a sense of ending and the next phrase a sense of beginning.

If you treat it only as an ending, the next phrase seems to have no strength; if you treat it only as a beginning, the cadence of the previous phrase is overlooked.

This needs the player to express two meanings on one note at the same time.

## Where elisions often appear

Elisions often appear where one section ends and a new section begins.

For example, in a sonata, between a cadence in the exposition and the transition that then begins.

They also often appear when the music is heading towards a climax, so that the momentum is not interrupted.

## The ordinary link between phrases

In most music, between one phrase and the next there is a clear cadence and a brief breath.

For example, a four-bar phrase ends in the fourth bar, and a new phrase begins in the fifth bar.

Such a structure is clear and symmetrical, and sounds very natural.

## What is an elision

In an elision, at the very moment the cadence note of the previous phrase sounds, the next phrase begins too.

That is to say, this note has a double identity: it is the end of the previous phrase and also the beginning of the next.

The pause that should have been there is "omitted", and the two phrases are joined tightly together.

## Changes in bar counts

Because one bar is shared by two phrases, the bar counts of the phrases become asymmetrical.

For example, two four-bar phrases, once overlapped, add up to only seven bars rather than eight.

When analysing the structure of a piece, if you find the bar count is "one short", you can think about whether there is an elision.

![A group of humanoid robots playing piano, synthesizer and drums on a neon street, with crystal towers behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa86gl3-qz2r3.webp)

## Contrast with an ordinary cadence

An ordinary cadence gives a feeling of "arrival" and "rest".

In an elision cadence, arrival and departure happen at the same time, and the rest is cancelled.

By comparing these two ways of writing, you can sense the composer's control over the rhythm and breathing of the music.

- The ending of the previous phrase is also the beginning of the next
- There is no pause between the two phrases
- It often appears at the boundary of a cadence and a new section
- When playing, you must both end and begin

## Understanding the breath of music

Elision reminds us that the breath of music is not always regular.

Composers can change the rhythmic feel of the music by omitting pauses, extending phrases and other techniques.

Understanding these techniques lets us control the breathing of phrases more consciously when we play.

## Trying an elision at the piano

You can write two simple four-bar phrases, with the first ending on the tonic and the second beginning on the tonic.

First play them separately, with a pause in between; then play the last note of the first phrase as the first note of the second.

**Listen**

Compare the two ways of playing and feel the continuous effect of the elision.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an elision?**
A: The closing note of one phrase is also the opening of the next.

**Q: What effect does it have on bar counts?**
A: There may be one bar fewer, for example eight bars becoming seven.

**Q: Where does it often appear?**
A: At the boundaries between sections or on the way to a climax.

**Q: What is the effect?**
A: The music is tighter and has more momentum.

**Q: How should it be handled in performance?**
A: Give the overlapping note a landing, while turning at once to the new phrase.

phrase-breathing-points.body:
Phrases in piano playing are similar to breathing in swimming. Swimming needs breaths taken in a fixed rhythm, and playing the piano also needs gaps for breathing between phrases. If you never breathe, the phrases get squeezed together; if you pause lightly in the right places, the music becomes more natural and more unhurried.

## Finding the breathing points in the score

Some markings in the score can help you find breathing points. The end of a slur, a rest, or the place after a long note is usually somewhere you can breathe.

Sometimes the score marks a breath mark directly, shaped like a small comma or tick, written above the staff.

The structure of the phrase is also a clue. Many phrases are four or eight bars long, and at the end there is often a cadence, after which a new phrase begins.

Changes in harmony can also give hints: when the harmony returns to the tonic chord, the phrase often comes to a close.

Putting these clues together, you can mark the approximate breathing points in the score.

## Making breathing points natural, not abrupt

A breathing point does not mean stopping for a long time. Usually you only need to ease off the last note of the phrase a little, or leave a very short gap between two phrases.

Your hand movement can go with the breath, for example by lifting the wrist gently at the end of a phrase and letting it drop at the start of the new phrase.

The rhythm still has to stay steady. The time for the breath should be "borrowed" from the value of the previous note, not added on top, unless the score has a fermata.

You can also really breathe along with the playing, taking a breath between phrases, and your body will be more relaxed.

Record yourself and listen to judge whether the breathing points are natural, and whether they are too long or too short.

## Finding breathing points in the score

You can first sing the melody through. The places where you naturally need to breathe are usually the ends of phrases. Draw a small mark in pencil in those places, to remind yourself to leave a little space lightly when you play.

A breathing point is generally very short and does not disturb the rhythm. It is more like ending the last note a little early, so the next phrase has a clear beginning.

Some phrases are very long, with no obvious pause in the middle. In that case you can use rises and falls in dynamics to give the phrase a feeling of "breathing" inside it, without actually stopping.

When practising, also pay attention to your own body. When playing a long phrase, many people unconsciously hold their breath, which makes the shoulders and arms tense. Keeping a natural breath helps you play in a relaxed way.

## Developing a sense of breathing in practice

You can sing first and then play. When you sing, you naturally pause where you need to breathe, and when you play you then imitate that feeling.

You can also listen to recordings of singers or wind players, noting where they breathe and how they handle the endings of phrases.

When practising, you can first play one phrase alone several times, then join two phrases together and feel the breath between them.

Gradually you will become more sensitive to the length and structure of phrases, and when reading a score you can find the breathing points more quickly.

This sense of breathing makes your playing more musical and more likely to move the listener.

![Person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8l62li-f76iu.webp)

## Why playing the piano needs breathing too

Playing the piano does not require blowing with the mouth, but music itself has breath. Phrases are like sentences in speech, and between sentences there need to be pauses and breaths.

If a piece has no pauses from beginning to end, it sounds like speaking non-stop in one breath, and the listener finds it hard to follow.

Good playing leaves suitable space between phrases, so that the music rises and falls and sounds more natural.

Singers and wind players have to breathe, so they are especially sensitive to the breathing of phrases. Pianists can learn from their experience.

**Try it**

Try singing a melody, and the places where you need to breathe are often the dividing lines between phrases.

- Phrases need suitable breaths between them
- Breathing points are often at the ends of phrases and after slurs
- You can sing the melody first to find where to breathe
- Breathing is not stopping but a very short gap

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: How do I know where a phrase ends?**
A: You can look at slurs, rests and cadences, and you can also feel it by singing the melody.

**Q: Do I have to pause between every phrase?**
A: Not necessarily a complete stop. Sometimes it is just a light ending, and you can handle it according to the tempo and style of the piece.

**Q: Must there be a pause between phrases?**
A: There does not have to be an obvious pause, but usually some space is needed so that the phrase has a clear beginning and ending.

**Q: Does a breath mark affect the rhythm?**
A: A breath mark usually takes a small part of the value of the previous note, and the overall rhythm must still stay steady.

**Q: How do I judge the length of a phrase?**
A: You can look at slurs, cadences and changes of harmony, and you can also sing the melody first to feel it.

**Q: Do fast pieces need breathing too?**
A: Yes, only the breaths are shorter and show up more in how the phrases are divided.

pause-on-thumb-notes-in-fast-runs.body:
When you play fast scales or runs, the thumb is often where things get unsteady: at the moment the thumb turns under, the hand easily wobbles, and the note can suddenly become louder or uneven. One practice method is to pause on every note played by the thumb: when the fingers reach a thumb note, stop, check whether your hand position is already ready for the next group of notes, and then continue. These thumb notes are like checkpoints along the way, helping you divide the run into sections and play it more steadily.

## Pausing on the thumb notes

When practising, first find all the notes in the run that are played by the thumb and circle them in pencil.

Then, as you play, pause on each thumb note when you reach it.

While you pause, keep your hand on the keys and feel the position of the hand.

## Runs in pieces

The fast runs in a piece do not necessarily have the same fingering as a scale, but the thumb is still the key position.

First settle the fingering, then circle the thumb notes and practise.

Sometimes you can also pause at other key points of change, not just at the thumb.

## Gradually speeding up

Practice with pauses on the thumb notes can start at a slow tempo.

Once you can do it steadily, raise the speed of each group of notes, but keep the pauses.

Finally, gradually shorten the pauses until the whole run is fluent and fast.

## Thumb notes in the left hand

In left-hand scales and runs, the position of the thumb is the mirror image of the right hand.

You can likewise circle the thumb notes first, then practise hands separately, pausing on the thumb notes.

The left hand is often less fluent than the right, so you can spend a little more time on it.

## Why the thumb causes trouble

In scales and runs, the thumb often has to pass under the other fingers, or the other fingers have to cross over the thumb.

If this movement is not fluent, the hand and arm easily wobble along with it.

The thumb itself is also quite strong, and if you are not careful, the notes it plays will be louder than the others.

## What to check during the pause

When you stop on a thumb note, check that the wrist is steady and not twisted to one side.

See whether the fingers you will use for the next group are already prepared above the right keys.

Then listen to the thumb note and see whether it is louder than the others.

## The group after the pause

When you continue from the thumb note, play the next group of notes through smoothly, and pause again only at the next thumb note.

This way, the run is divided into several small groups, each beginning with the thumb.

When every group is played clearly and evenly, the whole run becomes steady.

## Keep the thumb light

When you stop on a thumb note, pay special attention to the weight of the thumb.

If the thumb plays too heavily, individual notes will stick out in the run.

You can deliberately let the thumb play a little more lightly, keeping the same volume as the notes of the other fingers.

## Combining with rhythm changes

Thumb-pause practice can also be used with other methods, such as changing the rhythm or practising in groups.

But using only one method at a time makes the effect clearer.

Once you are fluent, go back to the original even rhythm.

## Don't depend on the pauses

Pausing on the thumb notes is only scaffolding, and it should be taken down once it has done its job.

When the thumb turn has become steady, cancel the pauses in good time and practise the run played continuously.

Otherwise, in performance you may get an unnatural hitch at the thumb.

![Illustration of Bangkok's city skyline at dusk with the elevated light rail](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa79lxw-aadum.webp)

## Thumb-pause practice summary

In fast runs, the thumb turn often makes the hand wobble and the notes uneven. You can circle the thumb notes and pause when you reach them.

During the pause, check that the wrist is steady, that the fingers for the next group are in place, and that the thumb note is not too loud. Both hands can be practised this way.

Pause from long to short, speed up gradually, and once the turn is steady, cancel the pauses in good time and restore the continuous run.

## Thumb notes in scales

Take the right hand of C major going up as an example. The thumb plays C and F, so you can pause on these two notes.

Each time you pause, check whether the thumb has turned under smoothly just after the third or fourth finger has played.

Going down, the other fingers cross over the thumb, and you can also stop on the thumb notes to check.

**Summary**
- The thumb is often the unsteady point in fast runs
- Pause when you reach a thumb note
- Check that the hand is ready for the next group of notes
- Once fluent, cancel the pauses and restore continuity

## How long to pause

At first you can pause for longer, with plenty of time to check.

Once you are fluent, gradually shorten the pause until it is just a very short "footing".

**Listen**

Going further, you can stop pausing altogether and restore the continuous run.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why is the thumb so often unsteady?**
A: The hand easily wobbles when the fingers change, and the thumb easily plays too loudly.

**Q: What do you do in practice?**
A: Pause on every note played by the thumb.

**Q: What do you check while paused?**
A: The wrist, the preparation of the next group of fingers, and the volume of the thumb.

**Q: Should the pauses always be kept?**
A: No, cancel them once the turn is steady.

**Q: Can the left hand be practised this way too?**
A: Yes, first circle the thumb notes and then practise hands separately.
