petrucci-odhecaton-music-print-1501.body:
In 1501, the Italian printer Ottaviano Petrucci published in Venice the first volume of Harmonice Musices Odhecaton ("One Hundred Songs of Harmonic Music"), often shortened to the Odhecaton, or "A Hundred Songs". It is one of the earliest surviving collections of polyphonic music printed with a movable-type system, which allowed multi-voice works to be copied and spread in a relatively uniform form. Before this, many polyphonic works circulated mainly in handwritten manuscripts, which were slow to copy and more likely to contain differences. Petrucci used a method of multiple impressions, printing the staves, the notes and the text onto the paper separately. The process was complicated, but it greatly improved consistency. For people learning the piano today, this reminds us that the score in our hands is not just "paper that was always there", but something that became easy to reproduce only after a long period of technical improvement. Knowing where printed music began also makes us value a clear score more.

## Odhecaton summary

Petrucci's Odhecaton, published in Venice in 1501, is one of the earliest surviving collections of polyphony in movable type. It used multiple impressions to print the staves, notes and text onto the paper, so that polyphonic works could be spread more uniformly.

Copying by hand did not disappear at once, but printing opened a more stable path of reproduction and also shaped our expectations today of a clear score.

How to choose between different editions is something you can look at together with Teacher Aum.

## From rare to gradually widespread

Even with printing, the number of early printed copies was still limited, and their prices and circulation cannot be imagined by today's standards.

But it opened a road, so that later printers could keep improving and print more kinds of scores.

Only in later centuries did printed scores gradually become something that many learners could get hold of.

## What it suggests for reading scores today

The relatively accurate scores we can buy or borrow now rest on centuries of craft and proofreading tradition.

This also reminds learners that choosing a carefully proofread score is safer than casually using a text of unknown origin.

When different editions disagree, you can ask where the difference comes from rather than picking one at random.

## It does not cancel out hand copying

After printing appeared, hand copying did not disappear at once.

People still copied scores for study, arrangement or preservation.

A more accurate way to put it is that printing offered a new, more stable way of circulation, which existed alongside hand copying for a long time.

![High-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a rainy neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdirwqq-qav2v.webp)

## Comparing editions in lessons with Teacher Aum

In lessons, you can ask Teacher Aum to look together at where the notes or markings differ when a piece has two editions.

Which one suits your current level better can also be discussed on the spot.

From the printed collection of 1501, we can think of being a little more careful when choosing scores today.

## What multiple impressions means

In the early days, it was not technically easy to print the staff lines, notes and text all clearly.

Petrucci printed these elements onto the same sheet in several passes so that each could be aligned.

This method took a lot of effort, but it gave a clearer result than a hasty single printing.

## The limits of the manuscript era

Before printed music became widespread, polyphonic works circulated mostly in handwritten manuscripts.

Copying took time, and differences easily arose in the notes, the words or the way the voices matched up.

A score was often used only within a limited circle, and it spread fairly slowly.

## Venice in 1501

Around the turn of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Venice was an important centre of printing and publishing.

Petrucci brought out the Odhecaton here, not by picking a city by chance but by drawing on the printing conditions already in place there.

The title of the first volume is rather long, and later people often used the short name "A Hundred Songs" to refer to it.

## Why it is said to be important

It was not the starting point of every page of music printing in human history, but it is a key example of polyphonic works being printed fairly completely as a collection in a movable-type system.

With a relatively uniform printed text, people in different places could more easily sing and study from the same text.

The more widespread printed scores that came later in music history were all built on early attempts like this.

**Before you play**
- Petrucci published the Odhecaton in Venice in 1501
- One of the earliest surviving collections of polyphony in movable type
- It used multiple impressions, printing the staves, notes and text separately
- It let polyphonic works be copied and spread more uniformly

## What kind of music was printed

The Odhecaton collects polyphonic secular songs that were popular at the time, and not the complete works of a single composer.

With several voices interwoven, printing had to meet strict alignment demands: if one voice is out of place, the chorus falls into confusion.

**Try it**

Precisely because it was so difficult, its success shows all the more that printing was beginning to be able to handle complex musical texts.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: In which year and where was the Odhecaton published?**
A: In 1501, in Venice.

**Q: Who was the publisher?**
A: Ottaviano Petrucci.

**Q: Why is it often mentioned in music history?**
A: Because it is one of the earliest surviving polyphonic collections printed with movable type, and it improved the consistency of copying scores.

**Q: What does multiple impressions mean?**
A: Printing the staves, notes and text onto the same sheet in several passes so that they are aligned and printed clearly.

**Q: Did hand-copied manuscripts disappear straight away once printing appeared?**
A: No. Hand copying and printing existed side by side for a long time.

practice-piece-from-the-end-backwards.body:
Many people always start practising a piece from the first bar. The opening gets more and more familiar, while the ending stays the least comfortable, and in performance they feel less and less sure as they go on. A simple adjustment is to plan your practice in reverse: first practise the last phrase, and once it is solid, add the phrase before it, then the one before that, working backwards one phrase at a time and playing through to the end each time. This way, the closer a section is to the end, the more often it gets played, so you feel more and more familiar and confident as you reach the final bars, instead of more and more nervous.

## Combine It with Practising from the Start

Practising backwards is not meant to replace practising from the beginning entirely. It is a complementary method.

**Summary**

You can focus on backwards practice for a period, and once the ending is solid too, play the whole piece from the start.

Within a single session, you can also practise backwards for a while and then play through from the beginning once.

## How to Divide the Phrases

Before you begin, mark the whole piece into phrases in the score, using a pencil and numbering them.

You can divide the phrases according to the natural structure of the music, usually a complete musical unit of a few bars.

If a phrase is especially difficult, split it again into two or three smaller pieces.

## Ask Your Teacher to Help Divide the Phrases

If you would like to try this method, tell your teacher and ask for help dividing the phrases, or for some suggestions.

Depending on the piece, your teacher may tell you which spots especially need backwards practice.

Using this method under a teacher's guidance works better.

## Always Play to the End

The key to backwards practice is that every time you add a new phrase, you play all the way to the end, rather than practising only the newly added phrase.

That way the new phrase gets practised, and so does its connection to everything after it.

Gradually, you will be able to start from any phrase and play fluently to the end.

## Helps with Memorising

Backwards practice also helps with memorising, because the start of every phrase becomes a starting point and you remember how each phrase begins.

These starting points are like landmarks in your memory. If you forget a spot while playing, you can pick up again from the next landmark.

When memorising, you can also work backwards: memorise the last phrase first, then add phrases one by one towards the front.

## Keep Track of Your Progress

In your practice notebook, you can note how far back you got each day, and next time continue adding from there.

If a phrase keeps going wrong once you add it, stay with it for another day and make it steady before moving on.

Watching the phrase numbers move gradually towards the beginning also brings a satisfying sense of progress.

## Do Not Forget the Music

When practising backwards, you often start in the middle, and you may sometimes lose the sense of the music as a whole.

While practising, think about where this phrase sits in the whole piece: is it building up, developing or closing?

Playing with that awareness, even when you start from the middle, gives the music the right direction.

## The Idea of Reversing

Practising from the end backwards means first making the last phrase solid, then adding the second-to-last phrase and playing from there to the end.

Next, add the third-to-last phrase and play from there to the end, and so on, all the way back to the beginning.

This way, every practice run passes through the ending, and the ending gets practised the most.

## Which Pieces Suit It

Backwards practice suits most pieces with a clear phrase structure, especially pieces whose ending is difficult or never quite settles.

For a very long work, you can first divide it into sections and practise backwards within each section.

For a very short piece, you can also use this method to make the whole piece more balanced.

## The Problem with Always Starting from the Beginning

If every practice session starts from the first bar, the opening gets played many times and naturally becomes very familiar.

But if practice time is limited, or you get interrupted midway, the later parts are often under-practised.

When it comes to performing, the opening goes smoothly, but the further you go the less familiar it feels, and the less sure you become.

- Starting from the beginning often leaves the ending least familiar
- Reverse it: start from the last phrase
- Add one phrase at a time towards the front, playing to the end each time
- The later the music, the more familiar it is, giving more confidence in performance

## More and More Confident Towards the End

Because the later parts get the most practice, the closer you come to the ending in performance, the more familiar it feels.

This is the opposite of starting from the beginning, and you do not end up getting more nervous as you play.

The ending is often the climax or summing-up of a piece, and playing it with confidence makes the whole piece more effective.

![Sketch of a golden grand piano on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa163p3-m78cb.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: Why practise from the end backwards?**
A: It lets the ending get the most practice, so you feel more confident as you play towards the end.

**Q: How do I practise backwards?**
A: Practise the last phrase first, then add phrases one at a time towards the front.

**Q: Where should I play to each time?**
A: Always play all the way to the end.

**Q: Do I still need to practise from the beginning?**
A: Yes. Backwards practice is a complementary method.

**Q: Does it help with memorising?**
A: Yes. The start of each phrase becomes a starting point in memory.

**Q: How do I use it for a long piece?**
A: Divide it into sections first, then practise backwards within each section.

pop-left-hand-bass-patterns.body:
When accompanying a pop song, the left hand usually takes care of the bass and gives the whole song a steady foundation. Beginners can start with the simplest approach: play just one root note for each chord, as a long note. When that is familiar, change the root to an octave to make the bass fuller; then go a step further and alternate between the root and the fifth, or add a simple rhythm pattern. At every step, first practise slowly until it is steady, then add the right-hand chords or melody. Progressing step by step like this, the left-hand accompaniment will have more and more groove.

## Step One: Play Only the Root

The simplest left-hand accompaniment is to play only the root of each chord: C for a C chord, G for a G chord.

You can play the root on the first beat of each bar and hold it to the end of the bar, or play it on every beat.

The point of this step is to get the left hand used to the chord changes and to move to the next root at the right time.

## Left Hand with Broken Chords

In a lyrical song, the left hand can also play broken chords, for example the root, the fifth and the octave one after another.

This kind of broken accompaniment sounds flowing and soft, and suits slow songs very well.

As you practise, make sure every note is even and let the root stand out a little.

## Practising the Left Hand from a Chord Chart

The sheet music for many pop songs is a chord chart, with only the melody and chord symbols and no specific left-hand notes.

In that case you can arrange the left-hand bass yourself from the chord symbols, for example by finding the root of each chord.

This practice builds your ability to accompany from a chord chart, so that with a new song you can quickly put an accompaniment together.

## Bass Notes in Slash Chords

Sometimes a chord chart shows a slash chord, such as C/E. Then the left hand plays the note after the slash, not the root.

Such a bass note is often there to make the bass line smoother, for example descending step by step.

Paying attention to the direction of the bass as you play makes the accompaniment sound more fluent.

- The left hand takes the bass and gives the song a steady foundation
- Start with one root note per chord
- When familiar, change to octaves to make the bass fuller
- Then add alternating root and fifth or a rhythm pattern

## Step Three: Root and Fifth

Going further, you can alternate between the root and the fifth. For a C chord, play C first, then G, then return to C.

This alternating bass gives the accompaniment a little flow, so it sounds less monotonous.

You can play the root on beat one and the fifth on beat three, forming a steady "one, three" pulse.

## Adding a Simple Rhythm

Once you are familiar with the basic notes, you can give the left hand some simple rhythm patterns, for example playing the bass on beat one and on the second half of beat two.

Songs in different styles have different rhythmic characteristics: ballads are more relaxed, up-tempo songs more springy.

Listen to more original recordings of songs, notice the rhythm of the bass, and try to imitate it.

## Step Two: Playing Octaves

When you can play the root well, change it to an octave, that is, use your little finger and thumb to play two roots an octave apart at the same time.

An octave bass is fuller and stronger than a single note, and especially suits sections that need more power, such as the chorus.

If your hands are small and octaves are difficult, you can keep playing single notes, or play the two notes one after the other.

![An illustration in red, orange and yellow lines on white of a grand piano, expressing the power of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0vaag-2w8az.webp)

## The Register of the Bass

Do not play the left-hand bass too low, or the sound may become muddy, especially when you use the pedal.

Generally, within one to two octaves below middle C the bass is clearer.

You can try the same bass in different registers and listen to which position works best.

## Step by Step

Every step of the left-hand accompaniment needs time to become familiar, so do not rush to use the most complex way all at once.

You can first play one song in a simple way until it is secure, then try changing to a richer bass.

Slowly you will build up several common left-hand accompaniment patterns and choose the right one for each song.

## Working with the Right Hand

Once the left-hand accompaniment is steady, add the right-hand chords or melody.

At first you can use the simplest left-hand approach, such as playing only the root, so that coordinating the two hands is easier.

When both hands are familiar, gradually change the left hand to a more complex accompaniment.

## The Job of the Left Hand

In pop accompaniment, the left hand usually does not play the melody but the bass, telling the listener which chord is sounding now.

A steady bass makes the whole song sound more solid and gives the right-hand chords and melody something reliable to rest on.

So the left-hand accompaniment does not need to be complicated, but it should be clear and steady.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What does the left hand do in pop accompaniment?**
A: It plays the bass and provides a steady foundation.

**Q: Where should beginners start?**
A: With just one root note per chord.

**Q: What if my hands are too small for octaves?**
A: Keep playing single notes, or play the two notes one after the other.

**Q: How do I alternate root and fifth?**
A: For example, play the root on beat one and the fifth on beat three.

**Q: How low is a good register for the bass?**
A: One to two octaves below middle C is clearer.

**Q: What if the chord chart does not show the left hand?**
A: Arrange the root notes yourself from the chord symbols.

practice-on-keyboard-with-fewer-keys.body:
A standard piano has 88 keys, but many beginner electronic keyboards have only 61 or 76 keys, so the range is narrower and the keys may be lighter than on a piano. At the beginner stage it is fine to practise on such a keyboard, since the range of many beginner pieces is not wide. Things to watch: when a note falls outside the range, you can use the octave-shift function or play it in the neighbouring octave; light keys may let your fingers get used to a light touch, so play on a piano when you have the chance; and before an exam or a performance, get used to a real piano in good time.

## The Weight of the Keys

On many beginner keyboards the keys are lighter than on a piano and do not need much force to press down.

**A small tip**

If you practise on light keys for a long time, your fingers may get used to touching the keys lightly, and when you switch to a piano the keys will feel very heavy.

Some keyboards have touch sensitivity, producing different volumes depending on how hard you press; you can pay attention to this function as you practise.

**Look from another angle**
- A standard piano has 88 keys
- Beginner keyboards often have 61 or 76 keys
- They can be used at the beginner stage, as beginner pieces do not have a wide range
- Play on a piano whenever you have the chance

## The Instrument Is Only a Tool

Whatever keyboard you use, steady practice and the right method are the key to progress.

Many people started learning on a simple keyboard and slowly made their way into music.

Making good use of the instrument at hand and enjoying the process of learning is a very good start.

## Keyboards with Different Numbers of Keys

A standard acoustic piano and many digital pianos have 88 keys, running from the A in the bass all the way to the C at the top, a very wide span.

Many beginner electronic keyboards have only 61 or 76 keys, missing some of the lowest and highest notes of a piano.

These keyboards are usually light and fairly moderately priced, and suit people who are just starting out on the keyboard.

## Finding Middle C

Because keyboards have different numbers of keys, the position of middle C differs too, and it is not necessarily in the exact middle of the keyboard.

You can check the manual, or find the marking on the keyboard, to confirm where middle C is.

Once you have found middle C, you can stick a small marker on it to help you find your position when you are starting out.

## Play on a Piano When You Can

Even if you usually practise on an electronic keyboard, whenever you have the chance, play on a real piano too, for example at your teacher's home, at school or in a practice room.

This lets you get used to the weight of the keys, the tone and the pedals of a piano, and reduces the discomfort of changing instruments.

If you are preparing for an exam or a performance, you should get used to a piano in good time, so that you do not feel at a loss on the day.

![A poster-style illustration of the city of Bangkok, with tall buildings and busy streets full of traffic](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1vytr-myx2k.webp)

## Is It Enough for Beginners?

At the beginner stage, the range of most pieces is concentrated around middle C and does not use the lowest and highest notes of the piano.

So a keyboard with 61 or 76 keys is generally enough for practising beginner pieces.

As your level rises, the range of pieces becomes wider and wider, and then you may need more keys.

## When to Think About Upgrading

If the pieces you are learning more and more often go beyond the range of the keyboard, or you need finer control of dynamics and pedalling, you can think about upgrading your instrument.

You can discuss it with your teacher and, depending on your level, budget and space, choose a suitable digital piano or acoustic piano.

An upgrade does not have to happen all in one step; you can consider it gradually as circumstances require.

## What If a Note Is Out of Range

If a note falls outside the range of the keyboard, see whether the keyboard has an octave-shift function, which raises or lowers the pitch of the whole keyboard by an octave.

You can also play that note in the neighbouring octave; the pitch is different, but it lets your practice continue.

If this happens more and more, it may mean you need to consider an instrument with more keys.

## Posture and Height

When using an electronic keyboard, pay attention to the height of the keyboard and where you sit, so that your forearms are roughly level with the keys.

You can use a stand and a chair with adjustable height to find a comfortable posture.

Sit roughly facing the middle of the keyboard, near middle C.

## The Sustain Pedal

Many beginner keyboards can be connected to a separate sustain pedal, which you can use to practise pedalling.

If the keyboard has a pedal socket, consider getting a pedal to make practice closer to a piano.

Place the pedal where your right foot can reach it easily, and set it firmly so that it does not slide.

## Practising Dynamics

If the keyboard has no touch sensitivity, the volume is the same however you press, and it is hard to practise changes of dynamics.

You can check the manual to see whether your keyboard supports touch sensitivity and how to set it.

If it does not, play on a piano and practise dynamics whenever you have the chance.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How many keys does a standard piano have?**
A: 88 keys.

**Q: Can I learn on 61 keys?**
A: At the beginner stage it is generally enough.

**Q: What if a note is out of range?**
A: Use the octave-shift function or play it in the neighbouring octave.

**Q: Do keys that are too light matter?**
A: You may get used to a light touch, so play on a piano when you have the chance.

**Q: Can I connect a pedal?**
A: Many keyboards have a pedal socket, and you can get one.

**Q: When should I upgrade my instrument?**
A: When the range is often not enough or you need finer control.

piano-competition-healthy-attitude.body:
A piano competition can give you a clear goal, performing experience and the chance to hear other people play, but it can also bring pressure. A healthier attitude is to treat a competition as one experience along the learning journey rather than a final verdict on yourself: focus on your preparation and progress, not only on the ranking; treat the judges' comments as a reference; and afterwards, whatever the result, reflect on what you gained. Before entering, you can talk with your teacher and family about whether the timing, the repertoire and your physical and emotional state are right. There is no need to compete just for the sake of competing.

## The Preparation Process

When preparing for a competition, you can prepare as you would for a performance: practise in sections, hold mock performances and try playing on different pianos.

Balance work and rest too. Leave plenty of time to recover, and do not overpractise because of the competition.

If you feel unwell physically or emotionally, adjust in good time and talk to your teacher and family.

## Treat It as an Experience

A competition is only one experience on the road of learning the piano. Its result does not represent all of your ability and worth.

The same person can play differently on different days and in different venues.

When you see a competition as a chance to learn, your mindset is more relaxed, and your playing may come across more naturally.

## Choosing the Right Competition

Different competitions have different requirements and levels, so you can choose one that suits your standard.

Read the rules carefully to understand the repertoire requirements, age categories and how to enter.

If anything is unclear, you can ask the organisers or your teacher, and go by the official instructions.

## Things to Consider Before Entering

Before deciding whether to enter, you can think through some questions with your teacher and family.

For example: is there enough time to prepare, is the repertoire suitable, and are your recent studies and life too busy?

If the conditions are not quite right, you can also choose to enter later. There is no need to force it.

## What a Competition Can Bring

A competition gives you a clear goal and deadline, so for a period of time you focus on preparing a few pieces.

It also gives you experience of playing in an unfamiliar venue in front of judges and an audience.

Hearing other people play at a competition also broadens your horizons and shows you different ways of approaching a piece.

## Focus on Your Own Progress

While preparing for a competition, pay attention to your own progress, such as pieces becoming more fluent and your playing becoming richer.

These improvements are real gains. Whatever the result, they belong to you.

You can keep a record of this progress as you prepare, and looking back later will give you a real sense of achievement.

## On the Day

On the day of the competition, you can arrive early, get used to the surroundings, and do your warm-up and mental preparation.

When you go on stage, keep your attention on the music rather than on the judges or the other competitors.

After you finish playing, however it felt, give yourself some credit.

## The Judges' Comments

Some competitions provide judges' comments, which are valuable learning material.

Treat the comments as a reference and discuss them with your teacher to see which areas can be improved.

Different judges may see things differently, so there is no need to doubt yourself because of a single comment.

## Reflecting Afterwards

After the competition, you can look back on the experience with your teacher and sum up what you gained and what needs improving.

If the result is disappointing, you can allow yourself to feel a little down, but also see the growth this experience brought.

If the result is great, keep a level head and carry on enjoying the process of learning the piano.

## The Parents' Role

When a child enters a competition, the parents' attitude matters a great deal.

Parents can focus on their child's effort and process, rather than only asking about the ranking.

Afterwards, you can talk with your child about the happy moments and what they learned from the experience, so that they feel supported.

- Competitions bring goals, performing experience and chances to connect with others
- Treat a competition as a learning experience, not a final verdict
- Focus on preparation and progress, not only on the ranking
- Before entering, consider timing, repertoire and physical and emotional state

## Competition Pressure

A competition's results come with rankings and evaluations, which inevitably bring pressure, especially for children.

If you care too much about the result, you may feel anxious during preparation and even lose interest in music.

So before entering, think clearly about why you are taking part.

![Watercolour of a white grand piano with sheet music and flowers](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1c43w-ouvfx.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What can a competition bring?**
A: A goal, performing experience and the chance to hear others play.

**Q: Does the competition result say everything about me?**
A: No. It is just one experience.

**Q: How should I view the judges' comments?**
A: Treat them as a reference and discuss them with your teacher.

**Q: When is it not a good time to enter?**
A: When there is not enough time to prepare, the repertoire is unsuitable or you are too busy.

**Q: What should I watch out for on the day?**
A: Arrive early and keep your attention on the music.

**Q: What should parents do?**
A: Focus on their child's effort and process, not only on the ranking.

pick-out-pop-melody-with-one-finger-firs.body:
When they want to play a favourite pop song on the piano, many people start by looking for the full accompaniment score, only to find there are too many notes to play. You can in fact begin with the simplest step: using just one finger, pick out the melody of the song on the piano, one note at a time. Once the melody is familiar, add fingering, then the left-hand chords. Picking out the melody with one finger helps us really remember the tune of the song, and also trains the ability to find notes by ear.

## Where the Chords Come From

The left-hand chords can be found from the chord chart of the song; in many pop songs the chord names are marked above the lyrics.

**Practice order**

You can also try finding them by ear, listening for which chord goes best with the melody.

The common triads, such as C, F, G and Am, can accompany many songs.

## Finding the First Note

First try to find the first note of the melody: play a few random notes on the piano and compare them with the pitch you sing.

If the note you play is higher than the one you sing, search to the left; if it is lower, search to the right.

The key that matches the pitch you sing is the first note.

## Start with a Simple Song

For your first try, you can choose a song with a simple melody and a small range.

For example, some children's songs or slow lyrical songs.

After you succeed in picking out the melody of one song, then take on more complicated ones.

## Find It Note by Note

After finding the first note, sing the second note, and listen to whether it is higher or lower than the first, and by how much.

Try searching upward or downward on the piano until you find the right note.

Searching note by note in this way, you find a whole phrase of the melody.

## Be Patient Finding Notes

When you first find notes by ear, it may be rather slow, and a phrase of melody can take several minutes.

This is normal; after practising a few more songs, you will get faster and faster at finding notes.

This ability will also help a great deal with improvising and arranging later on.

**Listen up**
- First use just one finger to pick out the melody
- Find it note by note
- Once the melody is familiar, add fingering and chords
- Practise finding notes by ear

## Hum the Pop Song Until It Is Familiar Before Finding Notes

Before finding notes, sing the melody of the song a few times, so that it is very clear in your head.

You can sing just the first line or two; you do not need to sing the whole song at once.

Once you know it well, you will know what sound you are searching for when finding notes.

## The Hurdle of the Full Accompaniment Score

The full piano score of a pop song often has melody, chords and accompaniment figures all at once, which is a heavy load for a beginner.

If you start with a score like that, it is easy to be unable to play on and lose interest.

Starting with the melody and adding step by step is much easier.

## The Benefits of One Finger

With just one finger, such as the index finger of the right hand, you do not need to think about fingering, and can put all your attention on pitch.

This lets you listen more intently and find the position of each note on the piano.

It is a very good ear-training exercise, and also helps us get to know the keyboard.

## When You Meet Black Keys

The melody of some songs uses black keys; when finding notes, if none of the white keys is right, try the black key next to them.

If a whole song has many black keys, it may be in a key with sharps or flats.

In that case you can also try moving the whole song to C major, and play it using only white keys, which is easier.

## Picking Out a Melody with One Finger: A Summary

When learning a pop song, you can first use just one finger to pick out the melody note by note, sing it until familiar first, find notes by comparing high and low, and write down the note names.

Once the melody is familiar, add five-finger fingering, then left-hand chords, which can be found from a chord chart or by ear.

Pay attention to rhythm, start with simple songs, and practise patiently, and your ability to find notes will grow stronger and stronger.

## Once the Melody Is Familiar, Add Fingering

After you can play the melody well with one finger, try playing it with five fingers.

Assign a suitable finger to each note, keeping hand movement to a minimum.

With fingering, the melody will play more smoothly, and feel more like real playing.

## Then Add Left-Hand Chords

Once the right-hand melody is familiar, you can add left-hand chords to the song.

At first you can play just a root note, or a simple chord, on the first beat of each bar.

Gradually, add richer accompaniment figures.

## Write Down the Notes You Find

After finding a phrase of melody, you can write the note names on paper, for example "E, E, F, G".

That way, next time you play it, you do not need to find it all over again.

You can also write it down using numbers from numbered notation (jianpu), for example "3, 3, 4, 5".

![A purple-blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6kyi2-ioopx.webp)

## Get the Rhythm Right Too

When finding a melody, you need to get not only the pitch right but also the rhythm.

Some notes are long, some are short, and in some places there is syncopation.

You can sing and play at the same time, letting your fingers follow the rhythm of your singing.

## FAQ

**Q: Why start with one finger?**
A: You do not have to think about fingering, and can concentrate on finding the pitch.

**Q: What should I do before finding notes?**
A: First sing the melody until it is familiar.

**Q: What if the note I play is higher than the one I sing?**
A: Search to the left.

**Q: What do I do once the melody is familiar?**
A: Add five-finger fingering, then left-hand chords.

**Q: What song should I choose the first time?**
A: A song with a simple melody and a small range.

practice-breaks-stretch-and-listening-re.body:
A break during practice means deliberately stopping for a few minutes after a spell of focused work, so your fingers, wrists, shoulders and ears can relax. Many people think the longer they practise the better, and play for an hour or two without getting up. In fact, suitable short breaks often let your attention recover, make your movements more natural and make your practice more consistent. This article shares some rest methods you can use every day. It is general advice on daily life and practice, not medical advice.

## Why You Need to Rest in the Middle of Practice

Playing the piano needs fine control of the fingers, while you also read the score, listen to the sound and count the beats. The brain and body work at the same time, and over time attention drops. When attention drops, people often shrug their shoulders, clench their teeth or stiffen their wrists without noticing, and the sound they produce becomes harsh. Pushing on at that point is not only inefficient, but can also build bad movement habits into your playing.

**Short, regular pauses**
Many teachers suggest stopping for three to five minutes after every twenty to thirty minutes of practice. You can adjust the exact time to how you feel. The point is to be regular, rather than waiting until you are very tired.

## Simple Upper-Body Stretches

![A piano in a quiet room in natural light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw6vb4bo-968zs.webp)

During a break, you can leave the piano bench, stand up and do some gentle stretches. Move slowly, and stop at what feels comfortable. There is no need to go for range. If a movement makes you uncomfortable, stop.

- Slowly raise both shoulders, hold for two seconds, then lower them gently. Repeat a few times.
- Interlace your fingers in front of you, palms facing out, and push gently forward, feeling your arms and back stretch.
- Bring one arm across your chest and support it gently with the other hand. Hold for a few seconds, then switch sides.
- Slowly tilt your head to the left and right to relax your neck.
- Gently draw circles with your wrists, a few circles clockwise and a few anticlockwise.

These movements only help your body come out of a fixed posture for a while. You do not need to treat them as training.

## Give Your Eyes and Ears a Break Too

When reading music, your eyes stay fixed on small notes close up. During a break, you can look out of the window at something far away, or close your eyes and take a few deep breaths. Your ears need rest too, especially if you practise on a digital piano with headphones. During a break, take the headphones off and let your ears be in a quiet environment, or listen to natural sounds around you.

**Keep the volume moderate**
When practising with headphones, do not turn the volume up too high. If your ears feel stuffy during a break, you can turn the volume down a little next time and shorten how long you wear headphones continuously.

## Use Break Time for "Thinking Practice"

Rest does not have to mean not thinking about music at all. Some people like to look at the score during a break, sing the melody silently in their head, and imagine how to handle the next section. This kind of practice without the hands can help you understand the structure of a piece without adding to the load on your hands. Taking a few sips of water and tidying the music on the stand are also small ways to calm down. You can also use the time to write down problems you found in the practice just now, so you can keep solving them afterwards.

## Adjust the Bench and Your Posture

A lot of tiredness comes from an unsuitable sitting posture. Before you sit down again after a break, check the height of the bench: when you sit, your forearms should be roughly parallel to the keys, and your feet should rest steadily on the floor or a footstool. Sit on the front half of the bench, with your back naturally upright and your shoulders relaxed. A good posture lets your body use less unnecessary effort when playing.

## Plan the Rhythm of Your Day's Practice

If you want to practise for a longer time in a day, you can split the practice into several sessions, for example one in the morning and one in the evening, instead of practising straight through at once. Each session has a clear goal, with rest in between, and your overall concentration will be higher. For children, practice time should be even shorter and more focused. Parents can stay nearby and remind the child to get up and move at suitable moments.

**Notice your body's signals**
If you often have persistent pain, numbness or discomfort while practising, you should stop practising and seek professional advice, rather than pushing on.

## FAQ

**Q: Will resting interrupt the feel of practice?**
A: A short break usually does not. It can actually help you be more focused when you come back to the piano.

**Q: How long should the stretches be?**
A: A few minutes is enough. Keep the movements gentle and stop at what feels comfortable.

**Q: Do children need rest when practising?**
A: Yes. Children's attention spans are shorter, so they suit short sessions several times.

**Q: Can I deal with sore wrists myself?**
A: If the discomfort persists, you should consult a doctor and not judge it yourself.

The above is only general reference for daily practice and is not medical advice. If your body has persistent discomfort, please consult a doctor or a licensed clinical music professional.

play-a-familiar-major-song-in-minor.body:
Two Tigers is a song many people have known how to sing since childhood, with a cheerful melody. What would it feel like to play it in a minor key? This is not actually a new idea: in the third movement of his First Symphony, the Austrian composer Mahler turned this tune (often known in Europe as Frère Jacques) into a minor-key version, making a piece of music with a gloomy colour. Turning a familiar major-key song into a minor key on the piano is a fun exercise that helps us understand the difference between major and minor.

- Lower the third, sixth and seventh notes of the major-key song
- Mahler's First Symphony uses a minor-key version of Frère Jacques
- You can directly feel the colour of major and minor
- Start with a simple song

## Starting with Two Tigers

The melody of Two Tigers is very simple. In C major it goes C, D, E, C, C, D, E, C, E, F, G, E, F, G.

**Something else to think about**

Change E to E♭ and it becomes C, D, E♭, C, C, D, E♭, C, E♭, F, G, E♭, F, G.

Play it, and you will find that the originally cheerful melody suddenly turns a little melancholy.

## Sharing in Lessons

In a lesson, you can play your own minor-key arrangement for Teacher Aum.

Your teacher can help check whether the harmony is suitable, or suggest improvements.

This kind of creative practice also makes lessons more fun.

## Help with Improvisation and Arranging

Being able to turn a song into a minor key is also a simple arranging skill.

When improvising or accompanying a song, you can use this method to bring a different colour to the music.

For example, in the second time through a song, you can try playing it in the minor.

## The Harmony Must Change Too

Changing only the melody is not enough. If the left hand has an accompaniment, the chords have to change to minor as well.

For example, the C major chord becomes a C minor chord, and the F major chord becomes an F minor chord.

The dominant chord, G major, often stays the same, because in harmonic minor the dominant chord is still a major chord.

## Major to Minor in Brief

The difference between major and minor lies in the pitch of several notes in the scale. In C natural minor, the third, sixth and seventh notes are a semitone lower than in C major. To start with, lower only the third, and after being changed to minor, Two Tigers becomes melancholy.

In the third movement of his First Symphony, Mahler has the double bass play a minor-key version of Frère Jacques. When arranging, the harmony must change too, the dominant chord often stays a major chord, and you can try the raised seventh of harmonic minor.

Nursery rhymes and folk songs can all be used, and you can also go the other way and turn minor into major. This helps you understand keys and is also an arranging skill. Try a few keys, write it out in notation, and bring it to a lesson to play for Teacher Aum.

## Other Songs Worth Trying

Besides Two Tigers, many simple nursery rhymes and folk songs can be tried in a minor key.

For example, Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star takes on a mysterious feeling in the minor.

Choosing a song with a simple melody that you know very well makes the change easier to hear.

## Trying It in Other Keys

Once you are familiar with doing it in C major, you can try it in other keys.

For example, to change a song in G major into G minor, you change B to B♭, E to E♭ and F♯ to F.

This helps us get to know the scales of different keys.

## Starting by Lowering Only the Third

To change a song in C major into C minor, to start with you can change every E in the melody to E♭.

The third is the key note that decides the colour of major or minor, and changing just this one note makes a clear difference in colour.

Then try lowering A and B as well, and hear what difference that makes.

## Mahler's Example

Mahler (1860-1911) was an Austrian composer, and his First Symphony was completed in the late 1880s.

In the third movement, he has the double bass play a solo minor-key melody, which is exactly the tune of Frère Jacques.

This music has a strange, somewhat gloomy colour, and is a famous example of this technique.

## Help in Understanding Keys

This exercise helps us understand the difference between major and minor directly.

Instead of only knowing in theory that "the third of the minor is a semitone lower", you hear with your own ears the change this semitone brings.

This understanding will be very helpful later when you study keys and harmony.

![Illustration in the style of a Bangkok city poster, with tall buildings and busy traffic in the streets](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9mx0l-jykqg.webp)

## The Difference Between Major and Minor

The difference between major and minor lies mainly in the pitch of several notes in the scale.

Take C major and C minor as an example: in C natural minor, the third, sixth and seventh notes are a semitone lower than in C major.

That is, E becomes E♭, A becomes A♭ and B becomes B♭.

## Try It the Other Way Round

You can also do the reverse and change a familiar minor-key song into a major key.

Raise the lowered third of the minor, and the originally sad melody may become bright.

This contrast lets us feel the different characters of major and minor more clearly.

## The Seventh Note of Harmonic Minor

In a minor key, to let the melody return to the tonic more smoothly, the seventh note is often raised, giving the harmonic minor.

For example, in C harmonic minor, B is not lowered and stays B natural.

When arranging, you can try both B♭ and B natural and hear which suits the song better.

## Writing Down Your Arrangement

You can write your own minor-key version on the staff.

When writing, pay attention to the change of key signature, or add accidentals in front of the notes that need them.

**Practice routine**

This is also a good exercise in notation.

## FAQ

**Q: When changing C major to C minor, which note do I change first?**
A: Change the third, E, to E♭.

**Q: In which work did Mahler use this technique?**
A: The third movement of his First Symphony.

**Q: What is Two Tigers often called in Europe?**
A: Frère Jacques.

**Q: What does the dominant chord often do in a minor key?**
A: It stays a major chord.

**Q: Can I practise the other way round?**
A: Yes. Change a minor-key song into a major key.

piano-rubato-beginner-boundaries.body:
Rubato (a slight stretching and squeezing of the tempo) can give a phrase a sense of breathing, but if a beginner has not yet settled the basic beat, the playing easily falls apart as soon as rubato is tried. A safer order is: first be able to play a passage evenly with the metronome, then add a very small amount of flexibility in bars the teacher chooses, always able to return to the grid.

## First Pass the "Steady Beat Test"

Choose four to eight bars and play them twice with the metronome without going astray. Once you pass, switch the metronome off, play once more, and listen back to a recording. Only if it is still broadly steady do you move on to limited rubato. Until you pass, put your energy into evenness and touch, not expressive speeding up and slowing down.

- Two steady runs with the metronome
- One run without the metronome that does not fall apart
- Difficult bars practised separately and slowly

## How to Do Limited Rubato

The teacher can circle the long notes or phrase endings that may "stretch", and everywhere else the original tempo stays. The stretch should be small, like lingering gently for half a beat, not suddenly twice as slow. After stretching, use the next two bars to return to the original tempo, as if paying back the time you borrowed.

**A workable exercise**
First run: stay completely with the metronome; second run: linger a little only on the circled long notes; third run: go back to the metronome. Comparing the three runs, your ears will understand the difference between flexibility and unsteadiness.

![A person practising with headphones in front of a white upright piano](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3ky6r0-415i0.webp)

## The Risk When Playing Hands Together

Three rules of discipline for flexibility practice:

- Stretch only at the circled places
- Always pay the beat back after stretching
- When it falls apart, go back to the steady beat

The most common loss of control is when the right hand wants rubato while the left-hand accompaniment keeps rushing on. You can first do the limited flexibility with the right hand alone, holding the left hand with a very simple rhythm, and then put the hands together. If it falls apart at once when the hands are together, the stretch is still too big.

## Awareness of Style

Some dance styles need a steady pulse and are not suited to casual rubato; only some lyrical short phrases suit a slight stretching and squeezing. The teacher should explain the style of the piece, so that the student does not apply the same rubato to every piece.

## Choices Before a Performance

Two weeks before a performance, make the rubato a little smaller again, giving priority to continuity. When nervous, a slight stretch can easily be magnified. A steady performance reassures the audience more than exaggerated speeding and slowing.

Write the rubato into your pencil markings: where it may stretch, and where it must return to the grid. The clearer the markings, the less the practice at home will go off course. You can also ask a family member to listen to the third recording and ask, "Where does it sound like breathing, and where like getting stuck?", using feedback from a non-specialist listener to correct your own impression.

## When Rubato and Dynamics Change Together

Beginners often slow down and at the same time suddenly get softer or louder, and the phrase collapses. In practice, first change only the tempo and keep the dynamics; then change only the dynamics and keep the tempo; only at the end allow both to change slightly in the same direction. Practising in separate parts reduces the chain reaction of "everything falls apart as soon as I slow down".

The teacher can use a hand gesture to draw the "stretch zone", and a student who can see the boundary with their eyes benefits more than from abstract explanation alone.

## Rubato and Playing from Memory

Adding rubato when the memory is not secure carries a higher risk, because without a visual reference it is easier to drag and keep slowing down. It is advisable to consolidate memorised passages with a steady beat first, and only then release a very small amount of flexibility. If you still need to look at your hands when playing from memory, the memory is not complete, and you should go back to slow practice in sections rather than use rubato to cover hesitation.

You can try a "shadow beat": count the beats in your head, let the hands and feet stretch slightly, but never stop counting. As soon as the counting breaks, restore the original tempo and start again.

## Suggested Lesson Wording

Instead of the abstract "be a bit freer", the teacher can say "linger a little in this circle, then come back within two bars". A concrete boundary is something the student can carry out. Write the same sentence on the home practice sheet, so that the boundary does not disappear once they are home.

If a student understands rubato as speeding up and slowing down all through the piece, go back to the metronome at once, rebuild the grid, and open up only one circle. Better a little less flexibility than losing the sense of the beat.

At the end of a flexibility exercise, finish with a minute of scales played completely on the beat, telling the brain "the grid is still there". This finish lowers the risk of rubato lingering into the next study.

Widen the circles of "may stretch" grade by grade: in the first year only at phrase endings, and only in the second year consider long notes inside phrases. Write the progression into the teaching plan, to avoid inconsistent standards among students in the same class.

A sentence to write in the homework book this week: steady first, then linger a tiny bit at the end of the phrase, then come back. Copy this sentence together with the circled bar numbers, so that the wording at home and in the lesson is consistent. If the whole piece still keeps speeding up and slowing down, cancel all flexibility this week and practise only the grid.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I practise rubato without a teacher?**
A: You can first practise a steady beat and check yourself with recordings; for larger flexibility, adding it under a teacher's guidance is recommended.

**Q: What if it clashes with the metronome?**
A: Switch the metronome off when practising flexibility, and switch it on when practising paying the beat back. Keep the two modes separate.

**Q: At what age can a child learn it?**
A: It varies from child to child. Introducing it once they can count beats steadily is usually smoother.

**Q: Does rubato mean having no beat?**
A: No. It is a slight stretching and squeezing on top of a perceptible beat, not the abolition of the beat.

practice-after-bad-day.body:
On a bad day, you do not have to force yourself to complete a demanding practice session as planned. You can shorten the practice, choose familiar pieces you like, or do only some simple scales and listening exercises, so that sitting down at the piano stays part of your day. If you really do not feel like playing, taking a day off is fine too, and you can return to your normal rhythm the next day.

## Simple Practice Still Has Value

If you do not want to play pieces, you can play just a few rounds of scales and arpeggios, or do the single-note listening exercise mentioned earlier.

**Summary**

These exercises do not need much thought, your fingers stay active, and the habit continues.

Sometimes, sitting down at the piano regularly is itself a persistence worth recognising.

## Shorten the Practice Time

If you had planned to practise for an hour, on a bad day you can change it to fifteen or twenty minutes.

A shorter session has a lower barrier to start and is easier to finish.

Finishing a small practice often feels more reassuring than giving up completely.

## Start with a Little Preparation

Before sitting down at the piano, you can drink a little water and tidy the piano bench and the music, giving yourself time to ease slowly into it.

After you open the lid, you can first play just a few long notes and listen to the sound, with no hurry to start the real practice.

These small actions take no effort, but they can help you move your attention slowly from what is bothering you to the music.

Note: the above is only general sharing about arranging daily practice, not professional advice. If your mood is troubled for a long time, consider asking a licensed clinical music practitioner, or seeing a doctor, to hear their opinion.

## Talk to Family or Your Teacher

When a child is in a bad mood, parents can first ask what has happened, rather than immediately asking for practice.

If an adult learner is under a lot of stress for a period, they can also tell the teacher, and together adjust the practice plan.

Saying how things are often makes people feel a little lighter, and can bring more suitable advice.

**Practice order**
- Allow yourself to adjust the length and content of practice
- Play familiar pieces you like first
- Keep the habit going with simple exercises
- When you need rest, you can rest for a day without worry

## Choose Familiar Pieces

On such days, you can first play pieces you already know and like, not aiming for perfection, just enjoying the playing.

Familiar melodies can help you relax, and sometimes, as you play, your mood slowly settles a little.

There is no need to practise the hardest passages now. Leave the challenges for days when you feel better.

![Illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background, expressing the strength of a song's ending](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xm8b6-3fvmc.webp)

## Allow Yourself to Rest

If you really are not in the mood to sit at the piano, taking a day off is perfectly fine. An occasional rest will not make you lose the progress you have made.

What matters is not to blame yourself for missing a day. Simply return to your usual practice rhythm the next day.

Long-term learning is a very long road, and it is normal to slow down now and then.

## Emotions Affect Practice

Everyone has days when their mood is low, perhaps because of exams, work or something in life.

When your mood is low, it is often hard to concentrate, and practising new, difficult material makes it easier to feel frustrated.

Knowing this, you can adjust your expectations of yourself on such days, and you do not need every day to go equally well.

There are also days when, as you practise, your mood slowly lifts. Then you can just let it be, and playing a little longer is fine too.

## Look After Yourself

This article shares general suggestions on arranging practice.

If the low feeling does not improve, and even eating and sleeping are affected, you can first talk to someone you trust.

You can also seek help from a doctor or other professional. Taking care of yourself comes before progress at the piano.

## Express Your Feelings Through Music

Some people, when they are in a bad mood, improvise a few chords, or play a melody at a slow tempo, letting their feelings come out through sound.

This kind of playing does not need to follow a score, and does not need to be heard by anyone. It is just spending a little time with your own feelings.

Improvising needs no rules. Just press a few notes that feel right to you.

## FAQ

**Q: Does practising help when I am in a bad mood?**
A: For some people, playing familiar pieces helps them relax, but there is no need to force it.

**Q: Will I go backwards if I take a day off?**
A: An occasional day off usually does not noticeably affect progress.

**Q: What if my child did badly in an exam and does not want to practise?**
A: First care about the child's feelings. You can shorten the practice or take a day off.

**Q: Can I play only the pieces I like?**
A: Yes. On such days, enjoying the music matters more.

**Q: Do I need to know theory to improvise?**
A: No. You can start with a few simple chords.

**Q: Should I tell my teacher?**
A: If you stay in a poor state, you can talk with your teacher and adjust the plan together.

practice-when-tired-shorter.body:
After sports day, a long journey or a full day of busy activity, you may feel physically tired, and there is no need to force yourself to practise for your usual length of time. You can cut your practice down to ten minutes or so and do only a warm-up and some review, avoiding new material that takes a lot of energy and attention. A short, easy session keeps the habit going without letting fatigue build up, and the next day, once you have recovered, you can go back to your normal schedule.

## Review Familiar Pieces

After the warm-up, you can play one or two pieces you already know well. For works you have long since mastered, there is no need to concentrate on reading the score, and your fingers almost find their own way.

While reviewing, you can pick one small thing to pay attention to, such as whether the end of a phrase is gentle, rather than aiming for a perfect performance of the whole piece.

Playing a piece you love can also give a tiring day a pleasant ending.

## Start with an Easy Warm-Up

To begin, you can play a few slow scales or some simple five-finger exercises to let your fingers loosen up gradually.

The warm-up does not need to be fast, and you can keep the touch light. The point is to get your hands and ears into practice mode.

If the warm-up itself already feels very hard, you can shorten today's practice even further, or even finish after the warm-up alone.

## Save New Material for When You Feel Good

Learning a new piece or tackling a technical difficulty takes a good deal of attention and patience, so it is best done when you are fresh.

When you are tired, you can leave these things alone for now, to avoid practising inaccurate movements while you are not at your best.

You can put a mark in the score to remind yourself to pick up from here next time you are in good form.

## Practice After You Have Recovered

Once you have rested well, you can go back to your usual practice length and content.

If your practice has been short for the last few days, you can review earlier material first on your return, then continue with the new parts.

Adjusting flexibly to how your body feels is an important way to keep practising for the long term.

## Tired Days for Adult Learners

Adult learners can also feel worn out in body and mind after a busy period at work or overtime.

At such times you can treat practice as a small way to unwind at the end of the day, playing a few familiar pieces without setting any goals.

If even that feels like too much, rest with an easy mind and start a little earlier the next day, which is also a perfectly reasonable arrangement.

## Arrangements for Children After Sports

Children who have taken part in sports day or a PE class are often already tired when they get home. Whether they play that day, and for how long, is something parents can decide by looking at how the child is doing.

You can let the child eat something and rest for a while first, and then decide whether to practise and for how long.

If the child is especially tired, they can play just one favourite piece, or simply take a day off.

**Quick tips**
- When tired, shorten practice to ten minutes or so
- Do only a warm-up and a review of familiar pieces
- Avoid passages that need a lot of physical effort, and new material
- Go back to your usual amount once you have recovered

![A golden sketch of a grand piano on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xv0jq-imlux.webp)

## How Tiredness Affects Practice

When your body is tired, it is often harder to concentrate, and your fingers may react more slowly than usual.

If you still force yourself to work on difficult passages then, you can easily make the same mistakes again and again, and the frustration can turn practice into a burden.

Understanding how tiredness affects practice lets you give yourself a more sensible plan on such days, instead of simply "pushing on" or "giving up".

## Watch Your Posture and Hands

When you are tired, it is easy to slouch, and your shoulders may rise without your noticing.

During practice you can stop now and then to check your posture, keeping your back straight and your shoulders relaxed.

If your fingers or arms feel clearly sore or achy, stop and rest first rather than pushing on.

## Shorten It Rather Than Cancel It

On tired days, you can cut a practice session that would normally be forty minutes or an hour down to ten minutes or so.

With less time, the mental pressure of sitting down at the piano is much smaller, and it is easier to begin.

**Before you start**

Even just ten minutes of playing keeps the daily practice habit going, which matters for long-term learning too.

## FAQ

**Q: Is it useful to practise when I am tired?**
A: A short, easy session can keep the habit going, but it is not a good time for demanding material.

**Q: Can I skip practice when I am tired?**
A: Yes, an occasional day off usually does not affect long-term progress.

**Q: How long counts as short?**
A: Ten to fifteen minutes is usually enough, as long as it does not feel forced.

**Q: Can my child practise right after sports?**
A: Let them rest and have something to eat first, then decide based on how they are doing.

**Q: Can I still play when my hands are sore?**
A: It is best to stop and rest first rather than pushing on.

**Q: When should I go back to normal practice?**
A: Once your body and mind have recovered, you can gradually return to your usual amount.

passepied-fast-three-eight-dance.body:
The passepied is a folk dance from Brittany in north-western France. In the seventeenth century it was taken into French dance and music, and it later appeared in many Baroque suites. It is fast, usually with a feel of 3/8, and often starts on an upbeat, like feet alternating lightly. In French, "passepied" roughly means "crossed feet". Bach's English Suite No. 5 contains two passepieds; in the early twentieth century, Debussy also wrote one in his Suite bergamasque, borrowing this old name.

## A dance from Brittany

The passepied began as a folk dance from Brittany in north-western France.

**Think again**

In the seventeenth century it was taken into French dance and music and became more elegant.

Later, together with the minuet, the gavotte and others, it became a common dance in the Baroque suite.

## Starting on the upbeat

Passepied phrases often begin on an upbeat, that is, they enter on the last beat of a bar.

This gives the music a feeling of springing forward, like a dancer lightly leaping up.

When you play, let this upbeat carry gently into the strong beat of the next bar.

## The passepied in Bach's partita

Bach's Partita No. 5 for keyboard is in G major, BWV 829, and it also contains a passepied.

This passepied is light and bright, with a rhythm full of energy.

Placed between the sarabande and the gigue, it brings a relaxed mood to the suite.

## Debussy's Passepied

Debussy's piano work Suite bergamasque was first written around 1890 and published in 1905.

Its last movement is called Passepied, borrowing the name of this old dance.

But Debussy's passepied is in 4/4, with a light staccato in the left hand and a flowing melody in the right, a very different style from the Baroque ones.

## An old name in a new use

Debussy and some other French composers liked to borrow the names of old dances.

They were not trying to revive the old dances, but to use the names to evoke a classical, elegant atmosphere.

This was a common practice in French music of the early twentieth century.

## The steps in the name passepied

In French, "passepied" roughly means "crossed feet".

The name describes the quick crossing of the feet in the dance.

When dancing it, the dancers' steps are light and nimble.

## Playing a Baroque passepied on the piano

To play a Baroque passepied, the tempo should be fast, but the touch should be light and clear.

Keep the upbeat of each phrase light, and the strong beats clear but not too heavy.

You can imagine a dancer's light steps, to give the music some spring.

## Asking your teacher to recommend a passepied

Whether to start with Bach's or Debussy's passepied is something you can ask Teacher Aum for advice on.

The teacher can also explain how to play the upbeat and the rhythmic character of Baroque dances.

From the passepied, you can get to know the light dances of the Baroque suite.

![A person wearing headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two city-at-night windows](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaeamqq-tnoub.webp)

## The passepied in summary

The passepied comes from a folk dance of Brittany in France and was taken into French music in the seventeenth century. Its name roughly means "crossed feet", it is usually in 3/8, much faster than a minuet, often starts on an upbeat and has short phrases. Bach's English Suite No. 5 in E minor, BWV 810, contains a pair of passepieds in E minor and E major, and the Partita No. 5 in G major, BWV 829, also has one.

Debussy's Suite bergamasque was first written around 1890 and published in 1905. Its last movement, Passepied, is in 4/4, with a light staccato in the left hand and a flowing right hand, borrowing the old name to evoke a classical atmosphere. A Baroque passepied should be fast and nimble with a light upbeat; for Debussy's, keep the left-hand staccato even and use little pedal. You can compare it with a minuet.

A suitable passepied to start with is something you can ask Teacher Aum to recommend.

- A folk dance from Brittany in France
- Fast, with a 3/8 feel
- Often starts on an upbeat
- Written by both Bach and Debussy

## Short phrases

Passepied phrases are usually short, four or eight bars long.

There are clear pauses between the phrases, like little sections of dance steps.

This makes the music sound light and neat.

## The passepieds in Bach's English Suite

Bach's English Suite No. 5 is in E minor, BWV 810, and it contains two passepieds.

The first is in E minor, the second in E major, and then the first returns.

This way of writing two dances as a pair is very common in Baroque suites.

## Comparing it with the minuet

You can play a passepied and a minuet side by side.

Both are in triple time, but their tempo and character differ: the minuet is elegant and unhurried, while the passepied is light and lively.

Comparing them helps you feel the character of each dance better.

## Playing Debussy's passepied on the piano

When playing Debussy's passepied, the left-hand staccato should be light and even, like gentle footsteps.

The right-hand melody should be smooth and flowing, floating above the left hand.

Use the pedal very little, so the left-hand staccato stays clear.

## Fast triple time

The passepied is usually in 3/8, though it is sometimes written in 3/4, but it is always fast.

Like the minuet it is in triple time, but it is much faster than a minuet.

Some people describe it as a "fast minuet".

**Order of practice**

## FAQ

**Q: Where does the passepied come from?**
A: The Brittany region in north-western France.

**Q: What does the name roughly mean?**
A: "Crossed feet".

**Q: What is its usual time signature?**
A: 3/8, and fast.

**Q: Which of Bach's English Suites contains a passepied?**
A: No. 5 in E minor, BWV 810.

**Q: Which work contains Debussy's passepied?**
A: Suite bergamasque.

polytonality-two-keys-at-once.body:
Polytonality means that in the same stretch of music, two or more different keys sound at the same time. A common kind is bitonality: for example, the right hand plays in C major while the left hand plays in F♯ major. To the ear, two colours are laid on top of each other, somewhat harsh yet with a strange brightness. In the early twentieth century, composers such as Stravinsky, Milhaud and Bartók all used this technique. In Stravinsky's 1911 ballet Petrushka there is a chord made of a C major triad and an F♯ major triad stacked together, often called the "Petrushka chord".

## Why Use Polytonality

Composers use polytonality to create new sound colours.

**Listen**

Two keys stacked together produce effects that traditional harmony does not have.

It can express conflict, humour or chaos, and it can also express a bright, strange kind of beauty.

## Polytonality and Dissonance

Polytonality often brings many dissonant intervals, and it can sound somewhat harsh.

But because each voice is in a key of its own, the music still has a certain order.

This is different from music with no tonality at all.

## White Keys and Black Keys

On the piano, the C major triad is C, E, G, all white keys.

The F♯ major triad is F♯, A♯, C♯, all black keys.

Play the black-key chord with the right hand and the white-key chord with the left, and you will hear the sound of the Petrushka chord.

## One Key and Two Keys

The music we usually play is mostly in a single key, such as C major or A minor.

In polytonality, two voices move at the same time, each in a different key.

So the listener hears the colours of two keys at once.

## Bartók's Microcosmos

The Hungarian composer Bartók wrote a set of piano teaching pieces called Mikrokosmos, in six volumes with more than one hundred and fifty pieces.

Some of the little pieces are designed specifically to practise bitonality: the right hand in one key and the left hand in another.

Each piece takes only a few lines of score, which makes them just right for a first taste of two keys sounding together.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwadx8m1-1yf24.webp)

## Polytonality: A Summary

Polytonality is two or more keys sounding at the same time. A common kind is bitonality, and the further apart the two keys are, the stronger the conflict. In Stravinsky's Petrushka of 1911, the chord made of a C major triad and an F♯ major triad stacked together is called the Petrushka chord. The two keys are three whole tones apart, and on the piano one is almost all white keys and the other almost all black keys.

Milhaud's 1920 piano suite Saudades do Brasil uses bitonality in many places, and Bartók's Mikrokosmos, in six volumes with more than one hundred and fifty pieces, has little pieces for practising bitonality. Polytonality is used to create new colours. Although there is dissonance, each voice is in one key. When listening, pay attention separately to the high and low voices. You can try playing Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star with the right hand and an F♯ major triad with the left, starting from closely related keys.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the Petrushka chord.

## From Close Keys to Distant Keys

If two keys are closely related, such as C major and G major, the conflict is small.

If two keys are distantly related, such as C major and F♯ major, the conflict is strong.

You can start by trying closely related keys and slowly get a feel for the effect of distant ones.

## Ask Your Teacher About Polytonality in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the Petrushka chord, so you can feel the sound of white keys and black keys stacked together.

Your teacher can also recommend bitonal pieces in Mikrokosmos that suit your level.

From polytonality, you can get to know the new colours of twentieth-century music.

## How to Hear Polytonality

When listening to polytonal music, try paying attention separately to the high and low voices.

First listen to the melody in the high voice and feel its key. Then listen to the accompaniment in the low voice and feel its key.

Gradually, you will be able to hear the two keys moving at the same time.

**Try it**
- Two or more keys sounding at the same time
- Bitonality is a common kind
- Many composers used it in the early twentieth century
- The "Petrushka chord" is a C major triad stacked with an F♯ major triad

## Bitonality

The kind of polytonality used most often is bitonality, which means two keys sounding at the same time.

For example, the right hand plays a melody in C major while the left hand plays an accompaniment in E♭ major.

The further apart the two keys are, the stronger the conflict sounds.

## Trying Bitonality with Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star

You can try it on the piano: play a simple C major melody with the right hand, such as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.

Play an F♯ major triad with the left hand as the accompaniment, and listen to the effect.

Then switch to other keys, such as G major or E♭ major, and compare the different effects.

## Milhaud's Saudades do Brasil

The French composer Darius Milhaud lived in Brazil for a time.

In 1920 he wrote the piano suite Saudades do Brasil, which uses bitonality in many places.

The right and left hands are often in different keys, and together with Brazilian dance rhythms the colours are very vivid.

## The Petrushka Chord

In 1911, Stravinsky wrote the ballet Petrushka, which tells the story of a puppet.

In the ballet there is a chord made of a C major triad and an F♯ major triad stacked together.

These two keys are three whole tones apart. On the piano, one is almost all white keys and the other almost all black keys.

## Playing Polytonal Works

When playing polytonal works, each hand needs to express its own key clearly.

Do not hesitate just because it feels unfamiliar. Play every note with confidence.

You can practise hands separately first, then put them together and slowly get used to the sound of two keys at once.

## FAQ

**Q: What is polytonality?**
A: Two or more keys sounding at the same time.

**Q: Which two triads make up the Petrushka chord?**
A: C major and F♯ major.

**Q: In what year was Petrushka written?**
A: 1911.

**Q: Which of Milhaud's piano suites uses bitonality?**
A: Saudades do Brasil, 1920.

**Q: Which of Bartók's teaching collections has bitonal pieces?**
A: Mikrokosmos.
