practice-softly-quiet-hours.body:
When someone at home or a neighbour needs to rest, you can switch to quiet practice: choose passages that call for soft playing and play them at a very light dynamic. On an acoustic piano you can use the soft pedal or a silencing device, and on a digital piano you can turn the volume down or wear headphones. You can also do silent fingering practice and score reading for a while. Quiet practice is not only about being quiet; it is also a great chance to train your control.

## When You Return to Normal Volume

After quiet practice, when you can play normally again, remember to play at your normal dynamic too, so you stay familiar with the full dynamic range.

Comparing quiet and normal-volume playing helps you grasp the dynamic changes in the piece better.

Combining both kinds of practice gives your playing more depth.

## Silent Practice

If even quiet playing is not suitable, you can do some silent practice, such as mentally running through the whole piece while looking at the score.

You can also rest your hands on the keys and press them down gently without making a sound, practising fingering and hand position changes.

Although there is no sound, these exercises help you become familiar with the piece.

## Choose Content Suited to Quiet Practice

Not everything suits quiet practice. Passages that need a lot of power are best left for times when you can play normally.

You can choose passages in the piece that are soft by nature, or sections with a gentle melody.

You can also practise fingering and slow scales, which do not need much volume.

## Soft Devices on Acoustic Pianos

Many upright pianos have a middle pedal. When pressed down or locked, it lowers a strip of felt between the hammers and the strings, making the sound noticeably quieter.

Some pianos also have a silent system that cuts off the sound of the strings completely, letting you hear an electronic sound through headphones.

With these devices the feel of the keys may change a little, so it is not a good idea to practise only this way for a long time.

**Summary**
- Practise soft passages at a very light dynamic
- Use the soft pedal, a silencing device or headphones
- You can do silent fingering practice and score reading
- Treat quiet practice as control training

## Talk with Your Family About Timing

You can talk with your family to find out which times need to be especially quiet and which times you can practise normally.

Schedule practice that needs more volume for times when everyone is awake and more active.

This arrangement looks after your family and also makes your practice better planned.

## Why Quiet Practice Is Needed

If there is a baby, an older person or someone who goes to bed early at home, practising in the evening or early morning may disturb them.

If you live in an apartment, neighbours may also need quiet at times.

Learning to practise quietly lets you stay in touch with the piano during these times while being considerate of the people around you.

## Stay Relaxed

When playing very softly, some people unconsciously tense their hands and arms, trying to "hold in" the sound.

In fact, controlling soft playing takes even more relaxation: let the weight of the arm fall lightly and let your fingers feel the keys sensitively.

If you notice your hands are tight, stop, shake them out, and continue once you have relaxed.

## The Convenience of a Digital Piano

A digital piano can turn the sound down or connect to headphones, which makes it a great helper during quiet hours.

When using headphones, remember that the thump of the keys can still carry, so try to touch the keys as lightly as possible.

Set the headphone volume just loud enough to hear clearly, and take them off now and then to rest your ears.

![Pointillist painting of an abstract figure playing a grand piano in a park](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9yhg9d-bd62p.webp)

## An Extra Benefit of Quiet Practice

Many teachers advise students to practise soft playing often, because controlling soft notes is often harder than playing loudly.

With regular quiet practice, your grasp of dynamics becomes finer, and the layers of tone colour in your playing become richer.

So practice in quiet hours is not just something you are forced into; it is also very valuable training.

## Play at a Very Light Dynamic

In quiet practice, try touching the keys very lightly, so that every note is clear but very gentle.

This takes good finger control, and the speed of each keypress should be slow and even.

You will find that playing very softly while still making every note sound is not easy, which is exactly why it is a great chance to train your control.

## FAQ

**Q: Does the soft pedal harm the piano?**
A: Not with normal use, but it is not a good idea to practise only with it for a long time.

**Q: Can neighbours hear me if I practise with headphones?**
A: The piano sound is barely audible, but the sound of the keys may carry.

**Q: What are the benefits of quiet practice?**
A: It trains your control of soft playing and dynamics.

**Q: What if I do not have a soft pedal?**
A: You can play at a very light dynamic, or do silent practice.

**Q: Can children practise quietly?**
A: Yes. Turn it into a game of "who can play the softest".

**Q: Can I practise loud passages during quiet hours?**
A: It is best to leave loud passages for times when you can play normally.

piano-in-silent-film-theatres.body:
Before sound films became widespread, the pictures in cinemas were often silent, and the music had to be supplied on the spot by live players. In the first twenty-odd years of the twentieth century, many venues hired a pianist to play to the story, pace and mood on screen: sometimes improvising, sometimes organising the music from ready-made lists of pieces or "cue sheets". A happy chase, a tense conflict, a lyrical exchange of glances could each become a different speed and texture on the piano. Looking back today, this also shows that the piano did not appear only in concerts and classrooms; it was once one of the most flexible accompanying instruments in public entertainment. It also reminds us that choosing a speed and a character by watching the picture is a very concrete kind of musical judgement. If you get the chance to try setting a few simple musical phrases to a short silent clip, you can feel quite directly the task those pianists faced. Agreeing beforehand where the beginning and end are makes this exercise easier.

## Why Live Piano Was Needed

Early films had no fixed soundtrack synchronised with the picture, and if a screening was completely silent, the atmosphere felt thin.

The piano has a moderate volume and can handle harmony and melody on its own, so it became the choice of many venues.

One player could cope with many kinds of scenes, which also suited the actual conditions of screening venues at the time.

## Improvisation and Cue Sheets

Some pianists relied mainly on improvisation, changing as they watched the picture.

Publishers and cinemas also prepared cue sheets or lists of pieces, matching situations such as "chase, lyrical, tense" to commonly used passages.

The two approaches were often mixed: first a prepared framework, then adjustments on the spot.

- Before sound films became widespread, many venues hired a pianist to play live
- Players often improvised, or relied on cue sheets and ready-made pieces
- Speed, texture and mood had to change with the picture
- The piano was a flexible accompanying instrument in public entertainment

## How to Follow the Picture

When the picture cuts quickly, the music often has to be tighter too; when the picture rests on a face, the melody may relax.

This correspondence is not mechanical, but it requires the player to keep watching, keep listening and keep deciding.

For practice today, it is very good training in "choosing a character".

![A golden grand piano sketch on a cream background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdixdzl-smecg.webp)

## Silent Film Piano: A Summary

Before sound films became widespread, many venues had a pianist provide live music for the picture, either improvising or following cue sheets, and changing speed and texture with the story.

The piano thus became a flexible accompanying instrument in public entertainment; this practice gradually declined as sound films rose, but it can still inspire today's choices of speed and character.

You can try setting music to a short clip together with Teacher Aum.

## What This Offers Everyday Practice

Even if you are not scoring a film, you can sometimes add a "scene" to your own practice: this passage is like walking, that passage is like a conversation.

The point is not to invent a story, but to make your choices of speed and touch more conscious.

Short character exercises are often remembered better than aimless repetition.

## Common Musical Material

Live pianists did not always compose entirely new themes; they would call on familiar marches, waltzes, lyrical songs or short mood passages.

Familiar tunes let the audience slip quickly into a certain atmosphere.

This also required the pianist to have a large enough repertoire to draw on at short notice.

## How It Differs from Concert Playing

In a concert, the pieces and their order are usually fixed in advance; silent film accompaniment had to follow the film.

The player did not necessarily face music listeners sitting quietly, but an audience watching a story, and had to serve that audience.

The standard of success was often "did it help the picture", not only "was it played completely".

## The Change Brought by Sound Films

In the late 1920s, sound films gradually became widespread, and the demand for live piano accompaniment fell markedly.

Many players who made a living this way moved on to other work, and this everyday form of public performance gradually left mainstream cinemas.

What remains are the cue sheets of the time, memories, and a few recordings and documents.

## Try a Short Passage with Teacher Aum in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to watch a very short silent clip with you and discuss what speed and texture to use.

After playing, you can also discuss where it matched and where it could be simpler.

From the work of the silent-era pianist, we come back to one conscious choice of character.

## How to Experience This Today

You can find a very short silent clip, watch it once, and then decide whether to use a march, a lyrical passage or a lighter figure.

It does not need to be complicated; getting the speed and mood right is already very close to the basic task of the time.

After playing, watch it again and check whether you matched the key moments in the action.

## FAQ

**Q: Where did the music in silent-era cinemas usually come from?**
A: It was supplied on the spot by a live pianist or other players.

**Q: What did the pianist base the playing on?**
A: Improvising while watching the picture, or following cue sheets and lists of pieces; the two were often combined.

**Q: How does live accompaniment differ from concert playing?**
A: It has to follow the picture, and its success depends first of all on whether it helps the story.

**Q: What happened after sound films became widespread?**
A: The demand for live accompaniment fell markedly, and this form of public performance gradually left mainstream cinemas.

**Q: How can learners today experience this kind of work?**
A: By choosing a speed and texture for a very short silent clip, then checking whether it matches the key moments in the action.

practice-phrase-loud-then-soft.body:
Here is a method to try when practising a phrase: play it once at a very loud dynamic, then once at a very soft dynamic, and finally at the dynamic the score asks for. When you play loudly, let your fingers land firmly at the bottom of the keys, which helps you find unsteady notes. When you play softly, you have to control every note with great care, which helps you find uneven spots. After practising both extremes, go back to your normal dynamic and you will notice that your control has improved a great deal.

## Listen for the Difference in Dynamics

While you practise, listen closely to the difference between dynamics.

**Listen**

The gap between loud and soft should be big enough. Do not just play a little louder and a little softer.

If the difference is not clear, record yourself, listen back, and adjust.

**Try it**
- Play the phrase loudly once, then softly once
- Finally, play it at the dynamic the score asks for
- Loud playing reveals unsteady notes
- Soft playing reveals uneven spots

## Different Dynamics in Each Hand

In more advanced practice, you can give each hand a different dynamic, for example the right hand loud and the left hand soft, then swap.

This builds independence between the hands and helps a lot when balancing melody and accompaniment.

It may be hard at first, so start slowly.

## Use It in Fast Passages

This method works especially well in fast passages, such as scale-like runs and broken chords.

Notes in fast passages are often uneven, and practising at both loud and soft dynamics makes every note clearer.

You can also combine loud and soft practice with slow practice.

## Do Not Overdo Loud and Soft Practice

Playing loudly for too long tires the hands, and playing softly for too long lets your attention drop.

One or two repetitions of each per phrase is enough.

Then go straight back to the normal dynamic to lock in the effect.

## A Note on Practising on a Digital Piano

On a digital piano, the feel of dynamics may differ from an acoustic piano.

Some digital pianos have a narrower dynamic range, so the difference between loud and soft is less obvious.

If you get the chance, try this exercise on an acoustic piano.

## Use It in Lyrical Melodies

This method also helps with lyrical melodies.

Playing loudly helps you feel the skeleton of the melody, while playing softly helps you appreciate its delicate expression.

Together, they give the rise and fall of the melody more depth.

## Fingers Reach the Bottom of the Keys in Loud Playing

When you play at a very loud dynamic, let your fingers land firmly at the bottom of the keys.

This helps you find which notes your fingers do not play strongly or steadily enough.

But loud playing does not mean brute force. Keep your arm and wrist relaxed and use weight rather than hard pressing.

## Crescendo and Diminuendo Practice

On top of loud and soft practice, you can also practise crescendo and diminuendo.

For example, start a phrase very softly, gradually grow to very loud, then gradually fade again.

This helps you control the transitions between dynamics and makes the music flow more naturally.

## Finally, Return to the Normal Dynamic

After playing loudly and softly, play once more at the dynamic marked in the score.

You will find that your fingers are steadier and your control of dynamics is finer.

This normal-dynamic pass is often the most comfortable of the three.

![Art Deco style illustration of someone practising at a deep red upright piano under a lamp at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwabr3hs-u1dbx.webp)

## Ask Your Teacher to Listen to the Contrast

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen and tell you whether the difference between your loud and soft playing is big enough.

Your teacher can also help decide which phrases suit this method.

Better control of dynamics makes the whole piece more expressive.

## Write the Method into Your Practice Plan

In your practice plan, you can schedule loud and soft practice for each phrase that needs more control.

For example: "Run in section three: once loud, once soft, once normal."

Using the method on purpose makes the results more noticeable.

## Control Every Note in Soft Playing

When you play at a very soft dynamic, every note must still sound and none can be dropped.

This takes very careful control: keep your fingers close to the keys and your movements small.

In soft playing, uneven notes stand out clearly, which is exactly how it helps you find problems.

## Why Use Two Extreme Dynamics

In everyday practice, people often use one medium dynamic and repeat it without noticing.

Practising at the two extremes, very loud and very soft, makes your fingers face different demands.

This reveals problems more clearly and widens your range of dynamic control.

## Summary: Loud Then Soft for Phrases

When practising a phrase, first play it very loudly, with fingers landing firmly at the bottom of the keys, using weight rather than force, to find unsteady notes. Then play it very softly, with fingers close to the keys and small movements, to find uneven spots. Finally play it at the dynamic the score asks for, and your control will be much better.

The method suits fast passages and lyrical melodies. One or two repetitions each of loud and soft are enough. At a more advanced stage, you can give each hand a different dynamic, or practise crescendo and diminuendo. Make the gap between loud and soft big enough, and remember that a digital piano may have a narrower dynamic range.

You can write the method into your practice plan, and ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the contrast is big enough.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the order of this method?**
A: Loud first, then soft, and finally the dynamic the score asks for.

**Q: What does loud playing help me find?**
A: Unsteady notes.

**Q: What does soft playing help me find?**
A: Uneven spots.

**Q: Should loud playing use brute force?**
A: No. Use weight and keep your arm relaxed.

**Q: What can I do in more advanced practice?**
A: Give each hand a different dynamic.

pedal-with-left-hand-only-first.body:
When you play a piece that needs the sustain pedal, starting with both hands and the foot together often means something gets neglected: the right-hand melody is not yet secure, the foot forgets to change the pedal, and the sound turns muddy. A practical method is to play the left hand alone first, adding the pedal at the same time. The left hand is often responsible for the bass and harmony, and pedal changes mostly follow changes in harmony. Once the left hand and pedal work well together, add the right hand, and the sound of the whole piece will be much clearer.

## Marking pedal changes on the score

When the score has no printed pedal markings, look at the harmony yourself and circle the places where the chord changes.

Make a small pencil mark at those places to remind yourself to change the pedal there.

In some places you may need to change the pedal several times within one chord, and you have to judge this with your ears.

## Listen for a connected bass

When you play the left hand alone, you can clearly hear the effect of the bass and the pedal.

A good pedal connects the bass notes without letting different harmonies blur together.

If you hear the sound of the previous chord dragging into the next one, the pedal was changed too late.

## Practising the syncopated pedal

Many pieces need a syncopated pedal (also called legato pedalling): after playing a new note, you quickly lift and press the pedal again.

With the left hand alone, you can practise this movement slowly: play the bass note, then lift the pedal, then press it down.

Once this movement is smooth, the sound can be both connected and clear.

## The right-hand melody may need adjusting

After adding the right hand, you sometimes find that certain right-hand notes are blurred by the pedal.

For example, some passing notes in the right hand mix with the chord notes under the same pedal.

When this happens, you can ask your teacher to judge whether you need to change the pedal more often, or use half-pedalling.

## The pedal follows the harmony

In many pieces, the sustain pedal is changed in step with the harmony.

When the chord changes, change the pedal once, so that the new harmony sounds out cleanly.

And a change in harmony can often be seen from the bass notes in the left hand.

## Hands and feet together make it easy to neglect something

Playing a piece that needs the pedal means looking after two hands and one foot at the same time.

If you do everything together from the start, it is hard to divide your attention.

The usual result is that the pedal is changed too early, too late, or forgotten altogether.

## Foot position and movement

Keep your heel on the floor as a pivot, with the ball of the foot resting on the pedal.

Pressing down and lifting up should both come from the ankle, not the whole leg.

Keep the movement quiet, and do not let the pedal make any thumping sound.

## Play the left hand alone first

Set the right hand aside and play only the left-hand part.

While you play, press the pedal following the pedal markings in the score, or following the changes in harmony.

This way, your attention only needs to be on the left hand and the foot.

## Use your ears, not your eyes

In the end, the pedal is controlled by the ears, and the markings in the score are only a reference.

Different pianos and different rooms give different pedal effects.

Every time you practise, listen carefully to whether the sound is clear.

- Play the left hand alone first, pressing the pedal at the same time
- The pedal often changes with the bass and harmony
- Add the right hand once the left hand and pedal are comfortable
- Use your ears to check whether the sound is clear

## Which pieces suit left hand plus pedal first

This method pays off clearly for pieces written with broken chords in the left hand and the melody singing in the right, such as many Romantic miniatures and piano accompaniments for pop songs.

For pieces where both hands are very complex, you can also play just the bass line with the pedal first.

For works that hardly need the pedal, this method is not really necessary.

![A close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa8wy0t-53lba.webp)

## Checking the pedal in lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your left hand with the pedal.

The teacher can help point out whether your pedal changes are well timed and whether your foot movement is relaxed.

With your teacher's confirmation, you will feel more confident when practising at home.

## Adding the right hand once the left is comfortable

Once the left hand and pedal work well together, add the right hand.

By then the movement of the foot is fairly automatic, and you can put more attention on the right-hand melody.

If the pedal goes wrong again after adding the right hand, go back to practising the left hand alone.

## Left hand plus pedal in summary

Using hands and feet together makes it easy to neglect something. The sustain pedal often changes with the harmony, and changes in harmony can mostly be seen in the left-hand bass, so you can play the left hand alone first while pressing the pedal.

With the left hand alone you can hear clearly whether the bass is connected, you can practise the syncopated pedal slowly, and you can mark the pedal changes on the score. Add the right hand once the left hand is comfortable, and after adding it check whether the melody has been blurred by the pedal.

This method suits pieces with broken chords in the left hand and a melody in the right. Pay attention to foot position and movement, control the pedal with your ears, and ask Teacher Aum to confirm in lessons.

## FAQ

**Q: Why play the left hand alone with the pedal first?**
A: The left hand is often responsible for the bass and harmony, and the pedal mostly changes with the harmony.

**Q: How can I tell the pedal was changed late?**
A: The sound of the previous chord drags into the next chord.

**Q: What is a syncopated pedal?**
A: After playing the new note, you quickly lift and press the pedal again.

**Q: How should the foot work the pedal?**
A: Keep the heel on the floor and use the ball of the foot and the movement of the ankle.

**Q: What controls the pedal in the end?**
A: The ears.

ponce-estrellita-1912-song-piano.body:
Estrellita ("Little Star") is a song written by the Mexican composer Manuel Ponce around 1912, later arranged for violin, piano and many other instruments. Its melody is simple and long-breathed, with a tone of longing, and it does not win by complicated technique. In piano arrangements, one hand usually sings while the other supports it with quiet chords or broken-chord figures. When learning it, it is closer to the character of the song to get the melody singing warmly first and only then think about accompaniment patterns, rather than playing it very full from the start. When listening, you can also softly sing the tune along first, and then listen to whether the lower notes make way at the places where the singer would breathe. If the arrangement has a lot of ornament, you can take the ornament away first and keep only the skeleton, to confirm that the song itself is still complete. When practising, even if the arrangement is written very ornately, you can prepare a version that keeps only the main phrases and simple chords, and fall back on it at any time to check whether the song is still there. If a phrase cannot breathe because of too much ornament, take the ornament away and set the breathing places again. The completeness of a short song is closer to its original character than piling on decoration. You can also sing the main phrases until you know them well before going to the piano, and then it becomes immediately clear which parts of the arrangement are ornament and which are skeleton.

## How the Accompaniment Makes Way

Chords or broken-chord figures should be light, and especially where the melody needs to breathe, the accompaniment should hold back a little.

**Notice the details**

Let the pedal follow the harmony, but do not let several chords pile up into one layer of mist that makes the outline of the song disappear.

If the accompaniment in the score is dense, you can first change it to simpler block chords, and add it back once the song is steady.

## How to Start Practising Estrellita

If you can already sing a fairly slow song smoothly, this Ponce arrangement is a suitable piece to start with.

Decide the speed by whether you can still sing a whole phrase to its end. There is no need to rush ahead at the beginning.

Feeling comes from the rise and fall of the phrases, not from a sudden thickening of volume.

## How to Connect the Main Melody

First play or sing the main phrase alone, and set the breathing places where the phrase really ends, rather than breathing at random.

Hold long notes firmly. Do not slip away early just because the accompaniment is still to come.

Play the same phrase twice in a row, and compare which time sounds more like a person singing.

## It Was Originally a Song

Estrellita first spread as a song. Its words and singable breath determine that, when arranged later, it should still keep its phrases whole.

A piano version is not meant to turn it into an étude. It is meant to let the keys keep telling that melody when there is no singing voice.

If you listen to arrangements for different instruments, you will find that the main phrase is often still there, and the changes are mainly in the accompaniment and the register.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdjq8ko-1t78x.webp)

## Ask Teacher Aum in a Lesson Whether the Song Is Still There

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the main melody is being covered by the accompaniment and whether the breathing places sound natural.

If an arrangement has too much ornament, you can also ask your teacher to help you trace the skeleton melody again.

From a short song of 1912, you can practise letting the piano finish singable phrases completely.

## What to Remember About Estrellita

This is a song by Ponce from around 1912, later often arranged for the piano, with a simple, long-breathed main phrase.

When playing the piano version, first keep the singable melody; let both the accompaniment and the pedal make way.

When you meet a more ornate score, fall back on the skeleton at any time to check whether the song is still there.

## Facing Different Arrangements

Piano scores on the market vary a great deal in complexity. Some are almost only melody plus chords, while others add many passing phrases.

Fix on one edition first, and do not pile the ornaments from different versions into a single playing.

Even if you choose a more ornate score, you can also keep a separate page with only the skeleton notes written down, and fall back on it at any time to see whether the song is still there.

## Ponce and the Place of This Song

Ponce wrote songs, guitar works and orchestral music, and also took part for many years in the musical life of Mexico at that time.

Estrellita is only one of his works, but because its melody is easy to remember, it has travelled further than many of his larger works.

**Slower**

When studying it, it is more suitable to treat it as a short singable song than as a showy arrangement.

- Its melody is simple and long-breathed, and it was later often arranged for the piano

pinghu-qiuyue-cantonese-music-piano.body:
Pinghu Qiuyue (Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake) is a famous piece of Cantonese music, written by Lü Wencheng, a representative figure of twentieth-century Cantonese music. The title comes from a scenic spot on Hangzhou's West Lake called "Pinghu Qiuyue". It is generally believed that Lü Wencheng wrote the piece after visiting West Lake, using a clear, flowing melody to paint the scene of moonlight lying like water on the lake on an autumn night. The piece was originally played on Cantonese music instruments such as the gaohu, and its melody contains many delicate ornaments and slides. Today there are also piano arrangements, which are a good way to experience the charm of Chinese folk music.

## The "Pinghu Qiuyue" of West Lake

Hangzhou's West Lake has many famous scenic spots, and "Pinghu Qiuyue" is one of them.

**Before You Begin**

On an autumn night the lake is calm and the moonlight spills over the water, a very beautiful scene.

Lü Wencheng borrowed this name and used music to paint such a scene.

## Who Was Lü Wencheng?

Lü Wencheng was born in 1898 and died in 1981. He was an important composer and performer of Cantonese music.

He improved the erhu and developed the gaohu, which has a clearer tone and became the lead instrument of Cantonese music.

He wrote many Cantonese music works, and Pinghu Qiuyue is one of the most widely known.

- A famous piece of Cantonese music, by Lü Wencheng
- The title comes from a scenic spot on Hangzhou's West Lake
- It paints moonlight on the lake on an autumn night
- Originally played on instruments such as the gaohu

## Pinghu Qiuyue in Brief

Cantonese music is a form of folk instrumental ensemble popular in the Guangdong region, and it flourished in the first half of the twentieth century. Lü Wencheng was born in 1898 and died in 1981. He improved the erhu to develop the gaohu. The name Pinghu Qiuyue comes from a scenic spot on Hangzhou's West Lake, and it is generally believed to have been written after his visit to West Lake.

The gaohu is clear in tone. The melody is based on the pentatonic scale and is flowing and fresh, with ornaments such as grace notes, slides and trills. The rhythm is steady and unhurried. The piano version keeps the charm with light harmony and delicate ornaments: the melody should be clear and flowing, and the accompaniment gentle and simple. You can listen to it together with Bubu Gao (Step by Step Higher) and Yu Da Ba Jiao (Rain Beating the Banana Leaves).

You can listen to the original performance first, and Teacher Aum can recommend piano scores.

## From Folk Instruments to the Piano

Arranging Pinghu Qiuyue as a piano piece means bringing out the charm of the folk instruments on the piano.

Arrangers often use light harmony and delicate ornaments to keep the character of the melody.

The piano version both keeps the mood of the original and shows off the tone of the piano.

## Comparing It with Other Cantonese Music

There are many other famous pieces of Cantonese music, such as Bubu Gao and Yu Da Ba Jiao.

Each of these pieces has its own character: some are cheerful, some delicate.

You can listen to them together and feel the richness and variety of Cantonese music.

## The Melodic Line of Pinghu Qiuyue

The melody of Pinghu Qiuyue is flowing and fresh, with both the elegance of the south of the Yangtze and the brightness of Cantonese music.

The melody is based on the pentatonic scale, often moving by step with some small leaps.

The whole piece gives a feeling of calm and ease.

## Listen to the Original First

Before you play, you can first listen to the original played on the gaohu and other folk instruments.

Notice the ornaments and slides in the melody, and how the instruments work together.

Then listen to the piano version and compare the two.

## The Ornaments in Pinghu Qiuyue

The melody of Cantonese music has many ornaments, such as grace notes, slides and trills.

These ornaments make the melody more lively and full of charm.

On the piano, use light ornaments to imitate these effects.

## The Accompaniment in the Piano Version

The left-hand accompaniment should be gentle and simple, creating a calm background for the melody.

Do not make the harmony too rich, or you will lose the light character of Chinese music.

You can use a moderate amount of pedal to make the sound warmer.

## Ask Your Teacher About the Charm of Pinghu Qiuyue in Lessons

If you want to play the piano version of Pinghu Qiuyue, you can ask Teacher Aum in a lesson to recommend a score that suits your level.

Your teacher can also help explain how to bring out the ornaments and charm of Chinese folk music on the piano.

This piece is very good for practising a clear, flowing melody.

## The Melody of the Piano Version

When playing the piano version, the melody should be clear and flowing, as if the gaohu were singing.

The ornaments should be light and natural, and should not overshadow the melody.

You can listen to the original performance first to find the charm of the melody.

## The Rhythm of Pinghu Qiuyue

The rhythm of the piece is steady and the tempo moderate, like a leisurely stroll by the lake.

In some places the rhythm is slightly free, as if you had stopped to admire the view.

When you play, keep the music flowing and do not make it too mechanical.

## What Is Cantonese Music?

Cantonese music is a form of folk instrumental ensemble popular in the Guangdong region, and it flourished in the first half of the twentieth century.

Its melodies are bright and beautiful, and often describe natural scenery and the pleasures of life.

Commonly used instruments include the gaohu, yangqin, qinqin and dongxiao.

## The Sound of the Gaohu

The gaohu has a higher, clearer tone than the erhu, which suits bright melodies very well.

In performance, techniques such as slides and trills are often used to make the melody more delicate.

**Summary**

The melody of Pinghu Qiuyue shows these qualities of the gaohu very well.

## FAQ

**Q: What kind of music is Pinghu Qiuyue?**
A: Cantonese music.

**Q: Who wrote it?**
A: Lü Wencheng.

**Q: Where does the title come from?**
A: A scenic spot on Hangzhou's West Lake.

**Q: What is the lead instrument of Cantonese music?**
A: The gaohu.

**Q: What should the harmony of the piano version be like?**
A: Light, not too rich.

phrase-extension-beyond-four-bars.body:
In much Classical music, phrases come in groups of four or eight bars, which sounds regular and balanced. But sometimes we find phrases of five bars, six bars or even longer. This is often because the composer has used phrase extension: within what would have been a four-bar phrase, repetition, sequence or a delayed cadence makes it longer. Phrase extension can create surprise and heighten expectation, so the music does not become too stiff. Haydn loved this technique, letting listeners feel surprise within a familiar pattern.

## Extending with a sequence

Another method is to use a sequence, repeating a fragment at a different pitch.

**Think again**

For example, a two-beat figure first appears on one note, then appears again one step higher.

A sequence lengthens the phrase while also giving it a sense of moving forward.

## Extension after the cadence

Sometimes, after the cadence, a phrase adds a few more bars that repeat the cadence chords.

This kind of extension is like finishing a sentence and then adding "Yes, exactly".

It makes the ending of the phrase firmer.

**Remember this**
- It lengthens a regular phrase
- It can be done through repetition, sequence or a delayed cadence
- It can create surprise and heighten expectation
- Haydn loved to use it

## Repeating a fragment

One of the common ways to extend a phrase is to repeat a fragment of it.

For example, if the third bar of a phrase is repeated once, the phrase goes from four bars to five.

This repetition is like stressing a particular idea, making it stand out.

## Try extending a phrase yourself

You can pick a simple four-bar melody and try to extend it to five or six bars using repetition or sequence.

You can also try using a deceptive cadence to lengthen the phrase.

Once you have written it, play it and compare the effect before and after the extension.

![Cyberpunk illustration: a person in futuristic clothes plays a black grand piano on a neon street, with a crystal synthesiser in front](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab7m32-tzqv5.webp)

## Haydn's phrase extensions

Haydn was a composer who loved to break regular phrases.

Often, just when listeners think a phrase is about to end, he adds some unexpected bars.

This technique fills his music with humour and surprise.

## What is phrase extension

Phrase extension means adding extra bars to a phrase that would otherwise be regular, making it longer.

An extended phrase may be five bars, six bars or longer.

The listener feels that the phrase did not end where it should have, but continued on a little further.

## How to spot an extension in a score

To spot a phrase extension in a score, first count the bars in the phrase.

If a phrase is not four or eight bars long, look for where the extra bars come from.

You can try taking out the extra bars and playing it, to see what the original phrase was like.

## Delaying the cadence

A composer can also extend a phrase by delaying the cadence.

For example, where a perfect cadence is expected, a deceptive cadence is used, such as the dominant chord moving to the vi chord instead of the tonic.

The phrase then needs a few more bars before it can really end.

## The regular four-bar phrase

In Classical-period music, phrases often come in groups of four bars.

Two four-bar phrases make up an eight-bar period, the first phrase like a question and the second like an answer.

This regular structure makes the music sound balanced and clear.

## Asking your teacher to find phrase extensions

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to point out where phrase extensions appear in the pieces you are learning.

The teacher can also help analyse which method of extension the composer used.

Understanding the structure of phrases makes your sense of phrasing in performance clearer.

## Extension at the beginning

Phrase extension can also appear at the beginning of a phrase, for example when one or two bars of introduction are added before the theme starts.

The phrase then begins with a "preparation" before it gets to the main matter.

This kind of extension often appears at the start of a piece or at the start of a new section.

## The effect of phrase extension

Phrase extension can give the music more tension, because the ending the listener expects is delayed.

It can also make the music more natural, so that it is not four bars after four bars all the time.

A good phrase extension sounds natural and does not strike the listener as abrupt.

## Phrase extension in summary

Classical phrases are often four or eight bars long. Phrase extension adds extra bars to a regular phrase. The methods include repeating a fragment, using a sequence, delaying the cadence with a deceptive cadence, repeating the cadence chords after the cadence, and adding an introduction at the beginning.

Haydn loved to use phrase extension to create humour and surprise. It adds tension and makes the music more natural. In a score, you can first count the bars of a phrase, then look for the extra part, and try removing it to compare.

When playing, you can change the dynamics on a repeated fragment and give some emphasis to the deceptive-cadence chord. You can also extend a four-bar melody yourself, and you can ask Teacher Aum to point out where the extensions are.

## Playing an extended phrase

When playing an extended phrase, let the listener feel the phrase stretching out.

For example, on a repeated fragment you can change the dynamics a little so that it sounds different.

**Order of practice**

At a delayed cadence, you can slightly emphasise the deceptive-cadence chord to bring out the feeling of surprise.

## FAQ

**Q: What is phrase extension?**
A: Adding extra bars to a regular phrase to make it longer.

**Q: What are the common methods of extension?**
A: Repetition, sequence, delaying the cadence and so on.

**Q: How do you delay a cadence?**
A: Use a deceptive cadence in place of a perfect cadence.

**Q: Which composer loved to use phrase extension?**
A: Haydn.

**Q: How do you spot an extension in a score?**
A: Count the bars of the phrase and look for the extra part.

phrase-ending-finish-cleanly.body:
The end of a phrase is often overlooked, and many players let go in a hurry as soon as they reach the last note. A good ending is like the final tie when wrapping a zongzi (a Chinese sticky rice dumpling): once everything inside is wrapped, the ending needs to be gently drawn in and set down steadily, so that the phrase feels complete and does not come loose.

## Making a phrase finish completely

You can take the last two or three notes of a phrase and practise them on their own, listening to whether the volume gradually fades and whether the last note is held for its full value. If you let go too early, the sound seems to break off suddenly.

At the end, the wrist can lift gently, drawing the fingers away from the keys. This movement should be soft; do not snatch the hand away, or the sound will feel stiff.

Before practising a piece, you can first find the beginning and end of each phrase and mark them in pencil. That way, when you play, you know clearly where to close a phrase and where a new one begins.

Listening back to a recording is also a good way to check your endings. A good ending makes the listener feel that a sentence has been completed, rather than cut off.

![Lights and buildings of a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8l73f9-o5vm4.webp)

## Connecting one phrase to the next

Once a phrase is finished well, the start of the next phrase also has to be ready. The join between two phrases needs both a clear separation and a continued flow of the music.

As you lift your hand at the end of a phrase, your eyes can already be looking at the start of the next one, and your hand ready to move to the new position.

If there is no rest between two phrases, the final note may need to be shortened very slightly to leave room to breathe; this space must be very small and must not disturb the rhythm.

In practice, you can practise two neighbouring phrases together, working specially on the transition between them.

When every phrase has a complete beginning and end, the whole piece will sound like a clear piece of storytelling.

**Quick tips**
- Close the end of a phrase deliberately
- The last note is usually a little softer
- The wrist can lift gently at the end
- Mark the ends of phrases on the score

## Practising backwards from the end

One effective method is to start from the last few notes of a phrase and then add more notes step by step towards the front.

For example, first practise the last two notes, making sure the dynamics and the length of the ending are right; then add the two notes before them and practise four notes; then keep expanding backwards until you have the whole phrase.

The benefit of this way of practising is that the ending gets practised the most and becomes the most secure, so it no longer remains a weak link.

The same method works for the end of a whole piece: start from the last section and work forwards section by section.

Once it is secure, play from the beginning all the way through and feel the overall direction of the phrase from start to finish.

## Dynamics and length of the final note

Most phrases end by getting naturally softer, like the tone slowing down at the end of a spoken sentence. When you play the last note, reduce the weight of your arm and let the sound settle softly.

The note must also be held for its full length. If the last note is a half note or a whole note, hold it for the written number of beats rather than lifting early.

The timing of the release matters too. The sound only truly ends at the moment the fingers leave the key, so lift gently and do not pull away abruptly.

In some phrases the ending may be strong, such as the close of a section. In that case, judge by the dynamics marked in the score and by the character of the piece itself.

You can record yourself and listen specifically to the ends of phrases, to see whether they sound complete and natural.

## Phrase endings are often overlooked

When practising, attention often goes to the start of a phrase and the difficult spots in the middle. By the time you reach the end, your hands and mind have already run ahead to the next phrase, and the last note gets rushed past.

Yet the end of a phrase decides the impression the sentence leaves. A cleanly finished ending lets the audience clearly feel that a sentence has been completed.

If the ending note is cut short, or its volume suddenly turns heavy, the phrase feels incomplete, as if it were interrupted halfway.

So in practice you need to pay special attention to the ends of phrases and treat them as just as important as the beginnings.

**A common mistake**

Once this habit is established, the continuity and completeness of the whole piece will improve noticeably.

## FAQ

**Q: Must the end of a phrase always get softer?**
A: In most cases it is a little softer, but some endings need emphasis, so refer to the dynamic markings in the score.

**Q: How long should the last note be held?**
A: Hold it for its full value, then release it gently.

**Q: Can I use the pedal at the end?**
A: Yes, but pay attention to when you lift the pedal, so that the final sound ends cleanly.

**Q: Must the end of a phrase always get softer?**
A: Not necessarily. It is usually a little softer, but it also depends on the dynamics marked in the score and the character of the piece.

**Q: Won't practising backwards from the end be slow?**
A: It may feel slower at first, but it makes the ending more secure, and the overall result is usually better.

**Q: How do I know where a phrase ends?**
A: Look at the slurs, cadences and rests, or sing the melody first to feel it.

play-melody-in-different-octaves-color.body:
Once you have learned a melody well, try moving it up an octave or down an octave. The same notes sound bright and light in the high register, deep and full in the low register, and warm in the middle. This simple exercise lets you feel the different tone colours of the piano and makes you more familiar with where things are on the keyboard. When arranging or improvising, changing octave is also a common way to bring variety to a repeated passage.

## Use in Arrangements

When arranging, changing octave is a common way to bring variety to a repeated section.

For example, if the verse of a song is repeated twice, you could lift the whole melody up an octave the second time, and it will sound fresh.

You can find this technique in many piano pieces too, where the same theme appears in different registers.

## The Sound of the Low Register

Play the same melody in the low register and the sound becomes deep and full.

The strings in the low register are longer, and the sound lasts longer too.

Do not play too fast, or the sounds will blur together and you will not hear each note clearly.

- Move the melody an octave higher or lower
- High is bright, low is deep, middle is warm
- Feel the different tone colour of each register
- Changing octave can bring variety to repeated sections

![A person wearing headphones practises at a white upright piano with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa4dqyw-vun2x.webp)

## Compare the Registers by Ear

When you play in a different octave, you can close your eyes and listen closely to the sound of each register.

Try describing what you hear in a few words, such as bright, warm, deep.

You can also record your playing in all three registers and compare them on playback.

## Summary: Changing Octave

Moving a well-learned melody up or down an octave lets you feel the different tone colours of the piano.

The high register is bright and light, the low register deep and full, and the middle register warm and rounded.

This exercise also helps you get to know the keyboard, and it is a simple, effective way to add variety when arranging and improvising.

## Use in Improvisation

When improvising, if you feel that staying in one register all the time gets a little dull, try moving a phrase up or down an octave.

The change is simple, but it can make the music much richer in colour.

You can also have a conversation between the high and low registers, like two people talking.

## Registers on a Digital Piano

If you practise on a digital piano, note that some have shorter keyboards and may not have all eighty-eight keys.

When you play in the low or high register, you may reach the edge of the keyboard.

You can also listen to how the digital piano sounds in different registers and compare it with an acoustic piano.

## The Sound of the High Register

Play the same melody in the high register and the sound becomes bright and light, sometimes like bells or birdsong.

The strings in the high register are shorter, and the sound fades more quickly.

As you play, try a lighter, quicker touch to make the sound crisper.

## The Left Hand Can Try It Too

Not only the right hand: the left hand can also play its accompaniment or bass line in a different octave.

For example, playing the bass lower gives the accompaniment more weight; playing it higher makes the accompaniment lighter.

Try several combinations and listen to which suits the piece best.

## How to Change Octave

Moving a melody to another octave is simple: shift every note up or down by eight white keys.

For example, if the melody starts on middle C, one octave up it starts on the C above, and one octave down it starts on the C below.

The fingering can usually stay the same; only the position of the hand moves.

## Getting to Know the Keyboard

Playing a melody in a different octave also helps you get to know the whole keyboard.

Many people are very familiar with the middle register, but in the high or low register they easily lose their place.

If you practise in different registers often, your feel for the keyboard becomes more complete.

## Adjusting Your Posture

When you play in the high or low register, lean your body a little towards that side instead of just stretching your arm.

Your hand will then sit more comfortably, and you will control the sound better.

You do not need to move the bench; a slight turn of the upper body is enough.

## The Registers of the Piano

The piano keyboard is very wide, covering more than seven octaves from the lowest note to the highest.

It can usually be divided into the low, middle and high registers, and each has its own character of sound.

Many people practising mostly play around the middle register and rarely experience the sound of the others.

## The Sound of the Middle Register

The middle register is where many melodies naturally sit. The sound is fairly warm and rounded, close to the range of the human voice.

Move a melody from the high or low register back to the middle register and you will feel its warmth even more.

**Pay attention to the details**

Comparing the sound of the three registers gives you a fuller understanding of the piano's tone.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How do I move a melody to another octave?**
A: Move every note up or down by eight white keys. The fingering usually stays the same.

**Q: What is the high register like?**
A: Bright and light.

**Q: What should I watch for in the low register?**
A: Do not play too fast, or the sounds will blur together.

**Q: What is changing octave good for?**
A: Feeling tone colour, getting to know the keyboard and adding variety to repeated sections.

**Q: How should my body be when I play in the high register?**
A: Lean your upper body slightly towards that side.

portato-dots-under-slur-articulation.body:
When notes have dots and are also covered by a slur, it indicates a way of playing between legato and staccato, often called portato. Each note is slightly separated, but not as short as ordinary staccato, so it sounds as if the notes are being gently "spoken" one by one. When playing, keep the wrist soft, press each note with a little arm weight and then release it lightly, leaving a small gap between the notes.

## The Difference from Staccato

Staccato notes are very short, and the fingers often seem to spring off the keys, so the sound is light and crisp.

Portato notes are longer, and the fingers leave the keys more slowly and softly.

You can play a passage staccato first, then portato, and compare the difference in sound.

## Use in Melodies

In some slow, lyrical pieces, composers use portato to make the melody more expressive.

For example, at the end of a phrase, several notes are played portato, like stressing words one by one in speech.

This treatment can make the melody sound warmer and more weighty.

## The Sound of Portato

Each portato note is slightly separated, but its length is a good part of the written value, so it is not as short and sharp as staccato.

It sounds as if the notes are being gently spoken one by one, with a tender yet weighty feeling.

It is often used in lyrical passages, or in melodies where every note needs to be emphasised.

## Use in Accompaniment

Portato also often appears in accompaniment, for example in repeated left-hand chords.

Playing these chords portato gives the accompaniment rhythm without being too stiff.

Compared with a staccato accompaniment, a portato accompaniment is softer and suits lyrical music.

## The Notation of Portato

The mark for portato is a dot above or below the note, with a slur covering the notes at the same time.

The dot means separate, the slur means connected, and together they mean "separated but connected".

Sometimes a short dash with a dot is used to indicate a similar effect.

## Imagine Speaking

You can imagine portato as speaking slowly, word by word, for example "I, miss, you, so, much".

There is a slight pause between the words, but the whole sentence is still connected.

Playing with this image in mind, portato will sound more natural.

![A black-and-white stippled sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa38x10-pf6cu.webp)

## Ways to Practise Portato

You can practise on a single note, pressing it again and again, holding it for a moment each time, then releasing it slowly.

Then practise on several neighbouring notes, making sure each note has the same length and volume.

When you are comfortable, put the portato into a piece and listen to whether it fits with the notes around it.

## Summary: Learning Portato

Portato is a touch between legato and staccato, notated with dots and a slur.

It makes music more expressive and is common in both melodies and accompaniment.

The keys to mastering it are a soft wrist, suitable weight and just the right gap.

## What the Wrist Does in Portato

When playing portato, keep the wrist soft; each note can come with a slight up-and-down motion.

When you press the key, use a little arm weight to make the sound full.

When you release, let the finger leave the key slowly; do not spring up suddenly.

## The Difference from Legato

In legato, the previous note is held until the moment the next note is pressed, with no gap in between.

In portato, a small gap is left between each note, so that there is breathing room between the notes.

The gap does not need to be large; it only has to be enough for you to hear that the notes are separate.

## Look for It in the Score

Open the piece you are practising and see whether there are any places with dots and a slur.

Circle them with a pencil as a reminder that portato is needed here.

When practising, pay special attention to these places so that the change of touch is clearer.

## The Three Basic Touches

There are three basic touches on the piano: legato, staccato and portato.

Legato connects the notes tightly, staccato makes each note very short, and portato lies between the two.

The score uses different marks to show these touches.

## Treatment in Different Styles

In works of the Classical period, portato is often quite light.

In Romantic works, portato may be fuller and more singing.

You can listen to recordings by several performers and compare how they treat the same portato passage.

**Common misunderstandings**
- Dots with a slur mean portato
- Between legato and staccato
- Each note slightly separated, but not too short
- Use a soft wrist and a little arm weight

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is the mark for portato?**
A: Dots with a slur.

**Q: How is it different from staccato?**
A: The notes are longer, and the fingers leave the keys more slowly and softly.

**Q: How is it different from legato?**
A: There is a small gap between each note.

**Q: How should the wrist be when playing?**
A: Keep it soft and use a little arm weight.

**Q: Where is portato often used?**
A: In lyrical melodies and soft accompaniment.

practice-dynamics-extremes-pp-ff.body:
Many people, when they play, stay at a middle volume: the soft places are not soft enough, the loud places are not loud enough, and the music sounds rather flat. An effective practice method is to practise the two ends of the dynamic range on purpose: use very little force to play a clear, steady pp, then use the weight of the arm to play a full ff that is not harsh. Once both ends are developed, the p, mp, mf and f in between have more room, and crescendos and diminuendos become clearer and more layered.

## Differences Between Pianos and Rooms

Different pianos and different rooms produce different softest and loudest sounds.

On a digital piano at home, the dynamic range may differ from an acoustic piano, and you can check the touch sensitivity settings in the manual.

When you meet an unfamiliar piano elsewhere, first try its softest and loudest ends, and adjust the way you control it.

## ff Does Not Mean Banging

Many people play too forcefully when playing loud, the sound turns harsh, and it can even make the hands hurt.

You can start with a medium dynamic, gradually add more arm weight, and listen for when the sound starts to turn harsh.

The limit where the sound is full but not harsh is the ff that suits you.

## Why the Sound Always Stays in the Middle

When we play, we often put our attention on the notes and the rhythm, and without noticing the dynamics settle at a habitual middle volume.

In the soft places we fear no sound will come out, so we play a little louder. In the loud places we fear it will be too harsh, so we play a little softer.

The result is that all the dynamics are squeezed into a very narrow range, and the rise and fall of the music shrinks.

## Keep pp Even

A very soft sound is easily uneven: some notes are almost inaudible, and others suddenly become louder.

You can use a simple scale or melody and play it only at pp, noticing whether every note has the same volume.

Keep your hand and wrist relaxed, and let every finger touch the key in the same way.

**Think again**
- The sound often stays at a middle volume
- Practise the two ends, pp and ff, on purpose
- pp should be clear and steady, ff full and not harsh
- With the two ends widened, the layers in the middle become richer

![A person in futuristic clothing playing a black grand piano on a neon street, with a small robot beside them](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa1259l-nuum8.webp)

## Practise a Full ff

When playing ff, do not just hit hard with the fingers. Let the weight of your arm and shoulder fall naturally onto the keys.

Your fingers should support that weight steadily, and your wrist should stay flexible, not stiff.

A loud sound played this way is full and strong, without sounding sharp or harsh.

## From the Two Ends to the Middle

Once both ends are developed, you can try playing several different levels between pp and ff, such as p, mp, mf and f.

Play these dynamics in turn on the same note or the same chord, and listen to whether the differences between them are clear.

This kind of practice makes your dynamic levels finer.

## Go Back to the Piece and Check the Contrast

Find the very soft and very loud places in a piece, and see whether you really play a clear contrast.

You can record yourself and listen. Sometimes you feel you are already very soft, but on the recording it still sounds like a medium volume.

Adjust according to the recording, so the dynamic contrasts in the piece become clearer.

## Practising a Very Soft pp

When playing pp, keep your fingers close to the keys and press the key down slowly, so the hammer reaches the string at a very low speed.

The point is to control the speed of the key press, not the amount of force. A slow, steady press can produce a very soft but clear sound.

If you press too slowly and too lightly, sometimes no sound comes out. Try several times and find the feeling where the sound just speaks.

## Crescendo and Diminuendo

With a wider dynamic range, crescendos and diminuendos also become more expressive.

You can use an ascending scale, starting at pp and gradually getting louder to ff, then an descending scale getting softer again.

Notice whether the change in dynamics is smooth, and do not jump suddenly to very loud or very soft.

## Protect Your Ears and Hands

Playing very loud for a long time can tire your ears, and can also make your hands and arms tense.

When practising ff, you can limit the time, practising only a short passage each time with a rest in between.

If your hands or arms feel uncomfortable, stop and relax, and ask your teacher to adjust your method if necessary.

## Put It into Your Daily Warm-Up

Dynamics practice can be built into your daily warm-up, for example playing a scale once at different dynamics.

You can also spend a few minutes while practising a piece specifically checking the dynamic contrasts.

**Slower**

After doing this for a few weeks, the contrast between loud and soft will appear naturally in your pieces.

## FAQ

**Q: Why does the sound always stay in the middle?**
A: Attention is on the notes and rhythm, and the dynamics are squeezed into a narrow range.

**Q: How do I play pp?**
A: Keep your fingers close to the keys, press down slowly, and control the speed of the key press.

**Q: How do I play ff?**
A: Use arm weight, with the fingers supporting steadily and the wrist flexible.

**Q: What if ff sounds harsh?**
A: Add weight gradually and find the limit where the sound is full but not harsh.

**Q: How do I practise the layers in the middle?**
A: Play p, mp, mf and f in turn between the two ends.

**Q: What should I watch for when playing ff for a long time?**
A: Limit the time and protect your ears and hands.

piano-duet-balance-listening.body:
To play a balanced piano duet, both players need to play their own part while listening to the other. In practice: first work out, section by section, who has the melody and who has the accompaniment, and have the accompanying player drop the dynamic one level; then agree on signals for starting and breathing, so you begin together and finish together. Do plenty of "listen only" and "swap parts" practice, and a natural understanding will build up.

Unlike playing solo, in a duet two people share one piano, one set of pedals and even one stool. Sitting close, the sounds also blend easily. If both players focus only on their own notes, the result is often a lively but indistinct jumble. The methods below suit duets between parent and child, classmates, or teacher and student.

## First, Work Out Who Is "Speaking"

**Draw a melody map**
Take out the score and, together, mark in pencil which part carries the melody in each section. Sometimes the melody is in the upper part (Primo), and sometimes it moves to the lower part (Secondo).

**Drop the accompaniment one level**
If the melody is mezzo forte, play the accompaniment mezzo piano; if the melody is piano, play the accompaniment even softer. This "one level down" rule is simple and easy to remember.

**Do not make the bass too heavy**
The sound of the bass part is naturally thick and heavy, and on the same piano it can easily cover the melody in the upper part. The player of the bass part needs to be especially careful about control.

## Start Together, Finish Together

- Agree that one person gives the starting signal, usually the player with the melody
- The signal can be a clear breath in, with a slight nod of the head
- Before starting, both players silently count a bar of the beat
- The ending of long notes and fermatas is also shown by the same person with a hand gesture
- Mark any slowing down or ritardando in the score in advance, and practise that passage together

## Who Takes the Pedal?

A piano usually has just one set of pedals, and it is generally the player of the bass part who takes it, because the bass part is closer to the pedals and changes of harmony often show up in the bass.

**The upper part should say what they need**
If the player of the upper part feels the sound is too blurred or too dry somewhere, they should tell their partner during practice, and you can decide together where to change the pedal.

**Practise without the pedal first**
When you first start playing together, you can play entirely without the pedal, get the rhythm and balance right, and only then add the pedal.

![Illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow lines on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-10/mvvo91k7-glap3.webp)

## Four Exercises to Build Understanding

**Listen only**
One person plays their own part while the other sits beside them, listening and following the score. Then swap. This helps you understand what your partner's part is doing.

**Swap parts**
If the difficulty allows, swap upper and lower parts and play each once. After playing your partner's part, you will better understand what kind of support they need.

**Take turns as "conductor"**
In each run-through, one person decides the tempo and dynamic changes, and the other follows. Swap roles for the next run.

**Record and listen back**
Record your duet on a phone and, when listening back, pay particular attention to these questions: Can you hear the melody clearly? Do your starts and endings line up?

## The Order for Learning a New Duet

**Learn your own part hands separately first**
Before playing together, each person should practise their own part until they can play it steadily. Duet time is precious, so do not spend it sorting out individual wrong notes.

**Play slowly together to find the alignment points**
The first time you play together, set the tempo at about half the usual speed. Mark the important beats where you both land at the same time. These are your "alignment points".

**Play in sections, then connect**
Divide the piece into several sections. Once each section lines up when played together, practise the links between sections, and only then play the whole piece.

## Small Reminders About Posture and Space

Two people on the same stool have limited space. Adjust your distance first so that both players' elbows can move freely. Where your arms cross, agree beforehand whose hand goes on top and whose underneath, to avoid collisions. If the stool height does not suit one of you, you can add a cushion to adjust it.

Playing duets is also an exercise in communication. During practice, use friendly language when giving each other feedback, for example "I'd like to hear more of your melody here" rather than "You're too loud". Good communication makes playing together more enjoyable. For parent and child duets, the adult can also use the chance to model how to listen and express themselves, so the child learns to cooperate through music.

## FAQ

**Q: Can two people of different levels play duets together?**

A: Yes. In many duet pieces the two parts differ in difficulty, and the more advanced player can take the more complex part.

**Q: One of us keeps speeding up. What should we do?**

A: First practise slowly together with a metronome, then gradually switch the metronome off and let the player giving the signals lead the tempo.

**Q: How old does a child need to be for duets?**

A: As long as the child can play a simple melody steadily, they can try duets with an adult. Start with pieces in a simple five-finger position.

**Q: How can I practise if I have no duet partner?**

A: You can first record one part, then play the other part while the recording plays, practising playing while listening to someone else's sound.

plum-blossom-three-variations-guqin.body:
Plum Blossom in Three Variations is an ancient piece for the guqin (the Chinese seven-string zither). It uses the image of plum blossoms opening in the depths of winter to praise a strong, noble character. One of the earliest surviving scores appears in a guqin collection compiled in 1425, during the Ming dynasty. The "three variations" in the title refer to a single theme played in harmonics, which appears three times in different registers of the guqin, like plum blossoms opening again and again in the wind. The piece is said to have originated as a flute tune from the Eastern Jin dynasty, and was only later adapted for the guqin. Its melody is elegant and its mood far-reaching, and on the piano it can help you explore a transparent, harmonic-like tone.

## Slower and Calmer

To play music with a guqin flavour, take the tempo a little slower and keep the mind a little calmer.

**Before you begin**

Leave a little space between the notes and let each sound fade away naturally.

Guqin music values the "lingering sound", and on the piano too you can learn to listen to each note as it slowly disappears.

## Try the Sound of Plum Blossom in Three Variations with Your Teacher in a Lesson

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate how to produce a transparent, harmonic-like sound in the high register of the piano.

You can also take turns with your teacher playing the theme in the three registers and compare how each one feels.

From one guqin piece, you can get a feel for the elegant mood of Chinese music.

- A guqin piece praising the character of the plum blossom
- One of the earliest surviving scores appears in a Ming dynasty guqin collection of 1425
- The same harmonics theme appears three times
- Said to come from a flute tune of the Eastern Jin dynasty

## Listen to the Guqin First

Before trying it on the piano, listen to several guqin players perform Plum Blossom in Three Variations.

Listen for the three appearances of the harmonics theme, and for how the stopped-note sections in between change.

Once you know it well, imitating it on the piano will feel more natural.

## How the Three Appearances Change

On the piano, try playing the theme once in each of three different registers.

The first time in the middle register, the second in the high register and the third in an even higher register.

Listen for how the same melody feels different in different registers.

## Plum Blossom in Three Variations: A Summary

Plum Blossom in Three Variations is an ancient guqin piece that praises a strong, noble character through plum blossoms opening in the cold of winter. It is said to come from a flute piece by a musician of the Eastern Jin dynasty, and one of its earliest surviving scores appears in a guqin collection compiled in 1425 in the Ming dynasty. The "three variations" refer to a theme played in harmonics that appears three times in different registers of the guqin. Harmonics are the clear sounds made by lightly touching the string at the hui markers with the left hand, and in the middle there are stopped-note sections with larger rises and falls. The mood is elegant and far-reaching.

On the piano, you can imitate harmonics with very soft notes in the high register and little pedal. You can play the theme once in each of the three registers, take the tempo slower, listen to the lingering sound, and listen to the original guqin version before you play.

You can ask Teacher Aum to demonstrate the harmonic-like tone.

## An Elegant Mood

The overall mood of Plum Blossom in Three Variations is elegant and far-reaching. It does not aim for liveliness or splendour.

It is like an ink painting, using simple lines to draw the spirit of the plum blossom.

When you listen to this piece, you can quiet your mind and take time to feel its atmosphere.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbis3gi-no42b.webp)

## From Flute Tune to Guqin Piece

According to old records, a musician of the Eastern Jin dynasty who was skilled at the flute once played a flute tune describing plum blossoms.

Later, this flute tune was adapted into a guqin piece, which is today's Plum Blossom in Three Variations.

Because so much time has passed, we can no longer know what the original flute tune was like.

## The Score of 1425

One of the earliest surviving scores of Plum Blossom in Three Variations appears in a guqin collection compiled in 1425, during the Ming dynasty.

This collection includes many ancient guqin pieces and is an important source for studying guqin music.

In later guqin collections, Plum Blossom in Three Variations also appears in many different versions.

## The Sections Between the Harmonics

Between the three appearances of the harmonics theme there are some sections played with stopped notes.

These sections have larger rises and falls in the melody, sometimes urgent and sometimes calm, like wind and snow blowing.

The clarity of the harmonics alternates with the changes of the stopped notes, like plum blossoms opening again and again in wind and snow.

## What "Three Variations" Means

In ancient times, "variation" (nong) could refer to a section of a piece or one playing of it.

In Plum Blossom in Three Variations, there is a theme played in harmonics, and it appears three times in the piece.

At each appearance the melody sits in a different register of the guqin, and each time it sounds fresher than the last.

## Harmonics on the Guqin

Harmonics on the guqin are the sounds made when a finger of the left hand lightly touches the string at a "hui" marker while the right hand plucks the string.

The sound of harmonics is clear and transparent, like a bell in the air or wind in the distance.

In Plum Blossom in Three Variations, the harmonics theme is as elegant and pure as the plum blossom itself.

## Imitating Harmonics on the Piano

The piano does not have harmonics like the guqin, but you can imitate their clarity with very soft notes in the high register.

Touch the keys lightly with your fingers, and use no pedal or only a little, so the sound stays transparent and clean.

This kind of tone practice helps you improve your control of piano tone.

## Plum Blossoms in Winter

Plum blossoms open in the cold of winter, often among the first flowers of the year.

In Chinese culture, the plum blossom symbolises strength and purity, and a lack of fear of wind and snow.

**Notice the details**

People in the past often used the plum blossom as a metaphor for a person of integrity, and plum blossoms are often described in poems and paintings.

## FAQ

**Q: What instrument is Plum Blossom in Three Variations for?**
A: The guqin.

**Q: In what year was the collection containing one of its earliest scores compiled?**
A: 1425, in the Ming dynasty.

**Q: What does "three variations" mean?**
A: A harmonics theme appears three times in different registers.

**Q: What is the piece said to have been originally?**
A: A flute tune from the Eastern Jin dynasty.

**Q: How can I imitate harmonics on the piano?**
A: Touch the keys very softly in the high register and use little pedal.
