practice-buddy-accountability.body:
Practising alone can be hard to keep up over a long time. Finding a practice buddy can add some motivation and fun. A buddy can be a classmate, a friend or a family member who also plays. You agree to share how your practice is going once a week, for example what you practised this week, what difficulties you met and what small progress you made, and you can also play for each other. The point is to encourage each other, not to compare who plays better. If you both want to, you can also work on a duet together.

## Online Buddies

If there is no one around you who is learning the piano, you can also find like-minded buddies online and share your practice by video or text.

When choosing an online buddy, take care to protect your privacy and do not casually give out information such as your address.

If a child wants to find an online buddy, it should be done with a parent's company and consent.

## Practice Buddies for Children

For children, learning the piano with friends of the same age often adds a lot of fun.

Parents can help the child contact classmates who also play, and agree to practise together or play for each other.

When children are together, they may come up with many fun practice games.

## A Buddy Is Not a Burden

The relationship with a practice buddy should be relaxed and happy, not a burden.

If you did not practise well one week, you can say so honestly, and your buddy will understand.

What matters is keeping your connection with music together, not making big progress every time.

## Play for Each Other

If it is convenient, you can arrange a time to play for each other, like a small concert.

This gives you a goal and makes you get a piece ready before the agreed time.

When you listen to the other person play, you can say what you liked and give sincere encouragement.

## Agree on How to Share

You can agree on a fixed time to share with your buddy, for example Sunday evenings, taking a few minutes to talk about the week's practice.

What you share can include which pieces you practised, how long you practised, what difficulties you met and what small progress you made.

You can also share by text or voice message, and you do not have to meet.

Sharing can be simple. A few sentences is enough. The key is to keep going.

## Do Not Compare, Just Encourage

When practising with a buddy, avoid comparing who has practised more or who plays better.

Everyone has a different pace and different goals. Comparing only brings pressure, and can even affect the friendship.

Keep your attention on each other's progress and be glad about every bit of growth the other makes.

**Listen**
- A practice buddy adds motivation and fun
- Agree to share your practice once a week
- You can play for each other
- Encourage each other rather than compare

## Set Goals Together

You can set some shared goals with your buddy, for example each learning a new piece within a month.

When the agreed time comes, play for each other and celebrate reaching the goal.

Shared goals let the two of you keep each other on track, and give you more motivation to keep going.

## What a Buddy Does for You

With a practice buddy, you know someone cares about your practice, and you will want to have some progress to talk about the next time you share.

Buddies can encourage each other and support each other when one meets a difficulty.

Sharing practice experience can also teach you new methods and ideas.

![A person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0x6sm-jcap1.webp)

## Practise a Duet Together

If you both play the piano, you can find some piano duet pieces for four hands to practise together.

If one plays the piano and the other plays another instrument, you can also find suitable ensemble pieces.

Playing together trains your listening and cooperation, and brings a lot of fun.

## The Difficulty of Practising Alone

When you practise on your own, it is easy to give up because you are busy, tired or have run into difficulty.

No one knows whether you practised today, and no one shares the joy of your progress with you.

Over time, practice can become a lonely thing that is easy to put off.

## Who Can Be a Buddy

A practice buddy can be a classmate in the same lessons, or a friend who plays another instrument.

Members of your household, such as a brother or sister, or a parent who is also learning, can also be buddies.

A buddy does not need to be at exactly your level. What matters is that you are both willing to share and encourage.

## FAQ

**Q: Why find a practice buddy?**
A: To add motivation and fun, and to encourage each other.

**Q: Who can be a buddy?**
A: A classmate, a friend or a family member.

**Q: How do we share?**
A: Agree on a fixed time and talk about what you practised and the difficulties you met.

**Q: Should we compare who plays better?**
A: No. Encourage each other instead.

**Q: Can I find an online buddy?**
A: Yes, but take care to protect your privacy, and children need a parent's consent.

**Q: What if I did not practise well?**
A: Say so honestly and keep the relationship relaxed.

piazzolla-libertango-1974-new-tango.body:
The Argentine composer Piazzolla devoted his life to combining traditional tango with classical music and jazz, and his style is called "nuevo tango" (new tango). In 1974 he recorded an album in Milan, Italy, and its title piece, Libertango, later spread around the world. The name "Libertango" was coined by joining the two words "libertad" (freedom) and "tango". In the piece, a 3+3+2 rhythm keeps pushing the music forward, and the melody is both fiery and tinged with sadness. Today it has countless arrangements for all kinds of instruments, and the piano versions are very popular.

## Piano Arrangements of Libertango

There are many piano arrangements of Libertango: solos, piano duets for four hands, and ensemble versions with other instruments.

Easy versions usually keep the main rhythm and melody, and suit intermediate learners.

Concert versions pack in counterpoint, harmony and virtuoso display.

## The Name Libertango

"Libertango" is a word Piazzolla coined, joining "freedom" and "tango".

The name reflects his wish to free the tango from old frameworks.

Some also understand it as a longing for freedom.

## The Sadness of the Melody

Above the ceaselessly driving rhythm, the melody is often long notes and descending lines.

The long notes carry a feeling of sadness and yearning, in contrast with the urgent rhythm underneath.

This mood of fire with sadness in it is a hallmark of Piazzolla's music.

## Who Was Piazzolla

Piazzolla was born in 1921 and died in 1992; he was an Argentine composer and bandoneon player.

As a child he lived with his family in New York, in the United States, and came into contact early with jazz and classical music.

Later he returned to Argentina and played in tango orchestras.

## Listen to the Original Recording First

Before playing, you can first listen to a recording by Piazzolla's own ensemble, to feel the rhythm and sound of the original.

You can also listen to versions played on different instruments, such as violin and cello.

After comparing, decide how you want to express it on the piano.

## The Repeating Bass

The bass of the piece often plays the same short figure over and over.

This repetition is like a machine that never stops running, keeping the music tense.

The left hand takes over this "machine", and must be steady yet a little springy.

- Piazzolla was born in 1921 and died in 1992
- Recorded in Milan in 1974
- The name is made by joining "freedom" and "tango"
- A 3+3+2 rhythm drives the music

## What Is "Nuevo Tango"

Traditional tango was mainly music to accompany dancing.

Piazzolla's "nuevo tango" added the counterpoint of classical music, the harmony of jazz, and a freer structure.

It is better suited to listening in a concert, not only to dancing.

## Libertango: A Summary

Piazzolla was born in 1921 and died in 1992; an Argentine composer and bandoneon player, he met jazz and classical music in New York as a child, and when studying composition in Paris in the 1950s he was encouraged by his teacher to make tango the core of his work, developing a "nuevo tango" that fuses classical counterpoint with jazz harmony; in 1974 he recorded Libertango in Milan.

The name is made by joining "freedom" and "tango", the rhythm is often divided 3+3+2, the bass repeats a short figure, the long notes of the melody carry sadness, you can imagine the sound of the bandoneon, the first note of each group is a little heavier, and the piano arrangements include solo, duet and ensemble versions.

You can listen to the original recording first, and Teacher Aum can help you practise the rhythm and accents.

## The Turning Point in Paris

In the 1950s, Piazzolla went to Paris to study composition with a famous composition teacher.

At first he wanted to write serious classical works, and was reluctant to mention his tango background.

After the teacher heard his tango, he encouraged him to follow his own path and make tango the core of his composing.

## Milan in 1974

In 1974, Piazzolla was living in Italy, and recorded an album in Milan.

The title piece of the album, Libertango, used electric instruments and percussion, and had a very modern sound.

The piece soon became popular, and became one of his best-known works.

## The Bandoneon

In tango music, an accordion-like instrument called the bandoneon is often used; its sound is somewhat like an organ, yet has a sense of breathing.

Piazzolla himself was a bandoneon player.

When playing on the piano, you can imagine the sound of this instrument, which gives the long notes more tension.

## The 3+3+2 Rhythm

The rhythm of Libertango often divides the eight quavers of a bar into 3+3+2.

This uneven grouping gives the music a strong driving force.

When playing, you can first clap this rhythm with your hands, counting "one two three, one two three, one two".

![An electronic keyboard and screens under neon lights](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwacvy8i-4j1eu.webp)

## The Accents of Libertango

Tango accents like to be "displaced", often not on the beat you think.

In the 3+3+2 grouping, the first note of each group usually needs to be a little heavier.

Play the accents clearly, and the flavour of tango comes out.

## Ask Your Teacher to Practise the Libertango Rhythm in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to help you practise the 3+3+2 rhythm and the positions of the accents.

Tango scores vary in difficulty, and you can ask the teacher which edition to choose.

This piece is very good for practising a sense of rhythm and strong expressiveness.

## FAQ

**Q: What nationality was Piazzolla?**
A: Argentine.

**Q: In which year was Libertango recorded?**
A: 1974, in Milan.

**Q: How did the name come about?**
A: By joining the two words "freedom" and "tango".

**Q: What rhythmic grouping does the piece often use?**
A: 3+3+2.

**Q: What is the accordion often used in tango called?**
A: The bandoneon.

pedal-six-four-neighbor-chord.body:
The six-four chord has several set uses, and the pedal six-four is one of the most common; it is also called the neighbour six-four. Its defining feature is that the bass stays still while the two upper voices move up a step and then return to where they started. For example, with the bass staying on C, the upper notes E and G first become F and A, then go back to E and G; the chord in the middle is the second-inversion (six-four) chord of F. This chord is like a gentle sway over one stable note, giving the music variety while keeping it steady. You can hear this harmony at the beginning and end of many pieces.

## The pedal six-four at the start of a piece

Many pieces begin with a pedal six-four over the tonic chord, creating a settled, warm atmosphere.

**A different angle**

For example, a lullaby can open with the chords C, F/C, C, so the music rocks gently.

This harmony is very well suited to expressing a calm mood.

## The shape of the pedal six-four

The pedal six-four is made of three chords: a root-position chord, a six-four chord, and then a return to the root-position chord.

Across these three chords, the bass stays on the same note.

The two upper voices act like neighbours: they step up and then come back.

## Using it on the dominant chord

A pedal six-four can also appear on the dominant chord.

For example, in C major, the bass stays on G while the upper chords go G, C/G, G.

This use often appears in the middle of a piece, prolonging the sense of expectation on the dominant chord.

## An example in C major

In C major, the most common pedal six-four is C, F/C, C.

The bass stays on C throughout, while the upper E and G first become F and A, and then return to E and G.

The F/C in the middle is the six-four chord of the F major triad.

## Playing the pedal six-four on the piano

At the piano, play the bass C continuously with the left hand and play C, F/C, C with the right.

The right hand's E and G change to F and A and back to E and G, and the movement should be smooth.

Listen for the feeling of the bass staying still while the upper notes sway.

## Telling it apart from the passing six-four

In a pedal six-four the bass stays still, while in a passing six-four the bass moves by step.

In both, the six-four chord sits in the middle, but they are formed differently.

When analysing a score, look first at what the bass is doing, and you can tell which kind it is.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon-lit street, with a drone flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwaar3x0-6qrwr.webp)

## The F/C sway in pop intros

In piano accompaniments for pop songs, the pedal six-four is also very common.

The left hand holds a C and does not let go, while the right hand rocks between the shapes of C and F/C, which gives the intro a groove.

This approach is often used in the intro or interlude of a song.

## Asking your teacher to listen to your pedal six-four

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your pedal six-four and check whether the connection in the upper voices is smooth.

You can also ask the teacher to help you find where pedal six-four chords appear in the pieces you are learning.

Applying harmony knowledge to real pieces makes it easier to understand.

## Improvising with the pedal six-four

You can try improvising a short piece of music over one bass note, using the pedal six-four.

Keep the bass C sounding, alternate the right hand between E, G and F, A, and choose the speed and length as you like.

It is a simple and attractive improvisation exercise.

## The pedal six-four in summary

The pedal six-four consists of a root-position chord, a six-four chord, and a return to the root-position chord. The bass stays still, and the two upper voices go up a step and come back. It is also called the neighbour six-four, and in C major the common version is C, F/C, C.

It makes the music sway gently over one chord. It can also be used on the dominant chord, such as G, C/G, G, and it often appears at the start of a piece to create a settled atmosphere, or at the end as a gentle farewell.

What distinguishes it from the passing six-four is that the bass stays still. At the piano, you can hold the bass in the left hand and move back and forth in the right; you can also use it to improvise and to play pop accompaniments. Whether the connection is smooth is something you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to.

## Why "pedal"?

It is called a pedal six-four because the bass stays still like a pedal point.

A pedal point is a note held for a long time in music, over which the upper harmony can change.

The pedal six-four can be seen as a very short pedal point.

## The pedal six-four at the end of a piece

At the end of a piece, a pedal six-four over the tonic chord is also very common.

After the final tonic chord, an F/C is added and then it returns to C, like a gentle farewell.

It sounds very close to the plagal "Amen cadence" (subdominant to tonic) at the end of a hymn.

- The bass stays still
- The upper voices go up a step and come back
- Also called the neighbour six-four
- For example C, F/C, C

## The effect of the pedal six-four

The pedal six-four creates a small ripple in the music over one chord.

The steadiness of the bass gives a feeling of stability, while the changes above add some colour.

It sounds like gently swaying in one place, rather than moving forward.

## Why is it also called "neighbour"?

It is also called the neighbour six-four because the movement of the upper voices is like a neighbour note.

A neighbour note starts from one note, steps to the adjacent note, and returns to the original note.

**Notice the detail**

In the pedal six-four, the two upper voices make this movement at the same time.

## FAQ

**Q: What does the bass do in a pedal six-four?**
A: It stays still.

**Q: How do the upper voices move?**
A: They go up a step and come back.

**Q: What is its other name?**
A: The neighbour six-four.

**Q: What is a common example in C major?**
A: C, F/C, C.

**Q: How is it different from the passing six-four?**
A: In the pedal six-four the bass stays still; in the passing six-four the bass moves by step.

practice-at-different-times-of-day.body:
The best time of day to practise differs from person to person. Some people are clear-headed in the morning and suit learning new pieces and technical difficulties; others are more relaxed in the evening and suit expressive playing and full run-throughs. Rather than chasing one "standard answer", a more practical approach is to observe how you feel at different times, put work that needs high concentration when you are alert, and put review and relaxed practice at other times, while also considering your family's routine and your neighbours' need for quiet.

**Slower**
- The right practice time differs from person to person
- Practise new pieces and technical difficulties when you are alert
- Schedule review and relaxed practice at other times
- Consider family routines and neighbours' need for quiet

## Try It for Two Weeks Before Deciding

You can spend a week or two trying practice at different times of day, noticing your concentration and how well the practice works.

For example, when you practise in the morning, do you read the score faster? When you practise in the evening, are you more willing to put feeling into it?

Write these observations down, and you will find your own pattern at different times.

## Split Practice into Two Sessions

If you have two times of day when you can practise, you can split your practice into two sessions, for example technique in the morning and pieces in the evening.

Split practice also gives your hands and brain time to rest, and avoids the tiredness of practising for a long time at once.

Many people find that two separate sessions work better than one long one.

## Everyone Has a Different Rhythm

Some people are used to getting up early and are most alert in the morning; others only get into the swing of things in the afternoon or evening.

Study, work and family arrangements also affect the time you have for practice.

So there is no practice time that suits everyone. You need to choose according to your own situation.

## Put Relaxed Work at Other Times

Reviewing pieces you have already learned, playing music you like and playing a piece straight through do not need so much concentration.

You can schedule them for times when you are more tired or have only scattered bits of time.

That way, different times of the day can all be used, and your practice has more layers.

## Consider Family and Neighbours

When choosing a practice time, also consider your family's routine and your neighbours' need for quiet.

For example, early in the morning and late at night, many people are resting, and practising then may disturb them.

If those are the only times you can practise, you can use headphones with a digital piano, or practise with a lighter touch.

![A purple and blue grand piano on a pink watercolour background, symbolising music theory and creative learning](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa0w7kl-y30yd.webp)

## Put Focused Work When You Are Alert

Learning new pieces, working on technical difficulties, slow practice and practising in sections all need a lot of concentration.

You can schedule these for the time when you are most alert, and your efficiency will be higher.

If that time is short, you can practise only the hardest parts and leave the rest for other times.

## Characteristics of Evening Practice

In the evening, after a day of study or work, you may be tired, but you may also feel more relaxed.

This is a good time for lyrical pieces, or for playing a piece straight through and enjoying the music.

If you are too tired, you can shorten the practice or do only some relaxed review.

## Children's Practice Time

For children, after school they may need to rest and have something to eat before they start practising.

You can also try practising for ten-odd minutes in the morning before school and see how the child is.

Discuss the practice time with your child and let the child take part in the decision, and it will be easier to stick to.

## Characteristics of Morning Practice

When you have just got up in the morning, your hands may be stiff and need a little more time to warm up.

But many people find that their minds are clearer in the morning and they learn new things faster.

If you choose to practise in the morning, you can first do some simple finger exercises and scales before the real practice.

## Adjust Whenever Needed

Life arrangements change with the season, the school term or work, and your practice time can change with them.

Every so often, you can observe your state again and see whether the current arrangement still suits you.

Only when you find a rhythm that suits you can you keep practising in the long term.

## A Fixed Time Is Easier to Keep

Once you find the time that suits you, you can try to fix it, for example half an hour after dinner every day.

A fixed time helps form a habit, and you do not need to decide again every day when to practise.

**Practice order**

Of course, if there is something special on a certain day, you can adjust flexibly.

## FAQ

**Q: When is practice most effective?**
A: It differs from person to person. Observe how you feel at different times.

**Q: When should I practise a new piece?**
A: At a time when you are alert and your concentration is high.

**Q: What can I practise when I am tired?**
A: Review, playing pieces you like, or full run-throughs.

**Q: Can I practise early in the morning or late at night?**
A: Consider your family and neighbours. You can use headphones or a light touch.

**Q: Can I split practice into two sessions?**
A: Yes, for example technique in the morning and pieces in the evening.

**Q: When should children practise?**
A: Discuss it with the child. It can be after rest following school.

piazzolla-oblivion-1982.body:
Oblivion is a slow tango that the Argentine composer Astor Piazzolla wrote for a film in 1982; its English and Italian title is often given as Oblivion. It does not win through fast syncopation, but through a long, slightly sad melody set over a slow, clear tango step. The original is often played by bandoneon and chamber ensemble, and many piano arrangements have followed. On the piano, singing that long melody through to the end first, and then letting the accompaniment support it gently, comes closer to the character of the piece than piling on many notes. It also reminds us that Piazzolla's nuevo tango is not only fiery fast pieces, but has a very quiet side too. After practising, you can listen again to a recording with bandoneon, and compare whether you are stretching the phrases long enough. If a particular phrase keeps breaking off midway, first sing that phrase through twice on its own, then go back to the piano and play it slowly to the end.

## The Pedal Helps the Breath

A long melody badly needs the pedal to connect it, but you still have to change it when the harmony changes, otherwise the sadness turns into blur.

A shallow pedal changed often is usually more suitable than pressing it all the way down.

When the phrase fades at its end, release the pedal cleanly in good time too.

## Oblivion: A Summary

Piazzolla's Oblivion was written in 1982 as a slow tango for a film; the original is often played by bandoneon and chamber ensemble, and there are many piano arrangements.

On the piano, first sing the long melody through, let the accompaniment hold the slow step steady and give way, change the pedal shallowly and often, and keep the dynamics restrained.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the long phrases and the step.

## The Bandoneon and Piano Arrangements

The bandoneon can draw out a very long breath, and the notes easily run on from one to the next.

A piano arrangement has to approach this connectedness through touch, phrasing and pedal, not just by playing the notes loudly.

If an arrangement adds many inner voices, it is all the more important to make clear which line is the main melody.

## The Tango Step Stays Underneath

The accompaniment should still feel the walking step of the tango, only slower, with smaller movements.

The left hand must be steady, yet must give way to the melody, especially in the soft opening and the quiet ending.

You can use the metronome to settle the slow step first, then place the right hand's long phrase on top.

## Ask Teacher Aum to Listen to the Long Phrases in Lessons

In a lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen whether the long melody breaks off midway, and whether the accompaniment makes the step too heavy.

Where the resonance builds up too thick, you can also ask the teacher to try changing the pedal more often with you.

From a slow tango of 1982, practise placing long phrases on top of a restrained step.

## Sing the Long Phrase Through

The melody of this piece often has very long phrases, which should not be broken up frequently midway.

You can first mark out the phrases by breath, then ease off gently at the phrase ends.

Singing first and then playing makes it easier to get a complete line than staring at each note and striking it.

## Keep the Dynamics Restrained

The strength of Oblivion comes from line and harmony, not from sustained loud playing.

Even when a phrase opens out a little, you should soon return to a rather inward sound.

If you find yourself getting louder and louder, try playing the whole piece once more at a very quiet volume, to rediscover its character.

## A Slow Piece Within Nuevo Tango

Piazzolla is often placed in the tradition of "nuevo tango", and his works include both tense, fast pieces and very slow, songlike ones.

Oblivion belongs to the latter: the syncopation is still there, but set within an unhurried tempo.

When listening, do not expect it to suddenly turn into lively dance-hall music.

## How to Start This Oblivion

An arrangement with a clear melody and a not-too-dense accompaniment is something an intermediate learner can begin; versions with very full voicing suit more advanced players better.

First settle on one edition, and do not mix the embellishments from different arrangements.

Set the tempo by what lets you sing a phrase through completely, and do not chase recordings that are too fast.

- Piazzolla wrote it in 1982 for a film
- A tango at a slow tempo
- The original is often played by bandoneon and chamber ensemble
- The melody is long, and the accompanying step is clear and restrained

## 1982 and Film Music

In 1982, Piazzolla wrote music for a film, including Oblivion.

This slow tango later often left the film and was played on its own in concerts.

**Summary**

Knowing the year it was written and what it was for helps in understanding that slow breath, suited to a picture that lingers.

## FAQ

A: 1982.

**Q: What was it originally written for?**
A: A score written for a film, later often played on its own.

**Q: What instruments often play the original?**
A: The bandoneon, often together with chamber ensemble.

**Q: What matters most to grasp on the piano?**
A: A complete long melody, and the slow, clear tango step underneath.

**Q: Why should you not get louder and louder?**
A: Because the strength of this slow tango comes mainly from line and harmony, not from sustained loud playing.

phone-away-during-practice.body:
When you practise, put your phone somewhere out of arm's reach, turn on Do Not Disturb mode, and bring it over only when you need the metronome or a recording. This can greatly reduce the number of times your practice is interrupted. Every time you check a message, your attention has to find its way back to the music, and after a few times a practice session that was once continuous has been cut into many fragments.

## Setting up Do Not Disturb

Before you start practising, set your phone to Do Not Disturb and allow only calls from emergency contacts to come through. That way you will not miss anything important, and everyday messages will not disturb you.

**Remember this**

You can also set a fixed time window, for example from seven to half past seven every evening, so that it goes into Do Not Disturb automatically and becomes a habit.

Turning off unnecessary app notifications reduces a lot of distraction in general, and all the more when you are practising.

- Set the phone to Do Not Disturb or silent mode
- Put it some distance from the piano
- Do the metronome and recording in a separate way where you can
- Check messages all together after you finish

## What about the metronome and recording

Many people use their phone as a metronome and recording device. In that case you can open only the app you need and keep Do Not Disturb on.

If circumstances allow, you can get a separate metronome, or use the metronome function built into a digital piano, to reduce the chances of using the phone.

When recording, once you have put the phone in a suitable position, do not touch it again, and listen back to everything together after you have finished.

## Put it in a suitable place

Do not leave the phone on the piano or beside the music stand. Even when it is silent, a screen lighting up draws the eyes.

You can put it on the other side of the room, or in another room. When you need it, you walk over to get it, and this small distance can reduce many urges to check it casually.

When children practise, parents can help by putting the phone away and giving it back to the child after practice.

## Check messages after you finish

Make yourself an agreement: look at the phone after you finish playing. If your practice time is thirty minutes, deal with messages all together after thirty minutes.

Most messages do not need an immediate reply, and half an hour later is usually fine.

After you keep this agreement a few times, you will find your concentration during practice clearly improves, and so does the effect of the practice.

## Cooperation from family

If your family know you are practising, you can ask them not to phone or call you during this time as far as possible.

When something needs to be discussed, it can wait until you have finished playing a section.

When a child is practising, parents can likewise keep their own phones further away, telling the child through action that this is a time for concentration.

## Keep your attention for the sound

Once the phone is further away, you can listen more carefully to your own playing: whether the tone is even, whether the phrases are connected, whether the dynamics are clear.

This kind of focused listening is a very important part of practising, and it is also the part most easily interrupted by the phone.

Treat practice time as a time away from the screen, which not only helps practice but also gives your eyes and brain some rest.

![Watercolour of a grand piano with its lid open in soft grey-purple tones](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9x59tj-8u1n1.webp)

## Why a phone interrupts practice so easily

The alert sounds and vibrations of a phone are hard to ignore. Even if you do not pick it up to look, you will be wondering "who sent that message", and your attention has already left the keys.

If you do pick it up, you often look at more than one thing and casually open other apps. By the time you put the phone down, several minutes may have gone by, and the feel in your hands from what you were just practising has faded.

Practice needs sustained concentration, especially when working on hard spots and memorising, and frequent interruptions reduce the effect.

## If you really must use your phone

Some people cannot do without their phone when practising, for example when they need it to read the score, run the metronome or compare with a demonstration recording. In that case you can set the phone to a "practice only" state.

Keep only a few apps related to practising on the home screen and move social and entertainment apps to other pages, so there is less chance of opening them casually.

After practice, restore your usual settings. That way the phone changes from a source of distraction into a tool with boundaries.

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What if I read my score on the phone?**
A: You can turn on Do Not Disturb, turn off notifications and open only the score app.

**Q: What if my child uses a tablet for online classes and also needs to practise?**
A: When the online class is over, put the tablet somewhere else, and when the score is needed, turn off notifications before using it.

**Q: Will Do Not Disturb make me miss an emergency call?**
A: You can set emergency contacts or a repeated-call alert, so important calls still get through.

**Q: Can I listen to demonstrations in a music app while practising?**
A: Yes, but once you have heard the demonstration, put the phone down and concentrate on your own playing.

**Q: Is it worth buying a separate metronome?**
A: If you are often distracted by your phone, a simple separate metronome can help a lot.

**Q: How long does practice need to be before I put the phone away?**
A: However long it is, if you want to concentrate, you can keep the phone further away.

perfect-vs-imperfect-authentic-cadence.body:
A cadence from the dominant chord to the tonic chord is called an authentic cadence, and it is a very common way of ending music. But even though both go from dominant to tonic, some sound completely final, like a full stop, while others leave a little room, somewhere between a comma and a full stop. The difference lies in the arrangement of the chords: whether the bass and the top note both land on the tonic. The former is usually called a perfect authentic cadence, and the latter an imperfect authentic cadence. Here is how to tell the two apart.

## Shaping perfect and imperfect cadences when you play

A perfect authentic cadence is often the end of a section or of the whole piece, and you can give it a clear close.

**Try it**

After an imperfect cadence there is often more music, so when you play it you can keep a little feeling of continuing.

Understanding how strong or weak a cadence is helps us express the structure of phrases better in performance.

## Steps for analysing a cadence

When analysing a cadence, first check whether its chords are V to I.

Then look at the bass notes of the two chords, and see whether they are the dominant and the tonic respectively.

Finally, look at whether the top note of the tonic chord is the tonic, to decide whether it is perfect or imperfect.

**Before you start**
- Authentic cadence: dominant chord to tonic chord
- Perfect: both chords in root position, with the top note on the tonic
- Imperfect: an inversion is used or the top note is not the tonic
- One sounds final, the other leaves a little room

## How it relates to other cadences

Besides the authentic cadence, there are also the plagal cadence, the half cadence and the deceptive cadence.

A half cadence ends on the dominant chord, like a question mark; a deceptive cadence moves from the dominant chord to a different chord.

Comparing these cadences side by side helps you understand more clearly what each one does.

## Common melodic endings

In a perfect authentic cadence, the melody often ends with a stepwise move of "2 to 1" or "7 to 1".

For example D to C, or B to C.

These melodic moves, together with root-position dominant-to-tonic chords, make up a typical ending.

## Finding them in real pieces

Take a familiar short piece, such as a children's song or a simple sonata movement, and find the authentic cadences in it.

Judge whether each cadence is perfect or imperfect, and see where in the piece each one occurs.

This kind of exercise helps us understand the structure of a piece.

![A cartoon character with glasses and headphones looks at sheet music while playing an upright piano in a night-time room, with a TIGA STUDIO neon sign on the wall](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa82vae-dgosn.webp)

## Conditions for a perfect authentic cadence

A perfect authentic cadence generally needs to meet several conditions: both the dominant chord and the tonic chord are in root position, that is, the bass notes are the dominant and the tonic respectively.

At the same time, in the final tonic chord, the highest voice must land on the tonic.

When these conditions are met, the sense of ending is very complete, like a full stop.

## What is an authentic cadence

An authentic cadence is a cadence from the dominant chord (V) to the tonic chord (I).

It is a strong way of ending in tonal music, and often appears at the ends of phrases and pieces.

In the dominant chord, the leading note resolves upwards to the tonic, and the bass goes from dominant to tonic, both of which strengthen the sense of ending.

## The imperfect authentic cadence

If a dominant-to-tonic cadence does not fully meet these conditions, it is called an imperfect authentic cadence.

For example, the top note of the final tonic chord may be the third or the fifth rather than the tonic.

Or one of the chords may be inverted, so the bass is not the dominant or the tonic.

## The two types of authentic cadence in summary

Among dominant-to-tonic authentic cadences, one where both chords are in root position and the tonic chord's top note rests on the tonic counts as a perfect authentic cadence, and it sounds like a full stop.

If there is an inversion, or the top note lands on the third or the fifth, it is an imperfect authentic cadence, often used in the middle of a section, leaving some room.

When analysing, look in turn at the chords, the bass and the top note. When playing, give a perfect cadence a clear close and keep a feeling of continuation in an imperfect one.

## Its role in phrase structure

In a period made of two phrases, the first phrase often ends with an imperfect cadence or a half cadence, like asking a question.

The second phrase ends with a perfect authentic cadence, like giving the answer.

By arranging the strength of cadences, a composer can make the structure of the music clearer.

## The role of the top note

The highest voice is often the melody, and listeners are especially sensitive to it.

If the melody ends on the tonic, you feel "back home".

If the melody lands on the third or the fifth, the harmony has returned to the tonic chord, but the melody seems not quite finished.

## Comparing a top note of C and E at the piano

In C major, play the bass G to C with the left hand, and with the right hand play a G major chord to a C major chord, ending with C as the top note.

Play it again, this time putting E as the final top note, and compare the two senses of ending.

You will find that the first is more complete, while the second still carries a hint of possible continuation.

## The change an inversion brings

If the dominant or the tonic chord is inverted, the bass is no longer the root, and the sense of ending is weaker.

For example, if the bass goes from the dominant to the third of the tonic chord in first inversion, it sounds less stable.

This kind of cadence is often used in the middle of a section, not at the end of the whole piece.

## FAQ

**Q: What is an authentic cadence?**
A: A cadence from the dominant chord to the tonic chord.

**Q: What are the conditions for a perfect authentic cadence?**
A: Both chords in root position, with the top note on the tonic.

**Q: What are the features of an imperfect authentic cadence?**
A: An inversion is used or the top note is not the tonic.

**Q: How is it arranged within a phrase structure?**
A: The first phrase mostly uses a weaker cadence, and the second phrase uses a perfect authentic cadence.

**Q: What do you look at when analysing?**
A: The chords, the bass and the top note.

piano-practice-timer-focus-blocks.body:
Practising in timed blocks means cutting one longer practice session into several focus periods of fixed length, for example twenty-five minutes of practice followed by five minutes of rest, with each period dealing with just one clear goal. The advantage is that when you know how long it is until your next break, it is easier to stay focused; and stopping at the end of each block to check what you have gained also stops you repeating the same spot without result. You can adjust the length of the blocks to age and habits: shorter for children, longer for adults. What matters is that every block has a clear task.

## The Basic Plan for Block Practice

- Before starting, write down two or three goals for this session
- Set a timer, for example twenty-five minutes
- During the timer, practise only one goal and stay off your phone
- When time is up, rest for five minutes and stand up to move around
- Review the progress you have just made, then start the next block

For an hour of practice, you can plan two focus blocks plus a relaxed review.

## What to Practise in Each Block

**Warm-up block**
Scales, arpeggios and finger exercises. This can be short, about ten minutes, to get your hands and ears ready.

**Difficult-passage block**
Concentrate on one or two hard passages in a piece, using methods such as slow practice, hands separately and changing rhythms. This block needs the most concentration, so it suits the time when you are fresh.

**Run-through block**
Play the piece through from start to finish once or twice, feeling its overall structure and mood, without stopping to make corrections.

**Relaxed block**
Play a favourite piece you can already play, or improvise for a few minutes, as an enjoyable end to practice.

## What to Do During a Break

A break is not time for your phone. You can drink some water, walk around, and stretch your arms and shoulders to relax your hands and eyes. You can also write down one thing you gained in a notebook, for example "fixed the fingering in bar twelve". A short rest makes the next block fresher.

![Wooden upright piano, green piano stool and orange books against a dark teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw3f6xvv-av312.webp)

## Adjusting the Length by Age

**Children**
Younger children can only focus for a short time, so you can set ten-minute blocks with two or three minutes of rest between. Parents can use an hourglass or a cute timer so the child can see time passing.

**Teenagers**
They can try blocks of fifteen to twenty minutes and lengthen them gradually.

**Adults**
Twenty-five minutes per block is common. On a busy day you can do just one block, which works equally well.

## Common Adjustments

**You finish the goal within a block**
You can move on to the next goal early, or use the remaining time to consolidate. There is no need to force yourself to wait for the timer.

**The block ends before you have finished**
Do not extend it. Rest first and continue in the next block. When you force yourself to carry on, your attention has often already dropped.

**You were interrupted**
If you are interrupted partway, you can pause the timer and carry on when you come back, or simply start a fresh block.

## Combining It with a Practice Log

After each session of block practice, write in your practice notebook how many blocks you did, the goal of each block and how it went. Looking back a week later, you can see clearly where the time went and which goals need more blocks. Some piano apps also record practice time automatically, so you can compare it with your own notes.

## A Sample Weekly Block Plan

Suppose an adult student practises five days a week, one hour a day. From Monday to Wednesday, each day has one warm-up block, one difficult-passage block and one run-through block. On Thursday, do just two difficult-passage blocks, concentrating on tackling the hardest passage. On Friday, do one run-through block and one relaxed block, and join up the week's results by playing for your family. This plan has both focus and variety, so the week does not feel monotonous.

## The Psychological Benefits of Block Practice

Many people dread practice because they feel it means a long, tiring session. Once practice is cut into small blocks, "just practise for twenty-five minutes first" sounds much easier to begin. After starting, you often find you are willing to do another block. The sense of completion from small blocks builds up bit by bit, and practice is no longer a heavy task.

## FAQ

**Q: Does it have to be twenty-five minutes per block?**
A: No. You can adjust it to your own span of focus. Anything from ten to forty minutes works.

**Q: Will a five-minute break interrupt my flow?**
A: A short break usually lets your attention recover, and it is often easier to get back into the groove afterwards.

**Q: What if my child does not want to stop for a break?**
A: If the child is enjoying the practice, you can extend it a little, but next time still encourage them to rest as planned.

**Q: I only have twenty minutes a day. How do I divide it into blocks?**
A: You can do just one block, focusing on a single goal. That is still better than playing aimlessly for twenty minutes.

**Q: Can I use my phone as the timer?**
A: Yes, but turn on Do Not Disturb so messages do not interrupt you.

**Q: Should I change pieces between blocks?**
A: Not necessarily. You can work on different passages of the same piece, or change pieces, according to your goals.

practice-while-traveling.body:
When you travel, there may be no piano nearby, but you can still stay connected to music. Save recordings and scores of the pieces you are learning on your phone, and use time spent waiting for trains or flights to listen and look. Replay the melody and fingering in your head. If there is a piano where you are staying, you can also play for a while once you have permission. When you get home, review familiar pieces first, then gradually return to your usual practice.

## Bringing a Portable Keyboard

If the trip is a long one, some people bring a small portable keyboard.

**Summary**

A portable keyboard has a different number of keys and a different feel from a piano, but it can be used to practise simple melodies and fingering.

Whether to bring one can depend on the length of the trip, the space in your luggage and your own needs.

## Preparing Before You Leave

Before you leave, you can photograph or scan the scores of the pieces you are learning and save them on your phone or tablet.

You can also download recordings of those pieces so you can listen whenever you like.

If your teacher has set particular practice points, you can note those down as well, to look at during the trip.

![A glowing teal grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9y96db-93nge.webp)

## Getting Back on Track at Home

When you get home, there is no need to jump straight into the hardest material. You can play a few familiar pieces first to find your feel again.

Over the next few days, gradually add the pieces you are learning and slowly return to your usual amount of practice.

If you did mental practice while travelling, you may find that you recover faster than you expected.

## Small Notes on the Road

If you have new ideas while practising in your head on a trip, such as a different way to shape a phrase, you can jot them down on your phone.

When you hear music you like, you can also note the title and the performer, then look it up when you get home, or ask your teacher to recommend a version that suits you.

These little notes tie your travels to your piano learning, and looking back at them at home may make you want to sit down and try it out.

## Enjoying Music on the Journey

Travel is also a good chance to come across different music.

You can pay attention to local music, go to a concert, or find inspiration in a melody you hear on the street.

These experiences can enrich your understanding of music, and you may have new ideas when you play at home again.

## Travelling and Practising

When you travel, your daily routine is disrupted, and often there is no piano nearby.

Some people worry that a few days or weeks without practice will leave their fingers rusty.

In fact, even when you cannot practise on a piano, there are many ways to stay in touch with music and make getting back into it easier when you are home.

- Save scores and recordings on your phone before you leave
- Use waiting time to listen to pieces and look at the score
- Replay the melody and fingering in your head
- When you get home, review first, then gradually return to practice

## Small Finger Exercises

Without a piano, you can also gently move your fingers on a tabletop or your knees, imitating some simple fingerings.

This kind of movement can keep your fingers fairly agile, but it does not need much force or much time.

In public places, keep the movements small so as not to disturb others.

## When Children Travel

When children go away on holiday, parents can prepare some music-related activities, such as singing the pieces they are learning together in the car.

You can also let your child listen to music they like, to keep their interest in music alive.

Travel is a time for rest and relaxation, so there is no need to put too much pressure on your child to practise.

## When Your Accommodation Has a Piano

Some hotels, guesthouses or friends' and relatives' homes may have a piano.

If you would like to play, first ask the owner or staff for permission and find out when you can play.

Mind the volume when you play, so you do not disturb other people's rest. You can also take the chance to feel how a different piano responds.

## Using Waiting Time

When waiting for a train or a flight, or while riding in a vehicle, you often have some spare time.

You can put on headphones and listen to the pieces you are learning, noticing how the performer handles tempo and dynamics.

You can also open the score and look at the structure, finding where things repeat and where they change.

## Practising in Your Head

Look at the score and "play" the piece through in your head, imagining the movements of your fingers and the sound.

If you cannot remember the fingering for a certain spot, mark it in the score and check it on the piano when you get home.

**Think about it**

Mental practice does not need a piano, but it can help you stay familiar with the piece.

## FAQ

**Q: Will I get worse if I do not practise for a week of travel?**
A: Your touch may be a little slower to return, but a few days of playing at home is usually enough to get it back.

**Q: Do I need to bring a portable keyboard?**
A: You can decide based on the length of the trip and your needs. It is not essential.

**Q: Can I play the piano at a hotel?**
A: Ask the staff for permission first, and pay attention to the rules of use.

**Q: What can I practise in the car?**
A: You can listen to recordings, read the score and do mental practice.

**Q: What should I practise first when I get home?**
A: Play familiar pieces first to find your feel again, then gradually return to your usual practice.

**Q: Should children practise while travelling?**
A: You can introduce music in a relaxed way, without putting too much pressure on them.

practice-on-the-acoustic-piano-voice-set.body:
Digital pianos usually have many sounds: piano, electric piano, organ, strings, synthesiser and so on. These sounds are fun, and trying them now and then can bring enjoyment. But when you are practising piano repertoire, you should normally choose a sound that imitates the acoustic piano, the familiar "grand piano" or "piano" sound. Different sounds differ in attack, sustain and response to touch, so practising with another sound may distort our sense of touch and tone.

## Summary: The Piano Sound

Digital pianos have many sounds. When practising piano repertoire, choose the sound that imitates the acoustic piano, because other sounds differ in attack, sustain and response to touch; for example, an organ sound has no dynamic variation, and an electric piano sound may lead you to misjudge your touch.

**Pay attention to the details**

Choose one natural piano sound with a rich response to touch and keep it unchanged, keep reverb low or turn it off, do not use effects such as chorus and delay or layered sounds when practising, and use other sounds for variety.

Check the sound before every practice, children can play with other sounds after practising, see the manual for how to set it, and tell Teacher Aum about your settings.

## The Electric Piano Sound

The electric piano sound is warm and rounded, and is often used in pop and jazz.

But its tone differs from the acoustic piano, and its response to touch is different too.

If you practise classical piano repertoire, using the electric piano sound may lead us to misjudge our own touch.

## Children and the Many Sounds

Children may be curious about all the different sounds and like to switch around.

Parents can agree with the child to use the piano sound while practising, and to play with other sounds for a while afterwards.

Practice is not compromised, and the child's curiosity has an outlet.

## Which Piano Sound to Choose

Some digital pianos have several piano sounds, for example bright, soft and concert.

You can choose one that sounds natural and has a rich response to touch as your everyday practice sound.

Once chosen, keep it unchanged as far as possible, so that your ears get used to this sound.

**Common misunderstandings**
- Choose the piano sound when practising piano repertoire
- Other sounds differ in response to touch and sustain
- Do not set reverb and effects too high
- Other sounds can be used for variety

## Reverb Settings

Many digital pianos can add a reverb effect, making the sound seem to come from a hall.

A moderate amount of reverb makes the sound more pleasant, but if it is set too high it hides the details of touch and pedalling.

When practising, you can set the reverb lower, or turn it off.

## Layering Two Sounds

Some digital pianos can layer two sounds together, such as piano and strings.

This sound is very full, but when practising piano repertoire it hides the sound of the piano itself.

You can use it when playing for fun, and turn it off when practising.

![A high-angle view of an older person playing an open grand piano on a rainy, neon-lit street at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa9w18a-vaesn.webp)

## Other Effects

Some digital pianos also have effects such as chorus and delay.

These effects are generally not needed when practising piano repertoire.

Keeping the sound clean makes it easier to hear the details of your playing.

## Tell Your Teacher About the Sound Settings

You can tell Teacher Aum which sound and settings you use on your digital piano.

If the lessons are on an acoustic piano, the teacher can help judge whether your touch has gone off because of the sound settings.

When needed, you can ask the teacher to suggest suitable settings.

## Other Sounds for Variety

Although you normally practise with the piano sound, trying other sounds now and then is also fun.

For example, play a piece by Bach with an organ sound, or a pop song with an electric piano sound.

This brings freshness and also lets us feel the characteristics of different instruments.

## Check Every Time You Switch On

Some digital pianos return to the default sound when switched on, while others keep the sound last used.

If other people at home also use the piano, the sound may have been changed.

Before each practice, you can first check whether it is set to the piano sound.

## The Many Sounds of a Digital Piano

Digital pianos usually have many built-in sounds that can imitate the sounds of all kinds of instruments.

For example electric piano, pipe organ, harpsichord, strings, voices and so on.

These sounds give a digital piano many more uses.

## Why Choose the Piano Sound

When practising piano repertoire, the aim is to learn to express music on the piano.

The piano sound imitates the sound of the acoustic piano, including attack, sustain and changes of dynamics.

Only by practising with the piano sound can you develop the right feel for the sound of the piano.

## How to Set the Sound

Different models of digital piano select sounds in different ways.

Some have dedicated buttons, and some need you to choose in a menu.

You can check the manual to find how to select the piano sound and how to restore the default settings.

## How Other Sounds Differ

Different sounds may respond to touch completely differently.

For example, with an organ sound, the volume is the same however you press the key, and the note keeps sounding as long as you hold it.

Practising with such a sound, you cannot practise the dynamic control and natural decay of the piano.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What sound should I use when practising piano repertoire?**
A: The sound that imitates the acoustic piano.

**Q: What is the problem with the organ sound?**
A: The volume does not change with touch, and it keeps sounding as long as you hold the key.

**Q: How high should the reverb be?**
A: Low, or turned off.

**Q: Can I use other sounds?**
A: Yes, for variety, trying them now and then.

**Q: What should I check before practising?**
A: Whether it is set to the piano sound.

practice-the-hardest-section-first.body:
Many people are used to starting every practice session at bar one. By the time they reach the difficult passage, they have already spent a lot of time and energy, and the hard part ends up with the least practice. The result is a piece whose opening is very familiar but which gets shakier the further it goes, with the hardest section staying a weak spot. One way to adjust is to practise the hardest section of the piece first, at the start of your session when your focus is strongest, and then move on to the rest. That way the difficult passage gets more practice, and better practice.

## Hard Spots Change

As you practise, the section that used to be hard may become comfortable, and a new difficult spot may appear.

So before each session, think again about which section most needs work today.

Adjust your focus according to where the piece stands.

## When Preparing for a Performance

When you are preparing for a performance, the hard spots need special attention.

Each day you can practise the hard spot first, then play the whole piece through to imitate the feeling of performing.

That way, when the performance comes, the hard spot will be something you can rely on.

## Do Not Neglect the Whole

Practising the hard section first does not mean you never need to play from start to finish.

Playing straight through helps you get to know the structure and the mood of the whole piece.

After you have worked on the hard spot, you can schedule one complete run-through.

## Start from Different Places

Besides practising the hard section first, you can also start from a different place in the piece each day.

For example, start from the second section today and from the third section tomorrow.

That way every part gets a chance to be practised when you are fresh.

## Find the Hard Section First

Before you practise, think about which section of the piece is the hardest or the least familiar.

It might be a technical difficulty, or it might be a passage you can never quite remember.

Mark it, and make it the first item of today's practice.

## Keep Track of Progress on the Hard Spot

Beside the score, you can write down the speed you reached on the hard spot each day, for example "played it smoothly at 60 beats per minute today".

Looking back a few days later, you will see the speed creeping up.

A record like this lets you see your progress clearly and know where to go next.

## When Your Focus Is Sharpest

The first stretch of a practice session is usually when your concentration is at its best.

Working on difficult material then is more effective and solves problems faster.

If you leave the hard spot until the end, you may already be tired, and the quality of your practice will drop.

- Always starting at bar one means the hard spot gets little practice
- The opening feels familiar, while the later parts and the hard spot do not
- Practise the hardest section first, while your focus is sharp
- The hard spot gets more practice, and better practice

## Familiar Opening, Unfamiliar Ending

Many people have had this feeling when performing: the opening goes smoothly, but the further they get, the less sure they feel.

This is often because, in everyday practice, the opening was practised a lot and the later parts only a little.

When they reach the hard spot, mistakes become even more likely.

## Hardest-First Practice: A Summary

If you always start from bar one, the hard spot often gets the least practice, so the opening is familiar while the later parts and the hard spot are not.

When your focus is sharp, you can do a short warm-up, then work on the hardest section of the piece, solving it slowly with suitable methods, and then practise the rest.

You can also start from a different place each day, re-judge which spot is hard as things change, keep the whole piece in mind, and give the hard spot priority even more when preparing for a performance.

![A person wearing headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two windows showing a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6t72y-i9yil.webp)

## A Short Warm-Up First

Before you work on the hard spot, you can warm up for a minute or two, for example by playing a few scales.

This loosens the fingers and avoids putting too much force into the difficult passage right away.

After the warm-up, go straight into practising the hard spot.

## Then Practise the Rest

After you have worked on the hard spot, practise the other parts of the piece, or play it through from the beginning.

You will notice that the hard spot now goes more smoothly than before.

The other parts still need practice too, but they can have less time.

## How to Practise the Hard Spot

When practising the hard spot, you can use slow tempo, hands separately, grouping notes, rhythm variations and similar methods.

Solve the problem a small piece at a time, and do not rush to join it up.

Once it feels fairly smooth, connect it with the parts before and after.

## How Far to Take the Hard Spot

Practising the hard spot first each day does not mean you have to get it completely right that same day.

As long as it is a little smoother than yesterday, that is progress, and you can use several correct repetitions in a row as the standard for the day.

After a few days, the hard spot will slowly become one of the more dependable parts of the piece.

## Give the Hard Spot a Name

You can give the hard spots in a piece a name, such as "the jump on page two" or "the fast scale in the middle".

That way, before each session, you can quickly remember what to practise first.

It also makes it easier to talk with your teacher.

## The Habit of Starting from the Beginning

Starting from bar one is a natural habit for many people, as if the piece would be incomplete otherwise.

But this means the opening gets practised especially often, and the later parts less and less.

**Another way to look at it**

If the hard spot is in the middle or toward the end of the piece, it often does not get enough practice.

## FAQ

**Q: What is the problem with always starting at bar one?**
A: The hard spot gets the least practice.

**Q: When should I practise the hard spot?**
A: When your focus is sharp, at the start of your session.

**Q: What should I do before practising the hard spot?**
A: A simple one-to-two-minute warm-up.

**Q: Do I still need to play from start to finish?**
A: Yes, schedule one run-through after you have worked on the hard spot.

**Q: Does the hard spot always stay the same?**
A: No, it changes, so judge it again each time.

purcell-dido-and-aeneas-chelsea-1689.body:
Dido and Aeneas is a short opera by the English composer Henry Purcell. The earliest performance we can now confirm took place around 1689 at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea, London, with the school's students taking part. The story is taken from the epic of the ancient Roman poet Virgil: the Trojan hero Aeneas arrives in Carthage and falls in love with Dido, the ruler of Carthage, but is then ordered to leave, and Dido is overcome with grief. At the end of the opera, Dido sings the famous When I am laid in earth, while the bass voice repeats a slowly descending melody, which has become a passage often mentioned in Baroque music.

## Dido and Aeneas

Dido, the ruler of Carthage, warmly welcomes Aeneas, and the two fall in love.

But Aeneas receives an order that he must leave Carthage to found a new city in Italy.

He decides to go, and Dido is heartbroken.

## What Is a Ground Bass

When the bass voice repeats the same melody over and over while the upper voices vary freely, this way of writing is called a "ground bass".

It is very common in Baroque music, and many dances and arias use it.

Purcell was especially skilled at writing ground basses, and When I am laid in earth is a very good example.

- A short opera by the English composer Henry Purcell
- Performed around 1689 at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea, London
- Based on Virgil's epic
- The closing When I am laid in earth uses a repeating descending bass

## The Repeating Descending Bass

The bass voice of When I am laid in earth repeats the same melody again and again.

This melody moves slowly downwards from high to low, one semitone at a time, like a long sigh.

It repeats over and over, while the singing above it keeps changing.

## A Short Opera

The whole of Dido and Aeneas lasts only about an hour, which is very short for an opera.

It is divided into three acts, with solos, choruses and dance passages.

In such a short span, it tells a complete and moving story.

## Keep the Left Hand Steady

When playing a ground bass, the left hand must be very steady, playing every repetition equally evenly.

The right-hand melody can be freer, with rise and fall and breath.

One hand steady and one hand flexible is exactly the charm of this way of writing.

## An Opera at a School

The earliest performance of Dido and Aeneas that we can now confirm was around 1689 at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea, London.

The school was run by a dancing master, and the students took part in the performance.

Some scholars also think it may have been written or performed earlier, but there is no definite record.

## Who Was Purcell?

Henry Purcell was an English composer of the second half of the seventeenth century who worked in London.

He wrote church music, incidental music for the theatre, songs and instrumental music, and is very important in the history of English music.

His life was not long, but he left a large number of works.

![A black grand piano and stool in front of a gold and red stippled background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbj3yb3-fa8vy.webp)

## An Opera in English

At that time, most opera in Europe was sung in Italian.

Dido and Aeneas uses English, with words by the poet Nahum Tate.

It is a very important early English-language opera in Britain.

## When I Am Laid in Earth

At the end of the opera, Dido sings a sad aria, When I am laid in earth.

She asks people to remember her but to forget her fate.

The melody of this aria is deeply felt and is often taken out and sung on its own.

## Playing a Descending Bass on the Piano

At the piano, you can use your left hand to play a descending chromatic bass slowly, from one note down to the note a fourth lower.

Repeat it several times and listen to the sad feeling it brings.

Then try playing a simple melody above it with your right hand, and experience this way of writing a ground bass.

## Dido and Aeneas Summary

Dido and Aeneas is a short opera by the English composer Henry Purcell of the second half of the seventeenth century, with words by Nahum Tate, sung in English. The earliest performance we can now confirm was around 1689 at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea, London. The story is taken from Virgil's Aeneid: the Trojan hero Aeneas arrives in Carthage, falls in love with its ruler Dido, and is then ordered to leave.

The whole opera lasts about an hour and has three acts. The closing aria When I am laid in earth uses a chromatically descending ground bass that returns again and again, with the singing above it constantly changing. At the piano, the left hand can play the steady ground bass while the right hand plays the melody freely.

You can try the ground bass together with Teacher Aum.

## Virgil's Epic

The opera's story is taken from the epic the Aeneid by the ancient Roman poet Virgil.

The epic tells how, after the fall of Troy, the hero Aeneas wanders with his companions in search of a new home.

On the way, he comes to the city of Carthage in North Africa.

In a lesson you can work with Teacher Aum, playing the ground bass with the left hand and improvising a melody with the right.

You can also chat with your teacher about the story of Dido and Aeneas and the history of English-language opera.

From an opera performed at a school, get to know the Baroque ground bass.

A: The English composer Henry Purcell.

**Q: Where was the earliest performance we can now confirm?**
A: A girls' boarding school in Chelsea, London, around 1689.

**Q: Which work is the story taken from?**
A: Virgil's epic the Aeneid.

**Q: What is the aria at the end of the opera called?**
A: When I am laid in earth.

**Q: What is a ground bass?**
A: The bass repeats the same melody while the upper voices vary freely.

practicing-in-shared-spaces.body:
When you play in a community activity room, a school practice room or another shared space, keep an eye on your volume, the time you take and the people around you. Find out the rules of the venue first, choose a suitable time, keep your volume under control, and tidy the piano and its surroundings when you finish. When you look after others, your own practice feels more relaxed too, and everyone can share the piano comfortably.

## Controlling Volume and Repertoire

A public space is different from your home, and the sound may carry further than you expect. You can play a few notes softly first, listen to the echo, and then decide on your overall volume.

**Another way to look at it**

When practising technical passages, hammering the same spot over and over may irritate the people nearby. You can play more softly, or save the repetitive work for home.

In an open space, choosing pieces with a clear melody and a calm mood often makes it easier to get along with the surroundings.

If the venue is very quiet, you can also give priority to practising slow, lyrical sections, and save the passages that need loud practice for home or a soundproofed practice room.

## Choosing a Suitable Time

Shared spaces have many users: some are reading, some are in meetings, some are resting. Try to choose times when few people are around or when playing is clearly allowed.

In the morning and at lunchtime, people nearby may need quiet; in the evening and at weekends there is more going on, and the sound of a piano is usually easier to accept.

If it is a shared practice room, you can agree on turns with the other users so that everyone gets a full session.

## Learn the Venue Rules First

Different shared spaces work in different ways. Some practice rooms need to be booked in advance, some activity rooms are only open at certain hours, and some places let you play at any time but would rather the sound was not too loud.

On your first visit, you can look at the notice at the door or ask a member of staff. Starting once you know the rules helps you avoid unnecessary misunderstandings.

If the venue has a sign-up sheet, remember to write down your time slot so that others can plan.

Some venues also have rules about whether you may bring food and whether you may record or film, and these details are worth asking about in advance.

## Take Good Care of the Piano

A piano in a shared space is used by many people, so it needs even more care. Wash your hands before playing, and do not put drinks or food on the piano.

Do not bang the keys or put heavy objects on the piano. If you notice a problem, such as a key that does not sound or a loose pedal, tell the staff rather than trying to fix it yourself.

Before you leave, close the lid, push the bench back into place, and take your music and belongings with you, so the next person finds a tidy piano.

If you adjusted the height of the bench, you can set it back roughly to where it was before you go, so the next player can sit down and start.

## When Someone Is Waiting

If you see someone waiting to use the piano, you can estimate how much longer you need and tell them, or give up your place at the end of a section.

A shared piano suffers most when one person occupies it for a long time. Set yourself a time limit, such as twenty or thirty minutes, and when it is up, finish or ask whether anyone else needs the piano.

Polite communication often makes everyone feel comfortable, and sometimes you meet someone who loves music too.

**Summary**
- Check the opening hours and rules of the venue first
- Control your volume and repertoire to suit the setting
- Watch how long you play when someone is waiting
- Before leaving, close the lid and tidy the bench and music stand

![A high-angle view of an open black piano being played on a neon-lit street on a rainy night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wv0le-v5kiz.webp)

## Treat It as a Small Performance

When you play in a shared space, people will inevitably pass by and stop to listen. You can treat this as a chance to practise playing in front of an audience.

There is no need to get so nervous that you stop just because someone is listening. Simply keep to your own pace.

If someone comes over to chat, you can respond in a friendly way. Sharing music is one of the reasons public pianos exist, but respect your own need to practise too, and do what you are comfortable with.

Every time you play a piece through successfully in a shared space, you build experience of playing for other people, which also helps a great deal when you perform on stage later.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I practise with headphones in a shared practice room?**
A: If it is a digital piano, yes. Headphones will not disturb others and make it easier to concentrate.

**Q: What if I get nervous when passers-by watch me?**
A: Start with a piece you know well and keep your attention on the music, and you will gradually get used to it.

**Q: Can I practise very difficult passages on a public piano?**
A: Yes, but watch your volume when repeating them, or save intensive repetition for a more private place.

**Q: What should I do if the piano is out of tune?**
A: Tell the staff, who can arrange for it to be tuned. Do not adjust it yourself.

**Q: What should children keep in mind when playing in a shared space?**
A: Parents can agree on the rules with the child beforehand, such as volume, time and looking after the piano.

**Q: Do I need to book a public piano?**
A: It depends on the venue. Some need a sign-up and some can be used at any time, so it is safest to ask before you go.
