progress-video-student-retention.body:
Progress in learning an instrument is often slow and subtle: the hand position a little steadier, the rhythm a little more accurate, the reading a little faster. Children change every day, but parents find it hard to notice, especially parents who are not musical and often see only "several months in, still the same few pieces." When parents cannot feel the value, they may hesitate at renewal time, and the student is lost. A progress video is a simple and effective method: every so often, record the child playing the same kind of material, and present the before-and-after comparison clearly. Growth you can see helps parents understand their child's effort, and gives the child more confidence to keep learning music.

## Forms a Progress Video Can Take

- Same-piece comparison: record the same piece once in week one and once in week four
- Skill clip: record just one skill, such as a left-hand accompaniment pattern or a scale passage
- Monthly highlights: cut together several of the month's best moments
- Term review: the changes from the first lesson to the last lesson at the end of a term

## Recording Tips

**Fixed camera position**
Film from the same angle every time, for example from above and to the side to show the hands and keys, so the before-and-after comparison is clear.

**Say what to look for before recording**
The teacher can use one sentence at the start of the video to explain what to watch for this time, for example "this time, notice whether the left hand is even", so parents know where to focus.

**Keep it short**
Keep each video under a minute. Parents are more willing to watch it all, and it is easier to save.

![An illustration of a grand piano in red, orange and yellow ink lines on a white background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw169qj4-kzbkt.webp)

## Add a Short Note

A video only shows what the playing looked like; a short written note is what helps parents truly understand. The note can have three parts: what was practised during this period, where the progress is, and what to practise next. The tone should be mainly encouraging but honest, neither exaggerating progress nor avoiding problems. For example: "This month the right-hand melody became more connected. The left-hand jumps still need more practice, and next month we will focus on coordinating both hands." A note like this is more convincing than vague praise.

## Privacy and Safety Come First

Progress videos involve images of minors and must be handled carefully. Obtain the parents' consent before recording and explain what the video will be used for: whether it is sent only to the parents themselves, or might be used in the studio's public promotion. By default, send videos privately only; public use requires separate written consent. When filming, try to show only the hands and keys, and avoid showing the child's face, school uniform, home address and similar information. Store video files carefully, and delete them or hand them back as agreed after a student stops lessons.

## Progress Videos and Retention

When parents receive progress videos regularly, they come to expect it: every month they can see how their child is changing. This ongoing communication makes parents feel that the studio is paying real attention to their child, and not just charging for lessons. At renewal time, parents already hold a series of records and can see directly what their investment has produced. Even if progress is not obvious for a while, the teacher can use the note to explain why, for example that they are working through a difficult spot, so parents stay patient.

## Let the Child Take Part Too

Progress videos are not only for parents. Letting children listen to a recording from a month ago and compare it with now is often more effective than a teacher saying "you've improved" a hundred times. Encourage the child to describe the changes they hear, which builds the ability to evaluate their own playing. Gradually, children learn to judge their own playing by ear, which matters a great deal for learning an instrument over the long term.

## How Parents Can Respond

After receiving a progress video, the parents' response also affects the child. Teachers can give parents some suggestions in the note:

- Name one specific improvement first, for example "this phrase is more connected than last time"
- Ask the child what was hardest about practising this piece
- Do not compare with other children; compare only with the child's own past
- Save the video, and look back at it together with the child at the end of the term

## Tools and Workload

You do not need professional equipment; a phone and a stable stand are enough. To keep the teacher's workload under control, schedule the recording for one fixed lesson each month and set aside a few minutes in that lesson to record everything together. Editing does not need to be complicated either; simply trimming the beginning and end is enough. Some practice apps can also log practice automatically and can serve as supplementary material.

## FAQ

**Q: How often should I make a progress video?**
A: Once a month is common. It is enough to show change without burdening teachers or parents.

**Q: Should I still send one when progress is not obvious?**
A: Yes, and explain in the note which difficult spot is being worked on, so parents understand the learning process.

**Q: What if a parent does not agree to filming?**
A: Respect the parent's decision. You can report progress with written notes or audio-only recordings instead.

**Q: Can progress videos be posted in a parents' group chat?**
A: This is not recommended. Each child's video should be sent separately to that child's own parents, to avoid comparisons and privacy problems.

puccini-o-mio-babbino-caro-1918-aria.body:
O mio babbino caro ("Oh my dear father") is an aria from the one-act comic opera Gianni Schicchi by the Italian composer Puccini, which premiered in New York in December 1918. In the opera, the daughter Lauretta sings it to beg her father to help her be with the one she loves. The whole aria lasts only a little over two minutes, and its melody is tender and broad, one of Puccini's best-loved tunes. It has many instrumental arrangements, and playing it on the piano lets you practise a singing melody and natural breathing.

## Lyricism in a Comedy

The whole of Gianni Schicchi moves quickly and is full of comic scenes.

This aria is like a quiet, gentle window suddenly opening in the middle of a lively comedy.

With this kind of contrast, Puccini makes his characters more alive.

## Who Was Puccini?

Giacomo Puccini (1858-1924) was an Italian opera composer, born into a musical family in Lucca.

His operas have beautiful melodies and sincere feeling, for example La bohème, Tosca and Madama Butterfly.

To this day, his works remain among the most frequently performed in opera houses around the world.

## Just Over Two Minutes

The aria lasts just over two minutes and is only a small part of the whole opera.

But its melody is very moving, and it is often taken out and sung on its own in concerts.

Many people know this song without knowing it comes from a comedy.

## Asking Your Teacher to Listen to Lauretta's Melody in a Lesson

You can play for Teacher Aum in a lesson and ask your teacher to listen to whether the melodic phrases rise and fall.

How long to linger on the high point of a phrase to make it sound natural can also be tried several different ways in the lesson.

From one aria, you experience the tenderness of Puccini's melodies.

## Lauretta's Long Phrases

The melody begins in the middle register, slowly rises, lingers at the top of the phrase, and then gently comes back down.

The phrases are long, and each one is like a long breath.

When playing, make every phrase rise and fall, as if you were singing.

**Notice the details**
- Puccini's one-act comic opera Gianni Schicchi
- Premiered in New York in December 1918
- The daughter Lauretta pleads with her father
- The whole piece lasts just over two minutes

## O mio babbino caro Summary

O mio babbino caro comes from Puccini's (1858-1924) one-act comic opera Gianni Schicchi. This opera is the comedy among a set of three one-act operas from 1918 and premiered in New York in December 1918. The story is set in thirteenth-century Florence and draws on a character mentioned in Dante's Divine Comedy. The daughter Lauretta sings this song to plead for her father's help, and the words mention an old street, an old bridge and the Arno river. The whole piece lasts just over two minutes.

The melody is broad and the phrases are long, like a quiet window opening in the middle of a lively comedy. In the piano version, the right-hand melody should be full, the left-hand accompaniment light and steady, and the tempo can broaden slightly at the high point of a phrase.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to the rise and fall of the melody.

## The Story of Gianni Schicchi

The story is set in thirteenth-century Florence. A rich old man has died, and his relatives discover that his will leaves all his property to a monastery.

The relatives have no choice but to ask the clever Gianni Schicchi to think of a solution.

The story draws on a character mentioned in Dante's Divine Comedy, which Puccini turned into a lively comedy.

![A person with headphones plays a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a neon tiga STUDIO sign between two windows showing a city at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwbi19la-1sevv.webp)

## Why So Many People Love It

This aria has a simple, moving melody and direct feeling, with no complicated technique.

It often appears in films and in all kinds of performances, so that many people who never listen to opera know it too.

For piano learners, it is a good piece for practising a singing melody.

## Florence in the Words

In the song, Lauretta says she wants to go to an old street in Florence to buy a wedding ring.

She also mentions the old bridge in the city and the Arno river that flows through it.

These place names give the aria a strong flavour of Florence.

## Playing O mio babbino caro on the Piano

Piano arrangements usually have the right hand play the melody and the left hand accompany with broken chords or block chords.

The melody should be played full and connected, and the accompaniment light and steady.

You can first sing the melody, feel the breathing of the words, and then imitate it at the piano.

## The Daughter's Plea

At first Gianni Schicchi is unwilling to help, because the relatives look down on him.

His daughter Lauretta has fallen in love with a young man from one of those families and is very anxious.

So she sings O mio babbino caro, saying how much she wants to be with the one she loves and asking her father to help no matter what.

## Flexible Tempo in an Aria

The tempo of an opera aria is often fairly free, and singers will linger slightly at the high point of a phrase.

When imitating this at the piano, you can pause a moment longer on the highest note of each of Lauretta's phrases.

But the accompaniment must not become disordered; it must always give the melody a steady support.

## Three One-Act Operas

In 1918, Puccini completed a set of three one-act operas, intended to be performed one after another on the same evening.

The three operas differ in style: one is a tragedy, one is set in a convent, and the last is a comedy.

**Slow down**

Gianni Schicchi is that last comedy, and it is also the most often performed of the three.

## FAQ

**Q: Which opera does O mio babbino caro come from?**
A: Puccini's one-act comic opera Gianni Schicchi.

**Q: In what year did the opera premiere?**
A: December 1918, in New York.

**Q: Who sings this aria?**
A: The daughter Lauretta in the opera.

**Q: In which city is the story set?**
A: Thirteenth-century Florence.

**Q: About how long is this aria?**
A: Just over two minutes.

pythagorean-tuning-stacked-fifths.body:
Pythagorean tuning is a very ancient tuning system, and its method is very simple: starting from one note, you stack pure fifths one after another, each with a frequency ratio of three to two, then move the resulting notes into the same octave to get a scale. In this tuning, the fifths and fourths are very pure, but the major third is considerably wider than in just intonation, and it sounds rather tense. Medieval European music often relied on fifths and fourths as its main consonant intervals, which fits the character of Pythagorean tuning well. Its name comes from Pythagoras of ancient Greece, who is said to have studied the relationship between pitch and numbers.

## Pythagorean Tuning in Brief

Pythagorean tuning starts from one note, stacks 3:2 pure fifths one after another, and moves the notes back into the same octave. Stacking six times gives a natural scale. Twelve pure fifths come out slightly higher than seven octaves, by about a quarter of a semitone, and this gap is called the Pythagorean comma.

**Before you try it**

The fifths and fourths are very pure. The major third is 81:64, wider than the 5:4 of just intonation. It suits medieval music, which treated the octave, fifth and fourth as its consonances. The blacksmith story is more legend; the claim that he studied pitch through string lengths is more reliable. In the Renaissance, thirds became more and more important, and people turned to meantone tuning.

The idea of the circle of fifths is similar to stacking fifths. Equal temperament narrows the fifths slightly so the circle closes. On the piano you can play a string of fifths to feel this, and you can chat about the topic with Teacher Aum.

## The Circle of Fifths and Pythagorean Tuning

The idea of the circle of fifths is very similar to the Pythagorean method of stacking fifths.

Line up C, G, D, A and so on all the way round, and the twelve keys form the circle of fifths.

In equal temperament, the fifths are narrowed by a tiny amount, which is why this circle can close perfectly.

## Feeling Fifths on the Piano

On the piano, you can play a string of pure fifths, such as C and G, G and D, D and A, and listen to the open, stable sound of the fifth.

The fifth in equal temperament is only a tiny bit narrower than a pure fifth, and it sounds almost equally pure.

Then play a major third, such as C and E, and notice its slight wobble.

## Talking About Pythagorean Tuning in the Lesson

In the lesson, you can chat with Teacher Aum about the relationship between Pythagorean tuning and the circle of fifths.

You can also play a string of fifths together on the piano and feel the process of stacking fifths.

This knowledge can help you understand the relationships between keys.

## The Limits of Pythagorean Tuning

Because the major third is too wide, Pythagorean tuning is not suited to music built on triads.

By the Renaissance, thirds and sixths were becoming more and more important in music.

People began looking for new tuning systems, such as meantone, to make the thirds purer.

## The Legend of Pythagoras

Pythagoras was a philosopher and mathematician of ancient Greece.

The story goes that he walked past a blacksmith's shop and heard hammers of different weights striking harmonious sounds, and so he began to study the relationship between pitch and numbers.

The story is very famous, but its details do not match physical fact, so it is more of a legend.

![Close-up of piano keys in soft light](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwab2wk0-1qoim.webp)

## String Length and Pitch

The more reliable account is that the ancient Greeks studied pitch using a single string.

Shorten the string by half and the pitch rises by an octave; shorten it to two thirds and the pitch rises by a pure fifth.

This way of understanding intervals through simple ratios influenced later music theory.

## Pythagorean Tuning Today

Today, some ensembles that perform medieval music use Pythagorean tuning.

String players, when playing melodies, sometimes also play the major third and the leading note a little higher, which resembles the character of Pythagorean tuning.

This shows that different approaches to tuning still exist in performance today.

## Comparing with Other Tunings

In Pythagorean tuning the fifths are purest and the thirds widest. In meantone the thirds are pure but the fifths are narrow. Equal temperament compromises between the two.

Every tuning system is a trade-off between different intervals.

Understanding these trade-offs helps us understand how sound has changed through music history.

## The Pythagorean Comma

If you keep stacking twelve pure fifths, in theory you should return to the note name you started from, for example from C back to C.

In reality, however, twelve pure fifths come out slightly higher than seven octaves, and this difference is called the Pythagorean comma.

This gap is about a quarter of a semitone, and it stops the twelve fifths from closing perfectly.

## Consonant Intervals in Medieval Music

In medieval European music, the octave, fifth and fourth were regarded as perfectly consonant intervals.

Thirds and sixths were seen as less consonant intervals and were rarely used at cadences.

This fits the character of Pythagorean tuning well: fifths and fourths are pure, while thirds are wide and tense.

## The Seven-Note Scale

Stack six pure fifths, from F to C, G, D, A, E and B, and you have seven notes.

Arrange them within one octave and you get F, G, A, B, C, D, E, which is a natural scale.

Keep stacking and you can also get the semitones such as F♯ and C♯.

## Stacking Pure Fifths

Pythagorean tuning starts from one note, say F, then stacks a pure fifth upward to get C, then another to get G, and so on.

Each pure fifth has a frequency ratio of three to two.

If a resulting note goes beyond one octave, lower it by one or more octaves to bring it back into the same octave range.

## The Wide Major Third

In Pythagorean tuning, the major third is built from four pure fifths, with a ratio of eighty-one to sixty-four.

This is considerably wider than the 5:4 major third of just intonation.

So in Pythagorean tuning, the major third sounds rather tense and not very consonant.

- Stack 3:2 pure fifths one after another
- Fifths and fourths are very pure
- The major third is wide, with a ratio of 81:64
- It suits medieval music built mainly on fifths and fourths

## FAQ

**Q: How does Pythagorean tuning produce a scale?**
A: By stacking 3:2 pure fifths one after another.

**Q: What is the ratio of the major third in Pythagorean tuning?**
A: 81:64.

**Q: What is the Pythagorean comma?**
A: The amount by which twelve pure fifths come out higher than seven octaves.

**Q: Why does it suit medieval music?**
A: Medieval music used fifths and fourths as its main consonant intervals.

**Q: Is the blacksmith story reliable?**
A: It is more of a legend; its details do not match physical fact.

pre-practice-desk-setup-one-minute.body:
You sit down at the piano, play for a few minutes, and only then find that your pencil is not within reach, you cannot find the metronome, or the music you are meant to practise today is still in your school bag. Getting up to look for it scatters your attention. You can build a one-minute habit: before you start practising, put out what you need, such as today's music, a pencil and eraser, the metronome, a glass of water and your practice notebook. Once everything is ready, start, and you will not need to keep getting up during practice.

## A Checklist for Children

Parents can help a child draw a practice-supplies card, with the music, pencil and water glass drawn as little icons, and stick it beside the piano.

Before each practice, the child looks at the list, puts each item out and ticks it off.

This gives the child a stronger sense of responsibility and helps them settle into practice mode more quickly.

## Getting Ready Before Practice: A Summary

Going off to find things halfway through practice interrupts your attention, so before you start you can spend one minute preparing: today's music, pencil and eraser, the metronome, a glass of water and your practice notebook.

While you are at it, adjust the bench, check the light and temperature, keep distractions such as your phone out of reach, and do not put the water glass on the piano.

Children can use a checklist with pictures, and tidy up after practice too, so that getting ready next time is quicker.

## The Practice Notebook

A practice notebook can be used to write today's plan, record how practice went, or note the first thing to do tomorrow.

Open it to today's page and put it where you can see it easily.

When you finish practising, jot down a few lines in it.

- Going to find things halfway through breaks your attention
- Spend one minute preparing before you start
- Music, pencil and eraser, metronome, water, practice notebook
- Start once everything is ready

## One Minute of Preparation

Before you begin practising, spend one minute getting what you need ready.

This minute looks very short, but it makes the practice that follows more continuous.

Gradually it becomes a natural little ritual before every practice.

## Move Distractions Away

While preparing, you can put away things you do not need, such as your phone, toys and snacks.

If you need your phone to record or to use as a metronome, set it to do-not-disturb mode.

The tidier your desk and the piano top are, the easier it is to concentrate.

![A glowing teal grand piano on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa76xhh-1l373.webp)

## Today's Music

First find the music you are going to practise today, and put it on the music stand or beside it in the order you will practise.

If you have several books, you can use bookmarks or sticky notes to mark today's pages.

That way, when you finish one piece, you can turn straight to the next.

## Light and Temperature

Check whether the light in the room is bright enough and whether the notes on the page are easy to see.

If the room is too cold or too hot, you can adjust that first as well.

A comfortable environment helps you concentrate on practice.

## Tidy Up After Practice Too

After practice, spend a minute putting things away: return the music to its usual place and the pencil to the music stand.

That way, getting ready next time will be quicker.

While you tidy, you can also think back over what you practised today.

## Glance at Your Plan While Preparing

Once everything is laid out, you can open your practice notebook and spend a few seconds looking at what you plan to practise first and what comes after.

With the order in mind, you know what the first thing to do is when you sit down, and you will not hesitate over the music for ages.

If you wrote down today's first task the day before, this step only needs a quick read.

## Pencil and Eraser

A pencil and eraser are tools you often use in practice, for marking fingerings, writing in beats and circling hard spots.

Keep them on the music stand or beside the piano, where you can reach them easily.

We use a pencil rather than a pen because marks may need to be changed or erased later.

## A Glass of Water

When a practice session is fairly long, keep a glass of water nearby so you can take a sip when you are thirsty.

But do not put the glass on the piano, in case it is accidentally knocked over and wets the keys or the body of the piano.

You can put it on a small table beside you.

## Adjust the Bench

While preparing, you can also adjust the height and position of the bench, especially if people of different heights share the same piano at home.

Sit down, let your arms rest naturally on the keys, and see whether it is comfortable.

Start once it is adjusted, so you do not discover halfway through that you were sitting wrongly.

## The Metronome

If today's practice needs a metronome, put it ready beforehand and set it to roughly the right tempo.

If you use a metronome app on your phone, you can open it first, then put the phone in a mode where messages will not disturb you.

That way you will not be distracted by phone notifications.

## Interrupted Practice

When practising, the worst thing is to just get into the flow and then be interrupted by having to look for something.

You get up to find a pencil or the music, and when you come back you often have to get back into the mood again.

Sometimes you get distracted while searching and go off to do something else, and the practice session is over.

## FAQ

**Q: Why prepare in advance?**
A: To avoid breaking your attention by going to look for things halfway through.

**Q: What should I prepare?**
A: Music, pencil and eraser, metronome, water, practice notebook.

**Q: Where should the water glass go?**
A: On a small table beside you, not on the piano.

**Q: What should I do about my phone?**
A: When you need it, set it to do-not-disturb mode.

**Q: How should a child prepare?**
A: Use a checklist with pictures and tick items off one by one.

questioning-techniques-piano-lesson.body:
Questioning technique in piano lessons means that the teacher does not rush to say "what is wrong and how to fix it", but uses well-chosen questions to guide the student to listen, observe and think for themselves, and finally find the answer. Telling the answer directly is of course faster, but students often remember only that one correction, and next time a similar problem comes up they still do not know what to do. Through questions, students gradually learn to judge their own playing, and when practising at home they can spot problems the way a teacher would.

## Why Questions Work Better Than Explanations

When students only listen passively in the lesson, they remember little. When a student has to answer a question, the brain must think actively and connect the sounds it hears with what it has learned. This process is a little slower, but the impression it leaves is deeper. More importantly, students spend only a short time with their teacher each week, and most of the time they practise alone, so the ability to judge themselves decides the quality of their practice.

**Give students time to think**
After asking a question, do not answer it yourself right away. Wait quietly for a few seconds and give the student time to think. Often the student actually knows the answer and just needs a little time to put it into words.

## Some Common Types of Questions

![A cartoon student wearing headphones playing a digital piano in a room at night](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw6vehxk-xahty.webp)

Depending on your teaching goal, you can choose different types of questions:

- Listening: "Of these two phrases you just played, which one sounds more connected?"
- Observation: "Look at this bar. What is different about the rhythm in the left hand and the right hand?"
- Comparison: "Play it once at each of two dynamic levels. Which do you prefer, and why?"
- Prediction: "If we play this place more slowly, what effect would that have?"
- Reflection: "In this week's practice, what did you find hardest?"
- Planning: "When you get home, which section will you practise first?"

None of these questions has a standard "right or wrong" answer, and they encourage students to share their own feelings and reasons.

## Start with Simple Questions

For beginners or younger students, questions should be simple and specific. For example, "Is this note long or short?" is easier to answer than "What do you think of how the rhythm is handled in this passage?" As the student's ability grows, the questions can gradually become more open, giving the student more room to express themselves.

**Avoid questions that make students nervous**
A question like "Why did you get it wrong again?" sounds more like criticism, and the student will only feel pressure. Ask in a calm, curious tone, so the student feels the teacher is exploring together with them.

## Using Recordings to Help Answer Questions

Sometimes it is hard for students to hear their own sound clearly while they are playing. The teacher can record the student's playing, play it back together, and then ask: "Can you hear where the rhythm speeds up?" Playback lets the student stand in the listener's position and makes it easier to spot problems. Recordings are used only in the lesson, or kept only after the parents have given their consent.

## When a Student Cannot Answer

If a student thinks for a long time and still cannot answer, the teacher can break the question into smaller parts, or give two options for the student to choose from. For example: "Do you think this place should be played a bit louder, or a bit softer?" When necessary, the teacher can demonstrate both ways of playing and then let the student judge. The aim is to involve the student in the process of judging, not to make the student feel that failing to answer is a failure.

## Bringing the Questioning Habit Home

At the end of the lesson, you can ask the student to sum up one or two things they learned today, and to name one question to ask themselves when practising at home, such as "Is my wrist relaxed?" Parents can also use the same question to gently remind their child while they practise, instead of constantly urging them on. Over time, students will form the good habit of thinking while they practise.

**Parents' questions should be gentle too**
When reminding their child at home, parents can learn from the teacher's way and ask in a curious tone rather than a commanding one.

## Balancing Questions and Explanation

Asking questions does not mean the teacher does not explain. New knowledge, technique and musical background still need to be explained and demonstrated clearly by the teacher. Questions suit places where the student already has some foundation and can judge for themselves. When explanation and questions alternate within a lesson, the student both gains new knowledge and practises thinking independently.

## FAQ

**Q: Will asking questions slow down the pace of the course?**
A: In the short term it may be a little slower, but once students' ability to judge themselves improves, their practice is usually more efficient.

**Q: Is question-based teaching suitable for very young children too?**
A: Yes, as long as the questions are simple and specific and are combined with demonstrations and games.

**Q: What if the student always says "I don't know"?**
A: You can break the question into smaller parts, or offer two options so that the student starts by choosing.

**Q: Will adult students find questions strange?**
A: Most adult students like being invited to think, and it makes them feel more involved.

prokofiev-troika-lieutenant-kije-1934.body:
Troika is the movement of Prokofiev's orchestral suite Lieutenant Kijé that is most often played on its own, catalogued as Op. 60 and completed around 1934. The suite comes from the music he wrote for a film. "Troika" refers to the scene of three horses pulling a sleigh forward; the music is light, with a clear rhythm, and you often hear bright, bell-like sounds. The piece was later arranged for piano as well. When playing the piano version, the most important thing is to keep the light stepping pulse and the clear rhythm steady, so that the sound is bright but not hard, without having to play every note heavily.

## Practise Slowly First, Then Gradually Bring the Tempo Up

The original sounds fast and light, but if you play at the speed of the recording from the very start, it is easy to rush and sound hard.

You can first fix the rhythm and fingering at a moderately slow tempo, then gradually approach the tempo of the score or the recording.

Speeding up a little each day is steadier than raising it too much at once.

## Bright but Not Piercing

The full score often has fairly bright, short sounds, and piano arrangements use staccato or light figures in the high register to approach this effect.

These notes should be bright and short, but not struck so that they sound sharp.

Move the fingertips down and up quickly while keeping the wrist relaxed, and the sound will be crisper.

## Asking Teacher Aum to Listen to the Pulse in Your Lesson

In your lesson, you can ask Teacher Aum to listen to whether the rhythm stays steady throughout and whether the short notes in the high register are being struck too hard.

Where the melody is covered up, you can also ask your teacher to mark which voices need to be played more softly.

From a piece of music depicting a sleigh, you practise playing a light rhythm clearly.

- From Prokofiev's Lieutenant Kijé suite, Op. 60
- The suite was arranged from film music, around 1934
- Depicts three horses pulling a sleigh forward
- Light, clear rhythm, often with bright, bell-like sounds

## Listen to Melody and Accompaniment Separately

Above the light background there is usually also a more singable melody.

First play the melody alone clearly, then add the accompaniment rhythm pattern lightly.

If, once the hands are together, all that is left is "bustle", it means the accompaniment is too heavy or the melodic phrases have not yet taken shape.

## A Light but Clear Rhythm

The beat of this music is quite clear, and the accents often follow a regular pattern, like a sleigh gliding forward one push at a time.

When playing the arrangement, count the beat steadily first, and do not add weight to all the notes at once just to make it "lively".

You can first tap the basic rhythm lightly with your hands, then go back to the piano and check it.

## From Film to Suite

Lieutenant Kijé was originally music Prokofiev wrote for a film, and he later selected several sections from it and arranged them into an orchestral suite.

The suite's opus number is 60 and it was completed around 1934; Troika is one of its most widely known movements.

Even if you have never seen the film, just listening to the music you can feel a scene moving forward, with a chill in the air and laughter.

## Troika Summary

Troika comes from Prokofiev's Lieutenant Kijé suite of around 1934. It comes from film music and depicts three horses pulling a sleigh forward, with a light, clear rhythm and bright tone colours.

For the piano arrangement, use little pedal, first steady the pulse, then let the melody be heard, and gradually increase the tempo.

You can ask Teacher Aum to listen to your pulse and touch.

## Use Little Pedal

In passages like this, with clear rhythm and short, crisp sounds, the pedal should be used sparingly.

If you use too much, the bell-like short notes will blur together and the pulse becomes indistinct.

If a long note needs a little resonance, you can touch the pedal lightly and change it cleanly straight away.

![A collage illustration of a hand in a high-tech glove playing a glowing keyboard against a neon city background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwdiava4-pf8vl.webp)

## What Is a Troika

In the traditional Russian way of travelling, a troika means three horses pulling a sleigh or carriage.

The music is not numbering each horse; it uses a steady rhythm and bright tone colours to approach the feeling of a sleigh moving over snow.

When you listen, you can first catch that pulse which keeps moving forward.

## How to Start with This Troika

The difficulty of piano arrangements depends on the version: some are fairly simple, and some write the orchestra's layers very fully.

An intermediate learner who can already play staccato lightly and keep the rhythm steady can start with a version whose layers are not too crowded.

Listening first to the original orchestral version, then learning the piano arrangement, gives you a better idea of which notes should be bright and which should give way.

## FAQ

**Q: Which work does Troika come from?**
A: Prokofiev's orchestral suite Lieutenant Kijé, Op. 60.

**Q: How is this suite related to the film?**
A: The suite was arranged from the music he wrote for a film.

**Q: What scene does "Troika" refer to?**
A: Three horses pulling a sleigh or carriage forward.

**Q: Why should the pedal be used little in the piano arrangement?**
A: So that the short, bright notes and the clear pulse do not blur together.

**Q: Is it a good idea to play it very fast from the start?**
A: No. First fix the rhythm and fingering, then gradually approach the original tempo.

piano-corner-layout-home.body:
When setting up a piano corner at home, start by thinking about three things: where the piano goes, where the light comes from, and where the music and supplies are kept. The position should be away from direct sun and damp, the lighting should light up the score without glare, and storage should keep the things you use often within easy reach. When the piano corner is set up conveniently, the barrier to sitting down and practising becomes much lower.

## Keep a Clear Path

The walk from the room door to the piano bench should have no obstacles to get around. If every practice begins with moving a chair or shifting a box, your willingness to start wears away little by little.

**Practice order**

Leave enough space around the bench too, so you can sit down and stand up easily and adjust your distance forwards and back.

Keep the area near the pedals clear, run cables along the wall, and avoid anything underfoot that could trip you.

## First, Choose a Good Position

An acoustic piano is sensitive to temperature and humidity. If it stands by a window in direct sun, or directly in front of an air conditioner vent, the wood and strings are easily affected. Placing it against a damp outside wall can also let moisture get into the piano.

An ideal spot is against an interior wall, some distance from windows and vents, with air circulating around it. A digital piano is less demanding about its surroundings, but should still avoid direct sun and water.

Also consider your family's daily habits. In the living room, the whole family can hear it; in a bedroom or study it is quieter. You can decide according to when you practise and the family's routine.

If there is no ideal spot for now, you can put it somewhere workable first, then watch how the piano holds up and how you use it, and adjust gradually.

## Keep the Piano Corner Inviting

When the piano corner is tidy and bright, people naturally want to sit down there. You can put a photo you like or a small plant that does not need frequent watering beside the piano, but do not put a flowerpot on top of it.

Tidy up regularly, put away music you have finished with, and wipe off the dust.

If a child is learning, let them help set it up, for example by choosing the colour of the lamp or displaying their certificates. When a child feels attached to the corner, they will also feel they belong there when practising.

A piano corner does not need to be large. A small space that is clean, bright and has a place for everything is enough to make people want to sit there for a while every day.

## Let the Light Fall on the Score

Reading music needs plentiful, even light. During the day you can use natural light, but take care that the sun does not shine directly on the score, because strong glare tires the eyes quickly.

For evening practice you need a lamp that lights the music stand. Light that comes from above and to one side, without casting the shadow of your hand or head on the score, works well.

Do not leave the rest of the room too dark either. If only the music stand is bright and everything around it is dark, your eyes must keep adjusting to light and dark as you look from score to keys and back, which is uncomfortable.

## Small Arrangements to Reduce Distraction

Try not to place the piano corner directly facing the television. With the TV on, both sound and picture pull attention away and also clash with the piano.

Keep your phone a little distance from the piano, and fetch it when you need the metronome or want to record.

If space at home is limited, you can use a rug or a bookshelf to separate the piano corner visually from the other areas, giving it its own "practice atmosphere".

- Keep the piano away from direct sun, air conditioner vents and damp walls
- The score needs steady, even lighting
- Keep the music you use often beside the piano and put the rest in a cabinet
- Keep the path from the door to the bench clear

![A person wearing headphones playing a dark upright piano by candlelight, with a tiga STUDIO neon sign between two city night windows](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9wt9f8-bousm.webp)

## Storing Music and Supplies

The two or three books you are working on can go on a small shelf beside the piano, or right next to the music stand. Books you have finished can go in a cabinet, arranged by category or difficulty so they are easy to find when you want to review.

Small items such as pencils, erasers and a metronome can live in a fixed little box at the side of the piano. Do not put the box on the piano lid, or it may vibrate off while you play.

**Think again**

Some piano benches have a storage compartment for music you use often, but do not stuff it too full, because a lid that is hard to open and close is less convenient.

## FAQ

**Q: Can a piano go next to a window?**
A: Yes, but avoid direct sunlight and drafts through gaps in the window, and close the curtains or adjust the position if needed.

**Q: How far from the wall should a piano be?**
A: Leave a small gap between the back of an acoustic piano and the wall to help ventilation and sound projection; for the exact distance, follow your piano tuner's advice.

**Q: Can a digital piano go in a bedroom?**
A: Yes. You can practise with headphones on a digital piano, so it is unlikely to disturb the family.

**Q: Does a piano corner need a rug?**
A: A thin, non-slip rug can reduce echo and protect the floor, but it should not be too thick, or the piano may not stand firmly.

**Q: What colour of light should the lamp give?**
A: Soft, neutral white light is best for reading music; light that is too yellow or too cool can tire the eyes.

**Q: What if the space is too small for a bench?**
A: You can choose a narrower bench, or push it under the piano when not in use, but pull it out to a suitable distance when you practise.

double-sharps-double-flats-when-notes-mo.body:
A double sharp raises a written note by two semitones, and a double flat lowers it by two semitones. In plain terms, each sign moves the pitch by a whole tone. You may see these marks in pieces that already use many sharps or flats, when a composer needs one more step in the same spelling. Once you know what the signs mean, finding the key is a short, practical task.

## What the two signs look like

A double sharp is often printed as a small cross, a bit like a sharp that has been drawn with two strokes. A double flat looks like two flat signs standing side by side. Both sit in front of the note they affect, just as a single sharp or flat would. If you meet one for the first time, pause and name the original note before you change it.

These signs are not ornaments. They are precise instructions about pitch, and they last until the end of the bar unless a natural, a sharp or a flat cancels them.

## Why a piece uses them at all

Music is spelled so that each scale degree keeps a clear letter name. If a passage is in a key that already has F sharp, and the line needs to go one step higher than F sharp, writing G natural would hide the fact that the note still functions as a raised F. Writing F double sharp keeps the letter F, which makes the harmony easier to read once you are used to it.

You do not need to accept this idea on trust. Compare a bar written with a double sharp and the same sounding bar written with a simpler letter. The sound can be identical, yet the first spelling shows how the line is moving.

## Finding the key on the keyboard

A reliable method is to start from the written letter, then move two semitones in the correct direction.

![Teal grand piano glowing on a dark grey stage floor](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwqwhs1f-selvo.webp)

- For F double sharp, begin on F, rise two semitones, and you will land on the key we also call G.
- For B double flat, begin on B, fall two semitones, and you will land on the key we also call A.
- For C double sharp, begin on C, rise two semitones, and you will land on D.
- For E double flat, begin on E, fall two semitones, and you will land on D.

The letter in the score and the name you might use in casual speech can differ. At the piano, press the key that matches the sound; when you talk about the score, keep the written letter.

## How long the sign lasts

Like other accidentals, a double sharp or double flat applies to that note, in that octave, until the next bar line. A natural sign cancels it and returns the note to its unaltered form, not to the key signature. If the key signature already has a sharp, a natural after a double sharp does not automatically restore the single sharp; some editions add the single sharp again to make the reading obvious.

When you practise, say the full name aloud: “C double sharp”, not only “D”. This habit keeps your eye and your ear connected to the spelling.

## A short reading drill

Open a score that uses these signs, or write a few short examples yourself. For each marked note, do three things in order: name the letter, state whether the sign raises or lowers the pitch by a whole tone, and point to the key. Then play a slow five-finger pattern that includes the note, so your hand learns the feel as well as the name.

If a chord contains a double sharp, find that note first, then add the others. Chords feel less crowded when the unusual spelling is settled before you build the rest of the shape.

## Common mix-ups and how to avoid them

Learners sometimes treat a double sharp as a single sharp and stop one semitone too low. Others see the cross and guess at a random black key. A third mix-up is to cancel the sign too early, in the same bar, because the shape looks heavy on the page. Slow reading prevents all three. Give the sign the same attention you would give a sudden change of clef.

It also helps to remember that a double sharp can land on a white key, and a double flat can do the same. The colour of the key is not a reliable clue; the distance of two semitones is.

## Putting the signs into everyday practice

You will not meet these marks in every beginner piece, and that is fine. When they do appear, treat them as a reading problem you can solve in a few seconds, not as a special difficulty. Add one short example to a practice session in the week you first see them, then return to your usual work. The goal is calm recognition, so the next time a cross or a pair of flats appears, your hands already know where to go.

## FAQ

**Q: Do double sharps and double flats always land on black keys?**
A: No. The move is two semitones, so the key you press may be white or black, depending on the starting note.

**Q: If F double sharp sounds like G, why not just write G?**
A: The spelling keeps the letter that belongs to the harmony or the scale degree, which makes the line easier to follow in context.

**Q: Does a bar line cancel a double sharp?**
A: Yes, in ordinary notation the accidental ends at the bar line, unless the next bar marks the note again.

**Q: What does a natural do after a double sharp?**
A: It cancels the double sharp and returns the note to its natural form. Some editions then add a single sharp or flat if the key signature needs it.

pygmalion-effect-teacher-expectations.body:
A teacher's expectations of their students can quietly influence the way they teach. The "Pygmalion effect", often mentioned in psychology, explores the relationship between expectations and performance. For piano teachers, paying attention to how they give feedback to different students is a useful form of self-check.

## Checking Yourself in the Lesson

With permission, a teacher can record their own lessons and watch them back, noticing how they respond to different students.

You can look at these questions: Do you wait the same length of time for each student to answer? Do you give the same number of hints? Is your tone of feedback equally patient?

You can also invite a colleague to sit in and offer some objective observations.

Once you spot differences, you can consciously adjust and give every student the same opportunities and attention.

This kind of self-check is not about criticising yourself. It is about making your teaching fairer and more effective.

You can simply note down the results, record another lesson after a while, and compare before and after to see whether the adjustments are working.

## Checking Your Expectations in the Lesson

A teacher can watch lesson recordings regularly and notice how long they wait, how many hints they give and what tone they use with different students. These details are often hard to notice during the lesson, but they can reveal unintended differences.

Give every student the same chance to finish playing, for example by waiting until the student has finished before giving feedback rather than interrupting halfway. This helps every student feel they are being taken seriously.

When giving feedback, try to point out specifically what the student did well and what needs improving, rather than offering general comments. Specific feedback helps every student.

The conclusions of psychological research have their own context and are open to debate. They can serve as a reference for reflection and need not be applied mechanically. What matters is staying open and continuing to observe your own teaching.

## A Balanced View of the Research

The Pygmalion effect is often cited, but later studies have not agreed on how large its influence is. Some found a small effect, and others found it only under certain conditions.

So it would be unwise to assume that "as long as the teacher believes, the student will certainly improve."

What is more valuable is the reminder the research gives us: a teacher's expectations may quietly affect their teaching behaviour.

For example, a teacher might give some students more waiting time, more hints and a warmer tone, and give others less.

These subtle differences are what deserve a teacher's reflection.

## Background to the Research

In the 1960s, the psychologists Rosenthal and Jacobson carried out a study in a primary school in the United States, later written up in the book Pygmalion in the Classroom.

In the study, they told teachers that certain students had shown, in a test, the potential to make great progress. In fact, those students had been chosen at random.

After a period of time, they reported that these students' results had improved more than those of the other students.

The researchers believed that teachers' expectations may have influenced students' performance through many small things in the way they taught. This phenomenon is called the "Pygmalion effect" or the "expectancy effect".

The study later sparked a great deal of discussion, and some researchers have also questioned its methods and results.

**Practice sequence**
- Expectations may influence how a teacher gives feedback
- You can check your own lessons through recordings
- Give every student the same waiting time and the same hints
- Focus on specific progress rather than first impressions

![A person wearing headphones practising at a white upright piano, with a neon sign behind](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8lwjqa-kgy3u.webp)

## Specific Feedback

When giving students feedback, try to point out specifically what they did well and what needs improving, rather than offering general comments.

For example, saying "your left hand in this passage is much steadier than last week" is more helpful than simply saying "good".

Specific feedback lets every student know both their progress and their direction.

When it comes to a student's progress, focus on their actual playing rather than first impressions.

Staying open and observant is a habit that pays off in teaching over the long term.

Students can borrow this way of thinking too, noticing whether their expectations of themselves are too low or too high, and using specific progress to adjust how they see themselves.

## FAQ

**Q: How can a teacher avoid first impressions?**
A: Review regularly through recordings, teaching notes and similar methods, and focus on changes in the student's specific performance.

**Q: Does the Pygmalion effect always exist?**
A: The research results are not consistent. You can treat it as a reference for reflecting on your teaching, not as a settled law.

**Q: Should a teacher have high expectations of students?**
A: You can keep reasonable expectations for every student and give them the same opportunities and support.

**Q: What should I watch out for when recording lessons?**
A: You need the consent of the student or their parents beforehand, and you should store the recordings safely.

**Q: Can students use this way of thinking?**
A: Yes. Use specific progress to adjust your expectations of yourself.

praise-effort-specific-feedback.body:
Compared with praising a child for being "talented", praising specifically the effort they put in and the methods they used usually makes them more willing to keep trying. For example, saying "You practised that left-hand part every day this week, and now it flows much better" lets the child know that progress comes from actions they can control, and they are less likely to shrink back from hard pieces out of fear of failing.

## What to Say About Mistakes and Difficulties

When a child plays a wrong note or runs into difficulty, you can focus on what to do next rather than on the mistake itself. For example, say "This bar is a bit tricky, so let's try again a little slower".

Avoid linking mistakes to ability, as in "How can you not even be able to do this?" Words like that easily make a child feel they are not good enough, and lose the courage to try.

You can also work with the child to analyse why it is difficult: are the fingerings unfamiliar, is the rhythm unsteady, or is the tempo too fast? Once you find the cause, think together about how to solve it.

When a child has overcome a difficulty through effort, you can point out that process specifically, so they feel the change that effort brings.

## Using It in Daily Practice

After the child finishes practising, parents can ask the child to talk about what they practised and what they feel has got better. The act of saying it out loud is itself a kind of self-affirmation.

You can also keep a simple notebook and note down the small improvements in each practice session. Over time, the child will see their own path of growth.

When talking with the teacher, you can find out what the child is currently focusing on, so that the feedback you give at home is more targeted.

Patience and consistency matter. Long-term, specific encouragement helps a child build confidence in learning more than occasional lavish praise.

**Practice order**
- Praise specific behaviour, not a vague label
- Link progress to practice methods
- Allow the child to make mistakes, and treat mistakes as clues
- Let the child say where they have improved

![A golden sketch of a grand piano on a beige background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw8juqlj-u0hse.webp)

## What Specific Praise Includes

Specific praise usually includes what the child did, and the change that this brought. For example, "You started with the left hand every day this week, and now the two hands fit together much more smoothly in this part" tells the child which approach works better than a plain "Great job".

You can also praise the methods the child has used, such as slowing down, practising in sections or recording themselves to check. The child will then be more willing to keep using those methods when they meet difficulties later.

Praise should be genuine and aimed at progress that really happened. If the child has not made obvious progress this time, you can still acknowledge their attitude of sticking with practice.

Keep your tone natural, with no need to exaggerate. A short, sincere sentence is often remembered better than a long speech of praise.

## How to Make Praise More Specific

Specific praise usually has three parts: what the child did, what change it brought, and that the adult noticed. For example, "Today you practised those two difficult bars slowly first, and the ending no longer gets stuck. I could hear it," carries more information than "Great job".

Some parents worry that not praising talent will leave the child without confidence. In fact, specific recognition can also build confidence, and this confidence is steadier, because the child knows that if they keep using the right methods, they can do it again next time.

You can also try judging less and asking more, such as "Which part felt most comfortable to play today?" This lets the child learn to observe and assess for themselves, which is very helpful for long-term piano learning.

## Parents' Own Mindset

Parents' expectations about learning the piano reach the child through words and attitude. When you focus on the process and on growth, not just on results, the child will enjoy the process of learning more too.

Avoid comparing your child with others. Every child has their own pace, and comparing with their own past performance shows real progress more clearly.

When parents themselves stay curious and interested in music, for example by listening to music together and chatting about favourite pieces, the child will feel that learning the piano is something fun.

**Another way to look at it**

A relaxed, supportive atmosphere at home is an important foundation for a child to keep learning the piano over the long term.

## FAQ

**Q: Can I not say my child is talented even when they play very well?**
A: You can express appreciation, but it is better to also mention the practice the child put in, so the child understands that results are linked to effort.

**Q: What should I say when my child has not improved?**
A: You can acknowledge the child's habit of sticking with practice, then work together to find one small thing to improve.

**Q: What is the problem with praising a child for being clever?**
A: This kind of praise may make the child care more about keeping up the image of being "clever", and less willing to try things that are difficult.

**Q: Should I praise my child even if they have not improved?**
A: You can acknowledge their effort and perseverance, while looking together for ways to improve.

**Q: Will too much praise make a child proud?**
A: Specific, genuine praise generally will not. The key is to focus on behaviour and methods rather than vague compliments.

**Q: How can I avoid comparing my child with others?**
A: You can compare the child's current performance with their own past, and focus on personal growth.

problem-bar-list-for-each-piece.body:
When you practise a piece, the difficult places are often only a small part of it. If you play from beginning to end every time, very little of your time goes to those places. A practical solution is to keep a problem-bar list for every piece: write down which bars need special practice and what the problem is. At the start of each practice session, look at the list, begin with the bars on it, and cross each one off once it is fixed. That way, more of your practice time goes where it is really needed.

## Don't Practise Too Much at Once

If there are many items on the list, you do not need to work through all of them in one session.

You can pick two or three each day, and choose a few different ones the next day.

If you try to practise too much at once, no spot gets worked on deeply enough, and the results are poorer.

## Where to Keep the List

The list can be written on a small card tucked into your music, or directly on the first page of the score.

You can also write it in your practice notebook, with one page for each piece.

What matters is that you can see it quickly every time you practise.

## How to Practise Each Problem Spot

When you work on the bars on your list, start by slowing down and practise just that one or two-bar passage.

Use methods such as hands separately, practising in small groups of notes, and changing the rhythm to solve the problems one at a time.

Once it plays smoothly, start from a bar or two before it and join it to what comes before and after.

## How to Find the Problem Spots

First play the whole piece through slowly. Whenever you meet a place that does not go smoothly or where you tend to make mistakes, note down the bar number.

You can also ask your teacher to point out, during a lesson, which places need more practice.

Recording yourself and listening back can also reveal things you did not notice while playing.

## Using It with Your Teacher

You can bring the list to your lesson and show your teacher which places have been fixed and which are still difficult.

Your teacher can then give more targeted advice based on the list.

This also helps you make better use of lesson time.

## Adding New Problem Spots

As your practice goes deeper, you sometimes find new difficulties, for example problems that appear once you speed up.

When that happens, you can add the new problem spots to the list.

The list is always being updated; it reflects what the piece needs right now.

## Problem Spots Are Only a Small Part

Look closely at a piece and you will find that most of the bars are not very hard, and there are only a few places where you really get stuck.

If you play from beginning to end every time, the easy parts get played many times while the hard parts are played only once or twice.

Finding the problem spots and practising them on their own makes your practice far more efficient.

![A wooden upright piano, green piano stool and orange books in front of a deep teal background](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa6bv7d-0thhj.webp)

## When You Are Practising Several Pieces

If you are practising several pieces at the same time, keep a list for each one.

When you practise, you can first deal with the one spot on each piece's list that most needs work.

That way every piece gets attention, instead of practising one and neglecting the others.

## Start with the List

At the start of every practice session, look at the list and begin with the bars on it.

This is when your mind is clearest and your attention is sharpest, which makes it the best time to deal with difficult places.

After you have worked on the places on the list, play the whole piece through.

## The Benefits of the List

A problem-bar list gives your practice a goal, so you do not just repeat things aimlessly.

It also helps you see your own progress: last week there were five problem spots, and this week only two are left.

Progress you can see makes practising more motivating.

**Summary**
- Problem spots are usually only a small part of a piece
- Write down the bars that need special practice and what the problem is
- Start every practice session with the list
- Cross each item off when it is fixed

## Problem-Bar List Summary

The difficult parts of a piece are usually only a small portion of it, so you can keep a problem-bar list, noting bar numbers and the specific problem.

Start every practice session with the list, practise slowly with suitable methods, cross each item off when it is fixed, and add new problem spots whenever they appear.

Pick a few each day, show the list to your teacher, and keep one list for each piece, so your practice has a clearer purpose.

## Cross Off Each One as You Fix It

When a problem spot has come out right and smoothly several times in a row, you can cross it off the list.

Watching the items on the list get crossed off one by one gives a real sense of achievement.

But a few days after crossing something off, check it again to make sure it has really stuck.

## What to Write on the List

On the list you can write the bar number and the problem at that spot, for example "bar 12, left-hand staccato unclear".

The more specific the problem, the better you know what to do when you practise.

If one place has several problems, you can write them separately and deal with one at a time.

## FAQ

**Q: What is a problem-bar list?**
A: A list of the bars that need special practice, with the problem at each one.

**Q: What should I write on the list?**
A: The bar number and the specific problem.

**Q: What should I practise first in a session?**
A: Start with the bars on the list.

**Q: When can I cross an item off?**
A: When you can play it correctly and smoothly several times in a row.

**Q: Do I have to practise every item in one session?**
A: No, just pick two or three each day.

prokofiev-peter-and-the-wolf-1936-instru.body:
In 1936, the Russian composer Prokofiev wrote Peter and the Wolf for a children's theatre in Moscow. It is a symphonic fairy tale with a narrator, in which every character is represented by an instrument or a group of instruments: the bird is a flute, the duck an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the grandfather a bassoon, the wolf three horns, and Peter is portrayed by the strings. The work premiered in Moscow in May of the same year and later became a classic for helping children get to know the instruments of the orchestra.

## Getting to Know the Sound of Instruments

Listening to Peter and the Wolf is a good way to get to know the tone colours of the orchestra's instruments.

**Remember this**

Try closing your eyes, listening only to the sound, and guessing which instrument is playing.

Once you are familiar with the tone colours of different instruments, you will be more interested when you listen to symphonies.

**Notice the details**
- Written in 1936 for a children's theatre in Moscow
- A symphonic fairy tale with narrator
- Each character is represented by an instrument
- Helps children get to know the instruments of the orchestra

## Good for the Whole Family to Hear

The work lasts about twenty-five minutes, a length at which children can listen quietly to the end.

Parents can listen together with their child and afterwards chat about which character and which instrument they liked.

This kind of listening experience will make children more interested in music.

## The Composer, Prokofiev

Sergei Prokofiev was a Russian composer and pianist, born in 1891 and died in 1953.

He wrote many works, including piano concertos, piano sonatas, ballets and symphonies.

In 1936 he returned to settle in Moscow, and in the same year wrote Peter and the Wolf.

## Written for a Children's Theatre

Peter and the Wolf was written at the invitation of a children's theatre in Moscow.

The theatre wanted a work that would help children get to know the various instruments of the symphony orchestra.

Prokofiev quickly completed the music and the story, reportedly in only a few weeks.

## One Instrument for Each Character

The work's greatest feature is that every character has its own instrument and melody.

The bird is played by the flute, with a light and nimble sound; the duck by the oboe, with a slightly clumsy sound; the cat by the low register of the clarinet, with soft footsteps.

The grandfather is played by the bassoon, with a deep sound; the wolf by three horns, with a dark sound; and Peter by the strings, with a bright melody.

## Imitating Instruments on the Piano

Although the piano has only one tone colour, you can imitate different instruments through touch, dynamics and register.

For example, when playing the bird's melody, you can play lightly and brightly in the high register; when playing the grandfather's melody, you can play steadily in the low register.

This kind of practice helps us enrich the piano's tone colour.

![A person in a high-tech jacket plays a glowing transparent grand piano on a wet neon street, with drones flying overhead](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mwa5clsi-04ajp.webp)

## Music That Tells a Story

Peter and the Wolf shows that music itself can tell a story.

Even without the narrator, listeners can sense the story developing from the changes in the music.

When playing piano pieces, you can also imagine a story, which makes the music more vivid.

## Narrator and Music

The work has a narrator who tells the story between the pieces of music.

The narrator first introduces each character and the instrument that represents it, so that listeners become familiar with the sounds before the story begins.

That way, when children hear a certain instrument, they know which character has entered.

## The Leitmotif Method

Using a fixed melody to represent a character is called a leitmotif in music.

Whenever the character appears, its melody sounds, sometimes changing according to the plot.

For example, the wolf's melody is always dark, while Peter's melody is always bright and lively.

## Peter and the Wolf Summary

In 1936, Prokofiev wrote the symphonic fairy tale with narrator Peter and the Wolf for a children's theatre in Moscow, and it premiered that May.

Each character is represented by an instrument, helping children get to know the instruments and tone colours of the symphony orchestra.

Piano learners can also imitate instruments at the piano with different registers and touches, or compose melodies for story characters.

## The Story of Peter and the Wolf

The story is about a boy called Peter who lives at his grandfather's house, with a meadow outside the door.

One day a wolf comes out of the forest and swallows the duck. With the help of the bird, Peter catches the wolf with a rope.

In the end the hunters arrive, and together they take the wolf to the zoo.

## Composing Music for Characters

You can play a game with your child: choose a story and compose a simple melody for each character.

Use different registers and tempos of the piano to portray different characters, for example an elephant walking slowly in the low register and a kitten hopping lightly in the high register.

This game is fun and also develops children's imagination and creativity.

## The 1936 Premiere

Peter and the Wolf premiered in Moscow in May 1936.

According to records, the premiere did not attract much attention, but the work soon spread around the world.

Today it has been translated into many languages and is performed and recorded with many different narrators.

## FAQ

**Q: Who wrote Peter and the Wolf?**
A: The Russian composer Prokofiev, in 1936.

**Q: Who was it written for?**
A: A children's theatre in Moscow.

**Q: Which instrument represents the bird?**
A: The flute.

**Q: Which instrument represents the wolf?**
A: Three horns.

**Q: How can you imitate instruments on the piano?**
A: With different registers, dynamics and touch.

practice-with-household-noise.body:
When there is television, cooking, a pet barking or neighbours renovating, it can be hard to concentrate on practising. You can choose a relatively quiet time and adjust what you practise: leave the parts that need careful listening for quiet times, and use noisy times for fingering, rhythm and familiar passages. You can also talk with your family and ask everyone to keep as quiet as possible during practice time.

## How Noise Affects Practice

Playing the piano relies heavily on your ears. When there is too much sound around you, you may not hear your own dynamic changes and tone clearly, and you are also more easily distracted.

Sometimes noise also makes people irritable, and the quality of practice drops with it.

Knowing what effects noise has lets you plan your practice more precisely, instead of forcing yourself to practise the same content in any environment.

## Give Yourself a Quiet Corner

If conditions allow, you can set up a relatively separate corner around the piano, for example partly screened off with a bookshelf or a curtain.

Such a space may not shut out sound completely, but it gives you a mental cue to "get into practice mode".

Putting a few music-related objects in the corner can also make the place more inviting.

## Neighbours and Outside Noise

If there is renovation or traffic noise outside, you can close the windows or move to a room farther from the source of the noise.

Renovation usually has set hours, so you can find out what they are and schedule your important practice for other times.

If you use a digital piano, you can also practise with headphones to reduce outside interference, but take care that the headphone volume is not too loud.

## Keep a Flexible Mindset

It is hard for a home environment to be perfect all the time, and accepting that can reduce the annoyance caused by noise.

Being able to practise with full focus when it is quiet, and to adjust the content when it is noisy, is itself a very practical practice skill.

Over time, you will find a practice rhythm that suits your household and strike a balance between life and music.

- Agree with your family on a relatively quiet practice time
- When it is noisy, practise fingering, rhythm and other things that do not depend on close listening
- When it is quiet, practise tone, dynamics and other things that need careful listening
- An occasional disturbance can be treated as concentration practice

## Plan Times Together with Your Family

If there are many people at home, you can agree with your family on a fixed practice slot, such as half an hour after dinner, and keep loud activities to a minimum during that time.

An agreement like this lets your family know when you need quiet, and lets you practise with more peace of mind.

In return, you can also respect your family's routines and avoid practising loud pieces while others are resting.

## Treat Distractions as Concentration Practice

An occasional small disturbance can also be treated as a chance to practise concentration. In a performance, there may be coughing or other sounds from the audience, and being able to stay focused despite distractions is a very useful ability.

You can try playing a familiar piece when there is a little noise, and see whether you can get from start to finish without stopping.

Of course, this is not suitable for learning new, difficult material, which is best left for quiet times.

## Pet Noises

Pets at home sometimes react to the piano, for example by barking along or running over to the piano.

You can play with your pet for a while before practising to settle it down, or take it to another room.

Some pets gradually get used to the sound of the piano and stop reacting so much, so you can give them time to adjust.

## Adjust What You Practise to the Environment

When it is rather noisy, you can practise things that do not depend much on detailed listening, such as learning fingering, working on rhythm, and repeating familiar passages.

When it is quiet, practise the parts that need careful listening, such as control of soft playing, the singing quality of a melody and the clarity of the pedal.

Dividing practice content this way means time is not wasted even when the environment is not ideal.

You can list the week's practice content and mark which items need quiet and which can be practised in ordinary surroundings, then choose flexibly according to the situation at home.

![Black and white pointillist sketch of a grand piano and a chair by a window](https://gsaqgbracxnucdmtmcxz.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/2026-11/mw9xkb19-yublw.webp)

## FAQ

**Q: What if it is too noisy at home to practise at all?**
A: You can temporarily switch to reading the score, listening to recordings or doing silent fingering practice.

**Q: Is it good to practise a digital piano with headphones?**
A: It reduces distractions, but keep the volume under control and take breaks.

**Q: What if my pet keeps barking along with the piano?**
A: Give your pet some time to adjust, or settle it down before you practise.

**Q: Is agreeing practice times with family useful?**
A: Usually very helpful, since everyone knows when quiet is needed.

**Q: Does practising in noise affect my listening judgement?**
A: Try to do detailed tone practice at quiet times.

**Q: Can I practise when neighbours are renovating?**
A: You can practise rhythm, fingering and so on, and leave important listening work for other times.
